## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library** of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, corrected with the greatest care; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with separate analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be surveyed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture and in which places of their works they have done so.

A most accurate edition, and one easily to be preferred to all others if the following matters are considered: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the exceptionally convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection, the first to assemble in one methodical and chronological library the six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**FIRST SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Under the direction of J. P. Migne, editor of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

## Expositions on the Psalms

*[The Complete Works of Augustine of Hippo]*

[Column 1033]

## Expositions on the Psalms

### Exposition of Psalm 80

## Sermon

*[Note: Addressed to the people of Carthage.]*

### 1. [Verse 1]

We have undertaken to speak to you about the present psalm. May your quiet aid our voice—for it is somewhat duller than usual; the attention of the listeners will give it strength, and the assistance of your command will enable me to speak.

*[Note: Thus the better manuscripts; the editions read, “and yours as well.”]*

This psalm has the following title: **“For the end, concerning the winepresses, on the fifth day of the week, a psalm for Asaph himself.”** Many mysteries are gathered together in this one title, yet in such a way that the threshold of the psalm points toward its interior.

When we are going to speak about winepresses, let none of you expect us to speak about the vat, the press, or the baskets; for the psalm itself does not contain these things, and therefore it points all the more strongly to a mystery. Even if the text of the psalm contained something of this kind, there would still be someone who thought that “winepresses” was to be understood literally, that nothing further should be sought there, and that nothing had been placed there mystically or signified sacramentally. He would say: “The psalm simply speaks about winepresses, and you are imagining I know not what else.”

You heard nothing of that kind when the psalm was read. Therefore understand the winepresses as a mystery of the Church that is now being enacted.

*[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “martyrdom.”]*

In a winepress we observe three things: pressure, and within the pressure two results—one to be stored up, the other to be thrown away. Thus, in the winepress there is trampling, affliction, and weight; and amid these the oil is secretly strained into the jars, while the dregs run openly through the streets.

Pay attention to this great spectacle. God does not cease to give us something to watch with great joy.

*[Note: Thus the Remigian manuscript. The editions read: “God does not abandon” (perhaps for “will not fail”) “to give us,” and so forth.]* Can the madness of the circus be compared with this spectacle? The former belongs to the dregs; this belongs to the oil.

Therefore, when you hear blasphemers muttering insolently and saying that afflictions abound in Christian times—for you know that they love to say this—do not be disturbed. There is an old proverb which began in Christian times: “God does not send rain; bring it against the Christians.” Although earlier people said these things, they now say also, when God does send rain: “Bring it against the Christians: if God does not send rain, we do not sow; if God sends rain, we do not thresh.”

*[Note: Edition of Erasmus has here: “Say it against the Christians.” The Louvain edition has: “Let a Christian say it.” Elsewhere below, instead of “bring it against the Christians,” both editions have “let the Christians say it.” Some books—namely those of Gemm., Pratell., and others—report the proverb in a different order, as follows: “The proverb began: ‘God does not send rain; we do not sow. God sends rain; we do not thresh.’” Then follows: “‘Let God not send rain,’ says the Christian; ‘and let God send rain,’ says the Christian. Although earlier people said these things, these people say them even now and wish to grow proud because of them,” and so on. The oldest and best manuscript, Corb., has this form: “The proverb began: ‘God does not send rain; we do not sow. God sends rain; we do not thresh. And if God does not send rain, let the Christian say it.’ Although earlier people said these things, these people now say also, when God does send rain, ‘Let the Christian say it.’” From this they wish to grow proud, and so on. But the reading of the manuscripts Reg. and Remig. seemed more suitable and easier than the others: “God does not send rain; bring it against the Christians,” and so on, and “because God does send rain, bring it against the Christians”—that is, attribute the cause to the Christians, in accordance with what Augustine also says in Book 2, chapter 3, of *The City of God*: “The popular saying arose, ‘There is no rain; the Christians are to blame.’” Hence also Tertullian, in *Apology*, chapter 40: “‘If the Tiber rises against the walls, if the Nile does not rise over the fields,’ he says, ‘the cry immediately goes up: Christians to the lion!’” And Cyprian, *To Demetrian*: “But when you say that many complain that wars arise more frequently, that pestilence and famine rage, and that long stretches of clear weather withhold showers and rains, and that all this is charged to us, it is no longer right to remain silent.”]*

And from this they wish to grow proud, from which they ought rather to pray more earnestly, choosing blasphemy over prayer.

Therefore, when they recall these things, boast of them, and say them insolently—not with fear, but with arrogance—do not let them trouble you. Suppose, then, that afflictions abound: be oil. Let the black dregs of ignorance insult you in the darkness, let them insult you publicly as though poured through the streets; but you, within yourself, in your heart, where he who sees in secret will repay you (Matthew 6:6), be strained into the jars.

The olive tree is shaken by certain storms, but it is not yet crushed by the pressures of the winepress. Thus both what is to be thrown away and what is to be stored hang together on the tree. But when they have reached the winepress and its pressures, the two are distinguished and separated: one is sought, the other rejected.

Would you like to know the force of these winepresses? I shall mention one thing, about which even those who produce these results complain. “How much plundering in our times,” they say; “how much oppression of the innocent; how much seizure of other people’s property!”

You are indeed looking at the dregs, because other people’s property is seized; but you are not looking at the oil, because gifts are made to the poor, even from people’s own possessions. Antiquity did not have such plunderers of other people’s property; but antiquity did not have such donors of their own property either.

Be somewhat more inquisitive in the winepress. Do not see only what flows publicly; there is something you will discover by searching. Investigate, listen, learn how many do what one rich man heard from the Lord and went away sorrowful.

Many hear from the Gospel: “Go, sell all that you possess, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21). Do you not observe how many do this?

“Few,” they say. Yet those few are the oil; and those who use well the possessions they have belong to the oil. Add them all together, and you will see the full storerooms of your master.

You see a plunderer such as you have never seen before; see also one who despises his own possessions such as you have never seen before.

Praise the winepresses. The prophecy from Revelation is being fulfilled: “Let the righteous person become more righteous, and let the filthy person become filthier still” (Revelation 22:11). Behold the winepresses in this saying: “Let the righteous person become more righteous, and let the filthy person become filthier still.”

### 2. [Verse 1]

Why also “on the fifth day of the week”? What does this mean? Let us return to God’s first works, lest we find there something by which we may understand the sacrament.

The Sabbath is the seventh day, on which God rested from all his works (Genesis 2:2), intimating the great mystery of our future rest from all our works.

“First of the week” means the first day, which we also call the Lord’s Day; “second of the week,” the second day; “third of the week,” the third; “fourth of the week,” the fourth. Therefore “fifth of the week” is the fifth day from the Lord’s Day; after it comes the sixth of the week, the sixth day; and the Sabbath itself is the seventh day.

Observe, then, to whom this psalm speaks. It seems to me that it speaks to the baptized.

On the fifth day God created living creatures from the waters. On the fifth day—that is, on the fifth of the week—God said: “Let the waters bring forth reptiles having living souls” (Genesis 1:20).

See, then, who you are, in whom the waters have now brought forth reptiles having living souls. You belong to the winepresses; and in you one thing is strained out and another is thrown away.

There are many who do not live worthily of the Baptism they have received. How many baptized people today preferred to fill the circus rather than this basilica! How many baptized people either build houses in the streets or complain that they should not be built!

This psalm, however, concerning the winepresses and the fifth day of the week, amid the pressure of discernment and in the sacrament of Baptism, is sung for Asaph himself.

Asaph was a certain man called by this name, as were Jeduthun, Korah, and the other names that we find in the titles of the Psalms. Yet the interpretation of the name discloses the mystery of hidden truth.

For in Latin, Asaph means **“Assembly.”** Thus, “concerning the winepresses, on the fifth day of the week,” it is sung for Asaph himself; that is, amid the pressure that makes the distinction, the psalm is sung for those baptized and reborn from water, for the Lord’s assembly.

We read the title at the threshold and have understood what it means in these presses.

*[Note: The Louvain edition and the manuscripts read *praediis*, “estates.” Erasmus’s edition more correctly has *prelis*, “presses”—that is, winepresses.]*

Now, if you please, let us also look at the house itself, the interior of the work—that is, the interior of the winepress. Let us enter, inspect, rejoice, fear, desire, and flee. You will find all these things in this inner house, that is, in the text of the psalm itself, when we begin to read and, with the Lord’s help, to speak what he grants us to speak.

### 3. [Verse 2]

Behold you, O Asaph, the assembly of the Lord: “Rejoice in God our helper.”

You who have assembled today—you are Asaph today, the Asaph of the Lord, since the psalm is sung for you: “Rejoice in God our helper.”

Others rejoice in the circus; you, in God. Others rejoice in their deceiver; you, rejoice in your helper. Others rejoice in their god, their belly; you, rejoice in your God, your helper.

“Shout joyfully to the God of Jacob,” because you too belong to Jacob—or rather, you are Jacob, the lesser people whom the greater serves (Genesis 25:23).

“Shout joyfully to the God of Jacob.” Whatever you cannot explain in words, do not therefore cease rejoicing. What you can explain, cry aloud; what you cannot, shout for joy.

For joy in abundance, when words cannot suffice, usually bursts forth into a shout of jubilation: “Shout joyfully to the God of Jacob.”

### 4. [Verse 3]

“Take up the psalm, and give the tambourine.” Both take and give.

What are you to take? What are you to give? “Take up the psalm, and give the tambourine.”

The Apostle Paul says in one place, reproving and grieving, that no one shared with him in the matter of giving and receiving (Philippians 4:15). What is “in the matter of giving and receiving,” unless it is what he explained openly elsewhere: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (1 Corinthians 9:11).

And it is true that the tambourine, which is made from skin, belongs to the flesh. The psalm, therefore, is spiritual; the tambourine, material.

Therefore, people of God, assembly of God, take up the psalm and give the tambourine: receive spiritual things and give material things.

This is what we urged you to do at that table of the blessed Martyr: that, receiving spiritual things, you should give material things.

*[Note: Namely, at the table of Cyprian the Martyr, who is expressly identified later, section 23. It was at Carthage, at the place where Cyprian completed his martyrdom. Augustine says in *Sermon 113 on Various Matters*, chapter 2: “At that same place a table was built for God. It is called Cyprian’s table, not because Cyprian ever feasted there, but because he was sacrificed there; and because by that sacrifice of his he prepared this table—not one at which he might feed or be fed, but one at which a sacrifice might be offered to God, to whom he too was offered.”]*

For these structures, which are built for a time, are necessary for receiving the bodies of either the living or the dead, but only for passing time. Shall we raise these buildings into heaven after God’s judgment? Nevertheless, without them we cannot at this time carry out the things that lead to the possession of heaven.

If, therefore, you are eager to receive spiritual things, be devoted in distributing material things. “Take up the psalm, and give the tambourine”: receive our voice and return your hands.

*[Note: Many manuscripts have: “You demand.” Others: “You receive.”]*

### 5. [Verse 3]

“A pleasant psaltery with the lyre.”

I remember that at some time we explained to Your Charity the difference between the psaltery and the lyre. Those who remember should review it; those who either did not hear it or do not remember should learn it now.

The difference between these two musical instruments—the psaltery and the lyre—is this: the psaltery has the hollow wooden resonator from which the sounding strings produce their notes in its upper part; the strings are struck below, so that they sound from above.

In the lyre, however, this same hollow wooden chamber occupies the lower part, as though the one instrument were from heaven and the other from earth.

The preaching of the word of God is heavenly; but if we hope for heavenly things, let us not be sluggish in doing earthly things, because it is “a pleasant psaltery, but with the lyre.”

This is another way of saying what was stated above: “Take up the psalm, and give the tambourine.” Here the psaltery stands for the psalm, and the lyre for the tambourine.

We are nevertheless admonished to respond to the preaching of God’s word with bodily works.

### 6. [Verse 4]

“Sound the trumpet.”

That is: preach more clearly and confidently; do not be frightened. As the prophet says in one place: “Cry aloud, and exalt your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58:1).

“Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month.”

It was commanded that a trumpet be sounded at the beginning of the month; and to this day the Jews perform this bodily, but do not understand it spiritually.

The beginning of the month is the new moon; the new moon is new life. What is the new moon? “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

What is meant by “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month, with trumpets”?

*[Note: This part of verse 4 is omitted: “on the notable day of your solemn feast.”]*

With complete confidence, preach the new life. Do not fear the tumult of the old life.

### 7. [Verse 5]

“For it is a commandment for Israel, and a judgment for the God of Jacob.”

Where there is a commandment, there is judgment. “For those who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Romans 2:12).

And the giver of the commandment himself is the Lord Christ, the Word made flesh. “For judgment,” he says, “I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

What does it mean, “so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind,” except that the humble are exalted and the proud cast down?

It does not mean that those who see should become blind, but that those who think they see should be convicted of blindness.

This is what the mystery of the winepress accomplishes: that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.

### 8. [Verse 6]

“He established it as a testimony in Joseph.”

Come, brothers: what does this mean? Joseph means **“Increase.”**

You remember and know that Joseph was sold into Egypt: Christ passed over to the Gentiles.

There Joseph was exalted after his tribulations (Genesis 37:28; 41:37 and following); here Christ was glorified after the passion of the martyrs.

Therefore the Gentiles belong especially to Joseph; and for that reason there is “increase,” because “the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” (Isaiah 54:1).

“He established it as a testimony in Joseph, when he went out from the land of Egypt.”

Here too, observe that the fifth day of the week is signified. When Joseph went out from the land of Egypt—that is, when the people multiplied through Joseph—it crossed the Red Sea (Exodus 14:22–31).

Then, therefore, the waters brought forth reptiles having living souls. The passage of the people through the sea prefigured nothing other than the passage of the faithful through Baptism. The Apostle is witness:

“I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1–2).

The passage through the sea signified nothing other than the sacrament of the baptized; the Egyptians who pursued them signified nothing other than the abundance of past sins.

You see the sacraments with complete clarity. The Egyptians press and pursue; sins therefore press upon us, but only as far as the water.

Why then are you afraid—still not having come—to come to the Baptism of Christ, to pass through the Red Sea? What does “red” mean? It is consecrated by the Lord’s blood.

Why are you afraid to come? Perhaps the consciousness of some monstrous sins pricks and torments your soul and tells you that what you have committed is so great that you should despair of forgiveness.

Be afraid lest something of your sins remain, if any Egyptian survives. But when you have crossed the Red Sea, when you have been led forth from your sins by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm (Psalm 135:12), you are going to receive mysteries you did not know.

For Joseph himself, when he went out from the land of Egypt, heard a language he had not known.

You will hear a language you did not know—a language which those who know it now hear and recognize, bearing witness and understanding.

You will hear where you ought to have your heart. When I said this just now, many understood and cried out; the rest stood silent, because they had not yet heard the language they did not know.

Let them hasten, then; let them cross over; let them learn: “He heard a language he did not know.”

### 9. [Verse 7]

“He turned his back away from burdens.”

Who turned his back away from burdens except the one who cried: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matthew 11:28)?

The same thing is signified in another way. What the pursuit of the Egyptians did is done by the burdens of sins.

“He turned his back away from burdens.” And as though you were to ask, “By what burdens?”—“His hands served at the basket.”

The basket signifies servile works. Cleaning, removing dung, and carrying earth are done with a basket; these are servile works, because everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:34, 36).

For good reason, then, the despised things of the world are counted as baskets. Yet God also filled baskets with fragments: he filled twelve baskets with fragments (Matthew 14:20), because he chose the despised things of the world to confound the strong (1 Corinthians 1:27).

When Joseph served at the basket, he carried earth there, because he made bricks: “His hands served at the basket.”

*[Note: The manuscripts read: “to clean dung.” The editions have: “to clean the dung.”]*

### 10. [Verse 8]

“In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you.”

Let each Christian conscience recognize itself—if it has devoutly crossed the Red Sea, if with the faith of believing and observing it has heard the language it did not know—and recognize that it has been heard in tribulation.

The great tribulation was the pressure of the burdens of sins. How greatly the relieved conscience rejoices!

Behold, you have been baptized. The conscience that yesterday was oppressed rejoices today. You were heard in tribulation; remember your tribulation.

Before you approached the water, what anxiety did you carry? What fasts did you undertake? What tribulations did you bear in your heart—what inward, devout, and dedicated prayers?

Your enemies have been slain; all your sins have been blotted out: “In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you.”

### 11. [Verse 8]

“I heard you in the hiding-place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction.”

Not in a storm at sea, but in the storm of the heart.

“I heard you in the hiding-place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction.”

Truly, brothers, the one who has been heard in the hiding-place of the storm ought to be tested at the water of contradiction.

For when he has believed, when he has been baptized, when he has begun to follow the way of God, when he has begun to be strained into the jars and to withdraw himself from the dregs running publicly, he will have many who harass him, many who insult him, many who disparage him, many who discourage him; they will even threaten him wherever they can, frightening and depressing him.

This whole thing is the water of contradiction.

I think that this is happening here today. I suppose that there are some here whose friends wanted to drag them to the circus and to I know not what trifles of today’s festival; perhaps those friends brought them here to the church.

Whether their friends brought them here or they were unable to be dragged by them to the circus, they have been tested in the water of contradiction.

Do not therefore be ashamed to preach what you know, or to defend among blasphemers what you have believed. For if you are heard in the hiding-place of the storm, “with the heart one believes unto righteousness”; if you are tested in the water of contradiction, “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

How great is this water of contradiction? It is now almost dried up.

Our ancestors experienced it when the nations fiercely resisted the word of God and the mystery of Christ. The water was stirred. Scripture in the Apocalypse clearly shows that waters are sometimes understood as peoples: when many waters appeared and the question was asked what they were, the answer was given: “They are peoples” (Revelation 17:15).

They endured the water of contradiction when the nations raged and the peoples devised futile things; when the kings of the earth stood up and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ (Psalm 2:1–2).

When the nations raged, that lion went roaring to meet the strong man Samson as he came to take a wife from among foreigners—namely, Christ descending to obtain a Church from the Gentiles.

But what did he do? He seized, held, broke, and scattered the lion; in his hands it became like a young goat.

For what could a roaring people be except a feeble sinner? Once that savagery had been slain, royal power no longer roars in this way, nor does the people of the Gentiles roar in opposition to Christ.

Indeed, within the kingdom of the Gentiles itself we find laws favorable to the Church, like honey in the lion’s mouth (Judges 14:5–8).

Why then should I now fear the water of contradiction, which has almost entirely dried up? It is now nearly silent, unless the dregs contradict.

However fiercely outsiders may rage, would that our own evils did not assist them!

“I heard you in the hiding-place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction.”

You remember what was said about Christ: that he was born “for the fall and rising of many, and as a sign that will be contradicted” (Luke 2:34).

We know it; we see it. The sign of the cross was raised, and it was contradicted. The glory of the cross was contradicted, but there was an inscription above the cross that was not destroyed.

There is an inscription in the psalm: “For the inscription of the title; do not destroy” (Psalm 59:1).

It was a sign that would be contradicted. For the Jews said, “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but that he himself said, ‘I am the King of the Jews.’”

The contradiction was defeated. The answer was given: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19:19–22).

“I heard you in the hiding-place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction.”

*[Note: Several manuscripts read: “he did not go to meet Christ.”]*

### 12. [Verses 9–10]

From the beginning of the psalm up to this verse we have heard everything concerning the oil of the winepress.

What remains is more grievous and must be guarded against. Up to the end it belongs to the dregs of the winepress—perhaps not without reason, with a *diapsalma* intervening.

Yet it is useful to hear this also, so that the one who already sees himself in the oil may rejoice, while the one in danger of running with the dregs may beware.

Hear both: love the one, fear the other.

“Hear, my people, and I will speak; I will testify to you.”

He is not speaking to a foreign people, nor to a people that does not belong to the winepress. “Judge,” he says, “between me and my vineyard” (Isaiah 5:3).

“Hear, my people, and I will speak; I will testify to you.”

*[Note: The editions read: “fall into the dregs.” All the manuscripts, however, read: “run in the dregs”; several have “run in the dregs,” meaning “run together with the dregs as they flow from the winepress.”]*

### 13. [Verse 10]

“Israel, if you will hear me, there shall be no new god among you.”

A new god is one made for a time. Our God, however, is not new but is from eternity to eternity.

And our Christ may perhaps be recent as man, but he is the everlasting God. What existed before the beginning? Certainly, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” And this same Christ our Lord was “the Word made flesh, so that he might dwell among us” (John 1:1, 14).

Far be it, then, that there should be a new god in anyone. A new god is either a stone or a phantom.

“‘It is not a stone,’ he says; ‘I have one made of silver and gold.’” He was right to wish to name the precious materials, for Scripture says: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold.”

They are great because they are golden and silver; they are precious; they shine. Yet “they have eyes and do not see” (Psalm 113:4–5).

These are new gods. What is newer than a god from a workshop? Even if spiders have already woven their aged webs around them, those that are not eternal are new.

This concerns the pagans.

Some other person, taking the name of the Lord his God in vain, has made for himself a Christ who is a creature, a Christ unequal and unlike the one who generated him—calling him the Son of God while denying the Son of God.

For if the only Son is what the Father is, and if he is from eternity, you have nevertheless imagined something else in your heart and have installed a new god.

Another has made for himself a god fighting against the race of darkness, afraid lest he be invaded, struggling lest he be corrupted; yet partly corrupted, so that he might be wholly saved—but not wholly, because he was partly corrupted.

The Manichaeans say these things. They too make for themselves a new god in their hearts.

Our God is not such a god; such is not your portion, Jacob. Rather, the one who made heaven and earth is your God—the one who does not need good things and does not fear evil things.

14. Therefore many heretics, together with the pagans, have made different gods for themselves and imagined different gods for themselves; and even if they have not placed them in temples, they have placed them—what is worse—in their own hearts, and have themselves become temples of false and laughable images. It is a great task to break these idols within and to cleanse a place for the living God, not for a recent one.

For all these people, thinking differently and making different gods for themselves, and varying the faith itself by falsehood, appear to disagree; but they all remain attached to earthly thoughts, and in earthly thoughts they agree with one another: their opinion is different, but their vanity is one. Of them it is said in another psalm, “They have united in vanity” (Ps. 61:10): although they disagree in the variety of their opinions, they are nevertheless gathered together by a similar vanity.

And you know that vanity is behind us, it is posterior; therefore the one who has forgotten what is behind—that is, has forgotten vanity—and has stretched himself toward what lies ahead, that is, toward truth, presses on toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus (Phil. 3:13–14). Thus these people agree with one another for the worse, although they appear to disagree among themselves.

That is why Samson tied together the tails of foxes (Judg. 15:4). Foxes signify the treacherous, and especially heretics: deceitful and fraudulent, hiding and deceiving in winding, cavernous passages, and stinking with a foul odor. Against this odor the Apostle says: “We are the good odor of Christ” [Note: [Col. 1040] The editions add *to God*, which is absent from the manuscripts] “in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15).

These foxes are signified in the Song of Songs, where it is said: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, hiding in crooked caverns” (Song 2:15). “Catch for us”: convict them for us; for you catch the one whom you convict of falsehood.

When the little foxes contradicted the Lord and said, “By what authority are you doing these things?” he replied: “Answer me also one question: The baptism of John—was it from heaven or from human beings?” Foxes, however, are accustomed to have dens such that they enter by one opening and leave by another. The fox-catcher has therefore set a net at both openings.

[Col. 1041] “Tell me: Was it from heaven or from human beings?” They perceived that he had stretched out a net on both sides by which to catch them, and they said among themselves: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’”—for John bore witness to Christ. “If we say, ‘From earth,’ the people will stone us, because they regard him as a prophet.” Perceiving, then, that on either side they would be caught, they answered, “We do not know.” And the Lord said: “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matt. 21:23–27).

You say that you do not know what you know; I will not tell you what you ask, because you have dared to leave by no opening, and have remained in your darkness.

Let us therefore obey, if we can, the word of God that says, “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.” Let us see whether we too can catch certain little foxes. Let us set a trap at both openings, so that wherever the fox wishes to escape, it may be caught.

For example, to a Manichaean who makes a recent god for himself and places in his heart what does not exist, let us say and ask: “Is God’s substance corruptible or incorruptible?” Choose whichever you wish and escape whichever way you wish, but you will not escape.

If you say, “Corruptible,” you will be stoned not by the people but by yourself. But if you say that God is incorruptible, how did the incorruptible God fear the race of darkness? What could a race of corruption do to the incorruptible? What remains except for you to say, “We do not know”?

Nevertheless, if this is said not through deceit but through ignorance, let him not remain in darkness. Let him change from a fox into a sheep; let him believe in the invisible, incorruptible, only God—not a recent one; in the *only* one, from the fact that he is “alone,” not from the fact that he is “sun,” lest we ourselves seem to have opened another cavern for the fleeing fox.

Yet we will not fear even the name “sun.” For it occurs in our Scriptures: “The sun of righteousness, and healing is in his wings” (Mal. 4:2). From the heat of this sun a shadow is sought; beneath the wings of this sun one flees from the heat, for healing is in his wings.

This is the sun of which the ungodly will say: “Therefore we wandered from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. 5:6). The worshipers of the sun will say, “The sun did not rise for us,” because although they worship the sun that he causes to rise upon the good and the wicked (Matt. 5:45), the sun that enlightens only the good did not rise for them.

Thus each person makes for himself recent gods, of whatever kind he wishes. For what prevents a deceived heart from fashioning whatever phantom it desires? But all these people agree in what is behind, that is, they are held by a similar vanity.

Hence our Samson—whose name also means “Their Sun,” namely, the sun of those upon whom he shines, not of everyone, as the sun rises upon the good and the wicked, but the sun of certain people, the sun of righteousness—who represented Christ, tied together, as I had begun to say, the tails of the foxes and fastened fire there. He fastened fire for burning, but for burning the harvests of the foreigners.

Therefore such people, agreeing in what is behind, like foxes tied together by their tails, drag along a destructive fire; but they do not burn our crops. For “the Lord knows those who are his; and let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.” “But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some indeed for honor, but others for dishonor. If anyone cleanses himself from such things, he will be a vessel for honor, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work” (2 Tim. 2:19–21). [Col. 1042] Therefore he will fear neither the foxes’ tails nor the foxes’ torches.

But let us consider this people: “If you listen to me,” he says, “there will not be in you a recent god.” The words “in you” move me. He did not say “from you,” as though an image had been brought in from outside; rather, “in you”: in your heart, in the image of your phantom, in the deception of your error, you will carry your recent god with you, while remaining old.

“If you listen to me”—to me, he says, “because I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14)—“there will not be in you a recent god, and you will not worship a foreign god.” For if he is not in you, you will not worship a foreign god. If you do not think of a false god, you will not worship a fabricated god; for there will not be in you a recent god.

15. [verse 11.] “For I am.” Why do you wish to worship what does not exist? “For I am the Lord your God,” because “I am who I am.” “And I indeed am,” he says, “who am above every creature; but what have I provided for you in time?—I who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

This is not said only to that people. For we have all been brought out of the land of Egypt; we have all crossed the Red Sea; our enemies, pursuing us, perished in the water. Let us not be ungrateful to our God; let us not forget the God who remains and fashion within ourselves a recent god.

“I who brought you out of the land of Egypt”: God is speaking. “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.” You suffer constriction within yourself because of the recent god established in your heart. Break the empty image; cast the fabricated idol down from your conscience. Open your mouth by confessing and loving, and I will fill it, because “with me is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:10).

16. [verse 12.] This is what the Lord says; but what follows? “And my people did not listen to my voice.” He would not say these things except to his people, for we know that whatever the Law says, it says to those who are under the Law (Rom. 3:19).

“And my people did not listen to my voice; and Israel did not attend to me.” Who? To whom? “Israel—to me.” O ungrateful soul! A soul through me, a soul called by me, a soul brought back by me to hope, a soul washed by me from sins: “And Israel did not attend to me.”

They are baptized and pass through the Red Sea; but on the way they murmur, contradict, complain, and are disturbed by seditions. They are ungrateful to the one who delivered them from pursuing enemies, who leads them through dry land and through the wilderness, yet with food and drink, with light by night and shade by day: “And Israel did not attend to me.”

17. [verse 13.] “And I let them go according to the desires of their hearts.” Behold the winepress: the openings have been opened, and the olive-lees flow out. “And I let them go,” not according to the salvation provided by my commandments, but “according to the desires of their hearts”: I gave them over to themselves.

The Apostle also says: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts” (Rom. 1:24). “I let them go according to the desires of their hearts; they will walk according to their desires.”

That is the source of what horrifies you—if indeed you are being strained out in the Lord’s hidden twin vessels, if indeed you have come to love his storehouses. Some defend the circus, others the amphitheater, others the little houses in the streets, others the theaters, others one thing, others another, and finally others their own recent gods: “They will walk according to their desires.”

18. [verses 14–15.] “If my people had listened to me; [Col. 1043] if Israel had walked in my ways.” For perhaps this Israel says: “Look, I sin; it is evident. I follow the desires of my heart; but what can I do? The devil does this; the demons do this.”

What is the devil? Who are the demons? Certainly, your enemies. “If Israel had walked in my ways, I would have humbled all their enemies to nothing.” Therefore: “If my people had listened to me.” Why are they my people if they do not listen to me? “If my people had listened to me.”

What does “my people” mean? Israel. What does “had listened to me” mean? “If it had walked in my ways.” It complains and groans beneath its enemies: “I would have humbled their enemies to nothing, and I would have laid my hand upon those who afflicted them.”

19. [verse 16.] But now, why do they complain about their enemies? They themselves have become worse enemies. How so? What follows? You complain about your enemies; what are you yourselves?

“The enemies of the Lord have lied to him.” Do you renounce? “I renounce”; and yet you return to what you renounced. What things do you renounce, if not evil deeds, diabolical deeds, deeds condemned by God— thefts, robberies, perjuries, murders, adulteries, sacrileges, abominable sacred rites, and curious investigations? You renounce all these things, and then again, bent beneath them, you are overcome.

“What happened to you afterward is worse than what came before”: a dog returning to its own vomit, and a washed sow returning to wallowing in the mire (2 Pet. 2:20, 22). “The enemies of the Lord have lied to him.”

And how great is the Lord’s patience! Why are they not thrown down? Why are they not slaughtered? Why are they not swallowed up when the earth opens? Why are they not burned when the heavens blaze? Because of the Lord’s great patience.

Will they remain unpunished? Far from it. Let them not flatter themselves so much because of God’s mercy as to presume upon his injustice. “Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works” (Rom. 2:4–6).

And if he does not repay now, he will repay then. For if he repays now, he repays for a time; but if a person is neither converted nor corrected, he will repay eternally.

See, then, that they will not remain unpunished; attend to what follows: “The enemies of the Lord have lied to him.” You will say: “And what has he done to them? Are they not alive? Do they not breathe the air? Do they not take in the light? Do they not drink from springs? Do they not eat the fruits of the earth?” “And their time will be forever.”

20. Let no one therefore flatter himself because he seems to belong to the winepress. It is good for him if he belongs to the oil in the winepress. Let no one who has wicked deeds—deeds that will not possess the kingdom of God—promise himself security and say: “Because I have the sign of Christ and the sacraments [Note: [Col. 1043] Most manuscripts have *the sacrament*] of Christ, I will not be destroyed forever; and even if I am cleansed, I will be saved through fire.”

For what does the Apostle say about those who have the foundation? “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.” What does what follows mean, they ask? “Let each person see what he builds upon the foundation. For one builds upon the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones; another with wood, hay, straw. The quality of each person’s work will be tested by fire; for the day of the Lord will reveal it, because [Col. 1044] it will be revealed in fire. If anyone’s work that he has built remains, he will receive a reward” (1 Cor. 3:10–15). That is, he built righteous works upon the foundation: gold, silver, precious stones.

“But if there are sins”: wood, hay, straw. “Nevertheless, because of the foundation he himself will be saved; yet as through fire.”

Brothers, I want to be exceedingly cautious. It is better not to give you a false assurance. I will not give what I do not receive. Fearing, I terrify you. I would make you secure if I were secure; I fear the eternal fire.

“And their time will be forever”: I understand this only as the eternal fire, of which Scripture says elsewhere: “Their fire will not be extinguished, and their worm will not die” (Isa. 66:24).

“But,” someone says, “he spoke of the ungodly, not of me. Although I am a sinner, although an adulterer, although a deceiver, although a robber, although a perjurer, I nevertheless have Christ as my foundation. I am a Christian; I have been baptized. I am cleansed through fire, and because of the foundation I do not perish.”

Tell me again: “What are you?” “A Christian,” you say. For now, proceed. “What else?” A robber, an adulterer, and the other things concerning which the Apostle says: “Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21).

Surely, then, without being corrected of such things and without repenting of such deeds, you hope for the kingdom of heaven? I do not think so, because “those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.”

And do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance? While promising yourself I know not what, “according to your hardness and impenitent heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works.”

Attend, then, to the Judge himself as he comes. Good: thanks be to God. He did not conceal the final sentence; he did not send the defendants outside and draw the curtain. He wished first to announce what he had determined to do.

“Indeed, all the nations will be gathered before him.” What will he do with them? He will separate them, and he will place some on his right and others on his left. Has any middle place been reserved?

What will he say to those on the right? “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom.” And to those on the left? “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:32–34, 41).

If you do not fear being sent to that place, look at whose company you will share. If, then, those deeds will not possess the kingdom of God—indeed, not the deeds themselves, but those who do such things, for such deeds will not be in the fire, since those burning in that fire will not be stealing and committing adultery—if those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God, then they will not be on the right with those to whom it will be said, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom.” For those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.

If, therefore, they will not be on the right, nothing remains except that they be on the left. And what will he say to those on the left? “Go into the eternal fire,” because “their time will be forever.”

21. “Explain to us, then,” someone says, “how those who build wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation do not perish but are saved, yet as through fire.”

That question is obscure, but I will speak briefly, as I can. Brothers, there are people who utterly despise this world, to whom nothing that flows away in time is pleasing [Note: [Col. 1044] Thus Erasmus and several manuscripts; others read *born*, or, with Lov., *known*]. They do not cling through any love to earthly pursuits [Note: [Col. 1045] The Ferrariense manuscript reads *wealth*]. They are holy, chaste, continent, righteous, perhaps even selling all they possess and distributing it to the poor, or possessing as though they did not possess, and using this world as though they did not use it (1 Cor. 7:30–31).

But there are others who cling somewhat through affection to things permitted because of human weakness. He does not seize another’s estate; but he loves his own so much that, if he loses it, he is disturbed. He does not desire another’s wife; but he clings to his own and is so joined to her that he does not observe the limit prescribed in the marriage contract for the procreation of children. He does not take what belongs to another; but he reclaims his own, and he has a lawsuit with his brother. For such people it is said: “It is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another” (1 Cor. 6:7).

Indeed, the Apostle commands that these lawsuits be conducted in the Church, not brought into the public courts; nevertheless, he calls them faults. For a Christian contends over earthly things more than is fitting for one to whom the kingdom of heaven has been promised. He does not lift his whole heart upward, but drags part of it upon the earth.

Finally, if the trial of being led to martyrdom should come [Note: Most manuscripts of good quality read *of speaking*], those who have Christ as their foundation and build with gold, silver, and precious stones say, “It is good for me to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). They run eagerly, and are either not at all or only slightly saddened by earthly frailty.

But those who love their own possessions and their own houses are deeply troubled. The hay, straw, and wood burn. Thus they have wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation, but things that are permitted, not things that are unlawful.

For I say, brothers: you possess the foundation; cling to heaven and trample upon the earth. If you are such a person, you build only gold, silver, and precious stones.

But when you say, “I love this possession; I fear that it may perish,” and loss threatens and you grieve, you do not indeed place it before Christ. For you love this possession in such a way that, if you were told, “Do you want that possession itself, or Christ?”—even if you lose it with sadness, you nevertheless embrace Christ more, whom you placed as your foundation. You will be saved as through fire.

Hear another case: You cannot retain this possession unless you give false testimony. Not doing this is to place Christ in the foundation, for Truth has said: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11).

Therefore, if you love your possession, yet do not commit robbery because of it, do not give false testimony because of it, do not commit murder because of it, do not swear falsely because of it, and do not deny Christ because of it, then, because you do not do these things for its sake, you have Christ as your foundation.

Nevertheless, because you love it and grieve if you lose it, you have placed upon the foundation not gold, silver, or precious stones, but wood, hay, and straw. You will therefore be saved when what you built begins to burn, yet as through fire.

Let no one who builds adulteries, blasphemies, sacrileges, idolatries, and perjuries upon this foundation think that he will be saved through fire, as though these were wood, hay, and straw. Rather, the one who builds the love of earthly things [Col. 1046] upon the foundation of the kingdom of heaven—that is, upon Christ—will have his love for temporal things burned up, and he himself will be saved through the sound foundation.

22. [verse 17.] “The enemies of the Lord have lied to him,” saying, “I am going to the vineyard,” but not going (Matt. 21:30). “And their time will be,” not for a time, but forever.

And who are these people? “And he fed them with the fat of wheat.” You know the fat of wheat, from which many enemies who have lied to him are fed.

“And he fed them with the fat of wheat”: he mixed them with his sacraments. He also fed Judas with the fat of wheat when he gave him the morsel (John 13:26); and the enemy of the Lord lied to him, and his time will be forever.

“And he fed them with the fat of wheat, and he satisfied them with honey from the rock.” O ungrateful people! He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock.

In the wilderness he brought water from the rock (Exod. 17:6), not honey. Honey is wisdom, holding the first place of sweetness among the foods of the heart.

How many enemies of the Lord, then, who lie to the Lord, are fed not only with the fat of wheat but also with honey from the rock, with the wisdom of Christ! How many delight in his word and in knowledge of his sacraments, in the explanation of his parables! How many delight in it; how many cry out!

And this honey is not from just any person, but from the rock; “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). How many, then, are filled with this honey, cry out, and say, “It is sweet”; they say, “Nothing better, nothing sweeter could either be understood or spoken”—and yet “the enemies of the Lord have lied to him.”

I do not wish to linger longer over painful matters. Although the psalm has ended on this note in a terrifying manner, nevertheless, I beg you, let us return from its end to its beginning: “Exult in God our helper, turned toward God” [Note: In the editions these words, “turned toward God,” had been omitted after “Exult in God our helper.” We have restored them from the manuscripts].

And after the word:

23. The divine spectacles, in the name of Christ, have held and suspended your minds to no small degree—not only toward desiring certain things, but also toward fleeing certain things. These are useful, healthy, edifying spectacles, not destructive ones; indeed, they are both destructive and edifying: destroying recent gods and building faith in the true and eternal God.

We also invite Your Charity for tomorrow. Tomorrow, as we have heard, they will have the sea in the theater; let us have a harbor in Christ.

But since on the day after tomorrow, that is, on Wednesday, we cannot meet at Cyprian’s table, because it is the festival of the holy martyrs, let us meet tomorrow at that same table.

# Exposition of Psalm 81

1. [verse 1.] The psalm is entitled, “A psalm belonging to Asaph.” The title of this psalm, like that of others similarly marked, either gives it the name of the man by whom it was written, or gives the interpretation of that name, so that its meaning may be referred to the Synagogue, which is what *Asaph* signifies: especially since its first verse also assigns this meaning to it.

[Col. 1047] For it begins in this way: “God stood in the synagogue of gods” [Note: This verse is also expounded in *Exposition of Psalm 94*, no. 6]. We must certainly not understand these gods as the gods of the Gentiles, whether idols or some heavenly or earthly creature other than human beings, since a little later this same psalm asserts and more clearly identifies which gods it intends to be understood, in whose synagogue God stood, when it says: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High; but you will die like human beings, and like one of the princes you will fall.”

God therefore stood in the synagogue of these sons of the Most High, of whom the same Most High says through Isaiah, “I fathered and exalted sons; but they themselves despised me” (Isa. 1:2).

By “the Synagogue” we understand the people of Israel, because their assembly is properly accustomed to be called the Synagogue, although it has also been called the Church. Our apostles, however, never called ours a synagogue, but always a Church—either for the sake of distinction, or because there is some difference between a gathering, from which the name “Synagogue” derives, and a calling together, from which the name “Church” derives.

For creatures such as sheep and cattle are accustomed to be gathered together, and we properly speak of their flocks; but to be called together is more characteristic of beings who use reason, such as human beings.

Hence, speaking in the person of Asaph, another psalm says: “I became like a beast before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. 72:23). This was the case because, although he seemed devoted to the one true God, he nevertheless sought from him carnal, earthly, and temporal things as great and supreme goods.

We also often find them called sons—not by the grace that belongs to the New Testament, but by that which belongs to the Old. For that too is grace: the grace by which he chose Abraham and propagated so great a people from his flesh; by which, before they were born, he loved Jacob but hated Esau (Mal. 1:2–3); by which he delivered them from Egypt; and by which, after expelling the Gentiles, he brought them into the promised land.

For if that too were not grace, the Gospel would certainly not say, regarding us, to whom power was given not to take possession of an earthly kingdom but to receive the kingdom of heaven, and to become sons of God, that “we have received grace for grace” (John 1:12, 16)—that is, the promises of the New Testament in place of the promises of the Old Testament.

It is therefore clear, as I think, in whose synagogue of gods God stood.

2. Next we must ask whether we should understand the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity itself as having stood in the synagogue of gods and as distinguishing the gods in their midst, because each one individually is God, and the Trinity itself is one God.

This is not easy to sift out, because it cannot be denied that God’s presence—spiritual, not bodily, and corresponding to his substance—is present to created things, in a marvelous manner scarcely intelligible to a few. To him it is said: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138:8).

Thus God is rightly said to stand invisibly in the assembly of human beings, just as he himself fills heaven and earth, as he himself declares through the prophet (Jer. 23:24). Indeed, he is not merely said to stand in the things he created; he is, in some way, understood to do so according to the capacity of the human mind [Col. 1048], if a person also stands and listens to him and rejoices with joy because of his intimate voice (John 3:29).

Nevertheless, as I judge, this psalm is attempting to suggest something that happened at a particular time: that God stood in the synagogue of gods. For that standing by which he fills heaven and earth belongs properly neither to the Synagogue nor to any change in time.

God therefore stood in the synagogue of gods—surely the one who said of himself, “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). The reason is also given: “But in the midst he distinguishes the gods.”

I therefore recognize that God stood in the synagogue of gods whose fathers they were, and from whom Christ came according to the flesh. For God stood in the synagogue of gods for this reason: that he might come from them according to the flesh.

But what kind of God? For he was not such as those in whose synagogue of gods he stood; rather, as the Apostle continues there, he is “God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

I recognize, I say, that he stood; I also recognize in the midst the divine Bridegroom, of whom one of his friends says: “In the midst of you stands one whom you do not know” (John 1:26). For concerning these people it is said shortly afterward in this psalm: “They did not know, nor did they understand; they walk in darkness.” The Apostle also bears witness: “Blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” (Rom. 11:25).

They saw him standing in their midst, but they did not see that he was God, as he wished to be seen when he said: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” [Note: Thus the manuscripts read. The editions have: “Whoever sees me sees,” and so forth] (John 14:9).

He distinguishes the gods, not according to their merits, but according to his grace, making from the same lump some vessels for honor and others for dishonor (Rom. 9:21). “For who distinguishes you? What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

3. [verses 2–3.] Hear also the voice of God who distinguishes; hear the voice of the Lord who divides the flame of fire (Ps. 28:7): “How long will you judge unjustly, and show favor to sinners?” As elsewhere: “How long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. 4:3).

Is it even until the coming of the one who is the light of the heart? I gave the Law; you resisted harshly. I sent prophets; you insulted them, killed them, or connived at those who did such things [Note: Erasmus reads *you restrained*; and below, where the text has “connived,” it reads “restrained.” So too the older books, in which *restrain* is consistently written for *connive*].

But to say nothing of those who killed the servants of God sent beforehand to them, what of you who kept silent when these things were happening—that is, you who wished to imitate those who were then silent as though they were innocent? “How long will you judge unjustly, and show favor to sinners?”

Is even the heir who is coming now to be killed? Did he not, for your sake, wish to be without a father, like an orphan? Did he not, for your sake, hunger and thirst like one in need? Did he not cry out to you, “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29)? Did he not, although he was rich, become poor so that you might become rich through his poverty (2 Cor. 8:9)?

“Judge for the orphan and the needy; justify the humble and the poor.” Do not believe that those who are proud and rich are just on their own account; believe and proclaim [Col. 1049] this one just for your sake, because he is humble and poor.

4. [verse 4.] But they will envy him and will not spare him at all, saying: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. 21:38). “Rescue the needy, and deliver the poor from the hand of the sinner.”

These words were spoken so that it might be known that, among that people in which Christ was born and killed, those who were not free from so great a crime were not only the wicked leaders. The others were such a great multitude that, as the Gospel says, the Jews feared them and therefore did not dare to lay hands upon Christ (Luke 22:2). Yet afterward they connived and allowed him to be killed by the evil and envious leaders of the Jews. If they had wished, they would always have been feared, so that the hands of the wicked could never have prevailed against him.

Concerning these people it is said elsewhere: “They are mute dogs that do not know how to bark” (Isa. 56:10). Of them also comes the saying: “Behold how the just man perished, and no one considers it” (Isa. 57:1).

He perished, insofar as they were concerned, because they wished to destroy him. For how could he perish by dying, when by that very means he was seeking what had perished?

Moreover, if those who allowed so great a crime to be committed by pretending not to notice it are rightly rebuked and deservedly accused [Note: The editions read *were silent*. The Corbie manuscripts more correctly read *allowed it*], with what severity must those be rebuked—or, rather, condemned—who did this through deliberate counsel and malice?

5. [verse 5.] Nevertheless, what follows applies most rightly to all: “They did not know, and they did not understand; they walk in darkness.”

For the first group, if they had known, would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8); and the second group, if they had known, would never have agreed to demand that Barabbas be released and Christ crucified.

But since the blindness mentioned above happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, through this blindness of that people, when Christ had been crucified, all the foundations of the earth would be shaken. They were shaken, and they will continue to be shaken, until the fullness of the Gentiles that has been predestined enters.

For at the Lord’s death the earth itself was shaken, and the rocks were split (Matt. 27:51). And if by “the foundations of the earth” we understand those who are happy because of an abundance of earthly goods, it was rightly foretold that they would be shaken—either by marveling that Christ’s humility, poverty, and death, which according to their standards seemed a great misery, should be loved and honored in such a way, or by themselves, after despising the empty happiness of this world, loving and pursuing that humility, poverty, and death.

Thus all the foundations of the earth are shaken, when some are astonished and others are transformed.

For just as we may not absurdly speak of the foundations of heaven—those upon which the kingdom of heaven is built in the saints and faithful, whom Scripture calls living stones (1 Pet. 2:5), whose foundation is first Christ himself, born of a virgin, concerning whom the Apostle says, “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11), and then the apostles and prophets, by whose authority the heavenly dwelling is chosen, so that by pursuing it we may be built together upon it—hence he says to the Ephesians: “You are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and [Col. 1050] members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Eph. 2:19–22):

so, in the same way, the foundations of the earth may not inappropriately be understood as those whose preeminent and powerful earthly happiness draws people, through envy of their authority, to desire such goods and, by attaining them, to be built together like earth upon earth, just as in that heavenly structure heaven is built upon heaven.

For it was said to the sinner, “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Gen. 3:19); and, “The heavens declare the glory of God,” when “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:2, 5).

6. [verses 6–7.] The kingdom of earthly happiness is pride, against which the humility of Christ came, reproaching those whom he wishes, through humility, to make sons of the Most High, and rebuking them: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High. But you will die like human beings, and like one of the princes you will fall.”

Perhaps when he says, “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High,” he is speaking to those who have been predestined to eternal life; but when he says to others, “But you will die like human beings, and like one of the princes you will fall,” he is distinguishing the gods in this way.

Or perhaps he rebukes everyone together, in order to distinguish those who obey and are corrected: “I,” he says, “said, You are gods and sons of the Most High”—that is, “I promised all of you heavenly happiness.” “But you, through the weakness of the flesh, will die like human beings; and through the exaltation of your spirit, like one of the princes”—that is, like the devil—“you will not be exalted, but you will fall.”

It is as if he were saying: “Since the days of your life are so few that you will soon die like human beings, this does not benefit you toward correction. Rather, like the devil, whose days in this world are many because he does not die in the flesh, you are lifted up so that you may fall.”

For through diabolical pride it happened that the perverse and blind leaders of the Jews envied the glory of Christ. Through this vice it has happened, and continues to happen, that the humility of Christ, who was crucified even to death, is despised by those who love the greatness of this world.

7. [verse 8.] Therefore, that this vice may be healed, it is said in the person of the prophet himself: “Arise, O God, judge the earth.” The earth was in uproar when it crucified you; arise from the dead and judge the earth. [Note: Col. 1050: Thus the better manuscripts; the editions read, “The earth feared.”] “For you will destroy among all the nations”—what, except the earth? That is, those who set their minds on earthly things; or else, destroying in believers the very inclination toward earthly desire and pride [Note: Col. 1050: The editions read *assumens*, “taking up”; the manuscripts correct this to *absumens*, “destroying”]; or discerning the unbelieving as earth destined to be crushed and destroyed. Thus, through his members, whose citizenship is in heaven, he judges the earth and destroys it among all the nations.

Nor should we pass over the fact that some codices read, “For you will inherit among all the nations.” This too can be understood without impropriety, and there is no contradiction in supposing that both readings may stand together. His inheritance is therefore brought about through love, by mercifully cultivating it through his commandments and grace, he destroys earthly desire.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 82

1. [verse 1.] The title of this psalm is: “A Song of the Psalm of Asaph.” We have often said what Asaph means, namely, “Assembly” (*Congregatio*). Thus the man called Asaph is placed in the titles of many psalms as a figure of the assembly of God’s people. In Greek, however, an assembly is called *synagōgē* (συναγωγή), a term that the Jewish people adopted almost as their proper name, so that it was called the Synagogue; just as the Christian people is more commonly called the Church, although it too is certainly an assembly.

2. [verse 2.] Accordingly, God’s people say in this psalm: “God, who will be like you?” I think this is more appropriately understood of Christ, because, having been made in the likeness of human beings, he was regarded by those who despised him as comparable with other human beings. Indeed, he was counted among the wicked (Isaiah 53:12)—but in order that he might be judged. When he comes to judge, then what is said here will take place: “God, who will be like you?”

For if the Psalms were not accustomed to speak to the Lord Christ, that statement also would not be made which no believer can doubt was spoken to him: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:7–8).

To him, then, it is now also said: “God, who will be like you?” You wished to be like many in humility, even like the robbers who were crucified with you (Luke 23:33); but when you come in glory, who will be like you? What significance would there be in saying to God, “Who will be like you?” unless it were said to the one who wished to be like human beings, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being (Philippians 2:7)?

For this reason he does not say, “Who is like you?”—which would certainly have been correctly said if the reference were to his divinity. But since the statement refers to the form of a servant, his dissimilarity from other human beings will become apparent when he appears in glory.

Therefore it follows: “Do not be silent, nor restrain yourself, O God.” At first he was silent in order to be judged; when, like a lamb before its shearer, he was without a voice, so he did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7), and restrained his power. To show that he was restraining himself, at the sound of his voice when he said, “I am,” those who were seeking to seize him drew back and fell (John 18:5–6).

When, then, he was being held and suffering, what was happening unless he himself restrained and checked himself, and in a certain sense moderated himself? Some have interpreted the words written here, “Nor restrain yourself, O God,” in this way: “Nor moderate yourself, O God.” Elsewhere he himself says, “I have been silent; shall I always be silent?” (Isaiah 42:14). Here he is told, “Do not be silent”; elsewhere it is said of him: “God will come openly, our God, and he will not be silent” (Psalm 50:3). Here it says, “Do not be silent”: he was silent in order to be judged when he came hidden; but he will not be silent in order to judge when he comes openly.

[Col. 1052] 3. [verse 3.] “For behold, your enemies have sounded forth, and those who hate you have raised their head.” This seems to me to signify the last days, when the things that are now restrained by fear will burst forth into unrestrained speech—but plainly irrational speech, so that it should be called a sound rather than an utterance or discourse.

They will not then begin to hate you; rather, those who hate you will then raise their head. It is not “their heads,” but “their head,” when they will reach the point of possessing even that head which is exalted above everything that is called God and worshiped—as the saying, “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11), will be fulfilled especially in him. And the one to whom it is said, “Do not be silent, nor moderate yourself, O God,” will kill him with the spirit of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming (2 Thessalonians 2:4, 8).

4. [verse 4.] “They have plotted wickedly against your people”; or, as other codices read, “They have devised a plot craftily,” “and have plotted against your saints.” These words are spoken mockingly. For when could they harm God’s people or nation, or his saints, who know how to say, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

5. [verse 5.] “They said, Come, let us destroy them from the nation.” He has used the singular number for the plural, as when one says, “Whose is this flock?” even when asking about a herd, with animals being understood. Accordingly, other codices read, “Let us destroy them from the nations,” where the translators have followed the sense more than the wording.

“Come, let us destroy them from the nation.” This is the sound with which they sounded forth rather than spoke, because they noisily uttered empty things to no purpose. “And let the name of Israel no longer be remembered.” Others have expressed this more plainly: “And let there no longer be remembrance of the name of Israel.” In Latin, “let remembrance be made of the name” is an unusual expression; it is more customary to say, “let the name be remembered.” But the meaning is the same, for the person who said “let remembrance be made of the name” translated a Greek expression.

Here Israel should certainly be understood as the seed of Abraham, to whom the Apostle says, “Then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:29)—not Israel according to the flesh, of whom he says, “Look at Israel according to the flesh” (1 Corinthians 10:18).

6. [verse 6.] “For they plotted together with one accord; together they established a covenant against you”—as though they could be stronger. In Scripture, *covenant* is not said only of that which has no force until the testators have died; every agreement and arrangement was also called a covenant. Thus Laban and Jacob made a covenant (Genesis 31:44), which plainly had force even between living persons; and countless such examples are read in the divine utterances.

7. [verses 7–8.] Then he begins to recall the enemies of Christ under certain names of nations; the interpretation of these names sufficiently indicates what is intended. For the enemies of truth are most suitably represented by such names.

The Idumeans are interpreted either as “Bloodied” or “Earthly.” The Ishmaelites mean “Obedient to themselves”—that is, not to God, but to themselves. Moab means “From the father.” This is better understood in a negative sense when the history itself is considered: the father, Lot, had intercourse with his daughter in an illicit union and begot him; because of this deed he received that name (Genesis 19:36–37). A father is good, however, as is the Law, if someone uses it lawfully (1 Timothy 1:8), not incestuously and unlawfully. [Note: Col. 1053: Thus the manuscripts; the Lovaniensis edition reads, “But the Law is a good father, as the Apostle says, if anyone,” etc.]

The Hagrites mean “Proselytes,” that is, “newcomers.” Among the enemies of God’s people, this name signifies not those who become citizens, but those who persist with a foreign and adventitious mind and reveal themselves when an opportunity to do harm is found.

Gebal means “A vain valley,” that is, “deceptively humble.” Ammon means “A turbulent people,” or “A people of grief.” Amalek means “A people who lick,” whence it is said elsewhere, “And his enemies will lick the earth” (Psalm 72:9).

The Foreigners, although the Latin name itself indicates that they are foreign and therefore, consistently, enemies, are called in Hebrew *Philistim* (פלשתים), which means “Falling through drink,” as though they were made drunk by worldly indulgence.

Tyre is called *Sor* in the Hebrew language. Whether this is interpreted as “Narrowness” or “Tribulation,” it should be understood of these enemies of God’s people in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Tribulation and anguish upon every soul of one who works evil” (Romans 2:9).

All these are therefore enumerated in this psalm: “The tents of the Idumeans and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, and the Foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre.”

8. [verse 9.] And, as if indicating the reason why they are enemies of God’s people, he adds and says: “For Asshur also came with them.” Asshur is figuratively understood as the devil himself, who works in the sons of disobedience (Ephesians 2:2), as though in his own vessels, so that they may attack God’s people.

“They became,” he says, “a help to the sons of Lot.” All the enemies, because their prince, the devil, works in them, became a help to the sons of Lot, whose name means “Declining.” The apostate angels are rightly understood as sons of Declining: by declining from the truth, they departed into the devil’s service.

These are the ones of whom the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities and the powers of this world’s darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12). Therefore these invisible enemies assist unbelieving human beings, in whom they work to attack God’s people. [Note: Col. 1053: The editions read, “Because these”; some manuscripts read “Therefore,” others “Because on account of.”]

9. [verses 10–13.] Let us now see what the prophetic spirit calls down—not so much cursing as prophesying. “Do to them,” it says, “as to Midian and Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon. They perished at Endor; they became like dung upon the earth.”

According to the historical account, the people of Israel, who were then God’s people, defeated and conquered all these men, as well as those whom he subsequently mentions, saying: “Make their princes like Oreb and Zeeb, and Zebah and Zalmunna” (Judges 4, 7, 8).

The interpretations of their names are as follows: Midian means “Declining judgment”; Sisera, “Exclusion of joy”; Jabin, “Wise.” Among these enemies overcome by God’s people, the wise one should be understood as the one of whom the Apostle says: “Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age?” (1 Corinthians 1:20).

Oreb means “Drought”; Zeeb, “Wolf”; Zebah, “Victim”—but a wolf’s victim, for the wolf too has its victims; Zalmunna means “Shadow of agitation.” All these meanings correspond to the wicked, whom God’s people conquer in what is good.

Kishon, at whose torrent they were defeated, means “Their hardness.” Endor, where they perished, means “Fountain of generation”—but plainly of carnal generation, to which they devoted themselves and in which they perished. They did not care about the regeneration that leads to life, where people neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot begin to die (Luke 20:35–36).
