It was therefore rightly said of them, “They became like dung upon the earth,” since nothing was propagated from them except earthly fertility. Thus, just as all those men were overcome figuratively by God’s people, so he prays that these enemies may truly be overcome.

10. “All their princes,” he says, “who said, Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.” This is the empty sound with which, as stated above, his enemies sounded forth. What should be understood as God’s sanctuary except the temple of God, of which the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17)?

For what else are the enemies attempting except to possess God’s people—that is, to subjugate them—so that the people may yield to their ungodly desires? [Note: Col. 1054: Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “fall.”]

11. [verse 14.] But what follows? “My God, make them like a wheel.” This can suitably be understood to mean that they should not remain stable in what they are planning. Nevertheless, I think it can also rightly be understood in this way: “Make them like a wheel,” because a wheel is lifted up by what is behind and cast down by what is ahead. Thus all the enemies of God’s people are made.

For this is not a wish but a prophecy. He adds: “Like stubble before the face of the wind.” By “face” he means presence. For what face does the wind have, when it possesses no bodily features, being a movement—that is, something like a wave of air? It is used here for the temptation by which light and empty hearts are swept away.

12. [verses 15–16.] The lightness by which people easily consent to evil is followed by severe torment. Hence he continues: “As fire that burns the forest, as a flame that burns the mountains, so you will pursue them in your storm, and in your wrath you will trouble them.”

He called them a forest because of their barrenness, and mountains because of their pride. Such are the enemies of God’s people: empty of righteousness and full of arrogance.

By mentioning fire and flame, he repeats the same idea under another name, intending us to understand God as judge and punisher. What he said above, “in your storm,” he subsequently explained by saying, “in your wrath”; and what he said earlier, “you will pursue them,” he later expressed as, “you will trouble them.”

Let us remember that God’s wrath must be understood without any turbulent emotion. His wrath is called the just reason for punishment, just as one might say that the law is angry when its ministers, moved according to it, inflict punishment.

13. [verses 17–19.] “Fill their faces,” he says, “with disgrace, and they will seek your name, O Lord.” This is plainly prophesied as something good and desirable for them. It would not be prophesied unless there were among the enemies of God’s people people of this kind, to whom this would be granted before the final judgment.

For even now they are the same people, and they constitute the same body of enemies in the envy with which they rival God’s people. Even now, wherever they can, they sound forth and raise their head; but only in parts, not universally as at the end of the age, when the final judgment is imminent.

Nevertheless, this same body exists both in those who will believe from among them and pass into another body—for their faces are beneficially filled with disgrace so that they may seek the Lord’s name—and in those who persevere in the same wickedness to the end. They are made like stubble before the face of the wind and are burned like unfruitful forests and mountains.

To these he returns again, saying: “Let them be ashamed and troubled for ever and ever.” Those who seek the Lord’s name are not troubled for ever and ever. Rather, as they look upon the disgrace of their sins, they are troubled for the purpose of seeking the Lord’s name, through which they will not be troubled.

14. Again he returns to those who, within the same fellowship of enemies, are to be confounded so that they may not be confounded forever, and are to be destroyed insofar as they are evil, so that, having been made good, they may be found forever.

For after saying of them, “Let them be confounded and perish,” he immediately added: “And let them know that the Lord is your name; you alone are the Most High over all the earth.” Coming to this knowledge, let them be confounded in such a way that they may please; let them perish in such a way that they may remain.

“Let them know,” he says, “that the Lord is your name,” as though all the others who are called lords were not truly designated by their own name, since they rule in a servile manner and, compared with the true Lord, are not lords at all. Thus it is said, “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14), as though things that have been made were not at all when compared with the one by whom they were made.

When he adds, “You alone are the Most High over all the earth”—or, as other codices read, “above all the earth”—this certainly also means “over all heaven” or “above all heaven.” But he preferred to say this in order to crush earthly pride.

The earth—that is, the human being to whom it was said, “You are earth” (Genesis 3:19), and “Why does earth and ash grow proud?” (Sirach 10:9)—ceases to be proud when it recognizes that the Lord is Most High above all the earth. That is, it recognizes that no human thoughts have power against those who are called according to God’s purpose, of whom it is said, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:28, 31).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 83

1. [verse 1.] This psalm is entitled “For the Winepresses.” And, as Your Charity noticed along with us—for we observed how intently you were listening—nothing in its text is said about a press, baskets, a vat, or the instruments or structure of a winepress. We heard absolutely nothing of this kind in it. Consequently, what its title, “For the Winepresses,” signifies is no small question.

Certainly, if after this title it said anything about such matters as those I have mentioned, carnal people would believe that it intended to sing about these visible winepresses. But because it imposed the title “For the Winepresses” and afterward said nothing throughout the psalm’s verses about those winepresses familiar to our eyes, there is no doubt that they are other winepresses which the Spirit of God wished us here to seek and understand.

Let us therefore recall what is done in these visible winepresses and see how it is spiritually enacted in the Church. A grape certainly hangs on vines, and an olive on trees—for winepresses are usually prepared for these two fruits. As long as they hang on their shrubs, they enjoy the open air as though in freedom. Before pressing, however, a grape is not wine, nor an olive oil.

So it is with human beings whom God predestined before the ages to be conformed to the image of his only-begotten Son (Romans 8:29), who was especially expressed as a great cluster in his passion. Such people, before they approach the service of God, enjoy the world as though in a delightful freedom, like grapes or olives hanging on their branches.

But since it is said, “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for testing” (Sirach 2:1), let everyone who approaches the service of God recognize that he has come to the winepresses. He will be afflicted, crushed, and compressed—not so that he may perish in this world, but so that he may flow into God’s storehouses.

He is stripped of the coverings of carnal desires, like grape skins. This is what has happened to him in regard to carnal desires [Note: Col. 1056: Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts; the Lovaniensis edition reads, “happens”], concerning which the Apostle also says, “Strip off the old person and put on the new” (Colossians 3:9–10). None of this takes place except through pressure. Therefore the Churches of God in this present age are called winepresses.

2. But who are we who have been placed in the winepresses? “The sons of Korah.” For it is added: “For the winepresses, of the sons of Korah.” We understand the sons of Korah to mean “sons of the Bald One,” insofar as those who know that language have been able to interpret it for us through the ministry they owed to God. Here I do not shrink from contemplating a great mystery and, with the Lord’s help, discovering it together with you.

For not every baldness is to be mocked, as though by sons of pestilence, lest someone who mocks a sacred baldness be scattered by demons. [Note: Col. 1056: Some manuscripts read “the sacred Calvary”; others, “the sacrament of the Bald One.”] Elisha was traveling, and foolish boys called after him, “Bald one, bald one!” And, in order that the mystery might be fulfilled, he turned to the Lord and asked that bears coming out of the forest might devour them (2 Kings 2:23–24).

Their childhood was indeed snatched from this world unto the destruction of life; the boys died, though the old would eventually die. [Note: Col. 1056: Many manuscripts read “unto departure,” and some “unto departures,” in place of “unto destruction.”] Nevertheless, the terror of the mystery was given to human beings. For Elisha then represented the person whose sons we are: the sons of Korah, namely, of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Your Charity will now recall from the Gospel why he was bald and represented Christ. Remember that he was crucified at the place of the Skull (Matthew 27:33).

Therefore, whether “the sons of Korah” is interpreted in this way, as we followed those before us in saying, or whether it means something else that perhaps escapes us, look meanwhile at what presents itself: it is full of mystery.

The sons of Korah are the sons of Christ. The bridegroom also calls them his sons when he says, “The sons of the bridegroom cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them” (Matthew 9:15). These winepresses, then, belong to Christians.

[Col. 1057] 3. But once established under pressure, we are crushed for this purpose: that through the love by which we were carried toward worldly, secular, temporal, fleeting, and perishable things, after suffering in this life the torments and tribulations of pressure and the abundance of temptations, we may begin to seek that rest which does not belong to this life or this earth.

And the Lord becomes, as it is written, “a refuge for the poor” (Psalm 9:10). What does “poor” mean? It means someone who is destitute, without resources, without help, without anything in which he may presume upon the earth. God is present to such poor people.

Even if people abound in money on this earth, they heed what the Apostle says: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Timothy 6:17). When they consider how uncertain is the source of their former joy, before they approached the service of God—that is, before they entered the winepresses—they see that from their very riches they either suffer the pressures of thought, wondering how these possessions may be managed and guarded, or, if they incline their desire even slightly toward loving them, they are filled more with fears than with benefits.

For what is as uncertain as a changeable possession? And not without reason is money itself represented as round, since it does not stand still.

Such people, even if they possess something, are poor. Those who possess none of these things but desire to possess them are counted among the reprobate rich. For God does not consider one’s resources but one’s will.

The poor, then, are destitute of every worldly resource. Even if such resources overflow around them, they understand how uncertain they are. Groaning toward God, having nothing in this world in which to delight or upon which to depend, and established in an abundance of pressures and temptations as in winepresses, they allow wine and oil to flow.

What are these things except good desires? God remains for them to desire; they no longer love the earth. They love the one who made heaven and earth; they love him, though they are not yet with him.

Their desire is delayed so that it may grow; it grows so that it may receive. For God is not going to give something small to the one who desires him, nor should one be exercised only a little to acquire the capacity for so great a good. [Note: Col. 1057: Thus the Remigian manuscript; other books read “only a little.”] God will not give something that he made, but himself, who made all things.

Exercise yourself to receive God; desire for a long time what you will always possess. Those in the people of Israel who hastened were rejected. This disposition of those who hurry is repeatedly censured in Scripture.

Who are those who hurry? Those who, having turned to God, do not find here the rest they were seeking or the joys that had been promised. They become weary as though on a journey, imagine that something long remains for them until this age or this life ends, and seek here some rest—which, if it is possessed, is false. They look back and fall away from their purpose, not considering with what terror it was said: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32).

Why was she made into a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26), unless to season human beings so that they may gain wisdom? Therefore her example, though bad, becomes good for you if you take care.

“Remember Lot’s wife,” he says. She looked back from the place from which she had been delivered—from Sodom—and remained there, the place toward which she looked. She herself remained in that place, while others passed by and were seasoned by her.

Having therefore been delivered from the Sodoms of our former life, let us not look back. For this is what it means to hurry: not to attend to what God has promised because it is far away, but to look toward what is near, from which you have already been delivered.

What does the Apostle Peter say about such people? “The true proverb has happened to them: The dog has turned to its own vomit” (2 Peter 2:22). [Note: Col. 1058: The editions read “returned”; the manuscripts read “turned.”] The conscience of sins was weighing upon the breast. Having received pardon, you vomited as it were, and your breast was relieved; a good conscience arose from a bad conscience. Why do you turn back again to your vomit? If a dog doing this is repulsive to your eyes, what will you be in the eyes of God?

4. Each person, dearest brothers, looks back from the stage of his journey to which he has advanced and which he has vowed to God when he abandons that stage.

For example, someone decides to preserve marital chastity—for justice begins from this point—and withdraws from fornication and that unlawful impurity. When he turns back to fornication, he has looked behind him.

Another, by God’s gift, vows something greater and decides not to enter marriage. If he had married without making this vow, he would not have been condemned; but if he marries after the vow he made to God, he will be condemned. He does what the other does, who had made no promise; yet the other is not condemned, while he is condemned.

Why, unless because he looked back? The other had already been there, whereas he had not yet reached that place.

So a virgin who would not sin if she married (1 Corinthians 7:28), if she is a consecrated woman and marries, will be regarded as an adulteress against Christ. For she has looked back from the place to which she had advanced.

Likewise, those who are pleased to abandon every worldly hope and every earthly activity and to join the fellowship of the saints, that common life in which no one calls anything his own, but everything is common to them, and in which they have one soul and one heart toward God (Acts 4:32): whoever wishes to withdraw from it is not regarded like someone who never entered it. The latter has not yet approached; the former has looked back.

Therefore, dearest brothers, vow as each person can, and repay the Lord your God whatever each person is able to repay (Psalm 76:12). Let no one look back; let no one delight in his former condition; let no one turn away from what lies ahead toward what lies behind. Let him run until he arrives. For we run not with our feet but with our desire.

No one should say that he has arrived in this life. For who can be as perfect as Paul? Yet he says: “Brothers, I do not consider myself to have apprehended it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead, according to my purpose I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:13–14).

You see Paul still running, and you already consider yourself to have arrived?

5. [verse 2.] If, therefore, you feel the pressures of this world even when you are prosperous, you have understood that you are in the winepress. Do you think, my brothers, that the world’s misfortune should be feared but its prosperity need not be feared? On the contrary, no misfortune breaks the person whom no prosperity corrupts.

How, then, must prosperity itself be avoided and feared, lest it deceive you by flattering you? Do not lean upon a staff of reed. For it is also written of certain people that they lean upon a staff of reed. Do not trust yourself to it (2 Kings 18:21). What you lean upon is fragile; it breaks and destroys you.

If, then, this world smiles upon you through prosperity, count yourself as being under pressure, so that you may say: “I found tribulation and pain, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 114:3–4).

He did not say, “I found tribulation,” except of a certain tribulation that lies hidden. A certain tribulation lies hidden from some people in this world, who think that things are going well for them while they are exiles from the Lord. “As long as we are in the body,” he says, “we are exiles from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6).

If you were an exile from your human father, you would be miserable. You are an exile from the Lord, and you are happy?

There are therefore people who think that things are going well for them. But those who understand that, amid any abundance of possessions and pleasures—although everything obeys their command and nothing unpleasant intrudes or adverse circumstances cause fear—they are nevertheless in an evil state as long as they are exiles from the Lord, have found tribulation and pain with the keenest vision, and have called upon the name of the Lord.

Such is the one who sings in this psalm. Who is he? The body of Christ. Who is this person? You, if you wish; all of us, if we wish; all the sons of Korah, and all one human being, because we are one body of Christ.

How could he not be one human being when he has one head? Christ is the head of all of us; all of us are the body of that head.

And all of us in this life are in the winepresses. If we have good understanding, we have already come to the winepresses.

Therefore, established amid the pressures of temptations, let us utter this voice and send our desire ahead: “How dearly loved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts!” [Note: Col. 1059: The editions read “lovely”; all our manuscripts read “dearly loved.”] He was in certain tabernacles, that is, in winepresses; but he desired other tabernacles where there is no pressure. From these he sighed toward those, and from these to those he flowed, as it were, through a channel of desire. [Note: Col. 1059: The editions and manuscripts read “through carnal desire,” except for the Remigian codex, which has “through a channel of desire,” doubtless in place of it.]

6. [verses 3–4.] And what follows? “My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord.” It is not enough to say, “It longs and languishes”; but where does it languish? “For the courts of the Lord.”

The pressed grape has flowed out; but where has it flowed? Into wine, into the vat, and into the peaceful storehouse, to be preserved in great rest.

Here there is longing; there possession. Here there is sighing; there rejoicing. Here there is prayer; there praise. Here there is groaning; there exultation.

Let no one here reject what I have called harsh; let no one be unwilling to suffer. We must fear that, while the grape fears the winepress, birds or wild beasts may eat it.

There appears to be great sadness when he says, “My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord,” for he does not possess what he desires. But is he therefore without joy? What joy? The joy of which the Apostle says: “Rejoicing in hope.”

There he will rejoice in reality; for now he rejoices in hope. And so those who rejoice in hope, because they are certain that they will receive what is promised, endure every pressure in the winepress.

Therefore, when that same Apostle had said, “Rejoicing in hope,” as though he were speaking to those who are already in the winepress, he immediately added: “Patient in tribulation.” “Patient in tribulation,” he says. What follows? “Persevering in prayer” (Romans 12:12).

What does “persevering” mean? It means that you are being delayed. You pray, and you are delayed; endure the fact that you are delayed. Let what is delayed be endured, because when it comes, it will not be taken away.

### 7.

You have heard the groaning in the winepress: “My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord.” Hear from what source it endures: rejoicing in hope. “My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God.” They have exulted here in what is to come. From what source comes exultation, unless from hope? In what have they exulted? “In the living God.” What things of yours have exulted? “My heart and my flesh.” From what source have they exulted?

“For even the sparrow,” he says, “has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest for itself, where it may place its young.” What does this mean? He had mentioned two things, and he answered with two birds as figures: he had said that his heart and his flesh had exulted, and he answered with the sparrow and the turtledove; the heart as the sparrow, the flesh as the turtledove.

The sparrow has found a house for itself; my heart has found a house for itself. It exercises its wings in the virtues of this present age—in faith, hope, and charity themselves—by which it will fly to its house. When it has arrived, it will remain there, and the plaintive voice of the sparrow, which is heard here, will no longer be heard there. For it is itself the plaintive sparrow of which he says in another psalm, “Like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Ps. 101:8). From the roof it flies to the house. Let it already be on the roof; let it trample the carnal house: it will have a heavenly dwelling, an everlasting home, and this sparrow will bring its complaints to an end.

But to the turtledove he gave young, that is, to the flesh: “The turtledove has found a nest for itself, where it may place its young.” The sparrow has a house, the turtledove a nest—and certainly a nest where it may place its young. A house is chosen, as it were, for eternity; a nest is constructed for a time. With the heart we think upon God, like a sparrow flying to its house; with the flesh, however, we perform good works. You see how many good things are accomplished through the flesh of the saints. Through it we perform what we have been commanded to perform, and by these works we are helped in this life: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; if you see someone naked, clothe him” (Isa. 58:7), and other such things that have been commanded us. We perform them only through the flesh.

Therefore that sparrow, which thinks upon its house, does not depart from the turtledove seeking a nest for itself where it may place its young. For it does not cast them down anywhere it happens to be; rather, it finds a nest for itself where it may place them.

But we say, brothers—as you know—how many seem to perform good works outside the Church! How many pagans feed the hungry, clothe the naked, receive strangers, visit the sick, and console the imprisoned! How many do these things? The turtledove seems to be producing offspring, but it does not find a nest for itself. How many things many heretics perform outside the Church, without placing their young in the nest? They will be trampled and crushed; they will not be preserved or guarded.

In the person of this flesh that performs works, the apostle Paul presents a certain woman when he says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived.” Adam afterward consented to the woman; for the woman was deceived by the serpent (Gen. 3:6). Nor can any evil persuasion now arise unless it first arouses the desire of your flesh [Note: [Col. 1060] Thus the manuscripts. Erasmus’s edition has *commoveret*; Lovaniensis has *commoverit*.], and if afterward you consent to it in your mind, the sparrow too has fallen. But if the desires of the flesh are overcome, the members are held ready for good works, the weapons of desire are taken away, and the turtledove begins to have young.

Therefore what does the Apostle say there? “She will be saved through the bearing of children.” Will a widowed woman, if she perseveres, not be happier? (1 Cor. 7:40). Will she not be saved because she does not bear children? Will a virgin of God not be better? Will she not be saved because she has no children? Or does she not belong to God?

The woman, then, who is understood figuratively as the flesh, will be saved through the bearing of children—that is, if she performs good works. But the turtledove must not find a nest for itself just anywhere where it may place its young. In the true faith, in the Catholic faith, in the fellowship of the Church’s unity, let it bring forth its works.

Therefore, when the Apostle was speaking of her, he added: “She will be saved through the bearing of children, if she remains in faith and love and holiness, with sobriety” (1 Tim. 2:14–15). By remaining in faith, then, faith itself is the nest of your young.

For on account of the weakness of the young of your turtledove, the Lord deigned to provide you with material from which you could make a nest: he clothed himself in the hay of flesh in order to come to you. In this faith place your young; in this nest perform your works.

What the nests are, or rather which nest it is, follows immediately: “Your altars, Lord of hosts.” When he had said, “The turtledove has found a nest for itself, where it may place its young,” as though you had asked, “Which nest?”—he answers: “Your altars, Lord of hosts, my king and my God.” What does “my king and my God” mean? The one who rules me, the one who created me.

### 8. [Verse 5]

But this is a nest, and here is our pilgrimage, here our sighing, here the threshing, here the pressing, because here is the winepress. What, then, does it desire? What does it long for? Where does our desire go? Toward what does it strive? Where does it carry us?

Placed here, it meditates upon those things; placed amid temptations, amid pressures, amid winepresses, sighing for the promises above, it already rehearses in advance, as it were, the future joys it will enjoy there. “Blessed,” he says, “are those who dwell in your house.” Why are they blessed? What will they possess? What will they do?

All those who are called blessed on earth possess something and do something. A man is called blessed because he has so many estates, so large a household, so much gold and silver: he is called blessed because of what he possesses. Another is called blessed because he has attained those honors, the proconsulate or the prefecture: he is called blessed because of what he does. Thus either because of possessing or because of doing.

But why are they blessed there? What will they possess? What will they do? What they will possess I have already said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house.” If you possess your own house, you are poor; if you possess the house of God, you are rich. In your own house you will fear robbers; the wall of the house of God is God himself. “Blessed, then, are those who dwell in your house.”

They possess the heavenly Jerusalem without narrowness, pressure, variation, or division of boundaries. All possess it, and each possesses the whole of it. Great are those riches! There one brother does not constrain another; there is no want.

What, then, will they do there? For necessity is the mother of all human activity. Brothers, I have already said briefly: run through in your mind every kind of activity and see whether anything gives birth to it except necessity. Those celebrated arts that seem so great in providing assistance—the advocacy of the tongue and the aids of medicine—are the outstanding activities of this present age. Remove the litigants: whom will the advocate assist? Remove wounds and illnesses: what will the physician treat?

All these activities of ours that daily life demands and brings about arise from necessity. Plowing, sowing, breaking up new ground, sailing—what work produces all such things except necessity and want? Take away hunger, thirst, and nakedness: for whom would all these things be needed?

The good works also that we are commanded to perform—for the things I have mentioned are honorable, though common to all human beings; I am excepting the worst works, detestable works, crimes and wicked deeds, murders, burglaries, adulteries, which I do not even count among human activities. I am speaking of honorable works: they arise only from the necessity of our bodily frailty.

Even the works we are commanded to perform—“Break your bread for the hungry”—for whom will you break it where no one is hungry? “Bring the homeless poor into your house”—which guest will you receive where everyone lives in his own homeland? Whom will you visit as sick where all enjoy perpetual health? With whom will you reconcile a quarrelsome person where eternal peace exists? Whom will you bury as dead where everyone lives forever?

You will therefore perform none of those honorable works common to all human beings; you will perform none of these good works, because these young of the turtledove will already have flown out of the nest.

What, then? You have already said what we shall possess: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house.” Say also what we shall do, because I do not see there any necessities that might compel me to act.

What I am saying and discussing now is produced by necessity. Will there be such discussion there, as though teaching the ignorant or reminding the forgetful? Or will the Gospel be recited in that homeland where the very Word of God will be contemplated?

Therefore, since this man, desiring and sighing with our voice, said what we shall possess in that homeland for which we sigh—“Blessed are those who dwell in your house”—let him also say what we shall do there: “They will praise you for ever and ever.”

This will be our entire occupation, an unceasing Alleluia. Do not suppose, brothers, that boredom will arise there. If you were to say this for a long time now, you would not endure it, because necessity turns you away from that joy. And since what is not seen does not delight us so greatly—if we praise with such eagerness, amid the very pressure and fragility of the flesh, what we believe, how shall we praise what we shall see?

When death has been swallowed up in victory, when this mortal has put on immortality and this corruptible has put on incorruption (1 Cor. 15:53–54), no one will say, “I have stood for a long time”; no one will say, “I have fasted for a long time; I have kept vigil for a long time.” There will be great stability there, and the immortality of our body itself will already be suspended in the contemplation of God [Note: [Col. 1062] The manuscripts have *contemplatione*.].

Even now, if this word that we distribute to you holds our bodily frailty upright for so long, what will that joy do to us? How will it transform us? “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Already like him—when shall we grow weary? From what shall we turn away?

Let us therefore be secure, brothers: the praise of God will not satisfy us [Note: [Col. 1062] The editions have *nisi laus Dei* (“unless the praise of God”). *Nisi* is absent from the better manuscripts. Among these, the Corbie manuscript also omits *laus Dei* (“the praise of God”), which most others have; but they do not add *amor Dei* (“the love of God”), nor does Erasmus’s edition have it.], nor will the love of God. If you grow weary of love, you will grow weary of praise. But if love will be everlasting, because that beauty will be insatiable, do not fear that you will be unable always to praise the one whom you will always be able to love.

Therefore: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will praise you for ever and ever.” Let us sigh for this life.

### 9. [Verses 6–7]

But how shall we get there? “Blessed is the man whose support comes from you, O Lord.” He understood where he was, because through the frailty of his flesh he could not fly to that blessedness. He looked around at his burdens, for it is said elsewhere: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15).

The spirit calls upward; the weight of the flesh draws downward. Between the two efforts—of suspension and of weight—there is a kind of struggle, and that struggle itself belongs to the pressure of the winepress.

Hear the Apostle expressing this very struggle from the winepress, because he too was crushed and pressed there: “I delight,” he says, “in the law of God according to the inner man; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members.”

Great is the struggle, and great the despair of escape, unless what follows comes to our aid: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:22–25).

Therefore here also, in this psalm, he saw those joys and considered them in his mind: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you for ever and ever.” But who will ascend there? What am I to do with the weight of the flesh?

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will praise you for ever and ever. For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man.” But what shall I do? How shall I fly? How shall I arrive? “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind.”

He declared himself wretched and said: “Who will free me from this body of death, so that I may dwell in the house of the Lord and praise him for ever and ever? Who will free me?” “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Therefore, just as in the Apostle’s words what came to the aid of that difficulty and apparently inextricable struggle was what he added—“The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord”—so here also, when he sighed with burning desire for the house of God and for those praises of God, and when he considered the heaviness of his body and the mass of his flesh, with a kind of despair arising, he awoke again to hope and said: “Blessed is the man whose support comes from you, O Lord.”

### 10.

What, then, does God provide in this grace for the one whom he has taken up in order to lead him to his destination? The psalm continues and says: “He has arranged ascents in his heart.”

He makes steps for him by which he may ascend. Where does he make these steps for him? In the heart. Therefore, the more you love, the higher you ascend. “He has arranged ascents,” he says, “in his heart.”

Who has done this? The one who has taken him up: “Blessed is the man whose support comes from you, O Lord.” Since he cannot do it by himself, your grace must take him up. And what does your grace do? It arranges [Col. 1064] ascents in the heart.

Where does it arrange the ascents? “In the heart, in the valley of weeping.” Behold, you have the winepress: the valley of weeping. Those pious tears of the afflicted are the new wine of lovers.

“He has arranged ascents in his heart.” Where, then, has he arranged them? “In the valley of weeping.” For here he has arranged ascents, in the valley of weeping; for here people weep where they sow: “Going forth,” he says, “they went and wept, casting their seeds” (Ps. 125:6).

Therefore let God arrange ascents in your heart through his grace. Ascend by loving. From this comes the singing of the Song of Ascents. And where has he arranged these ascents for you? “In the heart, in the valley of weeping.”

He has said where he arranged them and what he arranged [Note: [Col. 1064] Thus most printed editions. In B., *quo disposuit?* M.]. What did he arrange? Ascents. Where? Within, in the heart. In what region, and as though in what dwelling-place? “In the valley of weeping.”

For what shall we ascend? “To the place which he has appointed.” What does this mean, brothers: “To the place which he has appointed”? What place would he have named as the place he appointed, if it could be named?

You have been told: “He arranged ascents in the heart, in the valley of weeping.” You ask, “To where?” What answer can he give you? “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:9).

It is called a hill, a mountain, land, a meadow—nearly everything has been used to name that place. But who can explain what it is properly and not figuratively? For now “we see through a mirror in a riddle” what that place is; then “we shall see face to face” (ibid. 13:12).

Do not, then, ask to what place he has arranged them: “to the place which he has appointed.” He himself knows where; he knows, he who appointed it, where he will lead you, whose ascents he has arranged in your heart. Are you afraid to ascend, lest the one who leads you go astray?

Behold, “in the valley of weeping he arranged ascents, to the place which he has appointed.” We weep now. From where? From where our ascents have been arranged.

From where do we weep, unless from the condition that made the Apostle cry out that he was wretched, because he saw another law in his members warring against the law of his mind? And from where does this come to us? From the punishment of sin.

We thought that we could easily become righteous, as though by our own strength, before we received the commandment. But when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died—this is what the Apostle says.

For the Law was given to human beings, not to save them already, but so that through it they might recognize the sickness in which they lay. Hear the Apostle’s words: “For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly be from the Law. But Scripture imprisoned all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 3:21).

Grace was to come after the Law, and find a human being not only lying there but already confessing and saying, “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” Then the physician would come opportunely to the valley of weeping and say: “Certainly you have recognized that you have fallen. Listen to me, so that you may rise—you who disregarded me and therefore fell.”

The Law, then, was given to convict the sick person of his disease, since he seemed healthy to himself; it was given so that sins might be demonstrated, not so that they might be removed.

Once sin had been demonstrated through the Law that was given, sin increased, because sin is also committed against the Law: “Taking occasion,” he says, “through the commandment, sin worked in me every kind of covetous desire” (Rom. 7:7–8).

What does “taking occasion through the commandment” mean? Human beings attempted to fulfill the commandment as though by their own strength. Overcome by desire, they became guilty also through transgressing the commandment itself.

But what does the Apostle say? “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (ibid. 5:20): that is, the disease increased, and the medicine was commended.

Therefore, brothers, did those five porticoes of Solomon heal the sick, where the pool was located among them? “The sick,” he says, “lay in the five porticoes” (John 5:3); we have this passage in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1065] Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts. Lovaniensis has *dictum* (“said”).].

Those five porticoes are the Law contained in the five books of Moses. For this purpose the sick were brought out from their houses, so that they might lie in the porticoes. Thus the Law displayed the sick; it did not heal them.

But by God’s blessing the water was stirred, as though an angel were descending. When the water had been stirred, the one person who could descend was healed. That water surrounded by the five porticoes was the Jewish people enclosed by the Law. The Lord stirred this people by his presence, so that he might be killed.

For if the Lord had not stirred the Jewish people by his descent, would he have been crucified? Thus the stirred water signified the Lord’s passion, which occurred when the Jewish people were stirred up.

The sick person believes in this passion, descending into it as into stirred water, and is healed. One who was not healed by the Law—that is, by the porticoes—is healed by grace, through faith in the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ.

One, because there is unity.

Therefore what does he say here also? “He arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of weeping, to the place which he appointed.” There, in that place, we shall already rejoice.

### 11. [Verse 8]

Why, then, “in the valley of weeping”? And from what valley of weeping shall we come to that place of joy?

“For he will also give a blessing,” he says, “who gave the Law.” He afflicted us through the Law, pressed us through the Law, and showed us the winepress. We saw the pressure; we learned the tribulation of our flesh; we groaned while sin rebelled against our mind; we cried out, “Wretched man that I am!” Under the Law we groaned. What remains except that the one who gave the Law should give the blessing?

Grace will come after the Law; this is the blessing. And what has this grace and blessing provided for us? “They will go from virtue to virtue.”

Here, through grace, many virtues are given: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit; to another faith; to another gifts of healings; to another kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of utterances; to another prophecy” (1 Cor. 12:8–10).

There are many virtues, but they are necessary here; and from these virtues we go into virtue. What virtue? Christ, “the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (ibid. 1:24).

Here, in this place, he gives various virtues; but in place of all the virtues necessary and useful in the valley of weeping, he will give one virtue: himself.

Many also describe four virtues necessary for the conduct of our life, and they are found in Scripture. Prudence is that by which we distinguish good from evil. Justice is that by which we assign each person his due, owing nothing to anyone but loving all (Rom. 13:8). Temperance is that by which we restrain desires. Fortitude is that by which we endure everything painful.

These virtues are now given to us in the valley of weeping through the grace of God. From these virtues we go into that virtue.

And what will that virtue be, unless the contemplation of God alone? Prudence will not be necessary there, where no evils will arise for us to avoid. But what shall we think, brothers? Nor will this justice be necessary, where no one will lack anything whom we ought to assist. Nor will this temperance be necessary, where there will be no desire to restrain. Nor will this fortitude be necessary, where there will be no evils to endure.

Thus from the virtues of this active life we shall go into the virtue of that contemplation by which we contemplate God, as it is written: “In the morning I shall stand before you, and I shall contemplate” (Ps. 5:5).

And hear that from the virtues of this active life we shall go into that contemplation. It follows there: “They will go from virtue to virtue.” What virtue? The virtue of contemplation.

What does “of contemplation” mean? “The God of gods will appear in Zion.” The God of gods is Christ of Christians.

How is Christ the God of gods, the Christ of Christians? “I have said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). For he gave them the power to become children of God (John 1:12)—he in whom we have believed, the beautiful bridegroom who here appeared disfigured on account of our disfigurement. “We saw him,” it says, “and he had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53:2).

When every necessity of mortality has ended, he who is God with God, the Word with the Father, through whom all things were made, will appear to the pure in heart. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

“The God of gods will appear in Zion.”

### 12. [Verse 9]

Again, from contemplation of those joys he returns to his sighs. He sees what has preceded in hope and where he still is in reality. “Then the God of gods will appear in Zion”: this is the source of our joy; him we shall praise for ever and ever.

But for now it is still the time for praying, the time for supplication, and, if there is some measure of rejoicing, it is still in hope. We are on pilgrimage; we are in the valley of weeping.

Returning, then, to the groaning of this place, he says: “Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, God of Jacob.” For you also made that Jacob into Israel. God appeared to him, and he was called Israel (Gen. 32:28), “seeing God.”

Hear me, then, God of Jacob, and make me Israel. When shall I become Israel? When the God of gods appears in Zion.

### 13. [Verse 10]

“Look, O God, upon our protector.” “Under the shadow of your wings they will hope” (Ps. 35:8); therefore, “Look, O God, upon our protector.”

“And look upon the face of your Christ.” For when does God not look upon the face of his Christ? What does “Look upon the face of your Christ” mean?

We become known through the face. What, then, does “Look upon the face of your Christ” mean? Make your Christ known to everyone. “Look upon the face of your Christ”: let your Christ be known to all, so that we may go from virtue to virtue, so that grace may abound all the more, since sin abounded.

### 14. [Verse 11]

“For one day in your courts is better than thousands.” Those courts are the ones for which he sighed, in which his soul languished: “My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord.” One day there is better than thousands of days.

Human beings desire thousands of days and greatly wish to live here. Let them despise thousands of days and desire one day that has neither rising nor setting; one day, an everlasting day, to which yesterday does not yield and which tomorrow does not press upon. Let us desire that one day.

What have we to do with thousands of days? We go from thousands of days to one day [Note: [Col. 1067] The editions add here: “Let us hasten to the one day,” which the good manuscripts lack.], just as we go from virtues to virtue.

### 15.

“I have chosen to be cast down in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.”

For this man has found the valley of weeping; he has found humility from which he may ascend. He knows that if he wishes to exalt himself, he will fall, but if he humbles himself, he will be raised up. He has chosen to be cast down so that he may be lifted up.

How many people, wishing to be exalted apart from this tabernacle of the Lord’s winepress—that is, apart from the Catholic Church—and loving their own honors, refuse to recognize the truth [Note: [Col. 1067] Perhaps the decree of the Council of Carthage held on 13 September 401 had not yet been issued, providing that Donatist clergy should “be received in their own honors.”]?

If this verse were in their hearts—“I have chosen to be cast down in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners”—would they not cast aside their honors, run to the valley of weeping, find ascents in the heart there, and go from there from virtue to virtue, placing their hope in Christ and not in some unknown human being?

A good voice, a joyful voice, a voice to be chosen: “I have chosen to be cast down in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.”

He himself chose to be cast down in the house of the Lord. But the one who invited him to the banquet calls the person choosing the lower place to the higher and says to him, “Go up” (Luke 14:10). Nevertheless, he chose only to be in the house of the Lord, in whatever place—but not outside the threshold.

### 16. [Verse 12]

Why did he choose to be cast down in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners? “Because God loves mercy and truth.”

The Lord loves mercy, by which he first came to my aid; he loves truth, so that he may give the promised reward to the believer.

Hear mercy and truth in the Apostle Paul, formerly Saul the persecutor. He needed mercy, and he said that mercy had been shown to him: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy, so that in me Christ Jesus might display all patience toward those who would believe in him for eternal life” (1 Tim. 1:13, 16).

Thus, when Paul received pardon for such great crimes, no one would despair that whatever sins could be forgiven him [Note: [Col. 1067] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have *desperare posset* (“could despair”).].

Behold, you have mercy. At that time God did not wish to exercise truth by punishing the sinner. For if the sinner had been punished, would that not have been truth? Or would he dare to say, “I ought not to be punished,” when he could not say, “I have not sinned”? And if he said, “I have not sinned,” to whom would he say it? Whom would he deceive?

Therefore the Lord first bestowed mercy upon him; after mercy, truth. Hear him now demanding truth. First he says: “I obtained mercy, though I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10).

Afterward, when he was approaching his passion, he says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains for me the crown of righteousness.” The one who grants mercy preserves truth.

From where does he preserve truth? “Which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:7–8). He granted pardon; he will render the crown. He is the giver of pardon and the debtor of the crown.

How is he a debtor? Has he received something? Does God owe anything to anyone? We see that Paul holds him as a debtor: having obtained mercy, he demands truth: “The Lord will render to me,” he says, “on that day.”

What will he render to you, except what he owes you? How does he owe you anything? What have you given him? “Who has first given to him, that he may be repaid?” (Rom. 11:35).

The Lord made himself a debtor, not by receiving but by promising. He is not told, “Repay what you have received,” but, “Repay what you have promised.”

“He bestowed mercy upon me,” Paul says, “so as to make me innocent; for formerly I was a blasphemer and insolent, but by his grace I was made innocent.” But can the one who first bestowed mercy deny what he owes? “He loves mercy and truth.”

“He will give grace and glory.” What grace, except that of which Paul himself said, “By the grace of God I am what I am”? What glory, except that of which he said, “There remains for me the crown of righteousness”?

### 17. [Verse 13]

Therefore, “the Lord,” he says, “will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things.”

Why, then, do you refuse to preserve innocence, unless it is so that you may possess good things? He does not wish to preserve innocence so that he may not return what has been entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 1068] Thus several manuscripts. The editions have *non vultis* (“you do not wish”); and below, *quod ille assignat* (“what he assigns to him”), where most manuscripts have *quod illi assignatur* (“what is entrusted to him”), that is, the deposit entrusted to him.].

He wants to have gold and loses innocence. What does he gain? What does he lose? He has the profit of gold, but he has suffered the loss of innocence. Is anything more precious than innocence?

“But if I retain innocence,” he says, “I shall be poor.” Are innocence itself not great riches? If you have a chest full of gold, you will be rich; if you have a heart full of innocence, will you be poor?

But even now, while desiring the good things you long for, while in poverty, tribulation, the valley of weeping, pressure, and temptations, preserve innocence. What you desire will afterward also be your good: rest, eternity, immortality, freedom from suffering. These are the good things that God preserves for his righteous.

As for the good things you now desire as something great—the things for which you wish to be guilty rather than innocent—consider who possesses them and who abounds in such things.

You see riches among robbers, the impious, criminals, the shameful, the profligate, and the wicked. God gives them these things because of their participation in the human race and because of the abundance and overflowing generosity of his goodness [Note: [Col. 1068] Thus Erasmus and some manuscripts. Lovaniensis has “because of the abundance of generosity.”]. He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45).

He gives so much even to the wicked, and keeps nothing for you? Is what he promised you false? He keeps it. Be secure.

Did the one who had mercy on you when you were impious abandon you when you became devout? The one who granted the sinner the death of his Son—what does he preserve for the person saved through the death of his Son?

Be secure, then. Hold the debtor fast, because you have believed in the one who made the promise. “The Lord will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things.”

What, then, remains for us here in the winepress, in affliction, in hardship, in the dangerous condition of this life? What remains for us so that we may arrive there?

“Lord God of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you” [Note: [Col. 1069] Three manuscripts add to these words: “When you have turned to the Lord, O innocent one, what will be lacking to you if you are innocent for the Lord’s sake? For you possess the Lord himself, who is the source of all virtues and who gives virtues to those who persevere in innocence. Therefore blessed is the one who hopes in you, God.”].

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 84

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

#### 1.

We have entreated the Lord our God to show us his mercy and to give us his salvation. This was indeed said prophetically when these psalms were first spoken and written. But as far as the present time is concerned, the Lord has already shown his mercy to the nations and has given them his salvation.

He has shown it, certainly; but many do not wish to be healed so that they may see what he has shown. But because he himself heals the eyes of the heart so that they may see him, therefore, when he had said, “Show us your mercy,” as though many blind people might say, “How shall we see when he begins to show it?” he added, “And give us your salvation.”

By giving his salvation, he heals in us that by which we may see what he shows. This is not like a human physician, who heals people so that he may show them this light after he has cured them, while the light he will show is one thing and the physician who heals the eyes by which they may see the light is another—for the physician is not himself that light.

Our Lord God is not like this. He himself is the physician who heals that by which we may see, and he himself is the light that we may see.

Let us nevertheless run attentively through the whole psalm briefly, as far as we can and as far as the Lord grants, because of the limited time.

#### 2. [Verse 1]

Its title is: “To the end, for the sons of Korah, a psalm.” Let us understand “the end” to mean no other than the one of whom the Apostle says: “For Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4).

Therefore, when the title of the psalm first says, “To the end,” it directs our heart toward Christ. If we fix our attention on him, we shall not go astray, because he is the truth toward which we hasten, and he is the way by which we must run (John 14:6).

What does “for the sons of Korah” mean? *Korah* is translated from the Hebrew word into Latin as *Calvus*, “Bald.” Thus “for the sons of Korah” means “for the sons of the bald man.”

Who is this bald man? Not someone whom we should ridicule, but someone before whom we should weep. For certain people ridiculed him and were destroyed by demons. As the Book of Kings relates, when the boys ridiculed Elisha the bald man, saying after him, “Bald man, bald man,” bears came out of the forest and devoured the boys who laughed wickedly (2 Kings 2:23–24), boys to be mourned by their parents.

That event signified prophetically our future Lord Jesus Christ. For he was ridiculed by the Jews who mocked him as though he were bald, because he was crucified at the place of Calvary (Matt. 27:31).

But if we believe in him, we are his sons. This psalm, therefore, is sung for us, since it is inscribed “for the sons of Korah.” For we are the sons of the bridegroom (Matt. 9:15).

That bridegroom, giving his bride a pledge—his blood and the Holy Spirit, with which he has enriched us for the present during this pilgrimage—still keeps his hidden riches for us. If he has given such a pledge, what is it that he is keeping?

#### 3. [Verse 2]

Accordingly, the Prophet sings to him of the future, using words as though they referred already to past time. He speaks of things that were to happen as though they had happened, because with God even what is future has already happened.

There, then, the Prophet saw things future for us, but already accomplished in God’s most certain providence and predestination. In the same way he speaks in that psalm in which everyone recognizes Christ. It is recited as though the Gospel were being read [Note: [Col. 1070] Thus some manuscripts. Others, with the editions, have “the psalm was recited.”]:

“They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked and gazed upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots” (Ps. 21:17–19).

Who would not recognize the Gospel when the reader recites the psalm? Yet when this was said in the psalm, it did not say, “They will pierce my hands and feet,” but, “They pierced my hands and feet.” It did not say, “They will count my bones,” but, “They counted my bones.” It did not say, “They will divide my garments,” but, “They divided my garments among themselves.”

All these things that the Prophet saw as future he presented as though they were past. So here also: “You have blessed your land, O Lord,” as though he had already done so.

### 4. “You turned back the captivity of Jacob.”

His ancient people was Jacob, the people of Israel, born from the seed of Abraham and destined, in the promise, eventually to be God’s heir. There was indeed that people, to whom the Old Testament was given; but in the Old Testament the New Testament was prefigured.[^c0005-1] That was the figure; this is the expression of the truth.

In that figure, according to a certain foretelling of future things, a land of promise was given to that people, in a particular region where the Jewish people dwelt. There also stands the city of Jerusalem, whose name we have all heard. After that people had received this land, it suffered many hardships from its neighboring enemies, who attacked it on every side. And whenever it sinned against its God, it was handed over into captivity—not for destruction, but for discipline; not because the father condemned it, but because he chastised it.

When it had been conquered, it was liberated; and that nation was captured and liberated several times. Even now it is in captivity, and this is on account of the great sin it committed in crucifying its Lord.

What, then, according to these people, are we to understand by the words, “You turned back the captivity of Jacob”? Perhaps we should understand here another captivity, from which we all wish to be liberated. For we all belong to Jacob, if we belong to the seed of Abraham. The Apostle says this: “In Isaac shall your seed be called”—that is, “It is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed” (Rom. 9:7–8).

If the children of the promise are counted as seed, the Jews, by offending God, became degenerate; but we, by pleasing God, have become descendants of Abraham—not belonging to the flesh, but belonging to faith. For by imitating his faith we became children; whereas they, by degenerating from faith, deserved to be disinherited.

To make clear that they lost what they had received by being born from Abraham, consider how they arrogantly boasted before the Lord Jesus Christ, glorying in their bloodline and not in their life, saying to the Lord, “We have Abraham as our father.” The Lord, speaking to them as degenerates, said: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39).

If, then, they are no longer children because they did not do the works of Abraham, we are children because we do the works of Abraham. What are the works of Abraham that we do? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6; Gal. 3:6).

Therefore we all belong to Jacob, imitating the faith of Abraham, who believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.

What, then, is the captivity from which we wish to be liberated? I suppose that none of us is currently among the barbarians, nor has some armed nation invaded us and led us away captive. But now I shall show a certain captivity in which we groan and from which we desire to be liberated.

Let the Apostle Paul come forward and speak of it himself. Let him be our mirror; let him speak, and let us see ourselves there. For there is no one who does not recognize himself in these words. That blessed Apostle says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man”—within, the law of God delights me—“but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind.”

You have heard of the law; you have heard of the struggle. You have not yet heard of the captivity; hear what follows: “Warring,” he says, “against the law of my mind, and making me captive under the law of sin which is in my members.”

We recognize the captivity. Who among us does not wish to be liberated from this captivity? And from where will he be liberated? Because this Psalm itself sang of what was to come: “You turned back the captivity of Jacob.”

To whom did it say this? To Christ, on account of the words “For the end,” and “For the sons of Korah.” For he turned back the captivity of Jacob.

Hear Paul himself confessing this. When he said that he was being dragged captive by the law in his members, which warred against the law of his mind, he cried out under that captivity and said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” He asked who it was, and the answer immediately presented itself to him: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:22–25).

Of this grace of God the Prophet says to our Lord Jesus Christ: “You turned back the captivity of Jacob.”

Consider the captivity of Jacob; understand that this means, “You turned back our captivity”—not by freeing us from barbarians, among whom we have not been captive, but by freeing us from evil works and from our sins, through which Satan exercised dominion over us. For if someone has been freed from his sins, the prince of sinners has no basis on which to dominate him.

### 5. “[Verses 3–4.] You forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sins.”

How, then, did he turn back the captivity of Jacob? See that this liberation is spiritual; see that it takes place within: “You forgave,” he says, “the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sins.”

This is how he turned back the captivity: because he forgave the iniquity. Iniquity held the person captive; when iniquity is forgiven, you are liberated.

Confess, then, that you are in captivity, so that you may be worthy to be liberated. For one who has not understood his enemy—how can he call upon a liberator?

“You covered all their sins.” What does “you covered” mean? So that you would not see them. What does “so that you would not see them” mean? So that you would not punish them on account of them. You did not wish to see our sins; and therefore you did not see them,[^c0005-2] because you did not wish to see them: “You covered all their sins.”

“You calmed all your anger; you turned away from the anger of your indignation.”

### 6. “[Verse 5.] Turn us, Lord God of our salvations.”[^c0005-3]

And since these things are spoken of the future, although the words sound as though they referred to the past, he continues and says: “Turn us, Lord God of our salvations.”

What he had just narrated as though it had already happened—how does he now pray that it may happen? Unless it is because he wished to show that he had spoken the past-tense words prophetically.

That what he said had already happened is not yet accomplished is shown by the fact that he prays for it to happen: “Turn us, Lord God of our salvations, and turn away your anger from us.”

Were you not saying a little earlier, “You turned back the captivity of Jacob; you covered all their sins; you calmed all your anger; you turned away from the anger of your indignation”? How, then, do you now say, “Turn away your anger from us”?

The Prophet answers you: “I speak of those things as though they had happened because I see them as future; but because they have not yet happened, I pray that what I have already seen may come.” “Turn away your anger from us.”

### 7. “[Verse 6.] Will you be angry with us forever?”

Because of God’s anger we are mortal; and because of God’s anger, in this land, amid poverty and the labor of our faces, we eat bread. This is what Adam heard when he sinned: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. 3:19).

That Adam was all of us, because “in Adam all die.” What he heard has come upon us also. For we did not yet exist as ourselves, but we were in Adam. Therefore whatever happened to Adam also came upon us, so that we would die; for we were all in him.

The sins of parents do not pertain to children when the parents commit them after the children have already been born. Once children have been born, the children belong to themselves, and the parents belong to themselves. Therefore, if those who have been born continue in the evil ways of their parents, they necessarily bear their parents’ merits as well. But if they change themselves and do not imitate their evil parents, they begin to possess their own merit, not that of their parents.

Indeed, your father’s sin does not harm you if you change yourself—to such an extent that it does not even harm your father himself if he changes himself.

But what our root received for this mortality, it brought from Adam. What did it bring? This frailty of the flesh, this torment of pains, this house of poverty, this bond of death, and these snares of temptations. We carry all these things in this flesh; and this is God’s anger, because it is God’s punishment.

But because it was destined that we should be regenerated, and that by believing we should be made new; because in the resurrection all that mortality would be consumed, and the newness of the whole human being restored—for just as “in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22)—the Prophet, seeing this, said: “Will you be angry with us forever, or extend your anger from generation to generation?”

The first generation was mortal, arising from your anger; the second generation will be immortal, arising from your mercy.

### 8. “[Verse 7.] Will you not revive us again, so that your people may rejoice in you?”

What, then? Did you bring this about for yourself, O man—that because you turned to God, you deserved his mercy, whereas those who did not turn did not obtain mercy but encountered anger?

But in order that you might turn, could you have done so unless you had been called? Was it not the one who called you while you were turned away who himself enabled you to turn?

Do not, then, arrogate even your conversion to yourself. For unless he called you while you were fleeing, you could not turn.

Therefore, attributing even the benefit of conversion to God, the Prophet prays and says: “God, you who turn us, will revive us.”

He does not mean that we turn to you of our own will, without your mercy, and that you then revive us. Rather: “You who turn us will revive us,” so that not only our revival may come from you, but also the very conversion by which we are revived.

“God, you who turn us, will revive us; and your people will rejoice in you.”

A person rejoices in himself to his own harm; in you he will rejoice to his own good. When he wished to have joys from himself, he found mourning within himself. But now, because God is our entire joy, whoever wishes to rejoice securely should rejoice in him who cannot perish.

What, then, my brothers, do you wish to rejoice in—in silver? Either the silver perishes, or you do; and no one knows which will happen first. Yet this is certain: both will perish; which will perish first is uncertain.

For neither can a human being remain here forever, nor can silver remain here forever; so too gold, clothing, a house, money, broad estates, and finally this light itself.

Do not, then, wish to rejoice in these things. Rejoice in that light which has no setting; rejoice in that light which is preceded by no yesterday and followed by no tomorrow.

What is this light? “I am,” he says, “the light of the world” (John 8:12).

The one who says to you, “I am the light of the world,” calls you to himself. When he calls you, he turns you; when he turns you, he heals you; when he has healed you, you will see the one who turns you, to whom it is said: “And your people will rejoice in you.”

### 9. “[Verse 8.] Show us, Lord, your mercy.”

This is what we have sung[^c0005-9] and have already said here: “Show us, Lord, your mercy; and give us your salvation”—your salvation, your Christ.

Blessed is the one to whom God shows his mercy. The one to whom God shows his mercy cannot be proud. For by showing him his mercy, God persuades him that whatever good that person possesses, he possesses only from the one who is our entire good.

When a person sees that whatever good he possesses does not come from himself but from his God, he sees that everything praised in him comes from God’s mercy, not from his own merits. Seeing this, he does not become proud; not becoming proud, he is not lifted up; not being lifted up, he does not fall; not falling, he stands; standing, he clings; clinging, he remains; remaining, he enjoys and rejoices in the Lord his God.

The one who made him will himself be his delight. No one corrupts, interrupts, or takes away that delight. Who, being powerful, will threaten to take it away? What evil neighbor, thief, or ambusher can take God from you? He may be able to take away everything you possess in body, but he cannot take away the one whom you possess in your heart.

This is the mercy[^c0005-10] which—would that God would show it to us!—the Psalm asks for: “Show us, Lord, your mercy; and give us your salvation.” Give us your Christ; for in him is your mercy.

Let us also say to him: “Give us your Christ.” He has indeed already given us his Christ; nevertheless, let us still say to him, “Give us your Christ,” because we say to him, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. 6:11).

And what is our bread except the one who said, “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:41)?

Let us say to him: “Give us your Christ.” He has given us Christ, but as man; the very one whom he gave us as man[^c0005-11] he will give us as God. For he gave man to human beings, because he gave him to human beings in a form that human beings could receive. No human being could receive Christ as God.

He became man for human beings; he preserved himself as God for gods.

Or did I say this arrogantly? It would indeed be arrogant, unless he himself had said: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6; John 10:34).

We are renewed for that adoption,[^c0005-12] so that we may become children of God. We already are—but by faith. We are indeed so in hope; we are not yet so in reality. “For in hope we have been saved,” as the Apostle says. “But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25).

What do we await with patience except seeing what we believe? At present we believe what we do not see. By remaining in what we believe without seeing, we shall deserve to see what we believe.

Therefore, what does John say in his Epistle? “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be.”

Who would not rejoice if, suddenly, some traveler ignorant of his ancestry, enduring poverty and living in hardship and labor, were told: “You are the son of a senator; your father rejoices in a great estate and patrimony; I am restoring you to your father”? What joy he would feel, if the one making this promise were not deceitful!

So the truthful Apostle of Christ comes and says: “Why do you despair of yourselves? Why do you afflict yourselves and wear yourselves down with sorrow? Why, by following your desires, do you wish to be worn down in the poverty of these pleasures? You have a father, you have a homeland, you have an inheritance.”

Who is this father? “Beloved, we are children of God.”

Why, then, do we not yet see our Father? Because “it has not yet appeared what we shall be.” We already are, but in hope; for “what we shall be has not yet appeared.”

And what shall we be? “We know,” he says, “that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

But John said this about the Father; he did not say it about the Son, the Lord Jesus Christ.[^c0005-4] Perhaps, then, by seeing the Father and not the Son, we shall be blessed? Hear Christ himself: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”

When the one God is seen, the Trinity is seen: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Hear more explicitly that the vision of the Son himself will grant us blessedness, and that there is no difference between seeing him and seeing the Father. He says in the Gospel: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments, and I will love him and will show myself to him” (John 14:9, 21).

He was speaking to them and said, “I will show myself to him.” Why? Was he not himself the one who was speaking? The flesh was seeing flesh; the heart was not seeing divinity.[^c0005-13]

For this reason flesh saw flesh, so that the heart might be cleansed through faith, and from there might see God. It is said of the Lord: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). And the Lord said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

Therefore he promised that he would show himself to us.

What is his beauty, brothers? Consider it. All these beautiful things that you see and love—he made them. If these things are beautiful, what is he? If these things are great, how great is he?

Therefore, from these things that we love here, let us desire him more; and, despising these things, let us love him, so that by this very love we may cleanse our heart through faith, and our cleansed heart may encounter his vision.

The light that will be shown to us must find us healthy. This is what faith is doing now.

“Give us your salvation”: give us your Christ; let us know your Christ; let us see your Christ—not as the Jews saw him and crucified him, but as the angels see him and rejoice.

### 10. “[Verse 9.] I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me.”

The Prophet said this. God was speaking within him, while the world was making noise outside. Checking himself for a little while from the world’s noise, turning toward himself and, from himself, toward the one whose voice he heard within; as though stopping his ear against the tumult of this life’s restlessness, and against the soul weighed down by the body that is subject to corruption, and against the understanding depressed by its earthly dwelling and occupied with many thoughts (Wis. 9:15), he said: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me.”

And what did he hear? “For he will speak peace to his people.”

Therefore Christ’s voice, God’s voice, is peace; it calls us to peace.

“Come,” he says. “All of you who are not yet at peace, love peace. For what better thing can you find from me than peace?”

What is peace? Where there is no war.

What does “where there is no war” mean? Where there is no contradiction, where nothing resists, where nothing is hostile.

See whether we are already there. See whether there is no longer conflict with the devil. See whether all the saints and faithful are not wrestling with the prince of demons.

And how do they wrestle with one whom they do not see? They wrestle with their desires, through which he suggests sins to them. By not consenting to what he suggests, they fight, even if they are not conquered.

There is not yet peace, then, where there is struggle.

Or give me a person who suffers no temptation in his flesh, so that he may tell me that there is already peace. Perhaps he suffers no temptation in illicit pleasures; nevertheless, he at least suffers the suggestions themselves. Either something is suggested to him that he rejects, or something delights him from which he must restrain himself.

But suppose that nothing illicit now delights him. At least he struggles daily against hunger and thirst. For what righteous person is exempt from this? Hunger and thirst struggle; the weariness of the flesh struggles against us; the desire for sleep struggles; oppression struggles.

We wish to keep watch, but we grow drowsy. We wish to fast, but we hunger and thirst. We wish to stand, but we grow tired. We seek to sit; and if we do that for a long time, we weaken.

Whatever we provide for our refreshment, there again we find weariness.

Are you hungry? someone says to you. You answer, “I am hungry.” He sets food before you; he set it before you for refreshment. Remain in what he has set before you. Certainly you wanted to refresh yourself; keep doing this. By continuing to do it, in the very thing you had taken for refreshment, you find weariness.

You had grown tired from sitting for a long time; you rise and are refreshed by walking. Continue in what refreshes you; by walking for a long time, you become tired. You seek to sit again.

Find me something by which you can be refreshed, but in which, if you persist, you do not again become weary.

What kind of peace, then, is this which human beings possess here, amid so many resisting hardships, desires, needs, and wearinesses? This is not true peace; it is not perfect peace.
