What will perfect peace be? “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. Then shall come to pass the saying that is written: ‘Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your sting? O death, where is your contention?’” (1 Cor. 15:53–55).

For while mortality[^c0005-14] still exists, how can there be complete peace? This weariness, which we encounter in all our forms of refreshment, comes from death. It is from death because we carry a mortal body. Indeed, the Apostle calls the body dead even before the soul’s dissolution: “The body,” he says, “is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10).

For if you persist in what refreshes you, you will also die. Persist in eating excessively: the very thing will kill you. Persist in fasting excessively: you will die from it. Sit always, so that you do not wish to rise: you will die from it. Walk always, so that you do not wish to rest: you will die from it. Keep watch always, so that you do not wish to sleep: you will die from it. Sleep always, so that you do not wish to keep watch: you will die from it.

When, then, death has been swallowed up in victory, these things will no longer exist, and there will be full and eternal peace.

We shall be in a certain city. Brothers, when I speak of it, I do not want to stop—especially when scandals are increasing.

Who would not desire that city[^c0005-15] from which no friend departs, into which no enemy enters; where there is no tempter, no seditious person, no one dividing God’s people, and no one wearying the Church in the service of the devil? Then their own prince will be sent into eternal fire, together with all who agree with him and refuse to withdraw from him.

There will therefore be purified peace among the children of God, all loving one another, seeing one another filled with God, when God is “all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28).

God will be our common spectacle; God will be our common possession; God will be our common peace.

For whatever he now gives us, he himself will be for us in place of all that he gives. He will be perfect and complete peace.[^c0005-5]

This is the peace he speaks to his people—the peace that the one who said, “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me,” wished to hear: “For he will speak peace to his people, to his saints, and to those who turn their hearts toward him.”

Come, brothers: do you wish this peace that God speaks to belong to you? Turn your hearts toward him—not toward me, or toward that person, or toward any human being.

For whoever wishes to turn human hearts toward himself falls together with them. What is better: that you should fall with the one toward whom you turn, or that you should stand with the one with whom you turn?

Our joy, our peace, our rest, the end of all our troubles, is God alone. Blessed are those who turn their hearts toward him.

### 11. “[Verse 10.] Yet his salvation is near those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land.”

There were certain people among the Jewish nation who already feared him. Throughout all lands, idols were worshiped everywhere; demons were feared, not God. Among that nation, God was feared.

But why was he feared? In the Old Testament he was feared lest he hand them over into captivity, lest he take away their land, lest he crush their vines with hail, lest he make their wives barren, lest he take their children away from them.

These carnal promises of God still held small souls, and on account of these things God was feared. Yet he was near those who feared him even for these reasons.

The pagan sought land from the devil; the Jew sought land from God. What they sought was the same, but the one from whom they sought it was not the same.

By seeking what the pagan sought, the Jew was nevertheless distinguished from the pagan, because he sought these things from the one who had made everything.

And God was near to them, while he was far from the Gentiles. Yet he also regarded those who were far off and those who were near, as the Apostle says: “Coming, he preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near” (Eph. 2:17).

Whom did he call those who were near? The Jews, because they worshiped the one God.

Whom did he call those who were far off? The Gentiles, because they had abandoned the one by whom they were made and worshiped the things they themselves had made.

For no one is far from God by distance of place, but by disposition. You love God: you are near. You hate God: you are far away. Standing in one place, you may be both near and far.

The Prophet therefore regarded this. Although he saw God’s general mercy extending over all, he nevertheless saw something special and particular in the Jewish nation and said, “Yet.”

“I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me; for he will speak peace to his people.” And his people will not be the Jewish people alone, but will be gathered from all nations, because he will speak peace to his saints and to those who turn their hearts toward him—and to all who will turn their hearts toward him[^c0005-6] from the whole world.

“Yet his salvation is near those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land”—that is, in the land where the Prophet was born, greater glory may dwell, because from there Christ began to be preached.[^c0005-17]

From there came the Apostles, and there they were first sent. From there came the Prophets. There was the first temple; there God was sacrificed to; there were the Patriarchs. There also he himself came from the seed of Abraham. There Christ was manifested; there Christ appeared. For from there came the Virgin Mary, who bore Christ.

There he walked with his own feet; there he performed miracles.

Finally, he conferred such honor upon that nation that, when a certain Canaanite woman appealed to him, seeking healing for her daughter, he said to her: “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24).

Seeing this, the Prophet said: “Yet his salvation is near those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land.”

### 12. “[Verse 11.] Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed one another.”

Truth in our land came from the person of the Jews; mercy in the land of the Gentiles.

Where was truth? Where the utterances of God were.

Where was mercy? Among those who had abandoned their God and turned toward demons.

Did he despise them as well? It was as though he were saying: “Call these fugitives who are far away, who have withdrawn a long way from me. Call them, so that they may find me seeking them, since they did not wish to seek me.”

Therefore, “Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed one another.”

Do righteousness, and you will have peace, so that righteousness and peace may kiss one another. For if you do not love righteousness, you will not have peace.

These two love one another—righteousness and peace—and they kiss one another, so that the one who does righteousness may find peace kissing righteousness.

They are two friends. Perhaps you want one but do not practice the other. For there is no one who does not want peace, but not everyone wishes to work righteousness.

Ask all human beings, “Do you want peace?” The whole human race answers you with one voice: “I desire it, I long for it, I want it, I love it.”

Love righteousness as well, because righteousness and peace are two friends. They kiss one another. If you do not love the friend of peace, peace itself will not love you, nor will it come to you.

What great thing is it to desire peace? Any wicked person desires peace. Peace is a good thing.

But do righteousness, because righteousness and peace kiss one another; they do not quarrel.

Why do you quarrel with righteousness? Righteousness says to you, “Do not rage,” and you do not listen. “Do not commit adultery,” and you do not wish to listen. “Do not do to another what you do not want to suffer yourself.” “Do not say to another what you do not want said to you.”

“You are an enemy of my friend,” peace says to you. “Why do you seek me? I am a friend of righteousness. Whoever I find to be an enemy of my friend, I do not approach.”

Do you therefore wish to come to peace? Do righteousness.

For this reason another Psalm says to you: “Turn away from evil and do good”—that is, love righteousness—“and when you have turned away from evil and done good, seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. 33:15).

You will no longer seek it for long, because it too will meet you, so that it may kiss righteousness.

### 13. “[Verse 12.] Truth has arisen from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.”

“Truth has arisen from the earth”: Christ was born from a woman.

“Truth has arisen from the earth”: the Son of God proceeded from flesh.

What is truth? The Son of God.

What is earth? Flesh.

Ask from where Christ was born, and you will see that truth has arisen from the earth.

But this truth that arose from the earth existed before the earth, and through it heaven and earth were made. Yet so that righteousness might look down from heaven—that is, so that human beings might be justified by divine grace—truth was born from the Virgin Mary, so that he could offer a sacrifice in order to justify them: the sacrifice of his passion, the sacrifice of the cross.[^c0005-16]

And from where could he offer a sacrifice for our sins unless he died? But how could he die unless he received from us that by which he could die? That is, unless he took mortal flesh from us, Christ could not die. For the Word does not die; divinity does not die; the Power and Wisdom of God do not die.

How could he offer the sacrifice, the saving victim, if he did not die? And how could he die unless he assumed flesh? How could he assume flesh unless truth arose from the earth?

“Truth has arisen from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.”

### 14.

We can also give this another interpretation.

“Truth has arisen from the earth”: confession from a human being.

You were a sinner, O human being. O earth, when you sinned you heard, “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. 3:19). Let truth arise from you, so that righteousness may look down from heaven.

How does truth arise from you when you are a sinner, when you are unrighteous? Confess your sins, and truth will arise from you.

For if, although you are unrighteous, you say that you are righteous, how could truth arise from you? But if, although you are unrighteous, you say that you are unrighteous, truth has arisen from the earth.

Consider that tax collector praying in the temple, standing far away from the Pharisee. He did not dare even to lift his eyes to heaven, but was beating his breast and saying, “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

Behold, truth has arisen from the earth, because confession of sins has been made by a human being.

What follows? “Truly I tell you, that tax collector went down justified more than that Pharisee; for everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18:13–14).

Truth has arisen from the earth in the confession of sins; and righteousness has looked down from heaven, so that that tax collector went down justified more than the Pharisee.

To make clear that truth pertains to the confession of sins, the evangelist John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

How, then, does truth arise from the earth, so that righteousness may look down from heaven? Hear him continue and say: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John 1:8–9).

Therefore, truth has arisen from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.

What righteousness has looked down from heaven? It is as though God were saying: “Let us spare this man, because he did not spare himself. Let us forgive him, because he acknowledges. He has turned toward punishing his sin; I will turn toward freeing him.”

“Truth has arisen from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.”

### 15. “[Verse 13.] For the Lord will give sweetness, and our land will give its fruit.”

One verse remains. I ask that what I am about to say not seem tedious. Pay attention to something necessary, my brothers; pay attention, take it in, carry it away with you, and do not let the seed of God be empty in your hearts.[^c0005-7]

“Truth,” he says, “has arisen from the earth”: confession of sins by a human being. “And righteousness has looked down from heaven”: justification has been given by the Lord God to the one who confesses, so that he may acknowledge that the ungodly cannot make himself godly unless the one to whom he confesses does this—by believing in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5).

You can possess your sins; you will not possess good fruit unless the one to whom you confess gives it.

Therefore, after he had said, “Truth has arisen from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven,” it is as though someone said to him: “What is this that you have said, ‘Righteousness has looked down from heaven’?”

“For,” he says, “the Lord will give sweetness, and our land will give its fruit.”

Let us therefore look at ourselves. And if we find nothing in ourselves except sins, let us hate our sins and desire righteousness.

When we begin to hate sins, that very hatred of sins begins to make us like God, because we hate what God also hates.

When, therefore, you begin to hate your sins and confess them to God, when illicit pleasures seize and drag you toward things that do not benefit you, groan toward God. By confessing your sins to him, you will deserve to receive delight from him, and he will give you the sweetness of practicing righteousness.

Thus righteousness will begin to delight you, whereas iniquity formerly delighted you. You who once rejoiced in drunkenness will rejoice in sobriety. You who once rejoiced in theft, taking from another what you did not possess, will seek to give to one who does not possess what you have. You whom robbery delighted will be delighted by giving. You whom watching spectacles delighted will be delighted by praying. You whom foolish and adulterous songs delighted will be delighted to sing a hymn to God. You will run to church, although previously you ran to the theater.

From where did this sweetness arise, unless because “the Lord will give sweetness, and our land will give its fruit”?

For consider what I am saying. Behold, we have spoken to you the word of God; we have scattered seed among devoted hearts, finding your breasts, as it were, plowed by the plow of confession.

You received the seed with devotion and attention. Think about the word you have heard, as though breaking up clods, so that birds may not snatch away the seed and what has been sown may be able to sprout there.

And unless God sends rain, what benefit is there in what is sown?

This is what is meant by: “The Lord will give sweetness, and our land will give its fruit.”

May he visit your hearts by his visitations[^c0005-8]—in leisure, in business, at home, in bed, at table, in conversation, while walking—where we are not.

May God’s rain come and make fruitful what has been sown there. And where we are not present, while we rest securely or attend to something else, may God give growth to the seeds we have scattered, so that afterward, when we observe your good conduct, we too may rejoice in the fruit.

“For the Lord will give sweetness, and our land will give its fruit.”

16. [verse 14.] Righteousness shall go before him, and shall set his footsteps on the way. That righteousness is the one found in the confession of sins; for it is truth itself. You must be righteous toward yourself, so that you may punish yourself: this is the first righteousness of a human being—to punish yourself as evil, and for God to make you good. Since this, then, is the first righteousness of a human being, it becomes a way for God, so that God may come to you: make a way for him there, in the confession of sins. Therefore John too, when he was baptizing in the water of repentance and wanted penitents to come to him because of their former deeds, used to say this: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Matthew 3:3). You pleased yourself in your sins, O human being; let what you were displease you, so that you may be able to become what you were not. “Prepare the way of the Lord”: let this righteousness go before, so that you may confess your sins. He will come and visit you, because he will set his footsteps on the way; there is already a place for him to set his footsteps, there is a way by which he may come to you. Before you confessed your sins, however, you had blocked the way of God to yourself; there was no path by which he could come to you. Confess your life, and you open the way; and Christ will come and set his footsteps on the way, so that he may form you according to his footprints.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 85

### SERMON

[Note: [Column 1081] Delivered to the congregation on the vigil of a solemnity, perhaps that of Saint Cyprian, and preached at Carthage.]

1. God could bestow no greater gift upon human beings than to make the Word through whom he created all things their head, and to join them to him as members; so that he might be both the Son of God and the son of man, one God with the Father, one human being with human beings. Thus, when we speak to God in supplication, we do not separate the Son from him; and when the body of the Son prays, it does not separate its head from itself. Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is himself the one Savior of his body: he prays for us, he prays in us, and he is prayed to by us.

He prays for us as our priest; he prays in us as our head; he is prayed to by us as our God. Let us therefore recognize our voices in him, and his voices in us. And when something is said about the Lord Jesus Christ—especially in prophecy—that seems to pertain to a certain lowliness unworthy of God, let us not hesitate to attribute it to him who did not hesitate to join himself to us. For all creation serves him, because all creation was made through him.

Therefore, when we contemplate his sublimity and divinity, hearing, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3)—when we contemplate this divinity of the Son of God, most exalted and surpassing all the heights of created things, we also hear him, in some part of Scripture, as if groaning, praying, and confessing. We hesitate to attribute these words to him because our thought, recently occupied with his contemplation as God, is slow to descend to his lowliness. It often clings to the thought that it would do him an injury if, in his humanity, it recognized his words, when he was addressing them to the one whom he was beseeching as God; it tries to alter the meaning, and Scripture does not come to its aid except by leading it back to him and preventing it from straying from him.

Let it therefore awaken and rouse itself in faith, and see that the one whom it had just contemplated in the form of God [Column 1082] “took the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2:5–8). While hanging on the cross, he wanted the words of the Psalm to be his own, saying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 21:2).

Thus he is prayed to in the form of God, and he prays in the form of a servant: there the Creator, here the created one [Note: The word “created” was absent from the excellent Corbie manuscript.], assuming creation so that it might be changed, without himself being changed, and making us one human being with himself, head and body.

Therefore we pray to him, through him, and in him; we speak with him, and he speaks with us. We speak in him, and he speaks in us the prayer of this Psalm, which is entitled “A Prayer of David.” For our Lord, according to the flesh, is the son of David; according to his divinity, however, he is David’s Lord and David’s Creator—not only before David, but also before Abraham, from whom David came; and before Adam, from whom all human beings came; and before heaven and earth, in which all creation exists.

Therefore, when anyone hears these words, let no one say, “Christ is not speaking”; nor, again, let anyone say, “I am not speaking.” Rather, if one recognizes oneself in the body of Christ, let one say both: “Christ is speaking,” and “I am speaking.” Do not say anything without him, and he does not say anything without you. [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “He cannot say anything without him, and he says something without you.”]

Do we not have this in the Gospel? There, certainly, it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him.” There, certainly, we also have: “Jesus was sorrowful” (Matthew 26:38), “Jesus was tired” (John 4:6), “Jesus slept” (Matthew 8:24), “he was hungry” (the same, 4:2), and “Jesus was thirsty” (John 4:7; 19:28); and he prayed, and Jesus spent the night in prayer. “Jesus,” it says, “spent the night” (Luke 6:12), and continued in prayer [Note: Ferrara manuscript: “prostrated himself.”]; and globules of blood ran down through his body (Luke 22:43–44). What did he indicate when globules of blood dripped through the body of one who was praying, except that his body, which is the Church, was already flowing with the blood of martyrs?

2. [verse 1.] “Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear me.” He speaks from the form of a servant; you, servant, speak in the form of your Lord: “Incline your ear, O Lord.” He inclines his ear if you do not raise your neck; for he draws near to the humbled, but withdraws far from the exalted—unless he himself has exalted the one who was humbled.

God therefore inclines his ear to us. He is above, we are below; he is in exaltation, we are in lowliness—but we have not been abandoned. For “God demonstrates his love in us: indeed, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. For scarcely,” he says, “will anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person. But our Lord died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6–9).

Our merits had not gone before, on account of which the Son of God would die; rather, precisely because there were no merits, mercy was great. How certain, then, how secure a promise he makes to the righteous concerning their life—he who gave the unrighteous his own death! “Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear me; for I am poor and needy.”

He therefore does not incline [Column 1083] his ear to the rich; he inclines his ear to the poor and needy—that is, to the humble and the confessing, to the one who needs mercy—not to the one who is satiated, exalts himself, and boasts as though he lacked nothing, saying, “I thank you that I am not like this tax collector” (Luke 18:11–13). The rich Pharisee boasted of his merits; the poor tax collector confessed his sins.

3. Brothers, do not understand what I said—“He does not incline his ear to the rich”—as though God does not hear those who possess gold and silver, household servants, and estates, if they happened to be born into such circumstances or occupy that position among human affairs [Note: Thus several manuscripts; the editions read, “or when they gain [wealth].”]. Let them remember only what the Apostle says: “Command those who are rich in this present world not to be high-minded” (1 Timothy 6:17).

Those who are not high-minded are poor in God’s sight; and to the poor, needy, and destitute he inclines his ear. For they know that their hope is not in gold and silver, nor in those things with which they seem, for a time, to overflow. It is enough that riches do not destroy them; it is sufficient that they do not harm them, for they can provide no benefit. Certainly, an act of mercy is beneficial both in the rich person and in the poor: in the rich person, through will and deed; in the poor person, through will alone.

When someone is such as to despise in himself whatever normally inflates pride, he is God’s poor person. God inclines his ear to him, for he knows his contrite heart. Certainly, brothers, that poor man covered with sores who lay before the rich man’s gate was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom—we read it, and we believe it. But the rich man who dressed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day was taken to hell for torments (Luke 16:19–24).

Was that poor man really carried away by the angels because of his poverty, while the rich man was sent to torments because of his wealth? In the poor man, humility is understood to have been honored; in the rich man, pride is understood to have been condemned.

I prove briefly that it was not wealth but pride that was tormented in that rich man. Certainly, that poor man was lifted into Abraham’s bosom. Of Abraham himself Scripture says that he possessed much gold and silver and was rich on earth (Genesis 13:2). If every rich person is dragged off to torments, how had Abraham gone before the poor man, so as to receive him when he was carried into his bosom?

But Abraham was poor amid his riches: humble, trembling before all the commandments, and obedient. Indeed, he regarded those riches as nothing, to such an extent that, when commanded by the Lord, he offered his own son, for whom he had kept those riches (the same, 22:10).

Learn, therefore, to be needy and poor—both those of you who possess something in this world and those who possess nothing. For you may find a beggar who is proud, and a person with wealth who is confessing. God resists the proud, both those clothed in silk and those in rags; but he gives grace to the humble (James 4:6), whether they possess some substance of this world or possess none.

God is the examiner of the inner person; there he weighs, there he tests. You do not see God’s scales; your thought is lifted onto them. See that he placed the merit of being heard—that is, the reason why he would hear him—in this statement: “For I am poor and needy.”

Take care that you are not poor and needy: if you are not, you will not be heard. Whatever exists around you or within you from which you could presume, cast it away from you; let God alone be your entire confidence. Be needy of him, so that you may be filled by him. For whatever else you may have without him, the more widely spread you are, the emptier you are.

[Column 1084]

4. [verse 2.] “Guard my soul, for I am holy.” I do not know whether anyone else could perhaps say “for I am holy,” except the one who was without sin in this world—the one who did not commit all sins but forgave them all. We recognize the voice of the one saying, “For I am holy; guard my soul,” namely, in the form of a servant that he had assumed.

For there are flesh and soul there. It was not, as some have said [Note: the Apollinarians.], flesh alone and the Word; rather, there were flesh, soul, and Word. And all this is one Son of God, one Christ, one Savior: equal to the Father in the form of God, head of the Church in the form of a servant.

Therefore, when I hear, “For I am holy,” I recognize his voice. And here do I separate myself from it [Note: A Regius manuscript reads, “do I separate myself from it?”]? Certainly, he speaks inseparably from his body when he speaks in this way.

And shall I dare to say, “For I am holy”? If “holy” means one who sanctifies and needs sanctification from no one, then I am proud and a liar. But if “holy” means sanctified, according to what was said, “Be holy, because I too am holy” (Leviticus 19:2), then let the body of Christ also dare; let that one human being who cries out from the ends of the earth (Psalm 60:3), together with his head and under his head, dare to say, “For I am holy.”

For he received the grace of holiness, the grace of Baptism and the forgiveness of sins. “And these,” says the Apostle, listing many sins, both light and grave, customary and dreadful, “were what you were; but you were washed, but you were sanctified” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

If, then, he says that they have been sanctified, let each of the faithful say also, “I am holy.” This is not the pride of one who is elated, but the confession of one who is not ungrateful. For if you say that you are holy from yourself, you are proud; but again, if, as a believer in Christ and a member of Christ, you say that you are not holy, you are ungrateful.

When reproving pride, the Apostle did not say, “You do not have”; rather, he said, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (the same, 4:7). You were not reproved because you said that you had what you do not have [Note: The word “not” is absent from the reputable Remigius manuscript.], but because you wanted what you have to be from yourself. Rather, acknowledge both that you have it and that you have nothing from yourself, so that you may be neither proud nor ungrateful.

Say to your God: “I am holy because you sanctified me; because I received, not because I possessed; because you gave, not because I deserved.” For otherwise you begin to insult our Lord Jesus Christ himself. If all Christians, believers, and baptized people have put on Christ in him, as the Apostle says, “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27); if they have become members of his body and say that they are not holy, they insult the head itself, whose members are not holy [Note: Thus Erasmus and the better manuscripts. Lovanius, however, reads, “whose members are holy.”].

Now see where you are, and derive your dignity from your head. For “you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” “You were once,” he says, “darkness” ([Column 1085] Ephesians 5:8). But did you remain darkness? Did the Illuminator come so that you might remain darkness, or so that you might become light in him?

Therefore let each Christian say—or rather, let the whole body of Christ say it, crying out everywhere while enduring tribulations, various temptations, and countless scandals: “Guard my soul, for I am holy; save your servant, my God, who hopes in you.” See: that holy person is not proud, because he hopes in the Lord.

5. [verse 3.] “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I have cried to you all day long”—not on one day. Understand “all day long” as meaning at all times. From the moment when the body of Christ groans under afflictions until the end of the age, when the afflictions pass away, this human being groans and cries out to God; and each one of us has, in proportion, his own cry within this entire body.

You cried out during your days, and your days passed away; another succeeded you and cried out during his days; you are here, he there, another elsewhere. The body of Christ cries out all day long, as its members depart and are succeeded by others.

One human being extends to the end of the age. The same members of Christ cry out; some members already rest in him, some cry out now, some will cry out when we ourselves have come to rest, and after them others will cry out. The voice of the whole body of Christ is heard here saying, “I have cried to you all day long.”

Our head, however, at the right hand of the Father, intercedes for us (Romans 8:34). He receives some members, chastises others, cleanses others, consoles others, creates others, calls others, calls others back, corrects others, and restores others.

6. [verse 4.] “Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.” Gladden it because I have lifted it up to you. It was on earth and was experiencing bitterness on earth. So that it would not waste away in bitterness, so that it would not lose all the sweetness of your grace, I lifted it up to you; gladden it in your presence.

For you alone are gladness; the world is full of bitterness. Certainly, he rightly admonishes his members to have their hearts above. Let them hear, then, and do what he says; let them lift up to him what is ill on earth. For the heart does not decay there if it is lifted up to God [Note: Some manuscripts read, “For the heart decays there if it is not lifted up to God.”].

If you had grain in a lower place, you would lift it to a higher place so that it would not decay. You would move the grain to another place, and would you permit your heart to decay on earth? You would lift the grain to a higher place; lift your heart to heaven.

“And how,” you ask, “can I do so? What ropes, what machinery, what ladders are needed?” The steps are affections; your journey is your will. By loving, you ascend; by neglecting, you descend. Though standing on earth, you are in heaven if you love God.

For the heart is not lifted in the same way as the body. To lift the body, one changes its place; to lift the heart, one changes one’s will. “For to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.”

7. [verse 5.] “For you, O Lord, are sweet and gentle.” Therefore, “gladden” it. As though wearied by the bitterness of earthly things, he wanted to be sweetened; he sought the source of sweetness and did not find it on earth. Wherever he turned, he found scandals, fears, tribulations, and temptations.

In whom is there security? From whom is there [Column 1086] certain joy? Certainly not from oneself—how much less from another? Either people are evil, and it is necessary to endure them while hoping that they may be changed; or they are good, and one ought to love them in such a way as to fear—for they can be changed—that they may become evil. There, their wickedness makes the soul bitter; here, there is anxiety and fear lest the one who walks well should fall.

Wherever, then, the soul turns, it finds bitterness in earthly things; it has nothing by which to become sweet except to lift itself to God. “For you, O Lord, are sweet and gentle.”

What does “gentle” mean? Bearing with me until you perfect me. Indeed, my brothers, I shall speak as a human being among human beings and from among human beings: let each person bear with his own heart [Note: The Gatian manuscript reads, “let each seek his own heart.”] and look at himself without flattery and without fond self-caressing. Nothing is more foolish than for someone to flatter and deceive himself.

Let him pay attention and see what things are enacted in the human heart; how even prayers themselves are often obstructed by empty thoughts, so that the heart scarcely remains fixed on its God. It wants to hold itself steady, but somehow flees from itself; it cannot find the barriers by which to enclose itself, or certain restraints by which to hold back its flights and its wandering movements, and remain to be gladdened by its God.

It is rare for such prayer to occur amid many prayers. Each person would say that this happens to him and not to another, unless we found David in the Scriptures of God praying in a certain place and saying, “For I have found my heart, O Lord, so that I might pray to you” (2 Samuel 7:27).

He said that he had found his heart, as though it were accustomed to flee from him, and he pursued it like a fugitive, unable to catch it, crying out to God, “For my heart has forsaken me” (Psalm 39:13).

Therefore, my brothers, paying attention to what he says here—“You are sweet and gentle”—I seem to see what he means by “gentle.” “Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you I have lifted my soul; for you are sweet and gentle.” I seem to see why he called God gentle: because God endures these things of ours and nevertheless waits for prayer from us, in order to perfect us. When we give it to him, he receives it graciously and hears it; he does not remember the many prayers that we pour out disorderly, but receives the one that we scarcely manage to find.

For who is there, my brothers, who, if a friend began to speak with him and he wished to answer his conversation [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “did not wish to answer his conversation.”], would tolerate that friend turning away from him and speaking to someone else? Or suppose you appealed to a judge and placed him in a position where he was to hear you, but suddenly, while you were speaking to him, you left him and began chatting with your friend: when would he tolerate you?

And yet God tolerates so many hearts of people praying and thinking about different things. I say nothing of harmful thoughts; I say nothing of thoughts that are sometimes perverse and hostile to God. Even to think unnecessary things is an insult to the one with whom you had begun to speak.

Your prayer is speech addressed to God: when you read, God speaks to you; when you pray, you speak to God.

But what then? Are we to despair of the human race and say that every person into whose prayer some thought has slipped and interrupted his prayer belongs already to condemnation? If we say this, brothers, I do not see what hope remains.

[Column 1087] But since there is some hope in God, because his mercy is great, let us say to him: “Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, I have lifted my soul.” And how did I lift it? As I could, as you gave me strength, as I was able to seize it when it was fleeing from me [Note: Thus the manuscripts. Erasmus reads, “was able”; Lovanius, “you were able.”].

And you have forgotten that whenever I stood before you—imagine God speaking—I thought so many empty and unnecessary thoughts, and scarcely poured out a prayer that was fixed and steady: “For you, O Lord, are sweet and gentle.” You are gentle, bearing with me. I am wasting away from sickness; heal me, and I shall stand. Strengthen me, and I shall be strong. Until you do so, you bear with me: “For you, O Lord, are sweet and gentle.”

8. “And abundant in mercy.” For he is not merely merciful, but abundant in mercy: our iniquity abounds, and your mercy also abounds. “And you are abundant in mercy to all who call upon you.”

What, then, is the meaning of the many passages in Scripture saying that they will call and he will not hear them (Proverbs 1:28), while here it says, “merciful to all who call upon you”? Is it not because some who call do not call upon him himself? Of such people it is said, “They did not call upon God” (Psalm 52:6). They call, but they do not call upon God.

You call upon whatever you love; you call upon whatever you summon within yourself; you call upon whatever you want to come to you. If, then, you call upon God for the sake of money coming to you, or an inheritance coming to you, or worldly status coming to you, you call upon those things that you want to come to you; but you make God the helper of your desires, not the hearer of your longings.

God is good if he gives what you want. But what if you want something bad? Will he not be more merciful by not giving it? Yet if he does not give it, God is nothing to you, and you say, “How much I asked, how often I asked, and I was not heard!” What were you asking for? Perhaps the death of your enemy. What if he too was asking for yours? The one who created you created him as well. You are a human being, and he is a human being; but God is judge. He hears both and does not grant the request of either. You are sad because you were not heard against him; rejoice because he was not heard against you.

“I was not asking for that,” you say. “I was not asking for the death of my enemy, but for the life of my son. What evil was I asking for?” You were asking for nothing evil, as you understood it. But what if he was taken away lest wickedness change his understanding (Wisdom 4:11)?

“But he was a sinner,” you say, “and therefore I wanted him to live so that he might be corrected.” You wanted him to live so that he might become better. What if God knew that, if he lived, he would become worse? How do you know, then, what would have benefited him, to die or to live? If you do not know, return to your heart and leave God to his own counsel.

“What then,” you ask, “shall I do? What shall I pray for?” What your Lord taught you, what your heavenly teacher taught you. Call upon God as God; love God as God. Nothing is better than he; desire him, yearn for him.

See someone calling upon God in another Psalm: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek.” What does he ask? “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” Why? “That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord” (Psalm 26:4).

If, then, you want to be a lover of God, love him with the purest depths and chaste sighs; love him, cherish him, burn for him, yearn for him—in him you find nothing more delightful, [Column 1088] nothing better, nothing more joyful, nothing more lasting. For what is as lasting as that which is eternal? You need not fear that the one who prevents you from perishing will ever perish from you.

If, then, you call upon God as God, be confident: you are heard. You belong to this verse: “And abundant in mercy to all who call upon you.”

9. Therefore, do not say, “He did not give me that.” Return to your conscience; weigh it, question it, and do not spare it. If you truly called upon God, be certain that perhaps he did not give what you wanted temporarily precisely because it was not beneficial to you.

Let a Christian heart, a faithful heart, be built up in this, brothers, so that you do not begin, having become sad as though cheated of your desires, to grow angry against God. For “it is not beneficial to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:5).

Return to the Scriptures. The devil is heard, and the Apostle is not heard. What do you think? How are demons heard? They asked to go into the pigs, and it was granted to them (Matthew 8:31–32). How was the devil heard? He asked that Job be tested, and he received permission (Job 1:11–12; 2:5–6). How was the Apostle not heard?

“Because of the greatness,” he says, “of the revelations, lest I become exalted, a thorn in my flesh was given me, an angel of Satan to buffet me. Because of this I asked the Lord three times that he might take it away from me, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).

He heard the one whom he was preparing to condemn, and did not hear the one whom he wanted to heal. For a sick person also asks a physician for many things, but the physician does not give them. He does not hear according to the patient’s will, so that he may hear according to the patient’s health.

Therefore, make God your physician. Ask him for salvation, and he himself will be your salvation—not as though salvation were something external, but so that he himself may be salvation. Do not again love another salvation apart from him; instead, as you have it in the Psalm, “Say to my soul, ‘I am your salvation’” (Psalm 34:3).

What does it matter to you what he says to you, when he gives himself to you? Do you want him to give himself to you? What if, so that he may give himself to you, he does not want you to have what you want to possess? He removes the obstacles so that he may enter you.

Consider and reflect, brothers, on the good things God gives to sinners. From this understand what he keeps for his servants. To sinners who blaspheme him daily he gives heaven and earth, springs, fruits, health, children, resources, and abundance. God alone gives all these good things.

What do you think he keeps for the faithful, when he gives such things to sinners? Are we to think of him that the one who gives such things to the wicked keeps nothing for the good? On the contrary, he keeps heaven—not earth. Perhaps I am saying something too insignificant when I say “heaven”; he keeps himself, who made heaven.

Heaven is beautiful, but more beautiful is the maker of heaven. But I see heaven, and I do not see him. You have eyes with which to see heaven, but you do not yet have a heart with which to see the maker of heaven. Therefore he came from heaven to earth, so that he might cleanse the heart by which the one who made heaven and earth may be seen.

But certainly, await salvation with patience. He knows by which medicines he should heal you; he knows by which incisions and by which cauterizations. You brought sickness upon yourself by sinning. He came not only to soothe, but also to cut and cauterize.

Do you not see how much people endure under the hands of physicians, while a human being makes an uncertain [Column 1089] promise of hope? “You will be healed,” says the physician; “you will be healed if I cut you.” A human being says this, and says it to another human being; neither the one who speaks nor the one who hears is certain. For the speaker is speaking to a human being, although he did not make the human being and does not know perfectly what is happening within the human being.

And yet a person believes the words of another person who knows less about what is happening within a human being, submits his limbs, permits himself to be bound, or is often cut or cauterized without being bound. Perhaps he receives health for a few days, already healed but not knowing when he will die; perhaps he dies while being treated; perhaps he cannot be healed at all.

But to whom has God promised anything and failed him?

10. [verse 6.] “Fix my prayer in your ears, O Lord.” Great is the intensity of the one praying: “Fix my prayer in your ears, O Lord”—that is, let my prayer not go out from your ears; fix it there, in your ears.

How did he labor in childbirth, so to speak, in order to fix his prayer in God’s ears? Let God answer and say to us: “Do you want me to fix your prayer in my ears? Fix my law in your heart.”

“Fix my prayer in your ears, O Lord, and attend to the voice of my prayer.”

11. [verse 7.] “On the day of my tribulation I called upon you, for you heard me.” The reason you heard me was that on the day of my tribulation I called upon you.

A little earlier he had said, “I cried out all day long; I was troubled all day long.” Therefore, let no Christian say that there is a day on which he has not been troubled. We understood “all day” to mean the whole of time: he is troubled all day long.

What, then? Is there tribulation even when things are going well? Certainly there is tribulation. Why tribulation? Because, as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:6). However much may abound here, we are not yet in that homeland to which we hasten to return.

If the journey away from home is sweet, one does not love the homeland. If the homeland is sweet, the journey away from it is bitter; and if the journey is bitter, there is tribulation all day long.

When is there no tribulation? When there is delight in the homeland: “Delights are at your right hand forever.” “You will fill me with joy,” he says, “with your presence” (Psalm 15:11), “that I may contemplate the delight of the Lord” (Psalm 26:4).

There labor and groaning will pass away; there will be not prayer but praise; there, “Alleluia,” and there, “Amen,” a voice harmonious with the angels; there, vision without failure and love without weariness.

As long, then, as we are not there, you see that we are not yet in the good. But do all things abound? Let all things abound; see whether you are secure because all things do not perish. Let God say from above, “You will be eternal in these things; these things will be eternal with you, but you will not see my face.”

Let no one consult the flesh; consult the spirit. Let your heart answer you; let hope, faith, and love, which have begun to exist in you, answer you.

If we were guaranteed that we would always remain amid an abundance of worldly goods, and God said to us, “You will not see my face,” would we rejoice in those goods? Perhaps someone would choose to rejoice and say, “These things abound for me; I am well; I seek nothing more.” Such a person has not yet begun to be a lover of God; he has not yet begun to sigh like an [Column 1090] exile.

Far be it, far be it! Let all seductive things depart; let false flatteries depart; let those things depart that say to us daily, “Where is your God?” Let us pour out our soul upon ourselves, confess in tears, groan in our confessions, and sigh amid our miseries (Psalm 41:11, 4–5).

Whatever is present to us apart from our God is not sweet. We do not want all the things he has given if he does not give himself, who gave all things.

“Give heed to my prayer, O Lord, and attend to the voice of my prayer. On the day of my tribulation I called upon you, for you heard me.”

12. [verse 8.] “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord.” And what did he say? “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord.”

Let the pagans fashion for themselves whatever gods they wish. Let them bring in silversmiths, goldsmiths, polishers, and sculptors; let them make gods. What sort of gods? “They have eyes and do not see” (Psalm 113:5), and the other things that the Psalm says in sequence.

“But we do not worship these,” they say; “these are images.” And what do you worship? Something else that is worse: “For the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 95:5).

“And what then?” they say. “We do not worship demons either.” Clearly, you have nothing else in your temples; nothing else fills your prophets than a demon.

“But what do you say?” “We worship angels; we have angels as gods.” You plainly do not know angels. For angels worship one God, and they do not favor human beings who want to worship angels and not God. We find angels honored and forbidding human beings to worship them, directing them instead to the true God (Revelation 19:10).

Let them speak of angels; let them speak of human beings, because it was said, “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” (Psalm 81:6): “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord.”

Whatever else a human being may imagine, it is not like the one who made it. Except for God, whatever else exists in the nature of things was made by God. Who can worthily conceive how great is the difference between the one who made and what was made?

This person therefore said, “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord.” But he did not say how unlike God is, because this cannot be said.

Let your Charity pay attention: God is ineffable. We more easily say what he is not than what he is. You think of earth: this is not God. You think of the sea: this is not God. You think of all the things that are on earth—human beings and animals: this is not God. You think of all the things that are in the sea and that fly through the air: this is not God. Whatever shines in heaven—the stars, sun, and moon: this is not God. Heaven itself: this is not God.

Think of angels, Virtues, Powers, Archangels, Thrones, Seats, Dominations: this is not God.

And what is he? This alone I have been able to say: what he is not. You ask what he is? He is what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Corinthians 2:9). Why do you ask that to enter the tongue which has not entered the heart?

“There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and there is none according to your works.”

13. [verse 9.] “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord.” He announced [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “They announce.”] the Church: “All the nations that you have made.”

If there is any nation that God did not make, it will not worship him. But there is no nation that God did not make, because God made Adam and Eve, [Column 1091] the source of all nations; from them all nations were propagated.

God therefore made all nations: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord.”

When was this said? It was said when, before him, only a few holy people in one nation of the Hebrews worshiped. It was said then, and now what was said can be seen: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord.”

When these words were spoken, what they foretold could not be seen, but it was believed. Now that it is seen, why is it denied?

“All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and they shall glorify your name.”

14. [verse 10.] For you are great and do wondrous things; you alone are the great God. Let no one call himself great. There would be those who called themselves great; against them it is said: “You alone are the great God.” For what great thing is being said of God, that he alone is the great God? Who does not know that he is the great God? But because there would be those who called themselves great and made God small, against them it is said: “You alone are the great God.” For what you say is fulfilled, not what those say who call themselves great. What did God say through his Spirit? “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord.” What does some person say who calls himself great? “Far from it! God is not worshiped among all the nations; all the nations have perished, and Africa alone remains.” This is what you say, you who call yourself great; something else says he who alone is the great God. What does he say who alone is the great God? “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord.” I see what the only great God said. Let the falsely great man be silent—false in his greatness because he disdains being small. Who disdains being small? The one who says this. “Whoever wishes to be greater among you,” the Lord said, “shall be your servant” (Matthew 20:26). If he wished to be the servant of his brothers, he would not separate them from their mother; but since he wishes to be great and does not wish to be healthily small, God, who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6), because he alone is great, fulfills everything he foretold and refutes those who curse.

For such people curse Christ when they say that the Church has perished from the whole world and remains only in Africa. If you said to such a person, “You will lose your estate,” perhaps he would not refrain from laying hands on you; yet he says that Christ has lost his inheritance, redeemed with his own blood! Consider, brothers, what an insult he commits. Scripture says: “In a numerous nation is the glory of a king; in the diminution of a people is the ruin of the prince” (Proverbs 14:28). Thus you insult Christ by saying that his people have been reduced to this smallness. Is this why you were born, why you call yourself a Christian: to begrudge the glory of Christ, whose sign you claim to bear on your forehead but have lost from your heart?

“In a numerous nation is the glory of a king.” Recognize your king; give him glory; give him a numerous nation. “What numerous nation shall I give him?” you ask. Do not give one from your own heart, and you will give correctly. “From where shall I give one?” you ask. Give it from here: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord.” Say this, confess this, and you have given him a numerous nation, because all the nations are one in the One; this is unity. Just as there is one Church from the Churches—those Churches are the one Church—so there is one nation from the nations [Col. 1092]: formerly there were nations, many nations; now there is one nation. Why one nation? Because there is one faith, one hope, one love, one expectation. Finally, why should there not be one nation if there is one homeland? The heavenly homeland is Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1092] Regius manuscript: “if there is one heavenly homeland?”]. Whoever is not a citizen of that place does not belong to this nation; whoever is a citizen of that place belongs to God’s one nation.

And this nation stretches from east to west, from the north and the sea, through the four regions of the whole world. God says this: “From the east and the west, from the north and the sea, give glory to God.” He foretold this; he fulfilled it—he who alone is great. Let the one who refused to be small cease, therefore, to say this against the One who alone is great; for two great ones cannot exist, God and Donatus.

15. [verse 11.] “Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth.” Your way, your truth, your life [Note: [Col. 1092] All our manuscripts: “way”]: Christ. Therefore the body is toward him, and the body is from him. “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). “Lead me, O Lord, in your way.” In what way? “And I shall walk in your truth.”

It is one thing to lead someone to the way, another to lead him along the way. See how poor man is everywhere, everywhere in need of assistance. Those who are outside the way are not Christians, or are not yet Catholics; let them be led to the way. But once they have been brought to the way and made Catholics in Christ, let them be led by him along that very way, lest they fall. Certainly they are already walking in the way. “Lead me, O Lord, in your way”: certainly I am already in your way; lead me there. “And I shall walk in your truth”: with you leading me, I shall not go astray; if you abandon me, I shall go astray. Pray, therefore, that he not abandon you but lead you all the way to the end.

How does he lead? By always admonishing you, always giving you his hand. “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1). By giving his Christ, he gives his hand; by giving his hand, he gives his Christ. He leads to the way by bringing one to his Christ; he leads along the way by leading one in his Christ. Christ, however, is the truth. “Lead me, therefore, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth”—in him, certainly, who said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” For you who lead in the way and in the truth, where do you lead except to life? You lead, therefore, in him and to him. “Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth.”

16. “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name.” Therefore fear is found in rejoicing. And how can there be rejoicing if there is fear? Is fear not usually bitter? At some point there will be rejoicing without fear; for now there is rejoicing with fear [Col. 1093]. Full security does not yet exist, nor perfect rejoicing. If there is no rejoicing, we fail; if there is full security, we rejoice wrongly. Therefore let him sprinkle rejoicing upon us and instill fear, so that through the sweetness of rejoicing he may lead us to the dwelling of security. By giving fear, let him not make us rejoice wrongly and depart from the way.

For this reason the psalm says, “Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). So too the apostle Paul says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12–13). Whatever prosperity comes, brothers, ought rather to be feared; what you think prosperous is more truly temptation. An inheritance comes, possessions come, an abundance overflowing with some sort of happiness increases: these are temptations. Take care lest such things corrupt you.

Whatever is also prosperous according to Christ and the genuine love of Christ—if perhaps you have won your wife, who was of Donatus’s party; if perhaps your children, who were pagans, have come to faith; if perhaps you have won over your friend who wanted to lead you astray to the theaters [Note: [Col. 1093] Some manuscripts: “lead you with himself”], and you have led him to the church; if perhaps some adversary, your enemy, who contradicted you and raged violently, has laid aside his rage, become gentle, and recognized God, so that he no longer snarls against you but cries out with you against evil—these things are joyful. For how could we rejoice if we did not rejoice in such things? What other joys do we have except these?

But because tribulations, temptations, disagreements, schisms, and other evils also abound—without which this age cannot exist until iniquity passes away—let that rejoicing not make us secure. Rather, let our heart rejoice in such a way that it fears the Lord’s name, lest it rejoice from one source and be struck from another. Do not expect security in your pilgrimage. When we desire it here, it will be the body’s glue [viscum corporis] [Note: [Col. 1093] Three manuscripts: “the heart’s”], not human security. “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name.”

17. [verses 12–13.] “I shall give thanks to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart, and I shall glorify your name forever; for your mercy is great toward me, and you have rescued my soul from the lower hell.”

What we are saying, brothers, if I do not explain it to you as something certain, do not be angry with me. I am a human being, and I dare to say only as much as is granted to me from the holy Scriptures: nothing from myself. Neither have I yet experienced hell, nor have you; and perhaps there will be another way, and it will not be through hell. These things are uncertain.

Yet because Scripture says, and it cannot be contradicted, “You have rescued my soul from the lower hell,” we understand it as though there are two hells, an upper and a lower. For whence “lower hell” unless there is an upper hell? The lower one would not be called hell except in comparison with that higher region.

It appears, then, brothers, that there is a certain heavenly dwelling of the angels: there is life of indescribable joys, immortality and incorruption, and all things enduring according to God’s gift and grace. That region of reality is above. If that region is above, then this earthly region—where there are flesh and blood, corruption, birth and mortality, departure and succession, mutability and instability, fears, desires, terrors, uncertain joys, fragile hope, and a perishable substance—cannot, I think, be compared with that heaven of which I was speaking a little earlier. If this region cannot be compared with that one, then that is above and this is below.

And after death, where does one go from here, unless there is a lower hell beneath this hell in which we are in the flesh and in this mortality? “For the body is dead because of sin,” the Apostle says (Romans 8:10). Here, therefore, there are also the dead; so do not be surprised that it is called hell if it abounds in the dead. He did not say, “The body will die,” but, “The body is dead.” Our body still has life, certainly; yet compared with that body which will be like the bodies of angels, the human body is found to be dead, although it still possesses a soul.

But again, from this hell—that is, from this region of hell—there is another, lower region, to which the dead go. From there God wished to rescue our souls, sending his Son even there. For, brothers, the Son of God was sent because of these two hells, liberating us from every side. He was sent to this hell by being born, and to that one by dying. Therefore his voice is heard in that psalm—not through someone’s conjecture, but with the Apostle explaining it—where he says: “For you will not abandon my soul to hell” (Psalm 15:10; Acts 2:27). Thus either it is his own voice here also: “You have rescued my soul from the lower hell”; or it is our voice through Christ our Lord, because he reached even to hell for this reason: that we might not remain in hell.

18. I shall also give another interpretation. Perhaps among the hells themselves there is some lower region to which the wicked who have sinned greatly are thrust. For whether Abraham had not been in certain places among the hells, we cannot determine with sufficient certainty [Note: Several manuscripts read “whether Abraham had not been in certain places.” The editions, however, read “whether Abraham had already been in certain places.”]. The Lord had not yet come to hell to rescue from there the souls of all the preceding saints, and yet Abraham was there in a place of rest. And when a certain rich man was being tormented among the dead, he lifted his eyes and saw Abraham. He could not have seen him with his eyes lifted up unless the one were above and the other below.

And what did Abraham answer him when he said: “Father Abraham, send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger and let it drip onto my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame”? “Son,” he said, “remember that you received good things in your life, while Lazarus received evil things; but now he is resting here, while you are being tormented. And besides all this,” he said, “a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that neither can we cross to you nor can anyone cross from there to us” (Luke 16:22–26).

Between these two hells, then—perhaps in one of which the souls of the righteous rested and in the other the souls of the wicked were tormented—a certain person, praying here, already placed in the body of Christ and praying in the voice of Christ, said that God had rescued his soul from the lower hell because he had freed him from such sins as could have led him to the torments of the lower hell.

It is like this: if a physician sees that an illness is perhaps threatening you because of some exertion and says, “Spare yourself; treat yourself in this way; rest; use these foods, for if you do not, you will fall ill,” and you do what he says and remain healthy, you rightly say to the physician, “You have rescued me from illness”—not from an illness in which you already were, but from one in which you were going to be.

Suppose someone has a troublesome legal case and is about to be sent to prison; another person comes and defends him. What does he say in giving thanks? “You have rescued my soul from prison.” A debtor is about to be hanged [Col. 1095]; payment is made on his behalf, and he is said to have been freed from the gallows. In all these cases they were not yet in those things; but because their merits were leading them there, unless help had been given, they rightly say that they have been freed from the places to which their rescuers did not permit them to be led.

Therefore, brothers, whether this interpretation or that one is correct, regard me as an investigator of the word of God, not as a rash assertor. “And you have rescued my soul from the lower hell.”

19. [verse 14.] “O God, transgressors of the law have risen up against me.” Whom does he call “transgressors of the law”? Not pagans, who did not receive the law. No one transgresses what he did not receive. The Apostle states definitively: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Romans 4:15). By “transgressors of the law” he means violators of the law.

Whom, then, do we understand, brothers? If we take this as the voice of the Lord himself, the Jews were the transgressors of the law. “Transgressors of the law have risen up against me”: they did not keep the law and accused Christ, as though he himself were transgressing the law. “Transgressors of the law have risen up against me.” And the Lord suffered what we know.

Do you think that his body suffers nothing of this kind now? How could that be? If they called the head of the household Beelzebul, how much more his servants? “The disciple is not above his teacher, nor the servant above his lord” (Matthew 10:24–25). The body also suffers from transgressors of the law, and they rise up against the body of Christ.

Who are these transgressors of the law? Do the Jews perhaps dare to rise up against Christ? No; for they do not cause us much trouble either. They have not yet believed; they have not yet recognized salvation. The wicked Christians rise up against the body of Christ—those from whom the body of Christ suffers tribulation every day: all schisms, all heresies, all those within who live most wickedly, impose their practices upon those who live well, draw them over to themselves, and corrupt good morals through evil conversations (1 Corinthians 15:33). These are the transgressors of the law who have risen up against me.

Let every devout soul say this; let every Christian soul say it. Let the one who does not suffer this not say it. But if it is a Christian soul, it knows that it suffers evil. If it recognizes its own suffering in itself, let it recognize its voice here. If, however, it is outside the suffering, let it also be outside the voice. Yet in order not to be outside the suffering, let it walk along the narrow way (Matthew 7:14) and begin to live devoutly in Christ; it must necessarily suffer this persecution. “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ,” the Apostle says, “will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12).

“O God, transgressors of the law have risen up against me, and the assembly of the powerful have sought my soul.” The “assembly of the powerful” is the gathering of the proud. The assembly of the powerful rose up against the head—that is, against our Lord Jesus Christ—shouting and saying with one voice, “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6). Of these it was said: “The teeth of the children of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm 56:5). They did not strike him, but they shouted; by shouting they wounded, by shouting they crucified.

The will of those shouting was fulfilled when the Lord was crucified: “And the assembly of the powerful have sought my soul. And they have not set you before their eyes.” How did they not set him before their eyes? [Col. 1096] They did not understand God. They would have spared the man; they would have walked toward what they saw [Note: The editions read, “so that they might spare the man, so that they might walk toward what they saw,” whereas most and better manuscripts read, “They would have spared the man; they would have walked toward what they saw.” This is a mode of expression familiar and very frequent in Augustine throughout these popular sermons, but often corrupted in earlier printed editions. See below, section 23, where the manuscripts read “Then you would have left,” while the editions generally have “Then you would have left the shadow, so that you might be in the light.”]. Suppose he was not God but a man: was he therefore to be killed? Spare the man, and recognize God.

20. [verse 15.] “But you, Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and very merciful, and truthful.” Why patient, very merciful, and compassionate? Because, hanging on the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Whom does he entreat? On whose behalf does he entreat? Who is entreating? Where is he entreating? The Son entreats the Father; he is crucified for the ungodly; amid the very insults—not merely insults in words, but the death inflicted—he hangs upon the cross. It is as though he stretched out his hands for this purpose: to pray for them in such a way that his prayer might be directed like incense in the sight of the Father, and the lifting up of his hands like the evening sacrifice (Psalm 140:2). “Patient, very merciful, and truthful.”

21. [verse 16.] “Since you are therefore truthful, look upon me and have mercy on me; give power to your servant.” Because you are truthful, give power to your servant. Let the time of patience pass; let the time of judgment come. How does he say, “Give power to your servant”? “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

He will rise and himself come to earth to judge; he who was seen as contemptible will himself appear terrifying. He will display power, he who displayed patience: on the cross there was patience; in judgment there will be power. For a man will appear judging, but in glory; as the angels said, “As you saw him go, so will he come” (Acts 1:11).

He will come in that very human form to judgment; therefore the wicked will see him, for they will not see the form of God. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Appearing in human form, he will say, “Go into the eternal fire,” so that what Isaiah said may be fulfilled: “Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord” (Isaiah 26:10, according to the Septuagint). Let him be taken away so that he may not see the form of God. They will therefore see the form of a man.

He who, “being in the form of God, was equal to God” (Philippians 2:6): the wicked will not see this. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1): the wicked will not see this. For if the Word is God, and “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” while the wicked are impure in heart, they certainly will not see God.

And where is it written, “They shall see him whom they pierced” (John 19:37)? It means that they will see the form of a man, so that they may be judged; but they will not see the form of God—except those who will be separated to the right. For when they have been separated to the right, this will be said to them: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” But what will be said to the wicked on the left? “Go into the eternal fire, which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels.”

When the judgment has been completed, how did he conclude? “Thus the wicked shall go into everlasting burning, but the righteous into everlasting life” (Matthew 25:34, 41, 46). From seeing the form of a man, they will then proceed to seeing the form of God. “This is eternal life,” he says, “that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3)—understand: “and him also as the one true God,” because the Father and the Son are one true God. The meaning is therefore that they may know you and Jesus Christ, whom you sent, as one true God.

For they will not go to the vision of the Father without seeing the Son there also. If the Son were not present in the vision of his Father, the Son himself would not have said to his disciples that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. The disciples say to him: “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” [Col. 1097]. He says to them: “For so long a time I have been with you, and you do not know me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”

You see that in the vision of the Father there is also the vision of the Son, and in the vision of the Son there is also the vision of the Father. Therefore he added immediately and said: “Do you not know that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” That is: when I am seen, the Father is also seen; and when the Father is seen, the Son is also seen. The vision of the Father and the Son cannot be separated. Where nature and substance are not separated, the vision cannot be separated.

To show that the heart must be prepared there to see the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the divinity in which we believe without seeing it, and by believing cleanse the heart by which it may be seen—the Lord himself says elsewhere: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, that is the one who loves me; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I shall love him, and I shall reveal myself to him” (John 14:21).

Were they not seeing him when he spoke to them? They were seeing him, and they were not seeing him: they saw one thing and believed another; they saw a man and believed God. In the judgment, however, they will see the same Lord Jesus as a man together with the wicked; after the judgment they will see him as God, but the wicked will not. “Give power to your servant.”

22. “And save the son of your handmaid.” The Lord is the son of a handmaid. Whose handmaid? When his birth was announced to her, she answered and said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” [Note: The manuscripts read, “Let it be done to me as you will.”] (Luke 1:38).

He saved the Son of his handmaid, and his own Son: his own Son in the form of God; the Son of his handmaid in the form of a servant. The Lord was therefore born of God’s handmaid in the form of a servant, and he said, “Save the son of your handmaid.” And he was saved from death, as you know, when his dead flesh was raised again.

But so that you may see that he is God, and that he was not raised by the Father in such a way that he himself did not raise himself, because he too raised his own flesh, you have the statement in the Gospel: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up.” And lest we understand something else, the Evangelist follows and says: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21). Thus the Son of the handmaid was saved.

Let every Christian placed in the body of Christ also say: “Save the son of your handmaid.” Perhaps he cannot say, “Give power to your servant,” because that Son received power. But why should he not say this also? Was it not said to servants, “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28)? And servants say: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Corinthians 6:3).

Each of the saints, therefore, receives power, and each of the saints is the son of his handmaid [Col. 1098]. What if someone was born of a pagan woman and became a Christian? How can the son of a pagan woman be the son of that handmaid? Carnally he is indeed the son of a pagan woman, but spiritually he is the son of the Church. “And save the son of your handmaid.”

23. [verse 17.] “Work with me a sign for good.” What sign, except the sign of the resurrection? The Lord says: “This wicked and embittering generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:39–40).

Therefore the sign for good has already been worked with our Head. Let each one of us also say: “Work with me a sign for good,” because “at the last trumpet, at the coming of the Lord, the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52). This will be a sign for good.

“Work with me a sign for good, that those who hate me may see and be confounded.” At the judgment they will be confounded disastrously—those who now refuse to be confounded beneficially [Note: The word “who” is absent from the manuscripts]. Let them therefore be confounded now; let them accuse their evil ways and hold fast to the good way. None of us lives without confusion unless he first, having been confounded, rises again [Note: Several manuscripts read “without” rather than “unless.”].

God now offers them access to a salutary confusion, if they do not despise the medicine of confession. But if they refuse to be confounded now, they will then be confounded when their iniquities are led out against them (Wisdom 4:20). How will they be confounded? When they say: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. We fools considered their life madness; how were they counted among the sons of God? What did pride profit us?”

Then they will say it. Let them say it now, and they say it beneficially. Let each one turn humbly to God and say now, “What did pride profit me?” and let him hear from the Apostle: “What glory did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6:21).

You see that there is also now a salutary confusion in the place of repentance; then there will be a late, useless, fruitless confusion. “What did pride profit us? Or what did the boasting of riches contribute to us? All things passed away like a shadow” (Wisdom 5:3–9). What then? When you were living here, did you not see that all these things were passing away like a shadow?
