Then you should have left the shadow and been in the light; you should not have said afterward, “All things passed away like a shadow,” when you are about to go from the shadow into darkness.

“Work with me a sign for good, that those who hate me may see and be confounded.”

24. “For you, O Lord, have helped me and consoled me.” You helped me in the contest, and you consoled me in sorrow. For no one seeks consolation unless he is in misery. Do you not wish to be consoled? Say that you are happy.

And you hear: “My people”—you are already answering, and I hear the murmur of those who rightly hold fast to the Scriptures. May God, who wrote this in your hearts, confirm it in your actions. You see, brothers, that those who tell you, “You are happy,” are deceiving you. “My people, those who call you happy lead you into error and confuse the paths of your feet” (Isaiah 3:12).

So too in the Epistle of the apostle James: “Be miserable,” he says, “and mourn; let your laughter be turned into mourning” (James 4:9). You see what you have heard. When would these things be said to us in the region of security? Certainly this region is a region of scandals, temptations, and every evil, so that we may groan here and deserve to rejoice there; that we may be troubled here and consoled there, and say: “For you have removed my eyes from tears, my feet from sliding [labina]” [Note: The editions read “from falling” (a ruina), but the manuscripts read “from sliding” (a labina). See above, column 390, Exposition on Psalm 36, section 12], “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114:8–9).

This is the region of the dead. The region of the dead passes away; the region of the living comes. In the region of the dead there are toil, pain, fear, tribulation, temptation, groaning, and sighing. Here the happy are false and the unhappy are true, because false happiness is true misery. But whoever recognizes that he is in true misery will also be in true happiness. Yet now, because you are miserable, listen to the Lord saying, “Blessed are those who mourn” (Matthew 5:5).

O blessed mourners! Nothing is so closely joined to misery as mourning; nothing is so remote from and contrary to misery as blessedness. You say that mourners are blessed! Understand, he says, what I mean: I call mourners blessed. Why blessed? In hope. Why mourners? In reality. For they mourn in this death, in these tribulations, in their pilgrimage; and because they recognize that they are in this misery and groan, they are blessed.

Why do they mourn [Note: Some books read: “and groan. They are blessed; why do they mourn?”]? Blessed Cyprian was saddened in his passion; now he is consoled in his crown. Even now, while he is consoled, he is still sad. For our Lord Jesus Christ still intercedes for us (Romans 8:34); all the martyrs who are with him intercede for us. Their intercessions will not cease until our groaning has ceased. When our groaning has ceased, we shall all be consoled [Note: [Col. 1099] The word “we shall be consoled” is absent from all manuscripts], with one voice, in one people, in one homeland, thousands upon thousands joined with singing Angels and choirs of heavenly Powers living in one city.

Who groans there? Who sighs there? Who labors there? Who is in need there? Who dies there? Who shows mercy there? Who breaks bread for the hungry, where all are nourished with the bread of righteousness? No one says to you, “Receive a guest”: there will be no stranger there; all live in their homeland. No one says to you, “Reconcile your quarreling friends”: they enjoy God’s face in everlasting peace. No one says to you, “Visit the sick”: health and immortality endure. No one says to you, “Bury the dead”: all will be in eternal life. The works of mercy cease, because misery is not found there.

And what shall we do there? Shall we perhaps sleep? If now we fight against ourselves, although we carry this flesh as a house of sleep, and keep watch amid these lights, and this solemnity gives us courage to stay awake, what kind of vigils will that day give us? Therefore we shall keep watch; we shall not sleep.

What shall we do? These works of mercy will not exist, because there will be no misery. Perhaps the works of necessity that exist here—sowing, plowing, cooking, grinding, weaving—will exist? None of these, because there will be no necessity. Just as works of mercy will not exist because misery passes away, so where there is no necessity and no misery, works of necessity and mercy will not exist.

What will exist there? What will be our occupation? What our activity? Or will there be no activity because there is rest? Shall we therefore sit, grow numb, and do nothing? If our love grows cold, our activity will grow cold. How, then, will tranquil love in the presence of God—whom we now desire and for whom we sigh—kindle us when we come to him? How will the one whom we sigh for without yet having seen him illuminate us when we come to him? How will he change us? What will he make of us?

What shall we do, brothers? Let the psalm tell us: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house.” Why? “They shall praise you forever and ever” (Psalm 83:5). This will be our activity: the praise of God. You love [Note: [Col. 1100] An old Corbie codex: “Love, and you praise”], and you praise. You will cease to praise if you cease to love. But you will not cease to love, because the one whom you see is such that he never offends you by weariness: he satisfies you, and he does not satisfy you.

What I am saying is strange. If I say that he satisfies you, I fear that, as though satisfied, you may wish to depart, as from lunch or dinner. What, then, shall I say? Does he not satisfy you? Again I fear that if I say, “He does not satisfy you,” you may appear to be in need, as though you were emptier and there were less in you that ought to be filled.

What shall I say, then, except what can be said but scarcely thought? He satisfies you, and he does not satisfy you. For I find both in Scripture. When it said, “Blessed are those who hunger, for they shall be filled” (Matthew 5:6), there is also a statement about Wisdom: “Those who eat you shall hunger again, and those who drink you shall thirst again” (Ecclesiasticus 24:29). Indeed, it does not say “again,” but “still.” “He shall thirst again” might suggest that he first went away satisfied, digested, and returned to drink. But this means: “Those who eat you shall still hunger”; while eating, they shall hunger; and those who drink you shall, by drinking, thirst.

What does it mean to thirst while drinking? Never to grow weary. If, then, that sweetness will be ineffable and everlasting, what does it ask of us now, brothers, except sincere faith, firm hope, pure love, and that a person walk along the way the Lord has given, endure temptations, and receive consolations?

# Exposition of Psalm 86

## Sermon

[Note: Perhaps delivered to the people of Carthage on the day immediately following the exposition of Psalm 85, mentioned below, section 9.]

1. The psalm that has just been sung is short in its number of words but great in the weight of its meanings. For it was read in its entirety, and you see how it was brought all the way to its conclusion in so little time. This psalm has now been set before us for discussion, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant it, with your Charity, by our most blessed father, who is present [Note: Perhaps Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.].

The sudden assignment would have burdened me, unless the prayer of the one who assigned it had immediately strengthened me [Note: Two Corbie manuscripts read “continuous” rather than “immediately.”]. Let your Charity therefore attend.

A certain city is sung of and commended in this psalm. We are its citizens insofar as we are Christians; we are pilgrims from it for as long as we are mortal; and we journey toward it. Its king made himself the way by which we might reach the city, because the way had not been found, as though it were completely blocked by thickets and thorns [Column 1101: The Corbie manuscripts read “through whose way”; the editions read “through its way.”].

Therefore, as we walk in Christ and are still pilgrims until we arrive, sighing with desire for a certain ineffable rest that dwells in that city—a rest concerning which it was promised to us: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Corinthians 2:9)—as we walk, let us sing in such a way that we desire.

For whoever desires, even if his tongue is silent, sings in his heart; but whoever does not desire, even if he strikes human ears with whatever kind of shouting, is mute to God. See how ardent were the lovers of this city, those very people through whom these things were spoken and through whom they were commended to us, and with what affection they sang these things. Love of the city generated this affection in them; and the Spirit of God poured love of the city into them. “The love of God,” he says, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). Let us therefore, burning with this Spirit, hear what has been said about this city.

## 2. [verses 1, 2]

“Her foundations are in the holy mountains.” The Psalm had not yet said anything about her; here it begins and says: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains.” Whose foundations? There is no doubt that foundations, especially in mountains, belong to some city. This citizen, therefore, filled with the Holy Spirit and turning over within himself much concerning the love and desire for this city, as though he had meditated inwardly on many things, burst forth with this declaration: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains”—as though he had already said something about her.

How had he said nothing about her, when he had never been silent about her in his heart? How can she be called “her” if nothing has been said about her? But, as I said, giving birth in silence within himself to many thoughts about that city, and crying out to God, he burst forth even into the ears of human beings: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains.” And as though those who heard him were asking, “Whose?” he says: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion.” Behold whose foundations are in the holy mountains: those of a certain city, Zion, whose gates the Lord loves, as he says immediately afterward, “more than all the dwellings of Jacob.”

But what does “Her foundations are in the holy mountains” mean? Who are the holy mountains upon which this city has been founded? Another citizen explained this more clearly—the apostle Paul. The Prophet is a citizen of that place, and the Apostle is a citizen of that place; and for this reason they spoke, so that they might exhort the other citizens.

But how are they citizens—these Prophets and Apostles? Perhaps because they themselves are also the mountains upon which the foundations of this city are set, the city whose gates the Lord loves. Let another citizen state this openly, so that we may not seem to be merely conjecturing. Speaking to the Gentiles and reminding them that they should return and, as it were, be built into a holy structure, he says: “You have been built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets.” And because neither the Apostles nor the Prophets, in whom the city’s foundation rests, would rely upon themselves, he adds there: “Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone.”

So that the Gentiles would not think that they did not belong to Zion—for there was an earthly city called Zion, which by way of shadow bore the image of a certain Zion of which he now speaks, that heavenly Jerusalem of which the Apostle says, “which is the mother of us all” (Gal. 4:26)—so that, then, they would not be said to have no part in Zion because they were not of the Jewish people, he said to them: “Therefore you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets.”

You have the construction of so great a city. But where does this entire structure rest and lean, so that it may never fall? “Christ Jesus himself,” he says, “being the chief cornerstone” (Eph. 2:19–20).

## 3.

Someone may perhaps say: If Christ Jesus is the cornerstone, then two walls are joined together in him. For there can be no corner unless two walls, coming from different directions, meet as one. So also the two peoples—from circumcision and from uncircumcision—are joined together in Christian peace, in one faith, one hope, and one love.

But if Christ Jesus is the chief cornerstone, the earlier foundations and the later cornerstone seem to be distinct. Someone might therefore say that Christ rests more upon the Prophets and Apostles, rather than they upon him, if they are in the foundation while he is in the corner.

But let the person who says this consider that the corner is also in the foundation. The corner is not located only where it is visible, rising to a point; it begins from the foundation. For you may know that Christ is also the foundation, both the first and the greatest: “No one,” says the Apostle, “can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11).

How, then, are the Prophets and Apostles foundations, and how is Christ Jesus the foundation, beyond which nothing further exists? How can we understand this, unless just as he is plainly called the Holy of holies, so figuratively he is the foundation of foundations?

If, then, you think of the sacraments, Christ is the Holy of holies. If you think of the flock under authority, Christ is the Shepherd of shepherds. If you think of a structure, Christ is the foundation of foundations.

In these buildings, the same stone cannot be both at the bottom and at the top: if it is at the bottom, it will not be at the top; if it is at the top, it will not be at the bottom. For nearly all bodies are subject to spatial limitation; they cannot be everywhere or always. But because divinity is present everywhere, an analogy can be drawn to it from every direction, and it can wholly exist in analogies, because none of these things exists in its proper literal sense.

Is Christ a door in the way that we see doors made by a craftsman? Certainly not; and yet he said, “I am the door.” Or is he a shepherd in the way that we see those shepherds who oversee sheep? And yet he said, “I am the shepherd.” In one place he said both things. In the Gospel he said that the shepherd enters through the door; and there he said, “I am the good shepherd,” and there he said, “I am the door” (John 10:9, 11).

The shepherd enters through the door. And who is the shepherd who enters through the door? “I am the good shepherd.” Then what is the door through which you enter, good shepherd? “I am the door.” How, then, are you everything? How are all things through me? [Note: [Col. 1102] Thus the better manuscripts. The editions instead read: “How, then, are all things through you?”]

For example, when Paul enters through the door, does Christ not enter through the door? Why? Not because Paul is Christ, but because Christ is in Paul, and Paul is through Christ. He himself said: “Do you wish to receive proof that Christ is speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

When his saints and faithful enter through the door, does Christ not enter through the door? How do we prove this? Because Saul, not yet Paul, was persecuting his saints when a voice from heaven cried out to him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

Therefore the foundation and the cornerstone are the same; he rises from below—if indeed he rises from below. For the origin of this foundation occupies the summit. Just as the foundation of a bodily structure is at the bottom, so the foundation of a spiritual structure is at the top. If we were being built toward the earth, the foundation would have to be laid beneath us; but because the structure is heavenly, our foundation has gone before us to heaven.

Therefore the cornerstone himself, together with the mountains—the Apostles and great Prophets—who bear the structure of the city, forms a living building. Does this building now cry out from your hearts? Through our tongue, the skillful hand of God is working to make you squared and fitted for the construction of that building.

For it was not without reason that Noah’s ark was also built of squared timbers (Gen. 6:14, according to the Septuagint), since it likewise bore the figure of the Church. What does it mean to be squared? Consider the likeness of a square stone: the Christian ought to be like it. In every temptation, the Christian does not fall. Even if he is pushed and, as it were, turned over, he does not fall; for however you turn a square stone, it stands.

The Martyrs seemed to fall when they were struck, but what did a certain voice of the song say? “When the righteous falls, he will not be shaken, for the Lord strengthens his hand” (Ps. 36:24). Therefore be squared and fitted, prepared for every temptation; whatever pushes you, let it not overturn you. Let every calamity find you standing.

You are therefore raised into this structure by devout affection, sincere religion, faith, hope, and love; and being built is itself a way of walking. In these earthly cities, the structure of the buildings is one thing and the citizens who inhabit the structure are another. But that city is built from its citizens; they themselves are the stones who are its citizens, for they are living stones.

“And you,” he says, “as living stones are being built into a spiritual house” (1 Pet. 2:5). The voice is directed to us. Let us therefore continue concerning this city.

## 4.

“Her foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion.” I have already said this beforehand, so that you would not think the foundations and the gates were different. Why are the Apostles and Prophets foundations? Because their authority supports our weakness. Why are they gates? Because through them we enter the kingdom of God, for they preach to us.

And when we enter through them, we enter through Christ, for he is the door. Jerusalem is said to have twelve gates (Rev. 21:12); Christ is one gate, and Christ is twelve gates, because Christ is in the twelve gates. For this reason the number of the Apostles is twelve. Great is the mystery of this number twelve.

“You will sit,” he says, “on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). If there are twelve seats there, there is no place for the thirteenth, the apostle Paul, to sit, and there will be no way for him to judge. Yet he said that he would judge—not merely human beings, but also angels. “Do you not know,” he says, “that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3).

The crowd might therefore answer: “Why do you boast that you will judge? Where will you sit? The Lord spoke of twelve seats for the twelve Apostles. Judas fell; Matthias was appointed in his place; the number twelve of the seats was completed” (Acts 1:15–26). First find a place where you can sit, and then threaten to judge.

Let us therefore see what the twelve seats signify. It is the mystery of a certain universality, because the Church was destined to exist throughout the whole world; hence this structure is called into the unity of Christ. And because people come from every direction to judgment, there are twelve seats, just as, because people enter that city from every direction, there are twelve gates.

Therefore not only those twelve and the apostle Paul, but all who will judge, because of the signification of universality, belong to the twelve seats; just as all who will enter belong to the twelve gates.

There are four regions of the world: East, West, North, and South. These four regions are constantly named in Scripture. From all these four winds, as the Lord says in the Gospel, he will gather his elect (Mark 13:27); from all these four winds, then, the Church is called.

How is it called? It is called from every direction into the Trinity. It is called only through Baptism in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Four multiplied by three therefore gives twelve.

## 5.

Strike, then, with devotion at these gates, and let Christ cry out within you: “Open to me the gates of righteousness” (Ps. 117:19). For he went before in the Head; he follows himself in the body [Note: [Col. 1104] Erasmus and the Venetian edition do not have “himself.” M.].

See what the Apostle said: Christ was suffering in him: “That I may complete,” he says, “what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ in my flesh” (Col. 1:24). “That I may complete”—what? “What is lacking.” Lacking in whom? “In the afflictions of Christ.” And where are they lacking? “In my flesh.”

Was anything lacking in the afflictions of that man who was the Word of God, born from the Virgin Mary? He suffered whatever he ought to suffer, by his own will and not by the necessity of sin; and it seems that he suffered everything. For, hanging on the cross, he received the final vinegar and said, “It is finished”; then, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30).

What does “It is finished” mean? “Nothing is lacking for me from the measure of my sufferings; everything that was foretold concerning me has been fulfilled”—as though he had been waiting for those things to be completed.

Who departs in such a way as he departed from the body? But who could do this? The one who had first said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (John 10:17–18).

He laid it down when he willed; he took it up when he willed. No one took it away; no one forced it from him.

Therefore all the sufferings were fulfilled in the Head, but the sufferings of Christ in the body still remained. “You are the body of Christ and individually members of it” (1 Cor. 12:27). Since the Apostle was among these members, he said: “That I may complete what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ in my flesh.”

Therefore we are going where Christ has gone before, and Christ is still going there where he went before: Christ went before in the Head; he follows in the body.

And Christ still labors here; Christ was suffering here from Saul when Saul heard: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” As the tongue is accustomed to say when the foot is trodden upon, “You are treading on me.” No one has touched the tongue; it cries out through sympathy, not through physical abrasion.

Christ is still in need here; Christ is still a sojourner here; Christ is still sick here; Christ is still confined in prison here. We do him an injury if he himself did not say:

“I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; I was naked, and you clothed me; I was sick, and you visited me.”

And they said to him: “When did we see you suffering these things and minister to you?”

And he said to them: “Whenever you did it to one of the least of my brothers, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:35–40).

Therefore let us be built into Christ [Note: [Col. 1105] Thus the manuscripts. The editions instead read, “into Christ” in the dative form.] upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Christ himself being the chief cornerstone, because “the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob.”

Yet surely Zion itself was also among the dwellings of Jacob. And where was Zion except among the people of Jacob? Jacob, the grandson of Abraham, from whom the Jewish people descended, is called the people of Israel because Jacob himself was also called Israel (Gen. 32:28).

Your Holiness knows this well. But because there were certain temporal and figurative dwellings, while this speaker is speaking of a certain city that he understands spiritually, whose shadow and figure was that earthly city, he says: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob.”

He loves that spiritual city above all the figures by which that city, which always remains and is always heavenly in peace, was signified.

## 6. [verses 3, 4]

“Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God.” It was as though he were looking upon that Jerusalem city on earth. But consider what city he means—one of which some exceedingly glorious things have been spoken. For that earthly city has been destroyed; it fell to the earth after suffering its enemies, and it is no longer what it was. It expressed the image; the shadow passed away.

Why, then, “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God”? Hear why: “I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me.”

In that city, he says, now speaking in the person of God, “I will remember Rahab, and I will remember Babylon.” Rahab does not belong to the Jewish people; Babylon does not belong to the Jewish people. For he continues: “Indeed, foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians—these were there.”

Glorious things are rightly spoken of you, city of God, where that people alone is not present—the people born according to the flesh from Abraham—but all the nations are there, some of whom are named so that all may be understood.

“I will remember Rahab,” he says. Who is this Rahab? The prostitute in Jericho, who received the messengers and sent them out by another way; who trusted in the promise; who feared God; who was told to put forth scarlet from the window—that is, to have on her forehead the sign of the blood of Christ. She was saved there (Josh. 2 and 6:25), and she signified the Church of the Gentiles.

For this reason the Lord said to the proud Pharisees: “Truly I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of heaven before you” (Matt. 21:31). They go before because they use force: by believing they press forward, and way is yielded to faith, nor can anyone resist it; for “those who use force seize it.” For it is written there: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use violence seize it” (Matt. 11:12).

This is what the thief did—stronger on the cross (Luke 23:40–43) than in the throat [Note: [Col. 1106] Several books read “in the sickle,” incorrectly, as has been observed above, col. 655, note 12, near the end.].

“I will remember Rahab and Babylon.” Babylon is a city according to the present age. Just as Jerusalem is one holy city and Babylon one wicked city, all the wicked belong to Babylon, just as all the holy belong to Jerusalem.

But one slips down from Babylon into Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1106] Two manuscripts read *derivatur* (“is diverted”). Almost all the others read *delibatur* (“is diminished”).]. Through whom, if not through the one who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5)? Jerusalem is the city of the godly; Babylon is the city of the ungodly. But the one who justifies the ungodly has come; therefore he says, “I will remember” not only Rahab but also Babylon.

But whom will he remember—Rahab and Babylon? “Those who know me.” For this reason Scripture says in one place: “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that do not know you” (Ps. 78:6). Here it says, “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that do not know you”; elsewhere, “Extend your mercy to those who know you” (Ps. 35:11).

And so that you may know that he signified the Gentiles in Rahab and Babylon—as though someone were asking, “What is this that you have said: ‘I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me’? Why have you said this?”—he continues: “Indeed, the foreigners,” that is, those belonging to Rahab and those belonging to Babylon, “and Tyre.”

But how far do the Gentiles extend? To the ends of the earth. For he chose the people who are at the end of the earth: “And the people,” he says, “of the Ethiopians—these were there.”

Therefore, if Rahab was there, and those from Babylon were there, because the foreigners were there, and Tyre was there, and the people of the Ethiopians were there, then rightly the most glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.

## 7. [verse 5]

Now attend to the great mystery. Through the one by whom Rahab is there, Babylon is there—but is no longer Babylon; for she is freed from Babylon and begins to be Jerusalem.

“The daughter is divided against her mother,” and she will be among the members of that queen to whom it is said: “Forget your people and your father’s house; the king has desired your beauty” (Ps. 44:11–12).

For how could Babylon aspire to Jerusalem? How could Rahab reach those foundations? How could the foreigners, Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians reach them? Hear how:

“Mother Zion,” a man will say.

There is a certain man who says, “Mother Zion,” and through him all these people come. But who is this man? He says, if we listen and understand: “Mother Zion,” a man will say.

The passage continues, as though you were asking through whom Rahab, Babylon, the foreigners, Tyre, and the Ethiopians came. Behold through whom they came: “Mother Zion,” a man will say. “And a man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her.”

What could be clearer, brothers? Truly, glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God. Behold: “Mother Zion,” a man will say. Which man? The one who was made in her. A man was made in her, and he himself founded her.

How was he made in her, and how did he himself found her? In order that a man might be made in her, she had already been founded. Understand this, if you can.

For he says, “Mother Zion,” but “a man will say, Mother Zion.” The man, however, was made in her; yet he himself founded her—not a man, but the Most High.

He founded the city in which he was to be born, just as he created the mother from whom he was to be born. What is this, brothers? What promises we possess, what great hope! Behold, for our sake the Most High, who founded the city, says to the city itself, “Mother”; and a man was made in her, and the Most High founded her.

## 8. [verse 6]

As though someone were asking, “How do you know these things?” We have all sung them, and Christ, the man, sings in all of us—the man for our sake, God before us.

But what is so great about being before us? Before earth and heaven, before the ages. This man, then, who for our sake was made in her, is the very Most High who founded her.

How do we know these things? “The Lord will recount it in the record of the peoples.” For this follows in the Psalm: “Mother Zion, a man will say; and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her. The Lord will recount it in the record of the peoples and of princes.”

Which princes? Those who were born in her. The princes who were born in her became princes in her. For before they became princes in her, “God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong.”

Was a fisherman a prince? Was a tax collector a prince? Certainly they were princes—but because they became so in her.

What sort of princes were these? Princes came from Babylon. Believing princes came from the present age to the city of Rome, as though to the head of Babylon. They did not go to the emperor’s temple, but to the memorial of a fisherman.

From where did these princes come? “God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong; and God chose what is lowly and despised, even things that are not, to abolish things that are” (1 Cor. 1:27–28).

This is what he does who raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung heap. Why does he raise him? “To set him with princes, with the princes of his people” (Ps. 112:7–8).

A great thing, a great joy, a great gladness. Later orators also came to this city; but they would not have come unless fishermen had gone before them.

These things are great—but where are they found except in that city of God, of which the most glorious things have been spoken?

## 9. [verse 7]

Therefore, gathering together and blending all joys, how did he conclude? “As the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you.”

As the dwelling of all those who rejoice, of all those who are glad, is in this city. In this pilgrimage we are worn down; our dwelling will be joy alone. Labor and groaning will pass away; prayers will cease, and praises will take their place.

There, then, will be the dwelling of those who rejoice. There will not be the groaning of those who desire, but the joy of those who possess. The one for whom we now sigh will be present; we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

There our entire occupation will be nothing but praising God and enjoying God. And what else shall we seek, where the one through whom all things were made is sufficient alone? We shall be inhabited, and we shall inhabit; all things will be subjected to him, so that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28).

“Blessed, therefore, are those who dwell in your house.” From where does their blessedness come? From possessing gold, silver, a large household, numerous offspring? From where? “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; throughout the ages of ages they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5).

They are blessed in this one unoccupied task. Let us desire this one thing, brothers, when we come to it: let us prepare ourselves to rejoice in God and praise God.

The good works that now lead us there will not be there. We said yesterday, as far as we were able [Note: [Col. 1108] In the preceding exposition of the Psalm, no. 24.], that works of mercy will not be there where there is no misery. You will find no needy person; you will find no naked person; no one thirsty will come before you; there will be no stranger, no sick person whom you must visit, no dead person whom you must bury, no disputants between whom you must establish peace.

What will you do? Perhaps, because of the necessities of our bodies, will we plant, plow, conduct business, and travel? Great is the rest there. For all the works that necessity demands will be removed; when necessity has died, the works of necessity will perish.

What, then, will there be? How could the human tongue express it? “As the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you.” What does “as” mean? Why “as”? Because the joy there will be of a kind that we do not know here.

Here I see many joys, and many people rejoice in the present age, some in one thing and some in another. There is nothing with which that joy can be compared, but it will be “as” joy. For if I say simply “joy,” a kind of joy will immediately occur to the human mind such as people usually experience in drinking, banquets, greed, and the honors of the world.

People become elated and go mad with a certain joy; but “there is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord (Isa. 48:22, according to the Septuagint). There is a certain joy that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. 2:9).

“As the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you.” Let us prepare ourselves for another joy, because here we find something resembling it, but this is not it. Otherwise, we would prepare ourselves to enjoy there the things in which we rejoice here; and then our self-restraint would be greed.

There are people who are invited to a rich banquet, where many costly dishes are to be served, and they do not eat beforehand. If you ask them why they are not eating, they answer: “We are fasting” [Note: [Col. 1108] Supply: “they reply.”].

Fasting is a great work, a Christian work. Do not praise it too quickly; ask the reason. The matter concerns the belly, not religion. Why do they fast? So that cheap food may not fill their stomachs beforehand and prevent them from receiving the expensive food. Thus, in their fasting, they are engaged in the business of the throat.

Fasting is certainly a great thing: it fights against the belly and the throat, and at times it serves them. Therefore, my brothers, if you think that we will have something of this kind in that homeland to which the heavenly trumpet exhorts us, and if for this reason you abstain from present things in order to receive such things there more abundantly, then you are like those who fast for the sake of larger banquets and restrain themselves with greater lack of restraint.

Do not act in this way. Prepare yourselves for something ineffable. Cleanse your hearts from all your earthly and worldly affections. We shall see something which, once seen, will make us blessed, and it alone will be sufficient for us.

And what? Shall we not eat? Indeed we shall eat—and he himself will be our food, the one who both refreshes and does not fail.

“As the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you.” It has already been said from where our joy will come: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; throughout the ages of ages they will praise you.”

Let us praise the Lord even now, as much as we can, mingling our praises with groans; for by praising him we desire him, and we do not yet possess him. When we possess him, every groan will be removed, and only pure, sole, eternal praise will remain.

Turned toward the Lord.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 87

[Note: [Col. 1109] Dictated after the exposition of Psalm 41, discussed below in no. 7, and perhaps after Psalm 67.]

## 1. [verse 1]

The title of this eighty-seventh Psalm contains something that presents the interpreter with a new problem. Nowhere among the titles of the other psalms is there anything like what is read here: “For Melech, to respond.”

We have already said elsewhere what seemed to us concerning “a Psalm of a song” and “a song of a Psalm” [Note: [Col. 1109] He discussed this matter in Psalm 67, expounded in the year 415; he may be referring back to that discussion because the title of this Psalm contains “A song of a Psalm, for the sons of Korah,” and so forth.]. “For the sons of Korah” is customary in the titles of the Psalms and has often been discussed, as has the meaning of “to the end.” But what follows—“For Melech, to respond”—is unusual in this title.

“For Melech” can be rendered in Latin as “for the chorus,” for *melech* is a Hebrew word signifying “chorus.” What, then, is “for the chorus, to respond,” unless perhaps it means that the chorus should respond in harmony to the one singing?

We must believe that not only this Psalm but also other psalms were sung with a chorus responding, although they received different titles. I think this was done for the sake of variety, to relieve boredom. For this Psalm alone was not considered worthy of having a chorus respond, since it is certainly not the only one composed concerning the Lord’s passion.

Or if there is another reason for such great variety in the titles—a reason by which it could be shown that all the Psalms were given titles in such different ways that no title could fit any other—then I confess that, although I have tried hard, I have not been able to penetrate it. And if I have read anything on this matter written by those who discussed it before us, it has not satisfied either my expectation or my slowness of understanding.

I shall therefore explain in what mystery “For the chorus, to respond”—that is, so that a chorus may respond to the singer—seems to me to have been said.

Here the passion of the Lord is prophesied. The apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we should follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21). This is to respond.

The apostle John also says: “Just as Christ laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (1 John 3:16). This is to respond.

The chorus signifies harmony, which consists in love. Therefore, whoever, as though imitating the Lord’s passion, delivers up his body to be burned, but does not have love, does not respond in the chorus; and therefore it benefits him nothing (1 Cor. 13:3).

Accordingly, just as in musical art there are said to be—so far as learned men have been able to express these terms in Latin—a *praecentor* and a *succentor*, the *praecentor* being the one who gives the first voice in the song, and the *succentor* the one who follows by singing in response, so in this song of the passion Christ goes before, and the chorus of Martyrs follows him to the end, toward the heavenly crowns.

For this is sung “for the sons of Korah,” that is, for the imitators of Christ’s passion, because Christ was crucified at the place of the Skull (Matt. 27:33), which is said to be the interpretation of that Hebrew name, namely, “Korah.”

This is also the meaning of “Heman the Israelite” [Note: [Col. 1110] From his method of interpretation it is clear that Augustine read *Israeli tae*; in the Vulgate it is *Ezrahitae*, perhaps for *Zaraitae*. See below, Psalm 88, col. 1120, note (b).], which is placed at the end of this title. For Heman is said to be interpreted as “his brother.”

Christ has deigned to make those his brothers who understand the mystery of his cross and not only are not ashamed of it, but also faithfully glory in it—not exalting themselves on account of their own merits, but not being ungrateful toward his grace—so that it may be said to each of them: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47), just as Scripture commends Israel himself as being without deceit (Gen. 25:27).

Let us now listen to the voice of Christ, singing first in prophecy, to which his chorus may respond either by imitation or by thanksgiving.

## 2. [verses 2, 3]

“Lord, God of my salvation, I have cried out by day and by night before you. Let my prayer enter into your presence; incline your ear to my petition.”

The Lord also prayed—not according to the form of God, but according to the form of a servant; for according to this form he also suffered.

He prayed when he was engaged in joyful circumstances, which I think is signified by the name “day,” and when he was in adversity, which I think is signified by the name “night.”

The entry of prayer into God’s presence means its acceptance; the inclination of God’s ear means his merciful hearing. For God does not possess bodily members such as we have.

There is also the customary repetition: “Let my prayer enter into your presence” means the same as “Incline your ear to my petition.”

## 3. [verse 4]

“For my soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell.”

Do we dare say that Christ’s soul was filled with evils, when that affliction of the passion had power only in the flesh, whatever power it had? Hence, kindling his own people to endure suffering and exhorting his chorus, as it were, to respond, he says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

Can the soul not be killed by persecutors, but be filled with evils? If so, we must ask with what evils. We cannot say that that soul was filled with vices by which iniquity rules human beings; but perhaps it was filled with pains, through which the soul sympathizes with its flesh during its suffering.

For even what is called bodily pain cannot exist without the soul; sadness, which is the pain of the soul alone, inevitably precedes the bodily pain that is about to occur. The soul can therefore suffer even when the body does not suffer; but the body cannot suffer without the soul.

Why, then, should we not say that Christ’s soul was filled not with human sins, but nevertheless with human evils? Another prophet says of him that he suffered for us (Isa. 53:4). And the Evangelist says: “Taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled.” And the Lord himself then said to them concerning himself: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:37–38).

The Psalmist, foreseeing these future events, introduces him speaking: “For my soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell.” For he explained the same sentence entirely in other words when he said, “My soul is sorrowful unto death.”

What is meant by “My soul is sorrowful” is meant here by “My soul is filled with evils”; and what follows, “unto death,” is meant here by “My life has drawn near to hell.”

The Lord Jesus assumed these affections of human weakness, just as he assumed the flesh of human weakness and human bodily death—not by necessity of nature, but by the will of his compassion. He did so in order to transform in himself his body, which is the Church, of which he deigned to be the Head—that is, to transform his members in his saints and faithful people.

Thus, if someone among them should happen to become sorrowful and suffer amid human temptations, he would not on that account think himself alienated from Christ’s grace. The body, responding in harmony with the voice sung beforehand, would learn from its Head that these things are not sins but signs of human weakness.

For in this body we read and hear the foremost of its members, the apostle Paul, confessing that his soul was filled with such evils when he says that he has great sorrow and continual pain in his heart for his brothers according to the flesh, who are Israelites (Rom. 9:2–4).

If we say that the Lord also became sorrowful for them when his passion was drawing near, a passion in which they were to bind themselves to the most monstrous crime, I think we would not be speaking inappropriately.

## 4. [verses 5, 6]

Finally, what he said on the cross—“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)—is also said afterward in this Psalm:

“I have been counted among those who descend into the pit.”

He was counted among them by those who did not know what they were doing, who thought that he died in the way other human beings die, as though subject to necessity and overcome by that necessity.

By “the pit” he meant either the depth of misery or the depth of hell.

### 5.

“I have become,” he says, “like a man without help, free among the dead.” In these words the person of the Lord is especially apparent. For who else is free among the dead except the one who, in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3), alone among sinners was without sin? Hence, to those who foolishly thought themselves free, he says: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.” And because it was necessary that they be freed from sins through the one who had no sin: “If the Son,” he says, “sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:34, 36).

Thus he is free among the dead, who had authority to lay down his life and to take it up again; no one took it from him, but he laid it down of his own will (ibid. 10:18). He could also, whenever he wished, raise up his flesh as a temple released from them, that is, from the dead, when he said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (ibid. 2:19). When all had deserted him as he was about to suffer, he was not left alone, because the Father did not desert him, as he himself testifies (ibid. 8:29). Yet by his enemies—for whom he prayed because they did not know what they were doing—and by those who said, “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. Let him save him, if he wants him” (Matt. 27:40–43), he was made—that is, he was considered—as a man without help.

He was like the wounded who sleep in the tomb. But he adds, “whom you do not yet remember,” and here the distinction of the Lord Christ from the other dead must be observed. For he too was wounded and placed dead in the tomb (ibid. 50, 60); but those who did not know what they were doing—plainly not knowing who he was—thought him like others who had been killed by wounds and were sleeping in the tomb, “whom God does not yet remember,” that is, whose time for rising again had not yet come. Scripture is accustomed to call the dead “sleeping” for this reason: it wants them to be understood as destined to awaken, that is, to rise again.

But this wounded man, sleeping in the tomb, awoke on the third day and became “like a solitary sparrow on the housetop” (Ps. 101:8), that is, at the Father’s right hand in heaven; and now he dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9). Thus he is far different from those whom God does not yet remember for such a resurrection: what had to occur first in the head is reserved for the body at the end.

God is said to remember when he acts, and to forget when he does not act. For neither forgetfulness falls upon God, since he is changed in no way, nor remembrance, since he does not forget. “I have therefore become,” from those who did not know what they were doing, “like a man without help, while I was free among the dead. I have become, from those who did not know what they were doing, like the wounded sleeping in the tomb.”

“And they themselves have been driven from your hand.” That is: when they did these things to me, they themselves were driven from your hand; they were deprived of the help of your hand, those who thought me to be without help. For, as he says in another psalm, “They dug a pit before my face and fell into it” (Ps. 56:7).

I think this is better understood in this way than by referring the words, “And they themselves have been driven from your hand,” to those sleeping in the tomb, whom God does not yet remember. For among them are the righteous, of whom, although God does not yet remember them in order to raise them, it has nevertheless been said, “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wis. 3:1), that is, “they dwell in the help of the Most High and abide under the protection of the God of heaven” (Ps. 90:1).

Rather, those have been driven from the hand of God who believed that the Lord Christ had been driven from his hand, since they were able to kill him, reckoning him among the wicked.

### 6. [verse 7]

“They placed me,” he says, “in the lowest pit”—or rather, “in the deepest pit,” for that is how it is in Greek: *katôtatô* [the lowest or deepest]. What, then, is the deepest pit except the most profound misery, than which there can be nothing deeper? Hence it is said elsewhere, “You brought me up from the pit of misery” (Ps. 39:3).

“In darkness and in the shadow of death”: they placed him there, plainly thinking this when they did not know what they were doing, and they did not know him “whom none of the rulers of this age knew” (1 Cor. 2:8).

I am uncertain whether “the shadow of death” here should be understood as bodily death, or rather as that of which it is written, “Those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, light has arisen upon them” (Isa. 9:2), because, by believing in the light and in life, they were led out of the darkness and death of impiety.

Thus those who did not know what they were doing thought the Lord to be such a one, and unknowingly placed him among those whom he himself came to help, so that they would not remain such.

### 7. [verse 8]

“Your indignation has been confirmed upon me”—or, as other manuscripts have it, “your anger”; or, as others, “your fury.” The Greek word is θυμός (*thymos*), which our translators have rendered in different ways.

Where the Greek manuscripts have ὀργή (*orgē*), almost no translator has hesitated to render it in Latin as *ira*, “anger.” But where θυμός occurs, most have not thought that it should be called anger, although the great authorities of Latin eloquence, translating works of the Greek philosophers, have rendered even this term into Latin by the word for anger. There is no need to discuss the matter at greater length. Yet if we too ought to apply another name to it, I would say “indignation” more tolerably than “fury.” For fury, as the Latin language uses the word, is not usually found in sane people.

What, then, is “Your anger has been confirmed upon me” except what was thought by those who did not recognize the Lord of glory? Among them it was as though God’s anger had not merely been stirred up but actually confirmed against him whom they were able to bring even to death—not just any death, but the death they regarded as more accursed than all others, the death of the cross.

Hence the Apostle says: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us; for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree’” (Gal. 3:13). And because he wished to commend Christ’s obedience even to the extremity of humiliation, he says, “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death”; and because this seemed insufficient, he added, “even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8).

For this reason, as I see it, a verse of this kind follows in this psalm: “And you have brought all your suspensions”—or, as some have translated it, “all your waves”—or, as others, “all your upheavals upon me.”

It is also written in another psalm, “All your suspensions and your waves have entered upon me” (Ps. 41:8); or, as some have translated it better, “have passed over me.” For the Greek has διῆλθον (*diēlthon*), “they passed through” or “passed over,” not εἰσῆλθον (*eisēlthon*), “they entered.”

Where, then, both “suspensions” and “waves” are present, “waves” could not have been used in place of “suspensions.” We have explained these two terms by saying that “suspensions” signify threats, while “waves” signify the sufferings themselves [Note: Above, col. 474, no. 15]; both proceed from God’s judgment.

But there it is said, “All have passed over me”; here, “You have brought all upon me.” There, then, although certain things occurred, he said that all the evils signified by those words “passed over me.” Here, however, he says, “You have brought them upon me.” Things pass over either when they do not touch us, as threats do, or when they do touch us, as waves do.

But when he says, “All the suspensions,” he does not say, “have passed over me,” but, “You have brought them upon me”; he signifies that everything that was impending has come to pass. Everything concerning his passion was impending so long as it remained future in prophecy.

### 8. [verses 9, 10]

“You have put my acquaintances far from me.” If we understand “my acquaintances” to mean those whom he knew, they will all be included, for whom did he not know? But he calls them acquaintances because they too were acquainted with him, insofar as they were then able to know him—at least to the extent that they knew him to be innocent, even if they thought him merely human and not also God.

He could also have called those whom he approved “acquaintances,” just as he could call those whom he rejected “unknown,” to whom at the end he will say, “I do not know you” (Matt. 7:23).

When he adds, “They have made me an abomination to themselves,” this may indeed be understood of those whom he called his acquaintances, because they too recoiled from that kind of death. But it is better understood of those about whom he had been speaking above, his persecutors.

“I have been handed over,” he says, “and I was not going out.” Is this because his disciples were outside while he himself was being judged within? Or should “I was not going out” rather be understood in a deeper sense: “I was hiding within my inner being; I was not displaying who I was; I was not exposed or revealed”? And therefore it follows: “My eyes have grown weak from poverty.”

For whom are we to understand as his eyes? If they were his outward eyes, situated in the flesh in which he suffered, we do not read that during his passion they grew weak from poverty, that is, languished as though from hunger, as commonly happens. For he was handed over after his supper and crucified on that same day.

If they were his inward eyes, how did they grow weak from poverty, when unfailing light was within them? Clearly, then, he called “his eyes” those members which, in his body—of which he himself is the head—he loved as brighter, more eminent, and more important.

Speaking of this body, and using the likeness of our own body, the Apostle says:

> “If the whole body were an eye, where would be the hearing? If the whole were hearing, where would be the sense of smell? If all were one member, where would be the body? But now there are many members, yet one body. The eye cannot say to the hands, ‘I have no need of you.’ And if the hand should say, ‘Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body,’ is it for that reason not of the body?”

He expressed more clearly what he wished these words to mean when he said, “Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it” (1 Cor. 12:12–27).

Those eyes, therefore—that is, the holy Apostles—to whom flesh and blood had not revealed him, but his Father who is in heaven, so that Peter might say, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16–17)—when they saw him being handed over and enduring such great evils, grew weak from poverty. They did not see him as they wished, because he was not going out, that is, he was not being manifested in his power and might, but was hidden in his inner being and endured everything as though defeated and powerless.

Thus they grew weak from poverty, as though their food and their light had been taken away.

### 9.

“And I cried to you, Lord.” He did this most openly when he hung upon the tree. But what follows—“All day I stretched out my hands to you”—deservedly raises the question of how it should be understood.

If by “I stretched out my hands” we understand the punishment of the cross, how are we to understand “all day”? Did he hang upon the tree all day, when night also belongs to the whole day?

If by “day” he intended the period customarily called day as opposed to night, even of that day on which he was crucified a first and considerable part had already passed.

But if we wish to understand “day” as a period of time—especially since he used this noun in the feminine gender, which in Latin generally signifies nothing except time, although this is not so in Greek, where “day” is always feminine, and I think this is why our translators rendered it so—the question becomes more difficult. For how could he have stretched out his hands on the cross for the whole period, if not even for one entire day?

Moreover, if we say that “the whole” must be understood as “a part,” since Holy Scripture is accustomed to use this kind of expression, I do not find an example in which “the whole” can be taken for “a part” when the very word *whole* is added and it says “the whole.”

For in what the Lord said in the Gospel, “So will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matt. 12:40), “the whole” is not improperly understood as a part because he did not say, “for the whole of three days and the whole of three nights.” One middle day was complete; of the other two there were only parts—the final part of the first and the initial part of the last.

If, however, in this prophecy of the psalm he did not signify his cross by these words, but rather the prayer which, according to the Gospel testimony, we have learned that he poured out to God the Father in the form of a servant—we remember him praying long before his passion, on the day of his passion, and on the cross—we nowhere read that he did this for the whole day.

Accordingly, we may appropriately understand “stretched-out hands all day” as signifying the continuation of good works, from whose pursuit he never ceased.

### 10. [verse 11]

But because his good works benefited only those predestined to eternal salvation, not all human beings, nor even all among whom those works were performed, he consequently added:

“Will you work wonders for the dead?”

If we think this was said of those whose flesh became lifeless, great wonders were worked for the dead, since some of them even came back to life (ibid. 27:52). And that the Lord penetrated the realms below and rose from them victorious over death was a great wonder performed for the dead.

Therefore, by the words “Will you work wonders for the dead?” he signifies people so dead in heart that the great wonders of Christ did not move them to the life of faith. He did not say that wonders were not performed for them because they did not see them, but because they did not benefit from them.

For just as he says here, “All day I stretched out my hands to you,” because he refers all his works solely to the Father’s will, repeatedly testifying that he came for this purpose, to fulfill the Father’s will (John 6:38), so, because the unbelieving people also saw those same works, another prophet says, “All day I stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe and contradicted” (Isa. 65:2).

These are the dead for whom no wonders were performed—not because they did not see them, but because they did not come back to life through them.

What follows—“Or will physicians raise them up, and will they confess to you?”—means that people will not be raised by physicians so as to confess to you.

In Hebrew, however, the passage is asserted to read differently: it is said to refer not to physicians but to giants. Yet the authority of the translators of the Septuagint is so great that they are not without reason believed to have translated by the Holy Spirit. Because in Hebrew “giants” and “physicians” sound almost alike and are distinguished by a slight difference, they wished to indicate—not through error, but rather by means of the opportunity provided by the similarity of the words—how “giants” should be understood in this passage.

If we understand the proud to be signified by the name “giants”—those of whom the Apostle says, “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age?” (1 Cor. 1:20)—it was not inappropriate for the same people to be called “physicians,” as though they promised the salvation of souls through the art of their wisdom. Against them it is said, “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 3:9).

But if we understand “giants” in a good sense—for it was also said of the Lord himself, “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6)—because he is the giant of giants, namely, of the great and very strong who excel in spiritual strength within his Church, just as he is the mountain of mountains, since it is written, “In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, prepared on the top of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2), and also the Holy of holies—it is not absurd for these same great and strong people also to be called physicians.

Hence the Apostle Paul says, “If somehow I might stir my flesh to emulation and save some of them” (Rom. 11:14).

Yet even such physicians, although they do not heal from their own resources—for bodily physicians do not heal from their own resources either—however much they assist salvation through a faithful ministry, can heal the living, but cannot raise the dead. It is of such people that it is said, “Will you work wonders for the dead?”

For the grace of God by which human minds in some manner come back to life is exceedingly hidden, so that they may be able to hear commands concerning health from any of his ministers. He commends this grace in the Gospel when he says:

> “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”

And shortly afterward, repeating the same point more clearly, he says:

> “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life; but there are some among you who do not believe.”

Then the Evangelist inserts:

> “For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who believed” [Note: The printed editions have *credituri*, “who would believe”; the manuscripts have *credentes*, “who believed.” But in the Gospel the reading is *non credentes*, “who did not believe.”] “and who it was who would betray him.”

Then, continuing and joining this to the Lord’s own words, he says:

> “And he said, ‘This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted him by my Father’” (John 6:44, 64–66).

He had said above, “But there are some among you who do not believe.” And, as though explaining the cause of this, he says, “This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted him by my Father”: to show that even faith itself, by which a person believes and the soul comes back to life from the death of its heart, is given to us by God.

However outstanding preachers of the word may be, and however persuasive of the truth even through miracles, acting among people as great physicians, if those people are dead and have not come back to life by your grace:

> “Will you work wonders for the dead? Or will physicians raise them up, and will those whom they raise up confess to you?”

For this confession indicates the living, unlike what is written elsewhere: “From the dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes” (Sir. 17:26).

### 11. [verse 12]

“Will anyone declare your mercy in the tomb, and your truth in destruction?”

What was said above is understood here, so that this verse has the force of saying: “Will anyone declare your truth in destruction?” Scripture especially loves to join mercy and truth together, most of all in the Psalms.

When he says “in destruction,” he repeats in another word what he said above, “in the tomb.” “In the tomb” is said so that those who are in the tomb may be understood—those who were signified earlier by the name “the dead,” where he says, “Will you work wonders for the dead?”

For a dead soul’s body is a tomb. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says to such people:

> “You are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and of every impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matt. 23:27–28).

### 12. [verse 13]

“Will your wonders be known in darkness, and your righteousness in a forgotten land?”

What is “in darkness” is the same as “in a forgotten land.” Unbelievers are signified by the name “darkness.” Hence the Apostle says, “For you were once darkness” (Eph. 5:8).

So too “a forgotten land” is a person who has forgotten God. An unbelieving soul can reach such great darkness that the fool says in his heart, “There is no God” (Ps. 13:1).

The whole meaning, therefore, is continued and woven together in this way:

“I cried to you, Lord, amid my sufferings; all day I stretched out my hands to you”—that is, I did not cease to extend my works toward glorifying you.

Why, then, do the impious rage against me, unless it is because you do not work wonders for the dead—that is, they are not moved by them to faith, nor will physicians raise them up so that they may confess to you, since your hidden grace does not operate in them, drawing them to believe? For no one comes to me unless you draw him.

“For who will declare your mercy in the tomb”—that is, in a dead soul whose death lies beneath the burden of the body [Note: Perhaps *latet*, “lies hidden,” rather than *jacet*, “lies”]—“and your truth in destruction,” that is, in such a death, where the person is capable of neither believing nor perceiving any of these good things [Note: The manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions add *bonum*, “good,” here].

For will your wonders and your righteousness be known in the darkness of this death—that is, in a person who has lost the light of life by forgetting you?

### 13. [verse 14]

A question arose, however: what use are these dead people? What does God accomplish through them for the benefit of the body of Christ, which is the Church? It is so that the nature of God’s grace in the predestined, who are called according to his purpose, might be demonstrated.

Hence the body itself says in another psalm, “My God, his mercy will precede me. My God will show me among my enemies” (Ps. 58:11–12).

So here too it follows and says, “And I cried to you, Lord.” In these words the Lord Christ must now be understood as speaking from the voice of his body, that is, the Church. For what is “And I,” except that “we too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3)?

“But I cried to you,” so that I might be saved. For who distinguished me from the other children of wrath, when I hear the Apostle terrifyingly rebuking the ungrateful and saying:

> “For who makes you different? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

“Salvation belongs to the Lord.” But “a giant in the abundance of his strength will not be saved” (Ps. 32:16). Rather, as it is written:

> “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved. But how will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without someone preaching? And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written, ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things’” (Rom. 10:13–15).

These are the physicians who cure the man wounded by robbers; yet the Lord brought him to the inn (Luke 10:34). For they are also workers in the Lord’s field. Nevertheless, “neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

Therefore I too cried to the Lord; that is, I called upon the Lord so that I might be saved. But how would I call upon him unless I believed? And how would I believe unless I heard? Yet in order that I might believe what I heard, he himself drew me, because in secret he raised me from the death of my heart—not some physician, but he himself.

For many heard, since “their sound went out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5); but “faith does not belong to all” (2 Thess. 3:2), and “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19).

Accordingly, I could not have believed unless God’s mercy had preceded me. And because he raises the dead and calls things that do not exist as though they did, by calling me secretly, raising me, and drawing me, he brought me out of darkness and led me to the light of faith.

Therefore it follows: “And in the morning my prayer will come before you.”

Now it is morning, after the night and darkness of unbelief have passed. To make this morning exist for me, your mercy indeed preceded me. But because that glorification still remains when “the hidden things of darkness will be brought to light and the purposes of hearts will be revealed, and then each one will receive praise from you” (1 Cor. 4:5), now, in this life, in this pilgrimage, in this light of faith—which in comparison with the darkness of unbelievers is already day, but in comparison with the day in which we shall see face to face is still night—still my prayer will come before you.

### 14. [verse 15]

But so that this prayer may grow fervent and be exercised—a matter whose benefit to us, I think, cannot be explained in words—the good that will be given eternally is deferred, and the evils that will pass away grow more numerous.

Therefore it follows: “Why, Lord, have you rejected my prayer?”

This too was said in the words, “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21:2). The cause is put forward for investigation, not as though God’s hidden wisdom were being blamed for doing this without reason [Note: The manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions instead have *occulta*, “hidden”]. So here too: “Why, Lord, have you rejected my prayer?”

Yet if the reason for this is carefully considered, it was already indicated above. The prayers of the saints are apparently rejected through the delay of so great a benefit and through the adversity of tribulations, so that, like a fire beaten back by the breath of air, they may burn more intensely.

### 15. [verses 16–19]

He therefore briefly recounts also the tribulations of the body of Christ. For they did not occur in the head alone, since Saul too was told, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4), and Paul himself, already placed as an elect member in the same body, says:

> “That I may complete what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh” (Col. 1:24).

“Why, then, Lord, have you rejected my prayer? You turn your face away from me. I am poor, and in labor from my youth; but, having been exalted, I have been humbled and troubled [Note: Manuscripts of better quality have *confusus*, “confounded,” in accordance with the Septuagint. Yet below this corresponds to the phrase, “we shall neither be exalted nor be humbled and troubled.”]. Your angers have passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me. They have surrounded me like water all day; they have surrounded me together. You have put far from me friend and acquaintance from misery” [Note: The printed editions add “and neighbor”; this is absent from the manuscripts and the Septuagint].

All these things have happened and continue to happen in the members of Christ’s body.

God turns his face away from those who pray when he does not grant what they want, because they do not know that what they ask is not beneficial for them. The Church is poor when, as a pilgrim, she hungers and thirsts for what will satisfy her in her homeland.

She has been in labor from her youth; for the body of Christ says in another psalm, “Often they have attacked me from my youth” (Ps. 128:1).

And certain members of it are exalted even in this age so that greater humility may exist in them.

The angers of God pass over the body itself—that is, the unity of the saints and faithful, whose head is Christ—but they do not remain. For it was said not of the faithful but of the unbeliever, “The anger of God remains upon him” (John 3:36).

The terrors of God trouble the weakness of the faithful, because everything that can happen is wisely feared, even if it does not happen. Sometimes those very terrors so trouble the mind of one who considers the evils hanging over him that they seem to flow around him like water and to surround the one who fears on every side all at once.

And because such things are not absent from the Church as she journeys in this world, since they occur everywhere in one member or another, he therefore said, “all day,” signifying the continuation of time until this age comes to an end.

Often friends and acquaintances, endangered according to worldly standards, abandon the saints out of fear. Of these the Apostle says, “Everyone deserted me; may it not be held against them” (2 Tim. 4:16).

But why do all these things happen except so that the prayer of this holy body may, in the morning—that is, after the night of unbelief, in the light of faith—come before God until that salvation arrives in whose reality we are not yet saved but in whose hope we have already been saved, and which we faithfully await with patience (Rom. 8:24–25)?

Then the Lord will not reject our prayer, because there will be nothing left to ask for, but whatever was rightly requested will be obtained. Nor will he turn his face from us, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Nor shall we be poor, because God himself will be our abundance, all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). Nor shall we labor, because no weakness will remain.

Nor, after being exalted, shall we be humbled and troubled, because no adversity will exist there. Nor shall we endure even the passing anger of God, because we shall remain in his abiding kindness [Note: The better manuscripts have *manente*, “abiding”; the printed editions have *manentes*, “remaining”]. Nor will his terrors trouble us, because the promises, once fulfilled, will make us blessed [Note: The manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions have “will meet us”]. Nor will an acquaintance or friend who is terrified be put far from us, where there will be no enemy to fear.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXXXVIII

### SERMON I

[Delivered in the morning hours on the feast of certain martyrs.] On the first part of the Psalm.

### 1. [verse 1]

Receive, beloved, by the Lord’s gift, this psalm which we have undertaken to discuss, in the light of the hope which we have in Christ Jesus our Lord; and lift up your minds, because he who promised will fulfil the rest just as he has fulfilled much already. For what gives us confidence toward him is not our merit, but his mercy. And he himself is, I think, the “Understanding of Ethan the Israelite” [Note: The Vulgate here, as in the title of the preceding psalm, has *Ezrahitae*, perhaps for *Zaraitae*. For in 1 Chron. 2:6 Ethan and Heman are reckoned sons of Zerah; and in 1 Kings 4:31 Solomon is said in the Vulgate to be wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite and Heman, whereas the Septuagint has “the Zarite” for *Ezrahita*], from whom this psalm has taken its title.

You may see who the man called Ethan was; yet the interpretation of this name signifies “Strong.” And no one is strong in this world except through hope in God’s promise. For with respect to our merits we are weak; with respect to his mercy we are strong. Thus this man, weak in himself but strong in God’s mercy, began from this point.

### 2. [verse 2]

“I will sing your mercies, O Lord, for ever; from generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth.” “Let my members,” he says, “serve my Lord. I speak, but I speak what is yours; I will proclaim your truth with my mouth. If I do not serve, I am not a servant; if I speak from myself, I am a liar. Therefore, for me both to speak from you and to speak myself, there are two things: one yours, one mine—your truth, my mouth.” Let us hear, then, what truth he proclaims and what mercies he sings.

### 3. [verse 3]

“Because you have said: Mercy shall be built up for ever.” This I sing; this is your truth; my mouth serves to proclaim it: “Because you have said: Mercy shall be built up for ever.” “Thus,” you say, “I build, so that I do not destroy.” For you destroy some in such a way that you do not build them up; others you destroy in such a way that you do build them up.

For unless certain persons were destroyed in order to be built up, Jeremiah would not have been told, “Behold, I have set you for destruction and for building up” (Jer. 1:10). And surely all who worshipped idols and served stones would not be built up in Christ unless they were destroyed in their former error. Again, unless certain persons were destroyed so as not to be built up, it would not be said, “You will destroy them, and you will not build them up” (Ps. 27:5).

Therefore, on account of those who are destroyed and built up, lest they should think that the building up by which they are built was temporal, just as the ruin in which they are destroyed was temporal, this man, whose mouth serves God’s truth, held fast to the very truth of God. Hence I proclaim, hence I say, “Because you have said”; as one secure, I say it because you, God, have said it. For although I might waver in my own word, I would be made firm by your word. “Because you have said.” What have you said? “Mercy shall be built up for ever. Your truth shall be prepared in the heavens.”

As above, so in what follows. “I will sing your mercies, O Lord, for ever; from generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth.” He spoke of mercies; he spoke of truth; so again he joined the two: “Because you have said: Mercy shall be built up for ever. Your truth shall be prepared in the heavens.” Here too he repeated mercy and truth. For “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). Truth would not be displayed in the fulfilment of promises unless mercy had first gone before in the forgiveness of sins.

Further, many things were prophetically promised to the people of Israel, descended according to the flesh from Abraham’s seed; and that people was thus propagated, in which God’s promises might be fulfilled. Yet God did not shut the fountain of his goodness even to the nations of foreigners, whom he had placed under angels, while making the people Israel his own portion. The Apostle too distinctly distributes the Lord’s mercy and truth between these two.
