For he says that Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers. See: God did not deceive; see: he did not reject his people, whom he foreknew.

Indeed, when the fall of the Jews was under discussion, lest anyone should think them rejected in such a way that no grain from that winnowing would be carried into the barn, the Apostle says: “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew; for I too am an Israelite” (Rom. 11:1–2). If all of that people were thorns, from where does the grain which speaks to you come? Therefore God’s truth was fulfilled in those Israelites who believed, and one wall came from the circumcision and joined itself to the cornerstone (Eph. 2:20). But that stone would not make a corner unless it received another wall from the Gentiles. That wall, therefore, belongs as it were properly to truth; this other one to mercy. For, he says, “I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers; but that the Gentiles should glorify God for mercy” (Rom. 15:8–9).

Rightly, then, “Your truth shall be prepared in the heavens.” For all those Israelites called Apostles became heavens, which declare God’s glory. Of these heavens it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands.” And so that you may know that this is said of these heavens, certainly in what follows it is more expressly said: “There are no speeches nor words, whose voices are not heard.” Ask whose voices, and above you will find none but those of the heavens. Therefore, if they are the Apostles whose voice was heard in every language, they are those of whom it was said: “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:2, 4, 5). For although they were taken from here before the Church filled the whole world, their words nevertheless reached to the ends of the world. We rightly understand that what we now read was fulfilled in them: “Your truth shall be prepared in the heavens.”

### 4. [verse 4]

“I have established a covenant with my chosen ones.” “You have said”—understand this whole statement—“you have said, ‘I have established a covenant with my chosen ones.’” [Note: [Col. 1122] The printed editions read, “You have said, you have understood: you have said this whole thing.” But the manuscripts have *intelligitis* (“you understand”); some have *intelligimus* (“we understand”). Nothing else is intended than that the preceding word in verse 3, “you have said,” also refers to these following verses.]

What covenant, unless the new one? What covenant, unless that by which we are renewed for a new inheritance? What covenant, unless that whose inheritance we desire and love when we sing a new song? “I have established,” he says, “a covenant with my chosen ones. I have sworn to David my servant.”

How confidently this man speaks, who understands whose mouth serves the truth! “Because you have said it,” I speak confidently. If you make me confident because you have said it, how much more confident because you have sworn it! For God’s oath is the confirmation of his promise. Man is rightly forbidden to swear, lest, through the habit of swearing—since a human being can be deceived—he should also slip into perjury. God alone swears with security, because he cannot be deceived.

### 5. [verse 5]

Let us therefore see what God swore. “I have sworn,” he says, “to David my servant: I will prepare your seed forever.” What is David’s seed, unless Abraham’s seed? And what is Abraham’s seed? “And to your seed,” he says, “which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16).

But perhaps that Christ who is the head of the Church, the Savior of the body (Eph. 5:23), is Abraham’s seed, and therefore David’s; but are we not Abraham’s seed? Indeed we are, as the Apostle says: “But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3:29).

Let us therefore understand this passage, brothers: “I will prepare your seed forever”—not only that flesh of Christ born from the Virgin Mary, but also all of us who believe in Christ; for we are members of that head. This body cannot be decapitated: if the head is forever, the members also glory forever, so that Christ may be complete forever.

“I will prepare your seed forever; and I will build your throne for generation and generation.” Do we suppose that “forever” means the same as “for generation and generation”? For above he had also said, “For generation and generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth.” What does “for generation and generation” mean? For every generation. The word did not have to be repeated as often as a generation comes and passes. Thus the multiplication of generations is signified and emphasized by the repetition.

Or should two generations perhaps be understood, as you know and as you retain from what has already been suggested to your Charity? There is a generation now, of flesh and blood; and there will be a future generation in the resurrection of the dead. Christ is preached here; he will be preached there. But here he is preached so that he may be believed; there he will be preached so that he may be seen.

“I will build your throne for generation and generation.” Now Christ has his throne in us; his throne has been built in us. For unless he sat in us, he would not rule us; but if we were not ruled by him, we would be hurled down by ourselves. He therefore sits in [Col. 1123] us, reigning in us. He also sits in that other generation which will arise from the resurrection of the dead. Christ will reign forever in his saints.

God promised this; God said this. If that is too little, God swore this. Since the promise is therefore firm, not according to our merits but according to his mercy, no one ought to preach with hesitation what he cannot doubt.

Let that strength therefore come to be in our hearts from which Ethan received his name—“strong in heart.” Let us preach God’s truth, God’s utterance, God’s promises, God’s oath; and, strengthened in every way by these things, let us preach and, by bearing God, become heavens.

### 6. [verse 6]

“The heavens will confess your wonders, Lord.” The heavens will not confess their own merits, but “the heavens will confess your wonders, Lord.” For in every mercy shown to the lost, in the justification of the ungodly, what do we praise except God’s wonders?

You praise him because the dead have risen; praise him more because the lost have been redeemed. What grace, what mercy of God! You see a man who yesterday was a chasm of drunkenness and today is an ornament of sobriety. You see a man who yesterday was filth of lust and today is the glory of self-control. You see a man who yesterday blasphemed God and today praises God. You see a man who yesterday was a servant of creation and today worships the Creator.

People are turned away from all these forms of despair in this way: let them not look to their own merits; let them become heavens; let the heavens confess the wonders of him by whom the heavens were made. “For I shall behold,” he says, “the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8:4).

“The heavens will confess your wonders, Lord.” And so that you may know which heavens will confess, see where they will confess; for it follows: “And your truth in the assembly of the saints.” There can therefore be no doubt that by the heavens are understood the preachers of the word of truth.

And where will the heavens confess your wonders and your truth? “In the assembly of the saints.” Let the Church receive the dew of the heavens; let the heavens rain upon the thirsty earth, and let the earth, receiving the rain, bring forth good shoots, good works—lest, instead of good rain, it produce thorns and, instead of a granary, await fire.

“The heavens will confess your wonders, Lord, and your truth in the assembly of the saints.” The heavens, then, will confess your wonders and your truth. Everything the heavens preach is from you and about you; therefore they preach confidently. For they know whom they preach, since they cannot be ashamed of the one who is preached.

### 7. [verse 7]

What do the heavens preach? What will they confess in the assembly of the saints? “For who among the clouds will be equal to the Lord?” Is this what the heavens will confess, what the heavens will rain? What? “For who among the clouds will be equal to the Lord?”

The preachers are confident because no one among the clouds will be equal to the Lord. This seems to you a great praise, brothers: that the clouds are not equal to the Creator. If it is understood literally, without mystery, it is not great praise that the clouds are not equal to the Lord. For what? Are the stars above the clouds equal to the Lord? What of the sun, moon, angels, and heavens—could they even be compared with the Lord? What is meant by the statement, as though it were something great: “Who among the clouds will be equal to the Lord”?

We understand, brothers, that these clouds, like the heavens, are the preachers of truth: [Col. 1124] the Prophets, the Apostles, and the proclaimers of God’s word. We understand from that prophecy that all these classes of preachers are called clouds, where God, angry with his vineyard, said, “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it.” He explains and identifies this vineyard most clearly when he says, “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:6–7).

Do not understand the vineyard otherwise and, leaving aside the people signified, examine the earth: [Note: [Col. 1124] Thus the better manuscripts; the printed editions read, “all.”] “The vineyard,” he says, “of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” Let the house of Israel understand that it is itself my vineyard; let it understand that it gave me not grapes but thorns; let it understand that it proved ungrateful to the planter and cultivator, ungrateful to the one who irrigated it.

Therefore, if the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, what did he say in anger? “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it.” And in fact he did so: the Apostles were sent like clouds to rain upon the Jews. But when they rejected God’s word, because they had given thorns instead of grapes, the Apostles said, “We were sent to you; but because you rejected God’s word, we are going to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). From that time the clouds began not to rain upon that vineyard.

If, then, the clouds are the preachers of truth, let us first ask why they are clouds. They are the same as the heavens, and the same as the clouds: heavens because of the splendor of truth, clouds because of the hidden things of the flesh. All clouds are misty because of mortality; they come and pass away.

Because of these hidden things of the flesh—that is, the hidden things of the clouds—the Apostle says, “Do not judge anything before the proper time, until the Lord comes and brings to light the hidden things of darkness” (1 Cor. 4:5). Now you see what a person says, but you do not see what he carries in his heart. You see what is expressed from the cloud, but you do not see what is kept in the cloud. Whose eyes penetrate a cloud?

The preachers of truth are therefore clouds in the flesh. The Creator of all also came in the flesh. But “who among the clouds will be equal to the Lord?” Who, then, among the clouds will be equal to the Lord? And who will be like the Lord among the sons of God?

No one, then, among the sons of God will be like the Son of God. He is called the Son of God, and we are called sons of God; but who will be like the Lord among the sons of God? He is the only one, we are many; he is one, we are one in him; he was born, we were adopted; he is the Son begotten eternally by nature, equal to the Father, while we were made in time by grace; he is without any sin, while we have been freed from sin through him.

Who, then, among the clouds will be equal to the Lord? Or who will be like the Lord among the sons of God? We are called clouds because of the flesh, and we are preachers of truth because of the rain of the clouds; but our flesh came in one way, his flesh in another. We are also called sons of God, but he is the Son of God in another way. His cloud came from a virgin; he is the Son from eternity, equal to the Father.

Who, then, among the clouds will be equal to the Lord? Or who will be like the Lord among the sons of God? Let the Lord himself say whether he finds anyone like him. “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” For behold, because I appear, because I am seen, because I walk among you, and perhaps my presence has made me seem insignificant, say whom people say that the Son of Man is.

Certainly, because they see the Son of Man, they see a cloud. Let them say—or you [Col. 1125] say—whom people say that I am. And they answered with the answers of the people: “Some say Jeremiah, others Elijah, others John the Baptist, or one of the Prophets.”

Many clouds and sons of God were named. For since they were righteous and holy, they too were certainly sons of God: Jeremiah, Elijah, and John, sons of God; and clouds, because they were God’s preachers.

You have said which clouds people suppose me to be and among which sons of God people count me. Tell me also whom you say that I am. Peter answered for all, one speaking for unity: “You are,” he said, “the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:13–16).

“For who among the clouds will be equal to the Lord? Or who will be like the Lord among the sons of God? You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”—not like those sons of God who are not equal to you. You came in the flesh, but not like the clouds that are not equal to you. [Note: [Col. 1125] Erasmus, the Venice edition, and the Louvain edition omit *sed* (“but”), which is present in manuscript B.]

### 8. [verse 8]

Who are you, then, to whom the answer is given, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”—you whom other people thought to be one of the Prophets, though not holy or righteous, or Elijah, or Jeremiah, or John the Baptist? Who, then, are you?

Hear what follows: “God is to be glorified in the council of the saints.” “Who,” then, “among the clouds will be equal to the Lord? Or who will be like the Lord among the sons of God, when that God is to be glorified in the council of the saints?”

Since they cannot be his equals, let their counsel be to believe in him. Since the clouds and sons of God cannot be his equals, the counsel that remains for human weakness is that “the one who boasts should boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

“God is to be glorified in the council of the saints: great and terrible to all who surround him.”

God is everywhere. Who, then, are those who surround him, since he is everywhere? For if he has certain beings around him, he seems to be bounded on every side. But if it was truly said to God and about God, “There is no limit to his greatness” (Ps. 145:3), who remain around him except that he who is everywhere chose, through the flesh, to be born in one place, to live among one people, to be crucified in one place, to rise again from one place, and from one place to ascend into heaven?

Where he did these things, the Gentiles are around him. If he had remained where he did these things, he would not have become great and terrible to all who surround him. But because he preached there in such a way as to send preachers of his name from there throughout all the Gentiles and the whole world, performing miracles through his servants, he became great and terrible to all who surround him.

### 9. [verses 9–10]

“Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are mighty, Lord, and your truth is around you.”

Great is your power: you made heaven and earth and everything in them. But greater is your mercy, which displayed your truth around you. For if you were preached only where you chose to be born, to suffer, to rise again, and from where you chose to ascend, that truth of God’s promise would have been fulfilled, for the confirmation of the promises made to the fathers.

But the statement “the Gentiles glorify God because of his mercy” (Rom. 15:8–9) would not have been fulfilled unless that truth had been extended and spread around from the place where you chose to appear.

You indeed thundered from your own [Col. 1126] cloud in that place, but for the watering of the surrounding Gentiles you sent other clouds. Truly powerful, you fulfilled what you said: “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matt. 26:64).

“You are mighty, Lord, and your truth is around you.”

### 10.

But when your truth began to be preached around the world, surely the Gentiles raged, and the peoples meditated on vain things; the kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ (Ps. 2:1–2).

Certainly, when your truth began to be preached around you, as though you were coming to take a bride from foreign peoples, a roaring lion came out, and you suffocated him. This was prefigured in Samson (Judg. 14:5–6). [Note: [Col. 1126] Thus several manuscripts; others, with the printed editions, read “his.”] And you would not have applauded these words of mine, spoken without his name, unless you recognized them; for you heard them, you who are accustomed to be drenched by God’s clouds. Therefore, “your truth is around you.”

But when has there ever been no persecution, no opposition, since he was said to have been born as a sign that would be opposed (Luke 2:34)? Since that nation where you chose to be born and to live was like land separated from the waves of the Gentiles, so that dry land might appear, ready to be watered, while the remaining Gentiles were a sea in the bitterness of their barrenness, what do your preachers do when they scatter your truth around you, while the waves of the sea rage?

What do they do? “You rule the power of the sea.” For what did the sea accomplish by raging, except the day we celebrate today? It killed the martyrs, scattered seeds of blood, and the harvest of the Church sprang up.

Let the clouds therefore proceed confidently; let them spread your truth around you; let them not fear the raging waves: “You rule the power of the sea.” The sea is indeed stirred, the sea resists, the sea roars; but God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to endure (1 Cor. 10:13). Since he is faithful and does not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can endure, “you still the movement of its waves.”

### 11. [verse 11]

Finally, so that the sea might be calmed—or rather, so that the sea’s rage might be weakened—what did you do in the sea itself? “You humbled the proud one as though wounded.”

There is a certain proud dragon in the sea, of whom another Scripture says, “I will command the dragon there to bite him” (Amos 9:3). He is the dragon of whom it is said, “This is the dragon you formed to mock him” (Ps. 104:26), whose head he crushes upon the water.

“You humbled,” he says, “the proud one as a wounded man.” You humbled yourself, and the proud one was humbled. In his pride he held the proud; he was humbled when the great one became small, and the one who believed in him became small. While the small one was nourished by the example of the great one who became small, the devil lost what he held, because the proud one held only the proud.

By giving so great an example of humility, people learned to condemn their own pride and imitate God’s humility. Thus, by losing those whom he held, he himself was also humbled—not corrected, but overthrown.

“You humbled the proud one as a wounded man.” You were humbled, and you humbled him; you were wounded, and you wounded him. For your blood, poured out to erase the record of sins, could not fail to wound him.

[Col. 1127] For what did he grow proud except that he held a bond against us? You erased this bond, this record, with your blood (Col. 2:14). You therefore wounded him from whom you took away so much. Understand the devil as wounded—not in flesh pierced, for he has no flesh, but in the heart struck, where he is proud.

“And with the arm of your strength you scattered your enemies.”

### 12. [verses 12–13]

“Yours are the heavens, and yours is the earth.” From you they rain; upon what is yours they rain. [Note: [Col. 1127] This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “Let them rain; let them rain upon the earth.”]

“Yours are the heavens,” through which truth was preached around you; “yours is the earth,” which received the truth around you.

Finally, what came of that rain? “You founded the world and its fullness; you created the north and the seas.” For nothing can prevail against you, its Creator.

The world can indeed rage in its wickedness, through the perversity of its will; but can it exceed the limit set by the Creator who made all things? Why, then, should I fear the north? Why should I fear the seas?

The devil is indeed in the north, who said, “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14); but you humbled him as a wounded proud one. Therefore, what you did in them has greater force for your dominion than their will has for their wickedness.

“You created the north and the seas.”

### 13.

“Thabor and Hermon will exult in your name.” [Note: Some manuscripts have *Hermonim* here and below; others have *Hermoniim*.]

These mountains are understood literally, but they signify something. “Thabor and Hermon will exult in your name.”

Thabor is said to be interpreted as “coming light.” But from where does the light come of which it was said, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14), unless from him of whom it was said, “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9)?

That light, then, which is the light of the world, comes from that light which is not kindled from elsewhere, so that there is no danger that it might be extinguished. The light therefore comes from him: that lamp which is not placed under a bushel but upon a lampstand—Thabor, the coming light.

Hermon, however, is interpreted as “his anathema.” Rightly, the light came and became his anathema. Whose, unless that of the devil, who was wounded and proud? Thus, that we might be illuminated, it was given to us by you; that the one who held us in his error and pride might be an anathema to us, this too came to us from you.

Therefore, “Thabor and Hermon will exult in your name”—not in their own merits, but in your name. For they will say, “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory,” because of the raging sea, lest the Gentiles should say, “Where is their God?” (Ps. 115:1–2).

### 14. [verse 14]

“Your arm is with power.” Let no one claim anything for himself.

“Your arm is with power”: by you we were made; by you we were defended.

“Your arm is with power; let your hand be strengthened, and let your right hand be exalted.”

### 15. [verse 15]

“Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne.”

Your righteousness and judgment will appear at the end; now these things are hidden. And of your judgment it is said in another psalm, “For the hidden things of the Son” (Ps. 9:1). There will be a manifestation of your judgment and your righteousness.

Some will be placed [Col. 1128] at the right hand and some at the left (Matt. 25:33). The unbelievers will be terrified when they see what they now mock and do not believe; the righteous will rejoice when they see what, though they do not now see it, they believe.

“Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne”—certainly on the day of judgment.

What, then, now? “Mercy and truth go before your face.” I would fear the preparation of your throne, your righteousness and your judgment to come, unless your mercy and truth went before you. Why should I fear your judgments at the end, when, through your preceding mercy, you erase my sins, and by displaying your truth you fulfill your promises?

“Mercy and truth go before your face.” For “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 25:10).

### 16. [verses 16–17]

In all these things, shall we not exult? Or shall we comprehend the exultation in which we rejoice? Will words suffice for our joy? Will the tongue be able to explain our gladness?

If no words suffice, then: “Blessed is the people that understands jubilation.”

O blessed people! Do you suppose that you understand jubilation? You are in no way blessed unless you understand jubilation.

What does it mean to understand jubilation? Know from where you rejoice in something that you cannot explain in words. For your joy is not from yourself, so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

Do not therefore exult in your pride, but in God’s grace. See that grace itself is so great that the tongue is not capable of explaining it, and you have understood jubilation.

### 17.

Finally, if you have understood jubilation in grace, hear the praise of that grace itself.

“Blessed, certainly, is the people that understands jubilation.” What jubilation? See whether it is not about grace, whether it is not about God, and altogether not about yourself.

“Lord, they will walk in the light of your face.” That Thabor, “coming light,” unless it walks in the light of your face, has its lamp extinguished by the wind of pride.

“Lord, they will walk in the light of your face, and they will exult all day in your name.” Let Thabor and Hermon exult in your name. If they wish to exult all day, let them exult in your name; but if they exult in their own name, they will not exult all day. For they will not persevere in joy when they rejoice in themselves and fall through pride.

Therefore, in order that they may exult all day, they will exult in your name, “and in your righteousness they will be exalted.” Not in their own righteousness, but in yours, lest they be people who have zeal for God but not according to knowledge.

For some are reproved by the Apostle because they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge: ignorant of God’s righteousness, seeking to establish their own, and not exulting in your light, they are not subject to God’s righteousness. Why? Because “they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2–3).

But the people that understands jubilation—for those others are not according to knowledge, whereas the blessed people are not ignorant but understand jubilation—from where should it jubilate, from where should it exult, unless in your name, walking in the light of your face?

It will indeed deserve to be exalted, but in your righteousness. Let its own righteousness be removed from the midst, and let it be humbled; God’s righteousness will come, and it will be exalted.

“And in your righteousness they will be exalted.”

### 18. [verse 18]

“For you are the glory of their strength, and by your good pleasure our horn will be exalted”—because it pleased you, not because we are worthy.

### 19. [verse 19]

“For protection belongs to the Lord, and to the Holy One of Israel, our king.”

[Col. 1129] For I was pushed like a heap of sand and was about to fall; indeed, I would have fallen unless the Lord had received me.

“For the Lord’s is the protection; and the Holy One of Israel is our king.” He is the protection; he himself illuminates you. In his light you are safe; in his light you walk; in his righteousness you are exalted. [Note: [Col. 1129] The manuscripts have “you exult.”]

He received you; he himself guards your weakness. He makes you strong from himself, not from yourself.

### 20. [verse 20]

“Then you spoke in a vision to your sons, and you said.”

You spoke in your vision; you revealed this to your Prophets. Therefore you spoke to them in a vision—that is, in revelation. Hence the Prophets were called “Seers” (1 Sam. 9:9). They saw inwardly something they would proclaim outwardly; in secret they heard what they preached publicly.

“Then you spoke in a vision to your sons, and you said, ‘I have placed help upon a mighty one.’” You understand whom he means by “mighty one.”

“I have exalted the chosen one from my people.” You understand whom he means by “chosen one”—the one whom you already rejoice to see exalted.

### 21. [verse 21]

“I have found David my servant”—this David from the seed of David. [Note: This is the reading of most manuscripts. The printed editions have “this righteous David.”]

“With my holy oil I have anointed him.” For it is said of him, “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 45:8).

### 22. [verse 22]

“For my hand will assist him, and my arm will strengthen him”—in accordance with the assumption of human nature; in accordance with flesh being assumed in the Virgin’s womb (Luke 1:31); in accordance with the one who, in the form of God, is equal to the Father assuming the form of a servant and becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2:6–8).

### 23. [verse 23]

“The enemy will not profit against him.”

The enemy indeed rages, but he will not profit against him. He is accustomed to harm, but he will not harm.

What, then, will affliction accomplish? It will exercise, but it will not harm. His raging will be beneficial, because those against whom he rages will be crowned by conquering.

For what is conquered if nothing rages against us? Or where is God our helper if we do not fight? Let the enemy therefore do what belongs to him; but “the enemy will not profit against him, and the son of iniquity will not add to harming him.”

### 24. [verse 24]

“And I will crush his enemies before his face.”

They are crushed from their conspiracy, and they are crushed in what they believe. For they gradually come to believe. Like a calf’s head that has been crushed, they will come to drink for the people of God.

Moses crushed the head of the calf, scattered it in water, and gave it to the children of Israel to drink (Exod. 32:20). All unbelievers are crushed; they gradually come to believe, and they are drunk by the people of God, transferred into the body of Christ.

“And I will crush his enemies before his face; and those who hate him I will put to flight,” so that they may not harm.

But perhaps some of these fugitives say, “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. 139:7). When they see that they have nowhere to flee from the Almighty, they turn and flee to the Almighty.

“And those who hate him I will put to flight.”

### 25. [verse 25]

“And my truth and my mercy are with him.”

“All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” Remember, as far as you can, how often these two things are commended to us, so that we may render them to God.

For just as he showed us mercy, so as to erase [Col. 1130] our sins, and truth, so as to fulfill his promises, so we, walking in his way, ought to render mercy and truth to him: mercy, so that we may have mercy on the miserable; truth, so that we may not judge unjustly.

Let truth not take mercy away from you, nor mercy impede truth. For if through mercy you judge against truth, or, as though by a rigid truth, forget mercy, you will not walk in God’s way, where “mercy and truth have met one another” (Ps. 85:10).

“And in my name his horn will be exalted.” What need is there to linger? You are Christians; recognize Christ.

### 26. [verse 26]

“And I will place his hand upon the sea”—that is, he will rule the Gentiles.

“And his right hand upon the rivers.” Rivers run into the sea; covetous people slide into the bitterness of this age. Nevertheless, all these kinds of things will be subjected to Christ.

### 27. [verses 27–28]

“He himself will call upon me: ‘You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.’ And I will place him as firstborn, exalted among the kings of the earth.”

Our martyrs, whose anniversaries we celebrate, shed their blood because of these things believed but not yet seen. How much stronger ought we to be, seeing what they believed? [Note: [Col. 1130] The printed editions read, “seeing through what,” and so forth. “Through” is absent from the manuscripts.]

For they had not yet seen Christ exalted among the kings of the earth. The rulers were still gathering together against the Lord and against his Christ. What follows in that same psalm had not yet been fulfilled: “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, all you who judge the earth” (Ps. 2:2, 10).

Christ has therefore now become exalted among the kings of the earth.

### 28. [verse 29]

“Forever I will preserve my mercy for him, and my covenant will be faithful to him.”

For his sake it is a faithful covenant; in him the covenant was mediated. He is the mediator of the covenant, the one who ratifies the covenant, the guarantor of the covenant, the witness of the covenant, the inheritance of the covenant, and the co-heir of the covenant.

### 29. [verse 30]

“And I will establish his seed for age after age.”

Not only in this age, but for age after age—into which his seed, which is his inheritance, will surely pass: the seed of Abraham, which is Christ.

“But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Gal. 3:16, 29). And if they are to receive the inheritance forever, he will establish his seed for age after age.

“And his throne will be like the days of heaven.”

The thrones of earthly kings are like the days of earth. The days of heaven are one thing, and the days of earth another. The days of heaven are those years of which it is said, “But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. 102:27).

The days of earth are pressed forward by succeeding days: those that precede are excluded, and those that succeed do not remain. They come in order to go, and almost before they come, they go. Such are the days of earth.

But the days of heaven, those years that do not fail, have neither beginning nor end. No day there is narrowed between yesterday and tomorrow. No one there awaits the future; no one there loses the past. Rather, the days of heaven are always present, and there his throne will be forever.

For what remains, if it pleases you, let us reserve it. The psalm is long, and we still have something to do with you in the name of Christ. [Col. 1131]

Restore your strength, then. I do not mean the strength of your spirit, for I see that in spirit you are tireless, but the strength of the servants of the soul, so that your bodies may endure in their ministry. Refresh yourselves a little, and, refreshed, return to the food. [Note: Three manuscripts have “the senses of the soul”; and shortly afterward, “and return refreshed by food.” The Regius manuscript has “by foods”; that same manuscript and several others add, “Turned toward the Lord.”]

## SERMON II

[Note: Delivered on the same day as the preceding sermon.]

### On the second part of the Psalm

1. Direct your attention to the remaining part of the psalm about which we spoke in the morning, and demand the pious debt—the one who made both us and you will repay it through us.

In the earlier part of the psalm, the Lord Christ was announced on the basis of God’s promise; and in these words that we are about to expound, he is likewise announced. For a little earlier it had been said of him, among other things:

“And I will place him as firstborn, exalted among the kings of the earth. Forever I will preserve my mercy for him, and my covenant will be faithful to him. And I will establish his seed for age after age, and his throne like the days of heaven.”

Concerning these matters, and concerning everything above from the very beginning, we have said what we were able to say.

### 2. [verses 31–35]

It follows:

“If his sons abandon my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their offenses with scourges. But I will not scatter my mercy from him, nor will I harm” [Note: The printed editions add here only “them” or “those”; this is absent from most manuscripts and from the Septuagint. A little earlier, instead of “from him,” manuscript B has “from them,” with the following note: “Perhaps ‘from him’ should be read; this reading he later prefers in his explanation and indicates that it was the common reading.”] “in my truth. Nor will I profane my covenant, and what proceeds from my lips I will not reject.”

What a great foundation of God’s promise! The sons of this David are the sons of the bridegroom; therefore all Christians are called his sons.

God promises much. For he says that if Christians—that is, his sons—abandon his law and do not walk in his judgments; if they profane his statutes and do not keep his commandments, he will not despise them or abandon them to destruction. What, then, will he do? “I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their offenses with scourges.”

It is therefore not only the mercy of the one who calls, but also of the one who strikes and scourges.

Let the father’s hand therefore be upon you; and if you are a good son, do not reject discipline. For what son is there to whom his father does not give discipline? Let him give discipline, provided that he does not remove mercy; let him beat the rebellious, provided that he nevertheless return the inheritance.

If you have rightly understood the father’s promises, do not fear being scourged, but fear being disinherited. For “the Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:5–7).

The sinful son disdains being scourged, while he sees the Only-Begotten scourged though he was without sin.

“I will therefore visit,” he says, “their iniquities with a rod.” The Apostle also threatens in the same way: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Cor. 4:21).

Far be it from pious sons to say, “If you are coming with a rod, do not come.” For it is better to be instructed by the father’s rod than [Col. 1132] to perish under the robber’s caress.

3. “I will visit their iniquities with the rod,” he says, “and their transgressions with scourges. But I will not remove my mercy from him.” From whom? From that David, clearly, to whom I made such promises, whom I anointed with my holy oil above his companions (Ps. 44:8). Do you recognize the one from whom God will not remove his mercy?

Lest someone perhaps anxiously say, “Since he speaks of Christ, from whom he confirms that he will not remove his mercy, what then of the sinner?” For did he say, “I will not remove my mercy from them”? He says, “I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their transgressions with scourges.” You were expecting, for your security, the words, “But I will not remove my mercy from them.” Some manuscripts indeed have this, but the more correct ones do not. Nevertheless, those that have it are not without reason. For how does he not remove his mercy from Christ? Did the Savior of the body himself sin, either on earth or in heaven—he who sits at his right hand and intercedes for us (Rom. 8:34)?

Yet he does not remove it from Christ—from his members, from his body, which is the Church. For he says that he will not remove his mercy from him as something great, as though we did not recognize the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father [Note: [Col. 1132] So the manuscripts; the editions read, “as though we recognize.” A little later they read, “a human being is compared”; on the authority of some manuscripts of the best quality we restore, “a human being is reckoned.”]. For there a human being is not reckoned according to his own person, but there is one person, God and man. Therefore, he does not remove his mercy from him when he does not remove his mercy from his members, from his body, in which Christ himself suffered persecutions on earth even while he was already seated in heaven; and from heaven he cried out, “Saul, Saul,” not “Why do you persecute my servants?”; not “Why do you persecute my saints?”; not “Why do you persecute my disciples?”; but, “Why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4).

Thus, just as, when no one was persecuting him as he sat in heaven, he cried, “Why do you persecute me?” because the head recognized its members and love did not separate the head from the joining of its body, so, when he does not remove his mercy from him, he certainly does not remove it from us, who are his members and his body.

Yet for this reason we must not sin confidently and falsely promise ourselves that, whatever we do, we will not perish. There are, in fact, certain sins and certain iniquities about which it is either impossible for us to discuss and determine anything, or, if it were already possible, it would certainly take too long for the present occasion. No one can say that he is without sin; for if he says so, he will be lying: “For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

Therefore each person is necessarily scourged for his sins; but if he is a Christian, God’s mercy is not removed from him. Clearly, however, if you proceed into such great iniquities that you reject from yourself the rod of the one who strikes, if you reject the hand of the one who scourges, become indignant at God’s discipline, flee from the Father who chastises, and refuse to endure him as Father because he does not spare the sinner, then you have alienated yourself [Note: [Col. 1132] Ferrar Manuscript, “you alienate”; *alienas*.] from the inheritance; he himself has not cast you away. For if you remained under the scourging, you would not remain disinherited.

“But I will not remove my mercy from him,” he says, “nor will I harm him in my truth.” For this reason the mercy of the one who liberates will not be removed: so that the truth of the one who avenges may not cause harm.

### 4.

“And I will not profane my covenant; and the words that proceed from my lips I will not reject.” It is not because his children sin that I will be found a liar: I promised, and I act.

Suppose that they wish to sin even in despair, and to go altogether into sins, so that they offend the eyes of the Father and deserve to be disinherited. Is he not the God of whom it was said, “From these stones he is able to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:9)?

Therefore I say to you, brothers: many Christians sin in a tolerable way; many are corrected from sin by the scourge, amended, and healed; many, altogether turned away and resisting the Father’s discipline with stiff necks, and entirely rejecting God’s fatherhood [Note: [Col. 1133] So the manuscripts. The editions, however, read “inheritance.”], while nevertheless bearing the mark of Christ, proceed into such iniquities that the words must be recited against them: “Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21).

Yet because of them Christ will not remain without an inheritance. The wheat will not perish because of the chaff (Matt. 3:12); nor, because of the bad fish, will nothing from that net be placed in vessels (Matt. 13:47–48). “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19).

For the one who predestined us before we existed made his promise securely: “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:29–31). Let the despairing sin as much as they wish: let the members of Christ answer, “If God is for us, who can be against us?”

Therefore God will not harm in his truth, nor will he profane his covenant. His covenant remains immovable, because, knowing all things beforehand, he predestined heirs for himself; and the words that proceed from his lips he will not reject.

### 5. [Verses 36–38]

Listen for your confirmation; listen for your security, if you recognize that you are among the members of Christ. “Once I swore by my holiness: I will not lie to David. His offspring will remain forever.”

His offspring remains forever, because “the Lord knows those who are his.” “And his throne is like the sun before me, and like the full moon forever; and like a faithful witness in heaven.”

His throne means those over whom he rules, in whom he sits, in whom he reigns. If they are his throne, then they are his members, because our members too are the throne of our head. Consider how all our other members carry the head; but the head itself does not carry something above it. Rather, it is carried by the rest of our members, as though the whole human body were the throne of the head.

Therefore his throne—all in whom God reigns—will be, he says, before me like the sun, because “the righteous will shine in the kingdom of their Father like the sun” [Note: [Col. 1133] Corbie Manuscript, “their own.”] (Matt. 13:43). But this is spiritually, not bodily, as this sun shines from heaven, the sun that he makes rise upon the good and the evil (Matt. 5:45).

Indeed, this sun is before the eyes not only of human beings but also of cattle and the tiniest flies—for what animal, however insignificant, does not see this sun? But what does he say specifically about that other sun? “Like the sun before me.” Not before human beings, not before flesh, not before mortal animals, but “before me.”

“And like the moon”—but what moon? “Full forever.” For even if this moon that we know becomes full, on another day it begins to wane after it has become full. “Like the moon,” he says, “full forever.” Thus his throne will become full like the moon, but a moon full forever.

If the sun, why also the moon? Scripture commonly signifies the mortality of this flesh by the moon, because of its waxing and waning, because of its transitory appearance. Indeed, Jericho is interpreted as “moon”; and someone who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho fell among robbers (Luke 10:30), for he was going down from immortality to mortality.

This flesh, then, is like the moon, which at every time and in every month undergoes waxing and waning. But this flesh of ours will be perfected in the resurrection. “And a faithful witness in heaven.” Thus, if we were perfected in soul alone, he would compare us only to the sun; and if we were perfected in body alone, he would compare us only to the moon. But because God will perfect us both in soul and in body, it is said with reference to the soul, “like the sun before me,” because no one sees the soul except God; and with reference to the body, “like the moon,” now referring to the flesh, perfected forever in the resurrection of the dead. “And a faithful witness in heaven,” because everything that was said about the resurrection of the dead was true.

I beg you, listen to this once again more plainly, and remember it. For I know that some have understood, while others perhaps are still seeking what I have said. There is no point at which the Christian faith is so opposed as in the resurrection of the flesh.

Indeed, the one who was born as a sign against which contradiction would be spoken (Luke 2:34) also raised his own flesh from the dead, so as to confront the one who contradicted. And although he could have healed his members in such a way that it would not appear that they had been wounded, he preserved the scars on his body in order to heal the wound of doubt in the heart.

There is therefore no matter in which the Christian faith is opposed so vehemently, so obstinately, so insistently, and so contentiously as the resurrection of the flesh. Many of the philosophers of the Gentiles have discussed the immortality of the soul at length, and have handed down in numerous and extensive books the claim that the human soul is immortal. But when they come to the resurrection of the flesh, they do not hesitate; they oppose it most openly. Their opposition is such that they say it is impossible for this earthly flesh to ascend into heaven.

Therefore this moon is full forever, and against all who contradict it is a faithful witness in heaven.

### 6. [Verses 39–46]

These promises were made concerning Christ—how certain, how firm, how clear, how beyond doubt they are. For although some things are concealed in mysteries, others are so manifest that the obscure things are very easily opened through them.

Since this is so, see what follows:

> “But you rejected him and brought him to nothing; you delayed your Christ. You overturned the covenant of your servant; you profaned his holiness on the earth. You destroyed all his walls; you made his fortifications a terror. All who passed along the way plundered him; he became a reproach to his neighbors. You exalted the right hand of his enemies; you gladdened all his enemies. You turned away the help of his sword, and you did not assist him in battle. You released him from purification; you struck his throne to the ground [Note: [Col. 1135] So the manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. The editions read, “and you struck his throne to the ground.”]. You shortened the days of his throne; you drenched him with shame.”

What is this? You promised all those things, but you did these contrary things. Where are the promises at which we rejoiced a little earlier, over which we clapped so eagerly, about which we congratulated ourselves in security? It is as though one person had promised and another had overturned.

What is astonishing is that it was not another: “But you”—you who promised, you who confirmed, you who even swore an oath because of human doubt—you promised those things and did these things. Where shall I hold on to your oath? Where shall I find your promise? What is this? Would God really promise falsely, or swear falsely?

Why, then, did he promise those things and do these things? I say that he did these things in order to confirm the promises. But who am I to say this? Let us see whether the truth says it; then what I say will not be empty.

David had been set forth as the one to whom all these things were promised as destined to be fulfilled in his offspring, which is Christ. Therefore, because of the promises spoken to David, people expected them to be fulfilled in David. Accordingly, lest any Christian, saying, “He spoke about Christ,” should hear another say, “No, he spoke about that David,” and go astray by seeing all the promises fulfilled in David, God overthrew them in David. Thus, when you see that those things which must be fulfilled were not fulfilled in him, you seek another in whom they may be shown to be fulfilled.

In the same way, regarding Esau and Jacob, we find the elder worshiped by the younger, although it is written, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23). Thus, when you see that what was said was not fulfilled in those two who came first, you await two peoples in whom what God, who does not lie, deigned to promise may be fulfilled.

“Behold, from your offspring,” God said to David, “I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11). He promised that something from his offspring would remain forever. Then Solomon was born and became so wise that God’s promise concerning David’s offspring was thought to have been fulfilled in him. But Solomon fell, and he made room for hope in Christ. Since God could neither be deceived nor deceive, and since he knew that Solomon would fall, he did not place his promise in him. Instead, after Solomon’s fall, you were to turn your eyes toward God and demand the fulfillment of his promise.

“Then, Lord, have you lied? Will you not fulfill what you promised? Will you not provide what you swore? Perhaps God would have said to you here: ‘I did indeed swear and promise, but this man did not wish to persevere.’

“What then? Lord God, did you not foresee that he would not persevere? Surely you did. Why, then, were you promising me something eternal in one who would not persevere? Did you not say: ‘If they abandon my law, and do not walk in my judgments, and do not keep my commandments, and profane my covenant, nevertheless my promise will remain and my oath will be fulfilled’?

“Once I swore by my holiness”—within, in a certain secret place, at the very fountain from which the prophets drank and then belched forth these words to us—“Once,” he says, “I swore: I will not lie to David.”

Therefore, produce what you swore; give back what you promised. It was taken away from that David so that it would not be awaited in that David. Await, then, what I promised [Note: [Col. 1136] So the manuscripts. The editions read, “what he promised.”].

### 7.

David himself knows this. See what he says: “But you rejected him and brought him to nothing.” Where, then, is what you promised? “You delayed your Christ.”

Although he lists a number of sorrows, in this word he nevertheless restores us: what you promised, O God, remains altogether. For you did not take away your Christ; you delayed him.

Therefore, see what happened to this David, in whom the ignorant expected God to fulfill his promises, so that the promises of God might be fulfilled more firmly in another who was awaited: “You delayed your Christ; you overturned the covenant of your servant.”

Where, indeed, is the old covenant of the Jews? Where is that promised land in which those who inhabited it sinned, and from which, after it was destroyed, they departed? You seek the kingdom of the Jews—it is not there. You seek the altar of the Jews—it is not there. You seek the sacrifice of the Jews—it is not there. You seek the priesthood of the Jews—it is not there.

“You overturned the covenant of your servant; you profaned his holiness on the earth.” You showed that those holy things which they possessed were earthly.

“You destroyed all his walls,” with which you had fortified him. For when would he have been plundered unless the walls had been destroyed? “You made his fortifications a terror.” What does “a terror” mean? It means that it should be said to sinners, “If God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you” (Rom. 11:21).

“All who passed along the way plundered him.” All the Gentiles, plainly, passing along the way—that is, through this life—plundered Israel; they plundered David. First, see his fragments among all the Gentiles, for concerning them it was said, “They shall become portions for foxes” (Ps. 63:11).

Scripture called wicked kings foxes: deceitful and fearful men whom another’s strength terrifies. Therefore, when the Lord was speaking about Herod, who threatened him, he said, “Tell that fox” (Luke 13:32).

The king who fears no human being is not himself a fox: he is the lion from the tribe of Judah, to whom it is said, “You have gone up, lying down; you have slept like a lion” (Gen. 49:9). You went up by your power; you slept by your power, because you wished to, you slept [Note: [Col. 1136] Here the editions add, “because you wished to, you went up”; this is absent from the manuscripts.].

Therefore, in another psalm he says, “I slept.” Was the sentence not complete in the words, “I slept and fell into sleep; and I arose, because the Lord will receive me” (Ps. 3:6)? Why was “I” added? It must be pronounced with great emphasis: “I—I slept.” They raged; they persecuted. But if I had not wished it, I would not have slept. “I slept.”

Therefore, concerning those of whom it had been said, “They shall become portions for foxes,” it is now said, “All who passed along the way plundered him; he became a reproach to his neighbors.”

“You exalted the right hand of his enemies; you gladdened all his enemies.” Consider the Jews, and see that everything foretold was fulfilled.

“You turned away the help of his sword.” How had a few been accustomed to fight and bring down many? “You turned away the help of his sword, and you did not assist him in battle.” Rightly defeated, rightly captured, rightly deprived of his kingdom, rightly scattered: for he lost the land for which he killed the Lord.

“You turned away the help of his sword, and you did not assist him in battle. You released him from purification.”

What does this mean? Among all these evils, this is a great terror. However much God may strike, however angry he may be, however much he may beat and scourge, let him nevertheless scourge the one whom he is cleansing while bound; let him not release him from purification. For if he releases him from purification, then the person no longer has to be cleansed but must be cast away.

From what purification, then, is the Jew released? From faith. For “we live by faith” (Gal. 3:11), and it is said of faith, “cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). And because only faith in Christ cleanses, by not believing in Christ they were released from purification.

“You released him from purification; you struck his throne to the ground.” Rightly, then, you also broke him. “You shortened the days of his throne”: they thought that they would reign forever [Note: [Col. 1137] In the editions this line was repeated here, “You shortened the days of his throne,” but it is absent from the manuscripts.]. “You drenched him with shame.”

All these things happened to the Jews, yet Christ was not taken away but delayed.

### 8. [Verse 47]

Let us see, then, whether God fulfills his promises. After recounting these harsh things as having happened to that people and that kingdom, lest it be thought that God had fulfilled what he promised there and would not give another kingdom in Christ, whose kingdom will have no end, the Prophet addresses him and says:

“How long, O Lord, will you turn away forever?”

Perhaps it does not mean “forever” and “from them,” since “a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel may be saved” (Rom. 11:25). In the meantime, however, “your anger will burn like fire.”

### 9. [Verses 48–49]

“Remember what my substance is.”

This David, placed in the flesh among the Jews and placed in hope in Christ, says, “Remember what my substance is.” For it is not because the Jews failed that my substance failed. For from that people came the Virgin Mary, and from the Virgin Mary came Christ’s flesh—and that flesh was not sinful but the purifier of sinners. “There,” he says, “is my substance.”

“Remember what my substance is.” For the root did not utterly perish. The seed will come to whom the promise was made, “ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. 3:19).

“Remember what my substance is: for you did not establish all the children of human beings in vain.” Behold, all the children of human beings have gone into vanity; yet you did not establish them in vain.

Since all whom you did not establish in vain have gone into vanity, wherefrom would you cleanse them from vanity? Did you preserve nothing for yourself? That which you preserved for yourself, from which you would cleanse human beings of vanity—that holy one of yours—is my substance. From him, he says, all those whom you did not establish in vain are cleansed from their own vanity.

To them it is said, “Children of human beings, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” Perhaps, having become concerned, they would turn away from vanity; they would discover that they had been defiled by vanity and would seek the source of their cleansing. Come to their aid; make them secure.

“And know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful” (Ps. 4:3–4). He made his holy one marvelous; from him he cleansed everyone from vanity. “There,” he says, “is my substance; remember him.” For you did not establish all the children of human beings in vain.

Therefore you preserved something from which they might be cleansed. Who is the one you preserved? “Who is the person who will live and not see death?” Therefore that person who will live and not see death cleanses from vanity. For he did not establish all the children of human beings in vanity, nor can the one who made them disregard those whom he made, so as not to turn them and cleanse them [Note: [Col. 1138] The manuscripts omit the particle “so that”; *ut*.].

### 10.

“Who is the person who will live and not see death?” For, “having risen from the dead, he dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him” (Rom. 6:9).

Indeed, when it is written in another psalm, “You will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10), apostolic teaching takes up this testimony and argues against unbelievers in the Acts of the Apostles, saying:

“Men, brothers, we know that David the patriarch died, and his flesh saw corruption. Therefore it was not said about him, ‘You will not allow your holy one to see corruption’” (Acts 2:27–31).

If, then, it was not said about him, of whom was it said, “Who is the person who will live and not see death”? Perhaps there is no such person. On the contrary: “Who is he?” is said so that you may seek, not so that you may despair.

But perhaps there is some person who will live and not see death, and yet he did not speak of Christ, who died? There is no person at all who will live and not see death except the one who already died for mortals.

To know that he spoke of him, see what follows: “Who is the person who will live and not see death?” Did he therefore never exist in death? He did. How, then, will he live and not see death? “He will deliver his soul from the hands of the underworld.”

Behold: truly and uniquely, he alone will live and not see death; he will deliver his soul from the hands of the underworld. For even if his other faithful followers will rise from the dead and themselves live forever and not see death, they will not themselves deliver their souls from the hands of the underworld.

The one who delivers his soul from the hands of the underworld is himself the one who delivers the souls of his faithful; they cannot deliver themselves. Prove that he himself delivered his soul:

“I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me; for I slept” (Ps. 3:6). But I lay it down of myself, and I take it up again (John 10:17–18), because he is the one who delivers his soul from the hands of the underworld.

### 11. [Verse 50]

But even in the very faith of Christ there was some struggle, and for a long time the enraged Gentiles said, “When will he die, and his name perish?” (Ps. 40:6).

Therefore, for the sake of those who now believe in Christ but who would struggle for some time, the text continues and says:

“Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord?”

We have now recognized Christ as the purifier; we now hold fast to the one in whom you fulfill your promises. Manifest in him what you promised. He is the one who will live and not see death; he is the one who delivers his soul from the hands of the underworld. Yet we are still suffering.

The martyrs said these things, whose anniversaries we celebrate. He will live and not see death; he will deliver his soul from the hands of the underworld; yet, “for your sake we are put to death all day long; we are counted as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 43:22):

“Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord, which you swore to David in your truth?”

### 12. [Verse 51]

“Remember, Lord, the reproach of your servants.”

Now that he was living, now that he was seated at the right hand of the Father in heaven, reproaches were cast at Christians. For a long time Christians bore the charge concerning Christ.

That widow who gives birth and has more children than the woman who had a husband (Isa. 54:1; Gal. 4:27) heard disgrace; she heard reproaches. But the Church, having multiplied and stretching out to the right and to the left, no longer remembers the disgrace of her widowhood.

“Remember, Lord,” with whom there is an abundance of the sweetness of your remembrance; “remember,” do not forget.

What does “remember” mean? “Remember the reproach of your servants, which I held in my bosom from many nations.” I went, he says, to preach, and I heard reproaches and held them in my bosom, because I fulfilled the words, “We are blasphemed, yet we entreat”; “We have become as the refuse of the world, the scum of all” (1 Cor. 4:13).

For a long time Christians held reproaches in their bosom, in their hearts, and did not dare to resist those who abused them. Earlier, it seemed a crime to answer a pagan; now it is a crime to remain a pagan.

Thanks be to the Lord: he remembered our reproaches. He exalted the horn of his Christ; he made him marvelous among the kings of the earth. Now no one insults Christians—or, if someone does insult them, he does not do so publicly. He speaks in such a way [Note: [Col. 1139] The editions read, “so that he speaks evil.” The word “evil” is absent from the better manuscripts.] that he fears being heard more than he wishes to be believed.

“Which I held in my bosom from many nations.”

### 13. [Verse 52]

“What your enemies reproached, O Lord”—both Jews and pagans.

“What they reproached”: what did they reproach? “The change of your Christ.” This is what they reproached: the change of your Christ. For they objected that Christ had died, that Christ had been crucified.

“What are you objecting, you madmen?” Although now no one objects, if any still remain, why do you object that Christ died? He was not destroyed but changed. He is called dead because of the three days.

Behold what your enemies reproached—not the loss, not the destruction, but plainly “the change of your Christ.” He was changed from temporal life to eternal life; he was changed from the Jews to the Gentiles; he was also changed from earth to heaven.

Let your vain enemies go now and continue to reproach the change of your Christ. Would that they too might be changed; then they would not reproach the change of Christ.

But Christ’s change displeases them because they do not wish to be changed. For there is no change for them, and “they did not fear God” (Ps. 54:20).

“What your enemies reproached: the change of your Christ.”

### 14. [Verse 53]

They reproached him for his change; but what do you say?

“The blessing of the Lord is forever”—let it be so, let it be so [Note: [Col. 1139] Lovaniensis only in this place: “Blessed is the Lord.” Erasmus: “But the blessing of the Lord.” The better manuscripts consistently read: “The blessing of the Lord.”].

We give thanks for his mercy; we give thanks for his grace [Note: [Col. 1139] So most manuscripts. The editions read, “What else can I say but, Thanks be to his grace?”]. For we give thanks; we do not give, repay, return, or requite anything. We give thanks in words; in reality, we hold fast [Note: [Col. 1140] So the manuscripts of the best quality. Others read, “nor do we requite thanks, but give thanks only in words,” and so forth. The Lovaniensis edition reads, “nor do we requite grace; if we give thanks only in words”; shortly afterward, where the manuscripts read “we hold fast in reality,” it has, with Erasmus, “we repay.”].

He himself freely saved us; he himself did not take account of our ungodliness [Note: [Col. 1140] The particle “not” was absent from the editions and is found here only in the Regius Manuscript.]. He himself sought us when we were not seeking him, found us, redeemed us, and freed us from the dominion of the devil and the power of demons. He bound us so that we might be cleansed by faith; from that bondage he releases those enemies who do not believe and therefore cannot be cleansed.

Let those who remain say every day whatever they wish; day by day fewer and fewer of them will remain. Let them object, mock, and reproach—not the destruction, but the change of your Christ.

Do they not see that, when they say these things, they are failing either by not believing or by dying [Note: [Col. 1140] The editions read, “or by not believing.” The particle “not” is absent from the manuscripts and should be absent.]? Their curse is temporary, but “the blessing of the Lord is forever.”

And to confirm the blessing, so that no one may fear: “Let it be so, let it be so.” This is God’s signature of security.

Therefore, secure in his promises, let us believe what has passed, recognize what is present, and hope for what is future. May the enemy not turn us away from the way, so that the one who gathers us like his own chicks under his wings may shelter us; may we not wander from beneath his wings, lest the aerial hawk snatch away the chicks who are still featherless.

For a Christian must not hope in himself. If he wishes to be firm, let him be nourished by maternal warmth. She is the hen gathering her chicks, concerning whom reproach is directed at that unfaithful city, Jerusalem:

“How often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you did not wish it! Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:37–38).

Hence it was said, “You made his fortifications a terror.” Since they did not wish to be covered beneath the wings of this hen, and gave us such an example that we should fear the unclean aerial spirits who daily seek something to snatch away, let us enter beneath the wings of this divine Wisdom, because for the sake of her chicks she was weakened even unto death.

Let us love the Lord our God; let us love his Church: him as Father, her as Mother; him as Lord, her as his handmaid, because we are children of his handmaid. But this marriage is joined together by great love: no one offends one and wins the favor of the other.

Let no one say, “I do go to idols, I consult those possessed by spirits and sorcerers; but I do not abandon the Church of God—I am a Catholic.” By holding on to the mother, you have offended the Father.

Another says, “Far be it from me: I do not consult a sorcerer, I do not seek one possessed by spirits, I do not seek sacrilegious divinations, I do not go to worship demons, I do not serve stones; but I am nevertheless in the party of Donatus.”

What does it profit you that the Father is not offended, when he avenges the mother’s offense? What does it profit you if you confess the Lord, honor God, proclaim him, acknowledge his Son, and confess that he sits at the right hand of the Father, yet blaspheme his Church?

Do the examples of human marriage not correct you? If you had some patron whom you served every day, whose threshold you wore down by your service, whom you daily—not merely greeted but also worshiped—and to whom you offered faithful attentions, if you spoke one accusation against his wife, would you enter his house?

Therefore, beloved, hold fast: all of you with one accord, hold fast to God as Father and to the Church as Mother.

Celebrate the anniversaries of the saints with sobriety, so that we may imitate those who went before us and so that they may rejoice over you, they who pray for you; so that the blessing of the Lord may remain upon you forever: let it be so, let it be so.

# Exposition of Psalm 89

### 1. [Verse 1]

This psalm is prefaced with the title, “A prayer of Moses, the man of God.” Through this man of his, God gave the Law to his people; through the same man of his, he liberated them from the house of slavery and led them through the wilderness for forty years.

Moses was therefore a minister of the Old Covenant and a prophet of the New Covenant. For all those things happened to them in figure, as the Apostle says: “They were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11).

According to this dispensation, then, which was carried out through Moses, this psalm must be examined, since it received its title from his prayer.

### 2.

“Lord,” he says, “you have become our refuge from generation to generation”—whether in every generation or in two generations, the old and the new. For, as I said, Moses was a minister of the Covenant belonging to the old generation and a prophet of the Covenant belonging to the new generation.

The guarantor and bridegroom of the marriage that he received from that generation, Jesus himself, says: “If you believed Moses, you would also believe me, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46).

For we must not believe that this psalm was written altogether by Moses himself, since it is not contained in any of his writings, in which his songs are recorded. Rather, for the sake of some symbolic significance, the name of so great a servant of God was attached, so that the attention of the reader or hearer might be directed.

“You have therefore become our refuge,” he says, “from generation to generation.”

### 3. [verse 2]

But what kind of refuge he became—since he began to be for us what he had not previously been, namely, a refuge, though he himself did not come into existence only when he became a refuge for us—the text continues: “Before the mountains were made, and the earth and the world were formed, and from age to age, you are.” [Col. 1141; several manuscripts: “and from age and unto age,” etc.] You, therefore, who always are, and who existed before we existed and before the world existed, became a refuge for us when we turned toward you.

It does not seem to me that the words “Before the mountains were made, and the earth was formed” are to be understood in an ordinary way—or, as other manuscripts have it, using the word translated from a single Greek term, “was fashioned.” Mountains are, of course, the higher parts of the earth. And certainly, if God existed before the earth was formed, and the earth was formed by him, what great thing is said about mountains or any other parts of it, since God existed not only before the earth but also before heaven and earth, and before every bodily and spiritual creature? [Col. 1142]

Rather, perhaps the entire rational creation is distinguished by this difference, so that the heights of the angels are signified by the name “mountains,” and the lowliness of human beings by the name “earth.” Therefore, although everything that has been created may appropriately be called either made or formed, nevertheless, if these words have any precise distinction, the angels were made. When they are counted among his heavenly works, the enumeration is concluded in this way: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 148:5). But in order that human beings might be formed according to the body, the earth was fashioned. Scripture uses this word when we read either, “God fashioned,” or, “God formed man from the dust of the earth” (Genesis 2:7).

Therefore, before those things were made that are the highest and greatest in your creation—for what is greater than the rational heavenly creation?—and before the earth was fashioned, so that there might be one who would acknowledge and praise you on earth; and this is still not enough, because these things began either in time or together with time: “from age to age, you are.” More suitably this would be said, “From eternity to eternity.” For God is not “from an age,” since he existed before the ages; nor is he “unto an age” whose end comes, since he is without end.

But because of the ambiguity of the Greek word, it often happens in Scripture that the Latin translator renders either *age* (*saeculum*) for *eternity*, or *eternity* for *age*. Most appropriately, however, he does not say, “From age to age you were, and unto age you will be,” but uses a verb expressing the present, making known that God’s substance is altogether unchangeable. In him there is no “was” and “will be,” but only “is.” Hence it was said: “I am who I am,” and, “He who is has sent me to you” (Exodus 3:14); and, “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 102:27–28).

Behold the eternity that has become a refuge for us: remaining in it, we flee to it from this mutability of time.

### 4. [verse 3]

But since, while we are here, we live amid great and many temptations, and must fear being turned away from this refuge, let us consider what the prayer of the man of God asks next:

“Do not turn man toward lowliness”—that is, do not let man, turned away from your eternal and exalted things, desire temporal things and set his mind on earthly matters. He asks God for what God himself has commanded, using an entirely similar sentence to that in which we say in the prayer, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13).

Finally, he adds here: “And you said, ‘Return, children of men.’” It is as though he were saying: “I ask of you what you yourself commanded,” giving glory to his grace, so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31). Without his help, by the choice of our will, we cannot overcome the temptations of this life.

“Do not turn man,” he says, “toward lowliness”; and yet you said, “Return, children of men.” But grant what you commanded, by hearing the prayer of the one who asks and assisting the faith of the one who wills.

### 5. [verse 4]

“For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed.” Therefore we ought to turn from things that pass away and slip by to your refuge, where you are without any mutability. [Col. 1143] However long a period may be desired for this life, a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed—not even like tomorrow, which is still to come. Thus everything enclosed by the end of time must be regarded as already past.

Hence the Apostle also directed his intention away from the things that are behind, forgetting them—by which all temporal things are to be understood—and stretched it toward the things that are ahead (Philippians 3:13), which is the desire for eternal things.

But lest some suppose that God reckons a thousand years as one day in the sense that God has days of such length, he added, “And like a watch in the night,” since a watch lasts no longer than three hours. [Most manuscripts: “a watch,” singular.] He said this to diminish the apparent length of time.

Nevertheless, human beings have dared to presume knowledge of the times. To disciples who wished to know them, the Lord said: “It is not for you to know the times which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1:7). Yet they have defined this age as six thousand years, as though it could end after six days.

They did not consider that it was said, “Like one day, which has passed.” For when this was said, not merely a thousand years had passed. [Erasmus, Venice, and Louvain: “And that [fact] ought especially to have warned them.”] And the words “like a watch in the night” ought especially to have warned them not to be mocked by the uncertainty of the times. [Erasmus and Venice: “be enclosed”; manuscript reading: “be mocked.”] For just as they seem to have devised something plausible from the six days because of the first six days in which God completed his works, so they cannot adjust six watches—that is, eighteen hours—to their speculation.

### 6. [verses 5, 6]

Then this man of God—or rather, the prophetic spirit—seems in a certain way to recite the law of God written in his hidden wisdom, in which he established a limit for the course of sinful mortal life and the distress of mortality, when he says:

“Those things that are considered nothing will be their years. In the morning, like grass, let him pass away; in the morning let him bloom and pass away; in the evening let him fall, grow hard, and wither.”

The prosperity of the heirs of the Old Testament, which they sought from the Lord their God as a great good, deserved to receive this law in his hidden providence, which Moses appears to recite: “Those things that are considered nothing will be their years.”

Things are considered nothing because before they come they do not yet exist; when they have come, they will no longer exist.
