They do not come in order to be present, but in order not to be. “In the morning”—that is, beforehand—“like grass, let him pass away; in the morning let him bloom and pass away; in the evening”—that is, afterward—“let him fall, grow hard, and wither.” Let him fall, certainly, in death; grow hard, in the corpse; wither, in dust. [Col. 1144]

What is this, unless flesh, in which there is the condemned desire of carnal beings? “All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isaiah 40:6, 8).

### 7. [verse 7]

Without concealing that this punishment came from sin, he immediately added:

“For we have failed in your anger, and in your indignation we have been troubled.”

“We have failed,” in weakness; “we have been troubled,” by fear of death. We have become weak, and we tremble at the prospect of bringing our weakness to an end.

“Another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:18)—although by martyrdom one is not to be punished but crowned. [Several manuscripts: “a martyr, not to be punished but crowned”; editions: “by martyrdom, not to be punished but crowned.”]

The soul of the Lord himself, transforming us into himself, was “sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38), since the Lord’s departure is only through death (Psalm 67:21).

### 8. [verse 8]

“You have set our iniquities before your sight”—that is, you have not pretended not to see them.

“Our age in the illumination of your countenance”—“you have set” is understood. By “the illumination of your countenance” he has said what he earlier expressed as “before your sight,” and by “our age” what he earlier expressed as “our iniquities.”

### 9. [verses 9, 10]

“For all our days have failed, and in your anger we have failed.”

These words sufficiently show that this mortality is punitive. He says that the days have failed, either because human beings fail within them by loving what passes away, or because the days have been reduced to a small number. He appears to explain this in what follows:

“Our years were meditating like a spider.”

*The editions read* “will meditate.” It should be read, with some manuscripts, “were meditating,” in accordance with the Septuagint, *emeletōn*; for what follows he explains with verbs not in the future tense but in the past imperfect, “we were laboring, we were weaving.” The subsequent explanation uses not future-tense verbs but the imperfect: “we were laboring, we were weaving.”

“The days of our years are seventy years; but if there is strength, eighty years; and more than this is their labor and sorrow.”

These words seem to express the brevity and misery of this life, since in our time even those who have lived seventy years are called long-lived. Up to eighty they seem to retain some strength; but if they live beyond this, they live amid multiplied labor and sorrows.

Many, however, even within seventy years, endure an extremely weak and miserable old age; [the Regius manuscript reads “before”; perhaps “within” is to be read.] and it has often been shown that old people remain remarkably vigorous beyond eighty years.

It is better, therefore, to search for something spiritual in these numbers. For God’s anger toward the sons of Adam—through whom sin entered the world by one man, and death through sin, and thus death passed to all human beings (Romans 5:12)—is not greater because they live much shorter lives than the ancients did. The length of their lives was mocked when a thousand years were compared with yesterday and with three hours. And certainly they lived for a long time when they provoked God’s anger up to the flood in which they perished.

### 10

Seventy and eighty years make one hundred and fifty. That this is a sacred number is sufficiently indicated by this book of Psalms.

The number one hundred and fifty has the same significance as fifteen, since fifteen is formed by joining seven and eight. The first signifies the Old Testament because of the observance of the Sabbath; the second signifies the New Testament because of the Lord’s resurrection.

Hence there are fifteen steps in the temple; hence there are fifteen Songs of Ascents in the Psalms; hence the waters of the flood rose fifteen cubits above the highest mountains (Genesis 7:20); and this number is commended as sacred in various other passages as well.

Therefore he says: “Our years were meditating like a spider.” We labor amid corruptible things; we were weaving corruptible works, which, according to the prophet Isaiah, covered us not at all (Isaiah 59:6). [Col. 1145]

“The days of our years are seventy years; but if there is strength, eighty years.”

There is a difference between “in them” and “in strength.” “In them,” that is, in the years or days themselves, refers to what is understood in temporal matters. The number is seventy because temporal things appear to be promised in the Old Testament.

But if the years are not understood as years themselves, but as strength—that is, not in temporal matters but in eternal things—then the number is eighty. The New Testament exists in the hope of renewal and resurrection unto eternity.

“And more than this is their labor and sorrow”: whoever transgresses this faith and seeks something more finds labors and sorrows.

The passage can also be understood in this way: although we have been established in the New Testament, which the number eighty signifies, this life of ours has even more labor and sorrow while we groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption, the redemption of our body. “For we have been saved in hope; and what we do not yet see, we await with patience” (Romans 8:23–25).

This too belongs to the mercy of God. Hence the text continues and says: “For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be corrected.”

“The Lord corrects the one whom he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6). He also gives certain great men a thorn in the flesh, by which they are buffeted lest they become exalted by the greatness of their revelations, so that power may be perfected in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7, 9).

Some manuscripts do not have “we shall be corrected” but “we shall be instructed,” which refers to the same gentleness. No one can be instructed without labor and sorrow, because power is perfected in weakness.

### 11. [verses 11, 12]

“Who knows the power of your anger, and in accordance with your fear can reckon your anger?”

“It belongs to very few people,” he says, “to know the power of your anger.” For toward most people you are angry even when you spare them, in such a way that the labor and sorrow by which you correct and instruct those whom you love may be understood to belong not to anger but rather to your gentleness, lest they be tormented by eternal punishments.

As it is read in another psalm: “The sinner has provoked the Lord; according to the greatness of his anger he will not inquire” (Psalm 10:4).

Who, then, knows—that is, how many can be found who know—the power of your anger, and who can reckon your anger in accordance with your fear? Here too “who knows” is understood.

How difficult it is to find someone who knows how to reckon your anger according to your fear, so that he also understands that this belongs to it: that you seem to spare some people against whom you are more angry, allowing the sinner to prosper in his way and to receive greater punishments at the end.

Human anger, once it has killed the body, has no further power to act. God, however, has power both to punish here and, after the death of the body, to cast into Gehenna (Matthew 10:28).

Only a few instructed people understand that the prosperous happiness of the wicked is a greater form of God’s anger—empty and deceptive. The man whose feet almost slipped did not know this when he was jealous of sinners and looked upon the peace of the wicked. But he learned it when he entered the sanctuary of God and understood their end (Psalm 73:2–3, 17). Few enter there, so that they may learn, through fear of God, to reckon his anger and to count the prosperity of evil people among their punishments.

### 12

“Make your right hand known in this way.”

The Greek manuscripts have this more fully; some Latin manuscripts read, “Make your right hand known to me.”

What does “Make your right hand known in this way” mean, unless it refers to your Christ, of whom it was said, “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1) Make him known in such a way that your faithful may learn through him to ask and hope for those rewards of faith that do not appear in the Old Testament but are revealed in the New.

Let them not suppose that the happiness of earthly and temporal goods should be regarded as great, desired, or loved; let them not be disturbed when they see such happiness among those who do not worship you, and let their steps not be poured out into ruin because they do not know how to reckon your anger.

Accordingly, in keeping with the prayer of his man, he made his Christ known in such a way that, through his own sufferings, he showed that it is not the gifts that appear to be proclaimed in the Old Testament—where there are shadows of future things—but eternal gifts that must be desired.

In this sense, God’s right hand can also be understood as that by which he will separate his righteous from the wicked. It too is rightly made known in this way, when he scourges every son whom he receives and, by greater anger, does not permit him to prosper in his sins, but scourges him with his left hand in gentleness, so that, once corrected, he may place him at his right hand (Matthew 25:32–33). [Col. 1146; editions read “his left hand”; several manuscripts “the left”; some “with his left hand.”]

The reading found in many manuscripts, “Make your right hand known to me,” can refer to either matter, whether to Christ or to eternal blessedness. For God has a right hand no more in the form of a body than he has an anger disturbed by turbulent emotions.

### 13

As for what follows, “And those bound in heart by wisdom,” some manuscripts do not have “those bound” but “those instructed.” The Greek word sounds almost the same in both meanings, differing slightly in one syllable.

But when those are instructed in wisdom who “insert their foot into its fetters,” as it is written (Sirach 6:25)—not the foot of the body, but the foot of the heart—and, bound by its golden chains as it were, do not stray from the way of God or become fugitives from him, whichever reading is adopted, the truth of the meaning remains intact.

For God made those bound, or instructed, in heart by wisdom known in the New Testament in such a way that, for the sake of the faith which the impiety of Jews and Gentiles detested, they disregarded everything. They allowed themselves to be deprived of the things that those who judge carnally consider great promises in the Old Testament.

### 14. [verse 13]

Since they were made known in this way—so that they disregarded those things and, through their sufferings, bore witness to the eternal things that should be desired (hence they were called witnesses; for in Greek they are called *martyrs*)—they endured many and very great temporal evils, bitter and grievous.

The man of God observed this, as did the prophetic spirit represented under the name of Moses, and he said:

“Return, Lord; how long? And be entreatable toward your servants.” [Col. 1147]

This is their voice, or the voice spoken on their behalf, as they endure many evils while this age persecutes them, and are made known as those bound in heart by wisdom, so that even when compelled by such great evils they do not flee from the Lord to the good things of this age.

In accordance with what is written elsewhere, “How long do you turn your face away from me?” (Psalm 13:1), this too is said: “Return, Lord; how long?”

And so that those who attribute a very carnal human bodily form to God may know [the editions add “while thinking carnally,” absent from the manuscripts] that the turning away and turning back of his face do not occur through a movement like the movements of our bodies, let them recall the earlier words of this same psalm:

“You have set our iniquities before your sight; our age in the illumination of your countenance.”

How, then, does he say here, “Return,” so that he may be merciful, as though he had turned his face away in anger, when there he presents him as angry in such a way that he has not turned his face away from the iniquities and age of those with whom he is angry, but rather has set them before his sight and in the illumination of his countenance?

The word “how long” is the language of praying righteousness, not the impatient language of indignation.

The expression used here, “be entreatable,” has been translated by others word for word as “entreat.” But the one who says “be entreatable” avoids ambiguity, because *to entreat* is a common verb: both the one who pours out a plea and the one to whom it is poured out may be said to entreat. We say, “I entreat you,” and “I entreat from you.”

### 15. [verses 14, 15]

Then, anticipating future goods in hope and reckoning them as though they had already come to pass, he says:

“We have been filled in the morning with your mercy.”

Thus, amid these labors and sorrows that are like the darkness of night, prophecy has been kindled for us like a lamp in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts (2 Peter 1:19).

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Then the righteous will be filled with that good for which they now hunger and thirst (Matthew 5:8, 6), while they walk by faith and are pilgrims away from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:6).

Hence it is also said, “You will fill me with joy in your presence” (Psalm 16:11). “In the morning they will stand and contemplate” (Psalm 5:5); and, as other translators have said, “We have been satisfied in the morning with your mercy.” Then they will be satisfied, just as he says elsewhere: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm 17:15).

Hence it is said, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us”; and the Lord himself says, “I will show myself to him” (John 14:8, 21). Until this happens, nothing good is enough for us, nor ought it to be enough, lest our desire remain on the way. It must be stretched forth until it arrives.

“We have been filled in the morning with your mercy; and we have rejoiced and been glad in all our days.” [Many manuscripts: “and have taken delight.”]

That day is a day without end. All those days exist together; therefore they satisfy. They do not yield to successive days, since there is nothing there that, by not yet coming, is not yet present, and by coming, is no longer present. They all exist together because the one who stands and does not pass away is one. This is eternity.

These are the days of which it is said: “Who is the person who desires life and loves to see good days?” (Psalm 34:13). These days are also called years elsewhere, where it is said to God: “You are the same, and your years will not fail.”

They are not years that are considered nothing, nor days that have declined like a shadow (Psalm 102:28, 12). Rather, they are days that truly are. Their number was prayed to be made known by the one who said: “Make known to me, Lord, my end”—the end at which I may arrive, remain, and seek nothing further—“and the number of my days, what it is.” He says “what it is,” certainly, not what is not.

For those days, of which he says immediately elsewhere, “Behold, you have made my days old” (Psalm 39:5–6), do not truly exist because they do not stand or remain. They pass by in the swiftest mutability; not even one hour in them can be found in which we are so situated that one part of it has not already passed and another is not still to come, with no part standing still in existence.

But those years and days do not fail in which we too shall not fail, but shall be renewed without failing.

Let our soul burn with desire for those days; let it thirst for them ardently and intensely, so that there we may be filled and satisfied, and there say what we proclaim here:

“We have been satisfied in the morning with your mercy; and we have rejoiced and been glad in all our days.”

“We have rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, for the years in which we saw evils.”

### 16. [verse 16]

But now, amid days that are still evil, let us say what follows:

“And look upon your servants and upon your works.”

Your servants themselves are your works, not merely in that they are human beings, but also in that they are your servants, that is, obedient to your commands.

We are his workmanship—not only in Adam, but also created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them (Ephesians 2:10). For it is God who works in us both to will and to work, according to his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

“And direct their children,” so that they may be upright in heart, for God is good to those who are upright in heart.

God is good to Israel—but to those who are upright in heart. Not like the man whose feet were disturbed, because, when he looked upon the peace of sinners, God began to displease him, as though God were ignorant of these things, as though he did not care about them, and were neglecting the governance of the human race (Psalm 73:1–14). [Col. 1148; most manuscripts: “and neglecting human generation.”]

### 17. [verse 17]

“And let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us.”

Hence it is said: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, Lord” (Psalm 4:7).

“And direct the works of our hands for us,” so that we do not perform them in exchange for the reward of earthly things. For then they are not straight but crooked.

Many manuscripts end this psalm here. But in some there is another final verse: “And direct the work of our hands.” Careful and learned readers mark this verse with a star, which they call an asterisk. By this they indicate things that are found in the Hebrew or in other Greek translators but are not present in the Septuagint translation.

If we wish to explain this verse, it seems to me to have this meaning: all our good works are one work, the work of charity. “The fullness of the Law is charity” (Romans 13:10).

In the preceding verse, after saying, “And direct the works of our hands for us,” the final verse does not say “works” but “work”: “Direct the work of our hands.” It is as though, in the final verse, he wished to show that these works are one work, that is, that they are directed toward one work.

Our works are straight when they are directed toward this one end. “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5). [Col. 1149]

There is therefore one work in which all things are contained: faith working through love (Galatians 5:6). Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent” (John 6:29).

Since in this psalm the old life and the new life, mortal life and life that truly lives, the years that are considered nothing and the days that possess the fullness of mercy and true joy—that is, the punishment of the first man and the kingdom of the second—are sufficiently and clearly distinguished, I believe that the name of Moses, the man of God, was inscribed in its title so that those who piously and rightly search the Scriptures might understand that the law of God, administered through Moses, also contains beneath its veil something like what this psalm reveals.

In the Old Testament, God appears to promise, for good works, solely or almost solely the rewards of earthly goods. But when someone passes over to Christ, the veil is removed (2 Corinthians 3:16), and his eyes are opened so that he may contemplate the wonders of God’s law, by the gift of him to whom we say: “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Psalm 119:18).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 90

### SERMON I

### 1

This is the psalm concerning which the devil dared to tempt our Lord Jesus Christ. Let us therefore listen to it, so that, instructed, we may resist the tempter—not presuming upon ourselves, but upon the one who was tempted first, so that we would not be overcome in temptation.

Temptation was not necessary for him. Christ’s temptation is our instruction.

If we attend to what he answered the devil, so that we too may answer the same when the devil tempts us in a similar way, we enter through the door, as you heard in the Gospel reading. What does it mean to enter through the door? To enter through Christ. For he himself said: “I am the door” (John 10:7).

What does it mean to enter through Christ? To imitate Christ’s ways.

In what are we to imitate Christ’s ways? In the majesty by which he was God in the flesh? Does he exhort us to this, or demand from us that we perform miracles such as he himself performed?

Indeed, does not our Lord Jesus Christ even now, and always with the Father, govern the whole world? Does he call a human being to imitate him by governing heaven and earth with him, and all that is in them? Or does he call us to be creators ourselves, through whom all things may come to be, as all things came to be through Christ?

God our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, does not invite you to those works that he performed from the beginning, of which it is written, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3), nor to those which he performed on earth.

He does not say to you, “You will not be my disciple unless you walk upon the sea” (Matthew 14:25), or unless you raise a dead man who has been four days in the tomb (John 11:38–44), or unless you open the eyes of one born blind (John 9:1–7).

Nor does he say this. What, then, does it mean to enter through the door?

“Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

You must observe in him what he became for your sake, so that you may imitate it.

He performed miracles even before he was born of Mary. For who ever performed such things except the one of whom it is said, “He alone does great wonders” (Psalm 72:18)?

Through Christ’s power, those who came before him were also able to perform certain things. By the power of Christ, Elijah raised a dead man (1 Kings 17:22).

Or perhaps Peter is greater than Christ, because Christ raised a sick man by his voice (John 5:5–9), whereas, when Peter passed by, the sick were carried out so that his shadow might touch them (Acts 5:15). Is Peter, then, more powerful than Christ? What utterly foolish person would say this?

Why, then, was there such power in Peter? Because Christ was in Peter.

That is why he said: “All who came are thieves and robbers” (John 10:8)—that is, those who came of their own accord, who were not sent by me; those who came without me, in whom I was not, whom I did not introduce.

Therefore, whatever miracles were performed, whether by those who came before or those who came afterward, the same Lord performed them—the one who also performed them through his presence.

He does not exhort you even to those miracles, which he himself performed before he became human. To what, then, does he exhort you? To imitate what he could not have done unless he had become human.

Could he have endured sufferings unless he were human? Could he have died, been crucified, or humbled himself unless he were human?

So, when you suffer the troubles of this age, which the devil brings about either openly through human beings or secretly, as in the case of Job, be strong and patient. [Some editions read “if”; two manuscripts: “as Job most courageously endures”; one manuscript: “you will dwell.”] Dwell “in the help of the Most High,” as this psalm says. [Col. 1150] For if you withdraw from the help of the Most High, unable to help yourself, you will fall.

### 2

Many are strong when they suffer persecution from human beings and see them openly raging against them. They think that they imitate Christ’s sufferings when people openly persecute them. But when they are struck by the devil’s hidden persecution, they think that Christ does not crown them.

Do not be afraid when you imitate Christ. When the devil tempted the Lord, no human being was in the wilderness. He tempted him secretly, but he was overcome; and when he raged openly, he was overcome (Matthew 4:1–11).

Do the same if you wish to enter through the door, when the enemy tempts secretly, when he seeks to harm a person through bodily troubles, fevers, illnesses, or various physical labors, as he afflicted Job.

Job did not see the devil, but he understood God’s authority. He knew that the devil could do nothing against him unless permitted by the one whose authority is supreme. He gave all glory to God and did not grant power to the devil.

When the devil took everything away, Job said: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.” He did not say, “The Lord gave, and the devil has taken away,” because the devil would have taken nothing away unless the Lord had permitted it.

The Lord permitted it so that the human being might be tested and the devil overcome.

When the devil struck Job with a plague, the Lord permitted this too. Even when, from head to foot, he flowed with the corruption of worms, Job still attributed no power to the devil. [Manuscripts of better authority: “into the corruption of worms.”] [Col. 1151]

But when Job’s wife—the only person the devil had left him, not as a comforter for her husband but as his own assistant—suggested to him, “Say something against God, and die,” he answered her:

“You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:9–10).

### 3. [verses 1, 2]

The one who imitates Christ in this way—enduring all the troubles of this age, placing his hope in God, so that he is neither captured by enticement nor broken by fear—is the one who dwells in the help of the Most High and abides under the protection of the God of heaven.

You heard the psalm and sang it, for this is how the psalm begins.

When we come to the verses with which the devil tempted the Lord, you will recognize them, for they are familiar.

He says to the Lord: “You are my protector and my refuge, my God.”

Who says this to the Lord? The one who dwells in the help of the Most High.

Who is the one who dwells in the help of the Most High? The one who does not dwell in his own help.

Who is the one who dwells in the help of the Most High? The one who is not proud, unlike those who ate in order to become like gods and lost what they had been made to be: immortal human beings.

They wished to dwell in their own help, not in the help of the Most High. Therefore they listened to the serpent’s suggestion and despised God’s command. They discovered that what God had threatened had happened to them, not what the devil had promised (Genesis 3).

### 4. [vers. 3.]

Therefore you too say, “I will hope in him,” for he himself will rescue me—not I myself. See whether he teaches anything else than that all our hope should not be in ourselves, should not be in man. From what will he rescue you? From the snare of hunters and from an harsh word.

To be rescued from the snare of hunters is a great thing; but from an harsh word—what great thing is that? Many have fallen into the hunters’ snare through an harsh word. What do I mean? The devil and his angels stretch out snares; like hunters, they set traps. People who walk in Christ walk far from those very snares. He does not dare set a snare in Christ; he places it beside the way, not on the way. Let Christ be your way, and you will not fall into the devil’s snare. For one who wanders from the way, the snare is already there.

On this side and on that he places nooses; on this side and on that he places a snare: you walk among the nooses. But do you wish to walk safely? Do not turn aside to the right or to the left. Let him who was made your way be your way [Note: [Col. 1151] Here the editors add, “for you,” which is absent from the manuscripts], so that he may lead you to himself through himself; and you will not fear the hunters’ snares.

But what does “from an harsh word” mean? Through an harsh word the devil has sent many into the snare. For example, those who have wished to be Christians among pagans suffer the insults of pagans. They are ashamed among their insulters, and by withdrawing from the way because of the harsh word they fall into the hunters’ snares.

And what harm will an harsh word do to you? Nothing. Surely the snare into which the enemy drives you through an harsh word will do you no harm? Nets are often stretched for birds toward the head of a hedge, and stones are thrown into the hedge. Those stones will do the birds no harm. When does the one who throws a stone into the hedge strike the bird? Yet the bird, frightened by the empty sound, falls into the nets. So people, afraid of the vain and empty words of their insulters and ashamed of superfluous reproaches, fall into the hunters’ snares and are taken captive by the devil.

But why do I not say, brothers, what must not be left unsaid—what God compels me to say? However you receive this, God compels me to say it; and if I do not say it, I myself fall into the hunters’ snares. For if I fear people’s criticisms and therefore do not speak, I myself—who warn you not to fear people’s words—fall through an harsh word into the hunters’ snares.

What, then, am I going to say? Just as a Christian among pagans hears harsh words from pagans and, if he is ashamed of them, falls into the hunters’ snare, so among Christians those who wish to be more diligent and better will hear insults from Christians themselves.

And what benefit is it, brother, that you sometimes find a city where there is no pagan? No one there insults a Christian for being a Christian, because no pagan is found there. But there are many Christians living badly. Among them, someone who wishes to live well—to be sober among drunkards, chaste among fornicators, and to worship God sincerely among those who consult astrologers, seeking nothing of that kind; someone who refuses to go anywhere except to church among spectators of foolish theatrical shows [Note: [Col. 1152] Another manuscript from Corbie reads, “of theatrical frivolities”]—suffers insults from those very Christians and endures harsh words. They say, “What a great man you are! You are righteous; you are Elijah; you are Peter; you have come down from heaven.” They are mocking him. Wherever he turns, he hears an harsh word from this side and that.

But if he fears and withdraws from Christ’s way, he falls into the hunters’ snares. How, then, when such words are heard, does one not withdraw from the way? What does it mean not to withdraw from the way? When he hears harsh words, where is he to find consolation for himself, so that he does not care about the harsh words, does not withdraw from the way, and enters through the door?

Let him say: “What sort of words am I hearing, a servant, a sinner? My Lord heard: ‘You have a demon’” (John 8:48). You have just heard an harsh word spoken against the Lord. It was not necessary for the Lord to hear this, but he warned you concerning harsh words, so that you would not fall into the hunters’ snares.

### 5. [vers. 4.]

“He will overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings you will hope.” This means that your protection must not come from yourself, nor should you think that you can protect yourself. He will protect you in order to rescue you, and he will rescue you from the hunters’ snare and from an harsh word.

“He will overshadow you with his shoulders.” You may understand this both of the back and of the breast. For the shoulders are around the head. But since he says, “Under his wings you will hope,” it is clear that the protection of outspread wings causes you to be between God’s shoulders, so that God’s wings place you in the midst, on this side and on that. You will not fear that anyone may harm you; only do not withdraw from the place to which no enemy dares approach.

If a hen protects her chicks beneath her wings, how much safer will you be under God’s wings, both against the devil and against his angels—those aerial powers that fly around like hawks, seeking to carry off a weak chick?

For the comparison of the hen with the Wisdom of God was not made without reason. Christ himself, our Lord and Savior, spoke of himself as a hen: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling” (Matthew 23:37). That Jerusalem was unwilling; let us be willing. It was carried away by the aerial powers because, fleeing the hen’s wings, it presumed upon its own strength, although it was weak. Let us, confessing our weakness, flee beneath God’s wings. For he will be like a hen protecting her chicks.

The name “hen” is not insulting. Consider the other birds, brothers. Many birds lay eggs before us and warm their chicks, but no bird becomes so weakened with its chicks as a hen does. Let Your Charity consider this. We see swallows, sparrows [Note: [Col. 1153] The manuscripts read “geese”], and storks outside their nests, and we do not know whether they have offspring. But we recognize a hen in the weakness of her voice and the loosening of her feathers. She is wholly transformed by affection for her chicks: because they are weak, she makes herself weak.

Therefore, because we too were weak, the Wisdom of God made itself weak. For “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), so that we might hope under his wings.

### 6. [vers. 5–6.]

“His truth will surround you like a shield.” The wings are the shield; that is, the wings are not literally wings, nor is the shield literally a shield. If either of these were meant literally, could wings be a shield, or a shield be wings? But because all these things can be spoken figuratively through comparisons, they could therefore be both wings and a shield.

If Christ were literally a stone, he would not be a lion; and if he were a lion, he would not be a lamb. Therefore he is called both a lion (Revelation 5:5), a lamb (John 1:29), a stone (Acts 4:10–11), and a calf, and whatever else of this kind is said of him—not because he is a stone, a lion, a lamb, or a calf, but because he is Jesus Christ, the Savior of all. These are comparisons, not literal properties.

“His truth,” he says, “will surround you.” His truth is like a shield, so that it does not mingle those who hope in themselves with those who hope in God.

One person is a sinner, and another is a sinner. But consider a sinner who presumes upon himself, despises and does not confess his sins, and says, “If my sins displeased God, he would not allow me to live.” Another did not dare lift his eyes, but beat his breast, saying, “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13).

Both are sinners: but one mocks, while the other weeps; one despises, while the other confesses his sins. The truth of God, which shows no partiality, distinguishes the repentant from the one who defends himself, the humble from the proud, and the one who presumes upon himself from the one who presumes upon God.

Therefore his truth will surround you like a shield.

### 7.

“You will not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the business that walks in darkness, the ruin and the noonday demon.”

The two things he said above correspond to the two things he said below: “You will not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying by day”; and, in relation to the terror by night, “the business that walks in darkness”; and, in relation to the arrow flying by day, “the ruin and the noonday demon.”

What is to be feared at night, and what during the day? When someone sins in ignorance, he sins as though in the night; when someone sins knowingly, he sins as though in the day. The first two are therefore the lighter dangers; the dangers repeated afterward are the more serious.

Pay attention, so that, if the Lord grants it, this may be explained to you carefully. It is obscure, and there will be great profit if you understand it. He called the temptation that occurs among the ignorant, because it is lighter, “the terror by night”; and the temptation that occurs among those who know, because it is lighter, “the arrow flying by day.”

What are the lighter temptations? Those that do not press or drive so forcefully that they compel a person, but can be avoided and pass quickly. Now make the same temptations serious.

If a persecutor presses upon and greatly terrifies those who are ignorant—that is, those not yet firm in faith and unaware that they are Christians in order to hope for the future life—then, when they begin to be terrified by temporal evils, they think that Christ has abandoned them and that they are Christians without reason. For, as I have said, they do not know that they are Christians in order to overcome present things and hope for future things. The business that walks in darkness finds them and seizes them.

There are others, however, who know that they have been called to future hope; for what God promised us is not of this earth, nor of this life. All these temptations must be endured so that we may receive and obtain what God promised us for eternity. They know this. But when the persecutor begins to press more violently, acting through threats, punishments, and tortures, sometimes they yield; and, although they know, they fall as though in the day.

### 8.

Why “at noon”? Because the persecution burns intensely: he called the greater heat “noon.” Let Your Charity attend while I prove this from the Scriptures.

When the Lord spoke of the sower—how he went out to sow, and some seed fell on the way, some on rocky ground, and some among thorns—he graciously explained the parable himself. When he came to the rocky ground, he said: “These are those who hear the word and rejoice in the word for a time; and when tribulation occurs because of the word, they are immediately scandalized.” For what had he said about what fell on the rocky ground? “When the sun rose,” he said, “they were scorched, because they had no deep root” (Matthew 13:3–23).

These, then, are those who rejoice in the word for a time; and when persecution occurs because of the word, they wither. Why do they wither? Because they had no firm root. What is the root? Charity. For the Apostle says, “rooted and founded in charity” (Ephesians 3:17). Just as greed is the root of all evils (1 Timothy 6:10), so charity is the root of all good things.

You know this, and it has often been said. But why did I wish to recall it? So that you may understand the Psalm: the noonday demon is mentioned because of the heat of intense persecution.

For the Lord says: “The sun rose, and the grass withered, because it had no root.” And, explaining to us what it means for the grass to wither from the sun, he said that when persecution occurred they did not remain [Note: [Col. 1154] Here the editors add “in the faith,” which is absent from most manuscripts], because they had no deep root.

Here we rightly understand the noonday demon as intense persecution. Let Your Charity attend while I recall what that persecution was like at one time, from which the Lord deigned to deliver his Church.

First, the emperors and kings of this world thought that they could remove the name of Christ and the name of Christians from the earth by persecuting them. They ordered that anyone who confessed himself a Christian should be struck. Whoever did not wish to be struck denied that he was a Christian, knowing what evil he was doing; the arrow flying by day reached him.

But whoever did not care about the present life and confidently hoped for the future life avoided the arrow flying by day and confessed himself a Christian. Struck in the flesh, he was freed in the spirit; he began to await, placed with God in rest, even the redemption of his body in the resurrection of the dead. He escaped that temptation, the arrow flying by day.

Thus the command was: “Whoever confesses himself a Christian shall be struck.” That was the arrow flying by day. What faithful person would not avoid it by the speed of death [Note: [Col. 1155] Lov. reads “would avoid the speed”; Er. reads “would not avoid the speed.” The better manuscripts read “would not avoid it by the speed,” namely, the arrow flying by day]?

But the later command was: “If he confesses himself a Christian, he shall not be killed; he shall be tortured until he denies it. If he denies it, he shall be released.” That was the noonday demon.

Many, therefore, without denying Christ, failed under the tortures; for they were tortured until they denied him. But if they persevered in not denying Christ, what would the sword accomplish by killing the body with a single stroke and sending the soul to God? Long tortures did the same. Yet who could finally be found who would endure such great and prolonged agonies?

Many failed. And I believe that those who failed were those who presumed upon themselves, who did not dwell in the help of the Most High and in the protection of the God of heaven, who did not say to the Lord, “You are my protector,” who did not hope under the shadow of his wings, but relied too greatly upon their own strength.

They were cast down by God so that he might show them that he himself protects, he himself regulates temptations, and he permits only as much to come upon a person as the one to whom it comes can bear.

### 9. [vers. 7.]

Many, therefore, fell because of the noonday demon. Do you wish to know how many? What follows says: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; but it shall not come near you.”

To whom is this said, brothers, if not to the Lord Jesus Christ? The Lord Jesus is not only in himself, but also in us. Recall those words: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). When no one was touching him personally, he said, “Why are you persecuting me?” Did he not count himself among us? When he said, “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40), did he not count himself among us? For the members are not divided from one another—the head and the body.

What are the head and the body? The Savior and the Church.

How, then, is it said, “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand”? They will fall because of the noonday demon. Great is the terror of falling at Christ’s side, falling at Christ’s right hand.

How will they fall at his side? Why are some at his side and others at his right hand? Why a thousand at his side and ten thousand at his right hand? What does “a thousand at his side” mean? It means that there are fewer thousands than the ten thousand who will fall at his right hand.

Who are these? It will now become clear in the name of Christ; it will now be revealed.

Christ promised some that they would judge with him—namely, the Apostles, who left everything and followed him. Peter said to him, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.” And he promised them this: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:27–28).

Do not think that the Lord promised this to them alone. For where will the Apostle Paul sit, who labored more than all of them (1 Corinthians 15:10), if only twelve are to sit there? He is the thirteenth. Judas fell from the twelve, and Matthias was appointed in the place of Judas the betrayer; we read this in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1:15–26). The twelve thrones were filled.

Will the one who labored more than all of them not sit there? Or are the twelve thrones the perfection of the tribunal [Note: [Col. 1156] Hence the Master, *Sentences* IV, distinction 47, chapter “But not”: “The perfection of the tribunal—that is, the universality of those judging—is understood, namely, all the perfect who, having left everything, followed Christ”]? For thousands will sit upon the twelve thrones.

“But how do you prove to me,” someone says, “that Paul too will be among the judges?” Hear him saying: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Corinthians 6:3). “We shall judge,” he says. And he himself did not hesitate, in the confidence of his belief, to count himself among those who will judge with Christ [Note: The manuscripts read thus. The editors read, “because he believed that he himself would be counted among them”].

Those, then, who will judge with Christ are the leaders of the Church; they are the perfect. To such he said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor.” What does “Do you wish to be perfect?” mean? “Do you wish to judge with me and not be judged?” The man went away sorrowful (Matthew 19:21–22). But many did this, and many are doing it. Therefore these will judge with him.

But many promise themselves that they will judge with Christ because they leave all they possess and follow Christ, yet they presume upon themselves; they have a certain swelling and pride that God alone can know. They cannot avoid the noonday demon—that is, the fall caused by the burning heat of excessive persecution.

Many such people existed at that time. They had distributed all their possessions to the poor and already promised themselves that they would sit with Christ and judge the nations. When the heat of persecution burned like the noonday demon, they failed under the tortures and denied Christ.

These are the ones who fell at his side: although they expected to sit with Christ in judgment over the world, they fell.

### 10.

Now I shall say who fall at the right hand. You know that when the tribunal itself appears, where those who wished to be and truly were perfect will judge with Christ the Lord—those rooted and founded in charity, so that they would not wither from the sun and the noonday demon—the Lord says: “All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. He will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left; and they will be judged.”

Many will judge, but they will be fewer than those who will stand before the tribunal, because the former are like a thousand, while the latter are like ten thousand.

What will he say to those placed at the right? “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me.”

It is clear that he will say this to those who have the resources of this world with which to perform these human acts. Yet they too will reign with those others. For the former are like soldiers, the latter like provincials supplying provisions [Note: [Col. 1157] Compare *Tractate 122 on John*, no. 3, where he calls preachers of the Gospel “soldiers of Christ,” and the faithful from whom they receive their due support “provincials of Christ”]. Nevertheless, under one emperor, both soldier and provincial are in the kingdom.

The soldier is brave; the provincial is devoted. The brave soldier fights against the devil with prayers; the devoted provincial supplies provisions to the soldiers.

Let Your Charity understand. At the end those placed at the right will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

At that time, when the sun of persecution and the noonday demon had burned fiercely, there were many who promised themselves that they would judge with Christ. They could not endure the heat of persecution and fell at his side.

There were others who did not promise themselves seats among the judges, but through almsgiving promised themselves a place at the right hand. To them Christ would say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

And because many fell from that hope of judging, while many—and far more—fell from that hope of the right hand, therefore it was said to Christ: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.”

And because many will be with him who cared nothing for all those things, and with whom Christ is one as with his members, he says: “But it shall not come near you.”

Did he say this only to the head—that it would not come near? Certainly not. Nor did he say it only to Peter, or to Paul, or to all the Apostles, or to all the martyrs who did not fail under the tortures.

How, then, did it not come near them, when they were tortured in this way? The torture came near the flesh, but it did not reach the place of faith. Thus their faith was far removed from the terror of their torturers.

Let them torture; the terror will not come near. Let them torture, but the martyrs will mock the torture, trusting in the one who first conquered so that the others might conquer.

And who are those who conquer, if not those who did not presume upon themselves?

Let Your Charity attend. For this reason he said all the preceding things: “He will say to the Lord, ‘You are my protector and my refuge,’” and, “I will hope in him, for he himself will rescue me from the hunters’ snare.” He himself will rescue me, not I myself.

“He will overshadow you with his shoulders.” But when? When you hope under his wings.

“His truth will surround you like a shield.” Therefore, because you have presumed upon him and placed all your hope in him, what follows?

“You will not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the business that walks in darkness, the ruin and the noonday demon.”

Who will not fear? The one who presumes not upon himself but upon Christ.

But those who presume upon themselves—even if they already hoped for Christ’s side, as though they would judge; even if they already hoped to be at Christ’s right hand, as though he would say to them, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”—when the noonday demon came, that is, the burning heat of persecution, terrifying them violently, many fell from their hope of the judicial seat. Of these it was said, “A thousand shall fall at your side.” And many fell from their hope of reward for their services; of these it was said, “And ten thousand at your right hand.”

“But it shall not come near you”—that is, to the head and the body. Ruin and the noonday demon will not come near, “for the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19).

### 11. [vers. 8.]

“Nevertheless, with your eyes you will look on and see the recompense of sinners.”

What does this mean? Why “nevertheless”? Because the wicked were permitted to rage against your servants; the wicked were permitted to persecute your servants. Will it therefore go unpunished for the wicked that they persecuted your servants? It will not go unpunished.

Although you permitted it, and although your servants were thereby more greatly crowned, “nevertheless, with your eyes you will look on and see the recompense of sinners.” The evil they intended, not the good that was done through their ignorance, will be repaid to them.

For now we need the eyes of faith, and we need to see that they are exalted for a time but will weep forever. Those who are temporarily given power over God’s servants will be told: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:32–41).

But if someone has eyes, as he says, “With your eyes you will look on,” it is no small thing to see the wicked flourishing in this world and to have eyes fixed upon him, so that by faith you may consider what he will suffer at the end if he does not correct himself. For those who wish to thunder now will afterward be struck by lightning.

“Nevertheless, with your eyes you will look on and see the recompense of sinners.”

### 12. [vers. 9.]

“Because you are, Lord, my hope.”

Now he comes to the reason why one does not fall because of ruin and the noonday demon: “Because you are, Lord, my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.”

What does it mean that your refuge is in the heights? Many make God their refuge in such a way that they may flee from the heats of temporal things. God’s refuge is in the heights; it is very deeply hidden, a place to which you may flee from the coming wrath.

“Within, you have made the Most High your refuge. Evil will not approach you, and the scourge will not draw near your dwelling. For he has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will lift you up in their hands, lest you ever strike your foot against a stone.”

These are the words that the devil spoke to the Lord Jesus Christ when he tempted him. But because they need to be considered more carefully, and so that we do not weary you, let us postpone this until tomorrow—for tomorrow too a sermon is owed you [Note: [Col. 1158] So read the better and most manuscripts. Some others, with the editors, read: “for tomorrow too, if the Lord wills, a sermon on this will be owed you”—so that we may begin again from this point of the Psalm, out of consideration for your weariness. When we wish to finish obscure matters, let us not rush them and thereby prevent them from reaching your understanding.

## SERMON II

### 1.

As I do not doubt that Your Charity remembers—those of you who attended yesterday’s sermon—the Psalm we had begun to explain was prevented by the shortness of time from reaching its conclusion, and part of it was deferred until today. Those of you who were here yesterday, remember this; those who were not here, learn it.

For this reason we had the Gospel reading recited—the passage in which the Lord was tempted through the words of the Psalm that you heard here (Matthew 4:6). Christ was tempted so that the Christian would not be conquered by the tempter.

That teacher in all things wished to be tempted because we are tempted; just as he wished to die because we die, and wished to rise again because we shall rise again. Those things that he displayed in the human being who was made human for our sake, although he was God through whom we were made, he displayed for our sake.

We have often commended to Your Charity something that we are not tired of repeating: since perhaps many of you cannot read, either because you have no leisure to read or because you do not know letters, let them at least, through constant hearing, not forget their saving faith.

Certainly, by repeating these things we may seem troublesome to some, provided that we build up others. For we know that many possess strong memories and are devoted to divine reading, and already know what we are going to say; perhaps they want us to say things they do not know. But if they are quicker, let them observe that they are walking the way with those who are slower.

When two companions walk along the same road, one more quickly and the other more slowly, it is within the power of the quicker to walk with the slower, not within the power of the slower. For if the quicker wishes to go as fast as he can, the slower cannot follow him. It is therefore necessary for the quicker to restrain his speed and not abandon his slower companion.

This, then, is what I said I had often said, and now say again. As the Apostle says, “To write the same things to you is not burdensome for me, but is safe for you” (Philippians 3:1).

Our Lord Jesus Christ is like a wholly perfect man, both head and body. In him we recognize the head in that man who was born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, rose again, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and from there we await him as judge of the living and the dead. This is the head of the Church (Ephesians 5:23).

The Church is the body of this head—not only the Church that is here, but the Church that is here and throughout the whole world; not only the Church of this time, but the entire people of the saints, belonging to one city, from righteous Abel himself to those who will be born, believe in Christ, and exist until the end. This city is the body of Christ, and Christ is its head.

The angels too are our fellow citizens there. But because we are exiles, we labor; they, however, await our arrival in the city.

And from that city from which we are exiles, letters have come to us. These are the Scriptures, which exhort us to live well. Why do I say that letters have come? The King himself descended and became our way in our exile, so that by walking in him we may neither go astray nor fail, neither fall among robbers nor rush into the snares placed beside the way.

Knowing Christ, then, as the whole and complete Christ together with the Church, while he alone, born of the Virgin, is the head of the Church—the mediator, that is, between God and human beings, Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5)—let us understand that he is mediator in order to reconcile to himself those who had withdrawn. For a mediator is only between two parties.

We had withdrawn from the majesty of God and had offended him by our sin. The Son, the mediator, was sent so that by his blood he might loose our sins, by which we were separated from God, and, being placed between us, restore and reconcile us to the one from whom we had turned away and in whose grip we were held by our sins and transgressions.

He is our head. He is God, equal to the Father, the Word of God through whom all things were made (John 1:3): God in order that we might be created, man in order that we might be recreated [Note: [Col. 1160] The manuscripts read, “God in order that we might be created, man in order that we might be recreated”]; God in order that he might make, man in order that he might restore.

Looking to him, let us hear the Psalm in this way. Let Your Charity attend. This is the discipline and teaching of this school, useful to you not for understanding one Psalm only, but many, if you retain this rule.

Sometimes a Psalm—not only a Psalm, but every prophecy—speaks of Christ in such a way that it commends the head alone; sometimes it proceeds from the head to the body, that is, to the Church, without seeming to have changed the speaker. For the head is not separated from the body, but he speaks as though of one person.

Let Your Charity see what I mean. The Psalm in which the Lord’s Passion is described is certainly clear to everyone: “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my garment they cast lots.” Even when the Jews hear this, they are ashamed, for the prophecy concerning the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ was proclaimed with the utmost clarity.

Yet our Lord Jesus Christ had no sins, and nevertheless at the beginning of that Psalm he says: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? The words of my sins are far from my salvation” (Psalm 21:17–19, 2).

You see, then, what is said in the person of the head and what in the person of the body. The sins belong to us; the Passion endured for us belongs to the head. But because of his Passion for us, our sins are forgiven [Note: [Col. 1160] Am. and the manuscripts read thus. Er. and Lov. read, “he pays the debt of sins”].

So also in this Psalm.

## 2. [Verses 1–8]

We discussed these verses yesterday; let us recall them briefly. “He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide under the protection of the God of heaven.” In these verses we commended this to Your Charity: let no one place his hope in himself, but let him place all his hope in Him, in whom our strength lies; for we conquer through His help, not through our own presumption.

God therefore protects us if we say to the Lord what follows: “You are my protector and my refuge, my God; I will hope in Him, for He Himself will rescue me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word.” We said that many who fear the harsh word fall into the hunters’ snare. A man is mocked because he is a Christian; he regrets having become a Christian, and because of the harsh word he falls into the devil’s snare. A man is also mocked because he lives better than many Christians; and, fearing the harsh words of those who mock him, he falls into the devil’s traps, so that he is no longer wheat on the threshing floor but follows the chaff.

[Col. 1161] But he who hopes in God is rescued from the hunters’ snare and from the harsh word. How does God protect you? “He will overshadow you between His shoulders”—that is, He will place you before His breast, so that He may protect you with His wings; provided that you recognize your weakness, so that, like a feeble chick, you flee beneath the mother’s wings lest you be carried off by a kite.

For kites are the aerial powers, the devil and his angels: they want to carry off our weakness. Let us flee beneath the wings of Mother Wisdom, since Wisdom itself was made weak for our sake, because “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). Just as a hen becomes weak with her chicks in order to protect them with her wings (Matthew 23:37), so our Lord Jesus Christ, who, “though He was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped,” in order to be made weak with us, “emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in appearance as a man” (Philippians 2:6–7).

“And under His wings you will hope.” “His truth will surround you with a shield; you will not fear the terror of night.” The temptations of ignorance are the terror of night; sins committed knowingly are the arrow flying by day: for night signifies ignorance, and day manifestation. Some sin in ignorance; others sin knowingly. Those who sin in ignorance are overthrown by the terror of night; those who sin knowingly are struck by the arrow flying by day.

When these things occur amid more severe persecutions, until one reaches what is like midday, whoever falls from that heat will fall as though from the noonday demon. Many have fallen from that heat, as we already explained to Your Charity yesterday. For when persecution was raging, it was said: “Let Christians be tortured until they deny that they are Christians.” Formerly they were beaten after confessing; afterward they were tortured so that they would deny. And while every accused person is tortured until he denies, the Christians’ confession was tortured, while their denial was released.

There was then a great heat among the persecutors. Whoever fell in that temptation fell as though from the noonday demon. And how many fell! Many who had hoped to sit with the Lord and judge fell from His side. Likewise, many who had hoped to be at His right hand—among the holy people who serve Him like provincials providing provisions for soldiers, to whom it will be said, “I was hungry and you gave Me food” (for many will be at the right hand)—fell from that hope; and more fell from there, because there are more there. For fewer are those who will judge with the Lord, while more will stand before Him; but their condition will not be the same. Some will be at the left, others at the right; some to reign, others to be punished; some to hear, “Come, blessed of My Father, receive the kingdom,” others to hear, “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:32–41).

Therefore those who will fall from the ruin and the noonday demon will be “a thousand at your side and ten thousand at your right hand.” [Note: At “who,” Er., Ven., and Lov. omit “who.” M.] “But it will not approach you.” What does this mean? The noonday demon does not throw you down. Is it surprising if it does not throw down the Head? Yet it does not throw down those who cling to the Head in the manner of which the Apostle says, “The Lord knows those who are His” (2 Timothy 2:19).

[Col. 1162] For some are so predestined that the Lord knows who belong to His body. Since that temptation will not approach them in order to throw them down, they are understood in what is written: “But it will not approach you.” Yet lest those sinners who were permitted to inflict such things upon Christians be noticed by certain weak people, and someone say, “See what God wanted: that so much should be permitted to the impious and criminal against the servants of God,” consider for a little while with your eyes—with the eyes of faith—and you will see the punishment of sinners at the end, to whom so much is now permitted so that you may be tested. For what follows is this: “Nevertheless, with your eyes you will look on and see the repayment of sinners.”

## 3. [Verses 9–12]

“Because you, Lord, are my hope, you have made the Most High your refuge. Evil will not approach you.” He says to the Lord: “Because you, Lord, are my hope, you have made the Most High your refuge. Evil will not approach you, and the scourge will not come near your dwelling.”

Then come the words you heard, spoken by the devil: “For He has commanded His angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone.”

To whom does he say this? To whom did he say, “Because you, Lord, are my hope”? I suppose it need not be explained to Christians who the Lord is. If they understand the Father as God, how will angels lift Him up in their hands so that He does not strike His foot against a stone?

You see, then, that Christ the Lord, while speaking about the body, suddenly began to speak about the Head. Our Head is designated here when it is said: “Because you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.” You made the Most High your refuge because you are the Lord, my hope.

What does this mean? Let Your Charity attend: “Because you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.” It is no longer surprising. For this follows precisely because you have made the Most High your refuge: “Evil will not approach you,” and “the scourge will not come near your dwelling,” because you have made the Most High your refuge.

Yet we do not read in the Gospel that angels carried the Lord anywhere so that He would not strike His foot against a stone; nevertheless, we understand it. These things have already happened, and they were not prophesied without reason, except because they were going to happen. We cannot say, “Christ will come later, so that He may not strike His foot against a stone”; for He will come to judge. Where, then, was this fulfilled? Let Your Charity attend.

## 4.

First, hear these verses: “Because you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.” The human race knew that a human being could die, but did not know that he could rise again; therefore it had what it feared, but did not have what it could hope for. Thus, so that He who established the fear of death for the sake of discipline might give hope of resurrection for the reward of future eternal life, our Lord Jesus Christ rose first.

He died after many; He rose before all. In dying He suffered what many had already suffered; in rising He did what no one had done before Him. When will the Church receive this, except at the end? The Head has gone before in what the members hope for.

[Col. 1163] For Your Charity knows how they speak among themselves. Let the Church therefore say to her Lord Jesus Christ; let the body say to its Head: “Because you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.” That is: “You therefore rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, so that, ascending, you might set your refuge on high and become my hope. I was despairing on earth and did not believe that I would rise; now I believe, because my Head has ascended into heaven. Where the Head has gone before, the members will follow.”

I think it is now clear what was said: “Because you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.” I shall express it more plainly. So that I might have the hope of resurrection, which I did not have, you rose first, so that I might hope to follow you where you have gone before. It is the voice of the Church to her Lord; it is the voice of the body to its Head.

## 5.

Do not be surprised, then: “Evil will not approach you, and the scourge will not come near your dwelling.” The dwelling of God is flesh. The Word dwelt in flesh, and flesh became a dwelling for God. In that dwelling the Emperor fought for us; in that dwelling He was tempted by the enemy, so that the soldier would not fail.

And because He displayed that flesh to our eyes, because our eyes rejoice in this light and delight in this visible brightness, because He placed His flesh in manifestation so that all might see it, therefore the psalm says, “He placed His dwelling in the sun.” What does “in the sun” mean? In the open, in manifestation, in earthly light—that is, in the light which pours over the earth from heaven. There He placed His dwelling.

But how would He place His dwelling there unless He came forth like a bridegroom from His bridal chamber? For this follows: “He placed His dwelling in the sun.” And as though He were asked, “How?” it says: “And He Himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from His bridal chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run His course” (Psalm 18:6).

The dwelling is the bride herself. The Word is the bridegroom, the flesh is the bride, and the bridal chamber is the virgin’s womb. And what does the Apostle say? “The two shall become one flesh. This is a great sacrament; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5:31–32). And what does the Lord Himself say in the Gospel? “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6). From two, one; from the Word and flesh, one human being, one God.

His dwelling felt the scourges on earth; it is clear that the Lord was scourged (Matthew 27:26). Does it feel the scourges in heaven? [Note: At “feel,” Er., Ven., and Lov. read “felt.” M.] Certainly not. [Note: In B the word “Certainly not” is absent; Er., Ven., and Lov. transmit it. M.] Why? Because He made the Most High His refuge, so that He might be our hope; and evil will not approach Him, nor will the scourge come near His dwelling.

He is far above all the heavens, but He has feet on earth: the Head is in heaven, the body on earth. When His feet were being scourged and trampled by Saul, the Head cried out: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?” (Acts 9:4). Behold, no one persecutes the Head; behold, the Head is in heaven, because “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over Him” (Romans 6:9): “Evil will not approach you, and the scourge will not come near your dwelling.”

[Col. 1164] But let us not think that the Head has been separated from the body. They are separated in place, but joined in affection; that very union of affection cried out from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?” He cast him down by the voice that reproved him and raised him up by the right hand that showed mercy. The one who was persecuting Christ’s body became a member of Christ, so that he might himself suffer there what he was doing.

## 6.

What, then, brothers, was said about our Head? “Because you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge. Evil will not approach you, and the scourge will not come near your dwelling.” These things have been said.

“He has commanded His angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.” You heard this just now when the Gospel was read (Matthew 4:1–11). Attend carefully.

The Lord was baptized and fasted. Why was He baptized? So that we would not disdain baptism. For when John himself said to the Lord, “You come to me to be baptized, and I ought to be baptized by you,” and the Lord replied, “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:14–15), He wished to fulfill humility, so that the One who had no uncleanness might be cleansed.

Why this? Because of the pride of those who would come later. For sometimes there is a catechumen who perhaps surpasses many of the faithful in teaching and conduct. He observes many baptized people who are ignorant, and many who do not live as he does—not with such self-restraint, not with such chastity. He himself no longer seeks a wife, and sometimes sees a faithful man who, though he does not commit fornication, nevertheless uses his wife immoderately. He may raise the neck of pride and say: “Why do I now need to be baptized, in order to receive what this man has, when I already surpass him in life and teaching?”

To such a person the Lord says: “What have you surpassed? How far have you surpassed him? As far as I have surpassed you? A servant is not above his master, nor a disciple above his teacher. It is enough for the servant to be like his master, and for the disciple to be like his teacher” (Matthew 10:24–25). Do not become proud and refuse to seek baptism. You seek the Lord’s baptism; I sought the servant’s.

The Lord was therefore baptized, and after His baptism He was tempted. He fasted forty days in a mystery, as I have often recalled to you. Everything cannot be said at one time, lest necessary occasions be taken up. After forty days He became hungry.

He could also have never become hungry; but how would He be tempted? Or if He did not overcome the tempter, how would you learn to fight the tempter? He became hungry, and then the tempter said: “Tell these stones to become loaves, if you are the Son of God.”

What great thing would it have been for the Lord Jesus Christ to make bread from stones, when He satisfied so many thousands with five loaves (Matthew 14:17–21)? He made bread from nothing. For the great quantity of food that satisfied so many thousands—from where did it come? There were sources of bread in the Lord’s hands. [Note: The editions read “sources of loaves,” and shortly afterward “from five loaves, many loaves.” But Reg. and Remig., manuscripts of good quality, read “sources of bread,” and below, with other manuscripts, “much bread.” M.]

It is not surprising. He Himself made much bread from five loaves, enough to satisfy so many thousands, just as every day He makes immense harvests on earth from a few grains. These are the Lord’s miracles; but they have become cheap through constant repetition.

What, then, [Col. 1165] brothers, was it impossible for the Lord to make loaves from stones? He made human beings from stones, as John the Baptist himself said: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3:9). Why, then, did He not do it? To teach you how to answer the tempter, so that if perhaps you are placed in some difficulty and the tempter suggests to you, “If you were a Christian and belonged to Christ, would He now abandon you? Would He not have sent you help?”—you may know how to respond.

Perhaps the physician is still cutting, and for that reason he abandons you? But he does not abandon you. How did he fail to hear Paul precisely because he heard him? For Paul says that he was not heard concerning the thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan by whom he said he was beaten. “For this I besought the Lord three times, that He might take it away from me; and He said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).

It is as though someone were to say to a physician, after an ointment had perhaps been applied: “This plaster troubles me; I beg you, remove it.” And the physician replies: “No; it must remain there for a long time, for you cannot otherwise be healed.” The physician did not hear the sick man according to his wish, because he heard him according to his health.

Therefore be strong, brothers. When you are tested by some deprivation, while God chastises and instructs you—He who both prepares and preserves an eternal inheritance for you—let the devil not suggest to you: “If you were righteous, would He not send you bread by a raven, as He sent it to Elijah?” (1 Kings 17:6). Where is what you have read: “I have never seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread” (Psalm 36:25)?

You answer the devil: “Scripture speaks truly: ‘I have never seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread.’ For I have my bread, which you do not know.” What bread? Hear the Lord: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.”

Do you think the Word of God is bread? [Note: So the manuscripts. The editions read, “Do you think that the Word of God is not bread?”] If the Word through whom all things were made were not bread, He would not say, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41). You have therefore learned what to answer the tempter in the distress of hunger.

## 7.

What if he tempts you in such a way as to say: “If you were a Christian, you would perform miracles, as many Christians have done”? Deceived by the evil suggestion, you might tempt the Lord your God and say to our Lord God: “If I am a Christian, and I am before Your eyes, and You count me among Your people, let me also do something like the many things Your saints have done.”

You have tempted God, as though you were not a Christian if you did not do this. Many who desired such things have fallen. That magician Simon desired such things from the Apostles and wanted to purchase the Holy Spirit with money (Acts 8:18–19). He loved the power of miracles but did not love the imitation of humility.

Therefore, when a certain disciple, or someone from the crowd, wanted to follow the Lord, watching the miracles He performed, the Lord saw that he was proud and was seeking not the way of humility but the arrogance of power. He said: “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head” (Matthew 8:20).

Foxes have dens in you; the birds of heaven have nests in you. The fox is deceit; the birds of heaven are pride. Just as birds seek high places, so do the proud; and just as foxes have deceitful caves, so do all [Col. 1166] plotters.

What, then, did the Lord answer? Pride and deceit may dwell in you, but Christ has nowhere in you to dwell, nowhere to lay His head. For the laying down of the head is Christ’s humility. Unless He had laid down His head, you would not have been justified.

The disciples also desired such things, wishing already to seek [Note: Am., Er., the manuscripts, and Lov. read “to appear.”] the throne of the kingdom before taking the way of humility, when their mother requested on their behalf: “Command that one sit at Your right hand and the other at Your left.” They were seeking power; but through the suffering of humility [Note: Two manuscripts read “patience.”] one comes to the power of the kingdom.

The Lord said: “Can you drink the cup which I am going to drink?” (Matthew 20:21–22). Why do you consider the height of the kingdom and not imitate My humility?

What, then, if he tempts you in this way: “Perform miracles”? So that you do not tempt God, what should you answer? What the Lord answered.

The devil said to Him: “Throw Yourself down, for it is written, ‘He has commanded His angels concerning You, and they will lift You up in their hands, lest You strike Your foot against a stone.’ If You throw Yourself down, the angels will receive You.”

It could indeed have happened, brothers, that if the Lord had thrown Himself down, the angels would have rendered service to the Lord’s flesh. But what did He say to him? “Again it is written, ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’”

“You think I am merely a human being.” For the devil approached for this purpose: to test whether He Himself was the Son of God. He saw the flesh, but divinity was manifest in His works. The angels had borne witness. He saw a mortal being and tempted Him, so that, when Christ was tempted, the Christian might be instructed.
