What, then, is written? “You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” Therefore let us not tempt the Lord by saying: “If we belong to You, let us perform a miracle.”

## 8.

Let us return to the words of the psalm. “He has commanded His angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone.”

Christ was lifted up in the hands of angels when He was taken up into heaven—not because, if the angels had not carried Him, He would have fallen, but because they were rendering service to the King.

Do not say: “Those who carried Him are better than the One who was carried.” Are animals, then, better than human beings? But since animals carry human weakness, we should not say this either; for if the animals withdraw themselves, those who sit on them fall.

How should we speak? For it is also said of God: “Heaven is My throne” (Isaiah 66:1; Acts 7:49). Since heaven carries Him and God sits upon it, is heaven therefore better? In the same way we can understand the angels’ service in this psalm. It does not pertain to the Lord’s weakness, but to their honor and their service. [Note: Am., Er., and the manuscripts read “their”; Lov. reads “His.”]

Why did the Lord Jesus Christ rise? Hear the Apostle: “He died for our sins and rose for our justification” (Romans 4:25). Likewise, the Gospel speaks of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39).

What is Jesus’ glorification? He rose and ascended into heaven. Glorified by God through His ascension into heaven, He sent His Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost.

In [Col. 1167] the Law, in the book of Moses called Exodus, fifty days are counted from the day on which the lamb was killed and eaten; and the Law was given, written on tablets of stone by the finger of God (Exodus 12:19 and following).

What the finger of God is, the Gospel explains to us: the finger of God is the Holy Spirit. How do we prove this? When the Lord answered those who said that He cast out demons by the power of Beelzebub, He said: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matthew 12:28). Another Evangelist, recounting the same event, says: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11:20).

What is stated openly in one passage is stated obscurely in the other. You did not know what the finger of God was; the other Evangelist explains it, saying that it is the Spirit of God.

The Law was therefore given, written by the finger of God, on the fiftieth day after the lamb was killed; and the Holy Spirit came on the fiftieth day after the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. The lamb was killed, the Passover took place, fifty days were completed, and the Law was given.

But that Law was for fear, not for love. In order that fear might be turned into love, the righteous man was killed in reality—the one prefigured by that lamb which the Jews used to kill. He rose; and from the Lord’s Passover, just as from the Passover of the slain lamb, fifty days were counted, and the Holy Spirit came (Acts 2:1–4), now in the fullness of love, not under the punishment of fear.

Why have I said this? The Lord therefore rose and was glorified in order to send the Holy Spirit. I said earlier that the Head is in heaven and the feet on earth. If the Head is in heaven and the feet on earth, what are the Lord’s feet on earth except the Lord’s holy ones on earth?

Who are the Lord’s feet? The Apostles, sent throughout the whole world. Who are the Lord’s feet? All the Evangelists, in whom the Lord traverses every nation.

It was to be feared that the Evangelists might strike their feet against a stone. For with the Head placed in heaven, the feet laboring on earth could strike against a stone. Against what stone? Against the Law given on tablets of stone.

Therefore, lest they become liable under the Law, lacking grace and remaining held guilty by the Law—for this is the offense of guilt—the Lord absolved those whom the Law held guilty, so that they would no longer strike against the Law.

Lest the feet of this Head incur the guilt of the Law, the Holy Spirit was sent to produce love and free them from fear. Fear did not fulfill the Law; love fulfilled it. People feared and did not fulfill it; they loved and fulfilled it.

How did they fear and not fulfill it; how did they love and fulfill it? They feared, and they seized other people’s property; they loved, and they gave away their own.

Therefore it is not surprising that the Lord was taken up into heaven in the hands of angels for this reason: lest His foot strike against a stone. Lest those who labored on earth in His body, traversing the whole world, become liable under the Law, He removed fear from them and filled them with love.

By fear Peter denied three times (Matthew 26:69–75), for he had not yet received the Holy Spirit. Afterward, having received the Holy Spirit, he began to preach with confidence. He who had denied Him three times at the voice of a servant girl, after receiving the Holy Spirit confessed Him amid the beatings [Col. 1168] of rulers (Acts 2 and following).

This is not surprising, because the Lord dissolved that threefold fear by a threefold love. Rising from the dead, He said to Peter: “Peter, do you love Me?” He did not say, “Do you fear Me?” For if he still feared, he would strike his foot against the stone.

“Do you love Me?” He said; and Peter replied, “I love You.” Once would have been enough. It might have been enough for me, who do not see the heart; how much more would it have been enough for the Lord, who saw with what inner depths Peter was saying, “I love You”?

Yet it was not enough for the Lord to receive Peter’s answer once. He asked again, and Peter replied, “I love You” [Note: Erasmus, Venice, and Louvain have “I love You.” In B this is absent. M.]. He asked a third time, and Peter, now saddened, as though the Lord doubted his love, said: “Lord, You know all things; You know that I love You” (John 21:15–17).

But the Lord dealt with him as though He were saying: “You denied Me three times through fear; confess Me three times through love.”

With this love and charity He filled His disciples. Why? Because He made the Most High His refuge; because, having been glorified, He sent the Holy Spirit; because He freed believers from the guilt of the Law, so that their feet would not strike against the stone.

## 9. [Verse 13]

The remaining matters are now clear, brothers, because they have often been discussed. “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon” [Note: This verse was already discussed above, in *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 39, no. 1.].

You know who the serpent is; you know how the Church tramples upon him, since she is not overcome because she guards against his cunning. I think Your Charity also knows what the lion and the dragon are. The lion rages openly; the dragon lies in wait secretly. The devil has both kinds of force and power.

When martyrs were being killed, he was a raging lion; when heretics lie in wait, he is a creeping dragon. You conquered the lion; conquer the dragon also. The lion did not break you; let the dragon not deceive you [Note: All our manuscripts have “let the lion not break you.”].

Let us prove that he was a lion when he raged openly. Exhorting the martyrs, Peter said: “Do you not know that your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour?” (1 Peter 5:8). The openly raging lion sought someone to devour. How does the dragon lie in wait? Through heretics.

Fearing such people, lest the Church be corrupted by them from the virginity of faith which she carries in her heart, Paul said: “For I betrothed you to one man, to present a pure virgin to Christ; but I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the purity which is in Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2–3).

Few women in the Church possess bodily virginity; but all the faithful possess virginity of heart. He feared that this virginity of heart, which consists in faith, might be corrupted by the devil. Those who have lost it are virgins in body without cause. If the heart has been corrupted, what does she preserve in the body?

Thus a Catholic woman surpasses a heretical virgin. The former is not a virgin in body; the latter has become a woman in heart—and a woman not to God as husband, but to the serpent.

What, then, does the Church say? “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk.” The basilisk is king of serpents, just as the devil is king of demons. “And you will trample the lion and the dragon.”

## 10. [Verse 14]

Now come God’s words to the Church: “Because [Col. 1169] he hoped in Me, I will rescue him.” Therefore it is not only the Head, who now sits in heaven because He made the Most High His refuge, so that evil will not approach Him and the scourge will not come near His dwelling; it is also we who labor on earth and still live amid temptations, whose steps are feared lest they fall into snares.

Let us hear the voice of our Lord God consoling us and saying to us: “Because he hoped in Me, I will rescue him; I will protect him, because he has known My name.”

## 11. [Verse 15]

“He will call upon Me [Note: So Reg. manuscript; the editions read “He called upon Me.”], and I will answer him; I am with him in tribulation.”

Do not fear when you are in tribulation, as though God were not with you. Let faith be with you, and God is with you in tribulation.

The waves of the sea are rising; you are troubled in the boat because Christ is sleeping. Christ was sleeping in the boat, and the people were perishing (Matthew 8:24–25). If your faith sleeps in your heart, Christ sleeps in your boat, because Christ dwells in you through faith.

When you begin to be troubled, awaken Christ who is sleeping. Raise up your faith and know that He does not abandon you. But you think you are abandoned because He does not rescue you when you wish [Note: Perhaps “in the manner you wish”; that is, because He does not rescue you bodily.].

He rescued the three young men from the fire (Daniel 3:49–50). Did He who rescued the three young men abandon the Maccabees (2 Maccabees 7)? Certainly not. He rescued both: the former bodily, so that the unbelievers would be confounded; the latter spiritually, so that the faithful would imitate them.

“I am with him in tribulation; I will rescue him and glorify him.”

## 12. [Verse 16]

“I will fill him with length of days.” What is the length of days? Eternal life.

Brothers, do not think that “length of days” means what happens in winter, when the days are shorter, and in summer, when they are longer. Is He going to give us days of that sort? That length is the length which has no end: the eternal life promised to us in long days.

And truly, because it is sufficient, He did not say without reason, “I will fill him.” Nothing that is long in time is sufficient for us if it has an end; therefore it should not even be called long. And if we are greedy, we ought to be greedy for eternal life. Desire such a life as has no end. There is where our greed may extend itself.

Do you want silver without end? Desire eternal life without end. Do you not want your possession to have an end? Seek eternal life. “I will fill him with length of days.”

## 13.

“And I will show him My salvation.” This too, brothers, must not be passed over briefly. “I will show him My salvation”: this means, “I will show him Christ Himself.”

Why? Has He not been seen on earth? What great thing is it for Him to show us? But He was not seen with the kind of sight with which we shall see Him. He was seen with the kind of sight possessed by those who saw Him and crucified Him. Behold, those who saw Him crucified Him; we did not see Him, and we believed [Note: The printed editions have “we see and believe.” More manuscripts have “we saw and believed.”].

Did they have eyes while we do not? On the contrary, we also have the eyes of the heart; but for now we see through faith [Note: Nearly all manuscripts have “we live.”], not by sight. When will sight come? When we see face to face [Col. 1170] what the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 13:12), which God promises us as the great reward for all our labors.

Whatever you labor for, you labor in order to see. I do not know how great the thing is that we shall see, when our entire reward is vision—and the great object of that vision is our Lord Jesus Christ Himself.

He who appeared humble will Himself be seen as great and will make us rejoice, as He is now seen by the angels: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

Attend to the One who made this promise, the Lord Himself speaking in the Gospel: “Whoever loves Me will be loved by My Father, and I will love him.” And as though someone had said to Him, “What will You give the one who loves You?” He says: “I will show Myself to him” (John 14:21).

Let us desire and love; let us burn with longing, if we are the bride. The bridegroom is absent; let us endure. He whom we desire will come.

He gave so great a pledge: let the bride not fear that she will be abandoned by the bridegroom; He does not abandon His pledge. What pledge did He give? He poured out His blood. What pledge did He give? He sent the Holy Spirit.

Will that bridegroom abandon such pledges? If He did not love us, He would not give such pledges. He already loves us. If only we loved in the same way!

“Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). And how can we lay down our lives for Him? What benefit does it bring Him, since He has made the Most High His refuge and the scourge does not approach His dwelling?

But what does John say? “Just as Christ laid down His life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (1 John 3:16). Each person who lays down his life for his brother lays it down for Christ, just as one who feeds his brother feeds Christ: “Whatever you did for one of the least of Mine, you did for Me” (Matthew 25:40).

Let us love and imitate Him; let us run after His fragrances, as it is said in the Song of Songs: “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song of Songs 1:3). For He came and was fragrant, and His fragrance filled the world.

Where does the fragrance come from? From heaven. Follow, then, to heaven, if you do not answer falsely when it is said, “Lift up your hearts”: lift up your thoughts, lift up your love, lift up your hope, lest it rot on earth.

You would not dare to place wheat in damp earth lest it rot, because you worked, reaped, threshed, and winnowed it. You seek a place for your wheat, but do you not seek a place for your heart? Do you not seek a place for your treasure?

Do whatever you can on earth: distribute it. You will not lose it; you will store it away. And who preserves it? Christ, who also preserves you. Does He know how to preserve you but not how to preserve your treasure?

Why does He want you to change the place of your treasure, unless He wants you to change the place of your heart? For no one thinks except about his treasure.

How many are here now listening to me whose hearts are nowhere but in their purses? You are on earth because what you love is on earth. Send it to heaven, and your heart will be there. For “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

# Exposition of Psalm 91

[Col. 1171]

## Sermon

[Note: Delivered to the people on a Saturday; from no. 2.]

1. Attend to the Psalm: may the Lord grant us to open the mysteries contained here, since, because of the weariness of our minds, the same matters are treated in diverse and varied ways. For God teaches us no other song than that of faith, hope, and love: that our faith may be firm in him while we do not see him, believing in him whom we do not see, so that we may rejoice when we see him, and that the vision of his light may succeed our faith, when it will no longer be said to us, “Believe what you do not see,” but, “Rejoice because you see.”

May our hope also be unchanging and fixed in him; may it neither waver nor fluctuate nor be disturbed, just as the God in whom it is fixed cannot be disturbed. For now it is called hope; then it will not be hope but the reality itself. It is called hope only as long as what is hoped for is not seen, as the Apostle says: “But hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25).

For now, therefore, patience is necessary, until what has been promised comes. No one, however, is patient in good things. Whenever patience is demanded of a person, he is acting amid evils. When one is told, “Be patient, tolerate, endure,” there is distress beneath which God wants you to be strong, forbearing, long-suffering, and patient.

But surely the one who promised does not deceive? A physician draws out his instrument to cut wounds and says to the person whom he is about to operate on, “Be patient, endure, tolerate.” He demands patience amid pain, but after the pain he promises health. And the person who endures the pain of the physician’s instrument, unless he sets before himself the health he does not yet possess, fails amid the pain he suffers.

There are therefore many evils in this world, within and without; scandals simply do not cease, but abound. No one feels them except the one who walks in God’s way. Throughout all the divine pages he is told to endure the present, hope for the future, and love the one whom he does not see, so that he may embrace him when he sees him.

For love, which is joined to us as the third alongside faith and hope, is greater than faith and hope (1 Cor. 13:13). Faith concerns things that are not seen; but there will be vision when they have been seen [Note: Col. 1171. Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “there will be visions.”]. Hope concerns a reality that is not possessed; when that reality itself arrives, it will no longer be hope, because we shall possess it, not hope for it. Love, however, knows only how to grow more and more. For if we love one whom we do not see, how shall we love him when we see him? Let our desire, therefore, grow.

We are not Christians except for the age to come [Note: Col. 1171. Thus Am. and several manuscripts; Er. and Lov. read, “Let us not be Christians.”]. Let no one hope for present prosperity; let no one promise himself the happiness of this world because he is a Christian. Rather, let him use present prosperity as he can, how he can, when he can, and as much as he can. When it is present, let him give thanks to God’s consolation; when it is absent, let him give thanks to God’s justice. Let him be grateful everywhere and nowhere ungrateful: grateful to the Father when he consoles and caresses, and grateful to the Father when he corrects, scourges, and disciplines. For he always loves, whether he caresses or threatens. And let him say what you heard in the Psalm: “It is good to give thanks to the Lord, and to sing praises to your name, O Most High.”

2. [Verse 1.] The title of the Psalm reads: “A Psalm, a song, for the Sabbath day” [Note: Col. 1172. Thus the better manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint; the editions read, “on the Sabbath day.”]. Behold, today also is the Sabbath day. At the present time the Jews celebrate it with a certain bodily idleness that is sluggish, lax, and luxurious. They are free for trifles; and although God commanded the Sabbath (Exod. 20:8), they keep Sabbath in those things that God forbids. Our freedom is from evil works; their freedom is from good works. It is better to plow than to dance. They abstain from good work; they do not abstain from frivolous work.

God enjoins a Sabbath upon us. What kind? First, see where it is. It is within; our Sabbath is in the heart. Many are idle in their limbs, yet their conscience is in turmoil. No evil person can have a Sabbath, for his conscience never comes to rest anywhere; he must live in disturbances. But one whose conscience is good is tranquil, and that tranquility is the Sabbath of the heart.

He attends to the Lord who made the promise; and if he labors in the present, he is stretched toward the hope of the future, and every cloud of sadness is brightened, as the Apostle says, “Rejoicing in hope” (Rom. 12:12). This very joy in the tranquility of our hope is our Sabbath.

This is commended and sung in this Psalm: how the Christian is to be on the Sabbath of his heart—that is, in the freedom, tranquility, and serenity of his conscience, undisturbed. Hence it speaks here of what usually disturbs people, and teaches you to keep Sabbath in your heart.

3. [Verse 2.] The first thing is that you yourself, if you have made any progress, should give thanks to God for the progress you have made, because his gifts are involved, not your merits. Begin your Sabbath here: do not attribute to yourself what you have received, as though you had not received it (1 Cor. 4:7), and do not excuse yourself for the evil you do, because those things are your own.

For perverse and troubled people who do not keep Sabbath attribute their evils to God and their good deeds to themselves. If they have done something good, they say, “I did it.” If they have done something evil, they look for someone to accuse, so that they may not confess to God [Note: Several manuscripts read, “so that he does not confess to God.”].

And what does it mean, “He looks for someone to accuse”? If he is not extremely impious, he has Satan at hand to accuse: “Satan did it,” he says; “he persuaded me,” as though Satan had the power to compel. He has the cunning to persuade.

But if Satan were speaking and God were silent, you would have grounds for excusing yourself. Now your ears are placed between God, who warns, and the serpent, who suggests. Why are they turned this way and averted from that? Satan does not cease persuading you to evil, but God also does not cease admonishing you to good. Satan, however, does not compel one who is unwilling: it is in your power to consent or not to consent.

If, persuaded by Satan, you have done something evil, dismiss Satan and accuse yourself, so that by your accusation you may merit God’s mercy. Do you seek to accuse the one who has no forgiveness [Note: Col. 1172. The manuscripts read, “Do you await the one who has no forgiveness?”]? Accuse yourself, and you receive pardon.

Then there are many who do not accuse Satan but accuse fate. “My fate led me,” they say. When you ask, “Why did you do it? Why did you sin?” they reply, “Because of my evil fate.” In saying this they do not say, “I did it”; already they stretch out their hand toward God, while their tongue blasphemes.

They do not yet say this openly, but pay attention and see that this is what they are saying. Ask them what fate is, and they answer, “Evil stars.” Ask them who made the stars and who ordered the stars; they have nothing to answer except, “God.” It follows, then, that whether indirectly, or by a long reed, or through a neighbor [Note: Several manuscripts of excellent quality read, “through a female neighbor.”], they accuse God; and when God punishes their sins, they make God the author of their sins.

For it cannot be that he punishes what he has made; he punishes what you do, in order to free what he has made. Sometimes, however, leaving everything else aside, they go directly against God; and when they sin, they say, “God willed this. If God had not wanted it, I would not have sinned.”

Does he admonish you to this—that he should not merely not be listened to, so that you may not sin, but should be accused because you sin?

What, then, does this Psalm teach us? “It is good to give thanks to the Lord.” What does it mean to give thanks to the Lord? In both matters: in your sin, because you committed it, confess to the Lord; and in your good deed, confess to the Lord, because he accomplished it. Then you will sing praises to the name of God Most High, seeking God’s glory, not your own; his name, not yours.

For if you seek the name of God, he too seeks your name; but if you neglect the name of God, he also erases your name.

How did I say that he seeks your name? Consider how he spoke to his disciples when they returned after he had sent them to preach the Gospel. After they had performed many miracles and cast out demons in Christ’s name, they returned and said, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us.” They did indeed say, “in your name,” but he saw that they were rejoicing in that very glorification, exalting themselves and moving from it into pride because they had been permitted to cast out demons.

He saw that they were seeking their own glory, and said to them—himself seeking, or rather preserving, their names with him: “Do not rejoice in this, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:17, 20).

Behold where you have a name, if you do not neglect the name of God. Sing praises, therefore, to the name of God, so that your name may be fixed with God.

But what is it to sing praise, brothers? The psalter is a kind of instrument; it has strings. Our work is our psalter: whoever works with his hands at good works sings praise to God; whoever confesses with his mouth sings to God. Sing with your mouth; sing praise through your works. For what purpose?

4. [Verse 3.] “To proclaim your mercy in the morning and your truth by night.” What does it mean that God’s mercy is to be proclaimed in the morning and God’s truth by night?

“Morning” means when things go well for us; “night” means when there is the sadness of tribulation. What, then, did he say briefly? When things go well for you, rejoice in God, because it is his mercy.

Perhaps you would say: “If, then, I rejoice in God when things go well for me because it is his mercy, what shall I do when I am in sadness and tribulation? Is it his mercy when things go well for me, but his cruelty when things go badly? If I praise his mercy when things go well, should I accuse his cruelty when things go badly?”

No. When things go well, praise his mercy; when things go badly, praise his truth, because he scourges sins and is not unjust.

Daniel was in the night when he prayed: he was in captivity, for Jerusalem was under the power of its enemies. At that time the holy people were suffering many evils; Daniel himself was thrown into the lions’ den, and the three youths were cast into the fire (Dan. 6; 3). The people of Israel suffered these things in captivity: it was night.

By night Daniel confessed God’s truth. In prayer he said, “We have sinned, we have acted impiously, we have committed iniquity: to you, Lord, be glory; to us, confusion” (Dan. 9:5, 7). He proclaimed God’s truth by night.

What does it mean to proclaim God’s truth by night? It means not to accuse God because you suffer some evil, but to attribute it to your sins and to his correction: “To proclaim his mercy in the morning and his truth by night.”

When you proclaim mercy in the morning and truth by night, you always praise God, always confess to God, and sing praises to his name.

5. [Verse 4.] “Upon a ten-stringed psalter, with a song upon the lyre.” You have not merely heard of a ten-stringed psalter. The ten-stringed psalter signifies the ten commandments of the Law. But one must sing upon it, not carry it. The Jews also possess the Law: they carry it, but do not sing praise.

Who are those who sing praise? Those who act. That is not enough: those who act with sadness do not yet sing praise. Who are those who sing praise? Those who do good with gladness. For there is gladness in singing praise.

And what does the Apostle say? “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). Whatever you do, do it with gladness; then you both do good and do it well. But if you do it with sadness, it is done through you, not by you; you carry the psalter rather than sing.

“Upon a ten-stringed psalter, with a song upon the lyre”: that is, with word and deed. With a song means with the word; upon the lyre means through deed. If you speak words alone, you have, as it were, only a song and no lyre. If you act but do not speak, you have, as it were, only a lyre. Therefore speak well and act well, if you wish to have a song with a lyre.

6. [Verse 5.] “For you have gladdened me, Lord, by your work, and I shall exult in the works of your hands.” You see what he says. You made me live well; you formed me. If I perhaps do something good, I shall exult in the work of your hands, as the Apostle says: “For we are his workmanship, created for good works” (Eph. 2:10).

For unless he formed you for good works, you would know only your own evil works. “Whoever speaks falsehood speaks from his own” (John 8:44), the Gospel says. Every sin is falsehood. Whatever is against the law and against truth is called falsehood.

What, then, does he say? “Whoever speaks falsehood speaks from his own”: that is, whoever sins sins from his own. Pay attention to the contrary statement. If the one who speaks falsehood speaks from his own, it follows that the one who speaks truth speaks from God [Note: So the manuscripts read. The editions have “speaks of God”: an error that we have already corrected above.].

For this reason it is said elsewhere: “God alone is true, and every human being a liar” (Rom. 3:4). This sentence does not say to you, “Go, confidently lie, because you are human.” Rather, recognize that you are human because you are a liar; and in order to be truthful, drink truth, so that you may belch forth what is from God and be truthful.

Since you cannot have truth from yourself [Note: Col. 1175. Thus Am., Er., and the manuscripts; Lov. reads, “Since you cannot drink truth from yourself.”], it follows that you must drink it from where it flows. Just as, if you withdraw from the light, you are in darkness; and just as a stone does not become hot from itself but from the sun or from fire—if you withdraw it from the heat, it grows cold [Note: Three manuscripts read, “if you withdraw the heat from it.”]—and thus it becomes evident that what was hot was not its own, but that it was hot from the sun or from fire, so you, if you withdraw from God, will grow cold; if you approach God, you will grow fervent, as the Apostle says, “fervent in spirit” (Rom. 12:11).

Again, what does he say about light? If you approach him, you will be in the light. Therefore the Psalm says, “Approach him, and be enlightened; and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Ps. 33:5).

Since, then, you can perform no good work unless enlightened by God’s light and set aflame by God’s Spirit, when you see yourself doing good, confess to God and say what the Apostle says—say it to yourself, lest you become proud: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

Here, then, he confesses to God and teaches us a good confession, because he says [Note: Several manuscripts read, “by which he says.”]: “You have gladdened me, Lord, by your work, and I shall exult in the works of your hands.”

7. What are we to do about those who live wickedly and prosper? This is what troubles the mind of the one who loses the Sabbath [Note: So the better manuscripts read. Lov. has, “For these people have a troubled mind and lose the Sabbath. And the one who loses the Sabbath sees himself,” and Er. is similar, except that he has, “And he loses the Sabbath, who sees himself,” etc.].

He sees himself engaged daily in good works and laboring amid difficult circumstances—perhaps in poverty, perhaps in hunger, thirst, and nakedness, perhaps doing good while in prison—while the person who sent him to prison both does evil and rejoices. Then a very bad thought enters the heart against God and says: “God, why do I serve you? Why do I obey your words? I have not seized another’s property; I have not committed theft; I have not killed anyone; I have not coveted anyone’s possession; I have not given false testimony against anyone; I have not insulted my father or mother; I have not bowed down to idols; I have not taken the name of the Lord my God in vain. I have kept myself from sin.”

He counts the ten strings—that is, the ten commandments of the Law (Exod. 20:1–17)—and questions himself concerning each one. He sees that he has not sinned in any of them, and he is distressed because he suffers such evils.

Meanwhile those who, I will not say touch some of the strings, but do not even touch the psalter itself and do nothing good, consult idols. Perhaps they appear to be Christians when no evil afflicts their household; but when some tribulation occurs there, they run to a python, a diviner, or an astrologer.

The name of Christ is mentioned to such a person; he mocks and twists his mouth. He is asked, “A believer, and you consult an astrologer?” He replies, “Leave me alone. He disclosed my affairs to me; otherwise I would have lost everything and remained in mourning.”

My good man, do you not sign yourself with the sign of Christ’s cross? The Law forbids all these things. You rejoice because you found your possessions; are you not sad because you have perished? How much better that your tunic should perish than your soul!

He mocks at all these matters. He is insulting to his parents, hates his enemy, pursues him even to death, steals wherever he finds an opportunity, does not cease from false testimony, lays snares for another’s marriage, and covets his neighbor’s property. He does all these things and flourishes in wealth, honors, and the eminence of this world.

The wretched person who does good and suffers evil sees him, becomes troubled, and says: “God, I think you approve of evil and hate the good; you love those who practice iniquity.”

If he is shaken and consents to that thought, he will lose the Sabbath from his heart. He begins no longer to attend to this psalter; he has strayed from it and sings without reason, “It is good to give thanks to the Lord and to sing praises to your name, O Most High.”

Once the Sabbath has been lost from the inner person, the tranquility of the heart excluded, and the good thought rejected, he begins to imitate the one whom he sees flourishing in evil and turns to doing evil himself.

But God is patient because he is eternal, and he knows the day of his judgment, when he will examine everything.

8. [Verse 6.] Teaching us this, what does he say? “How greatly your works have been magnified, Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep.”

Truly, my brothers, no sea is as deep as this thought of God: that the wicked flourish while the good labor. Nothing is so deep, nothing so lofty. Every unbeliever is shipwrecked in this height, in this depth.

Do you wish to cross this deep? Do not spring away from the wood of Christ; you will not be submerged. Hold fast to Christ.

What do I mean by “hold fast to Christ”? For this reason he himself chose to labor on earth. You heard, when the prophet was read, that he did not turn his back from the scourges, did not turn his face from the spittle of men, and did not turn his cheek from their blows (Isa. 50:6). Why did he wish to suffer all these things except to console those who suffer?

He could also have raised his flesh at the end, but if you had not seen this, you would have had nothing to hope for. He did not delay his resurrection, lest you should still doubt.

With that end in view, therefore, endure and tolerate tribulations in the world—the end you have seen in Christ [Note: Col. 1176. Er. reads “as”; Am. and Lov., “which [tribulations]”; the manuscripts, “which [end],” with “end” understood]—and do not be disturbed by those who do evil and flourish in this world.

“Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep.” Where is the thought of God [Note: Col. 1176. Some manuscripts read, “There is the thought of God,” etc.]? For the present he loosens the reins; afterward he will tighten them.

Do not rejoice over the fish that leaps at its bait; the fisherman has not yet drawn out the hook [Note: Most manuscripts read, “hand”]—for the fish already has the hook in its throat.

And what seems long to you is brief: all these things quickly pass away. What is a human life, however long, compared with God’s eternity?

Do you wish to be long-suffering? Look to God’s eternity. You attend to your few days and want everything to be fulfilled within those few days. What things? That all the impious be condemned and all the good be crowned. Do you want this fulfilled within your days? God fulfills it in his own time.

Why do you suffer weariness and cause it [Note: Several manuscripts of good quality read, “But why do you suffer and cause it to continue for so long?”]? He is eternal; he delays because he is long-suffering. But you say, “That is why I am not long-suffering, because I am temporal.”

Yet it is in your power. Join your heart to God’s eternity, and you will be eternal with him.

For what has been said about temporal things? “All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls” (Isa. 40:6–8). Everything, therefore, withers and falls—not that word: “The word of the Lord remains forever.”

The grass passes away; the glory of grass passes away. But you have something to hold fast to: “The word of the Lord remains forever.”

Say to him, then: “Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep.” You have held fast to the wood and are crossing through this depth.

Do you see anything there? Do you understand anything there? “I understand,” you say. If you are now a Christian and well instructed, you say: “God reserves everything for his judgment. The good labor because they are scourged as sons; the wicked rejoice because they are condemned as outsiders.”

A man has two sons. He disciplines one and leaves the other alone. One does evil and is not corrected by his father; the other, as soon as he moves, is struck with blows and scourged. Why is one left alone and the other beaten, except because an inheritance is being preserved for the one who is beaten, while the one left alone has been disinherited?

He sees that the latter has no hope, and leaves him to do what he wishes. But the boy who is scourged, if he has no understanding and is foolish, congratulates his brother who is not beaten, groans over himself, and says in his heart: “My brother does so many evil things; he does whatever he wishes against my father’s commands, and no one says a harsh word to him. I, as soon as I move, am beaten.”

He is foolish and without understanding: he attends to what he suffers, but does not attend to what is being reserved for him.

9. [Verses 7–8.] Therefore, after saying, “Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep,” he immediately added: “The foolish person will not know, and the senseless will not understand these things.”

What are the things the foolish person will not understand and the senseless will not know? “When sinners spring up like grass.”

What does “like grass” mean? They are green while it is winter, but they will wither in summer. You attend to the flower of grass. What passes more quickly? What is brighter? What is greener? Do not take pleasure in its greenness; fear its dryness.

You have heard of sinners like grass; hear also of the righteous: “For behold” [Note: Er., Ven., and Lov. have, “How? Behold meanwhile,” etc.; M.].

For the moment, look at sinners: they flourish like grass—well and good. But who are those who do not know? The foolish and the senseless.

“When sinners spring up like grass, and all who practice iniquity flourish.” All who do not think rightly about God in their hearts have seen sinners springing up like grass—that is, flourishing for a time.

Why do they look upon them? “That they may perish forever and ever.” For they attend to their temporal flowering, imitate them, and, wishing to flourish with them for a time, perish eternally. This is what it means: “That they may perish forever and ever.”

10. [Verses 9–10.] “But you, O Most High, are forever, Lord.” From your eternity above, you await the passing of the time of the wicked and the coming of the time of the righteous.

“For behold.” Pay attention, brothers. The one who speaks [Note: Col. 1177. Thus the manuscripts, except one Corbie manuscript, which reads “the very one who”; the editions omit “who.”] has now joined himself to God’s eternity. He speaks from our person; he speaks from the person of Christ’s body, for Christ speaks in his body, that is, in his Church.

He has now joined himself to God’s eternity, just as I said to you shortly before: God is long-suffering and patient; he tolerates all these evils that he sees being committed by the wicked. Why? Because he is eternal and sees what he is reserving for them.

Do you also wish to be long-suffering and patient? Join yourself to God’s eternity; await with him the things that are beneath you. For when your heart has clung to the Most High, all mortal things will be beneath you, and you will say what follows: “For behold, your enemies will perish.”

Those who now flourish will afterward perish.

Who are God’s enemies? Brothers, perhaps you think that only those who blaspheme are God’s enemies. They certainly are, and they are terrible people who spare neither their tongues nor their evil thoughts in insulting God.

And what do they do to the exalted and eternal God? If I strike a column with my fist, I injure myself. Do you think that when blasphemy strikes God, you are not the one who is torn apart? You do nothing to God.

But God’s enemies are openly the blasphemers, and they are also found hidden every day. Beware of such enmity toward God.

Scripture reveals certain hidden enemies of God. Since you cannot know them by your own heart, you may know them in God’s Scripture and beware of being found among them.

James says openly in his Epistle: “Do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God?” (James 4:4). You have heard it. Do you not want to be an enemy of God? Do not be a friend of this world. For if you are a friend of this world, you will be an enemy of God.

Just as a wife cannot be adulterous without being an enemy of her husband, so the adulterous soul, through love of worldly things, cannot help being an enemy of God. It fears him but does not love him; it fears punishment but does not delight in justice.

Therefore all lovers of the world are God’s enemies, as are all seekers of frivolities and all who consult diviners, astrologers, and pythons. Whether they enter churches or do not enter churches [Note: Col. 1178. Thus Am., Er., and most manuscripts; Lov. reads, “They enter churches.”], they are God’s enemies.

They may flourish for a time like grass, but they will perish when he begins to inspect them and brings his judgment upon all flesh.

Join yourself to God’s Scripture and say this with the Psalm: “For behold, your enemies will perish.” May you not be found there where they will perish. “And all who practice iniquity will be scattered.”

11. [Verse 11.] What of you, who labor now, if God’s enemies will perish and all who practice iniquity will be scattered? You who groan amid these scandals and human iniquities, who are afflicted in the flesh but rejoice in the heart—what of you? What hope is there for you, O body of Christ?

O Christ, who sit in heaven at the right hand of the Father, but labor on earth through your feet and your members, and say, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4)—what hope will you have if God’s enemies perish and all who practice iniquity are scattered? What will happen to you?

“And my horn shall be exalted like that of the unicorn.” Why did he say, “like that of the unicorn”? Sometimes the unicorn signifies pride; sometimes the unicorn signifies the exaltation of unity, because unity is exalted and all heresies will perish with God’s enemies.

“And my horn shall be exalted like that of the unicorn.” And when will this be? “And my old age shall be in rich mercy.”

What did he mean by “my old age”? His final days. Just as old age is the final stage of our human life, so the whole period that the body of Christ now suffers in labors, hardships, vigils, hunger, thirst, scandals, iniquities, and pressures is its youth. Its old age—that is, its final condition—will be in joy.

Let your Love pay attention: he said “old age” so that you would not think of death. A person grows old in the flesh in order to die. But the old age of the Church will be white with rightly performed deeds and will not be corrupted by death. What the head of an old man is, our works will be.

You see how the head grows gray and becomes white as old age advances. When a person has aged well in its proper order, you look for a black hair on his head and do not find one. So when our life has become such that one looks for the blackness of sins and does not find it, this old age is youthful; this old age is green; it will always flourish.

You have heard of the grass of sinners; hear of the old age of the righteous: “My old age shall be in rich mercy.”

12. [Verse 12.] “And my eye has looked upon my enemies” [Note: Col. 1179. Thus the better manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek Septuagint; the editions read, “My eye [has looked] my enemies.”].

Whom does he call his enemies? All who practice iniquity.

Do not pay attention to the fact that an unjust person is your friend [Note: Er., Ven., and Lov. have, “that an unjust person is a friend to you.”]. Let a matter arise, and there you will test him. You begin to oppose his iniquity, and there you will see that when he was flattering you, he was an enemy. But you had not yet struck him—not in order to establish in his heart something that was not there, but to make what was there burst forth.

“And my eye has looked upon my enemies; and my ear shall hear those who rise against me in maliciousness.” When? In old age.

What does “in old age” mean? At the end. And what will our ear hear? Standing at the right hand, we shall hear what will be said to those at the left: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

The righteous will not fear this evil hearing. You know that it is said in a certain Psalm: “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear evil hearing” (Ps. 111:7).

What evil hearing? “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” “And my ear shall hear those who rise against me in maliciousness.”

13. [Verse 13.] The grass passes away; the flower of sinners passes away. What of the righteous? “The righteous shall flourish like the palm.”

They spring up like grass; the righteous shall flourish like the palm. In the palm he signified height. Perhaps the palm also signifies this because it is beautiful in its final form: its beginning is from the earth, but its end is at the top, where it possesses all its beauty. Its root appears rough in the earth, but its beautiful crown is beneath the sky.

Your beauty, then, will also be at the end. Let your root be fixed; but upward we have our root [Note: So Augustine and the manuscripts read. Er. and Lov. have, “let us have our root.”]. For our root is Christ, who ascended into heaven. “He will be humbled and exalted.”

“Like a cedar in Lebanon, he shall be multiplied.” See what trees he named: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm; like a cedar in Lebanon, he shall be multiplied.”

When the sun has risen, does the palm wither? Does the cedar wither? But when the blazing sun comes, the grass withers. Judgment will therefore come, so that sinners may wither and the faithful flourish.

“Like a cedar in Lebanon, he shall be multiplied.”

14. [Verses 14–16.] “Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God. They shall still be multiplied in abundant old age, and they shall be tranquil, so that they may proclaim.”

This is the Sabbath that I commended to you shortly before, from which the Psalm receives its title. “They shall be tranquil, so that they may proclaim.”

Why do the tranquil proclaim? The grass of sinners does not disturb them; the cedar and the palm are not bent even in storms. Therefore let them be tranquil, so that they may proclaim.

And truly, for now proclamation is to be made even to mocking people. O wretched lovers of the world! Those who are planted in the house of the Lord proclaim to you; those who confess to the Lord with song and lyre, in word and deed, proclaim to you and say:

“Do not be deceived by the prosperity of the wicked. Do not attend to the flower of grass. Do not attend to those who are blessed for a time but wretched forever. Nor is that happiness which now appears outwardly real; they are not blessed in their hearts, because an evil conscience torments them.”

But you be tranquil, hoping in the promises of the Lord your God.

For what will you proclaim in tranquility? “That the Lord God is righteous, and there is no iniquity in him.”

Pay attention, brothers. If you have been planted in the house of the Lord, if you wish to flourish like the palm and multiply like the cedar of Lebanon, and not wither like grass under the blazing sun—like those who seem to flourish while the sun is absent—then, if you do not wish to be grass but palm and cedar, what will you proclaim [Note: Several manuscripts read, “and cedar, so that you may proclaim.” The Regius manuscript has, “and cedar—see what you should proclaim.”]?

“That the Lord God is righteous, and there is no iniquity in him.”

How is there no iniquity? One person commits so many evils [Note: Er., Ven., and Lov. have, “whatever evils one commits.”]; he is healthy, has children, a full household, abundant glory, and exalted honors; he takes vengeance on his enemies and commits every kind of evil. Another, innocent in his affairs [Note: Manuscripts of good quality omit “his,” reading, “innocent in his affairs.”], who seizes no one else’s property and does nothing against anyone, labors in chains and prisons, burns and sighs in poverty.

How is there no iniquity in him?

Be tranquil and you will understand. You are disturbed, and in your own chamber you darken the light for yourself. The eternal God wishes to shine upon you; do not make a cloud for yourself out of your disturbance.

Be tranquil within yourself and see what I am telling you. Because God is eternal, because he now spares the wicked, leading them to repentance, and scourges the good, educating them for the kingdom of heaven, there is no iniquity in him. Do not be afraid.

“Behold, I have been scourged so much.” It is evident; I confess it; I have sinned—for I do not claim to be righteous.

This is what many people say. When someone is in some misery or pain, you enter to console him, and he says: “I have sinned, I admit it. They are my sins; I acknowledge them. But surely I have not sinned as greatly as that man? I know how much he has done; I know how much he has committed. They are my sins; I confess them to God, but they are smaller than his. And behold, he suffers no evil.”

Do not be disturbed; be tranquil, so that you may know that the Lord is righteous and that there is no iniquity in him.

What if he is scourging you now precisely because he is not reserving eternal fire for you? What if he is sparing that person now precisely because he will hear, “Go into the eternal fire”?

But when? When you have been placed at the right hand, then those placed at the left will be told: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Therefore do not let these things disturb you. Be tranquil, keep Sabbath, and proclaim that the Lord God is righteous and that there is no iniquity in him.

## Exposition of Psalm 92.

### Sermon to the People.

1. We heard the title of this Psalm when it was recited; and what it means is not difficult to discover from God’s Scripture, that is, from the book of Genesis. For in the title we are, as it were, warned at the threshold what we should seek within. It is therefore inscribed as follows: “A praise-song for David himself, for the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded.” [Note: [Col. 1181] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “of David himself.”] Let us then recall through all the days what God did when he created and ordered everything, from the first day through the sixth—for he sanctified the seventh, because on it he rested after all the works that he had made “very good”—and we find that on the sixth day, which is commemorated here because it says “before the Sabbath,” he made all the animals upon the earth; then, on that same day, he made man in his own image and likeness.

Those days were not ordered in this way without reason, except that the ages too were going to run in this fashion before we rest in God. We rest, however, if we perform good works. For this purpose it was written concerning God: “God rested on the seventh day, when he had made all his works very good” (Gen. I and II, 1–3). He was not fatigued, so that he needed to rest, nor is he now inactive, since the Lord Christ plainly says: “My Father is working until now” (John V, 17). He said this to the Jews, who thought about God in a fleshly manner and did not understand that God works in rest, always works, and is always at rest.

Therefore we also, whom God then intended to prefigure in himself, shall have rest after all good works. And indeed our good works, brothers, which we perform here in this world before rest, are carried out, as it were, with labor; and that rest is in hope, not yet possessed in actuality. If it were not in hope, we would fail in our labor. But laborious and good works pass away. What, indeed, is as good as extending bread to the hungry? And what we heard just now when the Gospel was read—what is as good as the general admonition: “Let everyone who has two tunics give to one who has none; and let whoever has food feed the hungry” (Luke III, 11)? To clothe the naked is a good work. Will this good work last forever? It involves some labor, but it has consolation in the hope of future rest.

How much labor does it take to clothe a naked person? A good work does not labor greatly; an evil work does. For whoever clothes the naked, if he has the means, does not labor; if he does not have the means, then: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14). But whoever wishes to strip one who is clothed—who can count how much he labors? Yet these things too will pass away when we come to that rest where no one is hungry who needs feeding, and no one is naked who needs clothing.

Therefore, because these good works too will pass away, and because this sixth day, on which “very good” works are completed, has an evening [Col. 1182], we do not find an evening in the Sabbath, because our rest will have no end: evening is used to signify the end.

Just as, then, on the sixth day God made man in his own image, so we find that in the sixth age the Lord Jesus came, so that man might be restored to the image of God. The first period, like the first day, extends from Adam to Noah; the second period, like the second day, from Noah to Abraham; the third period, like the third day, from Abraham to David; the fourth period, like the fourth day, from David to the Babylonian exile; the fifth period, like the fifth day, from the Babylonian exile to the preaching of John. The sixth day is now being enacted, from the preaching of John to the end; and after the end of the sixth day we arrive at rest.

The sixth day is therefore now being enacted. If the sixth day is being enacted, observe what the title contains: “For the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded.” Let us now hear the Psalm itself; let us ask it how the earth was founded, lest perhaps the earth was made at that time—for we do not read that in Genesis. When, then, was the earth founded? When, if not when what we have just read in the Apostle takes place: “Provided that you are standing firm in the faith,” he says, “stable and immovable” (I Cor. XV, 58)? When all who believe throughout the whole earth are immovable in faith, the earth is founded; then man is made in the image of God. This is signified by that sixth day in Genesis.

But how did God accomplish this? How was the earth founded? Christ came in order to found the earth. “For no one can lay a foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III, 11). Of him, then, the Psalm sings:

2. [Verse 1.] “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself.” We see that he put on two things: beauty and strength. But why? In order to found the earth. For it follows: “Indeed, he established the inhabited world, which shall not be moved.” From what did he establish it? Because he clothed himself with beauty. He would not establish it if he clothed himself only with beauty and not also with strength.

Why beauty? Why strength? He mentioned both: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself.” You know, brothers, that when our Lord came in the flesh [Note: [Col. 1182] Most manuscripts read “into the flesh, to whom.”], preaching the Gospel of the kingdom to those whom he addressed, he pleased some and displeased others. The tongues of the Jews were divided against one another. Some said, “He is good”; others said, “No, but he deceives the crowds” (John VI, 12). Some therefore spoke well; others reviled, tore at [Note: [Col. 1182] Here the editions add “barked,” which is absent from the manuscripts.], bit, and abused him. To those whom he pleased he put on beauty; to those whom he displeased he put on strength.

Imitate your Lord, then, so that you may be his garment: be beautiful toward those who are pleased by your good works; be strong against those who revile you. Hear the Apostle Paul imitating his Lord, and how he too possessed beauty and strength: “We are the good fragrance of Christ,” he says, “in every place, both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.” Those who are pleased by what is good are being saved; those who revile what is good are perishing. What belonged to him, he possessed as a good fragrance—indeed, he was a good fragrance; but woe to the wretched who die even from a good fragrance.

For he did not say, “To some we are a good fragrance, to others a bad fragrance”; but he said: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place, both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.” He immediately added: “To some we are the fragrance of life unto life, to others the fragrance of death unto death” (II Cor. II, 14–16). To those for whom he was the fragrance of life unto life, he had put on beauty; to those for whom he was the fragrance of death unto death, he had put on strength.

But if you rejoice when people praise you and your good works please them, while, when they reproach you, you fail in good works and suppose that you have lost, as it were, the fruit of your good works because you encounter critics, you have not stood immovably; you do not belong to the inhabited world “which shall not be moved.” “The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself.”

The Apostle Paul has another passage concerning this beauty and strength: “By the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left.” See where beauty is and where strength: “Through glory and dishonor.” In glory he is beautiful; in dishonor he is strong. Among some he was proclaimed glorious; among others he was despised as dishonorable. He brought beauty to those whom he pleased, and strength against those whom he displeased.

And so he lists everything to the end, where he says: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (II Cor. VI, 7, 8, 10). When he possesses everything, he is beautiful; when he has nothing, he is strong. It is therefore no wonder that what follows is: “Indeed, he established the inhabited world, which shall not be moved.” For how will the inhabited world not be moved? When all the faithful believe in Christ and are prepared for both possibilities: to rejoice with those who praise them, and to be strong against those who reproach them; not to grow soft under the tongues of those who praise, nor to be broken by the tongues of those who reproach.

3. Perhaps we should also ask about this word, why he said, “he girded himself.” Girding signifies work, for each person girds himself when he is about to work. But why did he not say, “He is girded,” but “He girded himself”? In another Psalm he says: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one; the peoples shall fall beneath you” (Ps. XLIV, 4, 6). There too he did not say “gird” or “gird yourself,” but “bind on”: you bind something to your side by girding; hence, “Bind your sword upon your thigh.”

The sword of the Lord with which he conquered the inhabited world by killing wickedness is the Spirit of God [Note: The manuscripts omit “is”; and after the word “of speech” they do not add “of God.” But the Regius manuscript reads: “With what did he conquer the inhabited world? By killing the wickedness of the spirit in the truth of God’s speech.”] in the truth of God’s word.

Why, then, is the sword said to be bound upon the thigh? We said one thing from another [Note: [Col. 1183] Ambrose omits “from another”; it is in the manuscripts, some of which below read “we have spoken,” or “we speak,” of binding on.], concerning girding in another Psalm; but since it has been mentioned, it must not be passed over. What is the binding of the sword upon the thigh? By the thigh he signifies the flesh. For the Lord would not otherwise conquer the inhabited world unless the sword of truth came in the flesh.

Why, then, is he girded here? Whoever girds himself places before himself something with which he girds himself. Hence it is said: “He was girded with a linen cloth and washed the feet of his disciples.” Because he was humble when he was girded with a linen cloth, he washed the feet of his disciples. All strength, however, lies in humility, because all pride is fragile. Therefore, when he spoke of strength, he added, “he girded himself,” so that you might recall God girded in humility when he washed the feet of his disciples.

Peter recoiled from his Lord and teacher—indeed, I have said too little in calling him his teacher, after having called him his Lord—when he saw him bending down to his feet and washing them. He was terrified and said: “Lord, will you wash my feet?” And he replied: “What I am doing, you do not know now; but afterward you will understand.” And he said: “You shall never wash my feet.” And he replied: “If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me.”

Peter, who at first had been terrified that his Lord was washing his feet, was still more terrified by the words “You will have no part with me.” He believed that the Lord was not doing this without reason, but that there was perhaps some sacrament involved, and he said: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my head and my whole body.” And he replied: “The one who has been washed once has no need to wash again, but is entirely clean.”

The washing of their feet therefore did not belong to the sacrament of cleansing [Note: So read Ambrose and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain editions have “merely,” or “only.”], but to an example of humility. For he had said: “What I am doing, you do not know; but afterward you will understand.” Let us see whether afterward they understood; let us see whether he disclosed to them what he was doing, so that we may see the Lord girded with strength, because all strength is in humility.

When he had washed their feet, he reclined again and said to them: “You call me Teacher, and you speak rightly, for I am; you call me Lord, and you speak rightly, for I am. If I, then, your Teacher and Lord, have washed your feet, how ought you to act toward one another?” (John XIII, 4–15).

If strength is therefore in humility, do not fear the proud. The humble are like a rock: the rock appears below, but it is solid. What are the proud like? Like smoke. Even if they rise high, they vanish. We should therefore refer the fact that he was girded to the Lord’s humility, in accordance with the Gospel’s recollection that he was girded in order to wash the feet of his disciples.

4. There is another meaning that we may understand in this word. We said that whoever girds himself places before himself what he attaches to himself, in order to gird himself with it. Those who revile us sometimes do so in our absence, as it were behind our back; sometimes openly to our face, as they did to the Lord hanging on the cross: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII, 40).

You do not need strength when someone reviles you in your absence, because you neither hear nor feel it. But if he says it to your face, you need to be strong. What does it mean to be strong? To endure. Do not suppose that you are strong because, when you hear abuse, you strike the one who has overcome you by his insult with your fist. That is not strength, if you strike after being insulted, since you have been overcome by anger [Note: Ambrose and all our manuscripts read: “if, overcome, you strike, since you have been overcome by anger.”]. It is extremely foolish to call a man strong when he has been overcome, since Scripture says: “The one who conquers anger is better than the one who captures a city” (Prov. XVI, 32).

It calls the conqueror of anger better than the captor of a city. You therefore have a great adversary within yourself. When, after hearing an insult, anger begins to rise so that you may repay evil for evil, recall the Apostle’s words: “Not returning evil for evil, nor abuse for abuse” (I Peter III, 9). By recalling these words you break your anger and retain your strength; and because the man cursed you to your face, not behind your back, you are girded with that strength.

5. Let us now hear the rest: “Indeed, he established the inhabited world, which shall not be moved.” You see, brothers, that many believe in Christ; the crowd is large. Yet within this great crowd you heard just now, when the Gospel was read, that the Lord will come carrying a winnowing shovel openly in his hand and will cleanse his threshing floor; he will store the grain in his barn and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt. III, 12).

There are therefore good and evil people throughout the whole earth: the good are grain, the evil are chaff. The threshing sledge enters the threshing floor; it crushes the chaff and cleanses the wheat. What, then, is the inhabited world that shall not be moved? He would certainly not say this unless there were also an inhabited world that would be moved. There is an inhabited world that shall not be moved, and an inhabited world that shall be moved.

The good, who are steadfast in faith, are an inhabited world, lest someone say, “They are only a part.” And the evil, who do not stand firm in faith when they experience some tribulation, are throughout the inhabited world. There is therefore a movable inhabited world and an immovable inhabited world, concerning which the Apostle speaks [Note: Perhaps, “concerning both.”].

See the movable inhabited world. I ask you: of whom was the Apostle speaking when he said, “Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have gone astray from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened, and they overthrow the faith of some”? Did these men belong to the inhabited world that shall not be moved? No; they were chaff: “They overthrow,” he says, “the faith of some.” He did not say “of all”; and if he had said “of all,” we should have had to understand all as belonging to the city of Babylon, which is destined to be condemned with the devil. Yet he said “the faith of some.”

And as though someone might say to him, “Who can resist them?” he immediately added: “But the firm foundation of God stands.” Behold the inhabited world that shall not be moved. What seal does this firm foundation possess? “The Lord knows those who are his.” This is the inhabited world that shall not be moved: “The Lord knows those who are his.” And what seal does it have? “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from injustice” (II Tim. II, 17–19).

Let him now depart from iniquity; for he cannot depart from the iniquitous, because the chaff is mixed with the wheat until the winnowing. What shall we say, brothers? Even in the threshing floor itself there is a marvelous fact concerning the wheat: it departs from the chaff when it is stripped, yet it does not depart from the threshing floor when it is threshed. When will it be separated completely? When the winnower comes.

For now, then, the threshing floor is in the inhabited world. If you are making progress, you must live among the iniquitous. You cannot depart from the iniquitous; depart from iniquity. “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity,” and he will be in the inhabited world that shall not be moved.

6. [Verse 2.] “Your throne is prepared, O God, from that time” [Note: In most manuscripts: “Your throne is prepared from that time; your throne, O God, from that time.” What does “from that time” mean?]. What is “from that time”? From then onward. It is as though he said: What is God’s throne? Where does God sit? In his saints. Do you wish to be God’s throne? Prepare a place in your heart where he may sit.

What is God’s throne except the place where God dwells? Where does God dwell except in his temple? What is his temple? Is it built with walls? Certainly not. Is this world perhaps his temple, because it is so great, a thing worthy to contain God? It does not contain the one by whom it was made. Where, then, is he contained? In a quiet soul, in a just soul; that soul carries him.

A great thing, brothers: certainly God is great; to the strong he is burdensome, but to the weak he is light. Whom did I call strong? The proud, who seem to have confidence in their own strength. For that weakness which exists in humility is greater strength. Hear the Apostle saying: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (II Cor. XII, 10).

This is what I commended [Note: The editions read, “the Gospel commended.” Some manuscripts have “I commended,” and several, together with Ambrose, read “he commended”; but they do not add “the Gospel.”], that the Lord was girded with strength when he taught humility.

That, then, is God’s throne, which is plainly described elsewhere by the prophet: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest?” That is, where shall God’s Spirit rest, except upon God’s throne? Hear how he describes that throne itself. Perhaps you expected to hear of a marble house, broad spaces of courtyards, great height and the splendor of roofs [Note: So read the manuscripts. The editions instead have: “broad, spacious courts, with the grandeur of the courtyards and the splendor of the roofs.”]. Hear what God prepares for himself: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest? Upon the humble and quiet one, who trembles at my words” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

Behold: you are humble and quiet, and God dwells in you [Note: Erasmus, Venice, and Louvain read this passage as follows: “Be humble and quiet, so that God may also dwell in you.” M.]. God is exalted; he does not dwell in you if you wish to be exalted. Certainly you wish to be exalted so that he may dwell in you: be humble and tremble at his words, and he dwells there. He does not fear a trembling dwelling, because he himself makes it firm.

“Your throne is prepared, O God, from that time.” “From that time,” that is, from then onward; that is, it signifies a certain time. From then onward—from what time? Perhaps from the day before the Sabbath. “From that time,” because the title of the Psalm indicates to us from what time. On the sixth day, that is, in the sixth age of this world, the Lord came in the flesh.

Therefore, “from that time”—plainly from that time according to his humanity, from that time from the womb. For what does another Psalm say? “In the splendor of the saints, from the womb.” “In the splendor of the saints,” that is, so that the saints may be enlightened, so that they may see God in the flesh, and so that the heart may be purified, by which he may be seen in his divinity. “In the splendor of the saints, from the womb.”

But what follows there? Lest you suppose that Christ began to exist from the womb: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3). When he had said, “In the splendor of the saints, from the womb,” he immediately added this, lest you suppose that Christ began from the time when he was born, as Adam, Abraham, and David began: “Before the morning star I begot you”—before everything that is illuminated [Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “before all things that illuminate.”]

By “the morning star” he either signifies all the stars, and by the stars the times, because God made the stars for signs of the times (Gen. I, 14), so that you may find Christ born before the times; and certainly one who was born before the times cannot be thought to have been born in time, because the times too are God’s creation. And certainly, if “all things were made through him” (John I, 3), the times too were made through him.

Or, certainly, by “before the morning star” he spoke of Wisdom, before every spirit that is illuminated. Let your Charity attend. Why, then, after saying “from the womb,” as though taking precaution for our faith lest we suppose that Christ began from the time when he was born from the Virgin’s womb, did he immediately add, “Before the morning star I begot you”?

So here too, after saying “from that time”—that is, from a certain time, from the day before the Sabbath, from that sixth age of the world when the Lord Christ came and was born in the flesh, because he graciously became man for our sake—since he was God [Note: So read the better manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain instead have: “And because he graciously willed to become man for our sake, God, not only …”], not only before Abraham, but before heaven and earth, he who said, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John VIII, 58); not only before Abraham, but before Adam; not only before Adam, but before all the angels, before heaven and earth, because all things were made through him—he immediately added, lest you, fixing your attention on the day of the Lord’s birth, from which he was born, suppose that he began to exist from that time: “Your throne is prepared, O God.”

But which God? “From eternity you are.” The Greek has *ἀπὸ αἰῶνος* (*apo aiōnos*): *αἰών* (*aiōn*) is sometimes used for “the age,” and sometimes for “eternity.” Therefore, O you who appear to have been born from that time, you are from eternity. Human birth must not be considered here; divine eternity must be considered.

Thus, from the time when he was born he began, he grew: you heard the Gospel. He chose disciples, filled them, and the disciples began to preach. Perhaps this is what he next says.

7. [Verses 3–4.] “The rivers have lifted up their voices.” What rivers are these that have lifted up their voices? We have not heard of them: neither when the Lord was born did we hear rivers speaking, nor when he was baptized, nor when he suffered. We did not hear rivers speaking. It is not merely that they spoke; they lifted up their voices. They not only spoke, but spoke powerfully, greatly, sublimely.

What rivers are these that spoke? We said that we do not read of them in the Gospel; nevertheless, let us seek them there. For if we do not find them there, where shall we find them? I could invent an answer for you and would suddenly be not a faithful steward [Note: Four manuscripts read “debater”], but a foolish storyteller. Let us seek in the Gospel; let us seek together what rivers these are that lifted up their voices.

“Jesus stood and cried out,” the Gospel says. What did he cry out? Behold, the very head of the rivers cries out; the fountain of life itself, from which the rivers were going to flow, first lifted up his voice. And what did Jesus cry out while standing [Note: In B: “Jesus stood and cried out.” Erasmus, Venice, and Louvain follow this reading. M.]?

“Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

The Evangelist immediately continues: “Now he said this concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII, 37–39).

But when Jesus had been glorified in the resurrection and ascension into heaven, as you know, brothers, after the ten days had been completed there for the sake of a certain sacrament, he sent his Holy Spirit and filled the disciples (Acts II, 4). That Spirit is the great river from which many rivers were filled. Concerning this river the Psalm says elsewhere: “The rushing of the river gladdens the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 5).

Rivers therefore began to flow from the bellies of the disciples when they received the Holy Spirit; these were the rivers that received the Holy Spirit. From where did the rivers [Note: So read Ambrose and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain instead have: “These rivers, having received the Holy Spirit, from where they lifted up …”] lift up their voices? Why did they lift them up? Because at first they were afraid.

Peter was not yet a river when, at the questioning of the maidservant, he denied Christ three times: “I do not know the man” (Matt. XXVI, 69–74). Fearing, he lies [Note: [Col. 1188] Some manuscripts read, “I do not know this man. Fearing, etc.”; others, “Fearing this, he lies.”]; he does not yet lift up his voice; he is not yet a river.

But when they had been filled with the Holy Spirit, the Jews summoned them and ordered them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. Peter and John, however, said to them: “Whether it is right before God to obey you rather than God, judge yourselves; for we cannot refrain from speaking of what we have seen and heard.”

Thus “the rivers lifted up their voice, from the voices of many waters.” The elevation of the voice is also indicated by what is written there: “Peter stood with the eleven, and lifting up his voice said to them, ‘Men of Judea’” (Acts II, 14), and the rest, in which he announces Jesus without fear and with great confidence.

“For the rivers lifted up their voice, from the voices of many waters.” When the Apostles had been released from the council of the Jews, they came to their own people and reported all that the priests and elders had said to them. When the others heard, “they lifted up their voice with one accord to the Lord and said, ‘Lord, you are the one who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them’” (Acts IV, 18–24), together with the rest that the rivers lifting up their voice were able to say.

“Wonderful are the swellings of the sea.” For when the disciples had lifted up their voices, many believed and many received the Holy Spirit, and many rivers began to cry out from a few. Therefore it follows: “From the voices of many waters, wonderful are the swellings of the sea”—that is, of this world.

When Christ began to be preached by such mighty voices, the sea began to grow angry, and persecutions began to increase. When the rivers had therefore lifted up their voice “from the voices of many waters, wonderful are the swellings of the sea.” Swellings are exaltations; for when the sea grows angry, its waves are raised up.
