Let the waves be raised as high as they will; let the sea rage as much as it will. “Wonderful indeed are the swellings of the sea,” wonderful are the threats, wonderful are the persecutions. But see what follows: “Wonderful is the Lord on high.”

Let the sea therefore restrain itself and at last become calm; let peace be granted to Christians. The sea was troubled; the little boat was tossed. The boat is the Church; the sea is the world. The Lord came, walked upon the sea, and pressed down the waves (Matt. XIV, 24–25). How did the Lord walk upon the sea? Upon the heads of those great, foaming waves. Powers and kings believed and were subjected to Christ.

Let us therefore not be afraid because “wonderful are the swellings of the sea”: “Wonderful is the Lord on high.”

8. [Verse 5.] “Your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy” [Note: [Col. 1189] Some manuscripts read “because.”]. They were so even more than the wonderful swellings of the sea and the Lord’s being wonderful on high. “Your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy.” “Your testimonies,” because he had said earlier: “I say these things to you so that in me you may have peace, but in the world you will have tribulation.”

Because the world was going to bring tribulation upon them, he said this to them. They began to suffer, and what the Lord had foretold to them was confirmed in them; they became still stronger. For when they saw sufferings being fulfilled in them, they hoped that crowns would also be fulfilled in them. Therefore: “Wonderful are the swellings of the sea; wonderful is the Lord on high. ‘So that in me,’ he says, ‘you may have peace, but in the world you will have tribulation.’”

What, then, shall we do? The sea rages, the waves rise up, and the furious waves roar; we suffer tribulations. Shall we perhaps fail? Certainly not. “Wonderful is the Lord on high.”

Indeed, when he said, “so that in me you may have peace, but in the world you will have tribulation,” as though they might say, “Surely the world will not crush us and destroy us?”, he immediately added: “But rejoice, because I have overcome the world” (John XVI, 33).

If he therefore says, “I have overcome the world,” cling to the one who overcame the world, who overcame the sea. Rejoice in him, because “wonderful is the Lord on high,” and “your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy.”

And what has become of all these things? “Holiness befits your house, O Lord.” Your whole house—not this part, or that part, or another part, but your entire house throughout the whole world. Why throughout the whole world? Because he “corrected the inhabited world, which shall not be moved” (Ps. XCV, 10).

The house of the Lord will be strong; it will be throughout the whole world. Many will fall, but that house stands; many will be troubled, but that house will not be moved. “Holiness befits your house, O Lord”—not for a short time. “For length of days.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XCIII

### SERMON

[Note: Delivered in another diocese at the request of a gathering of bishops, as can be understood from the conclusion.]

1. Just as we listened with the greatest attention when this Psalm was read, so let us listen attentively while the Lord reveals the mysteries that he has deigned to conceal here. For certain secrets of Scripture are closed, not so that they may be denied, but so that they may be opened to those who knock. If, then, you knock with devout feeling and sincere love of heart, he will open who sees from what motive you knock (Matt. VII, 7).

It is known to all of us—and would that we were not among their number—that many murmur against God’s patience and grieve that wicked and impious people either live in this world or even possess great power. What is more, they often possess great power against the good, and frequently the wicked oppress the good; the wicked exult while the good labor; the wicked are proud while the good are humbled.

Observing such things in the human race—and they are abundant—impatient and weak souls are perverted, as though it were useless to be good, because God turns away, or seems to turn away, his eyes from the good works of the devout and faithful [Col. 1190] and increases the wicked in the things they love.

Supposing, then, in their weakness, that it is useless for them to live well, they are either invited to imitate the wickedness of those whom they see flourishing, as it were; or, if through weakness of person or spirit they fear to do evil lest something evil befall them according to the laws of this world, they abstain from evil deeds—not because they love justice, but, to put it more plainly, because they fear being condemned among human beings by human beings. Yet they do not abstain from evil thoughts.

Among their unjust thoughts, that impiety especially occupies the chief place by which they seem to themselves to believe that God neglects and does not care about human affairs, and either treats good and evil alike—or, what is more pernicious to think, persecutes the good and favors the evil.

Whoever thinks such things, even if he does no evil to anyone, does great harm to himself and is impious toward himself; by his iniquity he does not injure God, but kills himself. Such people do not harm others because they are timid, yet God sees their murders, their adulteries, their frauds and robberies, and punishes them in their thoughts.

For he observes what they desire, whose eye is not obstructed by flesh so that it fails to see the will. If such people find opportunities, they do not become evil but are revealed as evil—not so that you may suppose that something then came into existence which became manifest, but so that you may understand what had been hidden within [Note: Erasmus, Venice, and Louvain read “what was.” M.].

A few years ago, almost yesterday, people saw these things, and even those who are slow to understand recognized them. There was here, for a time, a very powerful household, by which God had made a scourge for the human race; and the human race was chastised through it—if only it would recognize the scourge of a father and fear the sentence of a judge.

When that same great household was here, many groaned under it, murmured, criticized, detested, and blasphemed it. How people are constrained, and how many are handed over by that divine judgment to the desires of their hearts (Rom. I, 24)! Suddenly those who had murmured against that household became its own members [Note: So read the manuscripts of good authority. The editions have: “Suddenly they overthrew that household itself.”]; and people suffered at their hands the very things of which, shortly before, they had complained that they themselves suffered at the hands of such men.

Good, therefore, is the person who, even when he has the power to do harm, does not do so. Of him it is written: “Who could have transgressed, and did not transgress; and could have done evil, and did not do it. Who is he? We shall praise him. For he did wonders in his life” (Ecclus. XXXI, 10, 9).

Scripture was speaking of powerful men who were innocent. For the wolf desires to harm as much as the lion does. They harm differently, but they do not desire differently. The lion not only disregards a barking dog, but also drives it away, comes to the sheepfold, and, when the dogs have been silenced, seizes whatever it can. The wolf does not dare to do so amid the barking of the dogs.

Does it follow that, because it could not take anything from the dogs, frightened by them, it returned more innocent? God therefore teaches innocence, so that each person may be innocent not from fear of punishment, but from love of justice. Then the innocent person is free, and is truly innocent.

But whoever becomes innocent through fear is not innocent, although he does not harm the person whom he wishes to harm. For he does not harm another through an evil deed, but harms himself greatly through evil desire. Hear Scripture on how he harms himself: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X, 6).

And indeed people greatly err when they suppose that their injustice harms others but does not harm themselves. Anyone’s iniquity extends to another in order to injure his body, damage his property, invade his estate, carry off his slave, take away his gold or silver, or whatever else he possesses [Note: Louvain reads: “or whatever else he may be able to possess.” The other books read: “or whatever else he possesses.”].

That iniquity is therefore brought against another. Your iniquity harms another’s body, but does it not harm your own soul?

## 2.

Against this simple and truthful teaching—which urges good people to love justice itself and to desire to please God by means of it, and to understand that their soul is suffused by a certain intelligible light so that they may do what is just and prefer that light of wisdom to everything loved in this world [Note: [Col. 1191] The manuscripts read *ab illa* (“from/by that [feminine]”).]—there arise murmurs of the following kind among people; and even if they do not come forth in speech, they gnaw at the heart.

What do they say? “Am I really going to please God through justice? Or does he approve of the just, under whose rule the wicked flourish? They commit such great evils, and nothing bad happens to them.” Or, if some evil does happen, what do they say to you when you begin to tell them, “Look at how much evil he committed; how it was repaid to him; what an end he came to”? They begin to think of just people who have suffered misfortune, and set them against us, saying: “If something bad happened to that man because he was wicked, why did it happen to the other, who lived so justly? He gave so much alms; he performed so many good works in the Church. Why did he meet with such a fate? Why did he come to such an end, like that man who committed so many injustices?”

They say these things to show that they do not do evil because they are unable—or because they do not dare—to do so. For what the heart desires, the tongue reveals. Indeed, even if the tongue were silent, and were itself restrained by fear, God would see what a person was thinking within, even if it were hidden from another human being.

This psalm addresses such silent thoughts of people—or even such thoughts when they burst forth in words or deeds—if they are willing to be healed. Let them therefore pay attention and be healed. And would that in this entire multitude now gathered within these walls, hearing through us the word of the Lord, there were no such wounds requiring treatment—would that there were none! Yet it is not pointless to speak of the matter even if there are no wounds there. Let hearts be instructed, so that they may heal others when they begin to hear such things.

For I believe that every Christian who hears someone speaking in this way—if he is a good and faithful believer, if he believes rightly in God, and if his hope is in the future age rather than in this earth or this life, and if he does not listen in vain when told to have his heart above—laughs at and grieves over those who murmur in this way, and says to himself: “God knows what he is doing. We cannot know his purpose: why he spares the wicked for a time, or why the good suffer for a time. Yet this is enough for me to know: the good suffers for a time, and the wicked flourishes for a time.”

Whoever is such a person is secure. He patiently endures all the prosperity of the wicked, and patiently bears and tolerates the sufferings of the good, until this age comes to an end, until iniquity passes away. Such a person is already blessed; God has instructed him from his law and has calmed him during the evil days, until the pit is dug for the sinner.

But whoever is not yet such a person should hear through us what pleases the Lord. Let him himself say more within his heart—he who sees more clearly the wound requiring treatment.

## 3.

This psalm bears the following title, that is, this inscription: “A Psalm to David himself, on the fourth day of the week” [Note: [Col. 1192] The manuscripts read this way. The editors here have *sabbati* (“of the Sabbath”); afterward, however, they agree with the manuscripts.].

This psalm is going to teach patience amid the sufferings of the righteous; against the prosperity of the wicked it teaches and builds up patience. This is its meaning throughout, from beginning to end.

Why, then, does it bear the title “on the fourth day of the week”? The first day of the week is the Lord’s Day; the second day is the second weekday, which secular people call Monday; the third day is the third weekday, which they call Tuesday. The fourth day of the week, therefore, is the fourth weekday, which pagans and many Christians call “Mercury’s day.” But we would not wish them to do so; would that they corrected themselves and did not speak in this way. They have their own language, which they ought to use.

For these names are not used in every nation either: many other peoples call the days by different names, in one way or another. It is therefore better that an ecclesiastical manner of speaking proceed from a Christian mouth. Nevertheless, if habit has perhaps carried someone along so that something emerges from his mouth which his heart rejects, let him understand that all those after whom the heavenly bodies were named were human beings, and that these stars did not first begin to exist in heaven when those men began to exist. They were there earlier. But, through certain honors bestowed by mortals upon mortals, those men—who in their own time had great power and prominence in this world—were accorded divine honors, because they were dear to human beings, not on account of eternal life but on account of temporal advantage.

For the deceived men of ancient times [Note: [Col. 1192] This is the reading of Am. and the manuscripts, with a few exceptions reading “the men deceived by the age.” Erasmus and Lov. read “the ancient seers, being deceived.”], and those who wished to deceive others, in flattery of people who had provided them with some benefit according to the love of this world, pointed out stars in the sky, saying that this star belonged to one man and that one to another. But people who had not previously looked up, so as to see that those stars had been there before the men were born, were deceived and believed them; and an opinion of vanity was formed.

The devil confirmed this erroneous belief; Christ overturned it.

Accordingly, according to the way we speak, “on the fourth day of the week” means the fourth day counted from the Lord’s Day. Let Your Charity therefore pay attention to what this title signifies. Here there is a great mystery, and truly a hidden one. For most of the psalm’s words have an evident meaning, plainly move us, and are quickly understood. This title, however—as must be admitted—contains no small degree of obscurity. But the Lord will be present; he will clear away the cloud, and you will see the psalm and recognize it from the front of the psalm.

For at its front this psalm bears the words: “A Psalm to David himself, on the fourth day of the week.” The title is at the threshold; it is fixed upon the doorposts. People wish to know the title and then enter the house.

Let us therefore recall the Holy Scripture in Genesis. On the first day, what do we find was made? Light. On the second day, what do we find was made? The firmament, which God called heaven. On the third day, what do we find was made? The appearance of the earth and the sea, and the separation by which the whole gathering of the waters was called the sea, while the dry land was called earth. On the fourth day God made the luminaries in heaven (Gen. 1:3–19): the sun to rule the day, and the moon and stars to rule the night (Ps. 135:8–9). This he made on the fourth day.

What, then, does it mean that the psalm received its title from the fourth day—a psalm that teaches patience in the face of the prosperity of the wicked and the sufferings of the good?

You have the apostle Paul speaking to holy believers strengthened in Christ: “Do everything without murmuring and disputing, so that you may be blameless and sincere [Note: [Col. 1193] This is the reading of Am., Erasmus, and all our manuscripts. Lov. has *sinceri* (“sincere,” masculine plural).], spotless children of God in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like luminaries in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. 2:14–16).

The comparison with the luminaries is applied to the saints, so that they may be without murmuring in a crooked and perverse nation.

## 4.

But lest anyone therefore suppose that the luminaries of heaven ought to be worshiped and adored, because a comparison has been drawn from them to signify the saints, let us first explain in the name of Christ why it does not follow that the sun, moon, stars, or heaven should therefore seem worthy of worship by you merely because some comparison has been drawn from them by which the saints are signified. Many things have supplied comparisons for signifying the saints, yet they are not worshiped.

For if you think that whatever supplies a comparison for the saints ought to be worshiped, then worship the mountains and hills, because it is said: “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep” (Ps. 113:4). You are speaking about the saints; I am speaking about Christ himself. Worship the lion, because it is said, “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. 5:5). Worship the rock, because it is said, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4).

But if you do not worship these earthly things in Christ, although a comparison has been drawn from them, then, whenever a comparison has been drawn from any creature to signify the saints, understand the comparison as belonging to the creature, and worship the maker of the creature.

Our Lord Jesus Christ is called the sun (Wis. 5:6). Is this the sun which even the smallest animals see together with us? No; it is the one of whom it was said: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). For that light does not illuminate only human beings; it illuminates beasts, cattle, and every animal as well. But when it says that he illuminates every human being, it means that he illuminates the heart, where alone understanding is found.

## 5.

Let Your Charity understand that, when the Apostle said, “in a crooked and perverse nation”—that is, among the wicked—“among whom you shine like luminaries in the world, holding fast the word of life,” he in a certain way urged us both to understand this psalm and to anticipate its title.

For such are the saints who possess the word of life. From the manner of life they have in heaven, they look down upon all the wicked things done on earth. And just as the luminaries in heaven proceed by day and by night, completing their courses and following their appointed paths, while such great evils are committed and the fixed stars in heaven do not deviate from above as they travel through the heavenly regions which their Creator prescribed and appointed for them [Col. 1194], so the saints ought to act—provided their hearts are fixed in heaven; provided they do not hear and answer “we have our hearts above” in vain; provided they imitate the one who says, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

Because they are therefore in the heights and think about the things above, as it is said, “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matt. 6:21), they become patient through these thoughts of heavenly things. Whatever is committed on earth, they disregard in the same way that the luminaries of heaven disregard it, except insofar as they carry out the courses of day and night, although they see such great evils being done upon the earth.

It may perhaps be easy for the righteous to bear the wickedness of the wicked when it is not done against them personally. But just as they bear what is done against others, so let them also bear what is done against themselves. They ought not to endure and tolerate such things merely because they are done against others; and if they are done against them, they ought not to lose their endurance.

For whoever loses endurance has fallen from heaven. But whoever keeps his heart fixed in heaven has his earthly part laboring on earth. How many things do people invent even about the luminaries, and how patiently do the luminaries endure them? In the same way the righteous ought patiently to bear even all the false accusations made against them.

This very thing I mentioned earlier: when I say that one star belongs to Mercury, another to Saturn, and another to Jupiter, I am insulting the stars. What then? When they hear such great insults, are they moved, or do they not continue their courses? So too the person who has the word of God in a perverse and crooked nation is like a luminary shining in heaven [Note: [Col. 1194] Two manuscripts read this way. Others, with the editions, read “in the world.”].

How many people who think they honor the sun speak falsely about it? Those who say, “Christ is the sun,” speak falsely about the sun. The sun knows that Christ is its Lord and Creator. And if it could become indignant, it would be more bitterly indignant against the one who falsely honors it than against the one who insults it. For to a good servant an injury against his master is a greater insult.

How many false things do some people say about the luminaries themselves? They endure, tolerate, and are not moved. Why? Because they are in heaven.

But what is heaven? We must not pass over this either. How many lies do people tell when they see the moon becoming dark and say, “Sorcerers are bringing it down,” even though it undergoes its eclipse at fixed times according to God’s arrangement? Yet the moon in heaven does not concern itself with these human words.

But what does “in heaven” mean? It means “in the firmament of heaven.” Therefore the person whose heart is in the firmament of God’s book does not concern himself with such things.

## 6.

For heaven—that is, the firmament—is understood figuratively as the Book of the Law. Therefore it is said in one place: “He stretched out heaven like a skin” (Ps. 103:2). If it is stretched out like a skin, it is stretched out like a book, so that it may be read.

But when the time has passed, it is not read [Note: [Col. 1194] Erasmus, Venetus, and Lov. read: “for the time during which the law is read has therefore passed.” M.]. The Law is read because we have not yet come to that Wisdom which fills the hearts and minds of those who behold it; and then there will be no need for anything to be read to us there.

For in what is read to us, syllables sound and pass away. That light of truth does not pass away; remaining fixed, it fills the hearts of those who behold it, as it is said: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delights; for with you, Lord, is the fountain of life. And look at the fountain itself: ‘In your light,’ he says, ‘we shall see light’” (Ps. 35:9–10).

For now, therefore, reading is necessary, as long as we know in part and prophesy in part, as the Apostle says: “But when what is perfect has come, what is in part will be abolished” (1 Cor. 13:9–10). [Note: [Col. 1195] At this point Am. adds *legemus* (“we shall read”); other printed editions add, “a book will be necessary, nor shall we read,” which is absent from the manuscripts.] For in that city, Jerusalem, where the angels live, from which we are now exiles, and where our exile groans—though it groans only if we know that we are in exile, for the person who thinks he is well off while in exile hates his homeland greatly—is the Gospel read? Is the Apostle read? They are nourished by the Word of God. And that Word of God, so that it might sound to us for a time, “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

Nevertheless, the written Law itself is our firmament. If our heart is there, it is not shaken by the iniquities of human beings [Note: [Col. 1195] The better manuscripts read *non convellitur* (“is not shaken”); others, with Am. and Er., read *compellitur* (“is compelled”); Lov. reads *impellitur* (“is driven”).].

Thus it is said: “He stretched out heaven like a skin.” But when the times requiring books have passed, what is said? “Heaven will be rolled up like a book” (Isa. 34:4).

Whoever therefore has his heart above is himself a luminary: his heart shines in heaven and is not overcome by darkness. For darkness is below. But darkness is iniquity, not an unchangeable darkness. We mentioned this yesterday as well. Those who are darkness today can, if they wish, be light tomorrow; those who entered here as darkness can, if they wish, already become light.

The Apostle plainly said this, lest anyone think that iniquities are natural and cannot be changed: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light” (Eph. 5:8). He says, “light in the Lord,” not in yourselves.

Therefore, the heart is in the book; if the heart is in the book, the heart is in the firmament of heaven. If the heart is there, let it shine from there, and it will not be moved by the iniquities beneath it—not because it is in heaven according to the flesh, but because it is there according to its manner of life, as it is said: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

You cannot conceive of that city, because you do not yet see it. Do you wish to conceive of heaven? Think of the book of God. Hear the psalm: “And on his law he will meditate day and night.” And there the blessed person is described as one who “has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence; but his delight was in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 1:1–2).

Look at the luminary in heaven: “And on his law he will meditate day and night.” Does he wish to bear everything patiently? Let him not descend from heaven, and let him meditate on the law day and night.

Therefore his heart is in heaven. If his heart is in heaven, then all the iniquities committed on earth for a time, all the prosperity of wicked people, and all the sufferings of the righteous are nothing to the person who meditates on God’s law day and night. He patiently endures everything and will be blessed, instructed by God.

And how is he in the firmament of heaven? Because the Law is the firmament.

“Blessed is the man whom you instruct, Lord, and teach from your law, so that you may calm him during the evil days, until the pit is dug for the sinner.”

Pay attention, then, to how the luminaries proceed, set, and return; how they complete their courses, distinguish day from night, and turn the years and seasons, while such great evils are done on earth and they remain at rest in heaven [Col. 1196].

What, then, is God teaching us? Let us now attend to the psalm.

## 7. [verse 1]

“God of vengeance, Lord, God of vengeance has acted boldly.”

You think that he does not avenge? The God of vengeance does avenge. What does “God of vengeance” mean? The God of retribution.

You murmur because the wicked are not punished. Do not murmur, lest you be among those against whom vengeance is taken.

He commits theft and lives; you murmur against God because the man who stole from you does not die. If you no longer steal, consider carefully: for if you no longer do so, see whether you perhaps once did. If you are now day, remember your night. If you are now fixed in heaven, remember your earth.

Perhaps you discover that you were once a thief; and perhaps someone else was angry because you lived while committing theft and did not die. But just as you lived when you were committing theft so that afterward you might cease to do so, do not, because you have passed beyond it, wish to destroy the bridge of God’s mercy. Do you not know that many will cross by the path along which you crossed?

Would you now be the one murmuring if the man who first murmured against you were heard against you? And yet even now you desire God’s vengeance upon the wicked, so that the thief may die, and you murmur against God because the thief does not die.

Place the thief and the blasphemer on the scales of justice. You say now that you are not a thief; but by murmuring against God you are a blasphemer.

The thief watches for a person to fall asleep so that he may steal something; and you say that God is asleep and does not see the person. So you want him to correct his hand? First correct your tongue. You want him to correct his heart against a human being? Correct your heart against God, lest, when you desire God’s vengeance, it should come and find you first.

For he will come; he will come and judge those who persist in their wickedness, ungrateful for his merciful forbearance, ungrateful for his patience, “storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2:4–6).

Because God is the Lord of vengeance, the God of vengeance has therefore acted boldly.

For he spared no one when he spoke here. He himself was the Lord in the weakness of the flesh, but in the power of his word. He did not show partiality to the leaders of the Jews. How many things he says against them! And, as it is said [Note: [Col. 1196] This is the reading of Am. and the manuscripts. Lov. has: “as it is said, ‘he acted boldly’? Truly, with confidence.” Erasmus and Lov. read: “as it is said, ‘boldly’? He acted truly with confidence.” M.], truly with confidence, because it is written of him in the Psalms: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord.”

Who are the poor? Who are the needy? Those who have no hope except in him alone, in whom alone hope is not deceived.

Pay attention, brothers, to who the poor and needy are. Scripture does not always seem to mean people who possess nothing when it praises the poor. For you may find a poor man who, whenever he suffers some injustice, looks only to his patron, in whose house he perhaps lives, whose tenant he is, whose dependent or client he is; and he therefore declares that he is suffering unjustly because he belongs to that patron. His heart is in a human being, his hope is in a human being—ashes in ashes.

But there are others who are wealthy and are supported for a time by human honors; yet they place their hope neither in their money, nor in their estates, nor in their household, nor in the glory of a passing dignity. They place all their hope in him who has no successor, who cannot die, who can neither be deceived nor deceive. Such people, even if they seem to possess much according to the standards of this age, nevertheless manage it well for the refreshment of those in need; they are counted among the poor of the Lord.

They see that they live dangerously in this life and recognize that they are exiles. Thus they dwell amid the abundance of their riches as a traveler dwells in an inn: intending to pass through, not to possess.

What, then, does the Lord say? “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord: I will place him in salvation.” Our salvation is our Savior; he wished to place in him the hope of all the needy and destitute [Note: [Col. 1197] This is the reading of the manuscripts. The editions have: “the hope and groaning of all the needy.”].

And what does he say? “I will act confidently in him” (Ps. 11:6).

What does “I will act confidently” mean? He will not fear; he will not spare the vices and desires of human beings. Truly, he was a faithful physician, equipped with the medicinal blade of his word; he cut away all wounds. Therefore the one who was foretold and announced in this way was also found to be such.

He was speaking on the mountain, where he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” There he called blessed those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice; in that same discourse he said, “For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And in order to make them luminaries—that is, people who patiently endure all these passing iniquities—he said: “You will be blessed when they persecute you and say every evil against you. Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. 5:3, 10–12).

Then, as his discourse proceeded and he began to teach, although the crowd surrounded him, he said things to his disciples that struck at the face of the Pharisees and Jews. These people possessed—or thought they possessed—the authority to interpret all the Scriptures; they seemed, or believed themselves, to be just, and the obedience of the people appeared to conform to their authority.

He did not spare them. He said: “When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, who love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the corners of the streets, so that they may be seen by people” (Matt. 6:5), and other things of this kind. He touched them all; he feared no one.

When he had brought that discourse to an end, the Gospel concludes its account of it in this way: “When Jesus had finished these words, the crowds were astonished at his teaching. For he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. 7:28–29).

How many things did that man say of whom it was said, “He was teaching them as one having authority”: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!” (Matt. 23:13 and following); how many things did he say directly to their faces? He feared no one.

Why? Because he is the God of vengeance.

Therefore he did not spare them in his speech, so that afterward there might be people whom he would spare in judgment. For if they were unwilling to accept the medicine of the word, they were certainly going to encounter and experience the sentence of the Judge. Why? Because it says: “God of vengeance, Lord, God of vengeance has acted boldly”—that is, he spared no one in his word.

He who did not spare in his word when he was about to suffer—will he spare in his sentence when he comes to judge? He who feared no one in his humiliation—will he fear anyone in his glory?

From the fact that he has already acted boldly, consider how he will act at the end of the age. Do not therefore murmur against God, who seems to spare the wicked. Be good, so that he may perhaps not spare you for a time in chastisement, but spare you at the end in judgment.

“God of vengeance, Lord, God of vengeance has acted boldly.”

## 8. [verse 2]

And because he acted boldly, they did not tolerate his confidence; and because he had come in humility, clothed in mortal flesh, and had come to die—not to do what sinners do, but to suffer what sinners do—because he had come for this purpose, and because, after acting boldly, they could not bear his confidence in speech, what did they do?

They seized him, flogged him, mocked him, struck him with blows, smeared him with spittle, crowned him with thorns, lifted him upon the cross, and finally killed him.

But what follows, showing that he acted boldly? “Rise up, you who judge the earth. Repay the proud according to their deserts.”

Suppose that they seized him in his humility. Will they seize him in his exaltation? Suppose that they judged a mortal. Will they not be judged by the immortal?

What, then, does he say? “Rise up”—you who acted boldly, whose confidence in speech the wicked could not endure, and who thought they had accomplished something because they seized and crucified you. Those who ought to have seized you by faith seized you through persecution. You therefore who acted boldly among the wicked, who feared no one, and who suffered: “Rise up”—that is, rise again and go into heaven.

Let the Church also patiently endure what the head of the Church patiently endured.

“Rise up, you who judge the earth; repay the proud according to their deserts.”

He will repay them, brothers. For what does the saying mean, “Rise up, you who judge the earth; repay the proud according to their deserts”? It is the prophecy of one foretelling, not the audacity of one issuing a command.

It was not because the Prophet said, “Rise up, you who judge the earth,” that Christ obeyed the Prophet by rising and going into heaven. Rather, because Christ was going to do this, the Prophet foretold it. Christ did not do it because the Prophet had foretold it; the Prophet foretold it because Christ was going to do it.

He sees Christ in humility by the Spirit; he sees him humble, fearing no one and sparing no one in speech, and he says: “He acted boldly.” He sees how boldly he acted; he sees him seized, crucified, humbled, rising again, going into heaven, and coming from there to judge those among whose hands he suffered every evil. “Rise up,” he says, “you who judge the earth; repay the proud according to their deserts.”

He will repay the proud, not the humble.

Who are the proud? Those for whom it is not enough to do evil and who also wish to defend their sins.

Indeed, miracles were later performed among those who had crucified Christ, when some from that very number came to believe, and Christ’s blood was granted to them. They carried impious and bloodstained hands, stained with Christ’s blood; the very one whose blood they had shed washed those hands. They were joined to his body—that is, to the Church—although they had persecuted his mortal body, which they had seen. They poured out their price so that they might drink their price.

For many of them were later converted. When many miracles were performed by the Apostles, several thousand people believed in a single day [Col. 1199]. They were found so close to one another that they sold everything they possessed and placed the proceeds of their property at the feet of the Apostles; it was distributed to each according to his need, and they were of one soul and one heart toward God. They came from among those who had crucified the Lord [Note: [Col. 1199] Three manuscripts add here: “they were.”].

But why was retribution not rendered to them? Because it was said, “Repay the proud according to their deserts,” whereas they refused to be proud.

When they saw many miracles being performed through the name of Christ, whom they thought they had killed, they were moved by the miracles and heard from Peter in whose name they were performed. For the servants did not wish to claim their master’s power for themselves by saying that what he was doing in them had been done by them. They therefore gave honor to their Lord as servants. They said that the things they marveled at were being done in the name of the one whom they had crucified.

And they became humble; they were pierced in their hearts; they were troubled and confessed their sin; and they sought counsel, saying: “What, then, shall we do?” They did not despair of salvation but sought medicine.

Then Peter said to them: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 2; 4). Those who repented were humble; therefore retribution was not rendered to them.

For see what this psalm says: “Rise up, you who judge the earth; repay the proud according to their deserts.” Those people were therefore excluded from that number. In them the voice of the Lord hanging on the cross prevailed: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

“Rise up, you who judge the earth; repay the proud according to their deserts.”

Will he therefore repay them? He will repay them—but the proud.

## 9. [verses 3–4]

But when? When will he repay them?

Meanwhile the wicked triumph, the wicked exult, the wicked blaspheme, and they do every evil. Does this trouble you? Ask with devotion; do not criticize with pride.

Does this trouble you? The psalm sympathizes with you and asks along with you—not because it does not know, but because it asks with you precisely because it knows, so that in it you may find what you did not know.

When someone wishes to console another person, he does not raise him up unless he grieves with him. First he grieves with him, and then he restores him through consoling speech. But if he enters laughing at the other’s grief, he does not do what was just read, when the Apostle says: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15).

Therefore, in order to rejoice with you, he first weeps with you. He grieves with you in order to restore you. So too the psalm—and the Spirit of God, who certainly knows everything—asks with you, as though it were speaking your own words:

“How long, Lord, how long will sinners exult? They answer and speak iniquity; all who practice injustice speak?”

What will they speak except against God, when they say: “What benefit is it to us that we live in this way?” Because they live, they think that God does not know what they are doing.

See what evil befalls them! If a stationarius knew, he would seize them; and for that reason they avoid the eyes of the stationarius, lest they immediately be arrested. But no one can avoid the eyes of God, because he sees not only in your chamber but also the innermost parts of your heart.

They themselves think that nothing can be hidden from God; and because they do these things, know what they have done, and see that they are living while God knows, though they would not live if a stationarius knew, they say to themselves: “These things please God.”

And indeed, if our deeds displeased him as they displease judges, kings, emperors, and commentarienses, just as we avoid the eyes of those authorities, could we avoid the eyes of God? Therefore, these things please God.

For this reason, in another psalm it is said to the sinner: “You have done these things, and I was silent; you thought that I would be like you in wickedness” (Ps. 49:21).

What does “I would be like you” mean? It means: “Just as your evil deed pleases you, so you think it pleases me.”

And he threatens what will happen later: “I will reprove you.”

Therefore the one who said, “I was silent,” is not silent. When he said, “You have done these things, and I was silent; you thought that I would be like you,” he did not remain silent [Note: [Col. 1200] Erasmus, Venetus, and Lov. read: “When he says, ‘You have done these things …’ he is not silent.” M.].

When we speak, he is not silent; when the reader reads, he is not silent; when the psalm sings these words, he is not silent. All these voices of God are heard throughout the world.

How, then, is he silent, and how is he not silent? He is not silent in his word; he is silent in his vengeance.

What, then, does “You have done these things, and I was silent” mean? “You have done these things, and I did not punish you.”

“You thought that I would be like you in wickedness.” Concerning this silence of vengeance—that is, the suspension of punishment—he says elsewhere: “I have been silent; shall I always be silent?” (Isa. 42:14).

“How long, Lord, how long will sinners exult? They answer and speak iniquity; all who practice injustice speak?”

And he says that they perform all their works: “They answer and speak iniquity.”

What does “they answer” mean? They have something to say against the righteous person.

A righteous person comes and says: “Do not commit iniquity.”

“Why?”

“So that you may not die.”

“Look: I have committed iniquity. Why do I not die? He committed justice, and he died. Why did he die? I committed iniquity; why did God not take me away? Look, he practiced justice; why did God punish him in this way? Why does he suffer in this way?”

They answer; that is, they answer because they have something to say. Because they are spared, they find in God’s patience an argument for their response.

He spares them for one reason; they answer him for another, because they live.

Why he spares them, the Apostle explains by setting forth the purpose of God’s patience: “Do you suppose, you who do such things, that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s patience leads you to repentance?”

But you—that is, the person who answers and says, “If I displeased God, God would not spare me”—see what he is doing to himself. Hear the Apostle:

“But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2:3–6).

He increases his patience, and you increase your iniquity [Col. 1201].

His treasure will be found in everlasting mercy toward those who have not despised mercy; but your treasure will be found in wrath. What you put away little by little each day, you will later find as a mass. You put it away bit by bit, but you will find a heap.

Do not pay attention only to your small daily sins. Rivers are filled from tiny drops.

## 10. [verses 5–6]

What, then, do those people do who answer and speak iniquity because they commit sins and are spared?

“They have humbled your people, Lord”—that is, all who live justly, against whom all the wicked wish to exalt themselves.

“They have humbled your people, Lord, and afflicted your inheritance. They have killed the widow and the orphans, and murdered the proselyte”—that is, the foreigner, the stranger, the newcomer; this is what he calls the proselyte.

Each of these matters is clear, and there is no need to linger over them.

### 11. [verse 7]

And they said, “The Lord will not see.” He does not pay attention to these things; he neglects them; he cares about other matters; he does not understand. For these are the two voices of the wicked. One is the voice I have already mentioned: “You did these things, and I kept silent; you supposed that I was altogether like you” [Ps. 49:21]. What does “that I was altogether like you” mean? You think that I see your deeds and that they please me, because I do not punish them.

The other is the voice of the wicked: “God neither pays attention to these things nor takes notice, so as to know how I live; God does not care about me.” Does God then count me among anything? Or does God really number me? Or does he number human beings at all? Unhappy man! Did he care that you should exist, but not that you should live well? Such, then, is the voice of these people. “And they said, ‘The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.’”

### 12. [verse 8]

“Understand now, you who are foolish among the people, and you fools, become wise at last.” He instructs his people, whose feet can be shaken when a person sees the prosperity of the wicked—someone who is already living well among the number of God’s saints, that is, among the number of the children of the Church. He sees that the wicked flourish and commit iniquity, envies them, and is led to imitate their deeds, because he sees that it seems to profit him nothing to live humbly and well while hoping here for a reward. For if he hopes for that reward in the future, he does not lose it, since the time has not yet come for him to receive it.

You work in a vineyard: do your work, and you will receive your wages. Would you demand wages from the master of the household before you had worked, and do you demand them from God before you have worked? This endurance also belongs to your work, and it belongs to your reward. You want to do less in the vineyard because you do not want to endure; yet endurance itself belongs to the work, so that you may receive the reward.

But if you are deceitful, beware lest you not only fail to receive the reward, but also encounter punishment, because you wanted to be a deceitful laborer. Indeed, when a deceitful laborer begins not to work well, he watches the eyes of the master of the household; he looks toward the one who hired him, so that when the master turns his eyes away he may stop and not work well, but when the master turns his eyes back he may work well. But God, who hired you, does not turn his eyes away. You are not permitted to work deceitfully: the eyes of the master of the household are always upon you. Seek a place where you can deceive him, and stop, if you can.

Therefore, if some of you were perhaps thinking something of this kind when you saw the wicked flourishing, and your thoughts were making your feet waver on the way of God, this psalm speaks to you. But if none of you is such a person, it speaks through you to others, saying: “Understand now,” because they said, “The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.” “Understand,” he says, “now, you who are foolish among the people, and you fools, become wise at last.”

### 13. [verses 9–10]

“He who planted the ear, will he not hear? Does the one who made the means by which you hear lack the means to hear? He who planted the ear, will he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not observe? He who instructs the nations, will he not reprove?”

Pay very close attention to this, my brothers: “He who instructs the nations, will he not reprove?” This is what God does: he instructs the nations. That is why he sent his Word throughout the world to human beings. He sent it through angels, through patriarchs, through prophets, through servants—through so many heralds who went before the Judge. He also sent his very Word; he sent his very Son. He sent the servants of his Son, and in those servants he sent his Son.

Throughout the whole world the word of God is preached everywhere. Where are people not told, “Abandon your former iniquities; turn yourselves toward the straight paths”? That is why he spares you: so that you may correct yourselves. That is why he did not punish yesterday: so that today you may live well.

“He instructs the nations; will he not then reprove? Will he not hear those whom he instructs? Will he not judge those to whom he has sent and sown forth his word?”

If you were in school, would you receive something and not give it back? Certainly, when you receive instruction from a teacher, you are educated; the teacher entrusts to you what he provides. Will he not demand it back when you return it? Or, when you begin to return it, will you be free from fear of blows?

Now, then, we receive; afterward we are placed before the teacher, so that we may render an account of all our past deeds [Note: Two manuscripts read “our past deeds.”], that is, so that we may render an account of all that is now being entrusted to us.

Hear the Apostle saying: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that there each one may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (Rom. 14:10; and 2 Cor. 5:10).

“He who instructs the nations, will he not reprove—he who teaches knowledge to human beings?” Does the one who made you know not know? “He who teaches knowledge to human beings?”

### 14. [verse 11]

“The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain.” For although you do not know the thoughts of God, because they are just, he knows the thoughts of human beings, because they are vain.

Human beings, too, have come to know the thoughts of God—but those to whom he has already become a friend, he reveals his counsel. And you, my brothers, must not despise yourselves. If you approach the Lord in faith, you hear the thoughts of God. You are learning them now; this is what is being said to you, and for this you are being instructed: to understand why God now spares the wicked, so that you may not murmur against God, who teaches human beings knowledge.

“The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain.” Abandon, then, the thoughts of human beings, which are vain, so that you may grasp the thoughts of God, which are wise.

But who is the one who grasps the thoughts of God? The one who is placed in the firmament of heaven. We have already sung this; we have already said and explained it.

### 15. [verses 12–13]

“Blessed is the man whom you instruct, Lord, and whom you teach from your law,” “so that you may give him relief from the evil days, until a pit is dug for the sinner” (Ps. 93:12–13).

Here you have God’s purpose in sparing the wicked: a pit is being dug for the sinner. You already want to bury him; the pit is still being dug for him. Do not hurry to bury him.

What does “until a pit is dug for the sinner” mean? Or whom does he call “the sinner”? One individual? No. What, then? The entire class of sinful people—but the proud, for he has already said, “Repay the proud according to what they deserve.”

The tax collector was also a sinner, the one who had fixed his eyes upon the ground and was beating his breast, saying, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” But because he was not proud, and because God will repay the proud according to what they deserve, the pit is dug not for him but for such people, until he repays the proud according to what they deserve.

Therefore, when he says, “until a pit is dug for the sinner,” understand “the proud.” Who is proud? The one who does not repent by confessing his sins, so that he may be healed through humility.

Who is proud? The one who wants to claim for himself even the few good things he seems to possess, and detracts from the mercy of God.

Who is proud? The one who, even if he attributes the good things he does to God, nevertheless insults those who do not do them and exalts himself above them.

For that Pharisee also said, “I give thanks to you”; he did not say, “I do these things.” He gave thanks to God for what he did; therefore he recognized both that he was doing good and that God enabled him to do it. Why, then, was he condemned? Because he insulted the tax collector.

Pay attention, so that you may be perfected. First, whether a man or a woman, there must be a confession of sins, a salutary repentance capable of correcting a person, not of mocking God. But when, after repentance, a person begins to live well, there is still something he must consider: he must not attribute to himself what he does well, but give thanks to the one by whose grace he came to live well, because he called him and enlightened him.

Is this person already perfect? No; something is still lacking. What is lacking? That he not become proud over those who do not yet live as he does.

Whoever is such a person may be secure. The repayment of which it is said, “Repay the proud according to what they deserve,” is not made to him; he is not among those for whom the pit is being dug.

For look at the one who said, “I give you thanks that I am not like the rest of humanity: unjust, rapacious, adulterous—or even like this tax collector.” How greatly he exalted himself when he said, “that I am not even like this tax collector”! But the other, his face humbled, was beating his breast and saying, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

The one was proud in his good deeds; the other was humble in his evil deeds. See, brothers: God was more pleased with humility amid evil deeds than with pride amid good deeds. Such is God’s hatred of the proud.

And so he concluded: “Truly I tell you, the tax collector went down justified rather than the Pharisee.” And he says why: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:10–14).

My brothers, from this alone we learn [Note: Most manuscripts read “we do not learn.” A few have “we do not say.”] that Christ taught us humility, because God became human. This is the humility that displeases the pagans, and for which they insult us: “What sort of God do you worship, who was born? What sort of God do you worship, who was crucified?”

The humility of Christ displeases the proud. But if it pleases you, Christian, imitate it. If you imitate it, you will not labor, because he himself said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:28–29).

This, then, is Christian discipline: no one does anything good except by his grace. What a person does badly belongs to the person himself; what he does well, he does by God’s favor. When he begins to do well, let him not attribute it to himself. When he has not attributed it to himself, let him give thanks to the one from whom he received it.

But when he does good, let him not insult the one who does not do it, nor exalt himself above him. For God’s grace has not come to an end in him, so that it cannot reach someone else.

### 16

“so that you may give him relief from the evil days, until a pit is dug for the sinner.”

Be gentle, then, whoever you are, Christian, in the evil days. The days are evil in which sinners seem to flourish while the righteous suffer. But the suffering of the righteous is the scourge of the Father, and the prosperity of sinners is their pit.

Because God gives you relief from the evil days until a pit is dug for the sinner, do not imagine that angels are now standing somewhere with mattocks, digging this great pit, large enough to hold every kind of wicked person. Do not say to yourselves in a fleshly way, when you see that there are many wicked people: “Indeed, what pit could hold such a multitude of wicked people, such a crowd of sinners? When will a pit capable of holding them all be dug? When will it be emptied?” That is why God spares them.

This is not the meaning. The pit of sinners is their very prosperity, for they will fall into it as into a pit.

Pay attention, brothers, for it is a great thing that prosperity should be called a pit: “until a pit is dug for the sinner.” God spares the person whom he knows to be a sinner and ungodly, according to his hidden justice. And God’s very act of sparing him makes him elated through impunity.

He thinks himself exalted, and he falls. He falls precisely in that by which he thinks himself exalted. He thinks that this is an exalted path, but God calls it a pit.

A pit leads downward, not toward heaven. Proud sinners, however, seem to go up toward heaven, and they are plunged into the earth. The humble, by contrast, seem to lower themselves toward the earth, and they ascend to heaven.

Be gentle, then, whoever you are who are faithful, if you have been instructed from the law of God, so that your heart may be in the firmament of heaven [the supplied text appears to read *cortuum*, evidently “your heart”]. For God made the luminaries on the fourth day, which is called the fourth day of the week, from which this psalm received its title.

As you see the luminaries, with complete patience, directing their courses and not caring what people say about them, so you too should not care whatever flesh may do to you. For every human being is flesh and blood.

You are not insignificant in comparison with the other flesh by which you appear to be oppressed, because for you he assumed flesh, and for you he shed blood—he who will bring both you and that other person to his judgment [Note: The American edition and our manuscripts lack the words “who will bring both you and that other person to his judgment.”]. And if he granted so much when you were ungodly, what does he reserve for the faithful?

From this learn gentleness. How do you become gentle? When you say: “Because God wills this, that is why the wicked flourish” [Note: The words “that is why the wicked flourish” are absent from the manuscripts and from the American edition.]. He wants to spare the wicked; he leads those whom he spares toward repentance, but they are not corrected. He knows how to judge them.

A person is harsh when he wants to contradict either the goodness of the Lord, his patience, his power, or the justice of the Judge.

The proud man rises up against God, and God plunges him down; and he is plunged down in the very thing by which he rises up against God. For in another psalm he says: “You cast them down while they were exalting themselves” (Ps. 72:18). He did not say, “You cast them down because they were exalted,” or “You cast them down after they had become exalted,” as though their exaltation occurred at one time and their downfall at another. Rather, in the very thing by which they were exalting themselves, they were being cast down.

For the more a human heart is proud, the farther it withdraws from God; and if it withdraws from God, it goes into the depths. By contrast, a humble heart brings God down from heaven, so that he becomes near.

Certainly God is exalted; God is above all the heavens; he surpasses all the angels. How much must you exalt yourself to reach that height? I do not want you to strain yourself by stretching upward, lest in that stretching you perhaps crack through pride. God is indeed exalted: humble yourself, and he will descend to you.

### 17. [verse 14]

We have heard why he spares the wicked: this very thing is their pit. God says to you: “How and why the pit is being dug for them is not yours to know. But learn from my law that you ought to be patient until a pit is dug for the sinner.”

“And what about me?” you ask. “I suffer, and I suffer among those very sinners.”

The answer given to you is what follows: “For the Lord will not reject his people.” He disciplines them; he does not reject them.

How does Scripture say elsewhere? “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). He receives the one who has been scourged, and you say that he rejects him?

We see people doing this with their children. Sometimes, when they have already despaired of their children, they let them live as they wish. Those in whom they still have hope they scourge; those whom they see to be entirely hopeless and untamable they leave to do whatever they want.

Now, the one whom a father allows to do what he wants, he does not wish to admit to his inheritance. But the son whom he scourges is the one for whom he preserves the inheritance.

When God scourges his son, let him run beneath the hand of the scourging Father, because the one who scourges instructs him for the inheritance. He does not reject from the inheritance his son whom he chastises; rather, he scourges him so that he may receive him.

Do not be so foolish and childish as to say: “My father loves my brother more, because he allows him to do whatever he wants. If I move against my father’s command, I encounter blows.”

Rejoice beneath the blows, because the inheritance is being preserved for you: “For the Lord will not reject his people.” He corrects them for a time; he does not condemn them forever. But he spares the others for a time and will condemn them forever.

Choose for yourself: do you want temporal suffering or eternal punishment? Temporal happiness or eternal life? What does God threaten? Eternal punishment. What does God promise? Eternal rest.

In the scourging of the good, it is temporal; in the sparing of the wicked, it is temporal. “For the Lord will not reject his people, and he will not abandon his inheritance.”

### 18. [verse 15]

“Until justice is turned into judgment,” he says, “and all who possess it are upright in heart.”

Pay attention now, and possess justice, because you cannot yet possess judgment. First you must possess justice; but that very justice of yours will be turned into judgment.

The apostles possessed justice here and endured the wicked. But what is said to them? “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Therefore their justice will be turned into judgment.

For now, whoever is righteous here is meant to suffer evil and endure it. Let him endure the time of suffering, and the day of judgment will come.

But what should I say about the servants of God? The Lord himself, who is judge of the living and the dead, first wished to be judged, and then to judge.

“Until justice is turned into judgment, and all who possess it are upright in heart.” Those who now possess justice do not yet judge. First comes possessing justice, and afterward judging; first one endures the wicked, and afterward judges the wicked. Let justice exist now; afterward it will be turned into judgment.

And he endures evil people for as long as God wills, for as long as the Church of God bears with them, so that it may be instructed through their wickedness.

Yet God will not reject his people until justice is turned into judgment, “and all who possess it are upright in heart.”

Who are upright in heart? Those who want what God wants. God spares sinners, but you want him already to destroy sinners. You are crooked in heart and perverse in will when you want one thing and God wants another.

But God wants to spare the wicked, while you do not want them spared. God is patient with sinners, while you do not want to tolerate sinners.

But, as I began to say, you want one thing and God wants another. Turn your heart and direct it toward God, because the Lord also had compassion on the weak.

He saw in his body, that is, in his Church, weak people who at first tried to follow their own will. But when they saw that God’s will was different, they would direct themselves and their hearts toward accepting and following the will of God [Note: Erasmus, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read “when they see” and shortly afterward “they direct.”].

Do not try to twist God’s will toward your own will; correct your own will according to God’s will.

God’s will is like a rule. Suppose you have bent a rule: from where can you be corrected? The rule itself remains whole, for it is unchangeable. As long as the rule remains whole, you have somewhere to turn and correct your crookedness; you have something by which to correct what has been bent in you.

But what do human beings want? It is not enough that they have a crooked will; they also want to make God’s will crooked according to their own heart, so that God may do what they want, when they themselves ought to do what God wants.

### 19

How, then, did the Lord embrace two wills as one in the human being whom he bore?

He prefigured in his body, that is, in his Church, certain future people who would want to do their own will but would afterward follow God’s will. He showed that certain weak people belonged to him and prefigured them in himself.

For this reason he also sweated blood from his whole body (Luke 22:44), because in his body, that is, in his Church, he displayed the blood of the martyrs. Blood flowed from his whole body; so the Church has its martyrs, and blood has been poured out throughout his entire body.

Thus, prefiguring certain weak people in himself—or in his body [Note: Erasmus, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read “that is” instead of “or.”]—and sympathizing with them in the person of the weak, he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”

He displayed the human will. If he had remained in that will, he would already seem to be displaying a crooked heart. But if he has had compassion on you and frees you in himself, imitate what follows, saying: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matt. 26:39).

If a human will begins to creep secretly upon you—“Oh, if only God would kill this enemy of mine, so that he would not persecute me! Oh, if only it could happen that I did not suffer so much from him!”—if you persist and this pleases you, and you see that God does not will it, you are crooked in heart. You do not possess the justice that will be turned into judgment; for all who possess it are upright in heart.

And who are upright in heart? Those who are found as Job was found, who said: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). Behold an upright heart.

Again, what did he say to his wife during his grievous wound? The devil had left her alive for this reason and had not killed her: so that he might have her as an accomplice, not as a wife’s comfort. For the devil remembered that Adam had been deceived through Eve (Gen. 3:6), and considered this Eve necessary to himself.

She approached Job like another Eve; but Adam was better victorious on the dunghill than Adam defeated in paradise [Note: The manuscripts read “Job.” The editions read “Adam.”]. What did he answer that woman? See a prepared heart; see an upright heart.

Was he not suffering persecutions, and grievous ones? All Christians suffer. Even if human beings do not rage, the devil rages. And even if Christians have become emperors, has the devil become a Christian?

Let your Holiness, then, pay attention to what an upright heart is. She approached him and said: “Say something against God, and die.” She enumerated all his own and her hardships: “Say something,” she said, “against God, and die.”

But he, now recognizing Eve and wishing to return from where he had fallen, with his heart fixed upon God like a luminary in the firmament and dwelling in his heart in the book of God, said: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil?” (Job 2:9–10).

Because his heart was fixed upon God, it was upright. Since God is upright, when you fix your heart upon him, let him be your model, so that your heart may be upright. Fix your heart, then, upon him, and your heart will be upright.

But the human will was secretly creeping upon you; something from the weakness of the flesh was perhaps casting its spell upon your mind [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “was throwing” instead of “was casting its spell.”]. Do not despair now. The Lord prefigured you in his own weakness, not himself. The Lord was not afraid to suffer, since he was going to rise again on the third day.

If he were going to suffer wholly as a human being and not as God, and if he knew that he would rise again after three days, he would in no way have feared dying—something the Apostle Paul did not fear, although he would rise again at the end of the age.

For he says: “I am hard pressed between the two: my desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:23–24). Remaining in the flesh was burdensome to him; he was torn between two desires. He said that departing and being with Christ was much better.

Indeed, when that very suffering drew near, how he exulted! How he gloried! “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will give me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:7–8).

The Apostle rejoices because he is to be crowned, while the one who will crown him is sorrowful. The Apostle rejoices in this way, and Christ our Lord says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”

But he assumed sorrow in the same way as he assumed flesh. Do not think that by saying this we deny that the Lord was sorrowful. If we were to say that he was not sorrowful, when the Gospel says, “My soul is sorrowful even to death” (Matt. 26:38–39), then when the Gospel says, “Jesus slept” (Matt. 8:24), Jesus did not sleep; and when the Gospel says, “Jesus ate” (Luke 14:1, etc.), Jesus did not eat.

A little worm of corruption creeps in and leaves nothing sound, so that one might say that his body was not real and that he did not possess true flesh. Therefore, brothers, whatever has been written about him happened; it is true.

Was he therefore sorrowful? Absolutely, he was sorrowful—but he assumed sorrow by his will, just as he assumed flesh by his will. Just as he assumed true flesh by his will, so he assumed true sorrow by his will.

Thus, by his will, he displayed this in himself, so that if human weakness should secretly creep upon you and begin to want something other than what God wants, you might see the crookedness of your heart outside the rule, fasten it to the rule, and direct toward God your heart, which had begun to become crooked in the human being.

Thus, displaying you in himself, the Lord said, “My soul is sorrowful even to death,” and he said, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” But immediately do what he did for this reason, to teach you: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father.”

For if you do this, you will possess justice. If you possess justice, your heart is upright. If your heart is upright, that justice which now endures will be turned into judgment. And afterward, when your Lord judges, you will not only cease to fear evils, but will also glory in the crown.

Then you will see [Note: One Corbie manuscript reads “then you will see”; the editions read “then you see.”] how the patience of God has profited either for their punishment or for your crown. For now you do not see; believe what you do not yet see, so that you may not be ashamed when you do see.

“Until justice is turned into judgment, and all who possess it are upright in heart.”

### 20. [verse 16]

“Who will rise up for me against the wicked? Or who will stand with me against those who practice iniquity?”

Many persuade people to many evils. The serpent does not cease to whisper, so that you may commit iniquity. Wherever you turn—perhaps, if you have made progress, you seek to live well with someone and scarcely find anyone—many wicked people surround you, because there are few grains and much chaff.

This threshing floor has its grain, but it is still being worked. When the whole mass has been separated from the chaff, it will be great. The grains are few in comparison with the chaff, but many in themselves.

When the wicked clamor on every side and say, “Why do you live this way? Are you the only Christian? Why do you not do what the others do? Why do you not look at how the others live? Why do you not use remedies and amulets? Why do you not consult astrologers and soothsayers, as the others do?”—you make the sign of the cross and say, “I am a Christian,” to drive away these people of some sort.

But the adversary presses and urges you. What is worse, he suffocates Christians by the example of Christians. The Christian soul sweats, burns, and is troubled. Yet it must conquer. But does it conquer by its own strength?

Therefore see what it says. It answers: “What benefit is it to me that I now use remedies and gain a few days? I leave this world and go to my Lord” [Note: The manuscripts read, “I leave this place and go to the Lord,” and so forth.], “and he will send me into the fire, because I preferred a few days of life to the future life; he will send me into hell.”

What hell? The hell of God’s eternal judgment.

Surely you do not think that God does not care how people live? Perhaps a friend does not say this to you in the street, but a wife says it at home—or perhaps a husband says it to his faithful and good wife, deceiving her.

If a woman says this to her husband, she is an Eve to him; if a man says it to his wife, he is a devil to her. Either she is an Eve to you, or you are a serpent to her.

Sometimes a father wants to turn his mind toward his son. He finds the son himself evil and utterly wicked. He burns, he is tossed about, he seeks a way to conquer him; he is almost swallowed up, almost gives his consent. But may God be present.

Hear, then, the psalm: “Who will rise up for me,” it says, “against the wicked?” They are so numerous; wherever I look, they meet me. Who will confront the prince of iniquity, the devil, and his angels, and the human beings seduced by him?

### 21. [verse 17]

“Unless the Lord had helped me,” he says, “my soul would almost have dwelt in hell.”

I had almost fallen into the pit prepared for sinners. This is what is meant by “my soul would almost have dwelt in hell.” For it was already wavering, already almost giving consent, when it turned its gaze toward the Lord.

Suppose, for example, that someone was being insulted in order to make him commit iniquity. Sometimes the wicked gather together and insult the good, especially if they are more numerous and seize upon one person, as much chaff is sometimes around a single grain. They will not be together once the mass has been winnowed.

That one person is caught among many wicked people, insulted, and surrounded. They want to rise above him; they harass him as though he were righteous and insult him precisely on account of his righteousness: “A great apostle!” they say. “You have flown up to heaven like Elijah.”

People do these things, so that sometimes, when he pays attention to human speech, a good person may be ashamed to be good among the wicked.

Let him therefore resist the wicked, but not by his own strength, lest he become proud when he wants to escape the proud and increase the number of the proud.

But what should he say? “Who will rise up for me against the wicked? Or who will stand with me against those who practice iniquity? Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell.”

### 22. [verses 18–19]

“If I said, ‘My foot has slipped,’ your mercy, Lord, was helping me.”

See how God loves confession. Your foot slips, and you do not say, “My foot has slipped”; instead, when you are already falling, you claim to be standing.

Rather, if you have already begun to slip, if you have already begun to waver, confess the slipping, so that you may not have to mourn the fall; let him help you, so that your soul may not be in hell.

God wants confession; he wants humility. You are afraid as a human being; he helps you as God. But say nevertheless, “My foot has slipped.”

Why have you already begun to slip, yet say, “I am standing”? “If I said, ‘My foot has slipped,’ your mercy, Lord, was helping me.”

How Peter presumed—not in his own strength! The Lord appeared to be walking upon the sea, trampling the heads of all the proud in this world. His walking upon the swollen waves signified his path of trampling the heads of the proud.

The Church also tramples them, for the Church is Peter. Yet Peter did not dare to walk upon the waters by himself. What did he say? “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.”

The Lord was acting by his authority; Peter by the Lord’s command. “Command me,” he said, “to come to you.” He answered, “Come.”

The Church, too, tramples the heads of the proud. But because the Church also possesses human weakness, so that the words “If I said, ‘My foot has slipped’” might be fulfilled, Peter began to totter in the sea and cried out: “Lord, I am perishing.”

Therefore, what is placed here—“If I said, ‘My foot has slipped’”—is there expressed as “Lord, I am perishing.” And what is placed here—“Your mercy, Lord, was helping me”—is there expressed as “Jesus stretched out his hand and said, ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’” (Matt. 14:25–31).

It is remarkable how God tests human beings: our very dangers make the one who delivers us sweeter to us.

For see what follows. Because he said, “If I said, ‘My foot has slipped,’ your mercy, Lord, was helping me,” the Lord was certainly made sweet to him by rescuing him from dangers. And so, explaining that very sweetness of the Lord, he cries out: “Lord, according to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul.”

Many are the sorrows, but many also the consolations; bitter are the wounds, but sweet the medicines.

### 23. [verse 20]

“Can the seat of iniquity be joined to you, you who form suffering into a commandment?”

He said this: “No wicked person sits with you, nor will you have a seat of iniquity.” And he gives the reason by which this may be understood: “You who form suffering into a commandment.”

“For from this I understand that the seat of iniquity is not joined to you: you have not spared us either.”
