You find this in the Epistle of the Apostle Peter, where he also cited testimony from Scripture: “It is time,” he says, “for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord,” that is, it is time for those who belong to the house of the Lord to be judged now.

“If the children are scourged, what should the most wicked servants expect?” Therefore he added: “But if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God?”

Then he adds that other testimony: “And if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Pet. 4:17–18).

How, then, will the wicked be with you, when you do not spare even your faithful, so that you may discipline and instruct them?

But because he does not spare them for this reason—that he may instruct them—he said, “You who form suffering into a commandment.”

For *forms* means “makes forms,” “shapes,” or “molds.” Hence potters are so called, and a vessel is called “formed” (*fictile*). It does not mean something fabricated as a lie, but something shaped so that it may exist and have a form.

Thus he said earlier, “He who formed the eye, will he not see?” Surely “he formed the eye” is not a lie; it means “he fashioned the eye,” “he made the eye.”

Is he not the potter when he makes fragile, weak, and earthly vessels [Note: The American, Erasmian, and our manuscripts read “earthly.” The Louvain edition, together with three of its manuscripts, reads “eternal”]? Hear the Apostle saying: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7).

But perhaps someone else made these vessels for us? Hear the same Apostle: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God? Shall what is formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:20–21).

See also the Lord Christ himself, because he showed himself to be a potter. For he had made the human being from clay (John 9:1–6).

Therefore, what he said—“Can the seat of iniquity be joined to you, you who form suffering into a commandment?”—let us express in this way: “Can the seat of iniquity be joined to you, you who shape suffering into a commandment?”

“You form,” he says, “suffering into a commandment,” that is, from suffering you make a commandment for us, so that suffering itself becomes a commandment for us.

How is suffering commanded to us? When the one who died for you scourges you, does not promise you blessedness in this life, cannot deceive you, and does not give you here what you seek.

What will he give? Where will he give it? How much will he give—the one who does not give it here, who instructs here, who forms suffering into a commandment?

Your labor is here, and rest is promised to you. You notice that you have labor here; but consider what kind of rest he promises.

Can you even imagine it? If you could imagine it, you would see that your labor amounts to nothing in comparison with it.

Hear the one who saw it partially, who said, “Now I know in part” (1 Cor. 13:12). What does the Apostle say? “For this slight, momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure—an incomparably great and eternal weight of glory.”

What does “it is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory” mean? For whom is it preparing it? “For those who look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:17–18).

Do not be lazy in a brief labor, and you will rejoice without end. God is going to give you eternal life. Consider with what labor it must be purchased.

24. Pay attention, brothers; it is for sale. “What I have,” God says to you, “is for sale; buy it.” What does he have for sale? “I have rest for sale; buy it through labor.” Pay attention, so that we may be strong Christians in the name of Christ [Note: [Col. 1211] Most manuscripts: “in the name of Christ, brothers, Christians.”]. There is only a little left in the psalm; let us not grow weary. For how can someone be strong in doing who falters in listening? May the Lord assist us, so that we may explain what remains to you.

Pay attention: in a certain sense God has put the kingdom of heaven up for sale. You say to him, “How much is it worth?” Its price is labor. Just as, if he said, “Its price is gold,” it would not be enough merely to say this, but you would ask how much gold—for a solidus is gold, and so are a half-ounce, a pound, and other such amounts—so he specified the price lest you labor to discover how much you would need before you found it [Note: [Col. 1211] Thus the Regius Manuscript. Other manuscripts, with the editions, read: “how long the price of this thing would be,” omitting the verb “you would find.”].

The price of this thing is labor [Col. 1212]. How great is the labor? You must now discover for yourself how much labor is required. It is not yet being told you how great this labor will be, or how much labor will be demanded of you. God tells you this: “I show you how great that rest is; you judge by how much labor it must be purchased.”

Let God, then, say how great that rest will be. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5). This is everlasting rest: this rest will have no end, this joy will have no end, this gladness will have no end, this incorruption will have no end. You will have eternal life, rest that has no end. How much labor is a rest without end worth? If you want to make a true comparison and judge truly, eternal rest is rightly purchased by eternal labor.

This is true; but do not be afraid, for God is merciful. If you had eternal labor, you would never reach eternal rest. While always laboring, when would you arrive at that which can indeed rightly be purchased by eternal labor, since it is eternal rest? The price is equivalent: eternal rest is certainly worthy of being purchased by eternal labor. But if you labored forever, you would never reach rest. Therefore, in order that you may at last reach what you are buying, you are not to labor forever—not because it is not worth that much, but so that what is purchased may actually be possessed. It is indeed worthy of being bought with perpetual labor, but it must be bought with temporal labor.

Certainly the price should have been so great—namely, eternal labor for eternal rest. What do one million years of labor amount to? One million years have an end. “What I shall give you,” God says, “will have no end.” What mercy of God! He does not say, “Labor for one million years”; he does not say, “Labor for a thousand years”; he does not say, “Labor for five hundred years.” While you live, labor for a few years; thereafter there will be rest, and it will have no end.

And hear what follows [Note: [Col. 1212] Thus Augustine, Erasmus, and the manuscripts. Lovanius reads: “consonances.”]: “Lord, according to the multitude of the sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul.” You labor for a few years, and even amid those labors consolation is not absent; daily joys are not absent. But do not rejoice in the world: rejoice in Christ, rejoice in his word, rejoice in his law. What we are saying and what you are hearing belong to these very joys.

How great, then, are these consolations amid such great labors? True, therefore, is what the Apostle said: “For our present, light affliction, beyond all measure and in a manner beyond measure, is producing for us an eternal weight of glory.” Behold how small a price we give, as it were one carob, in order to receive everlasting treasures: a carob of labor for immeasurable rest, according to what was said, “beyond all measure and in a manner beyond measure, producing for us an eternal weight of glory.”

You rejoice for a time; do not put your trust in it. You are sad for a time; do not despair. Let prosperity not corrupt you, and let adversity not break you. Otherwise you may say in your heart: “It cannot happen that God admits the wicked to himself, since he corrects even the righteous in order to save them, and corrects them for the purpose of instructing them. If the righteous are scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?”

“Does the seat of iniquity cling to you?” That is, “Does the seat of the ungodly cling to you—you who fashion pain into the commandment, who wished to exercise and instruct these children in this way, who wished to give them commandments in such a way that they would not be without fear, lest they love something else and forget you, their true good?”

God is good. If God ceased, and did not mingle bitterness with the prosperities of the world, we would forget him.

25. But when the distress of troubles makes the soul’s waves rise, let that faith which was sleeping there be awakened. For it was calm when Christ was sleeping on the sea; while he slept, a storm arose, and they began to be in danger. Thus there will be tranquility and peace in the Christian heart, as long as our faith remains awake. But if our faith sleeps, we are in danger.

This is what the sleeping Christ signifies: that some people forget their faith and are endangered. But just as, when that boat was being tossed by the waves, Christ was awakened by those who were tossed and saying, “Lord, we are perishing,” and he arose, commanded the storms and the waves, the danger ceased, and calm was restored (Matt. 8:23–26), so also, when evil desires and evil persuasions disturb you, they are waves, and they will become calm.

You are already despairing and think that you do not belong to the Lord: let your faith awaken; rouse Christ in your heart. When faith rises, you recognize where you are. And if perhaps the waves of desire test you, you consider what God has promised; the sweetness of his promises will make you despise the world’s sweetness.

And if perhaps many threats from powerful evildoers press upon you, and those threats themselves drive you away from righteousness, you consider what God threatens: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41), and you do not abandon righteousness. Fearing eternal fire, therefore, you despise temporal pains; and for the sake of what God has promised, you despise temporal prosperity.

He promised rest: endure distress. He threatens eternal fire: despise temporal pains. When Christ awakens, let your heart become calm, so that you may also reach the harbor. For the one who prepared the ship would surely prepare the harbor as well.

“Does the seat of iniquity cling to you—you who fashion pain into the commandment?” He exercises us through evil people and instructs us through their persecutions. The good person is scourged by the wicked person’s malice, and the son is corrected through the servant. Thus pain is fashioned into the commandment. Whatever God permits them to do, evil people do, and he spares them for a time.

26. [Verse 21.] What follows? “They will lie in wait for the soul of the righteous.” Why will they lie in wait? Because they do not find a true crime to bring against him. What did they lie in wait for in the Lord? “They fabricated false charges” (ibid. 26:59), because they could not find true ones.

“And they will condemn innocent blood.” Why all this happens, he will make clear in what follows.

27. [Verse 22.] “And the Lord,” he says, “became my refuge.” You would not seek such a refuge if you were not in danger; but you were endangered for this very reason, so that you might seek it, because he fashions pain into the commandment.

“From the malice of the wicked he makes tribulation for me.” Pierced by tribulation, I began to seek the refuge that, in that worldly prosperity, I had ceased to seek. For who easily remembers God when he is always prosperous and rejoices in present hope? Let worldly hope withdraw, and let the hope of God draw near, so that you may say, “And the Lord became my refuge.” Let me suffer for this purpose: that the Lord may become my refuge.

“And my God became the help of my hope.” For now the Lord is hope; as long as we are here, we are in hope, not yet in possession. But lest we fail in hope, the Promiser is present, raising us up and tempering the evils that we suffer. For it was not said without reason: “God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond what you can bear, but with the testing he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure” (1 Cor. 10:13). Thus he sends you into the furnace of tribulation so that the vessel may be baked, not broken.

“And the Lord became my refuge, and my God the help of my hope.” Why, then, did he seem to you as though unjust because he spares the wicked? [Note: [Col. 1214] Erasmus and Venetus: “When, then, he who seemed to you…” Lovanius: “Why, then, did it seem to you…” M.] See how the psalm is now corrected, and correct yourself with the psalm. For this reason the psalm had your words.

What words? “How long, sinners, O Lord, how long will sinners glory?” The psalm had your words; now, therefore, have the words of the psalm. What are the words of the psalm? “And the Lord became my refuge, and my God the help of my hope.”

28. [Verse 23.] “And the Lord will repay them according to their works, and according to their wickedness the Lord our God will destroy them.”

It is not without significance that he says, “according to their wickedness.” Benefit is conferred upon me through them; nevertheless, their wickedness is mentioned, not their benefits. Certainly he exercises us through evil people and scourges us through them. For what purpose does he scourge us? Surely, for the kingdom of heaven. For he scourges every son whom he receives; and what son is there whose father does not discipline him (Heb. 12:6–7)?

When God does this, he instructs us for an everlasting inheritance. He often grants us this benefit through evil people, in whom he exercises and perfects our love, which he wishes to extend even to our enemies. For a Christian’s love is not perfect unless he fulfills what Christ commanded: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you” (Matt. 5:44). By this the devil himself is conquered; by this the crown of victory is received.

See how many benefits God grants us through evil people. Yet he will not repay them according to what he grants us through them, but according to their wickedness.

Consider how much he granted us through the very monstrous crime of Judas the betrayer. Judas handed over the Son of God to his passion, and through the passion of the Son of God all nations were redeemed for salvation. Yet Judas was not rewarded for the salvation of the nations; rather, the punishment due for his wickedness was repaid to him.

For if one considers Christ’s betrayal and not the betrayer’s intention, Judas did what God the Father did, of whom it is written that “he did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32). Judas did what the Lord Christ himself did, of whom it is written: “He handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma”; and again: “Christ,” he says, “loved the Church and handed himself over for her” (Eph. 5:2, 25).

And yet we give thanks to God the Father, who did not spare his only Son but handed him over for us; we give thanks to the Son himself, who handed himself over for us and thereby fulfilled the Father’s will. And we detest Judas, whose deed God used to grant us so great a benefit. Rightly we say: “The Lord repaid him according to his iniquity, and according to his wickedness he destroyed him.”

For he did not hand Christ over for us, but for the silver for which he sold him. Although Christ’s betrayal is our reception [Note: [Col. 1215] Thus in the manuscripts. The editions read: “redemption.”], and Christ’s sale is our redemption.

So also those who persecuted the martyrs, by persecuting them on earth, were sending them into heaven. Though knowingly inflicting the loss of the present life, they unknowingly bestowed the gain of the future life. Nevertheless, all who persisted in their unjust hatred of the righteous will be repaid by the Lord according to their iniquities, and according to their wickedness he will destroy them.

For just as the goodness of the righteous harms the wicked, so the iniquity of the ungodly benefits the good. The Lord says: “I have come so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). And the Apostle says: “To some we are the aroma of life leading to life, and to others the aroma of death leading to death” (2 Cor. 2:16).

The wickedness of the iniquitous is the left-hand weapon of the righteous, just as the same Apostle says: “Through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left,” that is, “through glory and dishonor” (ibid. 6:7–8). He then continues by describing the weapons on the right: the glory of God, a good reputation, and the truth [Note: [Col. 1215] Thus the Regius book. Other manuscripts read: “reputation, truth,” omitting “good.” The editions read: “the reputation of truth by which they were known,” etc.] by which it was known that they were living, that they were not being put to death, that they were rejoicing, that they were enriching many, and that they possessed all things.

The weapons on the left were that they were regarded as dishonorable and of bad reputation, thought to be deceivers, unknown, killed, restrained, saddened, needy, and apparently possessing nothing.

And what wonder is it if Christ’s soldiers attack the devil with both right- and left-hand weapons? Just as there is peace among people of good will (Luke 2:14), and yet for some they are an aroma of death leading to death, so destruction comes upon people of evil will, even when the weapons on the left become weapons of salvation for the righteous.

Therefore he will repay them not according to our benefit, which comes to us through them, but according to their own iniquity, by loving which they have hated their souls. He will not honor them according to the benefit he grants us through them—he who makes good use even of evil people—but according to their wickedness the Lord our God will destroy them.

29. Let the righteous, then, endure the unrighteous; let him endure the unrighteous person’s temporal impunity and the righteous person’s temporal labor. But “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17). For in this life there is no other righteousness for a human being than to live by faith, which works through love (Gal. 5:6).

If he lives by faith, let him believe that rest awaits him after present labor, and that everlasting torments await them after their present exultation. And if faith works through love, let him also love his enemies and, as far as it depends on him, wish to benefit them. In this way he will ensure that they do not harm him, even when they wish to do so.

And whenever they perhaps receive power as though to harm and rule, let him keep his heart above, where no one harms him. Let him be taught and instructed by God’s law, so that he may be comforted from the days of evil until the pit is dug for the sinner.

For if his delight is in the law of the Lord and he meditates on his law day and night (Ps. 1:2), and if his citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3:20), then he shines from the firmament over the earth. Hence this psalm received its title, “for the fourth day of the week,” when the lights were made (Gen. 1:14), so that he may do everything without murmuring, possessing the word of life amid a crooked and perverse generation (Phil. 2:14–16).

For just as night does not extinguish the stars in heaven, so iniquity does not overcome the minds of the faithful who cling to the firmament of Scripture. And the fact that our earthly possessions are sometimes handed over to the power of the wicked contributes not only to our instruction, so that the Lord may become our refuge and our God the help of our hope, but also to the sinner’s own pit. Of him it is said in another psalm: “He will be humbled and fall when he rules over the poor” (Ps. 9:10).

30. Perhaps the length of the sermon has been burdensome to you, although your eager attentiveness does not show this. But even if it has, forgive me: first, because I did it under orders, for our Lord God commanded me through those brothers in whom he dwells. God does not command except from his seat.

Second, because you were so eager for us, we confess that we too were eager for you. May our God, then, console this labor, so that our sweat may contribute to your progress in salvation and not serve as evidence against you.

I say this, brothers, so that you may profit from what you have heard and turn it over with yourselves. Do not allow yourselves to forget it, not merely by recalling and discussing these things, but also by living accordingly.

For the good life that is lived according to God’s commandments is like a stylus writing what is heard upon the heart. If it were written on wax, it would easily be erased. Write it on your hearts and in your conduct, and it will never be erased.

## Exposition of Psalm 94

### Sermon

[Note: [Col. 1216] Delivered at the command of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage—or rather of Valerius, bishop of Hippo—and therefore to Augustine, who was then a newly consecrated bishop or still a presbyter.]

1. [Verse 1.] I would rather, brothers, that we listen to our father; but it is also good that we obey our father. Since, therefore, he who deigns to pray for us has commanded it, let me speak to Your Charity about the present psalm, as the Lord God of us all will deign to grant.

The title of the psalm is, “Praise of a song, to David himself.” “Praise of a song” signifies both gladness, because it is a song, and devotion, because it is praise. For what should a human being praise more than that which pleases in such a way that it cannot displease?

The security of praise, therefore, lies in the praise of God. The one who praises is secure there, where he does not fear that he will be ashamed of the one praised. Let us therefore praise and sing; [Col. 1217] that is, let us praise with gladness and joy. What we are going to praise, however, the psalm itself indicates to us in the verses that follow.

2. “Come, let us exult in the Lord.” It invites us to the great feast of exultation—not in the world, but in the Lord. For if there were not an evil exultation in this world, which must be distinguished from good exultation, it would have been enough to say, “Come, let us exult.” But he distinguished them briefly.

What is it to exult well? To exult in the Lord. Therefore the evil exultation is to exult in the world; the good exultation is to exult in the Lord. You ought piously to exult in the Lord if you wish to insult the world without fear.

What does “Come” mean? From where does he call those whom he wishes to come and exult in the Lord, unless they are far away and must draw near by coming, approach by drawing near, and exult by approaching?

From where are they far away? Can a human being be far away in place from him who is everywhere? Do you wish to be far from him? Where will you go to be far away? For a certain sinner—yet a penitent who hoped for salvation, grieved over his sins, feared God’s anger, and wished to appease God—speaks in another psalm as follows: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there.”

What, then, remains? If he ascends into heaven, he finds God there. To flee far from God, where will he go? See what he says: “If I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138:7–8). If, by ascending into heaven, he finds God there, and by descending into hell he does not flee from God, where will he go, where will he flee from him who is angry, except to him who has been appeased?

And yet, although absolutely no one can flee from him who is everywhere, unless some people were far from God it would not be said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

No one, therefore, is far from God by place, but by unlikeness. What does “by unlikeness” mean? A bad life and bad conduct. For if one draws near to God by good conduct, one withdraws from God by bad conduct.

Thus one and the same person, standing bodily in one place, draws near to God by loving God and withdraws from God by loving iniquity. He moves his feet nowhere, yet he can both draw near and withdraw. For our feet on this journey are our affections. As each person’s affection is, as each person’s love is, so he either draws near to God or withdraws from him.

Do we not often say, when we find things that are unlike one another, “This is far from that”? When we compare two people, two horses, or two garments, and someone says, “This garment is similar; it is like that one,” what does someone else say who disagrees? “Certainly not; it is far from that one.” What does “it is far from that one” mean? It is unlike it.

They stand next to each other, and yet this one is far from that one. Two unrighteous people equal in life and conduct—if one is in the East and the other in the West—are close to each other. Two righteous people likewise, even if one is in the East and the other in the West, are together, because they are in God.

Conversely, one righteous and one unrighteous person, even if they are bound together by a single chain, are greatly separated from each other. Therefore, if we withdraw from God by unlikeness, we draw near to God by likeness.

By what likeness? By the likeness according to which we were made, which we had corrupted in ourselves by sinning, which we received again through the forgiveness of sins, and which is renewed inwardly in our mind, so that the image of our God may be, as it were, engraved again on the coin—that is, on our soul—and we may return to his treasures.

For why did our Lord Jesus Christ wish to show his tempters, by means of a coin, what God seeks? When they were seeking an occasion for slander and wished to consult the teacher of truth in order to test whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, what did he say? “Why do you test me, hypocrites?” He asked that a coin be brought to him, and it was brought. “Whose image,” he said, “does it bear?” They answered, “Caesar’s.” And he said to them: “Then give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Matt. 22:15–21).

It was as though he were saying: “If Caesar seeks his own image on a coin, does God not seek his own image in a human being?”

Inviting us to this likeness, our Lord Jesus Christ commands us also to love our enemies and gives the example of God himself: “Just as your Father,” he says, “who is in heaven, makes his sun rise on the good and the evil and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous, so be perfect as your Father is perfect” (ibid. 5:45, 48).

When he says, “Be perfect as he is,” he invites us to likeness. If, therefore, he invites us to likeness, it is clear that by becoming unlike we had withdrawn from God and had become far away through unlikeness, while by likeness we are made near, so that what is written may now be fulfilled in us: “Draw near to God, and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:5).

Thus to some who are far away and living badly this psalm says: “Come, let us exult in the Lord.” Where are you going? Where are you withdrawing? Where are you departing? Where are you fleeing by exulting in the world? “Come, let us exult in the Lord.” Where are you going to exult, where you are failing? Come, let us exult in him by whom we were made. Come, let us exult in the Lord.

3. “Let us shout for joy to God our salvation.” What does it mean to shout for joy? It means being unable to express joy in words, yet testifying with the voice to what has been conceived within and cannot be expressed in words. This is to shout for joy.

Let Your Charity consider those who shout for joy in every kind of song, as though in a certain contest of worldly gladness. You see how, amid songs expressed in words, overflowing joy seems to exceed what the tongue can say; see how they shout for joy, so that by that voice the feeling of the soul is indicated, although they cannot express in words what is conceived in the heart.

If, then, they shout for joy over earthly gladness, should we not shout for joy over heavenly gladness, which we truly cannot express in words?

4. [Verse 2.] “Let us come before his face in confession.” In Scripture, confession is understood in two ways. There is the confession of one who praises, and the confession of one who groans. The confession of one who praises pertains to the honor of the one praised; the confession of one who groans pertains to the repentance of the one confessing.

People confess when they praise God; they confess when they accuse themselves. Nothing is more worthy for the tongue to do. I truly think that these are the very vows of which he says in another psalm: “I will pay you my vows, which my lips have uttered” (Ps. 65:13–14).

Nothing is more sublime than this distinction, and nothing is so necessary both for understanding and for doing. How, then, do you distinguish the vows that you pay to God? You praise him and accuse yourself, because it is his mercy that he forgives our sins. For if he wished to act according to our merits, he would find only those whom he should condemn.

“Come,” therefore, he said [Note: [Col. 1219] Most manuscripts: “He came, therefore, saying.” Ambrose and Erasmus: “He came, therefore, teaching.”], so that we may now depart from our sins and so that he may not reckon with us concerning the past, but so that, as it were, new tablets may be made, after all the documents of our debts have been burned.

How great, then, is his praise, how great his mercy! Let us confess, certainly by praising. For if confession always belonged to the penitent, it would not be said in the Gospel of the Lord himself: “At that hour Jesus exulted in the Holy Spirit and said, ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones’” (Luke 10:21).

Was Christ penitent because he confessed? Nothing could make him repent, because he had done nothing culpably. Rather, he confessed in praise of the Father.

Since this, then, is also a place of exultation, perhaps we should understand here the confession that is praise of God. Hence also the title, “A song of praise,” so that we understand here not the confession of penitents but of those who praise.

And what does he immediately mean when he reminds us of a certain confession, saying: “Let us come before his face in confession”? What does “Let us come before his face in confession” mean? He is coming. Let us come before his face in confession beforehand: before he comes, let us condemn by confessing what we have done, so that he may find something to crown, not something to condemn.

Does this, too, not pertain to the praise of God, when you confess your sins? Indeed, it pertains above all to the praise of God. Why does it pertain above all to the praise of God? Because the more hopeless the sick person was thought to be, the more the physician is praised.

Confess your sins, therefore, insofar as you had despaired of yourself because of your iniquities. For the greater the confession of sins, the greater the praise of the one who forgives.

Let us not think, then, that we have departed from the praise of the song if we understand here the confession by which we confess our sins. This, too, pertains to the praise of the song, because when we recognize our sins, we proclaim God’s glory.

“Let us come before his face in confession.”

5. “And let us shout for joy to him in psalms.” We have already said what it means to shout for joy. It is repeated so that we may be strengthened in doing it; the repetition itself is an exhortation.

For we have not already forgotten and now wish to be reminded of what was said above, namely, that we should shout for joy. Rather, a word already known is often repeated in an emotional context, not so that it may become known, but so that the repetition itself may bring confirmation. It is repeated in order to convey the speaker’s feeling.

This is why the Lord says, “Amen, amen, I say to you” (John 1:51). One “Amen” would have sufficed. Why “Amen, amen,” unless the repetition itself is a confirmation?

“In psalms,” he says, “let us shout for joy to him.” And what shall we say in the psalms? What shall we say—or rather, what shall we feel—in the shout of joy? What things belong to the praise of this song? Listen now:

“For the Lord is a great God, and a great king above all gods.” Therefore let us shout for joy to him. “For the Lord will not reject his people.” Let us shout for joy to him. “For in his hand are the ends of the earth, and the heights of the mountains are his.” In all these things let us shout for joy to him. “For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.” Let us shout for joy to him.

What all these things mean, if they are examined appropriately, perhaps cannot be covered in the available time. But if they are entirely neglected, we will remain debtors. Therefore, briefly, in accordance with the time, receive as much as we can touch upon; for even a few seeds produce a very abundant harvest if the soil is fertile.

6. [Verse 3.] First he stated why we should shout for joy and why we should praise: “For the Lord is a great God, and a great king above all gods.”

There are, then, gods above whom our God is great, the one to whom we shout for joy, the one in whom we exult, the one to whom we sing songs of praise. There are such gods, but not for us.

The Apostle says: “For although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, from whom are all things and we through him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we in him” (1 Cor. 8:5–6).

If not for us, then for whom? Hear from another psalm: “For the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95:5).

The Holy Spirit, through the Prophet, could not commend your God and Lord to you more magnificently or more briefly. For it was little to say that God is terrifying above all demons. What is so great about being above all demons? “For the gods of the nations are demons.” But where is your God? “The Lord made the heavens.”

Your Lord made that place where demons cannot dwell; for the demons were cast down from heaven. The heavens are placed above the demons, and your Lord is above the heavens, because your Lord also made the heavens.

How much higher, then, is he than the gods of the nations, the demons, since he is higher than the heavens from which the angels fell to become demons?

And yet all the nations were under the demons. Temples were built for demons, altars constructed for demons, priests appointed for demons, sacrifices offered to demons, and possessed people introduced as prophets for demons. The nations offered all these things to demons; all these things are owed truly only to the one great God.

The nations made a temple for demons; God has a temple. The nations made priests for demons; God has a priest [Note: [Col. 1220] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “priests.”]. The nations offered sacrifices to demons; God has a sacrifice.

Indeed, those demons, wishing to appear to be gods, would not have demanded these things for themselves in order to deceive people unless they knew that such things were owed to the true God. For this is customarily owed to the true God which the false god demands for himself.

Therefore we recognize the true temple of God. “The temple of God is holy,” he says, “which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). If we are the temple of God, our soul is God’s altar.

What is God’s sacrifice? Perhaps we are performing it now: we place a sacrifice upon the altar when we praise God. The psalm teaches us this, saying: “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49:23).

But if you seek the priest [Col. 1221], he is above the heavens; he intercedes for you, the one who died on earth for you (Rom. 8:34).

Therefore, “the Lord is a great God, and a great king above all gods.”

Here understand human beings as gods; for the Lord is not king over demons. We have testimony from Scripture for this as well: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he distinguishes among the gods” [Note: [Col. 1221] The editions read: “he distinguishes.” The manuscripts read: “to distinguish”; so too Augustine in Psalm 81.] (Ps. 81:1).

He called them gods by participation, not by nature; by grace, through which he wished to make them gods. How great is the God who makes gods! Or what kind of gods are those whom a human being makes? As great as he is in making gods, so insignificant are those made by human beings.

The true God makes gods of those who believe in him, to whom he gave the power to become children of God (John 1:12). He himself is therefore the true God, because he was not made God. We, however, were made; we are not true gods, but we are nevertheless better than those whom human beings make.

“For the idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see” (Ps. 113:4–5). But our God made us with seeing eyes.

Yet he did not make us gods merely because he gave us seeing eyes; for he did this also for animals. Rather, he made us gods because he enlightened our inward eyes.

Therefore let there be praise to him, confession to him, shouting for joy to him: “For the Lord is a great God, and a great king above all gods.”

### 7. [verse 5]

For the Lord will not reject his people: praise to him, jubilation to him. Which people will he not reject? Here we are not permitted to interpret anything for ourselves; we have the Apostle’s prescription, and the Apostle explained where this was said (Rom. 11:1). There was the Jewish people: the people among whom the Prophets were found, the people among whom the Patriarchs were found, the people propagated according to the flesh from the seed of Abraham; the people in whom all the sacraments promising our Savior had gone before; the people among whom the temple, anointing, and priesthood were instituted as figures [Note: Col. 1221. Several manuscripts read “the anointing of the priest”], so that, when all those shadows had passed away, the light itself might arrive. This, then, was God’s people; to it the Prophets were sent, and in it those who were sent were born; to it the utterances of God were entrusted and committed.

What, then? Was all that condemned? God forbid. The Apostle called it the olive tree, for this tree began with the Patriarchs. But there were dry branches there, because they had risen too high through pride; so they were cut off because of their barrenness, and the wild olive was grafted in because of its humility. Nevertheless, beloved, lest the grafted wild olive should become proud, what does the Apostle say? “If you were cut from the naturally wild olive and, contrary to nature, grafted into the good olive, how much more will those who are natural be grafted into their own olive tree” (ibid., 16–24)? Thus, just as you, not remaining in unbelief, deserved to be grafted into the olive tree though you were a wild olive, so these people, once corrected, may more easily be grafted naturally into their own olive tree. This is what the Apostle says concerning them.

Therefore it is the same tree; and although some of its branches were broken, not all of them were. For if all the branches had been broken, where would Peter be? Where John? Where Thomas? Where Matthew? Where Andrew? Where would all those Apostles be? Where would Paul himself be—the Apostle who was speaking and, by his own fruit, bearing witness to the olive tree [Note: Col. 1222. Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “to the olive tree”]? Were not all these from that tree? And from where came the five hundred brothers to whom the Lord appeared after the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:6)? From where came the many thousands who responded to Peter’s voice when the Apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke in the languages of all nations? They were converted with such eagerness for God’s praise and accusation of themselves that those who had first shed the Lord’s blood in their fury learned, once they believed, to drink it. So all those thousands of people were converted that they sold their possessions and placed the proceeds of their property at the Apostles’ feet (Acts 2; 4).

What one rich man did not do when he heard it from the Lord’s mouth and went away from the Lord sorrowful (Matt. 19:21–22), those many thousands of the people whose hands had crucified Christ did immediately. The greater the wound in their hearts, the more eagerly they sought the physician.

Since, then, all those people came from that stock, the Psalm now says concerning them: “For the Lord will not reject his people.” The Apostle used this testimony from the Psalm when speaking on this subject, and said: “What then shall we say, brothers? Has God rejected his people, whom he foreknew? God forbid. For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew” (Rom. 11:1–2). Certainly, if the Lord had rejected his people, there would have been no source from which the Apostle himself came; and from where he came, so too did the others.

In these people is the Lord’s people—not in all of them; but, as it is written, “The remnant shall be saved” (Isa. 10:22; Rom. 9:27). Not in all of them: the threshing floor has been winnowed, the grain has been brought inside, and the straw lies there (Matt. 3:12). Whatever you see of the rejected Jews, you see straw. From the place where you see this straw, the grain has already gone out and has already been stored in the granary. Let us see both things; let us distinguish both.

### 8. [verse 4]

What does the Psalm add? “For in his hand are the ends of the earth.” We recognize the cornerstone: the cornerstone is Christ. There cannot be a corner unless it joins two walls in itself. They come to the corner from different directions, but at the corner they are not opposed to one another.

Circumcision came from one side, uncircumcision from the other; in Christ both peoples were reconciled, because he became the stone of which it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117:22). Since, then, Christ is the head of the corner, let us not attend to the difference between those who come from afar, but to the nearness of those who are joined together in Christ. There the matter is being accomplished; there let us see the words, “For the Lord will not reject his people.”

Here is one wall, in which, as we have said, the Lord did not reject his people. From there came the Apostles; from there came all the Israelites who believed and placed the proceeds of their sold possessions at the Apostles’ feet—poor by choice, rich in God. We have recognized one wall; there has been fulfilled what we said, “For the Lord will not reject his people.” Let us see the other wall also: “For in his hand are the ends of the earth.”

Here is the other wall, among all the nations: “In his hand are the ends of the earth.” All the nations also came to the cornerstone, where they recognized the kiss of peace, to that one who made the two one—not as the heretics do, who made one into two. For the Apostle says this very thing concerning the Lord Christ: “For he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14).

Therefore let us rejoice to him. Why? “For the Lord will not reject his people.” Again, why? “For in his hand are the ends of the earth, and the heights of the mountains are his.”

The heights of the mountains are the elevations of the earth. At one time these elevations—that is, the earthly powers themselves—opposed the Church. They promulgated laws against the Church and attempted to erase the Christian name from the earth. But after what had been prophesied was fulfilled, “All the kings of the earth shall worship him” (Ps. 71:11), what is said here came to pass: “The heights of the mountains are his.”

### 9. [verse 5]

But perhaps you are troubled by temptations, so that, established in such great grace of God’s promises, you are disturbed because of the world’s scandals. Yet those scandals themselves do nothing to you, because they have received their measure from the Lord: “For the sea is his.”

This world is indeed a sea, but God also made the sea; and its waves cannot rage except as far as the shore, where he himself set the boundary. Therefore no temptation exists unless it has received its measure from the Lord. Let there be temptations; let there be tribulations. Through them you are completed, not consumed.

See whether those very temptations are not beneficial. Listen to the Apostle: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13). He did not say, “He will not allow you to be tempted at all.” For if you refused temptation, you would refuse restoration.

You are therefore being restored; and if you are being restored, you are in the hands of the craftsman. He removes something from you, corrects something, smooths something, cleanses something. He works with certain instruments of his own; these are the scandals of this age. Only do not fall from the craftsman’s hand. No temptation will come upon you beyond your strength. God permits this for your benefit, so that you may progress through it.

Finally, hear the Apostle himself joining these words together: “But with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it.”

Was the sea, then, perhaps something you ought to fear? Do not be afraid: “For the sea is his, and he himself made it.” Do you fear scandals from the nations? He himself also made the nations; he will not allow them to rage beyond the measure he knows, the measure by which you may progress.

Does not another Psalm say, “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord” (Ps. 85:9)? If it says “all the nations that you have made,” it is clear that he himself made the nations also. Therefore: “The sea is his, and he himself made it, and his hands formed the dry land.”

Be yourself dry land, thirsting for God’s grace, so that sweet rain may come upon you and find fruit in you. He does not allow the waves to cover what he has sown.

“And his hands formed the dry land.”

Therefore here too let us rejoice to him.

**Note:** Thus several manuscripts. But Ambrosius and Erasmus have *quod servit* (“what serves”); Lovaniensis has *quos servat* (“whom he preserves”).

### 10. [verse 6]

Since these things are so, since we have unfolded so much pertaining to God’s praise, return to the point from which he had begun: “Come, let us worship and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us.”

For this reason let us rejoice: because he made this and that. He had recalled many things, and now he repeats the exhortation: “Come, let us worship and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us.”

Now that I have recalled God’s praises, do not be sluggish or stand far away in life and conduct: “Come, let us worship and fall down before him.”

But perhaps you are anxious about your sins, which had made you distant from God. Let us carry out what follows: “And let us weep before the Lord who made us.” Perhaps you are burning with the consciousness of your offense; extinguish the flame of sin with tears. Weep before the Lord. Weep before God confidently, before the God who made you; for he does not despise in you the work of his own hands.

Do not think that you can restore yourself. You can fall away from yourself; you cannot restore yourself. He restores you who made you.

“Let us weep before the Lord who made us.” Shed tears before him, confess to him, go before his face in confession. For who are you that you weep and confess to him, except one whom he made? It is no small confidence for a thing made to approach its maker—and not merely made, but made in his image and likeness.

“Come, let us worship and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us.”

### 11. [verse 7]

“For he is the Lord our God.”

But so that we may fall down and weep before him without fear, what are we? “But we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hands.”

See how elegantly he has changed the order of the words and, as it were, rendered them in an unusual way, so that we may understand that those who are the people are also the sheep. He did not say, “The sheep of his pasture and the people of his hands,” which might have seemed more fitting, since sheep belong to pasture; instead he said, “The people of his pasture.”

Therefore the people are sheep, because he says, “The people of his pasture”; the people themselves are sheep. But again, since we possess sheep that we have bought, not sheep that we have made—and since above he had said, “Let us fall down before him who made us”—he rightly said, “the sheep of his hands.”

No human being makes sheep for himself. He can buy them, they can be given to him, he can find them, gather them together, or finally steal them; he cannot make sheep. But our Lord made us. Therefore “the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hands” are those whom he himself deigned to make for himself by his grace.

For he also praises these sheep in the Song of Songs, describing certain perfect ones [Note: Col. 1224. Two manuscripts read “a certain perfect one.”] as the teeth of his holy bride, the Church: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep ascending from the washing, which bear twins, and none among them is barren” (Song 4:2; 6:5).

What does “Your teeth” mean? Those through whom you speak; for the teeth of the Church are those through whom the Church speaks.

What are your teeth like? “Like a flock of shorn sheep.”

Why shorn? Because they have laid aside the burdens of the world. Were not those sheep shorn of whom I was speaking shortly before—those whom God’s command had shorn when he said: “Go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21)? They carried out this command; shorn, they came.

And because they were baptized after believing in Christ, what is said there? “Ascending from the washing”—that is, ascending from cleansing.

And they all produce twins. What twins? Those two commandments on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

Therefore we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hands.

### 12. [verse 8]

Therefore, “Today, if you hear his voice.”

O my people, God’s people! God addresses his people—not only that people of his which he will not reject, but all his people. He speaks at the corner to both walls (Eph. 2:20); that is, in Christ prophecy speaks both to the people of the Jews and to the people of the Gentiles.

“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” At one time you heard his voice through Moses, and you hardened your hearts. He spoke through a herald when you hardened your hearts; now he speaks through himself. Let your hearts become soft.

He whom he used to send heralds before him has himself deigned to come; he speaks here with his own mouth, he who spoke through the mouths of the Prophets.

Therefore, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”

### 13. [verse 9]

Why did he say, “Do not harden your hearts”? Because you remember what your fathers used to do.

“Do not harden your hearts, as in that provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness.”

You certainly remember, brothers, that the people tempted God (Exod. 16:2–3; 17:2–7), received discipline, and were set straight in the wilderness as though by an excellent rider, by the reins of laws and the reins of commandments. Yet even while untamed, they were not abandoned by God—not only through present benefits, but also through the rod of correction, which did not cease.

Therefore do not harden your hearts: “as in that provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me.”

Let your fathers no longer be such; do not imitate them. They were your fathers; but if you do not imitate them, they will not be your fathers. Yet because you were born from them, they were your fathers.

And if the Gentiles coming from the ends of the earth, as Jeremiah says, “To you the Gentiles shall come from the ends of the earth, and they shall say, ‘Our fathers inherited lies, idols in which there is no benefit’” (Jer. 16:19)—if the Gentiles abandoned their idols in order to come to the God of Israel; and if those whom the God of Israel himself led out of Egypt through the Red Sea, in which he covered their pursuing enemies (Exod. 14:21–31), whom he led into the wilderness and fed with manna (ibid. 16:13–35), never removed his rod from their discipline and never withdrew the benefits of his mercy—must they themselves abandon their God when the Gentiles have come to their God?

“There your fathers tempted me; they tested me” [Note: Col. 1225. The editions read *probaverunt me* (“they tested me”). *Me* is absent from the manuscripts, most of which continue: “and they saw my works for forty years.” “They saw my works for forty years, and they provoked me.”]

“And they saw my works. For forty years they saw my works; for forty years they provoked me.” Before them I performed miracles through Moses’ hand, and they hardened their hearts more and more.

### 14. [verse 10]

“For forty years I was near this generation.”

What does “I was near” mean? I presented myself in my signs and mighty deeds—not for one day, not for two, but “for forty years I was near this generation.” And I said, “They are always straying in heart.”

Those forty years signified what is also meant by “always.” For this number forty indicates the completeness of the ages, as though the ages are perfected through this number.

Therefore the Lord fasted for forty days, was tempted in the wilderness for forty days (Matt. 4:1–11), and remained with the disciples for forty days after the resurrection (Acts 1:3). In the first forty days he showed temptation; in the later forty days, consolation, because when we are tempted, we are undoubtedly also consoled.

For his body, that is, the Church, must suffer temptations in this age; but the Consoler is not absent—the one who said, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

“And I said, ‘They are always straying in heart.’” I was with them for those forty years in order to show a kind of people that continually provokes me to the end of the age, since through those forty years he wished to signify the whole age.

### 15. [verse 11]

What then? Will there not be others in their place who enter into God’s rest? Those who displeased God’s mercy and resisted God with hardened hearts were rejected. But when they were rejected, did God lose his people? Will this not be true: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (ibid. 3:9)?

Therefore I said, “They are always straying in heart.” “And they did not know my ways, concerning whom I swore in my wrath, ‘They shall not enter into my rest.’”

“Concerning whom I swore in my wrath, ‘They shall not enter into my rest’”: a great terror. We began with rejoicing, but this Psalm concluded with great fear: “Concerning whom I swore in my wrath, ‘They shall not enter into my rest.’”

It is a great thing for the Lord to speak; how much greater for God to swear! You ought to fear a human being who swears, lest because of his oath he do something contrary to his will; how much more should you fear God, who cannot swear rashly about anything?

He wished an oath to serve as confirmation. And by whom does God swear? By himself, since he has no one greater by whom to swear (Heb. 6:13). By himself he confirms his promises; by himself he confirms his threats.

Let no one say in his heart: “What he promises is true; what he threatens is false.” Just as what he promises is true, so what he threatens is certain. You ought to be as certain of rest, happiness, eternity, and immortality, if you carry out his commandments, as you ought to be certain of destruction, the burning of eternal fire, and condemnation with the devil, if you despise his commandments.

Therefore he swore in his wrath that they should not enter his rest. Yet some must enter his rest; for his rest will not be given to no one. Once they have been rejected, we shall enter, because although some branches were broken off because of dissimilarity and unbelief, we shall be grafted in because of faith and humility (Rom. 11:19–20).

Let us therefore enter into his rest. But from where did those who entered—those who were chosen, who did not resist with hardened hearts—enter? Because it is true that the Lord will not reject his people.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 95

[Col. 1227]

### SERMON

**Note:** Probably delivered before the year 405, when the Donatists ruled by the violence of the Circumcellions, as appears from no. 11.

### 1. [verse 1]

The Lord and my brother Severus [Note: Col. 1227. That is, the bishop of Milevis, also praised in the exposition of Psalm 131, delivered on the day immediately before this sermon, in these words: “It was indeed right, beloved, that we should rather hear my brother and colleague, present among us all; and he has not refused even now, but has postponed it,” etc.] still delays our joy, in the sermon he owes us; for he acknowledges that he is held as a debtor. The Lord has gladdened all the churches through which he has passed by means of his mouth; therefore this church ought to be gladdened all the more, since the Lord propagated him from this church to the others.

But what shall we do except serve his will? Nevertheless, brothers, I said that he delays, not that he defrauds. Therefore hold him as your debtor, and do not release him until he has paid.

Let your Charity attend, then. Insofar as the Lord grants it, let us say something about this Psalm—something you already know, perhaps, but the recollection of truth is sweet.

Perhaps, when its title was proclaimed, some of you heard it with wonder. The title of the Psalm is inscribed: “When the house was being built after the captivity.”

Once this title had been announced, you perhaps expected, in the very text of the Psalm, to hear of stones being cut from the mountains, of masses being hauled, of foundations being laid, of beams being placed, and of columns being erected. It sings none of these things. And if it sings something else, does the Psalm therefore not correspond to its title, bearing one thing on its face and another in its voice?

On the contrary, it bears nothing else, but it seeks those who understand. For it speaks of the building of a house. Let all the stones of that house understand [Note: Col. 1227. Most manuscripts read “understand.”] what they have sung.

A house is being built for God—not in that place where Solomon built. He built a temple (1 Kings 6:1), and you have just heard what the Lord said concerning that temple. When the disciples were admiring the stones of the temple and its enormous masses, they pointed out their admiration and astonishment to the Lord. The Lord said to them: “Amen I say to you, not one stone will be left here upon another that will not be destroyed” (Matt. 24:1–2).

Such a house is not being built. For see where it is being built: not in one place, or in some particular part. Thus it begins:

### 2.

“Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.”

If all the earth sings a new song, it is built in this way, when it sings. To sing itself is to build—but only if it does not sing the old song.

The old song is sung by the desire of the flesh; the new song is sung by the love of God. Whatever you sing from desire, you sing an old song. Even if [Note: Col. 1227. The editions read “even if they do not sound”; *not* is absent from the manuscripts.] the words of the new song sound in your mouth, “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15:9).

It is better for you to be new and silent than to sing as one old. For if you are new and remain silent, it does not sound in human ears; but your heart does not cease from the new song, and it reaches the ears of God, who made you a new human being.

You love, and you are silent: love itself is a voice to God, and love itself is the new song. Hear that it is a new song. The Lord says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:34).

Therefore all the earth sings a new song; there the house is built [Note: Col. 1227. Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “where is the house built?”]. All the earth, then, is the house of God. If all the earth is the house of God, whoever does not belong to the whole earth is a ruin, not a house—the old ruin whose shadow that old temple possessed. For there the oldness was being destroyed so that newness might be built.

And how is the oldness destroyed? “Amen I say to you,” he says, “not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed.”

The stone is Christ. The Apostle says: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27). If everyone baptized in Christ has put on Christ, who places one stone upon another except someone who places one Baptism upon another?

But do not be afraid: “Not one will be left that will not be destroyed.” For the stones are gathered for the new structure that is being built after the captivity, and love binds them together in unity in such a way that it is not one stone upon another, but all the stones are one stone.

Do not be surprised: the new song has done this—that is, the renewal of love has done this. The Apostle fits us together into this structure and joins us together, bound in that unity, saying: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2–3).

Where there is unity of Spirit, there is one stone—but one stone made from many. How is one made from many? By bearing with one another in love.

Therefore the house of the Lord our God is being built; it is being built. This is what is happening, this is what is being accomplished. These voices accomplish it, the readings accomplish it, the preaching of the Gospel throughout the whole world accomplishes it. It is still being built.

This house has grown greatly and filled many nations; yet it has not occupied all nations. By growing, it has taken possession of many, and it will take possession of all. It is opposed by those who boast that they are its household members, and it is said, “It has already diminished.”

It is still growing. All the nations that have not yet believed will still believe. Let no one say, “Will that language believe too? Will the Barbarians believe?”

And what does it mean that the Holy Spirit appeared in fiery tongues (Acts 2:3), except that no language is so hard that it cannot be melted by that fire? For we already have many Barbarian nations that have believed in Christ. Where the Roman Empire has not yet extended, Christ already possesses the land. What remains closed to those who fight with iron is not closed to him who fights with wood.

“For the Lord reigned from the wood.” Who is he who fights with wood? Christ. From his cross he conquered kings; and after subjugating them, he fixed the cross itself upon their foreheads. They glory in it, because their salvation is there.

This is what is happening; this is how the house grows; this is how it is built. And so that you may know this, hear what follows in the Psalm. See those who are working and constructing the house:

“Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.”

### 3. [verses 2–3]

“Sing to the Lord, bless his name [Note: Col. 1228. The editions read “and bless”; *and* is absent from the manuscripts, which shortly afterward have “announce from day to day,” though elsewhere they read “from day into day.”], announce his salvation from day to day.”

How does the building grow? “Announce,” he says, “his salvation from day to day.” Let it be preached from day to day; let it be built from day to day; let my house grow, he says.

And as though the workers were saying, “Where do you command us to build? Where do you want your house to grow? Choose some level place for us, some spacious place, if you want a large house to be built for you. Where do you command us to announce from day to day?”

He shows them the place: “Announce his glory among the nations.” Announce his glory among the nations, he says—not your glory.

O builders, announce his glory among the nations. If you wish to announce your own glory, you will fall; if you are built upon his glory, you will be built while you build.

Therefore those who wished to announce their own glory did not wish to be in this house, and for this reason they do not sing the new song with the whole earth. They do not share communion with the entire world; and therefore they are not building in the house, but have erected a whitewashed wall.

How much does God threaten the whitewashed wall? The testimonies of the Prophets are innumerable, by which he curses the whitewashed wall [Note: Col. 1229. Most manuscripts read, “he says that he threatens the whitewashed wall.”]. What is a whitewashed wall except hypocrisy, that is, pretense? Outside it shines; inside it is mud.

What I am about to say has already been said. But because it was said by the same Spirit whom the Lord has also deigned to impart to us, we have said it; and whatever we say now by the same Spirit, those who came before us said. Therefore it must not be passed over, but must be said, because it was said by God’s gift.

Someone speaking about this whitewashed wall said the following: “Just as, in a wall not joined to other walls but erected by itself, if you make a doorway, whoever enters is outside, so in that group which did not wish to sing the new song with the house [Note: Col. 1229. Lovaniensis reads “with the Lord”; the other editions and manuscripts more correctly read “with the house.”], but wished to build a wall—and a whitewashed one, not a solid one [Note: Col. 1229. Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “a group … a whitewashed one, not a solid one,” and shortly afterward, “their door does not admit them.”]—what good is it that it has a door? If you enter, you are found outside.”

For they themselves did not enter through the door, and their door does not admit anyone. The Lord says: “I am the door; through me one enters.”

Who are those who enter through the door? Those who seek the Lord’s glory, not their own. Who enter through the door? Those who do what was said: “Announce his glory among the nations.”

“The one who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep,” says the Lord; “but the one who climbs in by another way is a thief and a robber” (John 10:7, 9, 1–2).

The one who enters through the door is humble; the one who climbs in by another way is proud. Therefore he said that one enters, while the other climbs. The one is received by entering; the other is cast down by climbing.

“Announce his glory among the nations.”

What does “among the nations” mean? Perhaps only a few are called nations, and that group which erected the whitewashed wall still has something to say: “Why are Getulia, Numidia, Mauretania, and Byzacium not nations? Provinces are nations” [Note: Col. 1229. The editions read, “Are Getulia … Byzacium not nations? Is a province a nation?” The text has been corrected from the manuscripts.].

Let God’s word remove speech from hypocrisy [Note: Col. 1229. Thus several manuscripts; the editions read “hypocrisy.”] and from the whitewashed wall, building the house throughout the whole world. It is not enough that he said, “Announce his glory among the nations.” Lest you think that some nations have been excluded, he continues and says, “Among all peoples, his wonders.”

### 4. [verse 4]

“For great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise.”

Who is the Lord except Jesus Christ, great and exceedingly worthy of praise? You certainly know that he appeared as a human being; you certainly know that he was conceived in a woman’s womb; you know that he was born from the womb; you know that he was nursed, carried in hands, circumcised, and that a sacrifice was offered for him; you know that he grew.

Finally, you know that he was struck in the face, spat upon, crowned with thorns, crucified, and killed; you know that he was pierced by a lance. You know that he suffered all these things. “He is great and exceedingly worthy of praise.”

Do not despise the little one; understand the great one. He became little because you were little. Let him be understood as great, and in him you will be great.

Thus the house is built; thus the masses are raised within the house. The stones being carried to the building grow.

Therefore grow; understand Christ as great. Though little, he is great—great exceedingly. He finished his words. He wished to say how great he is; but even if he said “great” all day long, what would he say? By saying “great” all day, he would eventually finish, because the day comes to an end. His greatness exists before the days, beyond the days, without a day.

What, then, could he say? “For great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise.”

What can a little tongue say in praising the great one? By saying “exceedingly,” he uttered a sound and gave something for the mind to savor, as though saying: “What I cannot make resound, consider; and when you have considered it, it will still be little.”

Can the tongue of anyone express what no thought can fully unfold? “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise.”

Let him be praised, let him be proclaimed, let his glory be announced, and the house is built [Note: Col. 1230. Thus several manuscripts; the editions read, “and let the house be built.”].

**Note:** Thus several manuscripts. But the editions have *et aedificetur domus* (“and let the house be built”).

### 5.

“He is terrible above all gods.”

Are there gods over whom he is terrible? Let us see whom he means, and we shall see why he says this [Note: Col. 1230. Some manuscripts here and in the following occurrence read “we shall see”; others read “let us see” in both places, as does the Maurist edition.].

Before he says it, beloved, attend. The one who seems almost terrified among human beings is terrible above all gods. Did the nations not rage? Did the peoples not meditate vain things against the Lord and against his Christ (Ps. 2:1)? Did those fat bulls not surround him? Did that roaring lion not roar over him (Ps. 21:13–14), entering the hearts of the raging and crying out, “Crucify, crucify” (Matt. 27:23)?

Was the one who is terrible—not above all human beings, but above all gods—terrified by that roaring?

For where he wishes to build the house, the place itself is wooded; hence what was said yesterday: “We found it in the fields of the wood” (Ps. 131). He was seeking that very house when he said, “We found it in the fields of the wood.”

And why is that place wooded? Human beings were worshiping idols. It is not surprising that they were feeding pigs. For he was that son who abandoned his father, consumed all he had among prostitutes, living wastefully; he was feeding pigs (Luke 15:12–15)—that is, he was worshiping demons. Through that very superstition of the Gentiles, the whole earth had become a forest.

But the one who builds the house uproots the forest. For this reason it was said, “When the house was being built after the captivity.” Human beings were held captive under the devil and served demons, but they were redeemed from captivity. They were able to sell themselves, but they could not redeem themselves.

The Redeemer came and paid the price. He poured out his blood and bought the whole world.

Do you ask what he bought? See what he gave, and discover what he bought. The blood of Christ is the price. How much is it worth? What else but the whole world? What else but all the nations?

They are exceedingly ungrateful toward their price—or exceedingly proud—who say either that it was so small that it bought only the Africans, or that they themselves are so great that it was given for them alone.

**Note:** The Donatists.

Therefore let them not rejoice arrogantly; let them not be proud. He gave as much as he gave for the whole. He knows what he bought, because he knows the price at which he bought it.

Thus, because we were redeemed from captivity, the house is being built after the captivity. And who are those who held us captive? Those to whom it is said, “Announce”: they are the uprooters of the forest, so that they may uproot the forest, free the earth from captivity, and construct and build by announcing the greatness of the Lord’s house.

From where is the forest of demons uprooted except by proclaiming the one who is above all? Therefore all the nations had demons as gods. Those whom they called gods were demons, as the Apostle states more explicitly: “What the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (1 Cor. 10:20).

Because they were in captivity for this reason—that they sacrificed to demons—and because for this reason the whole earth had remained forested, this one is announced as great and exceedingly worthy of praise.

### 6. [verse 5]

And how is his greatness shown, so that he may uproot those superstitions under which the captive people were held—the people whom he came to redeem, who is terrible above all gods? And as though someone were to say to him, “Why did you say, ‘above all gods’? Are there gods, then?” he continues and says: “For all the gods of the nations are demons.”

Let Your Charity pay attention. A little earlier he had said something great: “The Lord is great, and greatly to be praised.” And as though he were falling short in praising him—“and greatly to be praised”—did I not say that he allowed you to consider what he himself could not explain in words? But, explaining it himself in words, what great thing has he told me about the Lord Jesus Christ? That he is above all demons? For after saying, “Terrible above all gods,” he added, “For all the gods of the nations are demons.”

It is not a great thing to be above demons; you too, if you wish, will be—but only if you believe in him. Is that itself the greatness of the praise: “The Lord is great and greatly to be praised”? For, wishing to explain it as human speech could, although the Holy Spirit is a great player of the instrument, nevertheless he sounds through the narrow syllables of the human spirit, and generates thoughts. Wishing, then, to explain through this language what he means, what does he say? “The Lord is great and greatly to be praised.” Say, say how greatly he is to be praised; say it. “He is terrible,” he says, “above all gods.” Why did you say, “above all gods”? “For all the gods of the nations are demons.”

And is that the whole praise of him who is greatly to be praised—that he surpasses all the gods of the nations, which are demons? Wait, and hear what follows: “But the Lord made the heavens.” Therefore he is not merely above demons, but above all the heavens that he made.

If he had said, “Above all gods, for all the gods of the nations are demons,” and the Lord’s praise had stopped there, he would have said less than we are accustomed to think about Christ. But when he said, “The Lord, however, made the heavens,” see what difference there is between the heavens and the demons; and see what difference there is between the heavens themselves and him who made the heavens. Behold how exalted the Lord is.

He did not say, “But the Lord sits above the heavens.” Perhaps someone would then think that another had made the heavens above which he sat. Rather, he said, “But the Lord made the heavens.” If he made the heavens, he also made the angels; he himself made the angels, he himself made the apostles. The demons yielded to the apostles; but the apostles themselves were heavens, because they bore the Lord.

And what Lord did they bear? The one by whom they had been made. Hear that they are heavens: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:2). To these very heavens it is said: “Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples.”

“For the Lord is great and greatly to be praised; he is terrible above all gods.” Which gods? “For all the gods of the nations are demons.” And he himself is terrible above all these gods. “But the Lord made the heavens.” O heavens, whom he made, declare his glory among the nations! Let the house be built throughout the whole earth; let the whole earth sing a new song.

### 7. [verse 6]

“Confession and beauty are before him.” Do you love beauty? Do you wish to be beautiful? Confess. He did not say, “Beauty and confession,” but “Confession and beauty.” You were ugly: confess, so that you may be beautiful. You were a sinner: confess, so that you may be righteous. You were able to disfigure yourself; you cannot make yourself beautiful.

And what kind of bridegroom is ours, who loved the ugly in order to make her beautiful? “How,” someone says, “did he love the ugly?” “I did not come,” he says, “to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9:13).

“Do you call sinners so that they may remain sinners?” “No,” he says. And how will they not be sinners? “Confession and beauty are before him.” For they confess their sins; they vomit up the evils that they had greedily swallowed. They do not return to their vomit, like an unclean dog (2 Peter 2:22); and there will be confession and beauty.

We love beauty; let us first choose confession, so that beauty may follow.

Again, someone appears who loves power; he also loves magnificence and wishes to be great, as the angels are. There is a certain magnificence in the angels, and such power that, if the angels did everything they are able to do, it could not be endured. Every human being desires the power of angels, but does not love the righteousness of angels.

Love righteousness first, and power will follow you. For what follows here as well? “Holiness and magnificence in his sanctification.” You were already seeking magnificence: love holiness first. When you have been sanctified, you will also be magnificent.

For if you perversely wish to be magnificent first, you will fall before you rise. You do not rise; you are lifted up. You rise more safely if the one who does not fall raises you. For he who does not fall descended to you. You had fallen; he descended, and stretched out his hand to you. You cannot rise by your own strength. Clasp the hand of the one who descends, so that you may be raised by the strong one.

### 8. [verse 7]

What, then? If “confession and beauty are before him,” and “holiness and magnificence in his sanctification”—this is what we proclaim when we build the house; it has already been proclaimed among the nations—what must the nations do, to whom those who uprooted the forest have proclaimed it?
