Now he says to the nations themselves: “Bring to the Lord, families of the nations; bring to the Lord glory and honor.” Do not claim them for yourselves, because those who proclaimed to you did not proclaim their own glory, but his. You too, then, bring glory and honor to the Lord, and say: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Psalm 113:1).

Do not place your hope in a human being. If each one of you is baptized, let him say: “He baptizes me, of whom the friend of the bridegroom said, ‘This is the one who baptizes’” (John 1:33). For if you say these things, you bring glory and honor to the Lord: “Bring to the Lord glory and honor.”

### 9. [verse 8]

“Bring to the Lord glory for his name.” Bring glory not to the name of human beings, not to your own name, but to his name.

“Take up sacrifices, and enter his courts.” Take up sacrifices: what will you bring in order to enter his courts? For the house has already grown, and courts have been made; let those who bring sacrifices enter the courts.

Are we going to bring bulls, goats, or sheep? Far from it. If you had wanted a sacrifice, I would certainly have given you one. He was commending to us the sacrifice that we ought to offer. See whether it is that of which he said earlier: “Confession and beauty are before him.” Confession is a sacrifice to God.

O nations, then, if you wish to enter his courts, do not enter empty-handed. “Take up sacrifices.” What sacrifices are we to carry with us? “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 50:18–19).

Enter the house of God with a humbled heart, and you have entered with a sacrifice. But if you are proud, you enter empty. For how could you be proud unless you were empty? If you were full, you would not be swollen.

How could you be full? If you carried with you the sacrifice that you would bring to the courts of the Lord.

Let us not hold you for too long; let us hurry through the rest. See the house growing; see the building extending throughout the whole world. Rejoice, because you have entered the courts; rejoice, because you are being built into the temple of God. For those who enter are themselves being built; they themselves are the house of God. He is the inhabitant for whom the house is being built throughout the whole world—and this after the captivity.

“Take up sacrifices, and enter his courts.”

### 10. [verses 9–10]

“Worship the Lord in his holy court”: in the Catholic Church; this is his holy court.

Let no one say, “Look, here is Christ,” or, “Look, there.” For false prophets will arise. Say this to them: “Not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed” (Matthew 24:23–24, 2). You call people to a whitewashed wall; I worship my God in the holy court.

### 11.

“Let all the earth be moved before his face.” Say among the nations: “The Lord has reigned from the wood.” For he has set the world right, and it will not be moved.

What testimonies there are to the building of God’s house! The clouds of heaven thunder throughout the whole world that God’s house is being built, while frogs from the marsh croak, “We alone are Christians.”

What testimonies do I produce? Those of the Psalter. I produce what you sing while deaf: open your ears—you sing these words; you sing with me, but you do not agree with me. Your tongue sounds what mine sounds, but your heart is out of tune with mine.

Do you not sing these things? Look at the testimonies of the whole world: “Let all the earth be moved before his face”—and you say that it is not moved?

“Say among the nations: ‘The Lord has reigned from the wood.’” Or perhaps they will prevail here and say that they reign from the wood because they reign with the clubs of the Circumcellions? Reign from Christ’s cross, if you are going to reign from the wood.

For this wood of yours makes you wooden; the wood of Christ carries you across the sea.

You hear the Psalm saying, “He has set the world right, and it will not be moved,” and you say that it has not merely been moved after being set right, but has even diminished. Are you telling the truth and is he lying? Are the false prophets who cry, “Look, here is Christ; look, there,” telling the truth, while this prophet is lying?

Brothers, against these most explicit words you hear a din in the corners: “He handed him over,” and, “He handed him over.” What are you saying? Are your voices to be heard, or the voices of God? “For he has set the world right, and it will not be moved.”

I show you the world built up; take up a sacrifice and enter the courts of the Lord. You do not have a sacrifice; therefore you do not wish to enter.

What is this? If God had prescribed for you a bull, a goat, or a ram, you would find something to bring. He prescribed a humble heart for you, and you do not wish to enter. You do not find this in yourself because you have swollen with pride.

“For he has set the world right, and it will not be moved. He will judge the peoples in equity.” Then those who do not now wish to love equity will lament.

### 12. [verse 11]

“Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult.” Let the heavens rejoice, which declare the glory of God; let the heavens rejoice, which the Lord made. Let the earth exult, which the heavens rain upon.

For the heavens are preachers, and the earth is the audience.

“Let the sea and its fullness be moved.” What sea? The age, the world. The sea and its fullness were moved: the whole world was stirred up against the Church as it spread and was built throughout the whole earth.

You heard about this agitation in the Gospel: “They will hand you over to tribunals” (Mark 13:9).

The sea was moved; but when could the sea overcome the one who made the heavens?

### 13. [verses 12–13]

“The fields will rejoice, and everything in them.” All the gentle, all the meek, all the just are God’s fields.

“Then all the trees of the forest will exult.” The trees of the forest are the pagans.

Why do they now rejoice? Because “they were cut from the wild olive and grafted into the olive” (Romans 11:17).

“Then all the trees of the forest will exult”: because the immense cedar and cypress trees have been cut down, and imperishable timbers have been carried over for the building of the house.

They were trees of the forest, but before they entered the building; they were trees of the forest, but before they bore the olive.

### 14.

“Then all the trees of the forest will exult before the face of the Lord, because he has come, because he has come to judge the earth.”

He came first, and afterward he will come again. He first came into his Church in clouds. What are the clouds that carried him? The apostles preaching, of whom you heard when the Apostle was read: “We are ambassadors for Christ,” he says, “entreating you on behalf of Christ to be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20).

These are the clouds in which he came, apart from his later coming, when he will come to judge the living and the dead.

He came first in clouds. His voice first sounded thus in the Gospel: “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming in clouds.” What does “from now on” mean? Will the Lord not come afterward, when all the tribes of the earth will mourn?

He first came in his preachers and filled the whole world. Let us not resist his first coming, so that we may not fear the second.

And woe then to the pregnant and the nursing. You heard in the Gospel just now: “Take heed, because you do not know at what hour he will come” (Mark 13:26, 17, 33). These things were said figuratively.

Who are the pregnant, and who are the nursing? Souls that have hope in the world are called pregnant. Those who have already obtained what they hoped for are represented as nursing.

For example: someone wishes to buy an estate; she is pregnant, because the thing has not yet happened—the womb swells with hope. She buys it; she has given birth and is nursing what she bought.

“Woe to the pregnant and the nursing”: woe to those who have hope in the world; woe to those who cling to the things that they have brought forth from the hope of the world.

What, then, should a Christian do? Use the world, not serve the world.

What does this mean? “Having as though not having.” So he says; so he exhorts those whom he does not wish to be found on that day as pregnant and nursing. Thus he exhorts them:

> “From now on, brothers, the time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep as though they were not weeping; those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they were not using it—for the form of this world is passing away. I want you to be without anxiety” (1 Corinthians 7:29–32).

The one who is without anxiety awaits securely the coming of his Lord. For what kind of love for Christ is it to fear that he may come? Brothers, are we not ashamed? We love him, and we fear that he may come. Surely we love him? Or do we love our sins more?

Let us therefore hate those very sins, and love the one who will come to punish sins. He will come, whether we wish it or not. For the fact that he does not come now does not mean that he will not come.

He will come, and you do not know when. If he finds you prepared, the fact that you do not know will do you no harm.

“Then all the trees of the forest will exult before the face of the Lord, because he has come”—first. And afterward what? “Because he has come to judge the earth.”

“And all the trees of the forest will exult.” He came first, and afterward to judge the earth. He will find those who believed in his first coming exulting, because he has come.

### 15.

“For he will judge the world in equity”: not a part of it, because he did not purchase a part. He must judge the whole, because he paid the price for the whole.

You heard in the Gospel that, when he comes, “he will gather his elect from the four winds” (Mark 13:27). He gathers all his elect from the four winds; therefore, from the whole world.

For Adam himself also signifies the world—something I once mentioned. There are four letters: A, D, A, and M. And as the Greeks speak, the four regions of the world begin with these letters: *Anatolēn* (Ἀνατολήν), they call the East; *Dysin* (Δύσιν), the West; *Arktōn* (Ἄρκτον), the North; *Mesēmbrían* (Μεσημβρίαν), the South. You have *Adam*.

Adam himself, then, was scattered throughout the whole world. He was in one place and fell, and, in a certain way broken into pieces, filled the whole world. But God’s mercy gathered the fragments from everywhere, melted them together in the fire of love, and made one thing out of what had been broken.

That craftsman knows how to do this; let no one despair. It is a great work, certainly, but consider who the craftsman is. The one who made it restored it; the one who formed it reshaped it.

“He will judge the world in equity, and the peoples in his truth.” What are equity and truth? He will gather his elect with him for judgment, but he will separate the others from one another. For he will place some at his right hand and others at his left.

What is more equitable, what more truthful, than that those who refused to show mercy before the judge came should not expect mercy from the judge? But those who wished to show mercy will be judged with mercy.

For he will say to those placed at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” And he reckons to them works of mercy: “For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,” and so forth.

Again, what is reckoned against those placed at the left? That they refused to show mercy. And where will they go? “Go into the eternal fire.”

This dreadful sentence will produce a great groan. But what did another Psalm say? “The righteous will be in everlasting remembrance; he will not fear an evil report” (Psalm 111:7).

What is the evil report? “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:31–46).

The one who rejoices at the good report will not fear the evil report. How will they rejoice at the good report? “Come, blessed of my Father.” And from what report will they not fear? “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

This is equity; this is truth. “For he will judge the world in equity, and the peoples in his truth.”

Or is the judge not going to be just because you are unjust? Or is truth not going to be truthful because you are a liar?

But if you wish to have a merciful judge, be merciful before he comes. Forgive whatever has been committed against you; give from what you have in abundance.

And whose is it that you give, if not his? If you gave from what was your own, it would be generosity; when you give from what is his, it is repayment. “For what do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

These are the sacrifices most pleasing to God: mercy, humility, confession, peace, love. Let us bring these, and await securely the coming of the judge, who will judge the world in equity and the peoples in his truth.

## Exposition of Psalm 96

### Sermon to the People

### 1.

God provides great spectacles for the Christian heart, spectacles than which truly nothing more delightful can be found—provided that there is present a palate of faith capable of tasting the honey of God.

We believe that all of you who have believed wholeheartedly in our Savior possess his Spirit, which delights you when the prophecies are read—prophecies uttered from the mouths of the saints so many years ago and fulfilled after so many years in the faith of the nations.

For the holy prophets themselves experienced great delight when they saw these things in the spirit—not already fulfilled, but still future. It was a great pleasure for them. Yet because of the love with which they were inflamed for us, whom they did not yet see and whom they were bringing to birth in the spirit, they wished, if it could be done, to live with us in this age and see fulfilled what they prophesied in the spirit.

Therefore the Lord said to his disciples, who were already beginning to see these things: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Matthew 13:17).

Although they saw these things in the spirit, they were still, in a certain way, being formed for them as future events; for the apostles, however, they were already being made present.

Hence that Simeon, a certain righteous old man, rejoiced greatly when he saw the infant Jesus, recognizing the great in the small and acknowledging in that little body the Creator of heaven and earth. He rejoiced greatly because he had received the answer that he would not depart from this life before seeing the salvation of God.

He recognized him, was delighted, and exulted with joy; and he said this: “Lord, now you dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:25–30).

Great, then, is this delight, and love produces it.

We were delighted when this Psalm was sung. Some things in it were understood by everyone; others, as we judge, either by a few or certainly not by all.

Let us therefore consider it together in this sermon in which we serve you, and see with what great condescension God wished to make us joyful, presenting what he promised and displaying to us the truth of his promises.

### 2. [verse 1]

The Psalm is entitled: “For David, when his land was restored.”

Let us refer everything to Christ, if we wish to keep to the path of correct understanding. Let us not depart from the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), lest our understanding collapse. Let what was wavering in unstable motion be made firm in him; let what was hanging amid uncertainties lean upon him.

Whatever doubt a person has in mind when he hears the Scriptures of God, let him not depart from Christ. When Christ has been revealed to him in those words, let him understand that he has understood. Before he reaches an understanding of Christ, however, let him not presume that he has understood.

“For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4).

What, then, does “when his land was restored” mean, and how is it understood in Christ?

It is easy to recognize how David is understood as Christ. Christ is from Mary and from the seed of David; and because he was to come from his seed, he was therefore prophetically foretold under David’s name.

Thus David is Christ, because the interpretation of David is “strong of hand.” And who is as strong of hand as the one who conquered the world from the cross?

After his resurrection and ascension, when the Holy Spirit had been received and the apostles were speaking in various languages, the multitude of those who had crucified him was shaken. They sought a plan of salvation, received it, and believed. The guilt of Christ’s blood was forgiven them; they were given to drink Christ’s blood. They became faithful to the one whom they had persecuted. They believed in the one whom they had crucified and before whom, mocking him, they had shaken their heads. They wished to have that very one as their head (Acts 2).

Thus his land was restored, which is what the title of the Psalm contains.

For his land was Judea, and all Judea had perished when, in ignorance, they crucified their Lord—madly raging against the physician and rejecting salvation in their madness.

As though, then, the whole of Judea had perished—how entirely? The apostles themselves were shaken. Peter, who had followed with bold love, denied him three times in fearful agitation.

When he rose again, the Lord Jesus Christ found certain people on the road talking among themselves about him. When he asked what they were discussing, they said to him:

> “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and do you not know what has happened there in these days?”  
> He said to them, “What things?”  
> And they said: “About Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet powerful in deed and word before God and all the people; and how our chief priests and rulers handed him over to the sentence of death and crucified him. But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:18–21).

They had already lost hope in Christ. They did not say, “We hope that he will redeem,” but, “We were hoping that he would redeem Israel.” He was with them, but their hope in him was not.

He showed himself to them; he was also manifested to the other disciples, seen and touched, and found by those to whom he had already seemed to have perished. The faith of those who had fallen was restored; his land was restored.

Then, after spending forty days with them, he ascended into heaven (Acts 1:3, 9). And, as I mentioned a little earlier, having sent the Holy Spirit, he caused his disciples—uneducated men—to speak in the languages of all nations.

Then those for whom he had not said in vain, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34), were shaken, as we have said. They sought salvation and received the counsel that they should believe in him. Three thousand believed in one day, and then five thousand again (Acts 2:41; 4:4).

The Church of Christ began to blaze throughout Judea, where Christ’s reproach had blazed; and his land was restored.

But because he had said, “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16), the apostles were also sent to the nations, to whom the prophets had not been sent.

Those who had not sought were sought; those who expected nothing were found. They found as redeemer the God whom they had not held as the one who makes promises.

For the Jews already held God as the one who makes promises, because the prophets had proclaimed Christ there and promised Christ there. But although they had heard the promised one, they had not recognized him as present. To the nations nothing had been promised; nevertheless, even their faith had been spoken of in the prophets. It had not been spoken to them, but it had been spoken about them.

He was sent also to them. You heard, through God’s providential ordering, since the reading from the Acts of the Apostles was read to you just now, how the centurion Cornelius believed.

Cornelius the centurion was not of the Jewish nation. He prayed, fasted, and gave alms. God did not abandon him, although he was situated among the nations. An angel was sent to him to announce that his alms and prayers had been accepted before God. He believed after summoning Peter to himself (Acts 10).

Could the angel not have taught him? He sent him to Peter, so that faith might come to him more appropriately through a human being, because the Lord had deigned to visit human beings. He did not disdain to teach through a human being, although he had deigned to become human.

Thus his land was restored: one wall came from the Jews, another wall came from the nations, and from these two walls, coming from different directions, he himself was the cornerstone where both were joined together (Ephesians 2:20).

### 3.

Again, how do we understand “when his land was restored”? When his flesh was resurrected.

Another interpretation, which nevertheless does not depart from Christ, can present itself to us in this way: the land restored is the flesh resurrected.

For after his resurrection all the things sung in the Psalm took place.

Let us now hear a Psalm full of joy concerning the restoration of the land. May the Lord our God himself awaken in us an expectation and delight worthy of so great a thing. May he himself guide our discourse so that it is suited to your hearts, so that whatever in such spectacles makes our heart exult here may reach our tongue, and from there your ears, then your hearts, and from there your deeds.

### 4.

“The Lord has reigned.”

The one who stood before the judge; the one who received slaps; the one who was scourged; the one who was spat upon; the one who was crowned with thorns; the one who was struck with blows; the one who was hung upon the wood; the one who, while hanging on the wood, was mocked; the one who died on the cross; the one who was pierced with a spear; the one who was buried—he himself has risen.

“The Lord has reigned.”

Let kingdoms rage as much as they can. What will they do to the King of kings, the Lord of all kings, the Creator of all ages?

Is he despised because he appeared so submissive and so humble? It is mercy, not weakness. He appeared humble so that we might grasp him.

But now let us see: “The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult, let the many islands rejoice.”

This is certainly true, because the word of God was preached not only on the mainland, but also on the islands situated in the midst of the sea. They too are full of Christians, full of servants of God.

The sea does not separate the one who made the sea. Where ships can approach, can the words of God not approach? The islands have been filled.

Nevertheless, the islands can also rightly be understood figuratively as all the Churches.

Why islands? Because they are surrounded by the waves of every temptation. But just as an island can be battered by waves roaring all around it without being broken, and itself breaks the waves that come against it more than it is broken by them, so too the Churches of God, springing up throughout the whole world, have endured the persecutions of unbelievers roaring on every side. And behold, the islands stand, and the sea has now been calmed.

“Let the many islands rejoice.”

### 5. [verse 2]

“Cloud and darkness are around him; righteousness and judgment are the establishment of his throne.”

For whom are “cloud and darkness around him”? For whom are “righteousness and judgment the establishment of his throne”?

Cloud and darkness are for the impious, who did not understand him; righteousness and judgment are for the faithful, who believed in him. The former did not see because of pride; the latter deserved to be guided because of humility.

Hear of cloud and mist, and hear of righteousness and judgment. The Lord himself says: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

What does “those who see may become blind” mean? Those who think that they see, who consider themselves wise, who do not think that they need medicine—let them become blind; let them fail to understand. But let those who do not see see: let those who confess their blindness deserve to be enlightened.

Therefore let there be cloud and darkness around him for those who did not know him; but for those confessing and humbling themselves, “righteousness and judgment are the establishment of his throne.”

He calls those who believe in him his throne itself. For he has made his throne from them, because Wisdom sits in them; for the Son of God is the Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24).

We also heard a great testimony to this understanding from another Scripture: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.”

Therefore, because those who believed in him were made righteous—justified by faith—they became his throne. He sits in them, judging from them and guiding them.

Why? Because he found them gentle, like tame beasts—not kicking, not proudly throwing off their necks from his yoke, not refusing his whip. They became his good and gentle beasts, and deserved what is said in another Psalm: “He will guide the gentle in judgment; he will teach the meek his ways” (Psalm 24:9).

Therefore there is cloud and darkness for those who are not upright; but for the meek, “righteousness and judgment are the establishment of his throne.”

### 6. [verse 3]

“Fire will go before him, and it will burn his enemies round about.”

Of what fire does he speak, brothers, when he says, “Fire will go before him, and it will burn his enemies round about”?

I do not think he is speaking of that fire into which the impious will be sent by the final sentence of judgment, when those separated to the left, as we remember reading in the Gospel, will be told: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

I do not think he is speaking of that fire. Why do I not think so? Because he speaks of a certain fire that will go before him, before he comes to judgment.

For it is said that the fire will go before him and burn all around—that is, throughout the whole world—his enemies. That fire will be after his coming; but this fire will go before him.

What, then, is this fire? We can understand it as the punishment of the wicked; we can understand it as the salvation of the redeemed.

As punishment for the wicked, how? When Christ was preached, the nations grew angry and stirred up persecution. Their anger was a fire, consuming more those who persecuted than those whom they persecuted.

When we see two people, one becoming angry and the other enduring patiently, it is for you to judge which of them is burning. You can observe such a spectacle among human beings.

Place before your eyes an unjust person, agitated in mind, savage in appearance, with flaming eyes, words flashing like sparks, rushing toward the murder of another, plunder, injuries, insults; unable to contain himself or restrain himself.

Place beside him another person patiently receiving the words, blows, and whatever the first wishes to inflict, and, when struck on one cheek, offering the other as well.

When you see fury on one side and gentleness on the other; anger on one side and patience on the other; flames on one side and endurance on the other—will you hesitate to pronounce which of them is burning and suffering punishment? Is it the one whose body is being tormented, or the one whose spirit is being ravaged?

Therefore the prophet Isaiah also said: “And now fire will consume the adversaries” (Isaiah 26:11).

What does “and now” mean? Before that great day of judgment comes, those who will later burn in the punishment of that everlasting fire are already burning in their own fury.

Unless, perhaps, you think, my brothers, that the injustice proceeding from one person to harm another harms the one toward whom it proceeds, but does not harm the one from whom it proceeds. How could that happen?

Sometimes a burning torch is applied to damp, green wood. It does not set the wood on fire, but the torch itself continues to burn. So too with your enemy.

If an unjust person arises who plots against you or prepares some trouble for you, he is unjust. But if you are green wood—that is, if, vigorous and flourishing with spiritual sap, you resist the flames of enmity by praying for the one who persecutes you—he burns, while you remain unharmed. His injustice harms him; it harms you not at all.

Unless you think that it harms you if he does something to your body, while your patient and incorrupt soul reaches God to be crowned, following the example of its Lord, who chose to suffer at the hands of the Jews and, although he could have avoided death, died—because he who could have chosen not to be born was also born.

You were born by necessity; he by will. You die by necessity; he by mercy.

As, then, the Jews harmed him not at all, so no persecuting enemy will harm you, if you choose to be a member of that head.

Editorial notes and textual apparatus:

- [Col. 1231, §6] Thus Am., Er., and our manuscripts; LOV reads *per angustas* (“through narrow [syllables]”).
- [Col. 1232, §7] Fr. Ven. and LOV read: “Do you call sinners? Do you call them so that they may remain sinners?” M [has the printed wording].
- [Col. 1233, §8] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “what the nations ought to do.” The preceding question is: “What did those who uprooted the forest proclaim?”
- [Col. 1233, §9] Most manuscripts read “let them enter”; the editions read “they enter.”
- [Col. 1234, §11] The principal manuscripts read “choose equity” (*eligere*), rather than “love equity” (*diligere*).
- [Col. 1234, §13] Am. and our manuscripts read “they were cut off as wild olives” (*praecisi sunt oleastri*), rather than “from the wild olive” (*de oleastro*).
- [Col. 1235, §13] LOV reads *pararent* (“made ready the olive”); most manuscripts read *parerent* (“bore the olive”).
- [Col. 1235, §14] Thus the manuscripts: “the things which they have brought forth from the hope of the world”; the editions read “which they have brought forth from the world.”
- [Col. 1235, §14] The better manuscripts read “as though not possessing” (*quasi non tenentes*); Am. reads “not using”; LOV, “not buying”; Er., “neither buying nor using.”
- [Col. 1236, §15] See Tractate 9 on John, no. 11, and Tractate 10, no. 12.
- [Col. 1236, §15] Two manuscripts read “produces” (*habet*) rather than “will produce” (*faciet*).
- [Col. 1238, Psalm 96, §2] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “with which they also all …” (*cum qua tota ipsi etiam, etc.*).
- [Col. 1238, Psalm 96, §2] The manuscripts read “the chief priests” (*summi sacerdotum*).
- [Col. 1240, Psalm 96, §5] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “thus” (*sic*).
- [Col. 1240, Psalm 96, §5] Four manuscripts read “Let us hear” (*Audiamus*) rather than “We have heard” (*Audivimus*).
- [Col. 1240, Psalm 96, §5] Some manuscripts read “are guided” (*directi*), and others “are meek” (*mansueti*), instead of “are upright” (*recti*).
- [Col. 1241, Psalm 96, §6] Thus the manuscripts; LOV reads “stripes and blows” (*verbera ac plagas*).

7. Behold, we have understood the fire that goes before him—that is, at the present time it is to be understood as some punishment for unbelievers and the wicked. Let us understand the fire, if we can, also as the salvation of the redeemed; for this is what we had proposed. The Lord himself says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49). Fire, just as he says “sword”: for in another place he says that he did not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword (Matthew 10:34). The sword is for separation, the fire for burning; but both are beneficial, because the sword of his word has beneficially separated us from our evil way of life.

For he brought a sword and separated each of the faithful either from his father who had not believed in Christ, or likewise from his unbelieving mother; or, if he was born of Christian parents, at least from his former ancestry. None of us has failed to have either a grandfather, a great-grandfather, or some ancient origin among the Gentiles, and in that accursed unbelief toward God. We have been separated from what we were; but the sword intervened, dividing without killing.

So also with the fire: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.” Those who believed in him burned with enthusiasm and received the flame of love. Therefore, when the Holy Spirit was sent to the Apostles, he appeared in this way: “There appeared to them,” he says, “divided tongues as of fire, which also rested upon each one of them” (Acts 2:3). Inflamed by this fire, they began to go throughout the world, to inflame and set fire all around to his enemies.

Who are his enemies? Those who, having abandoned the God by whom they had been made, worshiped the images they had made. They were set on fire: if they were evil, for destruction; if they were good, for restoration. Either the one who refused to believe was himself burned by that fire, becoming worse after hearing the word of God and being consumed and destroyed by his own envy; or, if he was converted and believed, nothing in him remained unburned. The hay had burned so that the gold might be purified.

Gold is faith; hay is carnal desire. “All flesh is hay,” Isaiah says, “and all the honor of flesh is like the flower of hay” (Isaiah 40:6). Whatever there is in a carnal person that desires vain and worldly things is hay. How many, perhaps, even of our brothers have gone to the theater? They have been led by hay. Is not this fire to be desired for them, so that the hay may burn and the gold be purified? For the faith that is in them is pressed down by hay. It is therefore good for them to burn with holy fire, so that, once the hay has been consumed, what Christ redeemed may shine forth in its preciousness.

Thus: “Fire shall go before him, and shall burn up his enemies round about.” There are those who have burned beneficially and are his faithful today. They were his enemies, and now they are his faithful. You seek his enemies, but they are no more: they have been consumed; they burned. Love consumed in them what they were persecuting—Christ—and purified in them what they were to believe in Christ: “And shall burn up his enemies round about.”

[Note: [Col. 1242] Am. and the manuscripts read *quod persequebatur* (“what it was persecuting”); below, *quod crederet* (“what it was to believe”). But the reading seems to be *quo persequebantur* (“what they were persecuting”), *quo crederent* (“what they were to believe”).]

8. [Verse 4.] “His lightning flashes appeared to the world.” Great rejoicing! Do we not see it? Is it not evident? “His lightning flashes appeared to the whole earth”; his enemies were inflamed, his enemies were set on fire. Whatever opposed him burned, and “his lightning flashes appeared to the world.”

How did they appear? So that people might now believe. From where did the lightning flashes come? From the clouds. What are God’s clouds? The preachers of truth. You see a cloud in the sky: misty, dark, and containing within it I know not what hidden thing. If lightning flashes from the cloud, brightness leaps forth. From the very thing you had despised, there sprang forth what you would fear.

Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ sent his Apostles, his preachers, like clouds. They appeared to be human beings and were despised—just as clouds are seen and despised before something marvelous leaps forth from them. At first they were human beings carrying flesh, weak; moreover, they were uneducated, untaught, and of lowly status. But there was in them something that would flash; there was in them something that would glitter.

Peter, a fisherman, approached, prayed, and a dead man rose again (Acts 9:40). The human form was a cloud; the splendor of the miracle was a flash of lightning. So it was in their words, so in their deeds: when they said marvelous things and performed marvelous deeds, “his lightning flashes appeared to the world.”

The earth saw and was shaken. For if this is not true—if the whole earth does not now cry out, “Amen,” shaken by the lightning flashes bursting forth from those clouds—what is? It saw, and the earth was shaken.

9. [Verse 5.] “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord.” Who are the mountains? The proud. Every height that exalts itself against God trembled and collapsed before the deeds of Christ and of Christians; and when I say what was said—“melted”—no better word can be found.

“The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord.” Where is the height of the powers? Where is the hardness of unbelievers? “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord.” The Lord was fire to them; before his face they melted like wax. They remained hard only until that fire was brought near.

Every height has been leveled. Now the pagan does not dare to blaspheme Christ. He does not believe in him, but nevertheless he does not blaspheme him. Although he has not yet become a living stone, the hard mountain has nevertheless been conquered.

“The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord, before the face of the Lord of the whole earth”—not only of the Jews but also of the Gentiles, as the Apostle says (Romans 3:29): “For God is not the God of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles.”

The Lord, therefore, is Lord of the whole earth: the Lord Jesus Christ was born in Judea, but he was not born for Judea alone, because even before he was born he made all people; and he who made all has remade all. “Before the face of the Lord of the whole earth.”

10. [Verse 6.] “The heavens declared his righteousness, and all peoples saw his glory.” Which heavens declared it? “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:2). What are the heavens? Those who have been made his dwelling place. For just as God sits in the heavens, so he sits in the Apostles, so he sits in the preachers of the Gospel.

And you, if you wish, will be a heaven. Do you wish to be a heaven? Purge the earth from your heart. If you do not have earthly desires, and do not falsely answer that you have your heart above, you will be a heaven. “If you have risen with Christ”—the Apostle speaks to the faithful—“seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3:1–2).

You have begun to set your mind on the things that are above and not on those upon the earth. Have you not become a heaven? You carry flesh, but in your heart you are already heaven, for “your citizenship will be in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

Such a person also declares Christ. For who among the faithful is silent about Christ? Let your Charity attend: do you think that we alone, standing here, declare Christ, and that you do not declare him? From where do people come to us wishing to become Christians—people whom we have never seen, whom we do not know, to whom we have never preached? Did they perhaps believe without anyone declaring him? The Apostle says: “How will they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?” (Romans 10:14).

Therefore the whole Church proclaims Christ, and the heavens declare his righteousness, because all the faithful who take care to win for God those who have not yet believed, and who do this out of love, are heavens.

God thunders from them the terror of his judgment; the one who was unbelieving trembles, is afraid, and believes. Show people what Christ has accomplished throughout the whole world by speaking to them and leading them to love Christ.

How many people today have brought their friends either to a pantomime or to a flute-player? Why, except because they loved him? You too must love Christ. For he has provided such great spectacles that no one can say he finds anything blameworthy in them—he who conquered the world. Indeed, sometimes the one whom someone loves in the theater is defeated in that very thing. No one, however, is defeated in Christ; there is nothing of which to be ashamed.

Seize them, bring them, draw as many as you can. Be confident: you are bringing them to one who does not displease those who see him; and ask him to enlighten them and enable them to see well.

[Note: [Col. 1244] Thus the oldest Corbie manuscript. The editions read *exspectent* (“let them await”); and so do many manuscripts, but in this scribal usage *exspecto* and *exspectacula* are often preferred for *specto* (“I see”) and *spectacula* (“spectacles”).]

“The heavens declared his righteousness, and all peoples saw his glory.”

11. [Verse 7.] “Let all who worship carved images be put to shame.” Has this not happened? Have they not been put to shame? Are they not put to shame every day?

Carved images are idols made by hand.

[Note: [Col. 1244] Thus Am. and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain read *manifesta* (“manifest”).]

Why, then, are all who worship carved images now put to shame? Because “all peoples saw his glory.” Now all peoples confess the glory of Christ. Let those who worship stones be ashamed.

For those stones were dead; we have found the living stone. Indeed, those stones never lived, so that they should not even be called dead. But our stone is living, has always lived with the Father, died for us and rose again, now lives, and “death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Romans 6:9).

The peoples have come to know this glory of his: they abandon the temples and run to the churches. “Let all who worship carved images be put to shame.” Do they still seek to worship carved images? They were unwilling to abandon the idols; they have been abandoned by the idols.

“Let all who worship carved images be put to shame, who glory in their images.” But there arises some disputant who considered himself learned and says:

“I do not worship that stone, nor that senseless image. Surely your prophet could not have failed to know that ‘they have eyes and do not see’ (Psalm 113:5); and I know that the image has neither a soul nor eyes with which to see, nor ears with which to hear. I do not worship it; rather, I worship what I see and serve the one whom I do not see.”

Who is this? “Some invisible divinity,” he says, “that presides over that image.”

By giving this account of their images, they think themselves eloquent, because they do not worship idols but worship demons. For, brothers, as the Apostle says: “What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to become partners with demons” (1 Corinthians 10:19–20). For we know that “an idol is nothing” (1 Corinthians 8:4).

The Apostle himself said this: “We know that an idol is nothing”; but “what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God.” He said: “I do not want you to become partners with demons.”

Let them not therefore excuse themselves on the ground that they are not devoted to senseless idols; they are more devoted to demons, which is more dangerous. For if they worshiped only idols, then, just as the idols would not help them, so they would do them no harm. But if you worship and serve demons, they will be your masters.

And what kind of masters will they be? Your enemies, envious of you. They must envy your freedom; they always want to possess you, always want to make you such as they can drag away with themselves.

For these evil spirits have an innate malevolence and a certain destructive desire to harm. They rejoice in the evil of human beings, and they feed upon our deception if they have deceived us. And what do they seek? Not those over whom they will rule eternally, but those with whom they will be condemned eternally—just as a malicious robber is accustomed to name an innocent man.

If a living man were set on fire, would he burn less if two burned? Would he die less if two died? His punishment is not diminished, but his malevolence is nourished. “Let him die with me,” he says—not claiming that he will die less, but taking comfort in the evil of another.

Such is the devil. He wishes to lead astray those who will be punished with him. And because he cannot deceive God the Judge—for he cannot name an innocent person before him—he persuades people to sin, wanting to have genuine crimes to bring against them.

Behold what kind of masters those make for themselves who worship idols and demons: “What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to become partners with demons.”

12. What kind of God do we have? Hear what follows. For when he had said, “Let all who worship carved images be put to shame, who glory in their images”—

[Note: [Col. 1245] In the printed editions the word *addidit* (“he added”) appears here; it is rightly absent from the manuscripts. Since the words “when he had said” refer to the two preceding parts of verse 7, the text immediately shows, against the idolaters’ excuse that they worship not stones but divinities, that the words “Worship him, all his angels” follow here.]

—lest they should come forward as though giving an account of their images and say, “We do not worship stones but divinities”—what divinities do you worship? Tell me: do you worship demons, or good spirits such as the angels? For there are holy angels, and there are wicked spirits.

I say that in your temples none but wicked spirits are worshiped: spirits that arrogantly demand sacrifice for themselves and wish to be worshiped as gods. They are wicked; they are proud.

Such also are wicked human beings who seek their own glory and despise God’s glory. But consider holy people who are like the angels. When you find some holy servant of God, if you wish to honor and worship him as God, he forbids you. He does not wish to claim God’s honor for himself; he does not wish to be God to you, but to be with you under God.

The holy Apostles Paul and Barnabas did this. They were preaching the word of God in Lycaonia. After they had performed miracles in Lycaonia, the inhabitants of that region brought victims and wanted to sacrifice to them, calling Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercury. They were not pleased.

Did they perhaps refuse to have sacrifice offered to them because they abhorred being compared with demons? No, but because they shuddered at divine honor being offered to human beings. Their own words show this; we are not guessing. For the reading from that same book continues and says how they were moved:

“Then Paul and Barnabas tore their garments and said, ‘Men, brothers, what are you doing? We also are human beings subject to suffering, like you’” (Acts 14:13–14).

Pay attention. Just as good human beings forbid those who wished to worship them as gods, and instead wish the one God to be worshiped, the one God to be adored, and sacrifice to be offered to the one God rather than to themselves, so all the holy angels seek the glory of the one whom they love.

They strive to seize and inflame all whom they love for his worship, his adoration, and the contemplation of him. They proclaim him to them, not themselves, because they are angels. And because they are soldiers, they know no glory to seek except that of their Emperor. If they sought their own glory, they would be condemned as tyrants.

Such was the devil, and such were the demons—that is, his angels. He arrogated divine honor to himself and to all the demons, filled the temples of the pagans, and persuaded people to make images and offer sacrifices to them.

Would it not have been better for them to worship the holy angels rather than demons? They reply: “We do not worship evil demons. We worship the angels you speak of, the powers and ministers of the great God.”

Would that you wished to worship them! You would easily learn from them not to worship them.

Hear the angel who teaches. He was teaching a certain disciple of Christ and showing him many miracles in the Apocalypse of John. When the disciple had been shown a certain miraculous vision, he was terrified and threw himself at the angel’s feet. But that angel, who sought nothing except the glory of his Lord, said: “Rise; what are you doing? Worship him, for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers” (Revelation 19:10).

What then, my brothers? Let no one say: “I am afraid that the angel will become angry with me if I do not worship him as my god.” He becomes angry with you when you wish to worship him. For he is good and loves God. Just as demons become angry if they are not worshiped, so angels are indignant if they are worshiped in place of God.

But perhaps a weak and fearful heart will say to itself: “If demons become angry because they are not worshiped, I am afraid of offending demons.” What can even their prince, the devil, do to you? If he could do anything, not one of us would remain.

Are not so many things spoken daily against him by Christian mouths, while the Christian harvest grows? When you become angry with your most wicked servant, you give him this name: “Satan,” “devil.” This may be your error: you say this to a human being and, carried away by immoderate anger, rush to insult the image of God. Yet you choose as the name to call him what you detest intensely.

If he could, would he not avenge himself? But he is not permitted to do so; and he does only as much as he is permitted. He also wanted to tempt Job, and sought only the power to do so (Job 1:11); he could do nothing unless he had received permission.

Why, then, do you not confidently worship God, without whose will no one harms you, and by whose permission you are corrected rather than overthrown? For if the Lord your God should be pleased to permit some human being or some spirit to harm you, he will correct you so that you may cry out to him: “The Lord has chastened me severely, but he has not given me over to death” (Psalm 117:18).

Thus: “Let all who worship carved images be put to shame, who glory in their images. Worship him, all his angels.”

[Note: [Col. 1246] The editions read *sancti vel Angeli* (“the holy ones or angels”). The particle *vel* (“or”) is absent from the manuscripts.]

Let the pagans learn to worship God. They wish to worship angels; let them imitate the angels and worship the one whom the angels worship.

“Worship him, all his angels.” Let the angel who was sent to Cornelius worship him; for while Cornelius was worshiping him, he sent Cornelius to Peter (Acts 10:3ff.). Let him worship Christ the Lord of Peter, himself also Peter’s fellow servant.

[Note: [Col. 1247] The editions read: “for while Cornelius was worshiping him, he sent Cornelius to Peter, to worship Christ the Lord of Peter,” and so forth. We have corrected the passage according to the manuscripts.]

“Worship him, all his angels.”

13. [Verse 8.] “Zion heard, and rejoiced.” What did Zion hear? That all his angels worship him. What did Zion hear? Here is what it heard: “The heavens declared his righteousness, and all peoples saw his glory. Let all who worship carved images be put to shame, who glory in their images.”

For the Church did not yet exist among the Gentiles. In Judea, people from the Jews had believed, and those Jews who had believed thought that they alone belonged to Christ. The Apostles were sent to the Gentiles, and the Gospel was preached to Cornelius. Cornelius believed and was baptized, and those who were with Cornelius were baptized as well.

But you know what happened before they were baptized. The Reader has not yet reached this point, but some remember it; and those who do not remember may hear it briefly from me.

An angel was sent to Cornelius; the angel sent Cornelius to Peter; Peter came to Cornelius. Since Cornelius was from the Gentiles, both he and those who were with him were uncircumcised. Therefore, lest they hesitate to entrust the Gospel to the uncircumcised, before Cornelius himself and those who were with him were baptized, the Holy Spirit came upon them and filled them, and they began to speak in tongues.

The Holy Spirit had fallen upon no one except one who had been baptized; but upon these he fell before Baptism. Peter might have hesitated whether to baptize the uncircumcised. The Holy Spirit came, and they began to speak in tongues. An invisible gift was bestowed, and it removed the hesitation concerning the visible sacrament. They were all baptized.

And you have it written there: “The Apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God, and they glorified God.” This is what the psalm recalls here: “Zion heard, and rejoiced; and the daughters of Judea rejoiced.”

[Note: [Col. 1247] The editions read *filiae Judae* (“daughters of Judah”). Many manuscripts, following the Septuagint, read *filiae Judaeae* (“daughters of Judea”). The same reading is found in the better-quality codices at Psalm 47, verse 12.]

What did Zion hear and rejoice over? That the Gentiles had received the word of God. One wall had come, but the other had not yet come. Zion itself—the Church that was in Judea—is specifically named here.

“Zion heard, and rejoiced; and the daughters of Judea rejoiced.” Thus it is written: “The Apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard.” See whether the daughters of Judea did not rejoice. What did they hear? That the Gentiles also had received the word of God.

Where did this psalm say that? “The heavens declared his righteousness, and all peoples saw his glory.” And because the Gentiles believed—among whom idols had been worshiped—the psalm continues: “Let all who worship carved images be put to shame, who glory in their images. Zion heard, and rejoiced; and the daughters of Judea rejoiced.”

Afterward some of the circumcised wished to bring accusations against Peter and said to him: “Why did you enter the house of uncircumcised Gentiles and eat with them?” He gave them an account of how, while he was praying, a sheet hanging by four cords was shown to him. That sheet, which contained every kind of animal, signified all the Gentiles.

It hung by four cords because there are four regions of the world from which the future peoples were to come. For this reason the four Gospels proclaim Christ, so that it might be understood that his grace extends to all four regions of the world.

Since such a vision had been shown to Peter, he explained everything to them: how Cornelius had believed, because, before the Gentile was baptized, the Holy Spirit had come upon him. When they heard this, they were silent and glorified God, saying: “Then God has also granted repentance unto life to the Gentiles” (Acts 11:1–18).

Behold: “Zion heard, and rejoiced; and the daughters of Judea rejoiced because of your judgments, Lord.” What judgments? That God is not a respecter of persons. For Peter himself, when he saw the centurion Cornelius and those who were with him filled with the Holy Spirit, exclaimed and said: “Truly I understand that God is not a respecter of persons.”

Thus: “The daughters of Judea rejoiced because of your judgments, Lord.” What does “because of your judgments” mean? “In every nation, whoever serves him is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:34–35). For he is “not the God of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles” (Romans 3:29).

14. [Verse 9.] See whether this is not why the daughters of Judea rejoiced: “The daughters of Judea rejoiced because of your judgments, Lord. For you are the Lord Most High over all the earth.”

Not over Judea alone, not over Jerusalem alone, not over Zion alone, but over the whole earth. God’s judgments prevailed over this entire earth, so that he might summon peoples from everywhere. Those who have cut themselves off do not share in them; they neither hear what was foretold nor see it fulfilled: “For you are the Lord Most High over all the earth.”

“You are greatly exalted above all gods.” What does “greatly” mean? It is said of Christ. What, then, does “greatly” mean except that you are to understand him as equal to the Father?

What does “above all gods” mean? Who are they? Idols have neither understanding nor life. Demons have understanding and life, but they are evil. Is it a great thing that Christ is exalted above idols? He is exalted above demons; but even this is not yet very great. “The demons are the gods of the nations” (Psalm 95:5), but he is greatly exalted above all gods.

Human beings, too, have been called gods: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.” Again it is written: “God has taken his stand in the assembly of gods; in the midst he distinguishes among the gods” (Psalm 81:6, 1).

Above all these our Lord Jesus Christ has been exalted—not only above idols, not only above demons, but above all righteous human beings. And even this is little: above all the angels also. For what else is meant by “Worship him, all his angels”? “You are greatly exalted above all gods.”

15. [Verse 10.] What, then, do we all do who come together to him, to him who is greatly exalted above all gods? He has given us a brief command: “You who love the Lord, hate evil.”

Christ is not worthy to be loved together with greed. You love him; you must hate what he hates.

Your enemy is a human being, just as you are. You were created by one Creator and in one condition. Yet if your son were to speak with your enemy, come to your enemy’s house, and have frequent conversations with him, you would wish to disinherit him because he speaks with your enemy. And how would you put it? You would think you had a just complaint: “You are a friend of my enemy, and you seek something from my property!”

Therefore, pay attention. You love Christ; greed is an enemy of Christ. Why do you speak with it? I do not merely mean, Why do you speak with it? Why do you serve it? Christ commands many things, and you do not do them; greed commands, and you do them.

Christ commands you to clothe the poor, and you do not do it. Greed commands you to commit fraud, and this you do instead. If these things are so, if you are such a person, do not promise yourself too much of an inheritance in Christ.

But you say: “I love Christ.” “You who love the Lord, hate evil.” It becomes evident that you love what is good if you are found to hate what is evil: “You who love the Lord, hate evil.”

16. But when we begin to hate evil, persecutions will follow. We hate evil; some persecutor says to us, “Commit fraud”; he says to us, “Worship an idol”; he says to us, “Place incense before demons.” But we have heard: “You who love the Lord, hate evil.”

We have heard it, certainly, but if we do not do these things, he rages. How long does he rage? What will he take away? Answer: why are you a Christian? For the sake of an eternal inheritance, or for the sake of earthly happiness?

Question your faith. Place your soul upon the rack of conscience; torture yourself with fear of judgment; answer whom you have believed and why you have believed. You say to me: “I have believed in Christ.” What did Christ promise you except what he displayed in himself?

What did he display in himself? He died and rose again; he ascended into heaven. Do you wish to follow? Imitate his passion; await his promise.

What, then, will the raging persecutor take away from you when you begin to hate evil because you love the Lord? What will he take away? Your property? Surely not heaven!

Finally, whatever God has given you, let him take it away. He does not take it away unless God wills it; but if God wills it, he takes away what God gave, lest God himself be taken away from you. No one will take God from you; you take him from yourself if you flee from him.

17. Perhaps you reply: “I do not care about my property. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; I can say, ‘As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened’” (Job 1:21). “But I am afraid that he will kill me.” This is the whole matter.

Hear, then, the Psalm consoling you: “The Lord guards the souls of his servants.” Since he had said above, “You who love the Lord, hate evil,” lest you fear to hate evil because the evil one might kill you, he immediately added: “The Lord guards the souls of his servants.”

[Note: [Col. 1249] The old Corbie manuscript has here only: “the souls of his righteous ones.”]

Hear him guarding the souls of his servants and saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28).

He kills the body—the one who has been able to do the most against you. What has he done to you? What your Lord God also did. Why do you love to possess what Christ possessed if you fear to suffer what Christ suffered?

He came to bear your temporal life, weak and subject to death. Surely fear dying, if you can avoid dying. What you cannot avoid by nature, why do you not accept for the sake of faith?

Let the adversary who threatens you take this life from you; God gives you another life. For he himself gave you this life as well, and if he does not will it, even this life will not be taken away. But if he wills that it be taken from you, he has something to exchange with you. Do not fear being stripped for his sake.

Do you not wish to remove a ragged garment? He is going to give you a robe of glory. What robe do you mean? “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53).

This very flesh of yours will not perish. The enemy can rage only as far as death; beyond that he has no power, neither over the soul nor over the flesh itself. Even if he destroys the flesh, he does not prevent the resurrection.

People were afraid for their souls, and what did the Lord say to them? “Even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matthew 10:30). Do you fear losing your soul when you do not lose a hair? Everything is numbered for God. He who created everything will restore everything.

They did not exist, and they were created. They existed, and will they not be restored? Believe, then, with your whole heart, my brothers, and you who love the Lord, hate evil.

Be strong—not only in loving God but also in hating evil. Let no one terrify you. He who called you is more powerful; he is almighty.

[Note: [Col. 1250] Am., Erasmus, and several manuscripts read: “For let not more powerful ones terrify you; he who called you is almighty.”]

He is stronger than every strong one and higher than every exalted one.

The Son of God died for us. Be confident that you will receive his life, since you possess his death as a pledge. For whom did he die? Surely not for the righteous? Ask Paul. “Indeed, Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6).

You were ungodly, and he died for you. Now that you have been justified, will he abandon you? Will he who justified the ungodly abandon the godly?

“You who love the Lord, hate evil.” Let no one fear: “The Lord guards the souls of his servants; he will rescue them from the hand of the sinner.”

18. [Verse 11.] But perhaps you will say: “I am losing this light.” “Light has risen for the righteous.”

What light are you afraid of losing? Are you afraid of being in darkness? Do not fear losing this light. Rather, fear that, while taking care not to lose this light, you may lose the true light.

The light you fear losing is seen by those to whom it has been given, and it is shared with you. Do only the good see this sun, when he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45)?

The wicked see this light with you; robbers see it with you; the shameless see it with you; beasts, flies, and worms see it with you. What kind of light does he reserve for the righteous who gives this light even to them?

With good reason the martyrs saw this light in faith. For those who despised this light saw another light, which they desired, because they rejected this one.

“Light has risen for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart.” Do not think that they were truly in misery when they walked in chains. The prison was spacious for the faithful; the chains were light for those who confessed Christ. They had joys on the rack while proclaiming Christ amid torments.

[Note: [Col. 1250] Most manuscripts read *lenes* (“light”) rather than *leves*, which has the same meaning.]

“Light has risen for the righteous.” What light has risen for the righteous? The light that does not rise for the unrighteous—not this light, which he causes to rise upon the good and the evil.

There is another light that rises for the righteous. Of this light the unrighteous will say at the end, because it did not rise for them: “Therefore we went astray from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wisdom 5:6).

Behold: by loving this sun, they lay in the darkness of their hearts. What benefit was it for their eyes to see this one while their minds did not see that one?

Tobias was blind, yet he taught his son the way of God.

[Note: [Col. 1251] The old books consistently write *Tobis*. In the Septuagint, however, the name is *Tobit*.]

You know this, because Tobias admonished his son and said: “My son, give alms, because alms do not permit one to go into darkness” (Tobit 4:7, 11). He was speaking who was himself in darkness.

You see that there is another light that rises for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart. He did not have eyes, yet he said to his son, “Give alms; alms do not permit one to go into darkness.” Nor was he afraid that his son might say in his heart: “You did not give alms yourself; why are you speaking to me, blind man? Behold, your alms have led you into darkness, and yet you say to me, ‘Alms do not permit one to go into darkness’?”

Why did he say these things with confidence except because he saw another light? The son held his father’s hand so that he could walk; but the father taught his son the way so that he might live.

There is, then, another light that rises for the righteous: “Light has risen for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart.”

Do you wish to know it? Be upright in heart. What does “Be upright in heart” mean? Do not be crooked in heart toward God, resisting his will and wishing to bend him toward yourself instead of directing yourself toward him. Then you will feel the gladness known by all who are upright in heart.

“Light has risen for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart.”

19. [Verse 12.] Rejoice, you righteous. Perhaps the faithful who hear, “Rejoice, you righteous,” are already thinking about banquets, preparing cups, and waiting for the season of roses, because it has been said, “Rejoice, you righteous.” See what follows: “in the Lord.” “Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord.” You are waiting for springtime so that you may rejoice; you have the Lord as your joy. The Lord is always with you; he has no season. You have him by night, you have him by day. Be upright in heart, and your joy in him is always present.

For the joy that is according to the world is not true joy. Hear the prophet Isaiah: “There is no rejoicing for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. 48:22; and 57:21). What the wicked call rejoicing is not rejoicing. What sort of joy did the one who rejected this joy know? Let us believe him, brothers. He was a human being, but he knew both kinds of joy. Certainly he knew the joys of the cup, because he was human; he knew the joy of the table, he knew the joy of the bed; he knew these worldly and luxurious joys. He who knew those things boldly said: “There is no rejoicing for the wicked, says the Lord.” But it is not a human being who says this; the Lord says it: according to the truth of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1251] So Am., Er., and the manuscripts. Lov. instead has: “The Lord says according to the truth, ‘There is no rejoicing,’ etc.”], “There is no rejoicing for the wicked.” For they seem to themselves to rejoice; but “there is no rejoicing for the wicked,” he says—not a human being, but the Lord.

Accordingly, seeing that very joy, he said: “And I have not desired the day of men; you know” (Jer. 16:16). You show me another day; you teach me another light; you fill me with another joy; you instill something else within me. You have made me not desire the day of men. Isaiah certainly saw people drinking, indulging themselves, attending theaters and spectacles, the whole world luxuriating in various trivialities; nevertheless he cried out, “There is no rejoicing for the wicked, says the Lord.” If this is not rejoicing, what joy did he see in comparison with which this was not joy?

It is as if you knew the sun and, when someone praised a lamp, said to him, “That is not light.” Why is it not light? The other person considers it magnificent, rejoices, and exults; but you say, “That is not light.” Or if someone admired a monkey, you would say, “That is not beauty.” And if perhaps he were occupied with the arrangement of the limbs of that animal and admired all their proportions, you, who knew another beauty, would deny this one and say, “It is not.” Why? Because you know another.

But you say, “I do not see the one whom Isaiah saw.” Believe, and you will see. Perhaps you do not yet possess the means by which you may see; for there is an eye by which that beauty may be seen. Just as there is a bodily eye by which this light is seen, so there is an eye of the heart by which that joy is seen. Perhaps that eye is wounded, soiled, disturbed by anger, greed, covetousness, or senseless lust; your eye is disturbed and cannot see that light. Believe before you see: you will be healed, and you will see. “Light has dawned for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart.”

20. “Rejoice,” he says, “you righteous, in the Lord; and confess to the memory of his holiness.” Having rejoiced in the Lord, having now become joyful in the Lord, confess to him; for unless he had willed it, we would not rejoice in him. For the Lord himself says: “I have spoken these things to you, so that in me you may have peace, but in the world tribulation” (John 16:33).

If you are Christians, expect tribulations in this world; do not hope for more tranquil and better times. Brothers, you deceive yourselves. What the Gospel does not promise you, do not promise yourselves. You know what the Gospel says; we are speaking to Christians, and we must not betray the faith. The Gospel says that in the last times many evils, many scandals, many tribulations, and many iniquities will abound; “but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” “The charity of many will grow cold,” he says (Matt. 24:3–13). Therefore, whoever remains fervent in spirit, according to the Apostle who says, “fervent in spirit” (Rom. 12:11), will not have his charity grow cold, because “the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Let no one, then, promise himself what the Gospel does not promise. “Look, happier times will come, and I will do this, and I will buy that.” It is good for you to look to the one who is not deceived [Note: [Col. 1252] Am. and the manuscripts have “who does not deceive.”], nor has deceived anyone—who promised you not joy here, but joy in himself. When these things have passed away, hope that you will reign with him forever; otherwise, if you wish to reign here, you will have joy neither here nor find it there.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 97

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. [Verse 1.] “Sing to the Lord a new song.” The new human being knows it; the old does not. The old human being is the old life, and the new human being is the new life. The old life is drawn from Adam; the new life is formed in Christ.

In this psalm, the whole world is told to sing a new song. For elsewhere it is said more explicitly: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. 95:1), so that those who cut themselves off from communion with the whole world may understand that they cannot sing the new song, because the new song is sung in its entirety, not in a part.

Here too pay attention and see that this is being said. When the whole world is told to sing a new song, this is understood because peace sings the new song. “Sing to the Lord a new song, for the Lord has done marvelous things.”

What marvelous things? Just now the Gospel was being read, and we heard of the Lord’s marvelous works. The only son of his mother, who was a widow, was being carried out dead. The Lord had compassion and caused them to stop; they set him down, and he said, “Young man, I say to you, arise.” The dead man sat up and began to speak, and he gave him back to his mother (Luke 7:12–15).

Behold, the Lord has done marvelous things. But much greater is the marvel that he raised the whole world from everlasting death than that he raised the only son of a widowed mother. Therefore, “sing to the Lord a new song, for the Lord has done marvelous things.”

What marvelous things? Hear: “His right hand and his holy arm have saved him.” What is the Lord’s holy arm? Our Lord Jesus Christ. Hear Isaiah: “Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). His holy arm and his right hand are therefore one and the same.

Thus our Lord Jesus Christ is the arm of God and the right hand of God. For this reason it says, “His right hand has saved him.” It does not merely say, “His right hand has saved the world,” but, “has saved him”—for many are saved for themselves, not for him.

See how many desire this bodily health and receive it from him; they are healed by him, but are not healed for him. How are they healed by him and not for him? Once they have received health, they indulge themselves. Those who were chaste when sick become adulterers when healed; those who harmed no one while ill, after recovering their strength attack and oppress the innocent. They have been healed, but not for him.

Who, then, is healed for him? The one who is healed inwardly. Who is healed inwardly? The one who believes in him so that, after being healed inwardly and reformed into the new human being, he may afterward, at the end, receive perfect health also for this mortal flesh, which is sick for a time.

Let us therefore be healed for him. And in order that we may be healed for him, let us believe in his right hand, because “his right hand and his holy arm have saved him.”

2. [Verse 2.] “The Lord has made his salvation known.” That right hand, that arm, that salvation is our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it was said, “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6). Concerning him also spoke that Simeon who took the infant into his hands: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:28–30).

“The Lord has made his salvation known.” To whom did he make it known—to a part, or to the whole? Not to some part. Let no one deceive or mislead anyone by saying, “Behold, here is Christ; behold, there” (Matt. 24:23). The one who says, “Here he is, there he is,” points out parts.

To whom did the Lord make his salvation known? Hear what follows: “Before the nations he revealed his righteousness.” The right hand of God, the arm of God, the salvation of God, and the righteousness of God is our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

3. [Verse 3.] “He remembered his mercy to Jacob, and his truth to the house of Israel” [Note: [Col. 1254] So several manuscripts. The editions have “the house,” with a different grammatical form.].

What does “he remembered his mercy and truth” mean? He had mercy in order to make a promise; because he promised and fulfilled it, truth followed. Mercy sent the promise ahead; the promise brought forth truth. “He remembered his mercy to Jacob, and his truth to the house of Israel.”

And what then? Only to Jacob, and only to the house of Israel? The house of the Jews and that offspring of Abraham according to the flesh is customarily called the house of Israel, and Israel is Jacob. Jacob was the son of Isaac, and Isaac himself was the son of Abraham. Jacob, therefore, was Abraham’s grandson; and from Jacob came twelve sons, and from the twelve sons the whole Jewish lineage.

Was Christ promised only to them? If you examine what Israel means, Christ was promised to Israel. Israel means “seeing God.” We shall see by sight if now we see by faith. Let our faith have eyes, and the truth of faith will be displayed. Let us believe in him whom we do not see, and rejoicing we shall see him; let us desire the unseen, and we shall enjoy what is seen.

Therefore Israel exists now by faith; then Israel will exist by sight, face to face—not now through a mirror, not in an enigma (1 Cor. 13:12), but, as John said: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Prepare your hearts for this vision; prepare your souls for this joy. If God wished to show you the sun, he would warn you to prepare the eyes of your flesh. But because he deigns to show you the form of his wisdom, prepare the eyes of your heart. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

“He remembered his mercy to Jacob, and his truth to the house of Israel.” Who is this Israel? So that you do not perhaps think of one nation, the Jews, hear what follows: “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.” It does not say, “The whole earth,” but “all the ends of the earth,” as when we say, from end to end.

Let no one cut apart or disperse; the unity of Christ is strong. The one who paid such a price bought the whole. “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.”

4. [Verse 4.] Since they have seen it, “shout joyfully to God, all the earth.” You already know what it means to shout joyfully. Rejoice and speak. If you cannot speak what you rejoice in, shout joyfully; let your rejoicing be expressed by a shout if speech cannot express it. Yet let it not be a silent joy. Let the heart not be silent toward its God; let it not be silent about his gifts.

If you speak to yourself, you have been healed for yourself; if his right hand has healed you for him, speak to the one for whom you have been healed.

“All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God. Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing, exult, and sing psalms.”

5. [Verse 5.] “Sing psalms to the Lord our God on the lyre, on the lyre and with the voice of a psalm.” Sing psalms, not with the voice alone; add works, so that you may not merely sing but also act. The one who sings and acts sings psalms on the lyre and the psaltery.

6. [Verse 6.] And see what instruments are added in the comparisons: “With beaten trumpets and the voice of a horn-trumpet” [Note: [Col. 1255] So the inferior manuscripts. Others have “hammer.” The editions have “hammers.”].

What do beaten trumpets and horn-trumpets mean? Beaten trumpets are made of bronze; they are lengthened by hammering. If by hammering, then by being struck. You will be beaten trumpets, lengthened for the praise of God, if you make progress when you are afflicted. Tribulation is the striking; progress is the lengthening.
