Job was a beaten trumpet when, suddenly struck by such losses and by the bereavement of his children, he became, through that great blow of tribulation, a beaten trumpet and sounded: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

How he sounded! What a sweet sound he gave! This beaten trumpet is still being struck. He was handed over to be afflicted, so that his flesh too might be struck. It was struck; it began to decay and swarm with worms. His wife, preserved for the devil’s service rather than for the comfort of her husband, was placed beside him for his seduction and suggested blasphemy; but he did not obey her.

Adam obeyed Eve in paradise (Gen. 3:6); Job repelled Eve on the dung heap. Job was sitting on the dung heap while his flesh flowed and decayed with worms. Decaying Job on the dung heap was better than the sound man in paradise. But she was still Eve; he was no longer Adam.

He answered Eve, prepared for this overthrow and temptation, and said to her:

Behold how this trumpet is struck. The devil struck him with a grievous wound from head to foot, and, decaying with worms, he sat on the dung heap. We have heard how he was struck; let us hear how he sounds. If it pleases you, let us hear the sweet voice of this beaten trumpet.

“You have spoken,” he said, “like one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil?”

O strong sound! O sweet sound! Whom would this sound not awaken if he were not asleep? Whom would it not arouse to confidence in God, so that he might proceed securely into battle against the devil—not relying on his own strength, but on the strength of the one who tests him?

For he himself also strikes; the hammer would not act by itself. The prophet, recalling the future punishment of that devil, says: “The hammer of the whole earth has been crushed” (Jer. 50:23). By the hammer of the whole earth he intended the devil to be understood.

With that hammer placed in God’s hand—that is, under God’s power—the beaten trumpets are struck so that they may resound with God’s praises.

See how—I dare to say it, my brothers—even the Apostle was struck by this hammer. “So that I might not be exalted,” he says, “by the greatness of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (2 Cor. 12:7).

Behold, he is struck. Let us see how he sounds: “For this I besought the Lord three times, that he might remove it from me; and he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.’” [Col. 1256]

“I,” says that craftsman, “wish to perfect a trumpet; I shall not perfect it unless I strike it. Power is made perfect in weakness.” And now hear the beaten trumpet itself sounding well: “When I am weak, then I am powerful” (2 Cor. 12:8–10).

The Apostle himself, as an apostle clinging to Christ, clinging to that right hand by which the hammer is held so that the trumpet may be lengthened, placed in that right hand, also makes something from that hammer. He says concerning certain people: “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20).

He handed them over to be struck by the hammer. Before they were lengthened, they sounded badly; perhaps, once lengthened and made into beaten trumpets, having abandoned blasphemy, they resounded with the praises of the Lord. These are the beaten trumpets.

7. What is “the voice of a horn-trumpet”? The horn extends beyond the flesh. It must be firm enough to endure by rising above the flesh, and capable of producing sound. But how does this happen? Because it has risen above the flesh.

Whoever wishes to be a horn-trumpet must rise above the flesh. What does “rise above the flesh” mean? Let him transcend fleshly affections and conquer fleshly desires.

Hear the horn-trumpets: “If you have risen with Christ,” the Apostle says, “seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; think of the things that are above, not of those that are upon the earth” (Col. 3:1–2).

What does “seek the things that are above” mean? It means: rise above the flesh; do not think about carnal things.

Those to whom he was still speaking in this way were not yet horn-trumpets: “Brothers, I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not able. Indeed, you cannot even now, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1–2).

They were therefore not yet horn-trumpets, because they had not risen above the flesh. The horn clings to the flesh and extends beyond the flesh; although it arises from the flesh, it surpasses the flesh.

If, then, you are carnal and spiritual [Note: [Col. 1256] So the manuscripts. The editions have: “You will therefore become spiritual,” etc. Shortly afterward they have “you will burst forth into heaven.”], while you still tread the earth in the flesh, burst forth into heaven in spirit. “Although we walk in the flesh,” he says, “we do not wage war according to the flesh” (2 Cor. 10:3).

Let us not pass over what the Apostle said to those brothers. What did he say to prove that they were carnal, thinking carnally, and not yet made into horn-trumpets?

“When one of you says, ‘I am of Paul,’ and another, ‘I am of Apollos,’ and another, ‘I am of Cephas,’ are you not carnal and walking according to human standards? What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers of God, through whom you believed. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Cor. 1:12; 3:1–6).

He therefore wishes to raise them from the hope they had placed in a human being and to make them touch the spiritual things of Christ, so that they might be horn-trumpets if they rose above the flesh.

Brothers, do not mock brothers whom the mercy of God has not yet converted. Know that as long as you do this, you are thinking carnally. That trumpet which delights God’s ears is not such a trumpet; the trumpet of mockery produces a fruitless war.

Let the horn-trumpet raise you against the devil, not the fleshly trumpet against your brother.

“With beaten trumpets and the voice of a horn-trumpet, shout joyfully before the Lord, the King” [Note: [Col. 1257] Most manuscripts have: “Shout joyfully to the Lord before the Lord, the King”; some have: “Shout joyfully to God before the Lord, the King.” The Septuagint reads: “Shout joyfully before the Lord, the King.”].

8. [Verses 7–9.] While you are shouting joyfully and exulting with beaten trumpets and with the voice of a horn-trumpet, what follows? “Let the sea be moved, and its fullness.”

Brothers, when the Apostles preached the truth like beaten trumpets and horn-trumpets, the sea was moved: disturbances arose, storms increased, and persecutions of the Church occurred.

From what was the sea moved? When there was joyful shouting, when psalms were sung to God. God’s ears were delighted, and the waves of the sea were stirred up.

“Let the sea be moved, and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it.” Let the sea be moved by persecutions.

“Rivers shall clap their hands together.” Let the sea be moved, and let the rivers clap their hands together: persecutions arise, and the saints rejoice in God.

From what do the rivers clap their hands? What does “clap their hands” mean? It means to rejoice in works. To clap is to rejoice; hands signify works.

What rivers are these? Those whom God made rivers by giving them that water, the Holy Spirit. “If anyone thirsts,” he says, “let him come and drink. Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:37–39).

These rivers clapped their hands; these rivers rejoiced in their works and blessed God.

9. “The mountains will exult before the face of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1257] The manuscripts have “before the face of God.”], “because he has come, because he has come to judge the earth.”

Great are the mountains. God has come to judge the earth, and they rejoice. There are mountains that will tremble when the Lord comes to judge the earth.

There are therefore good mountains and bad mountains. The good mountains are spiritual greatness; the bad mountains are the swelling of pride.

“The mountains will exult before the face of the Lord, because he has come, because he has come to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in equity.”

Let the mountains therefore rejoice; he will not judge unjustly. If some human judge were coming, one to whom the conscience cannot be open, even innocent people might tremble if they expected from him the reward of praise or feared the punishment of condemnation. But when the one who cannot be deceived comes, let the mountains rejoice; let them rejoice securely. They will be enlightened by him, not condemned. Let them rejoice, because the Lord will come to judge the world in equity.

If the righteous mountains rejoice, let the wicked tremble. But behold, he has not yet come; why should they tremble? Let them be corrected and rejoice. It is in your power how you await Christ’s coming.

For this reason he delays coming: so that, when he comes, he may not condemn you. Behold, he has not yet come. He is in heaven, you are on earth. He delays his coming; do not delay your decision. His coming is harsh for the harsh, gentle for the devout.

See, then, who you are now. If you are harsh, you may become gentle; if you are gentle, rejoice already that he will come.

You are a Christian, then. “Yes,” you say. I believe you pray and say, “Your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10). You desire the one to come whom you fear will come. Correct yourself, so that you may not pray against yourself.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 98

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. Brothers, it ought now to be known to your Charity, as children of the Church and instructed in the school of Christ through all the writings of our ancient fathers who wrote the words of God and the mighty works of God, that those writers wished us—who were to be believers in Christ at this time—to consult them: Christ came to us at the appointed time, first in humility and later to come in exaltation.

For first he came to stand before the judge; afterward he will come as judge, seated, so that before him the human race may stand according to its deserts.

Many heralds went before him, as before a great judge, and proclaimed that he would still come in humility. Many heralds went before him while he was still to be born of the Virgin Mary, destined to be an infant and to suck milk [Note: [Col. 1258] So the manuscripts. The editions have “destined to be suckled.”]; while he was still to be a little child—the Word of God through whom all things were made. Many heralds went before him and foretold these times.

But they spoke in such a way that they covered their pronouncements with certain figures of things; and the very veil with which the truth was covered in the books of the ancients was to be removed when Truth itself would arise from the earth. Thus it is said in the psalm: “Truth has arisen from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84:12).

Therefore, whenever we hear a psalm, a prophet, or the Law—all of which were written before our Lord Jesus Christ came in the flesh—our entire concern now is to see Christ there and understand Christ there.

Let your Charity therefore attend with us to this psalm, and let us seek Christ here. Surely he will appear to those who seek him, though he first appeared to those who were not seeking him; and he will not abandon those who desire him, since he redeemed those who neglected him.

Behold, the psalm began with him; it speaks of him.

2. [Verse 1.] “The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry.” Our Lord Jesus Christ began to reign; he began to be preached after he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, after he filled his disciples with the confidence of the Holy Spirit, so that they would not fear the death which he had already killed in himself.

The Lord Christ therefore began to be preached, so that those who wished to have salvation might believe in him; and the peoples who worshiped idols became angry. Those who worshiped what they had made were angry because the one by whom they had been made was being announced.

Through his disciples, he was announcing himself—the one who wished them to be converted to him by whom they had been made and turned away from the things they themselves had made. They were angry on behalf of their idol against their Lord; yet if they had become angry on behalf of their idol against his servant, they would have been condemned.

Their servant is better than their idol: God made their servant, but a craftsman made their idol. They became so angry on behalf of their idol that they were not afraid to become angry against their Lord.

But “let them be angry” was foretold, not commanded. For in prophecy it is said, “The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry.” Something is to happen even from the peoples who are angry: let them be angry, and in their anger let the martyrs be crowned.

What did they do to the proclaimers of the word of truth, the clouds of Christ traveling around the world and raining upon God’s field? What did those who were angry do to them except afflict their flesh in their hands, while in Christ’s hands their spirit was crowned?

Nor did the very flesh which the persecutors were able to kill die in such a way that it perished forever. It will have its appointed time, when it too will rise, because the Lord has already shown the resurrection of the flesh in himself. He wished to receive it from us so that we might not despair concerning our own.

Therefore, brothers, the flesh of the servants whom the worshipers of idols killed will rise in its own time; but the idols which Christ shattered the craftsman will never make again.

You heard, when Jeremiah was read before the apostolic reading—if you lent your ear—you saw there the present times that we are now experiencing. For he said: “The gods that have not made heaven and earth shall perish from the earth and from beneath heaven” (Jer. 10:11).

He did not say, “The gods that have not made heaven and earth shall perish from heaven and from earth,” because they were never in heaven. But what did he say? “The gods that have not made heaven and earth shall perish from the earth.”

It is as though he answered the earth, while what he might have answered concerning heaven was absent, because they were not in heaven. He mentioned the earth twice because it is beneath heaven: “Let them perish from the earth and from beneath heaven,” from their temples.

See whether this is not happening, whether it has not already happened to a great extent. For what remains, or how much remains? The idols have remained more in the hearts of the pagans than in the sites of the temples.

3. Therefore, “the Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry.” “He who sits above the cherubim”—understand: “has reigned.” “Let the earth be moved.”

Again he said, “Let the peoples be angry.” For what he said by “the Lord,” he repeated by “he who sits above the cherubim”; and what he said by “has reigned,” he caused to be understood in another verse; and what he said by “let the peoples be angry,” he said by “let the earth be moved.”

For what are the peoples except the earth? Let the earth be angry as much as it can against him who now sits in heaven.

For the Lord was also on earth, and he assumed the earth in which he would be on earth. He clothed himself in flesh, and first wished to endure the anger of the peoples. So that his servants would not fear the anger of the peoples, he first wished to suffer it.

And because the anger of the peoples was necessary for his servants, so that through those very tribulations they might be cured and healed of all their sins, the physician first drank the bitter cup, so that the sick person would not fear drinking it.

Therefore, “the Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry.” Let the peoples be angry, because God brings many good things from their anger. They become angry, and God’s servants are purified; because they are exercised, they are crowned.

“Let the peoples be angry. He who sits above the cherubim has reigned; let the earth be moved.”

The cherubim is the seat of God, as the Scriptures teach: a certain heavenly and exalted seat which we do not see. But the Word of God knows it; it knows it as its own seat. The Word of God itself and the Spirit of God told God’s servants where God sits.

Not that God sits in the way a human being sits. But if you wish God to sit in you, if you are good, you will be God’s seat. For thus it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” For *thronus* is called *sedes* in Latin—that is, a seat.

Some have also interpreted what *cherubim* means in Latin—those who knew that Hebrew language—for *cherubim* is a Hebrew word. They said that cherubim means “fullness of knowledge.”

Therefore, because God surpasses all knowledge, he is said to sit above the fullness of knowledge. Let the fullness of knowledge be in you, then, and you too will be God’s seat.

But perhaps you will say: “When will the fullness of knowledge be in me? Who can reach such a height that the fullness of knowledge may be in him?” [Note: [Col. 1260] The word “height” is absent from the manuscripts; instead of “such a height,” some have “such a degree.”]

Do you suppose that God wishes us to have this fullness of knowledge so that we may know how many stars there are, or how many grains—not to mention grains of sand, but grains of wheat—or how many fruits hang upon a tree? God knows all things, because our hairs are numbered before God (Matt. 10:30).

But there is another fullness of knowledge which he wished human beings to know. The knowledge he wished you to have belongs to the Law of God.

And who can, you may say to me, know the Law perfectly, so as to possess within himself the fullness of knowledge of the Law and be able to become God’s seat?

Do not be troubled. You are briefly told what you must possess if you wish to have the fullness of knowledge and be God’s seat. The Apostle says: “The fullness of the Law is charity” (Rom. 13:10).

What, then? You have lost your entire excuse. Question your heart; see whether it has charity. If charity is there, the fullness of the Law is there; God already dwells in you, and you have become God’s seat.

Let the peoples be angry. What can the peoples do in their anger against one who has become God’s seat? You pay attention to those who rage against you, but you do not pay attention to the one who sits within you.

You have become heaven, and you fear earth? For Scripture says elsewhere that the Lord our God declares: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1).

Therefore, if by possessing the fullness of knowledge and possessing charity you have indeed become God’s seat, you have become heaven. It is not this heaven which we look upon with these eyes that is greatly precious to God. God’s heaven is holy souls; God’s heaven is the minds of the angels, and all the minds of his servants.

Therefore, “let the peoples be angry; let the earth be moved.” What can they do, or what can be done to God’s seat and the heaven in which God sits?

4. [Verse 2.] “The Lord is great in Zion, and he is exalted above all the peoples.”

“The Lord is great in Zion, and he is exalted.” Behold: if it was obscure to you when it said, “He who sits above the cherubim,” because you did not know what cherubim meant, and perhaps you imagined in your mind some immense, jewel-encrusted heavenly chair and called that cherubim, flying through fantasies according to the flesh, you have been told that cherubim is the fullness of knowledge.

You have also been told that the fullness of knowledge is not just any knowledge, but the fullness of knowledge of the Law, which is useful to a human being. And so that you would not despair of this knowledge of the Law, you have been told briefly: “The fullness of the Law is charity.”

Therefore, have charity toward God and your neighbor, and you will be God’s seat; you will belong to the cherubim.

But if you still do not understand, hear what follows: “The Lord is great in Zion.” The one whom I told you was above the cherubim is great in Zion.

Now seek what Zion is. We know Zion to be the city of God. The city that is Jerusalem is called Zion. It receives its name from a certain interpretation, because Zion is said to mean “watchtower,” that is, vision and contemplation.

To watch is to look ahead, or to look upon, or to direct one’s attention in order to see. Every soul is Zion if it directs its attention toward seeing the light that ought to be seen [Note: [Col. 1261] The ancient manuscripts have: “to see what ought to be seen.”].

For if it directs its attention toward itself, it is darkened; if it directs its attention toward his light, it is enlightened.

Yet since it is clear that Zion is the city of God, what is the city of God except the holy Church? Human beings who love one another and love their God, who dwells in them, make a city for God.

A city is held together by a certain law; their law itself is charity, and charity itself is God. For it is plainly written: “God is charity” (1 John 4:8).

Therefore, whoever is full of charity is full of God; and many who are full of charity make a city for God. This city is called Zion, and therefore it is the Church.

In her God is great. Be in her, and God will not be outside you. When God is in you—because you have become part of Zion, a member of Zion, a citizen of Zion, belonging to the fellowship of God’s people—God will be exalted in you above all peoples, above those who are angry or those who were angry.

Do you suppose that they were angry then but are not angry now? They were angry then; but because they were more numerous, they were openly angry. Now, because they have become few, they are angry secretly.

For the present their boldness has been broken; their anger too will come to an end.

5. For do you suppose, brothers, that those whose musical instruments clattered yesterday are not angry about our fasts? Let us not be angry with them, but fast for them. For our Lord God, who sits within us, told us—indeed, he commanded us—to pray for our enemies and for those who persecute us (Matt. 5:44). And when the Church does this, the persecutors are nearly finished. She was heard when she did this, and she is heard when she does it: they prevailed through their evil, but they have been finished through the good.

Would you like to know how they have been finished? They have been eaten by the Church. You seek them in themselves and do not find them; seek them in her who has eaten them, and they are found in her innermost parts. For, passing over to the Church, they became Christians; the persecutors perished, and the preachers increased.

Therefore, on the feast days of those people, because we see those who remain still raging in their pleasures, evil and perverse [Note: [Col. 1261] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read *voluntatibus* (“desires”).], we ask God on their behalf that those who listen with delight to the organ may listen with still greater delight to the voice of God. For if something that sounds without reason delights the ear, why should the word of God not delight the heart?

But we pray for them when we do not fast on their feast days, so that they may become a spectacle to themselves. For when they see themselves, they will displease themselves; but they do not displease themselves because they do not look at themselves. A drunkard does not displease himself, but he displeases the sober person. Consider a man who already rejoices in God, lives with gravity, and sighs for that eternal peace which God has promised him; you will see that when he looks upon a man dancing to the organ, he grieves more over that man’s madness than over the fever of a delirious person.

Therefore, if we know their evils—for we too have been freed from those very evils—let us grieve for them; and if we grieve for them, let us pray for them; and, in order that we may be heard, let us fast for them. We do not observe our own fasts during their feast days. Our fasts are other ones, which we observe during the future days of Easter and during the other solemn occasions we have in Christ. During these days, however, we fast for this purpose: that when they rejoice, we may groan for them. Their joy reminds us of our grief [Note: [Col. 1262] Two manuscripts read *movent* (“move” or “stir”).] and makes us remember how wretched they still are.

But because we see that many have been freed from that condition—the condition in which we too once were—we must not despair of them. And if they are still angry, let us pray; and if that fragment of the earth which remains is still stirred, let us remain in mourning for them, so that God may grant them understanding and they may hear with us these voices in which we now rejoice:

The Lord is great in Zion, and he is exalted above all peoples.

6. [vv. 3–4.] “Let them confess your great name.” Let all those peoples over whom you are great in Zion now confess your great name. Your name was small when they were angry; it has become great—let them now confess it.

How do we say that Christ’s name was small before Christ was widely and gloriously proclaimed? Because his name is called his fame. The name was small; now the name has become great. What nation has not heard the name of Christ?

Let the peoples who formerly were angry at your small name now confess your great name: “Let them confess your great name.” Why should they confess it? “For it is terrible and holy.” Your name itself is terrible and holy. The crucified one, the humbled one, the judged one is proclaimed in such a way that he will come exalted, he will come alive, he will come in power to judge.

For now he spares the peoples who blaspheme, because God’s patience leads to repentance (Rom. 2:4). The one who now spares does not necessarily spare forever; nor is the one now preached so that he may be feared not going to come to judge. He is coming, my brothers; he is coming. Let us fear him, and let us live in such a way that we may be found at his right hand. For he is coming to judge, so as to place some at the left and others at the right (Matt. 25:31–33).

And he does not do this in some arbitrary way, as though he might make a mistake among human beings, placing at the left the one who should be placed at the right, or, if God were to err, placing at the right the one who ought to stand at the left. He cannot err by placing the evil where he ought to place the good, or placing the good where he ought to place the evil.

If he cannot err, then we err if we do not fear. But if we fear now, then we will have nothing to fear at that time. “For it is terrible and holy; and the king’s honor loves judgment.” Thus let the peoples fear in such a way that they correct themselves. Let them not, presuming excessively upon his mercy, abandon themselves and live wickedly. For he loves mercy, but he also loves judgment.

What is mercy? That he now proclaims the truth to you, that he now cries out to you to turn back. Is it a small mercy that, although you have lived in evil deeds, he has not yet taken you away while you were sinning, so that he might forgive your sins when you believed? Is that a small mercy? Do you suppose that mercy will always be such that he punishes no one? Do not think so [Note: [Col. 1263] From Erasmus, Venice, and Louvain we have restored *putare* (“think”), which is said to be supplied in the margin of B. M.].

His name is terrible and holy; and the king’s honor loves judgment. For there is no just judgment—and indeed there is no judgment at all—unless each person receives what is deserved, according to what each has done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10). “And the king’s honor loves judgment.” Therefore let us fear; therefore let us do justice; therefore let us practice equity.

7. But who does equity? Who does justice? A sinful man, an unjust man, a perverse man, a man turned away from the light of truth? What must a human being do? He must simply turn himself toward God, so that God himself may form in him the equity which he himself cannot form, but can deform.

A human being is capable of wounding himself; is he perhaps capable of healing himself? When he wishes, he falls ill; he does not rise when he wishes. If he wishes, he may live intemperately in cold or heat, and he becomes ill on the day he chooses. But once, by living intemperately, he has begun to be ill, let him rise when he wishes. Let the one who lay down when he wished rise, if he can, when he wishes.

To become sick, the sick person needed only his own intemperance; but to rise he needs the physician’s medicine. So, in order to sin, a person is sufficient to himself for sinning; but in order to be justified, he is not sufficient to himself unless he is justified by the one who alone is just.

Therefore, so that people may surrender themselves to him to be formed in justice, after this psalm had terrified the peoples [Note: [Col. 1263] Three manuscripts read *terruit* (“terrified”).] and said, “Let them confess your great name, for it is terrible and holy; and the king’s honor loves judgment,” as though already seeking to know how those terrified peoples ought to live justly, since they cannot possess justice in themselves, it commended to them the author of their justice and continued:

“You prepared equity; you performed judgment and justice in Jacob.”

We too ought to possess judgment; we ought to possess justice. But he performs judgment and justice in us who made us so that he might perform them in us.

How ought we too to possess judgment and justice? You possess judgment when you distinguish evil from good; you possess justice when you follow the good and turn away from evil. By distinguishing, you possess judgment; by doing, you possess justice. “Turn away from evil,” he says, “and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. 33:15).

First you ought to possess judgment, and afterward justice. What judgment? That you first judge what is evil and what is good. And what justice? That you turn away from evil and do good. But you will not have this from yourself, because consider what he said: “You performed judgment and justice in Jacob.”

8. [v. 5.] “Exalt the Lord our God.” Truly exalt him; exalt him rightly. Let us praise and exalt the one who made the very justice that we possess; he made it in us. For who made justice in us except the one who justified us? Of Christ it is said: “He who justifies the ungodly” (Rom. 4:5).

We, therefore, are ungodly; he is the justifier. Since he himself also made in us the justice by which we please him, so that he may place us at the right and not at the left, so that he may say to those placed at the right, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,” and may not place us at the left among those to whom he will say, “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:34, 41)—he who will crown in us not our merits but his gifts, how greatly ought he to be exalted? “Exalt the Lord our God.”

9. “And worship the footstool of his feet, for he is holy” [Note: [Col. 1264] The editions read *sanctum est* (“it is holy”). The better manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint, read *sanctus est* (“he is holy”).].

What are we to worship? The footstool of his feet. A footstool is called a *suppedaneum*. What the Greeks call ὑποπόδιον (*hypopodion*), the Latins called *scabellum*; others called it *suppedaneum*.

But observe, brothers, what he commands us to worship. Elsewhere in Scripture it is said: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1). Does he therefore command us to worship the earth, because elsewhere he said that the footstool of God’s feet is the earth? And how shall we worship the earth, when Scripture plainly says: “You shall worship the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:13)? Here too it says, “Worship the footstool of his feet”; but, explaining what the footstool of his feet is, it says, “The earth is the footstool of my feet.”

I am perplexed. I fear worshiping the earth, lest the one who made heaven and earth condemn me; yet again I fear not worshiping the footstool of the feet of my Lord, because the Psalm tells me, “Worship the footstool of his feet.” I ask what the footstool of his feet is, and Scripture tells me: “The earth is the footstool of my feet.”

In my uncertainty I turn to Christ, because I am seeking him here, and I discover how the earth may be worshiped without impiety, how the footstool of his feet may be worshiped without impiety. For he took earth from the earth: flesh is from the earth, and from the flesh of Mary he received flesh. And because he walked here in that very flesh and gave us that flesh to eat for our salvation—yet no one eats that flesh unless he has first worshiped it—the way has been found in which this footstool of the Lord’s feet may be worshiped. Not only do we not sin by worshiping; we sin by failing to worship.

But does the flesh give life? The Lord himself said this while speaking of that very commendation of the earth: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” Therefore, whenever you bend and prostrate yourself before any earth, do not regard it as earth, but regard the Holy One whose footstool is what you worship; it is on account of him that you worship it. Thus here too he added: “Worship the footstool of his feet, for he is holy.”

Who is holy? The one in whose honor you worship his footstool. And when you worship him, do not remain in the flesh even in thought and fail to be made alive by the Spirit. For he says, “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.”

But when the Lord commended this, he was speaking about his flesh and had said: “Unless someone eats my flesh, he will not have eternal life within him.” Some of his disciples—nearly seventy—were scandalized and said: “This is a hard saying; who can understand it?” And they withdrew from him and no longer walked with him.

What he said seemed hard to them: “Unless someone eats my flesh, he will not have eternal life.” They received it foolishly; they understood it carnally and thought that the Lord was going to cut off certain pieces from his body and give them to them. And they said, “This is a hard saying.” They were hard, not the saying.

For if they had not been hard but gentle, they would have said to themselves: “He does not say this without cause; surely some hidden sacrament is present.” They would have remained with him as gentle people, not hard people, and would have learned from him what those who remained learned after the others departed.

For when the twelve disciples had remained with him and the others had gone away, they reported to him—as though grieving over the death of those who had departed—that they had been scandalized by his word and had withdrawn. But he instructed them and said: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:54–64).

Understand spiritually what I have said: you are not going to eat this body that you see, nor drink the blood that those who crucify me will shed. I have entrusted a sacrament to you; understood spiritually, it will give you life. Although it must be celebrated visibly, it must nevertheless be understood invisibly.

“Exalt the Lord our God, and worship the footstool of his feet, for he is holy.”

10. [vv. 6–8.] “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who invoke his name. They invoked the Lord, and he himself heard them; he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud.”

These ancient men—Moses, Aaron, and Samuel—were servants of God, great among the ancients. You know that Moses led the people of Israel out of Egypt by God’s power through the Red Sea and led them in the wilderness. Everyone who gladly hears these Scriptures in the Church, or reads them privately, or has learned them in any way, knows how many wonders God performed at that time through the hand of Moses.

Aaron was his brother, whom he also appointed priest. There he appears to be the only priest, namely Aaron. For in those writings Aaron is plainly called the priest of God (Exod. 28:1, etc.); Moses is not there said to have been a priest. But if he was not, what was he? Could he perhaps have been greater than a priest?

This psalm indicates [Note: [Col. 1265] Am., Er., and four manuscripts read *expropriat*, a word which already occurs in the manuscripts and in Am. in the exposition of Psalm 73, no. 5, above, col. 934, note 1.] that he too was a priest: “Moses and Aaron among his priests.” Therefore they were priests of the Lord.

Samuel is later read about in the Book of Kings. This is the Samuel of the time of David, for he anointed holy David. Samuel grew up in the temple from the beginning of his life. His mother was barren. Wishing to have a son, she prayed to the Lord with great groaning and, asking God to give her a son, showed that she did not wish to have him for carnal purposes, but as one whom God, who willed him to exist, gave to her when he was born.

For she vowed him to the Lord God and said, “If a male child is born to me, he shall serve in your temple.” And so she did. The holy Samuel remained with his mother during the period of nursing; as soon as she had weaned him, she gave him to the temple, so that he might grow there, be strengthened [Note: [Col. 1265] Some manuscripts read *probaretur* (“be tested”).] in spirit there, and serve God there. He became a great priest, a holy priest [Col. 1266] at that time (1 Sam. 1, etc.).

The psalm mentions these men, and through them wishes us to understand all the saints. But why did it name them here? Because, as we have said, we ought to understand Christ here.

Let Your Holiness pay attention. Above it said, “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship the footstool of his feet, for he is holy,” commending a certain person—namely our Lord Jesus Christ—whose footstool is to be worshiped because he assumed flesh, in which he would appear to the human race. And wishing to show us that the ancient fathers also proclaimed him, because our Lord Jesus Christ is the true priest, it mentioned these men, because God spoke to them in the pillar of cloud.

What does “in the pillar of cloud” mean? He spoke through figures. For if he spoke in a certain little cloud, those obscure sayings foreshadowed someone—I do not know whom—who would be made manifest. But that someone who was unknown is no longer unknown, because he is known to us: our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who invoke his name. They invoked the Lord, and he himself heard them; in the pillar of cloud he spoke to them.”

The one who first spoke in the pillar of cloud has spoken to us in the footstool of his feet—that is, in the earth assumed into flesh. From this we worship the footstool of his feet, for he is holy. He spoke from the cloud what was not then understood; he spoke in the footstool of his feet, and the words of his cloud were understood.

“In the pillar of cloud he spoke to them.”

11. Let us therefore pay attention, brothers. See what kind and what sort of saints he has named.

“They kept his testimonies and his commandments, which he gave them.”

They certainly kept them. Pay attention:

“They kept his testimonies and his commandments, which he gave them.”

He says this, and it cannot be denied. Did they have no sin? How could that be? When they kept his commandments, they kept his testimonies. Observe the sort of people he wants us to become, so that we do not presume as though we possessed perfect justice.

Behold, Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who invoke his name, to whom he spoke from the pillar of cloud, whom he heard so openly because they kept his testimonies and his commandments, which he gave them.

“Lord,” he says, “our God, you heard them; God, you were gracious to them.” God is not called gracious except in relation to sins: when he grants pardon, then he is called gracious. And what was there in these men for him to punish, so that he might be gracious by forgiving?

He was gracious by forgiving sins; he was also gracious by punishing. For what follows?

“You were gracious to them, and you punished all their inclinations.”

Even while punishing, you were gracious—not only by forgiving their sins, but also by punishing them.

Observe, my brothers, what he has commended here; pay attention. God is angry with the person whose sin he does not chastise. For the one to whom he is truly gracious not only forgives sins, so that they may not harm him in the future age; he also chastises him, so that he may not always delight in sinning.

12. Come, brothers. If we ask how they were punished, the Lord will be present so that I may speak. Let us seek these three persons—Moses, Aaron, and Samuel—and how they were punished, because he said, “Punishing all their inclinations,” meaning, certainly, those inclinations of theirs which the Lord knew in their hearts, but which human beings did not know.

For they lived among the people of God without any human complaint. But what shall we say? Did Moses perhaps have a sinful earlier life? For after striking a man, he fled from Egypt (Exod. 2:12, 15).

Aaron too had an earlier life that displeased God. For he allowed the frenzied and raging people to make an idol, and an idol was made for the people of God to worship (Exod. 32:1–4).

What did Samuel do? He was given to the temple as an infant. He spent all his years among God’s holy sacraments, a servant of God from the beginning of his life. Nothing was ever said about Samuel—nothing by human beings. Perhaps God knew something in him that needed cleansing, because what already appears perfect to human beings is still imperfect in relation to that perfection.

Craftsmen make many things and show them to the unskilled. When the unskilled have judged them to be perfect, the craftsmen polish them further, since they know what is still lacking, so that people marvel that such great refinement has been added to things they had already pronounced perfect. This happens with buildings, paintings, clothing, and almost every kind of art.

At first they judge the object to be already perfect, so that their eyes desire nothing more; but the unskilled eye judges one thing, while the rule of the art judges another.

So those saints lived before God’s eyes as though without fault, as though perfect, as though angels. Yet the one who punished all their inclinations knew what was lacking in them. He punished them not in anger, but graciously: he punished them in order to perfect what had been begun, not to condemn what had been cast away [Note: [Col. 1267] The Regius manuscript reads *electum* (“what had been chosen”).].

Therefore God was punishing all their inclinations.

How did he punish Samuel? Where is the punishment itself? I say this so that Christians who have already come to know Christ here—those to whom he came in the footstool of his feet, whom he loved so greatly, for whom he shed his blood—may know how they are chastised when they have made great progress.

Let us seek the punishment of Moses. He has almost none, except that at the end God said to him: “Go up into the mountain and die.” He said to an old man, “Die.” He had already completed his years. Was he never going to die? What sort of punishment was that?

He displayed his punishment there by saying, “You shall not enter the land of promise” (Deut. 32:49, 52), into which the people were going to enter. Moses bore a certain figure of certain people. For since he entered the kingdom of heaven, was it a great punishment for him not to come into that land which had been promised for a time, in order to show a shadow and pass away?

Did not many faithless people enter that land? Did they not do many evil things while living in that land and offend God? Did they not even practice idolatry in that very land? Was it a great matter that Moses was not given that land?

But Moses was intended to bear the figure of those who were under the Law, since the Law was given through Moses. He showed that those who wished to remain under the Law and did not wish to be under grace would not enter the land of promise.

Therefore what was said to Moses was a figure, not a punishment. What punishment is death for an old man? What punishment is not entering that land into which the unworthy entered?

What was said about Aaron? He too died an old man, and his sons succeeded him in the priesthood; his son afterward administered the priesthood (Num. 20:24–28; 33:38). How, then, did God punish him?

Samuel too, himself a holy old man, died, leaving sons as his successors (1 Sam. 8:1; 25:1). I ask what punishment was inflicted upon them, and according to human standards I do not find it. But according to what I know God’s servants suffer, they were punished every day.

Read and see the punishments, and you who are making progress, endure punishments [Note: [Col. 1268] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read *sed qui proficitis* (“but you who make progress”). Perhaps: “punishments every day,” etc.]. They suffered every day from peoples who contradicted them; they suffered every day from those who lived wickedly; and they were compelled to live among people whose lives they condemned every day.

This was the punishment. The person to whom it is small has not yet made progress. For injustice in another torments you to the degree that you have withdrawn from your own.

When you have become wheat—that is, good grass from good seed, a son of the kingdom—and begin to bear fruit, then the weeds will appear to you. For when the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds appeared.

When the weeds begin to appear, you will see yourself among the wicked. You will want, as it were, to separate the wicked from yourself and to separate all the wicked from the Church. The Lord’s judgment will answer you:

“Let both grow until the harvest, lest while you wish to uproot the weeds you uproot the wheat along with them” (Matt. 13:26–29).

By the Lord’s judgment it will be necessary to spare the weeds; by the condition of a servant it will be necessary to live among the weeds. You cannot separate them; you must endure them.

See how many blows you suffer in your heart, while with your body unharmed you live among the wicked. All of you who have made progress will recognize this; those who have already made progress recognize it.

These things must therefore be endured. Perhaps this belongs to the saying: “The servant who knew his master’s will and did not do what was required will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47–48) [Note: [Col. 1268] The Remigius manuscript lacks the particle *non* (“not”); the other books, including the printed editions, have it here, and the manuscripts have presented the same sentence to us in this form elsewhere.].

For to the degree that God’s will becomes known to us, our guilt also becomes known to us; and the more it becomes known to us, the more we enter into mourning and tears. We see how just is what God requires of us and in what great imperfection we still lie. And what was said comes to pass in us: “The one who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18).

Behold, let charity abound in you, and you will grieve more over the sinner. The greater the charity in you, the more the person whom you endure will torment you—not as though you were angry with him, but as though you were grieving for him.

13. Consider the apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 1268] Thus the Regius manuscript. The editions read *vidit* (“he saw”).] and what he suffered; consider who suffered what. “Besides those things which are external,” he says—for he had mentioned many things that he suffered and began to speak of inward matters, besides those external things that he suffered from the evil persecutors of Christ—“there is the daily pressure upon me, my concern for all the churches.”

And observe what sort of concern it was: how fatherly, how motherly. See how he was beaten, so that he might be punished in all his inclinations. We too shall speak of his inclinations, in which God punished him.

“Who is weak,” he says, “and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Cor. 11:28–29). The greater the charity, the greater the wounds inflicted by the sins of others.

He had also received a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan, by whom he was buffeted. Behold how gracious God was, punishing all his inclinations.

What were the inclinations in which he punished him so? He himself explained; he himself said: “So that I might not be exalted by the greatness of the revelations, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me.”

He was so perfect that it was nevertheless necessary to fear that he might be exalted. For God would not place medicine where there was no wound.

And he asked that it be removed. The sick man asked that the medicine be taken away:

“For this I besought the Lord three times,” he says, “that he might remove it from me”—that is, the thorn in the flesh by which he was buffeted, perhaps some bodily pain—“I asked,” he says, “that he might remove it from me; and he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Cor. 12:7–9).

I know whom I am treating; let the sick person not give me advice. Like a caustic plaster, it burns you, but it heals you. The patient asks the physician to remove the plaster, but he does not remove it until the wound upon which he placed it has been healed.

“Power is made perfect in weakness.”

Therefore, brothers, all of us who are making progress in Christ must not suppose that we shall be without the lash. However far we may progress, he knows our sins. At times he also shows them to us, and we too see our sins.

And when we begin to live among people such that they can no longer find anything in us to criticize, he who knows everything still criticizes us and punishes all our inclinations, because he is gracious toward us. For if he did not punish us and abandoned us, we would perish.

“God, you were gracious to them, and you punished all their inclinations.”

14. [v. 9.] “Exalt the Lord our God.” Again we exalt him. He is good even when he strikes [Note: [Col. 1269] Am. and Er. read *fuerit* (“will have struck”); Lov. reads *saevierit* (“will have raged”). The manuscripts more correctly read *ferit* (“strikes”). Moreover, Er., Ven., and Lov. read: “Again let us exalt him, because he is good; and when,” etc. M.]; how should he be praised, how exalted? You are able to show this toward your son, and God is not able?

You are not good when you caress your son and evil when you strike your son. When you caress him, you are a father; when you strike him, you are a father. You caress him so that he may not fail; you strike him so that he may not perish.

“Exalt the Lord our God, and worship on his holy mountain; for the Lord our God is holy.”

Just as above he said, “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship the footstool of his feet,” and we understood what it means to worship the footstool of his feet, so now, after exalting the Lord our God, lest anyone exalt him apart from his mountain, he also commended his mountain.

What is his mountain? Elsewhere we read about this mountain that a stone was cut from a mountain without hands, and it shattered all the kingdoms of the earth, and that stone grew. This is the vision of Daniel that I am recounting. This stone, which was cut from the mountain without hands, grew and became, he says, a great mountain, so that it filled the whole face of the earth (Dan. 2:34–35).

On that great mountain let us worship if we wish to be heard. Heretics do not worship on this mountain, because this mountain filled the whole face of the earth. They clung to a part and lost the whole. If they acknowledge the Catholic Church, they will worship on this mountain with us.

Indeed, we already see how greatly that stone which was cut from the mountain without hands has grown, how many regions of the earth it has occupied, and to what peoples it has reached.

What is the mountain from which the stone was cut without hands? The kingdom of the Jews—the people who first worshiped the one God. From there the stone was cut: our Lord Jesus Christ. He himself was called, “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Ps. 117:22; Acts 4:11).

This stone, cut from the mountain without hands, shattered all the kingdoms of the earth. We see all the kingdoms of the earth shattered by that stone.

What were the kingdoms of the earth? The kingdoms of idols, the kingdoms of demons, have been shattered. Saturn reigned over many people; where is his kingdom now? Mercury reigned over many people; where is his kingdom now? It has been shattered; those over whom he reigned have been brought into the kingdom of Christ.

What sort of kingdom did Caelestis have at Carthage? Where is the kingdom of Caelestis now? [Note: [Col. 1270] The editions read *regnum Veneris* (“the kingdom of Venus”) and below *regnum coeleste* (“the heavenly kingdom”). The manuscripts read *coelestis* in both places. Augustine has already discussed this Carthaginian pagan deity above, col. 752, *Enarrationes in Psalmum* 62, no. 7.]

That stone shattered all the kingdoms of the earth, the stone cut from the mountain without hands.

What does “cut from the mountain without hands” mean? He was born from the Jewish people without human intervention. For everyone who is born is born through marital intercourse; he was born of a virgin, born without hands. For “hands” signify human activity. Human hands did not intervene; there was no marital embrace, yet there was a child.

That stone, then, was born from the mountain without hands. It grew, and as it grew it shattered all the kingdoms of the earth. It became a great mountain and filled the whole face of the earth.

This is the Catholic Church, in communion with which you rejoice. But those who are not in communion with it, because they worship and praise God apart from this mountain, are not heard unto eternal life, even if they are heard in certain temporal matters.

Let them not therefore flatter themselves because God hears them in certain things. For he also hears pagans in certain things. Do pagans not cry out to God, and does it not rain? Why? Because he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45).

Do not therefore boast, pagan, that when you cry out to God, God sends rain, since he rains upon the just and the unjust. He has heard you concerning temporal things; he does not hear you concerning eternal things unless you worship on his holy mountain.

“Worship the Lord on his holy mountain, for the Lord our God is holy.”

15. Let these remarks on the Psalm suffice for Your Charity. We have spoken as much as the Lord has granted. And whatever we speak in the name of God, since it belongs to God who speaks through us, is God’s rain. Consider what sort of soil you are.

For when rain comes upon the earth, if the soil is good, it produces good fruits; if the soil is bad, it produces thorns. Yet the rain is sweet both upon the fruits and upon the thorns.

Let the person who becomes worse after hearing these words and produces thorns from the rain expect fire; let him not accuse the rain. But let the person who becomes better and produces crops from good soil expect the granary; let him praise the rain.

Or what are the clouds, or what is the rain, except God’s mercy, doing everything for those whom he loves and to whom he has granted that he be loved by them?

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 99

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. Brothers, you heard the Psalm when it was sung. It is short and not obscure—as though I had given you a guarantee, so that you would not fear the labor. Nevertheless, let us examine more attentively and, the more freely, the more diligently, what those things themselves that sound plainly may mean, so that they may be understood spiritually, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant it.

It is the voice of God sounding through whatever instrument, yet it is the voice of God. For it does not delight his ears unless it is his voice; and we too, when we speak, delight him when he himself speaks through us.

2. [v. 1.] “A Psalm in confession”—so it is inscribed; this is its title: “A Psalm in confession.” There are few verses, but they are pregnant with great things. May they bring forth seeds in your hearts, so that a granary may be prepared for the Lord’s harvest.

This Psalm, “in confession,” commands and urges us to do this: to jubilate to God. It does not urge one particular corner of the earth, or one particular dwelling-place or gathering of people. Rather, because it knows that it has sown blessing everywhere, it demands jubilation from everywhere.

3. [v. 2.] “Jubilate to the Lord, all the earth” [Note: [Col. 1271] The editions read *Deo* (“to God”). Most manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint, read *Domino* (“to the Lord”).].

Does all the earth now hear my voice? And yet all the earth has heard this voice. Already all the earth jubilates to the Lord, and whatever does not yet jubilate will jubilate.

For as the blessing advances, with the Church beginning from Jerusalem through all the nations (Luke 24:47), it everywhere overthrows impiety and everywhere builds piety. The good are mixed with the evil; the evil are throughout the whole earth, and the good are throughout the whole earth. In the evil, the whole earth murmurs; in the good, the whole earth jubilates.

What, then, is jubilation? The title of the present Psalm, which is inscribed “In confession,” makes us very attentive to this word. What does it mean to jubilate “in confession”?

There is a saying of another Psalm that says, “Blessed is the people who understand jubilation” (Ps. 88:16). Surely this is something great, since understanding it makes people blessed.

Therefore, may the Lord our God, who makes human beings blessed, grant me to understand what I say and grant you to understand what you hear: “Blessed is the people who understand jubilation.”

Let us therefore hasten toward this blessedness; let us understand jubilation and not pour it forth without understanding. What is the use of jubilating and obeying this Psalm, which says, “Jubilate to God, all the earth,” without understanding jubilation, so that only our voice jubilates while our heart does not?

For the sound of the heart is understanding.

### 4. What you know I am about to say

One who jubilates does not speak words, but produces a certain sound of joy without words. For it is the voice of a spirit overflowing with joy and expressing its feeling as best it can, without comprehending it in thought. A person rejoicing in exultation bursts forth from certain words that cannot be spoken or understood [Note: Col. 1272. Here, in several manuscripts, *non* (“not”) is absent.] into a kind of voice of exultation without words, so that it is evident that he does rejoice in the voice itself, but, as though filled with excessive joy, cannot explain in words what delights him.

Notice this in those who sing, even when they do not sing honorably. Our jubilation will not be like theirs: we must jubilate in justification, whereas they jubilate in iniquity. Thus we jubilate in confession, while they do so in confusion. Yet, so that you may understand what I am saying—or rather, remember something familiar—those who work in the fields jubilate most of all. Delighted by an abundance of crops, reapers, grape harvesters, or those gathering other fruits, rejoicing in the very fecundity and fertility of the earth, sing in exultation. Amid the songs they utter in words, they insert certain wordless cries in the exaltation of their rejoicing spirit; this is called jubilation.

If someone does not recognize this because he has never paid attention to it, let him pay attention from now on. And would that he find no one to whom he must pay attention, lest God find people whom he must overthrow. Nevertheless, because thorns do not cease to spring up, let us observe in those who exult wickedly a jubilation that must be condemned, and let us offer God a jubilation that will be crowned.

### 5. When, then, do we jubilate?

When we praise what cannot be expressed in words. We observe the whole of creation—the earth, the sea, the sky, and everything in them. We observe that each thing has its own origins and causes, the power of seeds, the order of coming into being, the manner of remaining, and the departure involved in perishing; that the cycles of the ages run without any disturbance; that the stars in a certain way revolve from east to west; that they complete the courses of the years. We see the dimensions of the months and the divisions of the hours.

Amid all these things, I do not know what invisible element—which is called spirit or soul—is present in all living creatures, enabling them to seek pleasure and flee distress, and giving them, for the preservation of their own well-being, a kind of trace of unity. We also see present in human beings something shared with God’s angels—not what they share with animals, such as living, hearing, seeing, and the rest, but the capacity to understand God, something that properly belongs to the mind [Note: Col. 1272. The editions read *pertineat* (“belongs”); several manuscripts, *pertinet*. Perhaps the latter is better.], and that distinguishes equity from iniquity just as the eye distinguishes white from black.

Amid this whole consideration of creation, which we have been able, in some fashion, to name and survey, let the soul ask itself: Who made all these things? Who created them? Who created you yourself among them? What are these things that you are considering? What are you, who are considering them? Who is the one who made both the things to be considered and the one who considers them? Who is this one? Name him. To name him, think of him.

For you can think of something and perhaps cannot say it; but in no way can you say what you have not been able to think. Therefore think of him before you name him. To think of him, draw near to him. When you wish to see something well, so that you may have something to speak about, you draw near in order to inspect it, lest you be deceived by seeing it from a distance. But just as bodily things are seen with the eyes, so he is perceived by the mind, attended to and seen by the heart.

And where is the heart by which he may be seen? “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). I hear this, and I believe it; insofar as I can, I understand that God is seen by the heart and can be contemplated only by a pure heart. But I hear another Scripture: “Who can boast that he has a pure heart? Or who can boast that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. 20:9).

I therefore attended to the whole of creation, insofar as I could. I observed the corporeal in heaven and on earth, and the spiritual in myself—the one who speaks, animates the limbs, raises the voice, moves the tongue, pronounces words, and distinguishes the senses. And when do I comprehend myself within myself? How, then, can I comprehend what is above me?

Yet the vision of God is promised to the human heart, and a certain work of cleansing the heart is enjoined [Note: Col. 1273. The editions read *inde dicitur* (“then it is said”); the manuscripts, *indicitur* (“is enjoined”)]. Scripture says this: Prepare the place from which you may see what you love, before you see it. For when God and his name are heard, to whom is what he hears not sweet—unless the wicked man has been removed and sent very far away? “For behold,” it says, “those who distance themselves from you shall perish”; and it follows: “You have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you” (Ps. 72:27).

But what is said to us? They are far away, and therefore in darkness; and their eyes are so wounded in the darkness that they not only do not desire the light but even dread it. What, then, is said to us who have been found far away? “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:6).

But in order that you may draw near and be enlightened, let your darkness displease you. Condemn what you are, so that you may deserve to be what you are not. You are unjust; you ought to be just. You will never attain justice if iniquity still pleases you. Crush it in your heart and cleanse it; drive it from your heart, where the one whom you wish to see wants to dwell. [Note: Col. 1273. The Regius manuscript reads: “Confess it in your heart; there he whom you wish to see wants to dwell,” etc.]

The human soul therefore draws near in some fashion, and the inner person is restored according to the image of God, because he was created according to the image of God. He had become so far away because he had entered into unlikeness. [Note: Col. 1273. Four manuscripts read: “As the human soul therefore draws near in some fashion, the inner person is restored according to the image of God; because, having been created according to the image of God, he had become so far away,” etc.] One does not draw near to God through distances of place, nor withdraw from God in the same way. Once you became unlike him, you withdrew far away; once you became like him, you drew near.

See how the Lord wishes us to draw near: first making us like him, so that we may draw near. “Be,” he says, “like your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise over the good and the wicked, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45). Learn to love your enemy, if you wish to avoid having an enemy. [Note: Col. 1273. The Colbert manuscript reads *friend*.]

Insofar as charity grows in you, making you and recalling you to the likeness of God, it extends even to enemies, so that you may be like the one who makes his sun rise not only over the good but over the good and the wicked, and sends rain not only upon the just but upon the just and the unjust. Insofar as you draw near to the likeness, you advance in charity, and you begin to perceive God to that extent.

And whom do you perceive: the one who comes to you, or the one to whom you return? For he has never departed from you. God withdraws from you when you withdraw from God. Everything is present to the blind just as it is to those who see. A blind person and one who sees stand in the same place, surrounded by the same forms of things. One is present to things, the other absent. Of two people standing in the same place, one is present and the other absent—not because the things themselves draw near to one or withdraw from the other, but because of the unlikeness of their eyes.

The one called blind, because that which is ordinarily attuned to the light [Note: Col. 1274. Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “to the light.”] clothing everything has been extinguished in him, is present in vain to the things he does not see. Indeed, he is more properly called absent than present: where his perception is not, he is rightly said to be absent. For this is what it means to be absent: to be absent in perception.

So too God is present everywhere, wholly present everywhere. “His wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). And what God the Father is, his Word and his Wisdom are also: light from light, God from God.

What, then, do you desire to see? What you wish to see is not far from you. The Apostle indeed says that he is “not far from each one of us: for in him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:27–28). How great, then, is the misery of being far from him who is everywhere?

### 6. Be like him, therefore, in devotion and attentive thought

“For his invisible things are understood and perceived through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20). Look upon the things that have been made, marvel, and seek their author. If you are unlike him, you will be repelled; if you are like him, you will exult.

And when you begin to draw near as one like him and to perceive God, insofar as charity grows in you—for “God is charity” (1 John 4:8)—you will perceive something that you were speaking of and yet were not speaking of. Before you perceived it, you thought you were able to speak of God. You begin to perceive him, and there you perceive that what you perceive cannot be spoken.

When you have learned there that what you perceive cannot be spoken, will you be silent and not praise? Will you therefore be mute in praising God and not return thanks to the one who wished to make himself known to you? You praised him when you were seeking him; will you be silent when you have found him? By no means. You will not be ungrateful. Honor is owed, reverence is owed, great praise is owed.

Consider who you are: earth and ashes. See who has been deemed worthy to see what; see who it is who sees what—humanity seeing God. I acknowledge not human merit but God’s mercy. Praise, therefore, the one who shows mercy.

“How,” you ask, “shall I praise him?” The little that I can perceive, “in part and in an enigma through a mirror” (1 Cor. 13:12), I can no longer explain. Hear the Psalm, then: “Jubilate to the Lord, all the earth.” You have understood the jubilation of all the earth if you jubilate to the Lord. Jubilate to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1274] So the manuscripts of better quality. But the editions have: “Of the earth? If you jubilate, jubilate to the Lord.”]

Finally, other things can be expressed in some fashion. [Col. 1275] He alone is ineffable who spoke, and all things came into being. “He spoke, and we were made”; but we cannot speak him (Ps. 32:9). His Word by which we were spoken into being is his Son. So that he might in some fashion be spoken by us, who are weak, he became weak. We can call jubilation a word, but we cannot call the Word a word. Jubilate, therefore, to the Lord, all the earth.

### 7. Serve the Lord with gladness

All servitude is full of bitterness. All who are bound by a condition of servitude [Note: Col. 1275. The word *servitude* is absent from most manuscripts.] both serve and murmur. Do not fear servitude under that Lord. There will be no groaning there, no murmuring, no indignation. No one seeks to have himself sold away from it [Note: Col. 1275. The Erasmus and Colbert manuscripts read “thinks”; the other books read *seeks*, which is better. Thus also in Tractate 41 on John, §4: “Often, when people suffer bad masters, they seek to have themselves sold; seeking not to have no master, but at least to change masters.”], because it is sweet that we have all been redeemed.

It is great happiness, brothers, to be a servant in that great household, even if with fetters. Do not fear, fettered servant; confess to the Lord. Attribute your fetters to your merits. Confess in fetters if you wish them to be turned into ornaments. It was not said without reason or without being heard: “Let the groaning of the prisoners come before you” (Ps. 78:11).

“Serve the Lord with gladness.” There is free servitude with the Lord—free servitude where charity serves, not necessity. “You have been called,” he says, “to freedom, brothers; only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through charity serve one another” (Gal. 5:13). Let charity make you a servant, [Note: [Col. 1275] So Am., Er., and most manuscripts. Lov. has “makes you.”] because truth has made you free.

“If you remain,” he says, “in my word, you are truly my disciples; and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (John 8:31–32). You are at once servant and free: servant because you were made; free because you are loved by the God by whom you were made; indeed, free for this very reason, because you love the one by whom you were made.

Do not serve with murmuring. Your murmuring does not make you cease to serve, but makes you serve as a bad servant. You are the Lord’s servant; you are the Lord’s freedman. Do not seek to be manumitted in such a way that you depart from the household of the one who manumits you.

### 8. Serve the Lord with gladness

That gladness will be full and perfect when “this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:54). Then gladness will be perfect; then there will be perfect jubilation, praise without defect, love without stumbling, fruit without fear, and life without death.

What of the present life? Is there no joy here? If there is no joy, there is no jubilation. How, then, does it say, “Jubilate to the Lord, all the earth”? There is certainly joy here too. Here we taste something of the future life, by which we shall be satisfied there.

But it is necessary that many grains endure among the weeds. There are grains among the chaff (Matt. 3:12; 13:30); there is a lily among thorns. What does the Church hear? “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song 2:2). It does not say, “among strangers,” but “among daughters.”

O Lord, how you console, strengthen, and terrify us! What is this that you say? “As a lily among”—among what thorns? “So is my beloved among”—among what daughters? Do you call the very daughters thorns? He answers: They are thorns because of their behavior, but daughters because of my sacraments.

Would that we groaned among the groans of strangers; we would groan less. The greater groaning is this: “For if an enemy had reproached me, I would surely have borne it; and if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would surely have hidden myself from him. But you, my equal, my guide, and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food” (Ps. 54:13–15).

Who are those who take sweet food with us but will not always be with us? What sweet food, if not this: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. 33:8)? Among such people we must groan.

### 9. But where will the Christian separate himself so as not to groan among false brothers?

Where will he go? What will he do? Should he seek the deserts? Scandals follow. Should one who is making good progress separate himself so as to endure no human being at all? What if, before he made progress, no one had been willing to endure him?

If, because he is making progress, he wishes to endure no one, then by the very fact that he does not wish to endure anyone, he is shown not to have made progress. Let Your Charity pay attention. The Apostle says: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2–3).

“Bearing with one another.” Do you have nothing in yourself that another must bear? I wonder whether that is so. But suppose it is: you are all the stronger for bearing with others, since you now have nothing in yourself that others must bear. If you are not being borne, bear others.

“I cannot,” you say. Then you have something in yourself that others must bear: “bearing with one another in love.”

You abandon human affairs and isolate yourself so that no one may see you. Whom will you benefit? Would you have reached this point if no one had benefited you? Or, because you think you have had swift feet for crossing over, are you going to cut off the bridge? I exhort everyone; the voice of God exhorts everyone: “Bearing with one another in love.”

### 10. “I shall separate myself,” someone says, “with a few good people; I shall be well off with them”

For it is impious and cruel to benefit no one. My Lord did not teach me this. [Note: Col. 1276. Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “Did not my Lord teach me this?”] He did not condemn the servant who misappropriated what he had received, but the one who did not distribute it.

Let the punishment of the misappropriator be understood from the punishment of the slothful servant. The Lord says in condemnation: “Wicked and lazy servant.” He does not say, “You misappropriated my money.” He does not say, “I gave it to you, and you did not return what I gave you intact.” Rather, “Because it did not increase, because you did not distribute it, for this,” he says, “I shall punish you” (Matt. 25:14–30).

“Then I shall separate myself with a few good people,” he says. “What have I to do with the crowds?”

Very well. Are these few good people those who have been sifted out of the crowds? If indeed they are already few, all good people. Nevertheless, the human thought is good and praiseworthy: to be with people who have chosen a quiet life, removed from popular clamor, restless crowds, and the great waves of the world; they are like people in a harbor.

Is that joy already there—the jubilation that is promised? Not yet: there are still groans and the anxiety of temptations. A harbor has an entrance from somewhere. If a harbor had no entrance on any side, no ship would enter it. Therefore it must be open on one side. Sometimes, however, through the side that is open, the wind rushes in; and where there are no reefs, ships are shattered by colliding with one another.

Where, then, is security, if not even in a harbor? Yet, in whatever way it may be, they are more fortunate in a harbor than on the open sea; this must be admitted, conceded, and acknowledged as true.

Let the ships love one another [Note: Col. 1277. Thus several manuscripts; the editions read, “Nevertheless, if ships …”; for “collide,” Erasmus and the Gatian manuscript have “are colliding,” while another manuscript has “will collide.”] and moor well alongside one another in the harbor; let them not collide with one another. Let equality of balance and constancy of charity be preserved there. And when perhaps the wind rushes in through the side that is open, let there be prudent steering.

### 11. For what will someone say to me who perhaps presides over such places—or rather, serves the brothers in them, in what are called monasteries?

What will he say? “I shall be cautious; I shall admit no evil.”

How will you admit no evil?

“I shall admit no evil person, no wicked brother who enters. I shall be well off with a few good people.”

Where do you know the person whom you perhaps wish to exclude? To discover that someone is wicked, he must be tested inside. How, then, do you exclude someone who is about to enter and must afterward be tested, but cannot be tested unless he enters?

Will you repel all the wicked? You say that you know how to inspect them. Do they all come to you with their hearts laid bare? Those who are about to enter do not know themselves; how much less do you know them?

Many have promised themselves that they would fulfill that holy life in which everything is held in common, where no one calls anything his own, and where there is one soul and one heart toward God (Acts 4:32, 35). They were sent into the furnace and cracked. [Col. 1277]

How, then, do you recognize someone who is still unknown even to himself? Do you exclude wicked brothers from the assembly of the good? Whoever you are who say these things, exclude from your own heart, if you can, all evil thoughts. Let not even an evil suggestion enter your heart.

“I do not consent,” you say.

Yet it entered in order to make its suggestion. [Note: [Col. 1277] Er., Venice, and Lov. have “so that it might be suggested.” M. has the present reading.] For we all wish to have fortified hearts, so that nothing may enter that is suggested for evil. But who knows from where it enters?
