Every day we fight within our one heart. One person struggles with a crowd within his own heart. Greed makes its suggestion, lust makes its suggestion, gluttony makes its suggestion, and this popular merriment makes its suggestion; everything makes its suggestion. He restrains himself from all of them, answers them all, and turns away from them all. It is difficult not to be struck by one of them. [Note: [Col. 1277] The Audoen manuscript has “by some one”; Reg. has “by some one” in the feminine form.]

Where, then, is security? Here, nowhere; in this life, nowhere, except in the sole hope of God’s promises. But there, when we have arrived, there will be perfect security, when the gates are closed and the bars of Jerusalem’s gates are strengthened (Ps. 147:13). There indeed will be full jubilation and great joy.

For now, do not confidently praise any way of life. “Before death, praise no one” (Sir. 11:30).

### 12. This is how people are deceived

They are deceived either into not undertaking the better life or into rashly undertaking it, because when people wish to praise it, they praise it in such a way that they do not mention the evils mixed into it; and when they wish to condemn it, they condemn it with such an envious and perverse spirit that they close their eyes to the good and exaggerate only the evils that are either present or imagined there.

Thus each way of life, when wrongly praised—that is, praised without caution—invites people by its praise. Those who come there find certain people unlike those whom they had believed would be there. Offended by the evils, they recoil from the good.

Brothers, apply this teaching to your own life, and hear it in such a way that you may live.

To speak generally, the Church of God is praised: great Christian people, Christians alone, the great Catholic Church. [Note: [Col. 1278] Er. and Lov. have “the Catholic Church.” The word “Church” is absent from Am. and the manuscripts.] They all love one another; each contributes what he can to the others; prayers, fasts, and hymns are practiced throughout the whole world; God is praised with a single agreement of peace.

Someone who does not know that the wicked are mixed in may hear this, come invited by the praise, and find wicked people mixed in—people whose presence was not announced to him before he came. Offended by false Christians, he withdraws from true Christians.

Then hateful and slanderous people rush into condemnation: “What kind of Christians are they? Which Christians? Avaricious people, usurers. Are they not the very people who fill theaters and amphitheaters with games and other spectacles, and fill churches on feast days? Drunkards, gluttons, envious people, persecuting one another.”

There are such people, but they are not the only kind. This condemner, in his blindness, is silent about the good; that praiser, in his carelessness, is silent about the wicked.

But if the Church of God is praised in this age in this way, how do the Scriptures of God praise it? Here is how, as I have just said: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.” A person hears this, considers it, and is pleased by the lily. He enters, clings to the lily, and endures the thorns. He will deserve to be among the praise and kisses [Note: [Col. 1278] Er. and Lov. have “in the eyes.” Am. has “in the kisses,” as do the manuscripts except a few, which have “in the kiss.”] of the bridegroom who says, “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.”

So also with the clergy. Those who praise the clergy point to good ministers, faithful stewards, people who endure everyone, who expend their own resources for those whom they wish to advance, seeking not what is theirs but what is Jesus Christ’s. They praise these things but forget that the clergy are mixed with the wicked.

Again, those who criticize the avarice, wickedness, and quarrels of the clergy—those who desire other people’s possessions, and are drunkards and gluttons—proclaim their faults. [Note: [Col. 1278] So Am. and most manuscripts. Er. and Lov. have “proclaiming.” The Regius manuscript has “proclaiming themselves.”]

You are envious when you condemn, and careless when you praise. You who praise, say that the wicked are mixed in. You who condemn, look also for the good there.

So too in that common life of the brothers which exists in a monastery: great and holy men live there daily in hymns, prayers, and praises of God; they occupy themselves with reading; they work with their hands and thereby support themselves; they do not avariciously demand anything; whatever is brought to them by devout brothers, they use with sufficiency and charity; no one claims for himself anything that another does not have; they all love one another and all bear with one another.

You have praised, you have praised. [Note: [Col. 1279] So the manuscripts. The editions have: “The one who does not know praises,” and so forth.] Whoever does not know what is happening within, who does not know how, when that wind enters, ships also collide in the harbor, enters as though expecting security and expecting to have no one whom he must endure. He finds wicked brothers there, who could not be found to be wicked unless they were admitted—and they must first be endured, lest perhaps they be corrected; nor can they easily be excluded unless they have first been endured. [Note: Col. 1279. Two manuscripts read “intolerable,” and some, together with Am., “not endured.” A little later “impatience” has been restored from the manuscripts; at that point the editions had [lacuna] “patience.”] [Note: [Col. 1279] Two manuscripts have “intolerable”; some, with Am., have “not endured.” A little later we have restored “impatience” from the manuscripts; in that place the editions had [lacuna]rat “patience.”]

And he himself becomes intolerably impatient. “Who was looking for me here? I thought charity was here.” Irritated by the annoyance of a few people, when he does not persevere in fulfilling what he vowed, he becomes a deserter from so holy a purpose and guilty of an unfulfilled vow.

Then, when he has left, he himself becomes a condemner and slanderer. He says only those things that he claims he could not endure—and sometimes they are true. But the true faults of the wicked must be endured for the sake of fellowship with the good.

Scripture says to him: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Sir. 2:16). And, what is worse, he belches forth the evil odor of indignation [Note: [Col. 1279] So most manuscripts. The editions have “indignations, the odor of evils.” Some manuscripts have “indignations of evil hatreds.”] in order to repel those who are about to enter, because he himself could not endure after he entered.

“What are they like?” “Envious, quarrelsome, enduring no one, avaricious. This person did such-and-such there, and that person did such-and-such there.”

You are wicked—why are you silent about the good? You proclaim those whom you could not endure; you are silent about those who endured you, though you were wicked.

### 13. Rightly, dearest brothers, that magnificent saying from the Lord’s Gospel comes from the Lord’s own mouth

“Two shall be in the field: one shall be taken, and one shall be left; two shall be at the mill: one shall be taken, and one shall be left; two shall be in bed: one shall be taken, and one shall be left” (Matt. 24:40–41; Luke 17:34–35).

Who are the two in the field? What the Apostle says: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. You are God’s husbandry” (1 Cor. 3:6, 9). We labor in the field. The two in the field are clergy: one shall be taken and one shall be left; the good shall be taken, and the wicked shall be left.

The two at the mill he referred to the people. [Note: [Col. 1279] Lov. has “I referred.” The other editions and the manuscripts have “he referred.”] Why at the mill? Because they are bound to the world and held fast by the cycle of temporal affairs, like a millstone. One shall be taken from there and one shall be left.

Which one shall be taken? The woman who performs good works, attends to the needs of God’s servants and the needs of the poor, is faithful in confession, secure in the joy of hope, watchful toward God, curses no one, loves as much as she can not only friends but also enemies, and knows no woman besides his wife and no man besides her husband. She too shall be taken from the mill; but the one who is otherwise shall be left.

Others say: “We want quiet; we do not want to endure anyone; we withdraw from the crowds; we shall be well off in a certain security.”

If you seek quiet, you seek something like a bed, so that you may rest without any anxiety. And from there one shall be taken and one shall be left.

Let no one deceive you, brothers. If you do not wish to be deceived and wish to love the brothers, know that every profession in the Church contains false people. I did not say that every person is false, but that every profession contains false persons. There are wicked Christians, but there are also good ones.

You seem to see more wicked people because they are chaff and prevent you from reaching the grain. There is grain there too. Draw near, test it, thresh it, and apply the judgment of the mouth.

You find undisciplined women religious. Does that mean that the religious life itself must be condemned? Many do not remain in their own houses; they go around other people’s houses, being busybodies, speaking things they ought not, proud, talkative (1 Tim. 5:13), and drunk. Even if they are virgins, what good is an intact body with a corrupt mind? A humble marriage is better than proud virginity. If she married, she would not have the title from which she could exalt herself, and she would have a restraint by which she could be governed.

But because of wicked virgins are we going to condemn those holy in body and spirit (1 Cor. 7:34)? Or because of the praiseworthy ones, will we be compelled to praise even those who deserve condemnation? From every group one shall be taken and one shall be left.

### 14. [Verse 2]

Therefore, brothers, let us finish the Psalm, because it is clear.

“Serve the Lord with gladness.” It addresses all of you who bear everything in charity and rejoice in hope. Serve the Lord not in the bitterness of murmuring but in the gladness of love.

“Enter into his presence with exultation.” It is easy to exult outwardly; exult in the presence of God. Let not your tongue exult greatly; let your conscience exult. “Enter into his presence with exultation.”

### 15. [Verse 3]

“Know that the Lord himself is God.”

Who does not know that the Lord himself is God? But he speaks of the Lord whom people did not think to be God: “Know that the Lord himself is God.” Let that Lord not seem insignificant to you. You crucified him, scourged him, smeared him with spittle, crowned him with thorns, clothed him in a garment of disgrace, hung him on the wood, fastened him with nails, pierced him with a spear, and placed guards at his tomb. He is God.

“Know that the Lord himself is God. He himself made us, and not we ourselves.” [Note: [Col. 1280] The editions have “and not we ourselves made us.” The word “ourselves” is absent from the manuscripts of better quality and from the Septuagint.]

He himself made us: “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). Why do you exult? Why are you proud? Another made you—and the one who made you suffers at your hands. Yet you boast and glory and exalt yourselves as though you had made yourselves.

It is good for you that the one who made you should complete you. “He himself made us, and not we ourselves.” We must not be proud. All the good that we have comes from our maker. Whatever we have made in ourselves is what condemns us; what he has made in us is what crowns us.

“He himself made us, and not we ourselves. But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.”

Sheep and a sheep: the sheep themselves are one sheep. And what a loving shepherd we have! He left the ninety-nine and descended to seek the one; he carries it back on his shoulders (Luke 15:4–5), redeemed by his blood. The shepherd died securely for the sheep, for by rising again he possesses the sheep.

“But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.”

### 16. [Verses 4–5]

“Enter his gates with confession.” In the gates there is a beginning; begin with confession. Hence the Psalm is “in confession”; there jubilate. [Note: [Col. 1281] The editions have: “Hence, jubilate the Psalm,” and so forth. The manuscripts read: “Hence the Psalm is in confession”—with “is inscribed” understood. The Remigius manuscript, however, reads: “Hence, jubilate the Psalm in confession.”]

Confess that you were not made by yourselves; praise the one by whom you were made. Let your good come from the one by departing from whom you made your evil.

“Enter his gates with confession.” Let the flock enter the gates; let it not remain outside among the wolves. And how is it to enter? With confession. Let confession be your gate—that is, your beginning.

Hence it is said in another Psalm: “Begin to the Lord with confession” (Ps. 146:7). What he calls “begin” there, he calls “gates” here: “Enter his gates with confession.”

And once we have entered, shall we no longer confess? Confess always; you always have something to confess. It is difficult in this life for a person to be so changed that nothing reprehensible is found in him. You must rebuke yourself, lest the one who will condemn rebuke you.

Therefore, even when you have entered his courts, confess. When will there be no confession of sins? In that rest, in that equality with the angels. But pay attention to what I said: there will be no confession of sins. I did not say there will be no confession, for there will be confession of praise.

You will always confess: him as God, yourself as a creature; him as protector, yourself as protected. In him you will in some fashion be hidden, as it is said: “You shall hide them in the hiding-place of your presence” (Ps. 30:21).

“In his courts confess to him in hymns.” At the gates confess; and when you have entered the courts, confess in hymns. Hymns are praises.

When you enter, rebuke yourself; once you have entered, praise him. “Open to me the gates of righteousness,” another Psalm says; “entering through them, I shall confess to the Lord” (Ps. 117:19). Does it say, “Once I have entered, I shall no longer confess”? Even after entering, he will confess.

For what sins was our Lord Jesus Christ confessing when he said, “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11:25)? He was confessing by praising him, not by accusing himself.

### 17. Praise his name, for the Lord is sweet

Do not think that you grow weak in praising. Your praise will be like eating: the more you praise, the more strength you gain, and the sweeter becomes the one whom you praise.

“Praise his name, for the Lord is sweet.”

“His mercy is forever.” When he has delivered you, he will not cease to be merciful. And that he may protect you forever in eternal life is also a work of his mercy.

“His mercy is forever, and his truth from generation to generation.” Either understand “from generation to generation” as every generation, or understand two generations: one earthly and the other heavenly. One generation gives birth to mortals; the other gives birth to the eternal. His truth is both here and there.

Do not think that his truth is not here. If his truth were not here, another Psalm would not say, “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. 84:12); nor would Truth itself say, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 100

[Col. 1282]

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE
1. [verse 1] We must seek throughout the whole body of this hundredth Psalm what it has in its first verse. “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.” Let no one flatter himself into impunity on account of God’s mercy, because there is also judgment; and let no one who has been changed for the better shrink from God’s judgment, because mercy comes first. For when human beings judge, sometimes, overcome by mercy [Note: [Col. 1282] Several manuscripts: “they show mercy.”], they act contrary to justice; and mercy seems to exist in them without judgment. Sometimes, however, wishing to maintain a strict judgment, they lose mercy. But God neither loses the severity of judgment in the goodness of mercy, nor, when judging with severity, loses the goodness of mercy.

Now, if we distinguish these two things—mercy and judgment—by their times, perhaps they were placed in this order not without reason, so that he did not say, “Judgment and mercy,” but “Mercy and judgment.” If, then, we distinguish these two according to their times, perhaps we shall find that the present is the time of mercy, while the future will be the time of judgment.

How is the present first a time of mercy? Consider first the matter in God, so that you too may imitate the Father insofar as he has bestowed upon you. For we do not arrogantly say that we ought to imitate our Father, since the Lord himself, the only-begotten Son of God, exhorts us to this when he says: “Be like your heavenly Father.” When he said, “Love your enemies, pray for those who persecute you,” he added, “so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, and sends rain on the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:48, 44–45).

Behold mercy. When you see the just and the unjust looking upon the same sun, receiving the same light [Note: [Col. 1282] Manuscripts: “gathering up” or “plucking.”], drinking from the same springs, being nourished by the same rain, being filled with the same fruits of the earth, breathing the same air, and possessing equally the good things of the world, do not think God unjust because he gives these things equally to the just and the unjust. It is the time of mercy, not yet of judgment. For unless God first spared through mercy, he would not find anyone whom he could crown through judgment. It is therefore the time of mercy when God’s patience leads sinners to repentance.

2. Hear the Apostle distinguishing the two times, and distinguish them yourself: “Do you suppose,” he says, “O man, who judges those who do such things and does the same, that you will escape God’s judgment?” Pay attention. He saw himself doing many evil things every day—though consider to whom he is speaking. He is not speaking to one individual, but to that kind of human race—and yet he saw himself living on, with no evil befalling him. He thought either that God was asleep, or that he paid no attention to human affairs, or that he approved of human beings’ evil deeds.

He removes this thought from the heart, but only from the hearts of those who understand rightly. What, then, does he say? “Do you suppose, O man,” he says, “who judges those who do such things and does them yourself, that you will escape God’s judgment?” [Col. 1283] And as though he were saying, “Why do I do so many evil things every day, and yet nothing evil happens to me?” he goes on to show him the time of mercy: “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering?” And indeed, this is what he was despising; but the Apostle made him anxious. “Do you not know,” he says, “that God’s goodness leads you to repentance?” Behold the time of mercy.

But so that he would not always think this would continue, how did he then terrify him concerning the time of judgment? “But according to your hardness and impenitent heart,” he says, “you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2:3–6). Behold: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.”

But he threatened judgment. Does that mean that God’s judgment is to be feared only, and not loved? It is to be feared by the wicked because of punishment, and loved by the good because of the crown.

Since, then, the Apostle terrified the wicked in the testimony I have recalled, hear where he gives the good hope concerning judgment. He presents himself and declares, showing in himself also the time of mercy. For unless he too had found the time of mercy, how would judgment have found him? A blasphemer, a persecutor, an insolent man. Thus he speaks, and commends the time of mercy in which we now live: “I was formerly,” he says, “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy.”

But perhaps he alone obtained mercy? Hear how he raises us up: “That in me,” he says, “Christ Jesus might display all long-suffering, as instruction for those who would believe in him for eternal life” (1 Tim. 1:13, 16).

What does “that he might display long-suffering in me” mean? It means that every sinner and criminal might see that Paul received forgiveness and might not despair of himself. Behold, he displayed himself and encouraged others. Where? In the time of mercy.

Hear what he says about the good in the time of judgment, speaking again about himself and about others. First he obtained mercy. Why? Because he had been a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man. The Lord came to give Paul a gift, not to repay him. For if he had wished to repay him, what would he have found to repay the sinner except punishment and torment? He did not wish to repay punishment, but gave grace.

Hear how the one to whom he gave this gift nevertheless holds the Lord as his debtor. He found him a giver in the time of mercy and holds him as a debtor in the time of judgment. See how he says this. “For I am already being offered,” he said, “and the time of my departure is near. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith.” This concerns the time of mercy; now hear about judgment: “From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day.”

He did not say “will give,” but “will render.” When he was giving, he was merciful; when he renders, he will be judge—because “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.” But by forgiving sins he made himself the debtor of a crown: “There I obtained mercy.” The Lord was therefore merciful at first, but now “he will render me the crown of righteousness.” From where will he render it? Because he is a righteous judge. Why [Col. 1284] is he a righteous judge? Because “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith.” Therefore, being righteous, he cannot do otherwise than crown these achievements. He finds things to crown. But what had he found before? “I was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor.” He gave those things; he will crown these. He gave the former in the time of mercy; he will crown the latter in the time of judgment—because “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.”

But did Paul alone deserve this? I had said that just as the Apostle terrified him in that testimony, so he raised him up in this one. After he had said, “The Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day,” he adds: “Not to me only, but also to all who love his manifestation and his kingdom” (2 Tim. 4:6–8).

3. Therefore, brothers, since we have the time of mercy, let us not flatter ourselves, let us not abandon ourselves, let us not say: “God always spares. Behold, I did it yesterday, and God spared me; I do it today, and God spares me; I will do it tomorrow, because God spares me.” You attend to mercy and do not fear judgment. If you wish to sing of mercy and judgment, understand that he spares you for this reason: so that you may be corrected, not so that you may remain in wickedness.

Do not store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment. For in the time of mercy it is said in another Psalm:

> “But God said to the sinner: ‘Why do you recite my ordinances and take my covenant upon your lips? You hate discipline, and you cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you made your portion with adulterers; sitting, you spoke evil against your brother, and you placed a stumbling block against your mother’s son. You did these things, and I was silent.’”

Behold the time of mercy. What does “I was silent” mean? Does it mean, “I did not rebuke”? Rather, “I did not judge.” For how can he be silent who cries out every day in the Scriptures, in the Gospel, and through his preachers? He was silent concerning punishment, not concerning the word.

“You did these things, and I was silent.” And because God was silent—that is, he did not take vengeance—what did the sinner say to himself in his heart? Hear: “You thought,” he says, “that I would be like you in wickedness.” That is: it was not enough that you were such; you thought me such as well.

And when he had shown him the time of mercy, he terrified him concerning the time of judgment: “I will rebuke you, and I will set you before your own face” (Ps. 49:16–21). You place yourself behind yourself; I will place you before yourself. For everyone who does not wish to see his own sins puts himself behind his back and observes the sins of others sharply—not through diligence, but through envy; not wishing to heal, but to accuse. He forgets himself.

Hence the Lord says to such people: “You see the splinter in your brother’s eye, but you do not see the beam in your own eye” (Matt. 7:3).

Since, then, mercy and judgment are sung to us, and since we who practice mercy confidently await judgment, let us be in his body and let us sing these things too. Christ sings this: if only the head sings, this song is from the Lord and does not concern us. But if it is the whole Christ—that is, his head and body—then be in his members, cling to him through faith, hope, and love, and in him you sing, in him you exult [Note: [Col. 1284] Thus most manuscripts. The editions have: “sing, in him exult.”], because he also labors in you, thirsts in you, hungers in you, and is afflicted in you. He is still dying in you, and you have already risen in him.

For if he were not dying in you, he would not wish himself to be spared in you by the persecutor when he said: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

Therefore, my brothers, Christ sings—but you know how. We have continually commended Christ to you, and I know that these things are not unfamiliar to you. The Lord Christ is the Word of God, through whom all things were made. This Word became flesh in order to redeem us and dwelt among us (John 1:3, 14). The God who is above all became man, the Son of God equal to the Father. He became man for this purpose: so that God-man might be mediator between human beings and God, reconcile those who were far away, join together those who were separated, call back those who had become estranged, and lead home those who were wandering. For this purpose he became man.

He therefore became the head of the Church, and he has a body and members. Seek his members: now they groan throughout the whole world; then they will rejoice at the end, in the crown of righteousness of which Paul says: “Which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day.”

Let us therefore now sing in hope, all gathered into one. Clothed with Christ, we are Christ together with our head, because certainly we are Abraham’s offspring. The Apostle says this. Since I said, “We are Christ,” the Apostle says: “Therefore you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise.” You are Abraham’s offspring. Let us see whether Christ is Abraham’s offspring:

> “In your offspring all the nations will be blessed.” He does not say, “In offsprings,” as though in many, but as though in one: “And to your offspring,” which is Christ (Gal. 3:29, 8, 16).

And he says to us: “Therefore you are Abraham’s offspring.” It is clear that we belong to Christ; and because we are his members and his body, together with our head we are one human being.

Let us therefore sing: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.”

4. [verse 2] “I will sing psalms and understand in the blameless way, when you come to me.” Unless you are in the blameless way, you cannot sing psalms or understand. If you wish to understand, sing psalms in the blameless way—that is, work cheerfully for your God.

What is the blameless way? Hear what follows: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house.” This blameless way begins with innocence and is also completed in it. Why seek many words? Be innocent, and you have fulfilled righteousness.

But what does it mean to be innocent? For, insofar as it lies within him, a person harms in two ways: either by making someone miserable or by abandoning someone miserable. For you do not want to be made miserable by another, and if you should become miserable, you do not want to be abandoned by another.

Who makes people miserable? The one who inflicts violence or lays snares, seizes what belongs to others, oppresses the poor, steals, solicits another’s marriage, is slanderous, wishes to inflict on people what will cause them pain, and does so out of deliberate ill will.

Who abandons the miserable? The one who sees a needy person requiring some help and, although he has the means to provide it, despises him, looks down on him, and turns his heart away. Even if that person were already entirely such that he needed no mercy, he would still be proud if he abandoned the miserable. He remains in the tribulation of the flesh, not knowing what may happen to him tomorrow, and he despises the tears of the miserable; he is not innocent.

But who is innocent? The one who, while harming no one else, does not harm himself either. For one who harms himself is not innocent.

Someone says: “Look, I have taken nothing from anyone, nor have I oppressed anyone. From my own property, from my honest labor, I will do what pleases me. I want to have a banquet prepared; I want to spend as much as delights me; I want to drink with whomever I wish, as much as delights me. Whom have I robbed? Whom have I oppressed? Who has complained about me?” He seems innocent.

But if he corrupts himself, if he overturns within himself the temple of God, what should you expect—that he will show mercy to others and spare the miserable? Can one who is cruel toward himself be merciful toward another?

All righteousness is therefore reduced to the single word “innocence.” “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6). When he loved iniquity, he thought that he was harming others. But see whether he was harming others: “Whoever loves iniquity,” he says, “hates his own soul.”

Therefore the one who wishes to harm others first harms himself. Nor does he walk, because there is nowhere for him to walk. Every wickedness suffers constriction; only innocence is broad, where one may walk [Note: [Col. 1286] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have: “because there is nowhere that does not suffer constrictions. Every wickedness is narrow; only innocence is broad. Where does he walk?”].

“I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house.” By “the midst of his house” he either means the Church itself, for Christ walks in it, or his own heart; for our inner house is our heart. Thus he may have explained what he said above, “in the innocence of my heart.” What is the innocence of his heart? “The midst of his house.”

Whoever has a bad house is driven out of it. For whoever is oppressed in his heart by an evil conscience cannot willingly dwell in his heart. Just as a person leaves his house because of dripping water or smoke and cannot endure living there, so the person who does not have a tranquil heart cannot willingly dwell in his own heart.

Such people go out from themselves by the intention of their minds and take pleasure in things outside, around the body. They seek rest in trifles, spectacles, luxuries, and every evil. Why do they want things to be good for them outside? Because things are not good for them within, where they could rejoice in their conscience.

Therefore, when the Lord had healed the paralytic, he said: “Take up your bed and go to your house” (Matt. 9:6). Let the soul that is, as it were, loosened by paralysis do this: let it be bound together in the members of good works, so that it may work well; let it take up its bed and govern its body. Now let it go to its house; let it enter its conscience. It will then find it broad, where it may walk, sing psalms, and understand.

5. [verses 3–4] “I did not set before my eyes an evil thing.” What does “I did not set before my eyes an evil thing” mean? “I did not love it.” For it is customary, as you know, to say of a person who is loved by someone, “He keeps him before his eyes.” And the one who is despised is accustomed to complain, “He does not keep me before his eyes.”

What, then, does it mean to keep something before one’s eyes? To love it. What does it mean not to love it? Not to dwell there in one’s heart.

He therefore said: “I did not set an evil thing before my eyes”—I did not love an evil thing. And he explains what that evil thing is: “I hated those who commit transgression” [Col. 1287] [Note: [Col. 1287] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “transgressions.”].

Pay attention, my brothers. If you walk with Christ in the midst of his house—that is, if you rest well either in your own heart or, in the Church itself, travel along the good road in the blameless way—you must not hate transgressors only when they are outside, but also wherever you find them within.

Who are transgressors? Those who hate God’s law. They hear it but do not do it; they are called transgressors. “I hated those who commit transgression”: drive them away from you.

But you ought to hate transgressors, not human beings. A single person who is a transgressor has two names: “human being” and “transgressor.” God made the human being; the person made himself a transgressor. Love in him what God made; pursue in him what he himself made. For when you have pursued his transgression, you kill what the human being made, and what God made is set free.

“I hated those who commit transgression.”

6. “A crooked heart did not cling to me.” What is a crooked heart? A twisted heart. What is a twisted heart? A heart that is not straight. What is a heart that is not straight? Look at what a straight heart is, and there you will find what a heart that is not straight is.

A person’s heart is called straight when he does not fail to will everything that God wills [Note: [Col. 1287] Augustine of Ancona and Lovaniensis have “he himself wills.” Erasmus and the manuscripts have “he himself does not fail to will.”]. Pay attention.

Someone prays that something—I do not know what—may not happen. He prays, and his request is not granted. Let him ask as much as he can [Note: [Col. 1287] Lovaniensis has “he asks”; the other editions and the manuscripts disagree.], but something happens contrary to his will. Let him submit himself to God’s will; let him not resist the great will.

For the Lord himself explains this in this way. Showing our weakness in himself, when he was about to suffer he said: “My soul is sorrowful even to death.” For he was not truly afraid of death, since he had the power to lay down his life and the power to take it up again (John 10:18).

And the Apostle Paul, his soldier and servant, cries out: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will render to me on that day, the righteous judge.”

He rejoices that he is going to die, while his Lord and commander is sorrowful because he is going to die? Is the servant then better than the Lord? And where is what the Lord himself said: “It is enough for the servant to be like his master, and for the disciple to be like his teacher” (Matt. 10:25)?

Behold, Paul is strong in the face of the death that is to come, while the Lord is sorrowful? “I desire,” he says, “to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). He rejoices because he is departing in order to be with Christ, while Christ himself is sorrowful, although Paul rejoices that he will be with him?

But what was that voice except the sound of our weakness? Many who are still weak are saddened by the death that is to come. But let them have a straight heart: let them avoid death as much as they can; but if they cannot, let them say what the Lord himself said—not for his own sake, but for ours.

What did he say? “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” Behold, you have the human will expressed. Now see the straight heart: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matt. 26:38–39).

If, then, the straight heart follows God, the crooked heart resists God. Let something adverse happen to it, [Col. 1288] and it cries out: “God, what have I done to you? What have I committed? What have I sinned?” It wants to appear just and God unjust.

What could be more crooked? It is not enough that it is twisted; it also thinks the rule is twisted. Correct yourself, and you will find the straightness from which you have deviated. He is just; you are unjust. Therefore you are perverse, because you call the human being just and God unjust.

Which human being do you call just? Yourself. For when you say, “What have I done to you?” you think yourself just. But God replies to you: “You speak truly: you have done nothing to me. You have done everything to yourself. For if you had done something to me, you would have done something good. Whatever is done well is done to me, because it is done according to my command. Whatever evil is done is done to you, not to me, because the wicked person does nothing except to himself, since I do not command it.”

When you see such people, brothers, rebuke them, accuse them, correct them. And if you cannot rebuke or correct them, do not agree with them, so that you may be able to say: “A crooked heart did not cling to me.”

7. “When the wicked turned away from me, I did not acknowledge him.” What does “I did not acknowledge” mean? I did not approve, praise, or take pleasure in him.

For we sometimes find “to know” used in the Scriptures in the sense of taking pleasure in something. What is hidden from God, brothers? Does he know the just and not know the unjust? What can you think that he does not know? I do not ask what you do; what can you think that he does not know? I do not ask what you think; what are you going to think that he has not seen beforehand?

God therefore knows everything. Yet at the end—that is, in judgment after mercy—he says of certain people:

> “On that day many will come and say, ‘Lord, Lord, in your name we cast out demons, in your name performed many mighty works, and in your name ate and drank.’ And I will say to them, ‘Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you’” (Matt. 7:22–23).

Does he not know someone? What, then, does “I do not know you” mean? “I do not recognize you according to my rule.” I know the rule of my righteousness; you do not conform to it. You have deviated from it; you are distorted.

Therefore he also says here: “I did not acknowledge him.” “When the wicked turned away from me, I did not acknowledge him.”

What does “I did not acknowledge” mean? Is it perhaps because, when a wicked man meets a just man in a narrow lane, he says to himself what is written in the Wisdom of Solomon, “He is grievous for us even to see” (Wis. 2:15), and changes his path so as not to see someone he does not wish to see?

But how many wicked people there are whom we see and who see us, who not only do not turn away from us but run to us, and sometimes desire that their wicked deeds be accomplished through us [Note: [Col. 1288] Erasmus and Lovaniensis continue after “they desire” as follows: “They often join themselves to us? It often happens to us.” The Regius manuscript has only: “They often join themselves to us.” Other manuscripts, with Augustine of Ancona, have only: “It often happens to us.” Perhaps, because the words were less understood, someone thought the earlier wording should be substituted. Augustine appears here to be referring to wicked litigants who desired to obtain unjust judgments from bishops.]? It often happens to us.

How, then, do they turn away? The person who is unlike you turns away from you. What does “he turns away from you” mean? He does not follow you. What does “he does not follow you” mean? He does not imitate you.

Therefore, “when the wicked turned away from me”—that is, when the wicked was unlike me, did not wish to imitate my ways, and did not wish to live as I had set myself before him for imitation—“I did not acknowledge him.”

What does “I did not acknowledge” mean? Not that I did not know him, but that I did not approve of him.

8. [verse 5] “The one who secretly slandered his neighbor, him I pursued.” Behold a good persecutor—not of the human being, but of sin.

“With one proud in eye and insatiable in heart, I did not eat.” What does “I did not eat with him” mean? I did not dine with him.

Let Your Charity pay attention, because you are going to hear something remarkable. If he did not eat with him, he did not dine; for “to eat” means to dine. Why, then, do we first find the Lord himself eating with the proud [Note: [Col. 1289] Augustine of Ancona, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis have: “with the proud and not with those publicans and sinners.” On the authority of the manuscripts we remove the conjunction “and” and place the question mark before the following sentence, “Not with the publicans…,” so that the sense is: “I do not mean with the publicans…”]?

Not with those publicans and sinners? For they were humble. They recognized their sickness and were seeking a physician. We find him eating with those proud Pharisees.

For a certain proud man had invited him. He was the one who was displeased because a sinful woman, who was notorious in the city, approached the Lord’s feet. And he said in his heart—for such was the purity of the Pharisees that no unrighteous person touched them; if any unclean person touched them even slightly, they recoiled, lest the unclean touch make them unclean—when that sinful woman, who was notorious in the city, approached the Lord’s feet weeping, and he saw her, he said in his heart:

> “If this man were a prophet, he would know what sort of woman this is who has approached his feet.”

How did he know that Christ did not know, unless he inferred that Christ did not know from the fact that Christ did not drive her away? For if he were truly a prophet, he would have driven her away.

But the Lord not only knew that sinful woman; as a physician he also saw the incurable wounds of that proud man [Note: [Col. 1289] All our manuscripts have “of his pride”; and shortly afterward most have, instead of “to show him,” “and to show him.”].

For when he heard what the man was thinking, in order to expose that proud man, he said: “Simon, I have something to say to you: Two debtors owed money to a certain lender; one owed him fifty denarii, the other five hundred. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both. Which loved him more?” He answered against himself, truth forcing a confession from him: “I suppose, Lord, the one to whom he forgave more.” And turning to the woman, he said to Simon: “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has washed my feet with her tears” (Luke 7:36–44), and the rest, which you know.

It is unnecessary to linger longer over the other details for which we have adduced this testimony. This Pharisee was proud, and the Lord ate with him. What, then, does he mean by saying: “With one proud in eye and insatiable in heart, I did not eat”? What does “I did not eat with him” mean? “I did not dine with him.”

How does he set before us things that he himself did not do? He urges us to imitate him. We see him dining with the proud; how does he prohibit us from dining with them?

We, brothers, sometimes refrain even from our brothers for the sake of correction, and do not dine with them, so that they may be corrected. If we see them living badly, we dine rather with outsiders, with pagans, than with those who cling to us [Note: [Col. 1290] Thus the manuscripts. Erasmus and Lovaniensis have: “who were with us and cling to us.”], so that they may be ashamed and corrected, as the Apostle says:

> “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of him, and do not associate with him; yet do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother” (2 Thess. 3:14–15).

We often do this as a remedy; and yet we frequently eat with many outsiders and with the impious.

9. What does he mean by saying: “With one proud in eye and insatiable in heart, I did not eat”? The devout heart has its banquets; the proud heart has its banquets. He said “insatiable in heart” because of the very foods of proud hearts.

What nourishes the proud heart? If it is proud, it is envious; it cannot be otherwise. Pride is the mother of envy: it can produce nothing but envy and must always remain with it. Therefore every proud person is envious; if he is envious, he feeds on the misfortunes of others.

Hence the Apostle says: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5:15). You see them eating one another; do not eat with them. Flee such a banquet. For they do not satisfy themselves by rejoicing in the misfortunes of others, because they are insatiable in heart.

Beware lest you be caught in their banquets by the devil’s snare.

The Jews fed on such foods when they crucified the Lord. They fed as though on the Lord’s punishment—for we too feed on the Lord’s cross, because we eat his body. When they saw him hanging on the cross, they insulted him, because they were insatiable in heart. They said:

> “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross; he saved others, but he cannot save himself” (Matt. 27:40, 42).

They fed on the food of their cruelty, while he fed on the food of his mercy. “Father,” he said, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

They therefore had one kind of banquet, and he another. But hear what is said concerning the table of the proud:

> “Let their table before them become a snare, a retribution, and a stumbling block” (Ps. 68:23).

They were fed, and they were caught. For just as birds are fed toward a trap, or fish toward a hook, but are caught, so were they.

The wicked therefore have their banquets, and the devout have theirs. Hear of the banquet of the devout: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

If, then, the devout person is nourished by the food of righteousness and the impious person by the food of pride, it is no wonder if the one who is insatiable in heart [Note: [Col. 1290] Augustine of Ancona, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis punctuated as follows: “It is no wonder if the insatiable in heart is nourished by the food of iniquity.” This is less suitable, for Augustine had proposed proving that “insatiable in heart” was said because of the foods of proud hearts.] is nourished by the food of iniquity.

Do not feed on the food of iniquity, and you will not eat with one who is proud in eye and insatiable in heart.

10. [verse 6] “And where were you nourished, and what delighted you, where he did not dine with you?” “My eyes,” he says, “are upon the faithful of the earth, so that they may sit with me.”

The Lord says: “My eyes are upon the faithful of the earth, so that they may sit with me”—that is, so that they may sit with me. How would they sit? “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

The faithful of the earth judge, those to whom it is said: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3).

“My eyes are upon the faithful of the earth, so that they may sit with me.”

“The one walking in the blameless way ministered to me.” He says “to me,” not “to himself.” For many preach the Gospel, but minister to themselves, because they seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21).

What does it mean to minister to Christ? To seek the things that belong to Christ. And indeed, when the wicked proclaim the Gospel, others are saved, while they are punished. For it is said: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:3).

Do not therefore be afraid when you hear the Gospel from an evil person. Woe to the one who ministers to himself—that is, who seeks his own interests there. You must receive what belongs to Christ.

“The one walking in the blameless way ministered to me.”

11. [verse 7] “He who acts proudly did not dwell in the midst of my house” [Note: [Col. 1291] Thus Augustine of Ancona, Erasmus, and the principal manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint. Lovaniensis has “he shall not dwell.”].

Refer this to that house—that is, to the heart. He did not dwell in my heart while acting proudly; no such person dwelt in my heart, for he recoiled from it. No one dwelt in my heart except the gentle and tranquil person; the proud person did not dwell there.

For the unjust person does not dwell in the heart of the just. Let the just person be separated from you by I know not how many thousands and dwelling places; if you have one heart, you dwell together.

“He who acts proudly did not dwell in the midst of my house. The one who speaks iniquity did not direct himself before my eyes.”

This is the blameless way, in which we understand when the Lord comes to us.

### 12. [verse 8]

“In the mornings I was killing all the sinners of the earth.” This is obscure; deign to pay attention, for this is now the end of the Psalm. “In the mornings I was killing all the sinners of the earth.” Why? “That I might destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity.”

There are therefore people working iniquity in the city of the Lord, and for the moment they are, as it were, spared. Why? Because it is the time of mercy. But the time of judgment will also come, since the Psalm began: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.” Above, he has already explained that only the good adhered to him. He did not adhere to the wicked, nor did he take pleasure in the banquets of their iniquity—those who ministered to themselves, not to the Lord, that is, who sought their own interests.

And it is as though someone were saying to him: “Why, then, have you tolerated such people in your city for so long?” He answers: “It is the time of mercy.” What does “the time of mercy” mean? Judgment has not yet been revealed: it is night. Day will appear; judgment will appear. Hear the Apostle: “Therefore do not judge anything before the time.” What does “before the time” mean? Before the day. Hear that he said “before the day”: “Until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will reveal the counsels of hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5).

For now, as long as you do not see my heart and I do not see yours, it is night. You asked something of a person; you did not receive it, and you think that you are being despised. Perhaps you are not being despised, for you do not see the heart. Yet you quickly blaspheme; in the night, forgiveness ought to be granted to you as you err. Someone loves you, and you think that he hates you; or he hates you, and you think that he loves you. Whatever the case may be, it is night.

Do not fear. Put your confidence in Christ; have your day in him. There is no evil to fear concerning what you think about him, because we are secure and certain that he cannot be deceived: he loves us. But we are not yet so certain about one another [Note: Thus Ambrose and several manuscripts; Erasmus and Louvain read: “not yet certain.”]. God knows our love for one another; but even if we love each other, who sees by what dispensation these things are done by us? Why does no one see the heart? Because it is night.

In this night temptations abound. The Psalm seems to have spoken of this very night: “You appointed darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forest will pass through: the young lions roaring to seize prey and to seek their food from God” (Psalm 103:20–21). At night the young lions seek food. Who are the young lions? The rulers and powers of this air, the demons and angels of the devil (Ephesians 2:2). How do they seek food for themselves? When they tempt. But because they do not approach unless God has given them power, it is said: “Seeking their food from God.”

Job was requested for temptation. What sort of food? Rich, fat [Note: A good Remigius manuscript reads “fat”; some read “rich.”], righteous Job, to whom God himself bore witness and said: “He was a blameless man, a true worshiper of God.” The devil requested him for temptation, seeking food from God; and he received him for testing, but not for crushing (Job 1:8, 12); for purification, not for overthrow—or perhaps not even for purification, but for proving.

Nevertheless, those who are tempted are sometimes handed over, because of some hidden merit of their own, into the hands of the tempter, since perhaps they have been handed over to their own desires. For the devil harms no one unless he has received power from God. But when? In the night. What does “in the night” mean? In this present time.

When the night has passed and the day has come, the wicked are sent with the devil into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life (Matthew 25:46). No tempter will be there, because the young lions are not there; because the night has passed.

Therefore the Lord said to his disciples: “This night Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; and I prayed for you, Peter, that your faith might not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). What does “to sift like wheat” mean? Just as a human being does not eat wheat unless it has first been crushed so that it may become bread, so the devil eats no one unless he has first overthrown him through tribulation. He crushes in order to eat. But when you are afflicted, if you remain a grain, do not be disturbed; nothing happens to you.

When oxen thresh, do they enter upon the wheat alone? They are sent together with the threshing instrument onto the threshing floor. But is the wheat to be afraid? Certainly not. Only the chaff is cut down; the wheat is stripped of what is superfluous [Note: Thus the better manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain read: “Only the chaff is cut down; it is stripped from the wheat; it is superfluous, and then will come,” etc.; Ambrose: “unless the chaff be stripped from the wheat, it is superfluous,” etc.]. Then the winnowing comes and finds the pure mass: the grain it finds, it puts into its granary; the heap of chaff it burns with unquenchable fire (Matthew 3:12).

### 13

Why did I say this? Because we possess the day in hope. Our day ought to be in Christ. For as long as we are amid temptations, it is night.

In this night God spares sinners, so that he does not remove them; he scourges them with temptations so that they may be corrected; he tolerates them in his city. Do we suppose that he will tolerate them forever? If it is always mercy, there is no judgment. But if, “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord,” then now he spares, and then he will judge.

But when will he judge? When the night has passed. Therefore he said: “In the mornings I was killing all the sinners of the earth.” What does “in the mornings” mean? When the day has already come, after the night has passed.

“In the mornings I was killing all the sinners of the earth.” Why does he spare them until morning? Because it was night. What does “it was night” mean? It was the time of sparing. He spared them while the hearts of human beings were hidden.

You see someone living badly, and you tolerate him. You do not know what he will become, because it is night: whether the one who lives badly today will live well tomorrow, or whether the one who lives well today will be evil tomorrow. It is night, and God tolerates everyone because he is patient. He tolerates them so that sinners may turn to him.

But those who do not correct themselves in this time of mercy will be killed. And why will they be killed? So that they may be scattered from the city of the Lord—from the fellowship of Jerusalem, from the fellowship of the saints, from the fellowship of the Church.

When will they be killed? “In the mornings.” What does “in the mornings” mean? When the night has passed. Why does he spare them now? Because it is the time of mercy. Why does he not always spare them? Because, “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.” [Column 1293]

Brothers, let no one flatter himself: all who work iniquity will be killed. Christ will kill them in the mornings and destroy them from his city. But now, while it is the time of mercy, let them hear him.

Everywhere he cries out—through the Law, through the Prophets, through the Psalms, through the Epistles, through the Gospels. See that he does not keep silent, because he spares and distributes mercy. But beware, because judgment is coming.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 101

### SERMON I

[Note: Delivered after the laws against the Donatists of the year 405; see Sermon 2, section 9.]

#### On the first part of the Psalm

### 1. [verse 1]

Behold, a poor man prays, and he does not pray in silence. It is therefore permitted to hear him and to see who he is. Perhaps he is the one of whom the Apostle says: “For your sake he became poor, although he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

If he is the one, how is he poor? For who does not see how he is rich? By what means are human beings rich? I suppose by gold, silver, household slaves, and land. But everything was made through him. Who, then, is richer than the one through whom riches were made—even those things that are not true riches?

Through him came those riches also: intellect, memory, character, life, the health of the body itself, the senses, and the harmonious arrangement of the limbs [Note: Ambrose and most manuscripts omit “memory”; some also omit “character.” The printed editions had “the strengthening of the limbs,” but a manuscript of the Fuliensians more correctly reads “the harmonious arrangement,” etc.]. Indeed, when these things are sound, even the poor are rich. Through him came also those greater riches: faith, piety, justice, love, chastity, and good character. No one possesses these either except through the one who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5).

Behold how rich he is. Who is richer: the one who has what he wants because another makes it, or the one who does what he wants while another possesses it? I think the richer is the one who made what you have, because you do not have what he possesses. Behold how rich he is.

How, in this one so rich, are we to recognize these words: “I ate ashes like bread, and I mixed my drink with weeping”? Have such immense riches come to this? That is exceedingly exalted; this is exceedingly lowly. What shall we do? How shall we bring these low things into harmony with those heights? They are very far apart.

I do not yet recognize this poor man; perhaps he is someone else. But let us continue our search. For how could he not seem to be that one, if you ask and do not stand in awe at these riches: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made”?

The one who said these things was rich when he said them. How much more rich was the one of whom he said, “In the beginning was the Word”—and not just any word, but the Word who was God; and not just anywhere, but with God; and not idle, since all things were made through him?

Did he eat ashes like bread and mix his drink with weeping? We must fear that our poverty may do violence to such riches.

Yet continue to inquire whether this poor man is indeed he, since “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1–3, 14). Consider also that saying: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Psalm 115:16).

Consider that chaste handmaid, both virgin and mother. There he accepted our poverty, where he took the form of a servant, emptying himself. He did this so that you would not be overwhelmed by his riches and would not dare approach him with your poverty. There, I say, he took the form of a servant; there he clothed himself in our poverty; there he made himself poor; there he enriched us.

Now, then, we are drawing near to understanding these things about him. Yet we must still not pronounce rashly. The virgin’s childbirth is the stone cut from the mountain without hands (Daniel 2:34), where no human being worked, where no desire was transferred, but only faith was kindled and the flesh of the Word conceived.

Then he came forth from the womb. The heavens spoke; angels announced him to the shepherds (Luke 2:7–14); a star drew the Magi to worship the king (Matthew 2:1–2); Simeon, filled with the Spirit, recognized the infant God in his mother’s hands.

Age increased—not in divinity, but in the flesh. The wisdom of the twelve-year-old boy amazes and astonishes unlearned elders [Note: Thus six manuscripts; others, with the editions, read: “the wisdom of God of the twelve-year-old boy.”] (Luke 2:25–47).

Or even if the elders were learned, what does their learning amount to in comparison with the Word of God? What does their learning amount to in comparison with the Wisdom of God? Even the learned, unless he comes to their aid, are surely destined to perish.

He continued to grow in bodily age. He came to the river to be baptized; the baptizer recognized God and confessed himself unworthy to undo the strap of his sandal (Mark 1:7–11). From that point onward, the blind are illumined, hearing is opened to the deaf, the mute speak, lepers are cleansed, paralytics are strengthened, the sick recover, and the dead rise (Matthew 11:5).

### 2

In comparison with that Word through whom all things were made, I now recognize the poverty of his riches. But how far is this still from ashes and weeping together with drink? I am still afraid to say, “It is he,” and yet I wish to say it.

There are things here that compel me to wish it, and again certain things that compel me to fear it. It is he, and it is not he. He is already in the form of a servant; he already bears mortal and fragile flesh; he has already come to die. Yet he is not yet understood in this destitution.

“I ate ashes like bread, and I mixed my drink with weeping.” Therefore let him add poverty to poverty and transfigure in himself the body of our humiliation (Philippians 3:21). Let him be our head, let us be his members, and let the two be one flesh.

For, in order that he might first become poor, “taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), he left the Father. But because he was born from a virgin, let him also leave his mother, cling to his wife, and let the two be one flesh (Ephesians 5:31–32).

Thus the two will be in one voice as well, and in that one voice we will no longer be astonished at our own voice: “I ate ashes like bread, and I mixed my drink with weeping.”

For he deigned to have us as members. There are also penitents among his members. They have not been excluded or separated from his Church. Nor would he join a spouse to himself at all except through that voice: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3:2).

Let us therefore hear what the head (Ephesians 4:15) and the body, the bridegroom (John 3:29) and the bride—Christ and the Church, the two made one—pray. The Word and flesh are not both one; the Father and the Word are both one; Christ and the Church are both one: one complete man [Note: The manuscripts read “a certain”; the editions, “indeed.”] in the form of his fullness: “Until we all attain to the unity of faith, to the knowledge of the Son of God, to a complete man, to the measure of the maturity of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13).

But until we attain this, our poverty is being enacted here; here there is still labor and groaning. Thanks be to his mercy.

Why should there be labor and groaning for the Word through whom all things were made? If he deigned to take our death upon himself, will he not give us his life? He raised us to great hope, and with great hope we groan.

Groaning contains sorrow; but there is also a groaning that contains joy. I think that barren Sarah groaned with joy when she gave birth [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read “gave birth”; more correctly Ambrose and the manuscripts read “groaned.”]. And we, from fear of you, conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation (Isaiah 26:18).

Let us therefore hear Christ poor in us, with us, and for us. The title itself indicates the poor man. Finally, suppose that I have guessed who this poor man is. Let us hear the prayer and recognize the person. Do not go astray when you hear something that cannot be fitted to his head. I have spoken beforehand so that, whenever you hear such a thing, you may understand that it sounds from the weakness of the body, and recognize the voice of the members in the head.

“The prayer of the needy,” says the title, “when he was troubled and poured out his prayer in the presence of the Lord.” This is that poor man who says elsewhere: “From the ends of the earth I cried out to you when my heart was troubled” (Psalm 60:3).

This is the same poor man, because he is the same Christ who, through the prophet, called himself both bridegroom and bride: “As a bridegroom he bound a mitre upon me, and as a bride he clothed me with adornment” (Isaiah 61:10).

He called himself the bridegroom; he called himself the bride. Why, unless he is called bridegroom on account of the head and bride on account of the body? The voice is therefore one, because the flesh is one.

Let us hear, and let us recognize ourselves in these voices as well. If we see that we are outside, let us work to be within.

### 3. [verses 2–3]

“Hear, O Lord, my prayer, and let my cry come to you.”

This is the same as “Hear, O Lord, my prayer,” namely, “Let my cry come to you.” The repetition expresses the petitioner’s earnest feeling.

“Do not turn your face away from me.” When would God turn his face away from the Son? When would the Father turn his face away from Christ? [Note: Supply: “turn his face away.”] But because of the poverty of the members: “Do not turn your face away from me.”

“On whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me.” I am troubled below, while you are above. If I exalt myself, you are far away; if I humble myself, you incline your ear to me.

But what does “On whatever day I am troubled” mean? Is he not troubled now? Or would he say this if he were not troubled [Note: An old, excellent Corbie manuscript reads: “Or would he not say this”]?  It would be enough to say, “Incline your ear to me, because I am troubled.”

“On whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me,” as though referring to the unity of the body: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26).

You are troubled today, and I am troubled. Another is troubled tomorrow, and I am troubled. After this generation, later generations that succeed one another will be troubled, and I am troubled. Until the end of the age, whoever is troubled in my body, I am troubled.

“On whatever day,” therefore, “I am troubled, incline your ear to me. On whatever day I call upon you, quickly hear me.”

This is the same thing. Even now I call upon you, but “on whatever day I call upon you, quickly hear me.” Peter prayed; Paul prayed; the other Apostles prayed. The faithful prayed in those times; the faithful prayed in succeeding times; the faithful prayed in the times of the martyrs; the faithful pray in our times; the faithful will pray in the times of those who come after us.

“On whatever day I call upon you, quickly hear me.” Quickly hear me, for I now ask for what you wish to give. I do not desire the kingdom of heaven as an earthly person desires earthly things, but as one already redeemed from the first captivity. “Quickly hear me.” You spoke with no other desire when you said: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Behold, I am here’” (Isaiah 58:9).

“On whatever day I call upon you, quickly hear me.” From where do you call upon him? From what tribulation? From what poverty? O poor man before the door of the rich God, with what desire do you beg? In what need do you seek him? In what poverty do you knock so that it may be opened to you?

Speak; let us hear this very poverty. Let us find ourselves in it and pray with you. Hear, and recognize it, if you can.

### 4. [verse 4]

“For my days have faded like smoke.”

O days—if they are days! For wherever day is heard, light is understood. “But my days have faded like smoke.” My days, my times: why “like smoke,” except because of the exaltation of pride?

Such days were rightly received by proud Adam, from whom Christ took flesh. Therefore Christ is in Adam, and Adam is in Christ. He surely delivered us from days of smoke, having deigned to possess the voice of the days of smoke.

“For my days have faded like smoke; and my bones have been roasted as in a frying-pan.”

My bones themselves, my strength itself, not without tribulation, not without burning. Where is the strength of Christ’s body greater than in the holy Apostles? And yet see the bones being roasted: “Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

They are strong, faithful, sound in understanding, and preachers of the word—living as they speak and speaking as they hear. They are indeed strong. But all who suffer scandals are their frying-pan.

For love is there, and especially in the bones. Bones are interior to all flesh and carry all the flesh. If someone suffers some scandal and his soul is placed in danger, the bone is burned to the degree that it loves.

Let love be absent, and no one is burned. Let charity be present, and if one member suffers with another suffering member, how are those burned who carry all the members?

“My bones have been roasted as in a frying-pan.”

### 5. [verse 5]

“My heart has been struck like grass, and it has withered.”

Look to Adam, from whom the human race comes. From whom, unless from him, did this misery spread? From whom, unless from him, did this inherited poverty come?

Let him therefore, now placed in the body of Christ with hope, who was once despairing in his own body, say: “My heart has been struck like grass, and it has withered.”

Rightly so, because “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6). But how did this happen to you? “Because I forgot to eat my bread.”

God had given the bread of the commandment. For what is the bread of the soul except the word of God? At the serpent’s prompting, the woman transgressing touched what was forbidden (Genesis 3:6); he forgot the commandment. Rightly, then, his heart was struck like grass and withered, because he forgot to eat his bread.

Forgetting to eat bread, he drank poison. His heart was struck and withered like grass.

He is the one struck in Isaiah, of whom it is said, and to whom it is said: “I will not be angry forever, for the spirit proceeds from me, and I made every breath. Because of sin I grieved him for a little while, and I struck him and turned my face away from him.”

Rightly, then: “Do not turn your face away from me”—that is, from the one who was struck, of whom you said, “I struck him,” and of whom you said, “I saw his ways and healed him” (Isaiah 57:16–18).

“My heart has been struck like grass, and it has withered, because I forgot to eat my bread.”

Now eat what you had forgotten [Note: The manuscripts read “what you had forgotten,” rather than “the bread which you had forgotten.”]. The bread itself has now come, in whose body you are permitted to remember the voice of your forgetfulness and to cry out from poverty so that you may receive riches.

Now eat, for you are in the body of the one who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41).

You had forgotten to eat your bread. But once he was crucified, “all the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord” (Psalm 21:28). After forgetfulness, let remembrance come. Let the bread from heaven be eaten so that one may live—not manna, as those ate who died (John 6:49), but the bread of which it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5:6).

### 6. [verse 6]

“Because of the voice of my groaning, my bones have clung to my flesh.”

Because of the voice that I understand, the voice that I know [Note: The editions add “probably,” which is absent from the principal manuscripts]:  “Because of the voice of my groaning,” not because of the voice of those for whom I suffer with compassion.

Many groan, and I also groan; and I groan because they groan wrongly. Someone loses money and groans; he loses faith and does not groan. I weigh money and faith, and I find a greater groaning in the one who groans wrongly—or does not groan at all.

He commits fraud and rejoices. With what profit? At what loss? He acquired money and lost justice. The one who knows how to groan groans over this; the one who draws near to the head, who rightly clings to the body of Christ, groans over it.

The carnal do not groan over it, and they make themselves objects of groaning because they do not groan over it. Yet we cannot despise them, whether they do not groan or groan wrongly. We want to correct them, amend them, and restore them [Note: Most manuscripts read “separate them.”]. When we cannot, we groan; and when we groan, we are not separated from them.

“For because of the voice of my groaning, my bones have clung to my flesh.” The strong have clung to the weak; the firm have clung to the infirm.

From where have they clung? From the voice of their own groaning, not from the voice of the groaning of those others. By what law have they clung, unless by the one that says: “We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak” (Romans 15:1)?

“My bones have clung to my flesh.”

### 7. [verses 7–8]

“I have become like a pelican dwelling in solitude; I have become like a night-raven among the ruins. I kept watch, and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof.” [Note: A Corbie manuscript reads “of a pelican”; and, where the text has “pelican,” it consistently reads “pelicans.”]

Behold three birds and three places. May the Lord grant that we may say what they mean, and that you may hear usefully what is spoken for your salvation.

What do the three birds and the three places mean? Which three birds? The pelican, the night-raven, and the sparrow. And which three places? Solitude, ruins, and the roof. The pelican is in solitude, the night-raven among the ruins, and the sparrow on the roof.

First, we must say what the pelican is. It is born in a region where this bird is unknown to us. It is born in desert places, especially along the River Nile in Egypt.

Whatever sort of bird this may be, let us attend to what the Psalm wished to say about it. “It dwells,” he says, “in solitude.” Why do you seek its form, its limbs, its voice, or its habits? As far as the Psalm gives you [Note: Ambrose and all the manuscripts read “gave”], it is a bird dwelling in solitude.

The night-raven is a bird that loves the night. Ruins are what we commonly call the remains of buildings, where walls stand without a roof and without inhabitants. There the night-raven dwells.

As for the sparrow and the roof, you know what they are.

I therefore find someone from the body of Christ, a preacher of the word, suffering with the weak, seeking Christ’s profits, mindful of the coming of his Lord, lest he hear: “You wicked and lazy servant, you ought to have put my money with the money-changers” (Matthew 25:26–27).

From this steward’s office let us examine the three birds. He comes among people where there are no Christians: he is the pelican in solitude. He comes to those who once existed and have fallen: he is the night-raven among the ruins. For he does not abandon the darkness of those who dwell in night, but wishes to gain them as well.

He comes to those who are indeed Christians, dwelling in a house—not as those who have not believed or have abandoned what they believed, but walking sluggishly in what they believe. The sparrow cries out to them, not in solitude, because they are Christians; nor among ruins, because they have not fallen; but they are nevertheless on the roof—more precisely, beneath the roof, because they are under the flesh.

That sparrow cries out above the flesh; he does not keep silent about God’s commandments, nor does he become carnal so as to be subjected to the roof. For “the one who is on the roof must not come down to take anything from his house” (Matthew 24:17); and, “What you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the roofs” (Matthew 10:27).

These are the three birds and the three places. One person may bear the role of the three birds, and three people may bear the role of the three birds. The three kinds of places are three kinds of people [Note: Some manuscripts omit: “of places are three kinds.”]. Nevertheless, solitude, ruins, and the roof signify only three kinds of people.

### 8

But why say so much about these? Let us look at the Lord himself, lest perhaps he is the one—and may he be better recognized as the pelican in solitude, the night-raven among the ruins, and the solitary sparrow on the roof.

Let this poor man, our head, speak to us: poor by his will, let him speak to the poor in their need. Let us not be silent about what is said or even read concerning this bird, the pelican—not rashly affirming anything, but nevertheless not keeping silent about what those who wrote these things wished both to be read and to be said.

Listen in this way: if it is true, let it fit; if it is false, let it not take hold of you.

It is said that these birds kill their young, as it were, with blows of their beaks, and then mourn over the young they themselves killed in the nest for three days. Finally, they say that the mother gravely wounds herself and pours her blood over her offspring, and that, drenched with it, they come back to life [Note: The manuscripts read, “so that, drenched with it, they come back to life,” with the singular referring to the blood].

Perhaps this is true; perhaps it is false. Nevertheless, if it is true, see how it corresponds to the one who gave us life through his blood. It corresponds to him that the mother’s flesh gives life to her offspring through her blood; it corresponds very well.

For he also calls himself a hen over her chicks: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matthew 23:37).

He possesses paternal authority and maternal affection. Paul likewise is both father and mother—not by himself, but through the Gospel. He is a father when he says: “Although you have many tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15). He is a mother when he says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).

If this bird is truly as described, it therefore bears a great likeness to the flesh of Christ, by whose blood we have been given life.
