But how does it fit Christ that the bird itself kills its young? Does this not also fit him: “I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39)? Or would Saul the persecutor have died unless he had been struck from heaven (Acts 9:4)? Or would the preacher have been raised up unless he had been given life by that blood?

Let those who wrote these things determine this. We must not establish our understanding upon uncertainty.

Let us rather recognize this bird in solitude; for this is what the Psalm wished to place there: “The pelican in solitude.”

I think that Christ born of a virgin is understood here. He alone was born in this way; therefore, solitude. He was born in solitude because he alone was born in this manner.

After his birth, the Passion was reached. By whom was he crucified? By those who stood there? By those who mourned [Note: One manuscript reads “by those who played.” Perhaps read: “by those who understood”]? No. He was crucified as if in the night of their ignorance and as if among the ruins of their fall.

Behold the night-raven among the ruins, loving the night [Note: Some manuscripts read: “and among the ruins he loves, and in the night.”]. For if he did not love it, why would he say: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)?

He was born in solitude because he alone was born in this way; he suffered in the darkness of the Jews as in night, and in their transgression as among ruins.

What happened afterward? “I kept watch.” Therefore, had you slept among the ruins and said, “I slept”? What does “I slept” mean? “I slept because I willed to”; I slept because I loved the night. But there follows: “And I rose” (Psalm 3:6). Therefore here: “I kept watch.”

But after he kept watch, what did he do? He ascended into heaven, becoming like a sparrow in flight—that is, in ascending—solitary on the roof, that is, in heaven.

Thus: the pelican in birth, the night-raven in death, the sparrow in resurrection. There, in solitude, as though alone; here, among the ruins, as though killed by those who could not remain standing in the building; but here, already awake and flying, solitary on the roof. There he intercedes for us (Romans 8:34).

For our head is the sparrow, and his body is the turtledove. Indeed, “the sparrow found a house for himself.” What house? He is in heaven, interceding for us. “And the turtledove a nest for herself”: the Church of God is a nest made from the wood of his cross, where she may place her young, her little ones (Psalm 83:4).

“I kept watch, and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof.”

### 9. [verse 9]

“All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me.”

With their mouths they praised; in their hearts they prepared ambushes. Hear their praise: “Teacher, we know that you teach the way of God in truth and do not show partiality. Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar?” (Matthew 22:16–17).

Whom you praise, you overthrow. Why, except because “those who praised me swore against me”?

And from where did this reproach arise, except because I came to make sinners my members, so that by doing penance they might be in my body? Hence the whole reproach; hence the persecution: “Why does your teacher eat with sinners and tax collectors?” “The healthy do not need a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 9:11–12).

Would that you knew yourselves to be sick, so that you might seek the physician! You would not kill him and perish through proud madness under the illusion of false health.

### 10. [verse 10]

“But why did my enemies reproach me all day long? Why did those who praised me swear against me?”

“Because I ate ashes like bread and mixed my drink with weeping.”

Because he wished to have these kinds of people among his members, to be healed and set free, reproach arose.

And today, what sort of reproach do the pagans direct against us? What do you suppose, brothers, that they say to us? “You corrupt discipline and pervert the morals of the human race.”

Why this attack? Say why; what have we done? “By giving people an opportunity for repentance,” they say, “and by promising pardon for every offense. Therefore people do evil, secure in the knowledge that, when they have turned back, everything will be forgiven them.”

Hence the reproach: “Because I ate ashes like bread and mixed my drink with weeping.”

O you who insult us, I invite you to this bread. You do not dare to say that you are not a sinner. Examine your conscience; ascend the tribunal of your mind; do not spare yourself; examine yourself; let the marrow of your heart speak to you. See whether you dare to profess your innocence.

If he looks at himself, he will certainly be disturbed; if he does not flatter himself, he will confess.

And what will you do, wretched man, if there is no harbor of pardon? If there was only permission to sin and no forgiveness of sins, where would you be? Where would you go?

Certainly, it was also for your sake that this poor man ate ashes like bread and mixed his drink with weeping.

“Such a banquet no longer pleases you?” “Yet,” he says, “people increase their sins through hope of pardon.”

Rather, they would increase their sins through despair of pardon. Do you not see with what reckless cruelty gladiators live? Why is this, except that, as though already destined for the sword and sacrifice, they wish to satisfy their lust before they shed their blood?

Would you not say the same to yourself: “I am already a sinner, already wicked, already condemned; there is no hope of pardon. Why should I not now do whatever I please, even if it is unlawful? Why should I not fulfill, as far as I can, all my desires, if after this nothing remains except torments”?

Would you not say this to yourself and become worse through that very despair?

Therefore the one who promises forgiveness corrects you more effectively, saying: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isaiah 46:8). “I do not desire the death of the wicked; rather, that he should turn back and live” (Ezekiel 33:11) [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “so much that he should turn back.”]

With this harbor certainly set before you, you lower the sails of iniquity, turn the prow around, and sail toward justice. Hoping for life, you do not neglect the medicine.

Nor should God displease you in this, as though by this promise of forgiveness he had made sinners secure. Indeed, so that people would not live worse through despair, he promised the harbor of forgiveness. Again, so that they would not live worse through hope of pardon, he made the day of death uncertain. In the greatest providence he established both: a place of reception for those who turn back, and uncertainty about the time, so that those who delay may be afraid.

Eat ashes as bread and mix your weeping with your drink. Through this banquet you will come to the table of God.

Do not despair; forgiveness has been promised to you.

“Thanks be to God,” he says, “because it has been promised. I hold to God’s promise.”

Then live well now.

“Tomorrow,” he says, “I will live well.”

God promised you forgiveness; no one promised you tomorrow. If you have lived badly, live well today.

“Fool! This very night your soul will be taken from you.” I do not say, “The things you have prepared—for whom will they be?” (Luke 12:20), but: “According to how you have lived, where will you be?”

Correct yourself, then, so that you may have in the body of Christ this voice—which, unless I am mistaken, you gladly recognize:

“Because I ate ashes like bread and mixed my drink with weeping.”

[Col. 1302] 11. [verse 11.] “Because of the face of your anger and your indignation, for you lifted me up and dashed me down.” [Note: The editions omit “your,” which the manuscripts have, in accordance with the Septuagint.] This is that anger of yours, Lord, against Adam: the anger with which we were all born, to which we were joined by being born; anger arising from the propagation of iniquity, anger from the mass of sin. In accordance with this the Apostle says, “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest”; and hence the Lord says, “The wrath of God remains upon him, because he has not believed in the only-begotten Son of God” (John 3:36). For he does not say, “The wrath of God will come upon him,” but “remains upon him,” because that condition in which he was born is not removed.

Why, then, and what does this expression mean: “For you lifted me up and dashed me down”? He does not say, “For you lifted me up and then dashed me down,” but, “For you lifted me up, you dashed me down.” You dashed me down because you lifted me up. How so? “Man, placed in honor, was made in the image of God”: lifted up to this honor, raised from the dust, raised from the earth, he received a rational soul and, by the vitality of reason itself, was set above all beasts, cattle, birds, and fish (Gen. 1:26). For which of these possesses the understanding of reason? None of them was made in the image of God. And just as none of them possesses this honor, so none of them possesses this misery. For what animal mourns over sin? What bird fears the hell of eternal fire? None has any share in blessed life, and therefore none has the goads of misery.

But man, because he was made capable of blessed life if he should live well, will therefore be in a miserable life because he lived badly. Thus: “Because you lifted me up, you dashed me down.” Punishment follows me because you gave me free will. If you had not given me free will, and by this reason had not made me better than the animals, just condemnation would not have followed me as a sinner. Therefore, through free will you lifted me up, and through the judgment of justice you dashed me down.

12. [verse 12.] “My days have declined like a shadow.” Your days could have been days that did not decline, if you had not declined from the true Day. You declined, and you received declining days. Is it surprising that your days became like you? They are declining days because you went astray; they are days of smoke because you became swollen with pride. Earlier he had said, “My days have failed like smoke”; and now he says, “My days have declined like a shadow.”

In this shadow the Day must be recognized; in this shadow the light must be seen, lest afterward, when repentance is late and fruitless, it be said: “What did our pride profit us? And what did the boasting of riches contribute to us? All things passed like a shadow” (Wis. 5:8–9). Say now, “All things will pass like a shadow,” and do not yourself pass like a shadow.

“My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass.” For earlier also he had said, “My heart was struck like grass and withered.” But the grass watered by the blood of the Savior will grow green again. “I have withered like grass”: I, the human being, after that transgression; this is what I am by your just judgment. But you—what are you?

13. [verse 13.] “But you, Lord, remain forever.” My days have declined like a shadow, but you remain forever: the Eternal saves what is temporal. It is not because I fell that you have grown old; rather, you are vigorous for my liberation, you who were vigorous for my humiliation.

“But you, Lord, remain forever, and your memorial from generation to generation.” Your memorial, because you do not forget; “from generation,” not from one generation only, but “from generation to generation.” For we have the promise of the present life and of the future life (1 Tim. 4:8).

14. [verse 14.] “You will arise and have mercy on Zion, because it is time to have mercy on her.” What time? “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law.” And where is Zion? “To redeem those who were under the Law” (Gal. 4:4–5).

At first, therefore, the Jews: from them came the Apostles; from them came those more than five hundred brothers (1 Cor. 15:6); from them afterward came that multitude whose soul and heart were one toward God (Acts 4:32). Thus: “You will arise and have mercy on Zion, because it is time to have mercy on her”—because the time has come. What time? “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2).

Who says this? The servant of God, the builder, who said, “You are God’s building”; who said, “As a wise architect I laid a foundation”; and, “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3:9–11).

14. [verse 15.] What, then, does he say here also? “Because your servants have taken pleasure in her stones.” The stones of whom? The stones of Zion. But there are also things there that are not stones. Whose are the non-stones? What follows, then? “And they will have mercy on her dust.”

Let us recognize the stones in Zion; let us recognize the dust in Zion. [Note: Here Lovaniensis has “we recognize,” against the other editions and the manuscripts.] For he does not say, “They will have mercy on her stones,” but what does he say? “Because your servants have taken pleasure in her stones, and they will have mercy on her dust.” They have taken pleasure in her stones; but they will have mercy on her dust.

I understand the stones of Zion as all the Prophets. There the voice of preaching was announced beforehand; from there the Gospel ministry was taken up; through that proclamation Christ was made known. Therefore your servants took pleasure in the stones of Zion.

But those transgressors who withdrew from the Lord and offended their Creator by their evil deeds returned to the earth from which they had been taken. They became dust; they became ungodly. Of them it is said, “Not so the ungodly, not so, but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4).

But wait, Lord; endure, Lord; be patient, Lord. Let the wind not rush in and carry this dust from the face of the earth. Let your servants come; let them come and recognize your words in the stones; let them have mercy on the dust of Zion; let the human being be formed in your image. Let the dust say, so that it may not perish, “Remember that we are dust” (Ps. 102:14). “And they will have mercy on her dust.”

This concerns Zion. Was there not also dust that crucified the Lord? What is worse, dust from the walls of ruins. It was truly dust; nevertheless, it was not said of that dust without purpose: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). From that very dust came a wall of so many thousands of believers who placed the price of their possessions at the feet of the Apostles.

Thus humanity was both formed and made beautiful from that dust. For who among the Gentiles did such a thing? How few among them do we admire for having done this, compared with those thousands? Suddenly there were first three thousand, then five thousand, all living in unity, all placing the prices of their possessions at the feet of the Apostles, so that it might be distributed to each according to each one’s need; they had one soul and one heart toward God (Acts 2:41; 4:4, 32, etc.). Who accomplished this even from that dust, except the one who also made Adam himself from dust?

This, then, concerns Zion, but not only within Zion.

16. [verse 16.] What follows, then? “And the nations will fear your name, Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory.” Now that you have had mercy on Zion; now that your servants have taken pleasure in her stones, recognizing the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets; now that they have had mercy on her dust, so that a living human being might be formed—or rather, reformed—from dust: from this point preaching grew among the nations.

“Let the nations fear your name, and all the kings of the earth your glory.” Let another wall come also from the nations; let the cornerstone be recognized (Eph. 2:20). There let the two, coming from different directions, adhere to one another, yet no longer holding contrary opinions.

17. [verse 17.] “For the Lord will build Zion.” This is what is now being done. Come, living stones, hasten into the structure, not into ruin. Zion is being built; beware of ruined walls. A tower is being built; an ark is being built; watch out for the flood. This is what is now being done: “For the Lord will build Zion.”

But once Zion has been built, what will happen? “And he will be seen in his glory.” In order to build Zion, in order that there might be a foundation in Zion, he was seen by Zion, but not in his glory: “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty” (Isa. 53:2).

But when he comes to judge with his angels, when all nations are gathered before him, when the sheep are separated to the right and the goats to the left (Matt. 25:31–33), will they not then see the one whom they pierced (Zech. 12:10)? And those who refused to be confounded by an earlier and salutary repentance will then be confounded too late.

“The Lord will build Zion, and he will be seen in his glory”—he who was first seen in it in his weakness.

18. [verse 18.] “He has regarded the prayer of the humble and has not despised their supplication.” In the building of Zion this is now taking place: those building Zion pray and groan. That one poor man is many poor people, because thousands throughout so many nations are one, because of the unity of the Church’s peace. He is one and he is many: one because of love, many because of breadth.

Therefore, prayer is now being offered; now we must hasten. Now, if anyone was one way and behaved another way, let him “eat ashes like bread and mingle his drink with weeping.” Now is the time, while Zion is being built; now the stones are entering into the structure. Once the building is complete and the house has been dedicated, why do you hasten then, seeking too late, asking in vain, knocking fruitlessly, and remaining outside with the five foolish virgins (Matt. 25:12)?

Therefore hasten now: “For he has regarded the prayer of the humble and has not despised their supplication.”

19. [verses 19–20.] “Let these things be written for another generation.” When these things were being written, they did not benefit those among whom they were written in the same way. For they were written to prophesy the New Testament among people who lived by the Old Testament.

Yet God had also given that Old Testament and had settled his people in that promised land. But because “your memorial is from generation to generation,” it does not belong to the wicked but to the righteous. In one generation it pertains to the Old Testament; in another generation it pertains to the New Testament.

And because what was prophesied announces the New Testament: “Let these things be written for another generation, and the people that will be created will praise the Lord.” Not the people who have been created, but “the people who will be created.”

What could be clearer, my brothers? Here that creation was foretold of which the Apostle says: “If, therefore, anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new; and all things are from God” (2 Cor. 5:17–18).

What does “all things are from God” mean? Both the old and the new, because “your memorial is from generation to generation”: “And the people that will be created will praise the Lord.”

“For he looked down from the height of his holy place.” He looked down from on high in order to come to the humble; from on high he became humble, in order to exalt the humble.

## SERMON II. On the Second Part of the Psalm

1. Yesterday we heard the groaning of a certain poor man in prayer, and we recognized him as the one who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake (2 Cor. 8:9), together with the members joined to him and speaking through their head. [Note: Erasmus, Venice, and Lovaniensis present this passage thus: “though he was rich, that we might be enriched by his poverty, and we saw the members joined to him and speaking through their head. We saw,” etc. M.] For there we saw ourselves also—if, that is, through his grace we are anything at all.

The words of groaning had already ended, and words of consolation had begun; but they could not be brought to an end yesterday in the course of our exposition. In what remains, let us hear today not the poor man groaning but rejoicing—rejoicing because he hopes, hoping because he does not presume upon himself.

He foretold the blessedness of human affairs in the Scriptures of God and added: “Let these things be written for another generation, and the people that will be created will praise the Lord. For he looked down from the height of his holy place.”

This is as far as yesterday’s sermon reached. See what follows.

2. [verses 20–22.] “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the earth, to hear the groaning of the fettered, to release the sons of those put to death.”

We find it said in another psalm, “Let the groaning of the fettered enter into your presence” (Ps. 78:11); and it was said in a passage where the voice of the martyrs was understood. [Note: Three manuscripts read, “is understood.”] From where are martyrs fettered? Were they not chained rather than fettered? We know that the holy martyrs of God were led before judges, taken around through the provinces, and sent into chains; [Note: Most manuscripts read, “taken around through the province into a chain,” etc.] we do not know them as having been put into fetters.

Yet the fetters of God’s discipline and fear are recognized—of that fear concerning which it is said, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Sir. 1:16). Through this fear the servants of God did not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul, because they feared him who has power to destroy both body and soul in the hell of fire (Matt. 10:28).

For unless the martyrs had been bound by the fetters of this fear, how would they have endured all those harsh and painful things from their persecutors, when it was within their power to do what they were compelled to do and escape what they were suffering? But God had bound them with these fetters: harsh and painful for a time, certainly, but tolerable because of his promises. To him it is said, “Because of the words of your lips I have guarded the difficult ways” (Ps. 16:4).

One must indeed groan in these fetters in order to obtain God’s mercy; hence the voice of the martyrs in another psalm: “Let the groaning of the fettered enter into your presence.” Yet such fetters must not be avoided in pursuit of a destructive freedom and the brief, fleeting sweetness of temporal life, which will be followed by everlasting bitterness.

Therefore Scripture, so that we may not refuse to be fettered by wisdom, addresses us as follows:

“Listen, my son, and receive my judgment, and do not reject my counsel. Put your foot into her fetters and your neck into her collar. Bend your shoulder and carry her, and do not hate her bonds. Approach her with all your soul, and keep her ways with all your strength. Investigate and seek, and she will be made known to you; and having become steadfast, do not abandon her. For in the last days you will find her rest, and she will turn into joy for you. And her fetters will be for you a protection of strength, and her collar a robe of glory. For she has a golden ornament, and her bonds are threads of hyacinth. You will put on her a robe of glory and place upon yourself a crown of exultation” (Sir. 6:24–32).

Let the fettered, then, cry out as long as they are in the bonds of God’s discipline, in which the martyrs were trained. The fetters will be released, and they will fly; and those very fetters will afterward be turned into adornment.

This happened in the case of the martyrs. For what did the persecutors accomplish by killing them, except that the fetters might be released and turned into crowns?

3. “The Lord therefore looked down from heaven to hear the groaning of the fettered, to release the sons of those put to death.” You have heard who those put to death were; you have heard who their sons were. What follows from this?

How are we released except when we say to him, “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115:16–17)? Each person is released from the bonds of evil desires or from the knots of his sins. The remission of sins is release.

For what would it have profited Lazarus that he had come out of the tomb, unless it had been said, “Release him, and let him go” (John 11:44)? He himself raised him from the tomb by his voice; by crying out he restored his soul; he himself overcame the earthly mass placed upon the buried man, and Lazarus came forth bound—not, therefore, by his own feet, but by the power of the one who brought him forth.

This takes place in the heart of the penitent. When you hear that a person repents of his sins, he has already come to life again. When you hear a person bring forth his conscience by confessing, he has already been led out of the tomb, but he has not yet been released.

When is he released? By whom is he released? “Whatever you loose on earth,” he says, “will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). It is rightly possible for the release of sins to be given through the Church; but the dead man himself can be raised only when the Lord cries out within. For God works these things inwardly.

We speak to your ears; how do we know what is happening in your hearts? But what happens inwardly is done not by us, but by him.

4. “He therefore looked down to release the sons of those put to death.” You have heard of whom those put to death were; you have heard who their sons were. For what purpose? “So that the name of the Lord might be proclaimed in Zion.”

At first the Church was oppressed, when the fettered were being put to death. After those pressures, the name of the Lord is proclaimed in Zion with great freedom, within the Church itself.

For this is Zion—not that one place, first proud and later taken captive, but Zion of which that Zion was a shadow. Zion is interpreted as “watchtower,” because, while we are placed in the flesh, we look toward what lies ahead, stretching ourselves not toward what is present but toward what is to come. Hence “watchtower.” For every watchman looks far ahead.

A watchtower is the place where guards are stationed. Such watchtowers are made on rocks, mountains, and trees, so that from a higher place one may see far away. Zion, then, is a watchtower; the Church is a watchtower.

What is the meaning of “watchtower”? To see far ahead—that is the watchtower. “I was troubled until I entered the sanctuary of God and understood the final things” (Ps. 72:16–17). What sort of watchtower is it to understand the final things? It is to cross the sea by seeing, not by sailing, and to dwell at the farthest end of the sea (Ps. 139:9) [Note: The editions read, “at the farthest ends”; the manuscripts, “at the farthest end”; and so below in Psalm 138.]—that is, to place one’s hope there, in what will be when the age has ended.

Therefore, if the Church is a watchtower, the name of the Lord is already proclaimed there. Not only is the name of the Lord proclaimed in this Zion, he says, but also his praise in Jerusalem.

5. [verse 23.] And how is it proclaimed? “When peoples gather together as one, and kingdoms, to serve the Lord.” From what did this come about, except through the blood of those put to death? From what did this come about, except through the groanings of the fettered?

Those who were in oppression and humility were therefore heard, so that in our times the Church might exist in the great glory that we see, and so that the kingdoms that once persecuted it might themselves now serve the Lord.

6. [verse 24.] “He answered him on the way of his strength.” To whom did he answer, if not the Lord? Let us look above to see who answered: “And his praise,” he says, “in Jerusalem, when peoples gather together as one, and kingdoms, to serve the Lord.”

“He answered him on the way of his strength.” What answered him, or who answered him, on the way of his strength? Let us first seek who answered, and then seek what his way of strength is.

The preceding words indicate that either his praise or Jerusalem answered him. For above he had said, “And his praise in Jerusalem, when peoples gather together as one, and kingdoms, to serve the Lord.”

We cannot say that “kingdoms” answered him, because he would have said, “They answered.” We cannot say that “peoples” answered him, because here too he would have said, “They answered.” Since he says, “He answered him,” we seek a singular noun above, and we find nothing except either his praise or Jerusalem.

Because this is ambiguous—whether it means his praise or Jerusalem—let us expound it in both senses.

How did his praise answer him? When those called by him give him thanks. He calls, and we answer—not with our voice, but with faith; not with our tongue, but with our life.

For if God calls you and commands you to live well, but you live badly, you do not answer his call, and his praise does not answer him through you. You live in such a way that he is not praised but rather blasphemed through you. But when we live in such a way that God is praised through us, his praise answers him.

Jerusalem also answered him, as one of his called and holy ones. For Jerusalem too was called, but the first Jerusalem was unwilling to listen, and it was said to her: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate. Jerusalem, Jerusalem”—he cries out, and there is no answer—“how often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23:38, 37)!

There is no answer. Rain falls from above, and thorns are produced instead of fruit.

But that other Jerusalem, of which it is said, “Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1; Gal. 4:27), answered him.

What does “she answered him” mean? She did not despise the one calling her. What does “she answered him” mean? He sent rain, and she produced fruit.

7. She answered him—but where? “On the way of his strength.” Was it in herself? For what would she have in herself, or what voice would she have in herself, from herself, except only the voice of sin, the voice of iniquity?

Examine her voice: what do you find except a great deal—“I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. 41:5)? [Note: Thus the better manuscripts; the editions read, “except tumult.”] But if she has been justified, she answered him not from her own merits but from his gifts. [Note: Perhaps, “from his gifts” (*muneribus*).]

Where? “On the way of his strength.” It is Christ; he himself is the way. “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Before the resurrection, however, he was not recognized by his people; and especially because he was crucified in weakness (2 Cor. 13:4), it remained hidden who he was, until he appeared strong by rising again.

The Church therefore did not answer him on the way of his weakness but on the way of his strength, because after the resurrection he called the Church from the whole world—not now weak upon the cross but strong in heaven.

For the praise of Christians’ faith is not that they believe Christ died, but that they believe Christ rose again. A pagan too believes that he died; indeed, he brings this against you as a crime, because you believed in one who died.

What, then, is your praise? To believe that Christ rose again and to hope that you will rise through Christ. This is the praise of faith. “For if you believe in your heart that Jesus is Lord and confess with your mouth that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” He does not say, “If you confess that God handed him over to be killed,” but, “If you confess that God raised him from the dead, you will then be saved.” “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:9–10).

Why, then, do we also believe that he died? Because we cannot believe that he rose again unless we first believe that he died. For who rises unless he has died? Who awakens unless he has first slept? But surely the one who sleeps “will add that he may rise again” (Ps. 41:9).

This is the faith of Christians. In this faith, then, by which the Church was gathered—the many children of the deserted woman, more numerous than those of her who had a husband—she answered him and gave him praise according to his commands: on the way of his strength, not on the way of his weakness.

8. You have already heard above how she answered him: “When peoples gather together as one, and kingdoms, to serve the Lord.” In this, then, she answered him—in unity. Whoever is not in unity does not answer him.

He is one; the Church is unity. Unity alone answers the One.

But there are some who say: This has already happened. The Church answered him among all nations, giving birth to more children than she who had a husband; she answered on the way of his strength, for she believed that Christ had risen, and all the nations believed in him. But that Church which once existed among all nations no longer exists; it has perished.

Those who are not in it say this. O shameless claim! It does not exist because you are not in it? See whether you are not in it for that very reason. For it will exist even if you do not.

The Holy Spirit foresaw this abominable and detestable claim, full of presumption and falsehood, supported by no truth, enlightened by no wisdom, seasoned with no salt—empty, reckless, headlong, and destructive. And, as though speaking against them when he proclaimed unity, he said: “When peoples gather together as one, and kingdoms, to serve the Lord.”

And when he had added, “He answered him”—certainly his praise, certainly Jerusalem our mother, to be recalled from her pilgrimage, fruitful with many children, more numerous than she who had a husband—because some would say in opposition, “She existed, but she no longer exists,” he continued: “Make known to me the shortness of my days.”

What is this? Certain people who have withdrawn from me murmur against me; those who are lost insist that I have perished. They certainly say this because I existed and no longer exist: “Make known to me the shortness of my days.” I am not asking you for those eternal days; they are without end, and I will be there. I am not asking about them. I am asking about temporal days; announce temporal days to me. “Make known to me the shortness of my days,” not the eternity of my days.

How long will I remain in this age? Announce it to me because of those who say, “She existed, but now she does not”; because of those who say, “The Scriptures have been fulfilled: all the nations believed, but the Church from all the nations apostatized and perished.”

What does this mean: “Make known to me the shortness of my days”? And he did announce it; that utterance was not idle. [Note: The editions read, “was not empty”; two manuscripts, “was not silent”; the rest, “was not idle.”]

Who announced it to me, if not the Way itself? How did he announce it? “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

9. But here they arise and say: “He says, ‘I am with you until the consummation of the age,’ because he foresaw us, because the party of Donatus will be on earth.”

Is it that Church which said, “Make known to me the shortness of my days”? Or is it rather the one that spoke above: “When peoples gather together as one, and kingdoms, to serve the Lord”?

Why are your hearts troubled? [Note: The editions read, “our hearts”; the manuscripts more correctly, “your hearts”: that is, the Donatists, against whom laws were enacted in 405.] Because emperors also issue laws against heretics. There it has been fulfilled: “And kingdoms, to serve the Lord.”

For you are not the sons of those put to death whose voice of the fettered was heard by the Lord. Far from it. Your deeds do not indicate this; your pride does not indicate this; your vanity does not indicate this. You have no taste, and you are outside; you are salt that has lost its savor, and therefore you are trampled by people (Matt. 5:13).

Hear what he says. Which Church? The one that gathered peoples as one. Which Church? The one that gathered kingdoms to serve the Lord.

Moved by your voices and your false opinions, she asks God to announce to her the shortness of her days, and she finds the Lord saying: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.”

Here you say: “He was speaking about us; we are the ones who will remain until the consummation of the age.” Let Christ himself be questioned, to whom it was said, “Make known to me the shortness of my days.” And he says: “This Gospel will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations; and then the end will come” (Matt. 24:14).

What is this that you were saying: “It certainly existed, and it has perished”? Hear the Lord announcing the shortness of her days. “This Gospel,” he says, “will be proclaimed.” Where? Throughout the whole world. To whom? As a testimony to all nations. What afterward? “And then the end will come.”

Do you not yet see that there are nations among whom the Gospel has not yet been proclaimed? Since what the Lord said must therefore be fulfilled—announcing to the Church the shortness of her days, so that this Gospel may be proclaimed among all nations and then the end may come—what do you mean by saying that the Church has already perished from all the nations, when the Gospel is being proclaimed for the very purpose that she may be present among all nations?

Therefore the Church will exist among all nations until the end of the age. This is the shortness of her days, because everything that ends is short, so that from this shortness one may pass at last into eternity.

Let heretics perish; let what they are perish, and let them be found to be what they are not. The shortness of her days will continue until the end of the age. It is called short because all this time—not merely from today until the end of the age, but from Adam until the end of the age—is a tiny drop when compared with eternity.

10. [verse 25.] Let heretics, then, not flatter themselves against me because I said, “The shortness of my days,” as though it would not remain until the end of the age. What did he add? “Do not call me back in the midst of my days.”

Do not deal with me, as heretics speak, in this way. Bring me to the end of the age, not to the midst of my days; and complete for me these short days, so that afterward you may give me eternal days.

Why, then, did you ask about the shortness of your days? Why? Do you wish to hear? “Your years are from generation to generation.”

That is why I asked about short days: although these days last with me until the end of the age, they are short in comparison with your days. “For your years are from generation to generation.”

Why does he not say, “Your years are unto ages of ages”? For eternity is more usually signified in the holy Scriptures in this way. Why, then, does he say, “Your years are from generation to generation”?

But whose years are these? Whose, except those that do not come and pass away? Whose, except those that do not come in order not to exist? Every day in this time comes in order not to be; every hour, every month, every year. None of these remains. Before it comes, it will be; [Note: Thus Amiens, Erasmus, most manuscripts, and Lovaniensis: “it will not be.” Some manuscripts read, “it was not.”] when it comes, it will not be.

Those, then, are your eternal years, your years that do not change; they will exist “from generation to generation.” There is a certain generation of generations; in it your years will be. What generation is this? There is one; and if we recognize it rightly, we will be in it, and God’s years will be in us.

How will they be in us? As God himself will be in us. Hence it is said, “That God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28). For God’s years are not one thing and God himself another; God’s years are God’s eternity. Eternity is God’s very substance, which has nothing changeable in it. There is nothing there that is past, as though it no longer existed; nothing future, as though it did not yet exist. There is nothing there except “is.” There is no “was” and “will be,” because what was no longer is, and what will be is not yet. Whatever is there is nothing but “is.”

Rightly, then, did God send his servant Moses in this way. Moses asked the name of the one who was sending him; he asked, and his desire was not disappointed. He asked not out of presumptuous curiosity but from the necessity of his ministry.

“What,” he said, “shall I say to the children of Israel if they say to me, ‘Who sent you to us?’”

And he, revealing the Creator to creation, God to man, the immortal to the mortal, the eternal to the temporal, said: “I am who I am.”

You would say, “I am.” Who? Gaius. Another: Lucius. Another: Marcus. Would you say anything other than your name? That is what was expected from God. That was what had been asked: “What are you called? By whom shall I say that I was sent when they ask?”

“I am.”

Who?

“He who is.”

Is this your name? Is this the whole of what you are called? Would “being” itself be your name, unless whatever else exists in comparison with you were found not truly to be?

This is your name. Express this same thing more clearly.

“Go,” he says, “and say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’ ‘I am who I am’; ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

Great is this “Is,” great indeed! What is a human being in comparison with that great “Is”—whatever he is? Who can grasp that being? Who can become a participant in it? Who can pant for it? Who can aspire to it? Who would presume that he could be there?

Do not despair, human frailty. “I am,” he says, “the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:13–15). You have heard what I am in myself; hear also what I am for you.

This eternity, then, called us, and the Word burst forth from eternity. Already eternity, already the Word—and not yet time.

Why not yet time? Because time too was made. How was time also made? “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

O Word before the ages, through whom the ages were made, born in time, yet being eternal life; calling temporal beings and making them eternal! This is the generation of generations.

“For one generation goes, and another generation comes” (Eccl. 1:4). And you see generations of human beings existing on earth like leaves on a tree—whether on an olive tree, a laurel, or any other tree that remains covered with foliage throughout the whole season.

Thus the human race is carried by the earth like leaves. The earth is full of human beings, but as some die, others succeed them by being born. The tree is always adorned with its green clothing; but look beneath and see how many dry leaves you are treading underfoot.

11. Thus there was a generation under Adam, and it passed away. From it were born some who would become participants in God’s eternity even at that time: from it came Abel, from it Seth, from it Enoch. That generation passed away; the Flood came, and one household remained. That generation produced some successors—Noah himself, his three sons [Note: [Col. 1312] Better manuscripts: “two.”], and his three daughters-in-law—for in that entire eight-member household only one sinner was found. An additional number was joined to the preceding generation. Then, from Noah’s three sons, as from three measures of flour, the world was filled. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were chosen; holy men, patriarchs, they pleased God (Gen. 4–28). That generation too produced those who followed and begot children [Note: [Col. 1312] Lovaniensis has *generationes* (“generations”); other editions and manuscripts have *generantes* (“those who beget”).]; they produced prophets, they produced heralds of God. Later our Lord Jesus Christ himself also came and put leaven into three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened (Matt. 13:33). In the times when his flesh was on earth there were Apostles, there were saints; after them there were other saints; and now, in the name of Christ, there are all who are saints, and after us there will be all who are saints, and so on to the end of the age, all who are saints. From so many generations you will gather together all the holy offspring of all generations and make from them one generation: in this “generation of generations” your years—that is, that eternity—will be present in the generation which is gathered from all generations and reduced to one; it will participate in your eternity. The other generations are generated as the ages are fulfilled, and from them that one is regenerated for eternity; transformed, it will be given life and become capable of bearing you, receiving strength from you. In the generation of generations are your years.

12. [Verses 26–28.] In the beginning you founded the earth, Lord. I know your eternity, by which you precede everything you have made. In the beginning you founded the earth, Lord; and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and they will all grow old like a garment, and like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same yourself [Note: [Col. 1312] The word *ipse* (“himself”) is absent from the principal manuscripts.]. Who are you? You are the same yourself. You who said, “I am who I am,” are the same yourself. And although even those things would not exist except from you, through you, and in you, yet they are not what you are: for you are the same yourself. And your years will not fail. Those years of yours will not fail, those years of yours which will exist in the generation of generations will not fail.

Knowing this, then, would I ask you about the shortness of my days, if I did not know that all the days of the age, from beginning to end, are short in comparison with your eternity? I know, therefore, from what standpoint I have asked. Let heretics not exalt themselves as though the days of the Church, spread throughout the whole world, were short; for even though they extend to the end, they are short. Why are they short? Because one day they will end.

Those years which will exist in the generation of generations are the years to be loved, desired, and longed for; for their sake we must remain in unity; for their sake we must avoid whatever evil belongs to the heretics; for their sake we must answer those who are lost, win those who had gone astray, and recall those who had perished. There ought our desire to be.

Nevertheless, to answer the verbose, the maliciously talkative, the slanderers, whisperers, and detractors, announce to me the shortness of my days; and do not cut me off in the middle of my days, taking me away from the earth before the whole world is filled with the Gospel, contrary to the answer of my Lord, who says: “This Gospel must be preached throughout the whole world, as a testimony to all nations; and then the end will come” (Matt. 24:14).

What shall we say to this, brothers? The words are plain and manifest: God founded the earth, we know that; the heavens are the works of his hands. Do not think that God makes one thing with his hand and another by his word. What he does by his word, he does by his hand; for he who said, “I am who I am,” is not divided according to bodily members. Perhaps his word is his hand. Certainly his hand is his power. For when it was said, “Let there be a firmament,” and the firmament came to be, he is understood to have made it by his word; but when he said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:6, 26), he seems to have made him as though by hand.

Listen, then: “The heavens are the works of your hands.” What he made by his word, he certainly also made by his hands, because he made it by his power and authority. Consider rather what he made, and do not ask how he made it. It is too much for you to comprehend how he made it, when he made you in such a way that you should first be an obedient servant and perhaps afterward an understanding friend. Therefore: “The heavens are the works of your hands.”

13. “They will perish, but you remain.” The Apostle Peter plainly said this: “The heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God; through these [Note: [Col. 1313] Erasmus, Venice, and Lovaniensis: *quod* (“through which”); manuscript: *quae* (“through which things”).] the world that then existed was destroyed, being flooded with water. But the heavens and the earth that now exist have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire” (2 Pet. 3:5–7).

Thus he has already said that the heavens perished through the Flood. We know that the heavens perished according to the extent and spaces of this air. For the water rose and occupied the whole expanse where the birds fly; and so the heavens near the earth certainly perished—the heavens, that is, according to which the birds are called “birds of heaven.” There are also the higher heavens of heavens in the firmament. But whether they too are destined to perish by fire, or whether only those heavens are meant which also perished in the Flood, is a somewhat more difficult matter of dispute among learned people and cannot easily, especially under pressure of time, be explained.

Let us therefore leave it aside, or postpone it. Let us nevertheless know that these things perish, while God remains. And if certain things that were made by God remain with God, they do not remain in themselves but in God, by not departing from God.

What then? Shall we say, brothers, that the angels are destined to perish in the fire by which the world will be set ablaze? God forbid. What then? Shall we say that God did not make the angels? God forbid. What shall we say, then? From where would they exist if they had not been made by him? “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32:9). This was said when his works were being recounted, among which the angels too were named.

The angels, then, will be with him even while the world burns with fire; and the conflagration of the world will not burn God’s saints. What the king’s furnace was for the three young men (Dan. 3), the burning world will be for the righteous marked with the Trinity.

14. Perhaps here we may also appropriately understand “the heavens” as the righteous themselves, God’s saints, in whom God, dwelling within them, thundered through his commands, flashed forth in miracles, and watered the earth with the rain of wisdom and truth; for “the heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:2).

But surely they too will perish? Or will they perish in a certain sense? In what sense? In the sense of a garment. What does “in the sense of a garment” mean? In the sense of the body. For the body is the garment of the soul; the Lord called it a garment when he said: “Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?” (Matt. 6:25).

How, then, does the garment perish? “Even though our outer person is being corrupted, the inner person is being renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16). Therefore they will perish, but according to the body; “you, however, remain.”

If, then, they will perish according to the body, where is the resurrection of the flesh? Where is the example of the members that went before in the Head? Where? Do you wish to hear? “It will be changed”; it will not be as it was. Hear the Apostle saying: “The dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” How shall we be changed? “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15:52, 44). It is sown mortal; it will rise immortal. It is sown corruptible; it will rise incorruptible.

We therefore await a change. Thus the heavens will perish and the heavens will be changed. But perhaps the bodies of the saints are not rightly called heavens? If they do not bear God, let them not be heavens. And how, he says, do you prove to me that they bear God? Have you forgotten: “Glorify God and bear him in your body” (ibid. 6:20)?

Such heavens, then, will perish, but not forever; they will perish in order to be changed. Does the Psalm not say this? Read what follows: “They will all grow old like a garment, and like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail.” You hear of a garment, you hear of a covering, and do you understand anything other than the body?

Let us therefore hope also for the transformation of our bodies, yet from him who existed before us and remains after us; from him from whom we are what we are, to whom we shall come when we have been changed; the one who changes, not the one who is changed; who makes, not the one who is made; who moves, yet remains.

And how can flesh and blood understand: “I am who I am”; “but you are the same, and your years will not fail”? But what are we, with these ragged years of ours, compared with those years? And what are those who exist in them? Yet we must not despair.

For already, with a certain greatness and excellence of wisdom, he had said, “I am who I am”; nevertheless, to console us he said: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” And we are Abraham’s offspring (Gal. 3:29); although we are rejected, although we are earth and ashes, we hope in him.

We are servants; but for our sake our Lord took the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7). For our sake, we mortals, the Immortal willed to die [Note: [Col. 1315] Here the word *mortales* (“mortals”), and at the next occurrence below the word *nos* (“we”), are absent from the manuscripts.]. For our sake he displayed this example of the resurrection.

Let us therefore hope that we shall come to those years, standing firm in them, in which the days do not pass through the circuit of the sun, but that which is remains as it is, because this alone truly is.

15. [Verse 29.] Tell us, then, whether we can ever be there. Listen and see whether you ought to despair; hear what follows: “The children of your servants will inhabit.” Where, unless in the years that do not fail? “The children of your servants will inhabit, and their offspring will be directed into the age” [Note: [Col. 1315] The editions have *in saeculum saeculi dirigetur* (“will be directed into the age of the age”). The word *saeculi* (“of the age”) is absent from the manuscripts.]; into the age of the age, into the eternal age, into the enduring age.

But he says, “the children of your servants.” We must fear that we are servants of God, while our children will be there, and not we. Or, if we are children of servants because we are children of the Apostles, what shall we say? What unhappy boldness of children yet to be born, boasting in a recent succession, would dare to say: “We shall be there; the Apostles will not be there”? Let this be far from the devotion of children, far from the faith of little ones, far from the understanding of the mature.

The Apostles will be there too: the rams go before, the lambs follow. Why then does he say, “the children of your servants,” and not, by way of abbreviation, “your servants”? They are your servants, their children are your servants, and the children of these—their grandchildren—what are they but your servants? You would include them all in an abbreviated expression if you said: “Your servants will inhabit.”

Let us see what he wished to remind us of. Something happened in earlier ages. For forty years the children of Israel were worn down in the wilderness; none of them entered the Promised Land, but their children did. In fact, two entered, as we remember, unless I am mistaken; the rest did not (Num. 14:29–30). Two entered from so many thousands.

Only so much labor was expended upon them; but God does not labor. Certainly his servants labored. How much did Moses endure, how much did he hear, on behalf of men who would not enter the Promised Land? Their children entered. What does this signify? New people entered; the old did not enter. Nevertheless, two entered from among them: one and unity, as head and body, Christ and the Church, together with all that newness, that is, of the children.

Therefore: “The children of your servants will inhabit.” The children of servants are the works of servants; no one will inhabit there except through his works. What, then, does “the children will inhabit” mean? Let no one boast that he will inhabit there if he says that he is a servant of God but has no works; for only children will inhabit.

What, then, does “the children of your servants will inhabit” mean? Servants will inhabit through their works; servants will inhabit through their children. Therefore, do not be barren if you wish to inhabit. Send ahead offspring whom you may follow—by sending them ahead, not by exalting them. Let your children lead you to the Promised Land, the land of the living, not of the dying. While you live here in this pilgrimage, let them go before you and receive you [Note: [Col. 1315] Some manuscripts read this way. Others have: “with you receiving the children for the sake of bodily refreshment. Joseph went before Jacob,” and so forth. The editions, however, generally read: “Let them receive you for the sake of bodily refreshment. Joseph, the son, went before Jacob,” and so forth.].

For the sake of bodily refreshment, Joseph went before Jacob into Egypt and said to his father and his brothers: “I went ahead to prepare food for you” (Gen. 45:7). Let your children go before you, then; let your works go before you. The kind of children you send ahead is the kind you will follow [Note: [Col. 1316] So the manuscripts. The editions, however, have *talis* (“such,” singular) instead of *tales* (“such,” plural).].

## Exposition of Psalm 102

### Sermon [Note: [Col. 1316] Delivered on the feast of the Martyrs.]

1. [Verse 1.] In every gift of our Lord God, in all his consolation, in all his correction, in the grace he has deigned to grant, in the pardon by which he has not repaid us what was owed, in all his works, let our soul bless the Lord.

For this is what we sang; from this begins the Psalm about which we shall speak, he himself granting that we are able to do so—he whom our soul blesses. Let each one of us awaken and exhort his soul and say to it: “Bless the Lord, my soul.” And let all of us, and the brothers in Christ who are everywhere, one human being whose head is in heaven, let this one human being exhort his soul and say to it: “Bless the Lord, my soul.”

It obeys, it submits, it does this; it is persuaded to do so not by our gifts but by the one whom our soul blesses. For this Psalm undertook to show us why our soul should bless the Lord, as though its own soul had answered him: “Why do you say to me, ‘Bless the Lord’?”

Let us hear, then; let our own soul hear; let it consider all the things by which it is stirred up, lest it be sluggish in blessing the Lord. Let it see whether what is said to it is just: “Bless, my soul, the Lord.” Let it see whether it ought to bless anything besides the Lord. “Bless,” he says, “my soul, the Lord.”

2. He repeats this and says more explicitly what he had said: “Bless, my soul, the Lord; and all my inward parts, his holy name.” I think he is not speaking about the inward parts of the body. I think he is not saying that our lungs and liver, and whatever intestines there are in the flesh, should burst forth into a voice blessing the Lord.

Indeed, the lung in our chest is like a kind of bellows, panting with reciprocal breath [Note: [Col. 1316] Some manuscripts: *anhelantis* (“of one panting”).]; this breath, formed from the air, is pressed out into voice and sound when we articulate words [Note: [Col. 1316] Most manuscripts have *dirigimus* (“we direct”).]. No sound of the voice can come from our mouth except what the compressed lung has emitted. But that is not what is meant here; all of this belongs to the ears of human beings.

God has ears, and he also has the sound of the heart. A person addresses his inward parts so that they may bless the Lord, and says to them: “All my inward parts, bless his holy name.” Do you ask what your inward parts are? Your soul itself. Thus, when he says, “Bless, my soul, the Lord,” he means the same as “all my inward parts, his holy name”—with “bless” understood.

Cry aloud [Note: [Col. 1316] Manuscripts: *clama* (“cry aloud”); Ambrosius and Erasmus: *clamat* (“he cries aloud”), and below, *silet* (“he is silent”); Lovaniensis: *clamas* (“you cry aloud”), *siles* (“you are silent”).] with your voice if there is a human being to hear; be silent with your voice when there is no one to hear. Your inward parts never lack one who hears them.

A moment ago, therefore, blessing was sounding from our mouths, and we were singing these very words: “Bless, my soul, the Lord; and all my inward parts, his holy name.” We sang for as long as the occasion allowed [Note: [Col. 1317] Ambrosius and the manuscripts read *tempori* (“for the occasion”); Erasmus and Lovaniensis, *temporis* (“of the time”).], and we became silent. Surely our inward parts ought not to be silent from blessing the Lord?

Let the sound of voices alternate according to the occasion; let the voice of the inward parts be perpetual. When you come together in church to sing a hymn, your voice sounds forth the praises of God. You have said as much as you could and departed; let your soul sound forth the praises of God.

You conduct business: let your soul praise God. You take food: hear what the Apostle says: “Whether you eat or drink, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Cor. 10:31). I dare to say: when you sleep, let your soul bless the Lord. Let not the thought of some disgrace awaken you; let not the planning [Note: [Col. 1317] Manuscripts: *dispositio* (“planning”); editions: *depositio*.] of a theft awaken you; let not some arranged adultery awaken you. Your innocence, even while you sleep, is the voice of your soul.

“Bless, my soul, the Lord; and all my inward parts, his holy name.”

3. [Verse 2.] “Bless, my soul, the Lord, and do not forget all his recompenses.” “Bless,” he says, “my soul, the Lord.” What is your soul? All your inward parts. “Bless, my soul, the Lord.” Repetition serves as exhortation.

But in order that you may always bless the Lord, “do not forget all his recompenses.” If you forget, you will be silent. Yet the Lord’s recompenses cannot be before your eyes unless your sins have been before your eyes. Let the pleasure of your past sin not be before your eyes; let the condemnation of sin be before your eyes—the condemnation from you, the forgiveness from God.

For this is what the Lord recompenses, so that you may say: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” (Ps. 115:12). Considering this, the martyrs, whose memory we celebrate today, and all the saints who have despised this life and, as you heard in the Letter of John, “laid down their lives for the brothers” (1 John 3:16)—which is the perfection of love, as the Lord says, “No one has greater love than this, that he should lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13)—considering this, the holy martyrs despised their lives here so that they might find them there, following the words of the Lord: “Whoever loves his life will lose it; and whoever loses it for my sake will find it unto eternal life” (ibid. 12:25).

For they wished to repay. Who wished to repay? And what? And to whom? Human beings repaid God with their service even unto death. But what did he not give? What did they give that they had not received?

He, then, truly recompenses, for he alone gives; but he does not recompense us according to our sins. Other recompenses were owed to us, and other recompenses were given. “Do not forget,” he says, “all his recompenses”—not “gifts,” but “recompenses.” For one thing was owed, and what was given was something that was not owed.

Hence he too says: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” (Ps. 115:12). He does not say, “for all that he has given me,” but “for all that he has repaid me.” You repaid evil for good; he repaid good for evil.

How did you, O human being, repay God evil for good? You who were first “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” (1 Tim. 1:13), you repaid him blasphemies.

For what good things? First, because you exist—but a stone exists too. Then, because you live—but an animal lives too. What will you repay the Lord for having made you above all cattle and all birds in his image and likeness (Gen. 1:26)? Do not ask what you will repay him: repay him his likeness; he asks for nothing more. He demands his own coin (Matt. 22:21).

But in place of thanksgiving, humility, obedience, and religious worship—that is, in place of all those good things which you owed your God, in place of the good things you received—you repaid blasphemies.

What, then, does he say? “Confess, and I forgive.” I too repay, but not what you repaid: you repaid evil for good; I repay good for evil.

4. Consider, then, O soul, all God’s recompenses by considering all your evil deeds. For as many as your evil deeds are, so many are his good recompenses.

And what will you perhaps offer him in gifts of hospitality? What gifts? What sacrifices? Since you will not forget his recompenses, he is pleased with this sacrifice: “Bless, O soul, the Lord.” “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me; sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High” (Ps. 49:14, 23).

God wishes to be praised, and this for your progress, not for his elevation. There is absolutely nothing to repay him [Note: [Col. 1318] The principal manuscripts read *retribuere* (“to repay”); some have *retribuere possis* (“you can repay”); the editions have *retribuos*.]; and what he demands, he demands not for himself but for you. It will benefit you; it is stored up for you. He does not love from you what would increase him, but what would bring you to him.

Therefore the martyrs were seeking; they were, in a sense, failing because they could not find it, and they said: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” They found nothing with which to repay except: “I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:12–13).

What will you repay the Lord? You were thinking, and you could not find anything: “I will receive the cup of salvation.” What? Did the Lord himself not give the cup of salvation?

Repay something of your own, if you can. No, I say: do not do it; do not repay from what is your own. God does not wish to be repaid from what is yours. If you repay from what is yours, you repay sin. For everything you have comes from him; the only thing you have that is your own is your sin.

He does not wish to be repaid from what is yours; he wishes to be repaid from what is his. It is like a farmer: if you bring him a crop from the land he sowed, you have repaid him from the farmer’s fruit; if you bring thorns, you have offered him something of your own.

Repay truth; praise the Lord in truth. If you wish to repay from what is yours, you will lie. “Whoever speaks falsehood speaks from what is his own” (John 8:44). If one who speaks falsehood speaks from what is his own, then one who speaks truth speaks from what belongs to God.

But what does it mean to receive the cup of salvation except to imitate the sufferings of the Lord? This is what the martyrs did. He said this to those who were proud and already seeking lofty seats and avoiding the valley of weeping, who wished to sit, one at his right hand and the other at his left.

What, then, did he say? “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20:22). The martyr, already prepared for the holy sacrifice, says: “I will receive the cup of salvation.” I will receive the cup of Christ; I will drink the passion of the Lord. Take care lest you fail. “And I will call upon the name of the Lord.”

Why, then, did they fail? Because they did not call upon the Lord; they presumed upon their own strength.

Repay in such a way that you remember that you received what you are repaying. Thus let your soul bless the Lord, so that it does not forget all his recompenses.

5. [Verses 3–5.] Hear all his recompenses:

“He who is gracious to all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases; who will redeem [Note: [Col. 1319] Most manuscripts consistently read *redimet* (“will redeem”).] your life from corruption, who crowns you with mercy and compassion; who satisfies your desire with good things: your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.”

These are the recompenses. What was owed to the sinner except punishment? What was owed to the blasphemer except the Gehenna of burning fire? He does not repay that. Do not be terrified; do not shudder; do not fear without love. Do not forget all his good recompenses, and change now, lest you experience his recompenses. What shall I say—bad ones? If they are just, they are not bad. They are bad for you [Note: [Col. 1319] So the better manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads: “Bad from you, but good from God. Nor are these things which you suffer, etc.” Ambrosius and Erasmus read the singular: “Bad from you, but good from God. Nor are these things, etc.”]; but to God even the evils you suffer are not evil. For if they are just, they are good; but to you, while you suffer them, they are evil.

You do not want those things that are just from God to be evil for you? Let your iniquity not be evil in the sight of God. For he did not cease to call; he did not neglect to instruct the one he had called; he did not cease to perfect the one he had instructed; he did not neglect to crown the one he had perfected.

What do you say? That you are a sinner? Turn back and receive these recompenses: “He is gracious to all your iniquities.”

After the forgiveness of sins, you bear an infirm body. There must be certain bodily desires that tickle you and suggest illicit pleasures; they come from your disease. For you still bear infirm flesh; death has not yet been swallowed up in victory; this corruptible body has not yet put on incorruption (1 Cor. 15:53–54). Even after the forgiveness of sins, the soul is still shaken by certain disturbances; it still moves amid the dangers of temptations; it takes pleasure in certain suggestions, not in others, and in those in which it takes pleasure it sometimes consents to certain things and is captured.

It is a disease; “he heals all your diseases.” All your diseases will be healed; do not fear. They are great, you say; but the physician is greater. No incurable disease confronts the almighty physician. Only allow yourself to be healed; do not push away his hands. He knows what he is doing.

Do not take pleasure only when he comforts you; also endure when he cuts. Endure the medicinal pain, thinking of the health that will come.

See, my brothers, how much people endure in these bodily diseases, although they are going to live only a few days and those few days are uncertain. For many, after enduring great pains and being cut by physicians, have died either in the hands of the physicians or, once already healed, when some illness suddenly overtook them.

If they expected death to be so near, would they undertake those immense pains to endure them? You do not endure for an uncertain outcome: the one who promised health cannot be deceived.

A physician is sometimes deceived and promises health concerning the human body. Why is he deceived? Because he did not make what he is treating. God made your body; God made your soul. He knows how to restore what he created; he knows how to reform what he himself formed.

Only remain beneath the hands of the physician; for he hates the one who repels his hands. This does not happen with the hands of a human physician. People want themselves to be bound and cut, giving certain pain for uncertain health and a great fee.

God, who made you, both heals you with certainty and does so freely. Therefore endure his hands, O soul that blesses him and does not forget his recompenses; for “he heals all your diseases.”

6. “Who redeems your life from corruption.” He heals all your diseases for this reason: he redeems your life from corruption.

“Behold, the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15). The soul, then, has life in a corruptible body. What kind of life? It bears burdens; it carries weights. How many things hinder the very thought of God—God as he ought to be thought of by a human being—interrupting it as though from the necessities of human corruption? How many things call it back? How many turn it away from lofty attention? How many interrupt it? What a crowd of imaginings! What a multitude of suggestions! All this, as though from the worms of this corruption, swarms in the human heart.

We have magnified the disease; let us also praise the physician. Will he not heal you, he who made you such that you would never have been sick if you had been willing to keep the law of health that you received? Did he not both establish and command you what to touch and what not to touch, in order to preserve your health (Gen. 2:16–17)?

You were unwilling to listen in order to preserve your health; listen in order to recover it. Through your illness you have learned how true was what he commanded. At last, then, let a human being hear through experience what he did not keep when warned. What hardness is this, which not even experience teaches?

Will he not heal you, who had made you such that you would never have been sick if you had been willing to keep his commands? Will he not heal you, who made the angels and will restore you so that you become equal to the angels? Will he not heal you, who made you in his image and who made heaven and earth?

He will heal you; what is necessary is that you wish to be healed. He heals every sick person, but he does not heal one who is unwilling.

What could be more blessed for you than to have your health in your will, as though in your own hand [Note: [Col. 1320] Erasmus and Lovaniensis add *vitam* (“life”): “as though you had your life in your own hand.” The word is absent from Ambrosius and the manuscripts.]?

If you wished to hold some lofty office in this world—command, a proconsulship, a prefecture—could you immediately possess it simply because you wished it? Would power immediately follow your will? Many wish to attain such things and cannot; but even if they attained them, what benefit is honor to the sick?

For who is not sick in this life? Who does not drag along a lasting disease? To be born here in a mortal body is to begin to be sick. Our needs are supported by daily medicines; the daily medicines are the replenishments of all our needs.

Would hunger not kill you unless you applied its medicine? Would thirst not destroy you unless, by drinking, you did not extinguish it completely but postponed it? For thirst will return after being moderated for a little while. We therefore temper the distress of our illness with these alleviations.

You were tired from standing, but sitting relieves you; sitting itself is medicine for weariness. In that very medicine you again become tired; you cannot sit for a long time. Whatever comes to the aid of weariness [Note: [Col. 1321] Manuscripts: *fatigato* (“the weary person”).] begins another weariness.

Why, then, do you desire these things while sick? Think first about your health.

Sometimes a person is sick in his own house, in his own bed, with a more obvious illness—although this illness too is obvious, though people do not wish to look at it. Yet with the illness for which human physicians are sought, each person is sick in his own house; he pants with fever in his own bed. He may wish to think about his household affairs, to give some order either in the house or on the estate, or to arrange something; immediately the care of his people, clamoring and murmuring around him, calls him back from such concerns, and he is told: “Leave these things; think first about your health.”

This, then, is said to you: Every human being, if you are not sick, think about other things; if your very illness proves that you are sick, think first about your health.

Your health is Christ. Think, then, about Christ. Receive his cup of salvation, “who heals all your diseases.” If you want this health, you will obtain it.

When you seek honors and riches, you will not immediately have them simply because you wish for them. This, however, is both more precious and follows your will [Note: [Col. 1321] The editions add here *ejus* (“of it” or “of him”), from which they continue: “and therefore it is added.” The word is absent from most manuscripts.].

“He who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from corruption.” There all your disease will be healed, when this corruptible body puts on incorruption. Your life has indeed been redeemed from corruption; now be secure. A contract in good faith has been entered into; no one deceives your Redeemer, no one circumvents him, no one oppresses him. He conducted the transaction here; he has already paid the price; he shed blood.

He shed blood, I say: the only Son of God shed blood for us. O soul, lift yourself up; you are worth so much. “He redeems your life from corruption.”

He showed by example what he promised as a reward: “He died for our sins and rose for our justification” (Rom. 4:25). Let the members hope for what was demonstrated in the Head. Will he not care for his members, whose Head he raised into heaven? Therefore: “He redeems your life from corruption.”

7. “Who crowns you with mercy and compassion.” Perhaps, when you heard “he crowns you,” you had already begun to become arrogant. “Then I am great; then I have struggled.” By whose strength? By yours, but strength supplied by him.

For it is clear that you struggle, and therefore you will be crowned because you will conquer. But see who first conquered; see who makes you victorious a second time as well. “I have conquered the world,” he says; “rejoice” (John 16:33).

And why do we rejoice if he conquered the world—as though we had conquered it? Let us indeed rejoice, because we have conquered. We who were conquered in ourselves conquered in him.

Therefore he crowns you because he crowns his gifts, not your merits. “I labored more than all of them,” says the Apostle; but see what he adds: “Not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

After all his labors he awaits the crown itself and says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness remains for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:7–8).

Why? Because I fought the fight. Why? Because I finished the course. Why? Because I kept the faith. From where did you fight? From where did you keep the faith? “Not I, however, but the grace of God with me.”

Therefore, even in being crowned, you are crowned by his mercy. Never be proud; always praise the Lord; do not forget all his recompenses.

It is a recompense when, though you were a sinner and ungodly, you were called so that you might be justified. It is a recompense when you were raised up [Note: [Col. 1322] The manuscripts have *rectus* (“upright”) instead of *erectus* (“raised up”).] and guided so that you would not fall. It is a recompense when strength was supplied to you so that you might persevere to the end.
