It is a recompense that even this flesh of yours, by which you were weighed down, should rise again, and that not a hair of your head should perish.

It is a recompense that after the resurrection you should be crowned. It is a recompense that you should praise God himself without failing for eternity.

Do not forget all his recompenses, if you wish your soul to bless the Lord, who crowns you with mercy and compassion.

## 8.

And what shall I do when crowned? Behold, I was being helped while I wrestled; when the contest is finished, I shall be crowned. No hostile suggestion or corruption will then remain with which I must wrestle. For in this life we are always wrestling with this corruption. But what is written? “The last enemy to be destroyed is death.” After the destruction of death, you will fear no enemy: “then death has been swallowed up in victory” (I Cor. 15:26, 54).

Then there will be victory; then, the crown. After the contest, therefore, I shall be crowned. After the crown, what shall I do? “He who satisfies your desire with good things.” For now you hear of something good and pant for it; you hear of something good and sigh. And even the fact that you perhaps sin arises because, in your eagerness to choose what is good, you are deceived; you are held guilty because you do not heed God’s good counsel concerning what should be rejected and what should be chosen—something you perhaps neglect to learn if you are deceived in choosing the good. Wherever you sin, you seek something as though it were good; you desire something as though it were refreshment. The things you seek are good, but they will be bad for you if you abandon him from whom good things are made.

Seek your own good, O soul. For one thing is good for one being and another for another, and all creatures possess a certain good of their own—the integrity and perfection of their nature. What is necessary for each imperfect thing in order that it may be perfected is different. Seek your own good. “No one is good except one, God” (Matt. 19:17). The highest good—that is your good. What, then, is lacking to one for whom the highest good is good?

There are also lower goods, which are good for different beings. What is good for cattle, brothers, except to fill the belly, to be free from want, to sleep, to enjoy themselves, to live, to be healthy, and to reproduce? This is good for them; and, up to a certain point, they possess a measure of their good, allotted and granted by God, the creator of all things. Is such a good what you seek? God gives this also; but do not seek only this. Co-heir with Christ, why do you rejoice because you are the companion of cattle? Raise your hope toward the good of all goods. He himself will be your good, from whom you were made good in your own kind and all things were made good in their own kind. For God made all things “very good.”

If, therefore, we call that good which is God “very good,” this has already also been said of creation: “God made all things very good” (Gen. 1:31). What, then, shall we say of that good concerning which it was said, “No one is good except one, God”? Shall we say that it is very good? Our recollection of all creatures returns to us, because it was said, “God made all things very good.” What, then, shall we say? We fail in speech, but not in feeling.

[Col. 1323] Let that recent exposition of the Psalm come to mind: we cannot explain it; let us jubilate. God is good. What kind of good—is there anyone who can say? Behold, we cannot speak, yet we are not permitted to remain silent. Therefore, if we cannot speak and, because of joy, are not permitted to remain silent, let us neither speak nor remain silent. What, then, shall we do, neither speaking nor remaining silent? Let us rejoice.

“Jubilate in God our savior; jubilate in God, all the earth” [Note: [Col. 1323] See *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 99.4–5.]. What does “jubilate” mean? Utter the ineffable voice of your joys, and belch forth your gladnesses before him. And what will that belching be after being filled, if even now, after these few refreshments, our soul is so deeply affected? What will it be when, after redemption from all corruption, what was said in this Psalm comes to pass: “He who satisfies your desire with good things”?

## 9.

And as though you were asking, “When does he satisfy it? For now I am not satisfied. Whatever I turn toward, what I have acquired becomes worthless to me, although what I desire has been kindled. When I do not possess anything, I love it; when I possess it, I despise it. What good will satisfy me?”—the praise of God.

Even when the body that is subject to corruption weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind occupied with many thoughts, my soul is not filled [Note: [Col. 1323] All our manuscripts read, “in my soul.”], it is not perfected; other pleasures arising from corruption and wants divert me from that good. When will my desire be satisfied with good things? You ask when? “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.”

Do you ask, then, when your soul will be satisfied with good things? When its youth has been renewed. And he added, “like the eagle’s.” Surely something is hidden here. Yet we do not remain silent about what is commonly said of the eagle, since it is not irrelevant to understand this in such a way. Let it merely be suggested to our hearts that the Holy Spirit did not say without cause, “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.” For he signified to us a kind of resurrection.

The eagle’s youth is indeed renewed, but not unto immortality. A likeness was given, insofar as something could be drawn from a mortal creature to signify, in some fashion, an immortal reality—not to demonstrate it. It is said that when the eagle has been weighed down by old age, it cannot take food because its beak has grown excessively. The upper part of its beak, which curves downward over the lower part, when it has grown too long through old age, does not allow it to open its mouth, so that there is no space between the lower part and the upper hook. Unless some space opens, it does not have a bite like a pair of pincers with which it can cut what it sends down into its throat. Thus, when the upper part grows and becomes excessively hooked, it cannot open its mouth or take anything.

Age causes this. It is weighed down by the weakness of old age, and lack of food makes it extremely feeble, as both conditions—age and want—come upon it [Note: [Col. 1323] Erasmus, the Venetian edition, and Louvain edition read: “as both conditions, age and want, come upon it.”]. Therefore, by a certain natural method, in order to restore what is, as it were, its youth [Note: [Col. 1323] Morel, *Elementa Critica*, p. 160, conjectures that the passage should be read: “Therefore, by a certain natural method—or rather, by care, etc.” M.], the eagle is said to strike and beat its upper beak against a rock—the beak whose excessive growth has closed the entrance to food. By grinding it against the rock, it knocks it off [Col. 1324] and is freed from the burden of its former beak, by which food was obstructed. It approaches food, and everything is restored. After old age it will be like a young eagle: the vigor of all its limbs, the brightness of its feathers, and the steering of its wings return; it flies high as before, and a kind of resurrection takes place in it.

This likeness has been set forth for this purpose: just as the moon is cited because, when diminished and in a certain way eclipsed, it is born again and becomes full—and signifies resurrection for us, although, once full, it does not remain so, but again wanes, so that it may always signify resurrection—so also with what has been said of the eagle. The eagle is not restored unto immortality, whereas we are restored unto eternal life. Nevertheless, the likeness was drawn from it for this reason: so that the rock might remove from us what impedes us.

Do not, therefore, presume upon your own strength. The firmness of the rock knocks old age from you. “The Rock was Christ” (I Cor. 10:4). In Christ our youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.

For we have grown old among our enemies, as that familiar verse of the Psalm says: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6:8). From what have we grown old? From mortal flesh, from this flesh of hay. Therefore, “My heart was struck like grass and withered, because I forgot to eat my bread” (Ps. 101:5). “I forgot,” he says, “to eat my bread.” Old age has grown; it has closed the mouth. Let it be worn away upon the rock.

## 10.

Thus also in the Psalm under discussion, when he had first said, “He who satisfies your desire with good things,” the soul seemed to reply: “I shall not be satisfied with mortal things; I shall not be satisfied with temporal things. Let him give something eternal; let him grant something eternal. Let him give me his Wisdom; let him give me his Word, God with God, and himself as God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

I stand as a beggar before his door. He whom I call upon does not sleep; let him give me three loaves. Recall the Gospel. Behold what it means to know the divine Scriptures; those who have read it have been moved. For recall that a certain needy man came to his friend’s house and asked for three loaves. And, it says, the other, sleeping, answered him and said: “I am already resting, and my children are sleeping inside with me.” But the one who persisted in asking extracted through his annoyance what he could not obtain by merit (Luke 11:5–8).

God wishes to give, but he gives only to one who asks, lest he give to one who cannot receive. He does not wish to be aroused by your annoyance [Note: [Col. 1324] So Ambrose, Erasmus, and several manuscripts. Louvain reads, “for.”]. For when you pray, you are not troubling him as though he were asleep: “He will neither slumber nor sleep who guards Israel” (Ps. 120:4).

Christ slept once, so that a spouse might be made for him from his side; he slept on the cross—it is evident. For he died, so that he might say, “I slept and took my rest.” But surely “the one who sleeps will not add that he should rise” (Ps. 40:9)? Therefore it follows there: “And I rose, because the Lord will receive me” (Ps. 3:6).

What, then, does the Apostle say? “Christ,” he says, “rising from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over him” (Rom. 6:9). He, therefore, does not sleep; see to it that your faith does not sleep.

Let the soul, then, already desiring to be satisfied with some lofty, ineffable good—a good over which one rather jubilates, and concerning which one jubilates, than explains anything—let it say, since it already wills and already senses something of it, and sees that it is hindered by the burden of the body and cannot be satisfied in this life: “What are you saying to me—that my desire will be satisfied with good things? I know the good that I should desire; I know what is sufficient for me. I see it in Philip: ‘Show us the Father,’ he says, ‘and it is enough for us.’”

He seemed to desire the Father alone. The Lord showed that three loaves were to be desired; he who is the one bread revealed the Father and said: “For so long I have been with you, and you do not know the Father? Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father.” He also promised the Spirit: “The Father will send him,” he says, “in my name” (John 14:8, 9, 26); and likewise he says, “Whom I shall send to you from the Father” (John 15:26)—his gift, equal to himself.

I know what I desire; but when will I be satisfied with it? Behold, now I think about the Trinity; however I think about the Trinity, I scarcely dare to apprehend anything of it, in a mirror and in an enigma, and only in part. When will I be satisfied? “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.”

You are not satisfied now because your soul is not capable of that solid and great food. Its beak is closed; it is not capable. Old age has closed your mouth; therefore the rock has been given to you. When old age has been worn away upon the rock and your youth has been renewed like the eagle’s, you will be able to eat your bread—the bread that says, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41). “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s”; then you will be satisfied with good things.

## 11. [verse 6]

“The Lord performs mercies and judgment for all who suffer wrong.”

He does this now, brothers, before we come to renewal like the eagle’s, before we are satisfied with good things. For what is there here, what is there in this pilgrimage, what is there in this life [Note: [Col. 1325] Several manuscripts read, “way.”]? Are we abandoned? No. “The Lord performs mercies.”

And see how he performs mercies: he does not leave us in the desert, he does not leave us in the wilderness, until we reach our homeland. He performs mercies—but for whom? “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.”

You heard this, brothers, when the Gospel was read. Let no one, then, think that God’s mercy will be shown to him if he himself is unmerciful. But hear what the measure of mercy is, lest it be directed toward a friend and not toward an enemy. It was said: “Love your enemies” (Matt. 5:7, 44).

You wish to be satisfied with God’s good things; let mercy be satisfied in you. Full mercy [Note: [Col. 1325] The editions read, “the mercy of God.” “Of God” is absent from the principal manuscripts.] is perfect mercy. It is the mercy that loves and cherishes even the one who hates it.

“But what shall I do?” you ask. “If I begin to love my enemy, I shall receive injuries and endure injuries, and I shall not avenge myself, although laws are available.” It is just that you avenge yourself; it is permitted, because it is just. But see whether there is not something in you that ought to be avenged, and avenge it. For you say, “Shall I not avenge myself?” as though God restrained the justice of vengeance and did not extinguish the pride of the avenger [Note: [Col. 1325] Most manuscripts omit the word “extinguish.”].

Surely that adulterous woman was not to be stoned? Or, if she were stoned, would something unjust have been done? If it would have been unjust, then it was unjustly commanded. But the Law commanded it; God commanded it. Yet, O avengers, see whether you are not sinners.

An adulterous woman was brought to be stoned according to the Law, but she was brought to the one who gave the Law. You rage, you who brought her; see against whom you rage and against whom you are raging. If a sinner rages against a sinful woman, stop raging; first confess. If a sinner rages against a sinful woman, leave her alone. He knows what he thinks about her, what he judges, how he spares, and how he heals.

Do you rage on the basis of the Law? The giver of the Law knows better what he is doing, the Law on the basis of which you rage. At that time, when she was brought before him, the Lord bent his head and was writing on the ground. He wrote on the ground when he bent down toward the ground. Before he bent down toward the ground, he had written not on the ground but on stone.

Now the ground was about to bring forth something fruitful from the Lord’s writings. On stone he had written the Law, signifying the hardness of the Jews; on the ground he wrote, signifying the fruit of Christians.

They came, therefore, bringing the adulterous woman, like raging waves against a rock; but they were shattered by his answer. For he said to them: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her.” And again, with his head bent, he was writing on the ground. And each one, now examining his own conscience, failed to appear (John 8:3–9).

It was not the weak adulterous woman who drove them away, but their adulterated conscience. They wanted to avenge; they desired to judge. They came to the rock and were swallowed up beside the rock, their judges (Ps. 140:6).

## 12.

“The Lord performs mercies”—but for whom? “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.”

Show mercy to everyone. What mercy will you show to a righteous person? Only in bodily necessities. If you fail to supply these to him, they will not fail to come from God. Whatever you do, therefore, benefits you more.

You give to a beggar who passes by and asks; but seek also a righteous person to whom you may give, through whom you may be received into eternal dwellings, because “whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive the reward of a righteous person” (Matt. 10:41).

The beggar seeks you; you seek the righteous person. Of one it was said, “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6:30); and of another it was said, “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may hand it over.” And if one is not found for a long time, seek for a long time; you will find him [Note: [Col. 1326] The principal manuscripts read: “Even if he is found after a long time, seek for a long time; you will find him.”].

But what will you provide? Is more not provided for you? “If we have sown spiritual things among you,” he says, “is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” Hence also that which we recently expounded by the Lord’s prompting: “He makes grass grow for cattle” (Ps. 103:14), that is, carnal things for those who thresh, because “you shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing” (I Cor. 9:11, 9).

For this reason we exhorted you to be diligent, careful, and sober in this matter, and to count your works as your treasures. But, brothers, do we say these things so that they may be done for us in this way? I think that, in the name of the Lord, this may be the voice of the weak, yet still an apostolic voice; but it benefits you, as the Apostle himself says: “Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit” (Phil. 4:17).

What alms, then, will you give to a righteous person? The widow did not feed him; the raven fed him, because the one who made the raven fed him (III Kings 17:6, 12)—I mean Elijah. God is not without means by which to give to his own. You, however, see what you are buying, when you buy, and at what price you buy. For you are buying the kingdom of heaven, and there is no time for buying except in this life. And consider how cheaply you buy it. It is worth as much to you as you are able to possess.

## 13.

Show mercy to the wicked, but not as wicked. For, insofar as he is wicked, do not receive the wicked person—that is, do not receive him with regard to, or out of love for, his wickedness. For it has also been forbidden to give to a sinner and to receive sinners.

And how, then, does it say, “Give to everyone who asks you”? And how does it say, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him” (Rom. 12:20)? These things seem contrary, but they are opened to those who knock in the name of Christ, and they will become clear to those who seek: “Do not give to a sinner” and “Do not receive a sinner” (Ecclus. 12:4–6), and yet, “Give to everyone who asks you.”

“But the one asking me is a sinner.” Give, but not as to a sinner. When do you give as to a sinner? When you approve in him what makes him a sinner, and wish to give it to him because of it.

Let your Charity attend for a little while, until the matter is unfolded through examples also; it is very useful for understanding. This is what he said [Note: [Col. 1327] The editions read, “I said.” Several manuscripts read, “he said”; refer it to the testimonies cited from Luke 6 and Romans 12.]: When someone is hungry, if you have something to give, give it; if you see that it ought to be given for assistance, give it. Do not let the bowels of mercy grow sluggish because a sinner has encountered you. For a sinful human being has encountered you.

When I say, “A sinful human being has encountered you,” I have uttered two names. These two names are not superfluous: one is “human being,” the other is “sinner.” That he is a human being is the work of God; that he is a sinner is the work of the human being. Give to the work of God; do not give to the work of the human being.

“And how,” you ask, “do you forbid me to give to the work of the human being?” What does it mean to give to the work of the human being? It means giving to the sinner on account of his sin, approving him because of his sin.

“And who would do this?” you ask. Who would do this? Would that no one did it! Would that only a few did it! Would that it were not done publicly!

Let those who give gifts to hunters tell me why they give them. Why does someone give to a hunter? He loves in him that in which he is most wicked; he feeds in him and clothes in him that very wickedness, making public his depravity for the spectacles of all.

Those who give to actors, who give to charioteers [Note: [Col. 1327] Ambrose and Erasmus read “soothsayers.” Louvain and the manuscripts read “charioteers.” Compare *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 39.8 and elsewhere, where he has already spoken of charioteers, hunters, and actors.], who give to prostitutes—why do they give? Do they not also give to human beings? Yet they do not attend there to the nature of God’s work, but to the wickedness of the human work.

Do you want to see what you honor in a hunter when you clothe him? Let someone say to you, “May you be such a one.” You love him, you rejoice in him, and you wish, in a certain sense, to strip yourself and clothe him. Do not take it as an insult if someone says to you, “May your sons be such” [Note: [Col. 1327] The editions read: “If someone says to you concerning prostitutes, ‘May your daughters be such.’ It is an insult,” etc. We have restored the passage from manuscripts of better quality.].

“It is an insult,” you say. Why is it an insult, except because that is wickedness? Why is it an insult, except because that is disgrace? Therefore, when you give, you do not give to courage but to disgrace [Note: [Col. 1327] So the manuscripts. The editions read, “when you do not give,” etc.].

Just as the one who gives to a hunter does not give to a human being but to a most wicked profession—for if he were merely a human being and not a hunter, you would not give to him; you honor the vice in him, not his nature—so, conversely, if you give something to a righteous person, to a prophet, or to a disciple of Christ who needs it, and you do not consider that he is a disciple of Christ, a minister of God, or a steward of God, but instead consider some temporal advantage, so that perhaps, when he is necessary to your case, he may be for sale to you because you have given him something, then you have no more given to a righteous person by giving in this way than the other gave to a human being when he gave to a hunter.

The matter, then, dearest ones, is set clearly before us, and I think that, although it was obscure, it is now manifest. For this reason the Lord bound you by saying, “Whoever receives a righteous person.” That would have been sufficient. But because a righteous person can be received with another intention, when it is thought that he may be useful for some temporal purpose—perhaps to satisfy greed, perhaps to provide assistance so that someone may be deceived or oppressed—and because you seek such a service from him and perhaps for that reason receive him, he denied you the reward of a righteous person except with an added qualification.

For he says, “Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person”—that is, receiving him for the reason that he is righteous. And, “Whoever receives a prophet”—not merely receiving a prophet, but “in the name of a prophet,” honoring in him the fact that he is a prophet. Finally: “Whoever gives one of these little ones only a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple”—that is, because he is a disciple of Christ, because he is a steward of the sacrament—“truly I say to you, he shall not lose his reward” (Matt. 10:41, 42).

As, therefore, you understand, “Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive the reward of a righteous person,” so understand, “Whoever receives a sinner in the name of a sinner shall lose his reward.”

## 14.

Therefore, brothers, exercise mercy. There is no other bond of love, no other vehicle by which we are brought from this life to that homeland. Extend your love even to your enemies; be confident.

For this reason Christ came, concerning whom it had long before been said: “From the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise, to destroy the enemy and the avenger” (Ps. 8:3). Some books have “defender,” but “avenger” is more accurate.

The Lord wished to destroy the avenger—that is, the one who wished to avenge himself, so that his sins might not be forgiven him. “What, then?” you ask. “Will discipline sleep? Will all correction be removed?” It will not be removed.

What, then, will you do with a dissolute son? Will you not discipline him, will you not beat him? And if you see your own servant living badly, will you not restrain him by some punishment or blows? Let this be done; let it be done. God permits it—or rather, he reproves you if it is not done. But do it with a spirit of love, not with a spirit of vengeance.

When you have suffered injuries from some people more powerful than yourself, however, where you are permitted neither to correct them by discipline nor perhaps even to admonish or command them, endure them; endure them confidently. Hear the Gospel that was read today: “Blessed shall you be when people persecute you and speak every evil against you, lying, because of my name” (Matt. 5:11).

There he also added the reason, lest you accept curses as deserved by you rather than for the sake of God’s justifications. For not everyone who is cursed is righteous; rather, the one who is righteous and is cursed unjustly—and if he is cursed unjustly, a reward is given to him.

Therefore be confident in being merciful; extend your love even to your enemies. Those who perhaps fall under your governance, avenge and restrain with love, with charity, keeping their eternal salvation in view, lest, while you spare the flesh, the soul perish.

Do this, and you will suffer many wicked people against whom you cannot exercise discipline [Note: [Col. 1328] Five manuscripts read: “and you will not suffer the wicked without retaliation, against whom,” etc.], because they do not belong to the jurisdiction of your governance. Endure their injuries; be confident.

For “the Lord performs mercies and judgment for all who suffer wrong.” He will show mercy in you if you have shown mercy. Thus you will be merciful, so that the injury you suffer will not go unpunished: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,” says the Lord (Deut. 32:35).

## 15. [verse 7]

“He made his ways known to Moses.”

What ways did he make known to Moses? Why did he choose Moses? Understand by Moses all the righteous, all the holy: he set down one, and let all be included. Nevertheless, the Law was given through Moses, and the very tradition of the Law contains something obscure.

For the Law was given for this purpose: so that the sick person might be convicted and implore the physician. This is God’s hidden way. A little earlier you had heard, “He who heals all your diseases.” The diseases lay hidden in the sick; the five books of Moses were given. The pool was surrounded by five porticoes. It brought forth the sick so that they might lie there and be exposed, not so that they might be healed.

The five porticoes exposed the sick; they did not heal them. The pool healed when one descended into it—and the pool was troubled (John 5:2–4). The troubling of the pool signified the Lord’s passion. For when he came and became unknown, with some saying, “He is the Christ,” and others, “He is not the Christ”; “He is righteous,” “He is a sinner”; “He is a teacher,” “He is a deceiver”—he troubled the water, that is, he troubled the people. And amid all that disturbance of the water, one person was healed, because in the Lord’s passion unity is healed.

Whoever is outside unity, even if he lies in the porticoes, cannot be healed. Even if he holds the Law, he does not attain salvation.

Therefore, since this mystery is present there, the Law was given to teach that sinners might be convicted and call upon the physician to receive grace. Thus the one who was convicted is represented by the Apostle Paul, who says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” For by the commandment a certain conflict within himself had been shown to him, which is why he says: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members.”

He recognized himself in misery, in groaning, in struggle and conflict—unable to agree with himself, discordant with himself, recoiling from himself. And what does he say, desiring peace, true and heavenly peace? “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:23–25).

“For where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.” But how did sin abound? “The Law entered in, so that sin might abound” (Rom. 5:20). Why did sin abound when the Law entered in? Because people were unwilling to confess that they were sinners; when the Law was added, they became transgressors as well. For no one is a transgressor except when he has transgressed the law. The Apostle himself says this: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15).

Sin therefore abounded so that grace might abound all the more. Thus, as I began to say, because this is the great mystery in the Law, it was given so that, as sin increased, the proud might be humbled; once humbled, they might confess; once confessing, they might be healed. These are the hidden ways that he made known to Moses, through whom he gave the Law by which sin might abound, so that grace might abound all the more.

God did not do this cruelly, but according to the strategy of medicine. Sometimes a person thinks himself healthy while he is sick; and because he is sick but does not feel it, he does not seek a physician. The disease increases, the distress grows, the physician is sought, and everything is healed.

“He made his ways known to Moses; his will to the children of Israel.” To all the children of Israel? To the true children of Israel—or rather, to all the children of Israel. For those who are deceitful, treacherous, and hypocritical are not children of Israel. And who are the children of Israel? “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47). “His will to the children of Israel.”

## 16. [verse 8]

“The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and abundant in mercy” [Note: [Col. 1330] The editions read, “of great mercy.” But the principal manuscripts read, “abundant in mercy.” Thus, we think, the Latin translator rendered the Greek word *polyeleos* (πολυέλεος).].

What is as patient as this? What is as abundant in mercy? People sin and live; sins increase, and life is prolonged. He is blasphemed daily, yet he makes his sun rise over the good and the wicked (Matt. 5:45). He calls from every side to correction; he calls from every side to repentance. He calls through the benefits of creation; he calls by granting time for living; he calls through the reader; he calls through the preacher; he calls through intimate reflection; he calls through the scourge of correction; he calls through the mercy of consolation. “Patient and abundant in mercy.”

But take care lest, by misusing the length of God’s mercy, you store up for yourself what the Apostle calls wrath “on the day of wrath.” For the Apostle says: “Do you despise the riches of his kindness and patience, not knowing that God’s patience leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2:5, 4).

Because he spares you, do you think that you please him? “You have done these things,” he says, “and I was silent; you suspected iniquity, thinking that I would be like you” (Ps. 49:21). Your sins do not please me, but by patience I seek right actions. If I punished sinners, I would not find confessors.

Therefore, by his patience and sparing, God leads you to repentance. But when you say every day, “This day is ending, and tomorrow I shall be the same; tomorrow will not yet be the last day”—and then the third day comes—suddenly his wrath arrives.

“Brother, do not delay turning to the Lord” (Ecclus. 5:8). For there are people who prepare for conversion but delay it, and in them the raven’s voice arises: “Tomorrow, tomorrow.” The raven sent from the ark did not return (Gen. 8:7). God does not seek delay in the raven’s voice, but confession in the dove’s groaning. The dove was sent out and returned.

How long will you say, “Tomorrow, tomorrow”? Pay attention to the final tomorrow, because you do not know which tomorrow will be the last. Let it be enough that, up to today, you have lived as a sinner.

You have heard—and often you are accustomed to hear; you have heard today also. As often as you hear, so often you are not corrected. “But according to the hardness of your heart and your unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each one according to his works” (Rom. 2:5, 6).

Do not imagine God to be merciful in such a way that he does not also appear just. “The Lord is compassionate and merciful.” I hear this and rejoice; so you say. Hear and rejoice: he added still further, “Patient and abundant in mercy”; and at the end, “And truthful.”

You rejoice at the earlier words; tremble at the last. He is merciful and patient in such a way that he is also truthful. When you have stored up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath, will you not experience as just the one whose kindness you despised?

## 17. [verse 9]

“He will not be angry forever, nor will he be indignant eternally.”

For the fact that we live amid scourges and the corruption [Note: [Col. 1331] Ambrose and several manuscripts read “correction.” More manuscripts, with Erasmus, read “chastisement.”] of mortality is also from his indignation. We have this punishment because of the first sin.

My brothers, we must not think only about escaping his future threats, but also about his present anger, because this anger too belongs to the one whose children, both he and we, the Apostle says we once were. For he says: “For we too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

Therefore, it is from his anger that this human being is a pilgrim here and that he labors. Is it not from his anger, my brothers, that it is said, “In sweat and toil you shall eat your bread, and the earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:19, 18)? This was said to our first parent.

Or is our life something else? If you can, turn toward some pleasure where you do not feel thorns. Choose what you wish: be greedy, be dissolute—to mention only these two [Note: [Col. 1331] So the manuscripts. The editions read: “Be greedy, be dissolute; not to mention only these two,” etc.]. Add a third: be ambitious. How many thorns there are in the desire for honors! How many thorns in the lust of sensuality! How many thorns in the ardor of greed! How many troubles shameful loves contain! How many anxieties there are here in this life!

I say nothing of hell. See whether you may already be a hell to yourself.

All this, then, my brothers, is from his anger. And when you turn, so that you may act justly, you will still be unable not to labor on the earth; your labor does not end until the journey has ended. We must labor on the way in order that we may rejoice in our homeland.

Therefore, by his promise he consoles your labor, your sweat, and your troubles, and says to you [Col. 1331]: “He will not be angry forever, nor will he be indignant eternally.”

## 18. [verses 10–11]

“He has not dealt with us according to our sins.”

Thanks be to God, because this is what he willed. We have not received what we deserved: “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. For as high as heaven is above the earth, the Lord has confirmed his mercy over those who fear him. The Lord has confirmed his mercy over those who fear him.” According to what? “As high as heaven is above the earth.”

What did he say? If heaven could ever withdraw from protecting the earth, then perhaps God could at some time cease protecting those who fear him. Consider heaven: everywhere and on every side it protects the earth, and there is no part of the earth that is not protected by heaven.

People sin under heaven; they do every evil under heaven, yet they are protected by heaven. From heaven comes light for the eyes, from heaven the air, from heaven breath, from heaven rain upon the earth for the sake of its fruits; from heaven comes every mercy. Remove heaven’s aid from the earth, and it will immediately fail.

Therefore, just as heaven’s protection remains over the earth, so the Lord’s protection remains over those who fear him. You fear God; his protection is above you.

But perhaps you are scourged and think that God has abandoned you. If heaven’s protection abandoned the earth [Col. 1332]: “For as high as heaven is above the earth, the Lord has confirmed his mercy over those who fear him.”

## 19. [verse 12]

And what did he do? Since he did not repay us according to our sins: “As far as the east is from the west, he has removed our sins far from us.”

“As high as heaven is above the earth, the Lord has confirmed his mercy over us.” I have said why: because of protection. From where? “As far as the east is from the west, he has made our sins far from us.”

Those who know the mysteries understand this; nevertheless, I shall say what everyone can hear. When sin is forgiven, your sins set; your grace rises. Your sins are as though at sunset; the grace by which you are freed is at sunrise. “Truth has risen from the earth” (Ps. 84:12).

What does “Truth has risen from the earth” mean? Your grace has been born; your sins have set; you are renewed in a certain way. You ought to attend to the rising; you ought to turn away from the setting. Turn away from your sins; turn toward God’s grace. As they set, you rise and make progress.

But the part of heaven that rises goes again toward setting. Likenesses cannot be drawn in every respect to perfection; the things themselves can be aligned with the realities to which they are applied: as he spoke of the eagle, as he spoke of the moon, so also here.

One part of heaven sets and another rises, but the part that rises now will set after twelve hours. The grace that rises for us is not like this: our sins set eternally, and grace remains eternally.

### 20. [verse 13]

But why, “As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our sins from us,” so that they might set and grace arise? Why do you think? “As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him.” Let him rage as fiercely as he wishes: he is a father. But he has scourged us, afflicted us, and crushed us: he is a father. My child, if you weep, weep under your father; do not do so in indignation, do not do so in the haughtiness of pride. What you suffer, and for which you lament, is medicine, not punishment; correction, not condemnation. Do not repel the scourge, if you do not wish to be rejected from the inheritance. Do not consider what punishment you endure in the scourge, but what place you have in the testament. “As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him.”

### 21. [verse 14]

“For he himself knows our formation”—that is, our weakness. He knows what he made, how it fell, how it must be restored, how it must be adopted, and how it must be enriched. Behold, we were made from clay: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47). He also sent his Son, who became the second man, though he was God before all things. He was second in coming, but first in returning; he died after many, but rose before all.

“He himself knows our formation.” What formation? Ourselves. Why do you say that he knows it? Because he has had compassion. “Remember that we are dust.” Turning to God himself, he says, “Remember,” as though God might forget. He knows and recognizes in such a way that he does not forget. But what does “Remember” mean? May your mercy toward us persevere. You have known our formation, in a certain sense; do not forget our formation, lest we forget your grace. “Remember that we are dust.”

### 22. [verse 15]

“Man is like grass; his days are like the days of grass.” Let him consider what man is; let man not grow proud: “his days are like grass.” Why does grass that is now blooming, but soon withers, grow proud? Why does grass that is green for a time [Note: [Col. 1333] So several manuscripts. Others, with the editions, read “vigorous.”]—and that too for a short time, until the sun grows hot—grow proud? It is good for us, then, that his mercy should be upon us, and that he should make gold out of grass.

“For man, his days are like grass; as the flower of the field, so he will bloom.” All the splendor of the human race—honors, powers, riches, arrogance, threats [Note: [Col. 1333] The editions add here “swelling,” which is absent from the manuscripts.]—is the flower of grass. That house is in bloom, and that great house is in bloom; that household is in bloom. And how many flourish [Note: [Col. 1333] The editions read, “for how many does it bloom.” Several manuscripts read, “how many flourish,” and so forth.], or for how many years do they live? Many years for you; a brief time for God. God does not count as you count.

In comparison with the long ages of those who live for a very long time, every flower of every household is like the flower of the field. At most, all the beauty of a year lasts for a year. Whatever is vigorous there, whatever shines there, whatever is beautiful there, does not endure [Note: [Col. 1333] “Endures forever” may perhaps be the better reading.]; indeed, it cannot be sustained through the whole year. How briefly the flowers pass away—and this is what is beautiful about plants. What is exceedingly beautiful falls quickly.

“All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:6–8). Since, then, the Father knew our formation—that we are grass and can bloom for a time—he sent us his Word; and he made his Word, which remains forever, a brother to grass, which does not remain forever. He made the Only-begotten, uniquely born from his substance, a brother to so many adopted brothers.

Do not be astonished that you will share in his eternity: he first chose to share in your grass. Will he deny you what is exalted, when he assumed from you what was humble? Therefore, as far as man is concerned, “man’s days are like grass; as the flower of the field, so he will bloom.”

### 23. [verse 16]

“For the spirit will pass through him, and he will be no more, and he will no longer know his place.” It is as though this were a kind of destruction, a kind of demise. Behold the man who puffs himself up; behold the man who swells with pride; behold the man who exalts himself: “The spirit will pass through him, and he will be no more, and he will no longer know his place.”

See those who are dying every day; this will be the whole matter, this will be the end. For he is not addressing grass, but the one for whose sake the Word also became grass. You are man; for your sake the Word became man. You are flesh, and for your sake the Word became flesh. “All flesh is grass, and the Word became flesh” (John 1:14).

How great, then, is the hope of grass, since the Word became flesh? That which remains forever did not disdain to take up grass, lest grass despair of itself.

### 24. [verse 17]

Therefore, when you consider yourself, think of your humility; think of your dust; do not exalt yourself. Whatever better condition you attain, you will owe to his grace; you will owe to his mercy. For listen to what follows: “But the mercy of the Lord is from age to age upon those who fear him.”

You who do not fear him will be grass, and in the grass, and in torment together with the grass; for the flesh will rise again for torment. Let those who fear him rejoice, because his mercy is upon them.

### 25. [verse 18]

“And his righteousness is upon the children’s children.” He speaks of recompense: “upon the children’s children.” How many servants of God have no children—how much less children’s children? But by “our children” he means our works; by “children’s children,” the reward of our works.

“His righteousness is upon the children’s children, upon those who keep his testament.” Let them beware lest they think that everything said applies to them; let them choose while it is permitted. “Upon those who keep his testament,” he says, “and remember his commandments, so as to do them.”

You were already preparing to exalt yourself, and perhaps to recite the Psalter to me, which I do not retain, or to pronounce the whole Law from memory. Certainly, in memory you are better than I am—better than any righteous person, if the righteous person does not retain the Law word for word. But see to it that you retain the commandments. How are you to retain them? Not by memory, but by life.

“Upon those who remember his commandments”—not so that they may recite them, but so that they may do them. Perhaps now the soul of each one is troubled. Who keeps all God’s commandments? Who retains all God’s Scriptures? Behold, I want not only to retain them in memory but also to carry them out in my works; but who can retain everything in memory? Do not be afraid; he does not burden you. “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40).

But I want to retain the whole Law. Retain it, if you can, when you can, as you can. Whichever page you ask, it will answer you this: Whatever you hold, hold; hold charity. “The end of the commandment is charity” (1 Tim. 1:5). Do not think about the multitude of branches; hold fast to the root, and the whole tree is in you. “And upon those who remember his commandments, so as to do them.”

### 26. [verse 19]

“The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven.” Who has prepared his throne in heaven, except Christ? He who descended and ascended, who died and rose again, who raised the assumed man into heaven—he himself prepared his throne in heaven.

A throne is the seat of a judge. Therefore observe, you who hear: “He has prepared his throne in heaven.” Let each person do what he wishes on earth; sin will not go unpunished, and righteousness will not be fruitless, because the Lord who was mocked before the throne of a human judge has prepared his throne in heaven.

“The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom will rule over all.” “The kingdom is the Lord’s, and he will rule over the nations” (Ps. 21:29). And his kingdom will rule over all.

### 27. [verse 20]

“Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, doing his word.” Therefore, you are not yet righteous or faithful through the word of God unless you do it. “Mighty in strength, doing his word, to hear the voice of his sayings” [Note: [Col. 1334] Our manuscripts omit “to hear the voice of his sayings.”].

### 28. [verse 21]

“Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers, doing his will.” All the angels, all the mighty in strength [Note: [Col. 1335] Several manuscripts read, “powers of strength”; others, “powers, strengths.”], doing his word; all his powers, all his ministers, doing his will—you, you bless the Lord.

For all who live wickedly, even if their tongue is silent, curse the Lord by their life. What does it profit that your tongue sings a hymn if your life breathes out sacrilege? By living wickedly you have sent many tongues into blasphemy. Your tongue is occupied with hymn, and the other tongues of those who look at you are occupied with blasphemies.

Therefore, if you wish to bless the Lord, do his word; do his will. Build upon the rock; do not build upon sand. To hear and not to do is to build upon sand; to hear and to do is to build upon the rock; neither to hear nor to do is to build nothing.

If you build upon sand, you build a ruin. If you build nothing, exposed to rain, rivers, and winds, you will be swept away before you have stood (Matt. 7:24–27). Therefore one must not cease, but build; nor build in such a way that a ruin is constructed, but build upon the rock, so that temptation does not overthrow it.

If this is how things are, bless the Lord. If it is not, do not flatter your tongue; question your life, and let it answer you. You discover what evil you are [Note: [Col. 1335] Several manuscripts read, “I discovered.”]; groan and confess. Your confession can bless the Lord, but let your transformation persevere in blessing.

### 29. [verse 22]

“Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion.” Therefore, in every place. Let him not be blessed where he does not rule: “in every place of his dominion.”

Perhaps someone may say, “I cannot bless the Lord in the east, because he has gone to the west”; or, “I cannot bless him in the west, because he is in the east.” He is not merely “from the east and from the west,” nor merely “from the desert mountains,” “because God is judge” (Ps. 74:7–8). He is everywhere in such a way that he is blessed everywhere; he is from every direction in such a way that he is praised everywhere; he is blessed everywhere in such a way that life is lived well everywhere.

“Bless the Lord, all his works.” For when you begin to bless the Lord by a good life, his works bless him, not your merits. He himself works the good through you and in you, as the Apostle says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you” (Phil. 2:12–13).

Therefore, lest you exalt yourself because you do his word and do his will, he wished to humble you by directing you toward his grace, from which you obtained this. “In every place of his dominion.” Bless the Lord, my soul.

This last verse is the same as the first: blessing at the beginning, blessing at the end. We have set out from blessing; let us return to blessing; let us reign in blessing.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 103

## SERMON I

[Note: [Col. 1335] Preached at Carthage, according to no. 13; Augustine was already an old man, according to sermon 2, no. 7.]

### 1.

The day before yesterday, as far as you are worthy to remember, you were abundantly refreshed. But since you dismissed us even after a long sermon with the greatest eagerness [Note: [Col. 1336] The editions read, “very eagerly.” The manuscripts’ “with the greatest eagerness” is better.], we did not think that Your Holiness should be deprived of today’s due, so that this may be from what was owed, while that was a gain.

The psalm that has been read is woven almost entirely from figures and mysteries, and requires not only our considerable attention but also yours—although everything that has been said can likewise be received reverently according to the literal sense.

For many, though not all, of God’s works are enumerated—works known to all who look upon them, who know how, from the things that have been made and are visible, to perceive intellectually the invisible things of him (Rom. 1:20). We see the vast structure of the world, made up of heaven and earth and all that is in them; and from the magnitude and beauty of this structure we already love, although we do not yet see, the immeasurable magnitude and beauty of its Maker.

For he has not ceased to place his works before our eyes, though he cannot yet be perceived by the purity of our heart, so that, seeing what we can see, we may love him whom we cannot see, and so that through the merit of that very love we may one day be able to see him.

Nevertheless, in all that has been said, a spiritual understanding must also be sought. In searching it out, your desires will help us in Christ’s name: with these, as though with invisible hands, you knock at an invisible door, so that it may be opened invisibly for you, and you may enter invisibly, and be healed invisibly.

### 2. [verse 1]

Therefore let us all say: “Bless the Lord, my soul.” Let us all address our soul, because the soul of all of us is one soul through one faith; and all of us who believe in Christ are, because of the unity of his body, one man.

Let our soul bless the Lord for his many benefits, for his so many and so great gifts of grace. We find these gifts in this psalm when we listen attentively, shake off the cloud of carnal thought, raise our mind as far as we can, direct our gaze as far as we can, and use the pure eye of our heart as far as we can—so far as the present life does not impede us, so far as the desires for present things do not occupy us, and so far as worldly desire does not blind us.

Raised up, then, we are about to hear great, joyful, beautiful, desirable gifts of his, full of gladness and joy. The one who had already conceived this psalm saw them in his mind and, exulting in that vision, poured them forth, saying: “Bless the Lord, my soul.”

### 3.

“Lord my God, you have been magnified exceedingly.” See the magnificent things he is about to say; and in these magnificent things, surely none other than the author of all magnificence is to be praised.

“You have put on confession and beauty.” O Lord my God, who have been magnified exceedingly: from what have you been magnified exceedingly? Are you not always great? Are you not always magnificent? Are you imperfect, so that you may grow? Do you fail, so that you may at some time become less?

But because you are what you are, and truly are, you certainly declared your name to your servant Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14). You are certainly great, and your greatness is eternal; it neither began nor ends. It does not begin with the beginning of time, nor run on until the end of time, nor undergo anything in between; for it is unchangeable greatness.

How, then, have you been magnified exceedingly? Another psalm reminds us. It says: “Your knowledge has been made wonderful from me” (Ps. 138:6). If it is rightly said, “Your knowledge has been made wonderful from me,” then it is rightly said, “You have been magnified exceedingly, Lord my God, from me.”

But this too must still be examined. Is my God magnified from me? Does he therefore become great from me? Our daily prayer for salvation teaches us something. “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. 6:9): every day we ask, every day we pray that this may happen.

If someone asks us, “What is it that you ask—that God’s name may be hallowed? Was it not holy at some time, so that it now needs to be hallowed?” And yet, unless we wanted it to happen, we would not ask that it happen.

For rejoicing is one thing and prayer another. We rejoice in what is; we pray that what is not yet may be. What, then, is “Hallowed be your name”? We understand it as what is said here: “Lord my God, you have been magnified exceedingly.” That is, “Hallowed be your name”: let your name be holy among human beings.

Your name is always holy, but for certain unclean people your name is not yet holy. The Apostle says: “To the pure all things are pure, but to the unclean and unbelieving nothing is pure.” If nothing is pure to the unclean and unbelieving, I ask the reason [Note: [Col. 1337] The editions add here, “but for certain unclean people it is not yet a cause,” which is absent from the better manuscripts.]. “Their mind and conscience,” he says, “are defiled” (Titus 1:15).

If nothing is pure for them, then neither is God—unless perhaps you think that God appears pure to those who blaspheme him every day. If he is pure, let him please; if he pleases, let him be praised. But if he is blasphemed, he displeases; and if he displeases, how can the one who displeases them be pure to them?

What, then, do we ask in saying, “Hallowed be your name”? We ask that God’s name may be holy to those who, through unbelief, do not yet possess it as holy—to whom he is not yet holy who is holy in himself, through himself, and in his saints.

We pray for the human race; we pray for the whole world; we pray for all nations, who sit every day and argue that God is not upright and that God does not judge rightly. We pray that they may at last correct themselves and bring an upright heart into conformity with his uprightness; and, cleaving to him and directed toward what is right [Note: [Col. 1337] So manuscripts of good quality. The editions read, “and cleaving to the same, from uprightness to uprightness.”], may they no longer find fault, but may the upright one please the upright—for “How good is the God of Israel, but to those who are upright in heart” (Ps. 72:1).

Therefore, when the one who sings this psalm saw how much God had bestowed upon the human race—to which God had previously appeared either nonexistent, or false, or not so great, but now appeared great when seen in his works—this one, who is ourselves, that is, the body of Christ, the members of Christ, said: “Lord my God, you have been magnified exceedingly.” That is: “I did not yet understand you; now I understand you as great.”

You were always great, even when hidden; but you became great to me when you appeared. You have therefore been magnified from me, just as “Your knowledge has been made wonderful from me,” for it has been made wonderful from me. I marvel at it because I have turned toward it; but whether I turn toward it or not, and whether after turning I turn away, it remains whole.

But I have now become great in it, and from being diminished I have become whole in it. I marvel at what I did not know—not because it has now become great when I learned it, but because I became great when I learned it.

Now hear where God appears to have been magnified exceedingly, though he is always great: he has been magnified exceedingly in his works for us.

### 4.

“You have put on confession and beauty.” He placed confession before beauty: beauty in loveliness. You seek beauty; you seek a good thing. But why do you seek beauty, O soul? So that your bridegroom may love you; for you displease him when you are ugly.

What is he like? “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.” You wish, though ugly, to kiss the beautiful one; but you do not consider that you are full of iniquities. “Grace has been poured out upon your lips.” For it was said of him: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, grace has been poured out upon your lips; therefore the young women have loved you” (Ps. 44:3).

There is, then, one who is lovely, one who is beautiful beyond the sons of men—although he is the Son of Man, he is nevertheless beyond the sons of men. You wish to please him, O human soul, O one soul in many. Let us hear the Church, because “they had one soul and one heart toward God” (Acts 4:32). The psalm addresses this soul.

Do you wish to please him? You cannot as long as you are deformed. What will you do to become beautiful? First let your deformity displease you, and then from the very one whom you wish to please you will merit beauty. For he himself will be your reformer, who was your former.

First, then, consider what you are, lest you dare to go, ugly, to kiss the beautiful one. “And looking at what,” you ask, “will I see myself?” He has placed his Scripture before you as a mirror. It is read to you: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

A mirror has been set before you in this reading. See whether you are what it said; if you are not yet, groan that you may be. The mirror will announce your face to you. Just as you will not sense a flatterer in a mirror, so do not flatter yourself. That brightness shows you what you are; see what you are, and if it displeases you, seek not to be so.

For if, while ugly, you still displease yourself, you already please the beautiful one. What, then? Since your ugliness displeases you, you begin with confession to him, as it is said elsewhere: “Begin to the Lord with confession” (Ps. 146:7).

First accuse your ugliness. The soul’s ugliness comes from sins and iniquities. By accusing your ugliness, begin to confess; from confession you begin to be adorned. And who adorns you, except the one who is beautiful in form beyond the sons of men?

### 5.

And in order to make her beautiful, I dare to say that he loved her even when she was ugly. What does “he loved her even when she was ugly” mean? “For Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:6). What life does he reserve for you, once justified, who gave his own death even to the ungodly?

Behold that beautiful one, “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,” because he is more righteous than the sons of men. Since he was coming to the ugly one in order to make her beautiful, he became ugly—I shall say this too, because I find it in the Scriptures.

Do not listen to me in this, lest I have rashly slipped into this expression. For just as I had said, “He loved her even when she was ugly,” not as though I had said it appropriately of certain people loving him, unless a witness came forward for me, I stated what the Apostle stated: Do you wish to know that he loved her even when she was ugly? “Christ died for the ungodly.”

So also now, when I say that, in order to come to the ugly one, he became ugly—became deformed—how shall I prove it, when the divine utterance has already told me, “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men”?

But in that same divine utterance I again find: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53:2). “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men”; “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty.” It did not say, “We did not see him, and therefore we did not know whether he had form or beauty.” Behold, we saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty.

Where, then, did the one who said, “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,” see him? And where did the one who said, “He had neither form nor beauty,” see him?

Listen to where the one who said “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” saw him: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped” (Phil. 2:6). Rightly beyond the sons of men, because equal to God.

Behold, I have received and recognized where he saw him who said, “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.” He answered us: “You ask where I saw him? In the form of God.” And from where did you see him in the form of God? How did you see him in the form of God? “Because his invisible things are perceived intellectually through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20).

Good, excellent. I have received and recognized whom you saw, what he was like when you saw him, where you saw him, and from where you saw him. Whom did you see? Our bridegroom. What was he like? “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.” Where did you see him? “When he was in the form of God.” From where did you see him? “Through the things that have been made, perceived intellectually.”

Let us see what another prophet says about him—not another spirit, for they do not disagree with one another. One showed us the one “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men”; let the other also show us the one of whom he said, “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty.”

The one Apostle Paul joins both prophets together; one passage of Paul bears witness to both prophets. There I have “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men”: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped.”

There he said what the other also saw: one who had neither form nor beauty, “because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:6–8).

Rightly they saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty. Rightly they shook their heads before the cross: “Is this the whole Son of God? If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:40). But he had neither form nor beauty.

Even so, O you who are displeased because he had neither form nor beauty! O you who shook your heads before the cross and did not fix your head upon the head that hung on the cross [Note: [Col. 1339] Several manuscripts read, “the cross.”]!

Rightly the head of those who insulted him wavers until he himself whom they insulted becomes their head. Behold, he takes up beauty again—and great beauty. Behold, what you say is less than what he did. You say, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross.” Behold, he did not come down from the cross, but rose from the tomb.

### 6.

Therefore, O soul, you cannot be beautiful unless you have confessed your ugliness to him who is always beautiful and who, for your sake, was for a time not beautiful. He was for a time not beautiful in the form of a servant, but he never departed from the beauty that is in the form of God.

Therefore, O Church, you possess beauty. It is said also to you in the Song of Songs: “O beautiful one among women” (Song 5:9). It is said of you: “Who is this who ascends, made white?” (Song 8:5, according to the Septuagint).

What does “made white” mean? Illuminated. Not made white as with cosmetics, as women whiten themselves when they wish to appear what they are not; not made white like a whitened wall—for a whitened wall, as the Apostle says, will be destroyed (Acts 23:3): hypocrisy and pretense. A whitened wall has plaster on the outside, but mud within.

She was not made white in this way, but made white and illuminated, because she was not white by herself. “Formerly,” he says, “I was a blasphemer” (1 Tim. 1:13); and again, “For we too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

Grace comes, illuminating and whitening. At first you were black, but by his grace you became white. “For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

Therefore it is said also of you: “Who is this who ascends, made white?” Already marvelous, already scarcely able to be contemplated. For it is the language of one who marvels: “Who is this who ascends, made white,” so beautiful, so luminous, so without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27)?

Is this not the one who lay in the filth of iniquities? Is this not the one who lay in the fornication of idols? Is this not the one who was unclean in every lust and carnal desire? Who, then, is this who ascends, made white?

Consider who it is who for her sake became one having neither form nor beauty, and you will understand the honor of this brightness [Note: [Col. 1340] Several manuscripts omit “and you will understand the honor of this brightness.”]. If you marvel at his humility on her account, no longer marvel at her exaltation on his account.

How great is the happiness of this woman made white, that even when she was black, he who would die for the ungodly lowered the beautiful one to her? Therefore our Lord God put on confession and beauty; he put on the Church. For the Church herself is confession and beauty: confession first, beauty afterward; confession of sins, beauty of right actions. “You have put on confession and beauty.”

### 7. [verse 2]

“Clothed with light as with a garment.” This is his garment, about which I have already spoken: “having neither spot nor wrinkle.” She is called light; and I have already said this too: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

Therefore, not in yourselves—for darkness is in you, but light is in the Lord. “Clothed with light as with a garment.”

“He stretches out heaven like a skin.” He wishes to enumerate through certain figurative mysteries how he did this: how the Church became light, how she became without spot or wrinkle, how she became bright, whitened, shining in the garment of her bridegroom while cleaving to him. Let us hear how this happened.

“He stretches out heaven like a skin.” I do indeed see this. For who stretched out this heaven that we behold with our bodily eyes, except God? And “he stretches it out like a skin”—if you take it literally, he has reduced it to a matter of ease [Note: [Col. 1340] Some manuscripts read, “he reduces it.” Others read, “you reduce it.”].

For when you see this great structure—since any human being who stretches out even a small room does so with great exertion, great labor, difficulty, and prolonged work—lest human weakness imagine such labor in God’s works, he has presented a kind of ease according to your capacity. Thus you may begin, in a certain way, to believe that God works easily and not think that he stretched out heaven as you stretch the roof of your house, but that it was as easy for him to stretch out such a great heaven as it is for you to stretch out a single skin.

Wonderful ease—and yet the Spirit still speaks to you who are slow [Note: [Col. 1341] Several manuscripts here and below read, “slowly.”]. Yes, I say, the Spirit still speaks to you who are slow. For God did not stretch out heaven even as you stretch out a skin.

If he stretched it out in that way, behold, a skin, either wrinkled or folded, is placed before you. Tell it to be stretched out; at your word, stretch out the skin. “I cannot,” you say. Therefore, even in stretching out a skin you are very far from God’s ease.

“For he spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148:5). He said, “Let there be a firmament between the water and the water,” and so it was made (Gen. 1:6). Nevertheless, to signify ease, for the moment you may receive something according to your understanding in the literal sense.

### 8.

But if, figuratively, we wish to uncover something covered and knock at what is closed, we find that God stretched out heaven like a skin, so that we may understand heaven as the holy Scripture.

God first established this authority in his Church; from there he began to carry out the rest. For he established heaven, and stretched it out like a skin—not without reason like a skin. First he stretched out the report of the preachers like a skin. Skin signifies mortality.

Therefore those two people, our first parents, Adam and Eve, the authors of the sin of the human race, after they had transgressed in paradise, having disregarded God’s commandment and yielded to the serpent’s suggestion and persuasion, were made mortal and sent out of paradise. To signify their mortality, they were clothed in tunics of skin; for they received tunics made from skins (Gen. 3). Skins are not usually removed except from dead animals. Therefore that mortality was represented by the name of skins.

What, then, if divine Scripture is signified here by the name of skin? How did God make heaven from skin, and stretch out heaven like a skin? Because those through whom Scripture was preached to us were mortal.

The Word of God, however, is always the same, always unchangeable and unfailing. Behold: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Was he present then but is he not present now? He is, and he will always be.

If, then, the Word of God is God with God, read, if you can. But what do you say? That it is above, and therefore you cannot read it? The Word of God is everywhere. “He reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things well through his purity” (Wis. 8:1; 7:24). “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:1, 10); and when he came, he was here. He came in the flesh, never absent in divinity.

Why, then, could you not read? Because “the world did not know God through wisdom in the wisdom of God,” being established there in the wisdom of God. For everything is there, and when it is withdrawn, nothing remains. Established there, you could not know God through wisdom.

Therefore what follows was necessary: “It pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. 1:21). If believers were to be saved through the foolishness of preaching, God chose certain mortal things; he chose mortal human beings, destined to die. By means of a mortal tongue he produced mortal sounds; by means of a dispensation involving mortals he employed mortal instruments.

And in this way heaven was made for you, so that in a mortal thing you might recognize the immortal Word, and so that you too might become immortal through participation in that same Word.

Moses lived [Note: [Col. 1342] The better manuscripts read, “said.”] and died. For God said to him, “Go up into the mountain and die” (Deut. 32:49). Jeremiah died, and so many prophets died. Their words remain to our posterity because they were not their own but belonged to him who stretched out heaven like a skin.

Behold the Apostle, released from this life, who said that to depart and be with Christ was much better (Phil. 1:23): he now lives with Christ, as all those prophets live with Christ. But through what did he administer to us what we read? Through what was destined to die: through his mouth, tongue, teeth, and hands.

All those things through which the Apostle carried out everything that we read are functions of the body, but they were directed by the soul, which God directed. Therefore heaven was stretched out like a skin.

We read now beneath heaven, as beneath the skin of the divine Scriptures, while it is being stretched out. For afterward “heaven will be folded up like a book” (Isa. 34:4). It is not without reason, brothers, that here it is like a skin and there like a book; something figurative is represented for us.

As far as divine Scripture is concerned, the speech of the dead is stretched out. Therefore it is stretched out like a skin—and it is stretched out all the more because those people have died. For after their death the prophets and Apostles became more widely known; they were not so well known while they lived.

While they were alive, only Judea possessed the prophets; once they were dead, all nations possessed them. For while they lived, the skin had not yet been stretched out; heaven had not yet been stretched out to cover the whole world.

Therefore, “he stretches out heaven like a skin.”

### 9. [verse 3]

“He covers its upper parts with waters.” [Note: [Col. 1342] Thus Am., Er., and most manuscripts. But Lov., “You cover.”]

We read this also, and it is properly understood literally. For when he commanded that a firmament be made between waters and waters, it came to pass that there are lower waters which inundate the earth, and upper waters removed from sight, yet entrusted to faith. “And let the waters,” he says, “which are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord; for he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:4–5). Thus the literal sense has been explained: he covers its upper parts with waters.

What does it mean figuratively? Since we have received the “skin” as a figure of Holy Scripture, and the authority of the divine word has been dispensed to us through mortals, whose fame, once they have died, is spread abroad together with that dispensation, how does he, according to this figure, cover its upper parts with waters? Whose upper parts? The heavens. And what are the heavens? Holy Scripture. What are the upper parts of Holy Scripture? What do we find that is higher in the holy Scriptures? Ask Paul: “I show you,” he says, “a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12:31). What way does he call more excellent?

“If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 13:1).

If, then, nothing more excellent than love can be found in Holy Scripture, how are the upper parts of heaven covered with waters, if the upper parts of Scripture are the commandment of love? Listen to how: “The love of God,” he says, “has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). From the very word “pouring,” understand the waters in the love of the Holy Spirit. These are the waters of which it is said in a certain Scripture: “Let your waters flow through your streets; let no stranger share them with you” (Prov. 5:16–17).

For all who are strangers to the way of truth—whether pagans, Jews, heretics, or any wicked Christians—may possess many gifts, but they cannot possess love. Why is this itself a gift? Let us say nothing for the moment about the other gifts outside, gifts that all human beings possess, since he makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked (Matt. 5:45): they are gifts of God, and are common not only to good and wicked people, but also to beasts and cattle. Existence itself, life, sight, feeling, hearing, and the other functions of the senses are gifts of God. But observe with whom, and with how many, they are shared, and with those whom you would not wish to imitate.

The worst people may possess a sharp intellect; the most shameful actors may possess skill and industry in the arts; thieves possess wealth; many wicked people possess marriages and children. All these are beautiful gifts of God—no one denies it—but observe with whom they are shared.

Consider the gifts belonging to the Church itself. What sort of gift is the gift of the sacraments in Baptism, the Eucharist, and the other holy sacraments? Simon Magus also obtained this gift (Acts 8:13). What sort of gift is prophecy? The wicked king Saul prophesied, and he prophesied while he was persecuting holy David. Pay close attention: I did not say, “after he had persecuted him.” Perhaps, after persecuting him, he repented and became worthy of the prophetic spirit. He prophesied neither after persecuting nor before he was going to persecute him, but while he was persecuting him.

He sent his servants to seize David. At that time David was among the prophets, where holy Samuel also was. Those who were sent were filled with the prophetic spirit and prophesied. Perhaps they had come with a good intention, either because of the necessity of their duty or because they would not do what had been commanded. He sent others also, and the same thing happened to them; let us interpret their intention in the same way.

When they delayed, Saul himself came, raging, panting for slaughter, thirsting for the blood of the innocent and holy man, to whom he was also ungrateful. He too was filled with the prophetic spirit and prophesied (1 Sam. 19:18–24).

Therefore let those who perhaps possess this holy gift of God without love—just as one may possess holy Baptism—not boast; let them consider what account they will have to render to God, who use holy things in an unholy manner. They will be among those who will say, “In your name we prophesied.” They will not be told, “You are lying,” but, “I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:22–23). For “if I have all prophecy but do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2). Saul also prophesied, but he was practicing iniquity.

But who practices iniquity except one who does not have love? “Love,” after all, “is the fullness of the Law” (Rom. 13:10).

What, then, did he say by “he covers its upper parts with waters”? In all the Scriptures, love occupies the most exalted way and the highest place. Only the good aspire to it; the wicked do not share it with us. They may share Baptism, they may share the other sacraments, they may share prayer, they may share these walls and this gathering; they do not share love with us.
