For love is the proper fountain of the good, the proper fountain of the holy, concerning which it is said: “Let no stranger share you.” Who are the strangers? All who hear, “I never knew you.” For if they are not known, they are certainly strangers—those to whom it is said, “I never knew you.”

The more excellent way of love, then, belongs to those who properly pertain to the kingdom of heaven. Therefore the commandment of love is above the heavens, above all books. For the books are subject to it; every tongue of the saints serves it, as does every movement of God’s ministers, both of soul and of body. It is therefore the more excellent way, and rightly it covers the upper parts of heaven with waters, because you find nothing more excellent than love in the divine books.

### 10.

But listen still more clearly to what the water is. We have said that the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us; we have also said, “Let your waters flow through your streets.” Someone might say to me, “It is not explicitly stated there whether I should understand love; what if someone else understands something else?”

Remember only what the Apostle says: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts.” Through what? “Through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

Now listen to the Lord, the teacher of the Apostles: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” Let him continue: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” What does this mean? Let the Evangelist explain: “Now this he said,” he says, “about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

Therefore, brothers, if the Spirit had not yet been given because Jesus had not yet been glorified, then, after he had been glorified and had ascended into heaven, the Holy Spirit was sent (John 7:37–39), and the Apostles were filled with love, poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit who had been given to them; for the upper parts of heaven are covered with waters.

And rightly so, because the Lord ascended into heaven in order to be above the heavens and from there to send love. God does not cover in such a way as though he were supported by the one whom he covers; he raises up the one whom he covers, he does not burden him. Thus he covers heaven with waters so that it may be raised up more greatly by the divine Spirit.

What raises is above; what is raised is below. The former suspends; the latter hangs. If, then, the former suspends and the latter hangs, listen to how this heaven of the Scriptures hangs upon love. There are, of course, those two most famous commandments of love: “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40).

“He covers its upper parts with waters.”

### 11.

“He makes clouds his ascent.”

This too is properly understood literally. The Lord visibly ascended into heaven. How were clouds made the ascent of heaven? “When he had said these things, a cloud received him” (Acts 1:9).

You also have a prediction concerning our resurrection: “And the dead,” he says, “in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:15–16). You have clouds as the ascent of heaven.

I will also show you clouds as the ascent of this heaven—that is, of the divine Scriptures. What does this mean, brothers? May the Lord my God deem me worthy to be numbered among those clouds, whatever sort they may be; he sees how misty a cloud I am. Yet receive all preachers of the word of truth as clouds.

Therefore, whoever is weak and cannot ascend into this heaven—that is, to the understanding of the Scriptures—let him ascend through clouds. Perhaps this is happening for you even now [Note: [Col. 1345] Thus most manuscripts; Am. and Er.: “may it be enough for you”; Lov.: “it is enough for you”]. If we are doing something, if our labor and sweat are not fruitless, you are ascending into the heaven of the divine Scriptures, that is, into their understanding, through our preaching.

How high was the heaven in this psalm! None of you could see what it meant figuratively: “He stretched out heaven like a skin, who covers its upper parts with waters.” This very statement, “He makes clouds his ascent,” has now been understood, insofar as the Lord has granted it through our preaching. For clouds do not rain from their own resources.

Ascend by understanding; bear fruit in that very understanding. Do not be like the vineyard of which the prophet says: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it.” A certain vineyard was accused because, when it ought to have produced grapes, it produced thorns, and did not return a worthy response to the sweet rain.

Whoever hears good things and does evil is drenched with sweet rain and produces thorns. Let us not suppose, brothers, that the Lord was speaking of some earthly and visible vineyard. For, so that an excuse for iniquity might not remain hidden beneath the obscurity of his speech, the Lord himself, through that same prophet, explained which vineyard he was addressing and of which vineyard he was speaking: “The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts,” he says, “is the house of Israel.”

Why do your hearts, O wicked people, wander through the mountains and hills of vine-dressers? “I know,” he says, “which vineyard I am speaking about; I know where I sought grapes and found thorns. You imagine and suppose one thing after another for no reason, unwilling to understand so that you may do good.”

For this too is written: “He was unwilling to understand, so that he might do good” (Ps. 35:4). Remove all your suspicions from the midst: “The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah his beloved young plant” (Isa. 5:1–7). Beloved when it was planted; condemned when it produced thorns.

Therefore, brothers, perhaps the house of Israel was the vineyard, and we are not the vineyard? Let us hear with fear what we see said to the Jews. See how the Apostle frightens the branches grafted in from the branches that were broken off, and in the broken branches commends a severity to be feared, while in the grafted branches he commends a goodness to be loved (Rom. 11:20–22).

Do not be fruitless in goodness, lest you experience severity in your barrenness.

“But I am not a vine,” you say to me. Where then is the Lord’s voice: “I am the vine, you are the branches; my Father is the cultivator” (John 15:1, 5)? Where is the Apostle’s voice: “Who plants a vineyard and does not partake of its fruit?” (1 Cor. 9:7).

You are therefore a vineyard, O Church, and you have God as your cultivator. No human cultivator drenches his vineyard.

Therefore, most beloved brothers, inward parts of the Church, pledges of the Church, children of the heavenly mother, listen while there is time. God threatened that vineyard with a most terrible threat: “I will command my clouds,” he says, “not to rain upon it.”

And it happened. The Apostles came to the Jews, and they rejected them. They said to them, “We were sent to you, but because you rejected the word of God, we are going to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

You see how, in the same Spirit of God, at the command of the one who dwells inwardly in the hearts of his people, the clouds of God were ordered not to drench the vineyard which, when it was expected to produce grapes, produced thorns.

Therefore he made clouds his ascent, and he stretched out heaven like a skin. You have no reason to complain: the authority of the Scriptures has been stretched over the whole world; clouds are not lacking; the word of truth is preached; all obscure things are explained, so that your hearts may ascend through the clouds.

See how you believe; see what you receive. After the preacher will come the judge; after the steward will come the exactor.

“He makes clouds his ascent.”

### 12.

“He walks upon the wings of the winds.”

It is dangerous now to understand this literally. What are the wings of the winds? Or how, in a picture, are we to make winds flying and possessing wings?

Wind, brothers, is nothing except what we feel: a certain movement and, as it were, wave of air, driving whatever it can according to its strength. What are the wings of the winds? Or truly [Note: [Col. 1346] The manuscripts read “truly” (*vere*).] what are the wings of God? Yet it is said: “Under the shadow of your wings they will hope” (Ps. 35:8).

Let us therefore try to understand this literally as something actually done in creation. Scripture perhaps commends the speed of the word. We spoke long ago in another psalm about this speed, where it is written: “His word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147:15). For human beings know nothing swifter than the winds.

Just as that ease was commended in the skin [Note: [Col. 1346] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “For nothing is swifter than the winds. You all know how greatly that ease …”]; for nothing is easier for a person to stretch than a skin—so here also, indicating that God, or his Word [Note: [Col. 1346] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read: “God through his Word.”], is present everywhere and leaves nothing untouched in the speed of its movement, because you know nothing swifter than the wind, he says: “He walks upon the wings of the winds.” That is, his speed surpasses the speed of the winds. Thus, by “the wings of the winds,” understand the speed of the winds, and understand the word of God as swifter than all winds.

And so, at the first level of consideration, let us knock at something deeper, and let these letters indicate something figurative to us.

### 13.

We understand winds figuratively, not unreasonably, as souls—not because the soul is wind, but because wind is invisible, although it is a bodily thing that drives bodies. Since it escapes the sight of human eyes, and the soul is invisible, we therefore properly understand souls as winds.

Hence it is also said that God breathed the breath of life into the formed human being, and “the human became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7). Therefore, in allegory, winds may reasonably be understood as souls.

But take care that, when you hear the word “allegory,” you do not suppose that I have said something about pantomimes. Certain words, because they are words and proceed from the tongue, are common even to amusing and dishonorable things; nevertheless, these words have their proper place in the Church and their proper place on the stage.

For I did not say what the Apostle did not say when, speaking of Abraham’s two sons, he said: “These things,” he says, “are an allegory” (Gal. 4:24). Allegory is spoken of when something else seems to sound in the words, but something else is signified in the understanding.

How is Christ called a lamb (John 1:29)? Is he a sheep? Christ is called a lion (Rev. 5:5): is he a beast? Christ is called a rock (1 Cor. 10:4): is he hardness? Christ is called a mountain (Dan. 2:35): is he a swelling of the earth? And so many things appear to sound one way and signify another; this is called allegory.

For the person who thinks I have spoken of the theater when I said “allegory” should also think that the Lord spoke of the amphitheater when he said “parable.” You see what a city does [Note: [Col. 1347] Carthage.], where spectacles abound. In the countryside I would speak more safely; perhaps people there would not have learned what allegory is unless they had learned it from the Scriptures of God.

Therefore, when we say that a figure is an allegory, a figurative sacrament is an allegory. And what do we understand here by “He ascended upon the wings of the winds”? We have said that the winds may properly be understood figuratively as souls.

What are the wings of the winds—the wings of souls—except those by which they are lifted upward? The wings of souls are therefore virtues, good works, rightly performed deeds.

All have their wings in two wings, for all the commandments are contained in two commandments. Whoever loves God and neighbor has a winged soul, with free wings, flying toward the Lord in holy love. Whoever is entangled in carnal love has birdlime on his wings.

For if the soul does not have wings, where does that person who groans amid tribulations get the words: “Who will give me wings like a dove?” And he continues: “Then I shall fly away and rest” (Ps. 55:7).

Likewise, elsewhere: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings like a dove and fly to the farthest limits of the sea…” He is as though saying: “Thus I can flee from the presence of your anger, if I take wings like a dove and fly to the farthest limits of the sea.”

To fly to the farthest limits of the sea is to extend hope to the end of the age, like the one who says: “This labor is before me until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand in the final things” (Ps. 73:16–17).

And how does he come to the farthest limits of the sea, even after taking wings? “For even there,” he says, “your hand will lead me, and your right hand will guide me” (Ps. 139:7–10). For even with my wings I shall fall unless you lead me.

Thus souls that work well and possess love from a pure heart and an unfeigned faith (1 Tim. 1:5) have good and free wings, bound by no birdlime. But however endowed with the virtues of love they may be, what are they compared with that love by which they were loved even when they were entangled in birdlime?

God’s love for us, therefore, is greater than our love for him. Our love is our wings, but he walks even upon the wings of the winds.

“He walks upon the wings of the winds.”

### 14.

The Apostle was saying to certain people: “I bend my knees before the Father for you, that he may grant you, according to the inner person, that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, so that, rooted and founded in love…”

He is already giving them love [Note: [Col. 1348] The editions add here “God”; this is absent from the manuscripts.]; he is already giving them wings and feathers. “So that you may be able,” he says, “to comprehend what is the breadth, length, height, and depth.”

Perhaps he signifies the cross of the Lord. There was breadth, where the hands were extended; length, rising from the earth, where the body was fastened; height, from the sloping wood extending upward; depth, where the cross was fixed, and where all our hope of life was located.

Breadth consists in good works; length in persevering to the end; height, because of “Lift up your heart,” consists in not performing all our good works—which we continue to perform to the end—with the breadth by which we do good and the length by which we persevere to the end, except in hope of heavenly rewards.

This is height: not seeking one’s reward here, but above. Otherwise it will be said to us: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2).

By depth I meant the place where the part of the cross was fixed and was not visible; from there arose the portions that were visible. What is hidden and not public in the Church? The sacrament of Baptism and the sacrament of the Eucharist.

The pagans see our good works, but the sacraments are concealed from them. Yet from what they do not see arise the things they do see [Note: [Col. 1348] Thus the manuscripts. The editions instead have: “but from the things they see they rise toward the things they do not see.”], just as from the depth of the cross, which is fixed in the earth, rises the whole cross that appears and can be seen.

And what follows? After the Apostle had said this, he added: “And to know the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ” (Eph. 3:14–19), after it had already been said, “rooted and founded in love.”

You love Christ, and therefore you work on the cross. But do you love him as much as he loved you? In loving, however much you can love, you fly toward him, so that you may know how he loved you. This is to know the surpassing greatness of Christ’s love.

You love as much as you can, and you fly as much as you can; but he walks upon the wings of the winds.

“He walks upon the wings of the winds.”

### 15. [verse 4]

“He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a blazing fire.”

This too, although we do not see the appearance of angels—for it is hidden from our eyes and exists in a certain great commonwealth of God the emperor—we know by faith that angels exist, and we read and hold firmly that they have appeared to many. It is not permitted for us to doubt this.

Angels are spirits; and when they are spirits, they are not angels. When they are sent, they become angels. For “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. Do you ask the name of this nature? It is spirit. Do you ask the office? It is angel. From what it is, it is spirit; from what it does, it is angel.

Consider this in a human being. The name of the nature is “human being,” the name of the office “soldier”; the name of the nature is “man,” the name of the office “herald.” A human being becomes a herald—that is, one who was a human being becomes a herald; it is not that one who was a herald becomes a human being.

Thus those who were already spirits, created by God the Creator, he makes his angels by sending them to announce what he has commanded. And he makes his ministers a blazing fire.

We read that fire appeared in the bush (Exod. 3:2); we also read that fire was sent from above and fulfilled what had been commanded. It therefore served when it fulfilled the command. When it existed, it belonged to its nature; when it did what had been commanded, it fulfilled its ministry.

Thus far, according to the literal sense, in created things.

### 16.

But what does this mean figuratively in the Church? How do we understand, “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a blazing fire”?

He calls spiritual people spirits. He rightly makes spiritual people his angels—that is, messengers of his word. “The spiritual person judges all things, but is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:15).

See how a spiritual person is made an angel of God. “I could not speak to you,” he says, “as spiritual people, but as carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1). He was sent from a certain spiritual disposition [Note: [Col. 1349] Some manuscripts read “effectuation” (*effectione*).] to carnal people, like an angel from heaven to earth.

How does he say, “and his ministers a blazing fire,” unless in the same way that he says, “fervent in spirit” (Rom. 12:11)? For every minister of God who is fervent in spirit is a burning fire.

Was Stephen not burning? With what fire was he burning? What sort of fire was it when he was being stoned and praying for those by whom he was being stoned (Acts 7:59)?

When you hear, “The minister of God is fire,” do you think he will burn you? Let him burn, but let him burn your hay—that is, let the minister of God, by preaching the word of God, burn away all your carnal desires.

Listen to him: “Let a person regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (1 Cor. 4:1).

But how was he burning when he said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:11)? He was burning and blazing with love, and he went toward them in order to set them on fire.

The Lord said that he would send this fire into the earth when he said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49). Just as the sword (Matt. 10:34), so also the fire: the sword divides carnal affection; the fire consumes it.

Understand everything in the word of God; recognize everything in the Spirit of God. Begin to burn with love through the word you hear, and see what the fire of God’s minister has done in you.

“He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a blazing fire.”

### 17. [verse 5]

“He founded the earth upon its firmness; it shall not be moved forever and ever.”

I do not know whether this can be understood of this earth in such a way that it yields any satisfactory meaning, or whether it is properly said, “It shall not be moved forever and ever,” when it is said elsewhere, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. 24:35).

There is difficulty here if you seek to understand it literally. For when he says, “He founded the earth upon its firmness,” perhaps there is some firmness hidden from us which holds the earth, and this is what he means by “founded.” Upon what? Upon the firmness of the earth itself, which he placed beneath it so that it might be held—something perhaps hidden from your eyes.

Let such things remain hidden in creation; the Creator will not remain hidden because of the obscurity of creation. Let us see what we can see; from what we see, let us praise and love him.

Let us turn to seek something placed here figuratively. “He founded the earth”: I understand the Church. “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 24:1); I understand the Church as earth.

It is the thirsty earth; it is the one that says in the Psalms—for one voice speaks from all: “My soul is like a waterless land to you” (Ps. 143:6). What does “waterless” mean? Thirsting. “My soul thirsts for you like a waterless land.” For unless it thirsts, it will not be properly watered.

For drunken souls, rain is a flood. They must thirst: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5:6). Let it say, “My soul is like a waterless land to you,” because elsewhere it says: “My soul thirsted for the living God” (Ps. 42:3).

I therefore understand the earth as the Church. What is its firmness upon which it has been founded except its foundation? Is it inappropriate to understand as the firmness upon which the earth has been founded the foundation upon which the Church has been established?

What is that foundation? “No one can lay another foundation,” he says, “besides the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3:11). We have therefore been made firm there.

Rightly, because we have been made firm there, we shall not be moved forever and ever; nothing is firmer than this foundation. You were weak, but the firm foundation carries you. You could not be firm in yourself; you will always be firm if you do not withdraw from that firm foundation.

“It shall not be moved forever and ever.” It is the predestined pillar and foundation of the truth (1 Tim. 3:15).

### 18. [verses 6–17]

“The abyss like a garment is its clothing; upon the mountains the waters will stand. At your rebuke they will flee; at the voice of your thunder they will be afraid. The mountains rise up, and the plains descend, to the place that you founded for them. You set a boundary that they shall not cross, nor shall they return to cover the earth.

“You send springs into the valleys; the waters will pass between the mountains. All the beasts of the field will drink; the wild asses will receive them for their thirst. Above them the birds of heaven will dwell; from the midst of the rocks they will give voice. Watering the mountains from his upper chambers, the earth will be satisfied with the fruit of your works.

“Producing grass for cattle and plants for the service of human beings, so that it may bring forth bread from the earth; and wine gladdens the human heart. So that it may brighten the face with oil; and bread strengthens the human heart. The trees of the field will be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon that he planted. There the sparrows will build their nests; the house of the coot is their leader.”

[Note: [Col. 1350] Am., Er., and several manuscripts: “so that you may bring forth.”]

[Note: [Col. 1350] The editions have: “and wine may gladden the human heart”; and shortly afterward, “and bread may strengthen the human heart.” But the better manuscripts have “gladdens” and “strengthens,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint, which Nobilius notes to be a Hebraism.]

[Note: [Col. 1350] The editions add here “all”; it is absent from the manuscripts.]

You perceive that heaven has been stretched out; you wish to ascend by understanding, and I see this. Yet I think that your Charity should consider with me how high it is. For this reason I wanted to recite many verses, so that you might see how highly the mysteries of God are set forth: so that we may not grow weary of what has been offered, nor regard what is readily available as worthless, but so that what is always sought, even with difficulty, may be found with greater delight.

Among other things, however, brothers, which may be understood literally, what of this statement: “There the sparrows will build their nests; the house of the coot is their leader”? Is the house of the coot the leader of sparrows? Or is the house of the coot the leader of cedars? For this too is found there: “And the cedars of Lebanon that he planted; there the sparrows will build their nests; the house of the coot is their leader.”

In Latin usage, we cannot understand “their”—that is, “of the cedars”—for cedars are feminine in gender. How, then, is the house of the coot the leader of sparrows?

This cannot in any way be understood in this creation that lies before our eyes. We know coots to be birds of the sea or marshes. Let the house of the coot be the nest of the coot; how, then, is the house of the coot the leader of sparrows?

Why does the Holy Spirit mingle certain things that seem absurd in visible realities, unless it is to compel us, from what we cannot understand literally, to seek them spiritually?

### 19.

Therefore, if you wish, as I said, to ascend by understanding to heaven, to the stretched-out skin, and he has made clouds its ascent, this cloud that speaks to you today is too weak to explain all these things. Forgive me, even if not for your weakness, then certainly for mine.

I see that your eagerness is so great that you are always ready to listen. But there are two matters whose consideration must not be neglected. We must consider both the weakness of our body and the memory required by the things being explained.

For the moment, think about what you have heard. What did I say? Chew over what you have eaten. Thus you will be clean animals, fit for God’s banquets.

Observe your fruit in your works. For one who hears well and does not act well digests very badly, because the Lord our God does not fail to feed us.

It is known to everyone that we shall have to render an account of the bread we have received and distributed. Your Charity knows this very well. The divine Page does not keep silent about it or flatter us; nor does God flatter us [Note: [Col. 1351] Several manuscripts: “flatter,” rather than “flatters.”].

You can observe how freely we speak to you from this place. And if perhaps I am less free, or all who speak to you in this place are less free, certainly the word of God itself fears no one.

Whether we fear or speak freely, we are compelled to proclaim the one who fears no one. God has granted you this: you hear not human beings but God, even through proud speakers.

You will have no excuse at God’s judgment unless you exercise yourselves in good works and give a suitable fruit for what you have heard, as for rain. Suitable fruit consists in good works; suitable fruit consists in sincere love—not only of a brother, but also of an enemy.

Do not despise any suppliant. If you cannot give him what he asks, do not despise him. If you can give, give; if you cannot, show yourself approachable. God crowns the will inwardly [Note: [Col. 1351] Am., Er., and most manuscripts: “goodness,” rather than “will.”] where he does not find the means.

Let no one say, “I do not have anything.” Love is not distributed from a purse. For whatever we say, whatever we have said, and whatever we may be able to say—whether we ourselves, those after us, or those before us—the end is always love, because “the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5).

When you ask God, question your hearts. See how you utter this verse: “Forgive us our debts, just as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

You will not be praying unless you say this [Note: [Col. 1352] “Prayer” is understood.]. If you say something else, he will not hear you, because the Jurist whom he sent did not dictate that to you.

It is therefore necessary that, when we speak our words in prayer, we speak according to this prayer; and when we speak these very words, that we understand well what we are saying, because God wished to make them clear.

If you do not pray, you will have no hope. If you pray otherwise than the Master taught, you will not be heard. Or if you lie in prayer, you will not obtain what you ask.

Therefore we must both pray and speak truthfully, and pray in the way he taught. Whether you wish it or not, every day you will say: “Forgive us our debts, just as we also forgive our debtors.” Do you wish to say this securely? Do what you say.

## Sermon II

### 1.

I know that you consider us your debtors, not out of necessity but, what is more powerful, out of love. First, however, we owe this to the Lord our God, who dwells also in you and demands these things from us; next, to the lord [Note: [Col. 1352] Thus the manuscripts: *domno*; the editions: *domino*.] and father who is present, commands, and prays for me; and then to the forcefulness of your demands, by which you extract this even from our feeble strength.

Nevertheless, insofar as the Lord grants it—may he also deign to grant those very powers at your prayers—since on the preceding day we recently treated the first parts of this psalm, we must also undertake what follows and, with his help, bring it to an end, in whose name we began.

We had commended to your Charity, who were present, that this entire psalm is woven together from figurative mysteries. Hence what is more difficult to seek is usually found more sweetly.

Do not think that these things have been withheld from you by obscurity, but that they have been stored up through difficulty, for the purpose we have often mentioned: “that it may be given to those who ask, found by those who seek, and entered by those who knock” (Matt. 7:7–8).

But we need somewhat more of both your silence and your patience, so that the few things we shall say may not occupy more time through disturbance. The shortness of time forces us to say only a few things; your Charity also knows that we ought to perform the solemn service owed at the funeral rites of a faithful body.

Let us not now be compelled to repeat and explain again what has already been said. If some who did not hear are absent, let them not be absent; perhaps it benefits them that they do not now hear what those who were present heard, so that they too may learn to be present [Note: [Col. 1352] Thus the manuscripts of good quality. The editions instead have: “but if some who did not hear are absent—would that they were not absent!—perhaps it benefits those who are not hearing now,” and so forth.].

Let us therefore read rapidly.

### 2. [verses 1–2]

“Bless the Lord, O my soul.”

Let the soul of all of us speak, made one in Christ.

“Lord my God, you have been greatly magnified.”

How have you been magnified? “You have put on confession and beauty.” Confess, so that you may be made beautiful, so that he may clothe you.

“You are clothed with light as with a garment.”

He is clothed with his Church, because it has become light in him, though previously it was darkness in itself, as the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

“Stretching out heaven like a skin”—

either as easily as you stretch a skin, if you understand it literally; or let us understand the authority of the Scriptures, spread throughout the whole world under the name of “skin.” For mortality is signified in the skin, and the entire authority of the divine Scriptures has been dispensed to us through mortal human beings, whose fame, now that they are dead, is spread abroad.

3. [v. 3.] “Who covers its upper parts with waters.” Whose upper parts? Heaven’s. What is heaven? We have said that it signifies divine Scripture, at least figuratively. What are the upper parts of divine Scripture? The commandment above which there is nothing: love. Why, then, is love compared with waters? Because “the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Why is the Spirit himself called water? Because “Jesus stood and cried out: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” How do we prove that he was speaking of the Spirit? Let the Evangelist himself say this, who continues: “Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who were to believe in him would receive” (John 6:37–39).

“Who walks upon the wings of the winds”—that is, upon the virtues of souls. What is the soul’s virtue? Love itself. How, then, does he walk upon it? Because God’s love for us is greater than our love for God.

4. [v. 4.] “Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a blazing fire”—that is, he makes those who are already spirits, who are spiritual and not carnal, his angels, sending them to preach his Gospel. “And his ministers a blazing fire.” For unless the minister who preaches is himself burning, he does not set on fire the person to whom he preaches.

5. [vv. 5–6.] “He founded the earth upon its firmament.” He established the Church upon the Church’s firmament. What is the firmament of the Church except the foundation of the Church? And what is the foundation of the Church except that of which the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11)? And therefore, supported upon such a foundation, what did it deserve to hear? “It shall not be moved forever and ever.”

“He founded the earth upon its firmness”—that is, he established the Church upon Christ the foundation. The Church will totter if the foundation totters; but how could Christ totter, when, before he came to us and assumed flesh, “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3); when he contains all things by his majesty and us by his goodness? Since Christ does not totter, “it shall not be moved forever and ever.” Where are those who say that the Church has perished from the world, when it cannot even be moved?

6. But how did the Lord begin to uphold this Church, to reveal it, to begin it, to display it, to spread it abroad? How did this begin? “He founded the earth upon its firmament; it shall not be moved forever and ever.”

“The abyss, like a garment, is its covering.” Whose? Surely perhaps God’s? But he had already spoken of his clothing: “You are clothed with light as with a garment.” I hear that God is clothed with light; and, if we are willing, we are that light itself. What do I mean, “if we are willing”? If we are no longer darkness.[^c0033-1]

Therefore, if God is clothed with light, whose garment is the abyss in turn? The abyss is called an immeasurable quantity of waters: all water, every moist nature and substance spread everywhere through seas, rivers, and hidden caverns is collectively called by one name, “the abyss.”

Therefore we understand the earth, of which he said, “He founded the earth upon its firmament; it shall not be moved forever and ever.” I believe that it is of this earth that he said, “The abyss, like a garment, is its covering.” For water is, as it were, the earth’s garment, surrounding and covering it. But at one time, in the Flood, this garment of the earth grew so greatly that it covered everything entirely and rose above the highest mountains, as Scripture testifies: by nearly fifteen cubits (Gen. 7:20). Perhaps this psalm indicated that very time when it said, “The abyss, like a garment, is its covering.”

[^c0033-1]: [Col. 1353] The better manuscripts read: “If we were already darkness.” Some have: “If we are already fleeing darkness.”

7. “The waters will stand above the mountains”—that is, the garment of the earth, which is the abyss, grew so greatly that the waters stood even above the mountains. We read, as I said, that this happened in the Flood. Was the Prophet speaking from that event? Was he recounting the past to us, or foretelling the future?

But if he were recounting the past, he would not say to us, “The waters will stand above the mountains,” but, “The waters stood above the mountains.” In Scripture we commonly read that the past tense is used for the future: the Spirit foresees what is to come as though it had already happened. Thus, in another psalm, in the passage that we all know, which is recited as though it were the Gospel, we read: “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones; they cast lots over my clothing” (Ps. 21:17–19). Everything is commemorated as though it had already happened, although it was certainly still to come.

But what can our diligence accomplish? What can such great occupation accomplish? Or when are we so at leisure that we can say with certainty, “It is so”? We often notice Prophets using verbs in the past tense to speak of things that are future. But the figure by which the past is spoken of as future does not readily present itself to the reader. I do not dare say, “It does not exist”; but certainly I would instruct those devoted to these Scriptures what they should seek. If they find it and bring it to us, we old men, occupied though the young have leisure, will rejoice in the studies of the young, and through their service we too will learn something. We are not disdainful, since Christ teaches about everything.

This, then, is what he says: “The waters will stand above the mountains.” The Prophet, concerned to foretell the future rather than narrate the past, said this because he wished the future Church to be understood in the flood of persecutions. There was once a time when the waters of persecutors had covered God’s earth, God’s Church; and they had covered it so completely that even those who were great—the mountains themselves—did not appear.

For when they were fleeing everywhere, how could they not appear smaller? Perhaps it is of those waters that the cry was uttered: “Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul” (Ps. 68:2). Especially are these the waters that make the sea: stormy and barren. For seawater does not make whatever land it covers fertile; rather, it brings it to sterility.

The mountains too were beneath the waters, because “the waters stood above the mountains.” The peoples who resisted had overcome the authority of all those everywhere who bravely preached God’s word; the waters had covered them, and the waters stood above them, saying, “Press, press,” and they pressed; “Extinguish them; let them not appear.” They said these things and prevailed against the martyrs; Christians fled everywhere, and the Apostles were concealed by a kind of flight.

Why were the Apostles concealed by flight? Because “the waters stood above the mountains.” Great was the power of the waters. But for how long? Hear what follows.

8. [v. 7.] “At your rebuke they will flee.” And this happened, brothers: at God’s rebuke the waters fled; that is, they withdrew from pressing upon the mountains. Now the mountains themselves stand forth—Peter and Paul. How they rise above! Those who formerly were pressed down by persecutors are now honored by emperors.

The waters fled at God’s rebuke, because “the heart of kings is in God’s hand”; he turned it wherever he wished (Prov. 21:1), and commanded through them that peace be granted to Christians. The apostolic authority emerged and became eminent.

Was the greatness of the mountains lacking even when the waters were above them? Nevertheless, my brothers, so that everyone might see the eminence of the mountains through whom salvation would come to the human race—for “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which my help will come” (Ps. 120:1)—“at God’s rebuke the waters fled.”

“At the sound of your thunder they will fear.” Who would not now be terrified by the voice of God through the Apostles, the voice of God through the Scriptures, through his clouds? The sea grew calm; the waters feared; the mountains were laid bare; the emperor gave the order. But who would have given the order unless God had thundered? Because God willed it, they gave the order, and it happened.

Therefore no human being should claim anything for himself. The waters feared, but “at the sound of your thunder.” For behold, when God willed it, the waters fled so that they would not press upon the mountains; before this happened, the mountains were firm beneath the waters.

9. [vv. 8–10.] “The mountains rise up, and the plains descend to the place that you founded for them.” He is still speaking about the waters. Let us not understand “mountains” here as earthly mountains, nor “plains” as earthly plains, but waves so great that they may be compared with mountains. At one time the sea was tossed, and its waves were like mountains, covering those Apostolic mountains.

But how long do “the mountains rise up, and the plains descend”? They raged, and then they were calmed. When they raged, they were mountains; when they were calmed, they became plains, for he founded a place for them.

There is a certain channel—a deep place, as it were—into which all the raging hearts of mortals have somehow been received.[^c0033-2] How many are now salty and bitter, and yet quiet! How many are unwilling to become sweet! Who are those unwilling to become sweet? Those who still refuse to believe in Christ.

And although there are many who have not yet believed, what do they do to the Church? Once they were mountains; now they are plains. Yet, my brothers, the sea is also calm.[^c0033-3] Why do they not rage now? Why are they not mad? Why do they not make the effort? If they cannot overthrow our land, surely they can cover it.[^c0033-4] Why do they not? Hear:

“You established a boundary which they will not cross, nor will they return to cover the earth.”

[^c0033-2]: [Col. 1355] All the manuscripts read *metus* (“fear”); the context requires *meatus* (“channel” or “passage”).

[^c0033-3]: [Col. 1355] The editions read *malitia* (“wickedness”), but *malacia* (“calm,” the term used of a dead sea when it is without winds or movement) should be read.

[^c0033-4]: [Col. 1355] Supply: “they can.”

10. [Col. 1356] Since, then, the most bitter waves have now received a limit, so that we may even preach such things freely; since they have received the limit assigned to them, since they cannot cross the boundary imposed upon them, nor return to cover the earth—what happens on the earth itself? What works are carried out there, now that the sea has laid it bare?

Although thin waves still roar along its shore, although the pagans still murmur, I hear the sound of the shores, but I do not dread a flood. What, then, what happens on the earth?

“You send forth springs in the valleys.” “You send forth,” he says, “springs in the valleys.”

You know what valleys are: depressed places of the earth. For valleys or lowlands are set over against hills and mountains as a contrasting figure. Hills and mountains are elevations of the earth; valleys or lowlands are the earth’s lowliness.

Do not despise lowliness; from it the springs flow: “You send forth springs in the valleys.” Hear the mountain: the Apostle says, “I labored more than all of them.” A certain greatness is being commended; yet immediately, so that the waters might flow forth, he made himself a valley: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

It is no contradiction for those who are mountains also to be valleys. For just as they are called mountains on account of spiritual greatness, so they are called valleys on account of the humility of their spirit.

“Not I,” he says—that is a valley; “but the grace of God with me”—that is a spring.

“You send forth springs in the valleys.” It was of the Spirit that what I have just recalled was said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” “Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who were to believe in him would receive.”

Let us see whether they are valleys, so that springs may be sent forth in the valleys. Hear the Prophet: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). What does “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one?” mean? Who will possess my spring? The valley.

11. “Between the mountains the waters will pass through.” Up to this point the Psalm has been recited by the Reader; let this suffice for Your Charity up to this point. We shall say this much, and in God’s name bring the sermon to an end.

What does “Between the mountains the waters will pass through” mean? We have heard who the mountains are: great preachers of the word, exalted angels of God, although they are still in mortal flesh; exalted not by their own power but by his grace. Yet as far as they themselves are concerned, they are valleys; in humility they send forth springs.

“And between the mountains,” he says, “the waters will pass through.” Let us suppose that this means: “Between the Apostles the preachings of the word of truth will pass through.”[^c0033-5]

What does “between the Apostles” mean? That which is said to be “between” is common. A common possession, from which all live equally, is “between”; it belongs neither to me nor to you, neither to you nor to me. For this reason we also speak in this way about certain people: “They have peace among themselves; they have faith among themselves; they have love among themselves.” This is certainly how we speak. What does “among themselves” mean? In their midst. And what does “in their midst” mean? It is common to them.

Hear of the waters “between the mountains.” Their faith was common to them; no one possessed the waters as his own and private property. For if they are not “between,” they are private and do not flow publicly: I have mine, and he has his; there is nothing between us that both he and I possess. But such preaching is not peaceful preaching.

Yet, so that the waters might flow between the mountains, hear the voice of the mountain: “May the God of peace grant you to have the same mind toward one another” (Rom. 15:5). And again: “That you may all have the same mind, and that there be no divisions among you” (1 Cor. 1:10). What I feel, you feel; the water flows in the midst. I do not possess something private as mine, nor do you possess something private as yours.[^c0033-6] Let truth be neither mine alone nor yours alone, so that it may be both yours and mine: “Between the mountains the waters will pass through.”

Hear the mountain himself, as I said, because “between the mountains the waters will pass through.” “Whether it was I or they,” he says, “so we preach, and so you believed” (1 Cor. 15:11). Securely he said, “Whether it was I or they, so we preach, and so you believed”: for the waters flowed between the mountains. There was no discord among the mountains concerning the waters, but peace of agreement and fellowship of love.

But if anyone wished to preach something else, he would already be preaching from his own possession, not from what was common. And hear what is said of him by the very one who sent forth springs in the valleys: “Whoever speaks falsehood speaks from his own” (John 8:44).

Therefore, lest some mountain be understood as flowing not from what was common but from its own source and wishing to pour in something private, the Apostle says: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.”

And observe how he refused to allow anyone to be presumed upon because of the mountain, lest the mountain depart from the waters flowing through the midst and wish to pour in something of its own.

“Even if we”—and what a great mountain said this! How abundantly the water flowed from his valley! Yet he wished it to run between the mountains, and for the peoples to possess there a sure faith[^c0033-7] that the Apostles held in common among themselves—“even if we,” he says.

And you, Paul, are you able to preach something otherwise? The question concerns Paul; hear what follows: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should announce to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:8–9).

If a mountain comes preaching another gospel, let him be accursed; if an angel comes preaching another gospel, let him be accursed. Why is this? Because he wishes to flow from what is private, not from what is common.

Perhaps a human being, obstructed by a carnal fog and led away from the common spring into his own falsehood, could do this; but an angel? Surely not even an angel? If an angel flowing from his own source in paradise had not been heard, we would not have been cast into death.

The common water had been set before human beings—the commandment of God: water in the midst, water, in a sense, public; it was effective without deceit, as we have said to Your Charity,[^c0033-8] flowing without stain and without mud. If that water were always drunk, one would always live.

An angel fallen from heaven came, made himself a serpent because he already desired craftily to scatter poisons. He poured out poison; he spoke from his own, from what was his, because “whoever speaks falsehood speaks from his own.” And the wretched, by listening, abandoned what was common, through which they were blessed; reduced to what was their own, they desired perversely to be like God—for this is what he had said to them: “Taste, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5)—and, desiring what they were not, they lost what they had received.

Therefore, brothers, let what we have said to Your Charity be of use concerning the springs: be valleys, so that springs may flow from you, and share with everyone what you have from God. Let the waters flow between the mountains; envy no one. Drink, be filled; once filled, flow forth.[^c0033-9] Everywhere let God’s common water have the glory, not the private falsehoods of human beings.

[^c0033-5]: [Col. 1356] So Ambrose, Erasmus, and the manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads: “the preachers.”

[^c0033-6]: [Col. 1357] Several manuscripts read: “as though my private thing, nor you your private thing.”

[^c0033-7]: [Col. 1357] All the manuscripts read this way. The editions have: “a sound faith.”

[^c0033-8]: [Col. 1357] Several manuscripts omit: “it was effective, as we have said to Your Charity.”

[^c0033-9]: [Col. 1358] The better manuscripts read: “flow forth once filled.” The editions have: “flow forth; fill others.”

## SERMON III

1. Your Charity remembers that we are debtors to you for treating the remaining parts of this psalm. Therefore there is no need for me to stir your attention with any preface.[^c0033-10] For I see you eagerly intent upon understanding the prophetic mysteries; nor is there any need for my sermon to make attentive those whom the Spirit of God has already made attentive.

Let us do rather what presses upon us. We have already spoken of the springs sent forth in the valleys and of the waters passing between the mountains; but we have spoken only up to that point. From here onward let us begin.

[^c0033-10]: [Col. 1358] So Ambrose, Erasmus, and the manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads: “to admonish.”

2. [v. 11.] For the Psalm continues: “All the beasts of the forest will drink.” What will they drink? The waters passing between the mountains. What will they drink? The springs sent forth in the valleys. And who will drink? The beasts of the forest.

We certainly see this also in the visible creation: the beasts of the forest drink from springs and from streams running between the mountains. But since it has pleased God to conceal his wisdom under the figures of such things—not to take it away from the diligent, but to shut it up from the negligent and open it to those who knock—it has also pleased our Lord God to exhort you through us to seek, in all these things that are spoken as though they concerned bodily and visible creation, something spiritually hidden, so that, when we find it, we may rejoice.

We understand the beasts of the forest as the Gentiles, and Scripture bears witness to this in many places. Yet two especially clear examples present themselves. In Noah’s ark, which no one among us doubts was a prefiguration of the Church, all kinds of animals would not have been enclosed (Gen. 7:2, 14) unless all the nations were signified in that unity of structure. Unless perhaps we suppose that, if all such creatures were completely destroyed by the Flood, God would have lacked the power to command the earth to produce them, just as it had produced them at his first word (Gen. 1:24).

Therefore it was not without reason, not rashly, and not because of any need or lack of power on God’s part that those animals were commanded to be enclosed in the ark.

For after the time came—and now we ought to add the second, most evident testimony—when the time came for what had been prefigured in the ark to be fulfilled in the Church, the Apostle Peter hesitated to give the Gospel sacrament to uncircumcised Gentiles. Rather, he did not hesitate, but thought that it should absolutely not be given. One day, being hungry and wishing to eat, he went up to pray.

This is known to all who read and hear the Acts of the Apostles attentively. While he was praying, a mental transport came upon him, which the Greeks call *ekstasis* (ἔκστασις): that is, his mind was turned away from its bodily habit in order to contemplate a certain vision, removed from present things.[^c0033-11]

Then he saw a certain vessel, like a linen cloth, being let down from heaven by its four corners; in it were all the animals, beasts of every kind. And a voice sounded to him: “Peter, kill and eat.”

But he, who had been instructed in the Law, had grown up in Jewish custom, retained the commandment given through Moses, God’s servant, and had faithfully observed his whole life, replied: “Far be it from me, Lord; never has anything common entered my mouth.”

Those who have learned the ecclesiastical Scriptures know well that “common” is what the Jews and the Law call unclean. And the voice said to him: “What God has cleansed, do not call unclean.” This happened three times, and the vessel that had been shown, lowered from heaven three times, was taken up again (Acts 10:9–16).

The vessel held by its four corners was the world in its four regions. Scripture often names these four regions: east and west, north and south. Therefore, because the whole world was being called through the Gospel, four Gospels were written.

The vessel lowered from heaven three times signifies this, because it was said to the Apostles: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

From this, as you already know, the number twelve of the disciples is also understood. It was not without reason that he wished to have twelve; and that number was so sacred that, when one had fallen, no one but another could be appointed in his place.

Why twelve Apostles? Because there are four regions of the world, and the whole world was being called in the Gospel, which is why four Gospels were written; and the whole world is called in the name of the Trinity, so that the Church may be gathered. Four multiplied by three makes twelve.

Therefore we should not be surprised that all the beasts of the forest drink from those waters passing between the mountains, from that apostolic teaching flowing in the midst because of the fellowship of concord.

For they were all in the ark; they were all in the vessel; Peter kills and eats them all, because Peter is the rock, and the rock is the Church.

What does “kill and eat” mean? To kill in them what they were, and to take them into his own body. You dissuaded a pagan from sacrileges: you killed what he was; by giving him Christ’s sacrament, you incorporated him into the Church—you ate him.

[^c0033-11]: [Col. 1359] So Ambrose, Erasmus, and the manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads: “alien.”

3. These beasts, then, drink those waters, but the waters are passing through: they do not remain; they pass through. For all the teaching administered throughout this present time passes away.

Thus the Apostle says: “Knowledge will be destroyed, and prophecy will be abolished.” Why will these be abolished? “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, what is in part will be abolished” (1 Cor. 13:8–10).

Surely Your Charity does not suppose that, in that city to which it is said, “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion, because he has strengthened the bars of your gates” (Ps. 147:12–13), once the bars have been strengthened and the city closed—of which we said previously that no friend goes out and no enemy enters—some book will need to be read or some sermon treated there in the way it is being treated for you now.[^c0033-12]

It is treated now so that it may be retained there; now it is divided syllable by syllable so that there it may be contemplated whole and entire.

The word of God will not be lacking there; yet it will not be there through letters, sounds, books, a reader, or a commentator. How, then? As it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.” For he did not come to us in such a way as to depart from there, because “he was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:1, 10).

We shall contemplate such a Word. “The God of gods will appear in Zion” (Ps. 83:8). But when? After the journey, when the road has been completed—provided that, after the road has been completed, we are not handed over to the judge, so that the judge may send us to prison.

But if, when the road has been completed, we come to our homeland, as we hope, desire, and strive to do, there we shall contemplate what we shall always praise. Neither what is present to us nor we who enjoy it will fail; neither will the one who eats grow weary, nor will what he eats fail.[^c0033-13]

Great and marvelous will that contemplation be. And who can speak worthily of it at this time, while the waters flow between the mountains?

For the present, then, let the waters flow between the mountains and pass through. While the waters pass through, one drinks during the journey, lest we fail from thirst on the road.

“All the beasts of the forest will drink.” From there you came; you were gathered from the forest. And what kind of forest? No human being passed through it, because no prophet had been sent there.

But wood was cut from the forests for the construction of the ark: from there came the wood, from there the beasts, from there you came. Therefore drink.

“All the beasts of the forest will drink.”

[^c0033-12]: [Col. 1360] Compare *Enarrationes in Psalmum* 84, §10, and on Psalm 147, at verse 13, where you will find this same statement.

[^c0033-13]: [Col. 1360] The editions read: “nor will what is eaten fail.” The manuscripts read: “nor will what he eats fail.”

4. “The wild asses will receive [the waters] for their thirst.” He calls certain large beasts wild asses. For who does not know that *onagri* means wild asses? He therefore speaks of certain great, untamed creatures.

The Gentiles had no yoke of the Law. Many nations lived according to their own customs, wandering about with proud boasting as in a desert. All the beasts are like this, but the wild asses are placed here to signify greatness.

They too will drink for their thirst; for the waters flow for them as well. From there the hare drinks, from there the wild ass: the hare is small, the wild ass large; the hare is timid, the wild ass fierce. Both drink from the same source, but each according to his thirst.

The water does not say, “I am sufficient for the hare,” and drive away the wild ass. Nor does it say, “Let the wild ass approach; if the hare approaches, he will be snatched away.” It flows so faithfully and temperately that it satisfies the wild ass without frightening the hare.

The sound of Tullian eloquence rings out; Cicero is being read, some book, one of his dialogues—or Plato’s, or someone else’s of that kind. The unlearned hear it, the weak, those of lesser courage; who dares aspire to it? It is the roar of water, perhaps troubled water; at any rate it flows so violently that the timid creature does not dare approach and drink.

To whom does it sound, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), and he does not dare drink? To whom does the Psalm sound, and he says, “It is too much for me”? Behold, the Psalm now sounds; certainly its mysteries are hidden. Yet it sounds in such a way that children delight to hear it, the unlearned approach to drink, and, once satisfied, belch forth in singing psalms.

The smaller and the larger beasts drink, then; but the larger drink more fully, because “the wild asses will receive [the waters] for their thirst.”

Let the smaller beasts drink what was said: “Men, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church. Women should be subject to their husbands” (Eph. 5:25, 24). Let the smaller drink.

But the Lord was asked: “Is it lawful to dismiss one’s wife for every reason?” The Lord forbade it and said that it was not lawful. “Do you not know,” he said, “that God made male and female from the beginning? What God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

Then he added: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and if he marries another, he commits adultery” (Matt. 19:3 and following). He tightened the fetter. This is useful for the person bound; he should first have acted so as not to be bound.

“Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife” (1 Cor. 7:27).

If you are not yet a wild ass, but are released from a wife, you have there something to drink as a hare; and if you take a wife, you have not sinned.

But when the disciples heard the Lord say that marriages could in no way be dissolved except on account of fornication, they said: “If such is the situation with a wife, it is not expedient to marry.” And the Lord said: “Not everyone grasps this word” (Matt. 19:10–12).

For you speak truly: if such is the situation with a wife, it is not expedient to marry. But will only the wild asses drink? “Not everyone grasps this word”; many do not grasp it. And who are those who grasp it? “The wild asses will receive [the waters] for their thirst.”

What does “The wild asses will receive [the waters] for their thirst” mean? Let the one who can grasp it receive it.

5. [v. 12.] Then the Psalm continues in its sequence: “Above them the birds of heaven will dwell.” Above whom? Above the wild asses, or rather above the mountains? For the meaning is directed from that point: “Between the mountains the waters will pass through; all the beasts of the forest will drink; the wild asses will receive [the waters] for their thirst; above them the birds of heaven will dwell.”

We understand more appropriately that it means above the mountains, because this too corresponds to the visible creation. Birds can dwell above mountains, but not above wild asses. We would understand it this way if necessity compelled us.[^c0033-14]

“Above the mountains, then, the birds of heaven will dwell.” We see birds dwelling on mountains; but many of them dwell in plains, many in valleys, many in groves, and many in gardens—not all on mountains. There are certain birds that dwell only on mountains.

This name signifies certain spiritual souls: the birds are spiritual hearts, which enjoy the free air. These birds rejoice in the clear sky; nevertheless, their food is on the mountains. There they will dwell.

You know the mountains; they have already been discussed. The mountains are the Prophets, the Apostles, and all preachers of the truth. Whoever wishes to be spiritual should dwell there; let him not wander in his own heart. Let him dwell there, reaching his goal in flight.[^c0033-15]

We have birds signifying something spiritual. It was not said without reason: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102:5). Nor was it said without reason concerning Abraham: “But he did not divide the birds.”

In that very mysterious sacrifice Abraham received three animals: a three-year-old ram, a three-year-old heifer, and a three-year-old she-goat, together with a turtledove and a pigeon. The ram was divided, and the pieces were placed opposite one another; the she-goat was divided, and likewise its pieces were placed opposite one another; the heifer was divided, and the same was done with its flesh. Then Scripture added: “But he did not divide the birds.”

It also says “a three-year-old ram, a three-year-old heifer, and a three-year-old she-goat”; but it says nothing about the age of the birds. Why, I ask you, unless certain spiritual people are signified in the birds, whose temporal age is therefore omitted because they contemplate eternal things and, in desire and understanding, transcend all temporal things?

They are spiritual men who judge all things and are judged by no one (1 Cor. 2:15). Therefore they alone are not divided into heresies and schisms.

The ram signifies the leaders, for they lead flocks. The heifer signifies the people of the Jews, for it had the yoke of the Law under which it labored. The she-goat signifies the Church from the Gentiles, which bounded about in certain free leaps and fed upon the bitter wild olive.

These animals are said to be three years old because grace was revealed in the third period. The first period was before the Law; the second was from the time when the Law was given; the third is the present period, from the time when the kingdom of heaven has been preached.

What, then, shall we say—that the ram is not divided? Were bishops not the authors of schisms and heresies? But if the peoples themselves were not divided—that is, if the heifer were not divided and the she-goat were not divided—perhaps those leaders would have been ashamed of their divisions and returned to unity.

Leaders are divided, and peoples are divided as well, so that “the blind may lead the blind, and both fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14). They are placed opposite one another.

“But he did not divide the birds.” Spiritual people have no division; they do not contemplate schisms. Peace is in them; they preserve it in others insofar as they can, and where others fail, they retain it in themselves.

“If there is a son of peace there,” he says, “your peace will rest upon him; if not, it will return to you” (Luke 10:6). He is not a son of peace; he wished to be divided; your peace will return to you, because “he did not divide the birds.”

The furnace will also come. For Abraham sat there until evening, and the great terror of the day of judgment came. That evening is the end of the age; and that furnace is the coming day of judgment. The furnace also divided what had been divided between the pieces (Gen. 15:9–17). When the furnace passed between the pieces, it separated some to the right and others to the left.

There are therefore certain carnal people who nevertheless are contained within the embrace of the Church. They live according to a certain manner of life, and we fear that they may be led astray by heretics. For as long as they are carnal, they are divisible.

“But he did not divide the birds”; carnal people are divided. “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people.” And how is it proved that carnal people are divided? He adds: “For when each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I to Apollos,’ or ‘I to Cephas,’ are you not carnal, and walking according to human ways?”

I ask you, brothers: listen and advance. Shake yourselves free from the carnal position; proceed into the turtledove and the pigeon. “For he did not divide the birds.”

But whoever remains such, living according to a certain manner suited to the carnal, and does not withdraw from the embrace of the Church, and is not led astray by heretics so as to be divided onto the opposite side—the furnace will come, and he cannot be placed on the right without passing through the furnace.

But if he does not wish to suffer the furnace, let him proceed into the turtledove and the pigeon. Let the one who can grasp it grasp it.

But if this does not happen, and he builds upon the foundation wood, hay, and straw—that is, if he builds worldly loves upon the foundation of his faith—nevertheless, if Christ is in the foundation, so that he holds the first place in the heart and nothing at all is placed before him, such people too are carried along and tolerated. The furnace will come; it will burn the wood, hay, and straw. “But he himself,” he says, “will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 1:12–13; 3:1–15).

This is what the furnace will do: it will separate some to the left, while it will in a certain manner purify others to the right.

“But he did not divide the birds.” Let the birds see whether they are such birds as dwell upon those mountains. They must not follow the height of their own hearts, concerning which it is said: “They have set their mouth against heaven” (Ps. 72:9). Lest they be lifted up by the winds, let them rest upon the mountains.

They have the authority of the saints; let them rest upon the mountains, upon the Apostles and the Prophets. Let such birds dwell there, because on the mountains they find rocks, certain firm supports of commandments.

For just as that one rock is Christ, the Word of God, so there are many words of God, many rocks; and these rocks are on the mountains.

See the birds dwelling there: “Above them the birds of heaven will dwell.”

6. But do not suppose that these birds of heaven follow their own authority; see what the Psalm says: “From the midst of the rocks they will give forth their voice.” Now, if I say to you, “Believe this, for Cicero said it; Plato said it; Pythagoras said it,” which of you would not laugh at me? For I would be a bird that does not send forth its voice from the rock. What ought each one of you to say to me? What ought one who has been instructed in this way to say? “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:9). Why do you speak to me of Plato, Cicero, and Virgil? You have before you the rocks of the mountains; from the midst of the rocks give me your voice. “From the midst of the rocks they will give forth their voice.” Let those be heard who hear from the Rock [Note: [Col. 1363] Thus several manuscripts. Some others read: “Let them hear who hear from the Rock.” But the editions read: “Let them be heard, because the rocks are heard.”]: let them be heard, because in those many rocks the Rock is heard also; for “the Rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). Let them therefore be heard gladly, giving forth their voice from the midst of the rocks. Nothing is sweeter than the voice of such birds. They sound, and the rocks resound: they sound—the spiritual persons discuss; the rocks resound—the testimonies of Scripture answer. Behold, from there the birds give forth their voice from the midst of the rocks; for they dwell in the mountains.

7. [verse 13] The mountains themselves, and those rocks, from where do they have their voice? In order that we may be watered by the Scriptures, we flee for refuge to the apostle Paul. From where does he have it? We flee for refuge to Isaiah. Isaiah, from where? Hear from where: “Watering the mountains from his upper places.”

Now, if an uncircumcised Gentile should come to us, intending to believe in Christ, we give him baptism and do not send him back to those works of the Law. And if a Jew asks us why we do this, we sound forth from the Rock and say, “Peter did this; Paul did this”: from the midst of the rocks we give forth our voice. That Rock itself—Peter, the great mountain—when he was praying and saw that vision, was watered from the upper places. The apostle Paul says to the Gentiles: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2). Paul says this as a mountain; from there we speak, sounding forth from the Rock.

The Lord waters that Rock itself from his upper places. For while this Rock was still rough in unbelief, and he wished to water it from his upper places so that water might flow into the valley, he cried out: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” He did not read him a prophet, nor did he read him another apostle; for the great mountain would have despised all these things. He watered him from his upper places, and immediately, having been watered and now desiring to pour forth, he said: “Lord, what do you command me to do?” (Acts 9:4, 6). Take that mountain, or rock, from which you can give forth your voice; take it, and see it watered from above and flowing forth below.

Hear this also in one passage: “Whether we were beside ourselves, it was for God; whether we are sober-minded, it is for you.” What he says, “we were beside ourselves,” you cannot grasp: for we have gone beyond all these carnal things, while you are still carnal. We were beside ourselves for God; and what we see when we go beyond ourselves we cannot express. For there he heard “inexpressible words, which it is not permitted for a human being to utter” (2 Cor. 12:4).

What then, those carnal people, those hares, say: “Will we not be watered? Will nothing reach us? And how does he send forth springs in the valleys? And how will the waters pass through the midst of the mountains?” To this, then, belongs the phrase, “Whether we are sober-minded, it is for you.” From where does this come [Note: [Col. 1364] Thus most manuscripts, supported by Ambrose and Erasmus. The Louvain edition has: “From where also this one whom he imitates.”]? Whom do we imitate? “The love of Christ,” he says, “constrains us” (ibid. 5:14).

You are a participant in the Word; even if today you are spiritual, yesterday you were carnal. Do you disdain to descend to the carnal, when the Word himself became flesh in order to dwell in you (John 1:14)?

8. Let us therefore bless the Lord and praise him who waters the mountains from his upper places. From there watering will come to the earth; from there the lowly also will be satisfied. For it follows: “From the fruit of your works the earth will be satisfied.”

What is “from the fruit of your works”? “Let no one glory in his works; but whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31). Your grace satisfies you when you are satisfied; let no one say that grace was given on account of his merits. If it is called grace, it is given freely; if it is repaid according to works, it is a reward that is repaid (Rom. 4:4–5). Receive it freely, therefore, because you are justified as an ungodly person. “From the fruit of your works the earth will be satisfied.”

9. [verse 14] “Producing grass for cattle, and plants for the service of human beings.” It is true; I see and recognize the creation: the earth produces grass for cattle and plants for the service of human beings. But I also see other cattle of the Lord, signified when it is said, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” For the animal itself says: “Is it for oxen that God is concerned?” Scripture says this for our sake.

How, then, does the earth produce grass for cattle? Because the Lord established that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. He sent preachers and said to them: “Eat whatever is set before you” (Luke 10:8); “for the laborer is worthy of his wage” (Luke 10:7). When he had said, “Eat whatever is set before you,” lest they should say, “We shall be shameless at other people’s tables when we are in need. Do you want us to be so bold?”—he said, “No; that is not their donation, but your wage.”

The wage of what? What do they give, and what do they receive? They give spiritual things and receive carnal things; they give gold and receive grass. For “all flesh is grass, and all the glory of flesh is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6). All temporal things that overflow and abound for you are grass for cattle. Why? Because they are carnal.

Hear whose cattle this grass belongs to. “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” The Apostle said this, such a preacher—so laborious, so diligent, so practiced—that he even gave that grass to the earth. “I,” he says, “made use of none of these things.” He showed that they were owed to him, but did not accept them; nor did he condemn those who accepted what was owed. Those who demanded what was not owed were to be condemned, not those who received their wage. Yet he gave away even his own wage.

Because someone else has given something to you, you must not therefore fail to give to another; otherwise you will not be the watered earth that produces grass for cattle. “From the fruit of your works,” he says, “the earth will be satisfied, producing grass for cattle.” Do not be barren: produce grass for cattle. If the cattle do not want your grass, let them nevertheless not find you barren. You receive spiritual things; repay carnal things. They are owed to the soldier; you repay them to the soldier. You are a provincial of Christ [Note: [Col. 1365] Concerning this term, see *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 90, Sermon 1, no. 10, and the note.]. Who has ever served as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who feeds a flock and does not receive milk from it?

I do not say this so that these things may be done for me. There was a certain soldier who even gave his provisions to a provincial; nevertheless, let the provincial repay the provisions. But to speak more appropriately here: they are cattle. “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” “Producing,” he says, “grass for cattle”; and, as though explaining this, he added, “and plants for the service of human beings.” So that you would not fail to understand what was said, “producing grass for cattle,” he explained it by repetition. What he called “grass” above, he later called “plants”; and what he had called “cattle,” he called “the service of human beings.” Therefore, service—and not freedom.

Where, then, is the saying, “You were called to freedom”? But hear the same man: “Although I am free from all, I made myself the servant of all, that I might win more” (1 Cor. 9:19). And to those to whom he said, “You were called to freedom,” what did he add? “Only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another” (Gal. 5:13).

Those whom he had made free, he made servants—not by condition, but nevertheless through Christ’s redemption; not by necessity, but by love: “Through love,” he says, “serve one another.” But, someone says, we serve one another for Christ, not peoples, not carnal persons, not the weak. You serve Christ well if you serve those whom Christ served. Is it not said of him, “Serving many well”? The Prophet is being read; this is usually understood of no one but Christ.

Let us nevertheless hear his own voice properly in the Gospel: “Whoever among you wishes to be greater will be your servant” (Matt. 20:26). He made you my servant, he who made you free by his blood. Tell us this, because you speak truly. Hear him elsewhere: “We are your servants through Jesus” (2 Cor. 4:5). Love your servants well, but in your Lord. May he grant us to serve well.
