For whether we wish it or not, we are servants; and yet, if we are willing, we serve not by necessity but by love.

A kind of pride among servants seemed to have been offended when the Lord said, “The one among you who wishes to be greater will be your servant.” For the sons of Zebedee were already seeking the highest seats: one wanted to sit at his right hand, the other at his left, expressing through their mother what they themselves desired. The Lord did not begrudge them the seats, but first showed them the valley of weeping, as if he were saying: “Do you wish to come there where I am? Come by the way I came.”

What does “Come by the way I came” mean? Through humility. “I descended from the heights, and in humiliation I ascend. I found you on earth, and you wish to fly before you have been nourished. First be fed, brought up, and carry the nest.”

For what did he say? How did he recall them to humility when they were already seeking exaltation? “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” And they, proud even in this, said: “We can.” As Peter said, “With you, even unto death” (Matt. 26:35). A strong man—until a woman said, “This man also was with them” (ibid. 26:69).

So also these men: “We can.” “Can you?” “We can.” And he said: “You will indeed drink my cup, even though now you cannot; you will drink it”—as he said to Peter, “You cannot follow me now; you will follow me afterward” (John 13:36). “You will indeed drink my cup; but to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you” (Matt. 20:20–27).

What does “It is not mine to give you” mean? It is not mine to give to the proud. At present, those to whom I am speaking, you are proud; therefore I said, “It is not mine to give you.” I did not say, “I will not give it to the humble,” but, “I will not give it to the proud.” But perhaps they might say, “We shall be humble.” Then it will not be you; I said, “to you.” I did not say, “I will not give it to the humble,” but, “I will not give it to the proud.” The king who becomes humble toward the proud will no longer be what he was.

10. Therefore the preachers of the Word are both cattle and servants. Let the earth, if it has been watered, produce grass for cattle and plants for the service of human beings. For this is the fruit, so that what was said in the Gospel may be fulfilled: “So that they may receive you into the eternal dwelling places” (Luke 16:9).

See what you should do with grass; see what you should buy with something of little value. “So that they may receive you,” he says, “into the eternal dwelling places”: where they themselves will be, there let them receive you. Why is this? Because “the one who receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward; and the one who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever gives one of these little ones only a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple—amen, I say to you, he will not lose his reward” (Matt. 10:41–42).

What reward will he not lose? “They will receive you into the eternal dwelling places.” Who would not hasten? Who would not run more eagerly?

If you are earth, be watered by the fruit of God’s works. Do not say, “There is no one with whom we can do this; our preachers, the cattle who tread out the grain, the serving men, do not need us.” Yet inquire whether someone is in need. Finally, let even one who does not need find in you what he does not wish to accept [Note: [Col. 1367] Thus the manuscripts of better quality. The editions read: “what he wishes to accept.”].

For he receives good will when you receive peace; even if he does not seek the gift, he seeks the fruit (Phil. 4:17). Yet inquire whether someone is in need, and do not say, “If he asks, I will give.” Are you waiting for him to ask? Do you feed God’s ox as though he were a passing beggar? You give to the one who asks because it is written, “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6:30). But what is written concerning this other matter? “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Ps. 40:2). Inquire whom you should give to: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor”—the one who anticipates the voice of the one about to ask.

If the soldiers of Christ are in such need among you that they even ask, see to it that they do not judge you before they ask. “How,” you say, “am I to inquire?” Be attentive; be provident. Look into how each person lives, from where he supports himself, what he possesses. Your attentiveness will not be reproved: you will be earth producing grass for cattle and plants for the service of human beings.

Be attentive and understand concerning the needy and the poor. One person comes to you in order to ask; another you should anticipate, so that he will not ask. Just as it is said of the one who seeks you, “Give to everyone who asks you,” so concerning the one whom you ought to seek it is said, “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give it.”

For although you must give also to these poor who ask [Note: [Col. 1367] The editions add here *patet* (“it is clear”), which is absent from the manuscripts], God did not forbid almsgiving to them. Christ himself says concerning them: “When you give a banquet, invite the blind, the lame, the weak, those who have nothing with which to repay you; and you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous” (Luke 14:13–14). Invite them also; feed them also. Feast when they feast; rejoice when they are filled. They have your bread; you have the justice of God.

Let no one say to you: “Christ commanded that one should give to a servant of God but not to a beggar.” Far be it from us; whoever says this speaks impiously. Give to him, but much more to the other. He asks, and in the voice of the one asking you recognize to whom you are giving. But the less the other asks, the more diligently you must watch so that you may anticipate the one who is about to ask—or perhaps the one who is not going to ask now but will one day condemn you.

Therefore be attentive to these matters, my brothers. You will find the neediness of many servants of God, if only you wish to find it. But because you enjoy the excuse by which you wish to say, “We did not know,” therefore you do not find them.

11. The Lord himself had a purse into which necessary things were put, and money was kept for the use of those who were with him and belonged to him. For when it is said that he was hungry (Matt. 4:2; 21:18), the Evangelist is not lying. He wished to be hungry for your sake, so that you would not hunger in him—he who, although rich, became poor so that we might be enriched by his poverty (2 Cor. 8:9).

He had a purse; and it is said of certain devout women that they followed wherever his feet went as he proclaimed the Gospel, and ministered to him from their possessions. Those women are named in the Gospel, among them the wife of a certain Chuza, Herod’s steward (Luke 8:3).

See what was happening. Paul was destined eventually to seek none of these things and to give everything to provincials. But because many weak people would seek such things, Christ assumed the person of the weak. Paul was more exalted—was Christ, then, not? Christ was more exalted because he was more merciful.

When he saw that Paul would not seek such things, he provided that the one who would seek them should not be condemned, and he offered an example for the weak. Just as he saw many eager and joyful people going to martyrdom, exulting in the very suffering—strong men, bearing a hundredfold, ripe for the granary—yet saw that some weak people might be troubled by the suffering that was to come, he wished to assume their person in his passion, so that they would not fail but would rather join the human will to the will of the Creator. Thus Christ said, “My soul is sorrowful even to death,” and again, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” He taught what the weak person should say, but then showed by following it what the weak person ought to do: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matt. 26:38–39).

Thus, just as in his passion he bore the person of the weak, prefigured in his own body—for they too are his members; indeed, it was not said without reason, “Your eyes saw my unfinished state, and in your book all shall be written” (Ps. 138:16)—so also, by having a purse and in a certain sense demanding provisions, not asking for them but allowing them to be provided [Note: [Col. 1368] Ambrose, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read: “not asking, but providing”], he assumed neediness.

Zacchaeus received him, and rejoiced (Luke 19:6). To whom was this good? To Christ, or to Zacchaeus? Truly, if Zacchaeus had not received him, was there no place for the Maker of the world to stay? Or if Zacchaeus had not fed him, would the one who satisfied so many thousands with five loaves have been in need?

Therefore, whenever someone receives a holy person, the benefit is bestowed not on the one received but on the one who receives him. Was Elijah not fed during that famine? Did not a raven bring him bread and meat, the creature serving the servant of God (1 Kings 17:6)? Yet he was sent to a widow to be fed—not so that something might be provided to a soldier, but so that something might be provided to a provincial.

12. Therefore, because we were speaking, brothers, also about feeding the poor: although the Lord had a purse, when he said to Judas, who was about to betray him, “What you are going to do, do quickly,” the others did not understand what he had said and supposed that he had told him to prepare something to be given to the poor. For he had a purse; this is written in the Gospel (John 13:27–29). They could not have supposed this unless the Lord had been accustomed to it.

From the things that were given and put into the purse, something was nevertheless given also to those poor whom God taught us not to despise. But if you do not despise that man, how much more should you not despise the ox by which this threshing floor is threshed? How much more your servant?

He does not need food; perhaps he needs clothing. He does not need clothing; perhaps he needs a roof. Perhaps he is building a church; perhaps he is undertaking something useful in the house of God. He waits for you to pay attention; he waits for you to understand concerning the needy and the poor.

But you, hard and stony earth, unwatered or watered in vain, preserve for yourself the excuse: “I did not know; I was unaware; no one told me.” No one told you? Christ does not cease speaking; the prophet does not cease speaking: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor.”

Do you not see the empty chest of your superior? Surely you see at least the building rising, the place into which you will enter and pray. Is it not brought before your eyes?

Unless perhaps you think, brothers, that your superiors are storing up treasures. We know that many do not store up treasures and are in need for their daily necessities—people whom no one at all suspects of this. You too would find them if you wished, if you looked around, if you watched for the purpose of producing fruit.

I have said what I could, as much as I could. I think we have been made clear to you, as the Apostle says—not that we say these things so that you may do them for us. May God grant that I have not said these things in vain. May God grant that you are watered earth, not stony earth like that of the Jews, from which they deserved to receive stone tablets, but fruitful earth—earth that, when watered, gives back to the farmer.

Those very people, with their stony heart signified by the stone tablets, gave tithes. You even groan, and nothing yet comes forth [Note: [Col. 1369] Ambrose, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read: “Even groan, and let nothing come forth here.”]. If you groan, give birth; if you give birth, bring forth. Why an empty groaning? Why a barren groaning? Are the entrails in torment, or is there nothing within to be brought forth?

“Watering the mountains from his upper places: from the fruit of your works the earth will be satisfied.” Blessed are those who act; blessed are those who hear these things fruitfully; blessed are those who do not cry out in vain. “From the fruit of your works the earth will be satisfied, producing grass for cattle and plants for the service of human beings.”

Why this [Note: [Col. 1369] Thus the principal manuscripts. The editions read: “Why does he call it? Why this?”]? “So that he may bring bread out of the earth.” What bread? Christ. From what earth? From Peter, from Paul, and from the other stewards of truth.

Hear that it is from earth: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels,” he says, “so that the surpassing greatness may be God’s power” (2 Cor. 4:7). He is the bread that came down from heaven (John 6:41), so that he might be brought forth from earth when he is proclaimed through the flesh of his servants.

The earth produces grass so that it may bring bread out of the earth. What earth produces grass? The devout peoples, the holy peoples. From what earth is bread brought forth? The Word of God from the Apostles, from the stewards of God’s sacraments, who still walk on earth and still carry an earthly body.

13. [verse 15] “And wine gladdens the human heart.” Let no one prepare himself for drunkenness; rather, let every person prepare himself for drunkenness. “How splendid is your cup, which makes one drunk!” (Ps. 22:5). We do not wish to say, “Let no one become drunk.” Become drunk, but see from what.

If the splendid cup of the Lord makes you drunk, this drunkenness will be seen in your works; it will be seen in a holy love of righteousness; finally, it will be seen in the alienation of your mind—but from earthly things toward heaven.

“So that he may gladden his face with oil.” I see what fruit this earth produces if it produces grass for cattle. These servants do not sell what they give; they are not sellers of the Gospel. They give freely because they received freely. They rejoice in your good works; for this benefits you. They do not seek the gift but seek the fruit.

What is the gladdening of the face with oil? The grace of God, a certain radiance made manifest, as the Apostle says: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:7). A certain grace that is visible among human beings, for the purpose of fostering holy love, is called oil, in divine radiance. And because it appeared most excellently in Christ, the whole world loves him. Although he was despised here, he is now worshiped by every nation: “For the kingdom is his, and he will rule the nations” (Ps. 21:29).

So great is his grace that many who do not believe in him praise him, and for that very reason say that they do not wish to believe in him, because no one can fulfill what he commands. Those who were raging against him by reviling him are hindered by praising him. Yet he is loved by all and proclaimed by all; because he was anointed excellently, therefore he is Christ. For Christ means “Anointed,” named from *chrism*. “Messiah” in Hebrew, “Christ” in Greek, “Anointed” in Latin; but he anoints his entire body. Therefore all who come receive grace, so that the face may be gladdened with oil.

14. “And bread strengthens the human heart.” What does this mean, brothers? It is as though he compelled us to understand what bread he was speaking about. This visible bread strengthens the stomach and strengthens the belly; there is another bread that strengthens the heart, because it is the bread of the heart.

He had already spoken above of bread: “So that he may bring bread out of the earth,” but he had not said what kind of bread it was. “And wine gladdens the human heart.” He now seems to be speaking of spiritual wine, for that gladdens the human heart. But let it still be thought that this refers to ordinary wine, because drunken people appear to be joyful in heart. Would that they were joyful and did not quarrel! You say to me, “What is more joyful than a drunk person?” Rather, what is more insane than a drunk person? What is usually more irritable?

There is therefore a wine that truly gladdens the heart and knows nothing except how to gladden the heart. But lest you think that this too should be understood of spiritual wine, while the bread should not, he explained that the bread also is spiritual: “And bread,” he says, “strengthens the human heart.”

Therefore understand the bread in the same way as you understand the wine. Hunger inwardly; thirst inwardly: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6). That bread is righteousness; that wine is righteousness. It is truth; truth is Christ (John 14:6). “I am,” he says, “the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41); and, “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15:5). “And bread strengthens the human heart.”

15. [verse 16] “The trees of the field will be satisfied,” but by that grace brought forth from the earth. The trees of the field are the peoples of the nations. “And the cedars of Lebanon, which he planted.” The cedars of Lebanon are the powerful of this age, and they too will be satisfied.

The bread, wine, and oil of Christ have reached senators, nobles, and kings; the trees of the field have been satisfied. First the lowly were satisfied, then also the cedars of Lebanon—but those whom he himself planted: devout cedars, religious believers; for he planted such trees [Note: [Col. 1370] The editions omit the word “devout.”].

For there are also ungodly cedars of Lebanon, since “the Lord will shatter the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. 28:5). Lebanon is a mountain; there, literally speaking, the trees are also very ancient and magnificent. Lebanon, however, is interpreted—as we read in those who wrote these things—as “whiteness” or “whitening.” Lebanon is called “whitening”; and it appears to be the whitening of this age, now shining and glittering in its pageantry.

There are cedars of Lebanon whom the Lord planted; they will be satisfied—those whom the Lord planted. For “every plant,” he says, “that my Father did not plant will be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13). “And the cedars of Lebanon, which he planted.”

16. [verse 17] “There the sparrows will build their nests. The house of the coot is their leader.”

Where will the sparrows build their nests? In the cedars of Lebanon. We have already heard what the cedars of Lebanon are: the nobles of the age, exalted by birth, wealth, and honors. They too are satisfied—the cedars whom he himself planted.

In these cedars the sparrows build their nests. Who are the sparrows? Sparrows are birds and flying creatures of heaven, but small birds are ordinarily called sparrows. There are therefore certain spiritual persons nesting in the cedars of Lebanon. That is, there are servants of God who hear in the Gospel, “Leave everything of yours,” or, “Sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

The great have heard this, but the small have also heard it, and the small have wanted to do it and to become spiritual: not to be joined to wives, not to be worn down by the care of children, not to possess private dwellings to which they would be bound, but to enter a certain common life.

But what did these sparrows leave behind? They appear to be small sparrows of this age. What did they leave? What great thing did they leave?

One person converts and leaves his impoverished father’s cell—scarcely one bed and one chest. Yet he converts, becomes a sparrow, and seeks spiritual things. Good—very good. Let us not mock him; let us not say, “You left nothing.” Let the one who left much not become proud.

We know that Peter was a fisherman when he followed the Lord; what could he have left? Or his brother Andrew, or the sons of Zebedee, John and James—these too were fishermen (Matt. 4:18, 21). And yet what did they say? “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Luke 18:27).

The Lord did not say to him: “You have forgotten your poverty. What did you leave in order to receive the whole world?” He left much, my brothers—he left much—not only because he left whatever he possessed, but because he left whatever he desired to possess. For what poor person does not swell with hope for this age? Who does not daily desire to increase what he has? That desire was cut off: it was advancing toward infinity, but received a limit.

And was nothing left? Peter truly left the whole world, and Peter received the whole world. “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. 6:10).

Many do this: those who have little do this; they come and become useful sparrows. They appear small because they do not possess the height of secular dignity; they nest in the cedars of Lebanon.

For the cedars of Lebanon too—the noble, rich, and exalted of this age—when they hear with fear, “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor,” pay attention to their possessions, their estates, and all their superfluous resources by which they appear exalted, and they provide these things to the servants of God. They give fields; they give gardens; they build churches and monasteries; they gather sparrows, so that the sparrows may nest in the cedars of Lebanon.

Therefore the cedars of Lebanon whom the Lord planted are satisfied, and there the sparrows will nest. Consider the whole earth, whether this is not so. In saying these things, I have not only believed but also seen; experience itself has given me understanding. Ask those who know the broadest lands, and see in how many cedars of Lebanon those sparrows of whom I have spoken build their nests [Col. 1372].

17. But nevertheless, my brothers, if those sparrows are spiritual, although they nest in the cedars of Lebanon, they ought not to value the cedars of Lebanon greatly or think that those from whom their necessities are supplied are superior to them.

For they are sparrows, while the others are cedars of Lebanon. Therefore, “the house of the coot is the leader of the sparrows.” Although the sparrows nest in the cedars of Lebanon, the cedars of Lebanon are not the leaders of the sparrows.

Behold, the trees of the field—all the peoples—will be satisfied; and the cedars of Lebanon whom the Lord planted—all the noble and exalted faithful—will be satisfied. There, that is, in the cedars of Lebanon, the sparrows will nest. They will offer the branches of their resources to gather the small spiritual people.

The cedars of Lebanon whom the Lord planted offer these things and do them; they do them willingly; they know what they are doing, and they know what they are receiving. But although the sparrows will nest in the cedars of Lebanon, “the house of the coot is their leader.”

What is the house of the coot? The coot, as we all know, is a sea bird; it lives either in ponds or in the sea. It has a certain house not easily found on the shore, or perhaps never there, but among things that are in the middle of the water—usually on rocks surrounded by water.

We therefore understand that a rock is a suitable house for the coot. Nowhere does it live more strongly or securely than on a rock. On what kind of rock? One situated in the sea. Although it is battered by the waves, it breaks the waves and is not broken by them. This is the great virtue of a rock situated in the sea.

How many waves have battered our Rock, the Lord Christ? The Jews were dashed against him; they were broken, but he remained whole. And let everyone who imitates Christ be in this age—in this sea, where he cannot help but feel storms and tempests—in such a way that he yields to no wind and to no wave, but receives everything and remains whole.

Therefore, the house of the coot is both strong and humble. The coot’s house is not in the heights; nothing is stronger than that house, and nothing is humbler. The sparrows nest in the cedars because of present necessity, but they have that Rock as their leader—the Rock that is battered by waves and is not broken—for they imitate Christ’s sufferings.

And if perhaps the cedars of Lebanon become angry and stir up some trouble or scandal against the servants of God in their branches, the sparrows will indeed fly away from there. But woe to the cedar that remains without sparrows’ nests! The sparrows will not be shipwrecked or perish, because the house of the coot is their leader.

18. [verse 18] What follows, then? “The highest mountains are for the deer.” The deer are great and spiritual, surpassing in their course all the thorny brambles and thickets. “He makes,” he says, “my feet like the feet of deer, and he will set me upon the heights” (Ps. 17:34).

Let them hold the high mountains, the lofty commandments of God. Let them think lofty thoughts; let them hold what stands very high in the Scriptures; let them be justified in the highest things. Those mountains are for the deer, because they are high.

What about the lowly animals? What about the hare? What about the hedgehog? The hare is a small and weak animal; the hedgehog is also covered with thorns [Note: [Col. 1372] The editions add here “the lesser of them,” which is absent from the manuscripts]. The one is a timid animal; the other is covered with thorns.

What do the thorns signify if not sinners? Whoever sins daily, even if the sins are not great, is covered with very small thorns [Col. 1373]. In what he fears, he is a hare; in what he is covered with the smallest sins, he is a hedgehog. He cannot hold those lofty and perfect commandments.

For “the highest mountains are for the deer.” What, then? Do these others perish? No. The highest mountains are for the deer in such a way that you may also see what follows: “The Rock is a refuge for hedgehogs and hares.”

For “the Lord has become a refuge for the poor” (Ps. 9:10). Place that Rock on the earth: it is a refuge for hedgehogs and hares. Place it in the sea: it is the house of the coot. The Rock is useful everywhere.

It is useful also in the mountains: without the foundation of the Rock, the mountains would collapse into the depths. Was it not said earlier of the mountains, “There the birds of heaven will dwell; from the midst of the rocks they will give forth their voices”?

Therefore the Rock is our refuge everywhere: whether it is raised up in the mountains, whether it is battered by waves in the sea and is not broken [Note: [Col. 1373] Erasmus, the Lyons edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read this way. In B, “be broken.” M.]; or whether it is made firm on the earth. To it belong the deer, to it the coot, to it the hare and the hedgehog.

Let the hares beat their breasts, and let the hedgehogs confess their sins. Although they are covered with small and daily sins, they are not without the Rock, which taught them to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). “The Rock is a refuge for hedgehogs and hares.”

19. [verse 19] “He made the moon for appointed times.” We understand this spiritually as the Church, growing from a small beginning and, in the mortality of this life, in a certain sense growing old, but so that it may draw near to the sun.

I am not speaking of the moon visible to the eyes, but of what is signified by that name. When the Church was obscure, when it had not yet appeared or become prominent, people were led astray, and it was said, “This is the Church; this is Christ,” so that they might shoot at the upright of heart in the obscure moon (Ps. 10:3).

Now, how blind is the one who goes astray when the moon is full? “He made the moon for appointed times.” For the Church passes through this age temporally; this mortality will not always exist here. Its waxing and waning will eventually pass away [Note: [Col. 1373] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “It can wax and wane; eventually it will pass away.”]. It was made for appointed times.

“The sun knew its setting.” And who is this sun, if not that sun of righteousness whose failure to rise the ungodly will lament on the day of judgment? They will say on that day: “Therefore we wandered from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. 5:6).

This sun rises for the one who understands Christ. But Christ withdraws from the understanding of the person who is so angry with his brother that he holds on to hatred. Therefore, “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). Even if love sometimes becomes angry in order to correct, it is not held guilty, because the anger has not grown old and turned into hatred.

But if anger has turned into hatred, the sun has set upon your anger. “Therefore, let the sun not set upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26).

20. And do not suppose, brothers, that the sun is to be worshiped on that account by some people, because in Scripture the sun sometimes signifies Christ. Such is the madness of human beings—as though something were said to be worshiped when it is said, “The sun signifies Christ.” Worship the rock, then, because it signifies Christ (I Cor. X, 4). “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII, 7); worship the sheep also, because it signifies Christ. “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. V, 5); worship the lion also, because it signifies Christ. See how many things signify Christ; all these are Christ by resemblance, not in their proper identity. Do you seek Christ’s proper identity? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.” Behold Christ’s proper identity, through whom you were made. Do you wish to hear also the proper identity through which you were restored? “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 1, 14). The rest are resemblances. Understand; be capable of Scripture, so that you may see one thing presented to your eyes and another thing signified to your heart.

21. Therefore, concerning that sun—the sun of righteousness—we may now say confidently: it is not without reason that it does not rise for the ungodly, even if they wish it to. Wisdom itself says, “The wicked will seek me, and will not find me. They will seek, and will not find me.” And why? “For they hated wisdom.” Wisdom itself speaks and says: “The wicked will seek me, and will not find me; for they hated wisdom” (Prov. I, 28–29). If they hated it, why do they seek it? They seek it not in order to enjoy it, but in order to inflate themselves; they seek it in words, but hate it in their conduct. “For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. I, 5). Therefore that sun does not rise for the ungodly; it does not rise for the wicked.

But what has been said about this sun? “Who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. V, 45). Therefore, this psalm signifies something concerning that sun of righteousness according to the mystery. For we see these things taking place in creation also, according to the appearance of visible things: “The sun has known its setting.” What does “The sun has known its setting” mean? Christ has known his passion: Christ’s setting is Christ’s passion. But does the sun set in such a way that it does not rise? “Will one who sleeps not add that he may rise again?” (Ps. XL, 9.) Did he himself not say, “I slept in turmoil”? And was it not said of him, “Be exalted above the heavens, O God” (Ps. LVI, 5–6)?

Therefore, “The sun has known its setting”: what does “has known” mean? It approved it; its setting pleased it. And from where do we show that he knew it—that is, that it pleased him? For what does God not know? What does Christ not know? And yet at the end he will say to certain people, “I do not know you” (Matt. VII, 23). How, then, is “I do not know you” there not to be understood as “You are unknown to me,” but rather as “You do not please me”? So here also, “The sun has known its setting” means that its setting pleased him. For if it had displeased him, how would he have suffered? A human being, since he is not that sun, suffers even when his suffering displeases him, and undergoes what he does not wish. But Christ would not have suffered unless it had pleased him—that is, unless he had known his setting, he would not have set. For he himself said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again; no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John X, 18). Therefore, he knew his setting.

22. [Verses 20–21.] And what happened when the sun set, when the Lord suffered? A certain darkness came over the apostles; their hope failed, although at first he had seemed to them great and the redeemer of all. Why? “You placed darkness, and it became night; there all the beasts of the forest will pass through. The lions’ cubs roar as they seek to seize prey, seeking from God their food” [Note: [Col. 1375] He has already expounded these verses above, in *Expositions of the Psalms* 100, §§ 12–13.].

What should I understand spiritually by the lions’ cubs except “the spiritual forces of wickedness” (Eph. VI, 12)? What should I understand except evil demons, which feed upon the errors of human beings? For there are princes of demons, and there are also certain contemptible demons. These demons seek to lead souls astray, but where the sun has not risen; for there is darkness. And when there is darkness, the lions’ cubs seek whom they may devour.

What was said about the greater lion himself, the prince of all such lions? “Do you not know that your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking whom he may devour?” (I Pet. V, 8.) Therefore, “seeking from God their food,” because no one can be tempted by the devil unless God permits it. The holy Job stood before the devil, and yet he was far from him: present to his sight, but removed from him in authority. When would the devil have dared to tempt either his flesh or the possessions he had, unless he had received power? Why, then, is power given? Either for the condemnation of the wicked or for the testing of the godly. The Lord justly governs all this; and the devil has power over no one, nor over anything belonging to anyone, unless he who possesses supreme and exalted power grants it.

Thus neither the devil nor human beings have power over another human being unless it is given from above. The judge of the living and the dead stood before a human judge; and the human judge, seeing Christ before him, puffed himself up and said: “Do you not know that I have power to kill you and release you?” But Christ, who had come to teach the very one by whom he was being judged, said: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John XIX, 10–11).

Human beings, the devil, and every kind of demon harm only by power they have received; but they do not harm those who are making progress. To the wicked they are like fire to hay; to the good they are like fire to gold. Judas was consumed like hay; Job was tested like gold.

“You placed darkness, and it became night; there all the beasts of the forest will pass through.” The beasts of the forest may now be understood in another way; for these things are always understood in different ways according to different contexts [Note: [Col. 1375] Three manuscripts: “often.”]. Thus the Lord himself is both lamb and lion. What is as different as a lamb and a lion? Yet what sort of lamb? One who would conquer the wolf and conquer the lion. He himself is rock, shepherd, and door. The shepherd enters through the door; and he says, “I am the good shepherd,” and he says, “I am the door” (John X, 7, 11).

The name “lion” signifies the Lord, because “the lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. V, 5); and it signifies the devil, because “you will trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. XC, 13). Learn to understand such expressions when they are used figuratively, lest, when you read that the rock signifies Christ (I Cor. X, 4), you suppose that everywhere the rock is Christ. Consider where a letter is placed in a word; there you understand its force. If you hear of the first letter in the name of God and suppose that it must always be placed there, you will erase it from the name of the devil. For the name of God begins with the same letter with which the name of the devil begins; yet nothing is as separate as God and the devil.

See, then, how absurd a person would be concerning both human and divine matters if he said of the single letter D, “It ought not to stand at the beginning of the devil’s name,” and, when you asked why, replied, “I read that letter in the name of God.” Such a person would be laughed at; indeed, he would not even be the sort of person to whom one would deem it worthwhile to give an answer.

Therefore, do not understand even these divine matters in such a childish way that one of you might suppose that, because I said earlier that the beasts of the forest signify the nations, whereas now I say that the beasts of the forest signify demons and rebellious angels, I am saying something contradictory. They are likenesses, and wherever they occur they are explained by their surrounding context.

“There all the beasts of the forest will pass through.” Where? In the night that the Lord established, because the sun knew its setting. “The lions’ cubs roar as they seize prey, seeking from God their food.” Rightly, the Lord, coming toward his setting—the sun of righteousness himself, acknowledging his setting—said to the disciples, as though darkness were about to come and a lion were about to prowl around seeking whom it might devour, though that lion would devour no one unless it asked permission [Note: [Col. 1376] Three manuscripts: “he said to his disciples.” Four continue: “as though they were about to be in darkness.”]: “This night Satan asked to sift you like wheat; and I prayed for you, Peter, that your faith might not fail” (Luke XXII, 31–32).

Was Peter not already between the lion’s teeth when he denied him three times (Matt. XXVI, 70–74)? “The lions’ cubs roar as they seize prey, and as they seek from God their food.”

23. [Verse 22.] “The sun has risen.” He who said, “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again,” knew his setting and laid down his life; the sun has risen and taken it up again. The sun has risen because the sun set, but the sun was not extinguished.

For those who do not understand Christ, it is still night; for them the sun has not yet risen. Let them persist in order to understand, lest they be seized by the roaring lion. For behold, the lions’ cubs do not dare to attack those for whom the sun has risen.

For the text continues: “The sun has risen, and they have gathered together, and they will lie down in their dens.” More and more, wherever [Note: [Col. 1376] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “there.”] this sun rises, so that it may be understood throughout the world and Christ may be glorified in the whole world, the lions’ cubs gather together. Those demons withdraw from persecuting the Church that were inciting the persecution of the house of God by working in the children of unbelief. For it was said: “According to the prince of the power of the air, who now works in the children of disobedience” (Eph. II, 2).

Now, because none of them dares to persecute the Church, the sun has risen and they have gathered together. And where are they? “And they will lie down in their dens.” Their dens are the hearts of unbelievers. How many carry lions lying down in their hearts? They do not burst forth from there; they do not attack this Jerusalem journeying as an exile. Why do they not attack? Because the sun has now risen and shines throughout the world.

24. [Verse 23.] See, then, what follows, because the sun has risen, they have gathered together, and they will lie down in their dens. What are you doing, O man of God? What are you doing, O Church of God? What are you doing, O body of Christ, whose head is in heaven? What are you doing, O human being who are its unity? “A man will go out,” it says, “to his work.” Let this man therefore perform good works in the security of the Church’s peace; let him work until the end.

For at some time there will be a certain darkening [Note: [Col. 1377] Several manuscripts: “a certain obscuration.”], and a certain attack will take place—but in the evening, that is, at the end of the world. For now the Church works in peace and tranquility, because “a man will go out to his work, and to his labor until evening.”

25. [Verse 24.] “How greatly magnified are your works, O Lord!” Rightly great, rightly exalted. Where were these works, so great, made? What was that standing-place of God where he stood, or what was that seat where he sat and performed these works? What place was it where he performed these things? From where did such beautiful things first proceed?

If you take it according to the literal sense, from where did all creation proceed—ordered, running in order, beautiful in order, rising in order, setting in order, and carrying out all times in order? And how did the Church receive growth, progress, and perfection? How is it directed toward a certain end of immortality? By what praises is it proclaimed? By what mysteries is it commended? By what sacraments is it concealed? By what preaching is it revealed?

Where did God do these things? I see great works: “How greatly magnified are your works, O Lord!” I seek where he made them, but I do not find the place. Yet I see what follows: “You made all things in wisdom.” Therefore you made all things in Christ.

That despised one, that one slapped, that one spat upon, that one crowned with thorns, that one crucified—you made all things in him. I hear, I hear what you announce about that soldier of yours to human beings; what you proclaim about that holy herald to the nations: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.” Let the Jews mock Christ crucified, because he is a stumbling block to them; let the pagans mock Christ crucified, because he is foolishness to them. “But we,” he says, “preach Christ crucified: to the Jews, indeed, a stumbling block; to the Gentiles, foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, 23–24). “You made all things in wisdom.”

26. “The earth is filled with your creation.” The earth is filled with Christ’s creation [Note: [Col. 1377] Thus several manuscripts. The editions have: “Your creation, O Christ.”]. And how? As we see: for what was not created by the Father through the Son? Whatever walks and crawls upon the earth, whatever swims in the waters, whatever flies in the air, whatever revolves in heaven—how much more the earth itself—the whole world is God’s creation.

But I do not know whether this signifies here something concerning a certain new creation, of which the Apostle says: “If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” [Note: [Col. 1377] The word “all things” is regularly omitted here in the manuscripts.]: “but all things are from God” (II Cor. V, 17–18). The new creation that has been made consists of all those who believe in Christ, who strip off the old person and put on the new (Eph. IV, 22, 24).

“The earth is filled with your creation.” In one place on earth he was crucified; in one small place that grain fell into the earth and died, but it bore abundant fruit. You were solitary, Lord Jesus, until you passed over; I recognize your voice in another psalm, where you said: “I am solitary until I pass over” (Ps. CXL, 10). You were therefore solitary until you passed over; you were solitary when you knew your setting. But from setting to rising you passed over. You rose, shone forth, and were glorified when you ascended into heaven, and the earth was filled with your creation.

Brothers, we have not yet finished the psalm; but let us defer something from it, in the name of Christ, until the Lord’s Day.

## SERMON IV

1. Your Charity remembers that, although there is one sermon of God spread throughout all the Scriptures, and although one Word sounds through the many mouths of the saints—though he is God with God in the beginning, and there has no syllables there because he has no temporal succession—we should not be surprised that, on account of our weakness, he descended into the fragments of our sounds, just as he descended to assume the weakness of our flesh (John I, 1, 14).

Nevertheless, your Charity remembers, as I said, that this psalm has already provided us with many sermons, and that the very mysteries enclosed here, so that they might be opened to those who knock, have occupied no small stretches of time for us over several days: as they are pronounced, commended, shown to be enclosed, opened, drawn out, and displayed. Thus you remember that even yesterday we could not reach the end of the psalm, and that we postponed it until today.

The Lord wished both to grant us the time for repayment, to enable me, a debtor, to satisfy the debt, and to make the exactors more secure. Let him himself therefore give us the good thing that we may repay, since he did not repay whatever evil we had done.

2. [Verses 24–25.] As you know, and as you recall with devotion and joy, the depths of our hearts cried out together with the psalm and said: “How greatly magnified are your works, O Lord! You made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your creation.”

Whatever was made by God was made in wisdom and through wisdom. Whatever knows wisdom, and whatever does not know wisdom but nevertheless exists within God’s creation, was made in wisdom and through wisdom.

Those who know wisdom possess the light of wisdom; those who do not know it nevertheless possess wisdom as the craftsman, although they themselves are held back by folly [Note: [Col. 1378] Several manuscripts omit “although they themselves are held back by folly.” Some have “wisdom” instead of “folly.” Others, with Am. and Er., have “in wisdom.”]. Those who possess its light also possess the craftsman; but not everyone who possesses the craftsman also possesses the light.

Among human beings, indeed, many become participants in it and are called wise; many are deprived of it and are called foolish. They are called foolish by a defective designation because, if they devote themselves to wisdom, seek it, ask for it, and knock, they can attain participation in it. For it is denied not by nature but by negligence.

There are other creatures that cannot become participants in wisdom: all beasts, all cattle, and all trees, which have no sensation at all. But because they cannot participate in wisdom, were they therefore not made in wisdom and through wisdom? God does not demand understanding from a horse or a mule; but he says to human beings, “Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. XXXI, 9).

[Col. 1379] What is nature in a horse is a crime in a human being. This, then, is what God says: “I do not demand participation in my wisdom from those whom I did not make in my image; but where I made it, from there I demand it, and I require the use of the thing I bestowed.”

Therefore human beings, returning to God what belongs to God, if they return to Caesar what belongs to Caesar (Matt. XXII, 21)—that is, returning to Caesar his image and returning to God his image—raise their own mind, not toward themselves, but toward their craftsman, toward the light from which they exist, and toward a certain spiritual warmth from which they burn, from which they grow cold when removed, from which they are darkened when they withdraw, and by which they are illuminated when they return.

And because they devoutly said to him, “You will light my lamp, O Lord; my God, you will enlighten my darkness” (Ps. XVII, 29), after the darkness of earthly folly has been dispelled, opening their mouths and drawing in the breath, they raise—as I have said—the confident eye of the heart. In the mind they survey the whole world: earth, sea, and heaven. Seeing all things beautifully arranged, running in order, divided into kinds, supported by seeds, changed through succession, and running through times, they take pleasure in the craftsman in these works, so that they too may please the craftsman in his work [Note: [Col. 1379] Thus several manuscripts. The editions have “in the craftsman.”].

And they cry out from great joy, because nothing can be compared with this gladness: “How greatly magnified are your works, O Lord! You made all things in wisdom.”

Where is that wisdom in which you made all things? By what sense is it reached? By what eye is it seen? By what effort is it sought? By what merit is it possessed? By what means, do you think, except by his grace? He who gave us existence gives us goodness. He gives it to those who turn back to him. Before they turned back, when they were going away after their own paths, did he not seek them? Did he not descend? Did not the Word become flesh and dwell among us (John I, 14)? Did he not light the lamp of his flesh while he hung upon the cross and seek the lost drachma (Luke XV, 8)?

He sought and found it, while the neighbors rejoiced—that is, the whole spiritual creation that draws near to God. With the neighbors rejoicing, the drachma was found; with the angels rejoicing, the human soul was found. It was found; let it therefore rejoice and say: “How greatly magnified are your works, O Lord! You made all things in wisdom.”

3. “The earth is filled with your creation.” With what creation of yours is the earth filled? With all trees and shrubs, with all animals and cattle; and with the whole human race itself, the earth is filled with God’s creation.

We see, we know, we read, we recognize, we praise, and in these things we proclaim him. Yet in these things we are not able to praise sufficiently, to the extent that our heart overflows from good contemplation.

But we must attend more closely to that creation concerning which the Apostle says: “If, then, anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (II Cor. V, 17). What old things have passed away? Among the Gentiles, all idolatry; among the Jews themselves, all that servitude of the Law, all those sacrifices that foretold the present sacrifice.

At that time the oldness of humanity abounded. He came who would renew his work; he came who would refine his silver, who would fashion his coin. And we see the earth full of Christians believing in God, turning away from their former impurities [Col. 1380] and idolatry, from their former hope toward the hope of the new age. And behold, it is not yet present in reality, but it is already possessed in hope; and through that hope we already sing and say, “The earth is filled with your creation.”

For we do not yet sing this in our homeland, not yet in that rest which is promised, not yet when the bars of the gates of Jerusalem have been secured (Ps. CXLVII, 13). We are still on pilgrimage, looking upon this whole world, and seeing people everywhere running toward the faith, fearing hell, despising death, loving eternal life, and scorning the present life. Filled with joy at such a spectacle, we say, “The earth is filled with your creation.”

4. This age is still shaken by waves of temptations; it is still disturbed by storms and squalls of tribulations and swelling [Note: [Col. 1380] Several manuscripts have “fears”; some have “swelling.”]. Yet this is the route by which we travel. Let the sea threaten and swell with waves; let it give birth to storms. This is the route by which we travel; a piece of wood has been given to us in which we may sail: “The earth is filled with your creation.”

But we are not yet in the land of the living; this is still the land of the dying. Yet we cry out and say: “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. CXLI, 6). In the land of the dying is my hope; in the land of the living is my portion. Behold this earth, which is filled with God’s creation.

The one who is still in this land of the dying, not yet in the land of the living—by what does he pass through? Hear what follows: “This sea is great and spacious; there are creeping things without number, small animals and great.”

The terrifying sea signifies something: there are creeping things without number. Ambushes creep through this age and suddenly seize the unwary. Who can count the creeping temptations? They creep; but beware lest they steal upon you.

Let there be watchfulness upon the wood; even in the waters [Note: [Col. 1380] The editions add: “we sail upon the cross”; this is absent from the better manuscripts.], even amid the waves, we are safe. Let Christ not sleep; let faith not sleep. And if it should sleep, let it be awakened. He will command the winds and calm the sea (Matt. VIII, 24–26); the journey will end, and there will be joy in our homeland.

“There are creeping things without number; small animals and great.” For I still see in this frightening sea those who do not yet believe. They move about in bitter and barren waters; yet they are both small and great. We know this: many of the small people of this age have not yet believed; many of the leading people of this age have not yet believed. Small and great animals are in this sea.

They hate the Church and are oppressed by the name of Christ; they do not rage because they are not permitted to do so. Their rage is shut up in the heart and does not break out into action. For all those, whether small or great—small and great animals—who now grieve that the temples are closed, the altars overturned, the images shattered, and laws enacted making sacrifice to idols a capital crime—all who grieve these things are still in the sea.

What, then, are we to do? Toward the homeland to which we are going? Through the sea—but upon the wood. Do not fear the danger; the wood carries you, and it contains the age.

Therefore pay attention: “This sea is great and spacious; there are creeping things without number, small animals and great.” Do not fear; do not be terrified. Desire the homeland; understand that you are on pilgrimage.

5. [Verse 26.] “There the ships will travel.” Behold, in the very thing that caused fear, ships float and are not sunk. By the ships [Col. 1381] we understand the Churches. They travel amid storms, amid the tempests of temptations, amid the waves of the age, amid small and great animals.

Christ is the pilot upon the wood of his cross. “There the ships will travel.” Let the ships not fear; let them not pay too much attention to where they are floating, but to whom they are entrusted to steer them. “There the ships will travel.” What passage could they find sorrowful when they perceive that Christ is the pilot? They will travel safely; let them travel perseveringly; they will come to their appointed end and be brought to the land of rest.

6. In this sea there is also something that surpasses all the small and great animals. What is it? Let us hear the psalm: “This dragon whom you formed to mock him.”

There are creeping things without number; there are small and great animals; there the ships will travel. And they will not fear—not only the creeping things without number, nor the small and great animals, but not even the dragon who is there: “Whom you formed,” he says to God, “to mock him.”

A great secret—but nevertheless I shall speak of something you know. You know a certain dragon who is the enemy of the Church. You have not seen him with the eyes of the flesh, but you see him with the eyes of faith. He is also called a lion. Scripture says of him: “You will trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. XC, 13). He has been subjected to your head, and he will be subjected to his body as well. Let the members cling only to their head, so that they may be his members.

It was said concerning the first woman whom this dragon deceived—namely, that Eve to whom he gave counsel of death, and who, through his cunning persuasion, entered the woman’s heart like a serpent. What happened is known to us; what happened there is also what we did, and what we mourn. For in those two human beings was the whole human race: from there came the offspring of death, and from there the guilt that is owed even by infants.

“For who is pure,” Scripture says, “in your sight? Not even an infant whose life upon the earth is a single day” (Job XIV, 4–5). The transmission of sin, the transmission of death, came from the first sin.

You know also what was said to the woman—or rather, to the serpent—when God heard of the sin of the first human being: “She will watch your head, and you will watch her heel” (Gen. III, 15). This was said in a great mystery, said in a figure of the future Church, made from the side of her husband—and from the side of one who was sleeping.

Adam was a form of the one who was to come. The Apostle says this: “He is a form of the one who was to come” (Rom. V, 14). What was to happen was prefigured: the Church was made from the side of the Lord sleeping upon the cross. For from the side of the crucified one, when it was pierced (John XIX, 34), the sacraments of the Church flowed forth.

What, then, was said to the Church? Listen now, understand, and beware: “She will watch your head, and you will watch her heel.”

O Church, watch the serpent’s head. What is the serpent’s head? The first suggestion of sin. Something illicit comes into your mind; do not keep your mind there; do not consent. That which comes into your mind is the serpent’s head. Trample the head, and you will escape the remaining impulses.

What does “trample the head” mean? Despise the suggestion itself. But it has suggested profit: “There is great profit there; there is great gold there. If you commit this fraud, you will be rich.” It is the serpent’s head; trample it.

What does “trample it” mean? Despise what it has suggested. But it has suggested great gold. “And what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI, 26.) Let the world’s profit perish, lest the soul suffer harm. By saying this, you have watched the serpent’s head and trampled it.

But that devil watches your heel. What does “he watches your heel” mean? He watches for when you slip from the way of God. You watch the first suggestion; he watches for your fall. For if you slip, you fall; if you fall, he will take possession. But so that you may not fall, do not leave the way.

God has laid out for you a narrow path; whatever lies outside it is slippery. Therefore Christ is light, and Christ is the way: “He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I, 9); and, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). Through me you go; you go to me [Note: [Col. 1382] The editions have: “if you go to me.” The particle “if” is absent from the manuscripts.]. If, then, he himself is the light and he himself is the way, if you withdraw from him, you will be neither in the light nor on the way. And what follows you? As a certain psalm says of the wicked: “Let their way be darkness and slipperiness” (Ps. XXXIV, 6).

7. This dragon, then, our ancient enemy, hot with rage and cunning in ambush, is in the great sea. “This dragon whom you formed to mock him.” Now you mock the dragon; for this is why the dragon was made here.

He fell through his own sin from the lofty dwelling of heaven, and from an angel became the devil. He received a certain place of his own in this great and spacious sea. His kingdom, which you suppose it to be, is his prison.

For many say: “Why has the devil received such great power that he rules in this age, and has such strength and ability?” How much strength or ability does he have? Unless he is permitted, he can do nothing. Act in such a way that he is not permitted to act against you; or, if he is permitted to tempt you, let him depart defeated and not take possession.

He was permitted to tempt certain holy men, servants of God. They overcame him because they did not withdraw from the way; they did not slip, although he watched their heels.

That holy Job sat upon a dung heap and was running along the way. See how Job watched the devil’s head and how the devil watched Job’s heel. Job repelled the one making suggestions; the devil hoped for one who might slip. The devil also seized Job’s wife; he took away everything Job possessed and left only his wife as his helper—not as a consolation for her husband, but rather as a tempter [Note: [Col. 1382] Several manuscripts omit “but rather as a tempter.”]. He even seized her because she was not watching his head. For she was still Eve; but Job was no longer Adam.

When everything had been taken away, Job remained with his wife, through whom he might be tempted, and with God, by whom he might be governed. What could be poorer than Job if you consider his household? What could be richer than he was if you consider his heart?

See the poverty of his house: everything had been taken away. See the riches of his heart: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

“The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away.” He knew his ruler and his tempter; he knew the one who permitted his tempter to act. “Let the devil claim nothing for himself,” he said. “He has the will to harm, but he would not have the power unless he received it. To the extent that he received power, to that extent I suffer. Therefore I do not suffer from him, but from the one who gave him power. Let the pride of my tempter be despised; let the scourges of my Father be endured.”

The tempter was repelled; his head was watched; he could not penetrate the heart. He attacked a walled city from outside, but he did not conquer it.

Another temptation followed. He was permitted to act against Job’s body; he struck it with a severe wound from head to foot. Job wasted away with corruption, teemed with worms, and, having lost his household, sat upon the dung heap.

There Eve, taken captive, was placed by the devil—not to assist her husband, but to bring about his fall [Note: [Col. 1383] Several manuscripts: “There Eve, taken captive, was made subject to the devil as a helper, and set over her husband for his fall.” The readings of Am. and Er. come close to this.]. She suggested that God be blasphemed. At first she had suggested in paradise that God be despised; now she suggested that God be blasphemed. Then he prevailed over one whole; now he was defeated by one covered in corruption. In paradise he cast him down; upon the dung heap he was overcome.

The dragon was watching to see whether Job would slip with his tongue. For every human being has feet in what he does; in whatever he moves, there he walks, as it were. Job said many things; those who read know how much Job said. In all those many words the serpent watched the heel of the one who might slip.

But the one who watched the serpent’s head repelled every suggestion. He answered his wife as it was fitting to answer her: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil?” And amid all that he said, he nowhere slipped (Job II, 10).

Many do not understand what is contained in those words, and interpret certain passages there as though Job had said something harsh against God.

### 8.

For among the many things he said this also, as though he were angry with God—so it seemed to those who did not understand—whereas he was bearing the great personage of a great prophecy:

“Would that there were an arbiter for us,” he says, speaking to God (ibid. IX, 33, according to the Septuagint)!

What does “Would that there were an arbiter for us” mean? [Note: [Col. 1383] *O mesitēs hēmōn* (“our mediator”).] As though there were someone who would judge between us, and, with him judging, my case would prevail. This is how it is understood at first hearing. But examine yourself, lest you slip; for that serpent is always watching your heel.

What did Job seem to have said? “Would that there were an arbiter! Would that there were someone in the middle who would judge between me and you!” This was said by a human being to God, by a human being in the dung heap, even by an angel in heaven to God: “Would that there were an arbiter for us!”

But what was he foreseeing? What was he desiring? “Many,” says the Lord, “have desired to see what you see, and have not seen it” (Matt. XIII, 17). He was desiring an arbiter. What is an arbiter? One who stands between the parties to settle a case.

Were we not enemies of God, with a bad case against God? Who could bring this bad case to an end except that mediator-arbiter, without whose coming the way of mercy would have perished? Of him the Apostle says: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (I Tim. II, 5).

If he were not human, he would not be a mediator, because as God he is equal to the Father. In another place he says: “Now a mediator is not of one party; but God is one” (Gal. III, 20). A mediator is between two; therefore Christ is mediator between the human being and God—not because he is God, but because he is human. For because he is God, he is equal to the Father; but if he is equal to the Father, he is not a mediator. [Note: [Col. 1384] Thus several manuscripts. But Erasmus and the Louvain edition have: “not because as God he is equal to the Father; but if he is equal to the Father, he is not a mediator.” Some manuscripts read: “not because as God he is equal to the Father, but because as human he is less than the Father. If he is equal to the Father, he is not a mediator.”]

To be a mediator, then, let him descend from what is higher to what is lower, from equality with the Father; let him do what the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. II, 7). Let him pour out his blood, erase our bond of indebtedness (Col. II, 14), and reconcile us with God [Note: [Col. 1384] The editions read, “establish peace.” The word “peace” is absent from the manuscripts.]—correcting our will toward righteousness and bending his judgment toward mercy.

As, then, we have explained this one passage, insofar as the Lord granted it, which seems to have been harshly spoken by Job, so also the other things there that seem almost harsh and blasphemous have their meanings. We would have thought otherwise if God had not borne witness—both before Job spoke and after he had spoken everything.

First God bore witness, saying: “A man without reproach, truthful, a worshiper of God” (Job I, 8). God said this before his temptation. But lest anyone, misunderstanding those words, should be scandalized and think that Job had indeed been a righteous man before the temptation, but that during the temptation he had failed gravely and fallen into sacrilegious blasphemy, after all the speeches had ended—both Job’s and those of his friends, by whom consolation was being offered to him—the Lord bears witness that they had not spoken the truth, as his servant Job had.

“For you have not spoken,” he says, “anything true before me, as my servant Job has.” Then he commands that Job offer sacrifices on their behalf, by which their sins might be loosed (ibid. XLII, 7, 8).

### 9.

Come, my brothers: whoever wishes to watch the serpent’s head and cross this sea safely—for this serpent must necessarily dwell here, and, as I had begun to say, the devil, having fallen from heaven, received this place—let him watch its head, away from fear of the world and desire for the world. For from these he suggests something: either from what you fear or from what you desire; he tests either your love or your fear.

If you fear Gehenna and love the kingdom of God, you will watch his head. Once you have avoided the head, you will be safe; he will neither hold your fall nor rejoice in your ruin.

But let no one say, as I said: “He possesses great power.” People see, as it were, how much power he has received; what he has lost they do not see. [Note: [Col. 1384] Here the editions add “of majesty,” which is absent from the principal manuscripts.]

But holy Job himself, in his mystical and deeply hidden words, speaking of this power that the devil is said to possess, and describing him in many ways through figures of comparison, explaining what he is or what he can do, says this also:

“Nothing similar to him has been made upon the earth, to be mocked by my angels.” God is speaking there in the Book of Job: “Nothing similar to him has been made upon the earth, to be mocked by my angels. He sees every high thing; and he himself is king over all that are in the waters” (ibid. XLI, 24–25, according to the Septuagint).

This testimony agrees with the following passage in the Psalm. When he had spoken of the great and spacious sea, where there are small and great creatures, where there are creeping things without number, where ships sail safely on wood, he says: “This dragon whom you formed to be mocked.”

But if he was formed to be mocked, how does God mock him? Or did God hand him over to be mocked—that is, so that he might be mocked? We would think that God mocked him if the Book of Job had not resolved the question. There it is said: “To be mocked by my angels.”

Do you wish to mock the dragon? Be an angel of God. But you are not yet an angel of God. Until you become one—if you pursue the course by which you may become one—there are angels who mock the dragon, so that he may not harm you.

For the Angels of heaven have been placed over the aerial powers, and from there proceeds the word by which what happens here is accomplished. They behold the fixed law, the eternal law, commanding without writing, without syllables, without sound—always fixed and abiding. The Angels behold it with a pure heart, and from it they accomplish whatever happens here; and the powers are ordered by it, from the highest to the lowest.

And if the powers of the highest heavens are governed by the word of God, how much more the lower and earthly powers? In evil beings, then, there remains only the desire to harm. A human being has this desire to harm in his power, a will directed toward destruction. But if he has been able to harm anyone, let him not boast: power was given to him. The sentence was spoken once; it is firm: “There is no power except from God” (Rom. XIII, 1).

What, then, do you fear? Let the dragon be in the waters; let the dragon be in the sea—you are going to cross there. He was formed so that he might be mocked; he was appointed to this place, assigned to these dwelling places.

Do you think these dwelling places are something great for him, because you do not know the dwelling places of the Angels from which he fell? [Note: [Col. 1385] Thus the better manuscripts; and some of them omit “he was assigned.” After these words the editions read: “If you think these dwelling places are something great, because you do not know the dwelling places of the Angels from which he fell, you marvel at the dwelling places of the dead from which he was cast down. What seems to you…”] What seems to you to be his glory is his condemnation.

### 10.

Receive a brief comparison, because truly it is something great to know and understand this. Imagine the whole administration of creation as a great house. This great house has a master; it has servants; and among those servants it has some close to itself, in better arrangements of clothing, treasures, storehouses, and great possessions. It also has servants in the lowest offices, subject to such authorities that some are assigned even to clean the sewers. From the highest stewards down to these final and lowest services, how many grades there are!

Suppose, then, that some great steward should give offense and, as a punishment from his master, become a doorkeeper in some remote place. If, exercising the power given to him, he should trouble those wishing to enter or leave, according to the measure of power he had received from his master, while they did not know that he had once been a great steward, they would think his power great because they did not know what he had lost.

And yet, my brothers, that doorkeeper of whom I spoke, by comparison with this great earthly house, could do something without his master’s knowledge and trouble someone without his master’s command. But this one has not even been placed at that door by which we enter to God.

For Christ is that door, and through Christ we enter into eternal life (John X, 9). But there is a certain door by which one enters this world, a certain door of mortality. Around the injuries and restorations of this weak flesh [Note: [Col. 1386] Am. and the manuscripts read “weak.”], he is, as it were, a kind of doorkeeper at this door. He has power in this sea through which ships travel, but not so much that he can do anything without the knowledge or will of his master.

Lest someone should say: “He has indeed lost the great power of the higher arrangements; but I am among these lower things, and here he can hold me in his power; I must serve him”—do not be deceived. Your Lord knows you, and knows you in such a way that he has counted the hairs of your head (Matt. X, 30).

What, then, do you fear? Perhaps he will try your flesh. It is the scourge of your Lord, not the power of your tempter. He wishes to harm the salvation that has been promised, but he is not permitted to do so. To ensure that he is not permitted, have Christ as your head; repel the head of the dragon; do not consent to his suggestion; do not slip from your path.

“This dragon whom you formed to be mocked.”

### 11. [verses 27–29]

Now do you wish to see how he cannot harm you unless he is permitted? “All things,” he says, “wait upon you, Lord, that you may give them food in due season.”

This dragon also wants to eat, but he does not eat whom he wishes. “All things wait upon you, Lord, that you may give them food in due season.” All things: both the creeping things without number, and the small and great creatures, and the dragon himself, and all your creation, with which you have filled the earth. “All things wait upon you, that you may give them food in due season,” each its own food.

You have your food, and the dragon has his food. If you live well, you will have Christ as your food; if you withdraw from Christ, you will be food for the dragon.

“All things wait upon you, that you may give them food in due season.” What was said to the dragon himself? “You shall eat earth.” It was said to the dragon: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life.” You have heard the dragon’s food.

You do not want God to give you to the dragon to eat; do not be the dragon’s food—that is, do not abandon the word of God. For where it was said to the dragon, “You shall eat earth,” it had already been said to the transgressor: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 14, 19).

You do not want to be the serpent’s food? Do not be earth. “How,” you ask, “shall I not be earth?” If you do not set your mind on earthly things. Hear the Apostle, so that you may not be earth. “If you have risen with Christ,” he says, “seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth” (Col. III, 1, 2).

If you do not set your mind on earthly things, you are not earth; if you are not earth, you are not eaten by the serpent, whose food was given as earth.

God gives the serpent its food when he wills and to whom he wills; but he judges well, he cannot be deceived, and he does not give it gold instead of earth.

“All things wait upon you, Lord, that you may give them food in due season.” When you give it to them, they gather it. It is before them, but they do not gather it unless you give it. Job was before the devil; and indeed he did not devour Job, but he did not even dare to tempt him until God had given him permission.

“They wait upon you”: when you give it to them, they gather it; if you do not give it, they do not gather it.

### 12.

And what of us, brothers? What food do we have? The Psalm continues concerning our food.

“When you open your hand, all things shall be filled with goodness.”

What does it mean, O Lord, that you open your hand? Your hand is Christ. “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1). To the one to whom it is revealed, it is opened, for revelation is an opening.

“When you open your hand, all things shall be filled with goodness.” When you reveal your Christ, all things shall be filled with goodness.

But they do not possess goodness from themselves; for at times this is proved to them: “When you turn away your face, they will be troubled.” [Note: [Col. 1387] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have: “for when are they good?” The manuscripts support the former reading.]

Many who were filled with goodness attributed to themselves what they possessed and wished to glory as though in their own justifications. They said to themselves: “I am just; I am great,” and became pleasing to themselves.

And the Apostle’s voice sounded against them: “For what do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

But wishing to prove to a human being that whatever he has comes from God, so that he might possess humility together with goodness, God sometimes troubles him. He turns his face away from him, and the person falls into temptation; and God shows him that his being just and walking rightly came about because God himself was guiding him.

“When you turn away your face, they will be troubled.”

See what he says in another Psalm: “I said in my abundance, ‘I shall not be moved forever.’” He presumed upon himself. He had been filled with goodness, and thought that all his goodness came from himself, and said in his heart: “I shall not be moved forever.”

But because he had already experienced that he had received God’s grace, in return for what he had experienced he gave thanks: “Lord, by your will you gave strength to my beauty; but you turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (Ps. XXIX, 7, 8).

So also here: “When you open your hand.” You will open your hand, and all things will be filled with goodness—not by their own hand, but by your open hand. “When you turn away your face, they will be troubled.”

### 13.

But why do you do this? Why do you turn your face away, so that they may be troubled?

“You will take away their spirit, and they will fail.”

Their spirit was their pride: they glory, attribute things to themselves, and justify themselves. Turn your face away, then, so that they may be troubled; take away their spirit, and let them fail. Let them cry out to you: “Hear me quickly, O Lord; my spirit has failed. Do not turn your face away from me” (Ps. CXLII, 7).

“You will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust.”

A human being, repenting of his sin, discovers that he did not have strength from himself and confesses to God, saying that he is earth and ashes.

O proud person, you have returned to your dust; your spirit has been taken away. You no longer boast, exalt yourself, or justify yourself. You see that you were made from dust, and that when the Lord turned his face away, you fell back into your own dust.
