Pray, then; confess your dust and your weakness.

### 14. [verse 30]

And see what follows:

“You will send forth your spirit, and they will be created.”

“You will take away their spirit; you will send forth yours.” You will take away their spirit; they will not have their own spirit.

Have they therefore been abandoned? “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V, 3). Yet they are not abandoned, because “the kingdom of heaven is theirs.”

They did not wish to have their own spirit; they will have the Spirit of God.

For this is what he said to the future martyrs: “When they seize you and bring you away,” [Note: [Col. 1388] Most manuscripts have “lead you away.”] “do not consider how or what you will speak; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (ibid. X, 19, 20).

Do not attribute strength to yourselves. “If it is yours,” he says, “and is not mine, it is hardness, not strength.”

“You will take away their spirit, and they will fail; you will send forth your spirit, and they will be created.”

“For we are his workmanship,” the Apostle says, “created in good works” (Eph. II, 10). From his Spirit we have received grace, so that we may live in righteousness, because he is the one who justifies the ungodly (Rom. IV, 5).

“You will take away their spirit, and they will fail; you will send forth your spirit, and they will be created; and you will renew the face of the earth”—that is, through new people who confess that they have been justified, not that they are just from themselves, so that the grace of God may be in them.

See what sort of people they are whose face of the earth has been renewed. Paul says: “I labored more than all of them.” What is this, Paul? Consider whether it was you—whether it was your spirit.

“Not I,” he says, “but the grace of God with me” (I Cor. XV, 10).

### 15. [verse 31]

What, then? Because when he has taken away our spirit, we shall return to our dust, usefully contemplating our weakness so that, once we have received his Spirit, we may be restored.

See what follows:

“May the glory of the Lord be forever.”

Not yours, not mine, not this person’s or that person’s: may the glory of the Lord be—not for a time, but forever.

“The Lord will rejoice in his works.”

Not in your works as though they were yours: if your works are evil, they are so through your iniquity; if they are good, they are so through the grace of God.

“The Lord will rejoice in his works.”

### 16. [verse 32]

“He looks upon the earth, and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains, and they smoke.”

O earth, you were exulting in your goodness and attributing strength to the abundance of your resources. Behold, the Lord looks upon you and makes you tremble.

May he look upon you and make you tremble, for the trembling of humility is better than the confidence of pride.

See how God looks upon the earth and makes it tremble. To the earth, as though it were presuming upon itself and exulting, the Apostle speaks:

“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. With fear and trembling: for it is God who works in you” (Phil. II, 12, 13).

You say, O Paul, “Work”; you tell us to work. Why “with trembling”? “For it is God,” he says, “who works in you.”

Therefore with trembling, because God is working. Since he gave it, and what you have is not from yourself, you will work with fear and trembling. For if you do not tremble before him, he will take away what he gave.

Work, then, with trembling. See another Psalm: “Serve the Lord in fear, and exult before him with trembling” (Ps. II, 11).

If one must exult with trembling, God looks upon the earth and an earthquake occurs. When God looks upon us, let our hearts tremble; then God will rest there.

Hear him elsewhere: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest? Upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

“He looks upon the earth, and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains, and they smoke.”

The mountains were proud; they boasted of themselves; God had not touched them. He touches them, and they smoke.

What does it mean that the mountains smoke? To offer prayer to the Lord.

Behold the great mountains, the proud and immense mountains: they did not pray to God. They wanted to be prayed to and did not pray to the one above.

For what powerful, swollen, and proud person on earth deigns humbly to pray to God? I am speaking of the ungodly, not of the cedars of Lebanon that the Lord planted.

Any ungodly person, an unhappy soul, does not know how to pray to God and wants human beings to pray to him. He is a mountain; it is necessary that God touch him and make him smoke.

When he begins to smoke, he will offer prayer to God like a sacrifice of the heart. He smokes toward God; then he beats his breast. He begins also to weep, because smoke drives out tears.

“He touches the mountains, and they smoke.”

### 17. [verse 33]

“I will sing to the Lord in my life.”

What will he sing? He will sing of everything that exists. [Note: [Col. 1389] The manuscripts omit “exists”; in its place the Colbertine manuscript has “lives.”]

Let us sing to the Lord in our life. Our life at present is hope; afterward our life will be eternity. The life of mortal life is hope of immortal life.

“I will sing to the Lord in my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist.”

Since in him I shall exist without end, as long as I exist I shall sing psalms to my God.

Lest perhaps, when we begin to sing psalms to God in that city, we should think that we will do something else, our whole life will be singing psalms to God.

If what we praise can become tiresome, our praise too can become tiresome. If he is loved forever, he is praised by us forever:

“I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist.”

### 18. [verse 34]

“May my discourse be pleasing to him; but I shall rejoice in the Lord.”

“May my discourse be pleasing to him.” What is a human being’s discourse with God other than confession of sins?

Confess to God what you are, and you have spoken with him. Speak with him; do good works, and speak with him.

“Wash yourselves, be clean,” Isaiah says; “remove your wickednesses from your souls, from before my eyes; cease from your wickednesses, learn to do good, judge for the orphan, and justify the widow; and come, let us argue together, says the Lord” (Isa. I, 16–18).

What does it mean to argue with God? Make yourself known to him who knows you, so that he may make himself known to you who do not know him.

“May my discourse be pleasing to him.”

Behold, this is pleasing to the Lord: your discourse, the sacrifice of your humility, the contrition of your heart, the burnt offering of your life. This is pleasing to God.

But what is pleasing to you?

“But I shall rejoice in the Lord.”

This is the mutual discourse of which I spoke: make yourself known to him who knows you, and let him make himself known to you who do not know him.

Your confession is pleasing to him; his grace is pleasing to you.

He has made himself known to you. How has he made himself known to you? Through the Word.

What Word? Christ.

He has spoken to you, and he has spoken himself. Because he sent Christ, he spoke himself.

Let us hear the Word himself: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also” (John XIV, 9).

“But I shall rejoice in the Lord.”

### 19. [verse 35]

“Let sinners fail from the earth.”

He seems to rage. O holy soul that sings and groans here! Would that our soul were with that soul! Would that it were joined, associated, and united with it! It will also see the mercy of the one who rages.

For who understands this except one who has been filled with love?

“Let sinners fail from the earth.”

You tremble because he curses. And who is cursing? A holy person. Without doubt he is heard.

But it was said to the saints: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII, 14).

What, then, does he mean by saying, “Let sinners perish from the earth”?

By all means, let them perish. Let their spirit be taken away, and let them perish, so that he may send forth his Spirit and they may be restored.

“Let sinners perish from the earth, and the wicked, so that they may no longer be.”

What does it mean that they may no longer be, except that they may no longer be wicked? Let them therefore be justified, so that they may no longer be wicked.

He saw this, was filled with joy, and recalls the first verse of the Psalm:

“Bless the Lord, O my soul.”

Let our soul bless the Lord, brothers, because he has deigned to give both ability and speech to us, and attention and eagerness to you.

Let each person, as he can, recall what he has heard. By speaking with one another, belch forth your nourishment; ruminate what you have received; do not let it pass into the entrails of your forgetfulness.

“Precious treasure rests in the mouth” (Prov. XXI, 20).

They were sought and found with great labor; they were announced and discussed with great labor. May our labor be fruitful for you, and may our soul bless the Lord.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 104

### 1. [verse 1]

The hundred-and-fourth Psalm is the first among those marked beforehand with “Alleluia.” The interpretation of this word—or rather, of these two words—is “Praise God.”

And therefore it begins from there:

“Confess to the Lord, and call upon his name.”

For this confession is to be understood as praise, as in: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI, 25).

After praise has been set forth, invocation ordinarily follows, where the one praying binds together his desires. Hence the Lord’s Prayer itself has at its beginning a very brief praise: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (ibid. VI, 9). Then the things requested follow afterward.

Therefore elsewhere in the Psalm it is said: “We shall confess to you, God; we shall confess, and we shall call upon your name” (Ps. LXXIV, 2).

Elsewhere it is clearer: “While praising, I shall call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies” (Ps. XVII, 4).

So also here: “Confess,” he says, “to the Lord, and call upon his name.” This is as though he had said: “Praise the Lord, and call upon his name.”

For he hears the one who calls upon him, whom he sees praising; and he sees the one praising whom he approves as loving.

And in what did the Lord wish the love of the good servant toward him to be shown especially, except in what he said to him: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI, 17)?

Hence here too it follows:

“Declare his works among the nations”—or rather, to express the Greek word literally, as certain other Latin manuscripts also have it, “Evangelize his works among the nations.” [Note: [Col. 1390] All the manuscripts have “Declare.”]

To whom is this said except to the Evangelists in prophecy?

### 2. [verses 2, 3]

“Sing to him, and sing psalms to him.”

Praise him in word and deed. One sings with the mouth; with the psaltery—that is, with the hands—one sings psalms.

“Tell of all his wonders; be praised in his holy name.”

These two verses can reasonably be understood as corresponding to the two preceding expressions: so that “Tell of all his wonders” refers to what was said, “Sing to him,” while what follows, “Be praised in his holy name,” refers to what was said, “And sing psalms to him.”

The former concerns the good word by which one sings to him and tells of all his wonders; the latter concerns the good work by which one sings psalms to him, so that no one should wish to be praised for a good work as though it were accomplished by his own strength.

Therefore, after saying, “Be praised”—which those who do good works may indeed deservedly be—the Psalm adds, “in his holy name,” so that “the one who glories may glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31).

Those, then, who wish to sing psalms to him and not to themselves should beware of doing their righteousness before human beings in order to be seen by them; otherwise they will have no reward with their Father who is in heaven (Matt. VI, 1).

Rather, let their works shine before human beings—not so that they themselves may be seen by them, but so that people may see their good works and glorify their Father who is in heaven (ibid. V, 16).

This is to be praised in his holy name.

Hence it is also read in another Psalm: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised; let the meek hear and rejoice” (Ps. XXXIII, 2, 3).

This too in a certain way follows here:

“Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.”

For thus the meek rejoice, who no longer rival those who are doing good works with bitter jealousy.

### 3. [verse 4]

“Seek the Lord, and be strengthened.”

This has been translated more expressly from the Greek, although the word may seem less Latin; hence other manuscripts have “be confirmed,” and others “be made strong.”

For it is also said: “My strength” (Ps. XVII, 2), and: “I shall keep my strength toward you” (Ps. LVIII, 10).

By seeking him and drawing near to him, we are both enlightened and strengthened, lest through blindness we fail to see what must be done, or through weakness fail to do even what we see.

What is said for seeing, “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII, 5), is said for doing, “Seek the Lord, and be made strong.”

“Seek,” he says, “his face always.”

What is the face of the Lord except the presence of God? As one speaks of the face of the wind and the face of fire: “As stubble before the face of the wind” (Ps. LXXXII, 14), and “As wax melts before the face of fire” (Ps. LXVII, 3).

Scripture uses many such expressions, wishing nothing else to be understood except the presence of those things whose face it names.

But what does “Seek his face always” mean?

I know indeed that “it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII, 28). But if he is always sought, when is he found?

Or did he say “always” of this whole life in which one lives here, from the time when we learned that we ought to do this—when, even after he has been found, he must still be sought?

Faith has already found him, but hope still seeks him. Love both finds him through faith and seeks to possess him through sight. There he will then be found in such a way that he will be sufficient for us and will no longer be sought further.

For unless faith found him in this life, it would not be said: “Seek the Lord”; and: “When you have found him, let the ungodly abandon his ways, and the unjust man his thoughts” (Isa. LV, 6, 7).

Likewise, if, once found by faith, he were not still to be sought, it would not be said: “If we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. VIII, 25).

Nor would John say: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2).

Or perhaps even when we see him face to face as he is, he will still have to be sought and sought without end, because he will be loved without end?

For we also say to someone who is present, “I am not seeking you”—that is, “I do not love you.”

And thus the one who is loved is sought even when he is present, as one acts through perpetual love so that he may not become absent. [Note: [Col. 1392] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “is desired.”]

Therefore, whoever loves someone, even when he sees him, always wishes him to be present without weariness. That is, he always seeks him to be present.

And surely this is what “Seek his face always” means: discovery should not bring an end to the seeking by which love is signified; rather, as the love of the one found grows, so should the seeking grow.

### 4. [verse 5]

From this point the ardent praiser moderates himself and descends to words accessible to the hearers, nourishing weak and infant love with God’s temporal wonders.

“Remember,” he says, “his wonders which he performed, his signs and the judgments of his mouth.”

This passage seems similar to the passage where Moses asked who God was. After he had said, “I am who I am,” and, “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you,’” which only a rare mind can grasp even in some small measure, God afterward, recalling his name, mercifully tempered his grace toward human beings, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; this is my name forever” (Exod. III, 14, 13).

There he wished it to be understood both that those whose God he said he was live with him forever, and he said what could also be grasped by little ones.

Thus, while “I am who I am” might be understood according to their capacity by those who, with great strength of love, know how always to seek his face, if what he himself is is too much for you to see or seek, then:

“Remember his wonders which he performed, his signs and the judgments of his mouth.”

### 5. [verses 6, 7]

And to whom is this said?

“O seed of Abraham, his servant; children of Jacob, his chosen ones.”

You are the seed of Abraham; you are the children of Jacob. Remember his wonders which he performed, his signs and the judgments of his mouth.

But lest anyone attribute this to one nation alone, to the Israelites according to the flesh, and fail to understand that the children of promise are more truly the seed of Abraham than the children of the flesh—of whom the Apostle says, when speaking to the Gentiles, “Therefore you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. III, 29)—the Psalm continues and says:

“He himself is the Lord our God; throughout all the earth are his judgments.”

This is said through Isaiah to free Jerusalem, our mother:

“He who redeemed you, he himself shall be called your God, the God of the whole earth” (Isa. LIV, 5).

Is he merely the God of the Jews? Certainly not (Rom. III, 29).

“He himself is the Lord our God; throughout all the earth are his judgments,” because throughout all the earth is his Church, where his judgments are preached.

What, then, does he say in another Psalm?

“He declares his word to Jacob, his righteousnesses and his judgments to Israel; he has not dealt so with every nation, and he has not revealed his judgments to them” (Ps. CXLVII, 19, 20).

This was said because he wished one nation to be understood as belonging to the seed of Abraham. It was indeed called from all the nations, and thus all the nations are said to be in it, so that it is one nation called into adoption.

To no nation outside this one has he revealed his judgments, because those who did not believe them, even if they were announced, did not have them revealed to them in truth: for unless they believe, they will not understand.

### 6. [verses 8–11]

“He remembered his covenant forever.”

Other manuscripts have “for eternity,” which arose from the ambiguity of the Greek. But if this is to be understood as “for this age,” not “for eternity,” how does the Psalm, explaining which covenant he remembered, add and say:

“The word which he commanded for a thousand generations”?

This can still be understood as having some limit; but afterward he says:

“Which he established with Abraham, and his oath with Isaac; and he appointed it for Jacob as a commandment, and for Israel as an eternal covenant.”

Here there is no room for ambiguity. The Greek has *aiōnion* (“eternal”), which our translators nowhere render except as “eternal”; only rarely have some rendered *aiōnion* somewhere as “age-long.”

Unless perhaps, because they more familiarly translate *aiōn* as “age,” they might wish to translate *aiōnion* not as “eternal” but as “belonging to the age.” I do not remember anyone having dared to do this.

But if in this passage the Old Covenant is to be understood, on account of the land of Canaan—for the wording is connected in this way:

“And he appointed it” to “Jacob as a commandment, and” to “Israel as an eternal covenant, saying, ‘I will give you the land of Canaan [Note: [Col. 1393] In the older manuscripts it is consistently “Chanan.”], the portion of your inheritance’”—how is “eternal” to be understood, since that earthly inheritance cannot be eternal?

And for this reason it is called the Old Covenant, because it is abolished through the New.

Nor does “a thousand generations” seem to signify anything eternal, because they evidently have an end, while they are far too many even for temporal matters.

However few years one may assign to a generation—for the Greeks call it *genea* (γενεά), and some have defined the smallest generation as fifteen years, from which a human being begins to be capable of begetting—what are these thousand generations, not only from the time of Abraham, when this promise was made to him, until the time of the New Testament, but from Adam himself until the end of the age?

For who would dare say that this age will last fifteen thousand years?

### 7.

Accordingly, it seems to me that the Old Testament is not meant here—the Testament that the prophet says is to be abolished by the New: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish a New Testament with the house of Jacob; not according to the Testament which I made with their fathers, when I led them out of the land of Egypt” (Jeremiah 31:31–32). Rather, the reference is to the testament of faith, which the Apostle praises when he presents Abraham to us for imitation and refutes those who glory in the works of the Law by showing that Abraham believed God even before circumcision, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Galatians 3:5–6).

Thus, after saying, “He remembered his covenant forever”—which we must understand as referring to eternity, namely, the covenant of justification and the eternal inheritance that God promised to faith—he adds: “the word which he commanded for a thousand generations.” What does “commanded” mean? For when he says, “I will give you the land of Canaan,” this is not a command but a promise. A command is [Col. 1394] what we must do; a promise is what we are to receive. The command, therefore, is faith, so that “the righteous shall live by faith” (Romans 1:17); and an eternal inheritance is promised to this faith.

The thousand generations, then, because of the perfection of the number, are to be understood as meaning all generations: that is, for as long as generation follows generation in succession, the command is that one should live by faith. The people of God observe this command, the children of promise coming into being by birth and departing by death, until the whole succession of generations comes to an end. This is signified by the number one thousand, since the solid square of the number ten—ten times ten, and this ten times again—reaches one thousand.

“He established,” he says, “with Abraham, and by his oath with Isaac. And he appointed it for Jacob,” that is, for Jacob himself, “as a commandment.” These are the three patriarchs concerning whom God says in a special way that he is their God. The Lord also names them in the New Testament, where he says: “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8:11). This is the eternal inheritance.

For here too, where he says, “He appointed it for Jacob as a commandment,” he makes clear that it is a commandment of faith; he would not call a promise a commandment. If the work belongs to the commandment, the reward belongs to the promise: “This is the work of God,” the Lord says, “that you believe in him whom he sent” (John 6:29). This word, therefore, which he commanded—“remembering his covenant forever”—that is, the word of faith which we preach (Romans 10:8), he appointed for Jacob himself as a commandment, and for Israel himself as an eternal covenant: namely, a covenant through which, from that word and from the fulfilled commandment, he would give something eternal.

He says, “I will give you the land of Canaan, the allotment of your inheritance.” How, then, is this eternal, unless it signifies something eternal? For that land itself was called the land of promise, “a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8, 17). All this signifies grace, in which one tastes “how good the Lord is” (Psalm 33:8); but not all people belong to it, for “faith is not possessed by all” (2 Thessalonians 3:2). Therefore he added, “the allotment of your inheritance.”

Hence, in another psalm, Abraham—understood to mean Christ—is likewise understood to speak when he says: “The cords have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is pleasant to me” (Psalm 15:6).

But why was it called the land of Canaan? The interpretation of this name makes it clear. For Canaan is interpreted as “Humble.” If this is related to the statement of the holy Noah, by which he declared that this same Canaan would be the servant of his brothers (Genesis 9:25), then servile fear is also signified here. “A slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever” (John 8:35). Therefore, once the Canaanite has been excluded, the land of promise is given to Abraham’s offspring. For “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18), so that the son may remain in the house forever. Hence it is said, “and for Israel himself as an eternal covenant.”

### 8. [verse 12]

Next he continues the history, which is very well known from the truth of the holy books: “When they were few in number, very few, and resident aliens in it”—that is, in the land of Canaan.

When Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob dwelt there, before they received it as an inheritance, they were very few in their offspring and resident aliens in it. Some manuscripts, however, do not read “very few and resident aliens,” but “very few persons and resident aliens.” It is evident that those who interpreted the passage in this way followed a Greek construction that cannot be transferred into Latin without an absurdity that is altogether intolerable.

If we tried to translate the entire construction, we would have to say: “In that they were few in number, very few and resident aliens in it” [Note: [Col. 1395] *En tô einai autous arithmô bracheis, oligostous kai paroikous en autê.*]. But what the Greek says, “in that they were,” is in Latin *cum essent*, “when they were.” This verb cannot be followed by the accusative case, but by the nominative. For who would say, “when they were very few persons” (*cum essent paucissimos*)? One says, “when they were very few” (*cum essent paucissimi*).

### 9. [verses 13–15]

“When,” therefore, “they were few in number,” or “few in number, very few and resident aliens in it, they passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people.”

This repeats what he had said, “from nation to nation.” “He did not permit anyone to harm them”—that is, he did not allow it. The Greek construction is “to harm them,” whereas the Latin is “to harm them” with the dative case.

“And he rebuked kings for their sake. Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets.”

These are the words of God rebuking or reproving kings, lest they injure [Note: [Col. 1395] Thus Am., Er., and most manuscripts. Others, with Lov.: “lest they neglect.”] the holy patriarchs while they were few in number, very few, and resident aliens in the land of Canaan. Although these words are not found in the books of that history, they must nevertheless be understood either as having been spoken secretly, just as God speaks in the hidden and truthful visions of human hearts, or as having been expressed through an angel.

For the king of Gerar and the king of Egypt were divinely warned not to harm Abraham (Genesis 12:17–20; and 20:3), another king not to harm Isaac (ibid. 26:8–11), and others not to harm Jacob (ibid. 31–33). They were very few and resident aliens, before Jacob moved with his sons into Egypt to dwell there. This is understood as being recalled in the words, “They passed from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people.”

But because one might ask how, before they passed over and multiplied in Egypt, they could have endured as few in number, very few, and resident aliens in a foreign land, he immediately added: “He did not permit anyone to harm them, and he rebuked kings for their sake. Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets.”

### 10.

It may rightly be asked how they were called “anointed ones” before there was an anointing from which this name was given to kings. This began with Saul, whose successor in the kingdom was David; thereafter the other kings of Judah and the kings of Israel were anointed through the continuation of the sacred custom. In that anointing the one true Christ was prefigured, to whom it was said: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8).

How, then, were they already called “anointed ones” at that time? We read that they were prophets, in the case of Abraham; and whatever is plainly said of him must certainly be understood of them as well.

Or were they called “anointed ones” because, even if secretly, they were already Christians? For although Christ’s flesh came from them, Christ existed before them—something he also answered the Jews when he said: “Before Abraham came to be, I am.”

How could they have been ignorant of him, or not believed in him, when they were called prophets precisely because, although more obscurely, they nevertheless foretold the Lord? Hence he himself openly says: “Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:58, 56).

For no one, apart from this faith which is in Christ Jesus—whether before his incarnation or afterward—has been reconciled to God, since the Apostle has most truthfully defined the matter: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

### 11. [verse 16]

Then he begins to recount how it happened that they passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people.

“And he called,” he says, “a famine upon the land; he broke every support of bread. He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold into slavery.”

Through this event it came about that they passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people.

But the expressions of the holy Scriptures must not be passed over carelessly. “He called a famine upon the land,” he says—as though famine were some person, or some animate body, or some spirit capable of obeying the one who called it—when famine is a destructive condition produced by lack of food, and exists in those who suffer it like an illness. Just as an illness is often brought to an end by medicine, so famine is, in a certain sense, cured by nourishment.

What, then, does “he called a famine” mean? Perhaps the evils that people suffer have certain angels appointed over them—evil angels, for in another psalm he says that God afflicted human beings “by the sending of evil angels” (Psalm 77:49), certainly not by an erroneous judgment—and perhaps “he called a famine” means “he called the angel appointed over famine,” who was named after the thing over which he was appointed.

From this opinion the ancient Romans consecrated certain gods, such as the goddess Fever and the god Pallor.

Or, what is more credible, “he called a famine” should be understood as “he said that there should be a famine,” so that to call is to name, to name is to say, and to say is to command. For he called the famine who calls things that are not as though they were [Note: [Col. 1396] Erasmus, the Venetian edition, and Lovanius read *tanquam sint* (“as though they were”). M.]. The Apostle did not say, “who calls things that are not so that they may be,” but “as though they were” (Romans 4:17).

For with God what will come to be by his disposition has already been accomplished, since elsewhere it is said of him: “He made the things that are to come” (Isaiah 45:11, according to the Septuagint). Here too, when the famine occurred, it was said to have been called—that is, it was made present, though it had already been arranged in his hidden governance.

Finally, he immediately explains how he called the famine, saying: “He broke every support of bread.” And this too is an unusual expression: he said “he broke” instead of “he consumed.”

### 12. [verse 17]

“He sent a man before them.” What man? Joseph. How did he send him? “Joseph was sold into slavery.”

When this happened, it was the sin of his brothers; nevertheless, God sent Joseph into Egypt. We must therefore contemplate a great and entirely necessary matter: how God makes good use of human beings’ evil deeds, [Col. 1397] just as they wickedly abuse God’s good works.

### 13. [verses 18–19]

He next weaves together the narrative, recalling what Joseph endured in his humiliation and how he was exalted.

“They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul, until his word came.”

We do not read that Joseph received fetters, but there can be no doubt that it happened. Certain things could have been omitted from that history which nevertheless were not hidden from the Holy Spirit, who speaks in these psalms.

When he says that iron passed through his soul, we understand this as the tribulation of harsh necessity; for he did not say that it passed through his body, but through his soul. There is a similar expression in the Gospel, where Simeon said to Mary:

“Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed; and a sword will pierce your own soul also, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:34–35).

The Lord’s passion, which was the ruin of many and in which the secrets of many hearts were disclosed—for what they thought about the Lord was made evident—undoubtedly also grieved his mother herself, who was grievously struck by the bereavement of her child according to the flesh.

Joseph was in such tribulation until his word came, by which he had truthfully interpreted dreams. Thus he was commended to the king, so that he might also foretell future events to him from his dreams (Genesis 41).

But because he said, “until his word came,” lest we understand this entirely in such a way that anyone might think such a great matter should be attributed to a human being, he immediately added: “The utterance of the Lord inflamed him”—or, as some manuscripts more accurately express it from the Greek, “The utterance of the Lord kindled him.” Thus he too was counted among those to whom it is said: “Praise his holy name.”

“The utterance of the Lord kindled him.” Fittingly, when the Holy Spirit was sent by the Lord, there appeared to them divided tongues as if of fire (Acts 2:3); and the Apostle says, “burning with the Spirit” (Romans 12:11). From this fire those depart of whom it is said: “The love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12).

### 14. [verses 20–22]

Finally, the text continues:

“The king sent and released him; the ruler of peoples, and he let him go.”

The king and the ruler of peoples are the same person: he released the man in fetters and let the prisoner go.

“He appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, to instruct his princes as himself and teach his elders wisdom.”

The Greek has: “and teach his elders wisdom.” This could be rendered word for word as: “to instruct his princes as himself, and make his elders wise.” For it has *πρεσβυτέρους* (*presbyterous*), which we ordinarily render “elders,” not *γέροντας* (*gerontas*), that is, “old men.” It has *σοφίσαι* (*sophisai*), a word that cannot be expressed by a single Latin word; it derives from wisdom, called *σοφία* (*sophia*) in Greek, not from prudence, which is called *φρόνησις* (*phronesis*).

Yet we do not read this in the account of Joseph’s exaltation, just as we do not read of fetters in the account of his humiliation. But how could it have happened that so great a man, a worshiper of the one true God, was concerned in Egypt only with feeding bodies and governing merely bodily affairs, without caring to make their souls [Col. 1398] better?

Those things were written in that history which, according to the purpose of the writer—in whom the Holy Spirit was present—were judged sufficient to signify future realities through that narrative.

### 15. [verse 23]

“And Israel entered Egypt, and Jacob was a resident alien in the land of Ham.”

What is Israel is Jacob; and what is Egypt is the land of Ham. Here it is shown most openly that the nation of the Egyptians also arose from the offspring of Ham, the son of Noah, whose firstborn was Canaan. Therefore, in the manuscripts that read “Canaan” here, the text must be corrected.

“Was a resident alien” is better translated than “dwelt,” as some manuscripts read. The latter would amount to the same thing as saying “was an inhabitant,” for it signifies nothing else. The Greek word at this point is the same as above, where it says, “very few and resident aliens in it.” Residence as an alien, or sojourning, indicates not a native but an outsider.

Behold how they passed from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people. What had been stated briefly has been explained by a brief narrative.

But from what kingdom did they pass into another people? This may rightly be asked. They were not yet reigning in the land of Canaan, since the kingdom of the people of Israel had not yet been established there. How, then, can this be understood, except perhaps according to anticipation, because a kingdom was to exist there through their offspring?

### 16. [verse 24]

Next the events that occurred in Egypt are narrated.

“And he greatly increased his people,” he says, “and made them stronger than their enemies.”

This too has been stated briefly, so that the manner in which it happened might subsequently be narrated. For the people of God were not made stronger than their Egyptian enemies when their male children were being killed or when they were being crushed in the making of bricks, but when, by the powerful hand of the Lord their God, through signs and wonders, they became objects of fear and honor, until the resistance of the cruel king was overcome and the Red Sea overwhelmed the pursuer together with his army.

### 17. [verse 25]

What was stated briefly—“he made his people stronger than their enemies”—as though we were asking how it happened, he now begins to explain, continuing until he has determined the matter by his narrative.

“And he turned their hearts so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants.”

Are we to understand or believe that God turns a human heart toward the committing of sins? Or is it not a sin—or only a small sin—to hate the people of God and deal deceitfully with his servants? Who would say that? Is God, then, the author of such grave sins, when he must not be believed to be the author of even the slightest sin? “Who is wise and will understand these things?” (Psalm 106:43).

This is that wonderful goodness of God, by which he makes good use even of evil beings, whether angels or human beings. Although they are evil through their own vice, he brings good out of their evil.

They were not good before they hated his people; rather, they were wicked and impious, such as would easily envy their own prosperous neighbors. By multiplying his [Col. 1399] people, therefore, God turned these evil persons toward envy through his beneficence. For envy is hatred of another’s happiness.

Thus he turned their hearts so that, through envy, they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants. He did not make their hearts evil; rather, by doing good to his people, he turned their hearts, already spontaneously evil, toward hatred. He did not pervert a sound heart, but turned one that was already spontaneously perverse toward hatred of his people, where he would make good use of that evil. He did not make them evil, but bestowed good things on those whom the wicked could very easily envy.

What use he made of their hatred, both for the discipline of his people and for the glory of his name—which is beneficial to us—the following events teach. These are recalled in his praise when the Alleluia is sung.

### 18. [verse 26]

“He sent Moses his servant, Aaron whom he himself chose.”

“Whom he chose” would have been sufficient; there is no special point to be sought in the addition of “himself.” It is a scriptural expression, as in: “In which they will dwell in it” (Numbers 13:20; and Leviticus 18:3, according to the Septuagint). The divine books are full of such expressions.

### 19. [verse 27]

“He placed in them the words of his signs and wonders in the land of Ham.”

We must not understand “the words of his signs and wonders” as though these were words by which signs and wonders were performed—that is, words spoken so that signs and wonders might occur. For many things happened without words: by means of a staff, an outstretched hand, or ashes thrown into the air.

But because the things that were done were not empty of meaning, just as the words we speak are not empty of meaning, they too were called “words”—not words of voices and sounds, but of signs and wonders.

“He placed in them,” that is, he did these things through them.

### 20. [verse 28]

“He sent darkness, and it became dark.”

This too is written among the plagues with which the Egyptians were struck. What follows, however, is read differently in different manuscripts. Some have: “And they embittered his words”; others: “And they did not embitter his words.” The former reading is found in more manuscripts. Where the negative particle has been added, we could scarcely find two manuscripts.

But perhaps the corruption arose because the sense seemed easier. For what is easier to understand than “and they embittered his words,” namely, by their obstinate contradictions? We have nevertheless tried to explain the other reading according to a sound interpretation. For the moment, this occurred to us: “They did not embitter his words,” that is, in Moses and Aaron, because they endured even their harshest words with the greatest patience until everything that God had determined to do through them had been completed in due order.

### 21. [verses 29–30]

“He turned their waters into blood and killed their fish. He gave their land frogs, in the inner chambers of their kings”—as though he were saying, “He turned their land into frogs.”

For the multitude of frogs had been so great that this could appropriately be said by *hyperbole* (*hyperbolē*, exaggeration).

### 22. [verse 31]

“He spoke, and the dog-fly and gnats came in all their territories.”

If one asks when he spoke, the word was in him before the event occurred, and it was there without time [Col. 1400] at the time when the event was to occur. Nevertheless, through angels and through his servants Moses and Aaron, he also in a certain sense spoke at that time so that it might happen, when it was about to happen.

### 23. [verse 32]

“He placed their rains as hail.”

This is an expression like the one in which he says, “He gave their land frogs,” except that there the whole land was not actually turned into frogs, whereas the rain could indeed have been wholly turned into hail.

“Fire that burns in their land”: “he placed” is understood.

### 24. [verse 33]

“And he struck their vines and their fig trees, and shattered every tree within their territories.”

This was done by the force of hail and lightning; hence he also said “fire that burns.”

### 25. [verse 34]

“He spoke, and the locust and the grasshopper came, of which there was no number.”

The locust and the grasshopper constitute one plague, since one is the parent and the other its offspring.

### 26. [verse 35]

“And it devoured every plant in their land, and it devoured every fruit of their land.”

Grass is also fruit, as Scripture is accustomed to speak; it calls even grain crops “grass.” But perhaps, in order to name two things, he wished the number to correspond to the two things he had mentioned—namely, the locust and the grasshopper.

All this belongs to a variety of expression that relieves weariness, not to any difference in meaning.

### 27. [verse 36]

“And he struck every firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their labor.”

This is the final plague, apart from the death in the Red Sea. I think “the firstfruits of their labors” was said because of the firstborn of the animals.

Although there were ten plagues, not all of them are mentioned, nor are they recounted in the same order in which they are said to have occurred there. Praise is free from the constraints governing a narrator who composes a history. Since the author and speaker of this praise is the Holy Spirit through the prophet, by the same authority with which he moved the human being who wrote that history, he both recalls something that is not recorded there and passes over something that is recorded there.

### 28. [verse 37]

He also adds to the praises of God the fact that he led the Israelites out of Egypt enriched with silver and gold. They were not yet such people as could despise the temporal, but nevertheless deserved and just, reward for their labors.

Nor, in the fact that they deceived the Egyptians by asking them to lend them gold and silver, should God be thought either to have commanded such deceit to those who have their hearts set on higher things, or to approve it if they committed it. Rather, through those words of God—spoken by the one who saw their hearts and examined their desires—they were permitted to do these things rather than commanded to do them.

Nevertheless, this was not without some advancement of the soul, still attached to bodily things. They did to those who deserved to suffer such things what they themselves had suffered by right; and although by deceit, they took from unjust people what was owed to them.

Just as God made use of the Egyptians’ injustice, so he made use of the Israelites’ weakness for the purpose of representing and foreshadowing through these events what was necessary.

“And he led them out with silver and gold.” This too is a scriptural expression. “With silver and gold” is said in place of “accompanied by silver and gold.”

“And there was no weak person among their tribes” [Col. 1401]—weak in body, not in spirit. This too was a great benefit of God: in that necessity of migration, no one was sick.

### 29. [verse 38]

“Egypt rejoiced at their departure, because fear of them had fallen upon them.”

The fear was certainly that of the Hebrews upon the Egyptians. It was not the fear by which the Hebrews were afraid, but the fear by which they were feared.

Someone may ask: How, then, did the Egyptians not want to let them go? How did they let them go as though they would return? How did they lend them gold and silver, as though they would return and repay them, if Egypt rejoiced at their departure?

It must be understood that, after the final death of the Egyptians and the great slaughter in the Red Sea of so vast an army of pursuers, the surviving Egyptians feared that the Hebrews might return and easily crush what remained of them.

Then what was said above was fulfilled: after saying, “He greatly increased his people,” he immediately added, “and made them stronger than their enemies.”

To explain this statement, which had been put forward in a single verse, and to show how it happened, he added all the other events in this account of the disaster, up to this point where he says: “Egypt rejoiced at their departure, because fear of them had fallen upon them.” Thus he assigns the fulfillment of what he had stated: that he made his people stronger than their enemies.

[Note: [Col. 1401] The word *cladis* (“disaster”) is absent from the manuscripts.]

### 30. [verse 39]

Accordingly, he now recounts the divine benefits bestowed upon them as they journeyed through the wilderness.

“He spread out a cloud for their protection, and fire to give them light by night.”

These things are as clear as they are familiar.

### 31. [verse 40]

“They asked” [Note: [Col. 1401] The editions read “They asked for meat.” The word “meat” is absent from the manuscripts.] “and quail came.”

They did not desire quail, but meat. Since quail is also meat, and since this psalm does not speak of the bitterness of those in whom God was not well pleased, but of the faith of the elect, who are the true offspring of Abraham, they should be understood as having asked that something might come by which the grumbling of the embittered would be silenced.

In the verse that follows—“and he satisfied them with the bread of heaven”—he did not name manna, but no one who has read those Scriptures is unaware of what is meant.

### 32. [verse 41]

“He split the rock, and waters flowed; rivers went through the dry land.”

This event is understood as quickly as it is read.

### 33. [verses 42–44]

Through all these benefits, God commends the merit of faith in Abraham. The text continues:

“For he remembered his holy word, which he had made to Abraham his servant. And he led out his people with rejoicing, and his chosen ones with gladness.”

What he says, “his people,” he repeats as “his chosen ones”; and what he says, “with rejoicing,” he repeats as “with gladness.”

“And he gave them the territories of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the peoples.”

What is expressed by “the territories of the nations” is expressed again by “the labors of the peoples”; and what is said as “he gave them” is repeated as “they possessed.”

### 34. [verse 45]

And as though we were asking for what purpose [Col. 1402] these things were given—lest the supreme good should be thought to consist in the very prosperity of temporal affairs granted to the people of God—he immediately referred that prosperity to something else, where the supreme good ought to be sought:

“So that they might keep his ordinances,” he says, “and seek his law.”

The servants of God and the elect children of promise, the true and genuine offspring of Abraham, are therefore to be understood as imitating Abraham’s faith and receiving these earthly goods from God for this reason: not to dissolve themselves in luxury through them or grow sluggish through perverse security, but because divine mercy has prepared all these things for them. By seeking them, they could be occupied with very demanding labors, so that they might be free for the purpose by which eternal good can be obtained: namely, “that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.”

Finally, because he wished the offspring of Abraham understood here to be those who truly were Abraham’s offspring—such people certainly were not absent even from that people—the Apostle Paul also makes this sufficiently clear when he says: “But God was not well pleased with most of them” (1 Corinthians 10:5). If not with all, then certainly there were some with whom God was well pleased.

Because this psalm commends such people, therefore, it says nothing here about the iniquities, provocations, and bitterness of those with whom God was not well pleased. But because the justice, and also the mercy, of almighty and merciful God appeared even toward the wicked, the following psalm speaks about them in its praises of God.

Nevertheless, both groups existed within one people, and the wicked did not contaminate the others with the contagion of their iniquities. “The Lord knows those who are his”; and if one cannot withdraw from the unjust in this world, “let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from injustice” (2 Timothy 2:19).

### 35.

To commend, as it were, the soul of this psalm, which lies hidden in its body—that is, its inner meaning within its outward words—it seems to me that the offspring of Abraham, namely all the children of promise who belong to the eternal inheritance of the eternal covenant, are admonished to choose God himself as their inheritance and to worship him freely: that is, for his own sake, not for some benefit or reward outside him.

They are to do this by praising, invoking, and proclaiming him; by working faithfully not for their own glory but for his; by rejoicing in hope and burning with love (Romans 12:11–12).

All this is expressed in these verses:

“Give thanks to the Lord, and call upon his name; proclaim his works among the nations. Sing to him and make music to him; tell of all his wonders. Glory in his holy name; let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually.”

### 36.

Next, for the nourishment of the hearts of little ones, so that they may be strengthened in faith, examples are set before them from the patriarchs: examples both of their faith and of God’s promise [Note: [Col. 1402] Most manuscripts read: “their faith and God’s promises are set before them.”]. By imitating and hoping, we are to be their offspring—not merely those of the Hebrew nation, but all who receive this grace throughout the whole earth.

All this is contained in the following verses:

“Remember his wonders which he performed, his signs and the judgments of his mouth. The offspring of Abraham his servant, [Col. 1403] the children of Jacob, his chosen ones. He himself is the Lord our God; throughout all the earth are his judgments. He remembered his covenant forever, the word which he commanded for a thousand generations. The covenant which he established with Abraham, and his oath with Isaac. And he appointed it for Jacob himself as a commandment, and for Israel himself as an eternal covenant, saying: ‘I will give you the land of Canaan, the allotment of your inheritance.’”

I have explained, according to the measure of my ability, how all these things should be understood.

### 37.

At this point a faith still small might wonder: If God is to be worshiped freely, and he himself is to be sought from himself as the inheritance of the eternal covenant, does he also not attend, with the abundance of his mercy, to the mortal life of those who seek him and to their temporal necessities? [Note: [Col. 1403] Thus the older manuscripts. Others, with the editions: “Why does he provide this mortal life for those who seek him, and their temporal necessities? Does he also not, by the abundance of his mercy, …?”] Listen attentively to what he provided for our fathers, whether those in whom he established examples of faith or those propagated from their flesh who also imitated their faith.

“When they were few in number, very few and resident aliens in it”—that is, in the land of Canaan—“they passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people. He did not leave anyone to harm them, and he rebuked kings for their sake. Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets.”

### 38.

But if you ask how they “passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people,” listen:

“He called a famine upon the land; he broke every support of bread. He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold into slavery. They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul, until his word came. The utterance of the Lord kindled him. The king sent and released him; the ruler of peoples, and he let him go. He appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, to instruct his princes as himself and teach his elders wisdom. And Israel entered Egypt, and Jacob was a resident alien in the land of Ham.”

Behold how they “passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people.”

### 39.

“And he greatly increased his people, and made them stronger than their enemies.”

But if you wish to know how he made them stronger than their enemies, listen:

“He turned their hearts so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants. He sent Moses his servant, Aaron whom he himself chose. He placed in them the words of his signs and wonders in the land of Ham. He sent darkness, and it became dark, and they embittered his words. He turned their waters into blood and killed their fish. He gave their land frogs, in the inner chambers of their kings. He spoke, and the dog-fly and gnats came in all their territories. He placed their rains as hail, fire that burns in their land. He struck their vines and their fig trees, and shattered every tree within their territories. He spoke, and the locust and the grasshopper came, of which there was no number. It devoured every plant in their land, and it devoured every fruit of their land. He struck [Col. 1404] every firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their labor. He led them out with silver and gold, and there was no weak person among their tribes. Egypt rejoiced at their departure, because fear of them had fallen upon them.”

Behold how he made his people stronger than their enemies.

40. But when his justice had inflicted these evils upon their enemies, hear what his mercy also bestowed upon them in temporal things: “He spread out a cloud for their protection, and fire to give them light by night. They asked, and quail came, and he satisfied them with the bread of heaven. He split the rock, and waters flowed; rivers ran through the dry land. For he remembered his holy word, which he had spoken to Abraham his servant. And he led out his people with rejoicing, and his chosen ones with gladness. And he gave them the territories of the nations, and they possessed the labor of peoples.”

Not so that they might worship him on account of these things, but so that they might also refer and direct these things toward the eternal good; that is: “So that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.” Whatever other goods God gives, therefore, must be referred to his gratuitous worship; his worship, however, must not be referred to the other goods God gives, for then it will be gratuitous. Challenging him to this contest, the enemy dared to say to God: “Does Job worship God for nothing?” (Job 1:9).

Moreover, if Joseph, sold into slavery, humbled, and then exalted, made room for temporal goods for the people of God, so that they might be strengthened against their enemies, how much more does Jesus, sold and humbled by his brothers according to the flesh, and exalted in heaven, make room for eternal goods for the people of God, triumphing over the devil and his angels?

Hear, therefore, seed of Abraham—not boasting in the flesh, but imitating faith; hear, servants of God and chosen of God, who have the promise of the present life and of the future (1 Tim. 4:8). If severe temptations afflict you in this age, think of Joseph in prison and Jesus on the cross. If prosperity in temporal affairs is at hand, do not worship God for its own sake, but use it for God’s sake; nor should you suppose that he is worshiped by his worshipers on account of the necessities of this life [Note: [Col. 1404] Most manuscripts read: “on account of the necessities of this life, which are necessary to his worshipers.”], since he gives these even to those who blaspheme him. Rather, seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matt. 6:33).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 105

1. Psalm 105 is likewise headed “Alleluia,” and this occurs twice. Some, however, say that one “Alleluia” belongs to the end of the preceding psalm and the other to the beginning of this one. They maintain this on the grounds that all the psalms marked “Alleluia” have “Alleluia” at the end, but not all at the beginning; therefore, whenever a psalm does not have “Alleluia” at the end, they do not want it to have it at the beginning either, and what appears at its beginning is to belong to the end of the preceding psalm.

But until they persuade us by some reliable evidence that this is true, we follow the practice of the many who, wherever they read “Alleluia,” attribute it to the psalm at whose beginning they find it. For there are very few manuscripts—and I found this in none of the Greek manuscripts I was able to examine—that have “Alleluia” at the end of Psalm 150 [Note: [Col. 1405] So the better manuscripts. But the editions read, except for the wording of Psalm 150: “after which there is already no other belonging to the same canon.”]. After it there is no further psalm belonging to the same sequence.

Yet even this could not override established practice, even if all the manuscripts contained it. It could have happened, for some reason connected with the praise of God, that the entire Book of Psalms—which is said to consist of five books, since they say that the divisions of the books occur where it is written, “Let it be, let it be”—was closed with a final “Alleluia” after all that had been sung. Nor do I see why, because of the ending of Psalm 150, all psalms marked “Alleluia” must have “Alleluia” at the end.

When “Alleluia” is doubled at the beginning of a psalm, I do not know why the Lord sometimes says “Amen” once and sometimes twice, and why “Alleluia” likewise could not sometimes be said once and sometimes twice—especially since both “Alleluia”s are placed after the numerical designation by which the psalm is identified, as in this case, Psalm 105. One ought to have been placed before the number itself if it belonged to the end of the preceding psalm, and the other “Alleluia,” belonging to the psalm bearing that number, ought to have been written after the psalm’s number.

But perhaps in this too unskilled custom has prevailed, and something may be offered that we do not yet know, which ought to guide us more by the judgment of truth than by the prejudice of custom. For now, however, before we learn this, wherever we find “Alleluia” written after the psalm number, whether once or twice, we attribute it, according to the Church’s most widespread practice, to the psalm marked by that number. We confess that we believe the mysteries of all the titles found in the Psalms, and of the order of those Psalms, to be great, and that we have not yet been able to penetrate them as fully as we wish.

2. [verse 1.] I see these two psalms, the 104th and the 105th, so closely joined to one another that in the first, the preceding one, the people of God are commended in his chosen ones, concerning whom no complaint is made. I think that these were those “in whom God was well pleased” (1 Cor. 10:5). In the psalm that follows, however, those are recalled who became bitter within the same people, though even to them God’s mercy was not lacking.

These words are spoken in the person of those who, having turned back, pray for pardon; and examples are recalled of those toward whom the rich mercy of God was displayed even though they were sinners.

This psalm, therefore, begins like the other: “Give thanks to the Lord.” But there it continues, “and call upon his name”; here, “for he is good, for his mercy is forever.” Accordingly, this can also be understood as a confession of sins, for a few verses later it says: “We have sinned with our fathers, we have acted unjustly, we have committed iniquity.” Yet in saying, “For he is good, for his mercy is forever,” there is certainly praise of God, and in his praise there is confession.

Indeed, when each person confesses his own sins, he ought to confess them with praise of God. A confession of sins is not devout unless it does not despair and asks for God’s mercy. Thus it contains his praise, either in words, when it calls him good and merciful, or in the disposition of the heart, when it believes this. For that tax collector, whose only words are recorded—“Lord, be merciful to me a sinner” (Luke 18:13)—although he did not say, “For you are good and merciful,” or anything similar, would not have said it unless he had believed it, since he prayed with hope, and hope could not exist without that faith.

There can therefore be true and devout praise of God where there is no confession of sins; this praise is very often called “confession” in Scripture. But there is no devout and useful confession of sins where God is not praised, whether in the heart or also with the mouth and in speech.

Some manuscripts read, “For he is good”; others, “For he is gracious” [suavis]. Thus one Greek word, χρηστός (*chrēstos*), has been rendered in different ways. Likewise, where it says, “For his mercy is forever,” the Greek has εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα (*eis ton aiōna*), which can also be translated “into eternity.” Therefore, if the mercy meant here is that by which no one can be blessed without God, “into eternity” is the better rendering. But if it is the mercy shown to the miserable, so that they are either comforted in misery or even delivered from it, “for the age” is better—that is, until the end of the age, in which there will not be a lack of miserable people to whom mercy may be shown.

Unless perhaps someone would dare to say that even those who will be condemned with the devil and his angels will not be entirely without some mercy from God—not mercy by which they are freed from that condemnation, but mercy by which their punishment is mitigated to some degree; and thus God’s eternal mercy could be understood as extending over their eternal misery. We read that some will receive a more tolerable condemnation in comparison with others; but who would dare say that the punishment of one who has been handed over to it will be mitigated, or that it will have some respite at intervals, when that rich man did not merit even a single drop? (Luke 16:24–26.) This very great matter must be discussed more carefully at leisure. For now, as far as this psalm is concerned, let what has been said about it suffice.

3. [verse 2.] “Who can speak of the mighty acts of the Lord?” Filled with consideration of God’s works, the one who seeks his mercy says: “Who,” he asks, “can make all his praises heard?” What was said above must be supplied, so that the sentence may be complete in this form: “Who can make all his praises heard?” That is, who is sufficient to make all his praises heard?

He said, “make heard,” meaning “cause to be heard,” showing that the mighty acts and praises of the Lord must be spoken in such a way that they are proclaimed to those who hear. But who can proclaim them all?

Or perhaps, because it follows, “Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice righteousness at all times,” he called those his praises that are understood as his works in his commandments. For, as the Apostle says, “It is God who works in you” [to will and to act] (Phil. 2:13).

It was said to the seed of Abraham, “Sing to him and sing psalms to him.” We understood this as though it had said: “Both speak and do good things to his praise.” These two words, “sing” and “sing psalms,” correspond to the two following verses: what is said, “Tell of all his wonders,” is “Sing to him”; while what is said, “Praise yourselves in his holy name” (Ps. 104:2–3), is “Sing psalms to him.”

To this seed the Lord himself also says: “Let your works shine before men, so that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

Considering, then, the commandments of God themselves—whose works are the praises of him who works in his own people—he says: “Who can speak of the mighty acts of the Lord?” For he works these things ineffably. “Who can make all his praises heard?” That is, who, having heard them, practices all his praises, which are the works of his commandments?

For insofar as they are practiced—even if not all that has been heard is practiced—he is to be praised who works in us both the will and the action, according to his good pleasure (Phil. 2:13). Therefore, although he could have said, “All his commandments,” or “all the works of his commandments,” he preferred to say, “his praises,” because, as has been said, he himself is to be praised insofar as they are practiced.

Yet who is sufficient to make these praises heard—that is, once they have been heard, who is capable of practicing them all?

4. [verse 3.] “Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice righteousness at all times”—certainly from the time when they begin and throughout their life in time. “For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

This may appear to be a repetition of the same thought, so that practicing righteousness is the same as keeping judgment. Thus in the preceding verse “at all times” may also be supplied, just as “blessed” is supplied in the following verse. When the omitted words are restored, the passage would read: “Blessed are those who keep judgment at all times; blessed are those who practice righteousness at all times.”

But unless there were some difference between judgment and righteousness, another psalm would not say: “Until righteousness is turned into judgment” (Ps. 93:15). Scripture does indeed like to place these two together, as in: “Righteousness and judgment are the foundation of his throne” (Ps. 96:2), and: “He will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like the noonday” (Ps. 36:6), even though there too a repetition of the same thought seems to occur.

Perhaps, because of the closeness of their meanings, one can also be used in place of the other—judgment for righteousness, or righteousness for judgment. Nevertheless, if they are used properly, I have no doubt that there is a difference: one is said to keep judgment when one judges rightly, and to practice righteousness when one acts rightly.

Nor do I think it absurd to understand this passage according to what is said, “Until righteousness is turned into judgment”: those are called blessed here who keep judgment in faith and practice righteousness in action. For the time will come when the judgment that is now kept in faith will also be exercised in action, when righteousness has been turned into judgment—that is, when the righteous receive the power to judge rightly those by whom they are now judged unjustly.

Accordingly, elsewhere the body of Christ is understood to say: “When I receive the appointed time, I will judge righteous judgments” (Ps. 75:2). More literally, this would be rendered, “I will judge equities.” He did not say, “When I receive the appointed time, I will practice righteousness,” because righteousness must be practiced at all times, just as he says here: “Those who practice righteousness at all times.”

5. [verses 4–5.] Then, because God justifies—that is, makes people righteous by healing them from their iniquities—there follows the prayer: “Remember us, Lord, in the goodwill of your people”; that is, grant that we may be among those in whom you are well pleased, because God is not well pleased in all of them.

“Visit us with your salvation.” For he himself is the Savior in whom sins are forgiven and souls are healed, so that they may be able to keep judgment and practice righteousness. Since those who speak these words understood that the people who do these things are blessed, they consequently ask for this in prayer.

Concerning this salvation it is said elsewhere: “So that we may know your way upon the earth”; and, as though we asked, “Upon what earth?” it follows, “Among all nations.” Again, as though we asked, “What way?” it follows, “Your salvation” (Ps. 66:2–3). For this salvation the aged Simeon spoke when he said: “For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:30). Of himself the Lord said: “I am the way” (John 14:6).

Visit us, therefore, with your salvation—that is, with your Christ—“to see the goodness of your chosen ones and to rejoice in the joy of your nation”; that is, visit us with your salvation for this purpose: that we may see the goodness of your chosen ones and rejoice in the joy of your nation.

Where this passage reads “in goodness,” other manuscripts read “in graciousness,” just as, where it says “For he is good,” others read “For he is gracious.” The Greek word is the same as in another passage: “The Lord will give graciousness” (Ps. 84:13), which some have translated “goodness” and others “kindness.”

But what does “Visit us, so that we may see the goodness of your chosen ones”—that is, the goodness you provide or grant to your chosen ones—mean, except that we should not remain blind, as those to whom it was said: “But now you say, ‘We see’; therefore your sin remains” (John 9:41)? “The Lord gives sight to the blind” (Ps. 145:8), not on account of their merits, but in the goodness of his chosen ones—that is, the goodness he displays or grants to his chosen ones.

Thus we say, “The salvation of my countenance is not from myself, but from my God” (Ps. 42:5); and we call it “our daily bread,” yet we add, “Give us” (Matt. 6:11). Visit us, therefore, with your salvation, so that we may see—in other words, for us to see—in the goodness of your chosen ones; so that we may rejoice—in other words, for us to rejoice—in the joy of your nation.

We ought to understand the one nation of God as the whole seed of Abraham—not the children of the flesh, but the children of the promise. Those whose voice this is desire to share in the joy of that nation. And what is the joy of this nation except its God? To him it is said: “You are my joy; redeem me” (Ps. 31:7); and to him it is said: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, Lord; you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4:6). This is the supreme, true, unchangeable, and blessed good, which is God himself.

“So that you may be praised with your inheritance.”

I am surprised that this verse has been translated in this way in many manuscripts, since the Greek expression is one and the same in all three verses. If the reading “so that you may be praised with your inheritance” is correct, then the two preceding verses could likewise correctly read: “So that you may see the goodness of your chosen ones, and rejoice in the joy of your nation.” The whole passage would then be connected in this way: “Visit us with your salvation, so that you may see the goodness of your chosen ones, so that you may rejoice in the joy of your nation, and so that you may be praised with your inheritance.”

According to the interpretation we have given—“Visit us, so that we may see the goodness of your chosen ones and rejoice in the joy of your nation”—this verse too ought consequently to say: “So that we may be praised with your inheritance.” For it was said to this inheritance: “Praise yourselves in his holy name.”

But since the expression appears ambiguous, if the interpretation preferred by the translators—“so that you may be praised”—is correct, the two preceding verses must also be understood in this way, because, as I said, the Greek expression is the same in all three verses. The whole passage would then be understood as saying: “Visit us with your salvation, so that you may see the goodness of your chosen ones”—that is, visit us for this purpose, so that you may make us be there and may see us there; “so that you may rejoice in the joy of your nation”—that is, so that you may be said to rejoice when they rejoice in you; “so that you may be praised with your inheritance”—that is, so that you may be praised with it, since it is praised only on your account.

Whether, therefore, the words “to see, to rejoice, to praise” are understood in the one way or the other, they desire to be visited with God’s salvation—that is, with his Christ—so that they may not be separated from his people and from those in whom God is well pleased.

6. [verses 6–7.] Let us hear what they next confess: “We have sinned with our fathers, we have acted unjustly, we have committed iniquity.”

What does “with our fathers” mean? Just as the Letter to the Hebrews says that Levi too was tithed in Abraham, because he was in Abraham’s loins when Abraham paid tithes to Melchizedek (Heb. 7:1–10), did these people likewise sin with their fathers because they were in their loins when those fathers were in Egypt?

For those who lived at the time when this psalm was written—and especially their descendants, since the words could have been spoken by those who were then alive or prophesied concerning those yet to come—were far removed in age from those who sinned in Egypt by failing to understand God’s wonders.

For this is what follows, explaining how they sinned with their fathers: “Our fathers,” he says, “did not understand your wonders in Egypt,” and then he recalls many other sins of theirs.

Or should the words “We have sinned with our fathers” rather be understood as though they said, “We have sinned like our fathers,” imitating their sins? If so, this must be supported by some example of such an expression. When I was looking for one at present, none occurred to me—an example in which someone says that he sinned with another person, or did something with him, because he later imitated him in a similar action after a long interval.

7. What, then, does “Our fathers did not understand your wonders” mean, except “They did not recognize what you intended to provide for them through those wonders”? What could this have been except eternal life and not a temporal but an unchangeable good, which is awaited through perseverance?

Therefore they murmured impatiently, became bitter, and sought to make themselves blessed by present, deceptive, and fleeting goods. “They did not remember the multitude of your mercies.”

This rebukes both understanding and memory. Understanding was needed so that they might consider the eternal goods to which God was calling them through those temporal things; memory was needed so that they would at least not forget the wonders performed in temporal affairs, and so that they might confidently believe that by the same power they had already experienced, God would deliver them from their enemies’ persecution.

But they forgot what he had provided for them in Egypt, through so many signs, in order to crush their enemies. “And they became bitter, going up in the sea” [Note: [Col. 1410] So the manuscripts. But the editions read, “into the sea.”], “the Red Sea.”

The manuscript I was consulting had the following reading: in the final two words, “the Red Sea,” a star had been placed before them. This indicates words that are present in the Hebrew but absent from the Septuagint translation.

Most of the manuscripts I was able to examine, both Greek and Latin, read as follows: “And they became bitter”—or, more explicitly from the Greek, “And they were embittered”—“as they went up in the Red Sea.”

Anyone who reads the account of their departure from Egypt and their passage through the Red Sea grieves over their unbelief, seeing how much fear and despair they experienced after so many great and recent miracles in Egypt. Yet he says that they did not remember the multitude of God’s mercies.

They are said to have “gone up” because the configuration of the land is such that the journey from the land of Canaan down into Egypt is called a descent, while the journey from there back into Canaan is called an ascent.

It should certainly be noted how Scripture wished to censure the failure to understand what ought to be understood and the failure to remember what ought to be retained in memory. People do not want this to be counted against their own fault, for no other reason than that they may pray less, be less humble before God, and fail to confess in his sight what they are, so that, having obtained his help, they may become what they are not.

For even sins of ignorance or negligence are better accused so that they may perish than excused so that they may remain; and they are better cleansed by calling upon God than strengthened by provoking him [Note: [Col. 1410] The manuscripts read “when he is angry.”].

8. [verse 8.] Yet he adds that God acted not according to their unbelief: “And he saved them,” he says, “for his name’s sake, to make his power known”—not because of any good merits of theirs.

9. [verse 9.] “And he rebuked the Red Sea, and it was dried up.”
