We do not read that any voice was sent from heaven to rebuke the sea. Rather, he called the divine power by which this was done a rebuke—unless perhaps someone says that it was rebuked secretly, in such a way that the water could hear while human beings could not.

Very hidden and mysterious is the power by which God acts, so that even things lacking sense immediately obey his will. “And he led them through the depths as through a desert.”

By “depths” he meant a great quantity of waters. For some, wishing to translate the whole verse, rendered it: “And he led them through many waters.” What, then, does “through the depths as through a desert” mean except that the place where the depths of the waters had been became dry, as though it were a desert?

[Col. 1411] 10. [verse 10.] “And he saved them from the hand of those who hated them.”

Some translated this verse circumlocutorily, avoiding less Latin phrasing: “And he saved them from the hand of those who hated them.”

“And he redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.”

What price was paid in this redemption? Or is this a prophecy, since the event occurred as a figure of Baptism, where we are redeemed from the hand of the devil by a great price, namely, the blood of Christ? Hence it was more appropriately represented not by just any sea but by the Red Sea, for blood is red in color.

11. [verse 11.] “And water covered their oppressors; not one of them remained”—not all the Egyptians, but those who were pursuing the departing Israelites, desiring to overtake or kill them.

12. [verse 12.] “And they believed in his words.”

The expression seems less Latin, because it does not say “his words” in the accusative or “into his words,” but “in his words”; nevertheless, this is extremely common in Scripture.

“And they praised his praise.”

Such expressions occur when we say, “He served this service,” or “He lived such a life.” By the praise of God he recalls that well-known praise in which it is said: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. 15:1).

13. [verse 13.] “They acted quickly; they forgot his works.”

Other manuscripts have the clearer reading: “They hastened; they forgot his works.” They did not await his counsel. They ought to have reflected that such great works of God toward them were not meaningless, but called them to some happiness without end, which must be endured through perseverance.

Instead, they hastened to become blessed through temporal things. These provide true happiness to no one because they do not extinguish insatiable desire: “Whoever drinks,” he says, “from this water will thirst again” (John 4:13).

14. [verse 14.] Finally: “And they lusted with lust in the desert, and they tempted God in the waterless place.”

What is expressed by “in the desert” is repeated in “in the waterless place,” that is, in a place without water. What is expressed by “they lusted with lust” is repeated in “they tempted God.” The expression “they lusted with lust” is like the earlier “they praised his praise.”

15. [verse 15.] “And he gave them their request”—that is, what they sought by asking—“and he sent fullness into their soul.”

Yet this did not make them blessed, for that was not the fullness of which it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled” (Matt. 5:6).

Accordingly, here he does not speak of the soul according to what is rational, but according to what makes an animate body an animal. Food and drink belong to the sustaining of this animal, in accordance with what is said in the Gospel: “Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?” (Matt. 6:25), as though eating belonged to the soul and clothing to the body.

In this sense it is said in Isaiah: “Why have we fasted, and you did not see? Why have we humbled our souls, and you did not know?” (Isa. 58:3).

16. [verse 16.] “And they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord.”

What kind of provocation he means—or, as others translated more explicitly, what kind of embittering—is sufficiently indicated by what follows.

[Col. 1412] 17. [verse 17.] “The earth opened,” he says, “and swallowed Dathan, and covered over the assembly of Abiron.”

What is expressed by “swallowed” is the same as “covered over.” Dathan and Abiron had one common cause: a most proud and sacrilegious schism.

18. [verse 18.] “And fire blazed in their assembly; the flame consumed sinners.”

In Scripture this term is not ordinarily used for those who, though they live justly and laudably, are not without sin. Rather, just as there is a distinction between those who mock and those who are mockers, between those who murmur and those who are habitual murmurers, between those who write and writers, and in other similar cases, Scripture ordinarily calls those who are very wicked and weighed down by great burdens of sins “sinners” [Note: [Col. 1412] Nearly all manuscripts read “serious” or “grave.”].

19. [verses 19–20.] “And they made a calf at Horeb, and worshiped a graven image. And they exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass.”

He does not say “for the likeness,” but “in the likeness.” The expression is like the one where he says, “And they believed in his words.”

He appropriately does not say, “And they exchanged the glory of God,” although that is what they did, just as the Apostle says: “And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man” (Rom. 1:23). Instead, he says, “their glory.”

God was their glory if they had awaited his counsel and had not hastened. To him it is said: “My glory, and the one who lifts up my head” (Ps. 3:4).

They exchanged this glory of theirs—that is, God—for the likeness of a calf that eats grass, so that they might be eaten by the one who eats those who think according to the flesh: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40:6).

20. [verses 21–22.] “They forgot God, who saved them.”

How did he save them? “He who did great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Cham, and awesome deeds at the Red Sea.”

The wonders are themselves the awesome deeds, for no wonder exists without a certain fear. Yet these could also be called awesome because they afflicted the adversaries and showed these people what they ought to fear.

21. [verse 23.] “And he said that he would destroy them.”

Because they had forgotten the one who had saved them by doing great things, and because they had made and worshiped a graven image, they deserved to perish for this monstrous crime and unbelievable impiety.

Therefore he said that he would destroy them, unless Moses, his chosen one, had stood in the breach before him.

He did not say that Moses stood in the breach as though he were breaking God’s anger, but “in the breach,” that is, in the calamity with which those people were about to be struck. That is, he would not have stood there unless he had offered himself on their behalf, saying: “If you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, erase me from your book” (Exod. 32:31–32).

Here it was shown how much the intercession of the saints avails with God on behalf of others. Moses was confident in God’s justice, by which God could not erase him, and so he obtained mercy: God did not destroy those whom he could justly have destroyed.

Thus he stood in the breach before him, to turn away his anger, so that he would not destroy them.

22. [verse 24.] “And they counted the desirable land as nothing.”

But had they seen it? How, then, did they count as nothing what they had not seen, unless in the way the following words explain: “And they did not believe his words”?

Certainly, unless that land called “a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exod. 3:8) signified something great—unless, through that visible sacrament, it led those who understood his wonders to invisible grace and the kingdom of heaven—these people could not rightly be censured for counting that land as nothing.

For we too ought to count as nothing the temporal kingdom of that land, so that we may truly love Jerusalem, our free mother, which is in heaven (Gal. 4:26), as the truly desirable land.

Rather, their unbelief is rightly rebuked here because, in counting the desirable land as nothing, they did not believe God’s words. Through certain small things he was leading them toward great things, but they hastened to be blessed by temporal goods, which they understood according to the flesh, and did not await his counsel, as was said above.

23. [verse 25.] “And they murmured in their tents; they did not hear the voice of the Lord”—who was strongly forbidding them to murmur.

24. “And he raised his hand over them, to overthrow them in the desert; and to cast down their seed among the nations, and scatter them throughout the lands.”

25. [verses 28–29.] Before saying that anyone had intervened in the face of God’s great indignation and had appeased him in some way, he continued by adding:

“And they were initiated into Beelphegor”—that is, consecrated to the idol of the nations—“and they ate the sacrifices of the dead” [Note: [Col. 1413] The older manuscripts read “sacrifice,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint]. “And they provoked him by their inventions, and destruction was multiplied among them.”

It is as though he postponed what he had begun by raising his hand over them, intending to overthrow them in the desert, cast down their seed among the nations, and scatter them throughout the lands, so that, having been given over to a reprobate mind, they would also commit the deed for which they would be punished with evident justice on account of its more monstrous crime.

As the Apostle says: “And since they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting” (Rom. 1:28).

26. [verse 30.] Finally, so great was their crime—that they were consecrated to an idol and ate the sacrifices of the dead—that is, because the nations sacrificed to dead human beings as though they were gods [Note: [Col. 1413] The word “nations” is absent from some manuscripts]—that God would not be appeased in any other way than by the manner in which Phinees the priest appeased him, when he killed together the man and the woman whom he found in an adulterous embrace (Num. 25:8).

If he had done this out of hatred rather than love, while zeal for God’s house consumed him, it would not have been counted to him as righteousness. By this act he struck that people, whose future destruction would be greater, as though it were one person, almost as with a rod, in order to save its soul from death.

The Lord Christ wished discipline to be milder after the New Testament had been revealed; yet the threat of Gehenna is more terrible than those threats of God which, according to the dispensation proper to those times, we read in that earlier period.

“Destruction was therefore multiplied among them,” since they were grievously devastated on account of their grave sins.

“And Phinees stood, and he appeased him, and the plague ceased.”

He stated the whole matter briefly, because here he is not teaching those who do not know, but recalling it to those who know [Col. 1414]. The “plague” mentioned here is the “breach” mentioned above, for there is one word in the Greek.

27. [verse 31.] “And it was counted to him as righteousness, from generation to generation, forever.”

God counted this to his priest as righteousness [Note: [Col. 1414] So the manuscripts. The editions read “to his priesthood”], not merely for as long as a generation exists, but forever. He searches the heart and knows how much this act was done out of love for the people.

28. [verses 32–33.] “And they provoked him at the water of contradiction, and Moses was troubled because of them, because they embittered his spirit. And he distinguished with his lips.”

What does “he distinguished” mean? It was not as though God, who had already done so many things, could not cause water to flow from the rock. Moses struck the rock with the rod in uncertainty, and therefore this miracle was distinguished from the other miracles, in which he had not doubted.

For this he took offense; for this he deserved to hear that he would die and not enter the promised land (Deut. 32:49–52). Troubled by the murmuring of the unbelieving people, he did not maintain the confidence he ought to have had.

Yet even after his death God gives favorable testimony to him as his chosen one, so that we may understand that his wavering in faith was corrected by this one punishment: he was not permitted to enter the land into which he himself was leading the people.

Far be it from us to believe that he was alienated from the kingdom of God’s grace, which that promised land signified, the land said to flow with milk and honey. For this is rather the eternal covenant that he established with Abraham—not according to the flesh, our father, but according to faith.

29. [verses 34, 36.] Those whose iniquities this psalm recounts, once they had entered that temporal promised land, “did not destroy the nations of whom the Lord had spoken to them. And they mingled with the nations, and learned their works, and served their graven images; and it became a stumbling block to them.”

The fact that they did not destroy those nations but mingled with them became a stumbling block to them.

30. [verses 37–40.] “And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons. And they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the graven images of Canaan.”

That historical account does not report that they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons and idols; but neither can this psalm lie, nor can the Prophets, who say this in many passages of their rebukes. The nations themselves did not conceal that they had this custom.

31. But what is it that follows? “And the land was slain with blood.” We might have supposed that this was a scribal error, and said that he had written *interfecta* (“slain”) instead of *infecta* (“stained”), had we not perceived, from the benefit of God, who willed that his Scriptures exist in many languages, that it was indeed written, “The land was slain with blood,” when we examined the Greek manuscripts. [Note: [Col. 1414] Greek: *ephonoctonêthê*.]

What, then, does “the land was slain” mean, unless this refers tropically to the people who inhabited the land—a manner of expression in which what is contained is signified by that which contains it? Thus we speak of a bad house in which bad people live, and of a good house in which good people live. For they themselves were killing their own souls by sacrificing their sons and spilling the blood of little ones who had no part in that crime; hence it is said, “They poured out innocent blood.” Therefore, “the land was slain with blood, and was defiled by their works,” since they themselves were slain in soul and defiled in their works.

“And they fornicated in their inventions.” He calls “inventions” what the Greeks call *epitēdeumata* (ἐπιτηδεύματα). For this is the word found in the Greek manuscripts both here and above, where it is said, “They provoked him by their inventions,” although in both places he calls “inventions” those things in which they imitated others. We must not therefore suppose that they are called inventions as though they had devised them themselves, with no preceding example in others for them to imitate. Hence some of our other translators preferred to say not “inventions” but “pursuits”; others, “affections” or “affectations”; and others, “pleasures.” Even those who used “inventions” in one place have put “pursuits” in another. I wished to mention this, lest the word “invention” should raise a question in relation to something they did not devise themselves but imitated from others.

32. [verses 40–43.] “And the Lord was enraged with fury against his people.” Some of our translators were unwilling to render the Greek *thymos* (θυμός) as “anger”; some rendered it “mind,” others “indignation,” and others “spirit.” Whatever term is used, however, no disturbance falls upon God; rather, this word, transferred from ordinary usage, has received the meaning of power to avenge.

33. “And he rejected his inheritance. And he delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them; and their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands.” When he called them God’s inheritance, it is clear that he rejected them and delivered them into the hands of their enemies not for destruction but for discipline. Finally, it follows: “He often delivered them.”

34. “Yet they provoked him by their counsel.” This is what he said above: “They did not endure his counsel.” But man’s counsel is destructive to man when he seeks what is his own rather than what is God’s (Philippians 2:21). In God’s inheritance—which is himself, when he graciously offers himself to us for our enjoyment—we shall suffer no narrowness of fellowship with the saints through loving our own possession as though it were private. For that most glorious city, having obtained the promised inheritance, in which no one will die and no one will be born, will not have citizens who rejoice individually in their own possessions, because God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28).

Whoever faithfully and ardently desires fellowship with that city during this pilgrimage learns to prefer common things to private ones, seeking not what is his own but what belongs to Jesus Christ. Thus he will not, by being wise for himself and consulting his own interests, provoke God by his counsel. Rather, hoping for what he does not see, he will not hasten to become blessed by visible things, but will patiently await that eternal reality which is not seen and follow the counsel of him whose help he implores in temptations. Thus he too will be humble in his confessions, lest he become like those of whom it is said: “And they were humbled in their iniquities.”

35. [verses 44–45.] Yet God, full of mercy, did not neglect them: “And he saw them when they were afflicted, when he heard their prayer. And he remembered his covenant, and he repented according to the multitude of his mercies.”

“Repented” is said because he changed what he seemed about to destroy. With God, indeed, all things are ordered and fixed; nor does he, as though by a sudden decision, do something which he did not foresee from eternity that he would do. Yet, in the temporal movements of the creature—which he governs wondrously—he himself, without being moved temporally, is said to do by a sudden will what, through the immutability of his most secret counsel, he established by an ordered sequence of causes. By that counsel, knowing each thing in its proper time, he both makes present things and has already made future things. [Note: [Col. 1416] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read, *agnita agit* (“having known, he acts”); thus also, “and he makes present things.”] And who is sufficient for such matters?

Let us therefore hear Scripture, which speaks lofty things humbly, offering them both for nourishment to the little ones and for investigation to the more mature: “And he saw them when they were afflicted, when he heard their prayer; and he remembered his covenant”—namely, the eternal covenant which he established with Abraham, not the old covenant that is abolished, but the new covenant that is also hidden within the old. “And he repented according to the multitude of his mercies.” He did what he had ordained, but he had foreknown that he would grant it to them when they were afflicted and praying; for their prayer itself, although it did not yet exist but was going to exist, was certainly not hidden from God.

36. [verse 46.] “And he gave them over to mercies,” so that they might be not vessels of wrath but vessels of mercy (Romans 9:22–23). I think that the plural “mercies” is used because he gave them over to different mercies: each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that (1 Corinthians 7:7).

He therefore gave them over to mercies “in the sight of all those who had taken them captive.” Now, whoever you are who read these words, and who recognize, by reading in the apostolic writings and searching the prophetic writings, the grace of God by which we are redeemed to eternal life through our Lord Jesus Christ, and who see the Old Testament revealed in the New and the New veiled in the Old, recall whom the apostle Paul called “the prince of the power of the air, who now works in the sons of disobedience” (Ephesians 2:2), and where he says of certain people that they may recover their senses from the snare of the devil, having been captured by him according to his will (2 Timothy 2:26). Recall also the words of the Lord Jesus Christ, when, expelling him from the hearts of the faithful, he said, “Now the prince of this world has been cast out” (John 12:31); and likewise the words of the same apostle: “He delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Colossians 1:13).

Reasoning through these and similar matters, turn your attention to the writings of the Old Testament and see what is sung in the psalm whose title is “When the house was built after the captivity.” For there it is said: “Sing to the Lord a new song.” And lest you think that this refers only to the Jewish people, he says: “Sing to the Lord, all the earth; sing to the Lord, bless his name, announce—or rather, proclaim the good news; indeed, to translate the very word used in the Greek, evangelize—day by day his salvation.”

For this is why it is called the Gospel: in it, day by day, the Day is announced—Christ the Lord, light from light, the Son from the Father. This too is “his salvation,” because Christ is the salvation of God, as we have already shown above. [Note: [Col. 1417] Above, no. 5.]

“Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples. For the Lord is great and exceedingly praiseworthy; he is to be feared above all gods. For all the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 95:1–5).

These enemies, therefore, together with their king, the devil, held God’s people captive. When we are redeemed from that captivity and the prince of this world is cast out, the house is built after the captivity. Its cornerstone is Christ, who made the two in himself into one new man, making peace; and, coming day by day, he proclaimed this peace as good news both to those who were near and to those who were far away, making both one (Ephesians 2:13–22). He also brought in other sheep that are not of this fold, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd (John 10:16).

Thus God gave his predestined ones over to mercies, because it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy (Romans 9:16), “in the sight of all those who had taken them captive.” These enemies—the devil and his angels—had taken the predestined captive for God’s kingdom and glory. But when they were cast out by our Redeemer, those who had been accustomed to rule inwardly over unbelievers attack the faithful outwardly.

They attack, but they do not overcome those who seize the tower of strength in the face of the enemy (Psalm 60:4). Yet, in order to attack, they perceive that remnants of weakness remain in us, because of which we say, “Forgive us our debts,” and because of which we say, “Do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:12–13).

After casting out these enemies, the Lord Christ completed healings in the body whose head is himself, the Savior of the body (Ephesians 5:23), so that in that same body the third completion might be brought about. For he said: “Behold, I cast out demons and complete healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am completed” (Luke 13:32)—that is, I am perfected, when all of us come together into a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4:13).

37. [verses 47–48.] Therefore, after the demons by whom we were held captive have been cast out, he completes the healings. For here too, after saying, “And he gave them over to mercies, in the sight of all those who had taken them captive,” as though the demons who had taken them captive had been cast out, a prayer follows that he may complete the healings:

“Save us, Lord our God, and gather us from the nations”—or, as other manuscripts read, “from the Gentiles”—“that we may confess your holy name and glory in your praise.”

Then he briefly adds the praise itself: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, from age to age.” We understand this as “from eternity to eternity,” because he will be praised without end by those of whom it is said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83:5).

This is the third completion of Christ’s body: after the demons have been cast out and the healings completed, it proceeds to the immortality of that body and the eternal kingdom of those who praise perfectly because they love perfectly—and who love perfectly because they contemplate face to face.

Then what was prayed for at the beginning of this psalm will be brought to perfection: “Remember us, Lord, in the favor of your people; visit us with your salvation, so that we may see the prosperity of your chosen, rejoice in the joy of your nation, and be praised together with your inheritance.”

For he gathers not only from the Gentiles the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24), but also those that are not of that fold, so that there may be one flock, as it was said, and one shepherd. [Note: [Col. 1418] Am. and Lov. read, “from the Jews.” Better Er. and the manuscripts: “from the Gentiles.”]

But the Jews, when they think that this prophecy refers to their visible kingdom, because they do not know how to rejoice in invisible blessings, will fall into the snares of him concerning whom the Lord says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John 5:43).

Of him the apostle Paul says: “For the man of sin, the son of destruction, will be revealed, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, presenting himself as though he were God.” And shortly afterward he says: “Then the wicked one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and will destroy by the illumination of his coming—him whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power and signs and lying wonders, and with every deceit of unrighteousness for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved. And therefore God will send them a working of error, so that they may believe the lie and all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to unrighteousness” (2 Thessalonians 2:3–11).

Through this apostate, through this one who exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped, it seems to me that the carnal people of Israel will suppose that the prophecy is fulfilled which says, “Save us, Lord our God, and gather us from the Gentiles.” Under his leadership, as though in the sight of their visible enemies who had visibly taken them captive, they will possess a visible glory.

Thus they will believe the lie, because they did not receive the love of the truth, so that they might desire not carnal but spiritual goods. For they were deceived by the devil into killing Christ when they said: “If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.” Then Caiaphas, one of them, being high priest that year, said to them: “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is expedient for us [Note: [Col. 1418] The editions read, “for you”; but the manuscripts, following the Greek, read, “for us.”] that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish.” But, as the Evangelist understood it, “he did not say this from himself; rather, being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation—and not only for the nation,” that is, for the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel, “but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John 11:48–52).

For he had other sheep that were not of that fold. All these sheep, both Israelites and Gentiles, had been taken captive by the devil and his angels. Therefore, after the devil’s dominion had been expelled from them, so that they might be saved and perfected eternally in the sight of the evil spirits who had taken them captive, their voice in the prophecy is:

“Save us, Lord our God, and gather us from the Gentiles.”

It is not, as the Jews think, to be fulfilled through the Antichrist, but through Christ our Lord, who comes in the name of his Father, day by day, as his salvation—the one of whom it is also said here, “Visit us with your salvation.”

And all the people will say—this people of the predestined, from circumcision and uncircumcision, a holy nation, a people for adoption:

“So be it, so be it.”

## Exposition of Psalm 106

1. This psalm commends to us the mercies of God, mercies proved in us; and therefore it is sweeter to those who have experienced them. It is astonishing if it can be pleasant to anyone except one who has learned in himself what he hears in this psalm. Yet it was written not for one or two individuals but for the people of God, and it is set before them as a mirror in which they may recognize themselves.

Its title need not now be discussed. It is “Alleluia,” and again “Alleluia.” It is our custom to sing this solemnly at a particular time, according to the ancient tradition of the Church; for we do not sing this without a sacrament on particular days. We sing “Alleluia” on particular days, but we think of it every day. For if this word signifies the praise of God, then, even if it is not in the mouth of the flesh, it is certainly in the mouth of the heart: “His praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33:2).

The fact that this title contains “Alleluia” not once but twice is not peculiar to this psalm; another psalm above also has it. As appears from its text, that psalm was sung concerning the people of Israel, whereas this one is sung concerning the universal Church of God, spread throughout the whole world.

Perhaps it rightly has “Alleluia” twice because of the cry we utter, “Abba, Father.” “Abba” means nothing other than “Father,” yet the Apostle did not say without reason, “In which we cry, Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15). One wall, coming from one side to the cornerstone, cries, “Abba”; the other, from the other side, cries, “Father”—in that cornerstone which is our peace and which made both one (Ephesians 2:14, 20).

Let us therefore see what we are instructed by here: what gives us cause for rejoicing, what gives us cause for groaning, and what gives us cause to seek help; how we are abandoned and how we are aided; what we are by ourselves and what we are by the mercy of God; how our pride is crushed so that his grace may be glorified.

Let each person, if possible, recognize in himself what I am about to say. I am speaking to people who walk in the way of God and have attained some degree of spiritual progress. If some, perhaps for that reason, understand me less, let them discover where they stand and hasten toward understanding by making progress.

I do not think that God will abandon our effort, so that what we say may reach everyone—both those who have experienced these things and those who have not: so that the experienced may approve, the inexperienced may desire them, and my discourse may be pleasant to all. It will first be pleasant to the Lord if it is truthful; and it will be truthful if it comes not from me but from him.

Thus the psalm begins.

2. [Verse 1.] “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is everlasting.”

Give thanks for this reason: “for he is good.” If you have tasted, give thanks. No one can give thanks who has refused to taste; for how will he say that something is sweet when he does not know it?

But if you have tasted how sweet the Lord is (1 Peter 2:3), “give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.” If you have tasted with eagerness, pour forth what you have tasted in thanksgiving.

“For his mercy is everlasting”—that is, eternal. Here it is expressed as “everlasting,” because in some passages of Scripture “everlasting”—in Greek, *eis aiōna* (εἰς αἰῶνα)—is understood to mean eternal. His mercy is not temporary rather than eternal, since this mercy is upon human beings precisely so that they may live eternally with the angels.

3. [Verses 2–9.] “Let those redeemed by the Lord say so.” The people of Israel also appear to have been redeemed from the land of Egypt, from the hand of slavery, from fruitless labors and works of clay. Let us nevertheless see whether it is they who say these things—the people whom the Lord freed from Egypt.

It is not so. Who, then, are these people? “Those whom he redeemed from the hand of their enemies.” Even here someone might still understand those redeemed from the hand of their enemies to be the Egyptians. Let the psalm state plainly who are intended, on whose behalf it wishes these things to be sung: “He gathered them from the regions,” which might still be regions of Egypt, for there are many regions even within one province.

Let it speak openly: “From the east and the west, from the north and the sea.” We therefore understand these people as already redeemed throughout the whole world.

This people of God, freed from the great and extensive Egypt, is led through the Red Sea, so that in Baptism the enemies may be brought to an end. Through the sacrament resembling the Red Sea—namely, Baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ—the pursuing Egyptians, that is, sins, are blotted out; and when you escape, no enemy who was oppressing you remains.

Let these people therefore say these things. And now let us hear, brothers, since this people of God is being led, what is happening in the gathering of all the nations redeemed through Christ. These things do not occur simultaneously in everyone, as though they were all happening at once, but in each individual believer; in that people, however, they occur in another way.

The whole people, that entire nation descended from Abraham according to the flesh, the entire multitude of the house of Israel, was led out of Egypt once, led through the Red Sea once, and brought to the promised land once. All were together in whom these things occurred: “All these things happened to them as a figure, but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

We, however, are not all gathered together at once. Rather, by believing gradually and individually, we are gathered into one city and one people of God. Yet in each one of us individually, these things that were written also occur; they occur in the people as well. For the people are made up of individuals, not individuals out of the people. Is one person ever made from peoples? Rather, a people consists of individual human beings.

Whatever, then, when I speak, you who have experienced these things recognize in yourself, do not remain absorbed in yourself in your thoughts and suppose that it happens only to you. Believe that it happens either to all or nearly all who come to this people and are redeemed from the hand of their enemies by the precious blood.

4. For he is about to repeat continually what we have just sung: “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men.” As far as I have been able to observe—and you can do so as well—he repeats these verses four times. In this number, as far as we have been able to investigate with the Lord’s help, he signifies four particular temptations from which the one to whom they confess his mercies delivers us.

Imagine a person at first seeking nothing, living according to his former life in a deceptive security, thinking that there is nothing after this life eventually comes to an end; negligent and sluggish, with a heart overwhelmed by the allurements of the world and lulled to sleep by deadly pleasures. To awaken this person so that he may seek the grace of God, become attentive, and awaken as though from sleep—is it not the hand of God that awakens him?

Yet he does not know who has awakened him. He begins already to belong to God when he comes to know the faith of the truth. [Note: [Col. 1421] Thus the manuscripts. But Am.: “He begins, however, to taste God’s sweetness when he has known,” etc. Er. and Lov.: “But he begins to belong to God, and to taste his sweetness,” etc.] But before he knows it, he grieves over his error. He discovers that he is in error, wishes to know the truth, knocks wherever he can, attempts whatever he can, wanders wherever he can, and even suffers hunger for the truth itself.

The first temptation, therefore, is that of error and hunger. When he has grown weary in this temptation and cries out to God, he is brought to the way of faith, from which he may begin to proceed toward the city of rest. He is brought to Christ, who said, “I am the way” (John 14:6).

5. When he has arrived there, already knowing what he ought to observe, he sometimes attributes too much to himself and, presuming on his own strength, begins to want to fight against sins, only to be overcome because of his pride.

He discovers himself bound by the difficulties of his desires and unable to walk along the way because of his chains. He feels enclosed by the difficulty of his vices; and, as though a wall of impossibility had been raised and the gates closed, he finds no way to escape and live rightly.

He already knows how he ought to live. Previously he was in error and suffered hunger for the truth; now he has received the food of truth and has been placed on the way. He hears: “Live well, according to what you know.” Previously you did not know how to live; now you have received this knowledge.

He tries, but cannot. He feels himself bound and cries out to the Lord. The second temptation, then, is difficulty in doing good, just as the first was error and hunger.

He cries out to the Lord in this temptation also. The Lord delivers him from his distresses, breaks the bonds of difficulty, and establishes him in the practice of righteousness. What had been difficult now begins to become easy for him: to abstain from evil, not to commit adultery, not to steal, not to murder, not to commit sacrilege, not to desire what belongs to another. What had previously been difficulty has become ability.

The Lord could have granted this without difficulty. But if we possessed it without difficulty, we would not recognize the giver of this good. For if, from the beginning, we could do what we wished whenever we wished, and did not feel desires resisting us, and our soul were not struck down by the weight of its chains, we would attribute to our own strength what we found ourselves able to do, and would not confess to the Lord his mercies.

6. After these two temptations—the first of error and lack of truth, the second of difficulty in doing good—a third temptation confronts the person. I am speaking to one who has already passed through these two.

These two are familiar, I admit, to many. Who does not know that he has come from ignorance to truth, from error to the way, from hunger for wisdom to the word of faith?

Then many struggle with the difficulties of their vices and, still bound by habit, groan as though confined and shackled. They recognize this temptation too, although they may already say, if they do say it: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24).

For see how tightly bound they are: “The flesh,” he says, “desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Galatians 5:17).

Therefore, one who has already been helped by the Spirit so that, just as he did not wish to be an adulterer, he is not one; just as he did not wish to be a thief, he is not one; and likewise with all the other things that people wish to overcome but are often bent and overcome by them, so that they cry out to God, asking him to deliver them from their distresses, and, once delivered, confess to the Lord his mercies—whoever is such a person, having overcome those difficulties and now living honorably among people, without any complaint concerning evil conduct, is confronted by the third temptation: a certain weariness with the delay of this life, so that at times he no longer takes pleasure either in reading or in praying.

The third temptation is contrary to the first. Previously he was endangered by hunger; afterward, by disgust. From what does this arise, unless from a certain sickness of the soul?

Adultery no longer entices you, yet the word of God does not delight you. After escaping the danger of ignorance and desire, over which you rejoice that you have prevailed, take care lest weariness and disgust kill you.

This too is no slight temptation. Recognize yourself in it and cry out to the Lord, so that here also he may deliver you from your distresses. When you have been freed from this temptation, let them confess his mercies to him.

7. Once freed from error, freed from difficulty in doing good, and freed from weariness and disgust with the word of God, perhaps you will be worthy to have the people entrusted to you and to be placed at the helm of the ship, governing the Church.

There is a fourth temptation there. Storms of the sea shaking the Church disturb the helmsman. Thus every devout believer among God’s people may experience those three temptations; this fourth one is especially ours. For the more we are honored, the more we are endangered.

It must be feared that the danger of error may turn any of you away from the truth; it must be feared that each person’s desire may overcome him, so that he chooses to follow it rather than cry out to the Lord concerning its difficulties; it must be feared that the word of God may become less pleasing to each of you, and that he may die of disgust.

But the temptation of governing, the temptation of the dangers involved in ruling the Church, touches us above all. Yet how will you be separate from us if the whole ship is endangered?

I have said this so that in this fourth temptation, as though it were our own particular concern—where it is necessary that you not cease from prayers, since you are the first to suffer shipwreck [Note: [Col. 1423] The words in parentheses are not found in all manuscripts. The editions, after “not cease,” continued as follows: “lest you first suffer shipwreck, if you are less attentive,” etc. The text has been corrected with the aid of several manuscripts.]—you may not be less attentive or pray less for us.

For what, brothers? Because you do not sit at the same helm, do you not sail in the same ship?

8. After these four temptations, four cries, four deliverances, and four confessions of the Lord’s mercies, the Church itself is then commended throughout this psalm, so that you may know most clearly which Church the psalm was speaking about from the beginning.

It is commended in such a way that God’s grace is proclaimed to us in all things [Note: [Col. 1423] Thus the manuscripts. But Am. reads, “to all of us”; Er. and Lov. have [lacuna], “to all of us.”]—he who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6). For he came so that those who do not see might see, and those who see might become blind (John 9:39); because “every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be humbled” (Isaiah 40:4).

After this commendation, something is said that may also be understood of heretics, by whom the Church is shaken as though by civil wars. Then the psalm, which I have already explained—perhaps more briefly than you expected—is brought to a conclusion.

Indeed, I think that I have explained this entire, somewhat lengthy psalm so thoroughly that you no longer expect from me the office of a disputant but almost that of a reader, if you retain what I have said. I think these matters have been placed before your eyes; but so that they may be better impressed upon you, let them be briefly repeated.

The first temptation is error and hunger for the word; the second, difficulty in overcoming desires; the third, weariness and disgust; the fourth, storm and danger in governing the Churches. In all these there are cries, deliverances, and confessions of God’s mercies.

Finally, the Church itself is commended. It has been saved by the grace of our God, not by its own merit. The affliction of its enemies because of their pride is recalled; once they have been destroyed, the Church has been raised up. There is also mention of certain plots by heretics to diminish it, of injuries inflicted, as it were, within the household, and of God’s benefits to the Church amid these things. Then comes the conclusion of the psalm.

Let us now read rather than discuss.

9. “Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of their enemies; whom he gathered from the regions, from the east and the west, from the north and the sea.”

Let Christians themselves, therefore, say this, summoned from the whole world. “They wandered in the wilderness, in a dry place; they did not find the way to a city of habitation.”

We have heard of a pitiable error. What shall we say about their lack? “Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them.”

But why did it faint? To what benefit? God is not cruel. Rather, he commends what is beneficial to us: when we fail, we are moved to pray, and when he comes to our aid, we learn to love him.

And so, after this error, hunger, and thirst: “They cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses.” What did he provide for them because they were wandering? “He led them by a straight way.” They did not find the way to a city of habitation; they were burning with hunger and thirst and were fainting. “He led them by a straight way, so that they might go to a city of habitation.”

He does not yet say how he relieved their hunger and thirst, but expect this also. “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men.” You who have experienced these things, tell them to those who have not: now placed on the way, now directed so as to find the city, and finally delivered from hunger and thirst:

“For he satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul with good things.”

10. [Verses 10–17.] Live well, then. You have now been placed on the way; you have heard what you ought to do and what you ought to hope for. What follows, since you strive and are overcome?

“Those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron.”

Why is this so, unless because you attributed it to yourself, because you did not recognize the grace of God, because you rejected the Lord’s counsel concerning you? For see what he adds:

“Because they embittered the words of the Lord”—through pride, “not knowing the righteousness of God and wishing to establish their own” (Romans 10:3). “And they provoked the counsel of the Most High. And their heart was humbled by labors.”

Now fight against desire. If God ceases to help, you can labor, but you cannot overcome. When you are oppressed by your evil habit, your heart will be humbled by labors, so that, with your heart now humbled, you may learn to cry out:

“Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?”

Their heart, therefore, “was humbled by labors; they were weakened, and there was no one to help them.”

What remains, then, except to understand why this happened?

“For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly have been from the Law. But Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through the faith of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 3:21–22). “The Law entered in so that the trespass might abound” (Romans 5:20).

You received the word; you received the commandment; yet you do not cease doing what you used to do badly. Having received the commandment, you increase your sins through transgression.

If you were proud because you did not know yourself, learn yourself now that you have been humbled. [Note: [Col. 1424] The editions read, “through the transgression of pride. If you did not know yourself, at least learn yourself; humbled, you will cry out,” etc. The text is corrected with the aid of the manuscripts.] You will cry out; you will be freed from necessity; once freed, you will confess the Lord’s mercies.

“And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he saved them from their distresses.”

They have been freed from the second temptation. The temptation of weariness and disgust remains. But first observe what he provided for those who had been delivered:

“He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds. Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men.”

Why? What difficulties did he overcome?

“For he shattered bronze gates and broke iron bars. He took them out of the way of their iniquity; for because of their injustices they were humbled.”

Because they attributed things to themselves rather than to God; because they established their own righteousness, ignorant of God’s righteousness, they were humbled. They discovered that they could not manage without the help of the one whose aid they had presumed upon by relying solely on their own strength.

### 11. [verses 18–22]

But what other kind remains? Their soul abhorred every kind of food. They are already suffering from loathing; weakened by loathing, they are in peril because of loathing. Unless perhaps you think that they could have been killed by hunger but could not be killed by loathing. See what follows after he had said, “Their soul abhorred every kind of food,” lest you should suppose that they were secure because of satiety and fail to see that they were instead [Col. 1425] dying from loathing: “And they drew near,” he says, “even to the gates of death.”

What, then, remains? Since the word of God delights you, do not attribute this to yourself, and do not puff yourself up with any arrogance on this account; nor, while greedily consuming the food, leap arrogantly upon those who are in peril from loathing. Understand also that this has been granted to you, not produced by you. “For what do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). Understanding this, and being in peril from this very fault and sickness, do what follows: “And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses.”

And since their sickness consisted in taking no delight: “He sent his word, and healed them.” See what evil loathing contains; see from what he delivers those who cry out to him in their loathing. “He sent his word, and healed them, and rescued them.” From what? Not from error, not from hunger, not from the difficulty of conquering sins, but from their corruption. It is a certain corruption of the mind to loathe what is sweet.

Therefore, for this benefit also, as for the preceding ones, “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the sons of men. And let them sacrifice a sacrifice of praise.” For now the Lord is sweet, so that he may be praised. “And let them declare his works with rejoicing”—not with weariness, not with sorrow, not with anxiety, not with loathing, but with rejoicing.

### 12. [verses 23–31]

That fourth kind remains, in which we are all in peril. For we are all in a ship: some work, others are carried along; nevertheless, all alike are endangered in the storm and saved in the harbor.

After all these things comes the following: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon many waters”—that is, among many peoples. That waters are often used for peoples is attested by the Apocalypse of John, where, when John asked what those waters were, he received the answer: “They are peoples” (Rev. 17:15).

Those, therefore, who do their work upon many waters themselves “saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.” For what is deeper than human hearts? From there winds often burst forth; storms of seditions and dissensions disturb the ship.

And what happens in these circumstances? God, willing that those who govern and those who are carried along should cry out to him, “spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood still.” What does “stood still” mean? It remained; it persisted. It still disturbs, tosses about for a long time, rages, and does not pass away. For he “spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood still.”

And what did this spirit of the storm do? “And its waves were lifted up.” They rise as far as the heavens in hearing; they descend as far as the abysses in fear. They rise as far as the heavens and descend as far as the abysses: outwardly, conflicts; inwardly, fears. “Their soul was wasting away in evils.”

They were disturbed and shaken as a drunken man. Those who sit at the helm and who faithfully love the ship understand what I am saying: “They were disturbed and shaken as a drunken man.” Certainly, when they speak, when they read, when they discuss matters, they appear wise. But woe from the storm! “And all their wisdom,” he says, “was swallowed up.”

Sometimes all human counsels fail. Whichever way one turns, the waves roar, the storm rages, and one’s arms grow weak. Where the prow should strike, to which wave the side should be exposed, where the ship should be driven and released, from which rocks it should be restrained lest it perish—none of this is seen at all by those at the helm.

And what remains [Col. 1426] except what follows? “And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he brought them out of their distresses. And he commanded the storm, and it became a gentle breeze.” It did not remain a storm, but became a gentle breeze. “And its waves were silent.”

Hear, concerning this matter, the voice of a certain helmsman who had been endangered, humbled, and delivered: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of our affliction which occurred in Asia, because we were burdened beyond our strength and beyond measure”—I see that all his wisdom had been swallowed up—“so that,” he says, “we were weary even of living” (2 Cor. 1:8).

And what then? Would he abandon them when they were thus failing? Or did they fail for this reason, so that he might find glory among them? Finally, what follows? “But we ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we should not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead” (2 Cor. 1:9).

“And he commanded the storm, and it became a gentle breeze.” They had already received within themselves, concerning themselves, the sentence of death—those whose entire wisdom had been swallowed up. “And its waves were silent. And they rejoiced because they were silent, and he brought them into the harbor of their desire. Let them confess to the Lord his mercies.”

Everywhere, absolutely everywhere, let them confess to the Lord—not our merits, not our powers, not our wisdom, but his mercies. Let him be loved in all our deliverance, the one who was invoked in all our affliction. “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the sons of men.”

### 13. [verses 32–38]

And see from where he says this, from where he has spoken all these things beforehand, from where he has enumerated them, and where these things take place: “And let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders.” And “let them exalt him”—that is, “let them praise him”; and “let them praise him”—that is, “let them exalt him.” Let peoples and elders, merchants and helmsmen, exalt and praise him.

For what did he do in this Church? What did he establish? From what did he rescue her? What did he grant her? “He opposed the proud and gave grace to the humble” (James 4:6): to the proud, namely, first to the Jewish people, arrogant and exalting themselves on account of their descent from Abraham and because the utterances of God had been entrusted to that nation (Rom. 3:2).

These things did not benefit them for healing, but for exaltation of heart—for swelling rather than greatness. What, then, did God do, resisting the proud and giving grace to the humble; cutting off the natural branches because of pride and grafting in the wild olive because of humility (Rom. 11:17–24)? What did God do? Hear these two things: first, how God resists the proud; then, how he gives grace to the humble.

“He made rivers in the desert.” Waters ran there; prophecies ran there. Now search among the Jews for a prophet: you do not find one. “He made rivers in the desert and outlets of waters in a thirsty land.” Let them say, “There is no longer a prophet, and he will not know us any more” (Ps. 73:9). “He made rivers in the desert and outlets of waters in a thirsty land, fruitful land into salt flats.”

You seek faith in Christ there, and do not find it; you seek a prophet, and do not find one; you seek a priest, and do not find one; you seek [Col. 1427] a sacrifice, and do not find one; you seek a temple, and do not find one. Why is this? Because “he made rivers in the desert and outlets of waters in a thirsty land; fruitful land into salt flats.” On account of what, and for what merit? “Because of the wickedness of those who dwelt in it.”

See how he resists the proud. Hear how he gives grace to the humble: “He made the desert into pools of water, and the dry land into outlets of waters. And he caused the hungry to dwell there.” For it was said to him: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 110:4).

For you seek a sacrifice among the Jews; you do not have one according to the order of Aaron, because “he made rivers in the desert.” [Note: [Col. 1427] The Erfurt and Louvain editions read, “For you seek a priest and a sacrifice,” etc.; the Am. edition and the manuscripts do not have “a priest and.”] You seek one according to the order of Melchizedek; among them you do not find it, but throughout the whole world it is celebrated in the Church. “From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is praised” (Ps. 113:3).

And God says to those whose rivers he made into a desert: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not accept sacrifice from your hands, because from the rising of the sun to its setting a pure sacrifice is offered to my name” (Mal. 1:10–11).

Where all sacrifices were unclean, when the nations were a desert, when they were desolate, when all the nations were salt flats—there are now springs; there are now rivers; there are now pools of water and outlets of waters.

Thus he resisted the proud, but gave grace to the humble. “And he caused the hungry to dwell there,” because “the poor shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. 22:26). “And they established a city for habitation”—for the present, habitation in hope, since he says, “Whoever hears me shall dwell in hope” (Prov. 1:33, according to the Septuagint). “And they established a city for habitation.”

“And they sowed fields, and planted vineyards, and produced the fruit of grain”—[Note: [Col. 1427] Supply: “fruit.”] the fruit for which that laborer rejoices who says, “Not because I seek a gift, but I seek the fruit” (Phil. 4:17).

“And he blessed them, and they multiplied exceedingly, and their cattle did not diminish.” This stands firm. For “the firm foundation of God stands, because the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19).

Cattle and sheep are said of those who walk simply in the Church but are useful: not very learned, but full of faith. Therefore he blessed both the spiritual and the carnal among them; they multiplied exceedingly, and their cattle did not diminish.

### 14. [verses 39–42]

“And they became few, and they were afflicted.” From where does this come, as though it were introduced from elsewhere? Rather, from within. For in order that they might become few, “they went out from us, but they were not of us.”

He speaks of them as though they were those about whom he had spoken earlier, so that they may be distinguished with understanding; for he speaks as though they were the same, because of their common sacraments. They belong to the people of God, if not in virtue, at least in outward appearance of piety. We have heard the Apostle speak of them: “In the last days grievous times will come; for people will be lovers of themselves” (2 Tim. 3:1–2).

The first evil is that they love themselves—that is, they please themselves. Would that they displeased themselves and pleased God! [Note: [Col. 1427] More manuscripts read, “and loved God.”] Would that, in their difficulties, they cried out [Col. 1428] and were delivered from their distresses. But, presuming greatly upon themselves, they became few.

It is clear, brothers: all who separate themselves from unity become few. They are many, indeed, but they are in unity so long as they are not separated from unity. [Note: [Col. 1428] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “but in unity, when they are not, they are separated from unity.”] Once the multitude of unity no longer belongs to them, they are few in heresy and schism.

“And they became few, and they were afflicted by the tribulation and pain of evils.” “Contempt was poured out upon princes.” For they were rejected by the Church of God. And even more: because they wished to be princes, they were therefore despised, and became salt that had lost its savor, thrown outside; therefore it is trampled by people (Matt. 5:13).

“Contempt was poured out upon princes. And he led them astray in a trackless place, and not on the way.” Those former ones were on the way; they were directed toward the city and finally led there, not led astray. But these were led astray in a trackless place.

What does “he led them astray” mean? “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts” (Rom. 1:24). This is what it means: he led them astray—he gave them over to themselves. For if you ask what the expression properly means, they lead themselves astray. “Whoever thinks he is something when he is nothing deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3).

What, then, does “he led them astray” mean? He abandoned them. “In a trackless place, and not on the way”: for how can people be on the way who hold a part and abandon the whole? How can they be on the way?

What, then, is the way, or where is the way recognized? “May God,” he says, “have mercy on us and bless us; may he make his face shine upon us, so that we may know your way on earth.” On what earth? “Among all the nations is your salvation” (Ps. 67:2–3).

Such people, then, in order to be diminished and become few, go out from here. They all went out from the multitude of unity, as I recalled shortly before in the saying about them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

But if perhaps they are ours in God’s hidden foreknowledge, they must return. How many are not ours, still apparently within; and how many are ours, still apparently outside! “The Lord knows those who are his.”

Those who are not ours but are within, whenever they find an opportunity, go out; and those who are ours but are outside, whenever they find an opportunity, return.

Accept, then, what God knows: according to this, “he led them astray in a trackless place, and not on the way.”

And what did he do with them? Hear attentively what I began to say. He could have tolerated them within forever, but we would not have benefited from them. Once they were separated and began to trouble us with malicious questions, they provided us with both zeal for inquiry and an example of fear. Each person trembles when he sees another depart, as though the following were being said to him through that person’s departure: “Therefore, whoever thinks he stands, let him see that he does not fall” (1 Cor. 10:12).

They are therefore beneficial because they go out. For if they were within and were so evil, they would provide no benefit.

What is said about them in a certain psalm? “The assembly of bulls”—that is, of stiff-necked and proud people—“the assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples” (Ps. 68:31). He calls the easily led souls “cows,” because they readily consent to the bulls who lead them astray.

But why is this? “So that those who have been tested as silver may be brought forth” (Ps. 68:31). What does “so that they may be brought forth” mean? So that they may appear, so that they may stand out [Col. 1429]—those who have been tested in the utterance of God.

When heretics must be answered out of necessity, Catholics are built up for their benefit. Paul plainly expressed this judgment: “For there must be heresies,” he says, “so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19).

There must also be bulls who lead others astray, “so that those who have been tested as silver” may become manifest—that is, “may be brought forth.”

What does “tested as silver” mean? “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances; silver tested by fire, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 12:7). Whoever has been tested in this silver—that is, in the utterance of the Lord—cannot fully bring forth this silver unless disturbed by the questions of heretics.

And here observe that nothing has been omitted: “Contempt was poured out upon princes”—upon those bulls. Why were they despised? Because they announced something else. What does “despised” mean? They were anathematized. For “whoever announces to you anything besides what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:9).

What is as despised as salt that has lost its savor, thrown outside and trampled? And see whether they are not princes. Hear Paul himself: “Even if we,” he says, “or an angel from heaven should preach to you anything besides what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:8–9).

They are princes; they are learned; they are great; they are precious stones. What more will you say? Are they perhaps angels? And yet, “even if an angel from heaven should announce to you anything besides what you received, let him be accursed”—because the devil himself was an angel who fell from heaven.

“Contempt was poured out upon princes. And he helped the poor man out of poverty.”

What does this mean, brothers? The princes were despised, and the poor man was helped. The proud were cast down, and the humble was instructed. He did this, and by doing so he helped the poor man out of poverty.

That beggar is the one who attributes nothing to himself and expects everything from the mercy of God. Every day he cries out before the Lord’s door, knocking so that it may be opened to him; naked and trembling, so that he may be clothed; lowering his eyes to the ground and beating his breast.

God greatly helped this beggar, this poor man, this humble person—even through the very separation of the heretics. For they became few, were afflicted, and were led astray in a trackless place and not on the way.

Finally, after those diminished, led astray, few, and afflicted people, what happens to the poor man who has been helped? “And he made families like sheep.”

You were thinking of one poor man and one beggar, of whom he said, “And he helped the poor man out of poverty.” This poor man consists of many families; this poor man consists of many peoples. Many Churches are one Church; one people, one family, one sheep.

“And he made families like sheep.” These are great mysteries, great sacraments—how profound, full of mysteries; how sweetly discovered, because they had long remained hidden.

Therefore, “the upright shall see and rejoice, and all iniquity shall shut its mouth.” That iniquity which chatters against unity and compels the truth to become manifest, once convicted, shall shut its mouth.

### 15. [verse 43]

“Who is wise? Let him keep these things, and understand the mercies of the Lord.”

See with what conclusion he closed: “Who is wise? Let him keep these things.” And what will the wise person keep? That is, if he is poor, he keeps them; if he is not rich—that is, if he is not proud, if he is not puffed up—[Col. 1430] he keeps these things.

Why does he keep them? Because he will understand the mercies of the Lord: not his own merits, not his own powers, not his own might, but the mercies of the Lord, who led the wandering and needy person onto the way and fed him; who freed and released the one fighting against the difficulty of sins and bound by the chains of habit; who restored the one loathing the word of God and almost dying from a certain weariness, by sending the medicine of his word; who brought the one in peril amid shipwreck and stormy dangers into harbor, after calming the sea; who finally established him among that people where he gives grace to the humble, not among those where he resists the proud; and who made him his own, so that, remaining within, he might be multiplied, rather than going out and being diminished.

The upright see this and rejoice. Therefore all iniquity shall shut its mouth, and the one who is wise shall keep these things.

How will he keep them? Through humility, by understanding the mercies of the Lord; for it was said everywhere: “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the sons of men.”

## ON PSALM 107  
### Why an Exposition Is Not Appended Here

### 1

I did not consider it necessary to expound Psalm 107, since I have already expounded it in Psalms 56 and 59, from whose concluding portions this psalm is composed.

For the concluding part of Psalm 56 is the beginning of this one, up to the verse where it says, “And your glory is over all the earth.” From there to the end is the concluding part of Psalm 59.

Likewise, the concluding part of Psalm 134 is the same as Psalm 113, beginning at the verse where it says, “The idols of the nations are silver and gold.” Similarly, Psalms 13 and 52, with some intervening changes, have everything in common from beginning to end.

Whatever, then, is placed somewhat differently in this Psalm 107 from the way it appears in those two psalms from whose parts it is composed does not have a difficult meaning.

Thus, in Psalm 56 it says, “I will sing and make melody; awake, my glory”; whereas in this psalm it says, “I will sing and make melody in my glory.” The word “awake” was therefore said there so that singing and making melody might take place in that glory.

Likewise, there it says, “For your mercy has been magnified up to the heavens”—or, as others have translated it, “has been lifted up”—whereas here it says, “For your mercy is great above the heavens.” For it was magnified up to the heavens so that it might be great in the heavens; this is what “above the heavens” means.

Likewise, in Psalm 59: “I will rejoice, and I will divide Shechem”; but here: “I will be exalted [Note: [Col. 1430] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. The editions read, “I will rejoice.”], and I will divide Shechem.”

This shows that what was signified concerning the division of Shechem was foretold as occurring after the Lord’s exaltation, and that the rejoicing pertains to this exaltation, so that he rejoices because he is exalted.

Hence elsewhere he says: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Ps. 30:12).

Likewise, there it says, “And Ephraim is the strength of my head”; here, “And Ephraim is the support of my head.” Through being received he becomes strength—that is, through receiving, he makes strong, bringing forth fruit in us. For Ephraim is interpreted as “Fruitfulness.”

“Support,” however, can refer to either of two things: either when we receive Christ, or when he himself receives us, since he is the head of the Church.

And where it says there, “Those who afflict us,” here it says, “Our enemies.” They are, of course, the very same people.

### 2

We are rightly admonished by this psalm to understand according to prophecy those titles that seem to have been set down as historical, in accordance with what we see about the composition of the psalms.

For what is more different, according to history, than what appears in the title of Psalm 56: “To the end; do not destroy; for David, in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave”; and in the title of Psalm 59: “To the end; for those [Note: [Col. 1431] Some manuscripts read “instead of ‘for those’”; and shortly afterward, “Mesopotamia of Syria.”] who will be changed; in the inscription of the title; for David, for instruction, when he burned Mesopotamia, Syria, and Syria of Zobah, and Joab turned back and struck twelve thousand in the Valley of Salt”?

For, apart from what is written, “in the inscription of the title,” “for David,” and “to the end,” the remaining details are so different that the one contains David’s humility, while the other contains his strength; the one, flight, and the other, victories.

And yet this psalm is composed from the concluding portions of these two psalms, whose titles are so different. This signifies that both converge upon one thing—not on the surface of history, but in the depth of prophecy—the ends of both being joined in this one psalm, whose title is “A song of a psalm, for David,” resembling neither of those titles except that this one also contains “for David.”

For, as the Epistle to the Hebrews says, “In many parts and in many ways, long ago God spoke to the fathers through the prophets” (Heb. 1:1). Yet it was through the one whom he afterward sent that he spoke, so that the utterances of the prophets might be fulfilled: [Note: [Col. 1431] Thus the better manuscripts. Others read, “in him”; the editions, “in it.”] “For however many the promises of God are, in him also” (2 Cor. 1:20).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 108

### 1

Whoever faithfully reads the Acts of the Apostles recognizes that this psalm contains a prophecy concerning Christ. There it is plainly evident that what is written here—“Let his days be few, and let another receive his episcopate”—was prophesied concerning Judas, Christ’s betrayer, when Matthias was appointed in Judas’s place and added as the twelfth in the number of the Apostles (Acts 1:15–26).

But if we attempt to understand everything spoken here in an evil sense as referring to that one man, the method of exposition will not altogether—or scarcely—succeed. If, however, everything is understood of such a class of evil people, namely Christ’s ungrateful enemies, the Jews, everything seems to me capable of being opened up more clearly.

For just as certain things are said that seem properly to pertain to the apostle Peter, yet do not have an evident meaning unless they are referred [Col. 1432] to the Church—whose person he is recognized to have represented figuratively because of the primacy he had among the disciples—as in “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:19), and other passages of this kind; so Judas, in a certain way, bears the person of Christ’s enemies, the Jews, who hated Christ then and now continue to hate him through the succession of that same impiety.

Concerning these people and this people, it is not inappropriate to understand not only those things that we read more openly about them in this psalm, but also those that are expressed more specifically concerning Judas himself, such as the passage I mentioned: “Let his days be few, and let another receive his episcopate.” This will become clear, with the Lord’s help, when we come to those verses in the order of exposition.

### 2. [verse 2]

The psalm therefore begins in this way: “O God, do not be silent about my praise, because the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful person have been opened against me.”

From this it appears both that the reproach which the sinner and the deceitful person do not keep silent is false, and that the praise about which God is not silent is true. For God is truthful, but every human being is a liar (Rom. 3:4), because no one is truthful except in the one in whom God speaks.

The greatest praise is that of the only-begotten Son of God, by which [Note: [Col. 1432] The Erfurt and Venetian editions read “because”; the Louvain edition, “who”; the Maurist edition, “by which.”] he is proclaimed to be precisely what he is: the only-begotten Son of God. This, however, was not apparent; it was concealed by the appearance of his weakness when the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful person were opened against him.

That mouth was opened because his power was hidden. He says, “The mouth of the deceitful person was opened,” because the hatred that had been covered by deceit burst forth into speech. This too is said more plainly in the following verses.

### 3. [verse 3]

“They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue”—certainly at the time when they praised him with deceptive flattery as a good teacher. Hence elsewhere it is said: “And those who praised me swore against me” (Ps. 102:9).

Then, because they burst forth, crying, “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6), he immediately added: “And they surrounded me with words of hatred.”

Those who, with a deceitful tongue, spoke words as though they were not words of hatred but of love, spoke against me because they did this while laying a snare. Later they surrounded me with words not of false and deceitful love but of open hatred, “and they fought against me without cause.”

Just as the godly love Christ freely, so the ungodly hate him freely. For just as the best people seek truth for its own sake, without any advantage proposed outside it, so the worst seek iniquity.

Hence even in authors of secular literature it was said of a certain thoroughly wicked man: “He was rather gratuitously evil and cruel” (Sallust, *The War of Catiline*).

### 4. [verse 4]

“Instead of loving me,” he says, “they slandered me.”

There are six distinctions in this category, which can readily be observed when they are mentioned:

- returning good for evil;
- not returning evil for evil;
- returning good for good;
- returning evil for evil;
- not returning good for good;
- returning evil for good.

The first two belong to the good, and of those two the first is better. The last two belong to the evil, and of those two the latter is worse. The middle two belong, in a certain way, to those in between; but of these, the first is close to the good, and the latter [Col. 1433] close to the evil.

These distinctions must be observed in the Holy Scriptures.

The Lord himself returns good for evil: he justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5), and, hanging on the cross, said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Following his footsteps, the holy Stephen, kneeling, prayed for those who were stoning him, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60).

To this belongs the command: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you” (Matt. 5:44).

That evil should not be returned for evil is stated by the apostle Paul: “Returning evil to no one for evil” (Rom. 12:17); and by the apostle Peter: “Not returning evil for evil or insult for insult” (1 Pet. 3:9). Hence we also read in the Psalms: “If I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil” (Ps. 7:5).
