Of the final two, the milder applies to the nine lepers who, after they had been cleansed by the Lord, did not give thanks (Luke 17:12, 18). But the final one, than which nothing is worse, applies to those of whom we read in this psalm: “Instead of loving me, they slandered me.”

They owed love because of such great benefits of the Lord; they not only failed to return it, but instead inflicted evil in return for that good.

The two middle cases, which we said belong in a certain way to those in between, are as follows. The first—returning good for good—is found among both good people and those who are moderately good or moderately evil.

Therefore the Lord does not condemn it, but he does not want his disciples to remain in it alone; he wants to lead them on to greater things. He says to them: “If you love those who love you”—that is, if you return good for good—“what reward will you have?” That is, “What great thing will you do? Do not even the tax collectors do this?” (Matt. 5:46).

He wants them to do this and much more: namely, to love not only their friends but also their enemies.

The latter case—returning evil for evil—is found among both evil people and those who are moderately evil or moderately good, to such an extent that the Law gave them a measure for vengeance: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Deut. 19:21). This is, if one may say so, the justice of the unjust.

It is not that it is unjust for each person to receive what he has done; otherwise the Law would never have established it. Rather, the desire for vengeance is vicious, and it belongs more properly to a judge to decree this among others than for a good person to seek it for himself.

Therefore, the ungodly, having fallen from that summit of kindness where good is returned for evil, have descended into what depth of wickedness by returning evil for good! By what precipitous fall have they crossed all the intervening steps!

It should not be considered a small matter that he does not say, “Instead of loving me, they killed me,” but “they slandered me.” For they killed him precisely because they slandered him, denying that he was the Son of God and saying that he cast out demons by the prince of demons (Luke 11:15), and, “He has a demon and is insane; why do you listen to him?” (John 10:20), along with other statements of this kind.

By this slander they turned away from him those whose conversion he was seeking. Therefore he said this in particular, to show that those who slander Christ do greater harm and thereby kill souls than those who, in their savagery, killed his mortal [Col. 1434] flesh, which was soon to rise again.

### 5

But after he had said, “Instead of loving me, they slandered me,” what did he say? “But I prayed.”

He did not say what he prayed for, but what can we better understand than that he prayed for those very people? They slandered him most of all when he was crucified, mocking him as a human being whom they seemed to have overcome. Concerning that cross he said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” Thus, while they were returning evil for good at the deepest level of wickedness, he returned good for evil at the highest level of kindness.

It may also rightly be understood that he prayed for his disciples, as he said even before his passion, that their faith should not fail (Luke 22:32). When he himself hung on the wood, in order to commend patience he did not display power amid the words of those who slandered him, although by divine power he could have destroyed them.

But what he offered as an example of patience was more useful to us than if, by destroying his enemies without delay, he had built us up in such a way that we would impatiently hurry to see those whom we suffer as evil people punished. For it is written: “The patient person is better than the strong” (Prov. 16:32).

The divine utterances therefore teach us, through the Lord’s example, when we hear, “Instead of loving me, they slandered me; but I prayed,” that whenever we perceive some people to be ungrateful—not merely failing to return good, but even returning evil for good—we should pray.

He prayed for others, whether they were raging, grieving, or endangered in faith; but we should first pray for ourselves, so that, with God’s mercy and help, we may overcome the disposition that carries us toward the desire for vengeance when we are slandered, whether we are present or absent.

Then, when we remember Christ’s patience, as though he himself had been awakened—as happened when he slept in the boat (Matt. 8:24–25)—the one who calms the disturbance and storm of our heart, let us pray with our mind stilled and pacified even for those who slander us, so that we may confidently say: “Forgive us, as we also forgive” (Matt. 6:12).

But he was forgiving—he who certainly had no sin that needed to be forgiven him.

### 6. [verse 5]

The text continues: “And they repaid me evil for good.” And as though we were asking, “What evil? In return for what good?” he says: “And hatred in return for my love.”

Here lies their entire and great guilt. For what harm could persecutors inflict on one who was dying voluntarily, not by necessity? Yet the hatred itself is the greatest crime of the persecutor, although it is a voluntary punishment for the one who suffers.

He sufficiently explained above how he had said, “Instead of loving me,” because they owed him love not just in some general way but because of his love, when he added here, “in return for my love.”

He recalls this love in the Gospel, where he says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23:37).

### 7

Next he begins to prophesy what they will receive in return for their impiety. He speaks of it in such a way that he seems, in a desire for vengeance, to wish that these things might happen, although they are spoken of as future events with absolute certainty and as things that, by God’s justice, will deservedly [Col. 1435] come upon such people.

Some who do not understand this manner of predicting future events under the appearance of an evil wish think that hatred is repaid with hatred and an evil disposition with an evil disposition. For it is truly the work of few to distinguish how the punishment of the wicked can please an accuser who desires to satisfy his hostility, and how, in a wholly different manner, it can please a judge who punishes sins with an upright will.

The former returns evil for evil; the latter, even when he takes vengeance, does not return evil for evil, because he returns what is just to the unjust. But what is just is certainly good.

He therefore punishes not from delight in another’s misery—which would be evil for evil—but from love of justice, which is good for evil.

Thus let the blind not slander the light of the Scriptures by supposing that God does not punish sins; nor let the unjust flatter themselves as though he returns evil for evil.

Let us therefore hear what the divine discourse next connects together. In the words that appear to wish for evil, let us understand the predictions of a prophet; and, lifting our minds toward his eternal law, let us behold God returning just recompense.

8. [verse 6.] “Set over him a sinful man, and let the devil stand at his right hand.” Earlier the complaint concerned many; now the Psalm speaks of one. Earlier it had said: “They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue, and with words of hatred they surrounded me, and they attacked me without cause; in return for loving me, they slandered me, but I prayed; and they repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love.” All this concerned many. But now, announcing what they deserved for these iniquities and what would befall them by divine judgment, he says, “Set over him a sinful man,” as though directing his words against the one who handed himself over to such people, the enemies of whom he had spoken above.

Since, then, here he foretells that Judas the betrayer would be punished with the punishment due to him, according to the Scripture of the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1:20), what is “Set over him a sinful man” except the one whom he identifies in the following verse when he says, “And let the devil stand at his right hand”? This, then, is what he deserved: to have the devil over him, that is, to be subject to the devil, because he did not wish to be subject to Christ. “Let him stand at his right hand” was said because he placed the devil’s works before God’s works. For that which each person places first is not improperly called his right, just as the right is placed before the left.

Therefore, of those who place the joys of this age before God and say, “Blessed is the people whose lot this is,” it is most rightly said, “Their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” Hence, when they said, “Blessed is the people whose lot this is,” their mouth spoke vanity, as was said of them above. But whoever’s mouth speaks truth, in opposition to what these people said—“Blessed is the people whose lot this is”—ought himself also to say what follows in the same psalm: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God” (Ps. 143:11, 15). For the Lord, not the devil, is at the right hand of this people, as he says elsewhere: “I kept the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, that I may not be shaken” (Ps. 15:8).

The devil, then, stood at Judas’s right hand when he placed greed before wisdom and money before his salvation, so that he might hand over the one by whom he ought to have been possessed, lest he be possessed by the one whose works Christ himself destroyed, although Judas did not wish to be possessed by him.

9. [verse 7.] “When he is judged, let him go forth condemned.” For he did not wish to be one to whom it would be said, “Enter into the joy of your lord,” but one of whom it is said, “Cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 25:21, 30). “And let his prayer become sin.” For there is no just prayer except through Christ, whom he sold through the enormity of his sin. A prayer that is not made through Christ cannot merely fail to blot out sin; it itself becomes sin.

One may ask when Judas could have prayed in such a way that his prayer would become sin.

[Note: [Col. 1436] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *would not become*. *Not* is absent from Ambrosianus and the manuscripts.]

I think it was before he handed over the Lord, when he had already begun to contemplate handing him over. For he could no longer pray through Christ. After he had handed him over and repented, if he had prayed through Christ, he would have asked for pardon; if he had asked for pardon, he would have had hope; if he had had hope, he would have hoped for mercy; and if he had hoped for mercy, he would not have fastened his neck with despair.

Accordingly, after he had said, “When he is judged, let him go forth condemned,” lest anyone think that he could free himself from the impending condemnation by the prayer he had learned with his fellow disciples—where it is said, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”—he added, “And let his prayer become sin,” because it was not made through Christ, whom he refused to follow but instead persecuted.

10. [verse 8.] “Let his days be few.” By “his days” he meant the days of his apostleship. They were few because, before the Lord’s passion, they were brought to an end by his crime and death.

And as though someone might ask, “What, then, will become of the sacred number twelve, in which the Lord did not wish without reason to have twelve chief Apostles?” he immediately added, “And let another take his episcopate”—as if saying: Let him be punished according to his deserts, and let that number be completed. Whoever wishes to know how this happened should read the Acts of the Apostles.

11. [verse 9.] “Let his children become orphans, and his wife a widow.” Certainly, when he himself died, his children became orphans and his wife was widowed.

12. [verse 10.] “Let his children be shaken and carried away, and let them beg.” “Shaken” means uncertain where to go, deprived of every support. “Let them be driven out of their dwellings.” This explains what he had said above, “Let them be carried away.” The following verses indicate how all this happened to his wife and children.

13. [verses 11–12.] “Let the creditor search out all his substance, and let strangers plunder his labors.” “Let there be no helper for him”—he says this concerning the preservation of his offspring. Therefore he continues, “Nor let there be anyone who has mercy on his orphans.”

14. [verse 13.] But since orphans, even without a helper or guardian, might nevertheless grow up amid hardship and poverty and preserve their family line through descendants, he continues and says: “Let his descendants be made for destruction; in one generation let his name be blotted out”—that is, what was generated from him should generate no further, but quickly pass away.

15. [verse 14.] But what does he add next? “Let the iniquity of his fathers return into the sight of the Lord, and let the sin of his mother not be blotted out.”

Is this to be understood as though even the sins of his parents were to be repaid to him? They are not repaid to one who has been changed in Christ and has begun not to be the son of the wicked, because he does not imitate their ways. For this also is written most truly: “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children”; and that which is said through the prophet: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins, it shall die.” This was said concerning those who turn to God and do not imitate the evils of their parents, as the prophet himself clearly shows: he says that the iniquities of their parents do not harm those who, by practicing righteousness, have become unlike them (Ezek. 18:4, 20).

But to what was said, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children,” there was added, “who hate me” (Exod. 20:5)—that is, as their parents hated me. Thus, just as imitation of the good causes even one’s own sins to be blotted out, so imitation of the wicked causes people to receive not only their own deserts but also those of the persons whom they have imitated.

If, then, Judas had held fast to that to which he was called, neither his own past sins nor the iniquity of his parents would in any way have pertained to him. But because he did not hold fast to adoption into God’s household and instead chose the iniquity of his ancient lineage, the iniquity of his fathers returned into the sight of the Lord, so that it too might be punished in him; and the sin of his mother was not blotted out in him.

16. [verse 15.] “Let them be continually before the Lord”—that is, let his fathers and his mother be continually before the Lord, not so that they might oppose the Lord, but so that the Lord might not forget their utterly evil deserts in this man, when he repays them also to him.

For by “against the Lord” he meant “in the sight of the Lord.” Other translators, however, rendered it, “Let them be continually in the sight of the Lord”; others, “Let them be continually before the Lord,” just as it is said elsewhere, “You have placed our iniquities in your sight” (Ps. 89:8).

He says “continually” so that this particular crime may be without remission, both in this age and in the age to come.

“Let their memory perish from the earth”—namely, the memory of his fathers and his mother. By their memory he means that which is preserved in the succession of descendants. He prophesied that this would perish from the earth, because Judas himself and his children, who were like the memory of his fathers and mother, were extinguished without continuation of offspring within the brief span of one generation, as was said above.

17. Someone may say: “Should this also be understood as pertaining to Judas’s punishment: that after his death his wife and children came to beg, were carried away and driven out of their dwellings, while the creditor searched out all his substance and strangers plundered all his labors, with no one helping or having pity on his orphans, and that they soon died without descendants? Does any pain concerning what happens to each person’s family after his death touch the dead? Or should we at least suppose that the dead know these things, whose consciousness, according to their deserts, whether good or evil, is elsewhere?”

I reply that this is indeed a great question, not to be discussed at present, since it would require a longer treatment: whether, and to what extent, and in what manner the spirits of the dead know what happens around us.

Nevertheless, to say briefly what can be said: if they had no concern for us, the Lord would not have said that the rich man who was suffering torments in the underworld had said, “I have five brothers there, lest they too come into this place of torment.” But however those who try to understand this differently may interpret it—and it must be admitted that it does not follow that, if the dead know that their relatives are alive, they therefore necessarily know also the joyful or sorrowful things that happen around their loved ones, since they neither see them in the places of punishment, where that rich man was, nor in the rest of the blessed, where he recognized Lazarus and Abraham, although from far away (Luke 16:28, 23)—this much I say: few are the people of such a disposition that, after their death, they neglect or utterly disregard what good or evil happens to their own, at least while those relatives are still alive. Many, however—as is shown even by the great care taken to commend one’s final wishes and to draw up wills of whatever kind—act sufficiently to ensure that, once they have died, their own may be well provided for.

As for the continuance of their descendants through successive generations, those alone laudably despise it who cut themselves off for the sake of the kingdom of heaven and wish or desire their children to do the same, longing for them to be crowned with martyrdom, so that none of them may remain on earth. All the rest, or nearly all, wish their own to be happy in this life after their death, and do not wish their family line to perish.

Therefore, if the dead perceive that, after Judas died so unhappily, his wife remained a widow and his children orphans, that the creditor searched out all his substance, that strangers plundered his labors, that they were driven from their dwellings, that his orphans found no one to pity them, and that they perished without descendants in a single generation, this is an accumulation of evils. If they do not perceive it, it is a terror for the living.

But if it troubles anyone how he could have possessed property for a creditor to search out and strangers to plunder, since he was already following the Lord with the other eleven, let that person believe that he left everything he possessed to his children and wife in such a way that he did not sincerely or consistently break the bond of greed. Even if he seemed to sell these possessions and distribute them to the poor, he would certainly have done what Ananias did after the Lord’s ascension (Acts 5:1–2). For he would not have feared that the Lord, whom he thought could be deceived when he took away what was being deposited from the money box, would know this by his divinity (John 12:6).

18. [verses 6–15.] But now let us see, insofar as the Lord helps us, how these words can also apply to the Jewish people, whose hostility persisted in stubborn hatred against the Lord. We have said that Judas represented this people figuratively, just as the Apostle Peter represented the Church.

“Set over him a sinful man, and let the devil stand at his right hand.” As in Judas, so this is to be understood in the case of this people: after rejecting Christ from itself, it became subject to the devil, preferring his persuasions in all wicked and earthly desires to eternal salvation.

“When he is judged, let him go forth condemned,” because, persisting in wickedness and unbelief, he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works (Rom. 2:5–6).

“And let his prayer become sin,” because it is not made through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), and the priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 109:4).

“Let his days be few.” This must be understood according to the kingdom, because the kingdom of the Jews did not continue long afterward.

“And let another take his episcopate.” I think that the Lord Christ may appropriately be understood as the episcopate of the Jewish people, because he was made flesh from the tribe of Judah. The Apostle says, “For I say that Christ became a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers” (Rom. 15:8). He himself also says, “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24), because he presented himself to them in the flesh.

The Magi who came from the east said this: “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?” (Matt. 2:1–2). This was also written in the title placed above the crucified man. Thus Pilate rightly answered those who wished to alter it, “What I have written, I have written” (John 19:19–22).

Another, then, namely the people of the Gentiles, received this episcopate of the Jewish people—that is, the Lord Christ.

“Let his children become orphans.” Of these it is said, “But the children of the kingdom will go into the outer darkness” (Matt. 8:12). They became orphans when they lost that kingdom, as though they had lost their father. It may also rightly be understood that they lost God as their Father: “Whoever does not have the Son,” says the Truth, “does not have the Father” (1 John 2:24).

“And his wife a widow.” The wife of the kingdom may be understood as the people over whom its kings rule as subjects; she became a widow when the kingdom itself was lost.

“Let his children be shaken and carried away, and let them beg.” Shaken by dangers and carried away under the pressure of enemies, the children of the kingdom of the Jews were conquered. What is it to beg except to live by the mercy of human beings, as they live under the kings of the nations to which they were carried away?

“Let them be driven out of their dwellings.” So it happened.

“Let the creditor search out all his substance”—that is, the substance of his people. Nothing is better understood here than that their debts are not forgiven, because they are forgiven only in Christ, whom they rejected, who also taught them to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). “All his substance” means his entire life, so that none of his debts—that is, none of his sins—may be forgiven.

“And let strangers plunder his labors”: the devil and his angels, because those who do not have Christ do not store up treasures in heaven.

“Let there be no helper for him.” Who is a helper to one for whom Christ is absent?

“Nor let there be anyone who has mercy on his orphans.” They remained as orphans after losing their father—that is, their kingdom—or after losing God, whose Son they persecuted and hated. No one has pity on them—not to provide or sustain temporal life, but to give true life, that is, eternal life.

“Let his descendants be made for destruction”—certainly, for eternal destruction.

“In one generation let his name be blotted out.” Because they were generated but not regenerated, they are blotted out in one generation. In another generation—that is, in regeneration—if they recognized it and held fast to it, they would not be blotted out.

“Let the iniquity of his fathers return into the sight of the Lord,” so that the Lord may repay this people, persisting in wickedness, with the iniquity of its fathers also. For he says to them: “You bear witness against yourselves, because you are sons of those who killed the Prophets.” And shortly afterward he says: “So that upon you may come all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah.” “And let the sin of his mother not be blotted out”: the sin of Jerusalem, which is in bondage with her children, which kills the Prophets and stones those sent to her (Matt. 23:31, 35, 37).

“Let their iniquity and sin be continually against the Lord”—that is, let them not be erased from the sight of the Lord, since God will avenge them eternally.

“And let their memory perish from the earth.” The earth of God is the field of God; the field of God is the Church of God. From this earth the memory of those who, although they were natural branches, were broken off because of unbelief has perished (Rom. 11:20–21).

[Note: [Col. 1440] The editions read *because*. But the manuscripts read *who*.]

19. [verses 16–17.] “Because he did not remember to show mercy”—whether that refers to Judas or to the people themselves. But it is better understood of the people when it says that he did not remember. For if he killed Christ, he should at least have remembered by repenting and shown mercy to his members, whom he persecuted with the greatest persistence.

Therefore he says, “Because he persecuted a poor and needy man.” This can indeed be understood of Judas, because the Lord did not disdain to become poor, although he was rich, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). But how am I to understand “needy,” unless perhaps because he said to the Samaritan woman, “Give me a drink” (John 4:7), and on the cross, “I thirst” (John 19:28)?

But I do not find how what follows can be understood of our Head himself, the Savior of his body, whom Judas persecuted. For after he had said, “And he persecuted a poor and needy man,” he added, “And to put to death the brokenhearted”—that is, “so that he might put him to death,” for some have interpreted it in this way also.

But “brokenhearted” is usually said only of one who is in the pain of repentance, pierced by the goads of sins. Thus it was said of those who, after the Lord’s ascension, heard the Apostles and “were pierced to the heart,” although they had killed the Lord. The blessed Peter addressed them, saying among other things: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins will be forgiven you” (Acts 2:37–38).

But since these very people became members of him whose members they had fastened to the wood, the Jewish people did not remember to show mercy. It persecuted a poor and needy man, but in his members. Of these, with reference to the very works of mercy, he will say: “When you did not do it for one of the least of mine, you did not do it for me” (Matt. 25:45). “And to put to death the brokenhearted”—plainly, “the brokenhearted,” but in his members.

Among those who persecuted them in order to put the brokenhearted to death was Saul, consenting to the killing of Stephen, who was brokenhearted (Acts 7:59), because Stephen himself belonged to those who had been pierced to the heart. But Saul remembered to show mercy; and he who in the morning was plundering divided food in the evening (Gen. 49:27). He himself, having been pierced to the heart, began to suffer the very things he had inflicted on those who were brokenhearted, so that in him too they might persecute the poor, wishing to put to death the brokenhearted.

For this they hated the Apostle Paul: because, having been pierced to the heart, he preached the one whom he had previously persecuted. As he himself was persecuting the poor, needy, and brokenhearted in his members, in order to put them to death, he heard from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” Having then become brokenhearted, he began to suffer the very things he had done to the brokenhearted (Acts 9:1–24).

20. [verse 18.] Then the Psalm continues: “And he loved cursing, and it shall come upon him.” Although Judas also loved cursing, by stealing from the money box and by selling and handing over the Lord, that people more openly loved cursing when it said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25).

“And he did not wish blessing, and it shall be far from him.” Judas did not wish blessing because he rejected Christ, in whom eternal blessing is found. But that people more openly refused blessing when the man enlightened by the Lord said to them, “Do you also wish to become his disciples?” They did not wish blessing and regarded it as a curse, replying, “You be his disciple” (John 9:27–28). Blessing became far from them because it passed over to the Gentiles.

“And he put on cursing as a garment”—whether Judas or that people. “And it entered like water into his inward parts.” Thus it is both outside and inside: outside like a garment, inside like water, because he fell under the judgment of the one who can kill both body and soul in Gehenna (Matt. 10:28)—the body outside, the soul inside.

“And like oil into his bones.” He shows that the man committed evil with delight and acquired for himself a curse, that is, eternal punishment, because blessing is eternal life. In the present, evil deeds delight people, like water in their inward parts and oil in their bones; but it is called a curse because God has foretold torments for such people. The curse is like oil in the bones when people consider themselves strong because they are permitted to commit evils as though with impunity.

21. [verse 19.] “Let it also be to him as a garment with which he is covered.” Since he had already spoken above about a garment, why does he repeat it? Is it because, when he said, “He put on cursing as a garment,” this differs from the garment with which one is not clothed but covered? One puts on a tunic, but one is covered with a cloak.

And what does this mean except that he also glories in his iniquity in the sight of human beings?

“And as a belt,” he says, “with which he is always girded.” People chiefly gird themselves so that they may be more ready for work and not be hindered by the folds of their clothing. Therefore, he girds himself with a curse who undertakes evil not suddenly but deliberately and learns to do evil in such a way that he is always ready for it. Hence he says here also, “And as a belt with which he is always girded.”

22. [verse 20.] “This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord.” He did not say, “their reward,” but “their work.” For it is clear that, by the garment, covering, water, oil, and belt, he was describing the very works by which eternal cursing is acquired.

It is therefore not one Judas but many of whom it is said, “This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord.” Although the plural number could also be used for the singular, as when, after Herod’s death, the angel said, “Those who sought the child’s life are dead” (Matt. 2:20).

But who slander Christ before the Lord more than those who slander the very words of the Lord, saying that he is not the one whom the Lord’s Law and Prophets foretold?

“And who speak evil,” he says, “against my soul”: denying that he was able to rise again when he wished, although he says, “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

23. [verse 21.] “But you, Lord, Lord, act with me.” Some thought that “mercy” should be supplied; some even added it. But the more accurate manuscripts read: “But you, Lord, Lord, act with me, for the sake of your name.”

Therefore, a deeper meaning must not be overlooked: the Son is understood to have said this to the Father, “Act with me,” because the works of the Father and the Son are the same. Even if we understand “mercy”—for it follows, “because your mercy is sweet”—since he did not say, “Act in me,” or “Act upon me,” or something similar, but said, “Act with me,” we rightly understand that the Father and the Son together show mercy to the vessels of mercy (Rom. 9:23).

This may also be understood in this way: “Act with me,” that is, “Help me.” We use this expression in ordinary speech when, concerning some matter that is on our side, we say, “He acts with us.”

The Father helps the Son insofar as God helps the man, on account of the form of a servant; God is God to that man, and the Father is also Lord to that form of a servant. In the form of God, the Son does not need assistance; for he is almighty equally with the Father, from whom he himself is also the helper of humanity.

For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wishes (John 5:21)—not that the Father raises some and the Son others, or that the Father acts in one way and the Son in another, because they do the same things and in the same manner.

Thus, insofar as the Son of God is human, God raised him from the dead—that is, the Father, to whom he says in the Psalms, “Raise me up, and I will repay them” (Ps. 40:11). But insofar as he is God, he also raised himself; for this reason he says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

He signified the same thing here, if one pays close attention. He commanded us to search the Scriptures, which bear witness to him (John 5:39), not to pass over them superficially. For he did not merely say, “You, Lord, Lord, act with me,” but said, “But you.” What is “But you” except “because I also” act? And in repeating not merely “Lord” but “Lord, Lord,” he expresses the affection of one praying, as in, “God, my God” (Ps. 21:2).

When, after saying, “Act with me,” he added, “for the sake of your name,” he commended grace. For without any preceding merits of works, human nature was raised to such an exalted state that the Word and flesh together—that is, God and man—were called the only-begotten Son of God. This happened so that, through what had not perished, what had perished might be sought by the one who had created it. Hence he continues, “Because your mercy is sweet.”

24. [verse 22.] “Deliver me, because I am needy and poor.” Need and poverty are the weakness through which he was crucified.

“And my heart is troubled within me.” This refers to what he said as his passion approached: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38).

25. [verse 23.] “Like a shadow when it declines, I have been taken away.” He signified death itself. For just as night comes from a declining shadow, so death comes from mortal flesh.

“I have been shaken off like a locust.” I think this is more appropriately understood in his members, that is, in his faithful ones. To express this somewhat more clearly, he preferred to say “like locusts” rather than “like a locust,” although even in the singular number many could be understood, as in the verse, “He spoke, and the locust came” (Ps. 104:34). But it would be less clear.

His faithful, then, were shaken off—that is, driven away by persecutors. By the name “locusts” he intended either to signify their multitude or the fact that they moved from place to place.

26. [verse 24.] “My knees have become weak through fasting.” We read that the Lord Christ fasted for forty days (Matt. 4:2). But did that hunger have such force in him that his knees became weak? Or is this also more appropriately understood in his members, that is, in his saints?

“And my flesh has been changed because of oil”—because of spiritual grace. Hence Christ is named from *chrisma*; *chrisma* means anointing. His flesh was changed because of oil, not for the worse but for the better: it rose from the dishonor of death into the glory of immortality.

When, therefore, he said, “My knees have become weak through fasting,” I think this signified those who appeared strong in his members but, as though the presence of the bread by which they were sustained had been taken away, failed in his passion even to the point of denial, as happened in Peter. Then, as if to strengthen them so that they would not fall utterly through weakness, he says, “And my flesh has been changed because of oil”: that is, “When they had failed through my death, I would strengthen them through my resurrection and anoint them by sending the Holy Spirit, who would not have come to them unless I had departed.”

For he had said, “He cannot come unless I depart” (John 16:7); and the Evangelist said, “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39). His flesh had not yet been changed.

Whether the Holy Spirit is signified by water, because of cleansing or irrigation, or by oil, because of exultation and the kindling of love, he is not thereby different from himself because the signs are different. The lion and the lamb are also very different, yet Christ is signified by both: by the lion for one reason and by the lamb for another, but he is not another Christ. For a lamb is not strong, nor is a lion innocent; but Christ is both innocent like a lamb and strong like a lion.

Jesus Christ himself says through Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61:1).

27. [verse 25.] “And I became a reproach to them”—through the death of the cross. For “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us” (Gal. 3:13).

“They saw me, and shook their heads.” They saw that he had hung there but did not see that he had risen; they saw when his knees became weak but did not see when his flesh was changed.

28. [verse 26.] “Help me, Lord my God; save me according to your mercy.” This can refer to the whole—that is, both to the Head and to the body: to the Head because of the form of a servant, and to the body because of those servants themselves.

For he could say to God even in them, “Help me” and “Save me”—in those concerning whom he said to Saul, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

When he added, “According to your mercy,” free grace is being recalled, not something owed on account of works.

29. [verse 27.] “And let them know that this is your hand, and that you, Lord, have made it.” He said “let them know” of those for whom he also prayed while they were raging. Among those who made him a reproach and shook their heads in mockery of him were also people who later believed in him.

But let those who attribute the form of a human body to God learn how God can have a hand. If he makes what he makes with a hand, does he also make that hand itself with a hand? How, then, is it said here, “Let them know that this is your hand, and that you, Lord, have made it”?

Let us understand the hand of God to be Christ. Hence it is said elsewhere, “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). This hand both existed and made it, because “in the beginning was the Word,” and “the Word became flesh” (John 1:1, 14). He existed without time according to his divinity, and he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3).

30. [verse 28.] “They will curse, and you will bless.” The curse of human beings, who love vanity and seek falsehood (Ps. 4:3), is therefore empty and false; but when God blesses, he brings about what he says.

“Let those who rise up against me be put to shame.”

[Note: [Col. 1444] Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read *be put to shame*. Lovaniensis reads *will be put to shame*.]

For they rise up because they think they can accomplish something against me; but when I have been exalted above the heavens and my glory has begun to be over all the earth, they will be put to shame.

“But your servant will rejoice”—whether at the right hand of the Father, or in his members, who rejoice both in hope amid temptations and eternally after the temptations.

31. [verse 29.] “Let those who slander me be clothed with shame”—that is, let them be ashamed that they slandered me. But this can also be understood in a good sense, when they are corrected.

“And let them be covered with their confusion as with a double cloak.” A *diplois* is a double cloak. Some have therefore also interpreted this verse in this way: “And let them be covered with their confusion as with a double cloak.”

It is understood, however, that they should be confounded both inwardly and outwardly—that is, both before God and before human beings.

32. [verse 30.] “I will confess greatly to the Lord with my mouth.” In ordinary Latin usage, *greatly* (*nimis*) is said of what is more than it ought to be; its opposite is *little*, what is less than it ought to be.

But *nimis* translates the Greek ἄγαν (*agan*). This verse, however, does not have ἄγαν but σφόδρα (*sphodra*). Some of our translators rendered this sometimes as *nimis* (“greatly”) and sometimes as *valde* (“very much”).

But if *nimis* is understood to mean *valde*, “very much,” it can also be used in praise, for this confession signifies praise.

For the verse continues: “And in the midst of many I will praise him.” He also says in another psalm, “In the midst of the Church I will sing to you” (Ps. 21:23).

But when the Church itself, which is the body of Christ, sings, how does the Church sing in the midst of the Church? Likewise here, although many are members of Christ, if he praises when they themselves praise because they are his members, how does he praise in the midst of many when he is said to praise while those many are praising?

Or does he praise in the midst of many because he is with his Church here until the consummation of the age (Matt. 28:20), so that when he says “in the midst of many,” we understand that he is honored by those same many? For someone is said to be in the midst of those to whom special honor is offered.

But if the heart is like the center of a human being, nothing is better understood than that he said, “In the hearts of many I will praise him.” For Christ dwells in our hearts through faith (Eph. 3:17). Therefore he says, “with my mouth”—that is, in the mouth of my body, which is the Church.

“With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

[Col. 1445]

33. [verse 31.] “Because he stood at the right hand of the poor.” It had been said of Judas, “And the devil stood at his right hand,” because he wished to increase his riches by selling Christ. Here, however, the Lord stood at the right hand of the poor, so that the riches of the poor might be the Lord himself.

He stood at the right hand of the poor not to lengthen his years of life, which would eventually end, nor to increase his money, nor to make him strong in bodily power, nor to preserve him in health for a time, but, he says, “to save my soul from those who persecute me.”

The soul is saved from persecutors when it does not consent to them in evil. It does not consent to them when the Lord stands at the right hand of the poor, lest he succumb through that very poverty—that is, through weakness.

This help was given to the body of Christ in all the holy martyrs.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 109

SERMON TO THE PEOPLE
1. Insofar as the Lord grants it—he who has appointed us ministers to serve you in word and sacrament, in the richness of his mercy—we have taken up this psalm that we have just sung: short in number of words, but great in the weight of its meaning. May he who made you attentive also make us capable of considering and expounding it as best we can. May your soul live, and may it keep watch toward God.

For God has appointed a time for his promises and a time for fulfilling what he promised. The time of promise lasted during the age of the Prophets, up to John the Baptist; from him onward, until the end, is the time for fulfilling what was promised. God is faithful, for he made himself our debtor—not by receiving something from us, but by promising us so much. The promise alone was not enough: he also wished to bind himself in writing, as though making with us a written acknowledgment of his promises, so that when he began to pay what he had [Col. 1446] promised, we might consider in the document the order in which the promises were to be fulfilled.

The time of prophecy, as we have often said, was the foretelling of the promises. He promised eternal salvation, blessed life with the angels without end, an unfading inheritance, everlasting glory, the sweetness of his countenance, the dwelling of his sanctification in heaven, and, through resurrection from the dead, freedom thereafter from all fear of dying. This is his promise as its final goal, toward which all our attention runs, and when we reach it, we shall seek and demand nothing more.

But he did not remain silent about the order by which we would come to that final state, both promising and foretelling it. He promised divinity to human beings, immortality to mortals, justification to sinners, and glorification to the despised. Whatever he promised, he promised to the undeserving, so that a reward might not be promised as though earned by works, but that grace might be given freely, from his own name. For even the fact that a person lives justly—insofar as a human being can live justly—is not a human merit but a divine benefaction [Note: Most manuscripts read: “not a merit, but a benefaction.”].

No one lives justly unless he has been justified, that is, made just. And a person is made just by him who can never be unjust. For just as a lamp is not kindled by itself, so the human soul does not provide its own light; rather, it cries out to God: “You will illuminate my lamp, Lord” (Psalm 17:29).

2. Since, then, the kingdom of heaven has been promised to sinners—not to those who remain in sin, but to those who have been freed from sin and serve righteousness—and since, as we have said, grace assists them so that they can do this, and they are justified by him who is always just [Note: The word “just” is absent from most manuscripts], it seemed incredible that God should take such care for human beings.

Even today, those who despair of divine grace and refuse to turn from their most wicked ways to God, so that they may be justified by him and, with all their sins erased through his forgiveness, begin to live justly in him who never lived unjustly—even today such people carry within themselves this destructive thought: they say that God does not care about human affairs, and that the creator and ruler of this world cannot possibly consider how each mortal lives on earth.

Thus a human being does not think that he is taken into account by God, although he was made by God. If we could address such a person—if he first admitted us to his ears and then to his heart; if, instead of resisting our search for him, he did not drive us away and allowed himself, though lost, to be found—we could say to him:

“O human being, how could God fail to take account of you, when he took care beforehand that you should come into existence? Why do you think you should not be counted among created things? Do not believe the deceiver: your hairs are numbered before your Creator” (Matthew 10:30). [Note: Thus the Amiens and Erasmus editions; most manuscripts read, “Do not yield”; the Louvain edition, “Believe no one.”]

Indeed, the Lord said this in the Gospel to his disciples so that they would not fear death or think that anything belonging to them would perish in death. They feared for their souls in death, while he gave them security even concerning their hairs. Can a soul perish whose hair does not perish?

Yet, brothers, because it seemed incredible to human beings that [Col. 1447] God promised that people would become, from this mortality, corruption, rejection, weakness, dust, and ashes, equal to the angels of God, he not only made Scripture with human beings so that they might believe; he also gave their faith a mediator—not just any prince, or any angel or archangel, but his only Son. Thus, through the very Son by whom he intended to lead us to the end he promised, he both revealed and provided the way.

For it would have been too little for God to make his Son merely a demonstrator of the way: he made him the way itself, so that you might go through him as he guides you, while walking by means of him.

3. He therefore promised that we would come to him—that is, to that unspeakable immortality and equality with his angels. How far away we were! How high he was, and how low we were! How he was at the summit, while we lay in despair at the bottom! We were sick without any expectation of salvation. A physician was sent, whom the sick man did not recognize. For if they had recognized him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8).

Yet this too contributed to the sick person’s cure: the sick man killed the physician. He came to visit us, and he was killed in order to heal us. He revealed himself to believers as God and human being: God, through whom we were made; human being, through whom we were restored.

One thing was visible in him; another remained hidden. And what was hidden was far more excellent than what was visible, but precisely because it was more excellent, it could not be seen. The sick person was healed through what could be seen, so that afterward he might become capable of seeing what had been deferred by being hidden, not taken away by being denied.

The only Son of God, therefore, was to come to human beings, assume humanity, and through what he assumed become human; he was to die, rise again, ascend into heaven, sit at the right hand of the Father, fulfill among the nations what he had promised, and, after fulfilling his promises among the nations, fulfill this also: that he would come, demand what he had advanced, distinguish the vessels of wrath from the vessels of mercy, repay the impious what he had threatened, and the just what he had promised.

All this, therefore, had to be prophesied and foretold; his coming had to be announced, so that he would not be dreaded when he suddenly arrived, but awaited in faith. This psalm belongs to these promises: it clearly and openly prophesies our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, so that we cannot at all doubt that Christ is announced in this psalm—especially since we are Christians and already believe the Gospel.

For when our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ asked the Jews whose son they said the Christ was, and they answered, “David,” he immediately replied to them:

“How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies beneath your feet’? If therefore,” he said, “he calls him Lord in the Spirit, how is he his son?” (Matthew 22:42–45).

This psalm begins with that verse.

4. [Verse 1.] “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet.”

We must therefore examine at the very beginning of the psalm the question that the Lord put to the Jews [Col. 1448]. For if what the Jews answered is demanded of us—whether we too confess it or deny it—far be it from us to deny it.

If we are asked, “Is Christ the son of David, or is he not?” and we answer, “No,” we contradict the Gospel. For Matthew, writing the Gospel, begins it this way: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David” (Matthew 1:1). The Evangelist says that he is writing the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David.

The Jews were therefore right, when Christ asked whose son they believed the Christ to be, to answer, “David.” The Gospel agrees with their answer. This is not merely the suspicion of the Jews but also the faith of Christians.

I see further confirmations. The Apostle says: “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3). He also says to Timothy: “Remember that Jesus Christ has risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my gospel.” And what does he say about this gospel? “For which I suffer even to chains, as though I were a criminal; but the word of God is not bound” (2 Timothy 2:8–9).

The Apostle therefore suffered even to chains for his gospel—that is, for the Gospel dispensation which he preached and administered to the peoples. He was the one who seized the prey in the morning and divided the food in the evening (Genesis 49:27). Thus he suffered even to chains for the gospel.

For what gospel? [Note: The editions read, “For what gospel did he preach?”; the words “did he preach” are absent from the manuscripts.] That “Jesus Christ has risen from the dead, from the seed of David.” For this gospel the Apostle suffered. And yet Christ was asking about this very matter. When the Jews gave the answer that the Apostle preached, Christ replied with a question that seemed to contradict it, saying: “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord?” And he inserted the testimony from this psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord.”

“If therefore,” he says, “he calls him Lord in the Spirit, how is he his son?”

The Jews fell silent under this question; they could find no further answer. Yet they did not seek him as Lord, because they did not recognize that he himself was the son of David.

But let us, brothers, believe and confess: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10). Let us believe and confess both that he is the son of David and that he is the Lord of David. Let us not be ashamed of the son of David, lest we find the Lord of David angered against us.

5. For it was precisely by calling him by this name as he passed by that the blind deserved to be illuminated. Jesus was passing by, and when they heard the sound of the passing crowd—already recognizing by their ears what they could not yet recognize with their eyes—they cried out with a loud voice: “Have mercy on us, son of David!”

The crowds rebuked them and told them to be silent. But they, moved by their desire for light and overcoming the crowd’s opposition by their persistence in crying out, continued. They held fast to the one who was passing by and deserved to be illuminated by the one who touched them.

For they were saying to the one who was passing by: “Have mercy on us, son of David.” He stood still, and, overcoming the cries of those who opposed them, said: “What do you want me to do for you?” They replied: “Lord, that we may see.” He touched their eyes and opened them. They saw him present whom they had perceived passing by (Matthew 20:29–34).

The Lord therefore did something transitory [Col. 1449]; but there is another thing that remains. I mean, the Lord’s transitory aspect is one thing, and the Lord’s abiding aspect another.

The Lord’s transitory aspect was the Virgin’s childbirth, the Word’s incarnation, his progression through the stages of life, the display of miracles, the endurance of sufferings, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. All of this was transitory. Christ is not still being born, nor is he still dying, rising again, or ascending into heaven.

Do you not see that these events took place and passed through time, presenting something transitory to travelers, so that they would not remain on the road but reach their homeland? Indeed, those blind men were sitting beside the road; there they perceived him passing by, and by crying out they held him fast.

On the road of this present age, therefore, the Lord carried out this transitory aspect of himself, and this transitory aspect pertains to the son of David. Thus they said to the Lord as he passed by: “Have mercy on us, son of David.”

It was as though they were saying: “We recognize the son of David in the one who is passing by; we learn that the son of David was made in passing” [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The editions instead have: “We recognize the one who is passing by.”].

Let us therefore recognize him too and confess him as the son of David, so that we may deserve to be illuminated. For we perceive the son of David passing by, and we are illuminated by the Lord of David.

6. Behold, then, our Teacher questioned the Jews; and they did not answer because they refused to be disciples. What if he questioned us? What would we answer?

The Jews failed in this question; let Christians make progress. Let them not be troubled but instructed. The Lord does not ask because he wishes to learn, but as a teacher he asks.

The wretched Jews might have said: “You tell us.” They preferred to burst apart in inflated silence rather than to be instructed through humble confession.

Let our Teacher therefore speak to us, and let us see what we should answer him when he asks: “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?”

Let us answer exactly what the Jews answered, but let us not remain where the Jews remained. Let us recall the Gospel that we believe: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David.”

When we are questioned, let us not forget that Christ is the son of David, as the Apostle commends to our memory: “Come, Christian, remember that Jesus Christ has risen from the dead, from the seed of David.”

Let us therefore be questioned and answer: “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” Let Christian voices answer in harmony: “David.”

Then let the Teacher reply and recall the matter to us:

“How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord? ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies beneath your feet.’”

How could we answer unless we learned from you? Now, because we have learned, we say:

“In the beginning you were the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. All things were made through you” (John 1:1, 3). Behold the Lord of David.

But because of our weakness—for we were lying as hopeless flesh—you became flesh, so that you might dwell among us (John 1:14). Behold the son of David.

Certainly, when you were in the form of God, you did not consider equality with God something to be seized; therefore you are the Lord of David. But you emptied yourself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7); hence you are the son of David.

Finally, even in your own question, when you said, “How is he his son?” you did not deny that you were his son, but asked how this could happen [Col. 1450]. “David,” you say, “calls him Lord; how is he his son?” I do not deny it; tell me how.

If they had recalled, from the Scriptures they read but did not understand, the manner of this in answer to that question, would they not have replied: “Why do you ask how? ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,’ which is interpreted, ‘God with us’” (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23).

A virgin would conceive in her womb; a virgin from the seed of David would bear a son, so that he might be the son of David. For Joseph and Mary were from the house and lineage of David (Luke 1:27, 32; 2:4–5).

That virgin therefore gave birth so that he might be the son of David. But the one whom she bore would be called Emmanuel, “God with us.” Behold: you have both the son of David and the Lord of David.

7. Perhaps this psalm itself will disclose something to us about how Christ is both David’s son and David’s Lord. Let us therefore listen to it and examine it; let us knock with devotion and draw it forth with love.

David himself speaks; for it is not permitted to contradict the Lord. “David,” he says, “in the Spirit calls him Lord.” What, then, does David himself say about Christ?

“A psalm of David himself”—and this is the entire title, simple, without any indication of a question, without any knot of difficulty.

What, then, does David say?

“The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet.”

What is “a footstool beneath your feet”? It means “under your feet,” since a footstool is beneath the feet.

“The Lord,” he says, “said to my Lord.”

David heard this; he heard it in the Spirit. We were not present when he heard it, but we believed the one who spoke what he heard and wrote it down.

He heard it, therefore, in a certain chamber of truth, in a certain sanctuary of mysteries—where the Prophets heard in secret what they proclaimed openly. There David heard it, and with great confidence he says:

“The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet.”

We know that Christ sat at the right hand of the Father after rising from the dead and ascending into heaven. It has already happened; we did not see it, but we believed it. We read it in the books, heard it proclaimed, and hold it by faith.

Thus, precisely through the fact that Christ was the son of David, he became the Lord of David. For that which was born from the seed of David was so honored that it became the Lord of David.

You marvel at this as though such things did not also occur in human affairs. If the son of some private citizen should become king, would he not be lord of his father? More marvelous still is what can happen: not only that the son of a private citizen, having become king, should be his father’s lord, but that the son of a layman, having become a bishop, should be his father’s father.

Thus, by the very fact that Christ took flesh, died in that flesh, rose again in the same flesh, ascended in it into heaven, and sat at the right hand of the Father—in that same flesh, so honored, so glorified, and so transformed into a heavenly state—he is both the son of David and the Lord of David.

In accordance with this dispensation of Christ’s passing [Note: Several manuscripts read “of Christ’s passages”], [Col. 1451] the Apostle also says:

“For this reason he exalted him from the dead and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians 2:9–10).

“He gave him,” he says, “the name that is above every name.” To Christ according to his humanity, to Christ according to the flesh—dead, rising, and ascending—he gave the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

Where will David be such that Christ is not his Lord? Whether in heaven, on earth, or under the earth, his Lord will be the one who is Lord of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

Let David therefore rejoice with us. He has been honored by the birth of his son and freed from subjection by his dominion. Let him rejoice and say; let him be heard by those who rejoice:

“The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet.”

8. “Sit”—not only on high, but also in concealment: exalted so that you may rule, hidden so that you may be believed. For what reward would there be for faith if what we believe were not hidden?

The reward of faith is to see what we believed before we saw it. As Scripture declares: “The just person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17). There would therefore be no righteousness of faith unless what we believed when it was preached was hidden, and unless by believing we came to see it.

“How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Psalm 30:20). You have hidden it, then, and they have remained without it? Far be it from us: “You have perfected it for those who hope in you.”

Wonderful, therefore, is the mystery of Christ sitting at the right hand of God: it was hidden so that it might be believed; it was withdrawn from sight so that it might be hoped for.

For we were saved in hope. But hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? These are the Apostle’s words. You recognize them, of course, but I commend them to those who are inexperienced.

What does the Apostle say? “In hope,” he says, “we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 7:24–25).

Since what is seen is not hope, he says: “You have hidden your sweetness from those who fear you.” Since we hope for what we do not see and await it with patience, he says: “You have perfected it for those who hope in you.”

Finally, beloved, listen attentively to what I am about to say. Since our righteousness comes from faith, and our hearts are cleansed by faith so that we may see what we have believed, both statements have been set forth: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8), and “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9).

Since, therefore, this is the righteousness of faith [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The editions instead have: “What, then, is this righteousness of faith? To believe …”]—to believe what you do not see, and by the very merit of faith to reach vision at the proper time—the Lord, when he promised the Holy Spirit in the Gospel, said:

“He will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment.”

Concerning what sin? Concerning what righteousness? Concerning what judgment? He continues and explains; he does not permit human conjectures:

[Col. 1452] “Concerning sin,” he says, “because they did not believe in me.”

How many other sins the Jews had! And yet he spoke as though this were the one sin: “Concerning sin, because they did not believe in me.”

This is the sin of which he says elsewhere: “If I had not come, they would not have sin” (John 15:22).

What does “If I had not come, they would not have sin” mean? Did you therefore come to the righteous and make them sinners? No. Apart from their other sins, which could be forgiven through faith, he named this one sin, and if it were not committed, all the others would be forgiven.

“Concerning sin,” he says, “because they did not believe in me”; and elsewhere: “If I had not come, they would not have sin.” By the very fact that he came and they did not believe in him, they fell into sin. If they had not fallen into it, all their other sins could have been forgiven through the indulgence of grace obtained by faith.

“Concerning sin,” therefore, “because they did not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me” (John 16:8–10).

This is righteousness: that you go to the Father and they will no longer see you. For this righteousness comes from faith. “The just lives by faith,” and he lives by faith precisely if he does not see what he believes.

Since, therefore, living by faith pertains to righteousness, and no one lives by faith unless he does not see what he believes, in order to establish that very righteousness in human beings—that is, so that they would believe what they did not see—he said: “Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me.”

“This,” he says, “will be your righteousness: to believe in the one whom you do not see, and, having been cleansed by faith, to see afterward, on the day of resurrection, the one in whom you have believed” [Note: Several manuscripts of good standing do not have the words “on the day of resurrection.”].

9. Christ therefore sits at the right hand of God; the Son at the right hand of the Father is hidden. Let us believe.

For here he says two things: both “God said, ‘Sit at my right hand,’” and he added, “until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet”—that is, under your feet.

You do not see Christ sitting at the right hand of the Father. Can you at least see how his enemies are placed as a footstool beneath his feet? [Note: Thus some manuscripts; the editions read, “nor can you see this.”] When this is fulfilled openly, believe that the other is taking place secretly.

Which enemies are placed as a footstool beneath his feet? Those who devise empty things, to whom it is said:

“Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise empty things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ.” And they said: “Let us tear apart their bonds and cast their yoke from us. Let them not rule over us; let them not subject us to themselves.”

“He who dwells in heaven will mock them.” You were an enemy; you will be beneath his feet, either adopted or conquered.

Seek, therefore, what place you will have beneath the feet of the Lord your God. You must have a place there, either by grace or by punishment.

He therefore sits at the right hand of God until his enemies are placed beneath his feet. This is happening; this is being carried out. Even if it is accomplished gradually, it is being accomplished without interruption.

For let the nations rage and the peoples devise empty things; let the kings of the earth stand forth and the rulers assemble together against the Lord and against his Christ. Will they, by raging, devising empty things, and assembling together against Christ, cause this not to be fulfilled?

“I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Psalm 2:1–8).

[Col. 1453] It will certainly be fulfilled, even while they rage and devise empty things: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.”

For it is not some empty talker who says this; the Lord said it to me [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The editions instead have: “not some empty talker spoke it.”].

Thus we can also say in this psalm: “He said”—not just anyone, not those who rage and devise empty things, but “the Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet.”

Let them rage, devise empty things, and make a din. Will it not be fulfilled? “Their memory has perished with a roar.” Another psalm also speaks, but it is not another Spirit:

“Their memory has perished with a roar, and the Lord remains forever” (Psalm 9:7–8).

The one, therefore, who remains forever while their memory perishes with a roar—he himself said to my Lord: “Sit at my right hand.” For he sits at the right hand of the Father until he places all his enemies as a footstool beneath his feet.

10. [Verse 2.] And what follows?

“The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your power.”

It is evident, brothers, it is most evident that the Prophet is not speaking of that kingdom of Christ by which he reigns forever with the Father, Lord of the things created through him. For when does the Word, God with God, not reign in the beginning?

It is written: “To the King of the ages [Col. 1453], invisible, incorruptible, the only God, be honor and glory for ages of ages” (1 Timothy 1:17). [Note: Here the editions add “immortal,” which is absent from the manuscripts.] “Honor and glory to the King of the ages, for ages of ages”—to which King of the ages? “The invisible, incorruptible one.”

For insofar as Christ is also invisible and incorruptible with the Father, because he is his Word, his Power, and his Wisdom, God with God, through whom all things were made, he is King of the ages.

Nevertheless, that dispensatory and transitory kingdom by which he called us into eternity through the mediation of his flesh begins with Christians; but his kingdom will have no end.

The enemies of the one sitting at the right hand of the Father are therefore placed as a footstool beneath his feet. As it has been said, this is being done, and it will be carried out fully until the end.

Let no one say that what has begun cannot be fulfilled. Why despair of the end of what has begun? The Almighty began it, and the Almighty promised that he would fulfill what he began.

From where did it begin?

“The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your power.”

What Zion? Jerusalem itself. Hear the Lord himself:

“It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day.”

From there he sits at the right hand of God the Father, rising again where he had been. Then, while he sits at the right hand of the Father, what is being done? What is being done so that his enemies may be placed as a footstool beneath his feet?

Hear him teaching and explaining:

“And repentance and forgiveness of sins will be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47).

For:

“The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your power.”

“The rod of your power”—that is, the kingdom of your might, because:

“You will rule them with an iron rod” (Psalm 2:9).

“The Lord will send it forth from Zion,” because:

“Beginning from Jerusalem.”

11. [Col. 1454] When, therefore, he has sent forth from Zion the rod of his power, what will happen?

“And rule in the midst of your enemies.”

First, rule in the midst of your enemies—among the raging nations. For will he rule in the midst of his enemies later, when the saints have received their honor and the impious their condemnation? What is surprising if he rules then, when the just reign with him eternally and the impious burn in everlasting punishments? What is surprising if he rules then?

Now, in the midst of your enemies; now, in this passing of the ages; now, in this propagation and succession of human mortality; now, while the torrent of time flows past: for this purpose the rod of your power has been directed forth from Zion, so that you may rule in the midst of your enemies.

Rule, rule in the midst of pagans, Jews, heretics, and false brothers. Rule, rule, son of David, Lord of David; rule in the midst of pagans, Jews, heretics, and false brothers. Rule in the midst of your enemies.

We do not understand this verse correctly if we do not already see it being fulfilled.

Sit, therefore, at the right hand of God; remain hidden so that you may be believed, until the times of the nations are fulfilled. For it is written: “Whom heaven must receive until the times of the nations are fulfilled” (Acts 3:21).

In order to rise again, you died; in order to ascend, you rose again; in order to sit at the right hand of the Father, you ascended. Thus, in order to sit at the right hand of the Father, you died.

From death comes resurrection, from resurrection ascension, and from ascension sitting at the right hand. All of this therefore began with death. The exaltation of this glory has humility as its beginning.

While you sit at the right hand of the Father, the times of the nations are fulfilled, all your enemies are placed as a footstool beneath your feet, and, in order to reach this point, you first rule in the midst of your enemies. For this purpose the Lord sends forth the rod of your power from Zion.

But in order that you might die, and through your death the record of sins might be erased (Colossians 2:14), and repentance and forgiveness of sins might be preached among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem, the blindness of the Jews brought this about.

The blindness of some served to illuminate others:

“Blindness in part has happened to Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter, and thus all Israel might be saved” (Romans 11:25).

“Blindness in part has happened to Israel”: it killed you. Having been killed, you rose again; by your blood you washed away the sins of the nations; sitting at the right hand of the Father, you gathered from every direction those who endure and take refuge in you.

“Blindness in part has happened to Israel; it happened so that the fullness of the nations might enter, and thus all Israel might be saved,” and so that all your enemies might be [Note: We restore the words “your” and “might be” from Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition. In their place, the B manuscript notes in the margin: “Supply, ‘might become.’”] a footstool beneath your feet.

But this is now. What afterward?

### 12. [verse 3]

“With you is the beginning on the day of your strength.” What is this day of his strength? When is the beginning with him—or what beginning, or how is the beginning with him, since he himself too is the Beginning? May the Lord help me, so that I may neither be disturbed in speaking nor you in hearing. For I see what has already happened, and with you I see it with the eyes of faith; with the eyes of the flesh as well I see what is now happening; and again, with the eyes of faith, I hope with you for what is to come.

What, then, has happened? What is happening? What is to come? Christ suffered, died, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven—as we know, on the fortieth day—and sits at the right hand of the Father. This has already happened; we did not see it, but we believe it.

What is happening now? He rules in the midst of his enemies, his rod of strength having been sent forth from Zion. This is taking place; this is being accomplished. At that time servants saw the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 1455] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions have: “this is being accomplished in the form of a servant; and the present form, etc.”] and now servants believe in the absent one. This is what we believe concerning the form of a servant, which we are able to grasp while we are still servants.

For this is that milk of little children which he prepared, passing the bread through the flesh. For that bread of angels was “the Word” in the beginning; yet, so that human beings might eat the bread of angels (Psalm 77:25), the Creator of angels became human. Thus the incarnate Word became receivable for us; we could not receive him if the Son, equal to God, had not emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being (Philippians 2:6–7).

Therefore, so that in some fashion we might grasp him who could not be grasped by mortals, the immortal became mortal, in order that, having completed his own death, he might make mortals immortal, and might give them something to inspect, something to believe, and something to see afterward. He gave the form of a servant to those present to inspect—not only to be seen with the eyes, but also to be handled with the hands. When that same form ascended into heaven, he commanded us to believe what he had allowed them to see.

But we too have something to see. They saw the rod sent forth from Zion; we see him ruling in the midst of his enemies. All this, brothers, belongs to the dispensation of the form of a servant, which servants can bear with tolerable ease and which future free persons love.

For the unchangeable Truth, which is the Word of God, God with God, through whom all things were made, while remaining in himself renews all things (Wisdom 7:27). To see this Truth, great and perfect purity of heart is necessary, and this purity comes through faith.

Once the form of a servant had been displayed, [faith] was enlarged for the displaying of the form of God [Note: [Col. 1455] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition have *dilatata*, “extended” or “spread out.” M.]. For the same person, speaking in the form of a servant to servants, says: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and I will show myself to him” (John 14:21). He promised that he would show himself to those who saw him.

What did they see? What did he promise? They saw the form of a servant; he promised the form of God. “I will show myself to him,” he says. This is the glory to which the kingdom is led, the kingdom that is now being gathered through the passing of this age. It is led toward a certain ineffable vision, which the ungodly will not deserve.

The form of a servant, however, was seen by the ungodly while he was here. Those who believed saw it, and those who killed him saw it. Do not think it a great thing to see that form: friends saw it, enemies saw it; and some who saw it killed him, while some who did not see it believed.
