Therefore this form of a servant, which here in humility both the devout and the ungodly have already seen, both the devout and the ungodly will see in the judgment. For when the Lord was being carried up into heaven before the eyes of his disciples, an angelic voice sounded to those gazing at him: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

Thus, in the same way—in that same form—for it was said concerning the ungodly: “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10). They will see as judge the one whom they mocked as he was judged. Therefore that form of a servant will be visible in the judgment to the just and the unjust, the devout and the ungodly, the faithful and the unbelieving.

What, then, will the ungodly not see? For of those concerning whom it was said, “They will look upon him whom they pierced,” it was also said: “Let the ungodly be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord” (Isaiah 26:10).

What does this mean, brothers? Let us distinguish and examine it [Note: [Col. 1456] All the manuscripts have *discamus*, “let us learn.”]. The ungodly is roused so that he may see something; the ungodly is taken away so that he may not see something.

We have already shown what he will see: that form of which it was said, “He will come in this way.” What, then, will he not see? “And I will show myself to him.” What does “myself” mean? Not the form of a servant. What does “myself” mean? The form of God, in which I “did not consider equality with God something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6–7).

What does “myself” mean? “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

This is the glory of God: ineffable light, the source of light without change, truth without defect, wisdom remaining in itself and renewing all things. This is the substance of God. Therefore the ungodly will be taken away, so that he may not see this honor of the Lord. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

### 13.

It seems to me, brothers, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant this to our capacity, that this concerns the time—if it is right to call it “time” [Note: [Col. 1456] Erasmus, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition have *temnus*, evidently an error. M.]. For at a certain time we shall come to what is not time. It seems to me that this is why it was said—and I say this without prejudice, if anyone can understand it better, more straightforwardly, or more plausibly—“With you is the beginning on the day of your strength.”

Indeed, the following verse, as I think, explains this sufficiently. For his strength was also spoken of here: the strength by which he subjected the nations to his yoke, by which he laid peoples low—not with iron, but with wood; although in the flesh, although in humility, although insofar as the form of a servant still permits and can contain it, his great strength is nevertheless grasped, because “what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25).

Since, then, his strength was also spoken of here, when it was said, “The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your strength, and rule in the midst of your enemies”—for how great is his strength, ruling in the midst of his enemies, who roar yet can do nothing against him, daily saying to one another, “When will he die, and his name perish?” (Psalm 40:6), while his glory increases among the peoples, while the nations are subjected to his name, while the sinner sees and is angry, gnashes his teeth, and wastes away (Psalm 111:10)—since this too is his strength, the Prophet, wishing to commend his strength in another way, as it truly is, “the Strength of God and the Wisdom of God,” Christ, in the perpetual light of unchangeable truth, to whose vision we are reserved, toward whose vision we are deferred, and through whose vision we are cleansed by faith, while the ungodly is removed from that vision so that he may not see the honor of the Lord—wishing, then, to show this, he says: “With you is the beginning on the day of your strength.”

What does “with you is the beginning” mean? Put in any meaning of “beginning” you wish. If it means Christ himself, it would more properly be said, “You are the beginning,” than “With you is the beginning.” For he answered those who asked, “Who are you?” and said, “The Beginning, because I am also speaking to you” (John 8:25).

But since the Father too is the Beginning, and the Son is the Beginning, are there two beginnings? Certainly not. For just as the Father is God and the Son is God, yet the Father and the Son are not two gods but one God, so the Father is Beginning and the Son is Beginning, yet the Father and the Son are not two beginnings but one Beginning.

“With you is the beginning.” Then it will be seen how the Beginning is with you. For the Beginning is not absent from you even now. Did you not say: “Behold, each of you will go to his own, and you will leave me alone; yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32)? Therefore the Beginning is with you here as well. For you also said elsewhere: “The Father, remaining in me, does his works” (John 14:10). “With you is the beginning”; the Father has never been separated from you.

But when it is seen that the Beginning is with you, then it will be evident to all who have already been made like you, because “they will see you as you are” (1 John 3:2). For here Philip saw you and was seeking the Father. Then what is now believed will be seen: the Beginning will be seen with you by the holy, by the just, when the ungodly have been removed from the midst so that they may not see the honor of the Lord.

### 14.

Let us now believe, brothers, what we shall then see. Philip too was rebuked because he sought to see the Father, while he did not recognize the Father in the Son himself: “Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”

But “whoever has seen me” means not whoever has seen in me the form of a servant. Whoever has seen me as I have hidden myself from those who fear me, as I perfect myself to be seen by those who hope in me (Psalm 30:20), has also seen the Father.

But because this vision will come later, what shall we have in its place now? Let us see what he says to Philip, to whom he had said, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” It is as though Philip silently replied: “How will I see you, if you are to be seen otherwise than in the form of a servant? Or how will I see the Father, a weak mortal human being, dust and ashes?”

Turning to him, deferring the vision and commanding faith—he who had said, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father”—because this was too much for Philip and seeing it was far beyond him, he says: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:8–11). What you cannot yet see, believe, so that you may deserve to see it.

When the time has come for us to see, then it will appear: “With you is the beginning on the day of your strength.” “Of your strength”—not of the strength of your weakness [Note: [Col. 1457] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “The strength of your strength, not the strength of your weakness.”], because strength is there.

“Of your strength.” Human beings now have their strengths in faith, hope, charity, and good works; but they will go “from strength to strength” (Psalm 84:7). Therefore the Beginning is with you: you will be seen with the Father, in the Father, so that the Father may be the Beginning with you on the day of your strength—that strength of yours which the ungodly will not see.

For even this weakness of yours “is stronger than human beings”: therefore, on the day of your strength, the Beginning is with you.

### 15.

“Of what strength do you speak?” Explain it. For here too, as has been said, his strength was named when the rod of his strength was sent forth from Zion, so that he might rule in the midst of his enemies.

“Of what strength do you speak?” “In the splendor of the holy.” “In the splendor,” he says, “of the holy.” He speaks of that strength, when the holy will be in splendor—not when they are still carrying earthly flesh and groaning in a mortal and corruptible body, which weighs down the soul and presses down the earthly dwelling that occupies a mind pondering many things (Wisdom 9:15); when thoughts themselves are not visible to one another. This is not “in the splendor of the holy.”

But what is “in the splendor of the holy”? It is when the Lord comes, “illuminates the hidden things of darkness, and reveals the counsels of hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5). This will be “in the splendor of the holy,” because then “the righteous will shine in the kingdom of their Father like the sun.”

For hear what “in the splendor of the holy” means. “The harvest will come,” he says; “the end of the age will come. The master of the household will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals, and they will cast them into the furnace of burning fire. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:39–43).

In what kingdom? See whether a certain vision is being reserved, concerning which it was said to us, “With you is the beginning.” In what kingdom? Certainly in eternal life. For to those placed at his right hand he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

Then, after the ungodly have been condemned and the righteous separated and praised, what follows the command, “Receive the kingdom”? “Then the ungodly will go into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:34, 46). What he had called the kingdom, he called eternal life—the place to which the ungodly will not go.

See whether eternal life is a certain vision: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3), because “with you is the beginning on the day of your strength.” Therefore: “With you is the beginning on the day of your strength, in the splendor of the holy.”

### 16.

But this is deferred; this will be given afterward. What now?

“From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” What is this? If God has a Son, does he also have a womb? Not in the manner of bodily flesh; for he does not have a bosom in that manner either. Yet it was said: “He who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him” (John 1:18).

What is a bosom? It is a womb; both “bosom” and “womb” are used for what is secret. What does “from the womb” mean? From the secret place, from the hidden place; from myself, from my substance. This is “from the womb,” because “who will recount his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8).

Let us therefore understand the Father saying to the Son: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” What, then, is “before the morning star”? “Morning star” is used for the stars, as Scripture signifies the whole by a part, and all the stars by the prominent star.

But how were those stars made? So that they might be “for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years” (Genesis 1:14). If, then, the stars were placed for signs and seasons, and “morning star” is used for the stars, what is “before the morning star” is “before the stars”; and what is “before the stars” is “before the times.” If before the times, then from eternity.

Do not ask “when”; eternity has no “when.” “When” and “at some time” are words belonging to times [Note: [Col. 1459] The printed editions have “adverbs”; the manuscripts have “words.”]. He was not born from the Father in time, through whom times were made. It was therefore said as it had to be said: figuratively and prophetically, so that “womb” might signify the hidden substance and “morning star” the times.

Or do you wish us also to consider David himself, who called his Lord his son? In order to say this, he heard it from his Lord; he heard it from one by whom he could not be deceived. And he already called him his Lord, because, he says, “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand.’”

He himself is speaking, and the discourse is, as it were, his own. If he himself is speaking, perhaps he himself could say: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you”—from the virginal womb, before the morning star, I begot you.

For if that virgin, deriving her lineage from the flesh of David, gave birth to Christ, then he was born from that womb as though begotten by David. “From the womb”—the womb to which no male had come; truly from the womb, properly from the womb, because he alone was from the womb alone.

Therefore he who had called him his Lord says: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” And this very phrase, “before the morning star,” was spoken symbolically and literally, and was fulfilled accordingly. For the Lord was born at night from the womb of the virgin Mary; this is indicated by the testimony of the shepherds, who were keeping watch over their flock (Luke 2:7–8).

“From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” O my Lord, sitting at the right hand of my Lord: from where are you my son, unless because “from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you”?

### 17. [verse 4]

And for what purpose were you born?

“The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

For this purpose you were born from the womb before the morning star: that you might be a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

If we understand “born from the womb” as referring to the virgin, and “before the morning star” as referring to the night, as the Gospels testify, then without doubt he was born from the womb before the morning star so that he might be a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

For insofar as he was born from the Father, God from God, coeternal with the one who begot him, he is not a priest; he is a priest because of the flesh he assumed, because of the victim that he would offer for us, received from us.

“The Lord has sworn.” What does “the Lord has sworn” mean? Does the Lord swear, when he forbids human beings to swear (Matthew 5:34)? Or perhaps he forbids human beings to swear all the more so that they may not slip into perjury, and God swears all the more because he cannot be perjured?

A human being, who through the habit of swearing can let his tongue slip into perjury, is rightly forbidden to swear. For the farther he is from swearing, the farther he will be from perjury. A human being who swears can swear falsely or truly; but one who does not swear cannot do so.

Why, then, should the Lord not swear, when the Lord’s oath is the confirmation of his promise? Let him indeed swear.

What do you do when you swear? You call God as witness. This is what swearing is: calling God as witness. And it is therefore dangerous, lest you call God as witness to some falsehood.

If, then, by swearing you call God as witness, why should God not by swearing call himself as witness? “As I live,” says the Lord: this is God’s oath.

Thus he swore concerning the offspring of Abraham: “As I live, says the Lord, because you have heard my voice and have not spared your only son for my sake, surely I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea; and all nations shall be blessed in your offspring” (Genesis 22:16–18).

And the offspring of Abraham who is Christ—that offspring of Abraham, taking flesh from the offspring of Abraham—will be a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

Concerning the priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, then, the Lord swore, and he will not repent.

What about the priesthood according to the order of Aaron? Does God repent as a human being does? Does he unwillingly fall into something that he does, or unwittingly slip so that afterward he regrets his lapse?

He knows what he is doing; he knows how far each thing will proceed. That it should be changed into something else lies within the power of the ruler. But repentance signifies a change in things.

For just as you, when you repent of something, grieve over what you have done, so when God changes something into something else beyond human expectation—that is, beyond what human beings expect—he is said to repent. Indeed, he is said to repent even of our punishment, if we repent of our evil life.

Therefore the Lord has sworn: he has sworn, he has confirmed; he will not repent, he will not change.

What has he confirmed? “You are a priest forever.” He is a priest forever because he will not repent.

But a priest in what respect? Will those sacrifices remain—the victims offered by the patriarchs, the altars of blood, the tabernacle, and those sacraments of the first, Old Testament? Certainly not. Those things have already been removed: the temple has already been overthrown, that priesthood removed, and their victim and sacrifice brought to an end. The Jews do not even possess these things.

They see that the priesthood according to the order of Aaron has already perished, yet they do not recognize the priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek.

“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

I am speaking to the faithful. If the catechumens do not understand something, let them cast off their sluggishness and hasten toward knowledge. There is therefore no need to disclose the mysteries; let the Scriptures announce to you what the priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek is.

### 18. [verse 5]

“The Lord at your right hand.”

The Lord had said, “Sit at my right hand”; now the Lord is at his right hand, as though they had exchanged seats.

Or perhaps this should rather be understood in this way: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever”—this was said to Christ. “You are a priest forever”: the Lord swore it. Which Lord? The one who said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand”—he himself swore it.

“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” And the words are addressed to the very Lord who swore: “The Lord is at your right hand.”

O Lord, who swore and said, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek”: he himself, the priest forever, is the Lord at your right hand. He himself, I say, the priest forever concerning whom you swore, is the Lord at your right hand, because you said to that same Lord of mine, “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.”

Therefore this Lord who is at your right hand, concerning whom you swore and to whom you swore, saying, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” “shattered” [Note: [Col. 1461] Most manuscripts have *conquassabit*, “will shatter.” Shortly afterward they also read: “What will the priest forever do? What will he do?”] kings on the day of his anger.

It is Christ himself, the Lord at your right hand, to whom you swore and will not repent. What does the priest forever do? What does he do who is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us (Romans 8:34), like a priest entering into the inner places, or into the Holy of Holies, into the hidden places of heaven—he alone without sin, and therefore easily cleansing from sins (Hebrews 9:12, 14, 24)?

He, then, at your right hand, shattered kings on the day of his anger.

Which kings, you ask? Have you forgotten: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2:2)? These kings he shattered by his glory and weakened by the weight of his name, so that they could not accomplish what they wished.

For they tried very hard to erase the Christian name from the earth, and they could not. For “whoever stumbles over that stone will be shattered” (Matthew 21:44).

They stumbled, then, over the stone of offense, and therefore were shattered. They say: “Who is Christ? Some Jew, some Galilean, killed in this way, dead in that way.” The stone lies before your feet, as though lying there contemptibly and humbly. Therefore, by despising it you stumble; by stumbling you fall; by falling you are shattered.

If such is the anger of the hidden one, what will the judgment of the manifest one be?

You have heard of the anger of the hidden one, concerning which the psalm is entitled “Concerning the hidden things of the Son.” The ninth psalm, if I remember correctly, is entitled “Concerning the hidden things of the Son”; and there the hidden judgment of hidden anger is displayed.

Those who stumble over that stone live under the anger of God; they are shattered. And what good does their being shattered do? Hear also about the future judgment: “Whoever stumbles over that stone,” he says, “will be shattered; but upon whomever that stone falls, it will crush him” (Luke 20:18).

When one stumbles over him, he lies there as though humble; then he shatters. But when he crushes, he will come from above.

See how, in these two words—“he will shatter” and “he will crush,” “he stumbles over him” and “he will come upon him”—two periods are distributed: Christ’s humility and his glory, hidden punishment and the future judgment.

The one whom he does not shatter while lying there will not be crushed when he comes. By “lying there” I mean appearing contemptible. For he is at the right hand of God, and from on high he cried out powerfully, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

Yet although he was in heaven, he would not have said, “Why are you persecuting me?”—when no one was touching him—unless he were seated at the right hand of the Father in heaven in such a way that on earth he was also lying, as it were, in us.

“The Lord is at your right hand; he shattered kings on the day of his anger.”

### 19. [verse 6]

“He will judge among the nations.”

But now the judgment is “concerning the hidden things”; for there will also be a manifest judgment: “He will judge among the nations.”

For now this is happening: “Their memory has perished with a noise.” In that same psalm, “Concerning the hidden things,” it says: “Their memory has perished with a noise, but the Lord remains forever; he has prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in righteousness.”

There it says: “You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly perished; their name you blotted out forever” (Psalm 9:6–9). This is being done secretly.

Therefore, on the day of his anger, he shattered kings. “He will judge among the nations.” How? Hear what follows: “He will fill the ruins.”

Now he judges among the nations in such a way as to fill the ruins; for when he judges at the end, he will condemn the ruins.

“He will fill the ruins.” What ruins? Whoever fears his name will fall. When he has fallen, what existed will be overthrown, so that what did not exist may be built.

“He will judge among the nations; he will fill the ruins.”

Whoever is rebellious against Christ has raised a tower on high that is destined to fall. It is good for you to cast yourself down, to become humble, to fall prostrate at the feet of the one sitting at the right hand of the Father, so that a ruin may come about in you that is to be rebuilt.

For if you remain in an evil elevation, you will be cast down when you will not be rebuilt. Indeed, Scripture says of such people elsewhere: “Destroy them, and you will not build them up” (Psalm 28:5).

Certainly it would not say of some, “Destroy them, and you will not build them up,” unless it destroyed some in such a way that it might build them up. This happens in the present time, when Christ judges among the nations in such a way as to fill the ruins.

“He will shatter many heads upon the earth.” Here, upon the earth—in this life—he will shatter many heads. He makes the proud humble. And I dare to say, my brothers: it is useful to walk humbly here with one’s head shattered rather than to enter into the judgment of eternal death with one’s head held high.

He will shatter many heads by making ruins, but by filling them he will build.

### 20. [verse 7]

“He will drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he will lift up his head.”

Let us also consider him drinking from the torrent on the way.

First, what is the torrent? The outflow of human mortality. For just as a torrent is gathered from rainwater, overflows, roars, runs, and in running flows away—that is, completes its course—so is the whole course of this mortality.

Human beings are born, live, and die; while some die, others are born; again, when those die, others arise. They succeed one another, enter, depart, and do not remain.

What is held here? What does not run? What does not, as though gathered from rain, go into the abyss?

For just as a river suddenly gathered from rain, from drops of showers, goes into the sea and disappears—and was not visible before it was gathered from the rain—so this human race is gathered from hidden places and flows forth; by death it goes again into the hidden place. The middle part resounds and passes away.

He drank from this torrent; he did not disdain to drink from this torrent. For him, to drink from this torrent was to be born and to die. This torrent has birth and death; Christ received these. He was born; he died. Thus he drank from the torrent on the way.

For he rejoiced “like a giant to run his course” (Psalm 19:5). Therefore he drank from the torrent on the way, because he did not stand in the way of sinners (Psalm 1:1).

Therefore, because he drank from the torrent on the way, “he lifted up his head”—that is, because he was humbled, “and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross; therefore God exalted him from the dead and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:8–11).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 110

[Col. 1463]

### SERMON

[Note: [Col. 1463] Delivered to the people on the solemnity of Easter.]

### 1.

The days have come for us to sing “Alleluia.” Be present in spirit, brothers, to receive what the Lord suggests for our exhortation and for nourishing that charity by which it is good for us to cling to God.

Be present in spirit, good singers, sons of the praise and everlasting glory of the true and incorruptible God. Attend carefully, you who know how to sing and make melody in your hearts to the Lord, always giving thanks for everything (Ephesians 5:19–20); and praise God. For this is “Alleluia.”

These days indeed come in order to pass away, and they pass away in order to come; and they signify the day that neither comes nor passes, because it is not preceded by yesterday so that it may come, nor pressed by tomorrow so that it may pass.

When we have come to that day, clinging to it, we too shall not pass away. As it is sung to God in a certain passage: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 84:5). This will be the business of those at leisure, this the work of those who are free from labor, this the activity of those at rest, this the care of those who are secure.

For just as these days, after the days of Lent—which signify the sorrow of this life before the resurrection of the Lord’s body—follow solemnly in welcomed joy, so that day which will be given after the resurrection to the Lord’s full body, that is, to the holy Church, when all the afflictions and pains of this life have been excluded, will follow in perpetual blessedness.

This life, however, demands continence from us, so that even when we groan under burdens, weighed down by labor and struggle, and long to be clothed over with our dwelling that is from heaven (2 Corinthians 5:2), we may restrain ourselves from worldly pleasures.

This is signified by the number forty, during which Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted (Exodus 34:28; 1 Kings 19:8; Matthew 4:2).

For we are commanded by the Law, by the Prophets, and by the Gospel itself—which has testimony from the Law and the Prophets, and hence the Savior shone on the mountain between those two persons (Matthew 17:3)—to restrain our appetite from all the enticements of the world by the fast of self-control, for through them captive human beings forget God.

This continues as long as the perfection of the Law’s Decalogue, like a ten-stringed psaltery, is proclaimed throughout the four parts of the world—that is, throughout the whole earth—so that ten multiplied by four marks the number forty.

But by the number fifty after the Lord’s resurrection, during which we sing “Alleluia,” not the end and passing of some period of time is signified, but that blessed eternity. For the ten added to the forty is the reward that is paid to the faithful laboring in this life—the reward that the master of the household prepared equally for the first and the last.

Let us therefore hear the breast of God’s people, full of divine praise [Note: [Col. 1463] The Royal manuscript has: “Let us therefore hear the psalm refreshing the breast of God’s people with divine praise.” Immediately afterward, with Ambrose and some manuscripts, it continues: “Behold, a person.” The Remigius manuscript instead has: “Behold, a certain person in this psalm,” etc. Finally, some manuscripts have: “Behold, it resounds in this psalm, and a certain person,” etc.].

Behold, in this psalm a certain person resounds, rejoicing with happy exultation, and prefigures the people who pour forth from their hearts in the love of God—that is, the body of Christ, liberated from every evil.

### 2. [verse 1]

“I will confess to you, Lord,” he says, “with my whole heart.”

Confession is not always confession of sins; the praise of God too is expressed through devout confession. The former mourns; the latter rejoices. The former displays a wound to the physician; the latter gives thanks for health.

This confession signifies someone not only liberated from every evil but also separated from all the wicked. Therefore let us see where he confesses to the Lord with his whole heart: “In the council of the upright,” he says, “and in the congregation”—I believe, those who will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28).

For no unrighteous person will then be among them. No thefts of any Judas will be tolerated; no Simon Magus will be baptized, wishing to buy the Spirit while considering selling him (Acts 8:13, 18–19); no Alexander the coppersmith will display many evils (2 Timothy 4:14); no one covered with a sheep’s skin will creep in under the guise of false brotherhood.

Among such people the Church must now groan, and such people it must then exclude, when all the righteous are gathered together.

“These are the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills”: through them mercy abandons no one who confesses, and no one’s iniquity remains unpunished, since he chastises every son whom he receives (Hebrews 12:6).

But if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear? (1 Peter 4:18).

Let a person choose whatever he wishes. The works of the Lord have not been arranged in such a way that a creature established in free choice can overcome the Creator’s will, even if it acts against his will.

God does not wish you to sin, for he forbids it. Yet if you sin, do not suppose that a human being has done what he wished and that something God did not wish has happened to God.

For just as he wishes a human being not to sin, so he wishes to spare the sinner, so that the sinner may return and live. Finally, he wishes to punish the one who persists in sin, so that the obstinate person may not escape the power of justice.

Thus, whatever you choose, the Almighty will not lack a means by which to fulfill his will concerning you. For “great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills.”

### 3. [verse 3]

“Confession and magnificence are his work.”

What is more magnificent than justifying the ungodly? But perhaps human work precedes this magnificence of God, so that, after confessing his sins, a person may deserve to be justified.

For “the tax collector went down from the temple justified more than the Pharisee,” because “he did not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven, but beat his breast, saying: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’”

This is the magnificence of the Lord: the justification of the sinner, because “whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 18:13–14).

This is the magnificence of the Lord, because “the one to whom more is forgiven loves more” (Luke 7:42–48).

This is the magnificence of the Lord, because “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

But perhaps this comes from works.

“No,” he says, “not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ for good works” (Ephesians 2:9–10).

A human being does not perform righteousness unless he has been justified. But by believing in him who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), he begins from faith, so that good works may show not what he earned beforehand, but what he received afterward.

From where, then, does that confession come? It is not yet the work of righteousness, but the rejection of sin. Yet whatever its condition may be, do not let the human being glory in himself even in this, so that “whoever glories may glory in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

For “what do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Therefore it is not only “magnificence,” by which the ungodly is justified, but also “confession and magnificence are his work.”

What, then, shall we say? “He has mercy on whomever he wishes, and he hardens whomever he wishes.” Is there injustice with God? Certainly not. For “his justice remains forever and ever. But you, human being,” belonging to this age, “who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:14, 18, 20).

### 4. [verses 4–5]

“He has made a memorial of his wonders”: humbling this person and exalting that one.

“He has made a memorial of his wonders,” reserving at an appropriate time extraordinary miracles which human weakness, attentive to novelty, would remember, although his daily miracles are greater [Note: [Col. 1465] The printed editions have: “which human weakness would remember, not being attentive to novelty.” The word “not” is absent from many manuscripts.].

He creates so many trees throughout the whole earth, and no one wonders. He withered one by a word, and mortal hearts were astonished (Matthew 21:19–20). Yet “he has made a memorial of his wonders.”

For this is the miracle that will especially remain fixed in attentive hearts: that constant repetition will not make it seem insignificant.

### 5.

But what benefit did the miracles bring, except that God should be feared? And what good would fear have done unless the merciful and compassionate Lord had given food to those who fear him—the food that does not perish, the bread that came down from heaven (John 6:27, 51), which he gave without any merits on their part? For Christ died for the ungodly (Rom. 5:6). No one, therefore, would give such food except the merciful and compassionate Lord. But if he has given so much to this life—if the sinner, who is to be justified, has received the Word made flesh—what will he receive in the world to come, when he has been glorified? “He will remember his covenant forever.” Yet he has not given everything who has given only the pledge.

### 6. [vv. 6–9]

“He will declare to his people the power of his works.” Let the holy Israelites not be distressed—those who have abandoned everything of their own and followed him; let them not be distressed, saying, “Who, then, can be saved?” For “it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:24–26). For he declared to them the power of his works, since the things that are difficult for human beings are easy for God.

“To give them the inheritance of the nations.” For the Gospel went also to the nations, and the rich of this world were commanded not to be proud-minded, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God (1 Tim. 6:17), for whom what is difficult for human beings is easy. Thus many were called; thus the inheritance of the nations was occupied; thus it came about that even very many who did not abandon all they possessed in this life in order to follow him nevertheless despised life itself for the confession of his name. And, humbling themselves like camels in order to carry the burdens of affliction, they entered as if through the eye of a needle, passing through the constrictions of piercing suffering. He himself accomplished these things, for whom all things are possible.

### 7.

“The works of his hands are truth and judgment.” Let truth be held by those who are judged here. The martyrs are judged here, and they are brought to that judgment in which they will judge not only those by whom they were judged, but even angels (1 Cor. 6:3)—against whom they had their struggle, even when they seemed to be judged by human beings.

“Let not tribulation, distress, famine, nakedness, or the sword separate [them] from Christ” (Rom. 8:35). For all his commandments are faithful: he does not deceive; he fulfills what he promised. Yet what he promised is not to be awaited or hoped for here; rather, these things “are confirmed forever and ever,” made in truth and righteousness. This is true and just: that one should labor here and rest there. For “he sent redemption to his people.” From what, then, are they redeemed, unless from the captivity of this pilgrimage? Let rest, therefore, be sought only in the heavenly homeland.

### 8.

God did indeed give the carnal Israelites the earthly Jerusalem, “which is in bondage with her children”; but this is the Old Testament, belonging to the old human being. Those who understood the figure there were even then heirs of the New Testament, because “the Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother” (Gal. 4:25–26), eternal in the heavens.

But through that old covenant it was proved in reality that God had promised transitory things: “He commanded his covenant forever.” But which covenant, unless the New? Whoever you wish to be its heir, do not deceive yourself. Do not think carnally of a land flowing with milk and honey; do not imagine pleasant estates, fruitful and shady gardens, or anything of the sort that the eye of avarice commonly desires here.

Since greed is “the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10), it must be put to death so that it may be consumed here, not postponed so that it may be satisfied there. First flee punishments; avoid Gehenna. Before you desire the God who makes promises, beware the God who threatens. For “holy and terrible is his name.”

### 9. [v. 10]

In place of all the pleasures of this world—whether those you have experienced or those you can increase and multiply in imagination—desire wisdom, the mother of immortal delights. Yet “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.” It will delight you, and without doubt it will delight you ineffably in the chaste and eternal embraces of truth; but debts must first be forgiven you before rewards are demanded.

“The beginning of wisdom,” therefore, “is the fear of the Lord.” “Good is understanding.” Who denies it? But to understand and not to act is dangerous. It is therefore good for those who act. Let it not lift the mind into pride. For “his praise endures forever” whose fear is the beginning of wisdom; and this will be the reward, this the end, this the permanent resting-place and seat.

There the faithful commandments are found, confirmed forever and ever; this is the inheritance of the New Testament—the commandments that endure eternally. “One thing I have asked of the Lord,” he says, “this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4). “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5), because his praise endures forever.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 111

[Col. 1467]

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1.

I believe, brothers, that you paid attention to the title of this psalm and committed it to memory. “The conversion,” it says, “of Haggai and Zechariah.” These men were not yet prophets when this was sung. For between the time of David and the deportation of the people of Israel to Babylon, fourteen generations are counted, as divine Scripture—and especially Matthew the evangelist—testifies (Matt. 1:17). The restoration of the ruined temple, according to the prophecy of the holy Jeremiah, was hoped for after seventy years from that deportation (Jer. 25:12; 29:10). When those years were completed, under Darius, king of Babylon, these two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, were filled with the Holy Spirit; and both began to prophesy one after the other within a single year. This appears to have concerned the restoration of the temple, as had been foretold so long before (1 Esd. 1, 5; Hag. 1; Zech. 1).

But whoever fixes the eye of the heart upon bodily events and does not extend it from there toward spiritual understanding dwells in thought among the stones of the temple, from which the visible structure rises, fashioned by human hands. Such a person is not himself made a living stone, fitted and suited to that temple which the Lord first prefigured in his own body when he said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

For the body of the Lord is, in its fuller sense, the holy Church itself, whose head has ascended into heaven. He is supremely the living stone, the cornerstone, of whom blessed Peter says:

> “Approaching the living stone, rejected by human beings but chosen and honored by God—and you yourselves, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. For Scripture says: ‘Behold, I lay in Zion a chosen, precious cornerstone, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame’” (1 Pet. 2:4–6).

[Note: The manuscripts read *accedimus*, “we approach,” instead of the printed *accedentes*, “approaching.”]

Therefore, in order that each person may become a living stone suitable for such a structure, let him understand spiritually the restoration of the temple from the ancient ruin that occurred in Adam, and the restoration of the new people according to the new and heavenly human being. Thus, “just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:49), so that, after all the ages of this world—like the seventy years that signify mystically the number of perfection—and as though after the captivity of a long pilgrimage, we may be constructed not as a mass destined to collapse but established in eternal immortality.

Do not suppose that the spiritual Jerusalem belongs to the Jews more than to you. For, as the Apostle says:

> “You are no longer strangers and resident foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone. In him the whole building, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in him you too are being built together into a dwelling-place of God in the Spirit” (Eph. 2:19–22).

This is the temple of God, to which the prophetic mystery of Haggai and Zechariah pertains. To this temple the same Apostle again says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. 3:17).

Whoever, therefore, turns from the ruinous corruption of this world toward the work of this joint building and toward the hope of a holy and firm structure, as a living stone, understands the title of the psalm; he understands “the conversion of Haggai and Zechariah.” Let him therefore sing what follows, not so much with the voice of his tongue as with his life.

[Note: Ambrosiaster and several manuscripts read *tam lingua et voce, quam vita*, “as much with tongue and voice as with life.”]

For the perfection of the building will be that ineffable peace of wisdom whose beginning is the fear of the Lord (Prov. 1:7). Let this conversion, therefore, begin with the one whom it is building together.

### 2. [v. 1]

“For blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly delight in his commandments.” Let God see—he alone judges both truly and mercifully—how much this person progresses in his commandments, since “human life upon the earth is a trial,” as holy Job says (Job 7:1). And again it is written: “The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15).

But “the one who judges us is the Lord.” We must not judge before the proper time, until the Lord comes, brings to light the hidden things of darkness, and reveals the purposes of hearts; then each person will receive praise from God (1 Cor. 4:4–5).

Let him, then, see how much each person progresses in his commandments. Nevertheless, the one who has loved the peace of that joint building will greatly delight in them; and he must no longer despair, because “he will greatly delight in his commandments,” and “peace on earth among people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

### 3. [vv. 2–3]

From this comes the statement: “His offspring will be mighty on the earth.” That the seed of the future harvest consists in works of mercy is attested by the Apostle, who says, “Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we shall reap” (Gal. 6:9). And again he says, “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Cor. 9:6).

What, brothers, is more powerful than this: that Zacchaeus should purchase the kingdom of heaven with half his possessions (Luke 19:8), but the widow with two small coins (Mark 12:42), and that each should possess just as much there? What is more powerful than that the same kingdom should be worth to the rich man with his treasures and to the poor man with a cup of cold water?

There are people who do these things while acquiring earthly possessions, either hoping for a reward from the Lord here or desiring to please human beings. But “the generation of the upright will be blessed”—that is, the works of those for whom the God of Israel is good, who are upright in heart.

An upright heart is one that does not resist the Father when he corrects it and believes him when he makes promises. It is not the heart of those whose feet are shaken, whose steps slip and wander, as is sung in another psalm, when they are jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners, and think that their own works are perishing because no imperishable reward is given them (Ps. 72:1–14).

But this man who fears the Lord and, through the conversion of an upright heart, is fitted into the holy temple of God seeks neither human glory nor earthly riches. Yet “glory and riches are in his house.” His house is his heart, where, with God praising him, he dwells more richly in the hope of eternal life than, with human beings flattering him, he dwells in marble and coffered houses with fear of eternal death.

“For his righteousness endures forever”; it is his glory, it is his riches. But the other man’s purple, fine linen, and splendid feasts, when they are present, pass away; and when the end has come, his burning tongue will cry out, longing for a drop of water from a finger (Luke 16:19–24).

[Note: The better manuscripts read *Deo laudante*, “with God praising him.” The printed editions read *Deo habitante*, “with God dwelling [in him],” and below *hominibus habitantibus*, “with human beings dwelling [there].” This latter reading, despite manuscript resistance, had also entered the book *Eight Questions to Dulcitius*, where, in question 4, the exposition of these first three verses is reproduced.]

### 4. [vv. 4–9]

“Light has risen in the darkness for the upright in heart.” They rightly direct their heart toward their God; rightly they walk uprightly with their God, preferring his will to their own and arrogantly presuming nothing upon themselves. For they remember that they were once darkness, but now are light in the Lord (Eph. 5:8).

“The Lord God is merciful, compassionate, and just.” It is pleasing that he is merciful and compassionate; but perhaps it is frightening that the Lord God is just. Do not fear in despair, blessed man who fears the Lord and greatly delights in his commandments: be gracious, show mercy, and lend.

For the Lord God is so just that he will judge without mercy the one who has not shown mercy (James 2:13). “The gracious man shows mercy and lends”; God does not drive him from his mouth as something tasteless. “Forgive,” he says, “and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38).

In what you forgive so that you may be forgiven, you show mercy; in what you give so that it may be given to you, you lend. Although, in the general sense, all mercy by which help is given to the wretched is called mercy, there is nevertheless a distinction: sometimes you expend neither money nor the effort of bodily labor, but by forgiving what someone has done against you, you freely acquire the forgiveness of your own sins.

These two duties of kindness—forgiving sins and distributing benefits—seem to me to be distinguished in this verse just as they are in the Gospel passage we mentioned: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.” Thus the verse reads: “The gracious man shows mercy and lends.”

Let us not be sluggish in these matters, brothers. The man who desires to be avenged seeks glory; but consider what is written: “The one who conquers anger is better than the one who captures a city” (Prov. 16:32). The man who does not wish to give to the poor seeks riches; but consider what is written: “You will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21).

You will therefore not be without glory when you forgive, because the triumph over conquered anger is more praiseworthy; nor will you be poor when you give, because the heavenly treasure is possessed more securely. This verse was brought forth by the preceding one: “Glory and riches are in his house.”

### 5.

The one who does these things, therefore, “will arrange his words in judgment.” The deeds themselves are the words by which he will be defended in judgment; and that judgment will not be without mercy for him, because he himself also showed mercy.

“For he will not be shaken forever”: he will be separated to the right and will hear, “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” For no other deeds are mentioned there except works of mercy.

He will therefore hear, “Come, blessed of my Father,” because “the generation of the upright will be blessed.” Thus: “The righteous will be in everlasting remembrance, and he will not fear evil tidings.” This is what those on the left will hear: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:34, 41).

### 6.

Therefore the one who here seeks not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ endures hardships with the greatest patience and confidently awaits the promises: “His heart is ready to hope in the Lord.” He is not broken by any temptations: “His heart is established; he will not be shaken until he sees above his enemies.”

His enemies wished to see earthly goods here; and when invisible things were promised them, they said, “Who will show us good things?” (Ps. 4:6). Let our heart, therefore, be established, and let us not be shaken until we see above our enemies. They wish to see the goods of human beings who are dying on earth; we believe that we shall see the goods of the Lord in the land of the living (Ps. 26:13).

### 7.

But it is a great thing to have an established heart and not be shaken when those who love what they see rejoice and mock the person who hopes for what he does not see. He will not be shaken until he himself sees—not below, as his enemies do, but above his enemies—what the eye has not seen, the ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him (1 Cor. 2:9).

How much is this unseen good worth? It is purchased for as much as each person is able to possess. For this reason that man also scattered and gave to the poor: he did not see, but he was purchasing. The one who kept the treasure in heaven was he who deigned to hunger and thirst in the poor on earth.

It is therefore no wonder that “his righteousness endures forever,” with the one who created the ages as its guardian. “His horn will be exalted in glory”—the horn whose humility was despised by the proud.

### 8. [v. 10]

“The sinner will see and be angry”: that is, his repentance will then be late and fruitless. For with whom will he be angry more than with himself, when he says, “What did our pride profit us? And what did the boasting of riches bring us?” He will see the horn of the one who scattered and gave to the poor exalted in glory.

“He will gnash his teeth and waste away,” because there will be “weeping and gnashing of teeth.” For he will not put forth leaves and flourish, as he would if he repented at the proper time; rather, he will repent then, when the desire for sins has passed away, with no consolation following.

The desire for sins will pass away when everything has passed like a shadow (Wis. 5:8–9), when, as the hay dries up, the flower falls. But the word of the Lord, which endures forever (Isa. 40:8), just as it was mocked by the vanity of the falsely blessed, will smile in derision at the destruction of those same people, who will then be truly miserable.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 112

[Col. 1471]

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1. [vv. 1–3]

You know, brothers, and you have often heard the Lord say in the Gospel, “Let the children come to me; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.” And again: “Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it” (Matt. 19:14; 18:3; Mark 10:14–15).

In many other passages also our Lord, through the singular example of humility, condemns the pride of the old human being by the likeness of childhood, in order to renew life humbly. Therefore, beloved, when you hear it sung in the Psalms, “Praise the Lord, children,” do not suppose that this exhortation does not concern you because you have already passed beyond bodily childhood, whether you are flourishing in youthful beauty or growing gray with the honor of old age.

The Apostle says to all of you: “Do not become children in your thinking; but be infants in evil, so that you may be mature in your thinking” (1 Cor. 14:20). And what evil is meant above all except pride? For pride, presuming upon empty greatness, does not allow a person to walk along the narrow way or enter through the narrow gate. But a child easily enters through what is narrow; and therefore no one enters the kingdom of heaven except as a child.

What is worse than the evil of pride, which does not wish even God to rule over it? For it is written: “The beginning of human pride is apostasy from God” (Sir. 10:14). Cast down, break, crush, and destroy this pride, which raises itself up against the divine commandments with a stiff neck and resists the Lord’s gentle yoke. Then “praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord.”

When that pride has been prostrated and extinguished, “praise is perfected from the mouth of infants and sucklings” (Ps. 8:3); when it has been crushed and destroyed, “let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

Those who think themselves great do not sing these things. Those who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks do not sing them. They praise themselves, not God; for they are not children. They want their own name proclaimed instead, and they do not praise the name of the Lord.

Thus “they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened; claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1:21–22). They wanted their own name to be spread far and wide for a very long time, though they themselves would soon pass into narrow straits.

[Note: This reading should be adopted with the better manuscripts, so that the antithesis with what follows may be clear. The printed editions read: “They wanted their name to be spread most widely and most highly.”]

God deserves, and the Lord deserves, to be proclaimed always and everywhere. Let him therefore always be proclaimed: “Let the name of the Lord be blessed, from this time forth and forever.” Let him be proclaimed everywhere: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, praise the name of the Lord.”

[Note: Some manuscripts read *laudabile*, “praiseworthy,” at this point.]

### 2.

Let one of the holy children who praise the name of the Lord question me and say: “Behold, I accept ‘forever’; I accept ‘unto eternity.’ But why is the name of the Lord blessed ‘from this time forth,’ and not before this and before all the ages?”

I shall answer the child who asks without defiance: “To you, lords and children”—[Note: Some manuscripts read *pueri*, “children”; the printed editions read *pueri Dominici*, “children of the Lord.”]—“to you it is said: ‘Praise the name of the Lord; let the name of the Lord be blessed.’ Let the name of the Lord be blessed by you, clearly from this time forth, from the time when this is said to you.

“You are beginning to praise, but praise without end. From this time forth, therefore, and forever, praise without end. Do not say, ‘We are indeed beginning to praise the Lord because we are children; but when we have grown and become great, we shall praise ourselves.’ No, children, no. For this reason the Lord says through Isaiah, ‘I am; and until you grow old, I am’ (Isa. 46:4).

“He who is is always to be praised. Praise him from this time forth, children; praise him, old men, and forever. For your old age will indeed grow white with the gray hairs of wisdom, but it will not wither through the decay of the flesh.

“Or, since in this passage childhood appears rather to signify humility, to which the empty and false greatness of pride is opposed—and since the proud do not know how to praise the Lord, and therefore only children praise him—let your old age be childlike and your childhood mature. That is, let neither your wisdom be accompanied by pride nor your humility be without wisdom, so that you may praise the Lord from this time forth and forever.

“Wherever the Church of Christ is spread among holy children, ‘praise the name of the Lord.’ For this is what is meant by: ‘From the rising of the sun to its setting, praise the name of the Lord.’”

### 3. [v. 4]

“The Lord is exalted above all nations.” The nations are human beings. What wonder is it if the Lord is exalted above human beings? Those who worship created things see with their eyes in the heavens the things they set above themselves: the sun, moon, and stars. They serve creation while abandoning the Creator.

But the Lord is not only exalted above all nations; “his glory is also above the heavens.” The heavens look up to him; and the humble have him with them—those who, established in the flesh beneath heaven, do not worship heaven in his place.

### 4. [vv. 5–6]

“For who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the humble?” Someone might suppose that he dwells in the high heavens, from which he looks upon earthly things below. But he looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth.

In what heights, then, does he dwell, from which he looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth? Or does he dwell in those heights and also look upon the humble themselves? For he exalts the humble in such a way that he does not make them proud.

Thus he also dwells in others whom he exalts and makes his heaven—that is, his throne. Yet, because he sees them as not proud but always subject to him, he looks upon the humble even in that heaven, among those heights in which he dwells.

For the Spirit speaks through Isaiah:

> “Thus says the Most High, who dwells in the heights; his name is eternal; the Most High, who dwells in holiness.”

He explained what he meant by “dwelling in the heights,” for, expressing it more fully, he said, “dwelling in holiness.” But who are the holy except the humble, those children who praise the Lord?

Therefore he adds: “Giving greatness of spirit to the fainthearted, and giving life to those who are humble in heart” (Isa. 57:15). In these holy people, in whom he rests, he gives greatness of spirit to the fainthearted. By giving greatness of spirit, he certainly makes them exalted; dwelling in them as in his place of rest, he dwells in the heights.

But because he gives greatness of spirit to the fainthearted, he looks upon as humble the same heights in which he dwells. “He looks,” he says, “upon the humble in heaven and on earth.”

### 5.

This also prompts us to ask whether the Lord our God looks upon the same humble people in heaven as on earth, or whether he looks upon some humble people in heaven and others on earth.

If they are the same, I see how this may be understood according to the Apostle, who says: “Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful before God” (2 Cor. 10:3–4).

Whence comes their power, unless it is because they are spiritual? Since the Apostle walks in the flesh and wages spiritual warfare, it is not surprising that his humility is looked upon in heaven because of the freedom of his spirit, and on earth because of the servitude of his body.

In another passage he says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). He also says that it would be “better” for him “to depart and be with Christ,” but that “to remain in the flesh is necessary” for the sake of others (Phil. 1:23–24).

Therefore, whoever understands both the Apostle’s citizenship in heaven and his remaining in the flesh on earth must also understand how the Lord our God dwells among exalted saints and nevertheless looks upon those same saints as humble, both in heaven—because they set their minds on the things above, having risen with Christ in hope (Col. 3:1)—and on earth—because they have not yet been released from the bond of the flesh, so that they can be with Christ with their whole life.

But if the Lord our God looks upon one group of humble people in heaven and another on earth, I believe that in heaven he now looks upon those whom he has called and in whom he dwells, while on earth he looks upon those whom he calls so that he may dwell in them. He possesses the former, who think upon heavenly things; he raises up the latter, who dream of earthly things.

### 6.

But because we have difficulty obtaining that those who have not yet joined their devout necks to the Lord’s gentle yoke should themselves already be called humble—since in this passage the divine words throughout the psalm admonish us to understand “the humble” as the holy Church—there is another interpretation, which your Charity should consider with me.

I think that “the heavens” here signify those who will sit upon twelve thrones and judge with the Lord (Matt. 19:28), while “the earth” signifies the rest of the multitude of the blessed, who will be placed on the right, so that, commended for their works of mercy, they may be received by those whom they made their friends from the mammon of unrighteousness during the mortality of this life, into eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9).

To these the Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9:11). This can also be expressed in these words: “If we have sown heavenly things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your earthly things?”

In heaven, therefore, he looks upon those who sow heavenly things; on earth, those who give back earthly things. Yet he looks upon both as humble. For “he looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth,” because both remember what they were through their own evil and what they have become through the Lord’s grace.

The Apostle, the “vessel of election,” does not say only to them, “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8), and again, “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast.” He immediately includes himself, saying, “For we are his workmanship, created for good works.”

Elsewhere he says concerning himself and those who are looked upon in heaven: “For we too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3). And again: “For we too were once foolish and disobedient, wandering astray, slaves to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, he saved us—not by works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:3–5).

Behold the humble whom he looks upon in heaven. They are spiritual and judge all things, yet they are humble, lest they be judged when cast down.

What does he say about himself in particular? Are these not the things he recalls? “I am not worthy,” he says, “to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9); “but I received mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1:13).

### 7. [vv. 7–9]

Finally, after these verses in which the Spirit says in the psalm, “Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells in the heights and looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth,” wishing to teach us why the humble in heaven are designated in such language, even though they are already spiritual, great, and worthy of judicial seats, he immediately adds:

> “He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to set him with the princes, with the princes of his people.”

Let the heads of the exalted, therefore, not disdain to be humble beneath the Lord’s right hand. For although the faithful steward of the Lord’s money will be placed with the princes of God’s people, although he will sit upon twelve thrones and even judge angels, nevertheless he is raised from the earth as a needy person and lifted from the dungheap as a poor man.

Or was the one who served various desires and pleasures not lifted from the dungheap? But perhaps, when he was already saying these things, he was neither needy nor poor. Why, then, does he still groan under his burden, longing to be clothed over with the dwelling that is from heaven (2 Cor. 5:2)? Why, lest he be exalted, is he buffeted and subjected to the angel of Satan by the thorn in his flesh (2 Cor. 12:7)?

He is indeed exalted because the Lord dwells in him and because he possesses the Spirit who searches all things, even the depths of God (1 Cor. 2:10). Thus he is in heaven; but even in heaven the Lord looks upon the humble.

### 8.

What, then, brothers? If we have now heard about the humble who are in heaven, raised from the dungheap so that they may be placed with the princes of the people, have we heard nothing consequently about the humble whom the Lord looks upon on earth?

Those who will judge with the Lord are fewer; those whom they receive into eternal dwellings are more numerous. Although the entire mass of grain, compared with the separated chaff, may appear to contain few, nevertheless, considered in itself, it is abundant.

“For the children of the forsaken woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1). There are many more children of the woman who conceived in old age through grace than of the woman who was married to the bond of the Law from the beginning of her life.

I say that she conceived in old age, looking to Sarah our mother in the one Isaac, the mother of the faithful among all nations.

But observe what person Isaiah presents: she seems altogether not to be a mother, not even one who has borne anyone. And yet what is said to her?

> “Your children whom you had lost will say in your ears: ‘This place is too narrow for us; make room for us now, so that we may dwell here.’ But you will say in your heart: ‘Who has begotten these for me, since I know that I am childless and a widow? Who, then, raised these for me? For I was left alone; where were these?’” (Isa. 49:20–21).

From this perspective, therefore, the Church says these things: she appears to bear nothing among those crowds who did not abandon everything in order to follow the Lord and sit upon twelve thrones.

But how many within that same crowd, making friends for themselves from the mammon of unrighteousness through works of mercy, will stand on the right?

Thus he not only raises from the dungheap the one whom he places with the princes of his people; he also “makes the barren woman dwell in a house as a joyful mother of children.” He who dwells in the heights and looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth: the seed of Abraham, like the stars of heaven—sublime holiness established in the heavenly seats—and, like the sand on the shore of the sea, the merciful and innumerable multitude separated from the waves on the left and from impious bitterness.

[Note: This is the reading of Ambrosiaster and the better manuscripts. The Louvain edition reads: “He places sublime holiness in the heavenly seats, and, like the sand on the shore of the sea, he separates the merciful ….” Erasmus has the same reading, except that he has *misericordiam*, “mercy,” instead of *misericordem*, “merciful.” Some manuscripts instead read: “He places holiness, sublime, in the heavenly seats.”]

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 113

## SERMON I: ON THE FIRST PART OF THE PSALM
1. [verses 1–6.] We read, and retain as very well known, dearest brothers, what is related in the Book of Exodus: that the people of Israel, liberated from the unjust domination of the Egyptians, passed through the divided waters of the sea on dry ground (Exod. 14:22). We also know that, when they were entering the promised land through the Jordan River, the river—touched by the feet of the priests carrying the Lord’s ark—stood above with its flow restrained, while below, what had been flowing ran off into the sea, until the whole people had crossed on dry ground while the priests stood there (Josh. 3:15–17). We know these things; nevertheless, we must not suppose that in this psalm, to which we have now responded after its Alleluia was pronounced and sung, the Holy Spirit intends, by our recalling those past events, that we should not at all think of future events of this kind. For those events, as the Apostle says, happened to them figuratively; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10:11).

Therefore, when we hear in the psalm, “When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion; the sea saw and fled, the Jordan turned backward,” do not suppose that past events are being recounted to us, but rather that future events are being foretold. For those miracles too, when they occurred among that people, were present events, but they were carried out not without signifying the future. And so, to show that the one who foretold these things by singing the psalm was carrying out in words the same things that had there been carried out in deeds—one and the same Spirit working both those deeds [textual note: Am. and nearly all manuscripts read “figures” (figuris)] and these words, so that what had been reserved to be revealed at the end of the ages might be announced beforehand through anticipatory figures of events and words—he did not say exactly what had happened there, but expressed some things differently from what we learned by reading there. Thus no one would suppose that he was merely recalling completed events rather than foretelling what was to come [textual note: nearly all manuscripts read “foreseeing” (praevidere)].

First, we read that the Jordan itself did not turn backward, but stood still on the side from which the waters flowed down from above, while that people was crossing. Next, we do not read that the mountains and hills leapt; these he added, so that he might repeat all those events as well. For after saying, “The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned backward,” he continued: “The mountains leapt like rams, and the hills like lambs of the sheep.” Then again he asks: “What is the matter with you, sea, that you fled; and you, Jordan, that you turned backward? Mountains, that you leapt like rams, and hills, like lambs of the sheep?”

2. Let us therefore attend to what we are being admonished about. Those events were figures of us, and these words urge us to recognize ourselves. If we hold firmly in our hearts the grace of God that has been given to us, we are Israel, the offspring of Abraham; the Apostle says to us, “Therefore you are Abraham’s offspring” (Gal. 3:29). For, as he says elsewhere, “Faith was counted to Abraham for righteousness, not in circumcision but in uncircumcision; and he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith that he had while uncircumcised, so that it might be counted also to those who are uncircumcised, that he might be the father of circumcision to those who are not only of the circumcision, but also to those who follow the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised.”

He was not made father only of the circumcised nation, to which it was said, “I have appointed you the father of many nations.” “Many,” moreover, means not merely some, but all (Rom. 4:9–17). This is openly stated when it is said to him, “In you all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Therefore, let no Christian think himself a stranger to the name of Israel. We are joined to those who believed from among the Jews—in whose number we find the Apostles foremost—in the cornerstone. Hence the Lord says elsewhere: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

Therefore the Christian people are Israel in the fuller sense, and they themselves are rather the house of Jacob. For Israel and Jacob are the same. But that multitude of Jews which was rightly rejected because of its unbelief sold its birthright for carnal pleasure, so that it might belong not to Jacob but rather to Esau. For you know that in this mystery it was said, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:33, 23).

3. Egypt, because its name is interpreted as “Affliction,” “the one afflicting,” or “the one constraining,” is often taken figuratively for this world, from which we must depart spiritually, lest we become unequally yoked with unbelievers (2 Cor. 6:14). Thus each person becomes a suitable citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem when he has first renounced this world, just as that people could not be led into the promised land unless it had first departed from Egypt.

But just as that people did not leave Egypt except by divine assistance and liberation, so no one turns his heart away from this world except by the gift of divine mercy. What was prefigured there once is fulfilled at this end of the world, in this “last hour,” as blessed John writes (1 John 2:18), through the daily offspring of the Church in each believer.

Hear the Apostle, the teacher of the nations, instructing and teaching: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses [textual note: the manuscripts, following the Greek, read “into Moses”; the editions read “in Moses”] in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ. But God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness. Now these things happened as figures of us” (1 Cor. 10:1–6).

What more do you want, dearest brothers? Surely it is evident—not by human conjecture, but by apostolic, that is, divine and lordly instruction. God was speaking through them, and although through clouds of flesh, the Lord was thundering—that all those events, performed figuratively, are now fulfilled in our salvation. Then the future was foretold; now the past is read and the present is recognized.

4. Hear something even more marvelous: the mysteries of the ancient Books, hidden and veiled, are revealed in part by the ancient Books themselves. For the prophet Micah speaks as follows:

“According to the days of their departure from Egypt, I shall show them marvels. The nations shall see, and they shall be confounded at all their strength; they shall put their hands over their mouths, their ears shall become deaf; they shall lick the earth like serpents, dragging themselves along the ground. They shall be disturbed by their strongholds; they shall fall in mind before the Lord our God, and they shall fear you. Who is a God like you, taking away iniquity and passing over the impiety of the remnant of your inheritance? He has not held his anger as a testimony, for he is willing and merciful. He himself shall turn and have mercy on us; he shall plunge our sins down, he shall plunge all our faults into the depths of the sea” (Mic. 7:15–19).

Surely you observe, brothers, that the sacred mysteries are opened here more plainly. Thus, although the Spirit of marvelous prophecy beholds future events in this psalm, he nevertheless seems to recount them as though they had already happened. “Judah became his sanctuary,” he says; “the sea saw and fled.” “Became” and “fled” are words of the past tense; likewise, “the Jordan turned backward,” “the mountains leapt,” and “the earth was moved” sound as though they refer to the past—without prejudice, however, to understanding them as future.

Otherwise we would be forced, contrary to the testimony of the Gospel, to understand even the following not as foretold of the future but as recalled from the past: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Ps. 21:19). Although these words too are expressed in the past tense, they foretold what was to be fulfilled much later in the Lord’s Passion.

Nevertheless, dearest brothers, the prophet I have mentioned also refined coarse hearts and confidently extended them toward understanding future events from past deeds. Thus we should believe not only, on apostolic authority, that those events were our figures, but also that this was not overlooked by the prophets themselves. As their eloquence discloses it [textual note: some manuscripts read “might disclose it” (panderetur)], we may see and rejoice, certain and secure, bringing forth from God’s treasury both new and old, harmoniously joined to one another.

Although he sang these things so long after that people’s departure from Egypt and so long before the times of the Church, nevertheless he unequivocally testifies that he is foretelling the future. “According to the days,” he says, “of their departure from Egypt, I shall show them marvels.
