They shall see, and they shall be confounded.” This is what is said here: “The sea saw and fled.” If here, through words of the past tense—“saw” and “fled”—future events are secretly foretold, then surely “they shall see and be confounded,” which are words of the future tense, cannot be understood as referring to past events.

A little later he makes our very enemies clear—those who followed us as we fled in order to kill us, namely, our sins—just as the Egyptians were drowned in the sea. He shows with the greatest clarity that our sins are submerged and destroyed in Baptism, saying: “For he is willing and merciful; he himself shall turn and have mercy on us; he shall plunge our sins down, he shall plunge all our faults into the depths of the sea.”

5. What then, dearly beloved? You who recognize yourselves as Israelites according to the offspring of Abraham, who are heirs as the house of Jacob according to the promise—recognize also that you have come out of Egypt, since you have renounced this world; that you have come out from a barbarous people, since by your confession of piety you have separated yourselves from the blasphemies of the nations.

For it is not your language but the language of the barbarians that does not know how to praise God, while you sing Alleluia to him. “Judah became his sanctuary” in you: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart” (Rom. 2:28–29).

Examine your hearts, then. If faith has circumcised them, if confession has purified them, then “Judah became his sanctuary” in you; in you “Israel became his dominion.” For he gave you power to become children of God (John 1:12).

6. Let each one of you now remember how, when he wanted to apply his heart to God and, turning away from the former desires of his ignorance, to submit his devoted spirit to God’s gentle yoke, he abandoned the carnal works of this world—in which he labored without fruit, as though making bricks in Egypt under the harsh domination of the devil. After hearing the Lord’s voice say, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28), he abandoned and rejected those things and ran beneath Christ’s light burden.

Let each one of you remember, then, how all worldly impediments gave way; how the voices of those who dissuaded him [textual note: Er. and Lov. read “the voices of those disagreeing and dissuading”; Am. omits “and dissuading”; the manuscripts omit “disagreeing and”] either did not dare to break out or, considering Christ’s name exalted and honored throughout all the lands, fell silent in fear.

Therefore, “the sea saw and fled,” so that the way might be opened to you without opposition toward spiritual freedom.

7. As for how the Jordan turned backward, I do not want you to seek outside yourselves; I do not want you to suspect anything evil. The Lord rebukes certain people who have turned their backs to him and not their faces (Jer. 2:27). Whoever abandons his beginning and turns away from his Creator flows, like a river into the sea, into the embittering wickedness of this world [textual note: three manuscripts read “embittering joy” (amaricantem laetitiam)].

It is therefore good for him to turn backward, so that God may be before the face of one who is returning—God whom he had placed behind himself. Then the sea of this world, which he had made to be before him as he flowed toward it, will be behind him. Thus he may forget what lies behind and stretch toward what lies ahead (Phil. 3:13)—which is beneficial once he has turned.

Before he turns, however, if he forgets what lies behind, he forgets God, because he had placed God behind himself by turning his back on him. And if he stretches toward what lies ahead, he stretches toward the world, because he had placed the world before his face and was rushing eagerly toward it.

The Jordan therefore signifies those who have received the grace of Baptism. The Jordan turns backward when they turn toward God, so that they no longer have him behind them but, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory (2 Cor. 3:18).

8. “The mountains leapt like rams”: the holy Apostles, faithful stewards of the word of truth, holy preachers of the Gospel. “And the hills like lambs of the sheep”: these are the ones of whom it is said, “In Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel”; these are the ones to whom it is said, “I do not write these things to shame you, but I admonish you as my dearest children” (1 Cor. 4:15, 14). They are the ones of whom it is said, “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28:1).

Look throughout all the lands, you who know how to marvel at these things, rejoice, and sing to the Lord your God. Observe these events being fulfilled throughout all nations, events that so long ago were performed and foretold figuratively.

9. Ask and say: “What is the matter with you, sea, that you fled; and you, Jordan, that you turned backward? Mountains, that you leapt like rams, and hills, like lambs of the sheep?”

What is the matter with you, world, that your impediments have given way? What is the matter with you, countless thousands of faithful people throughout the whole world, that you turn toward your Lord and renounce this world?

What is the matter with you who rejoice, to whom at the end it will be said, “Well done, good servant, because you were faithful in a few things, I will set you over many things”? What is the matter with you who rejoice, to whom at the end it will be said, “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:21, 34)?

10. [verse 7.] All these things will answer you, and you yourselves will answer yourselves: “The earth was moved at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob.”

What does “at the presence of the Lord” mean except the presence of the one who said, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20)? The earth was moved; but because it had remained sluggish in an evil way, it was moved so that it might be established more firmly by the presence of the Lord.

11. [verse 8.] “Who turns the rock into pools of water and the cliff into fountains of water.”

He melted himself, and a certain hardness of his own, to water his faithful, so that he might become in them “a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14). Previously, when he was unknown, he seemed hard. Because of this they were disturbed and did not wait until, once the Scriptures had been opened, he might flow and overflow into them—those who said, “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (John 6:61).

This rock, this hardness, was turned into pools of water, and this cliff into fountains of water, when, after rising again, he explained to them, beginning with Moses and proceeding through all the Prophets, why it was necessary for Christ to suffer (Luke 24:26–27). He also sent the Holy Spirit, of whom he said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).

## A Second Exposition of Psalm 113

12. [verse 1.] “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.”

For this grace of water bursting forth from the rock—“and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4)—was not given as though it were granted because of preceding works, but by the mercy of him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5). Indeed, Christ died for the ungodly (Rom. 5:6), so that human beings would seek the glory not of themselves but of God’s name.

13. [verse 2.] “Because of your mercy,” he says, “and your truth.”

Observe in the Holy Scriptures how often these two—mercy and truth—are joined together. In his mercy he called the ungodly, and in his truth he judges those who, once called, refused to come.

“Lest the nations should say, ‘Where is their God?’” At the last, his mercy and truth will appear, when the sign of the Son of Man appears in heaven. Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will not say, “Where is their God?” For he will no longer be proclaimed to them as one whom they must believe in, but will already be shown as one whom they must fear.

14. [verse 3.] “But our God is in heaven above.”

He is not in the heaven where they see the sun and moon, the works of God that they worship, but in heaven above, which transcends all heavenly and earthly bodies.

Nor is our God in heaven as though, with heaven removed, he feared a collapse without a place to stand. “In the heavens and on earth he has done whatever he willed.” He does not need his works, as though he were placed in them in order to remain. Rather, he persists in his own eternity, and while remaining there he made whatever he willed in heaven and on earth. They did not already carry him so that things might be made by him; for unless they had been made, they could not carry him.

Therefore, where he himself is present, he contains things as one who is not in need of them; he is not contained by them as one who needs them.

Or the words “In the heavens and on earth he has done whatever he willed” may be understood in this way: in the higher and lower ranks of his people he established his voluntary grace, so that no one might glory in the merits of works. For whether the mountains leap like rams or the hills like lambs of the sheep, “the earth was moved at the presence of the Lord,” so that they would not remain forever in earthly filth.

## Sermon II: On the Second Part of the Psalm

1. [verse 4.] Although, for those who examine them carefully, all the psalms perhaps form one continuous composition, so that no psalm follows which cannot be joined to the preceding one, let us nevertheless consider this psalm as though it and the preceding psalm were a single whole.

For when the preceding psalm said, “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory; because of your mercy and your truth; lest the nations should say, ‘Where is their God?’”—since we worship the invisible God, known to no bodily eyes but to the purest hearts—it was as though the nations could say, “Where is their God?” because they themselves could display their gods to the eyes. The psalm first taught that the presence of our God is perceived through his works: although he is in heaven above, “in the heavens and on earth he has done whatever he willed.”

And as though he were saying, “Let the nations display their gods,” he says: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands.” That is: although we cannot display our God to your bodily eyes, though you ought to have understood him through his works, nevertheless do not allow yourselves to be led astray by your vanities, because you can point with your finger to the things you worship.

It would be much more honorable for you to possess nothing that you could point out than for the blindness of your hearts to be displayed in what you point out with these eyes. For what do you display except gold and silver? They also have idols of bronze, wood, clay, and other materials of this kind; but the Holy Spirit preferred to mention their precious materials, because when someone is ashamed of what is more valuable to him, he is much more easily turned away from venerating what is less valuable.

Elsewhere in Scripture it is said of worshipers of idols: “Saying to wood, ‘You are my father,’ and to a stone, ‘You begot me’” (Jer. 2:27). But lest someone think himself wiser because he has not said this to wood and stone but to gold and silver, let him look here and direct here the ear of his heart: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold.”

Nothing worthless or contemptible has been named. To a mind that is not itself earthly, both earth and gold and silver are earth; yet gold and silver are more beautiful and brilliant, more solid and firm. Therefore do not add human hands, wishing to make a false god from the metal that the true God made—or rather, a false human being whom you may worship in place of the true God. Anyone who received such a being into friendship as though he were a real human being would be insane.

For the likeness of form and the structure that imitates limbs lead and, in a certain low affection, seize the weak hearts of mortals. But just as you display the individual things that have been fashioned, so display the functions of each one, whose likeness draws you, O human vanity.

2. [verses 5–7.] “They have mouths, and they will not speak; they have eyes, and they will not see; they have ears, and they will not hear; they have nostrils, and they will not smell; they have hands, and they will not touch; they have feet, and they will not walk; they will not cry out in their throats.”

The craftsman is therefore better than they are, since he was able to fashion these things with the movement and function of limbs—yet you would certainly be ashamed to worship such a craftsman. You too are better than they are, although you did not make them, because you do what they cannot do. Even an animal is better than they are. This is why the addition is made: “They will not cry out in their throats.”

For after saying above, “They have mouths, and they will not speak,” what need was there, once the limbs had been listed from head to foot, to repeat the matter of the throat’s cry? Surely it was because we understand that what he had mentioned concerning the other limbs is common to human beings and beasts. For beasts also see, hear, smell, and walk, and some, such as monkeys, touch with their hands.

But what he had said about the mouth belongs properly to human beings, since beasts do not speak. Yet lest anyone refer what was said only to the works of human limbs and place only human beings above the gods of the nations, he added after everything, saying, “They will not cry out in their throats”—something again common to human beings and animals.

If he had said this first, when he began to list the limbs from the mouth—“They have mouths, and they will not cry out”—then everything would also have been referred to human nature in this way, and a listener would not easily have noticed anything there concerning the fellowship of wild creatures.

But when he said of the mouth what is proper to human beings, and seemed to have ended the enumeration of the bodily parts with the feet, he added, “They will not cry out in their throats.” He thus made the reader or hearer attentive, so that, while asking why this had been added, he might discover that he was being warned that the idols of the nations should be placed below not only human beings but also beasts.

If one is ashamed to worship an animal—which God made seeing, hearing, smelling, touching, walking, and crying out in its throat—one should see how shameful it is to worship a mute image without life or sensation. It possesses a likeness of limbs for this purpose: that a soul devoted to bodily senses might attach its affection to a form as though it were living and animated, when it sees in that form what it experiences as living and animated in its own body.

How much better, then, do mice and snakes and the other kinds of living creatures, if one may speak in this way, in some sense judge the idols of the nations: since they find no human life in them, they do not care about their human form [textual note: the editions read, “How much more—or better—would mice and snakes and the other kinds of living creatures worship, which judge the idols …”]. Accordingly, they often build their nests in them and, unless they are frightened away by human movements, seek no more secure dwelling places.

A human being therefore moves himself in order to frighten a living beast away from his god; yet he worships as powerful the god that does not move itself, although he has frightened away from it something better than it is. He has frightened away one that sees from one that is blind, one that hears from one that is deaf, one that cries out from one that is mute, one that walks from one that is immobile, one that feels from one that is senseless, one that lives from one that is dead—indeed, from something worse than dead.

For just as it is obvious that a dead thing does not live, so it is obvious that it once lived. Therefore even a dead thing surpasses a god who neither lives nor has lived.

3. What could be clearer than this, my dearest brothers? What more evident? What child, when asked, would not answer that it is certain that “the idols of the nations have mouths, and they will not speak; they have eyes, and they will not see,” and the other things that divine speech has set forth?

Why, then, does the Holy Spirit take such care, in so many passages of Scripture, to suggest and inculcate these things as though to people who do not know them—as though they were not entirely obvious and well known to everyone? Is it not because the appearance of limbs, which we are accustomed naturally to see alive in living creatures and to experience in ourselves, when it has been fashioned as a sign and set upon a prominent platform—as they assert [textual note: Er. and Lov. read “fashioned in some sign, and set upon a prominent platform”]—and begins to be worshiped and honored by the multitude, produces in each person the most sordid affection of error?

Since such a person does not find vital movement in the image, he believes that a hidden divinity is present. Yet, deceived by its form and moved by the authority of supposedly wise institutions and obedient crowds, he cannot believe that an image resembling a living body exists without some living inhabitant.

From this affection of human beings, therefore, evil demons are invited to take possession of the idols of the nations. Through the varied deceit of those who preside over them [or, according to some manuscripts, “those who possess them”], deadly errors are sown and multiplied.

Elsewhere, accordingly, the divine Scriptures also stand guard against these things, lest anyone, when the idols have been ridiculed, say: “I do not worship this visible object, but the divinity that invisibly dwells there.” The same Scripture condemns those divinities in another psalm: “For the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95:5). The Apostle also says: “Not that an idol is anything, but that what the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to become partners with demons” (1 Cor. 10:19–20).

4. Those who say, “I worship neither the idol nor the demon, but I regard the bodily image as a sign of that reality which I ought to worship,” seem to themselves to practice a purer religion.

Thus they interpret the idols so that one represents the earth—which is why they commonly call a temple of Earth a temple of Tellus; another the sea, as in the statue of Neptune; another the air, as in that of Juno; another fire, as in that of Vulcan; another the morning star, as in that of Venus; another the sun; another the moon—whose statues they designate by the same names, just as they name the statue of Earth “Earth”; another this star, another that star, or this creature or that creature. For we are not able to enumerate everything.

When they are then challenged because they worship bodies—especially earth, sea, air, and fire, whose use is readily available to us (for concerning the heavenly bodies they are not so ashamed, since we cannot touch or reach them with our bodies except by the rays of our eyes)—they dare to respond that they do not worship the bodies themselves, but the divinities who preside over their governance.

Thus the Apostle’s single statement testifies to their punishment and condemnation: “They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. 1:25).

In the first part of this statement he condemned the idols; in the latter he condemned interpretations of the idols. By calling images made by craftsmen by the names of the things that God made, they exchange the truth of God for a lie. By treating the things themselves as gods and venerating them, they serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever.

5. Who worships or prays while looking at an idol without being affected in such a way that he thinks the idol hears him and hopes that it will grant what he desires?

Thus people bound by such superstitions often turn their backs to the sun and pour out prayers to the statue they call the sun. When the sound of the sea strikes them from behind, they strike the statue of Neptune—which they worship in place of the sea—as though it were capable of feeling, with their groans.

The likeness of limbs does this and, in a certain sense, compels it: a living mind, operating through bodily senses, is more inclined to think that the body it sees, so similar to its own body, feels something than that the rounded sun, the widely spread waves, or anything else not formed with the same features as those living things it is accustomed to see can feel.

Against this affection, by which human and carnal weakness can easily be captured, the Scripture of God sings things that are extremely well known, recalling and, as it were, awakening human minds that lie asleep in the habit of bodily forms: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold.” But God made silver and gold. “The work of human hands,” it says. For they worship what they themselves made from gold and silver.

6. Yet we too possess many instruments and vessels made from such material or metal for use in celebrating the sacraments. Consecrated by that very ministry, they are called holy, in honor of the one whom they serve for our salvation. Certainly these instruments or vessels are also nothing other than the work of human hands.

Nevertheless, do they have mouths and not speak? Do they have eyes and not see? Do we pray to them because through them we pray to God?

The principal cause of this insane impiety is that, in the affections of miserable people, a form resembling something living and making itself the object of prayer has greater power than the evident fact that it is not alive and therefore ought to be despised by something living.

For idols have greater power to bend an unhappy soul because they have mouths, eyes, ears, nostrils, hands, and feet than they have to correct it by the fact that they will not speak, see, hear, smell, touch, or walk.

7. [verse 8.] Therefore it follows that what comes next in this psalm should also take place: “Let all who make them and all who trust in them become like them.” Let them see with open and perceptive eyes, and worship with closed and dead minds, images that neither see nor live.

8. [verses 9–11.] “The house of Israel hoped in the Lord.” For “hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25).

But so that this patience may endure to the end, “he is their helper and their protector.” Or perhaps the spiritual—by whom the carnal are instructed in the spirit of gentleness, since the spiritual, as it were superior, intercede for those below—already see, and what is still hope for those below is already a present reality for them?

It is not so. For “the house of Aaron also hoped in the Lord.” Therefore, so that they too may continually stretch toward what lies ahead and persevere in running until they grasp that for which they were grasped (Phil. 3:12–14), and may know as they have been known (1 Cor. 13:12), he is their helper and protector.

Both groups fear the Lord and have hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector.

9. [verses 12–13.] We did not precede the Lord’s mercy by our merits. Rather, “the Lord remembered us and blessed us.” He blessed the house of Israel; he blessed the house of Aaron. Blessing both, he “blessed all who fear the Lord.”

You ask, “Which two?” The answer is: “The small with the great.” That is, the house of Israel with the house of Aaron—namely, those from that very nation who believed in the Savior Jesus. For “God was not pleased with all of them” (1 Cor. 10:5).

But if some of them did not believe, will their unbelief abolish the faithfulness of God? Certainly not (Rom. 3:3). For “not all who are from Israel are Israel, nor are all children because they are Abraham’s offspring”; but, as it is written, “the remnant shall be saved.”

Speaking in the person of those who believed from among them, it is said: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah” (Rom. 9:6–7, 27, 29). It is called offspring because it was scattered throughout the lands and multiplied.

10. [verses 14–18.] For the great ones of the house of Aaron [textual note: Lov. reads “great things”] said, “May the Lord add to you, to you and to your children” [textual note: the manuscripts read “to us, to us and to our children”]. And so it happened.

For children of Abraham were raised up even from stones (Matt. 3:9). Sheep that were not of this fold came, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd (John 10:16). The faith of all the nations came, and the number increased not only of wise bishops but also of obedient peoples.

The Lord added not only to the fathers—who would go before others so that the rest might imitate them in Christ—but also to their children, who would follow the pious footsteps of their fathers. For the one whom he had begotten in Christ through the Gospel said: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:15–16).

Thus the Lord added not only to the mountains leaping like rams but also to the hills leaping like lambs of the sheep [textual note: Lov. reads “the hills, that is, the nations, like lambs of the sheep”].

11. Therefore to both these groups, great and small, mountains and hills, rams and lambs, the prophet says what follows: “Blessed are you by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

It is as though he were saying: “Blessed are you by the Lord, who made you heaven among the great and earth among the small.” But this is not the visible heaven, filled with luminaries belonging to these eyes.

“For the heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord.” He has raised and exalted the minds of certain saints to such a degree that they became teachable not by any human being but by their own God. In comparison with this heaven, whatever is seen by bodily eyes must be called earth.

He gave this earth to the children of human beings so that, by contemplating it—whether in the part that shines above, as in what is called heaven, or in the part illuminated below, which properly bears the name earth—while everything, as we have said, is earth in comparison with what is called the heaven of heaven, they might infer, as far as they are able, the Creator, whom they cannot yet see with their weak hearts without this aid to inference.

12. There is also another interpretation of these words, which I must not conceal: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but the earth he gave to the children of men”—so that our attention does not depart from what we have said. For we had said that the great and the small are also signified by what is added: “Blessed are you by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” If, then, we understand the great by “heaven” and the small by “earth”—since the small, by growing, are destined to become heaven, and in that very hope are nourished with milk—then those great ones are the heaven of the earth when they nourish the little ones, so that they may also understand that they are the heaven of heaven, while they consider the hope in which the little ones are being nourished.

Yet because those great ones now draw the purity and abundance of wisdom not from man or through man, but from God himself, they have received as little ones those who are indeed destined to become heaven, so that they may know that they are the heaven of heaven; nevertheless, they are still earth to which they may say, “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Cor. III, 6). For to those very children of men whom he made heaven, he gave earth in which they might labor—he who knows how to provide for the earth through heaven.

Let heaven and earth, therefore, remain in their God who made them, and live from him, confessing and praising him. For if they wish to live from themselves, they will die, as it is written: “From the dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes” (Ecclus. XVII, 26). But, “The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all who go down into hell.” For your Scripture cries out elsewhere: “When the sinner comes into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3). But we who live bless the Lord, from this time forth and forever.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM CXIV

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. [Verse 1.] “I have loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my supplication.” Let the soul that is a pilgrim away from the Lord sing this; let that sheep which had gone astray sing this; let that son who had been dead and came to life again, who had been lost and was found (Luke XV, 6, 24), sing this; let our soul sing this, brothers and dearly beloved children. Let us be instructed, persevere, and sing this with the saints: “I have loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my supplication.”

Is the reason for loving itself that “the Lord will hear the voice of my supplication”? Is it not rather that we love because he has heard, or that we love in order that he may hear? What, then, is “I have loved, because he will hear”? Perhaps because hope commonly kindles love, he said that he had loved because he hoped that God would hear the voice of his supplication?

2. [Verses 2, 3.] From where, then, did he hope this? “Because,” he says, “he inclined his ear to me, and in my days I called upon him.” Therefore I loved because he will hear; he will hear because he inclined his ear to me. But how do you know, human soul, that God inclined his ear to you, unless you say, “I believed”? These three, then, remain: faith, hope, and love (1 Cor. XIII, 13). Because you believed, you hoped; because you hoped, you loved.

Now if I ask from where the soul believed that its God had inclined his ear to it, will it not answer: Because “he first loved us, and did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32)? “How,” says the Teacher of the Gentiles, “will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher? Or how will they preach unless they are sent?” (ibid. X, 14, 15).

When I saw all these things accomplished toward me, how could I not believe that the Lord had inclined his ear to me? And thus “he commended his love toward us, in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (ibid. V, 8, 9). When, therefore, those whose feet are beautiful announced these things to me—those who announced peace and announced good things (Isa. LII, 7)—because “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel II, 32), I believed that his ear was inclined toward me, and in my days I called upon him.

3. And what are your days, since you said, “In my days I called upon him”? Perhaps those in which the fullness of time came and God sent his Son (Gal. IV, 4), who had already said, “In an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. XLIX, 8)? You heard from the mouth of the preacher who came to you with beautiful feet, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. VI, 2). You believed, and in your days you called upon him, and said, “O Lord, deliver my soul.”

These things are indeed so. But I can more properly call my days, he says, the days of my misery, the days of my mortality, the days according to Adam, full of labor and sweat, the days according to the oldness of corruption. For I lay fallen, fixed in the mud of the deep (Ps. LXVIII, 3), and in another psalm I cried out, “Behold, you have made my days old” (Ps. XXXVIII, 6): in these my days I called upon him.

For my days differ from the days of my Lord. I call them my days because I made them for myself by the private boldness with which I abandoned him; and because he reigns everywhere and is almighty and holds all things, I deserved a prison—that is, I received the darkness of ignorance and the fetters of mortality. In these my days I called upon him, because elsewhere also I cry, “Bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. CXLI, 8). And because, in the day of salvation which he granted me, he helped me, “the groaning of the prisoners comes into his presence” (Ps. LXXVIII, 11).

[Note: [Col. 1488] Several manuscripts read “whom” instead of “which”; and, in place of “helped,” several read “helps.”]

For in these my days, “the pains of death surrounded me; the dangers of hell found me”—dangers which would not have found me unless I had wandered away from you. But now they found me, while I did not find them, because I was rejoicing in the prosperity of the world, in which the dangers of hell deceive more greatly.

4. [Verses 4–6.] But after I too found tribulation and sorrow, I called upon the name of the Lord. Useful tribulation and sorrow had been hidden from me: tribulation from which he gives help, to whom it is said, “Give us help in tribulation, for vain is the salvation of man” (Ps. LIX, 13). For I thought that one ought to rejoice and exult in the vain salvation of man. But when I had heard from my Lord, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5), I did not wait first to lose the temporal goods in which I took wrongful pleasure and then to mourn. Rather, I turned my attention to that very misery of mine in which I took such pleasure—a misery whose loss I feared, yet which I could not retain.

[Note: [Col. 1488] Thus Am., Er., and most manuscripts. Lov. reads: “my soul.”] I regarded it intensely and courageously, and saw that I was not only tormented by the adversities of this age but also bound by its prosperities. Thus I found the tribulation and sorrow that had been hidden from me, and I called upon the name of the Lord: “O Lord, deliver my soul.”

“For I am a wretched man; who will deliver me from the body of this death, except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord?” (Rom. VII, 24, 25). Let the holy people of God therefore say, “I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord.” And let the remnants of the Gentiles who do not yet call upon the name of the Lord hear, seek, find tribulation and sorrow, call upon the name of the Lord, and be saved.

We do not say this to them so that they may seek the misery they do not have, but so that they may find the misery they have without knowing it. Nor do we wish them to lack the earthly necessities they require while living a mortal life. Rather, we wish them to mourn that, having lost heavenly fullness, they have deserved to need earthly things—not for the enjoyment of lasting goods, but for the support of necessities.

Let them recognize and mourn this misery. He will make them blessed who mourn, though he did not wish them always to be miserable.

5. “The Lord is merciful and just, and our God has mercy.” Merciful, just, and merciful again. Merciful first, because he inclined his ear to me; and I did not know that the ear of my God had drawn near to my mouth unless I had been stirred up by those beautiful feet to call upon him. For who called upon him except one whom he himself first called? Hence he is merciful first.

He is just because he scourges; and again he has mercy because he receives. For he scourges every son whom he receives, and what he scourges ought not to be so bitter to me as what he receives ought to be sweet. For how could he not scourge those whom the Lord is guarding as little ones, while he seeks them as mature heirs?

[Note: [Col. 1488] Thus the better manuscripts. Er. and Lov. read: “For how does he scourge us?”] For what son is there to whom his father does not give discipline (Heb. XII, 6, 7)?

“I was humbled, and he saved me.” He saved me because I was humbled. For the pain which the physician causes by cutting is not punitive but healing.

6. [Verses 7–9.] “Return, then, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt graciously with you”—not because of your merits or your strength, but because the Lord has dealt graciously with you.

“Because,” he says, “he rescued my soul from death.” It is a remarkable thing, dearly beloved, that after saying that his soul should return to rest because the Lord had dealt graciously with him, he added, “Because he rescued my soul from death.” Would it return to rest because it had been rescued from death? Is rest not more commonly said to be in death? What, then, is the activity of one whose life is rest and whose death is unrest?

The activity of the soul, therefore, ought to be such as tends toward peaceful security, not such as increases restless labor. For the one who rescued it from death, having had mercy on it, said: “Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 28–30).

Gentle, therefore, and humble—following Christ as the way—the activity of the soul that tends toward rest ought to be.

[Note: [Col. 1489] Er. and Lov. read “humble of heart”; “of heart” is absent from the other books.] Yet it must not be sluggish or idle, so that it may complete its course, as it is written: “Complete your works in gentleness” (Ecclus. III, 19). For lest gentleness lead to sluggishness, “complete your works” has been added. For just as sleep in this life restores us to activity, so good activity leads us to ever-watchful rest.

7. God, however, is the one who grants and provides all things. Of him it is said here: “Because the Lord has dealt graciously with me, because he rescued my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling.” Whoever understands the bondage of this flesh sings these things as already accomplished with respect to himself in hope.

For it was truly said, “I was humbled, and he saved me”; but the Apostle also speaks truly: “For we have been saved in hope” (Rom. VIII, 24). With regard to death, it is rightly said that we have already been rescued, if we understand death as referring to unbelievers, of whom he said, “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. VIII, 22), and as in the preceding psalm: “The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all who go down into hell; but we who live bless the Lord” (Ps. CXIII, 17, 18).

A faithful person can therefore rightly understand that his soul has already been rescued from this death, precisely because he has been made faithful from unbelieving. Hence the Savior himself says, “Whoever believes in me passes from death to life” (John V, 24).

The remaining things, however, have been completed in hope for those who have not yet departed from this life. For now, when we consider our most dangerous falls, our eyes do not cease from tears. But then he will rescue our eyes from tears, when he also rescues our feet from falling. For there will then be no falling of walking feet, when there is no slipperiness of weak flesh.

But now, although our way is firm—for Christ is our way—nevertheless, because we place beneath ourselves the flesh which we are commanded to subdue,

[Note: [Col. 1489] Most manuscripts read “way”; the editions read “life.”] in the very work by which we chastise it into submission, it is a great thing not to fall in it. Yet who can avoid slipping in it?

8. Therefore, because we are both in the flesh and are not in the flesh—for we are in the flesh by that bond which has not yet been dissolved, although “to depart and be with Christ is much better” (Phil. I, 23)—we are not in the flesh because we have given the first fruits of the spirit to God, if indeed we can say that “our citizenship is in heaven” (ibid. III, 20), and, as though by our head, please God, while by our feet, as the extremities of the soul, we still feel slipperiness—hear how what is sung as though it had already been accomplished belongs to hope:

“He rescued,” he says, “my eyes from tears, my feet from falling.” Yet he does not say, “I please”; rather, “I shall please in the sight of the Lord, in the land of the living.” This sufficiently shows that, in that part of himself which is in the land of the dead—that is, in mortal flesh—he does not yet please in the sight of the Lord. For those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

Hence what the same apostle says next, “But you are not in the flesh,” he says according to this: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.” According to the spirit they pleased the Lord, because according to it they were not in the flesh. But who can please the living God in a dead body?

What, then, does he say? “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit who dwells in you” (Rom. VIII, 8–11). Then we shall be in the land of the living, pleasing in the sight of the Lord in every respect, and in no respect strangers to him.

For as long as we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from our Lord; and to the extent that we are pilgrims away from him, to that extent we are not in the land of the living. “But we are confident, and we consider it better to be pilgrims away from the body and to remain with the Lord; and therefore we strive, whether remaining with him or being pilgrims away, to be pleasing to him” (2 Cor. V, 6–9).

We strive now, while we still await the redemption of our body (Rom. VIII, 23). But when death has been swallowed up in victory, and this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality (1 Cor. XV, 53, 54), then there will be no weeping, because there will be no falling; and no falling, because there will be no corruption. Therefore we shall no longer strive to please, but shall altogether please in the sight of the Lord, in the land of the living.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM CXV

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. I believe that it is very well known to Your Holiness what the Apostle says: “For faith is not the possession of all” (2 Thess. III, 2);

[Note: [Col. 1490] Thus Er., Lugd., Venet., and Lov. In B., “because.” M.] and you are not unaware that the multitude of unbelievers is usually greater. For this reason it is said, “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. LIII, 1; Rom. X, 16).

Among them are also those of whom the same apostle says, “They all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. II, 21). Elsewhere he says that they preach the word of God not from truth but from rivalry, not purely (ibid. I, 17)—that is, not from the disposition of pure and sincere love. For they felt one thing, as their conduct showed, and preached another, in order to please people by the holy name. For of these he says again, “They do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own belly” (Rom. XVI, 18).

Yet he permits them to announce Christ. For although they preferred to believe the things they themselves did, so that they might perish, they nevertheless preached things which, if others believed and practiced them, would lead to salvation. For they announced nothing other than the rule of faith. The Apostle excludes those who preach otherwise, saying: “If anyone announces to you anything beyond what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. I, 9).

Those who announce falsehood do not announce Christ, because Christ is truth (John XIV, 6). But of these he says that they announce Christ, though not purely—that is, not with a simple and pure intention and sincere faith working through love (Gal. V, 6). For while pursuing earthly desires, they announced the kingdom of heaven, bearing falsehood in their heart and truth on their tongue.

Knowing, therefore, that believers had been set free even through Judas evangelizing, the Apostle permits these also in the same way: “Whether,” he says, “by pretext or by truth, Christ is announced” (Phil. I, 18). They announced the truth, even if not in truth—that is, not with a true intention.

These people speak what they do not believe, and for that reason they are rejected; yet they are useful to those whom the Lord instructs, saying: “Do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do” (Matt. XXIII, 3). Why, unless because they do not believe that what they say is useful?

There are others who believe but do not speak what they believe, whether through laziness or fear. For that servant, although he had received a talent, because he was unwilling to put it to use hears from the judging Lord: “Wicked and lazy servant.” And elsewhere in the Gospel it is said that many of the rulers of the Jews had believed in him, but did not confess him, lest they be expelled from the synagogues. They too were censured and rejected, for the Evangelist continues: “For they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God” (John XII, 42, 43).

If, then, both those who do not believe the truth they speak and those who do not speak the truth they believe are rightly rejected, who is to be called a truly faithful servant except the one to whom it is said: “Well done, good servant, because you have been faithful in a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your Lord”?

Such a servant neither speaks before he believes nor remains silent after he has believed, lest he either distribute in such a way that he himself does not possess, or, by failing to distribute what he possesses, lose it. For it is said: “To everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Matt. XXV, 21–29).

2. [Verse 10.] Let this good servant, then, singing “Alleluia”—that is, offering the sacrifice of praise to the Lord, from whom he is to hear, “Enter into the joy of your Lord”—exult and say: “I believed, therefore I spoke” (Ps. CXV, 10). That is, I believed perfectly.

For those who are unwilling to speak what they believe do not believe perfectly. To faith itself belongs also believing what has been said: “Whoever confesses me before men, I will confess him before the angels of God” (Matt. X, 32). For that servant was called faithful not merely because he received, but because he expended what he received and gained profit from it.

So here also he does not say, “I believed and therefore spoke,” but says that he spoke because he believed. At the same time he believed both what reward he ought to hope for by speaking and what punishment he ought to fear by remaining silent.

“I believed,” he says, “therefore I spoke. But I was humbled exceedingly.” For he suffered many tribulations on account of the word which he faithfully held and faithfully expended, and he was humbled exceedingly. Those who loved the glory of men more than the glory of God feared this.

But what does “But I” mean? He might rather have said, “I believed, therefore I both spoke and was humbled exceedingly.” Why did he add “But I,” unless because a man can be humbled by those who oppose the truth, whereas the truth itself cannot be humbled—the truth which he believes and speaks?

Hence the Apostle too, when speaking of his chain, says: “But the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. II, 9). Thus this man, because he is the one person of the holy witnesses—that is, of God’s martyrs—says: “I believed, therefore I spoke. But I”—not what I believed, not the word I uttered—“was humbled exceedingly.”

3. [Verse 11.] “But I said in my alarm, ‘Every man is a liar.’” He calls alarm ecstasy: the fear which human weakness suffers when persecutors threaten and the torments or death of suffering threaten.

For we understand that the voice of the martyrs appears in this psalm. Ecstasy is also used in another sense, when the mind is not alienated by fear but is lifted up by some inspiration of revelation.

“But I said in my alarm, ‘Every man is a liar.’” Terrified, he regarded his weakness and saw that he ought not to presume on himself. For insofar as man himself is concerned, he is a liar; but by the grace of God he has been made truthful, lest, yielding to the pressures of his enemies, he fail to speak what he had believed and instead deny it.

This happened to Peter, because he had presumed on himself and had to be taught that one must not presume upon man. And if no one ought to presume upon man, certainly no one ought to presume upon himself, because he is a man.

This man therefore rightly saw in his fear that every man is a liar. For even those who do not collapse under any fear, lest by yielding to persecutors they lie, are such through God’s gifts, not through their own strength.

Accordingly, it is most truly said, “Every man is a liar”; but God is truthful, who says: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’; but you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. LXXXI, 6, 7).

He comforts the humble and fills them not only with faith for believing the truth but also with confidence for proclaiming it, if they steadfastly submit themselves to God and do not imitate one of the princes, the devil, who did not stand in the truth and fell.

For if every man is a liar, they will be liars to the extent that they are men; but to the extent that they are not men, they will not be liars, because they will be gods and sons of the Most High.

4. [Verse 12.] Considering this, the most devout people of the faithful witnesses—considering how the mercy of God does not abandon human weakness, in whose fear it was said, “Every man is a liar”; how he consoles the humble and fills those who tremble with the spirit of confidence, so that, with their hearts almost dead, they may come to life again and not trust in themselves but in him who raises the dead (2 Cor. I, 9) and makes the tongues of infants eloquent (Wis. X, 21); who says, “When they hand you over, do not be anxious about how or what you should speak; for it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 19, 20)—considering all this, the one who had said, “I said in my alarm, ‘Every man is a liar,’” and seeing that by the Lord’s grace he had been made truthful, says: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?”

He does not say, “For all that he has given me,” but “for all that he has repaid me.” What, then, had preceded on the part of man, so that all God’s gifts could be called not an attribution but a repayment? What had preceded on the part of man except sins?

God therefore repays good for evil, while men repay evil for good. For this is what those people rendered who said, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him” (Matt. XXI, 38).

5. [Verses 13, 15.] But this man asks what he should repay the Lord and finds nothing except among the things which the Lord himself repays. “I will receive,” he says, “the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord.”

O man, made a liar by your sin and truthful by God’s gift, and therefore now no longer merely man—who gave you the cup of salvation, which, when you receive it and call upon the name of the Lord, you will repay him for all that he has repaid you? Who except the one who says, “Can you drink the cup which I am going to drink?” (Matt. XX, 22).

Who gave you the ability to imitate his sufferings except the one who first suffered for you? Therefore, “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.” He purchased it with his blood, which he first shed for the salvation of his servants, so that they would not hesitate to shed their blood for the name of the Lord—although this would benefit their own, not the Lord’s, welfare.

[Note: [Col. 1493] Verse 14, “I will pay my vows to the Lord before all his people,” is omitted.]

6. [Verse 16.] Let the servant purchased at so great a price confess his condition and say: “O Lord, I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid.”

Thus he is both purchased and born in the household. Or was he purchased together with his mother? Or, because he is born in the household, was he seized on account of the sin of his flight and therefore purchased because he was redeemed?

For he is the son of the handmaid insofar as every creature is subject to the Creator and owes true service to the true Lord. When she renders this service, she is free, receiving from the Lord this grace: that she serves him not by necessity but by will.

Therefore this man is a son of the heavenly Jerusalem, which is above and is the free mother of us all (Gal. IV, 26). She is free from sin, but a servant of righteousness. To her children who are still pilgrims it is said, “You were called to freedom”; and again he makes them servants, saying, “But through love serve one another” (ibid. V, 13).

To them it is likewise said: “When you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness; but now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. VI, 20, 22).

Let this servant therefore say to God: Many call themselves martyrs, many call themselves your servants, because they bear your name in various heresies and errors; but because they are outside your Church, they are not the children of your handmaid. “But I am your servant and the son of your handmaid.”

7. [Verse 17.] “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice the sacrifice of praise.” For I found no merits of my own when you broke my bonds; therefore I owe you the sacrifice of praise. And even if I glory in being your servant and the son of your handmaid, I will glory not in myself but in you, my Lord, who broke my bonds so that, returning from flight, I might be bound again to you.

8. [Verse 18.] “I will pay my vows to the Lord.” What vows are you going to pay? What victims did you vow? What incense? What burnt offerings?

Or do you have regard to what you said shortly before: “I will receive the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord”; and, “To you I will sacrifice the sacrifice of praise”?

And indeed, whoever rightly considers what he should vow to the Lord and what vows he should pay should vow himself and pay himself. This is what is required; this is what is owed.

Looking at the coin, the Lord says: “Give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God” (Matt. XXII, 21). Let Caesar receive his image; let God receive his image.

9. [Verse 19.] But whoever remembers that he is not only God’s servant but also the son of God’s handmaid sees where he should pay his vows, having been conformed to Christ through the cup of salvation.

[Note: [Col. 1494] Several manuscripts read “see”; some, “see yourselves.”]

“In the courts,” he says, “of the house of the Lord.” The house of God is the handmaid of God; and what is the house of God except all his people? Therefore it follows: “In the sight of all his people.”

And now he names the mother more openly. For what else is his people than what follows: “In the midst of you, Jerusalem”? The payment is pleasing, then, if it is made from peace and in peace. But those who are not children of this handmaid have loved war rather than peace.

Lest anyone think that the courts of the house of the Lord and all his people signify the Jews, because this psalm concluded by saying, “In the midst of you, Jerusalem,” a name in which the carnal Israelites glory, hear the following psalm, which consists of four verses.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM CXVI

## CONTINUATION OF THE PRECEDING SERMON

“Praise the Lord, all you nations; praise him, all you peoples.” These are the courts of the house of the Lord; that entire people is his; this is the true Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 1494] Most manuscripts read: “these words, Jerusalem.”]

Let those who refused to be children of this city hear, especially since they cut themselves off from the communion of all nations. “For his mercy has been confirmed upon us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever.”

These are those two things—mercy and truth—which I reminded you should be memorized in Psalm CXIII.

[Note: [Col. 1494] In *Exposition of Psalm CXIII*, sermon 1, no. 13.]

The mercy of the Lord has been confirmed upon us when the ravenous mouths of hostile nations yielded to the name by which we have been delivered. And the truth of the Lord remains forever, whether in the things he promised to the righteous or in the things with which he threatened the wicked.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM CXVII

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. We have heard, brothers, the Holy Spirit admonishing and exhorting us to offer God the sacrifice of confession. Confession is either of his praise or of our sins.

That confession by which we confess our sins to God is well known to everyone, so much so that the less-educated crowd thinks that this alone is called confession in the holy Scriptures. For whenever this word sounds from the reader’s mouth, it is immediately followed by the devout noise of people beating their breasts.

But they ought to notice how it is said in another psalm: “For I shall enter into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one keeping festival” (Ps. XLI, 5). Here it is certainly clear that the voice and sound of confession belong not to the sorrow of repentance but to the joy of a most solemn festival.

Or, if anyone still doubts in the face of such clear testimony, what will he say to what is written in Ecclesiasticus? “Bless the Lord, all his works; give greatness to his name, and confess in his praise with songs of the lips and with harps; and thus say in confession: ‘For all the works of the Lord are exceedingly good’” (Ecclus. XXXIX, 19–21).

Here no one, however slow, can doubt that confession is placed among the praises of God—unless perhaps someone’s mind is so perverse that he dares to say that the Lord Jesus Christ himself confessed his sins to the Father.

If some wicked person attempted to make this objection because of the word “confession,” the very context of the words would easily refute him. For he speaks as follows: “I confess to you,” he says, “Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because so it was pleasing before you.”

Who does not understand that he says this in praise of the Father? Who does not see that this confession belongs not to sorrow of heart but to joy, since the Evangelist has already said: “In that hour he exulted in the Holy Spirit and said, ‘I confess to you, Father’” (Luke X, 21)?

2. [Verse 1.] Therefore, dearly beloved, since it is in no way possible to doubt—given so many agreeing testimonies, similar examples of which you yourselves can observe throughout the Scriptures—that in the divine writings confession is customarily named not only in connection with sins but also in connection with the praises of God, what more appropriately should we understand ourselves to be admonished in this psalm, when we sing “Alleluia,” which means “Praise the Lord,” than when we hear, “Confess to the Lord”? That is, we are admonished to praise the Lord.

The praise of God could not be expressed more briefly than by saying, “For he is good.” I do not see what could be greater than this brevity, since it is so proper to God that he is good. When someone addressed the Son of God as “Good Teacher”—someone who looked upon his flesh and did not understand the fullness of his divinity, but regarded him as merely a human being—he replied, “Why do you question me about the good? No one is good except the one God” (Mark X, 17, 18).

What else is this than saying: If you wish to call me good, understand that I am also God?

But because this is said to a people, in anticipation of the future, delivered from all the labor and captivity of pilgrimage and from all mixture with the wicked—a deliverance granted to it by God’s grace, since he not only does not repay evil for evil but also repays good for evil—it is most suitably added: “For his mercy is forever.”

3. [Verses 2–5.] “Let the house of Israel say: ‘For he is good, for his mercy is forever.’ Let the house of Aaron say: ‘For he is good, for his mercy is forever.’ Let all who fear the Lord now say: ‘For his mercy is forever.’”

You recognize, I believe, dearly beloved, what the house of Israel is and what the house of Aaron is, and that both are those who fear the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1496] The manuscripts read “indeed.”] They are the small together with the great, already well commended to your hearts in another psalm. Let us all rejoice that we have been joined to their number by the grace of him who is good and whose mercy is forever.

For they have been heard who said, “May the Lord add to you—to you and to your children” (Ps. CXIII, 12–14): so that, among the Israelites who believe in Christ, from whose number the apostles, our fathers, come, the number of the Gentiles might be added both to the eminence of the perfect and to the obedience of the little ones.

Thus let us all, having been made one in Christ, having become one flock under one shepherd, and one body of that head, as though one man, say: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me in a spacious place.” The narrowness of our tribulation comes to an end; but the spacious place into which we pass has no boundary. For “who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” (Rom. VIII, 33).

4. [Verses 6, 7.] “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.” But does the Church have only human enemies? What is a man devoted to flesh and blood except flesh and blood?

But the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and authorities of this darkness”—that is, the rulers of the wicked, who love this world and are therefore called rulers of darkness, because “we too were once darkness, but now we are light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8).

He says, “against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (ibid. VI, 12)—that is, against the devil and his angels. Elsewhere he calls the devil “the prince of the power of the air” (ibid. II, 2).

Hear, then, what follows: “The Lord is my helper, and I will despise my enemies.” Whatever kind of enemies arise, whether from the number of wicked men or from the number of wicked angels, they will be despised through the help of the Lord, to whom we confess praise and to whom we sing “Alleluia.”

5. [Verses 8, 9.] Once the enemies have been despised, let no friend, as though a good man, oppose himself to me in such a way that he commands me to place my hope in him: “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man.”

Nor should anyone think of an angel—who can in a certain sense be called good—in such a way that I ought to trust in him. For no one is good except God alone. And when a man or an angel appears to help, if they do so with true love, it is he who acts through them, the one who made them good according to their measure.

“It is better, therefore, to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes.” For angels too are called princes, as we read in Daniel: “Michael, your prince” (Dan. XII, 1).

## 6. [verses 10, 11]

“**All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them; surrounding, they surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them.**” What he says, “All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them,” signifies the Church’s struggles and victory. But, as though the question were asked how it could have overcome such great evils, attention is directed to an example, and he says what it first suffered in its Head, adding what follows: “Surrounding, they surrounded me.” Here “all the nations” is rightly not repeated, since this was done by the Jews alone. “And in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them”: for there that devout people itself, which is Christ’s body, experienced the persecutors [Note: [Col. 1497] All our manuscripts read *senserit* (“will have experienced”); Am. reads *senserat* (“had experienced”). Soon afterward several books read *de cujus genere* (“from whose stock”); some, *de quibus generata* (“generated from whom”). Finally, Am. and most manuscripts omit *suscepta* (“assumed”), and what follows.], from whose stock that flesh was assumed and hung upon the cross, and for whom everything was done that was accomplished by that inner divinity through the external flesh, with immortal power yet mortally.

## 7. [verse 12]

“**They surrounded me like bees surround a honeycomb, and they blazed like fire among thorns, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them.**” Here the order of the words is already woven together according to the order of the events that occurred. For we rightly understand the Lord himself, the Head of the Church, to have been surrounded by persecutors as bees surround a honeycomb. The Holy Spirit speaks with mystical subtlety of what was done by those who did not understand. Bees produce honey in honeycombs; but the persecutors of the Lord, without knowing it, made him sweeter for us through that very passion, so that we might “taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. 33:9), he who “died for our sins and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4:25).

Now what follows, “And they blazed like fire among thorns,” is better understood of his body, that is, of the people spread everywhere. All the nations surrounded this people, since it was gathered from all nations. For they blazed like fire among thorns when, through the fire of persecution, they burned sinful flesh and the most grievous pricks of this mortal life. “And in the name,” he says, “of the Lord I took vengeance on them”: either because, once the malice that had persecuted the righteous in them had been extinguished, they too were joined to the Christian people; or because the rest of them, who in this age have despised the mercy of him who calls, will at the end experience the truth of him who judges.

## 8. [verse 13]

“**I was pushed so as to fall, like a heap of sand, and the Lord received me.**” Although there was already a great multitude of believers, comparable to innumerable sand and gathered into one fellowship as into a heap, nevertheless, what is a human being except “that you remember him” (Ps. 8:5)? He did not say, “The abundance of my number, the number of the nations, was unable to overcome”; but he says, “The Lord received me.” Therefore, the persecution of the nations had no means by which to push down the multitude of believers living together in the unity of faith, once faith had been placed in him who could receive each one, and all of them, and them everywhere; for he could not have been absent anywhere from those who called upon him.

## 9. [verse 14]

“**The Lord is my strength and my praise; and he has become my salvation.**” Who, then, fall when they are pushed, except those who want their strength to be their own and their praise to be their own? No one falls in the contest except one whose strength and praise fall. Therefore, whose strength and praise is the Lord does not fall any more than the Lord falls. And for this reason he became salvation for them—not because he himself became something that he had not previously been, but because, when they believed in him, they became what they had not been, and he himself began to be salvation for them, though not for himself, which he had not been for those who had turned away from him, but now was for those who had turned toward him.

## 10. [verse 15]

“**The voice of joy and salvation is in the tents of the righteous**”—where those who raged against their bodies thought there would be a voice of grief and destruction. For they did not perceive the inward joys of the saints concerning the hope of the future. Hence the Apostle also says, “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Cor. 6:10); and again, he says, “And not only this, but we glory in tribulations” (Rom. 5:3).

## 11. [verse 16]

“**The right hand of the Lord has displayed power.**” What power does he mean? “The right hand,” he says, “of the Lord has exalted me.” Great is the power that exalts the humble, deifies the mortal, grants perfection from weakness, glory from subjection, victory from suffering, and help from tribulation, so that the true salvation of God might be revealed to the afflicted, while the false salvation of humanity remained for those who inflicted affliction.

These things are great; but why are you surprised? Listen to what he repeats. It was not a human being who exalted himself; not a human being who perfected himself; not a human being who gave himself glory; not a human being who conquered; not a human being who was salvation for himself [Note: [Col. 1498] Am. and Er. read, “but why are you surprised if he repeats something? Listen to what he repeats.” Several manuscripts read, “but why are you surprised? If he repeats something, not a human being perfected himself,” and so forth. The Regius manuscript reads, “but why are you surprised? If something strikes you: not a human being conquered, not a human being was salvation for himself. The right hand,” and so forth.]: “The right hand of the Lord has displayed power.”

## 12. [verse 17]

“**I shall not die, but live, and I shall recount the works of the Lord.**” Yet those who were causing slaughter and death everywhere thought that the Church of Christ was dying. Behold, now it recounts the works of the Lord. Everywhere Christ is the glory of the blessed martyrs. He conquered those who struck him by being scourged; the impatient by suffering [Note: [Col. 1498] The manuscripts read *facientes* (“those doing it”).]; the savage by loving.

## 13. [verse 18]

But why did the body of Christ—the holy Church, the people adopted by God—endure such great and undeserved sufferings? Let it tell us. “The Lord,” it says, “correcting has corrected me, and has not handed me over to death.”

Let not, therefore, the rage of the ungodly suppose that anything was permitted to its own strength. It would not have had this power unless it had been given it from above. Often a householder commands that his sons be corrected by utterly wicked servants, while he prepares an inheritance for the sons and fetters for the servants. What kind of inheritance is this? Is it one of gold, silver, gems, estates, or pleasant properties? Observe by what entrance one comes to it, and understand what it is.

## 14. [verse 19]

“**Open for me,” he says, “the gates of righteousness.**” Behold, we have heard of gates. What is inside? “Entering into them,” he says, “I shall confess to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1499] So the manuscripts read *in eis* (“into them”), in accordance with the Greek. The editions read *in eas* (“into them”).]

That confession is the wondrous praise extending to the house of God, “in the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one celebrating a festival” (Ps. 41:5). This is the eternal blessedness of the righteous, by which those who dwell in the house of God are blessed, praising him forever and ever (Ps. 83:5).

## 15. [verse 20]

But observe how one enters the gates of righteousness. “These,” he says, “are the gates of the Lord; the righteous shall enter into them.” At least, let no unrighteous person enter these gates, into that Jerusalem which does not receive the uncircumcised, where it is said, “The dogs are outside” (Rev. 22:15).

Let it be enough that in my distant pilgrimage I have dwelt with the tents of Kedar, and that with those who hated peace I was peaceful (Ps. 119:5). I endured to the end the mingling with the wicked; but these are the gates of the Lord: the righteous shall enter into them.

## 16. [verse 21]

“**I shall confess to you, Lord, because you have heard me, and have become my salvation.**” How often it is shown that this confession is one of praise—not displaying wounds to a physician, but giving thanks for the health received. The physician himself is salvation.

## 17. [verse 22]

But whom do we mean by this one? “**The stone that the builders rejected**”; for “this one has been made the head of the corner,” so that “he might create the two in himself as one new human being, making peace, and might join both in one body to God” (Eph. 2:15–16)—namely, circumcision and uncircumcision.

## 18. [verse 23]

“**By the Lord it was made for him**” [Note: [Col. 1499] So the better manuscripts read, *factus est ei*. Am. and Er. read *factum est ei*. Lov. reads *factus est is*: that is, “the head of the corner,” and so forth.]—that is, he was made by the Lord the head of the corner.

Although he would not have been made this unless he had suffered, nevertheless he was not made this by those from whom he suffered. For those who were building rejected him; but in what the Lord was secretly building, he made him the head of the corner whom they had rejected.

“And it is wondrous in our eyes”: in the eyes of the inner human being, in the eyes of those who believe, hope, and love—not in the carnal eyes of those who rejected him by despising him as though he were merely human.

## 19. [verse 24]

“**This is the day that the Lord has made.**” This person remembers having said in the preceding psalms, “Because he inclined his ear to me, and in my days I called upon him” (Ps. 114:2), recalling his former days. Hence he now says, “This is the day that the Lord has made”—that is, the day on which he gave me salvation.

This is the day of which he said, “In an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49:8)—that is, the day on which that Mediator was made the head of the corner. Therefore, “let us exult and rejoice in it.”

## 20. [verse 25]

“**O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant good success; but prosper the journey**” [Note: [Col. 1500] The editions read, “grant good success” (*bene prosperare*). “But prosper the journey,” because it is the day. It should be read with the Corbie manuscript of excellent quality, “grant good success; but prosper the journey”; for in the Greek Septuagint there is *euodōson* (“grant success”), with the added particle *dē*, to which the word *autem* (“but”) corresponds above in verses 2 and 3.]

Because it is the day of salvation, save me; because, returning from our distant pilgrimage, we are separated from those who hated peace, with whom we had been peaceful, and when we spoke to them, they gratuitously waged war against us—grant good success to us who are returning, because you have become the way for us.

## 21. [verse 26]

“**For blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.**” Therefore cursed is he who comes in his own name, as he says in the Gospel: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 5:43).

“**We have blessed you from the house of the Lord.**” I believe that this is the voice of the great addressed to the little: namely, of those great ones who touch in mind the Word who is God with God, as far as they can in this life; yet they temper their speech for the sake of the little ones, so that they may sincerely say what the Apostle says: “Whether we have been beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are self-controlled, it is for you. For the love of Christ constrains us” (2 Cor. 5:13–14).

They bless the little ones from the inner house of the Lord, where that praise does not fail for ever and ever. Therefore observe what they proclaim from there.

## 22. [verse 27]

“**God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us.**” That Lord who came in the name of the Lord, whom the builders rejected and who was made the head of the corner (Matt. 21:9, 42)—that Mediator between God and humanity, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5)—is God, equal to the Father, and he has shone upon us so that we might understand what we have believed and proclaim it to you, who do not yet understand but already believe.

But so that you too may understand, “**Establish a festival day amid the throngs, up to the horns**” [Note: [Col. 1500] So the manuscripts read, in accordance with the Septuagint. The editions read, “up to the horn”; and shortly afterward, “the lofty altars.”] “of the altar”—that is, up to the inner house of God, from which we blessed you, where the heights of the altar are.

Establish a festival day—not sluggishly or negligently, but amid the throngs. For this is “the voice of exultation, the sound of one celebrating a festival,” of those walking in the place of the tabernacle, wondrous even to the house of God.

For if there is there a spiritual sacrifice, an everlasting sacrifice of praise, and an everlasting priest, then the everlasting altar is the peaceful mind itself of the righteous. We state this more plainly, brothers: whoever wishes to understand God the Word must not be satisfied with the flesh—the Word became flesh for their sake so that they might be nourished with milk—nor must this earthly festival, on which the lamb was slain, be sufficient for them. Rather, let the festival be established amid the throngs until we arrive, with our minds exalted by the Lord, at his inner divinity, he who graciously offered us his external humanity as milk for those needing nourishment.

## 23. [verses 28, 29]

And what else shall we do there except sing his praises? What else shall we say there except, “**You are my God, and I shall confess to you; my God, you are, and I shall exalt you. I shall confess to you, Lord, because you have heard me, and have become my salvation**”?

We shall not say these things with a clamor of words; rather, the love that clings to him cries out this voice by itself, and love itself is this voice.

Therefore, just as it began its praise, so it ends it: “**Confess to the Lord, because he is good, because his mercy is forever.**” The Psalm began from this and ends here; for just as, from the beginning that we have left behind, so at the end to which we return, there is nothing that delights more healthfully than the praise of God—and Alleluia always.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 118

## Preface

I have expounded, as the Lord granted and as I was able, all the other psalms that we know are contained in the book of Psalms, which ecclesiastical usage calls the Psalter, partly by speaking before the people and partly by dictating. But I had postponed Psalm 118—not so much because of its very well-known length as because of its depth, known to few.

When my brothers were greatly distressed that the exposition of this one psalm alone, insofar as it belongs to the same body of Psalms, was lacking from my little works, and when they pressed me urgently to discharge this debt, I did not yield for a long time to their requests and commands. For whenever I tried to think about it, it always exceeded the powers of our attention.

The more open it appears, the deeper it usually seems to me, so much so that I could not even demonstrate how deep it is. In the case of other passages that are difficult to understand, even if the obscurity of their meaning lies hidden, the obscurity itself nevertheless appears. But in this psalm even that does not appear, because it presents such a surface that it seems to require a reader and hearer, but not an expositor.
