And now, as I finally approach its treatment, I truly do not know what I can do in it. Nevertheless, I hope that God, who has been present and helped me, will enable me to accomplish something. For he has done this in all the works that I have sufficiently expounded, when they had previously seemed difficult and almost impossible for me to understand or explain. [Note: [Col. 1501] Several manuscripts read thus. The editions read, “I did this.”]

I have decided to undertake this through discourses to be delivered before the people, which the Greeks call *homilies* (ὁμιλίαι). For I consider it more just that ecclesiastical gatherings not be deprived of the understanding of this psalm, whose song, like that of the others, they are accustomed to enjoy.

But let the preface end here. We must now speak about the psalm itself, concerning which it seemed appropriate to offer this preliminary statement.

# SERMON I

## 1. [verse 1]

From its very beginning, this great psalm, dearly beloved, exhorts us to the blessedness that no one fails to desire. For who anywhere is, was, or will be found who does not wish to be blessed?

What need, then, is there for exhortation to something that the human mind desires spontaneously? Surely the one who exhorts acts so that the will of the person with whom he is dealing may be stirred toward that for which the exhortation is addressed.

Why, then, are we urged to desire what we cannot fail to desire? Because everyone indeed longs for blessedness, but very many do not know how one reaches it. Therefore this psalm teaches us, saying: “**Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.**”

It is as though it were saying: “I know what you want; you seek blessedness. If, then, you wish to be blessed, be undefiled.” Everyone wants the former, but few want the latter, without which one does not reach what everyone wants.

But where will anyone be undefiled except in the way? And in what way except in the law of the Lord? Accordingly, the statement “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” is not said to us needlessly; rather, necessary exhortation is applied to our minds.

What good is involved in this—something for which many are sluggish, namely, walking undefiled in the way that is the law of the Lord—is shown when those who do this are declared blessed, so that for the sake of what everyone wants, even what most people do not want may be done.

To be blessed is such a great good that both good and evil people desire it. It is not surprising that good people are good for this reason; what is surprising is that evil people are evil for this reason too: in order to be blessed.

For anyone devoted to lust, corrupted by luxury and sexual immorality, seeks blessedness in this evil and considers himself miserable when he does not reach the pleasure and joy of his desire, but does not hesitate to boast of himself as blessed when he does reach it.

Anyone who burns with the flames of greed gathers wealth by whatever means so as to be blessed. Whoever desires to shed the blood of enemies, whoever seeks domination, whoever nourishes his cruelty on the calamities of others—all seek blessedness in their crimes.

If this divine voice is heard, it calls these people back from their wandering—from seeking false blessedness in true misery—to the way: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.” It is as though it were saying: “Where are you going? You are perishing, and you do not know it. The road by which you are traveling does not lead where you desire to arrive. Certainly you want to be blessed, but these paths on which you run are miserable and lead to greater misery.

“Do not seek so great a good through evils. If you want to reach it, come here; go by this way. Abandon the wickedness of crooked ways, you who cannot abandon the desire for blessedness. You wear yourselves out by striving vainly toward the place where, upon arriving, you are defiled.”

The defiled are not blessed in error, walking in the perversity of the world; rather, “blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.”

## 2. [verses 2, 3]

Observe what he adds: “**Blessed are those who search his testimonies, who seek him with their whole heart.**”

It does not seem to me that these words mention any other kind of blessed people than the kind mentioned previously. For to search the Lord’s testimonies and to seek him with one’s whole heart is to be undefiled in the way and to walk in the law of the Lord.

Then he continues and says: “**For those who commit iniquity have not walked in his ways.**” If, therefore, those who walk in the way—that is, in the law of the Lord—are the very people who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart, then surely those who commit iniquity do not search his testimonies.

And yet we know that workers of iniquity search the Lord’s testimonies for this purpose: they prefer to be learned rather than righteous. We also know others who search the Lord’s testimonies for this purpose—not because they already live rightly, but so that they may know how they ought to live [Note: [Col. 1503] Lov.’s editions omit these words: “because they prefer to be learned rather than righteous; we also know others who search the Lord’s testimonies for this purpose.” They are present in the other editions and in the manuscript books.]

Such people therefore do not yet walk undefiled in the law of the Lord and, consequently, are not yet blessed. How, then, is “Blessed are those who search his testimonies” to be understood, when we see people who search his testimonies not to be blessed because they are not undefiled?

The scribes and Pharisees, who sat on Moses’ seat, are an example. The Lord says of them, “What they say, do; but what they do, do not do: for they say and do not do” (Matt. 23:3). They certainly searched the Lord’s testimonies so that they would have good things to say, although they did evil things.

But let us set them aside. The correct answer will be made to us that these people do not search the Lord’s testimonies. They do not seek the testimonies themselves, but seek something else through them: to be glorified by human beings or to become rich.

This is not to search the testimonies of God: it is not to love what they display, nor to wish to reach the one to whom they lead, namely, God.

Or, if they too do search God’s testimonies, although not in order to find him himself but to find and acquire something else through them, certainly they do not seek him with their whole heart. We plainly see that this was not added here without reason.

For the Spirit who speaks these words knew that many search his testimonies for another purpose, not for the purpose for which they were established. Therefore he did not say merely, “Blessed are those who search his testimonies”; he added, “who seek him with their whole heart,” as though teaching how, or for what purpose, the Lord’s testimonies should be searched.

Thus in the Book of Wisdom Wisdom itself says: “The wicked seek me and do not find me; for they hated wisdom” (Prov. 1:28–29). What else does this mean than, “They hated me”? “They seek me,” he says, “and do not find me—those who hate me.”

How, then, are they said to seek what they hate, unless they seek something else there? They do not wish to be wise for the glory of God; they wish to appear wise for human glory. How could they not hate wisdom, which commands and teaches that what they love must be despised?

Therefore: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search his testimonies, who seek him with their whole heart.” For by searching his testimonies in such a way that they seek him with their whole heart, they walk undefiled in the law of the Lord.

Yet was that man not searching his testimonies and seeking him who said, “Good Teacher, what good shall I do so that I may obtain eternal life?” But how did he seek him with his whole heart, when he preferred his riches to his counsel and, after hearing it, went away sad (Matt. 19:16, 22)?

The prophet Isaiah also says: “Seek the Lord; and when you have found him, let the impious abandon his ways, and the unjust man his thoughts” (Isa. 55:6–7).

## 3

The impious and the unjust therefore seek God so that, having found him, they may no longer be impious or unjust. How, then, are they already blessed, when they are still searching his testimonies and seeking him, since the impious and the unjust can do this as well?

Who would say that the impious and the unjust are blessed—whether an impious person or an unjust one?

They are therefore blessed in hope, just as blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness—not because of what is present, as long as they suffer evil, but because of what will be present, since the kingdom of heaven belongs to them; and blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness—not because they hunger and thirst, but because of what follows, since they shall be filled; and blessed are those who weep—not because they weep, but because of what follows, since they shall laugh (Matt. 5:10, 6, 5).

Accordingly, “Blessed are those who search his testimonies, who seek him with their whole heart”—not because they search and seek, but because they will find what they seek. For they seek with their whole heart, not negligently.

If they are blessed in hope, perhaps they are also undefiled in hope. For surely, in this life, even if we walk in the law of the Lord, search his testimonies, and seek him with our whole heart, if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (1 John 1:8).

But this must be examined more carefully. For what follows says: “For those who commit iniquity have not walked in his ways.” From this it may appear that those who walk in the way of the Lord—that is, in the law of the Lord—by searching his testimonies and seeking him with their whole heart, can already be undefiled, that is, without sin, because of the words that follow: “For those who commit iniquity have not walked in his ways.”

But “whoever commits sin also commits iniquity,” blessed John says; and he adds, “Sin is iniquity” (1 John 3:4).

But this discourse must now be brought to a close; such a great question must not be compressed into too narrow a space.

# SERMON II

## 1. [verse 3]

It is written, read, and true in this psalm: “For those who commit iniquity have not walked in his ways.” But, with God’s help—in whose hand are both we and our words (Wis. 7:16)—we must labor so that what has been rightly said, if not rightly understood, does not disturb the reader or hearer.

We must beware lest all the saints, whose voice is that of those who say, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” be thought either not to walk in the ways of the Lord, since sin is iniquity (1 John 3:4), and those who commit iniquity have certainly not walked in his ways; or, because there is no doubt that they do walk in the ways of the Lord, be believed to have no sin—which is unquestionably false.

For it was not written merely to avoid arrogance and pride: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” Otherwise, “And the truth is not in us” would not have been added; instead it would have said, “Humility is not in us.” This is especially clear because what follows illuminates the meaning more plainly and removes every ambiguity of doubt.

For when blessed John had said this, he added: “**But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity**” (1 John 1:8–9).

What does the condemned elevation of impiety say here? What does it oppose?

If the saints say that they do not have sin in order to avoid arrogance, and not in order to confess the truth, what are they confessing so that they may deserve forgiveness and cleansing? Is this too done in order to avoid arrogance? How, then, will true cleansing from sins be obtained if their confession is false?

Let the straw-like pride of the arrogant therefore fall silent and wither—pride that deceives itself, saying with feigned humility in the ears of human beings that it has sin, but saying within its heart with impious exaltation that it has no sin.

Those who say this deceive themselves, and the truth is not in them. When they say it in the ears of human beings, they deceive not only themselves but also others through the perversity of an unhealthy doctrine. But when they say it in their heart, there they deceive themselves; there the truth is not in them. Thus they deceive themselves in their heart and lose the light of truth in their own heart.

Let the holy family of Christ cry out, fruitful and growing throughout the whole world, humbly truthful and truthfully humble. Let it cry out, I say:

“**If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity.**”

Let these words be understood as they are spoken. For humility will then be true if it is not displayed only on the tongue, so that, according to the Apostle, “we may not be wise in high things, but consent with the humble” (Rom. 12:16). He does not say “converse with them,” but “consent with them”—something done not with the mouth but with the heart.

Hypocrite, if you say that you have sin while believing that you have no sin, outwardly you feign humility, but inwardly you embrace vanity. Therefore you have truth neither in your mouth nor in your heart.

What does it profit you to appear humble to human beings in what you say, if God sees that what you think is proud? Certainly, if a divine oracle sounded in your ears, “Do not speak proudly,” you would rightly be condemned if you spoke humbly with your mouth before human beings, but proudly in your heart before the Lord.

But when you hear, “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11:20)—for he does not say “speak,” but “be minded”—why are you not humble inwardly, where your thoughts are? Is the mind inflated by pride so that the tongue may pretend to humility?

You read or hear, “Do not be high-minded, but fear”; and you are so high-minded that you consider yourself to have no sin. Consequently, because you do not wish to fear, nothing remains for you except to swell with pride [Note: [Col. 1505] So the manuscripts read. The editions read, “to fear.”]

## 2

“And from where,” you ask, “is it written, ‘For those who commit iniquity have not walked in his ways’?”

Do the saints of the Lord not walk in the ways of the Lord? If they do walk in them, you say, they do not commit iniquity. If they do not commit iniquity, they have no sin, since sin is iniquity.

Rise to my aid, Lord Jesus, and help me against the arrogant heretic through the Apostle who confesses.

Behold your human being, emptying himself so that he may be filled with you. Let us hear him, my brothers; let us question him about this matter, if you please—indeed, because it pleases you.

Tell us, most blessed Paul: did you walk in the ways of the Lord while you were still living in the flesh?

He answers: “And from where did I say, ‘Nevertheless, let us walk according to that to which we have attained’?” (Phil. 3:16). From where did I say, “Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not walk in the same footsteps?” (2 Cor. 12:18).

From where did I say, “As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6–7)? What way of the Lord is more certain than faith, by which the righteous person lives (Rom. 1:17)?

Along what other way was I pressing toward the things above when I said, “One thing: forgetting what is behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, according to the aim I pursue the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 3:13–14)?

Finally, along what other way had I run when I said, “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the race” (2 Tim. 4:7)?

Let these answers suffice, by which we have learned that the Apostle Paul walked in the ways of the Lord. But let us ask him something else.

Tell us, I beg you, Apostle: when you were still living in the flesh and walking in the ways of the Lord, did you have sin, or were you without sin?

Let us hear whether he deceives himself, or whether he shares the understanding of blessed John, his fellow apostle—for the truth was in them.

He also answers: “Have you not read where I confess, saying, ‘For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do’?”

We have heard this. Let us now ask him: How were you walking in the ways of the Lord if you were doing the evil that you did not want, since the holy Psalm resounds with the words, “For those who commit iniquity have not walked in his ways”?

Listen to him immediately answering through the sentence that follows: “If I do what I do not want,” he says, “it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. 7:15–17).

Behold how those who walk in the ways of the Lord do not commit sin and yet are not without sin: for it is no longer they themselves who commit it, but the sin dwelling in them.

## 3

Someone will say here: How did he do the evil he did not want, and how was it not he himself who did it, but the sin that dwelt in him?

For the moment, the question has already been resolved, and it has sufficiently appeared, on the authority of canonical Scripture, that it is possible for those who walk in the ways of the Lord, although they are not without sin, nevertheless not to commit it themselves.

“For those who commit iniquity”—that is, sin, since sin is iniquity—“have not walked in his ways.”

But how it can be understood that he both commits that act because of the body of this death, in which the law of sin dwells, and does not himself commit it because of the ways of the Lord in which he walks, requires another discourse, since this one must now be brought to a close.

# SERMON III

## 1. [verse 3]

Because of what is written in this psalm—“For those who commit iniquity have not walked in his ways”—and because the Apostle John says that sin is iniquity (1 John 3:4), a difficult question has arisen: How can the saints in this life not be without sin, since this too is true: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8), and yet walk in the ways of the Lord, in which those who commit iniquity do not walk?

The question has been resolved by the Apostle Paul’s statement: “It is no longer I who commit it, but the sin dwelling in me.”

For how is the one in whom sin dwells without sin? Yet he walks in the ways of the Lord, in which those who commit sin do not walk, because it is no longer he himself who commits it, but the sin dwelling in him.

Nevertheless, the question has been resolved in such a way that another, more difficult question has arisen: How does a human being do what he himself does not do?

For he said both things: “I do not do what I want,” and “It is not I who commit it, but the sin dwelling in me” (Rom. 7:17, 20, 16).

From this we should understand that, when the sin dwelling in us works in us, we do not ourselves commit it—when our will in no way consents to it and even restrains the members of the body from obeying its desires.

For what does sin work in us against our will except illicit desires? If the assent of the will is not given to them, some movement of feeling is indeed stirred, but no action is granted to it.

The same Apostle commands this when he says: “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires; and do not offer your members as weapons of iniquity to sin” (Rom. 6:12–13).

There are therefore desires of sin to which he forbade us to be obedient. Sin works these desires [Note: [Col. 1507] Three manuscripts read *operatur* (“works”).]; if we obey them, we too commit sin. But if, obeying the Apostle, we do not yield to them, we do not ourselves commit it; rather, it is the sin dwelling in us that does so.

If we had no illicit desires, neither we nor sin would commit any evil in us. But the movement of illicit desire, which by not obeying it we do not ourselves commit, is nevertheless said to be done by us because it is not the vigor of an alien nature, but the weakness of our own.

From that weakness we shall be completely saved when we have become immortal in both soul and body.

Therefore, because we walk in the ways of the Lord, we do not obey the desires of sin; and because we are not without sin, we have the desires of sin.

Accordingly, by not obeying them, we no longer commit them ourselves; but it is the sin dwelling in us that stirs them.

“For those who commit iniquity”—that is, who obey the desires of sin—“have not walked in his ways.”

2. But it must still be asked what we are seeking to have forgiven when we say to God, “Forgive us our debts”: whether the sins we commit when we obey the desires of sin, or whether we wish those very desires to be forgiven—desires which we do not ourselves produce, but which the sin that dwells within us produces.

As far as I am able to understand, the whole guilt of that sickness and infirmity from which unlawful desires are stirred—the condition which the Apostle calls “sin” (Rom. VII, 7–25)—was dissolved through the sacrament of Baptism, together with all that we did, said, or thought in obedience to it. Nor would that sickness subsequently harm us, although it remained within us, if we never obeyed its unlawful desires, whether by action, speech, or silent consent, until the sickness itself also was healed, when what we ask was fulfilled—whether when we say, “Thy kingdom come,” or when we say, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. VI, 12, 10, 13).

But because “human life upon earth is a temptation” (Job VII, 1), even if we are far from serious crimes, there is nevertheless no lack of occasions on which we obey the desires of sin by deed, word, or thought. While we are watchful against greater dangers, certain minor offenses creep upon the unwary; and although, taken individually, they do not crush us by their own weight [Note: [Col. 1508] The manuscripts read *motibus* (“movements”); the printed editions read *molibus* (“weights”).], when gathered together they nevertheless overwhelm us by their accumulated mass. On account of these things, even those who walk in the ways of the Lord say, “Forgive us our debts.” For both the prayer itself and the confession itself belong to the ways of the Lord, although sins do not belong to them.

3. Therefore, in the ways of the Lord—which are all embraced by the one faith through which one believes in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. IV, 5), who also said, “I am the way” (John XIV, 6)—no one commits sin, but confesses it. Thus he deviates when he sins; and the sin committed by one who deviates is not attributed to the way. Yet in the way of faith those are regarded as non-sinners to whom sins are not imputed.

Concerning them, the Apostle Paul, commending the righteousness of faith, showed that it is written in the Psalm: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Rom. IV, 7; and Ps. XXXI, 1–2). This is what the ways of the Lord provide. Accordingly, since “the just person lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17), the iniquity that alienates a person from this way of the Lord is unbelief.

Whoever walks in this way—that is, in devout faith—either does not commit sin, or, if something is committed by one who has deviated, it is not imputed on account of the way and is treated as though he had not committed it. Thus the statement is rightly understood: “For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways,” since it signifies the iniquity that departs from faith or does not approach faith.

For just as the Lord said concerning the Jews, “If I had not come, they would not have sin” (John XV, 22)—not that they were entirely without sin before Christ came in the flesh and began to have sin after he came, but he wished a particular sin, namely unbelief, to be understood, because they did not believe in him—so those who work iniquity, not just any iniquity but this very iniquity of unbelief, have not walked in his ways. For “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10), and both are in Christ; apart from Christ they are nowhere.

“For I say,” the Apostle declares, “that Christ became a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers; but that the Gentiles should glorify God for his mercy” (Rom. XV, 8–9). In this, therefore, there is mercy, because he redeemed us; in this there is truth, because he fulfilled what he promised and will fulfill what he promises.

Those, then, who work iniquity—that is, unbelief—have not walked in his ways, because they did not believe in Christ. Let them therefore turn and devoutly believe in him who justifies the ungodly; and in him let them find, through sins forgiven, mercy, and through promises fulfilled, truth—that is, all the ways of the Lord [Col. 1509]. Walking in them, they will not work iniquity, because they will not hold unbelief but faith, “which works through love” (Gal. V, 6), and to which sin is not imputed.

# SERMON IV

1. [Verse 4.] Who is it, beloved, who says to the Lord, “You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly. Would that my ways might be directed toward keeping your statutes. Then I shall not be put to shame when I contemplate all your commandments”? Who is the one who says this, except each individual member of Christ, or rather the whole body of Christ?

And what does “You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly” mean? Does it mean, “You commanded exceedingly,” or “to be kept exceedingly”? Whichever of these we understand, the statement seems contrary to that famous and noble saying which the Greeks praise among their wise men, and which the Latins affirm by praising it: “Nothing in excess” (*Ne quid nimis*) (Terence, *Andria*, Act I, scene 1).

For if this is true—that nothing should be done in excess—how can what is said here be true: “You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly”? Why would God either command anything excessively or wish it to be kept excessively, if everything excessive deserved blame?

We might therefore say that we are bound by no authority of the Greek sages [Note: [Col. 1509] Am. and the manuscripts read *terreri* (“to be frightened”); the printed editions read *teneri* (“to be held”).], observing what is written: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (I Cor. I, 20). We might instead believe that the saying “Nothing in excess” is false, rather than the divine utterance in which we read and sing, “You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly”—unless true reason, rather than Greek arrogance, were to restrain us.

For “exceedingly” is said of whatever is more than it ought to be. “Too little” and “too much” are opposites. Too little is what is less than it ought to be; too much is what is more than it ought to be. Between these lies the proper measure, which is called “enough.” Since it is useful in life and conduct that we do absolutely nothing more than we ought, we should surely acknowledge rather than deny that the saying “Nothing in excess” is true.

Sometimes, however, the Latin language misuses this word, so that we find it used in the sacred writings, and use it in our own speech, to mean “very much.” Thus here, “You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly,” must mean “very greatly,” if we understand it correctly. And if we say to some very dear person, “I love you exceedingly,” we certainly do not mean that we love that person more than we ought, but that we love him or her very much.

Indeed, the Greek saying does not contain the word found here. There the word is ἄγαν (*agan*), which means “exceedingly”; here, however, the word is σφόδρα (*sphodra*), which means “very greatly.” But sometimes, as we have said, we find and use “exceedingly” to mean “very greatly.” Hence some Latin manuscripts do not read, “You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly,” but “very greatly.” Thus God commanded this very greatly, and God’s commandments ought to be kept very greatly.

2. [Verse 5.] But observe what humble devotion—or devout humility—and faith that does not forget grace add: “Would that my ways,” he says, “might be directed toward keeping your statutes.” You certainly commanded, but would that what you commanded might be accomplished in me [Col. 1510].

When you hear “Would that,” recognize the voice of one who desires; and once you have recognized the voice of one who desires, lay aside the pride of one who presumes. For who would say that he desires something that lies so entirely within his own power that he could accomplish it without any assistance?

Therefore, if a person desires what God commands, God must be asked to grant what he commands. From whom should it be desired, except from him from whom, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, “every good gift and every perfect gift” descends—the Father of lights (James I, 17)?

For the sake of those who think that divine assistance in doing righteousness consists only in bringing God’s commandments to our knowledge, so that once we know them we may fulfill them without any grace of God, by the powers of our own will alone: this person does not desire that his ways be directed toward keeping God’s statutes unless he has already received the commandments through God’s own command.

For this is the point of what he said earlier: “You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly.” It is as though he were saying: “I have already received the law; I already know it. For you commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly: your commandments are holy, just, and good; but sin works death in me through what is good (Rom. VII, 12–13), unless your grace comes to my aid. Would that, then, my ways might be directed toward keeping your statutes.”

3. [Verse 6.] “Then I shall not be put to shame when I contemplate all your commandments.” Whether God’s commandments are being read or recalled from memory, they should be regarded as a mirror, according to the Apostle James, who says:

“If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be compared to a man who observes the face of his birth in a mirror; for he observed himself, and went away, and immediately forgot what sort of man he was. But whoever looks into the perfect law of freedom and remains in it—not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work—this person will be blessed in his deed” (James I, 23–25).

This person wishes to be such that he may contemplate God’s commandments as in a mirror and not be put to shame, because he does not wish merely to be their hearer but their doer. Therefore he desires that his ways be directed toward keeping God’s statutes. From where are they to be directed, except by the grace of God? Otherwise he will possess God’s law not as a place for rejoicing but as a place for shame, if he wishes to contemplate commandments that he does not perform.

4. [Verse 7.] “I will confess to you,” he says, “with an upright heart, when I have learned the judgments of your righteousness.” This is not a confession of sins but of praise, just as he himself said in whom there was no sin: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI, 25). And as it is written in the book of Ecclesiasticus: “You shall say in confession, ‘All the works of the Lord are exceedingly good’” (Ecclus. XXXIX, 20–21).

“I will confess to you,” he says, “with an upright heart.” Certainly, if my ways are directed, I will confess to you, because you have done this, and this praise belongs to you, not to me. For then I will confess, when I have learned the judgments of your righteousness, if I have an upright heart—that is, if my ways have been directed toward keeping your statutes.

For what benefit will it be to me that I have learned them if, with a perverse heart, I depart along crooked paths? [Note: [Col. 1510] Most manuscripts read *habebo* (“I will have”).] I will not rejoice in them; rather, they will accuse me.

[Col. 1511] 5. [Verse 8.] Then he adds: “I will keep your statutes.” All these statements are connected with what he said: “Would that my ways might be directed toward keeping your statutes; then I shall not be put to shame when I contemplate all your commandments”; and, “I will confess to you with an upright heart”; and, “I will keep your statutes.”

But what follows? “Do not utterly forsake me”; or, as some manuscripts read, “Do not forsake me exceedingly,” with “exceedingly” used in the sense of “very greatly.” For the Greek word is used here too, namely σφόδρα (*sphodra*). It is as though he wished to be forsaken by the Lord, but not utterly. Far from it!

But because God had forsaken the world on account of its sins, he would have forsaken it utterly if even so great a remedy had not benefited it—namely, the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. As it is, in accordance with this prayer of the body of Christ, he has not forsaken it utterly, because “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V, 19).

This may also be understood as the voice of one who, when he had said in his abundance, “I shall never be moved,” as though trusting in his own strength, was shown by God that he had been granted the glory of his strength not by his own merit but by God’s will. God turned his face from him, and he became troubled (Ps. XXIX, 7–8).

When he therefore found himself no longer presuming upon himself, he cried out: “Do not utterly forsake me.” If you have forsaken me so that I may appear weak without your help, do not do so utterly, lest I perish.

You therefore commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly; I can no longer excuse myself on the ground of ignorance. But because I am weak: “Would that my ways might be directed toward keeping your statutes. Then I shall not be put to shame when I contemplate all your commandments”; then, “I will confess to you with an upright heart, when I have learned the judgments of your righteousness”; then, “I will keep your statutes.” And if you have forsaken me so that I would not glory in myself, do not do so utterly, and, justified by you, I will glory in you.

# SERMON V

1. [Verse 9.] Let us consider these verses, beloved, in the Psalm, and, as the Lord grants, let us search out his sacred Scriptures:

“With what does a young man correct his way? By keeping your words.”

He questions himself and answers himself. “With what does a young man correct his way?” extends as far as the question; then comes the answer: “By keeping your words.”

But here the keeping of God’s words must be understood as the practice of his commandments. It is useless to preserve them in memory if they are not also preserved in life. For some people, by holding on to God’s words, ensure that they do not forget them, but by living do not act so as to be corrected. Yet this person does not say, “With what does a young man exercise his memory?” but, “With what does he correct his way?” And he answers: “By keeping your words.” A way cannot in any manner be called corrected so long as life remains perverse.

2. But what does this “young man” mean? He could have said, “With what does a human being correct his way?” or, “With what does a man correct his way?” This is often expressed in Scripture so that “human being” is understood from the more honored sex, in a mode of expression by which the whole is signified through a part.

For neither is a woman who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly not blessed; yet it is said, “Blessed is the man” (Ps. I, 1). Here, however, he says neither “human being” nor “man,” but “young man.”

Is an older person to be despaired of? Or does an older person correct his way in something other than keeping God’s words? Perhaps this is an exhortation indicating the age at which it should most particularly be done, in accordance with what is written elsewhere: “My son, receive instruction from your youth, and you will find wisdom even to old age” (Ecclus. VI, 18).

There is also another interpretation, according to which we should recognize here the younger evangelical son who departed from his father into a distant country and squandered his substance by living prodigally with prostitutes. Afterward, having fed pigs and endured poverty and hunger, he returned to himself and said, “I will rise and go to my father.”

For with what did he correct his way, except by keeping God’s words, which he desired as one hungering for his father’s bread? His older brother certainly did not correct his way, since he said to his father, “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment.” The younger son, therefore, corrected his way, which he confessed that he had so corrupted and perverted that he said to his father, “I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke XV, 12–21).

A third interpretation also occurs to me, and, as far as I understand according to my limited capacity, I prefer it to the two preceding ones: the older person is to be recognized as the old human being, and the younger as the new; the older bears the image of the earthly human being, the younger that of the heavenly one. For “the spiritual was not first, but the animal; afterward, the spiritual” (I Cor. XV, 49, 46).

Thus, whoever he may be with respect to the age of his body—even if he is decrepit with the long old age of many years—he will be young in relation to God if he has been turned toward him through the newness of grace. And in this he corrects his way: by keeping his words. This is “the word of faith that we preach” (Rom. X, 8), and this is the faith that works through love (Gal. V, 6).

3. [Verse 10.] But observe what this younger people—the child of grace, the new human being, the singer of the new song, the heir of the new covenant—this younger one, not Cain but Abel; not Ishmael but Isaac; not Esau but Israel; not Manasseh but Ephraim; not Eli but Samuel; not Saul but David—adds:

“With my whole heart,” he says, “I have sought you; do not repel me from your commandments.”

Behold, he prays to be helped in keeping God’s words, in which he had said that the younger person corrected his way. For what else is “Do not repel me from your commandments” than this? For what is it to be repelled by God except not to be helped?

Human weakness cannot conform itself to his upright and demanding commandments unless his love, coming first, gives assistance. Those whom he does not help are therefore rightly said to be repelled by him, as though they were unworthy and were prevented by a flaming sword from extending their hand to the tree of life (Gen. III, 24).

But who is worthy, since through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, “in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12)?

Yet our deserved misery is healed by God’s undeserved mercy. For how could this speaker have sought God with his whole heart unless God himself had turned him, though he was turned away, toward himself? To him it is said, “O God, you will turn us and give us life” (Ps. LXXXIV, 7). And unless he had sought the lost and recalled the wandering one, who says, “I will seek what was lost, and I will bring back what had wandered” (Ezek. XXXIV, 16)?

4. [Verses 11–12.] This is why he corrects his way by keeping God’s words—with God directing him and accomplishing it. For he could not do it by himself, since the prophet Jeremiah acknowledges and says: “I know, Lord, that a human being’s way is not his own, nor does a man walk and correct his way” (Jer. X, 23).

This is also what the speaker earlier desired from the Lord, when he said, “Would that my ways might be directed.” And here, when he adds, “In my heart I have hidden your words, that I may not sin against you,” he immediately seeks divine assistance, lest God’s words be hidden in his heart without fruit if works of righteousness did not follow.

For after saying this, he added: “Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your statutes.” He says “teach me” in the sense in which those who do them learn them, not in the sense of those who merely remember them in order to have something to say. For he had already said, “In my heart I have hidden your words, that I may not sin against you.”

Why, then, does he still seek to learn what he already keeps hidden in his heart? He would not have hidden them there unless he had learned them. Why, then, does he add and say, “Teach me your statutes,” except because he wishes to learn them by doing them, not by speaking or retaining them in memory?

Therefore, since it is read in another Psalm, “He who gave the law will give blessing” (Ps. LXXXIII, 8), he says: “Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your statutes.” Because I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you, you gave the law; give also the blessing of grace, so that by doing I may learn what you commanded by making it known.

Let this suffice, so that your minds may be nourished without weariness. What follows requires another sermon.

# SERMON VI

1. [Verse 13.] The beginning of this sermon in the Psalm we are discussing is this verse: “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth.”

What does this mean, beloved? What does it mean? Who can declare all God’s judgments when he cannot investigate them? Or do we hesitate to exclaim with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and his ways past finding out” (Rom. XI, 33)?

The Lord says: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” And although he immediately promised them all truth through the Holy Spirit (John XVI, 12–13), blessed Paul nevertheless cries out, “We know in part.” We are thus to understand that through the Holy Spirit, of whom we have received the pledge, we are led toward all truth; but that we shall come into another life, after the mirror and riddle of this life, and then see face to face [Note: [Col. 1513] Am. and the manuscripts read: “but when, in another life, after the mirror and riddle of this life, we come face to face”; some have *aenigmata* (“riddles”) in place of *aenigma* (“riddle”).] (I Cor. XIII, 9, 12).

How, then, does this person say, “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth”? And he is the same person who, just one verse earlier, had said, “Teach me your statutes.”

How, then, did he declare all the judgments of God’s mouth, when he still wishes to learn his statutes? Did he already know all the judgments, while he still desired to learn the statutes? This would be even more remarkable, if he already knew God’s unsearchable judgments but did not know what he commanded human beings to do.

For statutes are not sayings but acts of righteousness—namely, the works of the righteous that God commands. They are called God’s, although they are done by us, because they are not done unless he grants them.

God’s judgments, moreover, are those by which the world is judged by him both now and at the end of the age. But since everything is contained in God’s words—both statutes and judgments—why does the one who says that he has hidden God’s words in his heart still ask to learn his statutes?

He says, “In my heart I have hidden your words, that I may not sin against you.” Then he adds, “Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your statutes.” And afterward: “With my lips,” he says, “I have declared all the judgments of your mouth.”

These two statements do not appear to be opposed to each other; rather, they seem friendly and connected, so that because he hides God’s words in his heart, he declares his judgments with his lips. “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10).

But how the statement placed between them—“Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your statutes”—fits with a person who already has God’s words in his heart and has declared all God’s judgments with his lips is not found except in this sense: he is understood to wish to learn them by doing them, not by retaining them in memory and speaking them. And he has shown that we must ask this of the Lord, without whom we can do nothing.

We have already discussed this before in another sermon. Now, however, we have undertaken, as God grants, to examine how he could say that he had declared all the judgments of God’s mouth with his lips, when those judgments are said to be unsearchable and when it is written elsewhere concerning their depth: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 7).

2. Pay attention, then, to what we should understand here. Does the Church not know God’s judgments? Certainly it does. For it surely knows to whom the Judge of the living and the dead will say, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom,” and to whom he will say, “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 34, 41).

It knows, I say, that neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor the other classes whom the Apostle Paul lists there, will possess the kingdom of God (I Cor. VI, 9–10). It knows the anger and indignation, tribulation and distress destined for every human soul that works evil, for the Jew first and also for the Greek; and glory, honor, and peace for everyone who works good, for the Jew first and also for the Greek (Rom. II, 9–10).

The Church knows these and similar judgments of God, clearly expressed. But these are not all of them, since some are unsearchable and, like a great abyss, deep and hidden.

Are even those judgments known to certain more excellent members of this Man who, together with his saving Head, is the whole Christ? Perhaps they are called unsearchable for human beings because human beings cannot investigate them by their own strength. But why should they be impossible for one to whom the Lord grants this through the gift of the Holy Spirit?

For it is said, “God dwells in inaccessible light” (I Tim. VI, 16), and yet we hear, “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII, 5). The problem is resolved in this way: he is inaccessible to our powers, but we approach him by his gifts.

Even if no saint is permitted to know all God’s judgments so long as “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. IX, 15)—for it is truly too much for a human being, since, to give one example by which the vastness of God’s judgments may be inferred, no one is slow in mind or lame in body without God’s judgment—the Church nevertheless has grounds to say, and to say truthfully, as the people of God’s possession:

“With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth.”

That is: “I have kept silent about none of your judgments that you wished to make known to me through your words, but I have declared them all completely with my lips.”

For this seems to be what he wished to signify by not saying, “all your judgments,” but “all the judgments of your mouth”—that is, those which you have spoken to me. By “his mouth,” therefore, we are to understand his utterance, which he has made to us in the revelations of many saints and in the two Testaments. The Church does not cease to declare all these judgments everywhere with her lips.

3. [Verse 14.] Then he continues and says: “I have rejoiced in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches.”

We understand the way of God’s testimonies to be nothing swifter, more certain, shorter, or greater than Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II, 3).

Hence this person also says that he rejoiced, or delighted, in this way as in all riches. God’s testimonies are those by which he deigns to prove to us how greatly he loves us. “God commends his love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. V, 8–9).

Since he himself says, “I am the way” (John XIV, 6), and since the humility of his carnal birth and passion are evident testimonies of God’s love toward us, Christ is unquestionably the way of God’s testimonies.

Through these testimonies, which we see fulfilled in him, we also await and hope that those future things promised to us eternally will be fulfilled. “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him freely give us all things?” (Rom. VIII, 32).

4. [Verses 15–16.] It follows: “I will prattle over your commandments and contemplate your ways.”

The Greek text has ἀδολεσχήσω (*adoleschēsō*). Some Latin translators have rendered it *garriam* (“I will prattle”), others *exercebor* (“I will exercise myself”). These two expressions appear different from one another; but if the exercise of the mind is understood, together with a certain delight in disputation, they are joined, and something is formed from both, so that loquacity is not foreign to such an exercise.

Loquacious people are commonly called prattlers. [Note: [Col. 1515] Thus Am. and the manuscripts; Er. and Lov. read “but if,” and below, “is prattling.”] Thus the Church exercises herself in God’s commandments, prattling against all the enemies of the Christian and catholic faith through the abundant disputations of her teachers. Those disputations are fruitful for the disputants if they consider in them nothing except the ways of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1515] The printed editions add here, “But all the ways of the Lord”; this is absent from the principal manuscripts.], as it is written: “Mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10). The fullness of both is found in Christ.

Through this pleasant exercise, what he adds also comes to pass: “I will meditate on your statutes; I will not forget your words.” I will meditate, precisely so that I may not forget. Hence that blessed person in the first Psalm “will meditate on the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. I, 2).

5. In all these matters that we have discussed as best we could, beloved, let us remember that the one who hides the Lord’s words in his heart, declares all the judgments of his mouth with his lips, delights in the way of his testimonies as in all riches, and, prattling or exercising himself in his commandments, contemplates his ways and meditates on his statutes so as not to forget his words—although through all this he plainly appears instructed in God’s law and teaching—nevertheless prays and says: “Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your statutes.”

Here he is understood to ask for nothing other than the assistance of grace, so that what he already knows in speech he may also learn in action.

# SERMON VII

1. [Verse 17.] If you remember the earlier parts of this Psalm, beloved, they should help us to understand what follows. For the words that speak as though from the person of one human being are members of Christ, and belong as one body to one head.

Earlier he had said: “With what does a young man correct his way? By keeping your words.” Now, more openly, he asks for assistance in order to do this:

“Reward your servant,” he says, “and I shall live, and I will keep your words.”

If he had asked that good be rewarded him for good, he would already have kept God’s words. But he did not say, “Reward your servant because I have kept your words,” as though he were demanding a good reward for the good of obedience. Rather, he said, “Reward your servant, and I shall live, and I will keep your words.”

What else does this mean than that the dead cannot keep them? These are the unbelievers, of whom it is said, “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. VIII, 22).

Therefore, if we understand the dead to be unbelievers and the living to be believers—for “the just person lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17), and God’s words cannot be kept except by faith, which works through love (Gal. V, 6)—then the one who says, “Reward your servant, and I shall live, and I will keep your words,” asks for this faith.

And because before faith human beings deserve nothing but evil in return for evil, while God rewards evil with good through undeserved grace, the person who says, “Reward your servant, and I shall live, and I will keep your words,” asks for this reward.

There are four kinds of recompense: evil is repaid for evil, as God will repay the ungodly with eternal fire; good is repaid for good, as he will repay the righteous with an eternal kingdom; good is repaid for evil, as Christ justifies the ungodly by grace; or evil is repaid for good, as Judas and the Jews persecuted Christ through wickedness [Note: [Col. 1516] The manuscripts read, “as the Jew persecuted Christ through wickedness.”].

Of these four recompenses, the first two belong to justice, so that evil is repaid for evil and good for good. The third belongs to mercy, so that good is repaid for evil. The fourth God does not know, for he repays no one evil for good.

The recompense I placed third is necessary first. For unless God repaid good for evil, there would be no one to whom he could repay good for good.

2. Consider Saul, afterward Paul. “Not according to works of righteousness,” he says, “which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration” (Titus III, 5).

And again: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (I Tim. I, 13).

And again: “I give this advice as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord, so that I might be faithful” (I Cor. VII, 25)—that is, so that I might live, because “the just person lives by faith.”

He was therefore dead beforehand through his own unrighteousness, before he lived through God’s grace. He confesses this very death in the following words: “When the commandment came, sin revived, but I died; and the commandment that was intended for life was found by me to be for death” (Rom. VII, 9–10).

God therefore repaid him good for evil—that is, life for death—a recompense of the kind requested here, where it says: “Reward your servant, and I shall live, and I will keep your words.”

He lived and kept God’s words, and began to belong to another recompense, in which good is repaid for good. On account of this he says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day” (II Tim. IV, 7–8).

He is certainly righteous in repaying good for good, because he was first merciful in repaying good for evil. Yet even that justice by which good is repaid for good is not without mercy, for it is also written: “He crowns you with compassion and mercy” (Ps. CII, 4).

When would the one who said, “I have fought the good fight” have conquered, unless God had granted it? Hence he says, “Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. XV, 57).

When would the one who finished the course have run, or reached the goal, unless God had helped him? Hence he says, “Therefore it is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16).

And when would the one who kept the faith have done so, unless—as he himself says—he had obtained mercy in order to be faithful?

3. Let human pride, therefore, nowhere exalt itself: God repays good rewards with his own gifts.

But if this person, who now prays and says, “Reward your servant, and I shall live,” were completely dead, he would not pray. Rather, he received the beginning of a good desire from the one from whom he asks for the life of obedience.

For those who said, “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke XVII, 5), had some faith. And the man who, when asked whether he believed, said, “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX, 23), confessed his unbelief but did not deny his faith.

Already beginning to live, the believer asks for life when he prays for obedience—not a reward because it has been preserved [Note: [Col. 1517] Am., Erasmus, and the manuscripts read, “not that a reward may be preserved for it”; Lov. reads, “not as though a reward were to be preserved for it.”], but assistance so that it may be preserved. As life grows, the person who is renewed day by day lives more fully each day (II Cor. IV, 16).

4. [Verse 18.] Knowing that God’s words cannot be kept through obedience unless they are seen through understanding, he adds this also to his prayer and says:

“Open my eyes, and I will contemplate wondrous things from your law.”

The same applies to what he adds: “I am a sojourner in the earth”; or, as some manuscripts have it, “I am a resident in the earth”; “do not hide your commandments from me.”

What he said earlier, “Open my eyes,” he expresses afterward as, “Do not hide from me.” And what he had said there, “wondrous things from your law,” he repeats in another form by saying, “your commandments.”

Nothing is more wondrous among God’s commandments than, “Love your enemies” (Matt. V, 44)—that is, “Repay good for evil.”

But the discussion of this sojourning or residence must not be confined to this point. Therefore this subject is not to be pursued here; another sermon must be awaited and, with the Lord’s help, delivered.

# SERMON VIII
### 1. [verse 19]

The discourse owed to your expectation of what follows in this great psalm must now be delivered, namely from the verse in which he says, “I am a sojourner in the earth; do not hide your commandments from me”—or, as some manuscripts read, “I am a tenant resident in the earth.” For the Greek word is πάροικος (*paroikos*), which some of our translators have rendered *inquilinus* (“tenant resident”), some *incola* (“inhabitant” or “sojourner”), and sometimes even *advena* (“newcomer” or “stranger”). Tenant residents, not having a house of their own, dwell in another’s; inhabitants or newcomers, on the other hand, are plainly people who have arrived from elsewhere.

Here a great question concerning the soul arises. For the statement “I am an inhabitant, or newcomer, or tenant resident in the earth” cannot seem to have been spoken according to the body, since the body derives its origin from the earth. But in this most profound question I do not dare to make a definitive pronouncement. For whether, on account of the soul—which God forbid anyone should think to be from the earth—it could rightly be said, “I am a tenant resident, or inhabitant, or newcomer in the earth”; or whether the statement is made according to the whole human being, because he was once a citizen of paradise, where, of course, the one speaking these words was not; or, which is freer from every controversy, whether not every human being can say this, but only one to whom an eternal homeland in heaven has been promised: this I know, that “human life upon earth is a temptation” (Job 7:1), and that “a heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam” (Ecclus. 40:1).

Yet I take greater pleasure in arguing according to this interpretation: that we say we are tenant residents or inhabitants in the earth because we have found the heavenly homeland from which we have received a pledge, and to which, once we arrive, we shall never migrate away. For the one who says in another psalm, “I am a tenant resident with you and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 38:13), does not say, “As all human beings”; but by saying “as all my fathers were,” he plainly wishes the righteous to be understood—those who preceded him in time and, in this pilgrimage, sighed with devout longing for the heavenly homeland.

Of them it is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> “According to faith all these died, without receiving the promises, but seeing them and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth. For those who say such things show that they seek a homeland. And indeed, if they had remembered that one from which they had departed, they would have had time to return; but now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them” (Heb. 11:13–16).

And what we read, “As long as we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord,” can be understood as not applying to everyone, but to the faithful: “For faith is not possessed by all” (2 Thess. 3:2). We see what the Apostle joins to these words. For after saying, “As long as we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord,” he says, “For we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6–7), so that we might understand this pilgrimage to belong to those who walk by faith.

Unbelievers, however, whom God did not foreknow and predestine to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8:29), cannot truthfully say that they are pilgrims in the earth when they are there where they were born according to the flesh. For they have no other city; and therefore they are not strangers in the earth but earthborn. Hence another Scripture says of a certain person: “For he has placed his house beside death, and his beams beside the underworld, with the earthborn” (Isa. 28:15).

They too are pilgrims and tenant residents—not of this earth, but of the people of God, from whom they are strangers. Therefore the Apostle says to those who believe and are beginning to possess the holy city, which is not of this world: “Therefore you are no longer pilgrims and tenant residents, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. 2:19).

Those, then, are earthly citizens who are pilgrims from the people of God; but those who are citizens among the people of God are pilgrims in the earth, because that whole people, as long as it is in the body, is on pilgrimage away from the Lord. Let him therefore say, “I am an inhabitant in the earth; do not hide your commandments from me.”

### 2

But from whom, after all, does God hide his commandments? Did God not wish them to be proclaimed everywhere? Would that they were clear to as many as they are clear. For what is clearer than this: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind”; and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”? “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:37–40). And who is unaware of these commandments? They are known both to all the faithful and to very many unbelievers.

Why, then, does the faithful person ask that what he sees is not hidden from him, although he sees that it is not hidden even from an unbeliever? Is it because knowing God is difficult, and consequently the commandment “You shall love the Lord your God” must be difficult to understand, lest one love something in place of him? For knowledge of one’s neighbor seems easier. Every human being is the neighbor of every other human being, and where there is a common nature no remoteness of kinship need be considered.

Yet even the one who said to the Lord, “And who is my neighbor?” did not know his neighbor. For a certain man was set before him who, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers. The one who had asked the question himself judged that the man’s neighbor was the one who showed him mercy (Luke 10:29–37). Thus it became clear that, in showing mercy, no one is to be considered a stranger by the person who loves his neighbor.

But many do not even know themselves. For to know oneself—as a human being ought to become known to oneself—is not granted to everyone. How, then, does someone love his neighbor as himself if he does not know himself?

It was not without reason, therefore, that the younger son, who had departed into a distant region and there squandered his substance by living wastefully, first returned to himself before saying, “I will arise and go to my father” (Luke 15:13–18). He had wandered so far that he had even left himself behind. Yet he would not have returned to himself if he had been wholly ignorant of himself; nor would he have said, “I will arise and go to my father,” if he had been entirely ignorant of God.

Accordingly, these things are known to some extent, and they are rightly requested in order that they may be known more and more. Therefore, if we are to know how to love God, God must be known; and if a person is to know how to love his neighbor as himself, he must first love himself by loving God. But how will he be able to do this if he does not know God, and does not know himself either?

Rightly, then, he says to God, “I am an inhabitant in the earth; do not hide your commandments from me.” For the commandments are rightly hidden from those who are not inhabitants in the earth: although they hear them, they do not relish them, because they relish earthly things. But those whose way of life is in heaven (Phil. 3:19–20), insofar as they live here, are certainly pilgrims.

Let them therefore ask that God’s commandments not be hidden from them—those commandments by which they may be freed from this tenancy by loving God, with whom they will be forever, and by loving their neighbor, so that he may be there [Note: [Col. 1520] Manuscripts: *sint* (“may they be”), instead of *sit* (“may he be”).] where they themselves will be.

### 3. [verse 20]

But what is loved by loving, if love itself is not loved? Accordingly, after this inhabitant in the earth had prayed that God’s commandments should not be hidden from him—commandments in which love is prescribed, either alone or above all—he declares that he wishes to possess love for that very love, saying: “My soul has desired to desire your justifications at all times.”

This is a praiseworthy desire, not a blameworthy one. It is not of this desire that it was said, “You shall not desire” (Exod. 20:17), but of that by which the flesh desires against the spirit (Gal. 5:17). As for the good desire by which the spirit desires against the flesh, look for where it is written; you will find: “Therefore the desire of wisdom leads to the kingdom” (Wis. 6:21), and many other testimonies to good desire.

There is, however, this distinction: when good desire is mentioned, what is desired is not left unstated; but when what is desired is not added and desire alone is mentioned, it is understood to be evil. Thus, in the passage I cited, “Therefore the desire of wisdom leads to the kingdom,” if it had not added “of wisdom,” it would in no way have said, “Desire leads to the kingdom.” But when the Apostle says, “I did not know desire except when the Law said, ‘You shall not desire’” (Rom. 7:7), he does not add desire for what thing, or what one should not desire. It is certain that, when said in this way, nothing but evil desire is understood.

What, then, did this soul desire? “To desire,” he says, “your justifications at all times.” I suppose he did not yet desire them when he desired to desire them. Justifications are righteous acts—that is, works of righteousness. If even the person who already desires them does not yet possess them, how far was he from them who was still desiring to desire them? And how much farther are those who do not yet desire even this?

### 4

It is remarkable how desire itself can be desired, when that whose desire is already in us is not yet in us. For it is not some beautiful body, such as gold, or some attractive flesh, that a person can desire without possessing because it is placed outside him and is not in him. Who does not know that desire is in a human being, that longing is in a human being? Why, then, is it desired in order to be possessed, as though it were introduced from outside? Or how can its desire be possessed without the desire itself, since the desire itself is nothing other than desire? For without doubt, to long is to desire.

What is this remarkable and inexplicable sickness? And yet it exists. A sick person suffering from loss of appetite, and wishing to escape this evil, certainly desires to desire food, while he desires not to lack appetite. But this loss of appetite is an illness of the body. The desire by which he desires to desire food—that is, to be free from loss of appetite—is in the mind, not in the body. He possesses it not through the pleasure of throat and palate, which are constricted by loss of appetite [Note: [Col. 1521] Several manuscripts read *restinguitur*, “is quenched.”], but through the intention of recovering health, by which provision is made to drive away his aversion to food.

It is therefore not surprising if the mind desires that the body should desire, when the mind desires and the body does not desire. But when both belong to the mind, and both are desire, why do I desire the desire for God’s justifications? [Note: [Col. 1521] The editions read, “why do I not desire”; *not* is absent from the better manuscripts.] How do I possess in one and the same mind both the desire for this longing and not the longing itself? Or how are these two things not one?

Why do I desire to desire the justifications, rather than desire the justifications themselves more than their desire? Or how can I desire the desire for the justifications and not desire the justifications themselves, when I desire their longing because I wish to possess them? If this is so, then surely I already desire the justifications themselves. What need, then, is there for me to desire their longing, when I already possess it and perceive that I possess it? For I could not desire the longing for righteousness unless, by desiring, I desired righteousness itself.

Or is this what I said above: that the very love by which what ought to be loved is loved must also be loved, just as the love by which what ought not to be loved is loved must be hated? We hate our desire by which the flesh desires against the spirit; and what is this desire except evil love? We love our desire by which the spirit desires against the flesh; and what is this desire except good love?

When it is said, “It must be loved,” what else is said than, “It must be desired”? Accordingly, since God’s justifications are rightly desired, the desire for God’s justifications is rightly desired. This can also be expressed in another way: if God’s justifications are rightly loved, the love of God’s justifications is rightly loved.

Or is it one thing to desire and another to long? Not because desire is not longing, but because not every desire is longing. For both things that are possessed and things that are not possessed are desired. By desiring, a person enjoys the things he possesses; by longing, he desires things that are absent. What, then, is longing except desire for absent things?

But how can God’s justifications be absent, unless they are unknown? Or should they be considered absent even when they are known but not performed? For what are justifications except righteous works, not words? Thus they can fail to be desired because of the soul’s weakness; yet, in the reasoning faculty, where their usefulness and healthfulness are seen, the desire for them can itself be desired.

Often we see what ought to be done and do not do it, because it does not delight us to do it; and we desire that it should delight us. Understanding flies ahead, while the human and infirm affection follows slowly, and sometimes does not follow at all. Therefore he desired to desire what he saw to be good, wishing to possess the delight of those things whose rationale he had been able to see.

### 5

He does not say, however, “My soul desires,” but, “My soul has desired to desire your justifications.” Perhaps this inhabitant in the earth was such that he had already reached what he had desired, and was now longing for those things whose desire he recalls having once desired.

But if he was already longing for them, why did he not possess them? For nothing prevents God’s justifications from being possessed except that they are not desired, when love for them does not burn, although love for them shines.

Or did he possess them and perform them? For shortly afterward he says: “Your servant was occupied with your justifications.” But he shows by what stages, as it were, one arrives at them. First, one must see how useful and honorable they are; then one must desire their longing; finally, as light and health advance, the performance of those things must become delightful, whereas previously only their rationale was delightful.

But what follows, since this discourse has already become lengthy, will be discussed more conveniently in another sermon, with the Lord’s help.

## SERMON IX

### 1. [verse 21]

The matters that follow in this great psalm remind us to recall the cause of our misery. For after saying, “My soul has desired to desire your justifications at all times”—that is, both in prosperous circumstances and in adverse ones, because righteousness ought to delight us in labors and pains as well; and it ought not to be loved only in tranquil times, so that it is abandoned in turbulent times, but embraced at all times—he immediately added: “You have rebuked the proud; cursed are those who depart from your commandments.”

For the proud depart from God’s commandments. It is one thing not to fulfill God’s commandments through weakness or ignorance; it is another to depart from them through pride, as did those who gave birth to us into these mortal evils. They were delighted by the words, “You shall be like gods,” and thus, through this pride, they departed from God’s commandment—a commandment they knew he had given them and which they could have fulfilled with the greatest ease, without any weakness holding them back, hindering them, or delaying them.

And behold, this whole harsh and unhappy misery of mortals is, in a certain sense, an inherited rebuke of the proud. For when God said, “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:5, 9), he was not ignorant of where he was; rather, he was rebuking the proud. He did not wish to learn where he then was—that is, to what misery he had come—but, by questioning him, he admonished him while rebuking him.

Observe, however, how, after saying, “You have rebuked the proud,” he does not say, “Cursed are those who departed from your commandments,” so that only the sin of the first human beings might come to mind. Instead he says, “Cursed are those who depart.” For it was necessary that everyone should be terrified by that example, so as not to depart from the divine commandments, and that, by loving righteousness at all times, they should receive even amid the labor of this world what we lost amid the pleasure of paradise.

### 2. [verse 22]

But since the proud do not lower their necks even under such a great rebuke, and although they have been cast down under the punishment of labor and death, they are lifted up by the swelling of pride, imitating the arrogance of those who are falling and mocking the humility of those who are rising, the body of Christ prays for them when it says: “Take away from me reproach and contempt, for I have sought your testimonies.”

In Greek, testimonies are called *martyria*, a word that we now also use in Latin. Hence those who have been humbled by various sufferings for the testimony of Christ, and who have struggled for the truth even unto death, we call not *testes*—although we could do so in Latin—but, in Greek, *martyrs*.

Since you hear this word more familiarly and more pleasantly, let us understand these words as though he had said: “Take away from me reproach and contempt, for I have sought your martyrdoms”—that is, your *martyria*.

When the body of Christ says this, does it regard it as any punishment to hear reproach and contempt from the impious and proud, when it reaches the crown precisely through these things? Why, then, does it ask that something apparently grave and intolerable be taken away from it, unless, as I have said, it is praying for its enemies themselves?

It sees that it is harmful for them to cast the holy name of Christ before Christians as a reproach, and to despise, with the same pride persisting and increasing, Christ’s cross—mocked by the Jews—and the whole medicine of Christian humility, by which alone that swelling is healed through which we fell when inflated, and through which, while lying prostrate, we became still more swollen.

Let the body of Christ therefore speak. It has now learned to love its enemies. Let it say to the Lord its God: “Take away from me reproach and contempt, for I have sought your *martyria*”—that is: “Take away from me the reproach that I hear, and the contempt with which I am despised, because I have sought your *martyria*.”

For my enemies—whom you command me to love, and who are dying and perishing more and more when they despise and condemn your *martyria* in me—will certainly revive and be found if they honor your *martyria* in me.

So it has happened; we see it. Behold, the martyrdom of Christ, among human beings and in this world, is not only not a reproach but a great ornament. Behold, not only in the sight of the Lord but also in the sight of human beings, the death of his saints is now precious (Ps. 115:15). Behold, his martyrs are not only not despised but are held in the highest honor.

Behold that younger son who, for the sake of the pigs he tended—that is, the unclean demons he worshiped—was persecuting his portion, which had gone before him in the few Christians. Now, among so many and such great nations, he most devoutly proclaims the martyrs whom he had reproached, and exalts with the greatest praises those whom he had despised. He was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found (Luke 15:12–24).

In view of this great gain through the correction, conversion, and redemption of his enemies, the body of Christ said to God, “Take away from me reproach and contempt.” And as though someone asked, “Reproach concerning what? Contempt concerning what?” he adds: “For I have sought your *martyria*.”

### 3. [verses 23–24]

Where is that reproach now? Where is that contempt? They have gone away and passed away; and because those who had been lost have been found, those things have perished.

But when the Church was praying such things, it was suffering them. “For princes,” he says, “sat and spoke against me.” The persecution was severe because princes decreed it while sitting—that is, occupying judicial seats and exercising authority.

Refer this to the head himself: you will find that the Jewish leaders sat in council, seeking how they might destroy Christ (Matt. 26:3). Refer it to his body, that is, the Church: you will find that the kings of the earth devised and ordered how Christians should exist nowhere.

“For princes sat and spoke against me; but your servant was occupied with your justifications.” What kind of occupation this was, if you wish to know, understand what he added: “For your testimonies are also my meditation, and your justifications are my counsel.”

Recall what I commended above: that testimonies are *martyria*. Recall that among the Lord’s justifications none is more difficult and more wonderful than that each person should love his enemies.

Thus the body of Christ was exercised both in meditating upon its *martyria* and in loving those from whom, because of those very *martyria*, it suffered reproach, contempt, and persecutions. For, as we have already explained, it was not praying for itself but rather for them, saying: “Take away from me reproach and contempt.”

“Princes therefore sat and spoke against me; but your servant was occupied with your justifications.” How? “For your testimonies are also my meditation, and your justifications are my counsel.”
