Counsel against counsel: the counsel of the princes who sat was to destroy the martyrs they had found; the counsel of the martyrs who suffered was to find again the enemies who had been lost. The former returned evil for good; the latter, good for evil.

What wonder, then, if the former were exhausted by killing, while the latter conquered by dying? What wonder, I say, if the martyrs bore temporal death with the greatest patience before the raging nations, and the nations, through the prayers of the martyrs, were able to reach eternal life, while the body of Christ was so exercised that it both meditated upon the *martyria* and prayed good things for the evil persecutors of the martyrs?

## SERMON X

### 1. [verse 25]

There follows in this great psalm a passage that we must consider and discuss as the Lord grants: “My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word.”

What does “My soul has clung to the pavement” mean? For when he adds and says, “Give me life according to your word,” why he asks to be given life he has certainly indicated beforehand by saying, “My soul has clung to the pavement.”

Since, then, he asks to be given life because his soul has clung to the pavement, it would be surprising if something good were intended by this. The whole statement is as though he were saying: “I am dead; give me life.”

What, then, is the pavement? If we wish to understand the whole world as one great house, we see the heaven as its ceiling; the earth, therefore, will be its pavement. He wishes, then, to be rescued from earthly things and to say with the Apostle, “Our way of life is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Accordingly, to cling to earthly things is the death of the soul, and against this evil the opposite life is requested when he says, “Give me life.”

### 2

But we must see whether these words suit someone who had previously said such things that he appeared to have clung to God more than to the pavement, so that his way of life was not in earthly things but in heavenly ones.

How can someone who says, “Your servant was occupied with your justifications; your testimonies are also my meditation, and your justifications are my counsel,” be understood to have clung to earthly things? These are the words that precede; and the words that follow them are, “My soul has clung to the pavement.”

Should we therefore understand from this that, however much anyone may progress in the Lord’s justifications, he still has an affection belonging to mortal flesh for these earthly things, in which “human life upon earth is a temptation” (Job 7:1), and that, if he perseveres in progressing, he is revived daily from this death by the one who gives life, through whose grace our inner self is renewed from day to day (2 Cor. 4:16)?

When the Apostle said, “As long as we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6), and desired “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23), his soul had clung to the pavement. Hence the body itself, because it is from the earth, can not improperly be understood as the pavement. Since it is still corruptible and weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15), we rightly groan in it and say to God, “My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word.”

For we shall indeed always be with the Lord with our bodies (1 Thess. 4:12–16). But then, because they will not be corruptible and will not weigh down the souls, if we consider the matter carefully, it will not be we who cling to them, but they will cling rather to us, while we cling to God.

Hence the words of another psalm: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 72:28), so that bodies may live from us by clinging to us, while we may live from God, because it is good for us to cling to God.

The clinging of which it is said, “My soul has clung to the pavement,” does not seem to me to signify the union of flesh and soul, although some have understood it in that way, but rather the soul’s carnal affection—the affection by which the flesh desires against the spirit (Gal. 5:17).

If this is rightly understood, then the person who says, “My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word,” is not praying to be released from this body of death through the death of the body itself, something that the final day of this life—whose brevity prevents it from being prolonged indefinitely—will eventually accomplish.

Rather, he is praying that the desire by which one desires against the spirit may diminish more and more, and that the desire by which one desires against the flesh may increase more and more, until the former is consumed in us and the latter is brought to perfection through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

### 3. [verse 26]

He rightly does not say, “Give me life according to my merit,” but says, “According to your word.” What else is this than “According to your promise”? He wishes to be a son of promise, not a son of exaltation, so that, according to grace, the promise may be secure for all the offspring.

For this is the word of promise: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called.” That is: “Those who are children of the flesh are not the children of God; rather, the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (Rom. 9:7–8).

What he was in himself he confesses in what follows: “I have declared my ways, and you heard me.” Some manuscripts read, “your ways”; but more manuscripts, and especially the Greek ones, read, “my ways”—that is, evil ways.

It seems to me that he is saying: “I confessed my sins, and you heard me”—that is, so that you might forgive them. “Teach me your justifications.” I confessed my ways; you erased them. Teach me your ways.

Teach me in such a way that I may do them, not merely know what I ought to do. For just as it is said of the Lord that he did not know sin (2 Cor. 5:21), and this is understood to mean that he did not commit it, so the person who does righteousness is truly said to know righteousness.

This is the prayer of one who is progressing. For if he did not do righteousness at all, he certainly would not have said the words above: “Your servant was occupied with your justifications.” He does not wish to learn from the Lord those in which he was occupied; rather, by progressing from these to others, as though growing, he desires to reach further ones.

### 4. [verses 27–28]

Finally he adds and says: “Make me understand the way of your justifications”; or, as some manuscripts read, “Instruct me.” This is expressed more precisely in Greek as, “Make me understand” [Note: [Col. 1526] Greek: *synetison me*.].

“And I shall be exercised in your wonders.” He calls the more profound justifications, which he desires to grasp by progressing, God’s wonders.

There are therefore certain justifications of God so wondrous that human weakness may believe that those who have not experienced them cannot reach them. Hence, while laboring and in a certain sense wearied by their difficulty, he adds: “My soul has grown drowsy from weariness; strengthen me in your words.”

What does “has grown drowsy” mean except that he has cooled from the hope by which he had believed he would grasp them? “But strengthen me,” he says, “in your words, lest by growing drowsy I fall even from those things to which I already feel that I have attained. Strengthen me, therefore, in those words of yours that I already hold and already practice, so that from them I may be able to advance toward others by progressing.”

### 5. [verse 29]

What prevents a person from walking in the way of God’s justifications in such a manner that he can easily reach even those wonders? What can we suppose except that he asks in what follows that it be removed from him, saying: “Take away from me the way of iniquity”?

And because the law of works entered in so that transgression might abound (Rom. 5:20), he continues and says: “And have mercy on me by your law” [Note: [Col. 1527] So Ambrose and the manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “and have mercy on me from the law.”].

By what law, unless the law of faith? Hear the Apostle: “Where, then, is your boasting? It is excluded. By what law? By the law of works? No, but by the law of faith” (Rom. 3:27).

This is the law of faith, by which we believe and pray that it may be granted to us through grace to do what we cannot fulfill by ourselves, lest, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish our own, we fail to submit to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10:3).

In the law of works, therefore, there is the righteousness of God who commands; but in the law of faith, there is the mercy of God who comes to our aid.

### 6. [verses 30–32]

After he had said, “And have mercy on me by your law,” he somehow—if it may be said so—claims, on the basis of the benefits he has already received, the remaining benefits that he has not yet received, in order to obtain them.

For he says: “I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments. I have clung to your testimonies; Lord, do not put me to shame.”

“I have chosen the way of truth in which I might run; I have not forgotten your judgments, so that I might run. I clung to your testimonies while I was running. Lord, do not put me to shame; may I reach the goal toward which I run and arrive where I am aiming.”

“For it is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16). Finally, he continues: “I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart.”

I would not run unless you had enlarged my heart. This verse plainly explains how it was said: “I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments; I have clung to your testimonies.” For this is the running of the way of God’s commandments [Note: [Col. 1527] Lovaniensis reads: “For these are the running and the way of God’s commandments,” differing from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.].

And because he brings before the Lord his benefits rather than his own merits, it is as though someone were saying to him: “How did you run this way by choosing it, by not forgetting God’s judgments, and by clinging to his testimonies? Were you able to do these things by yourself?”

“No,” he says. “What then?” “I ran the way of your commandments,” he says, “when you enlarged my heart.”

It was not, then, through my own will, as though it needed no help from you, but “when you enlarged my heart.” The enlargement of the heart is delight in righteousness. This is God’s gift: that in his commandments we are not constricted by fear of punishment, but enlarged by love and delight in righteousness.

For he promises us this breadth when he says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Cor. 6:16). How broad is the place where God walks! In this breadth, love is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5).

Hence it is also said: “And let your waters run freely in your streets” (Prov. 5:16). For *platea* (“street”) takes its name from the Greek word for breadth, since in Greek “broad” is called πλατύ (*platy*).

These are the waters concerning which the Lord cries out: “Let the one who thirsts come to me. The one who believes in me: rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” And the Evangelist, explaining what he had said, adds: “Now he said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive” (John 7:37–39).

Much could be said about this enlargement of the heart, but the length of this sermon is already being opposed by its own length.

## SERMON XI

### 1. [verse 33]

In this great psalm there follows a passage that, with the Lord’s help, must be considered and discussed: “Establish a law for me, Lord, the way of your justifications, and I shall seek it always.”

The Apostle says: “The law is not established for the righteous, but for the unrighteous and the disobedient,” and so forth; and, concluding what he says there, he adds: “And if there is anything else contrary to sound doctrine, which is according to the gospel of the glory of the blessed God, which has been entrusted to me” (1 Tim. 1:9–11).

Was this person, then, who says, “Establish a law for me, Lord,” such as the people for whom blessed Paul says the law was established? God forbid. For if he were such, he would not have said above, “I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart.”

What does he mean by praying that the Lord establish a law for him, if the law is not established for the righteous? Is it not established for the righteous in the way in which it was established for a rebellious people, on tablets of stone (Exod. 31:18), and not on tablets of hearts of flesh (2 Cor. 3:3); according to the old covenant from Mount Sinai, which gives birth to slavery (Gal. 4:24), and not according to the new covenant? [Note: [Col. 1528] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “but according to” (*sed secundum*); Ambrose and the manuscripts more correctly read “not according to” (*non secundum*).]

Of the new covenant it is written through the prophet Jeremiah:

> “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah—not according to the covenant which I established with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord. For this is the covenant which I will establish with the house of Israel: After those days, says the Lord, I will give my laws into their minds, and I will write them on their hearts” (Jer. 31:31–33).

Behold how this person wishes the Lord to establish a law for him—not as it was established for the unrighteous and disobedient, belonging to the old covenant, on tablets of stone, but as it is given to the holy children of the free woman—that is, of the heavenly Jerusalem—the children of promise and children of the eternal inheritance, by the Holy Spirit as the finger of God, in the mind and written on the heart.

It is not a law which they hold in memory and neglect in life, but one which they know by understanding and perform by loving, in the breadth of love and not in the narrowness of fear.

For the person who performs the work of the law out of fear of punishment and not out of love of righteousness certainly performs it unwillingly. What someone does unwillingly, he would prefer, if it could be done, not to be commanded at all. Accordingly, he is not a friend but rather an enemy of the law he would prefer not to exist; and the one who is impure in will is not cleansed by the work [Note: [Col. 1528] So Ambrose and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “by thought and will.”].

Such a person cannot say what this man said in the preceding verses: “I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart,” because that enlargement signifies love, which, according to the Apostle, is the fullness of the law (Rom. 13:10).

## 2.

Why, then, does he still ask that the law be imposed upon him—when, if it had not been imposed upon him, he certainly would not have run along the way of God’s commandments in the breadth of his heart? But since he speaks as one making progress, and knows that his progress is God’s gift, what else does he ask when he asks that the law be imposed upon him, except that he may progress in it more and more? It is as though you were holding a full cup and began giving it to someone thirsty: he both drinks by imbibing and asks by desiring.

But the law imposed upon the unjust and disobedient on tablets of stone makes them guilty of transgression, not children of the promise. Yet even the person who remembers it but does not love it is guilty in the same way; for, as it were, a stone is inscribed for him in his memory—not to adorn him, but to weigh him down: the burden of a load, not the title of an honor.

This man, however, called this law the way of God’s justifications. And there is no other way of his commandments than the one along which he had already said that he ran, when his heart was enlarged. Thus he both ran and runs, until he reaches the prize of God’s heavenly calling. Finally, after saying, “Impose your law upon me, O Lord, the way of your justifications,” he added, “and I shall always seek it.” For what does he seek that he already possesses, except that he possesses it by doing and seeks it by making progress?

## 3.

But what does “always” mean? Does seeking have no end, as it is said, “His praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm XXXIII, 2), because praising him will have no end? For we shall not cease to praise God when we have reached his eternal kingdom, since we read, “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; throughout the ages of ages they shall praise you” (Psalm LXXXIII, 5).

Or was “always” said to mean as long as one lives here, because progress continues for that long, whereas after this life the one who made good progress here is perfected there? Thus it was said of certain women, “always learning,” but of them in a bad sense, since he immediately added, “and never arriving at knowledge of the truth” (II Timothy III, 7). Whoever, however, continually makes progress here toward what is better reaches, by progressing, that place where he will no longer progress, because he remains perfect without end.

Yet it was not said of those women, “always learning,” so that they would continue after death to learn empty and fruitless things, when such teachings are followed not by study but by everlasting punishments. Here, therefore, God’s law is sought as long as one progresses in it, both by knowing and by loving; but there its fullness remains to be enjoyed, not to be sought.

The same is true of the saying, “Seek his face always” (Psalm CIV, 4). Where does “always” apply, if not here? For surely we shall not seek God’s face there, where we shall see face to face (I Corinthians XIII, 12).

Or, if it is rightly said that what is loved without weariness, and what one acts so as not to lose, is sought, then we shall seek God’s law—that is, God’s truth—always, entirely without end. For in this very psalm it is said, “And your law is truth.” It is sought now so that it may be held; then it will be held so that it may not be abandoned. Thus it is said of the Spirit of God that he searches all things, even the depths of God (I Corinthians II, 10)—not, of course, so that he may find what he does not know, but because he leaves absolutely nothing unknown.

## 4. [verse 34]

The grace of God, therefore, is especially commended to us when one who already knew the law according to the letter asks the Lord to impose it upon him. But “the letter kills, while the spirit gives life” (II Corinthians III, 6). He therefore prays that, through the Spirit [Note: [Column 1530] The editions read “through the Holy Spirit.” “Holy” is absent from the manuscripts.], he may do what he knew through the letter, lest the knowledge of a commandment that he does not observe bring upon him also the guilt of transgression.

Indeed, even in order to know the law as it ought to be known—that is, to understand what it means, why it was imposed upon those who would not keep it, and what benefit there is even in the fact that “the law entered in so that the trespass might increase” (Romans V, 20)—no one comprehends these things unless he has received understanding from the Lord. Hence this man adds and says, “Give me understanding, and I shall search your law, and keep it with my whole heart.”

For when someone has searched the law and reached its heights, on which the whole law depends, he must certainly love God with his whole heart, his whole soul, and his whole mind, and his neighbor as himself. “On these two commandments,” he says, “the whole Law and the Prophets depend” (Matthew XXII, 37–40). This is what he appears to have promised when he said, “And I shall keep it with my whole heart.”

## 5. [verse 35]

But since even this is of little avail through one’s own powers, unless one is helped by him who commands, so as to do what he commands, he says, “Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it.” My will is not enough for me unless you yourself lead me in what I have desired.

And certainly this is the path—that is, the way of God’s commandments—which he had already said that he ran after his heart had been enlarged by him. He calls it a path for this reason also: “Narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matthew VII, 14); and although it is narrow, no one runs along it unless his heart has been enlarged.

## 6. [verse 36]

But since he is still making progress and still running, he seeks divine assistance by which he may be led, because it is “not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans IX, 16). Finally, because God himself also works in us the willing [Note: [Column 1530] Thus Am. and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain read, “works in all good people.”]—for “the will is prepared by the Lord”—he continues and says, “Incline my heart toward your testimonies, and not toward greed.”

What does it mean to have one’s heart inclined toward something, except to will it? He therefore both willed it and prayed that he might will it. He willed it when he said, “Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it”; but he prayed that he might will it when he said, “Incline my heart toward your testimonies, and not toward greed.” He therefore prays that he may progress in that very will.

And what are God’s testimonies except those by which he himself bears witness to himself? Things are proved by testimonies; therefore God’s justifications and God’s commandments are proved by God’s testimonies. Whatever God wishes to persuade us of, he persuades us by his own testimonies. This man asks that his heart be inclined toward them, and not toward greed.

For God deals with us through his testimonies so that we may worship him freely; this is obstructed by greed, the root of all evils. Here he uses a Greek word from which general greed can be understood, by which each person desires more than is sufficient: πλέον (*pleon*) means “more” in Latin, and ἔξις (*hexis*) means “habit,” from the verb “to have.” Thus πλεονεξία (*pleonexia*) was named from “having more.” Some Latin interpreters in this passage have translated it as *emolumentum* (“gain”), others as *utilitas* (“advantage”), but those who translated it as *avaritia* (“greed”) did better.

The Apostle says, “For greed is the root of all evils” (I Timothy VI, 10). But in the Greek from which these words were translated into our language, the Apostle does not read πλεονεξία (*pleonexia*), which occurs in this passage of the psalm, but φιλαργυρία (*philargyria*), a word signifying love of money.

The Apostle should nevertheless be understood to have designated a genus by means of a species: by love of money he meant universal and general greed, which truly is the root of all evils. For the first human beings would not have been deceived and cast down by the serpent unless they had wished to possess more than they had received and to be more than they had been made. For the serpent had promised this, saying, “You shall be like gods” (Genesis III, 5). Thus they were overthrown by this πλεονεξία (*pleonexia*). By wanting to have more than they had received, they lost even what they had received.

A trace of this truth, which is scattered everywhere [Note: [Column 1531] Thus several manuscripts. The editions read, “by the laws that are scattered everywhere.” The word “laws” is absent from all the manuscripts.], has also been detected in forensic law, where it has been established that a person loses a case by claiming too much: that is, whoever claims more than is owed to him loses even what was owed to him.

All greed is cut away from us if God is worshiped freely. To this the holy Job was challenged by the enemy himself in the trial of temptation, when he said of him, “Does Job worship God for nothing?” (Job I, 9). The Devil thought that, in worshiping God, the righteous man’s heart was inclined toward greed, and that, for the sake of gain or advantage from the temporal possessions with which the Lord had enriched him, he served God like a hired laborer in exchange for such payment. But when he was tested, it became clear that he worshiped God freely.

If, therefore, we do not have our hearts inclined toward greed, we worship God only for God’s sake, so that God himself is the reward of his worship. Let us love him in himself; let us love him in ourselves; let us love him in our neighbors, whom we love as ourselves, whether they possess him or [Note: [Column 1531] Thus Am. and the manuscripts. Erasmus reads, “whether or not they seem to possess him.” Louvain reads, “whether or not they possess him.”] may come to possess him.

Since this is bestowed upon us by him who grants it, the words are therefore addressed to him: “Incline my heart toward your testimonies, and not toward greed.” But what follows must be treated in another discourse.

# SERMON XII

## 1. [verse 37]

The psalm that we have undertaken to explain continues: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity; give me life in your way.” Vanity and truth are opposites. The desire for this world is vanity; but Christ, who frees us from this world, is truth. He is also the way in which this man wishes to be given life, because he is also life. For he himself says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

But what does “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity” mean? As long as we are in this world, can we not see vanity? Every creature is subject to vanity, which is understood to exist in humanity; and, “All is vanity: what abundance has a person in all his labor with which he labors under the sun?” (Ecclesiastes I, 2–3).

Or perhaps this man prays that his life may not be under the sun, where all is vanity, but may be in him in whom he asks to be given life? For he ascended not only above the sun but above all the heavens, “so that he might fill all things” (Ephesians IV, 10). And those who do not hear the Apostle’s words in vain live in him rather than under the sun: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians III, 1–3).

Therefore, if our life is where truth is, our life is not under the sun, where vanity is. But we possess this great good more in hope than in reality. In accordance with our hope the blessed Apostle spoke these words; for after saying, “The creature was subjected to vanity,” he added, “not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope.”

In hope, therefore—that is, in the hope that we shall cleave to the contemplation of truth—we are meanwhile subject to vanity. For every creature—spiritual, animal, and bodily—is in humanity; indeed, it is humanity. Humanity sinned willingly and became hostile to truth; but, so that it might be punished deservedly, it was subjected to vanity unwillingly.

A little later the Apostle says, “And not only this, but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit”—that is, although we do not yet possess the whole of what we are, but only that part by which we are better than animals, we are subject to God, not to vanity, through the first fruits of the Spirit—“we ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body. For in hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.”

As long, then, as we are here according to the flesh, whose adoption and redemption we still await patiently in hope, so long are we subject to vanity according to that by which we are under the sun. As long, therefore, as we are in this condition, how can we fail to see the vanity to which we are subject in hope?

What, then, does this man mean when he says, “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity”? Does he ask, not that what we bear in hope may be fulfilled in this life, but that he may be in that condition which can someday be fulfilled in him, when he shall be freed from the slavery of corruption, in spirit, soul, and body, into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Romans VIII, 20–25), where he will no longer see vanity?

## 2.

These words can indeed be understood in this way, without departing from the rule of faith. But there is another meaning here, which I confess pleases me more.

The Lord says in the Gospel, “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark. Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be?” Accordingly, when we do something good, it matters greatly with what object of contemplation we do it.

Our action must be evaluated not by the action itself but by its end: we must consider not only whether what we do is good, but especially whether the reason for which we do it is good. He asks that these eyes with which we contemplate why we do what we do be turned away, lest they see vanity—that is, lest he regard this as the reason for which he acts when he does something good.

In this vanity the love of human praise holds a prominent place. On account of it, many people who were called great in this world and greatly praised in the cities of the nations performed great deeds, seeking glory not with God but with human beings. For this reason they appeared to live prudently, courageously, temperately, and justly. When they attained it, they received their reward: vain people, a vain reward.

Wishing to turn the eyes of his people away from this vanity, the Lord says, “Take care not to perform your righteousness before human beings in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.” Then, as he explained certain parts of righteousness—giving alms, prayer, and fasting—he everywhere warned that none of these things should be done for human glory. Everywhere he says that those who act for this reason have received their reward (Matthew VI, 1–23): not the eternal reward stored up with the Father for the saints, but the temporal reward sought by those who contemplate vanity in their works.

This is not because human praise itself is blameworthy. For what could people desire more than that others should approve what ought to be imitated? The fault lies in doing good works for the sake of that praise—that is, in looking to vanity in one’s works.

Even however much praise comes to a righteous person from human beings, the end of his good should not be found there. That praise too must be referred to the praise of God, for whose sake the truly good do good works, since they become good not from themselves but from him.

Indeed, in the same sermon the Lord had already said to them, “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V, 16). When we do something good, we ought to regard the end he established—that is, the glory of God—if our eyes are turned away from vanity.

The end of a good work, therefore, must not be human praise. Rather, we must correct human praise itself and refer everything to the praise of God, from whom we receive whatever is praised in us without the praiser’s error.

If it is vain to do good for the sake of human praise, how much vainer is it to do good for the sake of acquiring, increasing, or retaining money, or for the sake of any similar temporal advantage that comes to us from outside? For “all is vanity: what abundance has a person in all his labor with which he labors under the sun?”

Finally, we ought not to perform our good works for the sake of temporal health, but rather for the sake of the eternal health that we hope for, where we shall enjoy an unchanging good—one that will come to us from God, or rather, which God himself will be for us.

For if God’s saints performed good works for the sake of temporal health, Christ’s martyrs would never have completed the good work of confession at the cost of that very health. But they received help in tribulation, without regarding vanity, because “vain is the salvation of humanity” (Psalm LIX, 13). They did not desire the day of human beings (Jeremiah XVII, 16), because “humanity has been made like vanity; its days pass away like a shadow” (Psalm CXLIII, 4).

## 3. [verse 38]

When God is asked to grant us what appears to lie within our power—that is, the turning away of our eyes from seeing vanity—what is commended if not his grace?

Some people did not turn their eyes away from that vanity because they thought that they made themselves righteous and good, and they loved human glory more than God’s glory (John XII, 43). They are themselves human beings who took excessive pleasure in themselves and presumed upon the powers of their own free choice. Yet even this vanity and presumption is “a striving after wind” (Ecclesiastes VI, 9).

After saying, “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity; give me life in your way”—a way that is not vanity but truth—he then added, “Establish your word for your servant unto your fear” [Note: [Column 1534] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint. The editions read, “in your fear.”].

What else does this mean than, “Grant me that I may do what you say”? God’s word is not established in those who oppose it within themselves by doing the opposite; it is established in those in whom it remains immovable.

God therefore establishes his word in his fear for those to whom he gives the spirit of his fear—not that fear of which the Apostle says, “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear” (Romans VIII, 15), for “perfect love drives out fear” (I John IV, 18), but the fear of which the prophet says, “the spirit of the fear of God” (Isaiah XI, 3): the pure fear that “endures forever and ever” (Psalm XVIII, 10), the fear of offending the one whom one loves.

An adulterous woman fears her husband in one way; a chaste wife fears him in another: the adulterous woman fears that he will come, the chaste woman that he will leave her.

## 4. [verse 39]

“Take away,” he says, “my reproach, which I have suspected, because your judgments are sweet.”

Who is there who merely suspects his own reproach, and does not know his own reproach more clearly than anyone else’s? A person can rather suspect another’s reproach, since he is ignorant of what he suspects. But in one’s own reproach there is not mere suspicion but knowledge, where conscience speaks.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “My reproach, which I have suspected”? Clearly, this too must be drawn from the preceding meaning. As long as a person does not turn his eyes away lest they see vanity, he suspects in others what is being done in himself: he believes that another acts for the same reason for which he worships God or performs good works.

People can see what we do, but the object of our contemplation when we act is hidden. Therefore an opportunity for suspicions is created, so that a person dares to judge what is hidden in others and rashly suspects things that are usually false—or, even if true, still unknown.

For this reason, when the Lord spoke about the very end for which we ought to perform righteousness, turning our eyes away from contemplating vanity, he warned us not to perform good works for the sake of human praise, saying, “Take care not to perform your righteousness before human beings in order to be seen by them.”

He warned us not to act for the sake of money, saying, “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth,” and, “You cannot serve God and Mammon.” He warned us not to act for the sake of necessary food and clothing, saying, “Do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will wear” (Matthew VI, 1, 19, 24, 25).

And after giving all these warnings, since we can suspect that those whom we see living justly, although we do not see the end for which they act, perform good works for some such reason, he immediately added, “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Matthew VII, 1).

Thus here too, after saying, “Take away my reproach, which I have suspected,” he added, “because your judgments are sweet”—that is, your judgments are true. For the lover of truth cries out that what is true is sweet.

Human judgments about what is hidden in others, however, are not sweet, because they are rash. Therefore he called the reproach that he had suspected about others his own reproach. For they do not understand what the Apostle says, “Comparing themselves with themselves” (II Corinthians X, 12). A person more readily suspects in another what he feels in himself.

He was therefore asking that this reproach be taken away from him: what he had felt in himself and suspected in others, so that he might not be like the Devil, who suspected concerning the hidden things of holy Job that he did not worship God freely. He asked that Job be tested in order to discover a charge to bring against him (Job I, 9–11).

## 5. [verse 40]

But when a person readily suspects another’s reproach, nothing but rivalry is at work: a good work cannot be criticized, because it asserts what is evident, but the purpose for which it is done is criticized, because it does not reveal what is hidden. Thus anyone readily suspects another of wrongdoing, failing to see what is concealed and envying what stands out [Note: [Column 1535] Thus several manuscripts. Others read, “anyone may suspect, and so forth.” Erasmus and Louvain read, “no one ought to suspect, failing to see what is concealed and not envying what stands out.” In Am. and all the manuscripts, the words appear without the negation, “and envying what stands out.”].

Against this evil—by which each person readily suspects an evil that he does not see in another—there must be charity, which “does not envy” (I Corinthians XIII, 4). The Lord especially commends it, saying, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another”; and, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII, 34–35). Speaking of love of God and neighbor, he says, “On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend” (Matthew XXII, 40).

Hence, against the reproach of his own suspicion, which he desires to have removed, this man says, “Behold, I have desired your commandments; give me life in your righteousness.”

Behold, I have desired with my whole heart, my whole soul, and my whole mind to love you and my neighbor as myself. Give me life not in my righteousness but in yours—that is, fill me with this charity that I have desired. Help me to do what you commend; grant yourself what you command.

“Give me life in your righteousness,” because in myself I had what would cause me to die, but I find nowhere except in you that by which I may live. Your righteousness is Christ, “who was made for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption; so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord’” (I Corinthians I, 30–31).

And in him I find your commandments, which I have desired, so that in your righteousness—that is, in him—you may give me life. For he is the Word, God; and “the Word became flesh” so that he might also be my neighbor (John I, 14).

# SERMON XIII

## 1. [verse 41]

This passage must be joined to the preceding sermon, which we recently delivered on the psalm that is the longest of all, concerning the words that follow. These are the words: “And let your mercy come upon me, O Lord.”

This sentence appears attached to the preceding one. For he does not say merely, “Let it come upon me,” but “And let it come.” The preceding statement is, “Behold, I have desired your commandments; give me life in your righteousness.” Then follows, “And let your mercy come upon me, O Lord.”

What, then, does he ask here except that, through his mercy, he may do the commandments he has desired—the commandments he himself gave? He explains, in a certain sense, what he meant by “Give me life in your righteousness,” when he adds, “And let your mercy come upon me, O Lord, your salvation according to your word”—that is, according to your promise.

The Apostle wishes us to understand that we are children of the promise (Romans IX, 8), so that we may not suppose that what we are is our own, but may attribute everything to God’s grace. For “Christ was made for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption; so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord’” (I Corinthians I, 30–31).

Therefore, when he says, “Give me life in your righteousness,” he certainly desires to be given life in Christ; and this is the mercy that he asks to come upon him. Christ himself is also God’s salvation. By this word he explained what mercy he meant when he said, “And let your mercy come upon me, O Lord.”

If, then, we ask what this mercy is, let us hear what follows: “Your salvation according to your word.” For this was promised by the one who “calls into existence the things that do not exist as though they did” (Romans IV, 17). Those to whom the promise was made did not yet exist, so that no one might boast of merits. And those who were promised were themselves also promised, so that the whole body of Christ might say, “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Corinthians XV, 10).

## 2. [verse 42]

“And I shall answer,” he says, “those who reproach me with a word.”

It is ambiguous whether this means “those who reproach me with the Word” or “I shall answer with a word.” But either reading speaks of Christ [Note: [Column 1536] The manuscripts read *sonet* (“may sound”).]. For they reproach Christ to us—those for whom he is crucified either as a stumbling block or as foolishness (I Corinthians I, 23)—ignorant that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” the Word who “was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God” (John I, 14, 1).

Even if they do not reproach the Word himself, because he is hidden from them and his divinity is not recognized by those who despise his weakness on the cross, let us nevertheless answer those who reproach us with the Word, and let us not be terrified or ashamed by their reproach.

For if they had known the Word, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (I Corinthians II, 8). But the one upon whom God’s mercy has come answers those who reproach him with the Word: that is, his salvation comes to protect, not to crush.

For he will come to crush some people, those who now, while they despise his humility, are shattered by stumbling against him. Thus he says in the Gospel, “Whoever falls upon that stone will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Luke XX, 18).

Those who reproach us stumble and fall upon him. But so that we may not stumble and fall, let us not fear their reproaches; instead, let us answer them with the Word.

“This is the word of faith that we proclaim. For if you believe,” he says, “in your heart that Jesus is Lord, and confess with your mouth that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” (Romans X, 8–10).

It is not enough to have Christ in one’s heart and refuse to confess him out of fear of reproach. Those who reproach us must be answered with the Word. So that the martyrs might do this, it was promised and said to them, “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew X, 20).

Therefore, after saying, “I shall answer those who reproach me with a word,” he immediately continues, “because I have hoped in your words”—that is, in your promises.

## 3. [verse 43]

But since many who belonged to the very body whose words these are were unable, under the heavy pressure of persecution, to endure reproach, and denied Christ by falling away, the psalm therefore continues: “And do not take the word of truth utterly from my mouth.”

He speaks from his own mouth because the unity of the body is speaking. Among its members are counted even those who fell away for a time by denying Christ but later came back to life through repentance, or even regained, through restored confession, the martyr’s crown that they had lost.

Therefore, the word of truth was not taken utterly from the mouth of Peter, in whom the Church was represented, or—as some manuscripts read—not taken “altogether.” For although he denied Christ for a time, disturbed by fear, he was restored through weeping (Matthew XXVI, 70–75) and later crowned through confession.

Thus the whole body of Christ speaks—that is, the entire holy Church. Whether because, although many denied him, strong people remained who would fight for the truth until death, or because many of those who had denied him were restored, the word of truth was not taken utterly from its mouth.

When he says, “Do not take away,” this must be understood as, “Do not allow it to be taken away.” For this reason we pray, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew VI, 13). The Lord himself said to Peter, “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII, 32)—that is, that the word of truth might not be taken utterly from your mouth.

The psalm continues, “Because I have hoped in your judgments”; or, as some translators rendered the Greek more carefully, “I have hoped beyond hope” [Note: [Column 1537] Greek: *epēlpisa*.]. Although this word is less customary as a compound, it fulfills the need to interpret the truth.

We must therefore examine the meaning of this passage more attentively, so that, with God’s help, we may understand what is meant by “I have hoped in your words” and “I have hoped beyond hope in your judgments.”

“I shall answer,” he says, “those who reproach me with a word, because I have hoped in your words”—that is, because you yourself promised this to me.

“And do not take away the word of truth from my mouth utterly, because I have hoped beyond hope in your judgments”—that is, your judgments, by which you correct and scourge me, not only do not take away my hope but even increase it, because “the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews XII, 6).

Behold, the holy and humble in heart, presuming upon you, did not fail in persecutions. Behold also those who, presuming upon themselves, fell away, yet belonged to the same body: when they came to know themselves, they wept and found your grace more firmly, because they lost their pride.

Therefore, “Do not take away the word of truth from my mouth utterly, because I have hoped beyond hope in your judgments.”

## 4. [verse 44]

“And I shall keep your law always”—that is, if you do not take the word of truth from my mouth, I shall always keep your law.

“Throughout the age and throughout the age of the age”: this shows what he meant by “always.” Sometimes “always” means “as long as one lives here,” but this is not what “throughout the age and throughout the age of the age” means. It has been translated better in this way than as some manuscripts have it, “forever and throughout the age of the age,” since they could not say “and throughout the eternal eternity.”

This law must therefore be understood as the law of which the Apostle says, “The fullness of the law is love” (Romans XIII, 10). This law will be kept by the saints, from whose mouth the word of truth is not taken—that is, by the very Church of Christ—not only in this age, meaning until this age comes to an end, but also in the other age, which is called “the age of the age.”

For there too we shall not receive the commandments of the law, as we do here, so that we may keep them. Rather, we shall keep the fullness of the law itself, as I have said, without any fear of sinning, because when we see God we shall love him more fully, and we shall love our neighbor because “God will be all in all” (I Corinthians XV, 28). Nor will there be any room for a false suspicion concerning anyone, where no one will be hidden from anyone else.

# SERMON XIV

## 1. [verse 45]

The preceding verses of this psalm contain a prayer; but the verses that follow, which we must now discuss, contain a narrative.

Earlier, the man of God was asking for the assistance of God’s grace when he said, “Give me life in your righteousness,” and, “Let your mercy come upon me, O Lord,” along with other similar statements above and below.

Now, however, he says: “And I walked in breadth, because I sought your commandments. And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed. And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved. And I lifted up my hands toward your commandments, which I loved; and I was exercised in your justifications.”

Here the words belong to one narrating, not to one asking: as though, having obtained what he had asked for, he were confessing in praise of God what the Lord’s mercy—which he had asked to come upon him—had made him.

For he did not join these words to the preceding ones in such a way as to say: “And do not take away the word of truth from my mouth utterly, because I have hoped beyond hope in your judgments, and I shall keep your law always, throughout the age and throughout the age of the age, and I shall walk in breadth because I sought your commandments, and I shall speak of your testimonies before kings, and I shall not be ashamed,” and the rest in the same manner.

In that form, the following words would appear to have been connected with the preceding ones. But he says, “And I walked in breadth.” Here the conjunction—that is, “and”—has been placed, as it were, incongruously, because he does not say, “And I shall walk,” as he said, “And I shall keep your law always.”

Or certainly, if “I shall keep your law” is spoken in the optative mood, he does not say, “And may I walk in breadth,” as though he had desired and requested both; instead, he says, “And I walked in breadth.”

If this conjunction were absent, and the sentence were introduced freely and separately from the preceding connection—“I walked in breadth”—nothing here should disturb the reader because of an unusual manner of speech or lead him to suppose that some hidden meaning had to be sought.

Clearly, therefore, he wanted what he did not say to be understood: namely, that he had been heard. Then he added what he had become, as though he were saying: “When I prayed for these things, you heard me; and I walked in breadth,” followed by the other statements that he connected in this manner.

2. What, then, is “And I walked in a broad place,” except that I walked in love, which has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5)? He walked in this broad place who said, “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:11). This love is wholly and completely contained in those two commandments—namely, love of God and love of neighbor—upon which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:40). Accordingly, here too, when he had said, “And I walked in a broad place,” he added the reason, saying, “Because I sought your commandments.” Some manuscripts, however, do not read “commandments” but “testimonies.” Yet we find “commandments” in more manuscripts, and especially in the Greek ones. Who would doubt that this language, as the earlier one from which these words were translated, ought to be trusted more?

If, then, we wish to know how he sought these commandments, or how they are to be sought, let us attend to what the good Teacher, Master, and Giver says: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.” A little later he says: “If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (ibid. 7:7, 11). Here he clearly shows that what he had said—“Ask, seek, knock”—refers only to the persistence of petition, that is, of prayer.

Another Evangelist, however, does not say, “He will give good things to those who ask him”—things that can be understood in many ways, whether bodily or spiritual—but removes the ambiguity and carefully expresses what the Lord wished us to ask for earnestly and persistently. He says: “How much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke 11:13). This is the Spirit through whom love is poured into our hearts, so that by loving God and our neighbor we may fulfill the divine commandments. This is the Spirit in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15).

Therefore, it is he himself whom we desire to receive who makes us ask; it is he himself whom we long to find who makes us seek; it is he himself whom we strive to reach who makes us knock. The Apostle teaches this. While he says that in the Holy Spirit we cry, “Abba, Father,” he says again elsewhere, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4:6). How do we cry if he himself cries within us, unless he makes us cry when he begins to dwell in us? The Spirit received therefore also brings it about that he is sought through asking, seeking, and knocking, so that he may be received more abundantly.

Whether one asks that one may live well, or that one may conduct oneself well, “all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8:14). Thus he says, “I walked in a broad place, because I sought your commandments.” He had sought and found them because he had asked for and received the good Spirit, through whom, having been made good, he might do good things, from the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6).

[Col. 1540] 3. [v. 46.] “And I spoke,” he says, “of your testimonies in the presence of kings, and I was not ashamed”—like one who had asked and received the ability to answer those who reproached him with a word, so that the word of truth would not be taken from his mouth. Thus, fighting for it even unto death, he was not ashamed to speak of it in the presence of kings.

The testimonies of which he says he spoke are called in Greek *martyria*, a word that we now also use in Latin. Hence the term “martyrs” was derived, those to whom Jesus foretold that they would confess him before kings (Matt. 10:18).

4. [vv. 47–48.] “And I meditated,” he says, “on your commandments, which I loved, and I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I loved”—or, as some manuscripts read in both verses, “which I loved greatly,” “exceedingly,” or “very much,” as seemed appropriate for translating the Greek σφόδρα (*sphodra*).

He loved God’s commandments through that by which he walked in a broad place—namely, through the Holy Spirit, through whom love itself is poured out and the hearts of the faithful are enlarged. He loved them both by thinking and by doing. With regard to thought, he says, “And I meditated on your commandments”; with regard to action, “And I lifted up my hands to your commandments.” To both statements he added, “which I loved,” for “the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart” (1 Tim. 1:5).

When God’s commandment becomes an action through this end—that is, through the contemplation of this reality—it is then truly a good work; and then the hands are lifted up, because what they are lifted toward is above. Therefore, speaking of love itself, the Apostle says, “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12:31); and elsewhere, “to know the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge” (Eph. 3:19).

For if a reward of earthly happiness is sought from the work of God’s commandments, the hands are lowered rather than lifted, because that work seeks earthly benefits, which are not above but below. To both thought and action pertains what follows: “And I exercised myself in your ordinances.” More interpreters preferred this rendering to “I rejoiced” or “I prattled,” which some translated from the Greek ἠδολέσχουν (*ēdoleschoun*). A person exercises himself in God’s ordinances joyfully, and in a certain way prattles about them, when he keeps the commandments he loves with delight both in thought and in action.

SERMON XV

1. [v. 49.] Let us consider how much the Lord gives, and let us examine these verses of this great psalm: “Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope. This has consoled me in my humiliation, because your word has given me life.”

Does forgetfulness fall upon God as it does upon a human being? Why, then, is he told, “Remember”? Although in other passages of Holy Scripture the very word is used, as in, “Why have you forgotten me?” (Ps. 41:10), and “You will forget our poverty” (Ps. 44:24), and God himself says through the Prophet, “I will forget all his iniquities” (Ezek. 18:22), and this is read frequently elsewhere, such expressions are not understood in God as they occur in human beings.

For just as God is said to repent when he changes the course of events contrary to human expectation, though his plan has not changed—because “the plan of the Lord remains forever” (Ps. 32:11)—so he is said to forget when his help or promised gift appears to be delayed, or when he seems not to repay sinners according to their deserts, or when something of this kind occurs, as though what is hoped for or feared and does not happen had slipped from his memory. Such expressions are used in a figurative manner that moves human emotion, although God does these things according to a settled disposition, without defective memory, obscured understanding, or changed will.

When, therefore, he is told, “Remember,” the desire of the one praying is displayed and extended, because he is asking for what was promised. God is not being reminded, as though the matter had escaped his mind. “Remember,” he says, “your word to your servant”—that is, fulfill your promise to your servant—“in which you gave me hope”—that is, by that word, because you promised, you caused me to hope.

2. [v. 50.] “This has consoled me in my humiliation.” This refers, of course, to the hope given to the humble, as Scripture says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Pet. 5:5). Hence the Lord himself also says with his own mouth, “For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11; 18:14).

Here we may also rightly understand that humiliation which does not consist in a person humbling himself by confessing sins and not claiming righteousness for himself, but in being humbled by some tribulation or degradation deserved by his pride, or in having his patience exercised and tested. Hence this psalm says a little later, “Before I was humbled, I went astray.” And in the Book of Wisdom: “In pain endure, and in your humiliation have patience; for gold and silver are tested in the fire, but acceptable people in the furnace of humiliation” (Sir. 2:4–5). When it says “acceptable,” it means that hope was given there to console them in their humiliation.

When the Lord Jesus foretold to his disciples that this humiliation would come from persecutors, he did not leave them without hope. Rather, he gave them this consolation, saying, “By your patience you will possess your souls”; and, concerning the very body that enemies could kill and, as it were, utterly destroy, he said, “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:19, 18).

This hope was given to the body of Christ, which is the Church, so that it might be consoled in its humiliation. Because of this hope the Apostle Paul also says, “But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience” (Rom. 8:25). This is hope for eternal rewards.

There is also another hope that greatly consoles in the humiliation of tribulation. It has been given to the saints in God’s word, which promises the help of grace, so that no one may fail. Concerning this hope [Note: [Col. 1541] Am. Er. and all manuscripts, *re*.], the Apostle says: “God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also make a way out, so that you may be able to endure” (1 Cor. 10:13).

The Savior also gave this hope with his own mouth when he said, “This night Satan asked to sift you like wheat; but I prayed for you, Peter, that your faith might not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). He gave the same hope in the prayer that he taught, where he instructed us to say, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13). In a certain sense, he promised that he would give his endangered servants what he wished those who pray to ask for.

This psalm, then, should surely be understood as speaking especially of this hope: “This has consoled me in my humiliation, because your word has given me life.” Those who translated it more explicitly used not “word” but “utterance,” for the Greek has λόγιον (*logion*), which means “utterance,” not λόγος (*logos*), which means “word.”

3. [v. 51.] It follows: “The proud acted very wickedly; but I did not turn aside from your law.” By “the proud” he intended the persecutors of the godly. Therefore he added, “But I did not turn aside from your law,” because their persecution compelled him to turn aside from it.

He says that they acted extremely wickedly because they were not merely impious themselves but also forced the godly to become impious. In this humiliation—that is, in this tribulation—hope consoled him: the hope given in the word of God, which promised help so that the faith of the martyrs would not fail, together with the presence of his Spirit, who imparted strength to those laboring, so that, escaping the snare of the hunters, they might say: “If the Lord had not been among us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. 123:2–3).

4. Or does he perhaps mean by “This has consoled me in my humiliation” that humiliation by which humanity has been cast down and thrown into death because of that sin committed so disastrously in the happiness of paradise?

In this humiliation, in which humanity was made like vanity and its days pass away like a shadow (Ps. 144:4), all are children of wrath unless they are reconciled to God through the Mediator—those who were predestined for eternal salvation before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4–5). In this Mediator the ancient righteous also had hope, when they foresaw by the spirit of prophecy that he would come in the flesh.

Therefore, what word was spoken to them concerning him may also rightly be understood here as “the word,” if we take this utterance as theirs as well. Concerning that word it was said: “Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope. This has consoled me in my humiliation”—that is, in this mortality of mine—“because your utterance has given me life,” so that, cast down into death, I might have hope of life.

“The proud acted very wickedly,” since their pride was not subdued even by the humiliation of mortality. “But I did not turn aside from your law,” which the proud compelled me to do.

5. [v. 52.] “I remembered your judgments from of old, O Lord, and I was consoled”—or, as some manuscripts read, “and I was encouraged,” that is, “I received encouragement.” Either rendering could be given for the Greek word παρεκλήθην (*pareklēthēn*).

From the time when the human race first began, I remembered your judgments concerning the vessels of wrath, which are prepared [Note: [Col. 1542] Am. Er. and almost all manuscripts, *parata* (“prepared”).] for destruction; and I was consoled, because through these also you showed the riches of your glory upon the vessels of your mercy (Rom. 9:22–23).

6. [vv. 53–54.] “Weariness kept me from sinners who abandon your law. Your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my sojourning”; or, as some manuscripts read, “in the place of my pilgrimage.”

This is that humiliation in the place of mortality, where humanity wanders after being expelled from paradise and from that heavenly Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1542] So the manuscripts. But Er. and Lov. read, “and of the pilgrimage of humanity, expelled from paradise and from that heavenly Jerusalem.”], from which a certain man descended to Jericho and fell among robbers (Luke 10:30–37). Yet because of the mercy shown to him through that Samaritan, God’s ordinances were songs to him in the place of his pilgrimage, even though he was wearied by sinners who abandoned God’s law, since in this life he is sometimes compelled to associate with them, until the threshing floor is winnowed.

These two verses may also be joined individually to parts of the preceding verse. Thus what he says, “I remembered your judgments from of old, O Lord,” may refer to “Weariness seized me because of sinners who abandon your law”; while what he says there, “And I was consoled,” may refer to “Your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage.”

7. [v. 55.] “I remembered,” he says, “your name in the night, O Lord, and I kept your law.” That humiliation is night, in which there is the misery of mortality. It is night among the proud who act extremely wickedly; night in the weariness caused by sinners who abandon God’s law; and finally, it is night in this place of pilgrimage, until the Lord comes, illumines the hidden things of darkness, and reveals the counsels of hearts; then each person will receive praise from God (1 Cor. 4:5).

In this night, therefore, a person ought to remember the name of God, so that whoever boasts may boast in the Lord (ibid. 1:31). For this reason it is also written, “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 113:1).

Thus a person keeps God’s law not in his own glory but in God’s glory—not in his own righteousness but in God’s righteousness, that is, in righteousness given to him by God—just as this man says, “I remembered your name in the night, O Lord, and I kept your law.” He would not have kept it if, trusting in his own strength, he had not remembered the name of God, for “our help is in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 123:8).

8. [v. 56.] Therefore he continued: “This happened to me because I sought your ordinances.” Your ordinances, certainly, by which you justify the ungodly—not my ordinances, which never make me godly but make me proud.

This man was not one of those who, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, were not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10:3). Other translators therefore rendered these ordinances more appropriately as “justifications,” because the Greek has not δικαιοσύνας (*dikaiosynas*), that is, “righteousnesses,” but δικαιώματα (*dikaiōmata*), which are “justifications.”

But what does he mean by saying, “This happened to me”? What is “this”? Could it perhaps be the law, since he had said, “And I kept your law,” and then added, “This happened to me,” as though he were saying, “This law happened to me”? Yet there is no need to delay in explaining how God’s law came to be his.

The Greek expression from which these words were translated clearly indicates that “This happened to me” is not said of the law, because in that language “law” is masculine, whereas the feminine pronoun “this” is written there as well. We must therefore first ask what happened to him, and then how it happened to him, whatever it may be.

“This,” he says, “happened to me.” Certainly he does not mean, “This law,” because, as I have said, the Greek excludes that sense. Perhaps, then, he means, “This night,” because the whole preceding sentence runs as follows: “I remembered your name in the night, O Lord, and I kept your law”; and it continues, “This happened to me.” Since it is not the law, it is surely the night that happened to him.

What, then, does “Night happened to me because I sought your ordinances” mean? It was rather made light for him, not night, because he sought God’s ordinances. Thus “happened to me” is rightly understood as though it said, “happened for me,” that is, “came about for my benefit.”

For if that humiliation of mortality may reasonably be understood as night, in which the hearts of mortals are hidden from one another, so that countless and grievous temptations arise from such darkness—and in that same night the beasts of the forest pass through, the lion cubs roaring and seeking their food from God (Ps. 104:21)—and if, concerning that roaring lion seeking someone to devour (1 Pet. 5:8), the Lord says what I have already mentioned above, “This night Satan asked to sift you like wheat,” that is, “In this night in which the beasts of the forest pass through, that great lion sought you from God as food for himself”—then surely this very humiliation in the place of our pilgrimage, rightly understood as night, benefits those who are profitably exercised in it, so that they may learn not to be proud. For it was because of this evil that humanity was driven into this night. “The beginning of human pride is apostasy from God” (Sir. 10:14).

But once justified freely, and subjected to the various temptations of this night so that he may advance in this humiliation, a person who now understands may say what is stated later in this psalm: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your ordinances.” For what else is “It is good for me that you humbled me” than “This humiliation, which is called night, happened to me”—that is, “came about for my benefit”? But why? Clearly because “I sought your ordinances, not my own.”

9. We can also understand “This happened to me” in such a way that neither “law” nor “night” is supplied, but the pronoun “this” is taken in the same way as in that passage of another psalm where we read, “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I will seek” (Ps. 27:4).

He does not say what the one thing is, or which one thing he means when he says, “This I will seek.” The feminine gender is used as though it were neuter. For “I asked one thing; this I will seek” is an unusual expression, since it would more ordinarily be said: “I asked one thing of the Lord; this I will seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord.”

With neuter expressions, what is to be supplied is not usually demanded—such as “one good thing,” “one gift,” or anything of that kind. Whatever the thing may be, even if it is named with a masculine or feminine noun, or is indicated by words without a noun of any gender, it is ordinarily understood under the neuter gender.

Thus here also it could be said, “This happened to me,” as though it had been said, “This happened for me.” If we ask what that “this” is, what he said above comes to mind: “I remembered your name in the night, O Lord, and I kept your law.” “This happened to me”—that is, “This keeping of your law was not accomplished by me myself; it happened to me,” certainly through you, “because I sought your ordinances, not mine.”

“For it is God,” says the Apostle, “who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13). God also says through the Prophet: “And I will cause you to walk in my ordinances, and to observe my judgments and perform them” (Ezek. 36:27).

Therefore, since God says, “I will cause you to observe and perform my judgments,” this man most rightly says, “This happened to me.” When you ask what it was, he answers with what he had said above: “That I might keep the law of God.”

But since this discussion has grown long, what follows, with the Lord’s help, will be treated more suitably from another beginning.

SERMON XVI

1. [v. 57.] In God’s will we now undertake to examine these verses of this great psalm: “The Lord is my portion”—some manuscripts have, “My portion, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 1545] Most manuscripts, “my portion.”].

Is this said because whoever clings to God becomes a sharer in him, as it is written, “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 73:28)? Human beings do not become gods by their own existence, but become so by participating in the one who is truly God. Or is it because people choose portions for themselves in this world, or receive them by lot—one this, another that—from which each person lives, so that in a certain sense God is the portion of the godly, from whom they always live? Neither interpretation is unreasonable [Note: [Col. 1545] Er. and Lov. read, “as portions.” The word “as” is absent from Am. and the manuscripts.].

But let us hear what follows: “I said, ‘To keep your law.’” What is “The Lord is my portion; I said, ‘To keep your law,’” except that the Lord will be each person’s portion when he has kept his law?

2. [vv. 58–59.] But how does one keep it unless the life-giving Spirit grants this and helps him toward it, lest the letter kill (2 Cor. 3:6), and lest sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produce in a person every kind of desire (Rom. 7:8)? He must therefore be invoked. For faith obtains from the Spirit what the law commands, since “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel 2:32; Rom. 10:13).

Therefore see what he adds: “I entreated your face with my whole heart.” And, explaining how he entreated, he says: “Have mercy on me according to your utterance.” Then, as one who had been heard and helped by him whom he had entreated: “I considered,” he says, “my ways, and turned my feet toward your testimonies.” He turned them away, of course, from his own ways, which had displeased him, so that they might go toward your testimonies and find their way there.

Many manuscripts do not have “Because I considered,” as some read, but only “I considered.” What is here written, “And I turned my feet,” is read by some as, “Because I considered, and you turned my feet,” so that this may be attributed rather to God’s grace, according to what the Apostle says: “For it is God who works in you” (Phil. 2:13). To him it is also said, “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity.” If he turns away the eyes so that they do not see vanity, why not also the feet, so that they do not follow error? For this reason it is also written: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, because he will draw my feet out of the snare” (Ps. 25:15).

Whether the reading is “you turned my feet” or “I turned my feet,” it is brought about by him whose face he entreated in his heart, and to whom he said, “Have mercy on me according to your utterance”—that is, according to the word of your promise. For the children of promise are counted as Abraham’s offspring (Rom. 9:8–9).

3. [v. 60.] Finally, having obtained this benefit of grace, he says, “I am prepared, and I was not troubled, to keep your commandments.” Some translated this as “for keeping your commandments,” others as “that I might keep your commandments,” and others simply as “to keep your commandments.” The Greek has τοῦ φυλάξασθαι (*tou phylaxasthai*).

4. [v. 61.] He then showed how prepared he had become to keep the divine commandments, saying: “The cords of sinners have entangled me, but I have not forgotten your law.”

“The cords of sinners” are the impediments of enemies, whether spiritual enemies, such as the devil and his angels, or carnal enemies, among whose children of unbelief the devil works (Eph. 2:2). For the word “sinners” is not declined from the word meaning “sins,” but from the word meaning “sinners”; this is evident in the Greek [Note: [Col. 1546] Greek: *hamartōlōn*.].

When they threaten evil by which they may terrify the righteous, so that they will not suffer for God’s law, they entangle them, as it were, with cords, like a strong and sturdy rope. For “they draw iniquity like a long rope” (Isa. 5:18). By this means they attempt to entangle the saints, and sometimes they are permitted to do so. But if they entangle the body, they do not entangle the soul, where this man has not forgotten God’s law, because “the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2:9).

5. [v. 62.] “At midnight,” he says, “I rose to confess you because of the judgments of your righteousness.” For the very fact that the cords of sinners entangle the righteous is itself a judgment of God’s righteousness.

For this reason the Apostle Peter says that it is time for judgment to begin from the house of God. “And if it begins with us,” he says, “what will be the end of those who do not believe the Lord’s gospel? And if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Pet. 4:17–18).

He says this concerning the persecutions that the Church endured when the cords of sinners entangled it. Accordingly, I think that “midnight” should be understood as the more severe part of tribulation. He said, “I rose,” because the affliction did not crush him so as to cast him down; rather, it exercised him so that he might rise—that is, so that through that very tribulation he might advance toward confessing more courageously.

6. [vv. 63–64.] Since these things are accomplished by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, the Savior himself joins the voice of his own person to his body through this prophecy. I think what follows properly belongs to the head himself: “I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments.”

As it is written in the Epistle entitled “To the Hebrews”: “He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one; for this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers.” A little later it says: “Therefore, because the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of them in some manner” (Heb. 2:11, 14). What else does this mean except that he became their companion and sharer?

We would not become sharers in his divinity unless he himself became a sharer in our mortality. In the Gospel also, where it is said that we have become sharers in his divinity, we read: “He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.” And, to show how this came about—because he himself also became a sharer in our mortality—it continues there: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:12–14).

Through this sharing of his, grace is supplied to us, so that we may fear God chastely and keep his commandments. Accordingly, it is Jesus himself who speaks in this prophecy. Some things he speaks in his members and in the unity of his body, as in one human being spread throughout the whole world and growing through the succession of ages; other things he speaks in himself, our head.

This, then, is also what he says: “I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments.” And because he became the companion of his brothers—the God of human beings, the immortal one of mortals—“the grain fell into the earth” so that, dying, it might produce much fruit. Then, following from this fruit, he added: “The earth is full of your mercy, O Lord.” And from what does this come, unless when the ungodly is justified? So that he may advance in knowledge of this grace, he adds: “Teach me your ordinances.”

SERMON XVII

1. [v. 65.] These verses of this psalm, which we are now going to discuss according to God’s will, begin as follows: “You have dealt graciously with your servant, O Lord, according to your word,” or rather, “according to your utterance.”

The Greek word χρηστότητα (*chrēstotēta*) has been translated by our interpreters sometimes as “graciousness” or “pleasantness,” sometimes as “goodness.” But since pleasantness can also exist in evil, when unlawful and filthy things give pleasure, and can also exist in permitted carnal pleasure, we must understand the pleasantness that the Greeks call χρηστότητα as belonging to spiritual goods.
