For this reason our translators also wished to call it “goodness.”

I therefore think that “You have dealt graciously with your servant” means nothing other than, “You have caused the good to delight me.” When the good gives delight, that is a great gift of God [Note: [Col. 1547] So Am. and the manuscripts. Lov. reads, “the goodness of God is great.”].

But when the good work commanded by the law is done out of fear of punishment and not out of delight in righteousness—when God is feared, not loved—it is done slavishly, not freely. “The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever” (John 8:35), because “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

Therefore, “You have dealt graciously with your servant, O Lord,” by making a son of one who was a servant; “according to your utterance,” that is, according to your promise, so that the promise might be firm according to faith for all the offspring (Rom. 4:16).

2. [v. 66.] “Teach me graciousness, instruction, and knowledge,” he says, “because I have believed your commandments.” He asks that these things be increased and perfected in him. For since he had already said, “You have dealt graciously with your servant,” how does he now say, “Teach me graciousness,” unless he wishes God’s grace to become increasingly known to him through the sweetness of goodness?

Those who said, “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke 17:5), already had faith. And as long as one lives in this world, this is the song of those who are making progress.

He added “instruction,” or, as most manuscripts read, “discipline.” Wherever our Scriptures commonly use “discipline” for what the Greeks call παιδεία (*paideia*), instruction through hardships is to be understood, according to the saying: “The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives.” In ecclesiastical writings this is commonly called *disciplina*, translated from the Greek, where παιδεία is written.

This word occurs in the Greek of the Epistle to the Hebrews, where the Latin translator says: “No discipline at the time seems to be joyful but sorrowful; afterward, however, it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Heb. 12:6, 11).

Therefore, when God deals graciously with someone—that is, when he mercifully inspires in him a delight in the good—or, to explain this more clearly, when a person is given by God the love of God and, for God’s sake, love of neighbor, he ought certainly to pray earnestly that this gift may be increased in him so greatly that he may not only despise all other pleasures for its sake but also endure any sufferings for its sake.

Thus discipline is beneficially added to sweetness. It is not just any slight degree of sweetness or goodness—that is, of holy love—that must be sought and desired, but such a great degree that it cannot be extinguished beneath its pressure. Rather, like a great flame under the force of the wind, the more it is suppressed, the more ardently it is stirred up.

Therefore it was not enough to say, “You have dealt graciously with your servant,” unless he again asked that he be taught sweetness—sweetness so great that he might patiently endure discipline. Knowledge is placed third, because if knowledge surpasses love in greatness, it does not build up but puffs up (1 Cor. 8:1).

When love is so great in gracious goodness that it cannot be extinguished by the tribulations imposed by discipline, then knowledge will be useful. Through it a person comes to know both what he himself has deserved and what has been given to him by God, through which he may know that he is able to do what he did not know he could do and could not do at all by himself.

3. But he does not say, “Give me”; he says, “Teach me.” How is graciousness taught if it is not given? Many know what does not delight them, and although they possess knowledge of certain things, they do not possess graciousness. Graciousness cannot be learned unless it gives delight.

Likewise, discipline—which signifies corrective tribulation—is learned by receiving it; that is, not by hearing, reading, or thinking, but by experience. Knowledge, however, which he placed third among the things he says, “Teach me,” is given through teaching. For what else is teaching than giving knowledge?

These two are so connected that one cannot exist without the other. No one is taught unless he learns, and no one learns unless he is taught. Therefore, if a student is not capable of what the teacher says, the teacher cannot say, “I taught him, but he did not learn.” He can say, “I told him what needed to be said, but he did not learn,” because he did not perceive, comprehend, or understand.

For surely he would have learned if the teacher had taught him. Thus, when God wishes to teach, he first gives understanding, without which a person cannot learn what pertains to divine teaching. Hence this man says a little later, “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments.”

A person, when he wishes to teach someone, can indeed say what the Lord said to his disciples after he had risen from the dead. But he cannot do what the Lord did. The Gospel says: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures, and he said to them…” (Luke 24:45–46).

What he said to them is recorded there; but they grasped what he said because he opened the means by which it could be grasped. God therefore teaches sweetness by inspiring delight, teaches discipline by regulating tribulation, and teaches knowledge by imparting cognition.

Since some things are learned merely so that they may be known, while others are learned so that they may also be done, when God teaches them he teaches in such a way that we know what is to be known by opening the truth, and in such a way that we do what is to be done by inspiring sweetness.

For it is not without reason that it is said to him, “Teach me to do your will” (Ps. 143:10). “Teach,” he says, “in such a way that I may do it, not merely know it.” Right actions themselves are our fruit, which we return to our farmer. Yet Scripture says, “The Lord will give sweetness, and our land will give its fruit” (Ps. 85:13).

And what is this land except that of which it is said to the very one who gives sweetness: “My soul is like land without water to you” (Ps. 143:6)?

### 4.

But when he had said, “Teach me sweetness, discipline, and knowledge,” he added and said, “For I have believed in your commandments.” It may reasonably be asked why he did not say “I have obeyed,” but “I have believed.” For commandments and promises are different things. We undertake to fulfill commandments so that we may deserve to receive the promises. We believe the promises, therefore, and obey the commandments.

What, then, is meant by “I have believed in your commandments,” except: “I have believed that you commanded them, not some human being,” although they were administered to human beings through human beings? Since, therefore, I have believed that the commandments are yours, may the faith by which I have believed this obtain from you the grace by which I may do what you have commanded. For if a human being ordered these things externally, would he also help me internally to do what he ordered?

Teach me, then, sweetness by inspiring love; teach me discipline by granting patience; teach me knowledge by illuminating understanding: “For I have believed in your commandments.” I have believed that you, who are God, commanded them, and that you grant human beings the means by which they may do what you command.

### 5. [verse 67]

“Before I was humbled,” he says, “I went astray; therefore I kept your word”—or, as others express it more clearly, “therefore I kept your utterance”—namely, so that I would not be humbled again. This is better referred to that humiliation which took place in Adam, in whom the whole human creation, corrupted as though at its root because it did not wish to be subject to the truth, was subjected to futility (Rom. 8:20). It benefited the vessels of mercy to experience this, so that, with pride cast down, obedience might be loved and misery, never to return, might perish.

### 6. [verse 68]

“You are sweet, Lord”—or, as more manuscripts have it, “You are sweet, you, Lord.” Some also have, “You are sweet, you,” or, “You are good, you,” as we discussed above concerning this word. “And in your sweetness teach me your ordinances.” He truly wishes to perform God’s ordinances when he wishes to learn them in God’s sweetness, from the very one to whom he said, “You are sweet, Lord.”

### 7. [verse 69]

Finally, what follows is: “The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me”—that is, of those for whom it was no benefit that human nature had been humbled after it went astray. “But I will search out your commandments with all my heart.” However much iniquity may abound, he says, love will not grow cold in me (Matt. 24:12). He speaks as one who learns God’s ordinances in God’s sweetness. For the more pleasant are the things commanded by the one who gives help, the more eagerly the lover searches them out, so that, once known, he may practice them, and by practicing them come to know them; for they are known more perfectly when they are done.

### 8. [verse 70]

“Their heart has become curdled like milk.” Whose heart, except that of the proud, whose iniquity he said had been multiplied against him? By this expression and in this context he wishes their heart to be understood as hardened. Yet the expression is also used in a good sense, as in the sixty-seventh Psalm: “A mountain curdled like cheese, a fertile mountain” (Ps. 67:16); and it is understood as full of grace, for some have likewise translated the word as “curdled.”

But see what he sets against the hardness of their heart: “But I,” he says, “have meditated on your law.” What law? Surely, the most just and most merciful law; hence he says to it, “And by your law have mercy on me.” He resists the proud, so that they may be hardened, but gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4:6; 1 Pet. 5:5), so that they may love obedience and receive exaltation.

[Note: The editions read, “and that they may not receive.” The particle “not” is absent from the manuscripts.]

Through meditation on this law, voluntary humility is preserved, so that penal humiliation may be escaped—the humiliation of which he immediately speaks.

### 9. [verse 71]

“It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your ordinances.” He had already said something similar above: “Before I was humbled, I went astray; therefore I kept your utterance.” By that very fruit he shows that it was good for him to be humbled; but there he also stated the reason: by going astray, he had preceded penal humiliation.

What he said there, “Therefore I kept your utterance,” and what he says here, “So that I might learn your ordinances,” seem to me sufficiently to indicate that knowing them is the same as keeping them, and keeping them the same as knowing them. For Christ certainly did not fail to know the sin which he condemned, although it is said of him that he “did not know sin” (2 Cor. 5:21). He therefore knew it in one kind of knowledge, and again, in another kind of ignorance, he did not know it.

So also many learn God’s ordinances, and do not learn them. They know them in one kind of knowledge; and again, because they do not do them, they do not know them in another kind of ignorance. In this sense, therefore, he should be understood here to have said, “So that I might learn your ordinances”: with that knowledge by which they are practiced.

### 10. [verse 72]

But this does not happen except through love, when the one who performs an action takes pleasure in it. For this reason it was said, “In your sweetness teach me your ordinances.” The following verse shows this when it says: “The law of your mouth is good to me, above thousands of gold and silver”—so that love may love God’s law more than greed loves thousands of gold and silver.

## SERMON XVIII

### 1. [verse 73]

When God made the human being from dust and animated him with breath, it is not mentioned there that he made him with his hands. Why, then, some have thought that God made the other things by a word but made the human being, as though something especially important, with his own hands, I do not see—unless perhaps they think that the human body could not have been made except with hands because we read that the body of the human being was formed from dust (Gen. 2:7). They do not consider that it is written in the Gospel concerning the Word of God, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3), which cannot stand if the human body too was not made through the Word.

But they produce testimony from this Psalm and say: “Behold where the human being most plainly cries out, ‘Your hands made me and fashioned me.’” As though it had not also been plainly said, “I will behold the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8:4), and no less plainly, “The heavens are the works of your hands” (Ps. 101:26), and much more plainly, “His hands fashioned the dry land” (Ps. 94:5).

The hands of God, therefore, are the power of God. Or, if the plural number troubles them, because it does not say “your hand” but “your hands,” let them understand the hands of God as the power and wisdom of God, both of which are identified as one—Christ (1 Cor. 1:24). He is also understood as the arm of the Lord, where we read, “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1).

Or let them understand the hands of God as the Son and the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit too is a co-worker of the Father and the Son. Hence the Apostle says, “All these things the one and the same Spirit accomplishes” (1 Cor. 12:11). For this reason he said, “the one and the same,” so that people would not suppose there were as many spirits as there are works—not because the Spirit works without the Father and the Son.

It is therefore free to understand the hands of God in whatever way one wishes, provided that one neither denies that the things he makes with his hands are made by the Word, nor thinks that the things he makes by the Word are not made by his hands; and provided one does not believe that, because of the hands, God who works possesses a bodily form, one hand left and the other right, or, because of the Word, the sound of a mouth or some passing movement of the mind.

### 2.

There were also some who distinguished the two expressions “made me” and “fashioned me” in such a way that they said God made the soul but fashioned the body. For concerning the soul God said, “I have made every breath” (Isa. 57:16), while concerning the body we read, “And God fashioned the human being, dust from the earth” (Gen. 2:7)—as though everything that is fashioned is indeed made, but not everything that is made is fashioned.

For this reason they say that the soul is made rather than fashioned, because it is not a body but a spirit—as though it were not written, “He who fashioned the spirit of the human being within him” (Zech. 12:1).

Nevertheless, when both expressions are applied to the human being in one place, and it is not denied that both parts of the human being—that is, both soul and body—were created by God, it is not inelegant to distribute one expression to each, so that the soul is understood as made and the body as fashioned, whether formed or molded.

Some translators did not wish to say “fashioned me,” but “molded me,” preferring to decline the Greek less idiomatically rather than to say “fashioned,” since that word is sometimes used of pretense as well.

### 3.

But was this said concerning Adam, from whom all human beings have been propagated, so that, by reason of origin and seed, no human being could fail to say that he too was made when Adam was made? Or could it also rightly be said in this sense, “Your hands made me and molded me,” since each person is made from his parents not without the work of God—God himself creating, while they beget?

For if God’s operative power were withdrawn from things, they would perish; and nothing at all would be born, whether from the elements of the world, from parents, or from seeds, if God did not operate in them. For this reason he says to the prophet Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. 1:5).

But did God make the human being without understanding, whether the first human being or each one who is born, so that he now says to him, “Your hands made me and molded me; give me understanding”? Was understanding not implanted in human nature itself, so that by it human beings are distinguished from cattle? Or has it been so disfigured by sin that it too must be re-formed within it?

For this reason the Apostle says to all who belong to regeneration, “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind”; and certainly understanding is in the mind. Again he says, “Be re-formed in the newness of your understanding” (Rom. 12:2). But concerning those who did not share in this regeneration he says:

> “This I say and testify in the Lord: that you no longer walk as the Gentiles walk, in the futility of their mind, darkened in understanding, alienated from the way of God through the ignorance that is in them because of the blindness of their heart” (Eph. 4:17–18, 23).

It is therefore on account of these inner eyes, whose blindness consists in failing to understand, that hearts are cleansed by faith (Acts 15:9), so that they may be opened and become ever clearer. For although no one can believe in God without understanding something, nevertheless the very faith by which one believes is healed so that one may understand greater things.

There are things that we do not believe unless we understand them, and other things that we do not understand unless we believe them. For since “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. 10:17), how can someone believe the one preaching the faith if, to say nothing else, he does not understand the very language he speaks?

But if there were not again certain things that we cannot understand unless we first believe, the prophet would not say, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

Our understanding therefore advances toward understanding what it believes, and faith advances toward believing what it understands; and the mind itself advances in understanding so that these things may be understood more and more. Yet this does not happen through our own supposedly natural powers, but with God’s help and gift, just as healing comes not from nature but from medicine, so that an injured eye may recover its power of sight.

Therefore, the person who says to God, “Give me understanding, so that I may learn your commandments,” is not entirely without understanding, as though he were an animal. Nor is he in such a condition—although he is a human being—that he should be counted among those who “walk in the futility of their mind, darkened in understanding, alienated from the life of God.” For if he were such a person, he would not say this.

It is no small understanding to know from whom understanding must be requested. We must also consider how much more deeply the divine commandments are to be understood, since the person who already understands in this way—and who has already said that he kept God’s utterances—still asks that understanding be given to him in order to learn them.

### 4.

What our translators rendered as “Give me understanding,” the Greek expressed more briefly with **συνέτισόν με** (*synetison me*), because it comprehends in one word what is meant by “Give me understanding.” This cannot be said in Latin with a single word—as though Latin could not say “heal me” but had to say “give me health,” just as here it says “Give me understanding”; or as though one could not say here as well, “Make me understanding.”

An angel could indeed do this, for he said to Daniel, “I have come to give you understanding” (Dan. 10:14). The Greek has here the same verb as in this passage, **συνετίσαι σε** (*synetisai se*), as though a Latin speaker were to say “to give you health,” where a Greek speaker would say “to heal you.” The Latin translator would not use the circumlocution “to give you understanding” if, just as one can say “to heal you” from “health,” one could say “to make you understanding” from “understanding.”

But if an angel can do this, what is the reason that the psalmist asks God to make him so? Is it because God commanded the angel to do it? Indeed it is. For Christ is understood to have commanded the angel to do this at the place where the Prophet says:

> “And it happened, when I, Daniel, saw the vision and sought understanding, that behold, there stood before me what appeared like the form of a man. And I heard a man’s voice between the banks of the Ulai; and he called and said, ‘Make him understand the vision’” (Dan. 8:15–16).

[Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “and he said, Ulai.” “Ulai” is absent from Amerbach and from most manuscripts.]

The Greek there has the same verb as here, namely **συνέτισον** (*synetison*).

God therefore, because he is light (John 1:4, 9), illuminates pious minds by himself, so that they may understand the things that are spoken or revealed as divine. But if he uses an angel as a minister for this purpose, the angel can indeed do something in the human mind by which it becomes capable of receiving God’s light and understanding through it.

In this way the angel is said to give understanding to a human being, and, so to speak, to make the human being understanding, just as someone is said to give light to a house or illuminate a house when he makes a window in it—not because he enters and illuminates it with his own light, but because he merely opens an entrance through which it may be entered and illuminated.

Yet the sun, which illuminates the house through the window, did not itself create that house, or the human being who made the window in the house; nor did it itself command him to make it, or help the one making it, or do anything so that the opening might be made through which it would pour in its light.

God, however, both made the rational and intellectual mind of the human being, by which it could receive his light, and made the angel such that he could perform something by which the human mind might be helped to receive God’s light. He also helps that mind in such a way that it receives angelic action, and illuminates it from himself in such a way that it perceives not only the things shown by the truth but, by advancing, the truth itself as well.

But since we have discussed matters that, in my judgment, are necessary in a rather lengthy argument, let us defer the following verses of this Psalm and conclude this sermon here.

## SERMON XIX

### 1. [verse 73]

In this Psalm the Lord Jesus, through the Prophet, asked that understanding be given, as though on his own behalf, to his body, which is the Church, so that it might learn God’s commandments. For the life of his body—that is, of his people—is hidden with him in God (Col. 3:3), and in that same body of his he suffers need and asks for what is necessary to his members.

“Your hands,” he says, “made me and molded me; give me understanding, so that I may learn your commandments.” Because you formed me, he says, reform me, so that what the Apostle says may be accomplished in Christ’s body: “Be re-formed in the newness of your understanding” (Rom. 12:2).

### 2. [verse 74]

“Those who fear you,” he says, “will see me and rejoice”—or, as other manuscripts have it, “will be glad”—“because I have hoped in your words”: that is, in the things you promised, so that they might be children of the promise, the seed of Abraham, in whom all nations are blessed (Gen. 12:3; 26:4).

But who are those who fear God, and whom will they see and rejoice because he hoped in God’s words? If this is the body of Christ, that is, the Church, whose voice this is through Christ, or if this voice of Christ is spoken in and concerning the Church as concerning himself, are not those who fear God themselves included among them?

[Note: Five manuscripts read, “is not it itself among them,” and so forth.]

Who, then, is the one whom they see and rejoice? Does the people itself see itself and rejoice, so that it is said, “Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped in your words”? Or, as others have expressed it more carefully, “I have hoped beyond hope” [Greek: *epēlpisa*]? As though he were saying: “Those who fear you will see your Church and rejoice, because I have hoped beyond hope in your words,” even though those who see the Church and rejoice are themselves the Church.

But why did he not say, “Those who fear you see me and rejoice,” but used the present tense in “those who fear you,” while “they will see” and “they will rejoice” are future-tense verbs?

Is it because fear belongs to the present time, so long as human life on earth is a time of testing (Job 7:1), whereas the joy he wished to be understood here will come when the righteous shine in the kingdom of their Father like the sun (Matt. 13:43)? Hence we also read in another Psalm: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!”

Now, therefore, while they fear, they do not yet see; but “they will see” and “they will rejoice.” For there too it continues, “But you have perfected it for those who hope in you” (Ps. 30:20–21); and here, “because I have hoped in your words,” or “hoped beyond hope.” Thus, in this compound expression, carefully rendered by the more diligent translator, we may also understand what God is able to do “above all that we ask or think” (Eph. 3:20). Since these things surpass what we ask and understand, it is too little merely to hope for them; we ought to hope beyond hope.

### 3. [verses 75–76]

Since, therefore, the Church that is in this life still fears and does not yet see itself in that kingdom where its secure joy will be, but labors amid the dangerous temptations of this world, where it hears, “Let the one who thinks he stands beware lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12), it considers the misery of this mortality.

In this mortality, “a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam, from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb,” is imposed upon all and continues until the day of burial in the mother of all (Ecclus. 40:1). Because of the flesh’s desire against the spirit (Gal. 5:17), even those who have been regenerated are compelled to groan under its burden.

Considering this, therefore, it says:

> “I know, Lord, that your judgments are righteousness, and in truth you have humbled me” [so the better manuscripts read, according to the Septuagint. The editions have “and in your truth.”]. “Let your mercy come, and console me according to your word to your servant.”

Mercy and truth are commended in the divine utterance in such a way that, although they are found in many places, especially in the Psalms, one passage even says, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10).

Here he first placed truth, by which we have been humbled to death, when he judged whose judgments are righteousness; then mercy, by which we are restored to life, when he promises whose benefit is grace. Therefore he says, “according to your word to your servant,” that is, according to what you promised your servant.

Whether, then, it is regeneration by which we are adopted here as God’s children, or faith, hope, and love—the three things built up in us—although they come from God’s mercy, in this miserable and storm-tossed life they are consolations for the wretched, not the joys of the blessed. Therefore it is said, “Let your mercy come, and console me.”

### 4. [verse 77]

But because after these things and through these things those future realities will also come, the Psalm continues: “Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live.”

Then I shall truly live, when I can fear nothing lest I die. For that reality is called simply “life,” without any added qualification, and it is understood as eternal and blessed—as though only that should be called life, in comparison with which the life we now lead ought rather to be called death than life. Such is the saying in the Gospel: “If you wish to come to life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17).

Did he add “eternal” or “blessed”? Likewise, speaking of the resurrection of the flesh, he says, “Those who have done good will come to the resurrection of life” (John 5:29); here too he does not say “eternal” or “blessed.”

So also here: “Let your mercies come to me,” he says, “and I shall live.” He does not say, “I shall live forever,” or, “I shall live blessedly,” as though living were anything other than living without end and without misery.

But by what merit? “For your law,” he says, “is my meditation.” Unless this meditation were in the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6), no one could ever reach that life on its account.

I have thought this should be said so that no one, having committed the whole law to memory and recited it through constant recollection—never silent about what it commands, yet not living as it commands—might think that he has done what he reads: “For your law is my meditation,” and might imagine that he will thereby obtain what he requested above on the basis of this merit, where it was said, “Let your mercies come upon me, and I shall live.”

This meditation is the thought of one who loves, and of one who loves so greatly that love for this meditation does not grow cold, however greatly it may be surrounded by the abundance of another’s iniquity (Matt. 24:12).

### 5. [verse 78]

Finally, he continues and says: “Let the proud be put to shame, because they have acted wickedly against me in injustice; but I will be occupied with your commandments.”

Behold what he calls “the meditation of God’s law,” or rather, “the meditation that is God’s law.”

[Note: More manuscripts read “I act.”]

### 6. [verse 79]

“Let those who fear you,” he says, “and those who know your testimonies, turn to me.” In some Greek and Latin manuscripts we find, “Let them turn to me”; I think this has the same force as “to me” in the sense of “toward me.”

But who is this one who says this? No human being would dare say it, or, if he did say it, should be heeded. Clearly, then, it is the one who earlier inserted the distinctive character of his voice, saying, “I am a participant with all those who fear you.”

He became a participant in our mortality so that we might become participants in his divinity: we are participants with the one in life, while, in death, he became a participant with the many.

He is the one to whom those who fear God turn, and those who know God’s testimonies—testimonies foretold about him through the Prophets long beforehand and displayed shortly before in his presence through miracles.

### 7. [verse 80]

“Let my heart,” he says, “become blameless in your ordinances, so that I may not be put to shame.”

He returns to the voice of his body, namely, of his holy people, and now prays that its heart—this means the heart of its members—may become blameless in God’s ordinances, not through their own powers. He asked for this; he did not presume upon it.

What he added, “so that I may not be put to shame,” has something similar in the opening verses of this Psalm, where he said, “Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your ordinances; then I would not be put to shame when I look upon all your commandments.”

There, by saying “Would that,” he signified in one word the language of one making a request. Here he expressed the same thing more openly, in the language of one praying, by saying, “Let my heart become blameless.” Thus neither in that statement nor in this—although the two are one and the same—is there found the presumption of free will relying on itself against grace.

What he said there, “Then I would not be put to shame,” he says here, “so that I may not be put to shame.”

The heart of Christ’s members and body therefore becomes blameless by the grace of God, through the very head of the body, Jesus Christ our Lord: through the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5), in which all our past sins have been abolished; through the help of the Spirit, by which we desire what is against the flesh (Gal. 5:17), so that we may not be overcome in our struggle; and through the effect of the Lord’s Prayer [the manuscripts read “effect”; the editions have “affection”], in which we say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12).

Thus, once regeneration has been granted to us, our struggle helped, and our prayer poured out, our heart becomes blameless, so that we are not put to shame. For this too belongs to God’s ordinances, since among his other commandments he orders: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38).

## SERMON XX

### 1. [verse 81]

With the Lord’s help, we have undertaken to consider and explain this section of the great Psalm, where it says: “My soul has failed for your salvation, and I have hoped in your word.”

Not every kind of failure should be thought to be either guilt or punishment. There is also a praiseworthy and desirable failure. For although “to advance” and “to fail” are opposites, advancement is more commonly understood in a good sense and failure in an evil sense, when what one advances toward or fails from is not added or understood. But when this is added, advancing can be evil and failing can be good.

The Apostle plainly says: “Avoid profane novelties of words, for they will advance greatly toward ungodliness” (2 Tim. 2:16); and he says of certain people, “They will advance toward worse things” (2 Tim. 3:13). Thus failure from good into evil is bad, while failure from evil into good is good.

It was in the sense of a good failure that it was said, “My soul desires and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:3). So here too he does not say, “My soul has failed away from your salvation,” but, “My soul has failed toward your salvation,” that is, toward your salvation.

This failure is therefore good, for it indicates a desire for the good—not yet attained, but longed for with the greatest eagerness and intensity.

But who says this except the chosen race, the royal priesthood, the holy nation, the people of possession (1 Pet. 2:9), from the beginning of the human race to the end of this age, in those who lived, live, and will live here in their own times, longing for Christ?

The most holy old man Simeon bears witness to this. When he had received the infant into his hands, he said:

> “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation.”

For he had received a divine answer that he would not taste death until he had seen the Christ of the Lord (Luke 2:29–30, 26).

What the desire was in this old man must be believed to have been the desire of all the saints of earlier times. Hence the Lord himself also said to his disciples:

> “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. 13:17).

Thus their voice too is recognized in this passage: “My soul has failed toward your salvation.”

Nor did this desire of the saints cease then, nor does it now cease in Christ’s body, which is the Church, until the end of the age, until the one desired by all nations comes, as is promised through the Prophet (Hag. 2:8).

For this reason the Apostle says:

> “There remains for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to all who love his manifestation” (2 Tim. 4:8).

This desire of which we are now speaking arises from love of his manifestation. Concerning this he also says, “When Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4).

The Church’s earliest times, before the Virgin gave birth, therefore had saints who desired the coming of his incarnation. The present times, since he ascended into heaven, have saints who desire his manifestation for the judgment of the living and the dead.

Nor did this desire of the Church, from the beginning to the end of the age, ever rest for any length of time except while he lived here in the flesh with his disciples.

[Note: The manuscripts do not contain “voice”; “desire” may be understood in its place.]

Thus the voice of the whole body of Christ groaning in this life is rightly understood: “My soul has failed toward your salvation, and I have hoped in your word”—that is, in your promise. This hope causes what is not seen by believers to be awaited through patience (Rom. 8:25).

Here too the Greek has the word that some of our translators preferred to render as “I have hoped beyond hope” [Greek: *epēlpisa*], because what is to come will undoubtedly be greater than can be expressed.

### 2. [verse 82]

“My eyes,” he says, “have failed for your utterance, saying, ‘When will you console me?’”

Here again, in the eyes—but certainly the inner eyes—there is that praiseworthy and blessed failure, arising not from weakness of spirit but from the strength of desire for God’s promise. For he says, “for your utterance.”

But how do such eyes say, “When will you console me?” except when one prays and groans with such attention and expectation? It is the tongue that ordinarily speaks, not the eyes; but the desire expressed in prayer is, in a sense, the voice of the eyes.

Yet by saying, “When will you console me?” he shows that he is enduring delays. Hence there is also the expression, “And you, Lord, how long?” (Ps. 6:4). This happens either so that delayed joy may come more sweetly, or because this is the experience of those who desire: for the lover, even a period of time that is brief for one who comes to help is long.

[Note: Lovaniensis reads “one who comes suddenly”; the other editions and the manuscripts disagree.]

The Lord, however, knows what he should do and when, for he orders all things “by measure, number, and weight” (Wis. 11:21).

### 3. [verse 83]

When spiritual desires burn, carnal desires undoubtedly grow cold. For this reason it follows: “For I have become like a wineskin in the frost; I have not forgotten your ordinances.”

Clearly, by the wineskin he wishes the flesh of this death to be understood, and by the frost, the heavenly benefit by which the desires of the flesh are restrained, as though by cold, and grow numb. The result is that God’s ordinances do not slip from memory, since the mind is not occupied with something else; for what the Apostle says comes to pass: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14).

Therefore, after saying, “For I have become like a wineskin in the frost,” he added, “I have not forgotten your ordinances”—that is, “I have not forgotten them for this reason, because I have become such.”

The heat of desire has grown numb, so that the memory of love might burn.

### 4. [verse 84]

“How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment upon those who persecute me?”

This is the voice of the martyrs in the Apocalypse, and they are commanded to exercise patience until the number of their brothers and sisters is complete (Rev. 6:10–11).

The body of Christ therefore asks about its own days, which will be in this age. And lest anyone suppose that the Church would not exist here before the end of the age, and that some period would come in this world during which the Church would no longer be on earth, when it asked about its days it also added the question of judgment. In this way it clearly shows that the Church itself will remain on earth until the judgment, when vengeance against its persecutors will take place.

If anyone is troubled by the question why it asks what the Teacher answered when the disciples asked it—“It is not yours to know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts 1:7)—why should we not believe that this very question was prophetically foretold in this passage of the Psalm, and that the voice of the Church, predicted here so long beforehand, was completed through their question?

### 5. [verse 85]

What follows is: “The wicked have told me of delights, but not as your law, Lord.”

Our translators wished to render in this way what the Greeks call **ἀδολεσχίαι** (*adoleschiai*). It cannot by any means be expressed in Latin with a single word. Thus some called them “delights,” and others “talkings,” so that it may reasonably be understood that they are indeed exercises, but exercises in speech with a certain pleasure.

Such things are found in various sects and professions: both in secular literature and in the Jewish work called the *Deuterosis*, which contains thousands of stories apart from the canon of the divine Scriptures.

[Note: Some books have: “which are called *Deuteroses*, containing …” Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah 59, says: “The traditions of human beings, which they call *deuterōseis*.”]

The vain and wandering loquacity of heretics also contains such things. He wished all these people to be understood as “wicked,” by whom he says that **ἀδολεσχίαι**—that is, verbal exercises of delight—were recounted to him.

“But not as your law, Lord,” he says, because in your law it is truth, not words, that delights me.

### 6. [verse 86]

Finally, he adds: “All your commandments are truth; they have persecuted me unjustly; help me.”

The whole meaning depends on what came before: “How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment upon those who persecute me?”

In order to persecute me, they have told me the delights of their speeches; but I have set your law before them. It delighted me more because all your commandments are truth, whereas their speech abounds in vanity.

And therefore they persecuted me unjustly, because they persecuted nothing in me except the truth. Help me, then, so that I may fight for the truth unto death; for this too is your commandment, and therefore this too is truth.

### 7. [verse 87]

When the Church did this, it endured what he added: “They almost finished me upon the earth”—that is, when a great slaughter of martyrs took place as they confessed and preached the truth.

But because “Help me” was not said without reason, he continues: “But I did not forsake your commandments.”

### 8. [verse 88]

And so that it might persevere to the end, he says: “According to your mercy, give me life, and I will keep the testimonies of your mouth.” The Greek has *martyria*—“testimonies.”

This could not be passed over in silence because of the most sweet name of the martyrs. Clearly, when the cruelty of the persecutors raged so fiercely that the Church was almost finished upon the earth, they could in no way have kept God’s testimonies unless what is requested here had happened to them: “According to your mercy, give me life.”

They were given life so that, by loving life, they would not deny life, and by denying life, they would not lose life. Thus those who refused to abandon the truth for the sake of life lived by dying for the truth.

## SERMON XXI

### 1. [verse 89]

The human being who speaks in this Psalm, as though wearied by the mutability of human beings—from which this life is full of temptations—amid his tribulations, on account of which he had said above, “The wicked have persecuted me,” and, “They almost finished me upon the earth,” inflamed by desire for the heavenly Jerusalem, looked upward and said:

“Forever, Lord, your word remains in heaven”—that is, in your angels, who maintain an eternal service without desertion.

2. [verse 90.] The following verse, after heaven, consequently pertains to earth. For it is one of the eight verses belonging to this letter. Under each Hebrew letter, eight verses are set down, until the length of this psalm is completed. “Your truth is from generation to generation; you founded the earth, and it remains.” After heaven, therefore, looking upon earth with the gaze of a faithful mind, he finds generations in it that are not in heaven, and says, “Your truth is from generation to generation”—either signifying by this repetition all generations, from none of which God’s truth has ever been absent among his saints, whether they have been fewer or more according to the changing circumstances of the times; or wishing two particular generations to be understood, namely, one belonging to the Law and the Prophets, and the other belonging to the Gospel.

But, as though disclosing the reason why truth is never absent even from these generations, he says, “You founded the earth, and it remains,” calling those who are on earth “earth.” “No one can lay any other foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11). For the foundation of that generation belonging to the Law and the Prophets was not other than Christ, who has testimony from the Law and the Prophets (Rom. 3:21). Or are Moses and the Prophets to be reckoned sons born into slavery, belonging to the slave woman who gives birth, and not to the free woman who is our mother (Gal. 4:24, 26), to whom the man says, “Mother Zion,” and, “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5)? For he is both Most High with the Father and, for our sake, made most lowly in this mother, since he who was God above her became man in her.

“On this foundation, then, Lord, you founded the earth, and it remains,” because, established upon such a foundation, it will not be shaken forever and ever (Ps. 103:5), remaining, that is, in those to whom you will give eternal life. But those whom the slave woman bore, who belong to the Old Testament—in whose figures, nevertheless, the New Testament lay concealed—and who had no understanding beyond earthly promises, do not remain. “The slave does not remain in the house forever, but the son remains forever” (John 8:35).

3. [verse 91.] “By your ordinance the day remains.” All these things are indeed day [Note: Column 1560. Erasmus, Lyons, Venice: “For all these things, and every day.” M.]; and this is “the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 117:24), and “let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. 13:13). “For all things serve you.” All, certainly, of which he was speaking; all that belongs to this day serves you. The ungodly, however, of whom it is said, “I have likened your mother to the night” (Hos. 4:5, according to the Septuagint), do not serve you.

4. [verse 92.] Then he considered from what this earth might be delivered, so that it might remain founded, and added: “If your law had not been my meditation, then perhaps I would have perished in my humiliation.” This is the law of faith—not an empty faith, but one that “works through love” (Gal. 5:6). Through it grace is obtained, and grace makes people strong in temporal tribulation, so that they do not perish in mortal humiliation.

5. [verse 93.] “Forever,” he says, “I will not forget your righteous judgments, because by them you have given me life.” Behold why it happened that he did not perish in his humiliation. For, if God does not give life, what is a human being, who can kill himself but cannot give himself life?

6. [verse 94.] He then adds and says: “I am yours; save me, because I have sought your righteous judgments.” What was said, “I am yours,” must not be understood casually. For what is not his? Is it perhaps because God is said to be in heaven that one should think something on earth is not his, when another psalm cries out, “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. 23:1)?

What, then, is the meaning of this speaker’s commending himself to God in a somewhat more intimate manner by saying, “I am yours; save me,” unless he wishes it to be understood that, to his own harm, he had wanted to be his own—which is the first and greatest evil of disobedience? It is as though he were saying: “I wanted to be my own, and I destroyed myself.” “I am yours,” he says; “save me, because I have sought your righteous judgments”—not my own desires, by which I was my own, but your righteous judgments, so that I might now be yours.

7. [verse 95.] “Sinners,” he says, “waited for me in order to destroy me; but I understood your testimonies.” What does “they waited for me in order to destroy me” mean? Did they surround the road like ambushers, waiting for him to pass so that they could kill him? Was he afraid, then, of perishing through bodily death? Certainly not. What, then, is “they waited for me,” except that they waited for him to consent to their evil? For then they would destroy him.

He has said how he did not perish: “I understood your testimonies.” But here the Greek word sounds more familiarly to the ears of the Church: “I understood your martyries” [martyria]. For even if they killed me because I did not consent to them, I would not perish while confessing your martyries; but those who waited to destroy me, waiting for the moment when I would consent, tortured me even when I confessed.

Yet he did not abandon what he had understood, since he looked upon and saw, surely, an end without end, if he persevered to the end [Note: Column 1561. Several manuscripts read thus. Others, with the editions, read “although he persevered”: perhaps instead of “so that he might thus persevere.”].

8. [verse 96.] Finally, he followed this by adding: “I have seen the end of every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad.” For he had entered the sanctuary of God and understood in the last things (Ps. 72:17).

“Every consummation,” it seems to me, must here be understood as fighting for the truth even unto death (Sir. 4:33), and enduring every evil for the sake of what is true and supremely good. The end of this consummation is to excel in the kingdom of Christ, which has no end, and there to possess life without death, without pain, and with great honor—the life acquired through the death, pains, and reproaches of this present life.

As for what he added, “Your commandment is exceedingly broad,” I understand it as nothing other than love. For what would it have profited him, amid whatever impending death and whatever tortures, to confess those martyries, if love were not in the one confessing? Let us hear the Apostle: “Even if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

In this pouring out there is breadth; within it one also walks the narrow way without distress, through the gift of him to whom it was said, “You enlarged my footsteps beneath me, and my tracks were not weakened” (Ps. 17:37). The commandment of love, then, is broad: that twofold commandment by which we are ordered to love God and our neighbor. For what is broader than that on which [Note: Column 1562. Lyons, Venice, and Lovaniensis read “there” (*ibi*). M.] “the whole Law and the Prophets depend” (Matt. 22:37–40)?

SERMON XXII

1. [verse 97.] We have often pointed out that the praiseworthy breadth in which, when we perform God’s commandments, we suffer no distress is to be understood as love. For this reason, also, in this great psalm, after he had said above, “Your commandment is exceedingly broad,” in the following verse he shows from where it is broad, saying: “How I have loved your law, O Lord!” The breadth of the commandment, therefore, is love. For how can what God commands to be loved be loved, while the command itself is not loved? For that commandment is the law. “All day long,” he says, “it is my meditation.” Behold how I have loved it: so that it was my meditation all day long—or rather, as the Greek has it, “the whole day” [Greek: *olēn tēn hēmeran*], where the continuity of the one meditating is more clearly expressed.

This is understood as all time, that is, always. By such love, desire is overcome, for desire often contradicts the performance of the law’s commands, as the flesh lusts against the spirit. Against this the spirit, which lusts against the flesh (Gal. 5:17), must love God’s law so that its meditation is the whole day.

The Apostle says: “Where, then, is your boasting? It is excluded. Through what law? Of works? No, but through the law of faith” (Rom. 3:27). This is the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6), because by seeking, asking, and knocking it obtains the good Spirit (Luke 11:10, 13), through whom love itself is poured out in our hearts (Rom. 5:5). For “all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8:14), and they are received so that they may recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 8:11), while the slave is cast out—the one who does not remain in the house forever (John 8:35), that is, Israel according to the flesh, to whom it was said:

“When you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and all the Prophets in the kingdom of God, but yourselves being cast outside. And they will come from the east and the west and the north and the south, and will recline in the kingdom of God. And behold, those who were last will be first, and those who were first will be last” (Luke 13:28–30).

But “the Gentiles,” as the Chosen Vessel says, “who were not pursuing righteousness have attained righteousness, the righteousness that is from faith; but Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not arrive at the law of righteousness. Why? Because they pursued it not from faith but as though from works, and they stumbled over the stone of stumbling” (Rom. 9:30–32). Thus they became enemies of the one who speaks here in prophecy.

[Column 1563] 2. [verse 98.] He then joins this to what follows: “You have made me wiser than my enemies through your commandment, because it is mine forever.” For they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:2–3).

But this speaker, who is wiser than these enemies of his through God’s commandment, wishes to be found with the Apostle “not having his own righteousness, which is from the law, but the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness that is from God” (Phil. 3:9). This is not because the law that his enemies read is not from God, but because they do not understand it as this speaker does, who is wiser than his enemies through it by clinging to the stone over which they stumbled.

“For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4), so that they may be justified freely by his grace (Rom. 3:24)—not like those who think that by their own strength they fulfill the law and therefore seek to establish their own righteousness, although it is indeed from God’s law [Note: Column 1563. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “and therefore not from the law,” etc.; “not” is absent from the other editions.]. Rather, he is like the son of promise who, hungering and thirsting for it (Matt. 5:6), begs it from the Father, as it were, by asking, seeking, and knocking (Matt. 7:7), so that, adopted through the Only-Begotten, he may receive it.

But how would he have understood God’s commandment in this way, unless the one to whom he says, “You have made me wiser than my enemies through your commandment,” had himself made him understand it in this way? For his enemies, born as though from Hagar into slavery (Gal. 4:24), sought temporal rewards from the same commandment; and therefore it was not theirs forever, as it is this speaker’s.

Those who translated “forever” understood the passage better than those who translated “for the age,” as though, once this age had ended, there could no longer be any commandment of the law. There will indeed be none in the form written on visible tablets and in books; but the love of God and neighbor will remain forever on the tablets of the heart. Upon this twofold commandment the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:37–40). And the reward of keeping this commandment will be the commander himself, while the reward of love will be the beloved himself, when God will be “all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28).

3. [verse 99.] But what does the next statement mean: “I have understood more than all who teach me”? Who is this person who has understood more than all who teach him? Who, I ask, is he who dares to place himself above all the Prophets, who taught with such outstanding authority not only those who lived alongside them by speaking, but also later generations by writing?

Solomon was granted such great wisdom that he seems to have been preferred even to all who lived before him (1 Kings 3:12). Yet one cannot believe that he himself was prophesied here by his father David, especially since what is said here could not be spoken in the person of Solomon: “I have restrained my feet from every evil way.”

If, however, as is more acceptable, this prophet foretells Christ, arranging the prophetic words now from the perspective of the head, who is the Savior himself, and now from the perspective of his body, which is the Church, and making them speak as one, because of that great mystery in which it was said, “The two shall become one flesh” (Eph. 5:31–32), I clearly recognize the one who “understood more than all who teach him.”

This happened when, at twelve years of age, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem and, after three days, was found by his parents [Note: [Column 1564] Ambrosianus and the manuscripts: “by those seeking him.”] sitting in the temple among the teachers, listening to them and questioning them. All who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers (Luke 2:42–47). Nor is it without reason that he had said long beforehand through this prophecy, “I have understood more than all who teach me.”

By “all,” he clearly means human beings, not God the Father, concerning whom the Son himself says, “As the Father taught me, so I speak” (John 8:28). This is extremely difficult to understand as spoken in the person of the Word, unless someone can in some way grasp that the Son’s being taught by the Father is identical with his being begotten. For to him, being and being taught are not two different things; rather, what it is for him to be is what it is for him to be taught. Surely, then, from the one from whom he has being, from that same one he also has being taught.

But in the person of the human being, in whom he took the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), it is easier to understand that he learned from the Father what he spoke. In this form of a servant, especially as a boy, human beings could think that he needed to be taught by those of greater age; but he, whom the Father taught, understood more than all who taught him.

“For your testimonies,” he says, “are my meditation.” He understood more than all who taught him because he meditated on God’s testimonies. Who knew these testimonies about himself better than the one who said:

“You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth. But I do not receive testimony from man; I say these things so that you may be saved. He was the burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a time in his light. But I have a testimony greater than John’s” (John 5:33–36).

He was meditating on such testimonies when he understood more than all who taught him.

4. [verse 100.] Those teachers may also rightly be understood to be the elders themselves, of whom he immediately says, “I have understood more than the elders.” It seems to me that this is repeated in such a way that, when we read it, that period of his life might come to mind which became known to us through the Gospel: the period when, as a child, he sat among those older than himself—that is, as a younger person among elders—and understood more than all who taught him.

“Junior” and “senior” are commonly used in relation to one another as “younger” and “older,” even if neither has reached or approached old age. Yet, if we wish to look for the explicit designation “elders” in the Gospel, above whom he understood, we find it when the scribes and Pharisees said to him: “Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.”

Behold, he was accused of transgressing the tradition of the elders. But let us hear what the one who understood more than the elders replied to them: “Why do you also transgress God’s commandment on account of your tradition?”

Then, a little later, so that not only he who is the head of the body but also the body itself and its members might understand more than those elders whose tradition concerning the washing of hands was being upheld, he called the crowds to himself and said to them: “Hear and understand.” It was as though he were saying: “Understand more than those elders, you also, so that this prophecy may be shown to have been spoken in advance concerning you as well: ‘I have understood more than the elders.’” Thus it applies not only to the head but also to the body, and so to the whole Christ:

“It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth defiles a person.” Those elders did not understand this, although they had presented their own commands concerning the washing of hands as though they were great commandments. Nor had the members of this head, who understood more than the elders, yet understood what had been said by him.

Finally, Peter answered him shortly afterward: “Explain this parable to us.” He still thought that what the Lord had spoken without figures was a parable. But he said: “Are you also still without understanding? Do you not understand that everything that enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the sewer, but what proceeds from the mouth comes out of the heart, and these things defile a person?” (Matt. 15:1–18).

“Are you also still without understanding, and do you not understand more than those elders?” But now, having heard such a teacher, our head, each one of us can plainly say, “I have understood more than the elders.”

For what follows also suits the body: “Because I have sought your commandments.” Your commandments, not human commandments; your commandments, not the commandments of the elders, who, wanting to be teachers of the law, do not understand either what they say or the matters about which they make assertions (1 Tim. 1:7).

Rightly, concerning the commandments of God—which must be sought so that we may understand more than those elders—an answer was given to those who preferred their authority to the truth: “Why do you also transgress God’s commandment in order to establish your traditions?”

5. [verse 101.] What follows, however, seems to apply not to the head but to the body: “I have restrained my feet from every evil way, so that I may keep your words.” For our head, the Savior of the body, was not carried by carnal desire into any evil way, so that he would need to restrain his feet from it, as though his feet were moving there by their own impulses. We do this when we restrain our evil desires—desires that he did not possess—from taking hold of the evil ways.

For we can keep God’s words if we do not follow our evil desires until they arrive at the evil objects they desire (Sir. 18:30), but instead restrain them through the spirit that lusts against the flesh (Gal. 5:17), so that they do not drag us, once seized and overturned, along evil ways.

6. [verse 102.] “I have not turned aside,” he says, “from your judgments, because you established your law for me.” He has said what he feared, so that he might restrain his feet from every evil way. What else is “I have not turned aside from your judgments” than what he says elsewhere, “I feared your judgments”?

I have believed in them steadfastly, because you established your law for me. You, who are within the innermost parts of me, established your law within my heart by your Spirit, as by your finger, so that I would not fear it like a slave without love, but would love it with chaste fear as a son [Note: [Column 1565] Ambrosianus and the manuscripts omit “as a son.”], and fear it with chaste love.

7. [verse 103.] Therefore see what follows: “How sweet your words are to my throat!” Or, as the Greek expresses it more precisely, “your utterances”: “sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.”

This is that sweetness which the Lord gives, so that our earth may yield its fruit (Ps. 84:13), and so that we may truly do good well—that is, not from fear of carnal evil, but from delight in spiritual good [Note: [Column 1566] Perhaps “love.”].

Some manuscripts, it is true, do not have “honeycomb,” but more have it [Note: [Column 1566] Here some books add “honey,” in place of which “honeycomb” is implicitly understood.]. Open teaching of wisdom resembles honey; but what is drawn out from more hidden mysteries, as from waxen cells, by the mouth of one who speaks—or, as it were, chews—is like the honeycomb. Yet it is sweet to the mouth of the heart, not of the flesh.

8. [verse 104.] But what does he mean when he says, “From your commandments I have understood”? For “I have understood your commandments” is one thing, and “from your commandments I have understood” is another. He therefore seems to signify that he understood something else from God’s commandments.

This is what he says, as I see it: by performing God’s commandments, he reached an understanding of those things that he had desired to know. For this reason it is written: “You have desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and the Lord will provide it for you” (Sir. 1:33). No one, then, should perversely wish to reach the heights of wisdom before possessing the humility of obedience—a height that cannot be grasped unless one comes to it in the proper order.

Let him hear, therefore: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search out what is too powerful for you; but always consider what the Lord has commanded you” (Sir. 3:22). In this way a person reaches the wisdom of hidden things through obedience to the commandments.

When he had said, “Consider what the Lord has commanded you,” he added “always” because obedience must both be preserved in order to receive wisdom and, once wisdom has been received, must not be abandoned.

This, then, is the voice of Christ’s spiritual members: “From your commandments I have understood.” For the body of Christ rightly says this in those members who, while keeping the commandments, are granted richer teaching of wisdom precisely because they preserve the commandments.

“Therefore,” he says, “I have hated every way of iniquity.” Love of righteousness must hate every iniquity. That love is greater in proportion as it is more powerfully inflamed by the greater sweetness of wisdom, which is granted to the one who obeys God and gains understanding from his commandments.

SERMON XXIII

1. [verse 105.] With the strength that God grants, we now undertake to examine and treat these verses of the psalm. The first is: “Your word is a lamp for my feet, and a light for my paths.”

“What is a lamp” is repeated by “a light”; what is “for my feet” is repeated by “for my paths.” What, then, is “your word”? Is it perhaps that Word which in the beginning was God with God—the Word, namely, through whom all things were made? It is not so. For that Word is light, but it is not a lamp.

A lamp is a creature, not the Creator; it is kindled by participation in unchangeable light. This was John, of whom the Word who is God says, “He was the burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35). Yet he is both light and a lamp. Nevertheless, in comparison with the Word of whom it was said, “The Word was God,” he was not the light; rather, he was sent to bear witness to the light.

For that was the true light—not light that is illuminated, as a human being is, but light that illuminates every human being (John 1:1–9). Yet if a lamp were not also light, he would not say to the Apostles, “You are the light of the world.”

When they heard this, they were not to think that they were what the one who said it was. For he also said of himself in another place, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). He said to them concerning themselves: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden. Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house. In this way let your light shine before men” (Matt. 5:14–16).

Thus they were to know that they had been kindled like lamps from that light which shines unchangeably. For no creature, however rational and intellectual, is illuminated by itself; it is kindled by participation in eternal truth. Even if it is sometimes called “day,” it is not the Lord’s day but the day that the Lord made; and therefore it hears [Note: Column 1567. Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Lovaniensis: “And therefore he further added.” M.]: “Come to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:6).

Because of this participation, insofar as he is also human, the Mediator himself is called a lamp in the Apocalypse (Rev. 21:23). But this assumption is unique. For it could not be said divinely of any saint, nor is it in any way permissible to say it, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), except of the one Mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2:5).

Since, then, the Only-Begotten Word, equal to the one who begets him, is called light; and a human being illuminated by that Word is also called light, and is called a lamp—as John and the Apostles are—while none of them is the Word, and the Word by which they were illuminated is not a lamp, what is this word that is called light in such a way that it is a lamp? For he says, “Your word is a lamp for my feet, and a light for my paths.”

We must understand it as the word that came to the Prophets or the word preached through the Apostles—not Christ the Word himself, but Christ’s word, concerning which it is written: “Faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. 10:17).

The Apostle Peter likewise compares the prophetic word to a lamp: “We have,” he says, “the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1:19).

What is said here, then—“Your word is a lamp for my feet, and a light for my paths”—is the word contained throughout all the holy Scriptures.

2. [verses 106–107.] “I swore,” he says, “and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness,” as one walking well by that lamp and having straight paths.

In the following word what precedes is explained. For as though we were asking what “I swore” meant, he added, “and resolved.” He called that a sworn oath which he resolved by a solemn commitment, because the mind ought to be so firmly fixed on keeping the judgments of God’s righteousness that what he resolved should be equivalent to an oath.

3. The judgments of God’s righteousness are kept by faith, when, under God the righteous judge, one believes that neither a right deed is without its reward nor sin without punishment. But because Christ’s body endured many and very grievous evils for this faith, he says, “I have been humbled exceedingly.”

He does not say, “I humbled myself,” so that the humility enjoined as a command would necessarily be understood; rather, he says, “I have been humbled exceedingly”—that is, he suffered the greatest persecution because he swore and resolved to keep the judgments of God’s righteousness.

And so that faith itself would not fail amid such great humiliation, he added: “Lord, give me life according to your word,” that is, according to your promise. For the word of God’s promises is also a lamp for the feet and a light for the paths.

So also above, in asking God to give him life, amid the humiliation of persecution, he said: “They almost destroyed me on the earth; but I did not abandon your commandments. According to your mercy, give me life, and I will keep the testimonies”—that is, the martyries—“of your mouth.”

Here it is understood that, unless he himself gives life by granting endurance—for this reason it was said, “In your endurance you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19), and of him it was said, “My endurance is from him” (Ps. 61:6)—it is not merely the body that is put to death in persecution, but the soul also, by failing to keep the martyries and judgments of God’s righteousness.

4. [verse 108.] “Make acceptable,” O Lord, “the freewill offerings of my mouth.” That is, may they please you; do not reject them, but approve them.

The voluntary offerings of the mouth are rightly understood as sacrifices of praise, offered in the confession of love and not from fear of necessity. Hence it is said, “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily” (Ps. 53:8).

But what does he add, “And teach me your judgments”? Had he not said in the preceding verses, “I have not turned aside from your judgments”? How can this be, if he did not know them? And if he did know them, how can he say here, “And teach me your judgments”?

Is it like the statement, “You have made sweetness with your servant,” followed later by, “Teach me sweetness”? We explained this in such a way that we understood it as the language of one making progress, asking that what he had received be increased for him.

5. [verse 109.] “My soul is always in your hands.” Some manuscripts have, “in my hands,” but more have “in your hands,” and this is certainly clear. “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wis. 3:1), and “in whose hand are both we and our words” (Wis. 7:16).

“And I have not forgotten your law,” he says, as though his memory were assisted in not forgetting God’s law by his being in God’s hands, where his soul is.

But how “my soul is in my hands” is to be understood, I do not know. These are the words of the righteous, not of the unrighteous; of one returning to the Father, not of one departing from the Father.

The younger son may seem to have wanted to have his soul in his own hands when he said to his father, “Give me the portion of property that falls to me.” But for this reason he was dead; for this reason he had perished (Luke 15:12, 24).

Or was “my soul is in my hands” perhaps said because he was offering it to God to be given life? Hence it is said elsewhere: “To you I have lifted up my soul” (Ps. 24:1). For earlier he had also said here, “Give me life.”

6. [verse 110.] “Sinners,” he says, “laid a snare for me, but I did not stray from your commandments.” How could this be, except because his soul, whether in God’s hands or in his own to be given life, is offered to God?

7. [verse 111.] “I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance forever.” Some, wishing to express in Latin by one word what is expressed by one word in Greek, translated this as “I have inherited.” Even if that could be Latin, it would more likely signify the one who gave the inheritance than the one who received it, just as “I have enriched” refers to the one who enriched. The complete sense is therefore better conveyed by two words, whether one says, “I have possessed as an inheritance,” or “I have acquired as an inheritance”—not “an inheritance,” but “as an inheritance.”

If it is asked what he acquired as an inheritance, he answers, “Your testimonies.” What does he wish to be understood except that he became God’s witness and confessed his testimonies—that is, that he became God’s martyr and proclaimed his martyries, as martyrs say that this was bestowed upon them by the Father, whose heir they are [Note: Column 1569. Thus Ambrosianus and the manuscripts; Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “whose gift it is.”].

Many have wished to do this and have not been able; yet none have been able unless they wished to do so, because they could not have done it if they had wished to deny God’s testimonies [Note: [Column 1569] Thus the manuscripts. Ambrosianus: “if they had wished to deny the testimonies of faith.” Erasmus and Lovaniensis: “if God’s faith,” etc.]. But even their will was prepared by the Lord.

Therefore this speaker testifies that he acquired these things as an inheritance, and forever, because their glory is not the temporal glory of people seeking empty things. It is eternal glory: the glory of those who suffer for a brief time and reign without end.

Hence he continues: “For they are the rejoicing of my heart.” Even if there is affliction of the body, there is nevertheless rejoicing of the heart.

8. [verse 112.] Then he added: “I have inclined my heart to perform your righteous judgments forever, because of the reward.”

The one who says, “I have inclined my heart,” had already said, “Incline my heart toward your testimonies,” so that we may understand this to be at once a divine gift and an act of our own will.

But shall we perform God’s righteous judgments forever? Those works that we perform for the needs of our neighbors cannot be eternal, just as the needs themselves cannot. Yet if we do them without love, there is no righteousness; if we do them with love, the love itself is eternal, and an eternal reward is prepared for it.

For this reward, therefore, he says that he inclined his heart to perform God’s righteous judgments, so that, loving forever, he might forever deserve to possess what he loves.

SERMON XXIV

1. [verse 113.] The passage of this psalm on which, by God’s will, we are going to speak begins as follows: “I have hated the iniquitous, and I have loved your law.”

He does not say, “I have hated the iniquitous, and I have loved the righteous,” or, “I have hated iniquity, and I have loved your law.” Rather, after saying, “I have hated the iniquitous,” he explains why by adding, “and I have loved your law,” showing that he does not hate in wicked people the nature by which they are human beings, but the iniquity by which they are enemies of the law he loves.

2. [verse 114.] Then follows: “You are my helper and my protector.” A helper in doing good; a protector in escaping evil.

When he adds, “I have hoped beyond hope in your word,” he speaks as a son of promise.

3. [verse 115.] But what does the following verse mean: “Depart from me, evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God”? For he does not say, “I will perform them,” but “I will search them out.”

He desires the evildoers to depart from him so that he may know the commandments perfectly and diligently; indeed, he drives them away by addressing them. For evildoers train us in performing the commandments, but draw us away from examining them—not only when they persecute us or want to quarrel with us, but also when they obey and honor us, yet insist that we occupy ourselves with helping their vicious and burdensome desires and spend our time on them.

Or else they oppress the weak and compel them to bring their cases to us. To such people we do not dare say, “Man, who appointed me a judge or divider over you?” (Luke 12:14). For the Apostle has appointed churchmen as judges in such cases, while forbidding Christians to quarrel in court (1 Cor. 6:1–6) [Note: Column 1570. Most manuscripts omit “For the Apostle has appointed churchmen for such cases,” but retain “the Apostle [appointed] judges,” etc.].

Nor do we say to those who do not seize what belongs to others but greedily reclaim what is their own, “Beware of every kind of greed,” setting before their eyes the man to whom it was said, “Fool, this night your soul will be demanded from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).
