For even when we say this, they do not depart from us or withdraw; instead they persist, press, plead, cause tumult, and extort, so that we occupy ourselves with helping them obtain the things they love rather than with searching out God’s commandments, which we love.

Oh, with what weariness of turbulent crowds and with what desire for divine utterances was it said: “Depart from me, evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God”!

Let obedient and faithful people who rarely seek us for their secular affairs, and who readily submit to our judgments, forgive us. They do not crush us by quarreling, but rather console us by obeying.

Certainly, because there are those who act stubbornly against one another; who, when they oppress the good, disregard our judgments; and who make us lose time that ought to be spent on divine matters—certainly, I say, because of these people, may we too be permitted to cry out in this voice of Christ’s body: “Depart from me, evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God.”

### 4. [v. 116]

Then, after driving away—as though from the eyes of his heart—the flies that were rushing upon him, he returns to the one to whom he had said, “You are my helper and my protector; I have hoped in your word”; and continuing his prayer, he says, “Receive me according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation.”

He who had already said, “My protector,” asks to be received more and more, and to be brought to that for the sake of which he endures so many troubles, trusting that he will live there more truly than in these dreams of human affairs. For this is spoken of the future: “and I shall live,” as though one does not live in this dead body. For “the body is dead because of sin”; and “as we await the redemption of our body, we have been saved in hope,” and “hoping for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:10, 23–25). But hope does not put us to shame, “if the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). For the sake of receiving him more abundantly, he cries out to the Father, “Do not put me to shame in my expectation.”

### 5. [v. 117]

And as though an answer had been given to him in silence—“You do not wish to be put to shame in your expectation? Do not cease meditating on my justifications”—he recognizes that this meditation is often hindered by the languor of the soul and says, “Help me, and I shall be saved; and I shall meditate forever on your justifications.”

[Note: [Col. 1570] Er. Lugd. Ven. and Lov. read, “If not.” M.]

### 6. [v. 118]

“You have despised all”; or, as seems to be expressed more carefully from the Greek, “You have reduced to nothing all who depart from your justifications,” because their thought is unjust. Therefore he cried out, “Help me, and I shall be saved, and I shall meditate forever on your justifications”: for God reduces to nothing all who depart from his justifications.

But why do they depart? “Because,” he says, “their thought is unjust.” There one approaches; there one departs. All works, whether evil or good, proceed from thought: in thought each person is innocent, in thought each person is guilty. Hence it is written, “Holy thought will preserve you” (Prov. 2:11); and elsewhere we read, “There will be an inquiry into the thoughts of the ungodly” (Wis. 1:9); and the Apostle says, “Their thoughts accusing or even defending them” (Rom. 2:15).

But where is the person fortunate who is wretched in thought? Or how is the one who has been reduced to nothing not wretched there? For iniquity is a great barrenness. Rightly it is said, “Let the unrighteous who act vainly be put to shame” (Ps. 24:4), that is, uselessly, as though reduced to nothing.

### 7. [v. 119]

The Psalm continues: “I have reckoned”—or “thought” or “considered”—“all the sinners of the earth as transgressors.” Our translators have rendered the one Greek word ἐλογισάμην (*elogisamēn*) in many ways; but that sentence is profound, and, if the Lord helps, it must be penetrated more carefully in another discussion. The addition, “Therefore I have loved your testimonies forever,” makes it much more profound.

For the Apostle says, “The law produces wrath,” and, explaining the reason for this statement, he says, “For where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15), thus showing that not everyone is a transgressor. For not everyone has the law. That not everyone has the law he states more clearly elsewhere: “Those who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law” (Rom. 2:12).

What, then, does this mean: “I have reckoned all the sinners of the earth as transgressors”? For the moment it will be enough to have posed the question; it must be treated in another discourse, if God grants this, lest the length of the present discussion force it to be explained too briefly for what is explained to be properly understood.

## SERMON XXV  
### Reconciling the Psalm with the Apostle

### 1. [v. 119]

We ask, if God grants that we can find the answer, how we should understand what is said in this great Psalm: “Transgressors”—or rather, “those transgressing”; for the Greek says παραβαίνοντας (*parabainontas*), not παραβάτας (*parabatas*)—“I have reckoned all the sinners of the earth as transgressors.” The Apostle, however, says, “For where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

He said this when distinguishing the promise from the law. To gather the fuller meaning from what precedes: “For,” he says, “the promise to Abraham or to his offspring that he should be heir of the world did not come through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise nullified; for the law produces wrath, and where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:13–15). “Therefore it is by faith, so that the promise may be secure according to grace for all the offspring—not only for the one who is of the law, but also for the one who is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all” (Rom. 4:16).

Why does the Apostle say this, unless to show that the law, without the grace of the promise, not only does not remove sin but even increases it? Hence also the statement, “The law entered in so that the offense might abound.” But because everything is forgiven by grace—not only what is committed without the law, but also what is committed under the law—he immediately adds, “But where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20).

The Apostle therefore does not reckon all sinners as transgressors, but only those who transgress the law. “For where there is no law,” he says, “neither is there transgression.” Accordingly, according to the Apostle, every transgressor is indeed a sinner, because he sins against the law; but not every sinner is a transgressor, because some sin without the law: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

Moreover, if no one sinned without the law, the same Apostle would not say, “All who have sinned without the law will perish without the law.” According to this Psalm, however, if all the sinners of the earth are transgressors, then there is no sin without transgression; but there is no transgression without law; therefore there is no sin except under the law.

Thus the one who says, “I have reckoned all the sinners of the earth as transgressors,” wants sinners to be understood as none other than those who have transgressed the law, and for this reason contradicts the one who said, “All who have sinned without the law will perish without the law.” According to the Apostle, there are therefore some sinners who are not transgressors, namely, those who have sinned without the law: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression.” According to the Psalm, however, there is no sinner without transgression, because he reckons all the sinners of the earth as transgressors. Therefore, according to the Psalm, no one sinned without the law, since where there is no law, neither is there transgression.

Or shall we perhaps say that it is true that there is no transgression where there is no law, but untrue that some have sinned without the law? Or that it is true that some have sinned without the law, but untrue that where there is no law transgression cannot exist? The Apostle said both: both are therefore true, because Truth itself spoke both through the Apostle.

How, then, will it be true that in this Psalm the same Truth undoubtedly said, “I have reckoned all the sinners of the earth as transgressors”? For we are answered: Who, then, are those who, according to the Apostle, sinned without the law? Surely none of them can be reckoned a transgressor, since according to the same Apostle there is no transgression where there is no law.

### 2.

When the Apostle said, “All who have sinned without the law will perish without the law,” he was speaking of the law that God gave through his servant Moses to his people Israel. The words surrounding the statement themselves show this. For he was discussing Jews and Greeks—that is, Gentiles, who did not belong to circumcision but to uncircumcision. He calls them “without the law” because they had not received the law which the Jews gloried in having received. Hence he says to them, “But if you call yourself a Jew, and rest upon the law, and boast in God…”

Finally, we must consider how he arrived at this statement, “All who have sinned without the law will perish without the law.” “Wrath,” he says, “and indignation, tribulation and distress upon every soul of man who works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek; but glory and honor and peace for everyone who works good, for the Jew first and also for the Greek. For there is no partiality with God.”

To this he added the point that now gives rise to the question, saying, “For all who have sinned without the law will perish without the law; and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Rom. 2:8–17). He intends the Jews by the latter and the Greeks by the former, since these were the people under discussion. He shows that both are under sin, so that both may confess their need of grace. For this reason he says, “There is no distinction: for all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 3:22–24).

Whom does he mean by “all have sinned” except the Jews and the Greeks, concerning whom he had said, “There is no distinction”? For shortly before he says of these same people, “For we have already charged that Jews and Greeks are all under sin” (Rom. 3:9).

Accordingly, all who sinned without the law—namely, without the law in which the Jews gloried—will perish without the law; and all who sinned under the law—that is, the Jews themselves—will be judged by the law. Yet they will not therefore avoid perishing unless they believe in him who came “to seek what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

### 3.

Some Catholic commentators, failing to attend sufficiently to the actual meaning of the Apostle’s words, have understood them otherwise. They have said that those who sinned without the law perish, whereas those who sinned under the law are merely judged and do not perish—as though they were believed to be purified through temporary punishments, like the one of whom it is said, “He himself will be saved, but as through fire.”

But this is rightly understood from the foundation about which the Apostle was speaking when he said it. Earlier he had said, “As a wise architect I laid a foundation, and another builds upon it; but let each one see how he builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus”; and so forth, until the passage where he says that the one who builds upon this foundation not gold, silver and precious stones, but wood, hay and straw, is saved through fire (1 Cor. 3:10–15).

Such a person, however, neither rejects Christ so as not to receive him, nor abandons the foundation once received; and he places that foundation above all his carnal pleasures, by which he is captured and overcome, when the moment comes at which either those pleasures or Christ must be abandoned. If Christ is not placed first, he is not the foundation for that person. For the foundation is placed before all the later parts of a structure.

I do not think that those who held that the people of whom it is said, “They will be judged by the law,” do not perish thought this for any other reason than that they have Christ as their foundation. They paid too little attention, therefore, to what we have demonstrated; and Scripture itself cries out that the Apostle is speaking of the Jews, who are without Christ as their foundation.

What Christian, however, would say that a Jew who does not believe in Christ will not perish but will merely be judged, when Christ himself testifies to that same people that he was sent for the sake of the sheep that had perished from among them (Matt. 15:24)? And does he not say that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for Sodom than for the Jewish city that did not believe in him, though he performed such mighty miracles there (Matt. 11:23–24)?

[Note: [Col. 1574] Er. Lov. read: “testifies; more mildly and tolerably, etc.” Lugd. Ven. read: “testifies; and more mildly and tolerably, etc.” M.]

### 4.

If, then, the Apostle called the other nations “without the law” in relation to the law that God gave through Moses to the people of Israel but did not give to the other nations, what shall we understand the Psalm to mean when it says, “I have considered all the sinners of the earth transgressors,” unless we understand that there is some law according to which the sinners of the other nations are transgressors? “For where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

What law is this, unless perhaps the one about which the same Apostle says, “When Gentiles who do not have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, although they do not have the law, are a law to themselves” (Rom. 2:14)? According to the first statement, “not having the law,” they sinned without the law and will perish without the law; but according to the second, “they are a law to themselves,” all the sinners of the earth are rightly considered transgressors.

No one does injury to another except one who does not want it done to himself; and in this he transgresses the law of nature, which he cannot be allowed to claim ignorance of, since he does not want to suffer what he does.

But was this natural law not present among the people of Israel? Certainly it was, since they too were human beings. They would have been without natural law only if they could have existed outside the nature of the human race. They therefore became transgressors all the more through the divine law, by which that natural law was either restored, augmented, or confirmed.

### 5.

Moreover, if infants are not improperly reckoned among all the sinners of the earth because of the bonds of original sin, then they too, in “the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. 5:14), are shown to belong to that transgression which was first committed when the law was given in paradise (Gen. 3:6). Accordingly, with absolutely no exception, all the sinners of the earth are rightly considered transgressors.

“All have sinned and lack the glory of God.” Therefore the grace of the Savior finds all as transgressors—some more, others less. For the greater a person’s knowledge of the law, the less excuse there is for sin; and the less excuse there is for sin, the more evident the transgression.

[Note: [Col. 1574] Most manuscripts omit “the less excuse there is for sin.”]

It therefore remained for a righteousness belonging not to human beings but to God—that is, given by God—to come to the aid of all.

Hence the Apostle says, “Through the law comes knowledge of sin.” Not its removal, but its knowledge. “But now,” he says, “the righteousness of God has been manifested without the law, testified to by the Law and the Prophets” (Rom. 3:20–23).

Accordingly, the Psalmist also adds, “Therefore I have loved your testimonies,” as though he were saying:

Because the law—whether given in paradise, implanted by nature, or promulgated in written form—made all the sinners of the earth transgressors, therefore I have loved your testimonies, which are in your law and speak of your grace, so that the righteousness in me may not be mine but yours.

The law is useful for this purpose: that it may send us to grace. For not only does it testify to the manifestation of the righteousness of God, which exists without the law, but precisely by making people transgressors, so that “the letter kills,” it compels them through fear to flee to the life-giving Spirit (2 Cor. 3:6). Through that Spirit the totality of sins is erased and love for right actions is inspired. “Therefore,” he says, “I have loved your testimonies.”

Some manuscripts have “forever”; some do not. But if it is present, “forever” should be understood in the sense of “as long as this life is lived.” For here the testimonies from the Law and the Prophets are necessary, bearing witness to the righteousness of God by which we are justified freely. Here our own testimonies are also necessary, for the sake of which the martyrs have brought this present life to an end.

[Note: [Col. 1574] Nearly all manuscripts read “that human beings might have help,” rather than “that all might have help.”]

### 6. [v. 120]

Having recognized the grace of God, which alone frees from the transgression committed through knowledge of the law, he says in prayer:

“Pierce my flesh with nails because of your fear.”

Some of our translators rendered this more explicitly, since what could be expressed in Greek by one word—καθήλωσον (*kathēlōson*)—can be rendered, “Pierce with nails.” Others wished to translate it simply as “Pierce,” and did not add “with nails.” Thus, by trying to render one Greek word with one Latin word, they explained the meaning less fully. For the word “pierce” does not express the nails, whereas καθήλωσον cannot be understood without nails; in Latin it can be expressed only by two words, as in “pierce with nails.”

What does this mean except what the Apostle says: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14)? And again: “I have been crucified with Christ; nevertheless I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:19–20).

What else does this mean except: “The righteousness in me is not my own, which comes from the law, through which I became a transgressor, but the righteousness of God, that is, the righteousness that comes to me from God” (Phil. 3:9), not from myself?

Thus Christ lives in me—not I—“who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord’” (1 Cor. 1:30–31). He also says, “Those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (Gal. 5:24).

Although it is said here that they themselves crucified their flesh, in this Psalm God is nevertheless asked to accomplish it, when the prayer says, “Pierce my flesh with nails because of your fear.” We are thereby to understand that even what we rightly do must be attributed to the grace of God, who works in us both willing and working according to his good pleasure (Phil. 2:13).

### 7.

But what does it mean that, after saying, “Pierce my flesh with nails because of your fear,” he adds, “For I was afraid of your judgments”? What is meant by “Pierce me because of your fear; for I was afraid”? If he had already feared, or was fearing, why did he continue to pray that God would crucify his flesh because of fear?

Or did he wish fear to be added to him, so that he might fear as much as would suffice for crucifying his flesh—that is, his carnal desires and affections—as though he were saying, “Perfect your fear in me; for I was afraid of your judgments”?

But there is another and deeper meaning, which must be drawn out, as God grants, by searching the depths of this Scripture. “Pierce,” he says, “my flesh with nails because of your fear; for I was afraid of your judgments.” That is: Let my carnal desires be restrained by your chaste fear, which endures forever and ever (Ps. 18:10); for I was afraid of your judgments when the law threatened me with a punishment that could not give me righteousness.

But this fear, by which punishment is dreaded, is cast out by perfected love (1 John 4:18), which makes people free—not through fear of punishment, but through delight in righteousness. For this fear, in which righteousness is not loved but punishment is feared, is servile, because it is carnal; and therefore it does not crucify the flesh.

The will to sin remains alive. It appears in action when impunity is hoped for; but when punishment is believed to follow, it lives hidden—but it still lives. A person would prefer what the law forbids to be permitted, and grieves that it is not permitted, because he does not take spiritual delight in the law’s goodness but carnally fears the evil that it threatens.

By chaste fear, however, the love that casts out this fear is afraid to sin even if impunity should follow. It does not judge impunity to follow, because through love of righteousness it considers sin itself a punishment. By such fear the flesh is crucified: carnal pleasures, which are forbidden by the letter of the law rather than avoided, are conquered by delight in spiritual goods, and are destroyed as that victory grows toward perfection.

“Pierce,” therefore, he says, “my flesh with nails because of your fear; for I was afraid of your judgments.” That is: Give me chaste fear, to which that fear of the law, like a pedagogue, led me and by which I was afraid of your judgments.

## SERMON XXVI

### 1. [v. 121]

We have now undertaken to consider and discuss these verses of this great Psalm:

“I have done judgment and righteousness; do not hand me over to those who harm me.”

It is not surprising that the one who had earlier asked, because of the fear of God—and certainly chaste fear—to have his flesh pierced with nails, that is, his carnal desires, has done judgment and righteousness. Such desires usually obstruct our judgment so that it is not right.

Although in ordinary usage of our language “judgment” may be called either right or wrong—for in the Gospel people are told, “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a righteous judgment” (John 7:24)—in this passage “judgment” is placed in such a way that, unless it is right, it ought not to be called judgment at all. Otherwise it would not be enough to say, “I have done judgment”; one would have to say, “I have done righteous judgment.”

The Lord Jesus spoke in this manner when he said, “You have left the weightier matters of the Law: judgment, mercy and faith” (Matt. 23:23). Here too “judgment” is placed in such a way that there is no judgment if it is perverse. The same usage appears in many places in the divine Scriptures, as in, “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1), and in Isaiah, “I expected him to perform judgment, but he performed iniquity” (Isa. 5:7).

He does not say, “I expected him to perform righteous judgment, but he performed unrighteous judgment”; rather, it is as though judgment exists precisely because it is righteous, and what is unrighteous is not judgment.

Righteousness, however, is not ordinarily called good righteousness or bad righteousness, as good or bad judgment is sometimes mentioned. It is good by that very fact that it is righteousness. Thus ordinary speech allows us to say both “good judgment” and “bad judgment,” just as it allows us to say both “good judge” and “bad judge.” But one does not say “good righteousness” or “bad righteousness,” any more than one says “good just person” or “bad just person,” because anyone who is just is necessarily good.

Righteousness, therefore, is a great and especially praiseworthy virtue of the soul; there is no need to discuss it at length here. Judgment, when a more precise manner of speaking places it only in the good, is the activity of this virtue. For the one who has righteousness judges rightly—or rather, according to this manner of speaking, the one who has righteousness judges, because he does not judge at all unless he judges rightly.

The word “righteousness” in this passage signifies not the virtue itself but its work. For who makes righteousness in a human being except the one who justifies the ungodly—that is, who by his grace makes the ungodly righteous? Hence the Apostle says, “Being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3:24).

Therefore the one who has righteousness within himself—that is, the work of grace—does righteousness, that is, the work of righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 1577] Some manuscripts read “more exacting.”]

### 2.

“I have done,” he says, “judgment and righteousness; do not hand me over to those who harm me”—that is, “I have done righteous judgment; do not hand me over to those who persecute me for this reason.”

Some manuscripts also read, “Do not hand me over to those who persecute me.” What was said in Greek as τοῖς ἀντιδικοῦσι (*tois antidikousin*) has been translated by some as “those who harm,” by others as “those who persecute,” and by others as “those who slander.” I am surprised that, among all the manuscripts I have been able to consult, I have nowhere read “those who oppose,” since without controversy the Greek ἀντίδικος (*antidikos*) is called in Latin *adversarius*, “adversary.”

As he prays not to be handed over by the Lord to those who oppose him, what is he praying for except what we pray when we say, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13)? For the adversary is the one of whom the Apostle says, “Lest the tempter should have tempted you” (1 Thess. 3:5).

God hands over the person whom he abandons. The adversary does not deceive the one whom God does not abandon, preserving in him the virtue that adorns a human being according to his will. But from the one who had said in his prosperity, “I shall not be moved forever,” he turned away his face, and the man became troubled and was shown to himself (Ps. 30:7–8).

Whoever, therefore, has his flesh crucified by chaste fear of God and, uncorrupted by any carnal enticement, performs judgment and the work of righteousness, ought to pray not to be handed over to those who oppose him—that is, not to yield to his persecutors through fear of suffering evil, and thereby commit evil.

From the one who gives victory over desire, so that a person is not dragged along by pleasure, he also receives strength for endurance, so that he is not broken by pain. For of him it is said, “The Lord will give sweetness” (Ps. 85:13), and of him it is also said, “My patience is from him” (Ps. 62:6).

[Note: [Col. 1577] Some manuscripts read this way. The editions read, “And he hands over.”]

### 3. [vv. 122–123]

Finally, the Psalm continues:

“Receive your servant for good; let not the proud slander me.”

They drive me toward evil so that I may fall; but you receive me for good.

Those who translated the phrase as “Let them not slander me” followed a Greek expression less customary in the Latin language. Or perhaps the phrase “Let them not slander me” has the force it would have if one said, “Let them not seize me by slandering me”?

### 4.

Many slanders of the proud can be understood, from whom Christian humility is despised. But the greatest of them is perhaps present if the proud are understood here as human beings who slander us because we worship one who is dead.

Christian humility itself is indicated and divinely commended by the death of Christ. This slander is common to both kinds of unbelievers, Jews and Gentiles. Heretics too have their slanders, each particular to its own heresy; and schismatics have theirs, all of whom pride has cut off from the structure of Christ’s members.

How great and of what kind is the slander of the devil himself, who slandered the righteous man by saying, “Does Job worship the Lord for nothing?” (Job 1:9).

All these slanders of the proud, like the poisons of serpents, are overcome when Christ crucified is contemplated with the most watchful and devoted reverence. For this reason, as a prefiguration, at God’s merciful command Moses lifted up in the wilderness the likeness of a serpent on a tree (Num. 21:9; John 3:14), so that the likeness of sinful flesh, destined to be crucified, might be prefigured in Christ.

Looking upon this saving cross, we drive out all the venom of those who slander. This man too, gazing upon it with a kind of intense attention, says, “My eyes failed in longing for your salvation and for the word of your righteousness.”

For God made Christ himself, because of the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3), to be sin for us, so that we might be the righteousness of God in him (2 Cor. 5:21). He therefore says that his eyes failed in longing for the word of this righteousness of God, gazing ardently and thirstingly, while mindful of human weakness and desiring the divine grace in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1578] The manuscripts read this way. The editions have “the divine grace of Christ.”]

### 5. [v. 124]

Hence the Psalm continues:

“Deal with your servant according to your mercy”—certainly not according to my righteousness.

“And teach me your justifications,” he says: undoubtedly those by which God makes people righteous, not those by which they make themselves righteous.

### 6. [v. 125]

“I am your servant.”

For things did not go well for me when I wished to be my own free man rather than your servant.

“Give me understanding, and I shall know your testimonies.”

This request must never be interrupted. It is not enough to have received understanding and learned God’s testimonies unless one continues always to receive it, and in a certain sense continually drinks from the fountain of eternal light. For the more intelligent a person becomes, the more and more God’s testimonies are understood.

### 7. [v. 126]

“It is time,” he says, “for the Lord to act.”

Several manuscripts have this reading, rather than “It is time, Lord.” What time, then, or what action, did he wish to be understood as belonging to the Lord?

It is certainly the action he had mentioned shortly before: “Deal with your servant according to your mercy.” This is the time for the Lord to do this. What is it except the grace revealed in its own time through his Christ? Concerning this time the Apostle says, “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4).

For this reason, elsewhere, adding prophetic testimony, when he says, “At an acceptable time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you,” he immediately adds, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (Isa. 49:8; 2 Cor. 6:2).

But why, as though he wished to show that it was time for the Lord to act, did he immediately add, “They have dissipated your law”? It is as though the time for the Lord to act had come for this reason: because the proud had dissipated his law. They were “ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own,” and therefore “were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3).

What else is “They have dissipated your law” than this: “Through the wickedness of transgression they did not preserve its integrity”?

It was therefore necessary that the law be given to the proud who presumed upon the freedom of their own will, so that, after transgressing it, those who were pierced might be humbled and run—not through the law, but through faith—to the grace that comes to their aid.

Thus, after the law had been dissipated, it was time for mercy to be sent through the only-begotten Son of God. “The law entered in so that the offense might abound”; through this offense the law was dissipated; and at the appropriate time Christ came, so that “where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more” (Rom. 5:20).

### 8. [v. 127]

“Therefore,” he says, “I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz.”

Grace accomplishes this: that God’s commandments are fulfilled through love, since they could not be fulfilled through fear. For “the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Hence the Lord himself also says, “I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17); and the same Apostle says, “Love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13:10).

“Therefore, above gold and topaz.” For this too is read in another Psalm: “Above gold and a precious stone in abundance” (Ps. 19:11). Topaz, they report, is a very precious stone.

In the Old Testament, however, people did not understand the grace hidden beneath it, as though beneath a veil—the reality signified when they were unable to look directly at Moses’ face (Exod. 34:33–35; 2 Cor. 3:13–16). On account of an earthly and carnal reward they tried to obey God’s commandments, but they did not obey them, because they loved something else rather than the commandments themselves.

Thus those works were not the works of willing people, but rather the burdens of unwilling people. But when the commandments themselves are loved above gold and a very precious stone, every earthly reward is considered cheap in comparison with them; and no other goods of a human being can in any way be compared with those goods by which the human being himself becomes good.

### 9. [v. 128]

“Therefore,” he says, “I was corrected in relation to all your commandments.”

Certainly I was corrected because I loved them; and by loving those commandments, which are themselves right, I clung to them so that I too might become right.

What he adds follows naturally: “I hated every way of iniquity.”

For how could one who loves the right way fail to hate the wrong way? If he loved gold and a precious stone, he would surely hate whatever could inflict damage upon such things. Likewise, because he loved God’s commandments, he hated the way of iniquity, as one would hate some monstrous rock in a sea passage where it is necessary to suffer shipwreck involving such precious cargo.

To avoid this, the person who sails with the merchandise of the divine commandments on the wood of the cross sets his course far away from that rock.

## SERMON XXVII

[Col. 1580]

### 1. [v. 129]

These are the words of the Psalm that, with the Lord’s help, we shall discuss:

“Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul has searched them out.”

Who can enumerate even in general terms God’s testimonies? Heaven and earth, his visible and invisible works, in a certain sense bear witness to his goodness and greatness. Even the repeated and customary course of nature, by which the swiftness of time rolls onward through all kinds of things—even temporal and mortal things, which have certainly become cheap through familiarity—bears witness to the Creator if a devout observer notices it.

What of these things is not wonderful, if each is measured not by familiarity but by reason? But if, as though beneath the gaze of a single contemplation, we dare to look upon everything at once, does not what the prophet says happen within us: “I considered your works, and I was terrified” (Hab. 3:1)?

Yet this man was not terrified by the very wonder of things. Rather, he said that wonder was the reason why he ought to search them out, because they are wonderful. For after saying, “Your testimonies are wonderful,” he immediately adds, “therefore my soul has searched them out,” as though the difficulty of investigating them had made him more curious.

For the more hidden the causes of any thing are, the more wonderful it is.

### 2.

If, then, such a person should come before us—a person who says that he searches out God’s testimonies because they are wonderful, while the whole creation, both what is seen and what is unseen, is full of them—would we not restrain him by saying, “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search out what is too strong for you; but always think about what the Lord has commanded you” (Sir. 3:22)?

But suppose he answers us and says, “Those very things that the Lord has commanded, and that you order me to think about, are his wonderful testimonies. They testify that he is both Lord, because he commands, and good and great, because he commands such things.”

Would we dare to turn the man back from searching them out, rather than encourage him to do so diligently and devote as much effort as he can to so great a matter?

Or shall we perhaps acknowledge that God’s commands are testimonies of his goodness but deny that they are wonderful? What is surprising if the good Lord commands good things?

On the contrary, this very fact is entirely wondrous, and its reason must be carefully investigated: although the good God gave good commands, he nevertheless gave a good law to people whom that same law could not make alive, and from the good law there was no righteousness.

For if a law had been given that could make alive, righteousness would certainly have come from the law. Why, then, was a law given that could not make alive, and from which there was no righteousness? Surely this is wondrous; surely it is astonishing.

These, then, are the wonderful testimonies of God. For this reason the soul of this man searched them out, since it could not be said to him concerning them, “Do not search what is too strong for you; but always think about what the Lord has commanded you.” For these are precisely the things that the Lord has commanded us, and therefore they must always be considered.

Let us rather see what this soul, which searched them out, discovered.

3. [verse 130.] “The unfolding of your words,” he says, “gives light and grants understanding to little ones.” What is a “little one” except one who is humble and weak? Do not therefore grow proud; do not presume upon your own virtue, which is nothing; and you will understand why the good God gave a good law that nevertheless cannot give life. For it was given to make you little from being great, to show that you do not possess from yourself the strength to fulfill the law; and thus, needy and lacking assistance, you might flee to grace and cry out: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak” (Ps. 6:3). By searching into this, then, this little one understood what the least of the Apostles, Paul—that is, the “little” one—demonstrates: the law was given though it could not give life because Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ (Gal. 3:21–22).

Yes, Lord, do this—yes, merciful Lord: command what cannot be fulfilled; or rather, command what can be fulfilled only through your grace, so that when human beings cannot fulfill it by their own strength, every mouth may be stopped and no one may seem great in his own eyes. Let all be little, and let the whole world become guilty before you, because “no flesh will be justified before you by works of the law; for through the law comes knowledge of sin. But now your righteousness has been manifested apart from the law, attested by the Law and the Prophets” (Rom. 3:19–21). These are your marvelous testimonies, which the soul of this little one searched out; and he found them because he was humbled and became little. For who fulfills your commandments as they ought to be fulfilled—that is, from faith working through love (Gal. 5:6)—unless that very love is poured into his heart through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5:5)?

4. [verse 131.] This little one also confesses the same thing: “I opened my mouth,” he says, “and drew in the Spirit, because I longed for your commandments.” What did he long for except to fulfill the divine commandments? But the weak had no means of doing mighty things, nor the little one of doing great things. He opened his mouth, confessing that he could not do it by himself, and drew in that by which he could do it. He opened his mouth by asking, seeking, and knocking; and, thirsting, he drank deeply of the good Spirit, by whom he could do what he himself could not: the holy, righteous, and good commandment (ibid. 7:12). For if we, though evil, know how to give good gifts to our children, how much more will our heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:10, 13)? For it is not those who act by their own spirit, but all who are led by the Spirit of God, who are sons of God (Rom. 8:14)—not because they themselves do nothing, but lest they do no good: they are led by the Good One so that they may act. For each person becomes a good son all the more truly, the more generously the good Spirit is given to him by the Father.

5. [verse 132.] Finally, this person still asks. He opened his mouth and drew in breath, but he still knocks at the Father’s door and seeks; he drank, but the more sweetly he tasted, the more ardently he thirsts. Hear the words of the thirsty man: “Look upon me,” he says, “and have mercy on me according to the judgment of those who love your name”—that is, according to the judgment you exercised upon those who love your name, since, in order that they might love you, you first loved them. For the apostle John says: “We love God”; and as though the cause that made us love him were being sought, he added, “because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

6. [verse 133.] See what this man also says with complete clarity: “Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me.” What else does he say here than, “Make me upright and free according to your promise”? For the more God’s love reigns in anyone, the less iniquity rules over him. What else, then, does he ask than that, by God’s gift, he may love God? By loving God, he loves himself, so that he may be able to love his neighbor healthfully as himself; and upon these commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:37–40). What, then, does he pray for except that God may cause the commandments he imposes by commanding to be fulfilled by helping?

7. [verse 134.] But what does he mean when he says, “Redeem me from the slanders of men, and I will keep your commandments”? If those men bring true charges against him, they are not slandering him; if they bring false charges, why does he desire to be redeemed from slanders—that is, from false accusations—which cannot harm him? A false accusation, which is slander, does not make a person guilty except before a human judge. But where God is the judge, no one is injured by a false charge, because it is imputed not to the person against whom it is brought, but rather to the person who brings it.

Or is here foreshadowed the prayer of the Church and of the entire Christian people, who were redeemed from the slanders of men by which Christians everywhere were harassed? But does he therefore keep God’s commandments? Did not the holy people, amid those very slanders, when persecution was raging, preserve God’s commandments far more gloriously in their tribulations, refusing to yield to their persecutors in the commission of impiety? Surely this is the meaning: “Redeem me from the slanders of men, and I will keep your commandments”: Act within me by pouring in your Spirit, so that the slanders of men may not overcome me through fear and draw me away from your commandments into their evil deeds. For if you do this within me—that is, if in this way you redeem me from their slanders, granting me patience so that I do not fear the false accusations they bring against me—I will keep your commandments amid those very slanders.

[Note: [Col. 1582] The editions read, “I will not keep.” The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts.]

8. [verse 135.] “Make your face shine,” he says, “upon your servant”—that is, manifest your presence by coming to my aid and helping me. “And teach me your ordinances.” Teach me, certainly, so that I may do them; as is more explicitly read elsewhere: “Teach me to do your will” (Ps. 142:10). Those who hear, even if they retain in memory what they hear, are by no means to be considered to have learned if they do not do it. For the word of truth says: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” (John 6:45). Whoever therefore does not do—that is, does not come—has not learned.

9. [verse 136.] Recalling the pain of repentance for his transgression, this man says: “Streams of waters ran down my eyes, because they did not keep your law”—that is, my very eyes. For in some manuscripts this too is read: “Because I did not keep your law.” Thus “streams of waters ran down,” that is, outpourings of tears. This is the same construction by which one could say, “My feet descended mountains,” even without saying “through the mountains” or “onto the mountains”; just as one says, “He descended the stairs,” without saying “by way of the stairs,” or “He descended the pool,” without saying “into the pool.”

And he rightly says “ran down,” with the humility, that is, of repentance. For they had “risen” when, through proud obstinacy, they had stood erect and become exalted. They seemed to themselves to be above, when, ignorant of God’s righteousness, they wanted to establish their own (Rom. 10:3). Wearied by it and confounded by transgression of the law, they descended from that exaltation by weeping, so that through repentance they might rather obtain God’s righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 1583] Am. Er. and many manuscripts read, “by seeking.”]

There are manuscripts that do not read “ran down,” but “passed over,” as though he were saying with exaggeration that he had passed beyond fountains of water in weeping. By this we are to understand “streams of waters”—that is, that he wept more than waters flow from their sources.

[Note: [Col. 1583] Er. Lugd., Ven., and Lov. do not have “that is.”]

Why is there such weeping over the law not being kept, except so that grace may be obtained, which wipes away the iniquity of the repentant and assists the will of the believer?

SERMON XXVIII

1. [verses 137–138.] The singer of this psalm had said above: “Streams of waters ran down my eyes, because they did not keep your law,” thereby testifying that he had wept greatly over his transgression. Therefore, as though giving the reason why he ought to have wept so much and grieved deeply over his sin, he says: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right. You have commanded your testimonies in righteousness, and in your truth exceedingly.”

This righteousness of God, this right judgment, and this truth must be feared by every sinner. For by it all who are condemned are divinely condemned, and there is absolutely no one who can rightly complain against the just God about his own condemnation. Hence the weeping of the repentant is rightly ordered, because if his unrepentant heart were condemned, it would certainly be condemned most justly.

He properly calls God’s testimonies “righteousness”: by commanding righteousness, God proves himself righteous. There is also this truth: that God makes himself known through such testimonies.

2. [verse 139.] But what does the following mean: “My zeal has consumed me,” or, as other manuscripts read, “Your zeal”? Some also have “the zeal of your house,” and not “has consumed me,” but “has eaten me.” This seems to have been corrected from another psalm, where it is written, “The zeal of your house has eaten me”; we know that this was also recalled in the Gospel (Ps. 68:10; John 2:17). “Consumed” is nevertheless similar to “eaten.”

“My zeal,” which the majority of manuscripts have, raises no difficulty: for what is surprising if someone wastes away through his own zeal? But what some manuscripts have, “your zeal,” signifies a person zealous for God, not for himself; yet there is no contradiction if it is also called “my” zeal. For what else does the Apostle say: “I am jealous over you for God, with the jealousy of God”? By saying, “I am jealous over you,” what does he show except his own jealousy? But because he added “for God”—that is, not for himself but for God—he therefore added, “with the jealousy of God.”

God inspires this jealousy in his faithful through his own Spirit. It belongs to love, not envy. What, then, was the reason the Apostle said this?

[Note: [Col. 1583] Several manuscripts: “For this was the reason.”] “For I betrothed you,” he says, “to one husband, to present a pure virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and purity that is in Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2–3).

The zeal for God’s house was consuming him, although he was zealous for that house on Christ’s behalf, not his own. A bridegroom is rightly jealous for his bride on his own behalf; but the friend of the bridegroom ought not to be jealous for her on his own behalf, but for the bridegroom. This zeal, therefore, must be understood as good. For he adds the reason and says: “Because my enemies have forgotten your words.”

They were therefore repaying evil for good, because he was so vehemently and ardently zealous for them before God that he said he had been consumed by this zeal. Yet they therefore practiced hostility against him:

[Note: [Col. 1584] The manuscripts read: “For this very reason they practiced hostility,” omitting the particle “against.”]

For he wanted those for whom he was jealous, because he loved them, to love God. Not ungrateful for God’s grace, through which he had been reconciled to God from being an enemy, he himself also loved his enemies and was jealous for them before God, grieving and wasting away because they had forgotten his words.

3. [verse 140.] Then, considering what flame of love burned within him for the words of God, he says: “Your word is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant has loved it.” It was rightly that he was zealous against the impenitent heart of his enemies, who had forgotten God’s words; for he was burning to bring them to what he himself loved with the greatest ardor.

4. [verse 141.] “I am young,” he says, “and despised; I have not forgotten your ordinances”—not like my enemies, who have forgotten your words.

He seems to mean that, being younger in age, he did not forget God’s ordinances, and that he grieved for his enemies, who were older in age, because they had forgotten them. For what does “I, the younger, have not forgotten” mean except “those older have forgotten”? The Greek word is νεώτερος (*neōteros*), which also occurs in the passage: “By what means does a young man correct his way?” This is a comparative term, and therefore is rightly understood in comparison with someone older.

Let us therefore recognize here two peoples, who were also struggling in Rebecca’s womb, when it was said to her—not on the basis of works but of the one who calls—“The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:22–23; Rom. 9:12–13). The younger one here says that he is despised; for this reason he became greater, because God chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and things that are not, as though they were, in order to abolish the things that are (1 Cor. 1:28). And behold, those who were last are first, and those who were first are last (Matt. 20:16).

5. [verse 142.] Nor is it without reason that they forgot God’s words: they wanted to establish their own righteousness, being ignorant of God’s righteousness (Rom. 10:3). But this younger one did not forget, because he did not wish to have a righteousness of his own, but God’s righteousness, concerning which he now also says: “Your righteousness is righteousness forever, and your law is truth.”

How could the law not be truth, when through it comes knowledge of sin and when it bears witness to God’s righteousness? For the Apostle says: “The righteousness of God has been manifested, attested by the Law and the Prophets” (ibid. 3:20–21).

6. [verse 143.] Because of this righteousness the younger one suffered persecution from the elder, so that he might say what follows: “Tribulation and distress have found me; your commandments are my meditation.” Let them rage and persecute; provided that God’s commandments are not abandoned, and that even those who rage are loved on account of those commandments.

7. [verse 144.] “The righteousness of your testimonies is forever; give me understanding, and I shall live.” This younger one asks for understanding; if he did not possess it, he would not understand beyond the elders. But he asks for it amid tribulation and distress, so that he may understand how contemptible is what his persecuting enemies can take away from him, those by whom he says he has been despised.

Therefore he said, “and I shall live”: for if tribulation and distress should go so far that this life is ended by the hands of persecuting enemies, the one who prefers righteousness—which remains forever—to temporal things will live forever. That righteousness, in tribulation and distress, is God’s martyrdoms—that is, testimonies—for which the martyrs have been crowned.

SERMON XXIX

1. [verse 145.] The cry made to the Lord by those who pray—if it is made with the sound of bodily speech but without a heart directed toward God—who would doubt that it is made in vain? But if it is made with the heart, even while the bodily voice is silent, it may be hidden from any other human being, but not from God.

Therefore, whether with the voice of the flesh, when that is necessary, or in silence, when we pray we must cry to God with the heart. The cry of the heart is a great intensity of thought; when it occurs in prayer, it expresses the great feeling of one who desires and asks, so that he does not despair of obtaining what he seeks. A person cries with his whole heart when he thinks of nothing else.

Such prayers are rare for many and frequent for a few; whether they are found in everyone, I do not know. The singer of this psalm recalls such a prayer of his own, saying: “I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord.” He then added what his cry would accomplish: “I will seek your ordinances.” For this purpose he cried with his whole heart, and this he desired to be granted by the Lord who heard him: that he might seek his ordinances.

Thus what we are commanded to do, we pray to be able to seek. How far is the one who seeks still from the one who does! For it does not follow that the one who seeks will find, or that the one who finds will do. Yet no one can do unless he has found, nor find unless he has sought. But the Lord Jesus gave great hope when he said: “Seek, and you will find.”

Again, Wisdom says—and what is Wisdom except he himself?—“The wicked will seek me and will not find me.” Therefore “Seek, and you will find” was not said to the wicked, but to the good. Indeed, it was said to those concerning whom, shortly afterward in the same passage, he says: “If you, then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children” (Matt. 7:7, 11).

How, then, is it said to the wicked, “Seek, and you will find,” when it is also said, “The wicked will seek me and will not find me”? Or did the Lord intend them to seek something other than Wisdom when he promised that they would find if they sought? For in Wisdom are all the things that those who desire to be blessed ought to seek. There, therefore, are also God’s ordinances.

It remains for us to understand that not all the wicked fail to find Wisdom if they seek her, but only those who are so wicked that they hate her. For this is how the passage continues: “The wicked will seek me and will not find me; for they hated wisdom” (Prov. 1:28–29). They do not find her, therefore, because they hate her.

But if they hate her, how do they seek her? They do so because they do not seek her for her own sake, but for something the wicked love, and they think they will reach that more easily through her. For many eagerly seek the sayings of Wisdom and want to possess her in their teaching, not in their life, so that they may not reach the light of God—which is Wisdom herself—through the conduct Wisdom commands, but through the words Wisdom possesses, reach the praise of human beings, which is empty glory.

They do not therefore seek Wisdom even when they seek her, because they do not seek her herself; otherwise they would live according to her. They wish to be puffed up by her words, and the more they are puffed up, the farther they become from her.

But this man asks from the Lord precisely what the Lord commands him to do, so that God may himself work within him even what he commands. “For it is God,” says the Apostle, “who works in you both to will and to act, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13). “I cried,” he says, “with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord. I will seek your ordinances”—ordinances certainly to be practiced, not merely known, lest he become like that harsh servant who, even if he understands, will not obey (Prov. 29:19).

2. [verse 146.] “I cried; save me”—or, as some Greek and Latin manuscripts read, “I cried to you; save me.” What does “I cried to you” mean except “by crying out I called upon you”? But after he had said, “Save me,” what did he add? “And I will keep your testimonies”—lest, namely, through weakness, I deny you.

For salvation of the soul causes what one recognizes ought to be done actually to be done; and, even to the death of the body, if extreme temptation demands it, one must contend for the truth of the divine testimonies. But where there is no salvation, weakness succumbs and the truth is abandoned.

3. [verse 147.] But what follows contains a certain obscurity, which must sometimes be explained at greater length: “I anticipated the untimely night and cried out.” More manuscripts do not have “before dawn,” but “at an untimely hour”; only one, scarcely, was found to have the doubled preposition, that is, “at the untimeliness.”

“Untimeliness” here means the nighttime period that is not “mature”—that is, not suitable for doing anything by staying awake. This is also commonly called “an unsuitable hour.”

[Note: [Col. 1586] Thus most manuscripts; the editions read “an inconvenient hour.”] “Untimely night,” that is, midnight, when one ought to be resting, was undoubtedly given this name because it is unsuitable for the activities of those who stay awake.

The ancients called *tempestivum* “opportune” and *intempestivum* “inopportune,” deriving the word from *tempus*, “time,” not from that *tempestas* which, in the usage of the Latin language, is now called a disturbance of the sky. Nevertheless, historians readily use this word when they say *ea tempestate*, intending it to mean “at that time.” And when the excellent poet says:

> “Whence has this tempest so bright suddenly arisen?”

(Virg. *Aen.* 9.19–20),

he did not signify by this name a sky disturbed by rainstorms or winds, but rather one shining with sudden and brilliant calm.

What was said in Greek as ἐν ἀωρίᾳ (*en aōria*), not in one word but in two—that is, a preposition and a noun—some of our translators rendered *intempesta nocte*, “in the untimely night”; more rendered it *immaturitate*, “at untimeliness,” not in two words but in one, whose nominative is *immaturitas*. Others used two words, as the Greek does, *in immaturitate*, “at untimeliness.” For ἀωρία (*aōria*) means “untimeliness,” and ἐν ἀωρίᾳ (*en aōria*) means “at untimeliness”—as though the translator who said *intempesta nocte*, “in the untimely night,” also wished to express the doubled preposition by saying *in intempesta*: one preposition would indicate “at what hour,” while the other would belong to the composition of the noun.

There is, in fact, no difference in meaning between saying that someone did something “at cockcrow” and “in cockcrow.” Likewise, there would be no difference between saying that he cried out *intempesta nocte*, “in the untimely night,” or *in intempesta nocte*, “in the untimely night.” The Greek, however, says “in the untimely night,” which has the same meaning as *in immaturitate*, “at untimeliness,” that is, “in the immature nighttime period.”

Enough has now been said concerning the obscure expression. Let us examine its meaning.

4. [verse 147.] “I anticipated,” he says, “in the untimely night, and cried out; I hoped in your words.” If we apply this to each of the faithful and to the literal event, it often happens that at such a nighttime hour the love of God keeps watch, and, when the feeling of prayer presses intensely,

[Note: [Col. 1587] Several manuscripts read “arises.”] the time customarily devoted to prayer after cockcrow is anticipated rather than awaited.

But if we understand this entire age as night, then certainly in the untimely night we cry out to God and anticipate the maturity of the time when he will return to us what he promised, as it is read elsewhere: “Let us anticipate his face with confession” (Ps. 94:2).

Although, if we wish to understand this as the immature period of the present night, before the fullness of time had come—that is, before the maturity itself, when Christ would be manifested in the flesh (Gal. 4:4)—even then the Church was not silent. Anticipating that maturity, she cried out prophetically and hoped in the words of God, who was able to do what he promised: that all nations would be blessed in the seed of Abraham (Gen. 12:3; 22:18).

5. [verse 148.] The same Church says what follows: “My eyes anticipated the morning, that I might meditate on your words.” Let us take “the morning” to be the time when light arose for those who sat in the shadow of death (Isa. 9:2). Did not the eyes of the Church, in the holy people who previously lived on earth, anticipate this morning, because they foresaw beforehand that it would come, in order that they might meditate on God’s words, which already existed and announced these future events in the Law and the Prophets?

6. [verse 149.] “Hear my voice,” he says, “O Lord, according to your mercy; and according to your judgment give me life.” First, according to his mercy, God removes punishment from sinners; afterward, according to his judgment, he will give life to the righteous. For it is not without reason that this order is expressed elsewhere: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1).

Yet even the time of mercy is not without judgment. Concerning it the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Cor. 11:31–32). And his fellow apostle says: “It is time for judgment to begin with the household of God; and if it begins with us”—

[Note: [Col. 1587] Most manuscripts read “with you.”]

“what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of the Lord?” (1 Pet. 4:17).

The final time of judgment, too, will not be without mercy, because the psalm says: “He crowns you with compassion and mercy” (Ps. 103:4). But judgment is without mercy for those on the left who have not shown mercy (James 2:13).

7. [verse 150.] “Those who persecute me,” he says, “have drawn near in iniquity”—or, as some manuscripts read, “unjustly.” Those who persecute draw near when they advance so far as to torture and kill the flesh. Hence the twenty-first psalm, where the Lord’s passion was prophesied, says: “Do not depart from me, for tribulation is near” (Ps. 22:12), although the things described there were suffered not when the passion was imminent but when it was already present.

He called the tribulation “near” because it was taking place in the flesh; for nothing is closer to the soul than the flesh it bears. The persecutors therefore drew near by afflicting the flesh of those whom they persecuted. But observe what follows: “They have gone far from your law.” The nearer they came to persecuting the righteous, the farther they went from righteousness. Yet what harm did they do to those whom they approached by persecuting, since the inward approach of their Lord is closer, and from him they are never abandoned?

8. [verse 151.] Finally, the following comes next: “You are near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth.” Even in their tribulations, to attribute truth to God because they suffer them deservedly is the customary confession of the saints. Thus Queen Esther confesses it (Esth. 14:6–7), thus holy Daniel (Dan. 9:4, 15), thus the three men in the furnace (ibid. 3:24–31), and thus other companions of their holiness confess it.

But one may ask how it is said here, “All your ways are truth,” when another psalm reads, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 25:10). Yet toward the saints all the ways of the Lord are both mercy and truth: he helps them even in judging, and thus mercy is not absent; and in showing mercy he fulfills what he promised, so that truth is not absent.

Toward all, however, both those whom he saves and those whom he condemns, all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, because where he does not show mercy, the truth of retribution is displayed. He saves many who do not deserve it, but he condemns no one who does not deserve condemnation.

9. [verse 152.] “From the beginning,” he says, “I learned from your testimonies that you founded them forever.” What the Greek says as καταρχάς (*katarchas*), some of our translators rendered *ab initio*, “from the beginning”; some, *initio*, “at the beginning”; and some, *in initiis*, “in the beginnings.” Those who preferred the plural followed the Greek expression.

In Latin, however, it is more customary to say *ab initio* or *initio* for what is expressed in Greek by καταρχάς, which appears plural but is used adverbially. It is like our expression *alias hoc facio*: we seem to use the plural number of the feminine gender, but it is an adverb meaning “at another time.”

What, then, is meant by “From the beginning I learned,” or, to use the adverbial expression, “At the beginning I learned from your testimonies that you founded them forever”? He says that the Lord’s testimonies were founded by him forever, and testifies that he learned this from the beginning, learning it from no other source than the testimonies themselves.

What are these testimonies except those by which God testified that he would give his children an everlasting kingdom? And because he testified that he would give it in the Only-Begotten, of whom it was said, “His kingdom will have no end” (Luke 1:33), he said that these testimonies were founded forever, because what God promised through them is eternal.

For the testimonies themselves will not then be necessary, when the reality itself is seen for whose sake testimonies are now required in order that it may be believed. Thus he rightly says, “You founded them,” because they are shown to be true in Christ. “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3:11).

From where, then, did this man learn it “at the beginning,” except that the Church is speaking—the Church that has not been absent from the earth since the beginning of the human race, whose firstfruits is holy Abel, himself sacrificed (Gen. 4:8) as a testimony of the future blood of the Mediator to be shed by an ungodly brother?

For this also was said from the beginning: “The two shall become one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). Explaining this great mystery, the apostle Paul says: “I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32).

SERMON XXX

1. [verse 153.] No one who belongs to the body of Christ should consider this voice alien to him, since it truly speaks of the whole body of Christ placed in this humility. This is where the reading of the psalm begins, the meaning of which we have now undertaken to discuss: “See my humility and rescue me, because I have not forgotten your law.”

Here we understand no law of God more appropriately than that by which it is immutably established that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11; 18:14). The proud person, therefore, is ensnared by evils so that he may be humbled; the humble person is rescued from evils so that he may be exalted.

2. [verse 154.] “Judge my judgment,” he says, “and redeem me.” The preceding statement is repeated in a certain way. For “See my humility” means “Judge my judgment”; and “rescue me” means “and redeem me.” What was said above, “because I have not forgotten your law,” corresponds to what follows below, “because of your word, give me life.” For the word itself is God’s law, which he has not forgotten, so that he who is to be exalted might humble himself.

“Give me life” pertains to that exaltation, because the exaltation of the saints is eternal life.

3. [verse 155.] “Salvation is far from sinners,” he says, “because they have not sought your ordinances.” What distinguishes you, then, O you who have said, “Salvation is far from sinners”? What distinguishes you from sinners, so that salvation is not far from you but is with you?

This surely distinguishes you: you did what they did not do; that is, you sought God’s ordinances. But what do you have that you did not receive (1 Cor. 4:7)? Are you not the one who said shortly before: “I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord: I will seek your ordinances”? Therefore you received from the one to whom you cried the ability to seek them. He, then, distinguishes you from those from whom salvation is far precisely because they did not seek God’s ordinances.

4. [verse 156.] He himself also saw this. For I would not see it unless I saw it in him, unless I were in him. These are the words of the body of Christ, whose members we are. He saw this, I say, and immediately added: “Your mercies are many, O Lord.” Therefore even this—that we seek your ordinances—belongs to your mercies. “According to your judgment, give me life.” For I know that your judgment also will not come upon me without your mercy.

5. [verse 157.] “Many are those who persecute and trouble me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies.” It happened, as we know, remember, and acknowledge. The whole earth has been purpled with the blood of martyrs; heaven blooms with the crowns of martyrs; the churches are adorned with memorials of martyrs; the seasons are marked by the birthdays of martyrs; healings multiply through the merits of martyrs.

How has this happened, except because what was foretold has been fulfilled concerning this one man spread throughout the whole earth: “Many are those who persecute and trouble me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies”? We acknowledge it, and we give thanks to the Lord our God.

For you, O man—you yourself, in another psalm—said: “If the Lord had not been with us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. 124:2–3). Behold why you did not turn aside from his testimonies, and why you came to the palm of the heavenly calling amid the hands of many persecutors and tribulators.

6. [verse 158.] “I saw,” he says, “the senseless, and I wasted away”—or, as other manuscripts read, “I saw those who did not keep the covenant”; this reading is also found in many manuscripts.

But who are those who did not keep the covenant except those who turned aside from God’s testimonies, unable to endure the tribulations of their many persecutors? The covenant is this: that whoever conquers will be crowned. Those who did not tolerate persecution and, by denying God, turned aside from his testimonies did not keep this covenant.

This man therefore saw them and wasted away because he loved them. That zeal is good, proceeding from love, not envy. He then followed by explaining in what respect they did not keep the covenant: “Because they did not keep your words.” For they denied them in their tribulations.

7. [verse 159.] This man commends himself as different from them and says: “See that I have loved your commandments.” He does not say, “I have not denied your words or testimonies”—which the martyrs were forced to do, and, by refusing, endured intolerable sufferings. Rather, he says this where the fruit of all sufferings lies: “If I deliver my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

Commending this love, he says: “See that I have loved your commandments.” Then he asked for the reward: “Lord, in your mercy give me life.” They put to death; you give life. But if the reward is requested in mercy, though it ought to be given by justice, how much greater was the mercy by which the victory itself was obtained, so that the one to whom the reward was owed might receive it?

8. [verse 160.] “The beginning,” he says, “of your words is truth, and all the judgments of your righteousness are forever.” Your words proceed from your truth, he says, and therefore they are true and deceive no one, since through them life is announced to the righteous and punishment to the wicked. These, indeed, are the judgments of God’s righteousness forever.

SERMON XXXI

[Col. 1591]

1. [verse 161.] We know what persecutions the body of Christ—that is, the holy Church—has endured from the kings of the earth. Let us therefore recognize here also her words as she says, “Princes persecuted me without cause, and my heart was in fear of your words.” For what harm had Christians done to earthly kingdoms, although their King had promised them the kingdom of heaven? What, I ask, had they done to earthly kingdoms? Did their King forbid his soldiers to render and show what was owed to earthly kings? Did he not say to the Jews, who were contriving this accusation against him, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21)? Did he not himself pay the tribute from the mouth of a fish (ibid. 17:23–26)? Did not his forerunner, when soldiers of this kingdom asked what they should do for eternal salvation, say, “Unfasten your belt, throw down your weapons, abandon your king so that you may serve as soldiers of the Lord”? No, he said, “Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely; be satisfied with your pay” (Luke 3:14). Did not one of his soldiers and his most beloved companion say to his fellow soldiers, and in a certain sense to the provincial citizens of Christ, “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities”? And shortly afterward he says, “Render to all what is owed: tribute to whom tribute is due; revenue to whom revenue; fear to whom fear; honor to whom honor. Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom. 13:1, 7–8). Did he not command the Church to pray even for those kings themselves (1 Tim. 2:1–2)? What, then, did Christians do to offend them? What debt did they fail to repay? In what matter did Christians fail to obey earthly kings? Therefore earthly kings persecuted Christians without cause.

But pay attention to what he added: “And my heart was in fear of your words.” They too had threatening words: “I banish, I proscribe, I kill, I torture with claws, I burn with fire, I set upon them beasts” [Note: [Col. 1591] So Am. and the manuscripts. But Er. and Lov. read subigo, “subdue,” instead of subrigo, “set upon.”], “I tear their limbs apart.” But your words terrified me more: “Do not fear those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more that they can do; but fear him who has power to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28). My heart was in fear of these words of yours; and I despised my human persecutor and conquered my diabolical deceiver.

2. [verse 162.] Finally he continues: “I will exult over your words, as one who finds abundant spoils.” By those words he conquered, the words of which he had been afraid. For spoils are stripped from the conquered, just as the one about whom it is said in the Gospel was conquered and stripped: “No one enters the house of a strong man to plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (ibid. 12:29). But abundant spoils were found when even those who had persecuted the martyrs believed, in their wonder at the martyrs’ endurance; and those who had attempted to damage our King by diminishing his soldiers were instead acquired by him. Therefore whoever fears the words of God lest he be conquered in the contest exults victoriously over those same words.

3. [verse 163.] Now, lest we think that hatred of God’s words could have crept in because of that fear—for although he had already said, “I exulted over your words,” which he certainly would not have said if he hated them [Col. 1592], he nevertheless added further and says: “I have hated injustice and abhorred it; but I have loved your law.” Clearly that fear of his words did not produce hatred of those same words, but preserved an undiminished love. For God’s law is also God’s words and utterances.

Far be it, then, that love should perish through fear where the fear is chaste. Thus pious children both fear and love their fathers; thus a chaste wife fears her husband, lest she be abandoned by him, and loves him so that she may enjoy him. If, then, a human father and a human husband ought both to be feared and loved, how much more our Father who is in heaven (Matt. 6:9), and that Bridegroom who is not beautiful in the flesh above the sons of men, but beautiful in virtue (Ps. 44:3). For by whom is God’s law loved, unless by those who love God? And what does the law of a father have that is grievous to good sons? Is it because the one whom he loves he corrects, and scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12:6)? But whoever rejects these judgments does not receive the promises. Let paternal judgments therefore be praised even in the scourging, if the promises are loved in the reward.

4. [verse 164.] This is precisely what the one who says, “Seven times a day I praised you, because of the judgments of your justice,” does. What he says as “seven times a day” signifies “always.” For this number is customarily an indication of totality: hence six days were appointed for the divine work, with the seventh added as a day of rest (Gen. 2:2); and through seven days, moving forward and returning, all times revolve.

Nor was it for any other reason that it was said, “The just man falls seven times” [Note: [Col. 1592] So Am., Er., and the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint. Lov. reads cadit, “falls,” in the present tense.], “and rises again”: that is, the just man does not perish, though humbled in every way, provided that he has not transgressed—for otherwise he would not be just. For every kind of tribulation by which he is cast down in the sight of human beings, the phrase “he falls seven times” is used; and for the fact that he makes progress through all those tribulations, “he rises again” is used.

The sentence that follows in that book sufficiently illuminates the preceding one: “But the wicked will be weakened in evils” (Prov. 24:16). Thus for the just person to fall seven times and rise again means not to be weakened in all evils. Therefore the Church rightly praised God seven times a day because of his judgments of justice: when the time had come for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord (1 Pet. 4:17), she was not weakened in all her tribulations, but was glorified by the crowns of the martyrs.

5. [verse 165.] “Abundant peace,” he says, “belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them.” Is the law itself not a stumbling-block to those who love it, or is there no stumbling-block of any kind for those who love it? Both interpretations are rightly understood.
