For whoever loves God’s law honors even what he does not understand in it; and when something seems to sound absurd to him, he judges rather that he himself does not understand it and that something great lies hidden there. Therefore God’s law is not a stumbling-block to him.

But if he is to suffer no stumbling-block whatsoever, he must not regard people of every holy profession in such a way that his faith depends upon their conduct, lest, when some whom he esteemed highly fall, he himself perish through stumbling. Rather, let him love God’s law itself, and he will have abundant peace and no stumbling-block. For he loves it securely: even though many sin within it, it does not itself know how to sin.

6. [verse 166.] “I was awaiting your salvation, Lord, and I loved your commandments.” For what benefit would it have been for the ancient righteous to have loved God’s commandments, unless Christ, who is God’s salvation, had delivered them—and unless, by the Spirit imparted by him, they had also been able to love God’s commandments? If, then, those who loved his commandments awaited God’s salvation, how much more necessary was Jesus, that is, God’s salvation, for saving those who did not love his commandments?

This prophecy can also apply to the saints of these times, since grace has been revealed and the Gospel is preached. For those who love God’s commandments await Christ, so that when Christ, our life, appears, we too may appear with him in glory (Col. 3:4).

7. [verses 167–168.] “My soul has kept your testimonies, and I loved them greatly”; or, as some manuscripts have it, “it loved,” with “my soul” understood. God’s testimonies are kept when they are not denied. This is the duty of martyrs, because in Greek the testimonies are called *martyria*. But since to be burned in flames for God’s testimonies without love profits nothing (1 Cor. 13:3), he therefore added, “And I loved them greatly.”

Earlier he had said, “I loved your commandments”; then in the following verse, “Your testimonies I both kept and loved”; afterward, “Your commandments and your testimonies I kept,” for he says, “I kept your commandments and your testimonies.” For whoever loves them truly and willingly keeps them [Note: [Col. 1593] Am. and several manuscripts have a lacuna here.].

But often, while God’s commandments are being kept, enemies arise against whose will they are kept. Then the testimonies too must be guarded with courage, lest they be denied to persecuting enemies.

8. When, then, he had said that he had done both, he attributed to God the source of his action, adding and saying: “For all my ways are before you, Lord.” Therefore, he says, I kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are before you. It is as though he were saying: “If you had turned your face away from me, I would have become troubled and would not have kept your commandments and testimonies.” Therefore I kept them because all my ways are before you.

He intended God to be understood as seeing his ways with a merciful and assisting regard, just as the one who said, “Do not turn your face away from me,” prayed (Ps. 26:9). For certainly the face of the Lord is also upon those who do evil, but it is so that he may destroy their memory from the earth (Ps. 33:17). This man certainly did not say that his ways were seen by God in that sense, but in the sense in which “the Lord knows the ways of the righteous” (Ps. 1:6), and as he said to Moses, “I know you above all others” (Exod. 33:17).

For if the fact that his ways were before God did not assist the one who walked, he would not have said that he had therefore kept God’s commandments and testimonies because all his ways were before the Lord. He knows how to hear: “Serve the Lord in fear, and exult in him with trembling; embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry at some time and you perish from the righteous way” (Ps. 2:11–12)—because unless that way were before the Lord, it would not be a righteous way.

The Apostle Paul also imposes this fear and trembling upon those to whom he says, “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling”; and, explaining why he said this, he adds, “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13). Thus the ways of the righteous are before the Lord so that he may direct their steps, for these are the ways of which it is written in Proverbs: “The ways that are on the right hand the Lord knows; but those on the left are perverse”—so that we might understand that the Lord does not know them, on account of which he will say to the perverse, “I do not know you” (Matt. 7:23).

Moreover, to show with what benefit the Lord knows the ways that are on the right—that is, the ways of the righteous—he immediately added: “For he himself will make your steps straight, and will lead your paths forth in peace” (Prov. 4:27). This is why the man here also says, “I kept your commandments and your testimonies.” And as though we were asking how he was able to do this, he says: “Because all my ways are before you, Lord.”

## SERMON XXXII

1. [verse 169.] Let us now hear the voice of one praying. For we know who is praying, and, if we are not rejected, we recognize ourselves among the members of this praying person. “Let my prayer draw near in your sight, Lord”—that is, let my prayer, which is made in your sight, draw near to you. For “the Lord is near to those who have crushed the heart” (Ps. 33:19). “According to your word give me understanding.” He asks for what was promised. For by saying, “According to your word,” he means, as though he were saying, “According to your promise.” The Lord promised this when he said, “I will give you understanding” (Ps. 31:8).

2. [verse 170.] “Let my supplication enter into your sight, Lord; according to your word deliver me.” In a certain way he repeats what he had asked. For what he had previously said, “Let my prayer draw near in your sight, Lord,” corresponds to what he says afterward, “Let my supplication enter into your sight, Lord”; and what he had previously said, “According to your word give me understanding,” corresponds to what he says afterward, “According to your word deliver me.” For by receiving understanding, the person who is deceived through failing to understand by himself is delivered.

3. [verse 171.] “My lips,” he says, “will pour forth a hymn when you teach me your ordinances.” We know how God teaches those who are teachable by God. For everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to him who justifies the ungodly (John 6:45), so that he may keep God’s ordinances not merely by retaining them in memory, but also by doing them. Thus the one who glories glories not in himself but in the Lord (1 Cor. 1:31), and a hymn is poured forth.

4. [verse 172.] But now, because he has learned and praised God the teacher, he wants afterward to teach. “My tongue,” he says, “will proclaim your words, because all your commandments are justice” [Note: [Col. 1594] So according to several manuscripts. Ambrose likewise has this in his Commentary on this verse. The editions read “judgments.”].

When he says that he will proclaim these things, he is clearly made a minister of the word. For although God teaches inwardly, faith nevertheless comes from hearing; and how will they hear without someone preaching (Rom. 10:17, 14)? Nor, because God gives the increase (1 Cor. 3:7), is it therefore unnecessary to plant and water.

5. [verses 173–174.] He knows what dangers will follow from those who contradict and persecute him when he becomes a proclaimer of God’s words. Therefore he added: “Let your hand be present to save me, because I have chosen your commandments.” So that I might not be afraid, and so that fear might not merely hold my heart [Note: [Col. 1595] So Am. and the manuscripts, with a few exceptions, which read: “and so that my heart alone might not fear.” Er. and Lov. read: “and so that my heart might not fear.”], but my tongue might also proclaim your words, I chose your commandments and suppressed fear by love. Let your hand therefore be present, so that you may save me from a foreign hand.

In this way God saved the martyrs, when he did not permit them to be killed in soul; for according to the flesh, “the salvation of man is vain” (Ps. 59:13).

It can also be understood in this way: “Let your hand be with me,” so that the hand of God may be understood as Christ, in accordance with Isaiah’s words, “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). For the Only-Begotten was not made when all things were made through him (John 1:3); but he was made from the seed of David (Rom. 1:3), so that he might be Jesus, that is, Savior, who already was the Creator.

But since “Let your hand be with me” and “The hand of the Lord was made” are familiar expressions in Scripture (Ezek. 1:3, etc.), I do not know whether this meaning can be maintained in all those passages.

Certainly, when we hear what follows, “I longed for your salvation, Lord,” God’s salvation, Christ, presents himself to us even against the will of all our enemies. The ancient righteous most truthfully confess that they longed for him; the Church longed for him who was to come from the womb of his mother; the Church longs for him who is to come from the right hand of the Father.

This sentence is followed by, “And your law is my meditation,” because the law bears witness to Christ.

6. [verse 175.] But in this faith—when one believes with the heart unto righteousness, while confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:10)—let the nations rage and the peoples meditate on vain things (Ps. 2:1); let the flesh certainly be killed while it preaches you: “My soul shall live, and it shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me.”

Those are the judgments concerning which the time had come for them to begin from the house of the Lord (1 Pet. 4:17). “And they shall help me,” he says. Who does not see how greatly the blood of the Church has helped the Church? How great a harvest has sprung up throughout the whole world from that seed?

7. [verse 176.] Finally he reveals himself completely and shows what person was speaking throughout the whole Psalm. “I have gone astray,” he says, “like a sheep that is lost; seek your servant, because I have not forgotten your commandments.” Some manuscripts do not have “seek,” but “make alive.” Only one syllable distinguishes the two words in Greek: ζῆσον (*zēson*, “make alive”) and ζήτησον (*zētēson*, “seek”); hence the Greek manuscripts themselves vary.

But whichever of the two readings is correct, let the lost sheep be sought; let the lost sheep be made alive—for its sake its shepherd left the ninety-nine in the mountains and, while seeking it (Matt. 18:12), was torn by Jewish thorns. Yet it is still being sought; let it still be sought, though it has been found in part. For in that part of it which says, “I have not forgotten your commandments,” it has been found. But through those who choose, gather [Note: [Col. 1595] The word “gather” is absent from several manuscripts.], and love God’s commandments, it is still being sought; and through the blood of its shepherd, poured out and scattered, it is found among all nations.

8. As I have been able, and insofar as I have been helped by the Lord, I have treated and explained this great Psalm. Others wiser and more learned have certainly done so, or will do so, better; yet our ministry ought not therefore to have been lacking to it, especially since the brothers have earnestly requested this service from me, and I am indebted to them for it.

As for the Hebrew alphabet, under each of whose letters eight verses are placed, by which the entire Psalm is woven together: no one should be surprised that I have said nothing about it, since I found nothing that properly belonged to this Psalm. For it is not the only one that has these letters.

Let those who cannot find this feature in the Greek and Latin text—because it has not been preserved there—know that in the Hebrew manuscripts all eight verses begin with the letter placed before them, as we have been informed by those who know these letters. This was done much more carefully than our own poets, whether Latin or Punic, whom they call alphabetic Psalm-writers, are accustomed to do. For they do not begin all the verses, until the period is completed, with the same letter; they begin only the first verses with the letter they place before them.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 119

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. [verse 1.] The Psalm we have just heard sung and have answered by singing is short and extremely useful. You will not labor long in listening, nor will you labor fruitlessly in doing. For, as its title indicates, it is a “Song of Ascents.” In Greek it is written ἀναβαθμῶν (*anabathmōn*). Steps may be those of people descending or ascending; but the steps as they are set forth in these Psalms signify ascent.

Let us therefore understand ourselves as about to ascend. Let us not seek ascents with bodily feet, but as it is written in another Psalm: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of weeping, into the place which he established” (Ps. 83:6–7). He said “ascents”—where? That is, “in his heart.” From where? From “the valley of weeping.” And to what one ascends—here human speech seems to fail, and it cannot be explained, perhaps not even imagined. You heard just now, when the Apostle was being read: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:9). “It has not entered into the heart of man”: let the heart of man ascend there.

Therefore, since “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man,” how could one say where one must ascend? Since it could not be said, he said, “Into the place which he established.” What more can I say to you?—the man through whom the Holy Spirit was speaking asks. Into such and such a place, or such and such a place? Whatever I say, you imagine something earthly; you crawl upon the ground; you carry flesh. “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15).

To whom shall I speak? Who will hear? Who will grasp where we shall be after this life, if we ascend in the heart? Since no one can grasp it, hope for an ineffable place of blessedness, which the one who arranged ascents in your heart has established for you [Note: [Col. 1596] The editions read: “Since therefore no one hopes.” The Christinensis manuscript reads: “Since therefore no one can say, hope,” and so forth. But the reading seems to be: “Since therefore no one”—supply, “can grasp”—“hope.”].

But where? In the valley of weeping. The valley signifies humility; the mountain signifies loftiness. There is a mountain to which we may ascend, a certain spiritual elevation. And what is this mountain to which we ascend, if not the Lord Jesus Christ? By suffering he made the valley of weeping for you; by remaining he made the mountain of ascent.

What is the valley of weeping? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” What is the valley of weeping? He offered his cheek to the one who struck him; he was filled with reproaches (Lam. 3:30). What is the valley of weeping? He was struck with blows, smeared with spittle, crowned with thorns, and crucified. This is the valley of weeping from which you must ascend.

But in what direction must you ascend? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The Word itself became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14). Thus he descended to you in such a way that he remained in himself; he descended to you so that he might become for you the valley of weeping; he remained in himself so that he might be for you the mountain of ascent.

“In the last days,” Isaiah says, “the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, prepared at the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2) [Note: [Col. 1597] Er. and Lov. read “the mountain of the house of the Lord.” The word “house” is absent from Am. and the manuscripts.]. See to what we must ascend.

But do not imagine anything earthly. Because you have heard “mountain,” do not imagine some lofty part of the earth; when you hear “rock” or “stone,” do not understand hardness; when you hear “lion,” do not imagine ferocity; when you hear “lamb,” do not imagine an animal. None of these things is present in itself, yet he became all of them for you.

From here, then, there is an ascent; to there we must ascend—from his example to his divinity. For he gave you an example by humbling himself. Those who did not wish to ascend from the valley of weeping were checked by him. They wanted to have the ascent too quickly; they thought about high honors, but did not think about the way of humility.

Let Your Charity understand what I am saying. Two disciples wanted to sit beside the Lord, one at his right and the other at his left. The Lord saw that they were thinking prematurely and improperly about honors, when they ought first to have learned to humble themselves so that they might be exalted. And the Lord said to them, “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (Matt. 20:21–22). He was going to drink the cup of suffering in the valley of weeping; but they, without attending to Christ’s humility, wanted to grasp Christ’s height. He called them back to the way, as people who had gone astray—not to deny them what they wanted, but to show them by what route they should come.

2. Therefore, my brothers, let us sing this Psalm of ascent as we ascend in the heart, because in order that we might ascend, descent has come to us. For Jacob saw a ladder, and on that ladder ascending and descending beings were shown to him (Gen. 28:12): he saw both.

We may suppose that the ascending ones were those making progress and the descending ones those failing; for we truly find this among the people of God: some make progress, others fail. Those ladders could signify these people, but perhaps all good people are better understood in those ladders, both ascending and descending. For it was not without reason that they were not called “falling,” but “descending” [Col. 1598].

There is a great difference between descending and falling. For because Adam fell, Christ descended: the one fell, the other descended; the one fell through pride, the other descended through mercy.

Nor did he alone descend. He alone indeed descended from heaven, but many holy people, imitating him, descend and have descended to us. The Apostle was dwelling at a certain height of heart when he said, “Whether we were beside ourselves, it was for God.” What he had transcended in mind, he had transcended for God. Transcending in mind every human fragility, every temporal condition of the world, all things that vanish through coming into being and passing away—all these transitory things—he dwelt in his heart in a certain ineffable contemplation, insofar as he could. Of this he says that he heard ineffable words which it is not permitted to a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12:4).

But he could not speak those things to you; he could somehow see what he could not speak to you. Therefore, if he had always wished to remain in what he saw but could not speak, he would not have lifted you to where you too could see. What did he do? He descended. For there he says: “Whether we were beside ourselves, it was for God; whether we are self-controlled, it is for you” (ibid. 5:13). What does “we are self-controlled” mean? We speak in such a way that you can grasp it.

Christ too made himself such, by being born and suffering, that human beings could speak about him; for a human being easily speaks about a human being. When a human being speaks about God, how can he speak as God is? But a human being easily speaks about a human being.

Therefore, so that the great might descend to the small, and yet speak to them only of what is great, he who was great became small, so that the great might speak to the small about him [Note: [Col. 1598] Several manuscripts read: “so that they might speak to the small about him who was great.”].

You heard just now what I am saying, when the Apostle was being read. If you paid attention, he said this: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people.” Therefore he speaks to the spiritual in the heights; but in order to speak to the carnal, he descends.

To know that, when he descends, he speaks about the one who descended, consider how John speaks of him who remains in himself: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Grasp it, if you can; seize it—it is food.

But you will say to me: “That is indeed food, but I am an infant; I must be nursed with milk so that I may become capable of eating food.” Therefore, because you must be nourished with milk while he is food, that food was carried through flesh to your mouth.

Just as a mother eats food so that she may transmit it through her flesh as milk to the infant, so the Lord, the food of angels, the Word, became flesh and became milk. The Apostle says, “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able, and even now you are not able” (1 Cor. 3:1–2). Therefore, by giving milk he descends to the little ones; and because he descends, he gives the one who descended [Note: [Col. 1598] Most manuscripts read: “by descending he gave.”].

For he says: “Did I claim to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified?” (ibid. 2:2). If he had said only “Jesus Christ,” Jesus Christ also exists according to his divinity, according to what he was as the Word with God—the Son of God, Jesus Christ. But “him,” that is, spoken in this manner, the little ones do not grasp.

How, then, do those who receive milk grasp him? “Jesus Christ,” he says, “and him crucified.” Suck what he became for you, and you will grow toward what he is.

Therefore there are ascending and descending people. In that ladder there are both ascending and descending people. Who are the ascending? Those who make progress toward understanding spiritual things. Who are the descending? Those who, although they enjoy an understanding of spiritual things insofar as human beings can, nevertheless descend to the little ones, so that they may say to them things they are able to grasp; and, nourished with milk, the little ones may become capable and strong enough to receive spiritual food.

Isaiah too, brothers, belonged to those who descended to us; for the stages of his descent are also apparent. When he spoke of the Holy Spirit, he said: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11:2–3). He began with wisdom and descended all the way to fear.

As he who taught descended from wisdom all the way to fear, so you who are learning, if you make progress, ascend from fear to wisdom. For it is written, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 1:7).

Now, then, hear the Psalm. Let us place before our eyes a person about to ascend. Where is he about to ascend? In the heart. From where is he about to ascend? From humility, that is, from the valley of weeping. To what is he about to ascend? To that ineffable reality which, since it could not be said, was called “the place which he established.”

3. When a person has begun in this way to arrange his ascent—to state the matter more plainly, when a Christian has begun to think about making progress—he begins to suffer the tongues of adversaries. Whoever has not yet suffered those tongues has not yet made progress; whoever does not suffer them is not even attempting to make progress.

Do you want to know what we mean? Rather, let him experience it himself, together with us, and learn what we hear. Let him begin to make progress; let him begin to wish to ascend, to despise earthly, fragile, temporal things [Note: [Col. 1599] Several manuscripts read: “to despise earthly fragility, the temporal happiness of the world,” and so forth.], to regard the happiness of the world as nothing, to think only of God, not to rejoice in gains, not to waste away over losses, even to wish to sell all that is his and give it to the poor, and to follow Christ. Let us see how he suffers the tongues of those who slander [Note: [Col. 1599] So the manuscripts. The editions read “those who draw back.”], and of many who contradict him—and, what is more serious, of those who, as though giving advice, turn him away from salvation.

For whoever gives advice gives advice toward salvation, toward what is beneficial. But this person, while appearing to give advice, draws him back from salvation. Because he seems to wear the cloak of one giving counsel while possessing the poison of one who kills, he is called a deceitful tongue.

Therefore the one who is about to ascend first prays to God against these very tongues. For he says, “To you, Lord, when I was afflicted, I cried, and you heard me.” From what did he hear him? So that he might now establish him on the steps of ascent.

4. [verse 2.] And because the one who is already about to ascend has been heard, what does he pray? “Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue.” What is a deceitful tongue? A cunning tongue, one that bears the appearance of giving advice but brings destruction [Col. 1600].

These are the people who say: “And you are going to do what no one has done? And you alone are going to be a Christian?” And if he shows them that others have done this, and reads the Gospel where the Lord commanded it to be done, and reads the Acts of the Apostles, what do they say with their cunning tongue and wicked lips?

“You may not be able to fulfill it. What you are undertaking is too much.”

Some frighten people away by forbidding; others press them even more by praising them. Because this is a way of life that has now taken possession of the world, and Christ’s authority is so great that not even a pagan dares now to criticize Christ openly, they read the words of the one who cannot be criticized: “Go, sell all that you have, distribute it to the poor, and follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

Christ cannot be contradicted; the Gospel cannot be contradicted; Christ cannot be criticized. The deceitful tongue turns instead to praise in order to forbid.

If you praise, encourage. Why do you press someone down by praising him? It would be better for you to condemn than to praise deceitfully. For what would you say by condemning? “Away with it! This life is shameful; this life is evil.” But because you know that, if you say these things, you can be overwhelmed by evangelical authority, you turn to another kind of dissuasion: by falsely praising, you prevent me from receiving true praise; indeed, by praising Christ, you prevent me from following Christ.

You say: “What is this? Look, those people did it; perhaps you will not be able to. You begin to ascend, and you fall.” He appears to be giving advice; he is a serpent, a deceitful tongue; he contains poison.

Pray against it, if you wish to ascend, and say to your God: “Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

### 5. [vers. 3–5]

And your Lord says to you: “What will be given to you, or what will be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?” That is: What do you have against a deceitful tongue, what can you set against a deceitful tongue, with what can you protect yourself against a deceitful tongue? What will be given to you, or what will be added to you? He asked the question as an exercise; for he himself is about to say what he asks. He answered, supplying the answer to his own questioner: “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, together with desolating coals”—or, “destroying coals.” Whether you say “desolating” or “destroying” (for it is written differently in different manuscripts), the meaning is the same. Consider: coals are called destroyers because, by destroying and laying waste, they easily bring something to desolation.

What are these coals? Let Your Charity first understand what the arrows are. “The sharp arrows of the mighty one” are the words of God. Behold, they are shot and pierce hearts; but when hearts have been pierced by the arrows of God’s word, love is aroused [Note: [Col. 1600] Ambrosius and most manuscripts read: “is exercised.”], not destruction brought about. The Lord knows how to shoot toward love; and no one shoots more beautifully toward love than the one who shoots with the word. Indeed, he shoots the heart of the one who loves, so as to help the lover; he shoots in order to make someone a lover.

But what are the destroying coals? It is not enough to act with words against a deceitful tongue and unrighteous lips; it is not enough to act with words. One must also act by examples. Examples are the destroying coals. And why are they called destroying? Let Your Charity understand briefly. First, observe how one must act by examples.

A deceitful tongue knows nothing to say by which it is more deceitful than this: “See to it that you may not be able to fulfill it; undertaking this is too much for you.” You have received the evangelical commandment; you have the arrow, but you do not yet have the coals. It is to be feared that the arrow alone may not prevail against the deceitful tongue; there are also coals.

Suppose God begins to say to you: “Can you not? Why can he? Why could another? Are you more delicate than that senator? Are you weaker than that man—or than that sick man [Note: [Col. 1601] Some manuscripts read: “or than that invalid.”]? Are you weaker than women? Women have been able, and men cannot? Delicate rich people have been able, and poor people cannot?”

“But,” he says, “I have sinned greatly, and I am a great sinner.”

Those who have sinned greatly are also counted among them; and they loved all the more because more had been forgiven them, as it is said in the Gospel: “The one to whom little is forgiven loves little” (Luke 7:47). When all these have been listed, and the people who were able have been named individually, the one who has received the arrow in his heart, with the desolating coals also approaching, has the earthly thought within him laid waste.

What does “laid waste” mean? It is brought to desolation. There were many things in him that had grown wrongly green; there were many carnal thoughts and many worldly loves. These are burned by the desolating coals, so that a pure, desolate place may be made—a place in whose purity God may build his structure. For there had been a ruin of the devil there, and Christ is built there. As long as the devil remains there, Christ cannot be built.

The desolating coals approach and cast down what had been badly built; and, once the place has been laid waste, the structure of everlasting happiness is added. See, therefore, why they are called coals: because those who turn to the Lord rise again from the dead. When coals are kindled, they had been extinguished before they were kindled. Extinguished coals are called dead; burning coals are called alive. Thus the examples of many wicked people who have been converted to the Lord are called coals.

You hear people marveling and saying: “I knew that man—how drunk he was, how wicked, what a lover of the circus or the amphitheater, what a cheat! And now, how he serves God, how innocent he has become!” Do not marvel; he is a coal. You rejoice in one whom you had mourned as extinguished, now alive. But when you praise the living man, if you know how to praise him, apply him to the dead man so that he may be kindled. That is: whoever is still sluggish about following God, bring near to him the coal that had been extinguished; possess both the arrow of God’s word and the destroying coal, so that you may confront unrighteous lips and a deceitful tongue.

### 6.

What follows? This man has received the burning arrows; let him also receive the destroying coals. He is now repelling the deceitful tongue and unrighteous lips; he is now ascending the step and beginning to make progress. But he still lives among the wicked, among the unrighteous; the threshing floor has not yet been winnowed. Suppose that he has become wheat: is he already in the granary? Much chaff still needs to be pressed down. And the more he makes progress, the greater scandals he sees among the people. For if he does not make progress, he does not see iniquities; if he is not a true Christian, he does not see those who are false.

Indeed, brothers, the Lord teaches us this also through that likeness of the wheat and the weeds. “When the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds also appeared” (Matthew 13:26): that is, evil people appear to no one until he himself has become good; for when the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds appeared.

This man, then, has begun to make progress; he has begun to see the wicked and many evils that he had not previously known; and he cries out to the Lord: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has become long!” I have gone far away from you; my pilgrimage has become long. I have not yet come to that homeland where I shall live with no wicked person; I have not yet come to that company of angels where I shall fear no scandals.

Why, then, am I not yet there? “Because my sojourn has become long.” A sojourn is a pilgrimage; a sojourner is one who lives in a foreign land, not in his own city. “My sojourn,” he says, “has become long.”

And where is it long? Sometimes, my brothers, when a person is traveling abroad, he lives among better people than he might have lived among in his own country. But it is not so when we are traveling as exiles from that heavenly Jerusalem. A person changes his homeland, and sometimes fares well in exile: while traveling, he finds faithful friends whom he could not find in his own country. He had enemies, and so he was driven from his homeland; while traveling, he found what he had not possessed at home.

But that homeland, that Jerusalem where all are good, is not like this. Whoever journeys from it is among the wicked; nor can he withdraw from the wicked until he has returned to the company of angels, to the place from which he is now journeying. There are all the righteous and holy, who enjoy the Word of God without reading, without letters; what is written for us through pages, they see through the face of God.

What a homeland! A great homeland—and miserable are those who are exiles from that homeland.

### 7.

But what this man says—“My pilgrimage has become long”—is above all the voice of those who are the Church herself, who labors in this world. It is her voice that cries from the ends of the earth, saying in another psalm: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you.”

Who among us cries from the ends of the earth? Neither I, nor you, nor that man; but the whole Church herself, the entire inheritance of Christ, cries from the ends of the earth [Note: [Col. 1602] Ambrosius, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read: “the Church alone.”]. For the Church is his inheritance, and it was said of the Church: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8).

Therefore, if Christ’s possession extends to the ends of the earth, and Christ’s possession consists of all the saints [Note: [Col. 1602] Several manuscripts read: “Christ’s possession is holy people.”], and all the saints are one person in Christ, because holy unity exists in Christ, this one person says: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you, when my heart was distressed” (Psalm 60:3).

The long pilgrimage of this person, then, has taken place among the wicked. And as though someone said to him, “With whom, then, do you live, so that you groan?” he replies: “My pilgrimage has become long.”

But what if he were among the good? If he were among the good, he would not say, “Alas for me!” “Alas” is the voice of misery, the voice of calamity and unhappiness—yet in hope, because he has at least learned to groan. For many are miserable and do not groan; they are exiles and do not wish to return. But this man, now wishing to return, recognizes the unhappiness of his pilgrimage; because he has recognized it, he returns; and he begins to ascend, because he has begun to sing the Song of Ascents.

Where, then, does he groan, and among whom does he live? “I lived among the tents of Kedar.”

Because this word is Hebrew, you certainly did not understand it. What does “I lived among the tents of Kedar” mean? As far as we remember from the interpretation of Hebrew names, Kedar means “darkness.” Translated into Latin, Kedar is said to mean “darkness.”

You know that Abraham had two sons, whom the Apostle mentions and says are figures of the two covenants. One was from a slave woman and the other from a free woman. Ishmael was from the slave woman; Isaac was from the free woman, Sarah, whom Abraham received through faith after hope had failed. Both were from Abraham’s seed, but both were not Abraham’s heirs. One was born from Abraham but did not inherit; the other was both son and heir—not merely a son, but also an heir.

In Ishmael are all those who worship God carnally. The Old Testament also belongs to them. For the Apostle said: “You who wish to be under the Law, do you not hear the Law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one from the slave woman and one from the free woman; these things are an allegory. For these are the two covenants” (Galatians 4:21–24).

What are the two covenants? One is old, and the other new. The old covenant is from God, and the new covenant is from God—just as Ishmael and Isaac are both from Abraham. But Ishmael belongs to the earthly kingdom, and Isaac to the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore the Old Testament has earthly promises: an earthly Jerusalem, an earthly Palestine, an earthly kingdom, earthly salvation, the subjugation of enemies, an abundance of children, and fertility of crops [Note: [Col. 1603] Several manuscripts read: “of fruits.”]. All these are earthly promises. They are understood spiritually in figure: the earthly Jerusalem was a shadow of the heavenly kingdom, and the earthly kingdom was a shadow of the kingdom of heaven.

Ishmael is in shadow; Isaac is in light. If Ishmael is in shadow, it is not surprising that there is darkness there. For denser shadows are darkness. Thus Ishmael is in darkness, Isaac in light.

Whoever here, even within the Church, seeks earthly happiness from God still belongs to Ishmael. These are the people who contradict those making spiritual progress, slander them, and have unrighteous lips and deceitful tongues. Against them this man prayed as he ascended, and the desolating coals and sharp arrows of the mighty one were added to him.

For he still lives among them until the entire threshing floor has been winnowed. Therefore he said: “I lived among the tents of Kedar.” For the tents of Ishmael themselves are called Kedar. So the Book of Genesis has it; it says that Kedar belongs to Ishmael (Genesis 25:13).

Thus Isaac is with Ishmael: that is, those who belong to Isaac live among those who belong to Ishmael. The former wish to ascend upward; the latter wish to press them downward. The former wish to fly toward God; the latter try to tear out their wings.

For the Apostle says: “But just as then the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so it is also now.” The spiritual, therefore, suffer persecution from the carnal. But what does Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Genesis 16:15; 21:2, 3, 10; Galatians 4:21–30).

But when will this “Cast out” take place? When the threshing floor begins to be winnowed. For now, before he is cast out: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has become long! I lived among the tents of Kedar.” And he explains to us who those are who belong to the tents of Kedar.

### 8. [vers. 6]

“My soul has made a long pilgrimage.”

So that you would not understand a bodily pilgrimage, he said that the soul makes a pilgrimage. The body travels through places; the soul travels through affections. If you love the earth, you are on pilgrimage away from God; if you love God, you ascend to God.

Let us exercise ourselves in love of God and neighbor, so that we may return to love. If we fall to the earth, we wither and rot. But to this man who had fallen, someone came down so that he might ascend. Considering the length of his pilgrimage, he said that he was living among the tents of Kedar.

Why? “Because my soul has made a long pilgrimage.”

It makes its pilgrimage where it ascends. It does not make its pilgrimage bodily, nor does it ascend bodily. But where does it ascend? “Ascents,” he says, “are in the heart.” If it ascends in the heart, then only the soul that is on pilgrimage ascends by the ascents of the heart. But until it reaches its destination, “my soul has made a long pilgrimage.” Where? “Among the tents of Kedar.”

### 9. [vers. 7]

“With those who hated peace, I was peaceful.”

But, dearest brothers, so that you may hear this: you will not be able to prove how truly you sing unless you begin to do what you sing. However much I say, however I explain it, in whatever words I express it, it does not enter the heart of one in whom its work is absent. Begin to act, and see what we are saying. Then tears flow at each word; then the psalm is sung, and the heart does what is sung in the psalm.

How many sound with their voice while they are mute in their hearts? And how many are silent with their lips while they cry out in their affections? For God’s ears are directed toward the human heart: just as bodily ears are directed toward the human mouth, so the human heart is directed toward God’s ears. Many are heard with closed mouths, and many are not heard amid great shouting.

We must pray through our affections and say: “My soul has made a long pilgrimage; with those who hated peace, I was peaceful.”

What else do we say to these heretics except: “Recognize peace; love peace”? You call yourselves righteous. But if you were righteous, you would groan among the grain amid the chaff. Since there is grain in the Catholic Church, and true grain, it tolerates the chaff until the threshing floor is winnowed. For amid the chaff it cries: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has become long! I lived among the tents of Kedar.”

“I lived,” he says, “among the chaff.” But just as much smoke rises from chaff, so darkness comes from Kedar [Note: [Col. 1604] The word “from” is absent from the manuscripts]. “I lived among the tents of Kedar; my soul has made a long pilgrimage.” It is the voice of the grain groaning among the chaff.

This is what we say to those who hate peace: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful.” Who are those who hate peace? Those who tear apart unity. If they had not hated peace, they would have remained in unity.

But evidently they separated themselves for this reason: so that they might be righteous, so that they would not have the unrighteous mixed in with them. Either this voice is ours or theirs; decide whose it is.

The Catholic Church says: “Unity must not be abandoned; the Church of God must not be cut apart. God will judge the wicked and the good afterward. If the wicked cannot now be separated from the good, they must be tolerated for a time. The wicked can be with us on the threshing floor; they cannot be in the granary. And perhaps those who appear wicked today will be good tomorrow, while those who boast today of their goodness will be found wicked tomorrow.”

Whoever, therefore, humbly tolerates the wicked for a time will himself reach everlasting rest. This is the Catholic voice [Note: [Col. 1605] Perhaps: “the voice of the Catholic Church.”].

But what is their voice? They do not understand either what they say or the things about which they make assertions (1 Timothy 1:7): “Do not touch the unclean thing” (Isaiah 52:11), and “Whoever touches what is unclean will be defiled” (Leviticus 22:5). “Let us separate ourselves, lest we be mixed with the wicked.”

And we say to them: “Love peace; love unity.” You do not know from how many good people you separate yourselves while accusing those whom you regard as wicked. They rage and become violent when we say these things; indeed, they also seek to kill us. Their attacks have often appeared; their ambushes have appeared.

Therefore, while we live amid their ambushes, and those to whom we say, “Love peace,” oppose us, is this not our voice: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful”? “When I spoke to them, they fought against me without cause.”

But what does “they fought against me” mean, brothers? It would have been little if he had not added, “without cause.” To those to whom we say, “Love peace; love Christ”—are we saying, “Love and honor us”? No: “Honor Christ.”

We do not wish to be honored, but Christ. For what are we compared with the Apostle Paul? Yet he said to those little ones whom evil people and evil counselors wished to cut off from unity and lead into schisms: What did he say to them? “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Corinthians 1:13).

This is what we also say: “Love peace; love Christ.” For if they love peace, they love Christ. Therefore when we say, “Love peace,” we say, “Love Christ.”

Why? Because the Apostle says of Christ: “For he is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14). If Christ is peace because he made the two one, why have you made two out of one? How, then, are you peaceful, if Christ makes one out of two while you make two out of one?

But because we say these things, with those who hate peace we are peaceful; and yet those who hate peace, while we were speaking to them, fought against us without cause.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 120

### SERMON

[Note: [Col. 1605] Delivered to the people on the feast day of Saint Crispina the martyr.]

### 1.

This is the second of those psalms whose title is “Song of Ascents.” There are many of them signifying, as you heard already in the first, our ascent—which takes place in the heart toward God—from the valley of weeping, that is, from the humility of tribulation.

For an ascent cannot be useful to us unless we first humble ourselves [Note: [Col. 1605] Ambrosius, Erasmus, and several manuscripts have this reading. Lovaniensis reads: “of humility.” Some manuscripts read: “having been humbled.”] and remember that we must ascend from the valley. A valley is a depressed place in the earth: just as high places of the earth are mountains and hills, so a valley is a low place. We must beware lest, while we prematurely and perversely seek to be exalted, we ascend not at all but fall.

The Lord himself taught that one must ascend from the valley of weeping when he deigned to humble himself for us unto death, even death on a cross. Let us not abandon this example. The martyrs understood this valley of weeping.

How did they understand it? Why? Because they too ascended from the valley of weeping in order to be crowned.

### 2.

This psalm, “Song of Ascents,” also suits this day. For it was said of them: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds.” This is the valley of weeping, where seeds are cast by those who weep.

What are the seeds? Good works amid this earthly tribulation. Whoever acts well in the valley of weeping is like a person sowing during winter. Is he deterred from his work by the cold? In the same way, we must not be deterred from good works by the pressures of the world, because you see what follows: “Going,” he says, “they went and wept, casting their seeds.”

They would be very miserable if they always wept; they would be very miserable if they were never to be freed from tears. But see what follows: “But coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves [Note: [Col. 1606] All our manuscripts read: “their handfuls.”]” (Psalm 125:6).

### 3.

Nothing else, brothers, is taught to us by these songs except ascending—but ascending in the heart, in good affection, in faith, hope, and love, in the desire for immortality and eternal life. This is how one ascends.

It is fitting that we say how one must ascend. How many more terrifying things did Your Charity hear read from the Gospel! You certainly see that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. “If the master of the household,” he says, “had known at what hour the thief would come, I assure you, he would not have allowed his wall to be broken through.”

You say now: “Who, then, knows at what hour he will come, since the hour will be like that of a thief?” You do not know at what hour he will come; keep watch always, so that, because you do not know when he will come, he may find you prepared when he comes. Perhaps you do not know when he will come precisely so that you may always be prepared.

That hour will suddenly overtake the master of the household—who is represented as proud. Do not wish to be the master of the household, and that hour will not suddenly overtake you.

“And what shall I be?” you ask. Be what you heard in the psalm: “I am poor and sorrowful” (Psalm 68:30). For if you are poor and sorrowful, you will not be the master of the household whom that hour will find and suddenly crush.

Masters of the household are those who, trusting in their desires and flowing away in the pleasures of this age, swell with pride. They rise up against the humble and mock the saints who understand the narrow way that leads to life (Matthew 7:14).

That hour will come suddenly upon such people, because such people also existed in the days of Noah, whose days you heard recalled in the Gospel: “The coming of the Son of Man,” he says, “will be as it was in the days of Noah. They were eating, drinking, marrying, giving in marriage, planting, and building, until Noah entered the ark; and the flood came and destroyed them all” (Matthew 24:37–44; Luke 17:26–27).

What, then? Will all who do these things perish—those who marry, give in marriage, plant, and build? No; but those who put their confidence in these things, those who prefer these things to God, those who are quickly prepared to offend God for their sake.

But those who either do not use these things at all [Note: [Col. 1607] Some manuscripts, instead of “all,” have “empty.” Erasmus and the Corbie manuscript contain both words: “all the empty things.”] or use them as though they were not using them, placing greater confidence in the one who gave them than in the things given, and understanding in them his consolation and mercy without being possessed by the gifts, lest they fall away from the giver—such people will not be found unprepared by that hour like a thief.

The Apostle said to such people: “But you are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you like a thief; for you are all sons of light and sons of day.” Therefore, when the Lord said that the hour should be feared like a thief, he mentioned night; and the Apostle likewise says: “For the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.”

Do you not want it to find you? Do not be in the night. What does “Do not be in the night” mean? “You are sons of light and sons of day; we are not of night or darkness” (1 Thessalonians 5:2–5). Who are the sons of night and darkness? The unrighteous, the ungodly, and the unbelieving.

### 4. [vers. 1]

But let them also hear before the hour comes, and let the Apostle say to them: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8). As this psalm says, let them awaken.

The mountains have already been illuminated; why do they still sleep? Let them lift their eyes to the mountains, from which their help will come.

What does “the mountains have already been illuminated” mean? The sun of righteousness has already risen; the Gospel has already been preached by the Apostles; the Scriptures have been proclaimed; all the mysteries have been revealed; the veil has been torn (Matthew 27:51); the temple’s secret has been disclosed. At last, then, let them lift their eyes to the mountains, from which their help will come.

For this is what this psalm commands, the second among those entitled “Song of Ascents.” But let them not again put their confidence in the mountains, because the mountains themselves do not shine from themselves; they shine from the one of whom it was said: “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

The mountains may be understood as great people, illustrious people. And who is greater than John the Baptist? What a mountain he was, of whom the Lord himself says: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11).

You certainly see this great shining mountain; hear him confessing. What does he confess? “We all,” he says, “have received from his fullness” (John 1:16).

From whose fullness, then, did the mountains receive? Your help comes from him, not from the mountains [Note: [Col. 1607] Here some old Paris and Venetian editions continue after “not from the mountains” as follows: “Therefore our salvation and our help is Christ, Son of the Most High Father, and with that same Father almighty God, and abiding always with him according to what he is. Unless you lift your eyes toward those mountains I have mentioned…”], although unless you lift your eyes toward them through the Scriptures, you will not be brought near [Note: [Col. 1607] Most manuscripts read: “you will not be warned”], so that you may be illuminated by him.

### 5. [vers. 3]

Sing, then, what follows. If you wish to hear so that you may place your feet most firmly on the steps, lest you become weary during that ascent or slip and fall [Note: [Col. 1607] The old Venetian and Paris editions contain the following after “or slip and fall”: “ ‘My help,’ he says, ‘is from the Lord.’ Not from just any lord—for many lords are called lords: mortals, perishable, wretched—but from the Lord of lords, namely from the one who made heaven and earth. Behold the supreme Lord, who is God and Lord. He is called God because whatever things have been made are through him and from him, so that they may exist [Col. 1608]; he is called Lord because he ineffably possesses all things that exist. Therefore the good and supreme Lord, who is also God. If you lift your eyes to him through the mountains named above, your help will be everlasting. Therefore, if you wish your help to be with you, pray and say what follows: ‘Do not give…’ ”], say what follows: “Do not give my foot over to being moved.”

From what are feet moved? From what was the foot of the one who was in paradise moved? But first consider from what the foot of the one who was among the angels was moved. His foot was moved, he fell, and from an angel he became the devil. For when his foot was moved, he fell.

Ask from what he fell: he fell through pride [Note: [Col. 1608] Those Venetian and Paris editions read: “Pride caused him to fall from heaven to earth. He was an angel in heaven; falling to earth, he became the devil through his own pride. Whoever is proud shares in the devil; if he shares in him, he is the same. Therefore every proud person is the devil in a twofold portion—and this as long as he is proud. Therefore he does not move…”].

No one moves his foot except through pride; no one moves his foot toward ruin except through pride. Love moves the foot toward walking, progress, and ascent; pride moves it toward falling [Note: [Col. 1608] In those Venetian and Paris editions this gloss is also found here: “O lovely and limpid feet of love, which lead the humble to lofty heights! Dearly beloved, let us always follow and love these feet by imitation, so that we may deserve to reach the one whose feet they are, because, as John says, ‘God is love.’ Let us flee pride altogether, which moves feet toward falling, lest we too fall by becoming proud. Therefore that man also…”].

Thus what does that psalm say? “But the children of human beings will hope under the shelter of your wings.” If under your shelter, then always humble, always hoping in God, never trusting in themselves. “They will hope under the shelter of your wings.” For they are not satisfied from themselves so as to be blessed.

But what follows? “They will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delights.” Behold them thirsting; behold them intoxicated. Behold, they thirst; behold, they drink. But they do not drink from themselves, nor are they themselves a fountain for themselves.

From where do they drink? “They will hope under the shelter of your wings.” If they are under the wings, they are humble. Why? “For with you,” he says, “is the fountain of life.”

Therefore the mountains are not watered from themselves, just as the mountains are not illuminated from themselves. For see what follows: “In your light we shall see light.”

If, then, we shall see light in his light, who falls from the light except the one for whom he himself is not light? And whoever wishes to be light for himself falls from the light by which he is illuminated.

Therefore, knowing that only the one who wishes to shine for himself can fall, although he is darkness in himself, he immediately added: “Let not the foot of pride come to me, and let not the hand of sinners move me”—that is, let not the imitation of sinners move me so that I fall away from you.

Why did you fear, and say, “Let not the foot of pride come to me”? The following answers: “There all those who work iniquity have fallen” (Psalm 35:8–13). Those whom you now see working iniquity have already been condemned. But in order to be condemned, they fell there, when the foot of pride came upon them.

Rightly, then, this man, hearing how to ascend without falling, how to make progress from the valley of weeping without failing through the swelling of pride, says to God: “Do not give my foot over to being moved.”

And God says to him: “Nor let the one who guards you sleep.”

Let Your Charity pay attention. A single sentence has been made from two voices. The human being, ascending and singing the Song of Ascents, said: “Do not give my foot over to being moved.” And God, as though saying, “You say to me, ‘Do not give my foot over to being moved’; add, ‘Nor let the one who guards you sleep,’ and your foot will not be moved.”

[Col. 1609]

### 6. [vers. 4]

But that man may say: “Is it in my power to ensure that the one who guards me does not sleep? I want him neither to sleep nor to doze.”

Then choose for yourself the one who will neither sleep nor doze, and your foot will not be moved. God is never sleeping. If you wish to have a guardian who does not sleep, choose God as your guardian.

You say, “Do not give my foot over to being moved.” Good, very good. But he also says to you: “Nor let the one who guards you sleep.”

Perhaps you were about to turn toward human guardians and say: “Whom shall I find who does not sleep? What person will not doze? Whom shall I find? Where shall I go? Where shall I turn?” [Note: [Col. 1609] One Corbie manuscript reads: “Where shall I turn myself?”]

He points him out to you: “Behold, the one who guards Israel will neither doze nor sleep.”

Do you wish to have a guardian who neither sleeps nor dozes? Behold, the one who guards Israel will neither sleep nor doze. For Christ guards Israel.

Be Israel, then. What is “Israel”? Israel is interpreted as “Seeing God.”

And how is God seen? First through faith, afterward through sight. If you cannot yet see him through sight, see him through faith. If you cannot see his face, because there is the vision of his face, see his back.

This was said to Moses by the Lord: “You cannot see my face; you shall see my back when I have passed by” (Exodus 33:20, 23).

Perhaps you are waiting for him to pass by. He has already passed by; you see his back. Where did he pass by? Hear John: “When the hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13:1).

Our Lord Jesus Christ has already made the Passover. “Pascha” means “Passover” or “Passage.” For it is a Hebrew word; people think it is Greek, as though it meant “Passion,” but it does not. More diligent and learned people have discovered that Pascha is a Hebrew word; and they interpret it not as “passion” but as “passage.”

Through his passion the Lord passed from death to life, and he made a way for us who believe in his resurrection, so that we too may pass from death to life.

It is not a great thing to believe that Christ died. Pagans, Jews, and all the wicked also believe this. Everyone believes that he died. The faith of Christians is the resurrection of Christ. We consider this the great thing: that we believe he rose again.

Therefore he wished to be seen when he passed by—that is, when he rose again. He wished people to believe in him when he passed by, because “he was delivered up for our offenses and rose again for our justification” (Romans 4:25).

The Apostle especially commended faith in Christ’s resurrection. For he says: “If you believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9).

He did not say, “If you believe that Christ died”—which pagans, Jews, and all his enemies also believed. Rather, he said: “If you believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.”

To believe this is to be Israel; this is to see God. Although you still see his back, once you have believed in his back, you will arrive at the vision of his face.

What does this mean? When you have believed in what Christ became for you afterward; when you have believed in what Christ assumed afterward [Col. 1610].

For what is his face “in the beginning”? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” What is his back? “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14).

When, therefore, you believe in this—that the Word became flesh for you and rose again in the flesh so that you would not despair of your own flesh—you become Israel.

Once you have become Israel, the one who guards you will neither doze nor sleep, because you are already Israel and you have heard in the psalm: “Behold, the one who guards Israel will neither doze nor sleep.”

Christ himself slept, but he rose again. For what does he say in the psalm? “I slept and took my rest.” Did he remain in sleep? “I arose,” he says, “because the Lord will receive me” (Psalm 3:6).

If he has already risen, he has already passed over. If he has already passed over, see his back. What does “See his back” mean? Believe in his resurrection.

And because the Apostle says: “Although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4); and again: “Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and death no longer rules over him” (Romans 6:9), he rightly sings to you: “Behold, the one who guards Israel will neither doze nor sleep.”

Perhaps you still ask with carnal understanding: “Who is the one who will neither doze nor sleep?” And when you seek him among human beings, you are deceived; you will never find him. Do not, then, put your confidence in any human being. Every human being sleeps, and will sleep.

When does he doze? When he bears the flesh of weakness. When will he sleep? When he has died.

Do not, then, seek him among human beings.

### 7. [verse 5]

“And who,” you ask, “will guard me—the one who neither slumbers nor sleeps?” Hear what follows: “The Lord will guard you.”

[Note: [Col. 1610] The manuscripts consistently read this way, in agreement with the Greek Septuagint. The editions, however, read *custodit* (“guards”).]

It is not a human being who slumbers and sleeps, but the Lord guards you. How does he guard you? “The Lord is your shelter over the hand of your right hand.”

Come, brothers, let us understand, with the Lord’s help, what is meant by “The Lord is your shelter over the hand of your right hand.” It seems to me that there is a hidden meaning in why he did not say simply and absolutely, “The Lord will guard you,” but added, “over your right hand.” What does this mean? Does God guard our right hand but not our left? Did he not make us whole? Did the one who made our right hand not also make our left? Finally, if it pleased him to speak only of the right, why did he say, “over the hand of your right hand,” rather than simply, “over your right”? Why would he say this, unless he had concealed here some hidden meaning which we might reach by knocking? He could have said either, “The Lord will guard you,” and added nothing; or, if he wished to add “right,” “The Lord will guard you over your right.” Or, since he added “hand,” he could have said, “The Lord will guard you over your right hand,” not “over the hand of your right.”

What the Lord himself deigns to suggest, I will bring forth for you. He who also dwells in you undoubtedly makes you approve that what I say is true. For you do not know what we are going to say; but when we have said it, we will not demonstrate to you from ourselves that what we say is true. You yourselves will recognize that what we say is true. And how will you recognize it, unless he demonstrates it who dwells in you—insofar as you belong to that number whose voice says, “Do not let my foot be moved,” and to whom it is said, “Nor let him slumber who guards you”?

For Christ must not sleep in you, and now you will understand that what we say is true. “How,” you ask? Because if your faith sleeps, Christ sleeps in you. Christ in your heart is the faith of Christ. The Apostle says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Eph. 3:17). Where faith does not sleep, Christ is awake.

And if perhaps your faith was sleeping, and therefore you were wavering in this question, like that ship which was suffering the storm while Christ was sleeping, awaken Christ, and the storms will be calmed (Matt. 8:24–26).

### 8

I question your faith, dearly beloved. Since you are children of the Church, and have made progress in the Church—and those of you who have not yet made progress will make progress in the Church, while those of you who have already made progress are still to make progress in the Church—I ask you what you usually understand by what is said in the Gospel: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. 6:3).

[Note: [Col. 1611] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition read: “Since you are children of the Church, and have made progress in the Church, and are making progress in the Church, you who have not yet made progress, and are to be perfected in the Church, you who are already making progress.” The Louvain edition omits the words “and are making progress in the Church,” and continues: “You who have not yet made progress are to make progress in the Church. You who already…” M.]

When you understand this, you will discover what the right hand is and what the left hand is. At the same time, you will understand that God made both parts, the right and the left; and yet the left hand ought not to know what the right hand is doing.

Our left hand is called whatever we possess temporally; our right hand is called whatever the Lord promises us as eternal and unchangeable. But since the one who will give eternal life also provides present life with consolation from these temporal things, he made both the right and the left.

David says in a psalm concerning certain people: “Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” He therefore found some whom he reproved: they regarded the true right hand as their left, and had made the true left hand into their right. He explains next who they are.

Everyone who does not think human happiness consists in anything except temporal possessions, pleasures, and the abundance and plenty of this world is foolish and perverse. Such a person makes the left hand his right. Those were the sort of people of whom the psalm speaks—not because they had not also received from God the things they possessed temporally, but because they thought that life was blessed only in these things and sought nothing else.

For hear what he says about them next: “Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” And he continues:

“Their sons are like young plants, firmly established; their daughters adorned like the likeness of a temple; their storerooms full, bursting forth from one thing into another; their sheep fruitful, multiplying in their flocks; their oxen fat; there is no breach in the wall, nor any going out, nor any cry in their streets.”

He has described the great prosperity of certain people. Yet a just person could also possess this prosperity, as Job did. But Job regarded it as a left-hand possession, not as his right hand; for he had no right hand except the perpetual and everlasting happiness he possessed with God. Therefore the left hand was permitted to be struck, and the right hand was sufficient for him.

How was his left hand struck? By the devil’s temptations. The devil suddenly took everything away—though permitted by God, so that the just man might be tested and the ungodly man punished. He took everything away. But Job, who knew that the left was left and the right nothing other than right, how did he hold fast to the right? He rejoiced in the Lord and was consoled amid his losses, because he suffered no loss in his inward riches: his heart was full of God.

[Note: [Col. 1612] Thus the manuscripts. Erasmus and the Louvain edition read: “He did not suffer loss, for his heart was full of the inner riches of God.”]

“The Lord,” he says, “gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

This was his right hand: the Lord himself, eternal life itself, possession of that light, the fountain of life, light in the light. “They shall be inebriated with the abundance of your house”—that was his right hand. The left hand, however, existed for the assistance of consolation, not as the foundation of happiness. For his true and genuine happiness was God.

Those, however, of whom David says that “their mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity,” are not reproved because they abounded in all these things, but because their mouth spoke vanity. What follows? After enumerating their riches, he says: “They called the people blessed who have these things.”

This is the vanity their mouth spoke: they called the people blessed who have these things. What do you say, you who know what the left hand is and what the right hand is? He continues and says: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God” (Ps. 143:11–15).

### 9

Let your Charity pay attention. We have seen the left hand; we have also seen the right hand. Hear this confirmed in the Song of Songs: “His left hand,” she says, “is under my head.”

The bride speaks of the bridegroom, the Church speaks of Christ, in an embrace of piety and love.

[Note: [Col. 1612] Thus most manuscripts. The editions, however, read “in an embrace of chastity.”]

What does she say? “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6).

What does this mean? Was the right hand above and the left below, so that the bridegroom embraced the bride, placing the left hand beneath for consolation and laying the right hand upon her for protection?

“His left hand,” she says, “is under my head.” God gives it; therefore it is called his left hand, because God gives all these temporal things. How vain and impious are those who ask these things from idols and demons! How many ask such things from demons and do not receive them; and again, those who do not ask them from demons possess them—but these things are not given by demons. Many also ask them from God and do not receive them. For he knows how to distribute the left hand, he who calls us to the right.

Therefore, if there is a left hand, let it be the left hand; but let it be under the head. Let your head be above it—that is, let your faith be above it, where Christ dwells. Do not place temporal things before your faith, and the left hand will not be above your head. Rather, subject all temporal things to your faith, and place your faith before all temporal things. Then the left hand will be under your head, and rightly his right hand will embrace you.

### 10

Hear this same matter explained in Proverbs: what the left hand itself is and what the right hand is. Speaking of Wisdom, it says: “Length of days and years of life are in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and glory” (Prov. 3:16).

That length of days is eternity. Scripture calls what is eternal “long” in its proper sense; for whatever has an end is short. Elsewhere it says: “I will fill him with length of days” (Ps. 90:16).

And would it otherwise be said as something great: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Exod. 20:12)? What earth could this mean except that of which he says: “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6)? What does it mean to be long-lived there except to live there eternally?

For what does it mean to be long-lived here except to reach old age? Even if a lifespan seems long, once it has arrived it is shown to be short, because it comes to an end.

[Note: [Col. 1613] Thus Ambrosianus and the manuscripts. Erasmus and the Louvain edition read: “when death comes.”]

Many who curse their parents grow old in this land; many who obey their parents go quickly to the Lord. Is it therefore fulfilled that one should be long-lived according to this life? No: “long-lived” has been said with reference to that eternity.

[Note: [Col. 1613] The editions read “a long life.” The manuscripts read “long life” or “longevity.”]

Longevity is in her right hand; riches and glory, that is, the sufficiency of this life and what people regard as good, are in her left hand.

Someone comes and wants to strike your right hand—that is, to take away your faith. “You have received a slap on the right; offer the left also” (Matt. 5:39): let him take away what is temporal, not what you possess eternally.

Hear the Apostle Paul doing this. People were persecuting him because he was a Christian. His right hand was struck, but he offered the left: “I am a Roman citizen,” he said (Acts 22:25). They despised his right hand, and he frightened them with the left, because they could not fear his right hand: they had not yet believed in Christ.

What then does it mean that the right hand embraces and the left hand is under the head? What does “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” mean? It means: when you do a good work, do it for the sake of eternal life.

For if you do a good work on earth so that earthly things may abound for you, your left hand knows what your right hand is doing: you have mixed the right hand with the left. Do nothing except for the sake of eternal life. Do it for that reason, and you will act securely; for God commanded this.

[Note: [Col. 1613] All our manuscripts read: “For God tested him for this.”]

If you do what you do for the sake of merely human affairs and this life alone, only the left hand is working. But if you work for the sake of eternal life, only the right hand is working. If, however, you intend eternal life, but a desire for temporal life secretly creeps in, so that you pay attention to it as well when you perform a good work, seeking some reward for yourself here, the left hand mingles with the works of the right hand. God forbids this.

### 11

Let us now come to what the psalm says: “The Lord is your shelter over the hand of your right hand.” He calls the hand power. How do we prove this? Because the hand of God is also called the power of God.

For the devil, who tempted Job, said this to God: “Send your hand and touch all that he has, and see whether he will bless you to your face” (Job 1:11). What is “Send your hand” except “Give power”?

Listen more clearly, brother, lest you still think in a carnal way that God is divided into bodily members. Hear plainly how the hand is called power. Scripture says in one place: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21).

We know tongues as certain pieces of flesh. They move in the mouth and, striking the palate and teeth, distinguish the sounds by which we speak. Let the hands of the tongue be shown to me! The tongue therefore does not have hands—and yet it has hands. What are the hands of the tongue? The power of the tongue.

What does “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” mean? “By your mouth you will be justified, and by your mouth you will be condemned” (Matt. 12:37).

Therefore, if the hand is power, what is the hand of the right hand? I think it can be understood more appropriately in no other way than this: the hand of the right hand is the power God has given you, so that, if you wish, by God’s gift you may be on the right.

For all the ungodly will be on the left, while all the good children will be on the right. To them he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

In order that you may be on the right—that is, in order that you may become a child of God—you have received power. What power? The power of which John says: “He gave them power to become children of God.” From where did you receive this power? “To those who believe,” he says, “in his name” (John 1:12).

If you believe, then this very power has been given to you, so that you may be among the children of God. To be among the children of God is to belong to the right. Therefore your faith is the hand of your right hand: that is, the power given to you so that you may be among the children of God is the hand of your right hand.

But what benefit is the power a human being has received if the Lord does not protect him? Behold, he has believed and already walks in faith; yet he is weak and is shaken amid temptations, troubles, bodily corruptions, the suggestions of desire, and the deceits and snares of the enemy.

What benefit is it, then, that he has power and has believed in Christ so as to be among the children of God? Woe to that person unless the Lord also protects his faith—that is, unless he does not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, as the Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear” (1 Cor. 10:13).

He, therefore, who does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, protects us even though we are already faithful, even though the hand of our right hand is already within us. God protects us over the hand of our right hand. It is not enough for us to have the hand of our right hand unless he also protects that very hand.

### 12. [verse 6]

Behold, I have spoken about temptations. Pay attention to what follows: “May the Lord protect you over the hand of your right hand.”

[Note: [Col. 1614] Some manuscripts read *proteget* (“will protect”), and several read *protegit* (“protects”).]

I have spoken, and, as I think, you have recognized the matter. For if you had not recognized it, if you had not recognized it from the Scriptures, you would not have signified your understanding to me by your voices.
