Since you have understood, therefore, brothers, see what follows: why should the Lord protect us over the hand of our right hand—that is, over the very faith in which we have received the power to be children of God and to belong to the right? Why must the Lord protect us?

[Col. 1615] Because of scandals. From where do scandals arise? Scandals are to be feared from two sources, because there are also two commandments on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend: love of God and love of neighbor (Matt. 22:37–40).

The Church is loved for the sake of the neighbor; God is loved for the sake of God. In God, the sun is understood figuratively; in the Church, the moon is understood figuratively.

Whoever can go astray by believing something about God other than what ought to be believed—whoever does not believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance, deceived by the cunning of heretics, especially the Arians—has suffered scandal in God; he is burned by the sun.

[Note: [Col. 1615] The older Paris and Venetian editions add: “Especially the Arians, who introduced three *hypostases* (*upostaseis*), that is, three subsistent substances. But, by God’s merciful help, the first author of this error was condemned to exile by the perpetual sentence of the Catholic Fathers and, after his death, is said never to have returned to communion. Another, throughout the whole region of the East, was punished with a deserved and similar penalty. But if any of these or others, as I have said, deceived by the madness of error, should believe anything less in the Son or in the Holy Spirit than in the Father, etc.”]

Whoever, on the other hand, thinks that the Church exists in only one place and does not recognize it as spread throughout the whole world, and believes those who say, “Behold, here is Christ,” or “There” (Matt. 24:23), as you have just heard when the Gospel was read—although he purchased the whole world, because he paid so great a price—such a person is scandalized in the neighbor, and is burned by the moon.

Whoever therefore errs in the very substance of truth is burned by the sun, and is burned by day, because he errs in that very Wisdom of which it is said: “Day pours forth speech to day.” Hence the Apostle also says: “Comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. Day pours forth speech to day; comparing spiritual things with spiritual things: ‘We speak wisdom among the mature’” (1 Cor. 2:13, 6).

What is, “And night announces knowledge to night” (Ps. 18:3)? The humility of Christ, the flesh of Christ, and the crucifixion of Christ are preached to little ones, because this is the milk sufficient for little ones.

And therefore little ones are not abandoned in the night, because the moon also shines in the night. That is, the Church is preached through the flesh of Christ, because the flesh of Christ itself is the head of the Church. Whoever is not scandalized there, in that Church and in the flesh of Christ, is not burned by the moon.

Whoever is not scandalized by that unchangeable and undefiled truth is not burned by the sun.

[Note: [Col. 1615] Ambrosianus and most manuscripts continue after “undefiled”: “not by this sun which flies and cattle see together with us, but by that sun…”]

He is not burned by this sun, which flies and cattle see together with us, but by that sun of which the ungodly say at the end: “What did our pride profit us? What did the boasting of riches contribute to us? All these things passed away like a shadow.” And after saying this they add: “Therefore we have wandered from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. 5:6–9).

Does this sun not rise for all the ungodly, by the ordinance of him of whom it is said: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matt. 5:45)? God therefore made one sun which rises upon good and evil—the sun seen by both good and evil. But there is another sun, not made but begotten, through whom all things were made, where there is the unchangeable understanding of truth. Of him the ungodly say: “The sun did not rise for us.”

[Note: [Col. 1616] The older Paris and Venetian editions insert here: “Concerning this sun, Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, spoke beautifully as follows: ‘The Son of God is from the Father alone; not made, nor created, but begotten.’ From this, Possevinus, under the entry Athanasius in his *Apparatus*, Torrensis in his preface to Augustine’s *Confessions*, and Bellarmine in book 2, chapter 25, *On Christ*, think that the creed commonly called Athanasian was attributed to Athanasius himself on Augustine’s authority. Petavius, however, in *Dogmatic Theology on the Trinity*, book 7, chapter 8, section 7, says that those words were rashly attached to Augustine; and in fact they are absent from all our manuscripts and are not found in the editions of Ambrosianus, Erasmus, or Louvain.”]

Whoever does not err in that Wisdom is not burned by the sun. Whoever does not err in the Church, in the Lord’s flesh, and in those things accomplished temporally for our sake, is not burned by the moon.

Every human being, even if he has already believed in Christ, either errs there, or there [the printed text is incomplete], unless what is said is fulfilled in him:

[Note: [Col. 1616] Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read: “either errs there or does not err there.”] “The Lord is your shelter over the hand of your right hand.”

[Note: [Col. 1616] The Lyon and Venetian editions add here: “as though he were burned by the sun during the day and by the moon during the night.”]

For when he had said, “The Lord is your shelter over the hand of your right hand,” the person seemed to ask: “Now, behold, my right hand exists; I have chosen to believe in Christ; I have received power to be among the children of God. Why, then, is God still my shelter above—that is, over the hand of my right hand?” He continues: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.”

Your shelter over the hand of your right hand therefore exists for this purpose: so that the sun may not burn you by day, nor the moon by night.

Understand from this, brothers, that the words are figurative. In reality, if we think of the visible sun, it burns during the day. Does the moon burn during the night? But what is burning? Scandal.

Hear the Apostle say: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burned?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

### 13. [verse 7]

“By day, therefore, the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.” Why? “Because the Lord will guard you from every evil.”

[Note: [Col. 1616] Most manuscripts consistently read in this verse: “May he guard you”; and in the following verse, instead of “may he guard the entrance,” they read “he will guard the entrance.”]

He will guard you from scandals in the sun, from scandals in the moon, from every evil—the one who is your shelter over the hand of your right hand, who neither sleeps nor slumbers.

And for what purpose? Because we are in temptations: “The Lord will guard you from every evil.”

“May the Lord guard your soul”—your soul as well. “May he guard your entrance and your exit, from this time forth and forever.”

This does not mean your body; for the martyrs were killed in the body. Rather, may the Lord guard your soul, because the martyrs did not yield in soul.

The persecutors raged against Crispina, whose anniversary we celebrate today. They raged against a wealthy and delicate woman, but she was strong, because the Lord was her shelter over the hand of her right hand—he who guarded her.

[Note: [Col. 1616] The older Paris and Venetian editions read “Christiana.” Ambrosianus and Erasmus read “Christina.” But the Louvain edition and the manuscripts more correctly read “Crispina,” as again below in Psalm 137, at verse 7. She is commemorated as having suffered at Theveste in Africa on the Nones of December.]

For, brothers, is there anyone in Africa who does not know her? She was very famous, noble by birth, and rich in possessions. But all these things were left-hand things; they were under the head.

[Col. 1617] The enemy came to strike the head, and the left hand, which was under the head, was offered to him. The head was above, and the right hand embraced it from above.

What could the persecutor do, even against a delicate woman? She was indeed weak in sex, perhaps weakened by wealth, and physically weaker through habit; but what were these things against such great defenses? What were they against that bridegroom who placed his left hand beneath the head and embraced her with his right? When could the enemy strike one so fortified?

And yet he did strike—but the body. What does the psalm say? “May the Lord guard your soul.” The soul did not yield; the body was struck.

The body too was struck only for a time, for it will rise at the end. The one who deigned to be the head of the Church also offered his body to be struck for a time. He raised his own flesh on the third day, and at the end he will raise our flesh.

Therefore the head was raised so that the body might look to it and not fail. “May the Lord guard your soul.” Let the soul not yield; let it not be broken by scandals.

[Note: [Col. 1617] Several manuscripts read “in scandals.”]

In persecutions and tribulations, let it not yield by failing,

[Note: [Col. 1617] Thus Ambrosianus and the manuscripts. Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “let it not fall.”]

as the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who has power to kill both body and soul in the gehenna of fire” (Matt. 10:28).

[Note: [Col. 1617] Erasmus, the Lyon and Venetian editions, and the Louvain edition read: “to kill and cast into the gehenna of fire.” M.]

May the Lord therefore guard your soul, so that you do not yield to an evil persuader, yield to one who promises false things, or yield to one who threatens temporal things. May the Lord guard your soul.

### 14. [verse 8]

And then: “May the Lord guard your entrance and your exit, from this time forth and forever.”

Pay attention to your entrance for a time. “May the Lord guard your entrance and your exit, from this time forth and forever.” May the same one guard your exit.

What is the entrance? What is the exit? When we are tempted, we enter; when we overcome temptation, we leave.

Hear about the entrance; hear about the exit. “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter,” Scripture says, “and temptation in tribulation tests righteous people” (Sirach 27:6).

If righteous people are like vessels of the potter, the vessels of the potter must enter the furnace. And when they enter, the potter is not yet secure, but only when they have come out.

The Lord, however, is secure, because he knows those who are his (2 Tim. 2:19), and he knows which ones will not burst in the furnace. Those do not burst who do not possess the wind of pride.

Humility therefore guards us in every temptation, because we ascend from the valley of weeping while singing the Song of Ascents. The Lord guards the entrance, so that we may enter safely.

Let us be sound in faith when temptation occurs, and he guards the exit from this time forth and forever. For when we have come out from every temptation, no temptation will frighten us eternally, and no desire will even trouble us.

Hear the Apostle recalling the very thing I recalled a little earlier: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear.” Behold, your entrance is guarded. When God does not allow a temptation to happen to you which you cannot bear, he guards your entrance. See whether he also guards your exit.

“But he will make an escape with the temptation,” he says, “so that you may be able to endure” (1 Cor. 10:13). Can we, brothers, interpret these words in any other way than the very words of the Apostle have taught us?

Guard yourselves, therefore—but not by yourselves, because the Lord is the shelter, the one who guards, who neither slumbers nor sleeps.

He slept once for us; he rose again; now he will not sleep. Let no one presume upon himself. We ascend from the valley of weeping; let us not remain on the way. Steps remain on the road. We must not remain behind in laziness; we must not fall through pride.

Let us say to God: “Let not our foot be moved.” He will not sleep who guards us.

It is in our power, by God’s gift,

[Note: [Col. 1618] The manuscripts do not have the words “by God’s gift.”]

to make him our guardian who neither sleeps nor slumbers, who guards Israel. Which Israel? The one who sees God.

Thus your help will be from the Lord; thus your shelter will be over the hand of your right hand; thus your entrance and your exit will be guarded from this time forth and forever.

For if you presume upon yourself, your foot has been moved. If your foot has been moved, you now think yourself to be on some step; from there you fall if you are proud. For the humble person in the valley of weeping says: “Do not let my foot be moved.”

### 15

Although the psalm is short, the exposition and discourse have nevertheless been long. Consider, brothers, that on the anniversary of blessed Crispina I invited you, and that I was excessive in prolonging the banquet.

Could this not happen to you if some soldier invited you and compelled you to drink at the table without measure? Let us be permitted to do this in divine discourse, so that you may be inebriated and satisfied, just as the Lord has deigned by his temporal rain to water the earth, so that with greater joy he might allow us to go to the place of the martyrs, as we had promised yesterday.

For those martyrs are here with us without labor.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 121

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1

As impure love inflames the soul and calls it toward desiring earthly things and pursuing what perishes—things that themselves summon it toward destruction—and casts it down and plunges it into the depths, so holy love raises it toward what is above, inflames it toward eternal things, awakens it toward those things which neither pass away nor die, and lifts it from the depth of hell to heaven.

Every love nevertheless has its own force, and love cannot be inactive in the soul of one who loves; it must lead somewhere. But do you wish to know what kind of love it is? See where it leads.

We do not therefore warn you to love nothing; rather, we warn you not to love the world, so that you may freely love the one who made the world.

For a soul bound by earthly love is like a birdlime attached to its wings: it cannot fly. But when cleansed from the most filthy affections of the world, as though its wings were extended and its two wings released from every impediment—that is, by the two commandments of love of God and love of neighbor—it flies.

Where does it fly, except upward to God, since it ascends by loving? Before it can do so, if the desire to fly is already present in it, it groans on earth and says: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I will fly and rest?” (Ps. 54:7).

Where will it fly, except away from the midst of scandals—the very place where the one whose voice I have recalled also groaned? He wishes to fly away from the midst of scandals, from the mixture of evil people, from the chaff with which the grain has been mixed, where he will not suffer the association and fellowship of any wicked person, but will live in the holy society of the angelic citizens in the eternal Jerusalem.

### 2. [verse 1]

Therefore this psalm, which we have undertaken to expound today for your Holiness, desires Jerusalem itself—that is, the one who ascends in this psalm. For it is a Song of Ascents, as we have often said to your Charity: these are not steps of those descending, but of those ascending.

[Note: [Col. 1619] See Psalm 38, section 2, and Psalm 119, sections 1–3.]

This person therefore wishes to ascend. And where does he wish to ascend except into heaven? What does “into heaven” mean? Does he wish to ascend in order to be with the sun, moon, and stars? Far from it. In heaven there is the eternal Jerusalem, where our fellow citizens, the angels, are. We are pilgrims on earth, away from those fellow citizens of ours.

In pilgrimage we sigh; in the city we shall rejoice. Yet we also find companions on this pilgrimage who have already seen that city and invite us to run toward it.

This is why the person in the psalm rejoices, saying: “I rejoiced in those who said to me, ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’”

Brothers, let your Charity recall whether, when some festival of the martyrs and some holy place is announced, to which crowds will gather on a fixed day to celebrate the solemnity, those crowds do not stir themselves up and encourage one another, saying: “Let us go, let us go.”

And they ask: “Where shall we go?” The answer is given: “To that place, to the holy place.” They speak to one another and, as though set aflame, each one kindles a single flame. That one flame, formed from the conversation of those who kindle one another, carries them off to the holy place, and holy thought makes them holy.

If holy love carries people in this way to a temporal place, what kind of love must it be that carries those who are united into heaven, saying to one another, “We shall go into the house of the Lord”?

Therefore let us run, let us run, because we shall go into the house of the Lord. Let us run and not grow tired, because we shall reach the place where we will not grow weary. Let us run into the house of the Lord; let our soul rejoice in those who say these things to us.

For those who say these things to us saw the homeland first. From far away they call to those who come after them: “We shall go into the house of the Lord. Walk; run.”

The Apostles saw it, and they said to us: “Run, walk, follow. We shall go into the house of the Lord.” And what does each one of us say? “I rejoiced in those who said to me, ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’”

I rejoiced in the Prophets; I rejoiced in the Apostles. For all these people said to us: “We shall go into the house of the Lord.”

### 3. [verse 2]

“Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem.”

[Note: [Col. 1619] Only two manuscripts read: “in your courts.”]

Behold, you have the house of the Lord, if you were asking what the house of the Lord is. In that house of the Lord, the one who founded the house is praised. He himself is the delight of all who dwell in the house; here he alone is hope, and there he is possession.

What, then, should those who run think about? As though they were already there, and were standing there. For it is a great thing to stand there among the angels and not fail.

The one who fell from there did not stand in the truth (John 8:44). All who have not fallen stand in the truth. The one who enjoys God stands; but whoever wishes to enjoy himself falls.

And who wishes to enjoy himself? The one who is proud. Therefore the one who always wished to stand in the courts of Jerusalem says: “In your light we shall see light”—not “in my light”; and “With you is the fountain of life”—not “with me.”

And what did he add? “Let not the foot of pride come to me, and let not the hand of sinners move me. There all who work iniquity have fallen; they have been cast out and could not stand” (Ps. 35:10, 12–13).

Since they could not stand because they were proud, ascend humbly, so that you may say: “Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem.”

Consider what you will be like there. Although you are still on the way, place this before your eyes as though you were already standing there, as though you were already rejoicing indefatigably among the angels, and as though what was said were being fulfilled in you: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they shall praise you forever and ever” (Ps. 83:5).

“Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem.” Which Jerusalem? This Jerusalem is also commonly called Jerusalem, but this Jerusalem is a shadow of that one.

And what great thing is it to stand in this Jerusalem, when this Jerusalem could not stand, having been turned into a ruin?

The Holy Spirit therefore speaks this as something great from the inflamed heart of this lover, because he says: “Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem.”

Is this not the Jerusalem to which the Lord said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the Prophets and stone those who are sent to you” (Matt. 23:37)?

What great thing, then, was this person desiring—to stand among those who killed the Prophets and stoned those sent to them?

Far be it from one who loves in this way, who burns in this way, and who wishes to reach that Jerusalem, our mother (Gal. 4:26), to think in this way about this Jerusalem—the Jerusalem of which the Apostle says that it is “eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1).

### 4. [verse 3]

Listen, finally; do not believe me—listen to what follows, and what Jerusalem it designates in our minds. For when he had said, “Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem,” as though someone were saying to him, “Which Jerusalem do you mean? Of which Jerusalem are you speaking?” he immediately added, “Jerusalem, which is built as a city.”

Brothers, when David was saying these things, that city was complete; it was not being built. What city, then, is he speaking of, which is now being built, toward which living stones hasten in faith—of whom Peter says, “You also, as living stones, are being built together into a spiritual house” (1 Pet. 2:5), that is, God’s holy temple?

What does “you are being built together as living stones” mean? You are alive if you believe; but if you believe, you become God’s temple, because the apostle Paul says, “For God’s temple is holy, which temple you are.” That city, then, is now being built. Stones are cut from the mountains by the hands of those preaching the truth, and squared so that they may enter into the everlasting structure. Many stones are still in the craftsman’s hands; let them not fall from the craftsman’s hands, so that they may be perfected and built together into the structure of the temple.

This, then, is the Jerusalem that is being built as a city; its foundation is Christ. The apostle Paul says, “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3:17, 11).

When a foundation is laid in the earth, walls are built above it, and the weight of the walls presses downward, because the foundation has been placed below. But if our foundation is in heaven, let us be built toward heaven. Bodies built the structure that you see rising here, the spacious structure of this basilica; and because bodies built it, they placed the foundation below. But because we are being built spiritually, our foundation has been placed above.

Let us therefore hasten there, where we are to be built, because of that very Jerusalem it was said, “Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem.” But which Jerusalem? “Jerusalem, which is built as a city.”

He said too little, as though merely to identify Jerusalem, when he said, “which is built as a city”; that physical Jerusalem could still be understood. For what if someone should arise and say: “Even when these things were being said in David’s time and this song was being sung, that city was already complete; but he foresaw in the spirit that it would fall and be built again. For that city was conquered, and the captive people passed over into Babylon; and in Scripture this was called the transmigration into Babylon. Jeremiah prophesied that, after seventy years of captivity, it would be possible to build again that city which had been destroyed by those who waged war against it” (Jer. 29:4, 10).

Perhaps someone might say: “David saw this in the spirit: the city of Jerusalem would fall to its conquerors and, after seventy years, could be built again; and therefore he said, ‘Jerusalem, which is built as a city.’ Do not suppose, then, that he meant that city which consists of the saints as of living stones.”

What follows removes all doubt. He says, “Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem.” But which Jerusalem do I mean? “Do I mean this one,” he says, “which you see standing with walls erected in bodily form? No, but Jerusalem, which is built as a city.”

Why does he say not “a city,” but “as a city,” unless because that structure of walls which existed in Jerusalem was a visible city, as everyone properly calls it a city; whereas the other is built as a city, because those who enter it are like living stones? For are they really stones? Just as they are like stones but are not stones, so it is like a city but is not a city, because he said, “is built.” By the name of a building he intended the structure and joining together of bodies and walls to be understood. For properly speaking, a city is understood as people dwelling together. But he made clear to us that he had called this city a built-up urban community, because he said, “is built.” And because a spiritual building bears a certain likeness to a physical building, therefore it is built as a city.

### 5.

But let him say what follows and remove every doubt, since we must not understand carnally “Jerusalem, which is built as a city”: “whose participation is in the same thing.”

Now then, brothers, whoever raises the eye of the mind, whoever lays aside the darkness of the flesh, whoever cleanses the eye of the heart, let him raise it and see “the same thing.” What is “the same thing”? How shall I say it, except “the same thing”? Brothers, if you can, understand “the same thing.” For whatever else I say, I am not saying “the same thing.”

Nevertheless, let us try by certain neighboring words and meanings to lead the weakness of the mind toward contemplating “the same thing.”

What is “the same thing”? That which is always in the same condition; that which is not one thing now and another thing later. What, then, is “the same thing” except “that which is”? What is “that which is”? That which is eternal. For what is always otherwise and otherwise is not, because it does not remain. It is not altogether nonexistent, but it does not exist supremely.

And what is “that which is” except the one who, when he was sending Moses, said to him, “I am who I am”? What does this mean except the one whose servant said: “Behold, you are sending me; if the people say to me, ‘Who sent you?’ what shall I say to them?” He did not wish to state his name as anything other than, “I am who I am”; and he added and said, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

Behold “the same thing”: “I am who I am”; “He who is has sent me to you.” You cannot grasp it; it is too great to understand, too great to apprehend. Hold fast to what was made for your sake, whom you could not grasp. Hold fast to Christ’s flesh, into which you were lifted when sick and left half-dead from the robbers’ wounds, so that you might be brought to the inn (Luke 10:30, 34), and there be healed.

Let us therefore run to the house of the Lord and reach the city where our feet may stand: the city that is built as a city, whose participation is in the same thing. What must you hold fast to? To what Christ became for your sake, because he himself is Christ; and Christ himself is rightly understood as “I am who I am,” as he exists in the form of God. There, where he did not consider equality with God something to be seized (Phil. 2:6), there is “the same thing.”

But in order that you might become a participant in “the same thing,” he first became a participant in you; and “the Word became flesh,” so that flesh might participate in the Word. Since the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and came from the seed of Abraham—and since it was promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob that all nations would be blessed in their seed (Gen. 22:18)—we therefore see the Church spread throughout the whole world.

God speaks to the weak. He sought firmness of heart when he said, “I am who I am”; he sought firmness of heart and an upright eye of contemplation when he said, “He who is has sent me to you.”

But perhaps you do not yet possess contemplation. Do not fail; do not despair. He who is wished to become a human being, as you are; and therefore he continued by reminding Moses, as though Moses were afraid of the name. What name? That which is “is.” “And the Lord said to Moses,” he says, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; this is my name forever” (Exod. 3:13–15).

Do not despair of yourself because I said, “I am who I am,” and “He who is has sent me to you.” For you now fluctuate, and through the mutability of things and the variety of human mortality you cannot perceive what “the same thing” is. “I descend, because you cannot come.”

“I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Hope in the seed of Abraham for something, so that you may be strengthened to see the one who comes to you in the seed of Abraham.

### 6.

This, then, is “the same thing” of which it is said, “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. 101:27–28). Behold “the same thing,” whose years will not fail.

Brothers, do not our years fail every day, and do they not stand at all? Those that have come are no longer; those that are going to come do not yet exist. The former have already failed, and the latter, destined to fail, will come. On this one day, brothers—behold, what we are saying exists only for a moment. The past hours have passed; the future hours have not yet come; and when they come, they too will pass and fail.

What are the years that do not fail except those that stand? If, then, the years stand there, and those years that stand are one year, and that one year which stands is one day—because that one day has neither rising nor setting, is not begun by yesterday and is not shut out by tomorrow, but that day always stands—call it by whatever name you wish. If you wish, it is years; if you wish, it is a day. Whatever you conceive, it nevertheless stands.

That city participates in this very stability, its participation being in “the same thing.” Rightly, then, because it becomes a participant in that stability, the one who hastens there says, “Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem.” For everything stands there where nothing passes away.

Do you too wish to stand there and not pass away? Run there. No one possesses “the same thing” from himself.

Pay attention, brothers. What has a body is not “the same thing,” because it does not stand in itself. It changes through the stages of life; it changes through changes of place and time; it changes through bodily illnesses and failures. Therefore it does not stand in itself.

The heavenly bodies do not stand in themselves either. They have their own changes, even if hidden; certainly they move from place to place: they rise from east to west and again circle back to the east. Therefore they do not stand; they are not “the same thing.”

Nor does the human soul stand. Through how many changes and thoughts is it altered! By how many pleasures is it transformed! By how many desires is it struck apart and torn asunder! The mind itself, which is called rational, is changeable; it is not “the same thing.” Now it wills, now it does not will; now it knows, now it does not know; now it remembers, now it forgets. Therefore no one possesses “the same thing” from himself.

The one who wished to possess “the same thing” from himself, as though he himself were “the same thing” for himself, fell. The angel fell and became the devil. He offered human beings pride and, together with himself, cast down through envy the one who was standing.

These wished to be “the same thing” for themselves; they wished to rule themselves and be their own masters. They did not wish to have the true Lord, who truly is “the same thing,” to whom it was said, “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same.”

After so much sickness, after so many diseases, difficulties, and labors, let the humbled soul return to “the same thing” and be in that city whose participation is in “the same thing.”

### 7. [verse 4]

“For there the tribes went up.”

We were asking where the one who fell goes up, because we said that this is the voice of a human being going up, of the Church going up. Where, then, do we think he goes up? Where does he proceed? Where is he raised up?

“There,” he says, “the tribes went up.” Where did the tribes go up? Into the city whose participation is in “the same thing.” Therefore one goes up there, into Jerusalem.

But the human being who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho fell among robbers (Luke 10:30). He would not have gone down, and he would not have fallen among robbers. But because he fell among robbers by going down, let him come to the angels by going up.

Let him therefore go up, because “the tribes went up.” But what are the tribes? Many know; many do not know. But let us also, who know, descend to those who do not know about the tribes, so that they may go up with us to where the tribes went up.

Tribes may be called by another name, “curiae,” though not properly. Thus tribes cannot properly be called curiae by another name; they are called curiae by approximation. For if we properly say “curiae,” nothing is understood except the curiae existing individually in individual cities—whence “curiales” and “decurions,” that is, those who belong to a curia or decuria. You know that individual cities have individual curiae of this kind.

There are, or once were, also in these cities curiae belonging to peoples; and one city has many curiae, just as Rome has thirty-five curiae of the people. These are called tribes. The people of Israel had twelve of them, according to the sons of Jacob.

### 8.

There were twelve tribes of the people of Israel; but there were wicked people there, and good people there. How wicked were the tribes that crucified the Lord! How good were the tribes that recognized the Lord!

Those tribes, then, which crucified the Lord are tribes of the devil. When he therefore said here, “For there the tribes went up,” lest you understand all tribes, he added, “the tribes of the Lord.”

What are “the tribes of the Lord”? Those that recognized the Lord. From those same twelve wicked tribes there were good people—good people from the good tribes that recognized the maker of the city. They were the grain among those tribes in which they were mixed together among the chaff.

They went up, not with the chaff, but as tribes purified and chosen, as the tribes of the Lord: “There the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord.”

What are the tribes of the Lord? “The testimony of Israel.”

Listen, brothers, to what this means: “the testimony of Israel,” that is, those in whom it is recognized that he is truly Israel.

What is Israel? The interpretation of its name has already been stated, and let it be stated often; for even if it was stated recently, perhaps it has slipped from memory. By repeating it, let us ensure that it does not slip even from those who do not know or have not wished to read: let us be their book.

Israel is interpreted as “seeing God”—or, on more careful examination of the word, it is interpreted thus: Israel is “seeing God.” Both expressions mean: “seeing God.”

For a human being does not exist in himself; he is changed and turned if he does not participate in the one who is “the same thing.” He exists then, when he sees God. For he exists then, when he sees the one who is; and by seeing the one who is, he too becomes, according to his measure, one who is.

Therefore he is Israel; Israel is “seeing God.”

The proud person, then, is not Israel, because his participation is not in “the same thing”; he wishes to be “the same thing” for himself. Whoever wishes to be his own principle is not Israel.

Every pretender is therefore not Israel, because every proud person must be a pretender. I say this, brothers: every proud person must wish to appear to be what he is not. It cannot be otherwise, my brothers.

If only the proud person wished to appear to be what he is not in such a way that he wished to appear, for example, to be a flute-player when he was not a flute-player. He would quickly be exposed: someone would say to him, “Play; let us see whether you are a flute-player.” He could not; it would be discovered that he had falsely wished to appear to be what he was not.

If he said that he was eloquent, someone would say to him, “Speak, and prove it.” If he spoke, he would be found not to be what he had claimed.

The proud person, which is worse, wishes to appear righteous when he is not. And because it is difficult to understand righteousness, it is difficult to recognize the proud.

The proud therefore wish to appear to be what they are not. For this reason their participation is not in “the same thing”; they do not belong to Israel, which is “seeing God.”

Who, then, belongs to Israel? The one who is a participant in “the same thing.”

Who participates in “the same thing”? The one who confesses that he is not what God is, and that whatever good he can possess he has from God; from himself he has nothing but sin, while righteousness is from God.

Such a person is one in whom there is no deceit. And when the Lord saw Nathanael, what did he say? “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47).

If, then, the true Israelites, in whom there is no deceit, are those tribes that go up to Jerusalem, those tribes in which there is no deceit go up. They are the testimony of Israel—that is, through them it is recognized that there was grain among that chaff, when the threshing floor, as it appeared, was thought to be entirely chaff.

There was grain there. But when they have gone up into that height of splendor, when the threshing floor has been winnowed (Matt. 3:12), then there will be the testimony of Israel. Then all the wicked will say: “Truly there were righteous people among the wicked, when all seemed wicked to us, and we thought everyone was as we were.”

“The testimony of Israel.” Where do they go up? Why do they go up? “To confess your name, O Lord.”

Nothing more magnificent can be said. As pride presumes, so humility confesses. Just as the presumer is one who wishes to appear to be what he is not, so the confessor is one who does not wish to appear to be what he himself is, but loves what the other is.

For this purpose, then, the Israelites in whom there is no deceit go up: because they are truly Israelites, because in them is the testimony of Israel. For this purpose they go up: “to confess your name, O Lord.”

### 9. [verse 5]

“For there the seats for judgment sat.”

A remarkable riddle, a remarkable question, if it is not understood. He says “seats,” which the Greeks call *thronoi* (“thrones”). The Greeks call thrones seats, as honorable ones.

Therefore, my brothers, it is not surprising if human beings sit on seats, on chairs. But how can the seats themselves sit? How can we understand this? It would be as though someone were to say, “Let the chairs sit here,” or “Let the seats sit here.” One sits on a chair; one sits on seats; one sits on chairs. The seats themselves do not sit.

What, then, does this mean: “For there the seats for judgment sat”?

Certainly you are accustomed to hear God saying, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool for my feet” (Isa. 66:1). In Latin the whole statement is expressed as follows: “Heaven is my seat.”

Who are these, except the righteous? What are the heavens, except the righteous? Those who are heaven are themselves heavens, because just as there are many Churches and yet one Church, so also there are many righteous and yet one heaven.

God sits in them, and God judges through them. It was not without reason that it was said, “The heavens declare the glory of God.” The apostles became heaven. How did they become heaven? Because they were justified.

Just as the sinner became earth, to whom it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19), so those who were justified became heaven. They carried God, and through them God flashed miracles, thundered terrors, and rained consolations.

They were indeed heaven, and they declared the glory of God. So that you may know that they themselves were called heaven, the same psalm says: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world” (Ps. 18:2, 5). You ask whose, and you will find: of the heavens.

If, then, heaven is God’s seat, and the apostles are heaven, they too became God’s seats; they are God’s throne. It is said elsewhere: “The soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom.”

A great thing, a great thing has been said: “The soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom.” That is, wisdom sits in the soul of the righteous as in its own seat, as in its own throne, and from there judges whatever it judges.

They were therefore thrones of wisdom, and for this reason the Lord said to them: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Thus they too will sit upon twelve seats, and they themselves are God’s seats; for it was said of them, “There the seats sat.”

“For there the seats sat.” Who sat? The seats. And what are the seats? Those of whom it was said, “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.”

What are the seats? The heavens. What are the heavens? Heaven. What is heaven? That of which the Lord says, “Heaven is my seat.”

Those righteous people themselves are seats, and they have seats; and in that Jerusalem the seats will sit. For what purpose? For judgment.

“You will sit,” he says, “upon twelve seats, you seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

Whom will they judge? Those below who are on earth. Who will judge? Those who became heaven.

Those who are judged will be divided into two parts: one will be on the right, the other on the left. The saints will judge with Christ. “For he will come into judgment with the elders of the people,” says Isaiah (Isa. 3:14).

There are therefore some who will judge with him, and others who will be judged by him and by those who will judge with him.

These, then, will be divided into two parts. One will be placed on the right, and the works of mercy that they performed will be enumerated for them. The other will be placed on the left, and its cruelty and lack of mercy will be enumerated.

To those placed on the right it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” Why? “I was hungry,” he says, “and you gave me food.”

And they will say: “When did we see you hungry?” And he will say: “When you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (Matt. 25:31–45).

What, then, brothers? Those will judge of whom it was said that friends should be made from the mammon of unrighteousness, “so that,” he says, “they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

The saints will sit with the Lord to consider those who performed acts of mercy, and they will take those separated to the right into the kingdom of heaven. This is the peace of Jerusalem.

What is the peace of Jerusalem? That bodily works of mercy should be joined to the spiritual works of preaching, and that there should be peace through giving and receiving.

For the apostle, who spoke of the account of giving and receiving, says that these alms are such an account (Phil. 4:15). He says: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your bodily things?” (1 Cor. 9:11).

And he says elsewhere concerning the same matter: “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little.” Why did the one who had much not have too much? Because what he had in excess he gave to the needy. And what does it mean that the one who had little did not have too little? Because he received from the one who had abundance, “so that,” he says, “there might be equality” (2 Cor. 8:15, 14).

This is the peace of which it is said, “Let there be peace within your strength.”

### 10. [verse 6]

For when he had said, “For there the seats sat for judgment,” he added, “seats over the house of David”—that is, over the family of Christ, to which they gave food at the proper time. Immediately, as though addressing those seats, he says: “Ask what makes for the peace of Jerusalem.”

O you seats, who now sit in order to judge and have become the seats of the judging Lord—for those who judge ask questions, and those who are judged are questioned—“Ask,” he says, “what makes for the peace of Jerusalem.”

What will they find by asking? That some performed acts of mercy and others did not. Those whom they find to have performed acts of mercy they will call to Jerusalem, because they are what makes for the peace of Jerusalem.

Love is a powerful thing, brothers; love is a powerful thing. Do you wish to see how powerful love is? Whoever, through some necessity, has not been able to fulfill what God commands should love the one who fulfills it, and fulfill it in that person.

Let your Charity pay attention. For example, he has a wife whom he cannot dismiss. He ought to obey the apostle, who says, “Let the husband render the wife her due”; and, “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release.”

He remembers that the life which the same apostle describes is better: “I wish that all were as I myself am” (1 Cor. 7:3, 27, 7). He looks at those who have done this, loves them, and fulfills in them what he cannot fulfill in himself.

Love is a powerful thing. It is our strength, because if we are not in love, whatever else we possess is of no benefit.

“If I speak in the tongues of human beings,” the apostle says, “and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.” He adds another great thing: “And if I distribute all my possessions, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:1, 3).

But if love alone exists, even when it finds nothing to distribute to the poor, let it love; let it give only a cup of cold water (Matt. 10:42). It will be credited with as much as Zacchaeus, who gave half his property to the poor (Luke 19:8).

Why is this so? He gave so little, that one gave so much, and yet it will be credited to him with as much? Certainly with as much. Their means were unequal, but their love was not unequal.

### 11.

They therefore ask questions; consider what you are. Behold, it has already been said to us, “We will go into the house of the Lord.” Certainly we rejoiced in those who said to us, “We will go into the house of the Lord.” See, then, whether we are going.

For we do not go with our feet, but with our affections. See whether we are going. Let each one of you ask himself what he is like toward a holy poor person, toward a needy brother, toward a needy beggar. Let him see whether his inward compassion is not cramped.

For the seats that will sit in judgment will question you, and they must find what makes for the peace of Jerusalem. How do they question? As the seats of God. God questions. If anything is hidden from God, can it escape those seats when they question?

“Ask what makes for the peace of Jerusalem.” But what makes for the peace of Jerusalem? “And abundance,” he says, “for those who love you.”

He turns his voice toward Jerusalem itself. There is abundance for those who love it. Abundance comes from poverty: here they are poor, there abundant; here weak, there strong; here needy, there rich.

How did they become rich? Because here they gave what they received from God for a time, and there they received what God will later repay eternally.

Here, my brothers, even the rich are poor. It is good for the rich person to recognize that he is poor. For if he thinks himself full, that is swelling, not fullness. Let him recognize that he is empty, so that he may be filled.

What does he have? Gold. What does he not yet have? Eternal life. Let him consider what he has and see what he does not have.

Brothers, from what he has, let him give, so that he may receive what he does not have; from what he has, let him purchase what he does not have.

“And abundance for those who love you.”

### 12. [verse 7]

“Let there be peace within your strength.”

O Jerusalem! O city that is built as a city, whose participation is in “the same thing”! Let there be peace within your strength; let there be peace within your love, because your strength is your love.

Hear the Song of Songs: “Love is strong as death” (Song of Songs 8:6).

A great saying, brothers: “Love is strong as death.” The strength of charity could not have been expressed more magnificently than by saying, “Love is strong as death.”

For who resists death, brothers? Let your Charity pay attention. Fire, waves, and the sword can be resisted; powers can be resisted; kings can be resisted. One death comes—who resists it? Nothing is stronger than it.

Therefore love is compared with its strength, and it was said, “Love is strong as death.”

And because love kills what we were, so that we may be what we were not, love brings about a kind of death in us. By this death was dead the one who said, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). By this death were dead those to whom he said, “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3).

“Love is strong as death.” If, then, it is strong, it is powerful and of great force; it is itself strength. Through it the weak are governed by the strong, earth by heaven, and the peoples by the seats. Therefore, “Let there be peace within your strength”; let there be peace within your love.

And through this strength, through this love, through this peace, “let there be abundance in your towers,” that is, in your heights.

For few will sit in judgment, but many, placed on the right, will make up the people of that city. Many will belong to each of the exalted ones, by whom they will be received into eternal dwellings; and there will be abundance in its towers.

The fullness of delights and sufficiency of riches is God himself, he himself who is “the same thing,” he himself whose city’s participation is in “the same thing.” He will also be our abundance.

But how? Through love, that is, through strength.

In whom is love, brothers? In the one who does not seek what is his own in this life (Phil. 2:4, 21).

Hear the apostle possessing love: “Please all people in all things, just as I also please all people in all things.”

Where, then, is what you said, “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1:10)? Now you say that you please people; now you urge them also to please people.

But he did not set the limit there, so that anyone might please for his own sake rather than for the sake of love. Whoever seeks his own glory does not seek the salvation of others. For he says: “Just as I also please all people in all things, not seeking what benefits me, but what benefits many, so that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10:32–33).

### 13. [verse 8]

Therefore here also, when he was speaking of love, he said: “For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors, I was speaking of peace concerning you.”

O Jerusalem, city whose participation is in “the same thing”! I am in this life and on this earth; I am poor, a stranger, and groaning, not yet enjoying your peace, but proclaiming your peace.

I do not proclaim it for my own sake, as the heretics do, who seek their own glory and say, “Peace be with you,” while they do not possess the peace that they preach to the peoples. For if they possessed peace, they would not tear apart unity.

“I,” he says, “was speaking of peace concerning you.” But why? “For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors”: not for the sake of my honor, not for the sake of my money, not for the sake of my life. For “to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”

“But I was speaking of peace concerning you, for the sake of my brothers and my neighbors.” For he himself longed to depart and to be with Christ; and to those whom he preached these things—his neighbors and brothers—he says, “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:21, 23–24).

“For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors, I was speaking—however—of peace concerning you.”

### 14. [verse 9]

“For the sake of the house of the Lord our God, I sought good things for you.”

I did not seek good things for my own sake. For if I had not sought them for you, I would have sought them for myself; and therefore I would not have had them either, because I would not have sought them for you.

But: “For the sake of the house of the Lord my God,” for the sake of the Church, for the sake of the saints, for the sake of strangers, for the sake of the needy, so that they may go up—for we say to them, “We will go into the house of the Lord”—“for the sake of the house of the Lord my God, I sought good things for you.”

These things, brothers, which are more extensive and necessary, gather, eat, and drink. Grow strong, run, and take hold.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 122

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

I have undertaken, together with Your Holiness, to consider in order the Songs of Ascents: of one who ascends and loves, and therefore ascends because he loves.

Every love either ascends or descends. For by a good desire we are lifted toward God, and by an evil desire we are hurled down to the depths.

But because we have already fallen through evil desire, there remains for us—if we recognize who did not fall to us but descended to us—to ascend by clinging to him, because we cannot do so by our own strength.

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself said, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

It seems that he spoke only about himself. Have the others therefore remained behind, since the one who descended is the only one who ascended? What should the others do? They must be joined to his body, so that there may be one Christ, who descended and ascended.

The head descended; he ascended with the body, clothed in his Church, which he presented to himself without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27).

Therefore he alone ascended. But we too, when we are with him in such a way that we are his members in him, are alone with him; and thus he is one, and always one. Unity joins us to the one.

Those alone do not ascend with him who do not wish to be one with him.

Now, since he who is placed in heaven, with his flesh raised up immortal—the flesh through which he was mortal for a time—and who suffers nothing in heaven from persecutions, nothing from malice and reproach, as he willingly endured everything for us on earth, nevertheless sympathizes with his body laboring on earth, he said, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

No one was touching him then, yet from heaven he cried out that he was suffering persecution. We must not be without hope; indeed, we should confidently presume that if through love he himself is with us on earth, through that same love we too are with him in heaven.

But we have explained how he himself is with us on earth: we have spoken of his voice sounding from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” Saul was not touching him at all, nor even seeing him.

How, then, is it shown that we too are with him in heaven? The apostle Paul himself says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:1–3).

Therefore he is still below, and we are already above: he is below through the compassion of love, and we are above through the hope of love. For “in hope we have been saved” (Rom. 8:24).

But because our hope is certain, although it is something that will happen in the future, it is spoken of us as though it had already happened.

Textual notes:

- [Col. 1621] The manuscripts read *instructurom* [an uncertain, apparently corrupt reading].
- [Col. 1622] Most manuscripts read: “to lead the mind’s gaze, to lead the weakness of the mind.” One Corbie manuscript reads *fortem* (“strong”) for “perhaps you do not yet possess contemplation.”
- [Col. 1623] The Amiens manuscript and most manuscripts read: “it stands; yet it participates in that very stability,” etc. Some manuscripts read “wills” (*voluntatibus*) for “pleasures”; several read “is variously affected and stretched out” (*diversatur atque distenditur*) for “is struck apart and torn asunder.”
- [Col. 1624] Erasmus: “If he had not gone down, and not …”; the Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions: “If he had not gone down, he would not …,” etc. One Corbie manuscript reads: “Among those same twelve tribes there were wicked people, there were good people. From the good tribes, which recognized [the Lord], etc.”
- [Col. 1624] Some manuscripts read “who is” for “that he is truly Israel.” Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain omit “God” in “Israel is seeing God.”
- [Col. 1625] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read “if someone were to say to him” for “someone would say to him.” The Louvain edition alone reads: “does not belong to Israel, who is not …,” etc. The Amiens, Erasmus, and manuscripts read “that there was grain” for “that there were grain.” Six manuscripts read “what he is not” for “what he himself is.”
- [Col. 1626] Here the manuscripts read “will sit” for “sat.”
- [Col. 1628] The manuscripts read “that is swelling,” while the editions read “that is fullness.”
- [Col. 1629] Some manuscripts read “he himself” for “she herself.” The manuscripts read “cannot seek” for “does not seek.” The particle *autem* (“however/indeed”), deleted by the Louvain edition, is restored from the other editions and manuscripts, especially because it appears in the Greek Septuagint.
- [Col. 1630] The editions read “did not wish” for “will not have wished.” The Amiens and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts read “with flesh raised up”; Louvain reads “subsists in flesh.”

## 2. [v. 1]

Let this singer, then, ascend; but let this man sing from each of your hearts [Note: [Col. 1630] Thus the manuscripts. Lov., however: “but let him sing in each of us,” etc.], and let each person be this man. For when each of you says that verse individually, since all of you are one in Christ, one man is saying it—not, “To you, Lord, we have lifted up our eyes,” but, “To you, Lord, I have lifted up my eyes.” You should indeed think that each one of you is speaking; but that one speaks above all who is also spread throughout the whole world. That one speaks who says elsewhere, “From the ends of the earth I cried out to you when my heart was in anguish” (Ps. 60:3). Who is it that cries from the ends of the earth? What one man is spread as far as the ends of the earth?

[Col. 1631] Each individual person can cry out in his own region; but from the ends of the earth? Yet Christ’s inheritance, of which it was said, “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8), itself cries out and says, “From the ends of the earth I cried out to you when my heart was in anguish.” Let our heart be in anguish, and let us cry out. What should cause our heart anguish? Not the things that even the wicked suffer here—for example, because they suffer loss. If your heart is anguished for that reason, it is merely ash. You have lost one of your loved ones in accordance with God’s will: if your heart is anguished for that reason, what is so remarkable? The hearts of unbelievers are anguished for this reason too; those who have not yet believed in Christ suffer these things as well.

What, then, causes the Christian’s heart anguish? That he does not yet live with Christ. What causes the Christian’s heart anguish? That he is living as an exile and longs for his homeland. If this is why your heart is anguished, then even if you are prosperous according to worldly standards, you groan; even if every good thing flows to you and the world smiles upon you from every side, you still groan, because you see that you have been placed in exile. You realize that you already possess happiness in the eyes of fools, but not yet according to Christ’s promise. Seeking that happiness, you groan; seeking it, you long for it; and by longing you ascend, and by ascending you sing the Song of Ascents. As you sing the Song of Ascents, you say, “I have lifted up my eyes to you, who dwell in heaven.”

## 3

As he was ascending, where would he lift his eyes except to the place toward which he was striving and where he desired to ascend? For he ascended from earth to heaven. Behold the earth below, which we tread with our feet; behold also heaven above, which we see with our eyes. As we ascend, we sing, “I have lifted up my eyes to you, who dwell in heaven.”

Where, then, are the stairs? We see such great distances between heaven and earth, such a great separation and such vast spaces. We want to ascend there, but we see no stairs. Are we perhaps deceiving ourselves because we sing the Song of Ascents, that is, the song of ascent? We ascend to heaven if we think upon God, who has made ascents in the heart.

What does it mean to ascend in the heart? To make progress toward God. Just as everyone who fails does not descend but falls, so everyone who makes progress ascends—but only if he progresses without becoming proud; if he ascends without falling. If, however, he becomes proud through progressing, he falls again through ascending.

What must he do, then, in order not to become proud? Let him lift his eyes to him who dwells in heaven; let him not attend to himself. For every proud person attends to himself, and the one who pleases himself seems great to himself. But the person who pleases himself pleases a foolish man, because he himself is foolish when he pleases himself. The only one who pleases securely is the person who pleases God.

And who is the person who pleases God? The one to whom God is pleasing. God cannot be displeasing to himself; let him also be pleasing to you, so that you may please him. But he cannot be pleasing to you unless you are displeasing to yourself. If you are displeasing to yourself, take your eyes off yourself. Why do you attend to yourself? If you truly attend to yourself, you find in yourself something that displeases you, and you say to God, “My sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5).

[Col. 1632] Let your sin be before you, so that it may not be before God; and do not be before yourself, so that you may be before God. For just as we want God not to turn his face away from us, so we want him to turn his face away from our sins. Both things are sung to him in the Psalms. “Do not turn your face away from me” (Ps. 26:9)—that is the voice of the psalm, and therefore it is our voice. And the one who says, “Do not turn your face away from me,” see what he says elsewhere: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Ps. 50:11).

If you want him to turn his face away from your sins, turn your own face away from yourself, and do not turn it away from your sins. For if you do not turn your face away from them, you yourself become angry with your sins. But if you do not turn your face away from your sins, you acknowledge them, and he forgives them.

## 4

Lift your eyes away from yourself to him, and say, “I have lifted up my eyes to you, who dwell in heaven.”

My brothers, if we understand “heaven” bodily, as that which we see with bodily eyes, we shall truly go astray, thinking that we cannot ascend there except by placing stairs or using some kind of machinery. But if we ascend spiritually, we must understand heaven spiritually. If ascent [Note: [Col. 1632] Thus Am. and the manuscripts. Er. and Lov. read: “if there is ascent.”] is in the affections, heaven is in righteousness.

What, then, is God’s heaven? All holy souls, all righteous souls. For even though the Apostles were in the flesh on earth, they were heaven, because the Lord, seated in them, walked throughout the whole world. Therefore he dwells in heaven.

How? As he says in another psalm: “But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel” (Ps. 21:4). He who dwells in heaven dwells in the holy place. What is the holy place but his temple? “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. 3:17).

But all who are still weak and walk by faith (2 Cor. 5:7) are God’s temple according to faith; one day they will also be God’s temple according to sight. For how long are they a temple according to faith? For as long as Christ dwells in them through faith, as the Apostle says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Eph. 3:17).

There are, however, already heavens in which God dwells according to sight: they see him face to face. They are all the holy Angels, all the holy Virtues, Powers, Thrones, Dominions, and that heavenly Jerusalem from which we groan as exiles and which we pray for in longing. God dwells there.

There this man has lifted his faith; there he has ascended in affection, through longing. And this very longing [Note: [Col. 1632] Several manuscripts read “by this very longing”; and below some have “to abandon the filth.”] makes the soul sweat out the filth of sins and be cleansed from every stain, so that it too may become heaven, because it has lifted its eyes to him who dwells in heaven.

For if we understand this bodily heaven, which we see with our eyes, to be God’s dwelling place, God’s dwelling place will pass away, because “heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. 24:35). Furthermore, before God made heaven and earth, where did he dwell?

But someone may say: “And before God made the saints, where did he dwell?” God dwelt in himself, dwelt with himself, and is with himself. When he deigns to dwell in the saints, the saints are not God’s house in such a way that, if that house were removed, God would fall. We dwell in a house in one way, and God dwells in the saints in another. You dwell in a house; if it is removed, you fall. But God dwells in the saints in such a way that, if he departs, they fall.

Therefore, whoever carries God in such a way as to be God’s temple should not think that he carries God in such a way that he [Col. 1633] could frighten God if he withdrew from him. Woe to him if God withdraws, because he himself falls; God, however, always remains in himself.

The things in which we dwell contain us; the ones in whom God dwells are contained by him. See, then, how great the difference is between our dwelling and God’s. Let the soul say, “I have lifted up my eyes to you, who dwell in heaven,” so that it may understand that God does not need heaven as a dwelling place; rather, heaven needs him in order to be inhabited by him.

## 5. [vv. 2–4]

What follows, then, since he has said, “I have lifted up my eyes to you, who dwell in heaven”? How have you lifted up your eyes? “As the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are toward the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.”

We are both servants and a maidservant; he is both master and mistress.

Or [Note: [Col. 1633] Lov. reads “but” (*at*); Mss. as printed.] what do these words mean? What do these comparisons involving things mean? Let your Charity attend for a little while. It is not surprising that we are servants and he is master; but it is surprising that we are a maidservant and he is mistress.

Yet neither is it surprising that we are a maidservant, for we are the Church; nor is it surprising that he is mistress, for he is the power and wisdom of God. Hear, then, the Apostle saying: “But we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block and to the Gentiles foolishness, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:23–24).

Thus the people may be servants and the Church a maidservant: Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. You have heard both: Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. Therefore, when you hear “Christ,” lift your eyes to the hands of your master; when you hear “the power of God and the wisdom of God,” lift your eyes to the hands of your mistress. For you are both servant and maidservant: servant because you are the people, maidservant because you are the Church.

That maidservant, however, has found great dignity with God: she has become a wife. But until she comes to those spiritual embraces where she may securely enjoy the one whom she has loved and for whom she has sighed during this long exile, she is a bride. She has received a great pledge—the blood of the bridegroom—and she securely sighs for him.

She is not told, “Do not love,” as a betrothed virgin who is not yet married is sometimes told. It is rightly said to her, “Do not love; when you have become a wife, then love,” because it is an untimely and disorderly desire, and not chaste, to love someone when one does not know whether one will marry him. It can happen that one man betroths her and another takes her as his wife.

But since no one else can be preferred to Christ, let her love securely. Before she is joined to him, let her love him; let her sigh for him from afar and from her distant exile. He alone will take her as his wife, because he alone gave such a pledge. For who can take her as his wife in such a way that he dies for the one he wishes to marry? If he wished to die for her, there would be no one to marry her. But he securely died for his bride, whom, rising again, he was going to take as his wife.

Nevertheless, brothers, for the present let us be as servants and a maidservant. It was indeed said, “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15). But perhaps the Lord said this only to the disciples? Hear the Apostle Paul saying: “[Col. 1634] Therefore you are no longer a servant but a son; and if a son, also an heir through God” (Gal. 4:7). He was speaking to the people; he was speaking to believers.

Therefore, now that we have been redeemed in the name of the Lord by his blood and washed in his bath, we are sons—we are sons—because, though we are many, we are one in him.

What, then, does it mean that we still speak as servants? Can we possess as much merit in the Church, although we have already become sons from servants, as the Apostle Paul himself possessed? Yet what does he say in his Epistle? “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus” (Rom. 1:1).

If he still calls himself a servant—the one through whom the Gospel was preached to us—how much more ought we to acknowledge our condition, so that his grace may be greater in us? First he made servants of those whom he redeemed. For that blood is the price for servants; for the bride it is a pledge.

Acknowledging our condition, then, let us say—although we are already sons by grace, we are nevertheless servants because we are creatures, since every creature serves God:

“As the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are toward the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.”

## 6

He also explained why, just as servants have their eyes toward the hands of their master and maidservants have their eyes toward the hands of their mistress, so, he says, our eyes are toward the Lord our God. And as though you were asking, “Why?” he says, “Until he has mercy on us.”

What kind of servants, then, brothers, did he intend us to understand—those who have their eyes toward the hands of their masters? And what kind of maidservants—those who have their eyes toward the hands of their mistress until their mistress has mercy on them?

Who are these servants and maidservants who have their eyes in the hands of their masters, unless they are those who are ordered to be beaten? “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.” How? “As the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are toward the hands of her mistress.”

Thus both the male servants and the maidservants wait until either the master or the mistress has mercy.

Suppose, then, that a master has ordered a servant to be beaten. The servant is flogged and feels the pain of the blows; he looks toward his master’s hands until the master says, “Spare him.” For by “hand” he means power.

What, then, are we to say, brothers? Our Lord has ordered us to be beaten, and our mistress, the wisdom of God, has ordered us to be beaten. In this life we are flogged, and this whole mortal life is our wound.

Hear the voice of the psalm: “Because of iniquity you disciplined man, and you made my soul waste away like a spider” (Ps. 38:12). Consider, brothers, how frail a spider is, so that it is shattered and dies at the slightest touch.

And lest we think that only our flesh is made weak by the infirmity of mortality, he did not say, “You made me waste away,” lest we understand it according to the flesh; rather he said, “You made my soul waste away like a spider.” For nothing is weaker than our soul when it is placed amid the temptations of the world, amid the groans and travail of troubles. Nothing is weaker than it until it clings to heavenly solidity and is in God’s temple [Note: [Col. 1634] Most manuscripts read “into God’s temple”], from which it no longer falls.

For at first, in order to come to this weakness and wasting away, it became weak like a spider and was expelled from paradise. Then the servant was ordered to be beaten.

[Col. 1635] My brothers, see from when we have been flogged. In all who have been born from the beginning of the human race, in all who exist now, and in all who will be born afterward, Adam is being flogged. Adam is being flogged—that is, the human race. And many have become so hardened [Note: [Col. 1635] Am., Er., and many manuscripts read “have hardened themselves.”] that they do not even feel their blows.

Those, however, who from that race have become sons have received a sense of pain. They feel that they are being flogged, and they know who ordered them to be flogged. They have lifted their eyes to him who dwells in heaven, and thus their eyes are toward the hands of their master until he has mercy on them, as the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters and as the eyes of a maidservant are toward the hands of her mistress.

You see some happy people in this world laughing and boasting of themselves; they are not being flogged. Indeed, they are being flogged worse: they are beaten more severely precisely because they have now lost their sense.

Let them awaken and be flogged; let them feel that they are being flogged, know that they are being flogged, and grieve because they are being flogged. For “whoever increases knowledge increases pain”: Scripture has said this (Eccl. 1:18). Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

## 7

We shall hear the voice of the man who is being flogged, and let these be the voices of each one of us even when things are going well for us. For who does not understand that he is being flogged when he is ill, when he is in prison, when he is perhaps in chains, when he suffers at the hands of robbers? When some wicked people inflict troubles upon him, he feels that he is being flogged [Note: [Col. 1635] In several Paris editions, after “he feels that he is being flogged,” there is added: “Great is the fear of Christ’s enemies, but like smoke their terror vanishes. For who would doubt that recently, as we heard from the brothers who were present, that Boethius, the condemned enemy barking against the Lord, was deservedly scourged? Yet he did not recognize the Lord’s scourging when he chose condemnation rather than concord.” These words are absent from the editions of Am., Er., and Lov., and from the manuscripts.].

It is a profound understanding to see that he is being flogged even when things are going well for him. For Scripture does not say in Job, “Human life abounds in temptations,” but says, “Is not human life a temptation upon the earth?” (Job 7:1). It called the whole of life a temptation.

Therefore your whole life on earth is your wounds. Weep as long as you live on earth. Whether you live prosperously or are placed in some tribulation, cry out, “I have lifted up my eyes to you, who dwell in heaven.”

To the hands of the Lord who ordered you to be beaten, to whom you say in another psalm, “Because of iniquity you disciplined man, and you made my soul waste away like a spider,” cry out to the hands of the one who is beating you and say, “Have mercy on us, Lord; have mercy on us.”

Are these not the voices of one being flogged: “Have mercy on us, Lord; have mercy on us”?

## 8

“Because we have been filled exceedingly with contempt.” Our soul has been filled to overflowing: “reproach to those who abound, and contempt to the proud.”

The one who is despised is held in contempt. All who wish to live piously according to Christ must suffer reproaches; they must be despised (2 Tim. 3:12) by those who do not wish to live piously, whose entire happiness is earthly.

Those who call happiness what they cannot see with their eyes are mocked, and it is said to them: “What do you believe, madman? Do you see what you believe? Has someone returned from the underworld and reported to you what [Col. 1636] is happening there? Behold, I see what I love, and I enjoy it” [Note: [Col. 1636] Thus Er., Lugd., Venet., and Lov. In B. “and” is lacking. M.].

You are despised because you hope for what you do not see; and the person who seems to possess what he sees despises you. Consider whether he really possesses it. Do not be troubled; see whether he possesses it, and do not let him insult you. Do not, while thinking him happy in the present, lose the true happiness that is to come. Do not be troubled; consider whether he possesses it.

What he possesses slips away from him, or he himself slips away from what he possesses. Necessarily either he passes through his possessions or his possessions pass through him. Through whom do his possessions pass? Through the one who will be shaken while alive [Note: [Col. 1636] Thus several manuscripts. Others, with Am. and Er., “who will have shaken them.” Lov. has “who will have gone through them, shaken.”].

Who passes through his possessions? The one who dies rich, because when he dies he does not carry them with him to the underworld.

“I have my own house,” he boasts. You ask, “Which house is yours?” “The one my father left me.” And where did he get that house? “Our grandfather left it to him.” Go back to the great-grandfather, then to the ancestor before him, and soon he can no longer name them [Note: [Col. 1636] Er.: “You will go back … you can.” Lugd. and Venet.: “You will go back … he can.” Lov.: “Go back … you can.” M.].

Are you not rather frightened by seeing many people pass through that house, none of whom carried it with him to his eternal home? Your father left it here; he passed through it. You too will pass through it.

If, then, your house has a passage through it, it is an inn for travelers [Note: [Col. 1636] The editions have “for those journeying”; the manuscripts, “for those passing through.”], not a dwelling for permanent residents.
