And yet, because we hope for what is to come, sigh for future happiness, and what we shall be has not yet appeared—although we are already sons of God (1 John 3:2), because our life is hidden with Christ in God—we have been filled with contempt, that is, with scorn, by those who seek or possess happiness in this world.

## 9

“Our soul has been filled to overflowing: reproach to those who abound, and contempt to the proud.”

We were asking who those are who abound; he explained it to you when he said, “the proud.” What is “reproach” is “contempt”; and what is “those who abound” is “the proud.” It is a repetition of the same thought: “reproach to those who abound, and contempt to the proud.”

Why do the proud abound? Because they wish to be happy here. What? When they too are miserable, do they abound? Perhaps, when they are miserable, they do not insult us.

Let your Charity attend. They perhaps insult when they are happy, when they boast in the pomp of their riches, when they boast in the inflated emptiness of false honors. Then they insult us and say, as it were: “Look, I am doing well; I enjoy present things. Let those who promise what they do not show withdraw from me. What I see I possess; what I see I enjoy. Let me prosper in this life.”

You should be more secure, because Christ has risen and taught you what he will give in the other life. Be certain that he will give it. But that man insults because he possesses. Endure the one who insults, and you will laugh at the one who groans. For a time will come when those very people will say, “These are the ones whom we once held in ridicule.”

These are the words of the Book of Wisdom, because Scripture has disclosed to us what those very people will say who now mock us and despise us, and by whom we have been filled with reproach and contempt: what words they will have then, when they are despised by the truth [Col. 1637].

For they will see those whom they had despised when mingled with them shining at the right hand, when what the Apostle said has come to pass in them: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4). And they will say:

“These are the ones whom we once held in ridicule and for a reproachful example. We foolishly considered their life madness and their end without honor. How have they been counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints?”

They will continue in that speech and add:

“Therefore we went astray from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise for us. What did pride profit us? And what did the boasting of riches bring us?” (Wis. 5:3–8).

There you will not insult them, because they themselves will already be insulting themselves.

Until this happens, brothers, let us lift our eyes to him who dwells in heaven. Let us not take our eyes from him until he has mercy on us and frees us from every temptation, reproach, and contempt.

## 10

Furthermore, sometimes even those who are under the scourge of temporal misfortune insult us. You find someone who, because of the merit of his sins, whether by God’s hidden judgment or by an evident condemnation, is sent to prison and carries a chain—and he himself insults us.

When he is told, “Why did you not live well? Behold where you have come by living badly,” he replies, “Why do those who live well suffer these things?”

But they suffer them in order to be tested, to be exercised by temptations, and to make progress through scourges, because “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). And if he scourged the Only-Begotten who was without sin and handed him over for all (Rom. 8:32), how ought we to be scourged, who have done the things for which we are scourged?

When we say these things, they still become proud of their misfortune. Though afflicted, they have not been humbled, and they reply:

“These are the words of vain Christians, who believe what they do not see.”

If [Note: Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read “but even” (*sed et*)] even these people insult us, what are we to think, brothers? Are they not included in this psalm when it says, “Reproach to those who abound, and contempt to the proud”? Christians are insulted even by those who do not abound; although they are in poverty and distress, they too do not cease insulting us.

Certainly, then, it says, “Reproach to those who abound.” Or perhaps no one is found who insults even when placed in calamity? Did the thief who was crucified with the crucified Lord not insult him? (Luke 23:39).

If those who do not abound also insult us, why does the psalm say, “Reproach to those who abound”? If we examine carefully, they too abound.

In what way do they abound? For unless they abounded, they would not be proud. One person abounds in money and is proud because of it; another abounds in honors and is proud because of them; another thinks that he abounds in righteousness and is proud because of it—which is worse.

Those who seem not to abound in money think that they abound in righteousness against God. Placed in calamities, they justify themselves and accuse God, saying, “What have I done, or what have I committed?”

And you say, “Look back; remember your sins, if you have done nothing.”

Their conscience is somewhat stirred, and they return to themselves and consider their evil deeds. Yet, even after considering their [Col. 1638] evil deeds, they do not wish to confess that they are suffering what they deserve. Instead they say:

“Behold, I have plainly done many things; but I see many who have done worse and suffer no evil.”

He is righteous against God. He too abounds: his breast is full of righteousness, since God seems to him to be doing evil, while he himself seems to suffer unjustly.

If you gave him a ship to steer, he would go down with it in a shipwreck. Yet he wants to drive God from the governance of the world and hold the helm of creation himself, distributing pains and joys, punishments and rewards to everyone.

Wretched soul—and why are you surprised? [Note: Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read: “And why are you surprised? A wretched soul abounds, but …”; the manuscripts differ.] It abounds, but it abounds in wickedness; it abounds in malice. And the more it seems to itself to abound in righteousness, the more it abounds in wickedness.

## 11

But a Christian ought not to abound; he ought to acknowledge himself as poor. And if he has riches, he should know that they are not true riches, so that he may desire other riches.

For the one who desires false riches does not seek the true ones. But the one who seeks the true riches is still poor, and rightly says, “I am poor and suffering” (Ps. 68:30).

Again, the one who is both poor and full of wickedness—how is he said to abound? Because he is displeased that he is poor, and righteousness itself seems to abound in his heart against God’s righteousness.

And what is the abundance of our righteousness? However much righteousness there may be in us, it is some sort of dew beside that fountain; compared with that great nourishment, it is a few drops that soften our life and loosen its harsh iniquity.

For now, let us desire to be nourished from the full fountain of righteousness; let us desire to be filled by that abundance of which the psalm says: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35:9).

While we are here, let us understand that we are needy and lacking—not only in these riches, which are not true riches, but also in salvation itself.

And when we are healthy, let us understand that we are infirm. For as long as this body hungers and thirsts, as long as it is wearied by keeping watch, by standing, by walking, by sitting, and by eating; wherever it turns for relief from weariness, there it finds another weariness.

Therefore even in the body there is not perfect health. These are not riches, then, but beggary, because the more they abound, the more poverty and greed increase. This is not bodily salvation, but weakness.

We are daily soothed [Note: [Col. 1638] The editions have “paragorizamur.” Several manuscripts have “panegorizamur”; others, “paregorizamur.” In a manuscript of Christinaeus, the gloss “that is, we are soothed” is added. They evidently derived the word from Greek *parēgorein* (παρηγορεῖν), “to console,” and physicians used *paregorizein* to mean “to mitigate, ease, and temper.” An anonymous physician quoted by V. C. Cangio in the *Glossary* says: “Paregorics are things that soothe, so that the illness does not increase; they do not heal.”] by God’s medicines, because we eat and drink. The things placed before us are themselves medicines.

Brothers, if you wish to see what sort of illness afflicts us, observe that the person who fasts for seven days is consumed by hunger. Therefore hunger is there; but you do not feel it because you treat it daily. Thus our health itself is not yet perfect.

## 12

Let your Charity attend to how we are to understand ourselves [Col. 1639] as needy, so that we may rejoice in him and lift our eyes to him who dwells in heaven.

These are not true riches; they increase the desire of those who possess them. This is not true bodily health, because a failing weakness is carried everywhere. Wherever it turns, it fails. In the very thing that offers assistance you will not find stability. It grows tired while standing and wants to sit; but will it last even while sitting? What it chose in order not to be tired is where it finds itself failing.

It has grown tired from keeping watch and is going to sleep. Does it not fail simply because it has slept? It has grown tired from fasting and is going to eat. If it eats too much, it fails because of that.

This weakness can persevere in nothing. What of righteousness? How much righteousness is there amid so many temptations? We can restrain ourselves from homicide, adultery, theft, perjury, and fraud. But can we restrain ourselves from wicked thoughts? Can we restrain ourselves from the suggestions of evil desires?

What, then, is our righteousness? Let us hunger and thirst for everything—for true riches, true health, and true righteousness.

What are the true riches? That heavenly dwelling in Jerusalem. For who is called rich in this world? When a rich man is praised, what is said? “He is very rich; he lacks nothing.” That is the certain praise of the one who praises him. But it is not true, when it is said, “He lacks nothing.”

Consider whether he lacks nothing. If he desires nothing, he lacks nothing. But if he still desires more than he has, riches have been added to him so that his poverty may increase.

In that city, however, there will be true riches, because there we shall lack nothing; we shall need nothing, and there will be true health.

What is true health? When death has been swallowed up in victory, and this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality (1 Cor. 15:53–54)—then there will be true health. Then there will also be true and perfect righteousness, so that we shall be able not only to do nothing evil but not even to think anything evil.

But for now, needy, poor, lacking, and suffering, we sigh, groan, pray, and lift our eyes to God. Those who are happy in this world despise us, because they abound; and those who are unhappy in this world despise us, because they too abound, and righteousness is in their hearts—but false righteousness.

Therefore they do not reach the true righteousness, because they have been filled with the false. But if you are to reach the true, be needy and a beggar for that righteousness itself, and hear the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6).

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 123

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1. [vv. 1–5]

You already know well, dearly beloved brothers, that the Song of Ascents is the song of our ascent, and that this ascent is accomplished not by the feet of the body but by the affections of the heart. We have often impressed this upon you. Nor should the same things be repeated too often, so that there may be room to say what has not yet been said.

This psalm, then, which you have just heard sung, is superscribed “A Song of Ascents.” That is its title.

Those who ascend sing [Note: [Col. 1639] Lov. reads “sing!” (*cantate*), against the other editions and the manuscripts]. Sometimes they sing as though [Col. 1640] one person were singing; sometimes as though many were singing. For the many are one, because there is unity; Christ too is one, and in Christ the members of Christ together with Christ make one, while the head of all these members is in heaven.

Even though the body suffers on earth, it has not been severed from its head. For the head looks down from above and cares for the body. If he did not care for it, he would not have said to that persecutor who was still Saul, not yet Paul, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

You know these things very well, and they are familiar to you. Yet they should not be recalled with annoyance to those who have not forgotten them, so that through their patience they may return to the hearts even of those who had forgotten them. For these things are health-giving and should be said again and again.

Whether one person sings or many sing, the many are one man, because there is unity; and Christ, as we have said, is one, and all Christians are members of Christ.

## 2.

What, then, do these people sing? What do these members of Christ sing? For they love, and they sing because they love; they sing because they desire. Sometimes they sing amid tribulation, and sometimes they sing in exultation, when they sing in hope. Our tribulation belongs to the present age, but our hope to the age to come; and unless the hope of the future age consoles us amid the tribulation of the present age, we perish.

Our joy, then, brothers, is not yet in possession but already in hope. Yet our hope is as certain as if the reality were already accomplished, for we do not fear while Truth is making the promise. Truth can neither be deceived nor deceive. It is good for us to cling to it; it sets us free, but only if we remain in its word.

For now we believe; then we shall see. While we believe, there is hope in this age; when we see, there will be possession in the age to come. “We shall see face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). We shall see face to face when we have purified hearts. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

But how are hearts purified except through faith, as Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Purifying their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9)? Our hearts are purified through faith so that they may become capable of receiving the vision. For now we walk by faith, not yet by sight, as the Apostle says: “As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord.” And what does “we are away from the Lord” mean? “For we walk by faith,” he says, “not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6–7).

Whoever is away from home and walks by faith is not yet in the homeland, but is already on the way. Whoever does not believe is neither in the homeland nor on the way. Let us therefore walk as though we were on the way, because the King of the homeland has himself become the way. The King of our homeland is the Lord Jesus Christ. There is truth there; here there is the way.

Where are we going? To the truth. By what way are we going? By faith. Where are we going? To Christ. By what way are we going? Through Christ. For he himself said: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

At another time he said to those who believed in him: “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples; and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free” (John 8:31–32). “You shall know,” he says, “the truth”—but only if you remain in my word. In what word? As the Apostle says: “This is the word of faith which we preach” (Rom. 10:8).

First, then, there is the word of faith. If we remain in this word of faith, we shall know the truth, and the truth shall set us free. Truth is immortal; truth is unchangeable. Truth is that Word of which it is said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

And who sees this except one whose heart has been purified? How are hearts purified? “And the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14). The Word that remains in itself is the truth to which we come and which sets us free. But the word of faith that is preached, in which the Lord wills us to remain so that we may know the truth—this is: “The Word became flesh, and dwelt among us.”

You believe in Christ born in the flesh, and you will reach Christ born of God, God with God.  
[Note: Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Lovaniensis read *crede* (“believe”); the other books read *credis* (“you believe”).]  
[Col. 1641]

## 3.

Those whom we read about sing in exultation; these exultant members of Christ sing this psalm.  
[Note: Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Lovaniensis read “the psalms which”; the manuscripts read “those whom.”] And who exults here except in hope, as I said? Let that hope itself be certain for us, and let us sing in exultation.  
[Note: So most manuscripts. The editions read: “And so that this hope may be certain for us, let us sing in exultation.”]

Those who sing are not strangers to us, nor is our voice absent from this psalm. Listen as though you were hearing yourselves; listen as though you were observing yourselves in the mirror of the Scriptures. When you look into the Scriptures as into a mirror, your face brightens. When you find yourself, in the exultation of hope, resembling certain members of Christ—those members who sang these words—you too will be among those members, and you will sing them.

Why, then, do these people sing in exultation? Because they have escaped. Their song, therefore, is grounded in hope. While we are here and away from home, we have not yet escaped. Certain members of that body of which we too are members have gone before us, and they can sing in possession of the reality.

The holy martyrs also sang this. They have already escaped and are in exultation with Christ, awaiting the reception of bodies already incorruptible—the very bodies that were previously corruptible and in which they suffered punishments. Those bodies will then become ornaments of righteousness for them.

Therefore, whether they are already in possession of the reality or we are still in hope, let us unite our affection with their crowns and desire such a life as we do not have here, but cannot have unless we desire it here. Let us all sing together and say: “If it had not been that the Lord was among us.”

They looked back upon certain tribulations that they had suffered and, now established in that place of blessedness and security, considered what they had passed through and to what they had come. Since it was difficult to be delivered from those things unless the hand of the deliverer had been present, they said joyfully: “If it had not been that the Lord was among us.”

Thus they began to sing. They had not yet said from what they had escaped; such was their exultation: “If it had not been that the Lord was among us.”

## 4.

Let Israel now say: “If it had not been that the Lord was among us.” Let it say this now, because it has already escaped. For this psalm sets before us those who are escaping—that is, those who have already escaped—for our contemplation.

Let us establish them and ourselves in our hearts as already triumphing; and let us imagine that we too are there, just as it was said in the preceding psalm: “Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem” (Ps. 121:2). They were not yet there, but were on the way. Yet such was the joy of those hurrying onward, and such their hope of arriving, that although they were still on the way and laboring, they already seemed to themselves established there.

So now let us place ourselves in that triumph which will occur in the age to come, when we shall taunt death, already ended and destroyed; when we shall say: “Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15:55). Then we shall be joined to the angels and exult with our King, who was willing to rise first, although he had not wished to die first.

Many died before him, but no one rose before him to eternal life. Exulting with him, established there already in hope and in heart because we have escaped, let us consider what we have escaped: what scandals, what tribulations of the world, what persecutions by all the pagans, what deceits of all the heretics, what suggestions of the devil, what conflicts of desires.

Who could escape all these things except because the Lord was among us? Let Israel now say—for Israel says this securely—“If it had not been that the Lord was among us.” When? “When people rose up against us.”

Do not be surprised, then: they were defeated, for they were human beings. But the Lord was among us; it was not a human being among us. Human beings rose up against us. Nevertheless, human beings would have crushed other human beings unless, in those human beings who could not be crushed, it had been not a human being but the Lord.

## 5.

Therefore: “If it had not been that the Lord was among us, when people rose up against us.”

What could people do to you, exulting and singing and securely holding eternal blessedness?  
[Note: Most manuscripts read: “You exult, sing, and securely hold.”] What could people rising up against you do to you, unless the Lord were among you? What could they do? Perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.

They would have swallowed us alive; they would not have killed us first and then swallowed us. O monstrous ones! O cruel ones! The Church does not swallow in this way. To Peter it was said: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13), not, “Swallow alive.”

How, then, does Peter—that is, the Church—kill and then eat? And how would those who rose up against us perhaps have swallowed us alive, except because the Lord was among us?

No one enters the body of the Church unless he has first been killed. What was, dies, so that what was not may come to be. Otherwise, one who is not killed and not eaten by the Church may belong to the number of the people visible to human eyes. But in the number of the people known to God—of whom the Apostle says, “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19)—he cannot belong unless he has been eaten, and he cannot be eaten unless he has first been killed.

A pagan comes, and idolatry still lives in him. He is to be grafted into the members of Christ. In order to be grafted in, he must be eaten; but he cannot be eaten by the Church unless he has first been killed. Let him renounce the world: then he is killed. Let him believe in God: then he is eaten.

How, then, would they have swallowed us alive, except because the Lord was among us? Many persecutors have risen up at various times, and they are not absent even now. They rise up individually, and sometimes swallow people alive—but those in whom the Lord is not.

That is why they first said: “If it had not been that the Lord was among us,” because many are swallowed in whom the Lord is not. These are the people who are swallowed alive: they know that something is evil, yet consent with their tongue.

Certain persecutors rose up and said to people: “Offer incense. If you do not, we shall kill you.” Those people loved this life, and the sweetness of this life held them. They did not love what God had promised more than what they saw on earth. They were commanded to believe what they did not yet see, whereas they saw what they loved.  
[Note: Some manuscripts read: “They believed what they did not yet see.”]

By holding more tightly to what they saw, they shut the Lord out of their hearts. And because the Lord was not in them, they were swallowed alive.

What does “they were swallowed alive” mean? It means that they offered incense to idols while knowing that an idol is nothing. For if they had thought an idol to be something, they would have been swallowed dead. But when they think that an idol is nothing, and know that all those things of the Gentiles are empty, they are alive; yet when they do what their persecutors desire, they are swallowed alive.

They are swallowed alive for this reason: the Lord is not in them. Those in whom the Lord is present are killed and yet do not die. Those who consent and live are swallowed alive; once swallowed, they die.

But those who suffered and did not yield to tribulations exult and say: “Let Israel say”—let it say this exultantly, let it say this securely—“If it had not been that the Lord was among us, when people rose up against us, they would perhaps have swallowed us alive.”

## 6.

“When their fury was enraged against us.”

You know, brothers, that in one of the preceding psalms, at the very beginning of the Songs of Ascents, someone who had begun to ascend asked for help against a deceitful tongue and said: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

At first, when someone begins to ascend and make progress, at the very outset of his ascent he suffers deceitful tongues—flattering tongues aimed at destruction and at evil persuasion: “What are you doing? Why are you doing this? Can one not live otherwise? Can God not be served otherwise? You alone want to be what others are not!”  
[Note: Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Lovaniensis read: “Can you not live otherwise? Can you not serve God otherwise?”]

And if you find others who are with you, what does that flattering and deceitful tongue say? “Look, they were able to do it; perhaps you will not be able. You will undertake it and fail. It would have been better not to begin than to begin and fail.”  
[Note: Erasmus and Lyon read “if you undertake”; Lovaniensis, “if you will undertake.”]

The deceitful tongue still flatters. If you persevere, the deceitful and flattering tongue is defeated; then it begins to rage openly. What flattered in order to deceive now threatens in order to terrify.

But if the Lord is in you and you have not abandoned Christ from your heart, just as you overcame deceitful tongues through “sharp arrows and desolating coals” (Ps. 119:2–4)—that is, through the words of God by which your heart was pierced, and through the examples of the righteous who were brought to life from the dead and made righteous from sinners, like coals that revive from death—so you will conquer these people when they now rage and threaten, because they were unable to deceive by flattering.

They were defeated when they flattered; let them also be defeated when they threaten. But how are they defeated except because the Lord was among us? It is clear that you did not conquer; the one who is in you conquered.

You carry such a commander, and are defeated? Is he not the one you carry who said, “I have conquered the world” (John 16:33)? Did he not conquer the devil by dying first, although he had always been above every creature, because he is the Word, God with God?

Why did he conquer except to teach you to fight against the devil? And yet, although you have been taught, unless the one who first conquered for you is in you, you are defeated.

“If it had not been that the Lord was among us, when people rose up against us, they would perhaps have swallowed us alive. When their fury was enraged against us”—now they are enraged, now they rage openly—“the water would perhaps have engulfed us.”

He calls sinful peoples “water,” and we shall see what sort of water this is in what follows. Whoever consented to them would have been covered by the water. He would have died the death of the Egyptians, and would not have crossed over in the manner of the Israelites.

You know, brothers, that the Israelite people crossed through the water, and that the same water covered the Egyptian people (Exod. 14:22–29). “The water,” he says, “would have engulfed us.”

## 7.

But what sort of water is this? It is a torrent. It flows with force, but it will pass away. Torrents are rivers that swell because of sudden rains. They have great force; whoever falls into one is swept away—but only if the Lord is not present. If the Lord is present, the person’s soul crosses the torrent.

The torrent still flows, but the souls of the martyrs have already crossed it. As long as this age runs on through birth and death, it is a torrent; persecutions come from this torrent.

From this torrent our first Head drank, of whom it was said in the psalm: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way” (Ps. 109:7). From the torrent—the water that signifies the persecuting people—he drank, the one who said to his disciples: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20:22).

“He shall drink from the torrent on the way.” What does “on the way he drank” mean? He drank while passing through; he did not cling to it. He drank on the way, for perhaps this was said of him: “He did not stand in the way of sinners” (Ps. 1:1). He drank while passing through.

And what was said afterward? “Therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. 109:7). “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head.”

Our Head has already been lifted up, because he drank from the torrent on the way; for our Lord suffered. If, then, our Head has already been lifted up, what does the body fear from the torrent? Without doubt, because the Head has been lifted up, the body too will say afterward: “Our soul has passed through the torrent.” Perhaps “our soul has passed through water without substance.”

Behold what sort of water he meant when he said: “The water would perhaps have engulfed us.” But what sort of water is water without substance? What does “without substance” mean?

## 8.

First, what does “Perhaps our soul has passed through” mean? How could the Latins express what the Greeks say, namely ἄρα (*ara*)? For the Greek manuscripts have ἄρα. It is a word expressing doubt. It has indeed been rendered by a word of doubt, namely “perhaps,” but that is not entirely the sense.

We can express it with a word that is less idiomatic Latin but suitable for your understanding. What the Punic speakers say, *iar*—not the word for “wood,” but the word they use when they are in doubt—the Greeks say ἄρα. The Latins can or commonly do say *putas*, “do you suppose,” when they speak in this way: “Do you suppose I have escaped this?”

If one says, “Perhaps I have escaped,” you see that it does not convey the same sound. But what I have mentioned, *putas*, is commonly said; it is not said in that way in Latin. I could say it while explaining this to you, for I often use words that are not Latin so that you may understand.

But in Scripture this could not be put in a form that was not Latin. Because Latin lacked an exact equivalent, another word was placed there that did not convey precisely the same sound.

Understand it, then, as saying: “Do you suppose our soul has passed through water without substance?” And why do they say, “Do you suppose”? Because the magnitude of the danger scarcely makes their escape believable. They endured great slaughter and were in great peril. They were pressed so hard that they almost consented alive, almost were swallowed alive.

Now, as they escape and are already secure, but remember the magnitude of the danger itself, they say: “Do you suppose our soul has passed through water without substance?”

## 9.

What is water without substance except the water of unsubstantial sins? Sins have no substance. They have want, not substance; poverty, not substance.

In this water without substance, the younger son lost all his substance. You know that the younger son went away to a foreign land and said to his father: “Give me the portion of the substance that falls to me.”

“What do you want? It is better kept with your father. It is yours, but you want to squander it; you want to go far away.”

“Give it to me—give it to me.” And he gave it to him. He went off into a distant country, living prodigally with prostitutes, and lost his entire substance. He was left in need and fed pigs; in his poverty he remembered his father’s riches (Luke 15:12–17).

Unless want had driven him, he would not have desired that fullness. Let everyone, then, consider his sins and see whether sins themselves have substance.

“Why has the sinner provoked God?” (Ps. 9:13). If you do not see your sin before committing it, at least consider it once you have committed it. The sweetness of this age may for a time sweeten your throat; afterward it will be turned into great bitterness.

Look: you sinned and made a profit. What does it mean that you made a profit? To make a profit, you offended God. To increase your money, faith was diminished and gold increased. What did you lose, and what did you gain? What you gained is called gold; what you lost is called faith. Compare faith with gold. If faith were for sale in the marketplace, would it have a price?

You think about your profits but do not think about your losses. You rejoice over the treasury but do not mourn over the heart. Something or other abounds in your treasury, but see what has been diminished in your heart.

When you open your treasury, you find coins that were not there. Good: you rejoice that something is there which was not there. Examine the treasury of your heart. Faith was there, and is not there. If you rejoice over the former, why do you not mourn over the latter? You have lost more than you gained.

Do you want to see what you have lost? It could not have been taken from you even by shipwreck. Sometimes people lose everything at sea and come out naked. Many suffered shipwreck with Paul (Acts 27:41). The lovers of this age suffered shipwreck and all came out naked. They lost what they had outside, and found the house of their hearts empty.

But Paul carried the patrimony of his faith in his heart. No waves and no storms could take it away. He came out naked, and he came out rich. We ought to seek riches of this kind.

“But I do not see them,” you say to me. Foolish soul, you do not see them with the eyes of your flesh. Have an eye of the heart, and you will see them.

“But you do not see faith.” Why do you see it in someone else? Why do you cry out when someone breaks faith with you, if you do not see it? Let someone break faith with you: you cry out. Do you want faith to be displayed to you, and then you see it? When you are asked to display it, do you not see it?

What you cry out that another does not have toward you, mourn that you do not have toward another. And see that the sin you commit is without substance.

What is acquired through sin appears to be substance. But even this is not acquired. The person who knows how to use gold has gold; the person who does not know how to use gold is possessed by it, not its possessor. Be masters of gold, not slaves of gold. God made gold, and he made you above gold. He made gold for your support, and he made you in his image.

See what is above you, and trample what is beneath you. What, then, have you acquired? Do you want to see how insubstantial the water is? Take with you to the underworld what you acquired. What will you do? You acquired gold and lost faith. After a few days you depart from this life. You cannot take with you the gold you acquired by losing faith. Your heart empty of faith goes out to punishment; whereas, if full of faith, it would go out to a crown.

Look: what you did is nothing, and for nothing you offended God. The water that engulfed you is without substance. “Why has the sinner provoked God?” “Let those who act wickedly be confounded in vain” (Ps. 24:4). For no one acts wickedly except in vain, but no one considers this.

## 10.

People go along and hear that familiar proverb, while the proverbs of God sleep within them.  
[Note: So Am. and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “They hear the word of God and the proverbs of God, and they sleep within them; they hear that familiar proverb and remain awake to it. What proverb? ‘What I hold is better than what I hope for.’”]

What proverb? “What I hold is better than what I hope for.”

O unhappy person, what do you hold? You say, “What I hold is better.” Hold it, then, so that you do not lose it, and say: “What I hold is better.”

But if you do not hold it, why do you not hold what you cannot lose? What, then, do you hold? Gold. Hold it, then. If you hold it, let it not be taken from you against your will.

But if you are dragged by your gold to where you do not wish to go, and the greater robber therefore seeks you because he has found a lesser robber; if the greater eagle therefore seeks you because you first seized the hare—the lesser creature was your prey, and you will be prey to a greater one.

People do not see these things in human affairs; they are blinded by such great desire. It is a terrible matter, brothers; those who consider it shudder.

The powerful seek the weaker and seek to crush him for no other reason than that he has something which can be taken from him. The powerful see him suffering oppression beneath them for no other reason than what he possesses, and they gather to themselves the very thing on account of which he suffers.

The powerful person did not consider this when he persecuted the other. The other fled, was tormented, was afraid, and sought somewhere to hide. Why would he suffer these evils unless he possessed something? Learn from him what you should flee. The thing that tormented him, while you pursued him so that it might not be taken from you, will likewise torment you when someone else pursues you.

You notice that he is wealthy. If you seek him because he is wealthy, beware of becoming wealthy, lest another seek you. Everything is done in vain. Seek the end. Darkness comes upon you. Ask why. Nothing answers.

## 11. [Verse 6]

Let those who say, “Our soul has passed through water without substance,” therefore exult and rejoice in the Lord, and let them receive their substance.

They lost it while living prodigally. But has the Father become poor? Let them return, and they will find there the riches they squandered in their distant wandering with prostitutes. Let them escape the water without substance and say:

“Blessed is the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth.”

For the persecutors were hunters, and they placed bait in a trap. What bait? The sweetness of this life, so that each person, because of the sweetness of this life, might thrust his head into wickedness and the trap might close.

Those in whom the Lord was present did not fall into the trap—those who say, “If it had not been that the Lord was among us.” Let the Lord be in you, and you too will not be caught in the trap. Cry out: “Blessed is the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth.”

## 12. [Verse 7]

“Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the trap of the hunters.”

Because the Lord was in the soul itself, the soul was rescued like a sparrow from the trap of the hunters. Why “like a sparrow”? Because it had fallen carelessly, like a sparrow, and afterward it could say: “God will forgive me.”  
[Note: Lovaniensis reads: “Forgive me, God.”]

O unstable sparrow, fix your feet instead upon the rock; do not go into the trap. You will be caught, consumed, crushed.  
[Note: Lovaniensis reads “you will be caught”; the manuscripts read “you will be captured.”]  
[Note: Lovaniensis reads “fix the feet of faith”; the other books omit “of faith.”]  
[Note: Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice read “you will be held”; the manuscripts read “you will be crushed.”]

Let the Lord be in you, and he will rescue you from greater threats, from the trap of the hunters. If you see a bird seemingly already falling into a trap, you make a greater noise so that it may fly out of the trap.

So also with the martyrs: perhaps some of them were already stretching their necks toward the sweetness of this life.  
[Note: Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Lovaniensis read “of the martyrs.”] The Lord who was in them made the noise of Gehenna, and the sparrow was rescued from the trap of the hunters. “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the trap of the hunters.”

And what then? Will that trap always remain? The sweetness of this life was the trap. They did not remain caught in the trap, and they were killed. Once they had been killed, the trap was broken. The sweetness of this life, by which they could be caught again, no longer remained; it had been crushed.

But was the sparrow also crushed? Certainly not, because it was not in the trap. The trap was crushed, and we were rescued.

## 13. [Verse 8]

Let them therefore cry out because they have been rescued. Let them fly to God; let them triumph in God because they have been rescued, since the Lord was in them so that they would not be caught in the trap.

Why was the trap crushed, and we rescued? Do you want to know why? “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

For if this help were not present, the trap would indeed not remain forever; but once the sparrow had been caught, it would be crushed. This life is passing away, and those who are caught by its sweetness and offend God through that sweetness will pass away with this life.

The trap will indeed be crushed; be certain of it. All the sweetness of this present life will cease, having fulfilled the appointed course of its place. But one must not cling to it, so that when the trap is crushed you may exult and say: “The trap was crushed, and we were rescued.”

But do not suppose that you can do this by your own strength. Consider whose work it is that you may be rescued—for if you become proud, you fall into the trap—and say: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”  
[Note: So most manuscripts. Some others read: “Consider; be devout, so that you may be rescued.” Am. reads: “Consider whose help it is, that you may be rescued.” Erasmus reads: “Consider whose help it is; be devout, so that you may be rescued.” Finally, Lovaniensis reads: “Flee to the help of him whose work it is that you may be rescued.”]  
[Col. 1648]

## 14.

The psalm has been expounded, and, insofar as the Lord has deigned to help us, I think it has been explained. You know very well that tomorrow we also owe a sermon to Your Charity. Be present and assist us with your prayers.

You ought to remember our promise. I would not say what I was going to discuss unless I wished to be helped by the zeal of your faith and prayers. You remember that I promised to treat what is said in the Gospel: “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

Heretics—especially the Manichaeans—are accustomed to criticize the Law and to say that God did not give it.  
[Note: The manuscripts read “heretics”; the editions read “all heretics.”] This passage must therefore be explained, so that it may be understood that God did give the Law and that the Law was given through Moses—but for a definite purpose, so that it would not save.  
[Note: Lovaniensis reads: “so that it might save us.” The other books disagree because of the following words.]

The Law did not save so that the Lawgiver himself might be desired as the Emperor who would grant pardon to sinners. The Law was indeed given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

I wished to direct your attention to this. The Lord’s mercy will be present—not because of our merits, but perhaps in proportion to the merit of your desire; not from our resources, but from the abundance of his gifts—so that this very necessary matter may be treated for people living under the new testament in such a way that the enemy may find no hiding place in which to conceal himself for the purpose of deceiving the faithful.

# Exposition of Psalm 124

## Sermon to the People

### 1. [Verses 1–2]

This psalm, belonging to the number of the Songs of Ascents—about whose title we have already said much in other sermons, and which we do not wish to repeat lest we weary you rather than instruct you—teaches us, as we ascend and raise our souls to the Lord our God through affection of love and devotion, not to look toward people who prosper in this age with a false, empty, and thoroughly deceptive happiness.

Such people nourish nothing but pride; their hearts grow cold against God and become hard against the rain of his grace, so that they bear no fruit. Presuming that they possess in abundance everything that appears necessary for this life—and even more than necessary—they are lifted up. Although through wickedness they are lower than all human beings, through pride they consider themselves higher than all human beings.

And if only they would at least consider themselves to be like other human beings. But sometimes, by looking at and paying too much attention to such people, even those who worship God waver and totter, as though the reward for worshiping God had perished. They see themselves in labors, poverty, misery, sickness, pain, or some necessity, while they see others enjoying bodily health, abounding in temporal goods, rejoicing in the safety of their families, and flourishing in the splendor of their possessions—people who not only do not worship God but oppose all human beings.

When they look at such people, they waver and say to themselves what is openly written in a certain psalm: “How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High? Behold, these are sinners, and those who abound in the world have obtained riches.”

And it continues: “Have I then purified my heart in vain, and washed my hands among the innocent? Was I perhaps foolish, who desired to live justly and conduct myself innocently among human beings, when I know that those who do not wish to preserve innocence possess such happiness and, through their wickedness, insult the righteous who are happy?”  
[Note: Augustine’s edition and the manuscripts read “through their wickednesses.”]

### 2.

But who said that there in the psalm? Someone whose heart was not yet right. For the psalm from which we have just quoted—not this one that we have now undertaken to examine and explain, but the one in which it is said, “How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High? Behold, these are sinners, and those who abound in the world have obtained riches. Have I then purified my heart in vain, and washed my hands among the innocent?”—that psalm, in which you see the soul in danger and the feet wavering, began in this way:

“How good God is to Israel, to those who are upright in heart! But as for me,” he says, “my feet were almost moved; my steps nearly slipped.” Why? “Because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72:1–13).

He therefore said that his feet had been moved and his steps almost slipped—a fall toward ruin away from God—because he had looked upon and examined the happiness of sinners and had seen that they possessed peace while he had toil.

But he told this after he had escaped, after he had clung to God with a corrected heart. He recounted his former dangers. “God is good to Israel”—but to whom? To those who are upright in heart.

Who are upright in heart? Those who do not criticize God. Who are upright in heart? Those who direct their will toward God’s will, rather than trying to bend God’s will toward their own.

The command is brief: a person must make his heart upright. Do you want to have an upright heart? Do what God wills; do not wish God to do what you will.

Those, then, who have perverse hearts—that is, those who do not have an upright heart—sit and argue about how God ought to have acted, not praising what he did but criticizing it. They want to correct him. It is not enough that they do not wish to be corrected by him; they say: “God should not have made the poor. Only the rich should have existed, and only they should live. Why was a poor person made? Why does he live?”

He criticizes the God of the poor.  
[Note: Most manuscripts read: “He criticizes the poor man’s God.” The Fossatensis manuscript reads: “He criticizes God in the poor man.”]

How much better it would be for him to be God’s poor man and rich through God—that is, to follow God’s will and recognize that his poverty is temporal and passing, while his spiritual riches would come in such a way that they could never pass away in any manner.

He would possess faith among the riches of his heart, even if he did not happen to possess gold in his treasury. If he had gold in his treasury, he would fear the thief, and even unwillingly he could lose the gold from his treasury. But he would not lose faith from his heart unless he himself expelled it from there.

The answer can quickly be given, beloved. God made the poor person in order to test a human being, and God made the rich person in order to test him by means of the poor person.  
[Note: Four manuscripts read: “in order to test him by means of the rich person.”]

Everything God made, he made rightly. And if we cannot see his purpose—why he made this in one way and that in another—it is good for us to submit to his wisdom and believe that he acted well, even if we do not yet know why he acted as he did.

Then we shall have an upright heart, so that we may presume upon and trust in the Lord; our feet will not be moved; and, as we ascend, there will be fulfilled in us the beginning of this psalm:

“Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; they shall not be moved forever.”  
[Note: Some books read “it shall not be moved,” though below they consistently agree with the others in reading “those who inhabit.”]

3. Who are these people? Those who dwell in Jerusalem: they who dwell in Jerusalem will not be shaken forever. If we understand this Jerusalem as the earthly city, all who dwelt there were driven out by wars and the city’s destruction; now you look for a Jew in the city of Jerusalem and do not find one. Why, then [Note: [Col. 1650] Three manuscripts have: “and do not find one. How then,” etc. Others have: “certainly then.”], will those who dwell in Jerusalem not be shaken forever, unless it is because there is another Jerusalem, about which you often hear much? She is our mother, for whom we sigh and groan in this pilgrimage, so that we may return to her. We had wandered from her [Note: [Col. 1650] Thus several manuscripts. But the editions have: “We had wandered from the way.”], and had no way; her King came and became the way for us, so that we might be able to return to her. She is the one where our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem, as you heard in the preceding Psalm of Ascents, which has already been expounded and discussed for those of you who were present: the Jerusalem for which the singer sighed, “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose fellowship is in unity” (Ps. CXXI, 2, 3).

Those, therefore, who dwell there will not be shaken forever. But those who dwelt in this earthly Jerusalem were shaken—first in heart, afterward in exile. When they were shaken in heart and fell, then they crucified the King of that heavenly Jerusalem. Already they were spiritually outside, and they were excluding that King himself outside. For they cast him outside his own city and crucified him outside (John XIX, 17, 18). And he himself cast them outside his city, that is, outside the eternal Jerusalem, the mother of us all, which is in heaven.

4. What sort of Jerusalem is this? He describes it briefly: “The mountains are round about her.” Is it some great thing that we are in that city around which mountains have been set? Is all our happiness simply that we shall have a city surrounded by mountains? Surely we know what mountains are—or what are mountains except elevations of the earth?

There are, therefore, other mountains: lovable, lofty mountains, preachers of the truth, whether Angels, Apostles, or Prophets. They are around Jerusalem; they surround it and, as it were, make a wall for it. Scripture speaks continually of these lovable and delightful mountains. Pay attention when you hear or read: in more places than we can mention you will find delightful mountains. Nevertheless, insofar as the Lord suggests it, it delights us to say many things about these mountains; and divine testimonies from the Holy Scriptures have come before us [Col. 1651] [Note: [Col. 1651] The editions have *occurrunt* (“come before us” in the present tense). The manuscripts have *occurrerunt* (“came before us”).].

They are the mountains illumined by God. They are illumined first, so that light may descend from them to the valleys or hills, since these are not as high as the mountains. They are the ones through whom Scripture is provided to us, whether in prophecy [Note: [Col. 1651] More manuscripts have “in the Prophets”; and shortly afterward most have “whether in the Apostles.” The editions have “whether in the Epistles.”], in the Apostles, or in the Gospel. They are the mountains of which we sing, “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me,” because in this life we have help from the Holy Scriptures.

But because those mountains do not protect themselves, nor advise us of themselves, our hope ought not to be in the mountains, lest we be accursed, since we place our hope in a human being (Jer. XVII, 5), he had already said, “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me”; and he added, “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. CXX, 1, 2).

They are the mountains of which he says again: “Let the mountains receive peace for your people, and the hills righteousness” (Ps. LXXI, 3). The mountains are great, and the hills smaller. The mountains, therefore, see; the hills believe. Those who see have received peace and have brought it to those who believe. For those who believe receive righteousness, because “the just person lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17). The Angels see, announce what they see, and we believe. That John: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1)—he saw and preached to us so that we might believe.

And through the mountains receiving peace, the hills received righteousness. For what does he say about those mountains? He did not say, “They have peace from themselves,” or “They establish peace,” or “They generate peace,” but “They receive peace.” From where do they receive peace? From the Lord. Therefore lift your eyes to the mountains because of peace, so that your help may be from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

Again, recalling those mountains, the Holy Spirit says: “You, wondrously illuminating from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. LXXV, 5). He did not say, “The mountains illuminate,” but “You, illuminating from the everlasting mountains”: through these mountains, which you wished to be everlasting as they preach the Gospel, you illuminate [Note: [Col. 1651] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition have *illuminas* (“you illuminate”). M.], not the mountains. Such, then, are the mountains around Jerusalem.

5. And so that you may know what sort of mountains are around her: whenever Scripture mentions good mountains—which it does very rarely and with great difficulty, or perhaps never without immediately naming the Lord or indicating him at the same time—it does so lest hope remain in the mountains.

Look at how many examples I have mentioned. “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me”; and lest you remain there, it says, “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” Again, “Let the mountains receive peace for your people”: when it says “receive,” it shows that the source of peace from which they receive it is elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1651] Thus most manuscripts. The editions have “another mountain.”]. Again, “Illuminating from the mountains”; but it says, “You”: “You, wondrously illuminating from the everlasting mountains.” Likewise here, after it had said, “The mountains are around her,” lest you again remain in the mountains, it immediately adds, “And the Lord is around his people,” so that your hope may not be in the mountains but in him who illumines the mountains.

For when he dwells in the mountains—that is, in the holy ones—he himself is around his people; and he himself fortified [Note: [Col. 1652] Louvain has *mutavit* (“changed”) instead of this reading; other editions and manuscripts have *muravit* (“fortified”).] his people with a spiritual defense, so that they might not be shaken forever.

But when Scripture speaks of those evil mountains, it does not add the Lord to them. We have often told you that such mountains signify certain great souls, but evil ones. Do not think, brothers, that heresies could have arisen through some small souls. Only great men made heresies—but insofar as they were great, they were evil mountains. They were not such mountains as would receive peace, so that the hills might receive [Note: [Col. 1652] In B. the word *susciperent* (“might receive”) is missing; we have restored it from Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition. M.] righteousness. Rather, they received dissension from the devil, their father.

When such mountains appear, beware lest you flee to them. People will come and say to you: “That man was a great man, and that man was a great man. What a man Donatus was! What a man Maximianus was [Note: [Col. 1652] Thus Ambrosianus and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain have *Maximinianus*. Compare *Expositions on Psalm 36*, sermon 2.]! And some Photinus—what a man he was [Note: [Col. 1652] In Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition: “And do you not know what sort of man Photinus was?” M.]! And what a man Arius was!”

I have named all these mountains, but they are mountains of shipwreck. You see that some flame of speech shines from them and that some fire is kindled from them. If you are sailing in a wooden vessel and suffering through the night—that is, through the darkness of this life—let them not deceive you, and do not steer your ship there. There are rocks there; great shipwrecks occur there.

When these mountains have been praised to you and someone begins persuading you to go to those mountains as though to a place of help and to rest there, answer: “I trust in the Lord. How can you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountains like a sparrow’?” (Ps. X, 2).

It is good for you to lift your eyes to those mountains from which your help may come from the Lord, so that you may escape like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters, rather than migrate to the mountains. A sparrow is an unstable creature: it is quickly moved and quickly flies here and there. But trust in the Lord, and you will be like Mount Zion; you will not be shaken forever, and you will not migrate to the mountains like a sparrow.

Did he name the mountains there in such a way as to speak of the Lord?

6. But love such mountains in which the Lord is. Yet those mountains themselves love you if you do not place your hope in them. See, brothers, what the mountains of God are. For they are named in this way elsewhere: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Ps. XXXV, 7). It does not say “their righteousness,” but “your righteousness.”

Hear of such a mountain, the Apostle: “That I may be found in him,” he says, “not having my own righteousness, which comes from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ” (Phil. III, 9). But those who wished to be mountains through their own righteousness, like certain Jews or the Pharisees who were their leaders, are rebuked in this way: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X, 3).

Those who are subject, however, are so lofty that they are humble. And because they are great, they are called mountains; but because they are subject to God, they are valleys. And because they have a capacity for piety, they receive an abundance of peace and send its flood onward to the hills.

Now, however, see which mountains you should love. If you wish to be loved by the good mountains, do not place your hope even in the good mountains. For what sort of mountain was Paul? When will such a one be found? We are speaking of the greatness of human beings. Can anyone of such great grace easily be found? And yet he feared lest that sparrow place its hope in him. And what does he say? “Was Paul crucified for you?” (I Cor. I, 13).

But lift your eyes to the mountains, from which help may come to you, because “I planted, Apollos watered”; but your help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth, “for God gave the increase” (ibid. III, 6).

Thus, the mountains are around her. But just as the mountains are around her, so also the Lord is around his people, from this time and forever. If, therefore, the mountains are around her, and the Lord is around his people, the Lord binds his people together in one bond of love and peace, so that those who trust in the Lord, like Mount Zion, will not be shaken forever. And this is what is meant by “from this time and forever” [Note: [Col. 1653] Most manuscripts omit: “And this is what is meant by ‘from this time and forever.’”].

7. [Verse 3.] “For the Lord will not leave the sinners’ rod over the portion of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity.”

For the present, the righteous suffer to some extent, and at times the unrighteous rule over the righteous. In what ways? Sometimes the unrighteous attain the honors of this world. When they have attained them and have become judges or kings—for God does this for the discipline of his people and for the discipline of his nation—it cannot but be that the honor due to their authority is shown to them.

For God so ordered his Church that every authority established in this world should receive honor, sometimes even from better people. But I will give one example; from this infer the degrees of all authorities.

The first and daily authority of one human being over another is that of a master over a slave. Almost all households have such authority. There are masters and there are slaves; the names are different, but “human beings” and “human beings” are equal names.

And what does the Apostle say, teaching slaves to be subject to their masters? “Slaves, obey your masters according to the flesh,” because there is a master according to the spirit. He is the true and eternal master; these others are temporary, according to time.

When you walk along the road, when you live in this life, Christ does not wish to make you proud. It happened that you became a Christian and had a human master; you did not become a Christian for that reason, so that you would disdain serving. For when, at Christ’s command, you serve a human being, you are not serving that person but the one who commanded you.

And this is what he says: “Obey your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in simplicity of heart; not serving merely for the eyes, as though pleasing human beings, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, with good will” (Eph. VI, 5, 6).

See: he did not make slaves free, but he made bad slaves good slaves. How much do the rich owe Christ, who arranges their household for them! If there was an unbelieving slave there, Christ converts him; but Christ does not say to him, “Leave your master. You have now come to know the one who is the true master. That man is perhaps impious and unjust, whereas you are now faithful and just. It is unworthy that a just and faithful person should serve an unjust and unfaithful one.”

He did not say this to him, but rather: “Slaves”—and, to strengthen the slave, he said, “Serve by my example; I first served the unjust.”

For the Lord, who endured so much in his Passion—whom did he endure it from, if not a master from slaves, and from whom if not bad slaves? If they had been good slaves, they would have honored their master. But because they were bad slaves, they inflicted insults on him.

What did he do in return? He gave love in exchange for hatred. For he said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34).

If the Lord of heaven and earth, through whom all things were made, served the unworthy, prayed for those raging and raging madly, and presented himself as a physician when he came—for physicians, both in their art and in their health, serve the sick—how much more ought a human being not disdain, with all his heart, with complete good will, and with complete love, to serve even a bad master?

See: the better person serves the worse, but only for a time. What I have said about master and slave, understand also about authorities and kings, about all the heights of this world.

Sometimes authorities are good and fear God; sometimes they do not fear God. Julian was an unbelieving emperor, an apostate, unjust, and an idolater. Christian soldiers served an unbelieving emperor; but whenever the matter concerned Christ, they recognized only him who was in heaven.

Whenever Julian wished them to worship idols and offer incense, they placed God before him. But when he said, “Draw up the battle line; go against that people,” they immediately obeyed. They distinguished the eternal master from the temporal master; and yet, because of the eternal master, they were subject even to the temporal master.

8. But will it always be this way, that the unrighteous rule over the righteous? It will not be so. See what this Psalm says: “For the Lord will not leave the sinners’ rod over the portion of the righteous.”

The sinners’ rod is felt for a time over the portion of the righteous; but it is not left there and will not remain forever. The time will come when the one God will be acknowledged; the time will come when Christ, appearing in his glory, will gather all nations before him and divide them as a shepherd divides goats from sheep. He will place the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left (Matt. XXV, 32, 33).

And there you will see many slaves among the sheep and many masters among the goats; and again, many masters among the sheep and many slaves among the goats. It is not because we have consoled slaves in this way that all slaves are good, nor because we have thus restrained the pride of masters that all masters are bad. There are good and faithful masters, and there are bad ones; there are good and faithful slaves, and there are bad ones.

But as long as good slaves serve bad masters, let them endure for a time: “For the Lord will not leave the sinners’ rod over the portion of the righteous.” Why is this? “Lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity”: so that the righteous may endure unrighteous rulers for a time and understand that this is not eternal, but prepare themselves to possess an eternal inheritance.

What inheritance? Where every dominion and every authority is destroyed, “so that God may be all in all” (I Cor. XV, 28). Keeping themselves for this, contemplating this in their hearts, and still retaining it in faith [Note: [Col. 1655] Louvain has “and retaining this in faith”; the other editions and the manuscripts disagree.], and enduring so that they may see it, they do not stretch out their hands to iniquity.

For if they see that the sinners’ rod is always over the portion of the righteous, they think to themselves and say: “What benefit is it to me that I am righteous? The unrighteous will always rule me, and I will always be a slave? Then I too will commit iniquity, since holding to righteousness brings no benefit.”

But lest he say this, faith is made known to him: the sinners’ rod can be over the portion of the righteous for a time. The Lord will not leave it over the portion of the righteous, so that the righteous may not stretch out their hands to iniquity, but hold their hands back from iniquity and endure iniquity rather than commit it. For it is better to endure injustice than to commit it.

Why, then, will it not be forever? Because “the Lord will not leave the sinners’ rod over the portion of the righteous.”

9. [Verses 4, 5.] Those who are upright in heart think this—those of whom I spoke shortly before, who follow the will of God rather than their own will. But those who wish to follow God make him go before them and themselves follow; they do not go before themselves and make him follow them. And in everything they find him good, whether correcting, consoling, exercising, crowning, purifying, or illuminating them, as the Apostle says: “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Rom. VIII, 28).

And therefore it follows: “Do good, Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart.”

10. Just as the upright in heart turns away from evil and does good (Ps. XXXVI, 27), because he is not jealous of sinners when he sees the peace of sinners (Ps. LXXII, 3), so the crooked in heart [Note: [Col. 1655] Erasmus and Louvain have: “Thus it is with the crooked in heart, who …” The word *est* (“is”) is not found in Ambrosianus or in the manuscripts; some, with Ambrosianus, have *pravicordius*, while others have *pravus corde* (“crooked in heart”).], who is scandalized by the ways of the Lord, turns away from God and does evil. He is enticed by the sweetness of the world, and, ensnared and captured by it, pays bitter penalties.

For the one who turns away from God, unwilling to endure his discipline, the false happiness of evil becomes, by God’s judgment, a true snare. Therefore he immediately adds: “But those who turn aside into strangulation the Lord will lead away [Note: [Col. 1655] Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and most manuscripts have “will lead into strangulation”; Louvain has “will lead away.” The Greek Septuagint has ἀπάξει (“will lead away”).] together with those who work iniquity”—that is, those whose deeds they imitated, because they loved their present joys and did not believe in their future punishments.

Those, then, who are upright in heart and do not turn aside—what will they have? Let us now come to the inheritance itself, brothers, because we are sons. What shall we possess? What is the inheritance? What is our homeland called? Peace.

Through this we greet you; this we announce to you; this is what the mountains receive, and the hills, righteousness (Ps. LXXI, 3). It is Christ himself. For “he is our peace, who made both one and broke down the middle wall of the dividing barrier” (Eph. II, 14).

Because we are sons, we shall have an inheritance. And what shall that inheritance itself be called, if not peace? And see that those who do not love peace have been disinherited; but those who divide unity do not love peace. Peace is the possession of the pious, the possession of heirs. And who are the heirs? Sons.

Hear the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matt. V, 9).

Hear also the conclusion of this Psalm: “Peace be upon Israel.” Israel means “seeing God”; Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” Let Your Charity understand: Israel is interpreted as “seeing God”; Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.”

Who will not be shaken forever? Those who dwell in Jerusalem. Those who dwell in the vision of peace, therefore, will not be shaken forever. “And peace be upon Israel.” Therefore Israel, which is “seeing God,” is seeing peace; and that same Israel is also Jerusalem, because that people of God is itself the city of God.

If, then, seeing peace means seeing God, God himself is rightly peace. Therefore, because Christ, the Son of God, is peace, he came to gather his own and separate them from the unrighteous.

Which unrighteous? Those who hate Jerusalem, who hate peace, who wish to tear unity apart, who do not believe in peace, who proclaim a false peace among the people and do not possess it.

To them it is answered when they say, “Peace be with you”: “And with your spirit.” They speak falsely and hear falsely. To whom do they say, “Peace be with you”? To those whom they separate from the peace of the whole world. And to whom is it said, “And with your spirit”? To those who embrace dissensions and hate peace [Note: [Col. 1656] These words, “who embrace dissensions and hate peace,” are absent from Ambrosianus and all the manuscripts, as is the word *enim* (“for”) in the following sentence.].

For if peace were in their spirit, would they not love unity and abandon dissension? Therefore, proclaiming falsely, they hear falsely. Let us proclaim the truth and hear the truth. Let us be Israel and embrace peace, because Jerusalem is the vision of peace, and we are Israel, and peace is upon Israel.

[Note: [Col. 1654] Thus Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts. Louvain has “that he may serve.” And, “to strengthen him”: several manuscripts have “he will serve in order to strengthen.”]

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM CXXV

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. [Verse 1.] As you already remember, in our orderly exposition this Psalm is the one hundred and twenty-fifth. It belongs among those Psalms whose title is “A Song of Ascents.” It is, as you know, the voice of those ascending. Where else, unless to that heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of us all, which is in heaven (Gal. IV, 26)?

That Jerusalem which is heavenly is also eternal; but this one which existed on earth possessed its shadow. Thus this one fell, while the other remains; this one completed the time of preaching, while the other holds the eternity of our restoration.

We are pilgrims away from it in this life and sigh for our return to it: we remain wretched and laboring until we return to it. Nor have our fellow citizens, the Angels, abandoned us in our pilgrimage; rather, they announced to us that the King himself would come to us.

And he came to us, and among us he was despised by us, and afterward he was with us [Note: [Col. 1656] The editions have “he was with us.” The word “was” is absent from the manuscripts.]. He taught us to be despised, because he was despised; he taught us to endure, because he endured; he taught us to suffer, because he suffered; and he promised that we would rise again, because he rose again, showing in himself what we ought to hope for.

If, then, brothers, the ancient Prophets, our fathers, before the Lord Jesus Christ came in the flesh, before he died, rose again, and ascended into heaven, nevertheless sighed for that city, how much ought we to desire it, since he himself has gone before us to it and has never departed from it?

For the Lord did not come to us in such a way as to abandon the Angels. He remained with them and came to us; he remained with them in majesty and came to us in the flesh.

But where were we? [Note: [Col. 1657] Here Erasmus and Louvain add after “where”: “our Redeemer is said to have come there, and we were held captive”; this is absent from Ambrosianus and the manuscripts. Before “where,” they have “there.”] If it is said that our Redeemer came because we were held captive, where were we held captive, so that he might come to redeem captives? Where were we held? Perhaps among barbarians? The devil and his angels are worse than barbarians. They previously held the human race; he redeemed us from them who gave his blood for us—not gold or silver, but his own blood.

2. But how had a human being entered captivity? Let us ask the Apostle Paul. For he especially groans in this captivity, sighing for the eternal Jerusalem; and he taught us to groan by that same Spirit with which he himself, filled with it, groaned.

For this is what he says: “Every creature groans together and suffers in labor pains until now.” And again: “The creature was subjected to futility,” he says, “not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope.”

By “every creature” he meant that even among human beings who do not yet believe, but nevertheless will believe, creation groans in its labors. Does it groan only in those who have not yet believed? [Note: [Col. 1657] In B. the word *gemit* (“groans”) is missing; we have restored it from Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition. M.] But in those who have believed, does creation no longer groan or suffer labor pains?

“Not only that,” he says, “but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit”—that is, we who already serve God in the Spirit, who already believe God with the mind and, in that very faith, have given certain first fruits so that we may follow our first fruits—“we ourselves groan inwardly, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body.”

He too, then, was groaning, and all the faithful groan as they await adoption, the redemption of their body. Where do they groan? In this mortality. What redemption do they await? The redemption of their body, which has already occurred in the Lord, who rose from the dead and ascended into heaven.

Before this is given to us, it is necessary that we groan—even as faithful people, even as those who hope. Therefore he continues there and says, after saying, “We ourselves groan inwardly, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body,” as though someone were to say to him: “What benefit, then, has Christ brought you, if you still groan? How has the Savior saved you? Whoever groans is still sick.”

He added and said: “For in hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. VIII, 20–25).

See why we groan and how we groan: because what we hope for we are indeed already awaiting, but we do not yet possess; and until we possess it, we sigh in time, because we desire what we do not yet possess.

Why? Because “in hope we were saved.” The flesh taken from us in the Lord has already been saved—not in hope, but in reality. Our flesh has risen and ascended, saved in our Head; in the members it is still to be saved. Let the members rejoice securely, because they have not been abandoned by their Head.

For he said to his suffering members: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

Thus it happened that we were turned toward God. We had no hope except in the world, and therefore were wretched servants—and doubly wretched, because we had placed our hope in this life [Note: [Col. 1658] Ambrosianus and almost all the manuscripts omit “we had placed our hope.”] and had our face turned toward the world, our back toward God.

But when the Lord turns us around, so that we now begin to have our face toward God and our back toward the world, although we are still on the road, nevertheless we look toward our homeland. And whenever we perhaps suffer some tribulation, yet hold to the way and are carried by the wood, the wind is harsh, but the wind is favorable [Note: [Col. 1658] Thus Erasmus and several manuscripts. Other books have “it is our wind.”]; with labor indeed, but it quickly leads us and quickly brings us there.

Because, then, we were groaning over our captivity—and those who have already believed also groan—let us ask the Apostle Paul himself how we became captives. We had forgotten, but Scripture reminds us. For he says: “We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. VII, 14).

See from where we became captives: because we were sold under sin. Who sold us? We ourselves, who consented to the deceiver. We were able to sell ourselves, but we cannot redeem ourselves. We sold ourselves by consenting to sin; we are redeemed through faith in righteousness.

For innocent blood was given for us so that we might be redeemed.
