[Note: [Col. 1658] Erasmus and Louvain have: “Not whatever blood.” The word “not” is absent from Ambrosianus and the manuscripts.] Whatever blood he shed while persecuting the righteous—what sort of blood did he shed? He shed the blood of the righteous: the blood of the Prophets, our fathers, the righteous, and the martyrs. Yet all of them came from the stock of sin.

He shed the blood of one who was not justified but born righteous. When that blood was shed, he lost those whom he held. For those on whose behalf innocent blood was given were redeemed; and, turned from captivity, they sing this Psalm.

3. “When the Lord turned the captivity of Zion, we became as those who are comforted” [Note: [Col. 1658] Thus the Floriacensis manuscript here. The editions have “when the Lord has turned.”].

This means: “We became joyful.” When? “When the Lord turned the captivity of Zion.”

Which Zion? That same Jerusalem, the eternal Zion. How is Zion eternal, and how is Zion captive? It is eternal in the Angels and captive in human beings. For not all the citizens of that city are captives; those who are pilgrims away from it are the captives.

A human being is a citizen of Jerusalem, but, sold under sin, has become a pilgrim. From its stock the human race was born, and the captivity of Zion filled the earth [Note: [Col. 1658] Several manuscripts have “in captivity.” Some, with Erasmus, have “of Zion’s captivity.” Shortly afterward most manuscripts have “and this captive Zion.” “How, then, is this shadow …” The Noviomensis manuscript omits “and this captivity of Zion.”].

And how is this captivity of Zion a shadow of that Jerusalem? The shadow of that Zion, which the Jews received in image and figure, was in captivity in Babylonia; and after seventy years that people returned to its city (Jer. XXIX, 10; and I Esd. I).

The seventy years signify the whole period that revolves through seven days. When the whole period has passed, then we too return to our homeland, just as that people returned from Babylonian captivity after seventy years.

For this world is Babylon: Babylon is interpreted as “Confusion.” See whether the whole of human life is not confusion. Whenever people come to understand what they are doing in their vain hope, they are ashamed. Why do they labor? For whom do they labor? “For my children,” one says. And they themselves, for whom? “For their children.” And those, for whom? “For their children.” No one, then, is for himself.

From this confusion, therefore, they had already turned, to whom the Apostle says: “What glory did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI, 21).

This whole life of human affairs, insofar as it does not belong to God, is therefore confusion. In this confusion, in this Babylon, Zion is held captive; but the Lord turned the captivity of Zion.

4. “And we became,” he says, “as those who are comforted”—that is, we rejoiced, as though receiving consolation.

There is consolation only for the wretched; there is consolation only for those who groan and mourn. Why “as those who are comforted,” unless because we still groan? We groan in reality and are comforted in hope. When reality has passed [Note: [Col. 1659] Thus all the manuscripts. The editions have: “We groan in hope and are comforted in reality; when hope has passed.”], joy will come from groaning—eternal joy, where consolation will not be necessary, because no misery will wound us.

But why does he say “as those who are comforted,” rather than simply “comforted”? This word is not always used to indicate likeness. For when we say “as,” it sometimes refers to a reality and sometimes to a likeness. Here it refers to a reality.

Examples must also be given from ordinary human speech, so that this may be easily understood. When we say, “As the father lived, so also did the son,” we say this by way of likeness. And, “As an animal dies, so a human being dies”: this too is said by way of likeness.

But when we say, “He acted as a good man,” is he not a good man, but merely like a good man? “He acted as a righteous man”: this “as” does not deny that he is righteous, but shows his true character.

“You acted as a senator.” If someone says, “Then I am not a senator,” the reply is: “Rather, because you are one, you acted as a senator; and because you are righteous, you acted as a righteous person; and because you are good, you acted as a good person.”

Therefore, because these people truly were comforted, they rejoiced as those who are comforted. That is, their joy was great, like that of people who have been comforted by the one who died—the one who comforts those who are going to die.

For all of us groan when dying. He who died comforted us so that we would not fear dying. He rose first, so that we would have something to hope for. Because he rose first, he gave us hope. Because we are placed in misery, we have been comforted in hope; hence comes great joy.

And the Lord turned our captivity, so that now, after captivity, we may hold to the way and go to our homeland. Now that we have been redeemed, let us not fear our enemies lying in wait along the way.

For he redeemed us so that the enemy would not dare lie in wait for us, provided we do not depart from the way. Christ himself became the way (John XIV, 6).

Do you wish not to suffer from robbers? He says to you: “I have laid out the way for you to your homeland; do not depart from the way. I have fortified such a way that the robber does not dare approach you. Do not depart from it, and the robber will not dare approach you.”

Walk, then, in Christ and sing with joy; sing as one who is comforted, because he has gone before you—the one who commanded you to follow.

5. [verse 2, 3.] Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation. How is the mouth that we have in the body filled with joy? It is not ordinarily filled except with food, drink, or something of that kind put into the mouth. Sometimes our mouth is filled—and what we say to Your Holiness is more than this: when we have our mouth full, we cannot speak. But we have another mouth within, that is, in the heart, from which whatever proceeds—if it is evil, defiles us; if it is good, cleanses us.

You heard about this very mouth when the Gospel was being read. The Jews were insulting the Lord because His disciples ate without washing their hands. Those who possessed outward cleanliness but were inwardly full of stains were insulting Him; those whose righteousness existed only in the eyes of men were insulting Him. But the Lord was seeking our inward cleanliness, and if that is present, it is necessary that outward things also be clean. “Cleanse,” He says, “the things that are within, and the things that are without will be clean” (Matt. 23:26). The Lord Himself says elsewhere: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

But from where does almsgiving proceed? From the heart. For if you stretch out your hand but do not show mercy in your heart, you have done nothing; but if you show mercy in your heart, even if you have nothing to extend with your hand, God accepts your almsgiving.

Those wicked men, however, sought cleanliness outwardly. Among them was also that Pharisee who had invited the Lord, when a woman who was a sinner and notorious in the city approached; she washed the Lord’s feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment. The Pharisee who had invited the Lord, possessing cleanliness only outwardly in his body but inwardly full of iniquity and greed, said to himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would know what sort of woman is touching his feet.” How did he know whether the Lord knew or did not know? He judged that He did not know for this reason: He had not driven her away. If such a woman had approached the Pharisee himself, he who maintained cleanliness, as it were, in the flesh, would have blown her away, driven her off, and rejected her, lest the unclean touch the clean and contaminate his cleanliness.

Because the Lord did not do this, the Pharisee believed that He did not know what sort of woman had approached His feet. But the Lord knew not only her; He also heard the Pharisee’s thoughts. For even if bodily contact accomplishes something—O unclean Pharisee, could the Lord’s flesh be defiled by the woman’s contact, or could the woman be cleansed by contact with the Lord? The physician allowed the sick woman to touch the medicine; and she who had come knew the physician. She who had perhaps been brazen in her fornication became still more bold for the sake of salvation. She burst into a house where she had not been invited; but she had wounds, and she had come to the place where the physician was reclining.

The man who had invited the physician, however, considered himself well; for that reason he was not being healed. You know what follows in the Gospel: how the Pharisee himself was put to shame when the Lord showed him that He knew both the woman and the Pharisee’s thoughts (Luke 7:36–50).

6. But let us return to what has just been read from the Gospel, which concerns the present verse, where it says: “Our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation.” For we are asking which mouth and which tongue these are. Let Your Charity pay attention.

The Lord was insulted because His disciples ate without washing their hands. The Lord answered them as was fitting, and, calling the crowds, said: “Hear and understand, all of you. Whatever enters into the mouth does not defile a person, but what comes out.” What does this mean? When He said, “Whatever enters into the mouth,” He clearly meant the bodily mouth. Food enters it, and food does not defile people, because “all things are clean to the clean,” and “every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4:4).

Certain things had been set forth figuratively for the Jews and were called unclean (Lev. 11). But after the Light Himself came, the shadows were removed. We are not held to the letter but made alive in the spirit; and the yoke of observance imposed upon the Jews was not imposed upon Christians, because the Lord said: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30). The Apostle also says: “All things are clean to the clean; but to the unclean and unbelieving nothing is clean, but both their mind and their conscience are defiled” (Titus 1:15).

What did he mean? To a clean person both bread and pork are clean; to an unclean person neither bread nor pork is clean. “To the unclean and unbelieving,” he says, “nothing is clean.” Why is nothing clean? “Because,” he says, “both their mind and their conscience are defiled.” For if what is within is unclean, nothing outward can be clean. If, then, those whose inward parts are unclean cannot have clean outward things, cleanse what is within if you want what is outward to be clean.

There is the mouth that will be filled with joy for you, even when you are silent. For when you are silent and rejoice, your mouth cries out to God. But consider what your joy is about. If you rejoice in the world, you cry out to God with an unclean joy. But if you rejoice in redemption, as this psalm says, “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became joyful,” then your mouth is truly filled with joy and your tongue with exultation. It is clear that you rejoice in hope, and your joy is acceptable to God.

In that joy, or in that mouth which we have within, we both eat and drink: just as we eat through this mouth for the nourishment of the body, so through that mouth for the nourishment of the heart. Hence: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6).

7. But if only what comes out of the mouth makes a person unclean, and when we hear this in the Gospel we understand only the bodily mouth, it would be absurd and extremely foolish to think that a person is not made unclean when he eats, but is made unclean when he vomits. The Lord says: “Not what enters into the mouth, but what comes out, defiles.” When you eat, then, you do not become unclean, but when you vomit, you become unclean? When you drink, you are not unclean, but when you spit, you are unclean? When you spit, something comes out of your mouth; when you drink, something enters your mouth.

What, then, did the Lord mean by saying, “Not what enters into the mouth, but what comes out, defiles”? In the same passage, according to another evangelist, He went on to say what the things are that proceed from the mouth, so that you might understand that He was speaking not of the bodily mouth but of the mouth of the heart. For He says: “From the heart come evil thoughts, fornications, murders, blasphemies; these are the things that defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person” (Matt. 15:1–20; and Mark 7:5–23).

How, then, do those things come out of the mouth, my brothers, unless they come out of the heart, as the Lord Himself says? For they do not defile us only when we speak them. Let no one say: “When we speak, they come out of our mouth, because words and sounds come out of our mouth; and when we speak evil, we become unclean.” What if someone does not speak but merely thinks evil? Is he clean because nothing has proceeded from the mouth of his body? But God has already heard what came from the mouth of his heart.

Look carefully, my brothers, at what I am saying. I mention theft. I have just mentioned theft. Did theft defile me merely because I mentioned theft? Behold, it came out of my mouth, and it did not make me unclean. But a thief rises at night, says nothing with his mouth, and becomes unclean by what he does. He not only says nothing; he suppresses the crime in complete silence, and is so afraid that his voice will be heard that he does not even want his footsteps to make a sound. Is he therefore clean because he is so silent?

I say more, my brothers. Behold, he is still lying in his bed; he has not yet risen to commit the theft. He is awake and waiting for people to fall asleep. Already he cries out to God; already he is a thief; already he is unclean; already the crime has proceeded from the inner mouth. When does the crime proceed from the mouth? When the will to commit it is resolved. You have decided to do it; you have spoken; you have done it.

If you do not commit the theft outwardly, perhaps the person from whom you intended to take something did not deserve to lose it. He lost nothing, yet you will be condemned for theft. You decided to kill a person; you said in your heart, and murder sounded from your inner mouth. The person is still alive, yet you are punished as a murderer. What you are before God is at issue, not what has not yet appeared before human beings.

8. Certainly, then, we know—and must know and hold fast—that there is a mouth of the heart, and there is also a tongue of the heart. That mouth itself is filled with joy. With that mouth within we pray to God when our lips are closed and our conscience is open. There is silence, yet the breast cries out. To whose ears? Not to a human being’s, but to God’s.

So be secure: He hears who has mercy. And again, when no human being hears evil things, if they proceed from your mouth [Note: [Col. 1662] Seven manuscripts read, “from your heart”], do not be secure, because He hears who condemns.

Susanna was not heard [Note: [Col. 1662] Several manuscripts read: “Susanna was being judged.” More manuscripts omit the negation: “Susanna was heard.”] by the unjust judges; she was silent and prayed. Her mouth was not heard by human beings, but her heart cried out to God (Dan. 13:35ff.). Did she fail to deserve to be heard merely because her voice did not proceed from the mouth of her body? She was heard; when she prayed, no human being knew.

Therefore, brothers, consider what we have in our inner mouth. See to it that you say nothing evil there, and you will do nothing evil outwardly; for nothing can be done outwardly by a person except what has first been spoken inwardly. Guard the mouth of your heart from evil, and you will be innocent. The tongue of your body will be innocent; your hands will be innocent; your feet will also be innocent; your eyes will be innocent; your ears will be innocent [Note: [Col. 1663] In B., after “your eyes will be innocent,” the word “will be” is lacking; after “your ears,” the words “will be innocent” are omitted. We have followed Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions, and M.]. All your members will serve righteousness, because a righteous commander has taken possession of your heart.

9. “Then they will say among the nations: ‘The Lord has done great things for them.’ The Lord has done great things for us; we have become joyful.”

See, brothers, whether Zion is not now saying this among the nations, throughout the whole world. See whether people are not running to the Church. Throughout the whole world our price is received; “Amen” is answered.

Thus the captive Jerusalemites, the Jerusalemites who are going to return [Note: [Col. 1663] Four manuscripts read, “redeemed”], the pilgrims sighing for their homeland, say among the nations: “The Lord has done great things for us; we have become joyful.” Did they themselves do this for themselves? They did evil to themselves, because they sold themselves under sin. The Redeemer came and did good to them; “the Lord has done great things for them.” “The Lord has done great things for us; we have become joyful.”

10. [verse 4.] “Turn back our captivity, O Lord, like a torrent in the south.” Let Your Charity pay attention to what this means.

He had already said: “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion.” He seemed to be speaking of the past. But it is customary for a prophet, while speaking of the past, to announce the future. For he seemed to be speaking of the past when, in another psalm, he said: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 21:17). He did not say, “They will pierce”; he did not say, “They will count”; he did not say, “They will divide my garments among themselves”; he did not say, “They will cast lots for my garment.” These things were future, yet they were sung as though they had already happened. For everything that is future is already accomplished for God.

Here, therefore, when he said, “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became as those who are comforted; then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation,” to show that under the figure of the past he was thinking of the future, he said: “Then they will say among the nations.” “They will say”—this is already future. “The Lord has done great things for us; we have become joyful” [Note: [Col. 1663] Erasmus and Louvain add here, “in the past”; this is absent from the other books.]. When these words were being sung, they referred to the future; now they appear to be present.

Therefore he who sang of the future as though it were past prays as though speaking of future things: “Turn back our captivity, O Lord.” The captivity had not yet been turned back, because the Redeemer had not yet come. Thus, when the psalms were sung, what was then being prayed for has now been accomplished: “Turn back our captivity, O Lord, like a torrent in the south” [Col. 1664]—as torrents are made to flow in the south, so turn back our captivity.

What this means was being sought, but now, with the Lord’s help and through your prayers, it will become clear. In one passage Scripture, when it was commanding and exhorting people concerning good works, says: “As ice in fair weather, so your sins will be dissolved” (Ecclus. 3:17). Our sins, then, were binding us. How? As cold binds water so that it cannot flow. Bound by the cold of sins, we froze.

But the south wind is warm. When the south wind arises, the ice melts and the torrents are filled. Torrents are winter streams; filled by sudden waters, they flow with great force. We had therefore frozen in captivity; our sins were constricting us. The south wind, the Holy Spirit, blew; our sins were forgiven, and we were released from the cold of iniquity. Like ice in fair weather, our sins are dissolved. Let us run toward our homeland like torrents in the south.

For a long time we have labored, and we continue to labor even while doing good. The human life into which we have entered is wretched, full of labors, sorrows, dangers, hardships, and temptations. Do not let yourselves be deceived by the joy of human affairs; recognize what in human affairs must be mourned.

Could the child who is born have laughed first? Why does he begin to live with crying? He does not yet know how to laugh; why does he already know how to cry? Because he has begun to enter this life. But if he is one of those captives, here he weeps and groans; joy will come.

11. [verse 5.] For what follows is: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy.” In this life, which is full of tears, let us sow. What shall we sow? Good works. Works of mercy are our seeds. Concerning these seeds the Apostle says: “In doing good, let us not grow weary; for in due season we shall reap, if we do not faint. Therefore, while we have opportunity, let us do good to all, and especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Gal. 6:8–10).

Speaking of almsgiving itself, what does he say? “I say this: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Cor. 9:6). Therefore, he who sows abundantly will reap abundantly; he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and he who sows nothing will reap nothing.

Why do you desire broad estates where you may sow many seeds? You have no broader place in which to sow than Christ, who wished to be sown in Himself. Your field is the Church; sow as much as you can.

“But I have little with which to do it.” Do you have the will? Just as what you have would be nothing if good will were absent, so, because you have nothing, do not be sad if you possess good will. What are you sowing? Mercy. What will you reap? Peace.

Did the angels say, “Peace on earth to rich people”? No: “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

There was great willingness in Zacchaeus, great charity in Zacchaeus. He received the Lord into his house and received Him joyfully; he promised to give half his possessions to the poor and to restore fourfold anything he had taken from anyone (Luke 19:6, 8), so that you may understand that he kept half for himself not in order to have something to possess, but in order to have something from which to repay his debts.

Great was his willingness; he gave much and sowed much. Did that widow who put in two small coins sow little? On the contrary, she sowed as much as Zacchaeus. Her means were smaller, but her willingness was equal (Luke 21:1–4). She put in two small coins with as great a willingness as Zacchaeus gave half his possessions. If you consider what they gave, you will find them different; if you consider from what they gave, you will find them equal. She gave everything she had, and he gave what he had.

12. Suppose someone does not even have two coins. Is there something less valuable that we can sow in order to reap that harvest? There is. “Whoever gives a disciple a cup of cold water will not lose his reward.” A cup of cold water does not cost two coins; it costs nothing. Yet sometimes it costs nothing in such a way that one person has it and another does not. If, then, the one who has it gives it to the one who does not, he has given as much—if he gives what he gives out of complete charity—as that widow gave in two small coins, as Zacchaeus gave in half his possessions.

He did not add “cold” without reason, for he wanted to indicate poverty. That is why He said, “a cup of cold water,” so that no one might even make the excuse that he had no wood with which to heat the water. “Whoever gives a cup of cold water to one of the least will not lose his reward” (Mark 9:40; and Matt. 10:42).

But what if someone does not even have this? Let him be secure, even if he does not have this: “Peace on earth to people of good will.” Let him fear only having something and not doing it. For if he has something and does not do it, he has frozen inwardly; his sins have not yet been dissolved like a torrent in the south, because his will is cold.

What do the great good things we possess amount to? Let a fervent will be added, already released by the warmth of the south wind; even if a person has nothing, everything is credited to him.

How much do beggars provide for themselves? Let Your Charity pay attention to how almsgiving takes place. Certainly, those to whom you give alms are beggars; they are in need. You perhaps attend to your brothers if they lack something; if Christ is in you, you give even to strangers.

But if those who make a profession of begging are beggars, they too possess, amid their hardship, something with which they may assist one another. God has not deprived them of the means by which they may be tested, since they perform acts of charity. This man cannot walk; the one who can walk lends his feet to the lame. The one who sees lends his eyes to the blind. The young and healthy lend their strength to an old or sick person and carry him. One is needy; the other is rich.

13. Sometimes a rich person is also found to be poor, and a poor person provides him with something. Someone—I do not know who—comes to a river, all the more delicate because he is wealthy, and cannot cross. If he crossed with his limbs uncovered, he would become cold, fall ill, and die. A poor man, more physically practiced, approaches and carries the rich man across; he performs an act of charity for the rich man.

Therefore, do not think only those who have no money are poor. See each person as poor in whatever he is poor, because perhaps you are rich in what he is poor in, and you have something with which to assist him. Perhaps you lend him your limbs, and that is more than if you lent him money.

He needs counsel; you are full of counsel. In counsel he is poor, and you are rich. Behold, you neither labor nor lose anything: you give counsel, and you have performed an act of charity. [Col. 1666]

Now, my brothers, while we are speaking, you are like poor people coming to us; and because God has deigned to give to us, we give from what He has given us to you. And we all receive from Him who alone is rich.

Thus the body of Christ is held together; thus its associated members are joined and united in charity and in the bond of peace, when each person provides what he has to one who does not have it [Note: [Col. 1666] The Ambrosian and Erasmus editions, and most manuscripts, read: “when each person provides what he has to one who does not have it.”]. In what he has, he is rich; in what the other does not have, he is poor. Love one another in this way; cherish one another in this way. Do not attend only to yourselves; attend also to those in need around you.

But because these things are accomplished with labors and hardships in this life, do not grow weary. You sow in tears; you will reap in joy.

For what, my brothers? When the farmer goes out with the plow and carries seed, is the wind not sometimes cold, and does rain not deter him? He looks at the sky, sees that it is gloomy, trembles with cold, and nevertheless goes out and sows. For he fears that, if he observes the gloomy day and waits for a bright one, the season may pass and he may find nothing to reap.

Do not delay, my brothers. Sow in winter; sow good works even while you weep, because “those who sow in tears will reap in joy.” They send forth their seeds: good will and good works.

14. [verse 6.] “Going, they went and wept, scattering their seeds.” Why did they weep? Because they were among the miserable, and they themselves were miserable.

It is better, my brothers, that no one be miserable than that you should perform an act of mercy. For whoever wishes people to be miserable so that he may perform an act of mercy has a cruel mercy. It would be as though a physician, in order to practice his art, wished there to be many sick people: that would be cruel medicine.

It is better that all be healthy than that the physician’s art be exercised. It is better, then, that all should reign in blessedness in that homeland than that there should be people toward whom mercy must be shown.

Nevertheless, as long as there are people to whom mercy must be shown, let us not grow weary in this hardship of scattering our seeds. Even if we sow with weeping, we will still reap with joy. For in that resurrection of the dead each person will receive his sheaves, that is, the fruit of his seed, the crown of joys and exultation.

Then there will be the triumph of those who rejoice and mock death itself, over which they groaned. Then they will say to death: “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Cor. 15:55).

But why are they already rejoicing? Because they are carrying their sheaves. Because “going, they went and wept, scattering their seeds.” Why were they scattering their seeds? Because “those who sow in tears will reap in joy.”

15. By this psalm we have especially exhorted you to perform acts of mercy, because by this path one ascends; and you see that the one who sings the Song of Ascents is ascending. Remember this. Do not love descending and not ascending; think about ascent, because the man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho fell among thieves. He would not have gone down, and he would not have fallen among thieves [Note: [Col. 1666] Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions read: “If he had not gone down, he would not have fallen,” and so forth. M.].

Adam has already descended and fallen among thieves; for we are all Adam. But a priest passed by and despised him; a Levite passed by and despised him, because the Law could not heal. A certain Samaritan passed by—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ. For they said to Him: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” He did not say, “I am not a Samaritan”; rather, He said: “I do not have a demon” (John 8:48–49).

“Samaritan” is interpreted as “Guardian.” If He had said, “I am not a Samaritan,” He would have said, “I am not a guardian.” And who else would guard us?

Then, setting forth the parable: “The Samaritan passed by and showed mercy to him,” as you know. He was lying wounded on the road because he had descended. The Samaritan did not despise us as he passed by. He healed us, lifted us onto his beast, in his flesh [Note: [Col. 1667] So read the Ambrosian and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts. The Louvain edition reads: “that is, into his flesh.”], and brought us to the inn, that is, to the Church. He entrusted us to the innkeeper, that is, to the Apostle. He gave two denarii for our healing: the love of God and the love of neighbor. For on these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:37–40).

He said to the innkeeper: “If you spend anything more, when I return I will repay you” (Luke 10:30–37). The Apostle spent more, because although all the Apostles were permitted to receive support from Christ’s provincials as Christ’s soldiers, he labored with his own hands and gave his provisions to the provincials (1 Cor. 4:12; 1 Thess. 2:7, 9; and 2 Thess. 3:8–9).

Everything has been accomplished. If we have descended and been wounded, let us ascend, sing, and make progress, so that we may arrive.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 126

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. [verse 1.] Among all the songs bearing the title “Song of Ascents,” this psalm received something more in its title: the addition “of Solomon.” For it is headed in this way: “A Song of Ascents, of Solomon.”

Thus this unusual title, unlike the others, has made us attentive, so that we may ask why “of Solomon” was added. What the “Song of Ascents” is need not often be repeated, for much has already been said about it: it is the voice of one ascending in the affection of piety and charity toward that heavenly Jerusalem for which we sigh as long as we are pilgrims, and in which we will rejoice when we have returned from pilgrimage.

Everyone who makes progress ascends to it; everyone who falls away falls from it. Do not seek to ascend with your feet, nor think that you descend with your feet. By loving God, you ascend; by loving the world, you fall.

These, then, are songs of lovers, burning with a holy desire. Those who sing them from the heart are aflame; their burning heart is also found in their conduct, in good behavior, in works according to God’s commandments, in contempt for temporal things, and in love for eternal things.

But why “of Solomon” was added, I will say to Your Charity as far as the Lord inspires me.

2. In his own time Solomon was the son of David, that great man through whom the Holy Spirit produced many holy commandments, salutary admonitions, and divine mysteries in the divine Scriptures. For Solomon himself was a lover of women and was rejected by God. So great was the snare of that desire for him that he was even compelled by women to sacrifice to idols, as Scripture testifies concerning him [Col. 1668] (1 Kings 11).

But if, when he fell, what was spoken through him were erased, it would be judged that he himself had spoken those things, rather than that they had been spoken through him. Therefore, God’s mercy and His Spirit acted most fittingly in this also: whatever good was said through Solomon would be attributed to God, while the man’s sin would be attributed to the man.

What is surprising about Solomon’s falling among God’s people? Did Adam not fall in paradise? Did an angel not fall from heaven and become the devil? We are therefore taught to place our hope in no human being.

Since this Solomon had also built a temple for the Lord (1 Kings 6), in a type and figure of the future Church and the Lord’s body—hence He says in the Gospel, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19)—since he himself had built that temple, the true Solomon, our Lord Jesus Christ, the true peacemaker, built a temple for Himself.

For the name Solomon is interpreted as “Peaceful” or “Peacemaker.” He is the true peacemaker of whom the Apostle says: “For He Himself is our peace, who made both one.” He is the true peacemaker who joined together in Himself the two walls coming from opposite directions, making Himself the cornerstone: the people coming from the circumcision of believers and the people coming from the uncircumcision of the Gentiles who also believe. He made one Church from the two peoples and became their cornerstone (Eph. 2:14–22); therefore He is truly the peacemaker.

Because the true Solomon was this one, while that Solomon—the son of David by Bathsheba (2 Sam. 12:24), king of Israel—was a figure of this peacemaker when he built the temple, Scripture, lest you think that the one who built a house for God was the Solomon in question, showed you another Solomon and began the psalm in this way: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.”

The Lord, then, builds the house; the Lord Jesus Christ builds His house. Many labor in building, but unless He builds, “those who build it labor in vain.”

Who are those who labor in building? All who preach the word of God in the Church, the ministers of God’s sacraments. We all run, we all labor, and we are all building now; before us others ran, labored, and built. But unless the Lord builds the house, “those who build it labor in vain.”

For this reason, when the Apostles saw certain people falling, Paul said specifically: “You observe days, months, seasons, and years. I fear for you, lest somehow I have labored among you in vain” (Gal. 4:10–11) [Note: [Col. 1668] The manuscripts read this way. The editions lack “for you,” and below have “that I may have labored in you.”]. Because he knew that he himself was being built inwardly by the Lord, he mourned for these people, since he had labored among them in vain.

We speak outwardly; He builds inwardly. We notice how you hear, but only He knows what you are thinking, who sees your thoughts. He builds; He admonishes; He terrifies; He opens the understanding; He directs your mind toward faith. Yet we too labor as workers. But unless the Lord builds the house, “those who build it labor in vain.”

3. This house is also the city of God. For the house of God is the people of God, because the house of God is the temple of God. And what does the Apostle say? “For the temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). All the faithful, then, are the house of God—not only those who exist now, but also those who lived before us and have already fallen asleep, and those who will exist after us, including those who still have to be born into human affairs until the end of the age.

Countless faithful are gathered into one, though numbered by the Lord. Of them the Apostle says: “The Lord knows those who are His” (2 Tim. 2:19). They are the grains that now groan among the chaff, destined to become one mass when the threshing floor has been winnowed at the end (Matt. 3:12).

The entire number of the holy faithful, who are to be changed from human beings so as to become equal to the angels of God, together with the angels themselves, who are not now pilgrims but await us when we return from pilgrimage—all of them together constitute one house of God and one city. That city is Jerusalem.

It has guardians. Just as it has builders laboring so that it may be built, so it also has those who guard it. For guarding is what the Apostle refers to when he says: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds should be corrupted from the purity that is in Christ” (2 Cor. 11:3). He was guarding; he was a guardian [Note: [Col. 1669] Some manuscripts read this way. Others omit “he was a guardian”; in its place the editions have “he was cautious.”]. He watched over them, as far as he could, over those placed under his authority.

Bishops do this as well. For this reason a higher place has been established for bishops, so that they may oversee and, as it were, guard the people. Indeed, the Greek term *episkopos* is interpreted in Latin as *superintentor*, “overseer,” because he oversees and sees from above.

Just as a higher place is made for a vinedresser so that he may guard the vineyard, so a higher place has been made for bishops. From this elevated place, however, a dangerous account is demanded unless we stand here with such a disposition of heart that, through humility, we are beneath your feet and pray for you, so that He who knows your minds may Himself guard you.

We can see you entering and leaving; but we cannot see what you are thinking in your hearts, and indeed we cannot even see what you do in your homes. How, then, do we guard you? As human beings do, as far as we can and as far as we have received the ability.

And because we guard as human beings and cannot guard perfectly, will you therefore remain without a guardian? Far from it. For where is He of whom it is said: “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it labors in vain”?

We labor in guarding, but our labor is vain unless He guards who sees your thoughts. He guards you when you are awake; He guards you also when you are asleep [Note: [Col. 1669] Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions read, “when you sleep.”]. For He slept on the cross once and rose; now He does not sleep. “Be Israel,” because He does not sleep or slumber who guards Israel (Ps. 120:4).

Come, brothers: if we wish to be guarded under the shadow of God’s wings, let us be Israel [Note: [Col. 1669] These words, “let us be Israel,” are absent from the Ambrosian manuscript and from the other manuscripts; nor do they seem necessary if the preceding sentence is understood to refer to what is stated shortly afterward, namely, “let us be humble.”].

We guard you by the duty of our administration, but we wish to be guarded together with you. As your shepherds, we are under that Shepherd; together with you we are sheep. From this place we are your teachers, but under that one Teacher, in this school, we are fellow disciples with you.

### 4. [Verse 2]

If we wish to be guarded by him who was humbled for our sake and exalted in order to guard us, let us be humble. Let no one claim anything for himself. No one possesses anything good unless he has received it from him who alone is good. Whoever wishes to claim wisdom for himself is a fool. Let him be humble, so that wisdom may come and enlighten him. But if, before wisdom comes into him, he thinks himself wise, he rises before the light and walks in darkness.

And what does he hear in this psalm? “It is in vain for you to rise before the light.” What does “It is in vain for you to rise before the light” mean? If you rise before the light rises, you must remain in vanity, because you will be in darkness. Our light, Christ, has risen. It is good for you to rise after Christ; do not rise before Christ.

Who are those who rise before Christ? Those who wish to place themselves before Christ. And who are those who wish to place themselves before Christ? Those who wish to be exalted here, where he was humble. Therefore, let them be humble here if they wish to be exalted there, where Christ is exalted.

For he says concerning those who had clung to him by faith—and we too are among them, if we believe in him with a pure heart: “Father,” he says, “those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). A great gift, a great grace, a great promise, my brothers! And who would not wish to be with Christ where Christ is?

But Christ is now exalted. Do you wish to be where he is exalted? Be humble where he was humble. Therefore that very light says to them: “The disciple is not above the teacher, nor the servant above his lord” (Matthew 10:24). Those who wished to be disciples above their teacher, and servants above their lord, wished to rise before the light; they went in vain because they did not go after the light.

To them, then, this psalm says: “It is in vain for you to rise before the light.” Such were the sons of Zebedee. Before they were humbled in accordance with the Lord’s passion, they were already choosing places for themselves where they might sit—one at his right hand and the other at his left. They wished to rise before the light; therefore they went in vain.

When the Lord heard this, he recalled them to humility and said to them: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matthew 20:21–22). “I came to be humble, and you wish to be exalted before me? Where I go, follow,” he says. For if you wish to go by a way where I do not go, then “it is in vain for you to rise before the light.”

Peter too had risen before the light when he wished to give the Lord counsel, so that he would not suffer for us. The Lord had spoken of his passion, through which we were to be saved—of that very humility; for he suffered humbly. When, therefore, he spoke of his future passion, Peter, who shortly before had called him the Son of God, was terrified. He feared that he would die and said to him: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you” (Matthew 16:21–23). He wished to rise before the light and give counsel to the light. But what did the Lord do? He made him rise after the light: “Get behind me, Satan” (ibid.). You are called Satan for this reason: you wish to rise before the light. “Get behind me,” so that I may go before you and you may follow. Go by the way I go; do not wish to lead me along the way you want to take.

### 5

Therefore, to those who wished to rise before the light, the psalm says: “It is in vain for you to rise before the light.” And when shall we rise? When we have been humbled: “Rise after you have sat down.”

Rising signifies exaltation; sitting signifies humility. In some passages, sitting is understood as the honor of judging; in others, it displays humility.

How is sitting an honor of judging? “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

How is sitting a sign of humility? At the sixth hour, the Lord, weary, sat beside the well (John 4:6). The Lord’s weariness was the Lord’s weakness—the weakness of power, the weakness of wisdom. But that very weakness was humility. Therefore, since he sat because of weakness, that sitting signifies humility.

And that very sitting of his—that is, his humility—made us safe, because “what is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Corinthians 1:25). Therefore he says in a certain psalm: “Lord, you have known my sitting down and my rising” (Psalm 138:2), that is, my humility and my exaltation.

Why, then, do you wish to be exalted before the light, O sons of Zebedee? Let us speak in this way and name them especially, since they do not become angry with us: these things were written about them so that others might beware of the pride in which they themselves were reproved [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions instead read “were corrected.”].

Why, then, do you wish to rise before the light? It is in vain for you. Do you wish to be exalted before you have been humbled? Your own Lord, who is your light, was humbled in order to be exalted.

Hear Paul saying: “Who, being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.” Why was equality with God not something seized for him? Because it was his nature, because he was born for this: to be equal to the one by whom he was begotten [Note: Most manuscripts read “for this”; others, with the Ambrosian, “in this”; Erasmus and Lovaniensis, “for this.”]. But what did he do? “For our sake he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross.” This is his sitting.

But hear of his rising: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:6–9). You are already hurrying toward that name. Rise—but after you have sat down. You wish to rise, but first sit down; and, rising from humility, you will attain the kingdom. For if you seize the kingdom in advance, you fall from the kingdom before you rise.

“Can you drink,” he says, “the cup that I am about to drink?” And they said, “We can.” And he said: “You shall indeed drink my cup; but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give; it has been prepared for others by my Father” (Matthew 20:22–23).

What does “it is not mine to give you” mean? It is not mine to give to the proud—for they were still proud. But if you wish to receive it, do not remain what you are. It has been prepared for others; become others, and it will be prepared for you.

What does “Become others” mean? First be humbled, you who already wish to be exalted. They therefore understood that humility would benefit them, and they were corrected. Let us too hear this, because this is what the psalm says: “Rise after you have sat down.”

### 6

But lest anyone think that he is to sit in order to be honored—and lest, to show that by this sitting he intended to commend humility, anyone should think he was commanded to sit either for judging or for feasting and rejoicing, and should seek greater pride there—he added, as an indication of humility: “You who eat the bread of sorrows.”

Those, then, eat the bread of sorrows who groan in this pilgrimage. They are in the valley of weeping. For God makes ascents in the heart. But where does he establish them? “He established ascents,” he says, “in his heart.” Who established them? God.

If there are ascents in the heart, that is why they sing the Song of Ascents. Let us be humbled in the world; let us ascend [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The editions have “so that we may ascend.” Shortly afterward Erasmus and Lovaniensis add: “Because that ascent is in the hearts,” and so forth.]. How? In the heart. For that very ascent of the heart rises from the valley of weeping. “In the valley of weeping” (Psalm 83:6–7).

Just as mountains are raised up, so valleys are sunken. Valleys are called the depressed places of the earth; hills are higher places, though less high than mountains; very elevated places of the earth are called mountains.

But this is not enough. He does not say, “Rise from a hill”; nor does he say, “from a plain”; rather, “from a valley,” so that it may be something lower than a plain. If, therefore, in the valley of weeping you eat the bread of sorrows and say, “My tears have become my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’” (Psalm 41:4), you rise well, because you have sat down.

### 7

And as if you were to say, “When shall we rise? Now we are commanded to sit; when will our rising be, as the Lord’s rising was?” Look to him who went before you. For if you do not look to him, it is in vain for you to rise before the light.

When was he exalted? When he died. Therefore hope for your exaltation after death; hope in the resurrection of the dead, because he rose and ascended.

But where did he sleep? On the cross. When he slept on the cross, he bore a sign—or rather, he fulfilled what had been signified in Adam. When Adam slept, a rib was taken from him and Eve was made (Genesis 2:21–22). Thus, while the Lord slept on the cross, his side was pierced with a lance (John 19:34), and the sacraments flowed forth, from which the Church was made.

The Church was made the Lord’s spouse from his side, just as Eve was made from Adam’s side. But just as Eve was made only from the side of one who was sleeping, so the Church was made only from the side of one who was dying.

If, therefore, he did not rise except after dying, do you hope for exaltation except after this life? But to teach you this, the psalm, as though you were asking, “When shall I rise? Perhaps before I have sat down?” says: “When he gives sleep to his beloved.”

God gives this when his beloved have fallen asleep; then his beloved—that is, Christ’s beloved—will rise. For all will rise, but not in the manner of his beloved. There is a resurrection of the dead for everyone; but what does the Apostle say? “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51).

They rise for punishments; we rise as our Lord rose, so that we may follow our head, if we are his members. But if we are his members, then we are his beloved; then that resurrection which preceded in the Lord pertains to us, so that the light may rise before us and we may rise after the light. For it is in vain for us to rise before the light—that is, to seek exaltation before we die—since Christ our light was not exalted in the flesh until after he had died.

Therefore, established as his members, and as his beloved within his members, when we have received sleep, then we shall rise in the resurrection of the dead.

One person rose, never again to die. Lazarus rose (John 11:44), but he was to die; the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue rose (Matthew 9:25), but she was to die; the widow’s son rose (Luke 7:15), but he was to die. Christ rose, never to die.

Hear the Apostle: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Romans 6:9). Hope for such a resurrection; and for this reason be a Christian—not for the prosperity of this earth. For if you wish to be a Christian for the sake of the prosperity of this life, when your light did not seek worldly prosperity here, you wish to rise before the light; it is necessary that you remain in darkness.

Change; follow your light. Rise by the way he rose [Note: Thus Erasmus, Lugdunensis, Venetus, and Lovaniensis. In B.: “why he rose.” M.]; sit down first, and thus rise when he gives sleep to his beloved.

### 8. [Verse 3]

As though you were asking again, “Which beloved?”—“Behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb.”

When he says “the fruit of the womb,” these sons have been brought forth in labor. There is a certain woman in whom what was said to Eve is shown spiritually: “In groaning you shall give birth.” The Church, Christ’s spouse, gives birth to sons; and if she gives birth, she labors in childbirth.

In her figure, Eve too was called the mother of the living (Genesis 3:16, 20). In the members of the woman in labor was he who said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).

But she did not labor in vain, nor did she give birth in vain. There will be a holy seed in the resurrection of the dead; the righteous, who are now scattered throughout the whole world, will abound. The Church groans over them; the Church labors over them. But in that resurrection of the dead the Church’s birth will appear, and pain and groaning will pass away.

And what will be said? “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb.”

“Of this fruit” [Note: Greek: τοῦ καρποῦ, “of the fruit.”]—not “this fruit”—“the reward of the fruit of the womb.” What is this reward? To rise from the dead. What is this reward? To rise after you have sat down. What is this reward? To rejoice after you have eaten the bread of sorrows.

Whose womb? The Church’s. In whose womb—because Rebecca bore the type of the Church—those two twins, as two peoples, struggled with one another (Genesis 25:22–23). One mother held within her womb dissenting brothers, not yet born. They struck their mother’s womb with their internal conflicts; she groaned and suffered violence. But in giving birth she separated those whom, while pregnant, she had carried as twins.

So also now, brothers, as long as groaning has been given to the Church, as long as the Church is in labor, both the good and the wicked are within her. But the fruit of the womb was in Jacob, because the mother loved him. “Jacob I loved,” God says, “but Esau I hated” (Malachi 1:2–3; Romans 9:13).

Both came forth from one womb; one deserved to be loved, the other to be rejected. Therefore the fruit will be among his beloved. Thus: “the reward of the fruit of the womb.”

### 9. [Verse 4]

“Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those who have been shaken out.”

From where, brothers, did this inheritance come? From where did such a great inheritance come, of which at the end it is said, “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb”?

Some were shaken out from the Lord’s hand like arrows, went far away, and filled the whole earth, from which the saints spring up. For this is the inheritance of which it is said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8).

And how does this possession extend and grow as far as the ends of the earth? “Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those who have been shaken out.”

Arrows are shot from a bow, and the stronger the shooter, the farther the arrow travels. But who is stronger than the Lord who shoots? From his bow he sends his Apostles. There could be no remaining place to which an arrow shot by so powerful a shooter would not reach; it reached to the ends of the earth.

It goes no farther because there is nothing beyond the human race. For he has such strength that even if there were somewhere farther for the arrow to travel, he would shoot it there.

Thus are the sons of those who have been shaken out, just as those who were shaken out themselves. The earlier interpreters of these words also asked why they are called “sons of those who have been shaken out,” or who are to be understood as the sons of those who have been shaken out. Some thought, as I have just said, that the sons of those who have been shaken out are the sons of the Apostles.

### 10

Let Your Charity attend for a little while. It was asked why the Apostles were “shaken out.” Some said that they were called “shaken out” because the Lord commanded them: “If you leave a city where they do not listen to you, shake the dust from your feet” (Matthew 10:14).

But another said: “Then they ought not to be called the sons of those who have been shaken out, but the sons of those who shake out; for the Lord made them people who shake out when he said to them, ‘Shake the dust from your feet,’ not people who had been shaken out.”

He who had already discussed and stated these things seemed subtly to wish to contradict the preceding opinion [Note: After “the preceding opinion,” the Ambrosian manuscript and others add: “because these matters had already been discussed and stated,” which may be a gloss.]. Nevertheless, with the Lord’s help, as we seek how those to whom the Lord said, “Shake the dust from your feet,” could rightly also be called “shaken out,” we find that it can not unreasonably be said.

Although they themselves shook something out, they shook themselves out. I mean this: one who shakes something out either shakes himself out or shakes something else. If he shakes something else out, he is one who shakes out, but he is not shaken out; if he shakes himself out, he is both one who shakes out and one who is shaken out.

Attend; I shall explain it more clearly, if I can. If he shakes something else out, he is one who shakes out, not one who is shaken out. If he is shaken out by someone else, he is shaken out, not one who shakes out. But if he shakes himself out, he is one who shakes out, because he shakes himself, and he is shaken out, because he is shaken by himself.

The question, then, is: whom did the Apostles shake out? Surely themselves, for they shook the dust from their own feet.

But someone says: “They did not shake themselves out, but the dust.” This is plainly said captiously. For we use “shaken out” in two ways: either of that which is shaken out from something, or of that from which something is shaken out.

We say both, “The dust has been shaken out,” and “The garment has been shaken out.” Some people hold and shake a garment, and the dust that had clung to it leaps out. What do you say of the dust? “The dust has been shaken out.” What do you say of the garment? “The garment has been shaken out.”

If, therefore, both what leaps out through being shaken and that from which what had clung to it leaps out are called “shaken out,” then both the dust has been shaken out and the Apostles have been shaken out. Why, then, should “the sons of those who have been shaken out” not be called the sons of the Apostles?

### 11

But there is another interpretation that we must not pass over. Perhaps the expression was placed more obscurely for this reason: that it might generate many understandings, and people might depart richer [Note: Another manuscript from Corbie reads “more learned”], because they found something closed that could be opened in many ways, rather than something open in only one way.

We also say that something is shaken out so that what may be hidden within it comes out. Thus we speak in one way of shaking a garment, so that the dust may be shaken out of it, and in another way of shaking a sack, so that what was hidden inside may come out.

Therefore, brothers, I understand, as far as I can, that perhaps the Apostles themselves are called the sons of those who have been shaken out—the sons of the Prophets. The Prophets held closed and covered mysteries; they were shaken out so that manifest things might proceed from them.

Suppose, then, that the prophet said—as indeed he did: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me” (Isaiah 1:3). This is what occurs to me for the present as something to say about the prophet; if something else had occurred to me, I would have said that instead.

When a person hears this, if he thinks of the ass and the ox, the cattle and beasts of burden that he sees, he will handle outwardly something placed within, as it were, in a wrapping; he does not know what is there. The ass and the ox signify something.

What, then, is said to a person who already wishes to pronounce judgment? “Wait. What you are touching is closed; shake off the wrapping.” The Prophet has covered something—I do not know what—with the veils of names, and signifies—I do not know which ass and which ox.

For the ass, in the figure of God’s people, is God’s beast of burden, carrying its rider, the Lord, so that he does not go astray on the way. And that ox of which the Apostle says, “You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain”—does this concern oxen, he says, before God? But Scripture speaks this for our sake (1 Corinthians 9:9–10).

Therefore everyone who preaches the word of God admonishes, rebukes, and terrifies; he treads the threshing floor and performs the office of an ox. The ox came from the people of the Jews, for from there came the Apostolic preachers. And the ass came from the people of the uncircumcision, that is, from the Gentiles.

It came to carry the Lord. Therefore the Lord sat upon an ass that had never carried a human being, because the Law had not been sent to the Gentiles, nor had the Prophets.

Since, then, our Lord Jesus Christ wished to be our food, and for that reason was born and placed in a manger: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger.”

But would these things have emerged unless the sack had been shaken? Unless the prophecy, wrapped up, had been opened through careful attention, would its hidden contents have come forth to us?

All these things were closed before the Lord came. The Lord came and shook out those closed things, and they were made manifest. The Prophets were shaken out, and the Apostles were generated.

Therefore, because they were generated from the Prophets who had been shaken out, the Apostles are the sons of those who have been shaken out. They were placed in the hand of the mighty one like arrows and reached to the ends of the earth.

Thus at the end it is said: “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb.” This inheritance is gathered from the ends of the earth because “like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those who have been shaken out”—that is, the Apostles were the sons of the Prophets, like arrows in the hand of the mighty one.

If he is mighty, he shook them out mightily; if he shook them out mightily, those whom he shook out reached to the ends of the earth.

### 12. [Verse 5]

“Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire from them.”

Come, my brothers: who fulfills his desire from them? The one who does not love the world. The person full of worldly desire has no room for what they preached to enter him. Pour out what you carry, and become capable of what you do not have.

You desire riches; you cannot fulfill your desire from them. You desire earthly honors. You desire what God has given even to beasts of burden—that is, temporal pleasure, bodily health, and such things. You will not fulfill your desire from them.

But if you desire in the way the deer desires the springs of water (Psalm 51:2); if you say, “My soul desires and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 83:3), you fulfill your desire from them—not because they can already fulfill such a desire, but because by imitating such people you come to the one who fulfilled their desire.

### 13

“He shall not be confounded when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.”

Brothers, let us speak in the gate—that is, let everyone know what we are saying. Whoever does not wish to speak in the gate wishes to conceal what he says; and perhaps he wishes to conceal it for the reason that it is evil.

If he has confidence, let him speak in the gate, as it is said of Wisdom: “At the gates of the cities she speaks boldly” (Proverbs 8:3). As long as the innocent hold fast to righteousness, they will not be ashamed. This is to preach in the gate.

And who is the one who preaches in the gate? The one who preaches in Christ, because Christ is the gate through which we enter that city. I am lying if he himself did not say, “I am the door” (John 10:9). If he is the door, he is also the gate. A door is the entrance of a house; the gate is the entrance of a city, and the door is the entrance of a house.

But perhaps it is not properly called a gate if the city that was called a house is not properly called a city. Both were mentioned shortly before: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain”; and, lest you think this house something small when you hear it, he says: “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it labors in vain.”

That house, then, is the city. It has a door as a house and a gate as a city. Therefore he who is the door of the house is the gate of the city.

If, then, Christ is the city’s gate, the one who stands in Christ and preaches in this way is not ashamed. But whoever preaches against Christ finds the gate closed against him.

Who are those who preach against Christ? Those who deny that arrows were sent from the hand of the mighty one and reached to the ends of the earth; that this is the Lord’s inheritance, of which it was said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8).

It was preached and heard before it happened, and now that it has happened they refuse to acknowledge it. Those who argue against Christ, therefore, are outside the gate, because they seek their own honors, not Christ’s.

But the one who preaches in the gate seeks Christ’s honor, not his own. Therefore he who preaches in the gate says: “Do not put your confidence in me; for you will enter not through me, but through the gate.”

Those, however, who wish people to put their confidence in themselves do not want them to enter through the gate. It is no wonder that the gate is closed against them and that they idly knock for it to be opened.

Be attentive in spirit, then, brothers, also for tomorrow’s sermon, which, with the Lord’s help, we have promised to deliver to you from the Gospel concerning the dove [Note: See Treatise IV on the Gospel of John, section 16; and Treatises V and VI.]. In whose name we made the promise, in his mercy we shall fulfill it. But so that we may be capable fulfillers and not rash promisers, pray for us.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 127

### SERMON

[Note: Delivered to the people on the feast day of Saint Felix the martyr.]

### 1. [Verses 1–4]

As the Apostle says, dearly beloved brothers, “We compare spiritual things with spiritual things; but the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:13–14). We must therefore take care lest natural people, who do not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, be scandalized by this psalm rather than built up.

For, briefly—although we heard it when it was sung—because it is short, I shall run through it, not expounding it but reading it. And see this: if someone desires from God as something very great the things contained in this psalm, and perhaps does not receive them—not because he has been abandoned by God, but because he is loved more—and if he sees that those things which he heard here are rewards for those who fear God flourishing among those who do not fear God, let his steps falter, let his footprints be scattered in a fall, and let him say in his heart that he feared God without reason, since he did not deserve the gifts promised to those who fear him, while even those received them who not only did not fear him but also blasphemed him.

For see what it says: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. You shall eat the labors of your fruits; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you.”

Here we can still think, even if we are natural people, of the blessedness of the age to come. But see what follows: “Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house. Your sons shall be like olive shoots around your table. Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord.”

How? So that his wife may be like a fruitful vine on the sides of his house, and his sons may surround his table like olive shoots.

Have they, then, lost their reward who, for God’s sake, did not wish to marry? But the man who did not wish to marry says: “God will bless me in another way.” Indeed, either he will bless you in this way or he will not bless you: the statement has been made openly, “Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord.”

### 2

What, then, does this mean, brothers? So that, by desiring temporal and earthly happiness, we may not lose heavenly happiness, the Prophet has set before us something like a wrapping. This wrapping contains something inside. Your Charity remembers that, when I was expounding the preceding psalm, the one before this, we encountered an obscure verse where it was said: “Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those who have been shaken out” (Psalm 126:4).

When we asked who the sons of those who have been shaken out were, it seemed to us—through the Lord’s prompting, as we believe—that the Apostles were called the sons of those who had been shaken out, the sons of the Prophets. For the Prophets spoke in riddles and covered the meaning with figures of things, like wrappings of mysteries. That meaning could not come forth to human beings unless those wrappings were shaken out. Hence they were called the sons of those who had been shaken out, because they advanced from the Prophets who had been shaken out.

Let us, then, shake this psalm out too, lest we be deceived by its wrappings and, touching what is inside without seeing it, call wood gold or earthenware silver.

Let us shake it out, if it pleases Your Charity. The Lord will be present so that what is inside may come forth—especially, my brothers, because we are celebrating the birthdays of the martyrs.

What evils the martyrs suffered! What deaths, what torments, the squalor of prisons, the tightness of chains, the savagery of wild beasts, the heat of flames, the barbs of insults! Would they have suffered all these things unless they saw something toward which they were pressing, something that does not belong to the happiness of this age? [Note: The manuscripts, Erasmus, and the majority of copies read “toward which they were pressing.” Lovaniensis reads “by which they might hold themselves.”]

It would be shameful for us to celebrate the birthdays of the martyrs—of these servants of God who despised this world for the sake of eternal happiness—and to take what is written here as referring to present happiness. Then, if some faithful person of God, a citizen of that Jerusalem, happened to marry a wife and nevertheless have no children, we would say: “This man does not fear God. For if he feared God, his wife would be like a fruitful vine in his house, not barren, so that she would bear no child; and if this man feared God, his sons would surround his table like olive trees.”

If we say such things, we are natural people, not perceiving the things that belong to the Spirit of God.

Let us too begin to shake things out, so that we too may be sons of those who have been shaken out. For if we are sons of those who have been shaken out, we shall be in the hand of the mighty one like arrows, and he will shoot us by his command into the hearts of people who do not yet love, so that, pierced by the arrows of God’s words, they may love.

For if we begin to preach such things to them—“Children, or my brothers, fear the Lord so that you may have sons and grandsons, so that your household may rejoice”—we are not shooting so that that eternal Jerusalem may be loved. They will remain in love with earthly things, and, seeing these things abound among the wicked, even if they do not dare say so to us, they will say in their hearts: “Why does that man who does not fear God have a house full of children?”

Perhaps another person says to him: “You do not yet know what may happen to him. What if, because he does not fear God, he should bury them, and more were born to him for this reason, so that he might suffer greater grief over their death?”

But if you say such things, he will answer you: “I know an impious man, a pagan, a sacrilegious person, a worshiper of idols”—and perhaps he knows such a man and speaks the truth, and did not know only one, or only two or three [Note: Erasmus, Lugdunensis, Venetus, and Lovaniensis include the word “only” in the text, though it is not found in the Benedictine manuscript. The margin notes: “Supply ‘only.’”]—“whom a crowd of sons and grandsons led to the grave: an old man, decrepit, dead in his bed.

“Behold, he did not fear the Lord, and the most fertile offspring of his household closed his eyes.”

What shall we say to this? Nothing evil can happen to him, so that he should bury his sons while still alive, when, already dead, he has been led by his sons to an honorable burial.

### 3

Let us therefore shake it out—shake it out, if we wish to be sons of those who have been shaken out. Let something come forth here.

There is a certain man who is blessed in this way; and no one fears the Lord except one who is in the members of that man. There are many people, and there is one man: many Christians, and one Christ.

Those Christians, together with their head who ascended into heaven, are one Christ. It is not that he is one and we are many; rather, we many are one in that one. Therefore there is one man, Christ, head and body.

What is his body? His Church, as the Apostle says: “We are members of his body” (Ephesians 5:30); and, “You are the body of Christ and members” (1 Corinthians 12:27).

Let us therefore understand the voice of this man, in whose body we are one man; and there we shall see the true blessings of Jerusalem. For he says at the end: “And may you see the good things that are Jerusalem’s.”

But if you attend to these things with an earthly eye—the abundance of sons and grandsons, and the fruitfulness and fertility of a wife—they are not the blessings of that Jerusalem. These blessings belong to the land of those who die; that land belongs to the living.

Do not consider it something very great if you have children who will die—if not before you, certainly after you. Do you wish to have children who will never die and who will live forever? Be in the body of him of whom it was said: “You are the body of Christ and members.”

### 4

For the psalm itself also wished to show this. It is obscure in such a way as to urge us to knock; it is covered in such a way as to invite us to shake it out. It begins in the plural: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.”

It speaks to many. But because those many are one in Christ, it then proceeds and speaks in the singular: “You shall eat the labors of your fruits.”

Above it had said, “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.” Why now “You shall eat the labors of your fruits,” and not “You [plural] shall eat”? Why “the labors of your fruits,” and not “the labors of your [plural] fruits”? Has he so quickly forgotten that he was speaking to many?

But if you have now shaken it out, what answer did it give you? When I address many Christians, I understand one in the one Christ. Therefore you are many, and you are one; we are many, and we are one.

How are we many and one? Because we cling to him whose members we are, and whose head is in heaven, so that the members may follow.

### 5

Let him now describe that one, since it is clear whom he is describing. Everything that follows will thus become plain.

Fear the Lord, then, and walk in his ways, and do not envy those who do not walk in his ways when you see them to be unhappily happy. The people of the world are unhappily happy; but the martyrs were happily unhappy.

They were unhappy for a time, but happy forever. And in the very fact that they were unhappy for a time, they were thought more unhappy than they were.

For what does the Apostle say? “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6:10). Why “always”? Here and there—truly, here and there.

For what do we rejoice in here? In hope. From what shall we rejoice there? From the reality. Hope has great joy when it rejoices.

And if we rejoice in hope, see what follows: “Patient in tribulation” (Romans 12:12). The martyrs, then, were patient in tribulation because they rejoiced in hope.

But because what is promised did not yet exist, what does the Apostle say? “Hope that is seen is not hope. For if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25).

Behold why the martyrs endured everything: because they awaited with patience what they did not see. Those who killed them loved what they saw; those who were killed longed for what they did not see and hastened to grasp it. And when they were killed more slowly, they thought that delays were being imposed upon them.

### 6

Therefore, brothers, Felix—the martyr who is truly blessed both in name and in crown, whose day is today [Note: He is said to have suffered martyrdom at Thinnisa, or Thimisa, in Africa, not far from Hippo, on the eighth day before the Ides of November.] [Note: Thus all manuscripts; the editions, however, read, “whose feast-day is today.”]—despised the world. Or was he perhaps blessed because he feared the Lord, blessed because his wife was like a fruitful vine in the land and his sons surrounded his table? He possesses all these things perfectly, but in the body of the man described here; and because he understood this in such a way that he despised present things in order to receive future ones.

You should know, brothers, that he did not suffer the death which the other martyrs suffered. For he confessed, and he was remanded for torture; but on the following day his body was found lifeless. His persecutors had indeed shut the prison, but only against his body, not against his spirit. The executioners, who had prepared to torture him there, found him absent and lost the opportunity for their cruelty. He lay lifeless—without consciousness toward them, so that he might not be tortured, but conscious before God, so that he might be crowned.

Hence he too is blessed, brothers, not only in name but also in the reward of eternal life, if he loved these things [Note: Erasmus, the Lyons and Venetian editions: “but also in the reward of eternal life; thus this man loved.” M.].

### 7

Therefore let us listen to this psalm as though it were spoken about Christ. Let all who cling to Christ’s body and have become members of Christ walk in the ways of the Lord, and let us fear the Lord with a chaste fear, a fear that remains for ever and ever.

For there is another fear which love casts out, as John says: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). He does not say that every kind of fear is cast out by love. For you have the psalm saying: “The fear of the Lord is chaste, enduring for ever and ever” (Psalm 18:10). One fear, then, remains, while another is cast out. The fear that is cast out is not chaste; the fear that remains is chaste.

What is the fear that is cast out? Please pay attention. Some people fear only that they may suffer some misfortune on earth: that illness may come upon them, or loss, or bereavement, or the loss of someone dear, or exile, condemnation, imprisonment, or any other tribulation. That is why they fear and tremble. This fear is not yet chaste.

Listen further. Another person does not fear suffering on this earth, but fears hell—about which the Lord also warned us. You heard it when the Gospel was read: “Where their worm does not die and their fire is not extinguished” (Mark 9:43).
