People hear these words, and because these punishments truly await the wicked, they fear and restrain themselves from sin. They possess fear, and through fear they restrain themselves from sin. They do indeed fear, but they do not love righteousness.

When, however, through fear they restrain themselves from sin, the practice of righteousness develops; what was difficult begins to be loved, and God becomes sweet. The person then begins to live righteously not because he fears punishments, but because he loves eternity. Thus fear has been cast out by love, and chaste fear has taken its place.

### 8

What is this chaste fear? According to it, my brothers, we must understand what has been said: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.” If, with the help of our Lord God, I can speak worthily about this chaste fear, many perhaps will be inflamed by it to chaste love.

Perhaps I cannot explain it without proposing some comparison. Imagine a chaste woman who fears her husband; imagine another woman who is adulterous, and she too fears her husband. The chaste woman fears that her husband may leave; the adulterous woman fears that he may come. What if both husbands are absent? One fears that he will come; the other fears that he may delay.

The one to whom we are betrothed is absent in a certain sense; he is absent who gave us the pledge of the Holy Spirit, who redeemed us with his blood. He is the bridegroom more beautiful than anything, who appeared as though ugly amid the hands of his persecutors. Isaiah had said shortly before of him: “And we saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty” (Isaiah 53:2).

Is our bridegroom therefore ugly? Far from it. For how could the virgins love him, those who did not seek husbands on earth? He appeared ugly to his persecutors; and unless they had thought him ugly, they would not have attacked him, beaten him with whips, crowned him with thorns, and dishonored him with spittle. But because he appeared ugly to them, they did these things to him. They did not have eyes with which Christ could appear beautiful.

With what kind of eyes did Christ appear beautiful? What kind of eyes was Christ himself seeking when he said to Philip: “For so long a time I have been with you, and you have not seen me” (John 14:9)? These eyes must be cleansed so that they may be able to see that light. Yet, when they are lightly touched by its radiance, they are kindled with love, so that they desire to be healed and become enlightened.

To show you that Christ is beautiful to those who love him, the prophet says: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3). His beauty surpasses that of all human beings.

What is it that we love in Christ? His limbs crucified, his pierced side—or love? When we hear that he suffered for us, what do we love? Love is loved [Note: Am. and many manuscripts: “Why do we love, when we hear that he suffered for us? What do we love—his crucified limbs, his pierced side, or love? Love loves” (or “is loved”). “He loved us,” etc.].

He loved us so that we might love him in return; and so that we might be able to love him in return, he visited us through his Spirit. He is beautiful, and he is absent. Let the bride ask herself whether she is chaste.

We are all in his members, my brothers; we are in his members, and therefore we are one person. Let each person see what kind of fear he has: whether it is the fear that love casts out, or the chaste fear that remains for ever and ever.

He has tested it now [Note: Here Am. and several manuscripts read “he will test it.” Some books read “he has tested it” here and in the following passage.]. I speak, and he will test it. Our bridegroom is absent. Examine your conscience: do you want him to come, or do you still want him to delay?

See, brothers: I have knocked at the doors of your hearts; he heard the voice of those who dwell within. What the conscience of each person has said just now could not reach my ears, because I am human; but he who is absent in bodily presence and present in the power of his majesty heard you. How many, if told, “Behold, Christ is coming now; tomorrow is the day of judgment,” would not say, “Would that he would come!” Those who say this love him greatly. And if they are told, “He will delay,” they fear that he may delay, because their fear is chaste.

Just as now there is fear that he may delay, so when he has come there will be fear that he may depart. Yet this fear will be chaste, because it will be tranquil and secure. We will not be abandoned by him when he finds us, since he sought us before we sought him [Note: So the better manuscripts. Others, with Ambrose and Erasmus, read: “when he finds us, someone believing in him. When did he seek us? Before we sought him.” Lov. reads: “when the Lord finds us believing in him, when he sought us before we knew him.”].

This, then, is what chaste fear has, my brothers: it comes from love [Note: Erasmus, the Lyons and Venetian editions: “because it comes.” M.]. The fear that is not yet chaste fears his presence and punishments. Whatever good a person does, he does from fear—not from fear of losing that good, but from fear of suffering that evil. He does not fear losing the embrace of the most beautiful bridegroom; he fears being cast into hell.

This fear is good and useful. It will not, however, remain for ever and ever; but it is not yet that chaste fear which endures for ever and ever.

### 9

In what does the chaste fear consist? I ask again something that you should ask yourselves. Suppose God, coming in person—although he does not cease speaking through his Scriptures—were to speak to us and say to a person:

“Do you wish to sin? Sin. Do whatever delights you. Whatever you love on earth shall be yours. Whoever has angered you, let him perish; whoever you wish to seize, let him be seized; whoever you wish to beat, let him be beaten; whoever you wish to condemn, let him be condemned; whoever you wish to possess, possess him. Let no one resist you, let no one say to you, ‘What are you doing?’ Let no one say, ‘Do not do it’; let no one say, ‘Why did you do it?’ Let all these earthly things that you have desired abound for you, and live in them—not for a time, but forever. Only you will never see my face.”

My brothers, why did you groan, unless chaste fear—which remains for ever and ever—has already been born? Why was your heart struck? If God were to say, “You will never see my face,” and you were to have all this earthly happiness, abundance in every respect, and temporal goods flowing around you—if you neither lost nor abandoned any of them, what more would you want?

Chaste fear would nevertheless weep and groan and say: “Rather, let everything be taken away, so that I may see your face.” Chaste fear would cry out from the psalm and say: “God of hosts, restore us; show your face, and we shall be saved” (Psalm 79:8).

Chaste fear would cry out from the psalm and say: “One thing I have asked from the Lord; this I shall seek.” See how this chaste fear, this true love, this sincere love burns [Note: So Am., Erasmus, and the better manuscripts. Lov. reads: “true fear, sincere fear.” Some manuscripts read: “true fear, sincere love.”].

“One thing I have asked from the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” What if this were for the sake of earthly happiness? Listen to what follows: “That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord and be protected in his temple” (Psalm 26:4)—that is, I asked this one thing from the Lord: to be his temple and to be protected by him.

If you seek this one thing [Note: Lov. adds here: “you will receive it,” which is absent from the other books.], if you train your hearts toward this one thing [Note: Five manuscripts read: “if you raise them up.”], and if the only thing you fear losing is this, you will not envy earthly prosperities. You will hope for that true happiness, and you will be in the body of the one to whom is sung: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.”

### 10

“You shall eat the labors of your fruits.” O you—you many who are one—you shall eat the labors of your fruits. To those who do not understand, this seems to be said perversely. For he should have said: “You shall eat the fruit of your labors.” Many people eat the fruit of their labors. They work in a vineyard, but they do not eat the labor itself; rather, they eat what is produced by their labor. They work around fruit-bearing trees; who would eat the labors? But what those trees produce—the fruit of the labor—delights the farmer.

What does “You shall eat the labors of your fruits” mean? At present we have labors; afterward there will be fruit. Yet because even these labors are not without joy, on account of the hope of which we spoke shortly before—“Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation”—our labors themselves now delight us and make us glad because of hope.

If, then, our labor could be eaten and could bring joy, what will the fruit of that labor be like when it is eaten? Those who went forth sowing their seeds ate their labors as they went, weeping. How much more joyfully will those who come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves, eat the fruits of their labors (Psalm 125:6)?

And so that you may know, brothers, that this labor is eaten, in the preceding psalm you heard what was said to the proud, who wanted to rise before the light—that is, before Christ—not through the humility by which Christ rose. It was said to them: “Rise after you have sat down” (Psalm 126:2)—that is, humble yourselves, and then rise, because he too came to humble himself, he who was exalted for your sake.

And what was said? “You who eat the bread of sorrow.” This is the labor of fruits, the bread of sorrow. For if it were not eaten, it would not be called bread; but unless this bread possessed some sweetness, no one would eat it [Note: Am., Erasmus, and most manuscripts read: “no one would eat it with such sweetness. He weeps, etc.”]. With what sweetness does the one who prays weep amid groaning?

The tears of those who pray are sweeter than the joys of the theaters. And hear the flame of desire with which this bread is eaten, of which he says here: “You who eat the bread of sorrow.” Elsewhere this lover, whose voice we often recognize in the psalm, says: “My tears have become my bread day and night.” How have tears become bread? When it is said to me every day: “Where is your God?” (Psalm 41:4).

Before we see him who loved us and gave us his pledge, to whom we are betrothed, the pagans mock us and say: “Where is what Christians worship? Let them show us whom they worship.” Here I am, showing them my God; let them show me their god.

When the pagan says this to you, you find nothing to show him, because there is no one to whom you can show him. You return, therefore, and weep before God, because you sigh for him before seeing him and groan from longing for him. And because you weep in longing for him, those tears themselves are sweet and will be food for you, since they too have become your bread day and night while it is said to you every day: “Where is your God?”

But your God, of whom it is said, “Where is he?”, will come and wipe away the tears (Revelation 21:4). He himself will take the place of the bread of tears and will nourish you for eternity, because the Word of God, by whom the angels are fed, will be with us.

For now, then, there are the labors of fruits; afterward, the fruit of labor. “You shall eat the labors of your fruits; you are blessed, and it will be well with you.” “You are blessed” refers to the present; “it will be well with you” refers to the future. When you eat the labors of your fruits, you are blessed; when you reach the fruit of your labors, it will be well with you.

What did he say? For if it will be well with you, you will certainly be blessed; and if you are blessed, it will certainly be well with you. But there is a difference between hope and possession. If hope is so sweet, how much sweeter will possession be!

### 11

Now let us come to the words, “Your wife.” This is said to Christ. Therefore his wife is his Church; his Church is his wife; we ourselves are that wife. “Like a fruitful vine.” But among whom is she a fruitful vine?

We see many barren people entering these walls. We see many drunkards, usurers, dealers, people seeking diviners and going to male and female enchanters when their heads hurt, entering these walls. Is this the fruitfulness of the vine? Is this the abundance of the wife? It is not. These are thorns, but she is not thorny everywhere [Note: Most manuscripts: “but not everywhere. It has a thorny…”].

She has a certain fruitfulness and is a fruitful vine—but among whom? “In the sides of your house.” Not everyone is called the sides of the house. For I ask what these sides are. What shall I say? Are they walls, like strong stones? If he were speaking of this bodily dwelling, perhaps we would understand the sides in that way.

We call the sides of the house those who cling to Christ. It is not without reason that in ordinary speech we say of someone who perhaps acts badly because of the evil advice of his friends: “He has bad sides.” What does “He has bad sides” mean? Bad people cling to him. Likewise, we say of another: “He has good sides”—he lives by good counsel. What does this mean? He is governed by good advice.

Therefore the sides of the house are those who cling to Christ. Nor is it without reason that the wife herself was made from the side. While the man slept, Eve was made (Genesis 2:21–22); while Christ was dying, the Church was made. The former was made from the side of the man when a rib was taken from him; the latter was made from the side of the man when his side was pierced by a spear (John 19:34), and the sacraments flowed forth.

Therefore, “Your wife is like a fruitful vine.” But among whom? “In the sides of your house” [Note: Erasmus and Lov. add: “that is, in those who cling to Christ.”]. Among others who do not cling to Christ she is barren. But I will not count them among the vine.

### 12

“Your sons.” The wife and the sons are the same people. In these carnal marriages and unions, there is one wife and other sons; in the Church, those who are the wife are themselves the sons.

The apostles belonged to the Church and were among the Church’s members. Therefore they were in his wife, and they were the wife according to the portion they held among the members. Why, then, is it said of them: “When the bridegroom is taken away from them, then the bridegroom’s sons will fast” (Matthew 9:15)? Thus she is the wife, and they are the sons [Note: Erasmus, the Lyons and Venetian editions: “they are the sons.” M.].

I say something remarkable, my brothers. In the Lord’s words we find that the Church is his brothers, his sisters, and his mother. For when his mother and brothers were announced as standing outside, because they were standing outside they represented a type. What is represented by the mother? The synagogue. What is represented by the carnal brothers? The Jews standing outside. The synagogue stands outside.

Mary, however, is among the sides of his house, as are his relatives who came from the blood relationship of the virgin Mary and believed in him—not insofar as they were joined to him by carnal kinship, but insofar as they heard and did the word of God.

For the Lord answered and said: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” Thus some have attempted to say that Christ had no mother, because he said, “Who is my mother?” Why, then? Did Peter, John, James, and the other apostles have no fathers on earth? And yet what does he say to them? “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 23:9). What he taught the disciples concerning the father, he himself demonstrated concerning the mother.

The Lord wants us to place God before earthly relationships. Honor your father, because he is your father; honor God, because he is God. Your father generated you by contributing his flesh; God created you by exercising his power. Let the father not become angry when God is placed before him. Rather, let him rejoice that such honor is shown him that the one who ought to be placed before him has been found [Note: Perhaps one should read: “so that the one who alone should be placed before him has been found.”].

What, then, shall I say? What does the Lord say? “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” And he stretched out his hands toward his disciples and said: “Behold my mother and my brothers.” They were brothers; how were they his mother? He added: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother” (Matthew 12:46–50).

Suppose that “brother” refers to the masculine sex which the Church possesses [Note: The editions omit “whom here,” and also omit “sister, because of the women,” which is found in one Corbie manuscript.]; “sister,” because of the women whom Christ has here among his members. How is she his mother, unless it is because Christ himself is in Christians, whom the Church gives birth to as Christians every day through baptism?

Therefore, in those whom you understand as the wife, understand also the mother and the sons.

### 13

Let it therefore be said what kind of sons they ought to be. What kind? Peaceful. Why peaceful? Because “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).

Since the fruit of the olive is peace—for oil signifies peace, because it signifies love, and without love there is no peace—it is evident that those who divided peace did not possess love.

Hence I have already explained to Your Charity why the dove carried leaves with fruit to the ark (Genesis 8:11): to signify that those who were baptized outside, just as those pieces of wood were baptized outside the ark, if they possess not leaves alone—that is, words alone—but also fruit, which is love, are brought back to the ark by that same dove and come to unity [Note: Treatise 6 on John, no. 19.].

Such, then, ought the sons around the Lord’s table to be, like olive shoots. It is a perfect thing and a great blessedness. Who would not want to be there?

When you see a blasphemer with a wife, sons, and grandsons, while you perhaps have none, do not be jealous. See that this too has been fulfilled in you, but spiritually.

Or are you perhaps not among the members? If you are not there, weep, because you are neither here nor there. But if you are there, be secure; for even if you are there and not here, you are more fruitful there than here.

### 14

If, then, we possess these things, why do we possess them? Because we fear the Lord. “Thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord.” He is the man who consists of human beings, and those human beings are one man: many are one, because Christ is one.

### 15

**[Verses 5–6.]** “May the Lord bless you from Zion.”

You had begun to pay attention: “Thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord.” Perhaps your eyes were already passing over those who do not fear the Lord, and you were seeing there fertile wives and abundant children going around their father’s table. I do not know where you were going [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “I do not know what blessings you were seeking, and not from Zion.” Erasmus, the Lyons and Venetian editions: “I do not know where you were going, and not from Zion.” M.].

“May the Lord bless you—but from Zion.” Do not seek those blessings which are not from Zion.

Did the Lord not bless such things, my brothers? This blessing is indeed from the Lord. Or, if it is not from the Lord, who marries a wife if the Lord does not wish it? Who can be healthy if the Lord does not wish it? Or who could be rich if the Lord did not wish it? He gives these things—but do you not see that he has given them also to animals? This blessing, therefore, is not from Zion.

“May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem.” For those other things are not the good things of Jerusalem. Do you want to see that they are not Jerusalem’s good things? Even to birds it was said: “Increase and multiply” (Genesis 1:22). Do you wish to consider as something great what was given to birds? It was indeed given by God’s voice—who does not know this? But use these goods if you receive them, and think more about how you will nourish those who are born than about their being born.

For happiness does not consist in having children, but in having good children. Work at raising them if they are born; if they are not born, give thanks to God. Perhaps you will be less burdened with anxiety, and yet you have not remained barren of that mother. Perhaps [Note: Erasmus, the Lyons and Venetian editions, and Lov. read: “Perhaps children.” M.] through you spiritual children are born from this mother, children who are like olive shoots going around the Lord’s table [Note: Am., Erasmus, and the manuscripts read: “among young shoots.”].

Let the Lord therefore console you so that you may see the good things of Jerusalem. Those are the good things. Why are they good? Because they are eternal. Why are they good? Because the king is there: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14).

These other things are good, and yet they are not; for they do not stand: they slip and flow away. Children are little; you flatter the little ones, and the little ones flatter you. Do they remain in that condition? But you wish them to grow, and you wish their age to advance. Yet see that when one age arrives, another dies. When childhood comes, infancy dies; when adolescence comes, childhood dies; when youth comes, adolescence dies; when old age comes, youth dies; when death comes, every age dies. As many stages of life as you desire, so many deaths of stages of life you desire at once.

Therefore these things are not. Furthermore, were your children born on earth to live with you, or rather to remove and succeed you? You rejoice in those who are born so that you may be removed? For the children who are born seem to say to their parents: “Come, think about leaving here; let us too perform our little drama.”

The whole life of the human race is a drama of temptation, because it was said: “Every living human being is utter vanity” (Psalm 38:6). Yet if we rejoice in children who will succeed us, how much more should we rejoice in children with whom we shall remain, and in that Father to whom we were born—who will not die, but will enable us to live with him forever [Note: So the manuscripts. The editions read: “who will not die, but so that we may live with him forever.”]?

Those are the good things of Jerusalem, because they are what they are. Therefore, “May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem.” For these things which you regard as good, you see blindly [Note: The manuscripts: “not these things.”]. May you see—but those good things which are seen with the heart.

And for how long shall I see the good things of Jerusalem? “All the days of your life.” But if your life is eternal, you will see the good things of Jerusalem forever.

But, my brothers, if these are good things, you do not see them during all the days of your life [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “But these are good things, and you do not see them during all the days of your life,” omitting “if.”]. For when you leave the body, you do not die. Your life continues; the body dies, but the life of the spirit continues. The eyes do not see because the one who saw through the eyes has departed. Wherever the one who saw through the eyes is, he sees something.

That rich man who dressed in purple and fine linen on earth was not dead; if he had been dead, he would not have been tormented in the underworld (Luke 16:19, 23). Perhaps he wished that he might die, but he lived in the underworld to his own misfortune. He was tormented and did not see those good things which he had left on earth. His life was such, and he did not see those good things.

Desire, therefore, such good things as you may see throughout all the days of your life—that is, so that you may live forever with those good things.

### 16

What, then, are those good things? Pay attention, brothers. Could these things be called good: gold, silver, a pleasant estate, marble walls, paneled ceilings? Far from it. In this life the poor possess these things more abundantly. It is more for a poor person to see the starry sky than for a rich person to see a gilded ceiling.

What, then, brothers, is that good for which we are kindled, for which we sigh, by which we are inflamed, and for the sake of attaining and seeing which we endure such great labors? You heard it when the Apostle was read: “All who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12).

Christians do not fail to suffer persecution merely because the devil does not now rage through kings. If the devil is dead, persecutions are dead; but if our adversary lives, how does he not suggest temptations? How does he not rage? How does he not devise threats or scandals? If you begin to live piously, you will see that everyone who wishes to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution.

Why, then, do we suffer such great persecutions? For if we have hope in Christ only in this life, the Apostle says, “we are of all people most miserable” (1 Corinthians 15:19). Why were the martyrs condemned to the beasts? What is that good, if it can be expressed? From where does it come, or what tongue could speak of it, or what ears could hear it? Indeed, “neither has the ear heard it, nor has it entered into the human heart” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

Let us only love; let us only make progress. You see that there is no lack of battles, and we fight against our desires. Outside we fight with unbelieving and disobedient people; inside we fight with suggestions and carnal disturbances. We still fight everywhere, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15). We still fight because, although the spirit is life, the body is dead on account of sin.

But what will happen? “If the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, through his Spirit who dwells in you” (Romans 8:10–11).

When our mortal members have therefore been given life, nothing will resist our spirit. There will be no hunger and no thirst, because these arise from the corruption of the body. You restore yourself because something is lacking in you. The desires of carnal pleasures fight against us.

We carry death through the weakness of the body [Note: So Am., Erasmus, and most manuscripts. Lov. reads: “we carry weakness.”]. But when death itself has been transformed into that unchangeableness, and this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality, what will death hear then?

“Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Corinthians 15:53–55). Perhaps death itself dies, and someone says: “Do any enemies remain?” No; “the last enemy, death,” follows. When it has been destroyed, immortality will take its place. If there is no enemy, death will be destroyed as the last enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26).

Our good, for which we sigh, will be peace. Behold the good, brothers: it is called great good, peace. You were asking what it would be called. Is it gold, silver, an estate, or clothing? It is peace—not the kind of peace human beings have among themselves, faithless, unstable, changeable, uncertain; nor peace of the kind that one person has within himself.

For we said that a person also fights with himself. Until he has subdued all desires, he is still fighting. What kind of peace, then? The peace “which eye has not seen and ear has not heard.” What kind of peace? It is from Jerusalem, because Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.”

Thus, “May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things that are Jerusalem’s, and may you see all the days of your life.” And may you see not only your sons, but the sons of your sons.

What are your sons? The works you do here. What are the sons of your sons? The fruits of your works. You give alms: these are your sons. Through your almsgiving you receive eternal life; these are the sons of your sons.

“May you see the sons of your sons,” and then there will be what follows, with which the psalm concludes: “Peace upon Israel.”

This peace is preached to you by us; it is loved by us; and we desire that it be loved by you. Those who are peaceful here will reach that peace. They are peaceful here and there, those who go around the Lord’s table like olive shoots, so that the tree may not be barren, as was that fig tree on which the hungry Lord found no fruit.

And you see what happened to it. It had leaves alone and no fruit (Matthew 21:18–19). So are those who have words but do not have deeds. When the hungry Lord came, he found nothing there to eat, because the Lord hungers for our faith and good works.

Let us feed him by living well, and he will feed us by granting us to live forever [Note: So Erasmus, the Lyons and Venetian editions, and Lov. The B manuscript lacks the word “us.”].

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 128

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

#### 1

The psalm we have sung is short. But just as it is written in the Gospel about Zacchaeus that he was short in stature but great in action (Luke 19:2–9), and just as it is written about the widow who put two small coins into the treasury that her money was little but her love great (Mark 12:42–44), so this psalm, if you count its words, is short; but if you weigh its meanings, it is great.

It will not therefore keep us longer than is tolerable. Why? Let your prudence pay attention, and let Christian attentiveness be present. Let the word of God sound to those who wish and those who do not wish, in season and out of season. It finds a place for itself; it finds hearts in which to rest; it finds soil in which to sprout and bear fruit.

For it is clear that there are many evil and wicked people whom the Church bears until the end. For such people the word of God is useless. It falls upon them either as seed upon the road, which is trampled and gathered up by the birds; or as seed upon rocky places, where it has little soil, springs up immediately, and withers when the sun becomes hot because it has no root; or as seed among thorns, which, even if it sprouts and tries to rise into the air, is nevertheless choked by the multitude of thorns.

Such are those who despise the word of God like the road; or those who rejoice for an hour and, when tribulation comes, wither like plants under the sun’s heat; or those who, through thoughts, cares, and anxiety about this world, choke with the thorns of greed what had begun to sprout in them.

There is also good soil, in which the seed, when it has fallen, bears fruit—some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, some a hundredfold (Matthew 13:3–23). Whether little or much, all will be in the granary.

Such people exist, and for their sake we speak. For their sake Scripture speaks; for their sake the Gospel does not remain silent. But let those others also listen, lest they be one thing today and another tomorrow; lest by listening they change, or plow the road, or clear away the stones, or pull up the thorns.

Let the Spirit of God speak; let him speak to us and sing to us. Whether we wish to dance or do not wish to dance, let him sing. For just as someone who dances moves his limbs to the song, so those who dance to God’s command obey the sound with their deeds.

Therefore, what does the Lord say in the Gospel to those who did not wish to do this? “We sang to you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not lament” (Matthew 11:17).

Let him sing, then. We trust in God’s mercy [Note: Some manuscripts read: “in mercy.”], because there will be people about whom he will console us. For those who are obstinate and persist in wickedness disturb the Church daily with scandals, even though they hear the word of God.

The psalm speaks of such people. For this is how it begins:

#### 2

**[Verses 1–3.]** “Often they have attacked me from my youth.”

The Church speaks about those whom she tolerates. And as though someone were to say, “Only now?”—the Church has existed from ancient times. From the time when the saints began to be called, the Church has been on earth.

At one time the Church existed in Abel alone, and he was attacked by his wicked and lost brother Cain (Genesis 4:8). At one time the Church existed in Enoch alone, and he was taken away from the wicked (Genesis 5:24). At one time the Church existed in Noah’s household alone; it endured all those who perished in the flood, while the ark alone floated upon the waters and escaped to dry land (Genesis 6–8).

At one time the Church existed in Abraham alone, and we know how much he endured from the wicked. In Lot, his brother’s son, alone, and in his household, the Church existed in Sodom; it endured the iniquities and perversities of the Sodomites until God delivered him from their midst (Genesis 12–20).

The Church also began to exist among the people of Israel; it endured Pharaoh and the Egyptians. Then within that Church itself—that is, among the people of Israel—the number of saints began to increase. Moses and the other saints endured the wicked people of Israel, the Jews.

Then we came to our Lord Jesus Christ. The Gospel was preached, and he said in the Psalms: “I announced and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Psalm 39:6). What does “beyond number” mean? Not only did those who belonged to the number of the saints believe, but others beyond that number also entered: many righteous people, but even more wicked people. And the righteous endured the wicked.

When? In the Church. Is it only now, after all that she has enumerated and recounted? Therefore, lest the Church be surprised now, or lest anyone who wishes to be a good member of the Church be surprised at what occurs within the Church, let him hear the Church herself, his mother, saying to him:

“My son, do not be surprised at these things: ‘Often they have attacked me from my youth.’”

### 3.

A great feeling begins the Psalm in this way: “Often they have attacked me from my youth.” It is as though he were already saying something; for he seems not to have begun, but to have answered. Whom was he answering? Those who were thinking and saying: “How many evils we endure! How many scandals multiply every day, when wicked people enter the Church and we put up with them?” Let the Church answer concerning certain people—that is, let the complaints of the weak be answered by the voice of the strong; let the strong encourage the weak, the mature the little ones—and let the Church say: “Often they have attacked me from my youth.” Let Israel say this [Note: The editions read “Let Israel say this now.” The word “now” is absent from the manuscripts, and the particle “vero” (“indeed”) is sufficient in place of the Greek *de*.]: “Often they have attacked me from my youth.” Let it say this, and not fear it. For what purpose did he add “from my youth” after saying “Often they have attacked me”? The Church’s old age is now being attacked, but let it not fear; let it say: “Often they have attacked me from my youth.” Has it therefore failed to reach old age because they have not ceased attacking it? Have they been able to destroy it? Let Israel indeed say it; and let Israel console itself, let the Church itself console itself by recalling past examples, and let it say: “Often they have attacked me from my youth.”

### 4.

Why did they attack me? “For they could not prevail against me. Sinners worked upon my back; they prolonged their iniquity.”

Why did they attack me? Because they could not prevail against me. What does “they could not prevail against me” mean? They could not build. What does “they could not prevail against me” mean? I did not consent to them in evil. Every wicked person persecutes the good for this reason: the good person does not consent to him in evil.

Let him do some evil, and if the bishop does not rebuke him, the bishop is good. Let the bishop rebuke him, and he is a bad bishop. Let him seize something, and if the bishop keeps silent about the person from whom he seized it, the bishop is good. Let him at least speak and reprimand him, even if he does not demand its return, and he is bad. The one who rebukes the thief is bad, while the one who steals is good!

“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.” Against this the Apostle says: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals. Be sober, you just, [Col. 1691] and do not sin” (Isa. XXII, 13; 1 Cor. XV, 32–34). The word rings out; the speech that contradicts lust rings out. But the person who is a friend of his own lust and an enemy of the speech that contradicts it is hostile to his own beloved and hates the word of God.

Avarice has become a friend, and God an enemy. God contradicts avarice and wants nothing to be possessed by avarice. “Let me be possessed,” it cries. What do you want to be possessed by avarice? It commands hard things; I command easy things. Its burden is heavy; my burden is light. Its yoke is harsh; my yoke is gentle (Matt. XI, 30).

Do not wish to be possessed by avarice. Avarice commands you to cross the sea, and you obey. It commands you to entrust yourself to winds and storms; I command you to give the poor person something from what you possess at your own door. You are lazy when it comes to doing a good work before you, but energetic when it comes to crossing the sea. Because avarice commands, you serve; because God commands, you hate.

And what happens? When he begins to hate, he begins to want to accuse those from whom he hears good commandments, and to seek, through his suspicions, charges against God’s servants. “Do those who tell us these things not themselves do them?” And whether the things are done or not done, people say that they are done; things that are done well are said to be done badly; and what we endure is attributed to our guilt.

What do we answer? Do not pay attention to me; pay attention to this speech. It itself speaks to you through anyone whatever; you are hostile to it. “Agree with your adversary while you are with him on the way” (ibid. V, 25). You have made the word of God your adversary.

Do not pay attention [Note: Four manuscripts read: “Do not pay attention to the person through whom he speaks to you, but pay attention to the fact that he…”] to the person who speaks to you. The person through whom he speaks to you may be wicked, but the one who speaks to you—the word of God—is not wicked. Accuse God, if you can; accuse him.

### 5.

Do you believe, brothers, that those of whom it is said, “Often they have attacked me from my youth,” have gone so far as not even to hesitate to accuse God himself?

You accuse the miser, and he accuses God because God made gold. Do not be avaricious. “Then God should not have made gold.” This is what remains: because you cannot restrain your evil deeds, you accuse God’s good works. The Creator and Maker of the world displeases you.

“Then he should not have made the sun either,” because many people quarrel at their windows over sources of light and drag one another into court. If only we would restrain our vices! For all things are good, because God, who made all things, is good. His works praise him when they are contemplated as good by one who possesses the spirit of contemplation, the spirit of piety and wisdom.

God is praised everywhere by his works. How do his works praise him through the mouths of the three young men? What was omitted? The heavens praise him, the angels praise him, the stars praise him, the sun and moon praise him, days and nights praise him, everything that sprouts from the earth praises him, everything that swims in the sea praises him, everything that flies through the air praises him, all mountains and hills praise him, cold and heat praise him; and all the other things that God made—you heard that they praise God (Dan. III, 57–90).

Did you hear there that avarice praises God, or that lust praises God? Such things do not praise him, because he did not make them. Human beings praise God there; God is the creator of the human being. Avarice is the work of an evil human being; the human being himself is the work of God. And what does God want? To destroy in you what you yourself have made, and to save what he himself has made.

### 6.

Do not lend at interest. You accuse Scripture, which says: “The one who has not given his money at interest” (Ps. XIV, 5). I did not write that; it did not first come from my mouth. Listen to God.

And he says: “Clerics must not lend at interest.” Perhaps the person speaking to you does not lend at interest. But if he does lend at interest, grant that he too lends at interest: does the one who speaks to you through him lend at interest? If he does what he tells you, and you do not do it, you go into the fire [Note: Lyons, Venice, and Louvain include in the text the word “you go”; it is absent from B., but a marginal note reads: “Supply ‘you go.’”], while he goes into the kingdom. If he does not do what he tells you, but does the same evils that you do and says the good things that he does not do, then both of you go into the fire.

“Grass will burn [Note: Erasmus has: “the grass will burn in the fire.” Lyons, Venice, and Louvain have: “the grass will burn in the fire.”] but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. XL, 8). Surely the speech that spoke to you through him burns? Either Moses is speaking to you—that is, God’s good and righteous servant—or it is a Pharisee sitting on Moses’ chair.

You have also heard what was said about them: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII, 3). You have no grounds on which to excuse yourself when the word of God speaks to you. Because you cannot kill the word of God, you seek to accuse those through whom the word of God speaks to you. Seek as much as you want; say as much as you want; blaspheme as much as you want: “Often they have attacked me from my youth.” Let Israel indeed say: “Often they have attacked me from my youth.”

Even moneylenders dare to say: “I have no other way to live.” A robber caught at a narrow pass could say the same to me; a housebreaker caught near another person’s wall could say the same; a pimp who buys girls for prostitution could say the same; a sorcerer chanting evil spells and selling his wickedness could say the same. Whenever we tried to forbid such things, they would all answer that they had no other means of living, because that was how they supported themselves—as though the very thing that must be punished in them most severely were not this: that they had chosen an art of wickedness by which to pass their lives, and wished to nourish themselves by the very means through which they offend the one by whom everyone is nourished.

### 7.

But when you have cried out and said this, they answer: “If it is so, we will not come here; if it is so, we will not enter the Church itself.”

Let them come; let them enter; let them listen: “Often they have attacked me from my youth. For they could not prevail against me; sinners worked upon my back.” This means: They could not make me consent; they did what I had to bear.

How excellently this is said, how perfectly it expresses the meaning: “For they could not prevail against me; sinners worked upon my back.” At first they act toward us so that we may consent to their evil deeds. If we do not consent, they say: “Put up with us.”

Therefore, because you could not prevail against me, climb upon my back. I must carry you until the end comes; for I have been commanded to bear fruit with perseverance (Luke VIII, 15). I do not correct you; I tolerate you. Or perhaps, while I tolerate you, you are correcting yourself.

If you do not correct yourself to the end, I will tolerate you to the end; and to the end you will be upon my back, until the appointed time. Will you always be upon my back? The one who will shake you off will come. The time of harvest will come; the end of the age will come; God will send reapers.

The reapers are angels. They separate the wicked from among the righteous, as weeds from wheat; they store the grain in the barn, but burn the chaff in unquenchable fire. I have carried it as long as I could; now, rejoicing, I pass into God’s barn, and confidently sing: “Often they have attacked me from my youth.”

### 8.

For what could they do to me by attacking me from my youth? They exercised me; they did not crush me. They benefited me as fire benefits gold, not as fire benefits hay. When fire approaches gold, it removes its dross; when it approaches hay, it turns it to ashes.

“For they could not prevail against me,” because I did not consent; they did not make me like themselves. “Sinners worked upon my back; they prolonged their iniquity.” They did what I had to tolerate, but they did not bring it about that I should consent. Their iniquity, therefore, is far from me.

The wicked are mixed with the good, not only in the world, but also within the Church itself. You know this, and you have experienced it; and you will experience it even more if you are good. “When the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds appeared” (Matt. XIII, 27–43). The wicked in the Church are apparent to no one except the person who is good.

You know, therefore, that they are mixed together, and Scripture always and everywhere says that they will not be separated until the end. Although they are mixed together, they are far apart. Therefore, lest anyone should think, because the wicked are mixed among the good, that iniquity is close to righteousness, he says: “They could not prevail against me.” That is, they said—and said wrongly—“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.”

Evil words did not corrupt good morals. In what I heard from God, I did not yield to human speech. Sinners did what I had to bear, not what I would be united with; and their iniquity became far from me.

For what is as near as two people in one Church? And what is as far apart as iniquity and righteousness? Where there is agreement, there is nearness. Two people are bound and brought before a judge: a robber and one bound with him. One is criminal, the other innocent; they are bound by one chain, yet they are far apart. How far apart? As far as crime is from innocence.

Look: these people are far apart from one another. Another robber commits crimes in Spain; the one who commits them in Africa is close to him. How close? As close as crime is joined to crime, as robbery is joined to robbery.

Therefore let no one fear the wicked who are bodily mixed with him. Let him be far from them in heart, and confidently bear what he does not fear: “They have prolonged their iniquity.”

### 9. [verse 4]

What comes to mind [Note: Louvain has: “What will this be?” Erasmus and Aldus have “comes to mind,” in accordance with the manuscripts, some of which below have “the wicked” instead of “wickedly”]: Those who rule wickedly flourish; and, to use the language of the people, the wicked thunder, they puff themselves up in arrogance and in accusations.

What then? Is this always so? No. Listen to what follows: “The Lord, who is righteous, will cut off the necks of sinners.”

Let Your Charity pay attention. “The Lord,” he says, “who is righteous, will cut off the necks of sinners.” Who would not tremble? For who has not sinned?

“The Lord, who is righteous, will cut off the necks of sinners.” Trembling enters the hearts of all who hear this, if they believe the Scripture of God. If people beat their breasts without cause, they are lying when they beat their breasts, if they are righteous; and by lying to God in this, they become sinners. If, therefore, they truly beat their breasts, they are sinners.

And which of us does not beat his breast? Which of us does not cast his eyes down toward the ground like that tax collector and say: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII, 13)?

If, then, all are sinners, and no one is found without sin, the sword that cuts off necks is to be feared by all, because “the Lord, who is righteous, will cut off the necks of sinners.”

I do not think, my brothers, that this means all sinners; rather, in the member that he strikes, he indicates which sinners he strikes. For he did not say, “The Lord, who is righteous, will cut off the hands of sinners,” nor did he say, “The Lord, who is righteous, will cut off the feet of sinners.” Rather, because he wanted proud sinners to be understood—and all proud people are stiff-necked, since they not only do evil but do not even wish to acknowledge it, and when they are rebuked they justify themselves—consider this:

“You did it; at least acknowledge what you did. God hates the sinner; hate him too. Join yourself to God; persecute your sin together with him.”

“No,” he says. “I did well; God did badly.”

What does this mean? “I did nothing evil,” he says, “because Saturn did it, because Mars did it, because Venus did it. I did nothing; the stars did it.” You justify yourself and accuse God, who made the stars and adorned [Note: Aldus and most manuscripts have “ordered.”] the heavens.

And so, because you justify your sin and grow proud against God, making yourself free of guilt and God guilty, and because you have raised your neck and run against God, as it is written in Job—he was speaking of an impious sinner—“running against God with his thick neck and his shield” (Job XV, 26), and there he mentioned the neck:

Because you thus raise yourself up, and do not cast your eyes toward the ground, beat your breast, and say, “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner,” but boast of your merits and wish to contend with God in judgment—“You want,” God says, “to contend with me in judgment” (Jer. II, 29)—when you ought, in acknowledgment of your guilt, to make satisfaction to God and cry out to him with the words cried out in another Psalm: “If you observe iniquities, Lord; Lord, who will stand?” (Ps. CXXIX, 3);

to cry out to him with the words cried out in another Psalm: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. XL, 5);

because you do not wish to say these things, but justify your deeds against the word of God, what follows in Scripture comes upon you, and it says: “The Lord, who is righteous, will cut off the necks of sinners.”

### 10. [verse 5]

“Let all who hate Zion be confounded and turned backward.”

Those who hate Zion hate the Church; Zion is the Church. And those who enter the Church hypocritically hate the Church. Those who do not wish to observe the word of God hate the Church: “They worked upon my back.”

What is the Church to do except carry them until the end?

### 11. [verses 6, 7]

But what does he say about them? What follows is: “Let them become like the grass of the roofs, which withers before it is plucked up.”

The grass of the roofs is a plant that grows on roofs, on a roof covered with tiles. It appears high up, but has no root. How much better would it be to grow lower and flourish more vigorously! It now grows higher only so that it may dry out more quickly.

It has not yet been plucked up, and it has withered. They have not yet been condemned [Note: The manuscript of Corbie has “punished.”] in God’s judgment, and already they have no sap of greenness. Observe their works, and see that they have withered.

But they are alive and still here; therefore they have not yet been plucked up. They have withered, but they have not yet been plucked up. They have become like the grass of the roofs, which withers before it is plucked up.

### 12.

And reapers will come, but they will not fill their bundles from them. For the reapers will come and gather the wheat into the barn; they will bind the weeds and throw them into the fire.

So too the grass of the roofs is cleared away, and whatever is plucked from it is thrown into the fire, because it withered before it was plucked up. The reaper does not fill his hand from it.

For what follows says: “The reaper has not filled his hand, nor the one who gathers bundles his bosom.” The reapers are angels, the Lord says (Matt. XIII, 39).

### 13. [verse 8]

“And those who passed by on the road did not say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we have blessed you in the name of the Lord.’”

You know, brothers, that when one passes by people who are working, it is customary to say to them: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you.” This custom was even more common among the Jewish people. No one passed by and saw people doing some work in a field, vineyard, harvest, or anything of that kind without giving a blessing.

Some are those who gather the bundles; others are those who pass by on the road. Those who gather the bundles do not fill their hands from these people, because the grass of the roofs is not gathered into the barn.

Who are those who gather the bundles? The reapers. Who are the reapers? The Lord said: “The reapers are angels.”

Who are those who pass by? Those who have already passed along this road—that is, through this life—from here to their homeland. The Apostles were people passing through this life; the Prophets were people passing through it.

Whom did the Prophets and Apostles bless? Those in whom they saw the root of love. But when they found people rising above the roofs and growing proud in the neck of their shield, they spoke against them, saying what would happen to them; they did not pronounce a blessing upon them.

Therefore, all these wicked people whom the Church carries—you read about them in Scripture—are designated as belonging to the Antichrist, to the devil, to the chaff, and to the weeds. Innumerable things are said about them by way of comparison: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (ibid. VII, 21).

You will find no Scripture that speaks well of them, because those passing by on the road did not bless them. The Prophets, as they passed by, spoke every evil thing about them.

Look: David too, whom we carry, passed along the road. You heard what he said about them: “The Lord, who is righteous, will cut off the necks of sinners. Let all who hate Zion be confounded and turned backward. Let them become like the grass of the roofs, which withers before it is plucked up. The reaper has not filled his hand, nor the one who gathers bundles his bosom.”

He said these things about them. Therefore this passerby did not bless them, and what he himself said was fulfilled through him: “And those who passed by on the road did not say, ‘We have blessed you in the name of the Lord.’”

And these passersby—whether Prophets, Patriarchs, Apostles, or whoever has passed through—if we live well, brothers, have blessed us in the name of the Lord.

“When,” you ask, “did Paul bless me? When did Peter bless me?” Pay attention to the Scriptures; see whether you live well, and see there that you have been blessed. All those who live well have blessed us.

And how did they bless us? “In the name of the Lord,” not in their own name, as the heretics do. Those who say, “What we give is holy,” wish to bless in their own name, not in the name of the Lord. But those who say, “No one sanctifies except God, and no one is good except by God’s gift,” bless in the name of the Lord, not in their own name, because [Note: Many manuscripts have “who”] they are “friends of the bridegroom” (John III, 19), and do not wish to be adulterers of the bride.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM CXXIX

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1. [verses 1–3]

Since we presume that you are watchful not only with the eyes of the body but also with the heart, we ought to sing with understanding: “Out of the depths I have cried to you, Lord; Lord, hear my voice.”

For this is the voice of one ascending, belonging to the Song of Ascents. Each one of us ought therefore to see in what depth he is, from which he cries out to the Lord.

Jonah cried from the depths, from the belly of the sea creature (Jonah II, 2). He was not only beneath the waves but also inside the creature’s entrails; nevertheless, neither that body nor those waves shut in his prayer so that it could not reach God, and the belly of the beast could not hold back the voice of the one praying.

It penetrated everything, broke through everything, and reached the ears of God—or, if one must say that it reached God’s ears after breaking through everything, when God’s ears were in the heart of the one praying. For where is God’s presence absent from the voice of one who is faithful?

Nevertheless, we too must understand from what depth we cry out to the Lord. This mortal life is a depth for us. Whoever understands that he is in the depths cries out, groans, and sighs until he is drawn out of the depths and comes to the one who sits above all abysses, above the Cherubim, above everything he created—not only bodily things but also spiritual ones.

The soul must come to him, and his image, the human being, must be liberated by him. That image, impressed by God when he formed the human being, has been worn away in this depth as though by continual waves. Unless it is renewed and restored by God, who impressed it when he formed the human being [Note: Some manuscripts add: “he will always be in the depths.”]—the human being was capable of his own fall, but is not capable of his own resurrection—it remains always in the depths. Unless it is liberated, as I have said, it remains always in the depths.

But when it cries out from the depths, it rises from the depths, and that very cry does not allow it to remain long at the bottom. For those who do not cry out from the depths are very deeply sunk.

Scripture says: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3). Now see, brothers, what sort of depth it is where God is despised.

When someone sees himself overwhelmed by daily sins and weighed down by heaps and masses of iniquities, if he is told to pray to God, he laughs.

In what ways? First he says: “If crimes displeased God, would I be alive? If God cared about human affairs, would I not only be alive after committing such great crimes, but would things be going well for me?”

This commonly happens to those who are very deeply sunk and prosper in their iniquities. They sink all the more deeply the happier they appear to be; for deceptive happiness is itself the greater unhappiness.

Then people commonly say this too: “Since I have committed many things and condemnation is imminent, I lose this much if I do not do whatever I can. Since I am doomed anyway, why should I not do whatever comes to me?”

This is how desperate robbers are accustomed to speak: “The judge will kill me for ten murders just as he would for five, or for one. Why should I not now do whatever comes to me?”

This is what is meant by: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises.”

But the Lord Jesus Christ, who did not despise our depths, who deigned to come even into this life and promised the remission of all sins, also raised the human being from the depths, so that he might cry out from the depths beneath the masses of his sins and the sinner’s voice might reach God.

From what place does the sinner cry out, if not from the depths of evils?

### 2.

And see that it is the sinner’s voice crying from the depths: “Out of the depths I have cried to you, Lord; Lord, hear my voice. Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication.”

From where does he cry? From the depths. Who is it who cries? A sinner. With what hope does he cry? Because the one who came to destroy sins also gave hope to the sinner lying in the depths.

What follows these words? “If you observe iniquities, Lord; Lord, who will stand?” Here he has revealed [Note: Aldus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts have “appeared”] from what depth he would cry. He cries beneath the masses and waves of his iniquities.

He looked around himself; he examined his life. He saw it covered on every side with crimes and wicked deeds. Wherever he looked, he found nothing good in himself; nothing serene belonging to righteousness could appear before him.

And when he saw so many and such great sins on every side, and whole troops of his crimes, he cried out in fear: “If you observe iniquities, Lord; Lord, who will stand?”

He did not say, “I will not stand,” but “Who will stand?” For he saw almost the whole of human life surrounded by the barking of its sins; he saw every conscience accused by its own thoughts; he found no pure heart that presumed upon its own righteousness.

If, then, no pure heart can be found that presumes upon its own righteousness, let every heart presume upon the mercy of God and say: “If you observe iniquities, Lord; Lord, who will stand?”

### 3. [verses 4–6]

Why, then, is there hope? Because with you there is propitiation. And what is this propitiation, if not sacrifice? And what is sacrifice, if not that which was offered for us? Innocent blood, shed, wiped out all the sins of the guilty; so great a price, given, redeemed all captives from the hand of the enemy who held them captive. Therefore with you there is propitiation.

For if propitiation were not with you—if you wished to be only a judge and not merciful—you would observe all our iniquities and search them out. Who could endure? Who would stand before you and say, “I am innocent”? Who would stand in your judgment? Therefore there is one hope: because with you there is propitiation.

“Because of your law I have waited for you, Lord.” What law? The law that made people guilty? For a holy, just, and good law was given to the Jews (Rom. VII, 12), but it could make them guilty. A law was not given that could give life (Gal. III, 21), but one that would show sins to the sinner. For the sinner had forgotten himself and did not see himself; the law was given to him so that he might see himself. The law made him guilty; the Giver of the law set him free, for the Giver of the law is the Emperor.

A law was given that might frighten and bind one over to guilt; the law does not free from sins, but reveals sins. And perhaps, placed under that law, this man observed from the depths how many things he had done against the law, and thus cried out, saying: “If you observe iniquities, Lord; Lord, who will stand?” Therefore there is a law of God’s mercy, a law of God’s propitiation. That was a law of fear; another is the law of love.

The law of love grants pardon for sins, erases the past, warns about the future; it does not abandon its companion on the way, but becomes a companion to the one whom it leads on the way. But one must agree with one’s adversary while one is with him on the way (Matt. V, 25). For the word of God is your adversary as long as you do not agree with it. But you agree with it when you begin to take delight in doing what the word of God says. He who was an adversary now becomes a friend; thus, when the way is ended, there will be no one to hand you over to the judge.

Therefore, because of your law I have waited for you, Lord: because you deigned to bring a law of mercy, to forgive me all my sins, and henceforth to give me warnings lest I offend you. If in those warnings I should perhaps stumble, you have given me a remedy by which I may pray to you, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (ibid. VI, 12). You established this law for me: that as I forgive, so I may be forgiven. Because of this law I have waited for you, Lord. I have awaited your coming and your freeing me from every necessity, because in that necessity you did not abandon the law of mercy.

### 4.

Hear what law he means, if you have not yet understood that he now means the law of love. Hear the Apostle: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ.” Who bear one another’s burdens except those who have love? Those who do not have love are burdensome to themselves; those who have love bear one another.

Someone has injured you and asks forgiveness. If you do not forgive, you do not bear your brother’s burden; if you forgive, you bear one who is weak. And if you should perhaps fall, as a human being, into some weakness, he too ought to bear you in the same manner as you bear him. Hear what precedes: “Brothers,” he says, “if a person has been caught in some offense, you who are spiritual, instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness.” And lest, because he had called them spiritual, they should perhaps regard themselves as secure, he immediately added: “Watching yourself, lest you too be tempted.” Then he added what I mentioned: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. VI, 1–2). Hence he says: “Because of your law I have waited for you, Lord.”

They say that deer, when they cross straits to nearby islands for pasture, place their heads upon one another; and the one in front alone bears his head and does not place it upon another. But when he too becomes tired, he leaves the foremost position and returns behind, so that he too may rest upon another. Thus they all bear one another’s burdens and reach what they desire; and they do not suffer shipwreck, because love is, as it were, a ship for them.

Thus love bears burdens; but let it not fear to be weighed down by such burdens. Let each person take care not to be weighed down by his own sins. For when you bear your brother’s weakness, his sins do not burden you. Certainly, if you consent, then your own sins burden you, not another’s. For whoever consents to a sinner is burdened not by another’s sins but by his own. Consent to another’s sin becomes your own sin; nor is there any reason for you to complain that other people’s sins burden you. For it is said to you: “They burden you, but they are your own.” “You saw a thief and ran with him” (Ps. XLIX, 18). What does this mean? You walked with your feet to theft; indeed, you joined your mind to the thief. What belonged to him alone became yours, because it pleased you.

But if it displeases you, and you pray for him and grant the forgiveness he asks, so that you may be able with an untroubled countenance to say in your prayers, which the heavenly Jurist dictated to you, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” you have learned to bear your brother’s burdens. Thus another may bear yours, if you have any, and there may be among you what the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ.” Thus you securely sing what has just been said: “Because of your law I have waited for you, Lord.”

### 5.

But whoever does not keep this law does not wait for the Lord; nor, if he wishes to wait, has he any reason to wait: he waits in vain. For the Lord will come and find your sins; but he will not find that you lived in perfect righteousness. Perhaps he will not find murders—for they are grave and very great sins—nor will he find adultery, thefts, robbery, evil practices, or idolatry [Note: In B. the passage reads: “For the Lord will come and find your sins. But he will not find that you lived in perfect righteousness—perhaps murders. For they are grave and very great. He will not find adultery, thefts, robbery, evil practices, or idolatry; he will not find these things. Will he therefore find nothing? Hear the saying of the Gospel,” etc. We have restored this passage from manuscript Colbert, Royal Library of Paris, no. 1981. M.]. He will not find these things. Will he therefore find nothing? Hear the saying of the Gospel: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool!’” Who abstains even from these very slight sins of the tongue? But perhaps you say, “They are small.” “He will be liable,” he says, “to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. V, 22). If it seemed to you a small or slight matter to say to your brother, “Fool,” let the fire of Gehenna at least seem great to you. If you despised the lesser sin, let the greatness of the punishment deter you.

But you say: “They are lesser things, trifles, without which this life cannot exist.” Heap up trifles, and they make a huge pile. Grains are small, yet they make a mass; drops are small, yet they fill rivers and move great weights. Therefore the man who considers how many small daily sins a human being commits, if in no other way, at least by thoughts and speech, observes how many they are; and if he observes how small they are, he sees that many small things make a great heap. Thinking not, as it were, of his former sins, but of human frailty itself, he now cries as he ascends: “Out of the depths I have cried to you, Lord; Lord, hear my voice. Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication. If you observe iniquities, Lord; Lord, who will stand?”

I can avoid murders, adulteries, robberies, perjuries, evil practices, and idolatry; but can I avoid sins of the tongue? Can I avoid sins of the heart? It is written: “Sin is iniquity” (1 John III, 4). Who, then, will stand if you observe iniquities? If you wish to deal with us as a severe judge and not as a merciful father, who will stand before your eyes? But with you there is propitiation; because of your law I have waited for you, Lord. What sort of law is this? “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ.” Who bear one another’s burdens? Those who faithfully say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

6. My soul has waited for your word. No one waits except one who has not yet received what was promised; for one who has already received it, what is there to wait for? We have received the forgiveness of sins, but the kingdom of heaven has been promised to us; our debts have been erased, but our reward is still future; we have received pardon, but we do not yet possess eternal life. Yet the one who granted pardon also promised eternal life. If it were our word, we ought to fear; but because it is God’s word, it does not deceive. Therefore we confidently hope in the word of him who cannot deceive.

My soul has hoped in the Lord from the morning watch until night. What does he mean by this? Did he hope in the Lord for one day, and then his entire hope came to an end? “From the morning watch until night, my soul hoped in the Lord.” This morning watch is the end of night; from there until night my soul hoped in the Lord. Therefore we must understand this so that we do not suppose that we are to hope in the Lord for only one day: “From the morning watch until night.” What, then, do you think this means, brothers? “From the morning watch until night, my soul hoped in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1700] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and Louvain read: “What, then, do you think this means, ‘from the morning watch’?” M.]: because the Lord, through whom our sins were forgiven, rose from the dead at the morning watch, so that we might hope that what occurred beforehand in the Lord would also occur in us.

Our sins have already been forgiven, but we have not yet risen. If we have not yet risen, what occurred beforehand in our Head has not yet been accomplished in us. What occurred beforehand in our Head? The flesh of that Head also rose; but surely the spirit of that Head did not die? Yet what died in him rose again. He rose on the third day, and in a certain sense the Lord said this to us: “What you have seen in me, hope for in yourselves”; that is, “Because I have risen, you too will rise.”

7. But some say: “Behold, the Lord has risen. Does that mean that I too should hope that I can rise?” Certainly; for the Lord rose in that which he received from you. [Col. 1701] He would not have risen unless he had died, and he would not have died unless he had borne flesh.

What did the Lord receive from you? Flesh. What did he himself bring? The Word of God, who existed before all things, through whom all things were made. But in order to receive something from you, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 3, 14). He received from you what he might offer for you, just as a priest receives from you what he may offer for you when you wish to appease God on account of your sins.

It has already happened; it happened in this way. Our Priest received from us what he was to offer for us: he received flesh from us. In that flesh he became a victim, became a burnt offering, became a sacrifice. In his passion he became the sacrifice; in his resurrection he renewed what had been slain, and, as it were, gave it to God as your firstfruits. He said to you: “All that is yours has now been consecrated, since such firstfruits from you have been given to God. Therefore hope that what preceded in your firstfruits will also occur in you.”

8. Therefore, because he rose from the morning watch, our soul began to hope from that moment. And until when? Until night—until we die. For all our bodily death is, as it were, sleep.

You began to hope from the time when the Lord rose. Do not cease hoping until you depart from this life. For if you do not hope until night, everything you had hoped for is lost.

There are people who begin to hope but do not persevere until night. They begin to suffer tribulations and temptations; they see wicked and unjust people enjoying temporal prosperity. Since they had hoped for such things from the Lord—that they would be happy here—they notice that those who have committed crimes possess what they themselves desired to possess. Their feet falter, and they cease to hope. Why? Because they did not begin to hope from the morning watch.

What does this mean? They did not begin to hope from the Lord for what had preceded in the Lord from that morning watch. Instead, they hoped that, if they were Christians, their houses would be full of grain, wine, oil, silver, and gold; that none of them would die prematurely; that whoever had no children would receive them; that whoever had not married would marry; that not only would no woman in his household miscarry, but not even one of his animals; that his wine-casks would not turn sour, and that his vineyard would not be struck by hail.

The one who hoped in the Lord in this way noticed that those who did not worship the Lord abounded in such things. His feet faltered (Psalm 72:2–3), and he did not hope until night, because he had not begun to hope from the morning watch.

9. Who, then, begins to hope from the morning watch in this way? The one who hopes from the Lord for what he began to display at the morning watch when he rose. Before then no one had risen to live forever.

Let your Charity attend. The dead were raised before the Lord’s coming: Elijah also raised a dead man (1 Kings 17:22), and Elisha did likewise (2 Kings 4:35). But they rose only to die again. Those whom the Lord himself raised also rose to die: whether the young son of the widow (Luke 7:15), or the twelve-year-old girl, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue (Luke 8:55), or Lazarus (John 11:44). They were raised in a different way, all destined to die; they were born once but died twice.

[Col. 1702]

No one had risen never to die again except the Lord. When, then, did the Lord rise never again to die? At the morning watch.

Hope this also from the Lord: that you will rise—not as Lazarus rose, nor as the widow’s son or the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter rose, nor as those whom the ancient prophets raised—but hope that you will rise as the Lord rose, so that after the resurrection in which you rise, you will no longer fear dying. And you began to hope from the morning watch.

10. Hope, then, until night, until this life comes to an end, until the night of the entire human race arrives at the setting of the age. Why hope until then? Because after this night there will no longer be hope, but the reality itself.

“For hope that is seen is not hope,” the Apostle says; “for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25). If, then, we must patiently await what we do not see, let us hope until night—that is, until the end of this life or of the age.

When this night has passed, what we hoped for will come; and we will no longer hope, yet we will not be in despair. For lacking hope is considered blameworthy in those who despair, and sometimes we detest a person and say, “He has no hope.” Not having hope is not always evil. While we are in this life, it is evil not to have hope; for one who has no hope now will not possess the reality later. Therefore we ought to have hope now.

But when the reality has come, will there still be hope? “For what a person sees, why does he hope?” Our Lord God will come, first displaying to the human race the very form in which he was crucified and rose, so that the righteous and the impious alike may see him. The righteous will see and rejoice that they have found what they believed before seeing; the impious will be ashamed that they did not believe what they will see.

Those who are ashamed will be condemned, and those who rejoice will be crowned. It will be said to the confounded: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” It will be said to the joyful: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:41, 34). When they have received it, there will no longer be hope, because the reality will be possessed.

Thus, when hope has passed, that night will pass also; but until it happens, let our soul hope in the Lord from the morning watch.

11. He returns to the words: “From the morning watch let Israel hope in the Lord. From the morning watch until night, my soul hoped in the Lord.” But what did it hope for? [Note: [Col. 1702] The word “what” is absent from several manuscripts.] “From the morning watch let Israel hope in the Lord.” Let Israel not merely hope in the Lord, but let Israel hope from the morning watch.

Do I then condemn worldly hope when it is hoped for from God? No; Israel has another hope of its own. Let Israel not hope in riches as its supreme good, nor in bodily health, nor in an abundance of earthly things. Indeed, it will have tribulation here, if it happens to suffer some troubles on account of the truth.

The martyrs did hope in God, yet they suffered things such as robbers and wicked people suffer: they were exposed to beasts, burned in fires, struck by the sword, torn by claws, bound with chains, [Col. 1703] killed in prison. Having suffered all these evils, did they not hope in the Lord? Or did they hope for this—that, free from these evils, they might enjoy this life?

Certainly not, because they hoped from the morning watch. What does this mean? They considered that morning watch at which their Lord rose, and they saw that before he rose he himself had suffered such things as they were suffering. They therefore did not despair of rising after such sufferings to eternal life.

“Israel hoped in the Lord from the morning watch until night.”

12. [Verses 7–8.] “For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him is abundant redemption.” Magnificent! Nothing could have been said more appropriately, in response to what he had said: “From the morning watch let Israel hope in the Lord.”

Why? Because the Lord rose from the morning watch, and the body ought to hope for what occurred beforehand in the Head. But lest this thought be suggested: “The Head was able to rise because it was not burdened by sins; there was no sin in him. What are we to do? Shall we hope for a resurrection such as preceded in the Lord while we are weighed down by our sins?”—see what follows: “For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him is abundant redemption.
