And he himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities.”

Therefore, if it was weighed down by its own sins, God’s mercy is present. He went ahead without sin so that he might wipe away the sins of those who follow. Do not presume upon yourselves; presume upon the morning watch. See your Head risen and ascended into heaven. There was no guilt in him, but through him your guilt will be wiped away: “He himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities.”

Israel was able to sell itself and become sold under sin; it cannot redeem itself from its iniquities. He was able to redeem who was unable to sell himself. The one who committed no sin is himself the redeemer from sin.

“He himself will redeem Israel.” From what will he redeem it? From this iniquity or that one? “From all its iniquities.”

Let the person approaching God therefore not fear some of his iniquities. Let him approach with a full heart, cease doing what he used to do, and not say, “That iniquity will not be forgiven me.” If he says this, then, because of the very sin he thinks will not be forgiven him, he will not turn back; and by continuing to commit other sins, even what he did not fear will not be forgiven him.

“I have committed,” he says, “a great crime, and it cannot be forgiven me. I might as well commit the others too; for this is what I lose by not committing them.”

Do not fear. You are in the depths; do not disdain to cry to the Lord from the depths and say: “If you mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who will stand?” Look to him, await him, and endure for the sake of his law.

What law did he give you? “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Hope that you will rise, and that then you will be entirely without sin, since the one who was first without sin has risen. Hope from the morning watch. Do not say, “Because of my sins I am not worthy.” You are not worthy; but “with him there is abundant redemption,” and “he himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 130

[Col. 1704]

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. In this psalm the humility of God’s servant and faithful person is commended to us. Through his voice the whole body of Christ sings. We have often reminded your Charity that this should not be understood as the voice of one individual singing, but of all who are in Christ’s body. Since all are in his body, he speaks as one person; and he is one who is also many.

For many are many in themselves, but they are one in him who is one. This is also the temple of God, of which the Apostle says: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17)—all who believe in Christ, and believe in such a way that they love him.

For this is what it means to believe in Christ: to love Christ—not as the demons believed (James 2:19), though they did not love him. Therefore, although they believed, they said: “What have we to do with you, Son of God?” (Matthew 8:29).

Let us believe in such a way that we believe in him while loving him, and let us not say, “What have we to do with you?” but rather say, “We belong to you; you redeemed us.”

All who believe in this way are like living stones from which the temple of God is built (1 Peter 2:5), and like imperishable timbers from which that ark was constructed that could not be submerged in the flood (Genesis 6:14).

This temple—that is, the people themselves—is the place where God is entreated and hears. Whoever prays to God outside the temple of God is not heard with regard to the peace of the heavenly Jerusalem, even if he is heard with regard to certain temporal things, which God has also granted to pagans. For even the demons were heard and allowed to enter the pigs (Matthew 8:31–32).

To be heard with regard to eternal life is something else, and it is granted only to the one who prays in the temple of God. The one who prays in the temple of God is the one who prays in the peace of the Church, in the unity of Christ’s body. This body of Christ consists of the many believers throughout the whole world; therefore the one who prays in the temple is heard [Note: [Col. 1704] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and Louvain read “because.” M.].

For the one who prays in the peace of the Church prays in spirit and truth—not in that temple where there was a figure (John 4:21–24).

2. According to the figure, the Lord expelled from the temple those who sought their own interests—that is, those who went into the temple to buy and sell. But if that temple was a figure, it is clear that Christ’s body, which is the true temple of which the former was an image, also has buyers and sellers mixed within it—that is, people who seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21).

But they are driven out with a whip made of little cords. A cord signifies sins, as it is said through the prophet: “Woe to those who drag sins like a long garment” (Isaiah 5:18).

They drag sins like a long cord who add sins to sins. When they have committed one sin, they commit another to cover it. For just as, in order to make a cord, one strand of hemp is added to another, and it does not extend straight but is twisted, so all crooked deeds—which are sins—when they are added together, sin to sin and sin attached to sin, become a long cord.

[Col. 1705]

“Their paths are crooked, and their steps are twisted” (Job 6:18). What use is this cord except that one’s hands and feet may be bound with it and one may be cast into the outer darkness?

You remember what was said in the Gospel about a certain sinner: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 22:13). His hands and feet would not have been bound if he himself had not made the cord.

Therefore it is most plainly written elsewhere: “Each person is bound by the cords of his own sins” (Proverbs 5:22).

Since people are beaten because of their sins, the Lord therefore made a whip from cords and used it to drive from the temple all who sought their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ.

3. The voice in the Psalm belongs to this temple. In this temple, as I have said, God is entreated and hears in spirit and truth, not in that bodily temple. There was a shadow there in which what was to come was indicated; therefore that temple has now fallen.

Has the house of our prayer therefore fallen? Far from it. For the temple that fell cannot be called the house of prayer of which it was said: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations.”

You have heard what the Lord Jesus Christ said: “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations’; but you have made it a den of robbers” (Matthew 21:12–13; and John 2:14–16).

Did those who wished to make the house of God a den of robbers thereby cause the temple to collapse? In the same way, those who live wickedly in the Catholic Church, insofar as it lies within them, wish to make the house of God a den of robbers; but they do not therefore overthrow the temple.

For the time will come when they will be cast out because of the cord of their sins.

This temple of God, this body of Christ, this congregation of the faithful, has one voice, and as one person it sings in the Psalm. We have already heard its voice in many psalms; let us hear it in this one also.

If we wish, it is our voice. If we wish, we hear the singer with our ears and sing with our hearts. But if we do not wish this, we will be in that temple like buyers and sellers—that is, seeking our own interests. We enter the Church, but not for those things that please God’s eyes.

Let each person among you therefore see how he listens: whether he listens and mocks; whether he listens and puts it behind him; or whether he listens and harmonizes—that is, recognizes his own voice here and joins the voice of his heart to the voice of this psalm.

Nevertheless, the voice of this psalm does not fall silent. Let those who can—in fact, those who wish to—be instructed; let those who do not wish to be instructed not hinder others.

Let humility be commended to us. From there it began.

4. [Verse 1.] “Lord, my heart is not exalted.” He offered a sacrifice. How do we know that he offered a sacrifice? Because humility of heart is a sacrifice.

It is said in another psalm: “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it.” He very much wished to do something for God on account of his sins; he wished to appease him so that he might receive forgiveness of sins. And, as though seeking something with which to appease him, he says: “If you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings.”

Therefore he was seeking superfluously either rams, or bulls, or some such victim by which God might be appeased.

What, then? Since God does not delight in burnt offerings, does he not accept sacrifice, and is he appeased without sacrifice? If there is no sacrifice, there is no priest. But if we have [Note: [Col. 1706] Louvain: “but we have.” M.] a priest in heaven who intercedes for us with the Father—“For he entered into the Holy of Holies, within the veil, where the priest entered figuratively only once a year; so also the Lord was offered once for all time. He offered himself; he is priest and victim; and he entered into the Holy of Holies once” (Hebrews 9), and now he does not die, nor will death rule over him again (Romans 6:9)—we are secure because we have a Priest. Let us offer a sacrifice there also.

Let us see what sacrifice we ought to offer, since our God does not delight in burnt offerings, as you heard in the psalm. But what follows explains and shows what he offers: “A sacrifice to God is a spirit troubled; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 50:18–19).

If, then, a humbled heart is a sacrifice to God, the one who said, “Lord, my heart is not exalted,” offered a sacrifice.

See him offering in this way elsewhere: he says to God, “See my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (Psalm 24:18).

5. “Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up on high; I have not entered into great things, nor into things too wonderful for me.”

Let this be stated and heard more plainly: “I was not proud. I did not wish to become known among people as though I were engaged in wonderful things. I did not seek anything beyond my strength by which I might boast before the uninstructed.”

Let your Charity attend. A great matter is being commended. That magician Simon wished to enter into things wonderful beyond himself; for this reason the power of the Apostles pleased him more than the righteousness of Christians.

When he saw that through the laying on of the Apostles’ hands and through their prayers God gave the Holy Spirit to believers, and that the coming of the Holy Spirit was then demonstrated by a miracle, so that all upon whom the Holy Spirit came spoke in languages they had not learned—this does not mean that the Holy Spirit is not now given because those who believe do not speak in languages. At that time it was necessary for them to speak in languages so that they might signify that all languages would believe in Christ. Once what was signified had been fulfilled, the miracle was removed.

When Simon saw this, he wished to perform such things, not to become such a person. And you know that he even thought that the Holy Spirit could be purchased with money.

He was therefore one of those who enter the temple to buy and sell. He wished to buy what he intended to sell. And truly, my brothers, because he was such a person, he had entered among them in this spirit.

The Lord expelled from the temple those who sold doves; [Col. 1707] the dove signifies the Holy Spirit. Simon therefore wished to buy a dove and sell a dove. The Lord Jesus Christ, who dwelt in Peter, came and drove the evil merchant out with a whip of cords (Acts 8:18–23).

6. There are therefore people who delight in performing miracles and demand miracles from those who have made progress in the Church. Those who think that they themselves have made progress wish to perform such things and suppose that they do not belong to God if they have not performed them.

But the Lord our God, who knows what he should give to each person and how the body’s structure may be preserved in peace, addresses the Church through the Apostle: “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you’; nor again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need of you.’ If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If the whole body were hearing, where would smell be?”

Therefore, brothers, you see in our members how each member has its own function. The eye sees but does not hear; the ear hears but does not see; the hand works but neither hears nor sees; the foot walks but neither hears nor sees nor does what the hand does.

But if there is health in one body, and the members do not quarrel against one another, the ear sees in the eye, and the eye hears in the ear. Nor can the ear be reproached because it does not see, so that someone might say to it: “You are nothing; you are inferior. Can you see and distinguish colors as the eye does?”

The ear responds from the peace of the body and says: “I am where the eye is; I am in the same body. In myself I do not see, but in the one with whom I am I see.”

Thus, when the ear says, “The eye sees for me”; the eye says, “The ear hears for me”; the eyes and ears say, “The hands work for us”; the hands say, “The eyes and ears see and hear for us”; and the eyes, ears, and hands say, “The feet walk for us”—when all work together in one body [Note: [Col. 1707] Several manuscripts read “cooperate”], if there is health there and the members are in harmony, they rejoice and rejoice together.

If there is some discomfort in one member, they do not abandon one another but suffer together.

When the foot, which seems to be far from the eyes in the body—for the eyes are placed high, while the feet are positioned below—happens to step on a thorn, do the eyes abandon it? No. As we see, the whole body contracts; the person sits down; his back bends as he searches for the thorn that has pierced the sole.

All the members do whatever they can so that the thorn stuck in a low and insignificant place may be removed.

So, brothers, whoever in Christ’s body cannot raise the dead should not seek that gift, but should seek not to be discordant in the body [Note: [Col. 1707] Several manuscripts omit “but should seek”]. For just as the ear would become discordant if it sought to see, so would he. What he has not received, he cannot do.

But if someone objects and says, “If you were righteous, you would raise the dead, as Peter did”—for the Apostles seem to have done greater things in Christ than the Lord himself (John 14:12)—how can branches be more powerful than the root?

How, then, did they seem to do greater things than he? At the Lord’s voice the dead rose; at Peter’s passing shadow a dead man rose (Acts 5:15). This seems greater than the other.

But Christ could do this without Peter; Peter could do nothing except in Christ: “For without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

When the person who is making progress hears this, as though it were an accusation brought by ignorant pagans, by people who do not know what they are saying, let him respond within the structure of Christ’s body:

“You who say, ‘You are not righteous because you do not perform miracles’—you could also say to the ear, ‘You are not in the body because you do not see.’”

“You should do it too” [Note: [Col. 1708] Louvain reads: “do.” M.], he says, “as Peter did.”

“But Peter did it for me also, because I am in the body in which Peter acted. In that body, I can do what it can do, for I am not separated from it. What I can do less, it suffers with me; and what it can do more, I rejoice in.”

The Lord himself cried out from above on behalf of his body: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). No one was touching him, but the Head cried from heaven on behalf of the body laboring on earth.

7. If, then, brothers, each person justly does what he can, and does not envy what another can do more, but rejoices with him as one constituted with him in one body, this voice of the Psalm belongs to him: “Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up on high; I have not entered into great things, nor into things too wonderful for me.”

“For what exceeded my strength,” he says, “I did not seek; I did not stretch myself into that sphere; I did not wish to magnify myself there.”

How greatly this exaltation arising from an abundance of graces must be feared, lest anyone become proud of God’s gift, but instead preserve humility and do what is written: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Sirach 3:20).

How greatly pride in God’s gift must be feared should be commended again and again to your Charity, especially since the brevity of the Psalm allows us to speak.

The Apostle Paul, although he was made a preacher from being a persecutor, received more abundant grace in all his apostolic labor than the other Apostles, so that God might show more clearly that what he gives belongs to him, not to man.

As doctors customarily display the power of their art in desperate cases, so the Lord Jesus Christ, our physician and savior, displayed the greatness of his art in one who was desperate—one who had been a persecutor of the Church—in order not only to make him a Christian but also an Apostle; and not merely an Apostle, but, as he himself says, one who labored more than all the others (1 Corinthians 15:10).

He therefore received an exceedingly great grace.

And you see, brothers, that now in the Church the letters of the Apostle Paul are in use more than those of his fellow Apostles. The others did not write but merely spoke in the Church. For writings circulated by those in error under their names are rejected because they are not theirs and are not accepted by the Church. Others who did write did not write with such abundant or such great grace.

Since he possessed great grace and had received great gifts from God, what does he say in one place? “So that I might not be exalted by the greatness of the revelations”—pay attention; I am telling you something fearful—“so that I might not be exalted by the greatness of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me.”

What does this mean, brothers? So that he would not be exalted like a young man, he was buffeted like a child. And by whom? By an angel of Satan.

What does this mean? He was handed over to be violently afflicted by some bodily pain. Bodily pains are often inflicted by angels of Satan, but they can do this only when permitted. Thus holy Job was tested in this way. Satan was permitted to test him, and he struck him with a wound so that he rotted with worms. The unclean one was permitted, but the holy man was tested [Col. 1709] (Job 2:6–7).

The devil does not know what good comes from him, even when he rages. Raging, he entered the heart of Judas (John 13:27); raging, he handed Christ over; raging, he crucified him. And when Christ had been crucified, the world was redeemed.

Behold, the devil’s rage harmed the devil but benefited us. By raging, he lost those whom he held, redeemed by the Lord’s blood, which he shed in his rage. If he had known the great loss he would suffer, he would not have poured out upon the earth the price by which the human race was redeemed.

Thus that angel of Satan was permitted, as it were willingly, to buffet the Apostle; yet the Apostle was being healed.

And because what the physician had applied was troublesome to the sick man, he asked the physician to remove it. When a physician applies some strong, irritating, and burning poultice to the intestines, from which the swollen intestines will nevertheless be healed, and the patient begins to burn and suffer from the medicine, he asks the physician to remove it. But the physician comforts him and urges him to be patient, because he knows how beneficial what he has applied is.

So the Apostle continues and says, after he had said, “There was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me.” He had already stated why: “So that I might not be exalted by the greatness of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me.”

“For this reason,” he says, “I pleaded with the Lord three times that he might remove it from me.” This is to say: “I asked the physician to remove from me the troublesome poultice he had applied.”

But hear the physician’s voice: “And he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).

“I know what I have applied; I know from what you are sick; I know from what you will be healed.”

8. If, then, dearest brothers, the Apostle Paul could be exalted by the greatness of revelations unless he received an angel of Satan to buffet him, who could be secure about himself?

The one who has received less seems to walk more safely, provided that he does not perversely seek what he has not rightly received. Let him seek what without which he cannot be in Christ’s body, or without which he fares badly there.

A healthy finger is safer in the body than an inflamed eye. The finger is a small thing; the eye is magnificent and capable of much. Yet it is better to be a finger and be healthy than to be an eye and be troubled, inflamed, and blinded.

Therefore let no one seek anything in Christ’s body except health. According to his health, let him have faith. Through faith his heart is cleansed; through cleansing of heart he will see that face of which it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

The one who performed miracles and the one who did not perform miracles in Christ’s body ought to rejoice in nothing except the face of God.

The Apostles returned and said to the Lord, after they had been sent out by him: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.”

The Lord saw that pride arising from the power of miracles was tempting them. He who had come as a physician to heal our swellings and bear our weaknesses immediately said: “Do not rejoice in this, that the demons are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:17, 20).

Not all good Christians cast out demons; nevertheless, all their names are written in heaven. [Col. 1710] He did not wish them to rejoice in what they possessed uniquely, but in what they shared with the others: their salvation. He wished the Apostles to rejoice in what you also rejoice in.

Let your Charity attend. No believer has hope if his name is not written in heaven. The names of all the faithful who love Christ and humbly walk in his way, which he himself taught in humility, are written in heaven.

The name of every contemptible person in the Church who believes in Christ, loves Christ, and cherishes Christ’s peace is written in heaven—the name of anyone you may despise.

“And what resemblance is there between such a person and the Apostles, who performed so many miracles?” Yet the Apostles are restrained because they rejoiced in what was good in them personally, and they are commanded to rejoice in that from which even that contemptible person rejoices.

### 9. [verse 2]

Not without reason, my brothers, does he say with this humility, “Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up on high; neither have I entered upon great matters, nor upon things too wonderful for me.” If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul, “as one who has been taken from the milk, upon his mother, so be retribution upon my soul.” [Note: Col. 1710. Lov. has *ablactatus*, “weaned”; most manuscripts consistently have *ablatus*, “taken away,” a reading sometimes followed by Er.]

For he seems, as it were, to have bound himself under a curse. Just as elsewhere in the psalm he says, “Lord my God, if I have done this; if there is iniquity in my hands; if I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil, may I deservedly fall empty-handed before my enemies” (Ps. 7:4–5), and so forth, so here also he seems to have said: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul.” Come now, as though he were about to say, “Let that happen to me.” [Note: Col. 1710. Lov. omits *age*, “come now”; it is present in the other books.] Just as there: “If I repaid evil to those who repaid me evil, let this happen to me”—what? “May I deservedly fall empty-handed before my enemies”; so here also: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul, as one who has been taken from the milk, upon his mother, so let retribution be upon my soul.”

Pay attention. You know that to certain weak people the Apostle says, “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able to receive it; indeed, even now you are not able” (1 Cor. 3:2). There are weak people who are not fit for solid food. They want to stretch themselves toward what they cannot contain; and if they have somehow begun to grasp something—or if they have seemed to themselves to grasp what they have not grasped—they are lifted up by it and become proud. They seem wise to themselves.

This happens to all heretics. Although they were merely natural and carnal people, by defending their perverse opinions, which they were unable to see were false, they were excluded from the Catholic Church.

I shall say to your Charity what I can. You know that our Lord Jesus Christ is the Word of God, according to what John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” He is therefore bread; the angels live from him.

Behold, the bread is prepared for you; but grow from milk, so that you may reach the bread. And how, you ask, do I grow from milk? [Col. 1711] First believe firmly and hold fast to this: Christ was made for you according to your weakness.

How, then, does a mother act when she sees that her child is not yet fit to receive food? She gives the child the very foods themselves, but after they have passed through her flesh. For he himself is the bread by which the infant is nourished and by which its mother is also nourished; but the infant is not yet fit for the table, though it is fit for the breast. Thus the bread from the table passes through the mother’s breast, so that the same nourishment may reach the little infant.

So our Lord Jesus Christ, when he was the Word with the Father, through whom all things were made, and although he was “in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped” (Phil. 2:6)—the bread by which the angels could be nourished according to their capacity, from which the Powers and Virtues in heaven, intellectual spirits, were fed [Note: Am., Er., and the manuscripts read *spiritus*; Lov. omits it.]—while the weak human being, wrapped in flesh, lay upon the earth and could not reach the heavenly bread, so that “human beings might eat the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25), and manna might descend to the more genuine people of Israel: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1–3, 14).

### 10

Therefore the apostle Paul says this to those very weak people, whom he calls natural and carnal (1 Cor. 3:1): “Did I claim to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified?” (1 Cor. 2:2).

For Christ existed also without being crucified: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” And because that very Word became flesh, and that very Word was crucified—but he was not changed into a human being; rather, the human being was changed in him.

The human being was changed in him so as to become better than he was, not so that he might be converted into the very substance of the Word. [Note: Lov. reads, “so that the substance of the Word itself might be converted”; the other books disagree.]

Accordingly, in respect of what he was as a human being, God died; and in respect of what he was as God, the human being was raised, rose, and ascended into heaven. Whatever the human being suffered, it cannot be said that God did not suffer it, because, in assuming the human being, God was God; yet he was not changed into a human being. [Note: Four manuscripts add *homo* (“human being”) here.]

It is like this: you cannot say that you did not suffer an injury if your garment is torn. When you complain either to your friends or in court, you say this to the judge: “He tore me.” You do not say, “He tore my cloak,” but “He tore me.” If your garment could rightly be called “you,” although it is not you but your garment, how much more did the flesh of Christ—the temple of the Word, united with the Word—deserve to hear that whatever it suffered in the flesh, God himself suffered, although the Word could neither die, nor be corrupted, nor be changed, nor be killed, but whatever of these things was suffered, was suffered in the flesh?

And do not be surprised that the Word suffered nothing. Even the human soul cannot suffer anything when the flesh has been killed, as the Lord himself says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). If the soul cannot be killed, could the Word of God be killed?

And yet what does he say? “He scourged me, struck me with a blow, beat me, tore me apart.” None of this happens to the soul; and yet he says nothing but “me,” because of the unity of that fellowship.

### 11. [Col. 1712]

Our Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, being bread, made himself milk for us by becoming incarnate and appearing mortal. [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read, “made bread into milk for us, becoming incarnate and appearing to mortals.”] Thus death might be brought to an end in him, and we might not stray from the Word by believing that the Word became flesh.

Let us grow from this; let us be nourished by this milk. Before we are strong enough to receive the Word, let us not depart from faith in our milk.

But those heretics, wishing to argue about what they could not grasp, said that the Son is less than the Father, and said that the Holy Spirit is less than the Son. They established ranks and introduced three gods into the Church.

For they cannot deny that the Father is God; they cannot deny that the Son is God; they cannot deny that the Holy Spirit is God. But if the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, yet they are unequal and are not of the same substance, then there is not one God but three gods.

Arguing about what they could not grasp, they were lifted up in pride, and what is said in this psalm came to pass in them: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul, as one who has been taken from the milk, upon his mother, so let retribution be upon my soul.”

For the mother is the Church of God, from which they have separated themselves. There they ought to have been suckled and nourished, so that they might grow to receive the Word—God with God, equal to the Father in the form of God.

### 12

Those who before us expounded these matters seem to have discerned here another judgment and another meaning in these words. I shall not conceal it from your Charity.

They said this: Every proud person displeases God, and the human soul must humble itself lest it displease God; with all its heart it must attend to what is written: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things, and you will find favor before God” (Sir. 3:20).

But again there are certain people who, when they hear that they ought to be humble, abandon themselves and do not wish to learn anything, thinking that if they learn something they will become proud; and they remain only on milk. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “in their own milk.”]

Scripture reproves them, saying: “You have come to need milk, not solid food” (Heb. 5:12). God wishes us to be nourished with milk in such a way that we do not remain there, but, growing through milk, reach solid food.

A person therefore ought not to lift up his heart in pride, but ought to raise it toward the teaching of the Word of God. For if the soul were not to be raised, another verse of the psalm would not say: “To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul” (Ps. 24:1).

And unless the soul pours itself out beyond itself, it does not reach the vision of God and the knowledge of his unchangeable substance. For now, while it is still in the flesh, it is asked: “Where is your God?” Yet its God is within, and is within spiritually, and is spiritually exalted—not as though there were intervals of places, by which higher places are higher according to spatial intervals. For if such height were to be sought, the birds would surpass us in reaching God.

God is therefore high within, and high spiritually; nor does the soul reach out to touch him unless it passes beyond itself. For whatever you think about God according to the body, you are greatly mistaken.

You are very much an infant [Col. 1713] if you think of God even according to the human soul—if you think that God either forgets, or thinks in such a way that he becomes foolish, or does something and then repents. All these things are set forth in Scripture so that God might be commended to us as nursing infants; they are not there so that we should hear and understand them literally of him, as though God repented, or were now learning something he had not known, or understood what he had not understood, or remembered what he had forgotten. Such things belong to the soul, not to God.

Unless the soul therefore passes beyond even the measure of its own soul, it will not see that God is what he is—the one who said, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14).

Thus, when the man who was asked, “Where is your God?” sought him, what did he say? “My tears have become my bread day and night, while they say to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” But what did he do in order to find his God? “I meditated on these things,” he says, “and poured out my soul upon myself” (Ps. 41:4–5). In order to find God, he poured out his soul beyond himself.

You are not therefore told, “Be humble,” so that you may not think. Be humble because of pride; be lofty because of wisdom.

Hear a clear statement on this matter: “Do not become children in your minds; but be infants in wickedness, so that you may be mature in your minds” (1 Cor. 14:20).

Surely, my brothers, it has been explained where God wants us to be humble and where he wants us to be lofty: humble in order to avoid pride, lofty in order to receive wisdom.

Be suckled, so that you may be nourished; be nourished so that you may grow; grow so that you may eat bread. For when you begin to eat bread, you will be weaned—that is, you will no longer need milk, but solid food.

And this is what he seems to have said: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul”—that is, if I were little not in mind but in wickedness. Signifying this, he said the preceding words: “Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up on high; neither have I entered upon great matters, nor upon things too wonderful for me.” Behold: I was little in wickedness.

But because I was not little in understanding: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul,” let what is repaid to the little one who is weaned from his mother be repaid to me, so that now I may be fit to eat bread.

### 13

This interpretation, then, my brothers, is not displeasing, because it is not contrary to the faith. Yet I am troubled because it does not merely say, “As one who has been taken from the milk, so let retribution be upon my soul”; it adds, “As one who has been taken from the milk upon his mother, so let retribution be upon my soul.”

Here something of this sort occurs to me, so that I see it as a curse. For it is not an infant who is weaned, but one already somewhat grown. The one who is weak in earliest infancy—the true stage of infancy—is upon his mother; if he is taken from the milk, he perishes. It was therefore not without reason that “upon his mother” was added.

Everyone may be weaned by growing. For one who grows and is thus weaned, it is beneficial; but for one who is still upon his mother, it is harmful.

We must therefore beware and fear, brothers, lest anyone be weaned before the proper time. Every grown child is separated from milk; but let no one be separated from milk while he is still upon his mother.

When he is carried in his mother’s hands [Col. 1714]—he who was carried in the womb—for he was carried in the womb so that he might be born, and is carried in her hands so that he may grow, he needs milk; he is still upon his mother.

Let him not therefore wish to exalt his soul at the time when he is perhaps not yet fit to receive food, but let him fulfill the commands of humility. He has a place in which to exercise himself: let him believe in Christ, so that he may be able to understand Christ.

He cannot see the Word; he cannot grasp the equality of the Word with the Father; he cannot yet see the equality of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Word. Let him believe this and suck. [Note: So Am. Er. and the manuscripts; Lov. reads, “that is, let him rise.”]

He is secure, because when he has grown, he will eat what he could not eat before he grew by suckling. And he has room in which to stretch himself.

“Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you”—that is, matters which you are not yet sufficiently fit to grasp.

“And what shall I do?” you ask. “Shall I remain this way?” But “think continually about the commands the Lord has given you” (Sir. 3:22).

What has the Lord commanded you? Show mercy. Do not abandon the peace of the Church. Do not place your hope in a human being. Do not tempt God by seeking miracles.

If there is already fruit in you, you understand that you must tolerate the weeds along with the good grain until the harvest (Matt. 13:30), because you may be with the wicked for a time, but not forever. The chaff is mixed with you here, in this age, upon the threshing floor; it will not be with you in the granary.

Think continually about these things that the Lord has commanded you. You will not be separated from milk as long as you are upon your mother; do not die of hunger before you are fit to eat bread.

Grow. [Note: Lov. reads, “you will grow,” against the other printed editions and the manuscripts.] Your strength will become firm, and you will see what you could not see and grasp what you could not grasp.

### 14

What then? When I see what I could not see and grasp what I could not grasp, will I now be secure? Will I be perfect? No—not as long as you live here.

Our perfection is humility itself.

You heard how the apostolic reading concluded, if it has remained in your memory: how the one who received a blow lest he be exalted by revelations—so many things were revealed to him!—received an angel of Satan because of the greatness of his revelations, since he might otherwise have been exalted. And yet, to whom so many things were revealed, what did he say?

“Brothers, I do not consider myself to have apprehended it” (Phil. 3:13). Paul says, “Brothers, I do not consider myself to have apprehended it”—he who received the angel of Satan to strike him lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations.

Who dares to say that he has comprehended? Behold, Paul did not apprehend, and says, “I do not consider myself to have apprehended.” And what do you say, Paul? “I am still running,” he says, “so that I may apprehend.” [Note: Most manuscripts read, “And what are you doing, Paul? For this I am running,” and so forth.]

Paul is still on the way, and you think that you are already in your homeland?

“But one thing,” he says: “Forgetting what lies behind”—do this also, and forget your former wicked life. If vanity once delighted you, let it no longer delight you.

“Forgetting what lies behind,” he says, “and stretching forward to what lies ahead, according to my aim I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus.”

I hear the voice of God from above, and I run to apprehend. He has not allowed me to remain on the way, because he does not cease to address me.

Therefore, [Col. 1715] brothers, God does not cease to address us. For if he ceases, what is it that we are doing? What are the divine readings and divine hymns doing?

Forget, then, what lies behind, and stretch yourselves toward what lies ahead. Suck milk so that you may grow toward food. When you have reached your homeland, you will rejoice.

And continue to attend to the Apostle as he pursues the prize of the heavenly calling. For he says: “Therefore, let those of us who are perfect think this way.” He says, “I am not speaking to the imperfect, to whom I cannot yet speak wisdom, who are still given milk to drink and are not fed solid food; I am speaking to those who already eat solid food.”

They now seem to be perfect because they understand the equality of the Word with the Father; yet they do not yet see it as it must be seen, face to face, but only in part and in a mirror dimly (1 Cor. 13:12).

Let them therefore run; for when the way has been completed, then we shall return to our homeland. Let them run; let them stretch themselves.

“Therefore, let those of us who are perfect think this way; and if you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you” (Phil. 3:12–15). [Note: Some manuscripts read *vita*, “life,” rather than *via*, “way.”]

If perhaps you are mistaken about something, why do you not return to your mother’s milk? For if you do not exalt yourselves, if you do not lift up your heart, if you do not enter upon things too wonderful for you, but preserve humility, God will reveal to you that you think differently.

But if you wish to defend what you think differently, to assert it obstinately and against the peace of the Church, this saying becomes a curse for you: while you are upon your mother, you are separated from the milk outside; [Note: So some manuscripts; the editions read, “you will be separated.”] outside the mother’s womb you will die of hunger.

But if you persevere in Catholic peace, and if perhaps you think differently from what ought to be thought, God will reveal it to you in your humility.

Why? Because “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6; 1 Pet. 5:5).

### 15. [verse 3]

Therefore this psalm concluded with this: “Let Israel hope in the Lord, from this time now and forever.”

For what is written in Greek, ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν καὶ ἕως τοῦ αἰῶνος, has been rendered, “from this time now and forever.” But the word *age* does not always signify this present age; sometimes it signifies eternity. For “forever” is understood in two ways: “unto eternity,” either always without end, or until we come to eternity.

How, then, is it to be understood here? Let us hope in the Lord God until we come to eternity; for when we have come to eternity, there will no longer be hope, but the thing itself.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 131

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1. [verses 1–2]

It was indeed right, most beloved, that we should rather listen to my fellow bishop, who is present among us all. [Note: We have thought that Severus, bishop of Milevis, is being praised here, in view of the sermon on Ps. 95, §§1 and 5.]

Even now he did not refuse, but postponed it; and therefore I announce this to your Charity, so that you may hold him to his promise together with me.

It was not inappropriate for your Charity that I should first obey the one giving the command. For he compelled [Col. 1716] me to be his hearer today, on the understanding that I too am his, because in that very charity we are all his hearers, while we have one Master in heaven (Matt. 23:10).

Direct your attention, then, to the psalm which, as you know, we have undertaken to expound in order. It too bears the title “A Song of Ascents,” and is somewhat longer than the others under the same title.

Let us not therefore linger, except where necessity compels us, so that, if the Lord permits, we may explain the whole. You too ought not to hear everything as though you were inexperienced; something from your previous hearings ought also to help us, so that it is not necessary for everything to be said by us as though it were new.

And indeed we ought to be new, because old age ought not to creep over us [Note: Am., Er., and most manuscripts read *nobis* (“over us”); Lov. reads *novis* (“new”).]; but we must also grow and make progress. Concerning this very progress the Apostle says: “Although our outward person is being corrupted, our inward person is being renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16).

Let us not make progress in such a way that we become old from being new; rather, let this very newness grow.

### 2

“Remember, Lord, David, and all his meekness. As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.”

According to the historical reality, David was one man, king of Israel, the son of Jesse. He too was meek, as divine Scripture indicates and commends him; and he was so meek that he did not repay evil with evil even to his persecutor Saul.

He preserved such humility toward him that he acknowledged Saul as king and himself as a dog. Although he was more powerful in God’s sight, he did not answer the king insolently or proudly; rather, he sought to appease him by humility instead of provoking him by pride.

Saul was even delivered into his power, and this by the Lord God, so that he might do with him whatever he wished. But because he had not been commanded to kill him, and had merely been placed in his power—for a human being is permitted to use his own power—he turned what God had granted him toward gentleness instead.

If he had wished to kill him, he would have been rid of his enemy; but how then would he say, “Forgive me my debts, as I also forgive my debtors” (Matt. 6:12)?

Saul entered a cave where David was, not knowing that David was there. He had entered to attend to the needs of his belly. David rose quietly and slowly behind him and cut off a piece of his garment, which he showed him, so that Saul might know that David had had him in his power, yet had spared him not from necessity but by his own will, and had not wished to kill him (1 Sam. 24:4–15).

Perhaps it was this very meekness that the psalm now commends when it says, “Remember, Lord, David, and all his meekness.” This is according to the historical truth contained, as we have said, in divine Scripture.

But in the psalms, as in all prophecy, we are accustomed not to attend only to the letter, but to search through the letter for mysteries.

And your Charity remembers that in all the psalms we are accustomed to hear the voice of a certain person who has both a head and a body. The head is in heaven, the body on earth; but where the head has gone before, the body will follow.

I shall not now say who the head is or who the body is, for I am speaking to those who know.

### 3

David’s humility, then, is commended; David’s meekness is commended; and God is told, “Remember, Lord, David, and all his meekness.”

For what purpose, [Col. 1717] Lord, remember David? “As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.”

Remember him, therefore, so that he may fulfill what he promised.

David himself made a vow as though he possessed the power, and asks God to fulfill what he vowed. There is the devotion of the one making the vow, but there is also the humility of the one who begs.

Let no one presume to repay by his own strength what he has vowed. The one who encourages you to vow is himself the one who helps you fulfill it.

Let us see, then, what he vowed; and from this we shall understand how David is to be taken figuratively.

David is interpreted as “Strong of hand.” For he was a great warrior. Trusting in the Lord his God, he fought all his battles and struck down all his enemies, with God helping him, in accordance with the administration of that kingdom.

Yet he prefigured someone strong of hand for the defeat of enemies—the devil and his angels. The Church defeats these enemies.

And how does she defeat them? By meekness.

By meekness our own King conquered the devil. The devil raged; Christ endured. The one who raged was conquered; the one who endured conquered.

In this meekness the body of Christ, which is the Church, conquers its enemies. Let it be strong of hand; by its works let it conquer.

But since the body of Christ is both temple, house, and city, and the one who is the head of the body is also inhabitant of the house, sanctifier of the temple, and king of the city, as the Church is all those things, so Christ is all these things.

What, then, do we vow to God except that we are to be God’s temple? We can offer him nothing more pleasing than to say to him what is said in Isaiah: “Possess us” (Isa. 26:13).

Indeed [Note: Lov. reads *equidem* (“indeed”); B. and M. read *et quidem* (“and indeed”).], in the case of earthly possessions, a gift is made to the head of a household when possession is given to him. But possession is not like this when it is the Church; rather, the possession itself is given the privilege of being possessed by such a master.

### 4

What, then, does he say? “As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.”

Let us see what vow this was. [Note: Here the editions repeat the words already given six lines earlier, “that we may be God’s temple. We can offer him nothing more pleasing,” and then add, “than to swear” or “than to vow.” These words are not present in all the manuscripts.]

To swear is to promise firmly. Attend to this vow: with what ardor he made it, with what love, with what desire. Yet in order to fulfill it he begged the Lord, saying, “Remember, Lord, David, and all his meekness.”

In this meekness he made his vow, that he might be God’s house:

“If I enter into the tabernacle of my house, if I climb upon the bed of my couch; if I give sleep to my eyes”—it seemed too little to say, “sleep to my eyes”—“and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.”

Where was he seeking a place for the Lord? If he was meek, he was seeking it in himself.

For what is the Lord’s place? Hear the prophet: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest? Upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words” (Isa. 66:2).

Do you wish to be the Lord’s place? Be humble and quiet, trembling at the words of God, and you yourself will become what you seek. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “what you seek in another.”]

For if what you seek does not come to be in you, what benefit is it to you in another?

God sometimes works through an evangelist for the salvation of another alone, if the evangelist speaks and does not act; through his tongue [Col. 1718] another person becomes a place for the Lord, but he himself does not become the Lord’s place.

But one who does well what he teaches, and teaches in that way, becomes a place for the Lord together with the one he teaches, because all believers make one place for the Lord.

The Lord has his place in the heart, because there is one heart among all who are joined together in love.

### 5

How many thousands believed, my brothers, when they placed the prices of their possessions at the feet of the Apostles! But what does Scripture say about them?

Certainly they became God’s temple—not merely each one individually God’s temple, but all of them together God’s temple. Thus they became a place for the Lord.

And so that you may know that one place was made for the Lord in them all, Scripture says: “They had one soul and one heart directed toward God” (Acts 2:41; 4:4, 32, 35).

But many, so as not to make a place for the Lord, seek their own things, love their own things, rejoice in their own power, and desire what is private.

One who wishes to make a place for the Lord ought to rejoice not in what is private but in what is common.

They made their private possessions common. What they possessed, did they lose? If they had possessed things alone, and each person had possessed what was his own, each would have had only what he possessed. But when he made what was his own common, the things that belonged to the others also became his.

Let your Charity pay attention: because of the things each of us possesses individually, there arise quarrels, enmities, disputes, wars among human beings, disturbances, disagreements against one another, scandals, sins, iniquities, and murders.

Because of what? Because of the very things each of us possesses individually.

Do we quarrel because of the things we possess in common? We all breathe this air in common; we all see the sun in common.

Blessed, therefore, are those who make a place for the Lord in such a way that they do not rejoice in what is private.

This is the kind of person the psalmist was describing when he said, “If I enter into the tabernacle of my house.” This was something private.

He knew that what was private hindered him from making a place for the Lord, and he mentions the things that pertained to himself: “I will not enter into the tabernacle of my house until I find”—what? Once you have found a place for the Lord, will you enter your tabernacle? Or will that itself be your tabernacle, where you have found a place for the Lord? [Note: Some manuscripts read, “Will he himself be your tabernacle?”]

Why? Because you yourself will be the Lord’s place, and with those who are the Lord’s place you will be one.

### 6

Let us therefore abstain, brothers, from possessing private property—or, if we cannot abstain from possessing it, from loving it—and we shall make a place for the Lord.

“It is too much for me,” someone says.

But consider who you are [Note: Er., Lugd., and Ven. read *quid sis*, “what you are”; M. reads *quis sis*, “who you are.”] if you are going to make a place for the Lord. If some senator wished to stay as a guest with you—not the senator himself, but the steward of some important person according to this world—and said, “Something in your house offends me,” even if you loved that thing, you would nevertheless remove it so as not to offend the person whose friendship you sought.

And what benefit would a human being’s friendship bring you? Perhaps you would find there not only no assistance but even danger. For many people were not in danger before they joined themselves to the great; they desired the friendship of the powerful in order to incur greater dangers.

Seek the friendship of Christ without fear. He wishes to stay as a guest with you; make a place for him.

What does it mean, “Make a place for him”? [Col. 1719] Do not love yourself; love him.

If you love yourself, you close the door against him. If you love him, you open it to him. But if you open it and he enters, you will not perish by loving yourself; rather, you will be found together with the one who loves you.

### 7. [verse 3]

“If I enter into the tabernacle of my house, if I climb upon the bed of my couch.”

For private property itself, where a person rests, makes people proud. Therefore he said, “If I climb.”

In the thing that each person possesses privately, he necessarily becomes proud. From there a human being stretches himself against another human being, although both are flesh.

What is a human being, brothers? Flesh. And what is another human being? Another piece of flesh.

And yet rich flesh stretches itself against poor flesh—as though that flesh had brought something with it when it was born, or would take something away when it dies.

It had this advantage over the other: that it could swell more. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “so that it might fear more.”]

But the one who wishes to find a place for the Lord says, “If I climb upon the bed of my couch.”

### 8. [verse 4]

“If I give sleep to my eyes.”

For many people, when they sleep, do not make a place for the Lord. The Apostle awakens such people: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will illumine you” (Eph. 5:14). And elsewhere: “But since we belong to the day, let us be watchful and sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who become drunk, become drunk at night” (1 Thess. 5:5–8).

He calls the iniquity in which they fall asleep while desiring earthly things “night.”

And all those worldly prosperities that seem to exist are dreams of sleeping people. Just as one who sees treasures in a dream is rich while sleeping but will awaken and be poor, so people rejoice in their sleep over all these empty things of this age.

They will awaken when they do not wish to, if they do not awaken now when it is beneficial. They will discover that those things were dreams and have passed away, as Scripture says: “Like a dream of one awakening” (Ps. 72:20).

And elsewhere: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:6).

They slept their sleep; the sleep ended, and they found nothing in their hands, because in dreams they had seen passing riches.

This person, then, who wishes to find a place for the Lord, also said, “If I give sleep to my eyes.”

But there are some who do not sleep, yet doze. They withdraw somewhat from the love of temporal things, and then roll back into it again; like people dozing, they repeatedly let their heads droop.

Awaken; shake off sleep. By dozing you are about to fall.

The psalm does not wish the person who seeks to find a place for the Lord to give sleep to his eyes or slumber to his eyelids.

### 9. [verse 5]

“And rest,” he says, “to my temples.”

From rest for the temples, sleep comes to the eyes. The temples are around the eyes. As sleep is about to come, the temples become heavy.

For the temples of people who are about to sleep begin to grow heavy; and when they feel their temples growing heavy, sleep is already near.

If rest is given to the eyes, they give rest to their temples, and sleep comes. If they do not give rest to their temples, sleep does not come.

When something temporal therefore begins to delight you toward sin, your temples are already becoming heavy.

Do you wish to remain awake, neither sleeping nor dozing? Do not entrust yourself [Col. 1720] to such delight; it will have greater pains than sweetnesses. [Note: So Am. and most manuscripts; Er. and Lov. read, “you will have.” A little later Lov. has “by this delight,” where the other editions and our manuscripts have “by this thought.”]

By rubbing your forehead, as it were, with this thought, you shake off sleep and prepare a place for the Lord.

### 10

“Until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.”

Although sometimes God’s tabernacle is called God’s house, and God’s house God’s tabernacle, the distinction is nevertheless understood more precisely, most beloved brothers: the tabernacle is the Church according to this present time, while the house is the heavenly Church, the Jerusalem to which we shall go.

A tabernacle belongs to soldiers and combatants: soldiers’ tents are set up for battle and on campaign. Hence soldiers are called *contubernales*, as though they had and inhabited the same tents.

As long, therefore, as we have an enemy with whom we must fight, we make a tabernacle for God.

But when the time of battle has passed and that peace has come which surpasses all understanding, as the Apostle says, “the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4:7)—for however much you may think about that peace, the mind, still weighed down by the burden of the body, grasps less than it is—when that homeland has come [Note: Four manuscripts read, “when that has come, that homeland will already be,” and so forth.], it will already be the house. No adversary will tempt us, so that it should be called a tabernacle.

We shall not go forth to fight, but shall remain to praise.

For what is said about that house? “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5).

Here in the tabernacle we groan; in the house we shall praise.

Why? Because groaning belongs to those traveling abroad, while praise already belongs to those dwelling in their homeland.

Here, first, let a tabernacle be sought for the God of Jacob.

### 11. [verse 6]

“Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata.” What did we hear of? The dwelling-place of the Lord. “We heard of it in Ephrata. We found it in the fields of the forest.” Did he hear it there where he found it, or did he hear it in one place and find it in another? Let us therefore seek what Ephrata is, where he heard it; and likewise let us seek what “in the fields of the forest” means, where he found it.

Ephrata is a Hebrew word translated into Latin as “mirror,” as those have handed down who translated the Hebrew words placed in Scripture into another language, so that their meaning might reach us. For they translated from Hebrew into Greek, and from Greek it was translated for us into Latin. There were indeed people who kept watch over the Scriptures.

If, then, Ephrata means “mirror,” that house which was found in the fields of the forest was heard of in a mirror. A mirror bears an image: every prophecy is an image of things to come. Therefore the future house of God was proclaimed in the image of prophecy. We heard of it in the mirror—that is, “We heard of it in Ephrata.” “We found it in the fields of the forest.”

What are “the fields of the forest”? The fields of the woods. It does not mean what is commonly called a *saltus*, for example, an estate containing so many hundreds of acres. Properly, a *saltus* is a place still uncultivated and wooded. Indeed, some manuscripts read, “in the fields of the forest.”

What, then, were the fields of the forest except uncultivated nations? What were the fields of the forest except places where the thorns of idolatry still grew? Yet although the thorns of idolatry were there, there we found a place for the Lord, a dwelling-place for the God of Jacob. What was heard of in Ephrata was found in the fields of the forest; what was proclaimed in an image to the Jews was manifested in the faith of the Gentiles.

### 12. [verse 7]

“We shall enter into his dwellings” [Note: [Col. 1721] Am., Er., and several Mss., “we entered.” Lov., “we shall enter into the dwelling.” Other editions and most Mss., following the Greek LXX, “into the dwellings.”]—whose? Of the Lord God of Jacob.

Those who enter in order to dwell are themselves those who enter in order that they may be dwelt in. You enter your house so that you may dwell in it; you enter the house of God so that he may dwell in you. For the Lord is better: when he begins to dwell in you, he will make you blessed. But if you are not dwelt in by him, you will be miserable.

That son wanted to be in his own power who said, “Give me the share of the inheritance that belongs to me.” He was being kept safely with his father, lest he squander it with prostitutes. He received it, and it came under his control; he departed into a distant country and wasted everything with prostitutes. At last he suffered hunger and remembered his father; he returned so that he might be filled with bread (Luke 15:12–20).

Enter, therefore, so that you may be dwelt in; and do not belong to yourself, but to him: “We shall enter into his dwellings.”

### 13

“We shall worship” [Note: [Col. 1721] Several manuscripts, “we worshipped.”] “in the place where his feet stood.” Whose feet? The Lord’s, or those of the Lord’s house? For the house of the Lord is the place where he says that he ought to be worshiped. “We shall worship in the place where his feet stood.”

Apart from his house, God does not hear anyone unto eternal life. For that person belongs to the house of God who is joined in love to the living stones. But whoever does not have love causes a collapse; and when that person collapses, the house remains standing. Let no one threaten the house in which he has begun to be, as it were, a stone, as though he could harm the house by deciding to fall.

The first Jewish people had likewise grown proud, saying: “God will not defraud our father Abraham, to whom he promised so much from his offspring.” They did everything evil as though they were secure in God’s promise, believing that he would spare them—not on account of the merits of those committing crimes, but on account of Abraham’s merits—and would gather whatever sort of wicked children of Abraham into his house unto eternal life.

But what does John say? “Brood of vipers.” When those very children of Abraham came to him to be baptized in the water of repentance, he did not say to them, “Brood of Abraham,” but “Brood of vipers.” For they were like those whom they imitated: not children of Abraham, but children of the Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites, Jebusites, and all those who offended God. They were their children because they followed their deeds.

“Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance. And do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3:7–9).

I do not know what stones he was then seeing in the fields of the forest, from which children of Abraham were raised up. For those who imitate his faith are more truly children than those who were born from his flesh.

Let no one, then, threaten the house of God, as though saying, “I withdraw myself, and the house will fall.” It is good for that person to be built together with it and to have love. For if he himself falls, the house will stand.

Thus, brothers, the house of God consists of those whom he predestined and foreknew would persevere. It is of them that it was said, “Where his feet stood.” For there are some who do not persevere, and his feet do not stand in them [Note: [Col. 1721] Am. and the Mss. read, “and indeed there are some who,” etc., and do not contain *sunt* (“there are”).] They are therefore not the Church; they do not belong to that which is now the dwelling-place and will then be the house.

But where did his feet stand? [Note: [Col. 1722] Er. and Lov. read, “But where did his feet not stand?” The word “not” is absent from Am. and the Mss.] “Because iniquity abounded, the love of many will grow cold.” His feet do not stand in those in whom love grows cold. But what follows? “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:12–13).

Behold in whom his feet stood: worship in that place—that is, be among those in whom the feet of the Lord have stood.

### 14

But if you wish to understand “where the feet of his house stood” of the house itself, let your feet [Note: [Col. 1722] Am. reads, “the feet of the Lord’s house.” Er. and Lov. read, “the feet of the Lord,” omitting “house.” The Mss. reading, “the feet of his house,” is better.] stand in Christ. Your feet will stand if you persevere in Christ.

For what is said about the devil? “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44). The devil’s feet, therefore, did not stand.

And what does he say about the proud? “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of sinners move me. There the workers of iniquity fell; they were driven out and could not stand” (Psalm 35:12–13).

Therefore the house of God is that whose feet stand. Hence what does John say in his joy? “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him.” If he does not stand, he does not hear him. “And he rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29).

He rightly stands because he rejoices because of the bridegroom’s voice. For if he rejoiced because of his own voice, he would fall. You now see why those who rejoice at their own voice have fallen.

That friend of the bridegroom said, “This is he who baptizes” (John 1:33). Some say, “We baptize.” Rejoicing in their own voice, they were unable to stand, and they do not belong to this house of which it is said, “Where his feet stood.”

### 15. [verse 8]

“Arise, O Lord, into your rest.” He says to the sleeping Lord, “Arise.” You already know who slept and who rose again. In one place he says in the psalm, “I slept in turmoil” (Psalm 56:5).

He is rightly told, “Arise, O Lord, into your rest.” You will no longer be troubled, because Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him (Romans 6:9). His voice is heard in another psalm: “I slept and took my sleep, and I arose, because the Lord will receive me” (Psalm 3:6).

He slept; to him it is said, “Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification”—that is, arise so that the ark of your sanctification, which you sanctified, may also rise.

He is our head; his ark is his Church. He rose first, and the Church will also rise. The body would not dare to promise itself resurrection unless the head rose first.

“Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification.”

Some have understood the body of Christ born from Mary as the ark of sanctification, so that the meaning would be: “Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification”—arise with the body, so that those who did not believe may touch you.

“Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification.”

### 16. [verse 9]

“Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your holy ones rejoice.”

When you have risen from the dead and gone to the Father, let that royal priesthood be clothed with faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17). Having received the pledge of the Holy Spirit, let the members rejoice in the hope of the resurrection, which preceded in the head; for the Apostle says to them, “Rejoicing in hope” (Romans 12:12).

### 17. [verse 10]

“For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.”

This was said to God the Father: “For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.”

The Lord was crucified in Judea; he was crucified by the Jews; he slept, troubled by them. He slept among the hands of those raging against him, and he rose to judge them. In one place he says, “Raise me up, and I will repay them” (Psalm 40:11). He has repaid, and he will repay. For how much the Jews suffered afterward, when they had killed the Lord, they themselves know.

They were all expelled from the very city where they killed him. What then? Did everyone from David’s line perish, and everyone from the tribe of Judah? No. Some believed from among them, and many thousands of people believed from among them—and this already after the Lord’s resurrection.

They raged so as to crucify him, and afterward they began to see miracles being performed in the name of the crucified one. They trembled even more at the power of the name of the one who had seemed to be powerless in their hands. Cut to the heart, they now believed that divinity had been hidden in the one whom they had thought was like other human beings. Seeking counsel from the Apostles, they heard: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Therefore, because Christ rose to judge those by whom he was crucified, he turned his face away from the Jews and turned it toward the Gentiles. God is, as it were, entreated on behalf of the remnant of Israel, and it is said to him: “For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.”

If the chaff has been condemned, let the wheat be gathered. “The remnant will be saved,” as Isaiah says (Isaiah 10:21). And indeed a remnant was saved: from there were the twelve Apostles; from there were more than five hundred brothers to whom the Lord showed himself after the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:6); from there were the many thousands who were baptized and placed the value of their possessions at the Apostles’ feet (Acts 2 and 4).

Thus what God was asked for here was fulfilled: “For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.”

### 18. [verse 11]

“The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not repent of it.”

What does “he swore” mean? He confirmed the promise by himself. What does “he will not repent of it” mean? He will not change it.

God does not suffer the pain of repentance, nor is he mistaken in anything so that he would wish to correct what he had done in error. But just as a human being, when he repents, wishes to change what he has done, so when you hear that God repents, expect a change. God brings it about in a different way from you, although he calls it by the name of repentance. You do it because you had erred; he does it because he punishes or because he delivers.

God changed Saul’s kingdom when he repented, as it is said. In the very passage where Scripture says, “It repented him,” it says shortly afterward, “For he is not as a human being, that he should repent” (1 Samuel 15:11, 29).

When, therefore, he changes his works through his unchangeable plan, he is said to repent because of the change of the work itself, not of the plan. Yet he promised this in such a way that it would not be changed.

Just as it is said, “The Lord swore, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4), so here, because it was promised in such a way that it would not be changed, because it necessarily had to happen and endure, he said:

“The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not repent of it: From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne.”

He could have said, “From the fruit of your loins.” Why did he wish to say, “From the fruit of your womb”? If he had said the former, he would have spoken truly; but he wished to speak more significantly by saying, “From the fruit of your womb,” because Christ was born of a woman, without a man’s intervention.

### 19. [verse 12]

What then? “The Lord swore truth to David: From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne. If your sons keep my covenant and these testimonies of mine which I will teach them, their sons also will sit forever upon your throne.”

“If your sons keep it, their sons will sit forever.” Parents establish merit for their children. But what if his sons kept it and their sons did not keep it? Why is the blessedness of the children promised on the merit of their fathers?

What does he say? “If your sons keep it, their sons will sit forever.” He does not say, “If your sons keep it, they will sit upon your throne; and if their sons keep it, they too will sit upon your throne.” Rather, he says, “If your sons keep it, their sons will sit upon your throne.” Why, unless he wished the children here to be understood as their fruits?

“If your sons,” he says, “keep my law and preserve these commandments of mine which I will teach them, their sons will sit upon your throne.” That is, this will be their fruit: that they sit upon your throne.

At present, brothers, all of us who labor in Christ, all who tremble at his words, who in whatever way try to do his will, and groan while asking him to help us fulfill what he commands—do we already sit upon those seats of blessedness that are promised to us? No. But while holding fast to the commandments, we hope that this will come to pass.

That hope itself is spoken of, as it were, in children [Note: [Col. 1724] Several Mss. read, “is given.”], because for a person living in this life, children are hope and children are fruits. Hence people who excuse their greed say that they are preserving what they preserve for their children; and when they do not wish to give to the needy, they excuse themselves in the name of affection, because their children are their hope.

All people who live according to this world say that their hope is to beget children and leave them behind. Therefore he designated hope itself by the name of children and said: “If your sons keep my covenant and these testimonies of mine which I will teach them, their sons will sit forever upon your throne.” That is, they will have such fruits that their hope will not deceive them, but they will come to the place where they hope to come.

At present, therefore, they are like fathers—people of future hope. But when they have obtained what they hope for, they are children, because they have brought forth and generated in their works that which they attain [Note: [Col. 1724] The editions read, “in good works.” The manuscripts read, “in their works.”] And this is preserved for them in the future, because posterity itself is also customarily called children.

### 20

Or, if you understand the children themselves as human beings, understand it as having been said about them also.

“If your sons keep my covenant and these testimonies of mine which I will teach them”—so that the meaning is this: “If your sons keep my covenant and these testimonies of mine which I will teach them, and their sons also”—that is, if they keep them; here you should place the pause, and then continue—“they will sit forever upon your throne.” That is, both your sons and their sons will sit, but only if they keep them.

What, then, if they do not keep them? Has God’s promise perished? No. It was said and promised for this reason: God foresaw—what, except that they would believe? But lest anyone should, as it were, threaten God’s promises and wish to place in his own power what God promised to fulfill, he therefore swore and said [Note: [Col. 1725] The manuscripts read thus. The editions read, “therefore he swore to him and said.”] This shows that it will undoubtedly come to pass.

Why, then, did he place there the condition, “If they keep it”? So that you may not already boast of the promises and then abandon the keeping of them. You will be a son of David if you keep them; but if you do not, you will not be a son of David.

God made the promise to David’s sons. Do not say, “I am a son of David,” if you degenerate. If the Jews do not say this, although they were born from that very line—or rather, they do say it, but they are delirious—for the Lord plainly says, “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39), and he denied that they were his children because they did not do his works: how can we call ourselves sons of David, who are not descended from his line according to the flesh?

It remains that we are not his children except by imitating his faith and worshiping God as he worshiped him. If, then, you do not hope to attain by your deeds what you do not hope for through lineage, how will it be fulfilled in you that you will sit upon David’s throne? And if it is not fulfilled in you, do you suppose that it will not be fulfilled?

How, then, was it found in the fields of the forest? And how did his feet stand? Whatever kind of person you may be, that house will stand.

### 21. [verse 13]

“For the Lord chose Zion; he chose her beforehand as his dwelling.”

Zion itself is the Church; it is also that Jerusalem toward whose peace we run, which is a pilgrim not in the angels but in us, and from its better part awaits the return of the other part. From there the Scriptures came to us, which are read every day.

That city itself is Zion, whom the Lord chose beforehand.

### 22. [verse 14]

“This is my rest forever and ever.”

These are now God’s words: “My rest; there I rest.”

How greatly God loves us, brothers, that because we rest, he says that he rests! He is not ever troubled, nor does he rest in this way; but he says that he rests there because we will have rest in him.

“Here I will dwell, because I chose her beforehand.”

### 23. [verse 15]

“Blessing her widow, I will bless her, and I will fill her poor with bread.”
