Every soul that understands that it is deserted of every help except that of God alone is a widow. How does the Apostle describe a widow? “But she who is truly a widow and desolate has hoped in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1725] Lovaniensis reads, “will hope”; and below, “will persist in prayers.” The Ambrosian manuscript, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read, “has hoped,” “persists,” in accordance with the Apostle’s Greek text.]

He was speaking of those widows whom we all call widows [Note: [Col. 1725] Seven manuscripts read, “had called.”] in the Church. He had said, “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives,” and he did not count her among the widows.

Describing holy widows, what does he say? “But she who is truly a widow and desolate has hoped in the Lord, and persists in prayers and supplications night and day.” Then he added, “But she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Timothy 5:5–6).

Why, then, is she a widow? Because she has no help from anywhere except God alone. Those who have husbands are, as it were, proud of their husbands’ help; widows seem deserted, but their help is stronger.

The whole Church, therefore, is one widow—whether among men or women, whether among married men or married women, whether among the young, the old, or virgins. The whole Church is one widow, deserted in this world, if she perceives and knows her widowhood. Then help is present to her.

Do you not recognize this widow in the Gospel, my brothers, when the Lord said that we ought always to pray and not grow faint? There was a judge in a city, he said, who neither feared God nor respected human beings. A certain widow kept appealing to him daily, saying, “Vindicate me against my adversary.” By appealing to him daily, the widow wore him down.

The judge himself said within himself—he who neither feared God nor respected human beings—“Although I do not fear God and do not respect human beings, nevertheless, because this widow is troubling me, I will vindicate her.”

If an evil judge heard a widow so as not to be troubled, will God not hear the Church, whom he urges to pray? (Luke 18:1–8.)

### 24

Likewise, “I will fill her poor with bread.” What does this mean, brothers? Let us be poor, and then we shall be filled.

Many people who rely upon the world and are proud are Christians. They worship Christ, but they are not filled; for they are filled already, and they abound in their pride. Of such people it is said, “Reproach to those who abound, and contempt for the proud” (Psalm 123:4). They abound, and therefore they eat, but they are not filled.

And what is said of them in the psalm? “All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped.” They worship Christ, honor Christ, and plead with Christ, but they are not filled with his wisdom and righteousness. Why? Because they are not poor.

But the poor—that is, those humble in heart—the more they hunger, the more they eat. And they hunger all the more because they are empty of the world. Whoever is full rejects whatever you may give him, because he is full.

Give me a hungry person; give me those of whom it is said, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled” (Matthew 5:6). These will be the poor of whom he now says, “I will fill her poor with bread.”

For in that same psalm where it is said, “All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped,” it is also said of the poor, precisely as in this psalm: “The poor will eat and be filled, and they will praise the Lord who seek him” (Psalm 22:30, 27).

Where it says, “All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped,” it also says, “The poor will eat and be filled.” Why, when the rich are said to have worshiped, are they not said to have been filled, whereas when the poor are mentioned, they are said to have been filled?

And with what are they filled? What sort of fullness is this, brothers? God himself is the bread. In order to become milk for us, the Bread descended to earth; and he said to his own, “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (John 6:41).

Therefore it is said there in the psalm, “The poor will eat and be filled.” With what will they be satisfied? Hear what follows: “And they will praise the Lord who seek him.”

### 25

Therefore be poor; be among the members of that widow. Let your help be in the one God alone.

Money is nothing; you will not have help from it. Many have been plunged into ruin because of money; many have perished because of money. Many, because of their great wealth, have been sought by robbers; they would have been safe if they had not possessed anything for which they might be sought.

Many have relied upon more powerful friends. Those upon whom they relied fell and dragged down those who had relied upon them. Look at the examples of the human race.

Is what is said to you something great? We do not speak of these matters only from the Scriptures; read them throughout the world. Take care not to rely upon money, upon a human friend, upon worldly honor and boasting.

Take all these things away. But if you have them, give thanks to God if you despise them. If you are puffed up by them, do not wait until you become the prey of human beings; you are already the devil’s prey.

But if you do not rely upon these things, you will be among the members of that widow who is the Church, of whom it is said, “Blessing her widow, I will bless her.” You will also be poor, of the kind of whom it is said, “I will fill her poor with bread.”

### 26

Sometimes, however—and this must not be left unsaid—you find a proud poor person and a humble rich person. We encounter such people every day.

You hear a poor person, as though groaning under a rich person; and when a more powerful person oppresses the rich person, then you see him being humble—sometimes not even then, but proud even then. From this you see what he would be if he had something.

The poor person of God is poor in spirit, not in his purse. A man may come forward who has a full house, fertile lands, many estates, and much gold and silver. He knows that he must not rely upon these things; he humbles himself before God and uses them well. Thus his heart is lifted toward God, so that he knows that these riches not only do him no good, but even impede his feet unless God guides and assists him. He is counted among the poor who are filled with bread.

You find another beggar puffed up—or perhaps not puffed up because he has nothing, yet seeking something by which he may become puffed up. God does not consider means but desire. He judges him according to the desire with which he craves temporal things, not according to the means that he has been unable to acquire.

Hence the Apostle says concerning the rich: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment.”

What, then, should they do with their riches? He continues: “Let them be rich in good works; let them give readily and share.” And see that here they are poor: “Let them lay up for themselves,” he says, “a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Timothy 6:17–19).

When they have taken hold of it, then they will be rich. But while they do not yet possess it, let them know that they are poor.

Thus it comes about that all those who are humble in heart and established in twofold love [Note: [Col. 1727] Lov. reads thus. Other editions and the Mss. read, “in genuine love.”], whatever they may possess in this world, God counts among his poor, whom he fills with bread.

### 27. [verses 16–17]

“I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her holy ones will rejoice with rejoicing.”

We are now at the end of the psalm; let your Charity pay attention for a little while.

“I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her holy ones will rejoice with rejoicing.”

Who is our Savior except our Christ? What, then, does “I will clothe her priests with salvation” mean? “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27).

“And her holy ones will rejoice with rejoicing.” From what will they rejoice with rejoicing? Because they have been clothed with salvation—not in themselves. For they have become light—not in themselves, but in the Lord [Note: [Col. 1728] Er., Lugd., Ven.: “for they became light not in themselves.” M.]; previously they were darkness (Ephesians 5:8).

Therefore he added, “There I will raise up the horn of David,” so that the height of David may be understood as reliance upon Christ. The horn signifies height. And what kind of height? Not a fleshly one. For all the bones are covered with flesh; the horn projects beyond the flesh. The horn is spiritual height.

And what is spiritual height except to rely upon Christ, not to say, “I act; I baptize,” but, “This is he who baptizes” (John 1:33)? There is the horn of David.

And so that you may know that the horn of David is there, pay attention to what follows: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.” What is the lamp? You already know the Lord’s words concerning John: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35).

And what does John say? “This is he who baptizes.” In him, therefore, the holy ones will rejoice; in him the priests will rejoice, because whatever good belongs to them does not belong to them, but to him who has the power to baptize.

Therefore everyone who has received Baptism approaches his temple without fear [Note: [Col. 1728] The manuscripts read thus. The editions read, “but to him. And because he has the power to baptize, everyone who receives Baptism approaches his temple without fear.”], because it belongs not to a human being but to him in whom the horn of David has been raised up.

### 28. [verse 18]

“Upon him, however, my sanctification will flourish” [Note: [Col. 1728] The first part of verse 18, “I will clothe his enemies with shame,” is omitted.].

Upon whom? Upon my Christ.

When he says, “my Christ,” it is the voice of the Father, who says, “Blessing her widow, I will bless her, and I will fill her poor with bread. I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her holy ones will rejoice with rejoicing.”

He who says, “There I will raise up the horn of David,” is God. He himself says, “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ,” because Christ is both our Christ and the Father’s Christ.

He is our Christ when he saves and rules us, just as he is also our Lord; but he is the Son of the Father. Christ, however, is both ours and the Father’s. For if Christ did not belong to the Father, it would not have been said above, “For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.”

“Upon him my sanctification will flourish.” It flourishes upon Christ. Let no human being claim it for himself, because he himself sanctifies; otherwise the statement “Upon him my sanctification will flourish” would not be true.

The glory of sanctification will flourish. Therefore Christ’s sanctification is in Christ himself; the power of God’s sanctification is in Christ.

For “will flourish” refers to glory, because when trees flower, they are beautiful. Sanctification, therefore, is in Baptism; from there it flourishes and shines [Note: [Col. 1728] Ambrose, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read, “from which it flourishes.”].

How could the world yield to this beauty? Because it flourishes in Christ. But place it in human power: how does it flourish, when “all flesh is grass, and all the glory of flesh is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6)?

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 132

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1. [verse 1]

The psalm is short, but very well known and celebrated.

“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one.”

The sound of this verse is so sweet that even those who do not know the Psalter sing the verse itself. It is as sweet as the love that makes brothers dwell together as one.

This, brothers, does not require interpretation or explanation: how good and how pleasant it is to dwell together as one. But what follows contains something that can be opened to those who knock.

Nevertheless, so that an understanding of the whole structure of the psalm may descend to us from this verse, let us first consider this point again and again: Is “How good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” spoken of all Christians? Or are there certain and perfect people who dwell together as one, so that this blessing does not belong to everyone but to some, although from them it descends to the others?

### 2

These words of the Psalter, this sweet sound, this pleasant melody, both in song and in understanding, also gave birth to monasteries. Brothers who desired to dwell together as one were awakened by this sound; this verse was their trumpet.

It sounded throughout the whole world, and those who had been divided were gathered together. The cry of God, the cry of the Holy Spirit, the prophetic cry was not heard in Judea; and it was heard throughout the whole world.

The deaf were opposed to this sound while it was being sung among them; but people with opened ears were found, of whom it was said: “Those to whom he was not announced will see him, and those who have not heard will understand” (Isaiah 52:15).

Nevertheless, beloved, if we consider the matter, this blessing first arose from that wall of circumcision. Did all the Jews perish? And from where came the Apostles, sons of the Prophets, sons of the shaken-off ones (Psalm 126:4)? I speak as to people who already know.

From where came the five hundred who saw the Lord after the resurrection, whom the Apostle Paul mentions (1 Corinthians 15:6)? From where came the one hundred and twenty who were together in one place after the Lord’s resurrection and ascension into heaven? While they were gathered in one place, the Holy Spirit sent from heaven came upon them on the day of Pentecost—sent in the manner in which he had been promised.

They all came from there. They were the first to dwell together as one: they sold everything they possessed and placed the value of their goods at the Apostles’ feet, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles. It was distributed to each according to each one’s need; no one called anything his own, but everything was common to them.

And what does “as one” mean? “They had,” he says, “one soul and one heart toward God” (Acts 1, 2, and 4).

They were therefore the first to hear, “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one.” They heard it first, but they did not hear it alone. For this love and unity of brothers did not come only to them. This rejoicing of love and vow to God also came to later generations.

For something is vowed to God, and it is said [Note: [Col. 1730] Several manuscripts read: “and they vowed a vow to God. For they vowed something to God, as it is said,” etc.]: “Vow, and repay your vows to the Lord your God” (Psalm 76:12). It is better not to vow than to vow and not repay (Ecclesiastes 5:4).

But the mind ought to be eager, so that it both vows and repays; it should not be sluggish in vowing because it considers itself less capable of repayment. Certainly, it will never repay if it thinks that it will repay from its own resources.

### 3

From the voice of this psalm the monks also received their name, so that no one may insult Catholics because of this name.

When you rightly begin to insult the heretics concerning the Circumcellions [Note: [Col. 1730] Several manuscripts read, “Circilliones”; some read, “Cercelliones.”], so that they may be ashamed and be saved, they insult you concerning the monks.

First, if they are to be compared, you may judge; if your words are needed, you are already laboring. Nothing is needed except that you admonish each person to pay attention—simply to pay attention and compare.

What need is there of your words? Let drunkards be compared with sober people, reckless people with thoughtful people, frenzied people with simple people, wanderers with those gathered together.

Nevertheless, they are accustomed to say: “What does the name ‘monks’ mean?”

How much better for us to say: “What does the name ‘Circumcellions’ mean?” But, they say, they are not called Circumcellions. Perhaps we call them by a corrupted form of the name.

Shall we tell you their complete name? Perhaps they are called *circumcelliones*, not *circilliones*. Certainly, if that is what they are called, let them explain what they are.

For they are called *circumcelliones* because they wander around the cells. They are accustomed to go here and there, having no fixed dwelling anywhere, and to do the things you know—and the things they know, whether they wish it or not.

### 4. [verse 1]

Nevertheless, dearly beloved, there are also those who are false monks; and we know such men. Yet the pious brotherhood has not perished because of those who profess to be what they are not. For there are false monks just as there are false clerics and false believers. All three classes, my brothers—the three that we have at some time commended to you, and, I think, more than once—have their good members and their bad members. [Note: [Column 1730] Above, on Psalm 99, no. 13.]

For concerning these very three classes it was said: “Two will be in the field; one will be taken and one will be left: and two in a bed; one will be taken and one will be left: and two at the mill; one will be taken and one will be left” (Luke 17:34–35).

Those in the field are the ones who govern the Church. Hence the Apostle says—see whether he was not in the field—“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6).

By those in the bed, however, he wanted us to understand those who loved quietness; for by “bed” he wanted quietness to be understood: they do not mix with the crowds or with the tumult of the human race, but serve God in leisure. Yet even there one will be taken and one will be left. There are the upright, and there are the reprobate. Do not be alarmed when reprobates are found there; for some are hidden and are not discovered until the end.

Likewise, he called the two at the mill by a feminine form, because he wanted the common people to be understood. Why at the mill? Because they move about in this world, where the mill is understood to be; for this world turns as a mill does. Woe to those whom it crushes. Thus good believers move about there: one of them will be consumed, and the other will be taken.

Lovers of this age, deceivers, and pretenders engage in certain activities of the world. Others, however, are there as the Apostle says: “Those who use this world as though they did not use it; for the outward form of this world is passing away. I want you to be free from anxiety” (1 Corinthians 7:31–32).

Do you hear who will be taken from the mill? Certainly, many sins seem to belong to the rich. For when they conduct more business, administer more affairs, and have more extensive property dependent upon them, it is difficult for them not to contract more sins. And of them it was said that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.

When the disciples were saddened on their account—for they had already despaired of them—the Lord consoled them, saying: “What is impossible for human beings is easy for God” (Matthew 19:24–26).

But how does God make that easy? Listen to the Apostle, provided you do not neglect what he commanded: “Command,” he says, “the rich of this age not to be proud in their thinking.” For you find a poor man who is proud and a rich man who is humble; a Christian who carefully considers that all those things pass away and flow past, that he brought nothing into this world and can take nothing away from the world; who considers how that rich man who was burning in the flame of hell desired that a drop be distilled for him from the finger of the man whose crumbs from his table he had once coveted.

Thinking on these things, they do what the Apostle says: “They must not place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us abundantly with all things for enjoyment. Let them be rich,” he says, “in good works, generous in giving, sharing, and storing up treasure.” And what profit do they gain from this? “Let them store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life” (1 Timothy 6:17–19).

Behold who will be taken from the mill. But that rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen, who feasted splendidly every day and despised the poor man lying at his gate (Luke 16:19–24), will be left. For from the mill one will be taken, and the other will be left.

### 5.

Thus Ezekiel also speaks of three persons, in whom we may reasonably understand these three classes: “When the Lord sends a sword upon the land, even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in their midst, they would not deliver sons or daughters; they alone would be saved” (Ezekiel 14:13–16).

Those men were delivered long ago, but by these three names he signified certain three classes. Noah signifies the rulers of the Church, because he himself guided the ark in the flood (Genesis 7).

Daniel, however, chose a quiet life, serving God in celibacy—that is, not seeking a wife. He was a holy man, living his life amid heavenly desires; tested in many things, he was found to be refined gold. How quiet was he, who was secure even among lions (Daniel 6; and 14:28–39)!

Therefore, in the name of Daniel—who is also called “a man of desires” (Daniel 10:11), specifically of chaste and holy desires—the servants of God are signified, of whom it is said: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.”

In the name of Job is signified that one at the mill who will be taken. For he had a wife, he had children, and he had great wealth. He possessed so much in this age that the devil made this an accusation against him, claiming that he did not worship God freely, but because of what he had received.

The adversary brought this charge against the holy man; and through his temptations it was proved that Job worshiped God freely—not because of what he had received, but because of the One who had given it. After everything had been lost through sudden affliction and trial—his inheritance lost, his heirs lost, with only his wife left to him, not for consolation but for temptation—he said what you know: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

What is sung every day was fulfilled in him, provided our conduct also agrees with it: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33:2).

Therefore, in these three names three classes of human beings were signified, and once again in those three whom I mentioned in the Gospel.

### 6.

What, then, do those people say who taunt us concerning the name “monks”? Perhaps they will say: “Our people are not called circumcellions. You call them that by an insulting name; we do not call them that.”

Let them say what they do call them, and you will hear. They call them *agonistici*—“combatants.” We too admit that this is an honorable name, if only the reality corresponded to it.

But meanwhile let your Holiness consider this: those who say to us, “Show us where the name ‘monks’ is written,” should show us where the name “agonistici” is written.

“We call them that,” they say, “because of the contest. For they fight, and the Apostle says, ‘I have fought the good fight’” (2 Timothy 4:7). Since there are those who fight against the devil and prevail, they are called the agonistic soldiers of Christ.

Would that they were soldiers of Christ, and not soldiers of the devil, whose cry “Praise be to God!” is feared more than the roar of a lion. [Note: [Column 1732] The word “circumcellions.”]

These men also dare to taunt us because, when brothers see human beings, they say, “Thanks be to God.” [Note: [Column 1732] The word “monks.”]

“What does ‘Thanks be to God’ mean?” they say. Are you so deaf that you do not know what “Thanks be to God” means? Whoever says “Thanks be to God” gives thanks to God.

See whether a brother ought not to give thanks to God when he sees his brother. Is there not a place for rejoicing when those who dwell in Christ see one another? And yet you laugh at our “Thanks be to God,” while people weep at your “Praise be to God.”

But certainly you have given an account of the name: you have explained why you call them *agonistici*. Let it be so, as you call them; let it truly be so—we entirely approve. May the Lord grant that they fight against the devil and not against Christ, whose Church they persecute.

Nevertheless, because they fight, you call them *agonistici*, and you have found the source of the name, since the Apostle said, “I have fought the good fight.”

Why, then, should we not also call them “monks,” when the Psalm says, “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity”?

For *monos* (μόνος) means “one,” but not just any kind of one. Even in a crowd there is one; one may be called “one” together with many, but he cannot be called *monos*—that is, “alone.” For *monos* means one alone.

Those, therefore, who live together in such a way that they make one person, so that what is written may truly apply to them—“one soul and one heart”—many bodies but not many souls, many bodies but not many hearts—are rightly called *monos*, that is, “one alone.”

Hence that one man was also healed in the pool. Let those who taunt the name “monks” answer us and explain why the man who was found to have been ill for thirty-eight years gave the following answer to the Lord: “When the water is stirred, I have no one to put me into the pool; another goes down before me” (John 5:5, 7).

One had gone down; another was no longer going down. One alone was healed; he represented the unity of the Church.

It is fitting that those who have cut themselves off from unity taunt the name of unity. It is fitting that the name “monks” displeases them, because they do not wish to dwell together with their brothers; but, by following Donatus, they abandoned Christ.

Your Love has heard these things about the one and the one alone. Let us now rejoice with the Psalm, so that we may see what follows. It is brief; with the Lord’s prompting, we can run through it. For I think that from what has been said it can be clear what follows, although those words may appear obscure.

### 7. [verse 2]

“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.”

The one who was speaking showed what he saw when he said, “Behold.” We too see it, brothers, and bless God; and we pray that we too may say, “Behold.”

And let the Psalm say what they resemble: “Like ointment on the head, which ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which ran down upon the edge of his garment.”

What was Aaron? A priest. Who is the priest, except the one priest who entered the Holy of Holies? Who is this priest, except the one who was both victim and priest? Except the one who, when he found nothing clean in the world that he could offer, offered himself?

The ointment is on his head, because the whole Christ is with the Church; but the ointment came from the head. Christ is our head: crucified and buried, he rose again and ascended into heaven; and the Holy Spirit came from the head.

Where? To the beard.

The beard signifies the strong; the beard signifies the young, energetic, tireless, and joyful. Therefore, when we describe such men, we say, “He is a bearded man.”

Thus that first ointment descended upon the Apostles; it descended upon those who endured the first assaults of the age. The Holy Spirit therefore descended upon them.

For those who first began to dwell together also suffered persecution. But because the ointment had descended upon the beard, they suffered without being conquered. Indeed, the head itself had already gone before them in suffering, from which the ointment descended. With such an example preceding them, who could conquer the beard?

### 8.

Holy Stephen belonged to that beard. And this is what it means not to be conquered: that love is not conquered by enemies.

Those who persecuted the saints seemed to themselves to have won. They were striking, and they were being struck; they were killing, and they were being killed. Who would not have thought that the former were winning and the latter losing?

But because love was not conquered, the ointment descended upon the beard.

Consider Stephen. Love raged in him. It raged against them while they were listening; it prayed for them while they were stoning him.

For what did he say while they were listening? “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit.” See the beard. Did he flatter them? Did he fear?

When they heard these things spoken against them [Note: [Column 1734] Here the editions add after “spoken against them” the words “they raged”; these are absent from all manuscripts.]—for Stephen seemed to rage—he raged with his mouth, but loved in his heart; and love itself was not conquered in him.

They, recoiling from the word like darkness fleeing from light, began to run toward the stones in order to stone Stephen. Just as Stephen’s words had previously stoned them, so afterward their stones stoned Stephen.

When ought Stephen to have been more angry: when he was being stoned, or when he was being heard? Behold, he became gentle while he was being stoned, and he raged while he was being heard.

Why did he rage while he was being heard? Because he wanted to change those by whom he was being heard.

When the stones came against him, love was not conquered, because the ointment had descended from the head upon the beard, and he had heard from that very head: “Love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).

He had heard it from that very head hanging upon the cross and saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Thus the ointment had descended from the head upon the beard, because when Stephen too was being stoned, he knelt and said: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:51–59).

### 9.

Therefore, they were like the beard. For many were strong, and they endured many persecutions. But if the ointment had not also descended from the beard, we would not now have monasteries.

But because it descended also upon the edge of the garment—for thus he says, “which descended upon the edge of his garment”—the Church followed, and from the Lord’s garment she gave birth to monasteries.

For the priestly garment signifies the Church. It is the garment of which the Apostle says: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27).

It is cleansed so that it may have no spot; it is stretched out so that it may have no wrinkle. Where does the fuller stretch it out, except upon wood? Every day we see tunics being, in a manner of speaking, crucified by fullers: they are crucified so that they may have no wrinkle.

What, then, is the edge of the garment? My brothers, what are we to receive in the edge of the garment? The edge is the end of the garment. What are we to receive at the end of the garment? Is it because at the end of time the Church was to have brothers dwelling together? Or should we understand perfection in the edge, because the garment is perfected at its edge, and those are perfect who know how to dwell together?

Those are perfect who fulfill the law. But how is Christ’s law fulfilled by those who dwell together as brothers? Listen to the Apostle: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). This is the edge of the garment.

How, my brothers, are we to understand which edge he means, the one to which the ointment could descend? I do not think he meant the edge of the garment at the sides. There are edges at the sides. But the ointment could descend from the beard to the edge that is at the head, where the opening for the head is. [Note: [Column 1734] All manuscripts read “the head.”]

Those who dwell together are like this: just as the head of a person enters through these edges so that he may put on the garment, so Christ, who is our head, enters through fraternal harmony so that he may clothe himself, so that the Church may cling to him.

### 10. [verse 3]

What else does he say? “Like the dew of Hermon, which descended upon the mountains of Zion.” [Note: [Column 1735] The editions read “the mountain.” But it is clear that Augustine read “the mountains,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint.]

He wanted this to be understood, my brothers: that the grace of God is what makes brothers dwell together—not their own strength, not their own merits, but his gift and his grace, like dew from heaven.

For the earth does not rain upon itself; nor does whatever it has produced fail to wither unless rain descends from above. In one place in the Psalm he says: “You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance” (Psalm 67:10).

Why did he say “voluntary”? Because it is not according to our merits, but according to his will.

For what good have we deserved, sinners that we are? What good have we deserved, unrighteous as we are? From Adam comes Adam, and many sins arise upon Adam. Whoever is born is born Adam, condemned from one condemned, and by living badly adds further sins to Adam. [Note: [Column 1735] The Corbie manuscript reads: “and many sins arise upon Adam. He is born condemned from one condemned, and by living badly adds further sins to Adam.”]

For what good did Adam deserve? Yet the merciful one loved, and the bridegroom loved—not something beautiful, but in order to make it beautiful.

Therefore he called the grace of God the dew of Hermon.

### 11.

But you ought to know what Hermon is. It is a certain mountain far removed from Jerusalem—that is, from Zion. Thus it is surprising that he says, “Like the dew of Hermon, which descended upon the mountains of Zion,” since Mount Hermon is far removed from Jerusalem; for it is said to be beyond the Jordan.

Let us therefore seek something through the interpretation of “Hermon.” For it is not a Hebrew word, and we have its interpretation from those who know that language. Hermon is said to be interpreted as “Exalted Light.”

For the dew comes from Christ; there is no exalted light except Christ.

How was he exalted? First upon the cross, afterward in heaven. He was exalted upon the cross while he was being humbled; but his humiliation could not be anything other than exalted.

The dispensation of the human being was becoming less and less, as was signified in John; the dispensation of God in our Lord Jesus Christ was increasing. This is also shown by their birthdays.

For John was born, as the Church teaches, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, when the days are already beginning to grow shorter. But the Lord was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, when the days are already beginning to grow longer.

Listen to John himself confessing: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

Their passions also indicate this. The Lord was exalted upon the cross; John was diminished when his head was struck off.

Therefore Christ is the exalted light; hence comes the dew of Hermon.

But all of you who wish to dwell together, desire this dew; be rained upon by it. Otherwise you will not be able to keep what you profess, nor will you be able to dare to profess it unless he thunders; nor will you be able to persevere unless his nourishment is not lacking for you. For this nourishment descends upon the mountains of Zion.

### 12.

Now the mountains of Zion are great in Zion. What is Zion? The Church. And who are the mountains there? The great ones.

The beard signifies those whom the mountains signify; the edge of the garment signifies the same. The beard is understood only in the perfect.

Therefore they dwell together only in those in whom the love of Christ has been perfected. [Note: [Column 1736] Most manuscripts read “Christian love.”]

For those in whom the love of Christ is not perfect—even when they are together—are hateful, troublesome, and turbulent; they disturb the others with their anxiety and ask what they should say about them. They are like an unruly animal in a yoke, which not only fails to pull but also breaks with its kicks what has been yoked together.

But if he has the dew of Hermon, which descended upon the mountains of Zion, he is peaceful, calm, humble, and patient; instead of murmuring, he pours out a prayer.

For all murmurers are magnificently described in one passage of Scripture: “The inward parts of a fool are like a cartwheel” (Sirach 33:5).

What does “The inward parts of a fool are like a cartwheel” mean? It carries hay and murmurs; for a cartwheel cannot rest from murmuring.

So are many brothers: they dwell together only in body. But who are those who dwell together? Those of whom it was said: “They had one soul and one heart toward God; and no one said that anything was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4:32).

They have been designated and described as belonging to the beard, belonging to the edge of the garment, and being counted among the mountains of Zion.

And if there are other murmurers there, let them remember the Lord’s saying: “One will be taken, and one will be left” (Matthew 24:40).

### 13.

“For there the Lord commanded blessing.”

Where did he command it? Among brothers who dwell together. There he commanded blessing; there those who dwell harmoniously bless the Lord.

For in discord you do not bless the Lord. You say in vain that your tongue sounds with the Lord’s blessing if you do not sound with it in your heart: with your mouth you bless, and in your heart you curse.

“With their mouth they blessed, and with their heart they cursed” (Psalm 61:5). Are these merely our words? Certain people were signified.

You bless the Lord when you pray, and then, in your prayer, you curse your enemy. Is this what you heard from the Lord himself: “Love your enemies”?

But if you do this—if you love your enemy and pray for him—there the Lord has commanded his blessing; there you will have life forever, that is, eternally.

For many who love this life curse their enemies. For what reason, if not for this life and its worldly advantages? Where has your enemy constrained you, so that you are forced to curse? You have been constrained on earth; move away, dwell in heaven.

“How,” you will say, “do I dwell in heaven, a human being clothed in flesh and devoted to the flesh?”

Go ahead in your heart to the place where you will follow with your body. Do not hear “Lift up your hearts” as one who is deaf. Have your heart above, and no one will constrain you in heaven. [Note: [Column 1736] The Christin manuscript reads “on earth.”]

And therefore another Psalm follows appropriately:

## Exposition of Psalm 133

### Continuation of the preceding sermon

### 1. [verse 1]

“Behold now, bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.”

Why did he add “in the courts”? The courts are understood as the more spacious areas of a house. Whoever stands in the courts is not constrained or pressed; in a certain way he is enlarged.

Remain in expansiveness, and you can love your enemy, because you do not love those things in which you suffer constraint from your enemy.

How are you understood to stand in the courts? Stand in love, and you stand in the courts. In love there is breadth; in hatred, narrowness.

Listen to the Apostle: “Wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress upon every soul of a human being who works evil” (Romans 2:8–9).

But what does he say about the breadth of love? “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

Where you hear of being poured out, understand breadth; where you hear breadth, understand the courts of the Lord. And you will have the Lord’s true blessing when you do not curse your enemies.

For the Spirit addresses those who suffer tribulation, so that they may glory in tribulations, and says to them: “Behold now, bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord.”

What does “Behold now” mean? At this time. For after the tribulations have passed, it is clear that we shall devote ourselves to the Lord’s blessing, as it is said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83:5).

Those who will then bless without failing begin here to bless the Lord: here, amid tribulations, temptations, and troubles; amid the adversities of the age, the ambushes of the enemy, and the deceits and assaults of the devil.

This is what is meant by: “Behold now, bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord.”

What does “who stand” mean? Those who persevere. For it was said of a certain one who was an archangel, “He did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44). And it was said of the bridegroom’s friend: “But the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29).

### 2. [verse 2]

Therefore: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God, in the nights lift up your hands toward the holy places and bless the Lord.”

It is easy to bless in the days. What does “in the days” mean? In prosperous circumstances. Night is a sorrowful thing; day is a joyful thing.

When things go well for you, you bless the Lord. When you desire a son and he is born, you bless the Lord. Your wife is delivered from the danger of childbirth; you bless the Lord. Your son was ill and is restored; you bless the Lord.

Your son was ill; perhaps you consulted an astrologer or a diviner. Perhaps a curse against the Lord came not from your tongue but from your behavior; it came from your conduct and your life.

Do not boast because you bless with your tongue if you curse with your life.

“How,” you ask, “do I curse with my life?”

Because your life is observed, and people say: “Look, a Christian; look at what Christians are like.” Christ is blasphemed on your account.

When your life curses, what good does it do that your tongue blesses? Therefore bless the Lord.

When? In the nights.

When did Job bless? When the night was sorrowful. Everything he possessed was taken away; his children, for whom he had cared, were taken away. What a sorrowful night!

But let us see whether he did not bless in the night: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:14–21).

How dark the night was! Struck with an ulcer from head to foot, he rotted and melted within himself. Then Eve dared to tempt him: “Say something against your God and die.”

Hear him blessing in the nights: “You have spoken,” he said, “like one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:7–10)

Behold what is meant by: “In the nights lift up your hands toward the holy places and bless the Lord.”

What did Job say? “You have spoken like one of the foolish women.”

Rotten Adam repelled Eve, as if saying: “Let it be enough that because of you I became mortal. You had power in paradise, but you are defeated in the dung heap.”

Great is the grace of God! But whence did this come, unless the dew of Hermon had rained upon that soul and the Lord had given sweetness, so that our earth might yield its fruit (Psalm 84:13)?

“In the nights lift up your hands toward the holy places and bless the Lord.”

### 3. [verse 3]

“May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth.”

He encourages many to bless, and he blesses one, because he made one from many; because “it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132:1).

The word “brothers” is plural, but “to dwell together in unity” is singular. Therefore: “May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth.”

Let none of you say, “It does not reach me.” Do you think, then, who is the one to whom he said, “May the Lord bless you from Zion”? He blessed one. Be one, and the blessing reaches you.

## Exposition of Psalm 134

### Sermon to the People

### 1. [verse 1]

It ought to be very sweet to us, and we ought joyfully to rejoice in the sweetness with which this Psalm exhorts us. For it says: “Praise the name of the Lord.”

And it immediately adds the reason why it is right for us to praise the Lord’s name: “Praise, servants, the Lord.”

What could be more just? What more worthy? What more grateful? For if servants do not praise the Lord, they will be proud, ungrateful, and irreligious.

And what do they accomplish by not praising the Lord except that they will experience the Lord as severe? For even if an ungrateful servant refuses to praise his master, he does not thereby cease to be a servant.

Whether you praise or do not praise, you are a servant; but if you praise, you will make him favorable; if you do not praise, you will offend him.

This, then, is a good and useful exhortation. We should therefore take greater care to learn how God is to be praised than to doubt whether he should be praised.

Therefore: “Praise the name of the Lord.” The Psalm exhorts us, the Prophet exhorts us, the Spirit of God exhorts us, and finally the Lord himself exhorts us to praise the Lord.

For he does not grow through our praises, but we do. God does not become better if you praise him, nor worse if you reproach him. But by praising what is good, you will become better; by reproaching it, worse. He himself remains good as he is.

For if he teaches his servants themselves—those who have deserved well of him, the preachers of his word, the rulers of his Church, the worshipers of his name, and the obedient to his command—to have the sweetness of their good life in their conscience, so that they are not corrupted by human praise or broken by human reproach, how much more does he himself, unchangeable above all things, who teaches these things, not become greater if you praise him, nor lesser if you reproach him?

But because it is advantageous for us to praise the Lord, he mercifully commands us to praise him, not arrogantly.

Let us therefore hear what he says: “Praise the name of the Lord; praise, servants, the Lord.”

For you do nothing inappropriate by praising the Lord as servants. Even if you were always nothing but servants, you ought to praise the Lord. How much more ought you, as servants, to praise the Lord so that you may deserve to become sons as well?

### 2. [verse 2]

But since it is written in another Psalm, “Praise is fitting for the upright” (Psalm 32:1), and elsewhere it is written, “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sirach 15:9), and again it is said, “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me, and there is the way in which I will show him the salvation of God”; and consequently: “But to the sinner God said, ‘Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take up my covenant in your mouth? You hate discipline, and you cast my words behind you’” (Psalm 49:23, 16–17)—lest someone, since it is said, “Praise, servants, the Lord,” think that the praise of the Lord benefits him even if he is a wicked servant in this great house, he immediately adds and teaches what sort of people ought to praise the Lord:

“You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.”

Those who stand, not those who fall. [Note: [Column 1739] Some manuscripts read “not those who lie.”]

Those are said to stand who persevere in his commands; who serve God in sincere faith, firm hope, and genuine love; who honor his Church; and who, by living badly, do not give offense to those who wish to enter and encounter stones of stumbling on the way. [Note: [Column 1739] Thus most manuscripts. The editions read “of living.”] [Note: [Column 1739] Seven manuscripts read “and do not find them.”]

Therefore: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, praise the name of the Lord.”

Be grateful. You were outside, and you stand within. [Note: [Column 1739] Thus most manuscripts. The editions instead read: “Be grateful, so that you do not wander outside. Since, therefore…”]

Since you stand, is it not enough for you that here you praise the one who raised you when you were lying down, made you stand in his house, and enabled you to recognize and praise him? Is it a small benefit that we stand in the house of the Lord?

For the present, here, in this pilgrimage, in this house—which is also called the tabernacle of pilgrimage—since we stand here, ought we not to be very grateful?

Should we not consider that we stand here? Should we not consider what we had become? Should we not consider where we were lying and to where we have been gathered?

Should we not consider that all the impious were not seeking the Lord, and that he himself sought those who were not seeking him; that he himself raised those whom he found, called those whom he raised, brought in those whom he called, and made them stand in his house?

Whoever considers these things and is not ungrateful utterly despises himself out of love for his Lord, by whom such great benefits have been bestowed upon him.

And since he has nothing with which to repay God for such great benefits, what remains for him except to give thanks rather than to repay?

To this very thanksgiving belong both receiving the Lord’s cup and invoking his name. For “what shall the servant repay the Lord for all that he has repaid him?” (Psalm 115:12–13)

Therefore: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God, praise the Lord.”

### 3. [verse 3]

What am I going to say about why you should praise him? “Because the Lord is good.”

In one brief word the praise of the Lord our God has been explained: “The Lord is good.”

But he is good in a way unlike the good things he made. For God made all things very good (Genesis 1:31): not merely good, but very good. He made heaven and earth and all that is in them good, and he made them very good.

If he made all these things good, what must he himself be who made them? And yet, although he made good things, and although the one who made them is much better than the things he made, you cannot find anything better to say about him than that “the Lord is good”—provided that you understand “good” properly: the one from whom all other good things come.

For he himself made all things good; he is the good one whom no one made. He is good through his own goodness, not through goodness received from elsewhere. He is good through goodness that is himself, not by clinging to another good.

“But it is good for me to cling to God” (Psalm 72:28)—to him who did not need anyone by whom he might be made good, but whom all other things needed in order to be made good.

Do you wish to hear how uniquely good he is? When the Lord was questioned, he said: “No one is good except the one God” (Matthew 19:17).

I neither wish to pass over this uniqueness of his goodness too briefly nor am I sufficiently capable of commending it appropriately. I fear that if I move quickly beyond it, I may be found ungrateful; and I likewise fear that if I undertake to explain it, I may become exhausted beneath the burden of the Lord’s praise.

Nevertheless, brothers, receive me as one who both praises and is insufficient, so that even if the explanation of his praise is not completed, the devotion of the one praising may be accepted.

Let him approve that I wished to do it; let him forgive me for not having completed it.

### 4.

I am held by ineffable sweetness when I hear, “The Lord is good”; and when I consider and examine everything that I see outwardly, since all things are from him, even when these things please me, I return to him from whom they are, so that I may understand that the Lord is good. Again, when I have entered into him as far as I can, I find him interior and superior to me; for the Lord is so good that he does not need these things in order to be good.

Finally, I do not praise these things apart from him; but I find him, apart from these things, perfect, without need, unchangeable, seeking no one’s good by which he might be increased, fearing no one’s evil by which he might be diminished. And what more shall I say? In creation I find a good heaven, a good sun, a good moon, good stars; a good earth, and the things that are generated in the earth and are supported by roots, good; those that walk and move, good; those that fly through the air and swim in the waters, good.

I also call the human being good: “For a good person brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart” (Id. XII, 35). I also call the angel good, who did not fall through pride and become the devil, but remains obediently attached to him by whom he was made [Note: [Col. 1740] Thus Am., Er., and most manuscripts. Lov. reads: “And having become the devil, he is good, and would be so if he remained attached to him in obedience,” etc.].

I call all these things good, but with their particular names: a good heaven, a good angel, a good human being. But when I turn my attention to God, I think that nothing is better to say than “good.” For the Lord Jesus Christ himself said, “A good man”; and he himself also said, “No one is good except the one God.” Did he not urge us to seek and distinguish what it means for something to be good through another good, and what it means to be good through itself?

How good, then, is the one from whom all good things come? You will find [Note: [Col. 1741] Lov. reads “you will find”; M. reads “you will find”] absolutely no good thing that is not good from him. He who makes good things is himself properly good, just as he is properly good [Note: [Col. 1741] Er., Lugd., and Ven. read “good” (bonus); M. reads “good” (bonum)]. For the things he made do exist; nor is he wronged when we say that the things he made do not exist [Note: [Col. 1741] The Vindocinensis manuscript omits “not.”]. Why would he have made them if the things he made did not exist? Or what did he make, if what he made does not exist?

Since, then, those things also exist which he made, nevertheless we come to a comparison with him; and as though he alone existed, he said, “I am who I am,” and, “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you.’” He did not say, “The Lord God, that omnipotent, merciful, just one”—although, had he said these things, he would certainly have spoken truly. Removing from consideration all the names by which God could be called and described, he answered that his name was “To be,” as though this were his name: “This is what you shall say to them,” he said; “‘He who is’ has sent me.”

For he exists in such a way that, in comparison with him, the things that have been made do not exist. Without comparison with him, they do exist, because they are from him; but compared with him, they do not exist, since true being is unchangeable being, which he alone possesses [Note: [Col. 1741] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “they are not to be compared with him, because they are from him; but when not compared with him, they are, because they are from him. For compared with him they are not, because true …”]. “He is” means that he is; just as the good of good things is good [Note: [Col. 1741] The word “of good things” (bonorum) is absent from Am. and the manuscripts.].

Consider and see that whatever else you praise, you praise because it is good. Anyone who praises what is not good is insane. If you praise an unjust person precisely insofar as he is unjust, will you not also be unjust? If you praise a thief precisely insofar as he is a thief, will you not also be his accomplice? If you praise a just person precisely insofar as he is just, do you not share in that very justice by praising him? For you would not praise the just person unless you loved him; and you would not love him if you possessed nothing of that goodness yourself.

If, then, whatever else we praise, we praise because it is good, no greater, better, or firmer reason could be given to you for praising God than that he is good. Therefore: “Praise the Lord, for he is good.”

### 5.

How long shall we speak of his goodness? Who can conceive in his heart or comprehend how good the Lord is? But let us return to ourselves, recognize him in ourselves, and praise the craftsman in his works, since we are not capable of contemplating him himself. And if someday we shall be capable of contemplating him, when our heart has been cleansed by faith so that at last it may rejoice in the truth, nevertheless now, since he cannot be seen by us, let us look upon his works, lest we remain without praising him [Note: [Col. 1741] Several manuscripts read: “And if we shall contemplate him, capable,” etc.].

Therefore I said, “Praise the Lord, for he is good; sing psalms to his name, for he is sweet.” He might perhaps be good without being sweet, if he did not grant you the ability to taste. But he presented himself to human beings in such a way that he even sent bread from heaven (John 6:32–51), and gave his Son, equal to himself and identical with himself, to become human and to be killed for human beings, so that through what you are, you might taste what you are not.

For it was very difficult for you to taste the sweetness of God, because that sweetness was remote and exceedingly high, while you were exceedingly low and lying in the depths. Into this great separation a Mediator was sent. You, a human being, could not come to God; God became human. Thus, since as a human being you can [Col. 1742] come to a human being, though you could not come to God, you might come to God through a human being. And “the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus,” came to be (1 Timothy 2:5).

But if he were human only, by following what you are you would never arrive; if he were God only, because you could not grasp what you are not, you would never arrive. God became human so that, by following what you can follow—the human being—you might reach what you could not reach—God. He is the Mediator, and for this reason he became sweet.

What is sweeter than the bread of angels? How could the Lord not be sweet, when a human being ate the bread of angels (Psalm 77:25)? For a human being does not live by one thing and an angel by another. He is truth itself, wisdom itself, the power of God itself [Note: Am., Er., and most manuscripts read “the truth itself, the wisdom itself, the power of God itself.” Lov. reads “the truth of God.”]. But you cannot enjoy these things in the way the angels do.

How do they enjoy them? As it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” through whom all things were made. But how do you touch him? “Because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 3, 14). In order that a human being might eat the bread of angels, the Creator of angels became human.

Sing, therefore, to his name, for he is sweet. If you have tasted, sing; if you have tasted how sweet the Lord is, sing; if what you have tasted is good, praise him. Who is so ungrateful to the one who cooks or feeds him that, after being delighted by some dish, he would not give thanks by praising what he tastes? If we do not remain silent about these things, shall we remain silent about the one who gave everything?

Sing to his name, for he is sweet.

### 6.

And now hear of his works. Perhaps you were striving to see the good of all good things, the good from which all good things come, the good without which nothing is good, and the good that is good without the others; you were striving to see him, and perhaps you were failing as you extended your mind’s vision. I infer this from myself, for I experience it.

But if there is someone—as can indeed happen, and very readily happen—whose mental vision is stronger than mine and who fixes the gaze of his heart for a long time upon what truly is, let him praise as he can, and in the way we cannot, let him praise. Yet thanks be to the one who moderated his praise in this psalm, so that it might belong both to the strong and to the weak.

When, in the sending of his servant Moses, he said, “I am who I am,” and, “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you,’” because it was difficult for the human mind to grasp what it means properly to be, and because a human being was being sent to human beings, though not by a human being, God immediately moderated his praise. He said of himself something that could be grasped with sweetness; he did not wish to remain in that which was being praised, but which the one praising could not reach.

“Go,” he said, “say to the children of Israel, ‘The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever.” Certainly, Lord, you have that name, since you also said, “I am”; “He who is has sent me to you.” Why, then, have you now changed the name, saying, “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”?

Does it not seem that reason itself answers and says: What I said, “I am who I am,” is true, but you do not grasp it. What I said, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:14–15, 6), is both true and comprehensible to you. For “I am who I am” concerns what I am for myself; but “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” concerns what I am for you. If you fail to grasp what I am for myself, grasp what I am for you.

And lest anyone perhaps think that what God said, “I am who I am,” and “He who is has sent me to you,” was his only eternal name, while what he said, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” was a temporal name, God did not take care, after saying, “I am who I am,” and, “He who is has sent me to you,” to say that this was his name forever, because even had he not said so, it would have been understood.

For he is, and truly is; and precisely because he truly is, he is without beginning and without end. But because of the human being he says, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” And lest human anxiety arise there, since this appears temporal rather than eternal, he made us secure because through temporal things he leads us to eternal life.

“This is my name forever,” he says—not because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are eternal, but because God will make them eternal afterward, without end. They had a beginning, but they will have no end.

### 7.

In Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, consider his whole Church; consider the entire seed of Israel. The entire seed of Israel means not only what is from the flesh, but also what is from faith. For the Apostle was speaking to the Gentiles when he said: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:29).

We are all therefore blessed in the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He blessed a certain tree and created it as an olive tree, as the Apostle said, meaning the holy Patriarchs, from whom the people of God blossomed. But this olive tree was pruned, not cut down, and from it the proud branches were broken off: this is the blasphemous and impious people of the Jews.

Nevertheless, good and useful branches remained, for the Apostles came from there. And while useful branches had been left there, by God’s mercy the wild olive of the Gentiles was grafted in. To it the Apostle says: “Although you were a wild olive, you were grafted in among them and became a sharer in the rich root of the olive tree. Do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, remember that you do not support the root; the root supports you” (Romans 11:17–18).

This is the one tree belonging to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And, what is more, the wild olive has been grafted into Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob more fully than the broken branches. They are no longer there because of their brokenness; the wild olive was not there, and now it is there. They deserved to be broken off through pride; it deserved to be grafted in through humility. They lost the root; it retained the root.

When, therefore, you hear “Israel of God,” Israel belonging to God, do not make yourselves strangers to it [Note: Some manuscripts read, “when you hear Israel, concerning Israel that belongs…” Am. reads, “you heard Israel, and Israel belonging…” Er. reads, “and concerning Israel belonging…”]. You were indeed a wild olive, but you are an olive tree, sharers in the richness of the olive tree.

For do you wish to know how the wild olive was grafted into Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, lest you think that you do not belong to this tree because you do not belong bodily to Abraham’s seed? When the Lord marveled at the faith of that centurion who was not from the people of Israel but from the Gentiles, he said: “Therefore I tell you, many will come from the east and the west.” Behold, the wild olive is already in the hand of the one who grafts: “Many will come from the east and the west.”

We see what he is bringing to be grafted; let us see where he will graft it: “They will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” We see both what he grafted in and where he grafted it.

And what does he say concerning the natural branches that were proud? “But the children of the kingdom will go into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:11–12). The matter was foretold; the matter was fulfilled.

### 8. [verse 4]

Therefore, “Sing to the Lord, for he is sweet.” And consider what he has done around us: “For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession.” Praise him, sing, because he has done these things. I speak of things that you are able to grasp.

He placed the other nations under angels; “the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession.” He made his own nation a field for himself to cultivate and sow. Although he created all the nations, he entrusted the others to angels, while he appointed this one for himself to possess and preserve: this people, this Jacob.

Was it on account of his merit, or by God’s grace? Concerning those not yet born he said, “The elder shall serve the younger,” as the Apostle said. What merit could those not yet born have possessed, before either of them had done anything good or evil? Let Jacob, therefore, not exalt himself, not boast, not attribute this to his own merits. He was foreknown beforehand, predestined beforehand, chosen beforehand—not chosen for his merits, but found and given life by God’s grace (Romans 9:11–13).

The same is true of all the nations. For what merit did the wild olive possess, with the bitterness of its berries and the sterility of its wildness, that it should be grafted in? It was a tree of the forest, not of the master’s field; and yet by his mercy he grafted the wild olive into the olive tree. But the wild olive had not yet been grafted in when the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession.

### 9. [verse 5]

And what does the Prophet say? “For I have known that the Lord is great.” With his mind flying upward, raised above the flesh and transcending creation, he came to know that the Lord is great.

Not everyone can know this by seeing. Let them praise what he has done: “He is sweet”; “the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession.” And praise him for this too [Note: So read most manuscripts. The editions read, “And here you praise him.”], for “I too have known that the Lord is great.”

The Prophet was speaking—the one who entered into the sanctuary of God, who perhaps heard ineffable words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak (2 Corinthians 12:4), who said what could be said to human beings and kept to himself what could not be said.

Therefore let what we can receive be heard, and let what we cannot receive be believed. Let what we can receive be heard: “For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession.” Let what we cannot receive be believed: that he himself knew that the Lord is great.

If we said to him, “We ask you, explain his greatness,” would he perhaps not answer us: “He whom I see is not very great if I can explain him”? Let him therefore return to his works and speak to us. Let him retain in his own conscience the greatness of the Lord which he saw and commended to us for belief, but to which he could not lead our eyes; and let him enumerate certain things that the Lord did here, so that for us also, who cannot see his greatness as he did, it may become sweet through his works, which we can grasp.

“For I,” he says, “have known that the Lord is great, and that our God is above all gods.” Which gods? As the Apostle says: “Although there are those called gods in heaven and on earth, as indeed there are many gods and many lords, yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we for him, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him” (1 Corinthians 8:5–6).

Human beings may be called gods. For it is written, “God has taken his stand in the assembly of the gods”; and, “I said, ‘You are gods, all of you sons of the Most High’” (Psalm 81:1, 6). Is God not above human beings? But what great thing is it if God is above human beings? God is also above angels. For angels did not make God; God made angels. And he who made must necessarily be above everything he made.

Recognizing, therefore, the greatness of the Lord and seeing that he is above every creature—not only bodily but also spiritual—the Prophet says: “The great King above all gods.” He is the supreme God, who has no god above him. Let him speak of his works; those can be grasped.

### 10. [verse 6]

“Whatever the Lord willed, he made in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses.”

Who, however, can comprehend these things? Who can enumerate the works of the Lord in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses? Nevertheless, although we cannot comprehend everything, we must believe and hold firmly, without hesitation, that whatever creatures exist in heaven, whatever exist on earth, whatever exist in the sea and in all the abysses, were made by the Lord. For “whatever he willed, he made in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses,” as we have already said.

He was not compelled to make everything he made; rather, “whatever he willed, he made.” His will is the cause of everything he made.

You build a house because, if you did not wish to build it, you would remain without a dwelling. Necessity compels you to build a house, not free will. You make clothing because, if you did not make it, you would go about naked. You are therefore driven to make clothing by necessity, not by free will. You plant a mountain with vines and scatter seed because, unless you do so, you will have no food. You do all these things out of necessity.

God made by goodness; he needed none of what he made. Therefore “whatever he willed, he made.”

### 11.

Do you think that we too have something we can do by free will? We do the things we have mentioned out of necessity, because if we did not do them, we would remain needy and destitute. Can we find something that we do by free will? Certainly: when we praise God himself by loving him.

You do this by free will when you love what you praise—not out of necessity, but because it pleases you. This is why God pleased the righteous and holy, even when he scourged them. When he displeased all the wicked, he pleased them; and while they were under his scourge, in distress, labors, wounds, and poverty, they praised God. Even the one who tormented them did not displease them.

This is to love freely, not as though a reward had been placed before you to receive. For God himself will be your highest reward, whom you love freely. And you must love in such a way that you do not cease to desire him as your reward, since he alone satisfies you, as Philip desired him when he said, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8).

Rightly so, because we do this by free will, and ought to do it by free will: we do it because we delight in it, we do it by loving. For even if we are corrected by him, he must never displease us, since he is always just.

His praiser said this: “My vows are upon me, O God; I will repay them as praises to you” (Psalm 55:12). And elsewhere: “Freely I will sacrifice to you” (Psalm 54:8). What does “Freely I will sacrifice” mean? “Freely I will praise you.” For, he says, “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me” (Psalm 49:23).

If you were compelled to offer your Lord a sacrifice pleasing and acceptable to him, as sacrifices had previously been commanded [Note: [Col. 1746] Several manuscripts read “a sacrifice was commanded.”] under the shadow of things to come, perhaps you would not find in your flock a bull that pleased him, or among your goats a he-goat worthy of the Lord’s altar, or in your sheepfold a ram worthy to be offered as a victim to your Lord. And, not finding one, you would be anxious about what to do; perhaps you would say to God, “I wanted to, but I did not have one.”

Can you say the same of praise: “I wanted to, but I did not have it”? To have wanted to praise is itself to have praised. God does not seek words from you, but your heart.

Finally, you can say, “I did not have a tongue” [Note: So read most manuscripts. The editions read, “Nor can anyone say…”]. If someone loses the power of speech through illness, he has no tongue, yet he has praise. For if God had bodily ears and needed the sound of your body, then when you remained without a tongue you would also remain without praise. But now, because he seeks the heart, examines the heart, and is within as witness, judge, approver, helper [Note: Some manuscripts read “hearer”], and crown-giver, it is enough for you to offer your will.

When you can, you confess with your mouth for salvation [Note: [Col. 1746] Thus Am. and the manuscripts. Er. and Lov. read “confess,” and below, “believe.”]; when you cannot, you believe in your heart for righteousness (Romans 10:10). In your heart you praise, in your heart you bless, in your heart you place sacred victims upon the altar of conscience; and the response is made to you: “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

### 12.

That God, then, who is omnipotent, made in heaven and on earth everything whatever he willed. You do not do in your own house everything you will. He made in heaven and on earth everything whatever he willed; you should at least do in your own field everything you will.

You will many things, but you cannot do everything you will in your own house. Perhaps your wife objects; your children object; sometimes even a servant obstinately objects, and you do not do what you will.

“But I do what I will,” you say, “because I punish the one who does not obey and contradicts me.” You do not even do this whenever you will. Sometimes you want to punish and cannot; sometimes you threaten, and before you do what you threaten, you die.

Do you think you do what you will within yourself? Do you restrain all your desires? Perhaps you restrain them—but do you thereby make those desires, which you restrain, cease to arise? Certainly you want not to be troubled by the irritation of your desires; and yet “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Galatians 5:17).

You do not do what you will even within yourself; but our God, in heaven and on earth, made everything whatever he willed. May he himself give you the grace to do within yourself what you will. For unless he helps you, you do not even do within yourself what you will.

Indeed, when the one who said, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish,” was unable to do within himself what he willed; when he himself groaned over himself, saying, “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members”—because he had not fulfilled what he willed not only in his house or field, but in his flesh and spirit—he cried out to God, who made everything whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, and said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?”

And as though that good and sweet one were answering him, he immediately added: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:22–25).

Love this sweetness, then; praise this sweetness. Understand that God, who made everything whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, will also do in you what you will. With his help you will fulfill your will.

But while you cannot, confess; when you can, give thanks. Lying down, cry out; when raised up, do not become proud.

He, then, made in heaven and on earth everything whatever he willed, in the sea and in all the abysses.

### 13. [verse 7]

“Raising clouds from the end of the earth.”

We see these works of the Lord in his creation. Clouds come from the end of the earth toward the middle and rain; you do not know from where they arose. The Prophet therefore indicates that he raises them from the end of the earth, whether from below or from the circumference of the earth’s boundaries; nevertheless, he raises them from the earth.

“He made lightning into rain.” For lightning without rain would terrify you and give you nothing [Note: Most manuscripts read, “and would give you no food.”]. “He made lightning into rain.” There is lightning, and you tremble; it rains, and you rejoice. “He made lightning into rain”: the one who terrified you made the same thing so that you might rejoice [Note: Several manuscripts read, “he himself refreshed you.”].

“He brings the winds out of his treasuries”—from hidden causes, from a source you do not know. You feel that the wind blows; but by what cause it blows, or from what treasury of reason it has been brought forth, you do not know. Nevertheless, you owe God the piety of believing, because it would not blow unless the one who made it had commanded it, unless the one who created it had brought it forth.

### 14. [verses 8–12]

We see these things, then, in creation; we praise, marvel at, and bless God. Let us see what he did among human beings for the sake of his people.

“He struck the firstborn of Egypt.” Those divine words were spoken which you would love, and the words you would fear were not spoken. Pay attention: even when he is angry, he does what he wills.

“He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from human being to beast. He sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt.” You know and have read how much the hand of the Lord did through Moses in Egypt, to terrify, crush, and cast down the proud Egyptians—in Pharaoh and in all his servants.

It is little to say “in Egypt”; what happened after the people had been led out from there? “He struck many nations,” which possessed the land that God wished to give to his people. “And he killed mighty kings: Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan.”

The Psalm recalls all these things briefly; we read them in the other divine books, where the hand of the Lord is greatly manifested.
