When you see what was done to the impious, take care that such things do not happen to you. They were done to them so that you might pass by, not imitate them, and not suffer such things.

Yet see that the scourge of the Lord is upon all flesh. Do not think that you are unseen when you sin; do not think that you are disregarded; do not think that the Lord sleeps. Consider examples of God’s benefits when you recall them, and when you recall God’s vengeance, be afraid. He is omnipotent both for consoling and for chastising.

This is why these things are useful when they are read. When the devout person sees what the impious person suffered, he purifies himself from all impiety, lest he too fall into such punishment and vengeance.

You have therefore received these things well. What did God do next? “He drove out the impious and gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his servant.”

### 15. [verse 13]

Then comes the exultation of his praise: “Lord, your name is forever,” after all these things that you have done.

What do I see that you have done? I look upon your creation, which you made in heaven; I look upon this lowest region where we dwell; and from this I see your benefits—the clouds, the winds, and the rains. I consider your people: you led them out of the house of bondage, performed signs and wonders among their enemies, punished those who afflicted them, expelled the impious from their land, killed their kings, and gave their land to your people.

I saw everything, and filled with praise I said: “Lord, your name is forever.”

## Mystical exposition of the preceding verses

### 16. [verse 6]

We see, know, and praise how these things are written according to the literal sense. But if they signify something, let me not be burdensome as I explain them as best I can.

Behold, in human beings themselves I can recognize that in heaven and on earth he made everything whatever he willed. By “heaven” I understand spiritual people; by “earth,” carnal people. The Church of God consists of these two, as of heaven and earth. Preaching belongs to the spiritual, obedience to the carnal.

For “the heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Psalm 18:2). But if the people of God were not God’s earth, the Apostle would not say, “You are God’s building, God’s cultivation. Like a wise architect I laid a foundation; another builds upon it.”

We are therefore God’s building and God’s field. “Who plants a vineyard,” he says, “and does not eat of its fruit?” (1 Corinthians 9:7). “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:9–10, 6).

Thus in his Church, in his preachers, and in his peoples, as in heaven and earth, he made everything whatever he willed.

But this is not enough: “In the sea and in all the abysses he made everything whatever he willed.” The sea is all unbelievers, all who do not yet believe; and in them he made everything whatever he willed. For unbelievers do not rage unless they are permitted to do so; nor is vengeance taken against them when they are perverse unless the one who made all nations commands it.

Suppose it is the sea and not the earth: is it therefore outside the power of God almighty? “In the sea and in all the abysses he did what he willed.”

What are the abysses? The hidden hearts of mortals, the deep thoughts of human beings. How does God do what he wills there as well? Because “the Lord examines the righteous and the impious, but the one who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6).

And where does he examine him? Elsewhere it is written: “There will be an examination in the thoughts of the impious” (Wisdom 1:9). Therefore, “in all the abysses he made everything whatever he willed.”

A good heart is hidden; an evil heart is hidden. There is an abyss in the good heart and an abyss in the evil heart; but these things are naked before God, from whom nothing is hidden. He consoles the good heart and torments the evil heart.

Therefore he made everything whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses.

### 17. [verse 7]

“Raising clouds from the end of the earth.”

What clouds? The preachers of his word of truth. Concerning these clouds, in another place, becoming angry with his vineyard, he says: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isaiah 5:6).

And it is not enough that he raised clouds from Jerusalem or from Israel and sent them to preach his Gospel throughout the whole world. Concerning these clouds it was said: “Their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5). This is not enough; for the Lord himself says, “This Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14). He raises clouds from the end of the earth.

For as the Gospel grows, from where will there be preachers of the Gospel at the ends of the earth unless he raises clouds there from the end of the earth?

What does he do through these clouds? “He made lightning into rain”: he turned threats toward mercy; from terrors he brought refreshment.

How did he bring refreshment from terrors? When God threatens you through a prophet or an apostle and you are afraid, did the flash of lightning not terrify you? But when you correct yourself through repentance and recognize that this has happened through mercy, the terror of the lightning is turned into rain.

“He brings the winds out of his treasuries.” I think that the same people are preachers, clouds, and winds: clouds because of the flesh, winds because of the spirit. Clouds are seen; winds are felt but not seen.

Finally, because we see that the flesh is from the earth, he says, “He raises clouds from the end of the earth.” He had expressed where he raises the clouds; he comes to the winds, because the origin of the human spirit is unknown: “Bringing forth,” he says, “the winds from his treasuries.”

Pay attention for a little while, and let us examine what follows.

### 18. [verse 8]

“He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from human being to beast.”

May our firstborn be safe for the Lord, since he himself gave them to us. The punishment is grievous and the blow exceedingly terrible: the death of the firstborn.

What are our firstborn? These present ways of life by which we now serve God—they are our firstborn. For we possess faith itself as firstfruits, from which we begin. It was said to the Church, “You will come and pass through from the beginning of faith” (Song of Songs 4:8, according to the Septuagint); and no one begins to live well except from faith.

Our faith, therefore, is among our firstborn. When our faith is guarded, other things can follow. For people are purified daily as they progress toward what is better and live better, while the inner person is renewed day by day, as the Apostle says: “Although our outer person is being corrupted, the inner person is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). This happens because the firstborn faith lives.

Concerning this firstborn faith the Apostle also says: “And not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit”—that is, who are already giving God the firstfruits of our spirit, namely faith itself, as our firstborn—“yet we groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body” (Romans 8:23).

If it is therefore a great grace of God that our faith is preserved, it is a great punishment to kill the firstborn, when people placed in the affliction of the Church lose their faith.

For they afflict the Church in order to destroy faith. Egypt itself is interpreted as “affliction.” Whoever therefore afflicts the Church, whoever introduces scandals into the Church—even if they are called Christians—their firstborn die.

They become unbelievers, empty people, possessing only the name and the sign. In their hearts, however, they have buried their firstborn. To such an extent that when you say something to them for the sake of a good life, the hope of eternal life, and fear of eternal fire, they mock inwardly; or, if they are such as to dare do so in your presence, they twist their mouths and say, “Who has come back from there?” People say to themselves whatever they wish.

And he is a Christian; but because he afflicts the Church, his firstborn has been killed and his faith has died. This extends “from human being to beast.”

I will say, brothers, what I understand. By “human beings” I understand spiritually those who are learned, because of the rational soul, which constitutes the human being; by “beasts,” the unlearned, though nevertheless possessing faith, since otherwise they would not have firstborn.

There are learned people who afflict the Church by creating schisms and heresies. Consequently, you do not find faith even in them, because they have become Egypt—that is, affliction—for the people of God. Their firstborn have been killed. They drag unlearned crowds behind them; these are the beasts.

In this affliction by which the Church is afflicted, faith dies in those who afflict her. The firstborn die both in the learned and in the unlearned, because God killed the firstborn of the Egyptians, from human being to beast.

### 19. [verse 9]

“He sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants.”

Pharaoh was the king of the Egyptians. Consider the name and see how God does these things. The king is first in every nation. Egypt means “Affliction”; Pharaoh means “Dissipation.” Affliction therefore has Dissipation as its king, because those who afflict the Church afflict her in a state of dissipation.

For in order to afflict, they are scattered. The king leads, and the people follow. Dissipation goes before; affliction follows.

Listen—listen to these names, rich in typical interpretation [Note: Some manuscripts read “mystical interpretation”] and wisdom. You will not find one of these names interpreted as anything good where God exercised his anger.

20. [verses 10, 11.] He struck many nations and slew mighty kings. Which kings and which nations, tell me? Sihon, king of the Amorites. Hear names laden with mysteries. “He slew Sihon,” it says, “king of the Amorites.” He certainly slew him; and now may he slay him from the hearts of his servants and from the temptations of his Church, nor may his hand cease from slaying such kings and such peoples. For Sihon is interpreted as “temptation of the eyes” [Note: Almost all manuscripts consistently have here and below “temptation of colors.” Moreover, later, in Psalm 133, section 9, the same name is said to be interpreted as “useless shoot or burning temptation.”]; the Amorites are interpreted as “those who make bitter.” Now see whether we can understand how those who make bitter could have “temptation of the eyes” as their king. Temptation of the eyes is nothing other than falsehood: it has color, but it does not have truth. What wonder, then, if those who make bitter have such a king—a lying king? For unless falsehood and pretense go before, they are not those who make bitter in the Church; they make bitter precisely because they pretend. Temptation of the eyes goes before, and bitterness follows; and it went before even in the devil himself, for “temptation of the eyes” is what “transfigures himself as an angel of light” (II Corinthians 11:14) [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions, however, have: “For if there is no temptation of the eyes, how does he transfigure himself as an angel of light?”].

May the hand of the Lord slay both him and them: him, so that he may not lead others astray; them, so that they may be corrected. Indeed, in every individual that king is slain when one condemns pretense and loves truth. The hand of God does not cease doing this. For just as he acted then literally, so now he acts spiritually, in order to fulfill what he then prophetically foretold.

He also slew another king and his people: “And Og, king of Bashan.” How wicked this one is too! Og is interpreted as “conclusion”; Bashan is interpreted as “confusion.” That king is wicked who blocks the way to God. For this is what the devil does: by continually setting his fabrications in the way, setting his idols in the way, setting himself up as necessary through those possessed [Note: Some manuscripts have: “making his idols, setting himself up,” and so forth. Others have: “setting his idols in the way, without ceasing, through those possessed,” and so forth. Certain manuscripts have: “setting his idols in the way, making [them] without ceasing through those possessed,” and so forth.], through fortune-tellers, augurs, haruspices, magicians, and the sacred rites of demons, he blocks the way.

Christ brings this about in the opposite way, so that the way which had been blocked may be opened. For one redeemed through him says, “And in my God I will leap over a wall” (Psalm 17:30). Thus the devil does nothing else except block the way, so that people may not believe in God. For if one believes in God, the way is open—and Christ himself is the way (John 14:6). But if one does not believe in God, the way is blocked. And if it has been blocked because people do not believe, what remains except that, when the one in whom they did not believe comes, those who did not believe will be put to shame? Why? Because “conclusion” goes before, and “confusion” follows: conclusion goes before as king, and confusion follows like the people. Those whom he now blocks, so that they may not believe in Christ, will all be put to shame when Christ appears, and their iniquities will bring them forth in opposition to them. Then the impious, put to shame, will say: “What profit did pride bring us?” (Wisdom 5:8).

Great are the mysteries, my brothers. “Dissipation” is the king of “affliction”; they are scattered so that they may be afflicted. Great are the mysteries. “Temptation of the eyes,” that is, deceit, is the king of those who make bitter; for they deceive in order to make bitter. “Conclusion” is the king of confusion; for they are shut off so that they may not pass over to faith, and when the one in whom we believe comes, they will be put to shame.

And God slew all the kingdoms of Canaan. Canaan is interpreted as “prepared for humiliation.” Humility appears to signify something good, but only if it is beneficial humility; for an evil humiliation is punitive. If humiliation did not pertain to punishment, it would not be said, “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11; 18:14). For no benefit is bestowed on him when he is punished so that he may be humbled.

Canaan, then, is now proud. Every impious person, every unbeliever, exalts his heart; he does not wish to believe in God. But this exaltation is prepared for humiliation on the day of judgment. Then he will be humbled when he does not wish to be humbled, for “they are vessels of wrath, perfected for destruction” (Romans 9:22). For now let them exalt themselves, chatter, stretch themselves above the faithful, mock the faithful, and blaspheme Christians; let them say, “What they say about the day of judgment is old wives’ tales.” Their arrogance is prepared for humiliation. When the judge comes—the one who is now proclaimed and mocked—then the one who is now proud will be humbled, not beneficially but punitively. For now he is not humbled, but prepared for humiliation; that is, he is prepared for condemnation, prepared as a sacrificial victim.

21. [verse 13.] God therefore overturned all these things: bodily at that time, when our fathers were led out of the land of Egypt; spiritually now, and his hand does not cease until the end. Therefore do not suppose that these manifestations of God’s power were then completed and have ceased. “Lord, your name,” he says, “is forever.” That is, your mercy does not cease, nor does your hand cease forever to do the things that you then foretold by means of figures: “For all those things happened to them in figure, but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Corinthians 10:11).

“Your memorial, O Lord, is from generation to generation.” This generation and that generation: the generation by which we are made faithful and reborn through Baptism, and the generation by which we shall rise from the dead and live forever, joined to the angels. “Your memorial, O Lord,” both over this generation and over that generation: for even now you have not forgotten us, so as to call us; nor will you then forget us, so as to crown us. “Your memorial, O Lord, is from generation to generation.”

22. [verse 14.] “For the Lord judged” [Note: The editions, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint, have “will judge.” But the manuscripts consistently have “judged,” and Augustine appears to have read it in this way from his manner of interpretation.] “his people.” Certainly he completed all those things among the Jewish people. Have his works now remained unfinished, after he led his people into the promised land? By no means; he will still judge: “The Lord judged his people, and he will be invoked among his servants.”

He has already judged that people; apart from the future judgment, the Jewish people has been judged. What does “judged” mean? The righteous have been separated from that people, and the unrighteous have remained. But if I am lying, or am thought to be lying because I said, “It has already been judged,” hear the Lord saying: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). The proud have been blinded; the humble have been enlightened. The Lord therefore judged his people.

Isaiah spoke of this very judgment: “And now you, house of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord.” This is too little; but what follows? “For he dismissed his people, the house of Israel” (Isaiah 2:5–6). That is the house of Jacob which is the house of Israel; for the one who is Jacob is himself Israel. You know the holy Scriptures, and I think it comes to your mind that Jacob himself, when he saw the angel wrestling with him, then received the name by which he was to be called Israel (Genesis 32:28). It is one man, whether Jacob or Israel; it is one person: the house of Jacob and the house of Israel are one nation, one people. He invites this one and dismisses this one.

And now, surely, you have killed Christ, O house of Jacob; you have killed Christ; you have already shaken your head before the cross; you have mocked him as he hung there; you have already said, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross.” The physician has already prayed for the frenzied: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Matthew 27:39–43; Luke 23:34–35). Surely you have already done all these things, and now believe in the one whom you killed; drink the blood that you poured out.

“And now you, house of Jacob”—I wish to explain from Isaiah’s testimony what he said here: “For the Lord judged his people, and he will be invoked among his servants” [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions have: “to explain the testimony from you.”]. For he is understood to have judged his people by separating, within that very people, the good from the evil, the faithful from the unfaithful, the Apostles from the lying Jews.

This he signified, as I had begun to say, through the Prophet, saying: “Now, after all your evils, O house of Jacob, come; let us walk in the light of the Lord.” Why do I say to you, “Come; let us walk in the light of the Lord”? So that, by remaining in Judaism, you may not fail to reach Christ. Why? Was Christ not always prophesied there? “But now he dismissed his people, the house of Israel.”

Come, house of Jacob, because he dismissed his people, the house of Jacob; come, house of Israel, because he dismissed his people, the house of Israel. Who is it that comes, and who is it that has been dismissed, except because this is the judgment: “that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind”? The Lord therefore judged his people.

He separated them, then; and will he not find there those whom he may restore to his kingdom? Certainly he will find them: “And he will be invoked among his servants.” The Apostle says, “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” And how does he prove this? “For I too am an Israelite” (Romans 11:1–2).

Therefore, “the Lord judged his people,” separating the good from the evil. This is: “And he will be invoked among his servants.” By whom? By the nations. For how many nations have come by believing! How many estates, how many remote places are now coming! From there countless people come—I do not know how many—and they wish to believe. We say to them, “What do you want?” They reply, “To know the glory of God.”

Believe me, brothers, we marvel and rejoice at hearing such a declaration from country people. They come from who knows where, stirred up by who knows whom. What am I saying—by who knows whom? Indeed, I know by whom: because he says, “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him.”

They come suddenly from the forest, from the desert, from the most remote and rugged mountains to the Church, and most or nearly all of them have this utterance, so that we may truly see God teaching within: the prophetic Scripture is fulfilled in which it was said, “They shall all be taught by God” (Isaiah 54:13; John 6:44–45).

We ask them, “What do you desire?” And they say, “To see the glory of God.” For “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). They believe, they are consecrated, and they insist that clergy be ordained for them. Is not this fulfilled: “And he will be invoked among his servants”?

23. [verses 15–17.] Finally, after this entire arrangement and administration, the Spirit of God turns to reproaching and mocking the idols, which are already mocked by their own worshipers: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold.”

Since God does all these things—he who made in heaven and on earth everything whatsoever he willed, who judged his people [Col. 1754] and will be invoked among his servants—what remains except a thing fashioned, to be mocked rather than worshiped?

Perhaps, when he was about to say “the idols of the nations,” he intended us to despise all these things. Perhaps he was going to say, “The idols of the nations are stones and wood, plaster and clay.” I do not say these things; the material is cheap. I speak of what they greatly love, or what they greatly honor: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold.”

Certainly it is gold; certainly it is silver. Because silver shines and gold shines, do they therefore have eyes and see? Insofar as it is silver, insofar as it is gold, it may perhaps be useful to the miser, but not to the religious person; indeed, not even useful to the miser, but useful to one who uses it well and, by distributing it, acquires a heavenly treasure. Yet, since these things are now senseless, why do you make gods out of silver and gold, human beings? When you make them gods, do you not see that they do not see (Wisdom 15:15)?

“They have eyes, and they do not see” [Note: The manuscripts have “they do not see,” and likewise below in the present tense: “they do not hear, they do not smell, they do not speak, they do not act, they do not walk.”]; “they have ears, and they do not hear; they have nostrils, and they do not smell; they have a mouth, and they do not speak; they have hands, and they do not act; they have feet, and they do not walk.”

The craftsman—the silversmith and goldsmith—could make all these things: eyes, ears, nostrils, a mouth, hands, and feet. But he could not give light to the eyes, hearing to the ears, a voice to the mouth, sensation to the nostrils, movement to the hands, or a path to the feet.

24. [verse 18.] O human being, without doubt you now laugh at what you made, if you have recognized by whom you were made. But what is said about those who have not recognized him? “Let all who make them and all who trust in them become like them.”

And do you believe, brothers, that some likeness to the idols is expressed in them—not in their flesh, certainly, but in their inner person? For “they have ears, and they do not hear.” God cries out to them: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 11:15). “They have eyes, and they do not see”: they have bodily eyes, but they do not have the eyes of faith.

Finally, this prophecy is fulfilled throughout all the nations. See how it was spoken through the Prophet. I am not recalling anything allegorical or figurative; hear the proper, explicit, simple, manifest prophecy foretold, and see it fulfilled. “The Lord prevailed against them,” says the prophet Zephaniah. Against those who resisted, against those who rebelled, and who, by killing the faithful, made martyrs—yet without knowing what they were doing—“the Lord prevailed against them.”

And how did he prevail? In his Church we see that he prevailed against them. They wanted to extinguish and kill the few Christians; they shed blood. From the blood of those who were killed, so many arose that those very slayers of the martyrs were overcome. Even now those who once slaughtered Christians because of idols are looking for places where they can hide their idols. Did the Lord not prevail against them?

See whether he does what follows: “The Lord prevailed against them.” And what did he do? “He exterminated all the gods of the nations from the earth, and they shall worship him, each one from his own place, all the islands of the nations” (Zephaniah 2:11).

What is this? Was it not foretold? Was it not fulfilled? Does it not appear just as it is read? [Col. 1755] And those who remained “have eyes, and they do not see; they have nostrils, and they do not smell.” They do not perceive that fragrance. “We are the good fragrance of Christ,” as the Apostle says, “in every place” (II Corinthians 2:15). What does it profit them to have nostrils and not smell the fragrance of Christ, so sweet? Truly this has happened in them, and truly it was said of them: “Let all who make them and all who trust in them become like them.”

25. [verses 19, 20.] Yet daily they believe through the miracles of Christ the Lord. Daily the eyes of the blind are opened, the ears of the deaf are opened, the nostrils of the senseless are given breath, the mouths of the mute are loosened, the hands of the paralyzed are released, the feet of the lame are straightened, and from these stones children of Abraham are raised up (Matthew 3:9). To all of them let it now be said: “House of Israel, bless the Lord.”

They are all children of Abraham. And if children of Abraham are raised from these stones, it is clear that those are rather the house of Israel who belong to the house of Israel, who belong to the seed of Abraham not according to the flesh but according to faith: “House of Israel, bless the Lord.”

But suppose this is said of that house, and the people of Israel are called by that name. From there the Apostles and thousands of the circumcised believed. “House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord.”

Bless the Lord, peoples—that is, the house of Israel in general. Bless the Lord, those set over others—that is, the house of Aaron. Bless the Lord, ministers—that is, the house of Levi. What of the remaining nations? “You who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.”

26. [verse 21.] Let us all therefore say with one voice what follows: “Blessed is the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem.”

“From Zion” and “Jerusalem.” Zion means “watchtower” or “contemplation”; Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” In which Jerusalem will he now dwell? In the one that fell? No, but in that mother of ours who is in heaven, of whom it was said, “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” (Isaiah 54:1; Galatians 4:26–27).

Now, therefore, the Lord is “from Zion,” because we are watching until he comes [Note: Am. and the manuscripts have “until he comes.”]. Yet, as long as we live in hope, we are in Zion. When the journey is finished, we shall dwell in that city which will never fall, because the Lord both dwells in it and guards it. It is the vision of peace, eternal Jerusalem—the peace, my brothers, whose praise no tongue is sufficient to express, where we shall no longer feel any enemy, either in the Church or outside the Church, either in our flesh or in our thoughts.

“Death will be swallowed up in victory” (I Corinthians 15:54), and we shall have leisure to behold God in eternal peace, having become citizens of Jerusalem, the city of God.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM CXXXV

1. [verse 1.] “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is for ever.” This psalm contains the praise of God, and in all its verses ends in the same manner. Accordingly, although many things are said here in praise of God, his mercy is especially commended; and the Holy Spirit, through whom the psalm was composed, would not have any verse conclude without the most explicit commendation of it.

I remember that, in the one hundred and fifth psalm, which begins similarly, because the codex at which I was looking read not “for ever” but “his mercy is unto the age,” I examined which interpretation we ought rather to understand. For in Greek it is written εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, which may be translated both “unto the age” and “for ever.” But it would take too long to repeat here what I discussed there as best I could.

In this psalm, however, even that very codex reads not “unto the age,” as most do, but “his mercy is for ever.” Although after the judgment in which, at the end of the age, the living and the dead are to be judged—when the righteous have been sent into eternal life and the unrighteous into eternal burning—there will thereafter be none upon whom God may still have mercy, it can nevertheless rightly be understood that his mercy, which he bestows upon his holy and faithful ones, will be for ever: not because they will be miserable for ever and therefore need his mercy for ever, but because that blessedness which he mercifully grants to the miserable, so that they may cease to be miserable and begin to be blessed, will have no end; therefore his mercy is for ever.

For our becoming righteous from unrighteous, sound from infirm, living from dead, immortal from mortal, blessed from miserable, is his mercy. And our being thus will be for ever; therefore his mercy is for ever.

Accordingly, “Confess to the Lord,” that is, praise the Lord by confessing him, “for he is good.” Nor will you receive anything temporal for this confession, “for his mercy is for ever,” that is, the benefit which he mercifully bestows upon you is eternal.

Where it reads, “for he is good,” the Greek has ἀγαθός, not as in the one hundred and fifth psalm, where the Greek for “for he is good” is χρηστός. Hence some translated the latter, “for he is sweet.” But ἀγαθός means not merely good, but supremely good.

2. [verses 2, 3.] Then follows: “Confess to the God of gods, for his mercy is for ever. Confess to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is for ever.”

Who these gods and lords are, of whose gods and lords he is God and Lord—the true God—is rightly often asked. In another psalm we find even human beings called gods: “God stood in the assembly of gods; but in their midst he distinguishes gods”; and a little later, “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High; but you shall die as human beings, and fall like one of the princes.”

The Lord also recalls this testimony in the Gospel, saying: “Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, You are gods’? If he called those gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken, do you say to him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John 10:34–36).

Thus they were called gods not because all were good, but because the word of God came to them. For if all were good for that reason, he would not judge them in this way. When he had said, “God stood in the assembly of gods,” he did not say, “In their midst he distinguishes gods and human beings,” as though showing the difference between gods and human beings; rather, “In their midst,” he says, “he distinguishes gods.”

Then follows: “How long will you judge iniquity?” (Psalm 81:1, 2, 6, 7), and the rest—things which he surely says not to all, but to some, because he speaks while distinguishing them; yet in their midst he distinguishes gods.

3. But if human beings to whom the word of God came are called gods, the question is whether angels also should be called gods, since equality with angels is promised as the greatest reward to righteous and holy human beings.

In the Scriptures, indeed, I do not know whether angels are anywhere, or readily can be found, expressly called gods. But when it had been said of the Lord God, “Terrible above all gods,” the text immediately added, as if explaining why this was said: “For the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 95:4, 5).

The Lord was called terrible above such gods in his saints, whom he made heavens, and by whom demons might be terrified. For it follows: “But the Lord made the heavens.”

Thus it does not say simply “gods,” but “the gods of the nations are demons”; yet above it says, “Terrible above all gods,” not “above all gods of the nations,” although this is what it means by adding what follows: “For the gods of the nations are demons.”

It is said, however, that this is not written so in Hebrew, but: “The gods of the nations are images.” If this is true, the Septuagint must all the more be believed to have translated by the divine Spirit, by whose Spirit the things in the Hebrew writings were also spoken.

For, with the same Spirit at work, it was fitting that it should also be said, “The gods of the nations are demons,” so that we might understand the Hebrew wording, “The gods of the nations are images,” as indicating rather the demons which are in the images.

For as regards the images themselves, which in Greek are called εἴδωλα, “idols,” a word which we now use as Latin, they have eyes and do not see, and the other things said of them precisely because they lack every sense. Therefore they cannot be terrified, since only things that have sensation can, of course, be terrified.

How then was it said of the Lord, “He is terrible above all gods, for the gods of the nations are images,” unless demons, which can be terrified, are understood through the images?

Hence the Apostle also says, “We know that an idol is nothing,” referring to lifeless earthly material. Again, lest anyone suppose that there is no living and sentient nature delighted by the sacrifices of the nations, he adds: “What the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not wish you to become partners with demons” (I Corinthians 10:20).

If, therefore, nowhere in the divine utterances are holy angels found to be called gods, the chief reason that occurs to me is that human beings might not, by this name, be built up to render to holy angels the ministry or service of religion called in Greek λειτουργία [leitourgia] or λατρεία [latreia], which they themselves do not wish to receive from human beings except for that God who is God both of themselves and of human beings.

Thus angels are much more usefully called angels, which in Latin are termed messengers, so that by the name—not of their substance but of their office—we may sufficiently understand that they wish us to worship the God whom they announce.

The Apostle therefore briefly resolves this whole question when he says: “For although there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him” (I Corinthians 8:4–6).

4. [verse 4.] Let us therefore confess to the God of gods and the Lord of lords, for his mercy is for ever: to him who alone does great wonders.

As at the ends of all the verses there stands, “for his mercy is for ever,” so at the beginnings of all of them, though it is not written, “Confess” must be understood. This is clearer in Greek. It would also be clear in Latin had our translators been able to translate the same construction.

In this verse they could have done so, had they said, “to him doing wonders”; for where we have, “Who did wonders,” the Greek has “to him doing wonders” [Note: Τῷ ποιήσαντι.], where “Confess” must necessarily be understood.

Would that they had at least added the pronoun, so as to say, “To him who does,” or “to him who did,” or “to him who established”; for then it would readily have been understood that “Confess” must be supplied.

But now it has been made so obscure that one who either does not know how, or neglects, to consult the Greek codex may think that “Who made the heavens,” “Who established the earth,” “Who made the lights,” is followed by “for his mercy is for ever” because he made them on account of his eternal mercy.

Yet those whom he frees from misery pertain to his mercy; we should not understand his making heaven, earth, and lights as an act of mercy, since that belongs to his goodness, who created all things very good (Genesis 1:31). He created in order that all things might exist (Wisdom 1:14); but it belongs to mercy that he cleanse us from our sins and free us from misery for ever.

Thus the psalm addresses us: Confess to the God of gods; confess to the Lord of lords; confess to him who alone does great wonders; confess to him who made the heavens in understanding; confess to him who established the earth above the waters; confess to him who alone made the great lights. Why we should confess, it sets at the end of every verse: “For his mercy is for ever.”

5. [verses 5–10.] But what does “who alone does great wonders” mean? Is it because he performed many wonders through angels and human beings? There are certain great things which God alone does, and the text itself proceeds to specify them: “Who made the heavens in understanding; who established the earth above the waters; who alone made the great lights.”

This is why “alone” is also added here: because he performed the other wonders it will mention through human beings. For after saying, “Who alone made the great lights,” it explains what those lights are: “The sun for the rule of the day, the moon and stars for the rule of the night.”

Then it begins to say what he did through angels or human beings: “Who struck Egypt with their firstborn,” and the rest.

God therefore made the whole creation—not through any creature, but alone. He mentioned certain more excellent parts of creation, from which we might think of the whole: the intelligible heavens and the visible earth; and, since there are also visible heavens, he mentioned their lights to remind us that the whole corporeal heaven was made by him.

6. Yet the phrase, “Who made the heavens in understanding,” or, as others translated it, “in intelligence,” may be examined as to whether it means intelligible heavens, or that God made the heavens in his own understanding or intelligence—that is, in his own Wisdom—as is written elsewhere, “You made all things in Wisdom” (Psalm 103:24), thus indicating the only-begotten Word.

But if we understand that God made the heavens in his own understanding, why does it say this only of the heavens, when he made all things in that same Wisdom? Or was it necessary to express it there alone, so that it might be understood even where unspoken in the other clauses?

The sense would then be: “Who made the heavens in understanding, who founded the earth above the waters”—so that here too you supply “in understanding”—“who alone made the great lights, the sun for the rule of the day, the moon and stars for the rule of the night,” surely in understanding.

How then did he make them alone, if “in understanding” or “in intelligence” means in Wisdom, that is, in the only-begotten Word? Is it because the Trinity is not three gods but one God, that the statement that God alone made them refers to the fact that he did not make a creature through a creature?

7. But what does “Who established the earth above the waters” mean? It is an obscure question, because the earth seems heavier, so that it is believed not to be borne by waters but rather to bear the waters.

To avoid seeming to defend our Scriptures contentiously against those who think they have ascertained these matters by certain reasons, whether this is so or otherwise, we have a nearby interpretation: the earth inhabited by human beings and containing terrestrial animals—called “dry land” elsewhere in Scripture, as it is written, “Let the dry land appear,” and “God called the dry land Earth” (Genesis 1:9, 10)—is established above the waters because it rises above the waters that flow around it.

For a coastal city [Note: Most manuscripts: “littoral.”] is said to be founded above the sea not because the sea is beneath it as waters are under vaulted caverns or under floating ships, but because it rises above the lower sea [Note: Thus Am. and some manuscripts. The Royal manuscript reads, “rises above the first sea at its boundaries.” Erasmus and Louvain: “rises above the lower sea at the first boundaries.”].

So Pharaoh is said to have gone out above the water—the Greek has this, where some Latin texts have “to the water” (Exodus 7:15)—and so the Lord sat above the well (John 4:6): both were higher than the river and the well, the former beside the river and the latter beside the well.

8. But if these sayings also signify something else more relevant to us: God made the heavens in understanding, namely his spiritual saints, to whom he granted not merely believing but also understanding divine things.

Those not yet able to do this, but holding only the most steadfast faith, are figured as earth below the heavens. And because they stand in unshaken belief in the Baptism they have received, it is said, “He established the earth above the waters.”

Again, since it is written of the Lord Jesus Christ that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him (Colossians 2:3), and other utterances of Scripture also testify that these two, wisdom and knowledge, differ in some respect—especially holy Job speaking, where the individual terms are, as it were, defined—he says: “But he said to man: Behold, piety is wisdom, and to abstain from evil is knowledge” (Job 28:28).

We rightly understand wisdom as the knowledge and love of that which always is and unchangeably remains, namely God. For the Greek calls what he says, “Behold, piety is wisdom,” θεοσέβεια [theosebeia], which may be rendered fully in Latin as “the worship of God.”

But “to abstain from evil,” which he calls knowledge, is what else than cautiously and wisely conducting oneself in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, as in the night of this age (Philippians 2:15), so that by abstaining from iniquity one may not be confounded with darkness, being distinguished by the light of one’s proper gift?

Accordingly, when the Apostle wished in one place to show the harmonious variety of gifts in the people of God, he put these two first: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom”—I take this to be “the sun for the rule of the day”; “to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit”—this is the moon.

Then I think the stars are mentioned, as it were, in what follows: “To another faith in the same Spirit; to another the gift of healings in one Spirit; to another workings of powers; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of utterances” (I Corinthians 12:8–10).

None of these is unnecessary in the night of this age; when that night has passed, these necessary things will no longer be so. Therefore they are “for the rule of the night.”

For he says “for the rule,” whether of day or night, so that there may be power to shine by day or by night [Note: Am. and most manuscripts: “so that there might be power for the day to shine, or for the night.”]. In spiritual gifts this is understood thus: “He gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

“Who struck Egypt with their firstborn.” He also struck the world, together with those things considered foremost in the world.

9. [vers. 11–26.] He who brought Israel out from among them. He also brings his saints and faithful ones out from among the wicked. With a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. What is mightier, what more exalted, than he of whom it was said: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1). He who divided the Red Sea into sections. He also divides it, so that one and the same Baptism may be life to some and death to others. And he led Israel through its midst. He likewise leads his renewed people through the laver of regeneration. And he shook off Pharaoh and his power in the Red Sea. Through Baptism he swiftly destroys the sin and guilt of his own people.[^c0073-1]

He who led his people through the desert. He also leads us through the aridity and barrenness of this age, lest we perish in it. He who struck down great kings and slew mighty kings. He also strikes and kills, through us, the devil’s powers, those harmful powers. Sihon, king of the Amorites. “Useless shoot” or “heated temptation,” which is the interpretation of Sihon; “king of those who embitter,” which is the interpretation of “the Amorites.” And Og, king of Bashan. “He who heaps up,” which is the interpretation of Og; and “king of Confusion,” which is the interpretation of Bashan—for what does the devil heap up except confusion? And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his servant. He also gives as an inheritance to the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, those whom the devil possessed.

For he remembered us in our lowliness. And he redeemed us from our enemies: by the blood of his Only-Begotten Son. He gives food to all flesh—that is, to the whole human race, not only to the Israelites but also to the Gentiles. Of this food it is said: “My flesh is truly food” (John VI, 56).

Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his mercy is everlasting. Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is everlasting. By saying here “God of heaven,” I believe he wished to express differently what he had already said above, “God of gods”; for what he then added afterward, he repeats here also: “Give thanks to the Lord of lords.” Yet although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—just as there are many gods and many lords—still, for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist (I Cor. VIII, 5–6). To him we give thanks, because his mercy is everlasting.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM CXXXVI

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. [vers. 1.] I do not think you have forgotten that we commended—or rather, reminded—you of something which every educated person in the holy Church ought to know: where we are citizens, where we are pilgrims, that the cause of our pilgrimage is sin, and that the gift of our return is the forgiveness of sins and justification by the grace of God.

You have heard and know that two cities, for the present mingled bodily but separated in heart, run through the successive ages of the world until the end: one whose end is eternal peace, called Jerusalem; the other whose joy is temporal peace, called Babylon. You also retain, I believe, the interpretations of their names: Jerusalem is interpreted as “Vision of peace,” Babylon as “Confusion.”

Jerusalem was held captive in Babylon, but not in its entirety, for its citizens include the angels. Yet as regards those human beings predestined for the glory of God, destined by adoption to be fellow heirs with Christ, whom he redeemed from that very captivity by his blood: we explained that this portion of the city of Jerusalem is held captive in Babylon on account of sin, but begins to depart from it first in heart, through confession of iniquity and love of righteousness, and afterward, at the end of the age, is to be separated from it bodily as well.

We commended this in the psalm which we first treated here with Your Charity, which begins: “Praise is due to you, O God, in Zion, and to you the vow shall be paid in Jerusalem” (Ps. LXIV, 2). Today, however, we sang: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion.” Observe that in the former it says, “Praise is due to you, O God, in Zion”; here, however: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion”—that Zion where praise is due to God.

2. What, then, are the rivers of Babylon, and what does it mean for us to sit and weep in remembrance of Zion? For if we are citizens of that place, we do not merely sing this, but also act upon it. If we are citizens of Jerusalem—that is, of Zion—and in this life, in this confusion of the present age, in this Babylon, we do not dwell as citizens but are held as captives, we ought not merely to sing these words but also to enact them with devout feeling and religious longing for the eternal city.

This city called Babylon also has its lovers, people who care for temporal peace, hope for nothing beyond it, fix all their joy there, and bring it to an end there. We see them laboring greatly for the earthly commonwealth. Yet if anyone conducts himself faithfully within it, without seeking pride, perishable arrogance, or hateful boasting there, but exhibiting true faith as far as he can, for as long as he can, to whomever he can, in accordance with what he sees of earthly things and understands of the city’s appearance, God does not allow him to perish in Babylon. For he has predestined such people to be citizens of Jerusalem.

God understands their captivity and shows them another city, the one for which they ought truly to sigh, for which they ought to strive in every way, and toward which they ought to exhort their fellow citizens and fellow pilgrims, as far as they are able, so that they may attain it. Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ says: “The one who is faithful in very little is faithful also in much”; and again: “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke XVI, 10, 12).

3. Yet, beloved, attend to the rivers of Babylon. The rivers of Babylon are all the things that are loved here and pass away. Someone, for example, has loved practicing agriculture itself, becoming rich from it, occupying his mind with it, and deriving pleasure from it. Let him consider the end, and see that what he loved is not the foundation of Jerusalem but a river of Babylon.

Another says: “It is a great thing to be a soldier. All farmers fear soldiers, obey them, and tremble before them. If I am a farmer, I shall fear the soldier; if I am a soldier, I shall be feared by the farmer.” O madman, you have thrown yourself into another river of Babylon, one more turbulent and rapacious. You wish to be feared by someone lesser; fear someone greater. The one who fears you can suddenly become greater than you; but the one whom you ought to fear will never be lesser.

“Being an advocate,” he says, “is a great thing: possessing the most powerful eloquence, having everyone dependent upon the tongue of his eloquent patron and awaiting from his mouth either losses or gains, death or life, destruction or safety.” You do not know where you have cast yourself. This too is a river of Babylon; and because it makes a great sound, the noise of the water beats upon the rocks. Observe that it flows; observe that it slides away; and if you observe that it flows and slides away, beware, because it carries you along.

Another says: “It is a great thing to sail and engage in commerce: to know many provinces, to gather profits from everywhere, not to be subject in one’s city to any powerful person, always to travel abroad, to nourish the mind through the variety of business and peoples, and to return rich through the increase of profits.” This too is a river of Babylon. When will your profits stand firm? When will you become secure, when will you be confident because of what you acquire? The richer you become, the more fearful you will be. In a single shipwreck you will emerge naked, and rightly lament yourself in the river of Babylon, because you did not wish to sit and weep by the rivers of Babylon.

4. Other citizens of holy Jerusalem, therefore, understanding their captivity, observe human desires and the various cravings of people, which seize, drag, and drive them this way and that into the sea. They see these things and do not throw themselves into the rivers of Babylon; rather, they sit by the rivers of Babylon and weep—either for those who are being swept away, or for themselves, who deserved to be in Babylon—yet they sit, that is, they are humbled.[^c0073-2]

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion.” O holy Zion, where everything stands firm and nothing flows away! Who threw us into this place? Why did we abandon your Creator and your fellowship? Behold, set amid things that flow and slide away, scarcely anyone who has been seized by the river will escape if he can hold on to a piece of wood.

Therefore, humbled in our captivity, let us sit by the rivers of Babylon; let us not dare to throw ourselves into those rivers. Nor let us dare, in the evil and sorrow of our captivity, to raise ourselves up proudly. Let us sit, and thus let us weep. Let us sit by the rivers of Babylon, not beneath the rivers of Babylon: let our humility be such that it does not drown us.

Sit above the river; do not be in the river, do not be beneath the river. Yet sit humbly; do not speak as though you were in Jerusalem. For there you will stand, since another psalm speaks from that very hope and sings: “Our feet were standing in your courts, O Jerusalem” (Ps. CXXI, 2). You will be raised there if here you humble yourself through repentance and confession.

“Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem”; but “by the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion.” From there you ought to weep, remembering Zion.

5. Many weep with Babylonian weeping because they also rejoice with Babylonian joy. Those who rejoice in profits and weep over losses derive both from Babylon. You ought to weep, but while remembering Zion. If you weep in remembrance of Zion, then even when things go well for you according to Babylon, you ought to weep.

Therefore it is said in a certain psalm: “I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXIV, 3–4). What does he mean by saying, “I found”? He found some tribulation as though it were to be sought, as though he had found what he was seeking. And when he found it, with what gain did he find it? He called upon the name of the Lord.

It makes a great difference whether you find tribulation or are found by tribulation. For elsewhere he says: “The sorrows of hell found me” (Ps. XVII, 6). What does “The sorrows of hell found me” mean? What does “I found tribulation and sorrow” mean?

When sadness suddenly takes hold of you, when the worldly affairs in which you delighted have been thrown into confusion; when that sudden sadness itself finds you where you did not think you could become sad, it happens, and you are made sad: the sorrow of hell has found you. You thought you were above; yet you were below. And when the sorrow of hell found you, there you discovered yourself below, though you had thought yourself above.

You found yourself deeply afflicted with sorrow, grieving over some evil from which perhaps you had presumed you would not become sad; the sorrow of hell found you.[^c0073-3]

But when things go well for you, when all worldly matters smile upon you, when none of your loved ones has died, when nothing in your vineyard has perhaps withered, been struck by hail, or proved barren, when your wine-jar has not soured, your livestock has not suffered miscarriage, you have not been stripped of honor in any worldly dignity, your friends everywhere are alive and remain your friends, clients are not lacking, your children obey, servants tremble, your wife is harmonious, and your household is called happy—there, if you can, find tribulation,[^c0073-4] so that, having found tribulation, you may call upon the name of the Lord.

The divine discourse seems to teach something perverse: to weep in joy and rejoice in sorrow. Hear one who rejoices in sorrow: “We glory,” he says, “in tribulations” (Rom. V, 3). But as for one who weeps in joy, see whether he finds tribulation.

Let each person consider his own happiness, by which his soul exulted and was, as it were, swollen with joy, lifting itself up and saying, “I am happy.” Let him consider whether that happiness does not flow away, whether he can be certain that it will remain forever. But if he is not certain, and sees that the source of his joy is flowing away, it is a river of Babylon: let him sit above it and weep.

He will sit and weep if he remembers Zion. O that peace which we shall see with God! O that holy equality of the angels! O that beautiful vision and spectacle! Behold, in Babylon the things they hold are beautiful; let them not hold them, let them not be deceived by them. The consolation of captives is one thing; the joy of the free is another.

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion.”

6. [vers. 2.] “On the willows in its midst we hung up our organs.” The citizens of Jerusalem have their organs: the Scriptures of God, the commandments of God, the promises of God, and a certain meditation upon the age to come. But while they live in the midst of Babylon, they hang their organs upon its willows.

Willows are fruitless trees; and in this passage they are placed so that nothing good can be understood by “willows,” although elsewhere perhaps the term may have another sense. For the present, understand them as sterile trees growing beside the rivers of Babylon. These trees are watered by the rivers of Babylon, yet bear no fruit. Such are greedy and avaricious people, sterile in good works. The citizens of Babylon, who are also the trees of that region, are nourished by the pleasures of passing things, as though watered by the rivers of Babylon: you seek fruit and find it nowhere.

When we suffer from such people, we are living among those who are in the midst of Babylon. For there is a great difference between the midst of Babylon and the outskirts of Babylon. There are some who are not in its midst—that is, they are not overwhelmed by such great desire for the age and its pleasures.[^c0073-5] But those who, to put it plainly and briefly, are very wicked are in the midst of Babylon: they are sterile trees, like the willows of Babylon.

When we see them and find them so barren that it seems difficult to find in them anything from which they might be led to right faith, good works, hope for the age to come, or longing for liberation from the captivity of mortality, we know the Scriptures to speak to them. But because we find no fruit in them from which to begin,[^c0073-6] we turn our face away from them and say: “These people do not yet understand; they do not grasp anything. Whatever we say to them, they will regard as hostile and adverse.”

Therefore, by postponing the Scriptures in their case, we hang up our organs on the willows. For we do not consider them worthy to bear our organs. We do not fasten our organs to them by inserting them into them; rather, by postponing them, we hang them up. The willows are the fruitless trees of Babylon, fed by temporal pleasures as though by the rivers of Babylon.

7. [vers. 3.] And see whether the Psalm does not continue in this way: “On the willows,” it says, “in its midst we hung up our organs. For there those who took us captive asked us for words of songs, and those who led us away asked us for a hymn”—you must understand, “they asked us.”

Those who took us captive asked us for words of songs and a hymn. Who are those who took us captive, brothers? Whom have we experienced at some time as our captors?

That Jerusalem certainly experienced Babylonians, Persians, Chaldeans, and the people of those nations and regions as its captors; but this happened later, not when these psalms were being sung. Yet we have already told Your Charity that everything which occurred literally in that city was a figure of our own condition. It can easily be shown that we are captives.

For we no longer breathe the air of that freedom; we do not enjoy the purity of truth and that wisdom which, while remaining in itself, renews all things (Wis. VII, 27). We are tempted by the pleasures of temporal things, and every day we struggle with suggestions of unlawful delights. We scarcely draw breath even in prayer; we understand that we are captives.

But who took us captive? What people? What nation? What king? If we have been redeemed, we were captives. Who redeemed us? Christ. From whom did he redeem us? From the devil. Therefore the devil and his angels took us captive; and they would not have done so unless we had consented. We were led away as captives.

I have said who our captors are. They are also the robbers who wounded that traveler who descended from Jerusalem to Jericho and left him half-dead. He is the one whom our guardian—that is, the Samaritan (for “Samaritan” is interpreted as “Guardian”)—was confronted with by the Jews, who said to him: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” He rejected one of these two accusations and accepted the other: “I do not have a demon,” he said (John VIII, 48–49). But he did not say, “I am not a Samaritan.” For if that Samaritan does not guard us, we certainly perish.

Thus the Samaritan, passing by, saw the wounded man who had been abandoned by the robbers and, as you know, took him up (Luke X, 30–35). Just as those who inflicted upon us the wounds of sins are sometimes represented under the name of “robbers,” since our captivity involved our consent, so our captors are also said to be those same powers.

8. These people, then, who took us captive—the devil and his angels—when did they speak to us, and when did they ask us for words of songs? What are we to understand?

When such people question us—people in whom the devil is at work—we must understand that it is the devil himself who questions us, the devil who works in them. The Apostle says: “And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once lived according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who is now at work in the children of disobedience, among whom we also once conducted ourselves” (Eph. II, 1–3).

He shows that, having been redeemed from Babylon, he had already begun to depart from it. Yet what does he still say? That we are struggling with our enemies. And lest we become angry with the people who inflict persecutions upon us, the Apostle removed our attention from hatred of human beings and directed it toward a struggle against certain spirits whom we do not see, with whom we contend.

For he says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood”—that is, against the people whom you see, from whom you seem to suffer evil, who bring persecutions upon you. Indeed, we have been commanded to pray for them. “Our struggle,” he says, “is not against flesh and blood”—that is, against human beings—“but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (ibid. VI, 12).

What did he mean by “of this world”? He meant the lovers of the world. He also called them “darkness,” that is, unrighteous, wicked, unbelieving, sinful people. But when they come to believe, he rejoices over them in this way: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (ibid. V, 8). Thus he establishes that we must struggle against those principalities; they took us captive.

9. Just as the devil entered the heart of Judas (John XIII, 27) so that he might betray the Lord—and he would not have entered unless Judas had given him room—so many wicked people from the midst of Babylon, through carnal and unlawful desires, give room to the devil and his angels in their hearts, so that he may work in them and through them. At times they question us and say to us: “Explain to us the reason.”

Many pagans say these things to us: “Explain to us the reason why Christ came, and what benefit Christ brought to the human race. Are not human affairs worse since Christ came than they were before? Were not human affairs happier then than they are now? Let Christians tell us what good Christ brought. Why do they think human affairs happier because Christ came?”

For you see: if theaters, amphitheaters, and circuses stood unharmed; if nothing in Babylon collapsed; if an abundance of overflowing pleasures existed for people singing and dancing to shameful songs; if the lust of fornicators and prostitutes had peace and security; if the man who cries out for pantomimes to be clothed did not fear hunger in his household; if all these things flowed along without stain or disturbance, and there were great security for vanities, then times would be happy, and Christ would have brought great happiness to human affairs.

But because iniquities are cut down, so that when desire has been uprooted, the love of Jerusalem may be planted; because bitterness is mingled into temporal life, so that eternal things may be desired; because people are disciplined through scourges, receiving a father’s correction lest they encounter a judge’s sentence, they say that Christ brought no good and brought only hardships.

You begin to tell a person how many good things Christ has done, and he cannot understand. You set before him those who do what you have just heard in the Gospel: they sell all that they possess and give to the poor, so that they may have treasure in heaven and follow the Lord (Matt. XIX, 21). You say to him: “Behold what Christ brought.” How many do these things, distributing their possessions to the needy and becoming poor, not from necessity but by choice, following God and hoping for the kingdom of heaven!

Such people laugh at them as though they were fools: “What sort of good things did Christ bring,” they say, “that a person should lose his possessions and, when he gives to the needy, remain needy?”

What, then, will you do? You do not understand Christ’s good things. Another has filled you—the adversary of Christ, to whom you gave room in your heart. You look back to earlier times, and the former times seem to you happier, when things were like olives hanging on a tree, enjoying, as it were, the freedom of the breeze in the air through a kind of wandering desire.

The time has come for the olive to be put into the press; for it was not always going to hang on the tree. The year has already reached its end. It is not without reason that certain psalms are entitled “For the winepresses” (Ps. VIII, LXXX, and LXXXIII): freedom on the tree, pressure in the winepress.

When human affairs are crushed and pressed, you notice that greed increases; notice also that self-restraint increases. Why are you so blind that you see the amurca flowing through the streets but do not see the oil in the oil-vessel?[^c0073-7] This too is not without reason. Those who behave badly are publicly known; those who turn to God and are cleansed from the filth of evil desires are hidden. For even from the winepress itself, or out of it, the amurca flows openly, while the oil is secretly filtered out.

10. You applaud these things and rejoice at them, because you can now sit by the rivers of Babylon and weep. But those who took us captive, when they enter people’s hearts and question us through the tongues of those whom they possess, say to us: “Sing to us words of songs; give us an explanation of Christ’s coming and what the other life is. I want to believe.[^c0073-8] Teach me the reason why you command me to believe.” I answer him and say: “O man, why do you not want me to command you to believe?

You are full of evil desires.” If I speak of those good things of Jerusalem, you cannot understand them. You must be emptied of what fills you, so that you can be filled with what you lack.

Therefore do not readily say anything to such a person. He is a willow, a sterile tree. Do not strike the organ so that it sounds; hang it up instead.”

But he will say: “Tell me; sing to me; give me an explanation. You do not want me to learn?”[^c0073-9] You do not listen with a good disposition; you do not knock in a way that makes it fitting for the door to be opened to you. The one who took me captive has filled you; he himself is questioning me about you. He is crafty; he asks deceitfully. He does not ask what he may learn, but what he may criticize. Therefore I will not speak; I will hang up my organ.

11. [vers. 4.] But what will he say afterward? “Sing to us words of songs; sing to us a hymn; sing to us from the songs of Zion.” What do we answer?

Babylon carries you, Babylon holds you, Babylon nourishes you, Babylon speaks through you. You know how to grasp only what shines for a time; you do not know how to meditate upon eternal things. You do not understand what you are asking.

“How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”

Truly, brothers, this is how it is. Begin to wish to preach whatever small amount of truth you know, and see how necessary it is for you to endure such mockers, exactors of truth, and people full of falsehood. When they demand from you what they cannot understand, answer them and say, with the confidence of your holy song: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”

12. But see how you conduct yourself among them, O people of God, O body of Christ, O noble pilgrimage—for you are not from here; you belong elsewhere. Take care lest, when those who say to you, “Sing to us words of songs; tell us a hymn; sing to us from the songs of Zion,” seem to be loved by you, and you desire their friendship and fear displeasing such people, Babylon begin to delight you and you forget Jerusalem.

Fearing this, see what he adds; see what follows. The man who was singing suffered these things. And we are that man, if we wish to be. He suffered from people everywhere asking such questions, flattering with praise, biting with criticism, falsely commending, demanding what they could not understand, and refusing to pour out what filled them.

Amid crowds of such people, as though endangered, he raised his mind toward the remembrance of Zion. He bound himself with a kind of oath, and said: “If I forget you, Jerusalem”—amid the words of the captors, the words of the deceitful, the words of those who question wickedly, who ask but do not wish to learn.

13. From there came that rich man[^c0073-10] who asked the Lord: “Good Teacher, what shall I do to obtain eternal life?” Was he not asking about eternal life and, as it were, asking for a song of Zion?

“Keep the commandments,” the Lord said to him. And he, in his pride, when he heard this, said: “I have kept all these things from my youth.” Then the Lord said something to him from the songs of Zion, knowing that he would not understand it. But he gave us an example of how many people ask as though seeking counsel about eternal life and praise us only as long as we answer what they want.

He gave us a lesson through that man, as though we might one day say to such people: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”

“Do you wish to be perfect?” he said. “Go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me.” To learn many songs from the songs of Zion, let him first cast away his impediments and walk unencumbered, lest he be weighed down by any burden; then he will learn something from the songs of Zion.

But he went away sorrowful. Let us say after him: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”

The Lord nevertheless gave hope to the rich. For the disciples, saddened, said: “Who, then, can be saved?” And he answered them: “What is impossible for human beings is easy for God” (Matt. XIX, 16–26).

The rich, too, have a certain song of their own, and they have received a song from Zion—a song of which the Apostle says: “Command those who are rich in this present age not to be proud, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us with everything abundantly for enjoyment.”

Adding what they ought to do, he now touches the organ; he does not hang it up: “Let them be rich in good works, generous in giving, sharing, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (I Tim. VI, 17–19).

The rich received this song from the songs of Zion: first, not to be proud. Riches raise people up; and those whom they raise up, those rivers carry away.[^c0073-11] What, then, is commanded to them? Above all, not to be proud. Let them beware of doing with riches what riches do; let them beware of pride in riches.

For this is the chief evil that riches bring upon unwary people. Gold itself is not evil, for God created it; but the avaricious person is evil, abandoning the Creator and turning toward the creature. Let him therefore guard against being proud in this matter and sit above the river of Babylon.

This is what is said to him: “Do not be proud”—therefore let him sit. “Nor place your hope in the uncertainty of riches”—therefore let him sit above the rivers of Babylon. For if he places his hope in the uncertainty of riches, he is dragged along by the river of Babylon.

But if he humbles himself, does not become proud, and does not place his hope in the uncertainty of riches, he sits above the river, sighs for eternal Jerusalem in remembrance of Zion, and, in order to reach Zion, gives away his possessions.

Behold the song which the rich received from the songs of Zion. Let them work; let them touch the organ; let them not be idle when they encounter someone saying to them: “What are you doing? You are wasting your possessions by giving so much away. Store them up for your children.”

When they see that such a person does not understand, and realize that he is a willow, let them not readily explain why they act or what they are doing; let them hang their organs on the willows of Babylon. Apart from the willows, however, let them sing; let them not cease; let them work. For they do not lose what they give away. They entrust it to a servant, and it is safe; they entrust it to Christ, and it perishes?

14. You have heard the song of the rich from the songs of Zion; hear also the song of the poor. Paul himself speaks: “We brought nothing into this world, and we cannot take anything out of it. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge a person into destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evils; by desiring it, some have shipwrecked their faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (ibid., 7–10).

Are these songs therefore contrary to one another? They are not. Observe what was said to the rich: “Do not be proud, nor place your hope in the uncertainty of riches”; do good works, give, and store up for yourselves a good foundation for the future.[^c0073-12]

But what was said to the poor? “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation.” He did not say, “Those who are rich,” but “Those who wish to become rich.” For if they were already rich, they would hear another song: the rich person hears that he should give away; the poor person hears that he should not desire.

15. [vers. 5.] But while you live among such people, who do not understand the song of Zion, hang up, as I said, your organs on the willows in its midst; postpone what you are going to say. They begin to become fruitful trees; the trees are changed, and they will bear good fruit. Then we may sing into the ears of those who listen.

But while you live among these people who make noise, question wickedly, and resist the truth, bind yourselves not to wish to please them, lest you forget Jerusalem. Let your one soul, made one from many through the peace of Christ, let captive Jerusalem itself, living here on earth, say:

“If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand forget me.”

He bound himself most forcefully, my brothers: “May my right hand forget me.” He bound himself with terrible severity. Our right hand is eternal life; our left hand is temporal life. Whatever you do for the sake of eternal life, the right hand performs.

If, in your works, you mingle with love of eternal life a desire for temporal life, human praise, or some worldly advantage, then your left hand has learned what your right hand is doing. And you know that this is contained in the Gospel commandment: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. VI, 3).

“If I forget you,” he says, “Jerusalem, may my right hand forget me.” And this truly happens. He foretold it; he did not wish it: for those who forget Jerusalem, what he said happens—their right hand forgets them. Eternal life remains in itself; they remain in temporal pleasure and make their right hand what is left.

16. Attend to these matters, brothers. For the sake of the right hand, let me explain this to you, insofar as the Lord grants it, for the salvation of all. Perhaps you remember that I once spoke here about certain people who make what is left into what is right—that is, who possess greater temporal goods and place their blessedness in them, not knowing what true happiness is, what the true right hand is.[^c0073-13]

Scripture calls these people “sons of strangers,” as though they were citizens not of Jerusalem but of Babylon. For in one place the psalm says: “Lord, deliver me from the hand of the sons of strangers, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.”

It continues and says: “Their sons are like young plants, firmly established; their daughters adorned like the likeness of a temple; their storerooms full, overflowing from one thing to another; their sheep fertile, multiplying in their exits; their oxen fat. There is no breach in the wall, nor any outcry in their streets.”

Is possessing this happiness, then, the same as sinning? No. But it is making the left hand into the right, though it is left. Therefore, continuing, what does he say? “They called the people blessed who have these things.”

Behold the source of the vanity spoken by their mouth: they called the people blessed who have these things. But you are a citizen of Jerusalem, who do not forget Jerusalem, lest your right hand forget you. Behold, those whose mouth has spoken vanity called the people blessed who have these things. Tell me, then, the song of Zion.

“Blessed,” he says, “is the people whose Lord is their God” (Ps. CXLIII, 11–15).

Question your hearts, brothers, whether you desire God’s goods, whether you desire that city of Jerusalem, whether you long for eternal life. Let all this earthly happiness be your left hand; let that be your right hand which you will always possess. And if you possess the left hand, do not presume upon it.
