Do you not rebuke someone who wants to eat with his left hand? If you think an insult is done to your table when a guest eats with his left hand, how is no insult done to God’s table if you make what is right left, and what is left right?

What, then? “If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand forget me.”

[^c0073-1]: Note: [Col. 1760] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read *suum* (“its own”) instead of *suorum* (“of his own”).

[^c0073-2]: Note: [Col. 1763] The editions read *humilitate humiliati* (“humbled in humility”). The word *humilitate* is absent from the manuscripts.

[^c0073-3]: Note: [Col. 1763] The editions add *et quibus delectabaris* (“and in which you delighted”); this is absent from some manuscripts.

[^c0073-4]: Note: [Col. 1764] Nearly all the manuscripts read *inveni tribulationem* (“find tribulation”). The editions read *invenis tribulationem* (“you find tribulation”). Shortly afterward Erasmus and several manuscripts read *si aliquando potes* (“if at some time you can”).

[^c0073-5]: Note: [Col. 1764] Three manuscripts read *tota* (“the whole”) instead of *tanta* (“such great”).

[^c0073-6]: Note: [Col. 1765] The text appears to mean “from which to begin” or “with which to begin”; the construction is somewhat compressed.

[^c0073-7]: *Amurca* is the dark, watery residue separated from olive oil during pressing; *gemellaria* appears to refer to a vessel or receptacle for the oil. The precise technical sense of the latter term is uncertain.

[^c0073-8]: Note: [Col. 1767] Erasmus and most manuscripts read *volo credere* (“I want to believe”). Ambrose and Lovaniensis read *nolo credere* (“I do not want to believe”).

[^c0073-9]: Note: [Col. 1767] Some manuscripts read *Non vis, inquit, ut discam?* (“You do not want me to learn?”). Ambrose and Erasmus, with four manuscripts, read *Non vis, inquit, ut dicam* (“You do not want me to speak?”). Lovaniensis reads *Novi quis dicat* (“I know who is speaking”).

[^c0073-10]: Note: [Col. 1768] The Corbie manuscript reads *dives ille* (“that rich man”). The editions read *civis ille* (“that citizen”). Most manuscripts read *civis et ille* (“that citizen also”).

[^c0073-11]: Note: [Col. 1769] The Corbie manuscript reads *tollunt* (“carry away”). Other manuscripts, together with the editions, read *extollunt* (“raise up”).

[^c0073-12]: Note: [Col. 1769] Lund, Venice, and Lovaniensis read: “riches; but rather to do good works,” and so forth. Manuscript M has this reading.

[^c0073-13]: Note: [Col. 1770] In *Exposition of Psalm CXX*, no. 8.

[^c0073-14]: Note: [Col. 1761] Thus the manuscripts. The Lovaniensis edition reads *nos* (“us”) instead of *vos* (“you”).

[^c0073-15]: Note: [Col. 1762] Most manuscripts read *odiosamque* (“hateful”) before “boasting”; the editions read *otiosamque* (“idle”).

[^c0073-16]: Note: [Col. 1762] Most manuscripts omit *negotiorum et* (“of business and”).

[^c0073-17]: Note: [Col. 1770] The Amarbacensis edition and seven manuscripts read *hinc* (“from here”) instead of *hic* (“here”).

17. [Verse 6.] “Let my tongue cleave to my throat, if I do not remember you.” That is, he says, “Let me become mute if I do not remember you.” For why does one speak, why does one make a sound, if one does not sing the songs of Zion? Our tongue itself is the song of Jerusalem. The song of love [Note: [Col. 1771] Thus most manuscripts. The editions read “of delight.”] of this age is a foreign tongue, a barbarous tongue, which we learned in captivity. Therefore, he will be mute before God who has forgotten Jerusalem.

And it is not enough to remember; for even the enemies have remembered her, wishing to overthrow her. “What city is this?” they say. “Who are the Christians, and what sort of people are the Christians? Would that there were no Christians!” The captive multitude has already conquered its captors, and yet they murmur and rage and wish to kill the holy city while it sojourns among them—just as Pharaoh wished to kill that very people when he killed the male children at birth and left the females alive: he was suffocating virtues and nourishing desires.

It is therefore not enough to remember; see how you remember. For we remember some things with hatred and others with love. Thus, after he had said, “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget me. Let my tongue cleave to my throat, if I do not remember you,” he immediately added, “If I do not set Jerusalem above the beginning of my joy.”

For there is the highest joy, where we enjoy God, where we are secure in a united brotherhood and civic fellowship. No tempter will violate us there; no one will be able even to strike us with any enticement; nothing there will delight us except what is good. Every necessity will die there, and the highest happiness will arise there. “If I do not set Jerusalem above the beginning of my joy.”

18. [Verse 7.] And he turns to the Lord against the enemies of that city: “Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom.” Edom is the one who was also called Esau. For you heard just now, when the Apostle was read: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” There were two sons in one womb, twins together, in Rebecca’s womb, sons of Isaac, grandsons of Abraham. Both were born: one for inheritance, the other for disinheritance.

Now this Esau became the enemy of his brother, because the younger son forestalled his blessing; and it was fulfilled: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Romans 9:10–13; Genesis 25:23). Who, then, is the elder, who is the younger, and who is the elder who will serve the younger? We understand it now. The Jewish people appeared to be the elder, and the Christian people, later in time, the younger.

And see how the elder serves the younger. They carry our books; we live from their books. But so that you may understand “elder” and “younger” in a general sense, brothers, the carnal person is called the elder, and the spiritual person the younger, because the carnal comes first and the spiritual afterward. You have the Apostle saying plainly: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven.” Earlier he had said: “But it is not the spiritual that is first, but the animal; afterward, the spiritual” (1 Corinthians 15:46–49).

By “animal” he means the one whom he shows to be carnal. The human being who is born begins as an animal, begins as carnal. If he turns from Babylonian captivity toward the return to Jerusalem, he is renewed, and a renewal takes place according to the new and inner person; he becomes younger in time, but greater in power.

Thus Esau signifies all carnal people, while Jacob signifies all spiritual people: the younger are the elect, the elder those who are rejected. Does such a person himself wish to be chosen? Let him become younger.

Edom, moreover, was named from a certain red, that is, somewhat rosy, food. The lentil dish had been well cooked and mashed. This Esau desired it from his brother Jacob, and yielded his birthright to him, overcome by his desire to eat that lentil dish. The other yielded the food of pleasure and received the honor of rank. Thus, by a certain agreement made between them, it came about that one would be elder and the other younger, so that the elder would serve the younger; and he was called Edom (Genesis 25:29–34; 27:36–37).

As those who know that language say, Edom is interpreted as “Blood”; for in Punic also *Edom* means “blood.” Do not be surprised [Note: [Col. 1772] Am. and most manuscripts read: “Do not be surprised if they pertain to blood,” etc.]. All carnal people pertain to blood. “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15:50). Edom does not belong there; Jacob belongs there, the one who went without carnal food and received spiritual honor.

But he became an enemy. All carnal people are enemies of spiritual people: all such people, desiring what is present, persecute those whom they see contemplating eternal things. Against these, turning his attention to Jerusalem and asking God to rescue him from captivity, he says: “Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom.” Deliver us from the carnal, from those who imitate that Edom, who are elder brothers but enemies. They were born first; but those born later conquered them in precedence, because desire of the flesh cast the former down, while the latter were raised up by rejecting that desire.

They live [Note: [Col. 1772] Most manuscripts read “They see”; some read “They are envious.”], and they are envious, and they persecute.

19. “Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom, unto the day of Jerusalem.” Is this the day of Jerusalem in which she labored and was taken captive, or the day of Jerusalem’s happiness, when she is freed, reaches her destination, and is joined to eternity? “Remember,” he says, “Lord; do not forget the sons of Edom.” Which sons? “Those who said, ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundation in her.’”

Remember, then, that day when they wished to overthrow Jerusalem. For how many persecutions the Church has suffered! How the sons of Edom—that is, carnal people, subject to the devil and his angels, worshiping stones and wood, following the desires of the flesh—used to say: “Destroy the Christians; remove the Christians; let not one remain; overthrow them down to the foundation!”

Were these things not said? And when such things were being said, the persecutors were condemned, while the martyrs were crowned. “Those who said, ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundation in her.’” The sons of Edom say, “Lay it bare, lay it bare”; but God says, “Serve.” Whose words can prevail except those of God, who said, “The elder shall serve the younger”? “Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundation in her.”

20. [Verse 8.] And he turns to her: “Unhappy daughter of Babylon.” Unhappy because of your exultation, your presumption, and your hostilities: “Unhappy daughter of Babylon.”

The city itself is called Babylon and the daughter of Babylon, just as Jerusalem and the daughter of Jerusalem, and as Zion and the daughter of Zion. In the same manner the Church is called the daughter [Note: [Col. 1773] Most manuscripts read “sons.”] of the Church. She is called “daughter” because of succession, and “mother” because of precedence.

There was once an original Babylon; did that same people remain in it? Through Babylon’s succession, the daughter of Babylon came into being. O unhappy daughter of Babylon, you! “Blessed is the one who will repay you with the repayment you made.”

You are unhappy; he is blessed.

21. [Verse 9.] What did you do, and what will be repaid to you? Listen: “Blessed is the one who will repay you with the repayment you made to us.” What repayment does he mean? The Psalm closes with this: “Blessed is the one who will seize and dash your infants against the rock.”

He calls her unhappy, but blessed the one who will repay her with the repayment she made to us. We ask what repayment this is: “Blessed,” he says, “is the one who will seize and dash your infants against the rock.” That is the repayment.

For what did this Babylon do to us? We have already sung in that Psalm: “The words of the wicked prevailed against us” (Psalm 64:4). When we were born, this confusion of the present age found us as little children and suffocated us, while we were still infants, with the vain opinions of various errors.

An infant was born who was destined to become a citizen of Jerusalem—and already, in God’s predestination, a citizen—but who was meanwhile held captive for a time. What does he learn to love except what his parents whisper into him [Note: [Col. 1773] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions read: “An infant is born … to love what his parents whisper into him.” M.]?

They instruct and teach him greed, theft, daily lies, various forms of worship of idols and demons, and unlawful remedies of incantations and amulets. What is an infant still to do, a tender soul watching what his elders do, except follow what he sees them doing?

Babylon therefore persecuted us when we were little; but God gave us knowledge of himself when we had grown up, so that we would not follow the errors of our parents. I also recalled this at that time [Note: [Col. 1773] In the exposition of Psalm 64, no. 6.], as it had been foretold by the prophet: “To you the nations will come from the ends of the earth, and they will say, ‘Truly our fathers worshiped falsehood’” [Note: [Col. 1773] Manuscripts read “possessed”; according to the Greek Septuagint, *ektēsanto*], “vanity that did not profit them” (Jeremiah 16:19).

Those who had been killed as infants by following these vanities now speak as young men. By casting away vanities and coming back to life in God, let them advance and repay Babylon [Note: [Col. 1773] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice editions read: “They will advance and repay.” M.]. What repayment will they make to her? The repayment she made to us.

Let her infants likewise be suffocated; rather, let her infants likewise be dashed and die. Who are Babylon’s infants? Evil desires as they are born. For there are people who struggle against an old desire. When desire is born, before evil habit gains strength against you, when desire is still small, do not let it acquire the strength of wicked habit; while it is small, dash it to pieces.

But you fear that, once dashed, it may not die. Dash it against the rock: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

22. Brothers, let the instruments not cease in their work; sing the songs of Zion to one another. As gladly as you listened, so much more gladly practice what you heard—if you do not wish to be willows of Babylon, fed by its rivers and producing no fruit.

But sigh for the eternal Jerusalem. Let your life follow [Note: [Col. 1774] Am. and several manuscripts read “it will follow”; some, “it follows.”] where your hope goes ahead; there we shall be with Christ. Christ is now our head; he now governs us from above. He will embrace us with himself in that city; we shall be equal to the angels of God.

We would not dare to hope this about ourselves unless the Truth promised it. Desire this, then, brothers; think about this day and night. Whatever may smile upon you from the world in apparent prosperity, do not presume upon it; do not converse fondly with your desires.

If the enemy is great, let it be killed against the rock; if the enemy is small, let it be dashed against the rock. Kill the greater ones against the rock, and dash the lesser ones against the rock. Let the rock prevail.

Be built upon the rock, if you do not wish to be swept away either by a river, or by winds, or by rain. If you wish to be armed against temptations in this age, let the desire for eternal Jerusalem grow and become strong in your hearts.

Captivity will pass; happiness will come; the final enemy will be condemned; and with the king who cannot die we shall triumph.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 137

### SERMON [Note: [Col. 1774] Preached to the people on the feast of Crispina the Martyr.]

1. [Verse 1.] The title of this Psalm is brief and simple. It does not hold us back, since we know whose figure David bore, and recognize ourselves in him as well, because we too are members of that body.

Let us therefore recognize here the voice of the Church, and rejoice together that we have been found worthy to be in that Church whose singing voice we have heard. The entire title is: “For David himself.” Let us therefore see what is said to David himself.

2. “I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart.” The title of a Psalm usually indicates what is taking place within it. Here, however, since the title does not indicate this but only shows for whom it is sung, the first verse announces what takes place throughout the Psalm: “I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart.”

Let us therefore hear this confession. But first I remind you that in Scripture, when we confess to God, confession is usually spoken of in two ways: either confession of sins or confession of praise. Everyone knows confession of sins, but few pay attention to confession of praise.

For confession of sins is so familiar that whenever the words “I will confess to you, Lord,” or “We will confess to you,” are heard anywhere in Scripture, people immediately, by force of habit, move their hands toward their breasts to beat them. To such an extent do people usually understand confession as nothing except confession of sins.

But was our Lord Jesus Christ himself a sinner, when he said in the Gospel, “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth”? He went on to say what he was confessing, so that we might understand that this was confession of praise, not of iniquity: “I confess to you,” he says, “Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11:25).

He praised the Father; he praised God, because he does not despise the humble but despises the proud. Here too we are going to hear such confession: praise and thanksgiving to God.

“I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart.” I place my whole heart upon the altar of your confession; I offer you a sacrifice of praise. A *holocaust* is a sacrifice in which everything is burned completely; for in Greek ὅλον (*holon*) means “whole,” and in Latin, *totum*.

See how he offers a spiritual holocaust who says, “I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart.” “Let the flame of your love,” he says, “set my whole heart ablaze. Let nothing in me be left for myself, nor anything by which I may turn my attention toward myself; but let me burn wholly toward you, be wholly aflame in you, love you wholly, as one inflamed by you.”

“I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart, because you have heard the words of my mouth.” Whose mouth, if not my heart’s? For there we have the voice that God hears, which the human ear entirely does not know.

Certainly those who accused Susanna were shouting and did not raise their eyes to heaven; she was silent, but cried out in her heart. From where she deserved to be heard, from there they deserved to be punished (Daniel 13).

There is therefore an inner mouth. There we ask; from there we ask. And if we have prepared lodging or a house for God, there we speak and there we are heard. For he is not placed far from each one of us, in whom “we live and move and are” (Acts 17:27–28).

Nothing makes you far from God except iniquity alone. Cast down the intervening wall of sin, and you are with the one whom you ask. “You have heard,” he says, “the words of my mouth”; “I will confess to you.”

3. “And before the angels I will sing to you.” I will not sing before human beings, but before the angels I will sing. My psaltery is my joy. But my joy from below is before human beings; my joy from above is before the angels.

For the ungodly person does not know the joy of the righteous: “There is no rejoicing for the wicked,” says the Lord (Isaiah 48:22; 57:21). The wicked man rejoices in the tavern [Note: [Col. 1775] Am., Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “in the procession.”]; the martyr rejoices in chains.

How did that holy Crispina rejoice, whose feast is celebrated today [Note: [Col. 1775] A sermon was preached on the feast of the same martyr in the exposition of Psalm 120, as may be seen above, col. 1605.]? She rejoiced when she was seized, when she was led before the judge, when she was sent to prison, when she was brought out bound, when she was raised onto the scaffold, when she was heard, and when she was condemned. In all these things she rejoiced; and wretched people thought her wretched, although she was rejoicing before the angels.

4. [Verse 2.] “I will worship toward your holy temple.” What is your holy temple? Where we shall dwell, where we shall worship [Note: [Col. 1775] Some manuscripts read “where you dwell.”]. For we run in order to worship. Our pregnant heart labors to give birth and seeks where it may deliver.

What is that place where God is to be worshiped? What world? What building? What dwelling, finally, in heaven and among the stars? We search the holy Scriptures and find the answer in the words of Wisdom: “I was with him; I was the one in whom he rejoiced daily.” And he speaks of his works and explains to us his dwelling. What dwelling?

“When he made firm,” he says, “the clouds above, when he set apart his dwelling above the winds” (Proverbs 8:30, 27–28).

His dwelling is his temple. Where, then, shall we go? Are we to worship above the winds? If worship takes place above the winds, the birds surpass us.

But if we understand “winds” as souls—that is, souls signified under the name of winds—as Scripture says in one place, “He flew upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm 17:11), meaning above the powers of souls; hence the breath of God is also called a soul (Genesis 2:7), as though it were wind—not that this should be understood as the wind by which we feel the body being driven, but that something invisible is signified by its name, something that cannot be seen with the eyes, perceived by the ears, tracked by smell, tasted by the palate, or touched by the hand.

That invisible thing is a certain life by which we live, which is called the soul. If we understand these as the winds, there is no reason for us to seek visible wings in order to fly with the birds to worship at the temple of God. Rather, we shall find God seated above ourselves, if we are willing to be his faithful people.

See whether this is not so: “The temple of God is holy,” the Apostle says, “which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

Nevertheless, what is clear is that God dwells in the angels. Therefore, when our joy takes its song from spiritual things, not earthly goods, so that it may sing before the angels, the congregation of angels itself is the temple of God, and we worship toward the temple of God.

There is a Church below and a Church above: the Church below in all the faithful, the Church above in all the angels. But the Lord of angels descended to the Church below, and the angels ministered on earth to the one who was ministering to us (Matthew 4:11). For he says, “I did not come to be ministered to, but to minister” (Matthew 20:28).

What did he minister to us except what even today we eat and drink [Note: [Col. 1776] Three manuscripts read “what we ate.”]? Since the Lord of angels ministered to us, let us not despair of becoming equal to the angels.

For one greater than the angels descended to human beings; the Creator of angels took on humanity; the Lord of angels died for humanity. “Therefore I will worship toward your holy temple.” I understand your temple to be not one made by human hands, but one that you made for yourself.

5. “And I will confess to your name, in your mercy and your truth.” We confess in these two things; for it is also written in another Psalm: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10).

We confess in these two things: in your mercy and in your truth. In your mercy you regarded the sinner; in your truth you fulfilled the promise. Therefore, in your mercy and truth I will confess to you.

I too render these, according to the strength you have given me, by practicing mercy and truth: mercy in helping, truth in judging. By these we are aided by God; by these we merit God. Rightly, then, mercy and truth are all the ways of the Lord.

There are no other ways by which he comes to us [Note: [Col. 1776] Am. and several manuscripts read “by which he came.”]; there are no other ways by which we come to him.

6. “For you have magnified your holy name above everything.” What kind of thanksgiving is this, brothers? He magnified his holy name above Abraham. For Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3).

All the other nations sacrificed to idols and served demons. Isaac was born from Abraham; God was magnified over that household. From there came Jacob; God was magnified, the God who says, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6).

From there came twelve sons; from there the people of Israel, freed from Egypt, led through the Red Sea, trained in the wilderness, and, after the nations had been expelled, settled in the promised land. The name of the Lord was magnified over Israel.

But from there also came the Virgin Mary; from there the Lord Christ, who died because of our sins and rose again because of our justification (Romans 4:25), filling the faithful with the Holy Spirit and sending the message to be preached among the nations: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3:2).

And behold, he magnified his holy name above everything.

7. [Verse 3.] “On whatever day I call upon you, hear me quickly.” Why “quickly”? Because you said, “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isaiah 58:9).

Why “quickly”? Because I no longer ask for earthly happiness; I have learned holy desire from the New Testament. I do not ask for land, bodily fertility, temporal health, the subjection of enemies, riches, or honors. I ask for none of these things; therefore hear me quickly.

Because you have taught me what to ask, give me what I ask.

Let us say to this person: “Are you asking for something of this kind?” Let us hear ourselves; let him pour out his petition, and let us see what he asks, so that we may learn through him to ask and thus deserve to receive.

You came to the Church. I do not know what you intended to ask for today. What do we suppose you came to ask for? You came with your desire, whatever it was—would that it were innocent, even if carnal!

But remove iniquity; remove carnality. Learn what you should ask for. Pay attention to what you are celebrating today. You are celebrating the feast of a holy and blessed woman, and perhaps you desire earthly happiness [Note: [Col. 1777] Some manuscripts read “celebrity.”].

For the sake of holy desire she abandoned the happiness she had on earth. She left behind sons who wept and grieved as though she were a cruel mother, because she appeared to have lost human compassion while hastening toward the divine crown.

Did she not know what she desired, what she was treading underfoot? Indeed, she knew how to sing before the angels of God, and she desired their fellowship, a holy and pure friendship where she would no longer die and where she would know a judge before whom falsehood could have no power.

What, then? Are there no good things in that life? Indeed there are; there alone are good things—not goods mixed with evils, but securities [Note: [Col. 1777] Most manuscripts read: “not goods mixed with evils, but goods of security, in which…”] in which you may rejoice as much as you wish, and no one will say to you, “Moderate yourself.”

Here, however, rejoicing in earthly goods is troublesome and exceedingly dangerous, lest you rejoice in such a way that you cling to them and perish through rejoicing wrongly [Note: [Col. 1777] Am. and several manuscripts read “lest you cling to them.” Perhaps the reading is “and by clinging perish miserably.”].

For why does God mix tribulations with earthly joys, unless it is so that, feeling tribulation and bitterness, we may learn to desire eternal sweetness?

[Col. 1778] 8. Let us see, then, what he asks, and by what merit he said, “Hear me quickly.” What are you asking, so that you may be heard quickly? “You will multiply me.”

“Multiplication” can be understood in many ways. There is the multiplication of earthly generation, according to the first blessing of our nature that we heard: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, and rule it” (Genesis 1:28).

Did he wish to be multiplied in this way when he said, “Hear me quickly”? Certainly this multiplication too is fruitful, and it comes only from the Lord’s blessing.

What shall I say now about the other kinds of multiplication? One person has been multiplied in gold, another in silver, another in cattle, another in servants, another in possessions, another in all these things.

There are many earthly multiplications, but that of children is more fortunate—although even fertility itself is troublesome to greedy people. For they fear that they will be left poor because many children may be born.

This anxiety has driven many to impiety, so that they forget that they are parents. Stripped of every feeling of humanity, they expose their children in order to make them strangers: the woman who gave birth casts them away, while the one who did not give birth gathers them; one despises them, the other loves them; one is a mother in the flesh in vain, the other more truly in the will.

Since, then, there are many multiplications and many kinds of multiplication, what multiplication does the one who said, “Hear me quickly,” seek? For he says, “You will multiply me.”

We wait to hear in what respect. Listen, then: “In my soul.” Not in my flesh, but in my soul: “You will multiply me in my soul.”

Is there still something to be added, lest multiplication in the soul itself be immediately understood as happiness? For people are multiplied in their souls by anxieties [Note: [Col. 1778] Here Erasmus and Louvain add “and frenzies”; Am. and the manuscripts omit this.].

A person in whom vices have also multiplied appears to be multiplied in his soul. One is merely greedy, another merely proud, another merely lustful; this person is greedy, proud, and lustful all at once. He has been multiplied in his soul, but to his own harm.

This multiplication is poverty, not abundance.

What, then, do you mean, you who said, “Hear me quickly,” and removed yourself from every body, from every earthly thing, and from every worldly desire, so that you might say to God, “You will multiply me in my soul”?

Explain further what you desire: “You will multiply me,” he says, “in my soul, in strength.” The vow is explicit; the desire is explicit, cut away from every confusion.

If he had said, “You will multiply me,” you might have thought of some earthly things. He added, “in my soul.” Again, lest you think of vices in the soul, he added, “in strength.”

There is nothing more that you should desire from God if you wish to say with a good and sincere face, “Hear me quickly.”

9. [Verse 4.] “Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, Lord.” So it will happen; indeed, so it is happening, and it happens every day. It was not said without reason, except because it was going to happen.

“Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, Lord.” But when they confess to you and praise you, let them not desire earthly things from you. For what will the kings of the earth desire? Do they not already possess power itself?

Whatever more a person desires on earth, his desire extends up to power. What more can he attain? A higher exaltation is required. But perhaps the higher it is, [Col. 1779] the more dangerous.

Therefore, the greater the earthly exaltation of kings, the more they ought to humble themselves before God. Why do they do this [Note: [Col. 1779] Thus the manuscripts. Louvain reads, “And what should they do?” Am. and Erasmus read, “Why should they do this?”]? “Because they have heard all the words of your mouth.”

O Lord, all the words of your mouth! I do not know in what hidden nation the Law and the Prophets were concealed—all the words of your mouth. But in the Jewish nation alone were all the words of your mouth. Praising that nation, the Apostle says: “What advantage, then, has the Jew? Or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them” (Romans 3:1–2).

There were the words of God.

But give me that holy man Gideon in the time of the Judges. See what sign he asked from the Lord: “I will place,” he says, “a fleece on the threshing floor; let the fleece be drenched with rain, while the floor remains dry.” And it happened: the fleece alone was drenched with rain, while the floor was dry.

He asked for a second sign: “Let the entire floor be drenched with rain, and let the fleece alone be found dry.” This too happened: the floor was drenched with rain, while the fleece was dry (Judges 6:36–40).

First the fleece was drenched with rain and the floor was dry; afterward the floor was drenched with rain and the fleece was dry.

What does the floor seem to signify to you, brothers? Is it not the whole world? What is the fleece? It is like the Jewish nation in the midst of the whole world, possessing the sacrament of grace not in manifestation but in the cloud of secrecy, as though rain were contained in the fleece under a veil [Note: [Col. 1779] Most manuscripts read “as though in the fleece there were rain.”].

The time came when the rain was to be revealed upon the floor; it was made manifest, not kept covered. Thus what was said came to pass: “Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, Lord, because they have heard all the words of your mouth.”

What is this, Israel, that you were concealing? How long were you concealing it? The fleece was wrung out, and rain came forth from you.

Christ alone is the sweetness of the rain. Him alone you do not recognize in the Scriptures, although the Scriptures were made for his sake. But let all the kings of the earth confess to you, Lord, because they have heard all the words of your mouth.

10. [Verse 5.] “And let them sing in the ways of the Lord, because great is the glory of the Lord.” Let the kings of the earth sing in the ways of the Lord.

In what ways should they sing? In those of which it was said above, “In your mercy and your truth,” because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.”

Therefore, let the kings of the earth not be proud, but humble. Then let them sing in the ways of the Lord, if they are humble. Let them love, and they will sing.

We know travelers who sing; they sing and hasten to arrive. There are evil songs, like those of the old person; but the new song belongs to the new person.

Let the kings of the earth therefore walk in your ways; let them walk and sing in your ways. What should they sing? “Because great is the glory of the Lord”—not of kings.

11. [Verse 6.] See how he wished the kings to sing in the ways, humbly carrying the Lord and not exalting themselves against the Lord. For if they exalt themselves, what follows? “Because the Lord is exalted, and he regards the humble.”

Do kings wish to be regarded? Let them be humble.

What if they exalt themselves in pride? Can they hide from his eyes? Perhaps because you heard that he “regards the humble,” you may wish to be proud and say in your soul: “God regards the humble; he does not regard me. I will do what I want. Who sees me?”

A human being does not see me; God does not wish to see me, because I am not humble, while he regards the humble. I will do what I want.

O insolent one, would you say this if you knew what you ought to love? Look: if God does not wish to see you, do you not fear precisely that he does not wish to see you?

If you greet some great patron of yours and, intent on something else, he does not see you, how your soul aches! But if God does not see you, do you consider yourself secure?

The Savior does not see you, but the plunderer sees you [Note: [Col. 1780] Am., with one manuscript, reads “and the condemner sees you.” Erasmus reads “and the plunderer and condemner sees you.”].

And yet God himself does see you. Do not suppose that you are unseen; rather, pray that you may deserve to be seen by the one by whom you are seen.

For it is said: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.” Since they are not upon the unrighteous, let the unrighteous therefore do what they want. “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.” Let the passage continue: “And his ears are open to their prayers.”

Do the unrighteous, who thought themselves secure because the eyes of the Lord were not upon them, not fear because his ears are not open to their prayers? Is it not better that both his eyes should be upon us and his ears open to our prayers?

But when you do those things upon which you do not wish the eyes of the Lord to rest, you do not deserve that the Lord’s ears be open to your prayers [Note: [Col. 1780] Erasmus and the Regius manuscript read: “When you do those things upon which you wish the eyes of the Lord to rest, then you deserve…”]. And yet, by doing evil, you do not turn the eyes of the Lord away from yourself.

For what follows there? “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.” But to what end? “To destroy their memory from the earth.”

Do you see that you are seen? Do you see that you cannot remain hidden? Since whatever you do is seen, why do you not do that by which you may deserve to please him?

What, then, is said here as well? “Because great is the glory of the Lord; because the Lord is exalted, and he regards the humble.”

The exalted he seems not to regard, for he regards the humble. What of the exalted? “He knows them from afar.”

What, then, does the proud person gain for himself [Note: [Col. 1780] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read: “What does the proud person gain except that he…”]? He gains being seen from afar, not remaining unseen.

Do not think that you ought therefore to be secure because he sees you less well [Note: [Col. 1780] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read “sees you.” M.]. He who sees from afar sees you less well; but God, even if he sees you from afar, sees you perfectly, and he is not with you.

You are acting not so that you may be seen less perfectly, but so that you may not be with the one by whom you are seen.

But what does the humble person gain for himself? “The Lord is near to those who have crushed their heart” (Psalm 33:16–17, 19).

Let the proud exalt himself as much as he wishes. Certainly God dwells on high; God is in heaven. Do you wish him to draw near to you? Humble yourself. For he will be so much higher than you as you are more exalted: “But the exalted he knows from afar.”

12. [Verse 7.] “If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will revive me.” It is true: whatever tribulation you are in, confess and call upon him; he frees you and revives you.

Nevertheless, we ought to understand something more deeply here, so that we may cling to God more intimately and say to him, “Hear me quickly.”

For he had said, “He knows the exalted from afar”; and the exalted, the proud, do not know tribulation. They do not know the tribulation of which it is said elsewhere: “I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 114:3–4).

What is so remarkable if tribulation finds you? If you are capable of anything, find tribulation yourself.

“And who,” you ask, “is able to find tribulation? Or who would even seek it?” You are in the midst of tribulation and do not know it?

Is this brief life not tribulation? If it is not tribulation, it is not a pilgrimage; but if it is a pilgrimage, then either you love your homeland too little, or you are certainly in tribulation. For who is not troubled by not being with what he desires?

But why does this tribulation not seem so to you? Because you do not love. Love the other life, and you will see that this life is tribulation. However brightly it may shine with prosperity, however abundantly it may overflow with pleasures [Note: [Col. 1781] Thus most manuscripts. The editions read “however richly it may flower.”], since that most certain joy without any temptation, which God preserves for us at the end, is not yet here, this life is undoubtedly tribulation.

Let us therefore understand the tribulation of this life as well, brothers: “If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will revive me.”

He does not speak as though he were saying, “If some tribulation should happen to me, you will free me from it.” Rather, how does he speak? “If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will revive me”; that is, “You will not revive me in any other way unless I walk in the midst of tribulation.”

“If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will revive me.” Woe to those who laugh; blessed are those who mourn (Luke 6:21, 25): “If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will revive me.”

13. “You have stretched out your hand over the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand has saved me.” Let enemies rage: what can enemies do? They can take away money, strip one of possessions, proscribe, send into exile, torture with pains and torments, and, finally, if permitted, even kill. Can they do anything more? But you, Lord, have stretched out your hand over the wrath of my enemies: over what my enemies can do to me, you have stretched out your hand. For enemies cannot separate me from you; but you avenge more fully, because you still defer me: “You have stretched out your hand over the wrath of my enemies.” Let the enemy rage as much as he can: he does not separate me from God. Yet you, Lord, do not yet receive me [Note: [Col. 1781] The Regius manuscript reads, “look upon me.”]; you still wear me down in pilgrimage; you still do not grant your joy and sweetness; you have not yet made me drunk from the abundance of your house, nor have you yet given me to drink from the torrent of your delight. For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light (Ps. XXXV, 9–10). But behold, I have given [Note: [Col. 1781] Lovaniensis reads, “you have given.” But the Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read, “I have given.” This reading is confirmed by the passage above, in Psalm 134, no. 18: “giving to God the firstfruits of our spirit, that is, faith itself as our firstborn.”] the firstfruits of the Spirit, and I have believed in you, and I serve the law of God with my mind (Rom. VII, 25); nevertheless, we still groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body (ibid. VIII, 23). God gave us sinners this life, in which Adam must also be worn down in the sweat and labor of his face, when the earth brings forth thorns and thistles for him (Gen. III, 18–19). Could any enemy have brought about more? “You have stretched out your hand over the wrath of my enemies”; yet not unto despair. For what follows is: “And your right hand has saved me.”

14. It may also be understood thus: “You have stretched out your hand over the wrath of my enemies”: my enemies were angry; you avenged me upon my enemies. “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away” (Ps. CXI, 10). Where are those who said: “Let the Christian name [Note: [Col. 1782] Several manuscripts consistently read, “the Christian.”] perish from the earth”? Certainly, they either die or are converted. Therefore, “You have stretched out your hand over the wrath of my enemies,” while it was said what is written: “My enemies have spoken evil against me: When shall he die, and his name perish?” (Ps. XL, 6)—when shall the Christian name be erased from the earth? While they say these things, some have believed, some have perished, and a few fearful ones remain. How great was the wrath of enemies when the blood of martyrs was being shed! How they thought that they would erase the Christian name from the earth! “You have stretched out your hand over the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand has saved me.” Behold, those who persecuted martyrs seek out the memorials of martyrs, whether to worship [Note: [Col. 1782] Some manuscripts read, “pray.”] there or to make themselves drunk there; yet they seek them. “You have stretched out your hand over the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand has saved me.” Your right hand has saved me according to its desire. There is one kind of salvation at the right hand, for there is another salvation at the left: temporal and carnal salvation is at the left; eternal salvation with the angels is at the right. Therefore Christ, now placed in immortality itself, is said to sit at the right hand of God (Mark XVI, 19). For God does not have within himself a right or a left; but the right hand of God is called that blessedness which, because it cannot be shown to the eyes, has received such a name. By this your right hand you have saved me, not according to temporal salvation. For Crispina was killed; but did God abandon her? He did not save her at the left, but he did save her at the right. What torments the Maccabees endured! (II Macc. VII). But the three children, walking amid the flames, praised God (Dan. III, 24). Their salvation was at the right; that of the others was also at the left. Thus he sometimes does not save his saints at the left, but he always saves them at the right. The ungodly, however, he often saves at the left, but does not save at the right. For those who persecuted Crispina were sound in body: she was killed; they live. Their salvation is at the left, hers at the right: “And your right hand has saved me.”

15. [verse 8.] “Lord, you will repay for me.” I do not repay; you will repay for me. Let enemies rage as much as they please: you will repay what I cannot. “Lord, you will repay for me.” Consider this in our Head himself. For he left us an example, that we might follow his footsteps. “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth; when he was reviled, he did not revile in return,” saying, “Lord, you will repay for me”; “when he was judged, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to him who judges justly” [Note: [Col. 1782] Ambrosianus with one manuscript reads, “unjustly.” But the other editions and manuscripts read, “justly,” in accordance with the Greek δικαίως.] (I Pet. II, 21–23). What is meant by, “Lord, you will repay for me”? “I,” he says, “do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges” (John VIII, 50). “Beloved, do not avenge yourselves,” the Apostle says, “but give place to wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Rom. XII, 19). “Lord, you will repay for me.”

[Col. 1783] 16. There is another interpretation here which must not be neglected, and perhaps is to be preferred: “Lord Christ, you will repay for me.” For if I pay what is due, I have taken by robbery; you paid what you did not take by robbery: “Lord, you will repay for me.” See him repaying for us. Those came who demanded the tribute; they demanded the didrachma tax, that is, two drachmas for one person. They came to the Lord for him to pay the tax—or rather, not to him himself, but to his disciples—and they said to them: “Does your master not pay the tribute?” They reported this to him. And he said: “From whom do the kings of the earth exact tribute? From their own sons, or from strangers?” They answered: “From strangers.” “Therefore,” he said, “the sons are free. Yet, lest we offend them,” he said to Peter, “go, cast a hook into the sea; and when the first fish comes up, open its mouth, and you will find a stater”—that is, two didrachmas. A stater is a unit of weight containing four drachmas. “You will find it there; give it to them for me and for yourself” (Matt. XVII, 23–26). “Lord, you will repay for me.” Rightly do we have the first fish caught by the hook, caught by the hook [Note: [Col. 1783] Two manuscripts read, “caught by love.”]; the first to rise from the sea, the firstborn from the dead. In his mouth we find two didrachmas, that is, four drachmas: in his mouth we find the four Gospels. By these four drachmas we are freed from the exaction of this world; through the four Gospels we shall not remain debtors, for there all our sins are paid. Therefore he repaid for us: thanks be to his mercy. He owed nothing; he did not pay for himself, but paid for us. “Behold,” he says, “the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me.” What is meant by, “He will find nothing in me”? He will find no sin in me; he has no reason why he should kill me. “But,” he says, “that all may know that I do the will of my Father, arise, let us go from here” (John XIV, 30–31). What is meant by, “Arise, let us go from here”? That is, I suffer not by necessity but by will, paying what I do not owe: “Lord, you will repay for me.”

17. “Lord, your mercy is everlasting.” What should I desire? Not the day of humankind [Note: [Col. 1783] The Christinaean manuscript reads, “You know what I desire: the day of humankind?”]. “I have not labored in following you, Lord, and I have not desired the day of humankind; you know” (Jer. XVII, 16). Behold, if the holy martyr Crispina had desired the day of humankind, she would have denied Christ: she would have lived longer here, but would not have lived eternally. She preferred to live eternally rather than to live a little longer in time. Thus: “Lord, your mercy is everlasting”; I do not wish to be delivered for a time. “Your mercy is everlasting,” by which you delivered the martyrs and yet so quickly took them away from this life. “Lord, your mercy is everlasting.”

18. “Do not despise the works of your hands.” I do not say, Lord, “Do not despise the works of my hands”; I do not boast of my works. “Indeed, I sought the Lord with my hands by night before him, and was not deceived” (Ps. LXXVI, 3); nevertheless, I do not commend the works of my hands: I fear that, when you examine them, you will find more sins than merits. This alone I ask, this I say, this I desire to obtain: “Do not despise the works of your hands.” See your work in me, not mine; for if you see mine, you condemn; if you see yours, you crown. For whatever good works are mine come from you, and therefore they are yours more than mine. For I hear from your Apostle: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. II, 8–10). Therefore, whether in that by which we are human beings, or in that by which we have been changed and justified from our ungodliness, “Lord, do not despise the works of your hands.”

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 138

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. We had prepared a short psalm for you, which we had instructed the Reader to sing; but, apparently confused at the time, he read one psalm in place of another. We preferred to follow God’s will in the Reader’s mistake rather than our own intention in our own plan. If, therefore, we keep you here for some time because of its length, do not charge it to us; but believe that God wished us to labor without fruitlessness. For it was not without reason that we received punishment for our first sin, so that we should eat our bread in the sweat of our face (Gen. III, 19). Only, if it is bread, pay attention. It is bread if it is Christ: “I am,” he says, “the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI, 41). Let us seek in the Prophets the one whom we have had revealed in the Gospel. Those whose hearts are still covered by a veil do not see him there (II Cor. III, 14), as your Charity heard yesterday. But for us, because the evening sacrifice of the Lord’s cross tore the veil (Matt. XXVII, 51), so that the temple’s hidden things are now open, as long as Christ is preached to us, bread must be eaten, even with labor and sweat.

2. Our Lord Jesus Christ sometimes speaks in the Prophets in the person of our Head, who is Christ the Savior himself, seated at the right hand of the Father; he was also born of a virgin for our sake and suffered under Pontius Pilate, as you know. By the shedding of his innocent blood, which is our price, he redeemed the guilty from the captivity in which the devil held us, granting us forgiveness of sins and, by that same price—his blood—erasing the bond by which we were held as debtors (Col. II, 13–14).

He is the ruler, bridegroom, and redeemer of the Church, our Head. And certainly, if he is the Head, he has a body. His body is the holy Church, which is also his wife; to her the Apostle says, “You are the body of Christ and members of it” (I Cor. XII, 27). Thus the whole Christ is Head and body, as one complete man. For woman was made from man and belongs to man; and it was said of the first marriage, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24). The Apostle interprets this as a mystery, saying that it was not without reason that this was spoken of those two human beings, since Christ and the Church were already being signified in them. For the Apostle explains it this way: “The two shall be one flesh”—“this is a great mystery; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. V, 31–32).

He also says that Adam himself was “a type of the one to come” (Rom. V, 14). Therefore, just as Eve was made from the side of the sleeping Adam (Gen. II, 21–22), so from the side of the sleeping Lord—that is, of the Lord dying in his passion and pierced by a spear on the cross (John XIX, 34)—the sacraments flowed by which the Church would be formed. For he speaks of this future passion of his in another psalm: “I slept and took my rest; and I rose again, because the Lord will receive me” (Ps. III, 6). Thus sleep signifies the passion: Eve from the side of the sleeping man, the Church from the side of the suffering man.

Our Lord Jesus Christ therefore speaks in the Prophets sometimes in his own voice, sometimes in ours, because he makes himself one with us, as it was said, “The two shall be one flesh.” Hence the Lord himself also says in the Gospel, when speaking about marriage, “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matt. XIX, 6). One flesh, because he assumed flesh from our mortality; but not one divinity, because he is the Creator and we are creatures.

Whatever, therefore, the Lord speaks in the person of the flesh he assumed belongs both to that Head which has already ascended into heaven and to those members which still labor in earthly exile. On behalf of these laboring members, when Saul was persecuting them, he cried from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4).

Let us therefore hear the Lord Jesus Christ speaking prophetically. These psalms were sung long before the Lord was born from Mary, but not before the Lord existed; for he was always the Creator of all things, though at a certain time he was also born from a creature. Let us believe that divinity and, as far as we can, understand it as equal to the Father. But that divinity, equal to the Father, became a participant in our mortality—not from what was his, but from what was ours—so that we too might become participants in his divinity, not from what is ours, but from what is his.

3. [verse 1.] “Lord, you have examined me and known me.” Let the Lord Jesus Christ himself say this; let him himself say it to the Father: “Lord, you have examined me and known me.” The Father is not his Lord except because he graciously consented to be born according to the flesh. He is the Father of God and the Lord of man. Do you wish to know whose Father he is? He is the Father of the Son equal to himself.

The Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.” God is Father to this form, the form equal to himself, the only-begotten Son born from his substance. But for our sake, so that we might be restored and made participants in his divinity, renewed for eternal life—for, as I said, he himself became a participant in our mortality—what does the Apostle say of him in the passage where he had said, “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized”? “He emptied himself,” he says, “taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II, 6–7).

He was in the form of God, equal to the Father; and he took the form of a servant, in which he was less than the Father. Hence he says both things in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30), and “The Father is greater than I” (ibid. XIV, 28). “I and the Father are one,” according to the form of God; “The Father is greater than I,” according to the form of a servant.

Since, therefore, he is both Father and Lord—the Father of the form of God, the Lord of the form of a servant—let him say this himself, and let us neither marvel nor take offense that the only Son of God says: “Lord, you have examined me and known me.” “You have examined and known me”—not because he did not know, but because he made him known to others. “You have examined me,” he says, “and known me.”

4. [verse 2.] “You have known my sitting down and my rising up.” What is this sitting down? What is this rising up? One who sits humbles himself. The Lord therefore sat in his passion and rose in his resurrection. “You,” he says, “have known this”: that is, you willed it, you approved it; it happened according to your will.

If, however, you wish to understand the voice of the Head in the person of the body, let us too say, “You have known my sitting down and my rising up.” A human being sits when he humbles himself in repentance; he rises when, with sins forgiven, he is raised up in hope of eternal life. Therefore it is said in another psalm: “Rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. CXXVI, 2). Penitents eat the bread of sorrow; they sing in another psalm and say, “My tears have become my bread day and night” (Ps. XLI, 4).

What, then, does “Rise after you have sat down” mean? Do not exalt yourselves unless you have first been humbled. For many wish to rise before they have sat down; they wish to appear righteous before they have confessed that they are sinners.

Therefore, if you understand it as spoken in the person of our Head, interpret it this way: “You have known my sitting down and my rising up”—my passion and my resurrection. If you understand it as spoken in the person of the body: “You have known my sitting down and my rising up”; before your eyes I have confessed my sins and have been justified by your grace.

5. [verse 3.] “You understood my thoughts from afar; you searched out my path and my boundary, and foresaw all my ways.” What does “from afar” mean? While I am still in exile, before I come to that homeland, you knew my thought.

Consider the younger son, because he too became the body of Christ, the Church coming from the Gentiles. The younger son had gone into a far country [Note: [Col. 1786] Several manuscripts read, “He was in a far country”; shortly afterward, “he was not far away.”] For a certain head of a household had two sons. The elder had not gone far, but worked in the field, and signifies the saints who perform the works and commandments of the Law. But the human race, which had turned aside [Note: [Col. 1786] So many manuscripts; the editions read “had flowed away.”] into the worship of idols, had journeyed into a far country.

What is so far from the one who made you as the image that you yourself made for yourself? The younger son therefore went into a far country, carrying his property with him. As we know from the Gospel, he squandered it by living prodigally with prostitutes; then, suffering hunger, he attached himself to a certain ruler of that region, who put him in charge of feeding pigs. He longed to fill himself with the pods they ate, but he could not [Note: [Col. 1786] Erasmus and Lovaniensis add “and scraps,” which Ambrosianus and the manuscripts do not have.].

After labor, threshing, tribulation, and poverty, the thought of his father came to him, and he wanted to return. Thus he said, “I will rise and go to my father.” He said, “I will rise,” for he had been sitting. Recognize his voice here, then, when he says, “You have known my sitting down and my rising up.” I sat in poverty; I rose in desire for your bread.

“You understood my thoughts from afar.” I had gone far away, but where is the one whom I had abandoned not present? “You understood my thoughts from afar.” Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel that his father ran to meet him as he came (Luke XV, 11–20). Truly, he had understood his thoughts from afar.

“You searched out my path and my boundary.” “My path,” he says—but which path except the evil one along which he had walked in order to abandon his father, as though he could be hidden from the eyes of the avenger? Or would he have been worn down in that poverty and put in charge of feeding pigs unless the father had wished to scourge the one who was far away so that he might recover the one who was near?

Thus, like a fugitive discovered, with God’s lawful vengeance following him—God who avenges our desires wherever we go and however far we advance [Note: [Col. 1787] In the editions, after “however far we advance,” there is an added “we are recognized”; it is redundant and absent from the manuscripts]—he speaks like a fugitive who has been caught: “You searched out my path and my boundary.”

What is “my path”? The way along which I went. What is “my boundary”? The point to which I arrived. “You searched out my path and my boundary.” My farthest boundary was not far from your eyes: I had gone a long way, and you were there. “You searched out my path and my boundary.”

6. [verse 4.] “And you foresaw all my ways.” He did not say, “You saw,” but “You foresaw.” Before I went them, before I walked them, you foresaw my ways; and you allowed me to walk my ways in labor, so that, if I did not wish to labor, I might return to your ways.

“For there is no deceit in my tongue.” Why did he say this? Because, behold, I confess to you: I walked my path; I became far from you; I departed from you, with whom it was well for me, and without you my good became evil for me. For if it were well for me without you, perhaps I would not wish to return to you.

Thus this person, confessing his sins and declaring the body of Christ justified not in itself but in his grace, said, “There is no deceit in my tongue.”

7. [verse 5.] “Behold, you, Lord, have known all my last things and my first things.” You knew my last things, when I fed pigs; you knew my first things, when I asked you for my share of my property. My first things were the beginnings of my later evils. The ancient sin was when we fell; the final punishment was when we reached this laborious and dangerous mortality.

Would that this be our final state! It will be our final state if we now wish to return. For there is another final state for certain ungodly people, to whom it will be said: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

But we, brothers, have abandoned God only this far: let our labor suffice until the mortality of this life. Let us remember the bread of our Father; let us recall the blessedness of our Father’s house. Let us not be delighted by the pods of pigs, the doctrines of demons.

“Behold, you, Lord, have known all my last things and my first things”: my last things, where I arrived; my first things, where I offended you. “You formed me and placed your hand upon me.”

You formed me—where? In this mortality, already for the labors to which we were all born. For no one is born whom God has not formed in his mother’s womb; nor is there any creature of which he is not the maker.

But you formed me in this labor, and you placed your hand upon me: an avenging hand, weighing upon the proud. For he cast down the exalted in such a health-giving way that he might raise up the humble. “You formed me and placed your hand upon me.”

8. [verse 6.] “Your knowledge has become wonderful because of me; it has prevailed; I cannot attain it.” What is obscure here, yet understood with no small sweetness, hear attentively.

Moses, the holy servant of God, with whom God spoke through a cloud—since, when he spoke temporally, he spoke to his servant through an assumed creature; that is, not through his substance, but through some assumed bodily creature by which those voices would be produced and resound in human and mortal ears—knew that this speech of God came about through certain assumed bodily creatures. God was speaking then in this way, not as he speaks in his substance.

How does he speak in his substance? God’s speech is the Word of God; the Word of God is Christ. That Word does not sound and pass away, but remains forever, unchangeably, the Word through which all things were made (John I, 3). To this Word it is said—and this Word is also the Wisdom of God—“You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same” (Ps. CI, 27–28). And elsewhere, when Scripture speaks of Wisdom, it says: “Remaining in herself, she renews all things” (Wis. VII, 27).

That Wisdom, therefore, standing—if “standing” is the right word, since it is said because of its unchangeability, not because of immobility—and always existing in the same manner, altered in no place or time, never otherwise here than there, never otherwise now than before: this itself is God’s speech.

But the speech that came to Moses came to a human being through syllables and passing sounds. These things would not occur unless God assumed such a creature through which he might emit speech and voices.

The holy Moses knew that God’s speech took place through assumed bodily creatures. He desired and longed to see God’s own form, and he said to God who was speaking with him, “If I have found favor before you, show me yourself.” Since he greatly desired this and, if one may say so, wished by a certain friendly intimacy—which God himself had graciously granted him—to compel God to let him see his majesty and face, God said to him: “You cannot see my face; for no one shall see my face and live. But I will place you in a cleft of the rock, and I will pass by, and I will place my hand over you; but when I have passed by, you will see my back” (Exod. XXXIII, 9–23).

From these words arose another riddle, that is, a certain obscure figure of things. “When I have passed by, you will see my back,” God says—as though he had a face on one side and a back on the other. Far be it from us to think anything of that sort about such Majesty. For one who thinks this about God gains nothing from the fact that temples [Note: [Col. 1788] Ambrosianus and Erasmus read “temples of God.” The word “of God,” which is absent from some manuscripts, was rightly removed by the Louvain editors, lest the passage be understood as referring to any temples other than those of idols, which had been closed by the emperors’ laws because their worship was forbidden, from the year 391.] have been closed. He makes an idol in his heart.

There are therefore great mysteries in those words. As I said, the Lord spoke through a creature, as he wished, to his servant. The person of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was understood there. According to the form of God, by which he is equal to the Father, he too is invisible to human eyes, just as the Father is. If human wisdom cannot be seen by the eyes, can the Power and Wisdom of God be seen by bodily eyes?

But because the Lord was to assume flesh at the proper time, so that, for the sake of healing the mind within, he might also appear to bodily eyes whenever it was necessary for him to appear in this way, he foretold this figuratively to Moses: “You cannot see my face; you will see my back, but only when I have passed by. And so that you may not see my face, my hand will be over you.”

What was it for the Lord to pass by except what the Evangelist says: “When the hour had come for Jesus to pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII, 1)? For the Passover signifies this very passing-over. What is called Pascha in the Hebrew language is interpreted in Latin as “Passover.”

What does “You shall not see my face, but you shall see my back” mean? Whose person did Moses represent when it was said to him, “You shall not see my face, but you shall see my back, and this when I have passed by; and so that you may not see my face, I will place my hand over you”? He called his face his first things, and, in a certain way, his back the passing-over from this world through his passion.

He appeared to the Jews, but they did not recognize him. Moses represented them when it was said to him, “You cannot see my face.” Why did they not see God present in the flesh? Because the Lord’s hand had been laid heavily upon them. For Isaiah had said of them: “Make the heart of this people dull, and weigh down their eyes” (Isa. VI, 10). Their voice is also heard in another psalm: “For your hand has been heavy upon me” (Ps. XXXI, 4).

Therefore, so that they would not then recognize the divinity of Christ [Note: [Col. 1789] The editions add here “they were weighed down,” which is absent from the principal manuscripts]—for if they had recognized it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (I Cor. II, 8), and if the Lord had not been crucified, his blood would not have redeemed the world—what did God do except what the Apostle says concerning the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, when he exclaims: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how untraceable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever and ever.”

The Apostle says this because he had earlier said: “A partial blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI, 33–36, 25–26).

The Jews were therefore partially blinded because of their pride, since they called themselves righteous; and, blinded, they crucified the Lord. He placed his hand over them so that they would not see him until he passed from this world to the Father.

Let us see whether, after he had passed by, they saw his back. The Lord rose and appeared to his disciples (John XX–XXI) and to all who had already believed in him—not to those by whom he had been crucified, because he had placed his hand over them until he passed by.

He ascended into heaven after spending forty days with his disciples. When the day of Pentecost was fulfilled, he sent them the Holy Spirit. Filled with the Holy Spirit, they began to speak in the languages of all those who had been born together and had learned only one language. Those who had crucified the Lord were astonished and terrified at so great a miracle. Cut to the heart by this great wonder, they sought counsel from the Apostles about what they should do, after Christ had been preached to them, while they marveled at how uneducated men could speak in every language.

Through the Apostle Peter, therefore, Christ was announced to them—the one whom they had despised on the cross and mocked as though he were a mortal man. They had insulted him because he did not descend from the cross, although what he did was far greater: to rise from the tomb rather than to descend from the cross.

When Christ had thus been announced to them, they said, “What shall we do?” Those who had raged against the Lord whom they saw now sought the counsel of salvation. They were told: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; and your sins will be forgiven you” (Acts I–II).

Behold, they saw the back of the one whose face they had been unable to see. His hand had been over their eyes—not forever, but until he passed by. After he had passed by, he removed his hand from their eyes. With the hand removed from their eyes, they said to the disciples, “What shall we do?” First savage, afterward devout; first angry, afterward fearful; first hard, afterward bent; first blind, afterward enlightened.

9. I think we recognize in this psalm too such voices of the Gentiles remembering their unbelief. For God has enclosed all in unbelief, so that he might have mercy on all (Rom. XI, 32).

“You formed me and placed your hand over me. Your knowledge has become wonderful because of me; it has prevailed; I cannot attain it.” It is as though you placed your hand over me: you have become wondrous to me; I cannot comprehend you, though I was once with you.

How easy your fatherly face was for me when I said, “Give me my property, the portion that falls to me.” Behold, after I went into a far country and was crushed by hunger (Luke XV, 12–17), much lies before me, and there is labor before me; I cannot grasp what I abandoned.

“For your knowledge,” he says, “has become wonderful because of me.” Because of my sin it became wondrous to me and incomprehensible to me. For it was easy for me to contemplate you when I had not abandoned you through pride.

“Your knowledge has become wonderful because of me; it has prevailed; I cannot attain it”—but understand “from myself.” I cannot attain it from myself. When, therefore, I can attain it, I can do so only from you.

10. [verse 7.] Behold, you find in the far country that the fugitive is not hidden from the eyes of the one from whom he flees. And where will he go now, whose boundary has been searched out? See what he says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” For “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. I, 7). Who can flee in the world from that Spirit by which the world is filled?

“Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” He seeks a place in which to flee from God’s anger. What place will receive God’s fugitive? When people receive fugitives, they ask them from whom they have fled. If they find that the slave belongs to some master who is less powerful, they receive him without fear, saying in their hearts, “This man does not have such a master that he could be tracked down.”

But when they hear of a powerful master, they either do not receive the fugitive or receive him with great fear, because even a powerful human being can be deceived. Where is God not? Who can deceive God? Whom does God not see? From whom does God not reclaim his fugitive?

Where, then, will this fugitive go from the face of God? He turns this way and that, as though seeking a place for his flight.

11. [verse 8.] “If I ascend into heaven,” he says, “you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.” At last you have learned, wicked fugitive, that you cannot in any way become far from the one from whom you wished to distance yourself. Behold, he is everywhere; where will you go?

He finds counsel, and this counsel is inspired in him by the one who already deigns to call him back. “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.” If I exalt myself, I find you as my restrainer; if I hide myself, I find you as my investigator—and not merely an investigator, but one who tracks me down.

For if I become proud of my righteousness, you are there, whose righteousness is true. If, by sinning, I come into the depths of evils and refuse to confess (Prov. XVIII, 3), saying, “Who sees me?” (Ecclus. XXIII, 25), “Will anyone confess to you in hell?” (Ps. VI, 6), you are there even there, to avenge.

Where, then, shall I go so that I may flee from your face—that is, so that I may not experience you as angry?

12. [verse 9.] He finds this counsel: “Thus,” he says, “I shall flee from your face; thus I shall flee from your Spirit—from the avenging Spirit, from the vindicating face.” How? “If I take up my wings in the right direction and dwell at the farthest limits of the sea” [Note: [Col. 1791] So the manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek Septuagint. The editions read “at the farthest limits of the seas.”]—“in this way I can flee from your face.”

If he wishes to flee from God’s face to the farthest limits of the sea, will the one from whom he flees not be there, of whom he said, “If I descend into hell, you are present”? It would be strange if he were not at the farthest limits of the sea, when he is not absent even in hell.

“But I know,” he says, “how to flee from your anger. My wings must be taken up not toward what is crooked, but in the right direction, so that I may neither be lifted up in proud presumption nor plunged into destructive despair.”

What wings does he wish to take up except the two wings, the two commandments of love? On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. XXII, 40).

“If I take up these wings, these feathers, in this way, and dwell at the farthest limits of the sea, I can flee from your face to your face—from the face of the angry one to the face of the reconciled one.”

What is the farthest limit of the sea except the end of the age? Let us fly there now by hope and desire, possessing the wings of twofold love. Let there be no rest for us except at the end of the sea. For if we wish for rest elsewhere, we shall be thrown into the sea. Let us fly until the sea comes to an end; let us suspend ourselves upon the wings of twofold love. In the meantime, let us fly toward God by hope, and by faithful hope let us anticipate that end of the sea.

13. [verse 10.] But consider who will lead us there: the very one whose angry face we wish to flee. For what follows? “If I descend into hell, you are there.” [Col. 1792] “If I take up my wings in the right direction.” “I shall take them up,” he says; therefore he had lost them. “If I take up my wings in the right direction, and dwell at the furthest limits of the sea. For there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will bring me there.”

Let us meditate on this, dearest brothers; let this be our hope, let this be our consolation. Let us take up through love the wings that we lost through desire. For desire became birdlime for our wings; it struck us down from the freedom of our air—that is, from those free breezes of the Spirit of God. Struck down from there, we lost our wings and were, in a sense, taken captive under the power of the fowler; from there he redeemed us by his blood, from whom we fled in order to be captured. He nourishes wings for us from his commandments; now we raise them without birdlime. Let us not love the sea, but let us fly to the furthest limits of the sea.

Let no one tremble; but let no one presume upon his wings either. For even those who have wings, unless he himself raises them—[Note: [Col. 1792] Am. and several manuscripts read *pennati*, “winged”; shortly afterward the Corbie manuscript reads, “unless he himself guides them.”]—unless he himself leads them, we shall be hurled into the depths of the sea, exhausted and weary, as though presuming upon our own strength. It is therefore necessary that we have wings, and it is necessary that he himself lead us; for he is our helper. We possess free will; but with that very free will, how much can we do unless he helps us who commands? “For there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will bring me there.”

14. [verse 11.] And considering the length of the way, what did he say to himself? “And I said, Perhaps darknesses will trample me.” For behold, I have already believed in Christ; I am already being raised up on the two wings of the twofold love; and the iniquity of this age abounds. And because iniquity has abounded, the love of many grows cold. Thus the Lord said: “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold.” In this life, amid so many scandals, amid so many sins, amid such great crowds of daily temptations and daily evil suggestions, what shall I do? he says. How shall I reach the furthest limits of the sea? I hear the Lord’s terrifying words: “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold.” Then he added: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:12–13).
