Considering the length of the way, I said to myself, “Perhaps darknesses will trample me.” “And night will be illumination in my delights.” Night has become illumination for me, because in the night I had despaired of being able to cross so vast a sea, to traverse so long a road, and to come to the end by persevering to the end. Thanks be to him who sought me when I was a fugitive, who struck my back with the blow of a scourge, who recalled me from destruction by calling me, who made the night illuminated for me.

For it is night as long as this life continues. How has night been illuminated? Because Christ descended into the night. Christ took flesh from this age and illuminated the night for us. That woman had lost a drachma; she lit a lamp (Luke 15:8). The Wisdom of God had lost a drachma. What is a drachma? A coin on which there was the image of our Emperor himself. For man was made in the image of God (Gen. 1:27), and he had been lost.

And what did the wise woman do? She lit a lamp. [Col. 1793] The lamp is made of clay, but it has light by which the drachma may be found. Thus the lamp of Wisdom, the flesh of Christ, was made of clay; but it shines by his Word and finds the lost. “And night will be illumination in my delights”: night has become a delight for me. Christ is our delight. See how we rejoice in him now. Whence come these cries of yours, these joys of yours, if not from delight? And whence comes this delight, if not because the night has been illuminated, if not because the Lord Christ is proclaimed to us? Because he sought you before you sought him, and found you so that you might find him. “And night will be illumination in my delights.”

15. [verse 12.] “For darknesses will not be darkened by you.” Therefore, do not darken your own darknesses; and God does not darken them, but rather illuminates them. For it was said to him in another psalm: “You will illuminate my lamp, Lord; my God, you will illuminate my darknesses” (Ps. 17:29).

Who, then, darken their darknesses, which God does not darken? Evil people, perverse people. When they sin, they are indeed darknesses; but when they do not confess the sins they have committed, and instead defend them, they darken their darknesses. Therefore, if you have sinned, you are in darkness; but by confessing your darknesses, you will deserve to have your darknesses illuminated. By defending your darknesses, however, you darken your darknesses. And when will you escape from double darknesses, you who were struggling in single darknesses?

Why, moreover, does the Lord not darken our darknesses? Because he does not allow us to have our sins go unpunished: he scourges us in these labors and disciplines us. You should know, brothers, that all this misery of the human race in which the world groans is medicinal pain, not a penal sentence. You see pain everywhere, fear everywhere, necessity everywhere, labors everywhere. Avarice increases, but amid evils.

If God rescues us here through such scourges so that our darknesses may not be darkened, let us recognize that we are under the punishment of the scourge, and let us bless God, who mingles bitterness with the sweetness of temporal life, lest, blinded by delight in temporal pleasures, we fail to desire eternal delights, and fail to wish for the sea to end and to dwell at the furthest limit of the sea. [Note: [Col. 1793] The better manuscripts read thus. The editions have: “to bring the sea to an end and to dwell at the furthest limit of the sea.”]

Let the waves of the sea rage, then; the more fiercely the waves of the sea rage, the more that dove suspends itself with its wings. [Note: [Col. 1793] The Corbie manuscript reads: “the more that the dove of it suspends itself with its wings.” Perhaps *in illa* should be understood with *novissima*, “at the furthest limit.”] God therefore does not darken our darknesses, because he mingles scourges with our sins and bitterness with our perverse delights. Let us not darken our darknesses by defending our sins. “And night will be illumination in our delights. For darknesses will not be darkened by you.”

16. “And night will be illuminated like day.” Night like day: prosperity in this age is day for us; adversity in this age is night for us. But if we recognize that we suffer adversities deservedly because of our sins, and if the Father’s scourges are sweet to us, lest the Judge’s sentence be bitter, then we shall possess the darknesses of this night in such a way that we also possess the light of this night.

If it is night, how is there light there? It is night because the human race goes astray here; it is night [Col. 1794] because we have not yet come to that day which yesterday and tomorrow do not constrain, but which is perpetual day, without rising because without setting. It is night here, then; but this night has a certain light of its own, and its own darknesses.

We have explained why it is generally night. What is the light of this night? The prosperity and happiness of this age, temporal joy, temporal honor—these are like the light of this night. Adversity, however, and the bitterness of tribulations, or lowliness, are like the darknesses of this night.

In this night, in this mortality of human life, people have light and people have darkness: prosperity is light, adversity is darkness. But when the Lord Christ comes, dwells in the soul through faith, promises another light, breathes into us and grants patience, and warns a person not to delight in prosperity lest he be broken by adversity, then the faithful person begins to use this world impartially. He is neither lifted up when prosperity occurs nor broken when adversity comes, but blesses the Lord everywhere—not only when he abounds, but also when he suffers loss; not only when he is healthy, but also when he is sick—so that this true song may be fulfilled in him: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2).

If, then, always—both when this night shines and when this night is dark; when prosperity smiles and when adversity is sorrowful—let his praise always be in your mouth. And what has just been said will come to pass for you: “As his darknesses are, so also is his light.” His darknesses do not trample me, because his light does not exalt me.

17. Behold, you have his light in Job. He abounded in all things. The light of his night is first described in his riches: the abundance and multitude of his possessions overflowed, and this was the light of his night. The enemy thought that this man worshiped God because God had given him all those things, and he asked that they be taken away from him. The darknesses of his night, which had first possessed light, came upon him.

Yet he knew that, whether light was present there or darkness, it was still the night in which he was a pilgrim away from his God. And he possessed an inner light—God himself—by which he would regard impartially either the darknesses of that night or its light. Therefore, because he worshiped God in the light of that night, that is, in the abundance of his possessions, when all his possessions had been taken from him and his darknesses had come, what did he say?

“The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened: blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

I am in a certain night of this life. “My Lord,” he says, “dwells in my heart. He illuminated this night for me with certain consolations when he gave me an abundance of temporal possessions. He withdrew that temporal light, and the night was, as it were, darkened. But because ‘as his darknesses are, so also is his light’: the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened: blessed be the name of the Lord.”

I am not sad in this night, because “as his darknesses are, so also is his light.” Both pass away, so that “those who rejoice may be as though they did not rejoice, and those who weep as though they did not weep” (1 Cor. 7:30), because “as his darknesses are, so also is his light.”

[Col. 1795] 18. [verse 13.] “For you possessed my inward parts, Lord.” Not without reason: “As his darknesses are, so also is his light.” The possessor is within. He holds not only the heart but also the inward parts; not only thoughts but also delights. He himself, therefore, possesses that from which some light might delight me in the night; he himself holds my inward parts. I do not know how to delight except in the inner light of his wisdom.

What, then? Do you not delight in prosperity of circumstances, in the happiness of the times, in honors, in riches, in family? “I do not delight,” he says. Why? Because “as his darknesses are, so also is his light.”

Whence comes this impartiality in you, so that his darknesses are for you as his light is? Whence? “For you possessed my inward parts, Lord; you received me from the womb of my mother.”

While I was in my mother’s womb, I did not regard the darknesses of that night and the light of that night impartially. For my mother’s womb was the custom of my city. What city is that? The one that first gave birth to us in captivity. We know that Babylon of which we spoke yesterday, from which all those depart who believe in and sigh for that light, the heavenly Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 1795] Several manuscripts read *coelestis*, “heavenly.” Shortly afterward the Royal manuscript reads: “Therefore I said, ‘From the womb…’”]

I therefore said: From the womb of my mother I was received by the Lord; from there the darknesses of this night and the light of this night became indifferent to me. But whoever is in the womb of that mother, Babylon, rejoices in the prosperities of this age and is broken by the adversities of this age. He does not know how to rejoice unless something prosperous occurs according to time, nor does he know how to grieve unless something adverse occurs according to time.

Come out now from the womb of Babylon; begin to sing a hymn to the Lord. Come forth and be born; God will receive you from the womb of your mother. Which God? That God of the apostle Paul, who said: “But when it pleased God, who separated me from my mother’s womb, to reveal [Note: [Col. 1795] Am. and the manuscripts read *praedicare*, “to proclaim.” Shortly afterward, several manuscripts omit “and had learned.”] his Son in me” (Gal. 1:15–16).

For who was his mother? The synagogue. And what had he learned there, except what those Jews themselves and that people had and had learned? The name of the praise of God remained among them, but deeds were not found in them. The words of God were in them like leaves on a tree, but fruit nowhere. When the Lord found such a fig tree, as you know, he dried it up by a curse. For he found leaves on it and did not find fruit; it represented for us a certain tree. For the time of those fruits had not yet come (Matt. 21:19; Mark 11:13–14). Did all human beings know this, while the Maker of heaven and earth did not?

Therefore, he who separated Paul from the womb of his mother also separated us from the womb of our mother. From the womb of which mother? Of that Babylon. Having therefore been received from that womb, let us now begin to have another hope. He promised, brothers, why you should rejoice. [Note: [Col. 1795] Most manuscripts read: “we now begin to have another hope. May it profit, brothers, why do you rejoice?” Some continue: “act fruitfully.”] Bear fruit, having been placed in another hope.

Now we know no evil except offending God and failing to be brought to what he has promised; nor do we know any good except pleasing God and being brought to what he promises. What of the good things of this world, and what of the evils of this world? Let us regard them impartially, because, having now been received from the womb of that mother of ours and regarding these things impartially, we say: “As his darknesses are, so also is his light.”

Neither does the happiness of this age make us blessed, nor does adversity make us miserable. It is necessary to hold fast to righteousness, love faith, hope in God, love God, and love one’s neighbor. After these labors we shall have unfailing light; we shall have a day without setting. Whatever is luminous or dark in this night passes away. “For you possessed my inward parts, Lord; you received me from the womb of my mother.”

19. [verse 14.] “I will confess to you, Lord, because you are wondrously awe-inspiring.” You are wondrously awe-inspiring: by the very fact that we marvel at you, you inspire awe; we rejoice with trembling. For we fear that, lifting ourselves up through pride because of your gifts, we may deserve to lose what we received through humility.

“I will confess to you, Lord, because you have been wondrously made terrible: your works are wonderful, and my soul knows them exceedingly well.” Now my soul knows them exceedingly well, because you received me from the womb of my mother. Previously, however, your knowledge was made wondrous from me: it had grown strong, and I could not reach it. Therefore, from me it had grown strong, and I could not reach it.

Whence does my soul now know exceedingly well, except because “night is illumination in my delights”? Except because your grace came to me and illuminated my darknesses? Except because you possessed my inward parts? Except because you received me from the womb of my mother?

20. [verse 15.] “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret.” He says “his bone”; what is commonly called *ossum* is called *os* in Latin. This is found in Greek [Note: [Col. 1796] *Ostoûn*, “bone.”] For here we might think that *os* means “mouth,” from *ora*, “mouths,” rather than *os*, pronounced with a short vowel, from *ossa*, “bones.” [Note: [Col. 1796] Thus the manuscripts. Am. and Er. read: “*os* improperly.” Lov. reads: “*ossum* improperly.”]

“Therefore,” he says, “my bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret.” I have a certain bone within, in secret. Let us speak this way instead; it is better for grammarians to criticize us than for the people not to understand. There is, then, he says, a certain bone of mine within, in secret. You made a bone for me within, in secret, and it was not hidden from you.

You made it in secret; but did you also hide it from yourself? This bone of mine, made by you in secret, human beings do not see; human beings do not know it. But you know it, because you made it.

What bone does he mean, brothers? Let us seek it; it is in secret. But because we Christians speak to Christians in the name of the Lord, we now find what this sort of bone is. It is a certain inner firmness, because firmness and strength are understood in bones. There is therefore a certain inner firmness of the soul, where it is not broken. [Note: [Col. 1796] Thus Am. and the manuscripts. Er. and Lov. read: “an inner force, where firmness is not broken.”]

Let whatever torments, whatever tribulations, whatever adversities of this age rage on every side; what God made firm in secret cannot be broken in us; it does not yield. For a certain firmness of our patience has been made by the Lord, concerning which it is said in another psalm: “Nevertheless my soul shall be subject to God, because my patience is from him” (Ps. 61:6).

And consider the apostle Paul, possessing within this kind of firmness: “As though sorrowful,” he says, “yet always rejoicing” (2 Cor. 6:10). Whence “as though sorrowful”? Through insults, reproaches, persecutions, scourges, blows, stonings, prisons, chains. Who would not then have considered them miserable? Nor would those persecutors themselves have raged against them unless they thought that they were being made miserable by their persecutions.

They judged them from their own weakness, since they did not possess a hidden bone within. But those who possessed it appeared sorrowful to human beings outwardly, while inwardly they rejoiced in God, to whom their bone was not hidden—the bone he had made in secret.

The same apostle Paul reveals this bone, made by God in secret, in these words: “But not only so,” he says, “we also glory in tribulations.” Is it a small matter that you are not sad, but that you also glory? “It is too little,” he says, for Christians. He made such a bone for me in secret that it is not enough not to be broken unless I also glory.

Where do you glory? “In tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience; patience, proven character; and proven character, hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:3–5).

Thus that hidden bone was formed and strengthened, so that it even makes us glory in tribulations. But we appear miserable to human beings because what we possess within is hidden from them.

“My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret; and my substance is in the lower parts of the earth.” Behold, my substance is in the flesh; my substance is in the lower parts of the earth. Yet I possess within a bone that you formed, which makes me yield to none of the persecutions [Note: [Col. 1797] Am. and several manuscripts read “persecutors.”] of this lower region, where my substance still is.

For what great thing is it if an angel is strong? It is a great thing if flesh is strong. And whence is flesh strong, whence is a strong earthen vessel, except because a bone was made there in secret? “And my substance is in the lower parts of the earth.”

21. [verse 16.] What does he say about those who are less firm? For, as I have already pointed out, Christ is speaking. But many things are spoken from the person of the body; hear also what is spoken from the person of the head—not as though he distinguishes them by introducing the persons, now the head and now the body. For if he distinguishes them, he seems to divide them; “the two will not be one flesh.” But if “the two are one flesh” (Eph. 5:31–32), do not be surprised if the two are in one voice.

When our Lord Jesus Christ suffered, the disciples did not yet possess that inner bone; the strength of patience had not yet been established in them. They hid themselves; they did not know their own strength. Peter dared to promise fellowship in death with the Lord’s passion, and he did not know that he was sick; but the physician knew the sick man.

What happened? “With you even unto death,” he said. “Truly I tell you, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (Matt. 26:34–35; Luke [Col. 1798] 22:33–34). The physician’s answer proved truer than the sick man’s presumption.

Of these, then, he says: “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret.” In them that bone itself was strengthened inwardly, and especially the strength of suffering in our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself. When he wished, he sat; when he wished, he rose; when he wished, he slept; when he wished, he awoke, because he said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

What does he say about those in whom that strength had not yet been formed and strengthened? See what he says to God the Father: “My imperfect state your eyes saw.” My imperfect state—Peter promising and denying, presuming and failing—your eyes nevertheless saw.

For after the third denial, when the Lord looked upon him, as it is written in the Gospel, and Peter was reminded of what the Lord had foretold, he went outside and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62). That weeping resulted from God’s looking upon him, because he says: “My imperfect state your eyes saw.”

For that imperfect man, stumbling in the Lord’s passion, would undoubtedly have perished. But your eyes saw him—not him alone, but all who were imperfect until they were strengthened by Christ’s resurrection. It appeared to their eyes that what had died in the Lord had not perished; and that bone was made in secret within them, so that they themselves no longer feared dying.

“My imperfect state your eyes saw; and in your book all will be written”—not only the perfect, but also the imperfect. Let the imperfect not fear, provided that they make progress. Nor, because I have said “let them not fear,” should they love imperfection and remain where they were found. Let them make as much progress as lies within them. Let them add daily, advance daily; nevertheless, let them not withdraw from the body of the Lord, so that, joined together in one body and fitted among these members, they may deserve to have this utterance spoken of them: “My imperfect state your eyes saw; and in your book all will be written.”

22. “By day they will go astray, and no one among them.” Here the day was still our Lord Jesus Christ; hence he said: “Walk while you have the day” (John 12:35). But his imperfect followers will go astray by day. They too thought that our Lord Jesus Christ was merely a human being; that he did not possess hidden divinity within himself, that he was not secretly God, but only what he appeared to be. They thought this too.

For Peter himself—we speak especially of him, since in him an example of weakness that is nevertheless not without hope has been set before us [Note: [Col. 1798] Thus five manuscripts. Others, with the editions, read: “an example of firmness that is not without hope.”]—had said to the Lord, when he asked what people said about him: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” And the Lord had said to him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.”

Why? Because he had called him the Son of God. Shortly afterward, in the same place and in the very sequence of the words, the Lord began to speak of his future passion. But Peter, who had already confessed him as the Son of God, feared that he would die as the Son of Man.

He was the Son of God, and he was also the son of man: the Son of God in the form of God, equal to the Father; the son of man in the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7), in which he is less than the Father (John 14:28). He was going to come to his passion precisely in the form of a servant. What did Peter fear—that the form of God would perish in the form of a servant? Why did he not rather presume that the form of the servant would rise again from the form of God?

He said to him: “Far be it from you, Lord; may God be merciful to you.” And the Lord, who had called him blessed in that earlier utterance, said: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not understand the things of God, but the things of human beings” (Matt. 16:13–23).

Earlier, because he had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” he had heard: “Flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” Therefore, he was a rock; therefore, he was blessed. But now, because he had answered not from the Father’s revelation but from the weakness of flesh, he was called Satan: “You do not understand the things of God, but the things of human beings.”

And here was Christ, brothers. He had walked among them; he had commanded the winds (Matt. 8:26); before their eyes he had walked upon the waves (Matt. 14:25); before their eyes he had raised a man dead for four days (John 11:39–44); before their eyes he had performed so many miracles. Yet they trembled at his passion, as though they had lost the one in whom they had presumed in vain.

“But by day they will go astray [Note: [Col. 1799] Thus most manuscripts. The editions read: “they were going astray.”], and no one among them.” No one at all—not even the one who had said, “With you even unto death.” For he had said to them: “The hour is coming when you will leave me alone, and each one will go his own way. But I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32).

The Father was with him, and he himself was with the Father; the Father was in him, and he himself was in the Father; he and the Father were one (John 10:30, 38). Yet they were afraid when he died. Why, unless because they went astray by day, and no one was among them? “By day they will go astray, and no one among them.”

23. [verse 17.] But what does “they will go astray by day” mean? Will they perish? And where is it said: “My imperfect state your eyes saw, and in your book all will be written”? When, then, did they go astray by day? When they did not understand the Lord, who was placed here.

And what follows? “But your friends, God, have been greatly honored by me.” Those very same people who went astray by day, and no one was among them, became your friends, and “have been greatly honored by me.” That bone was made in secret within them after the Lord’s resurrection, and they suffered for his name, in whose passion they had trembled.

“But your friends, God, have been greatly honored by me; their rule has been greatly strengthened.” Having become apostles, having become leaders of the Church, having become rams leading the flocks, their rule was greatly strengthened.

24. [verse 18.] “I will number them, and they will be multiplied beyond the sand.” Through those who went astray by day, and no one was among them, behold, this great multitude was born, which can no longer be numbered like sand except by God.

He said, “They will be multiplied beyond the sand,” and yet he had said, “I will number them.” Those who were numbered themselves will be multiplied beyond the sand. For the sand was numbered by him who has numbered the hairs of our head (Matt. 10:30). “I will number them, and they will be multiplied beyond the sand.”

25. “I arose, and I am still with you.” “I arose, and I am still with you”—what does this mean? “I have suffered,” he says; “I have been buried. Behold, I have risen, and still they do not understand that I am with them.” “I am still with you,” that is, not yet with them, because they do not yet recognize me. For thus it is read in the Gospel: after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, those to whom he appeared did not immediately recognize him (Matt. 28:17).

There is another meaning as well: “I arose, and I am still with you.” Perhaps he wished this to signify the time during which he is still hidden at the right hand of the Father, before he is revealed in the glory in which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

26. [verses 19–20.] Then he says what he suffers during all this time—now that he has risen and is still with the Father—through the mixture of sinners in his body, which is the Church, and through the separation of heretics.

For he continues and says: “If you kill sinners, God; men of blood, depart from me, for you will say in your thought, ‘They will receive their cities in vanity.’”

The order of the words seems to be connected in this way: “If you kill sinners, God, they will receive their cities in vanity.” For he wishes them to be understood as killed when, through the pride with which they swell, they lose the grace by which they live.

“For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. 1:5). Thus sinners are killed, because, darkened in their understanding, they are alienated from the life of God (Eph. 4:18). For through their arrogance they lose confession; and thus, in those who have been killed, what is written comes to pass: “From the dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes” (Sir. 17:26).

And so they receive their cities in vanity—that is, their vain peoples, who follow their vanity. Swollen with the name of righteousness, they persuade the blind and inexperienced to follow them as though they were more righteous, after breaking the bond of unity.

And because they often find here an occasion for separating themselves from the unity of Christ, while they accuse the wicked with whom they pretend they do not wish to have communion; and because it can happen that they not only slander the innocent, whom they pretend to flee as wicked, but also speak truth about certain wicked people like themselves, among whom Christ’s wheat groans while preserving the bond of unity—therefore he inserted: “Men of blood, depart from me, for you will say in your thought, ‘They will receive their cities in vanity.’”

That is, they will therefore lead their peoples into their own separation, to be corrupted by their own vanity, because you will say in your thought: “Men of blood, depart from me.” Thus, sinners killed in spirit because of the merit of their pride receive their cities—that is, their peoples—in vanity; that is, they lead them away into the vanity of error by separating them. As though offended by the mixture of chaff, they abandon the wheat after breaking unity.

For this reason the wheat itself—that is, the good faithful—are warned not to separate themselves openly from the wicked before the final winnowing, which is to occur at the end, lest they abandon the good who are still mixed with them. Rather, by good conduct and a life unlike theirs, let the wheat somehow say silently to them: “Men of blood, depart from me.” [Note: [Col. 1800] The editions read: “let the body of Christ say silently to them, ‘Men of blood…’” The manuscripts do not contain “the body of Christ”; in its place “wheat” is understood.]

For the voice of God says this to them—a voice that is in thought, just as God speaks it in the thought of his holy people. And who are the men of blood except those who hate their brothers, as John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15)?

Not understanding this, the sinners who have been killed accuse the communion of the wicked: they do not understand how God says to the wicked in the thought of the good, “Men of blood, depart from me.” And by separating themselves through these accusations, they receive their cities in vanity.

This voice, which is now spoken in the thought of the good to the wicked, will be open on that day when our very head says to them: “I never knew you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (Matt. 7:23).

27. [verse 21.] But now the body of Christ, which is the Church, says: Why do the proud accuse me, as though the sins of others defile me, and therefore, by separating themselves, they receive their cities in vanity?

“Have I not hated those who hate you, Lord? Why do they demand from me even a bodily separation from the wicked, so that before the time of the harvest the wheat may be uprooted together with the weeds (Matt. 13:30); so that before the time of the winnowing I may lose the endurance required to tolerate the chaff (Matt. 3:12); so that, before all kinds of fish reach the end of the age, as though to the shore, where they are to be separated, I may tear apart the nets of peace and unity (Matt. 13:47)?

Are the sacraments I receive the sacraments of the wicked? Do I share in communion with them by consenting to their lives and deeds? “Have I not hated those who hate you, Lord, and was I not wasting away over your enemies? When zeal for your house consumed me (Ps. 68:10), did I not see the senseless and waste away? Did disgust not also seize me because of sinners who abandon your law (Ps. 118:139, 158, 53)?

For who are your enemies except those who show by their life that they hate your law? Since, then, I hated them, why do those who receive their cities in vanity accuse me, because the sins of those whom I hated and over whom I wasted away in zeal for God’s house could be imputed to me?

But where is it written, ‘Love your enemies’? Or is it because he said ‘your enemies,’ not God’s? ‘Do good,’ he says, ‘to those who hate you’; he did not say, ‘to those who hate God.’ Therefore this man, following that distinction, said [Note: [Col. 1801] Er. reads *securus*, “confidently”; M. has the present reading.]: ‘Have I not hated those who hate you, Lord?’ He did not say, ‘those who hate me.’ ‘And I was wasting away over your enemies’: he said ‘your enemies,’ not ‘mine.’

But those who hate us for this reason, and are therefore our enemies, because we serve God—what else do they do but hate him and become his enemies? Should we therefore not love such enemies of ours [Note: [Col. 1801] Thus Am., Er., and several manuscripts. Lov. reads: “should we not love such enemies?”]? Or do they not suffer persecution for God’s sake, to whom it is said: ‘Pray for those who persecute you’ (Matt. 5:44)?”

Therefore, consider what follows.

28. [verse 22.] “With perfect hatred I hated them.” What is “with perfect hatred”? I hated their iniquities in them; I loved your creaturely nature in them. This is to hate with perfect hatred: neither to hate human beings because of their vices, nor to love vices because of human beings.

For see what he adds: “They became enemies to me.” He now shows that they are not only God’s enemies but also his own. How, then, will he fulfill in them both what he himself said, “Have I not hated those who hated you,” and what the Lord commanded, “Love your enemies”? How will he fulfill this except through that perfect hatred, so that he hates in them what makes them wicked, but loves what makes them human?

Even in the time of the Old Testament, when the carnal people were restrained by visible punishments, Moses, the servant of God, a man who belonged through understanding to the New Testament—how did he hate sinners while praying for them? And how did he not hate them when he killed them, unless he hated them with perfect hatred? For with that perfection he hated the iniquity which he punished in such a way that he loved the humanity for which he prayed.

29. [verse 23.] Since, then, the body of Christ—although at the end it must also be separated bodily from the impious and wicked—now meanwhile groans among them; and since those sinners, when slain, slander the good concerning their association with the wicked and separate themselves, as though on the occasion of the wicked, still further from the good and innocent, and thus “receive their cities in vanity,” so that many wicked people still remain who do not follow their separation but, to be endured by the good until the end, remain in the same mixture: what does the body of Christ do, whether bearing fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold, with perseverance (Matt. XIII, 23; Luke VIII, 15)? What does Christ’s neighbor (*proxima*) do in the midst of the daughters, “like a lily among thorns” (Song II, 2)? What are her words? What is her conscience? What is the appearance of “the king’s daughter within” (Ps. XLIV, 14)?

Listen to what she says: “Prove me, O God, and know my heart.” You, God, prove; you know—not man, not the heretic, who neither knows how to prove nor can know my heart, where you prove and know that I do not consent to the deeds of the wicked, while they think that I can be contaminated by the sins of others. Thus, while in my distant pilgrimage I do what I lament in another psalm—that is, while “with those who hate peace I am peaceful” [Note: [Col. 1802] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read *eram* (“I was”) instead of *sum* (“I am”).] (Ps. CXIX, 7)—until I reach that vision of peace whose interpretation is Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, the eternal city in heaven, they, by quarrelling and slandering and separating themselves, “receive their cities,” not, indeed, in eternity but in vanity.

“Prove me, therefore, O God, and know my heart; examine me, and know my paths.” Why this? Attend to what follows.

30. [verse 24.] “And see,” he says, “whether there is in me any way of iniquity, and lead me in the eternal way.” “Examine,” he says, “my paths”—that is, my counsels and thoughts—“and see whether there is in me any way of iniquity,” whether in doing or consenting; “and lead me in the eternal way.”

What else does he say than, “Lead me in Christ”? For what is the eternal way except the one who is eternal life? Eternal is he who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). If, therefore, you find in my way something that displeases your eyes, since my way is mortal, lead me in the eternal way, where there is no iniquity. For even “if anyone should sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the atonement for our sins” (I John [Col. 1803] II, 1). He is the eternal way without sin [Note: [Col. 1803] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “life.”]; he is eternal life without punishment.

31. Great are the mysteries, brothers. How does the Spirit of God speak with us? How does he provide us with delights on this night? What is this, we ask you, brothers? Why are things sweeter the more obscure they are? [Note: [Col. 1803] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read this passage as: “They are sweeter from the fact that they are more obscure.”] He prepares for us, by wondrous methods, a drink that leads us to love him. He makes his very words wondrous, so that although we say things you already knew, nevertheless, because they were drawn out from passages that had seemed obscure, the knowledge itself becomes, as it were, new.

Did you not know, brothers, that the wicked must be tolerated in the Church of God and that schisms must not be made? Did you not already know that within those nets which catch both good and bad fish we must remain until the shore, and that the nets must not be torn, because on the shore the good will be separated into vessels and the bad thrown away? You already knew these things; but you did not understand these verses of this psalm. What you did not understand has been explained, and what you knew has been made new.

## Exposition of Psalm 139

### Sermon to the People

1. The lords, my brothers [Note: [Col. 1803] From these words one may rightly infer that the sermon was delivered at some gathering of bishops.], and in them the Lord of all, have ordered me to bring this psalm to you for understanding, insofar as the Lord grants it. May he assist me through your prayers, so that I may say what I ought to say and you hear what you ought to hear, so that the divine sermon may be useful to all of us. For it is not useful to everyone, because “faith is not possessed by all” (II Thess. III, 2). Faith, however, is in the soul like a good root that turns rain into fruit; but faithlessness, diabolical error, and desire—the evil root of all evils (I Tim. VI, 10)—like a root of thorns, turns even sweet rain into pricks.

2. What this psalm contains, I believe you noticed when it was sung, since it complains and groans and pours out a prayer to God: the body of Christ, placed among the wicked. For its voice is heard in every such prophecy, like the voice of that poor man—that is, the needy man, not yet satisfied, hungering and thirsting for righteousness (Matt. V, 6)—for whom a certain fullness is reserved at the end. Meanwhile, here and now, let him thirst and hunger, groan and knock and seek. Let him not delight in the attractions of his pilgrimage; let him not regard the world as his homeland, from which Christ came to set him free. For Christ wished to be our head, the head, that is, of a certain body. He cannot be called a head where there is no body of which he is the head. Therefore, if Christ is the head, Christ is the head of some body. The holy Church is the body of that head, and we are among its members if we love our head.

Let us therefore hear the voices of Christ’s body—that is, our own voices, if we are in Christ’s body—because whoever is not there will be among those amid whom that body groans. Therefore either you will be in that body, groaning among the wicked, or you will not be in that body and will be among those amid whom the body groans, the body that groans among the wicked: either a member of Christ or an enemy of Christ’s body.

Nor are these enemies and adversaries of Christ’s body understood in only one way, or do they act in only one way. The one who rules among them and uses them as his vessels is deceitful and many-sided. Yet many are freed from him and pass into Christ’s body; who they are and how many they will be is known to the one who redeemed them by his blood, though they did not know him [Note: [Col. 1804] The editions read “what”; some manuscripts, “that”; others, “how many.”]. But some will persist in their wickedness, not belonging to Christ’s body; and they too are known to him, for nothing is unknown to him.

Meanwhile, those who have already been joined to his members, not yet possessing the future resurrection in which all groaning will perish and praise will take its place, in which all tribulation will die and there will be rejoicing without end—not yet possessing this in reality, but nevertheless holding it in hope—groan out of a certain longing and pray to be freed from wicked people, among whom the good must necessarily live as well. For separation is not yet safe for anyone. Separation belongs to the one who cannot err.

What does “the one who cannot err” mean? It means one who neither transfers evil to the right nor good to the left. But in this life it is difficult for us to know even ourselves; how much less should we pass a hasty judgment on anyone else! If today we know someone to be wicked, we do not know what he will be tomorrow; and perhaps the one we hate intensely is our brother, though we do not know it.

Therefore, let us safely hate wickedness in the wicked and love the creature, so that we may love what God made in that person and hate what the person himself made there. God made the person himself; the person made sin. Love what God made; hate what the person made. For in this way you persecute what the person made so that what God made may be freed.

3. [verse 1.] “For the end; a psalm to David.” Understand “the end” as nothing other than what the Apostle has prescribed for you: “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4). Therefore, when you hear the psalm say, “For the end,” let your hearts be turned toward Christ.

For the title of the psalm is, as it were, the psalm’s herald, saying: “Behold, he will come” [Note: [Col. 1804] Thus most manuscripts. The editions instead read: “Behold, I have come,” and so forth.]; from there I shall speak, from there I shall sing of Christ. For by “to David” I understand only the one who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. I, 3). Meanwhile, the name corresponds to the lineage. His carnal lineage is from David; his spiritual lineage is above David—not only before David, but before Abraham; not only before Abraham, but before Adam; not only before Adam, but before heaven and earth, before all angels, before all powers and virtues, before all visible and invisible things.

Why? Because, for these things to exist, “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3). Therefore, because he was from the seed of David—not according to his divinity, by which he is the Creator of David himself, but according to the flesh—David was deemed worthy to be named in prophecy. Fix your attention on this end, because the psalm is sung to David; hear the voice of his body, and be in his body. Let the voice you have heard become your own voice; pray, and say what follows.

[Col. 1805] 4. [verse 2.] “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man”—not from one man, but from the whole kind; not only from the vessels, but from the prince himself, that is, from the devil himself.

Why “from the man,” if from the devil? Because he too is called a man figuratively: “An enemy man came and sowed weeds over it.” When the servants said to the master of the household, “Did you not sow good seed? From where, then, have the weeds appeared?” the answer was: “An enemy man has done this” (Matt. XIII, 25, 27, 28).

Pray, therefore, as much as you can, to be delivered from this evil man: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph. VI, 12), that is, the rulers of sinners. Indeed, we too once were such, for we have just heard the Apostle’s voice: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8).

Now, therefore, having become light—not in ourselves, but in the Lord—let us pray not only against the darkness, that is, against sinners whom the devil still possesses, but also against the devil himself, their prince, who works in the children of disobedience (Eph. II, 2).

“Rescue me from the unjust man.” This is the same as “from the evil man”—what is evil is unjust. He called him evil because he is unjust, lest you perhaps think that some unjust person is good. Many are unjust as though they were harmless. They are not savage, harsh, or persecutors who cause people distress; yet they are unjust in another way, because they are lustful, drunk, and devoted to pleasures.

How can one who does not spare himself harm no one? He is innocent who harms no one, not he who harms himself. But how can one who harms himself fail to harm you? You reply: “How does he harm me? He has not invaded my property or sought my life. He feeds on his own lust and delights in his own pleasures. But if his pleasures are polluted, he himself is polluted. What does that concern me, when he is not troublesome to me?”

He harms you at least by his example, because he lives with you and invites you to do what he does. When you perhaps see him prospering amid those filths, are you not drawn by the pleasure of such deeds? Even if you do not consent, at least you have found something to overcome. How, then, did he not harm you, when you are struggling to conquer what he produced in your heart?

Every unjust person, therefore, is evil, and necessarily harmful, whether gentle or savage. Whoever encounters him, whoever is caught in his snares, will discover how harmful is what he had thought mild. For, brothers, thorns do not prick at their roots. Pull thorns from the earth, touch their roots, and see whether you feel pain; yet that from which you feel pain at the surface has come from that root.

Therefore, do not be pleased by people who seem gentle and agreeable but are lovers of carnal pleasures and followers of polluted desires. Do not be pleased by them. Although they still appear gentle, they are roots of thorns.

For by such deeds, through lust, they often squander what they possess. And how do they seek to replenish what they have squandered? Do they then spare robbery and schemes of fraud, or refrain from seeking every kind of wickedness? Now you see the evil man whom you previously thought gentle.

When you saw him getting drunk, he was good; now you see a thief and fear a robber. Thorns have emerged from those roots. When you perceived the gentle roots of the thorns, if you could have burned them then, there would have been no source from which what now pricks you could emerge.

Therefore, my brothers, you who are Christ’s body, or Christ’s members, groaning among such wicked people: whenever you find people inclined to rush into evil lusts and destructive pleasures, rebuke them then, correct them then, burn them then. Let the root be set on fire, and there will be no source from which a thorn may grow.

But if you cannot do this, be certain that you will have them as enemies. They may keep silent; they may conceal their hostility; they cannot love you. But since they cannot love you, and since those who hate you must necessarily seek evil for you, let not your tongue and heart cease to say to God: “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man; free me from the unjust man.”

5. [verse 3.] “Who have devised injustices in their heart.” What of it, then, that they do not dare to bring them forth on their tongue but keep them in their heart? He said this on account of those who often speak good things with their lips. You hear the voice of a just man, but it is not the heart of a just man.

For what purpose was it useful to add this, saying, “Who have devised injustices in their heart”? Deliver me from them; let your hand be most powerful there to rescue me. It is easy to avoid open hostility; easy to turn away from an enemy who is ready and manifest, whose iniquity is already even on his lips. That enemy is troublesome; that enemy is hidden and difficult to avoid, who carries good things on his lips and conceals evil in his heart: “Who have devised injustices in their heart.”

“All day long they were preparing wars.” What is “wars”? They were preparing throughout the day things against which I would fight. For whatever exists against which a Christian struggles arises from such hearts. Whether sedition, schism, heresy, or turbulent contradiction, none of this bursts forth except from those thoughts that were concealed. While their lips were speaking good things, “all day long they were preparing wars.” You hear words of peace, but the preparation for war does not depart from their hearts.

What is said by “all day long” signifies “without interruption,” that is, throughout the whole time.

6. [verse 4.] “They sharpened their tongues like serpents.” If you are still seeking the man, look at the likeness. The serpent is characterized especially by cunning and the deceit of causing harm; therefore it also crawls. It does not even have feet, so that its tracks might be heard when it comes. Along its path its movement seems gentle, but it is not straight.

So they crawl and creep in order to do harm, carrying hidden poison beneath a gentle touch. And therefore it follows: “The poison of asps is under their lips.” See, it is under their lips, so that we may understand one thing as being beneath their lips and another thing as being on their lips.

Another passage openly reveals such people when it says: “They speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts” (Ps. XXVII, 3).

7. [verse 5.] “Preserve me, O Lord, from the hand of the sinner; rescue me from unjust men.” They are known; they are known [Note: [Col. 1806] Am. and the manuscripts read: “They themselves are; they themselves are known.” This perhaps refers to what he said immediately before: “But evil is in their hearts.” The same books shortly afterward read: “not to ask what it is.”]. Here there is no need to understand who they are, but to act; there is need to pray, not to ask who they are.

But how you should pray against such people, he reveals in what follows. For many pray ineptly against the wicked. “They have devised,” he says, “to trip up my steps.” This can still be understood in a carnal sense. Everyone has an enemy who plots to defraud him in a business transaction and take money from him while engaged with him in a common enterprise. Everyone has an enemy who is a neighbor and plots to bring harm upon his household, to diminish something belonging to him. Certainly he plots deceitfully and fraudulently and seeks to accomplish these things by the devil’s devices; no one doubts this.

Yet such people must not be feared on account of these things, but lest by lying in wait for you they draw you over to themselves—that is, separate you from Christ’s body and make you part of their body. For just as Christ is the head of the good, so the devil is their head.

“They have devised,” he says, “to trip up my steps.” What does “to trip up my steps” mean? It does not mean that you should err in the business you conduct with him, or that he should deceive you in a case you share with him in court. He has tripped up your steps if he has hindered you on God’s way, so that what you were directing rightly should stumble, slip from the way, fall on the way, depart from the way, remain on the way, or turn back from where it had come. Whatever of this he does to you, he has tripped you and deceived you.

Pray against such snares, lest you lose your heavenly inheritance, lest you lose Christ as your co-heir, because you are going to live forever with the one who made you an heir. For he did not make you heir of one whose death you will succeed to, but of one with whom you will live forever.

8. [verse 6.] “The proud have hidden a snare for me.” He briefly disclosed the whole body of the devil when he said “the proud.” Hence they often call themselves just, although they are unjust. Hence nothing is so harmful to them as confessing their sins.

They are false just people, and therefore necessarily envy true just people. For no one envies another in something he does not wish either to be or to appear to be. One person envies you because you are rich; either he wants to be rich so that he may envy you, or he wants to be thought rich. Another envies you because you are distinguished and noble; either he strives to be this, or he wants to be thought to be this.

And so, with everything that appears or is thought good in this world, whatever someone wants to possess, whatever he wants to excel in, or whatever reputation he seeks, he envies you in that respect. But these people, who are falsely just, want to appear just although they are not; and when they see someone truly just, they necessarily envy him and contrive with him how he may lose what he glories in.

From this come all seductions and trippings. The devil himself first wished this: when he fell, he envied the standing human being. And because he himself lost the kingdom of heaven, he did not wish man to reach it (Gen. III), nor does he wish it now. He is working so that man may not reach the place from which he himself was cast down.

Therefore, because he himself is proud, and because he is envious on account of his pride, the whole body of such people is his body. But let us pray against the one who cannot be corrected, and on behalf of those who can, so that we may say to the unjust man: “Why do you envy the just man, unjust man? Because you wish to appear just? Quickly do what is better, and you will more easily become what you wish to appear to be. Be just.”

[Note: [Col. 1807] Thus several manuscripts. The editions read: “What you wish to appear to be, be in reality, and so forth.” The Regius manuscript reads: “Be so; love,” and so forth.]

Then you will love the one you envied, because what you grieve that he is, you too will be, and you will love yourself in him and him in yourself.

For if you envied a rich person, it would not be in your power to become rich; if you envied some honorable, noble senator, it would not be in your power to become noble and distinguished; if you envied a handsome person, you could never make yourself handsome; if you envied a strong and vigorous person, you could never give yourself strength. But if you envy the just person, the matter lies within your will: become what you grieve that another is.

You will not have to buy what you are not and another is. It comes freely; it comes quickly: “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke II, 14).

9. But those proud people “hid a snare; they sought to trip up my steps” [Note: [Col. 1808] The manuscripts at this point read: “straight steps.” Erasmus reads: “my straight steps.”]. And what did they do? “They stretched out ropes as snares for my feet.”

What ropes? This word is familiar in Scripture, and elsewhere we find what ropes signify. The Lord made a whip from little cords and drove from the temple those who were behaving badly there (John II, 15). He showed us how to understand the ropes, because another Scripture says: “Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. V, 22); and Isaiah says plainly: “Woe to those who draw sins like a long rope!” (Isa. V, 18).

Why is it called a rope? Because every sinner who persists in his sins adds sins to sins. Although he ought to be corrected by an accusation of his sin, he doubles through defense what could have been removed through confession; and often he wishes to be protected by other sins because of those he has committed.

He committed adultery, and so that he may not be killed he prepares murder; he adds sin to sin. Again, if he happens to commit murder, the man who previously feared one crime now fears two. And when he sees himself fearing more things than before, he does not consider reducing what he has done but adding what he has not yet done; perhaps he also seeks sorcery. Behold, he has three.

Who can now imagine an end? Who can cut short the rope of sins? The word “rope” is used very appropriately. For, in order for a rope to be twisted, something is added; and straight strands are not added but twisted ones. Perversity is joined to itself and drawn out at length, and he does not consider cutting off what he has woven badly, but adding to it, extending it, stretching it out, so that in the end he may have something with which his hands and feet will be bound and he will be thrown into the outer darkness (Matt. XXII, 13).

These sins of theirs they stretch out toward the just when they persuade them to do the evils they themselves do. Therefore he said: “They stretched out ropes as snares for my feet,” that is, they wished to cast me down through their sins.

And where did they do this? “Beside the paths they placed a stumbling-block for me,” not on the paths but beside the paths. Your paths are God’s commandments. They placed stumbling-blocks beside the paths; do not depart from the paths, and you will not rush into the stumbling-blocks.

Nor do I want you to say: “Would God have prevented them from placing stumbling-blocks beside my paths, and then they would not have placed them there?” On the contrary, God permitted them to place stumbling-blocks beside the paths, while you do not depart from the paths. “Beside the paths they placed stumbling-blocks for me.”

10. [verse 7.] And what remains? What remedy is there amid so many evils, in these temptations, in these dangers? “I said to the Lord: You are my God.” Those people are men, and not mine; but you are both God and mine. “I said to the Lord: You are my God.”

This is a great voice of prayer; it moves confidence. Is he not the God of those people? For whose God is he not, since he is the true God? Yet he belongs properly to those who enjoy him, who serve him, who willingly remain under him.

The wicked too, though unwillingly, are under him. They call upon the God from whom they may receive a crown; under him they flee from the one by whom they will be condemned. And the unjust person who does not wish to have the Lord as his God—where will he flee from the God of all?

It is good for him, therefore, to turn to the God of all and make him his own through conversion. Placed among such sinners, seducers, hypocrites, and proud people, let him say to God, whom he has made his own God through his conversion: “I said to the Lord: You are my God.”

“Give ear, O Lord, to the voice of my supplication.” The statement is simple and easy to understand, but perhaps it is nevertheless pleasing to consider why he did not say, “Give ear to my supplication,” but, as though expressing the feeling of his soul more clearly, said, “the voice of my supplication.” He means the life of my supplication, the soul of my supplication—not what sounds in my words, but that from which my words live.

Other noises, being without a soul, can be called sounds, but they cannot be called voices. A voice properly belongs to animate and living things. How many people, however, beseech God but do not perceive God, nor think rightly about God? They may have the sound of supplication, but they cannot have its voice, because life is not there.

But this person was alive: he understood his God, saw from what he was to be delivered, and perceived from whom he was to be delivered. This itself was the voice of his supplication.

11. [verse 8.] Commending that voice to God’s ears, let him say: “Lord, Lord.” You, Lord, Lord—that is, you who are truly Lord—not lords such as human beings are, not lords such as those who buy with a small purse, but the Lord who purchased with blood.

“Lord, Lord, the strength of my salvation”—that is, you who give strength to my salvation. What does “the strength of my salvation” mean?

He was complaining about the stumbling-blocks and snares of sinners, about wicked people, the devil’s vessels, barking and lying in wait all around him, and about the proud who envy the just. Among such people he must necessarily lead his life while living here in this pilgrimage.

The Lord foretold that such stumbling-blocks would abound and said: “Iniquity will abound, and because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold.” But he immediately added consolation: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXIV, 12–13).

This man paid attention and was afraid; troubled by the abundance of iniquities, he looked toward hope, because “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” He stretched himself toward perseverance and saw a long road. And because perseverance is a great and difficult thing, he prayed to the one who had commanded him to persevere for the perfection of his perseverance [Note: [Col. 1809] Several manuscripts read: “for his perseverance.”].

“Certainly I shall be saved if I persevere to the end. But perseverance belongs to strength, so that I may deserve salvation. You are the strength of my salvation; you make me persevere so that I may reach salvation. Lord, Lord, the strength of my salvation.”

And from where do I hope that you are the strength of my salvation? “You have overshadowed my head on the day of battle.”

Behold, I am still fighting. I fight outside against those who pretend to be good; I fight within against my desires, because “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin that is in my members.” “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 23–25).

Therefore, struggling in this battle, he looked toward the grace of God. And because he had begun to burn and dry up, he found, as it were, a shade under which he might live: “You have overshadowed my head on the day of battle,” that is, in the heat, so that I would not grow weary or dry up.

12. [verse 9.] “Do not hand me over, O Lord, to the sinner through my own desire.” This is how your shade will benefit me: I will not suffer heat from myself. And what could that sinner do to me, however fiercely he might rage?

The wicked raged against the martyrs. They dragged them, bound them with chains, shut them in prisons, struck them with the sword, threw them to wild beasts [Note: [Col. 1810] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read “subjected them”; the manuscript reads “threw them to wild beasts.”], and consumed them with fire. They did all these things, but God did not hand them over to sinners, because they were not handed over to their own desire.

Pray for this, therefore, as much as you can: that God may not hand you over to the sinner through your own desire. For you give the devil a place through your desire.

Behold, the devil has proposed profit and invited you to fraud: you cannot have the profit unless you commit fraud. But the profit is bait, and the fraud is a snare. Look at the bait in such a way that you also see the snare. You cannot obtain the profit unless you commit fraud; but if you commit fraud, you will be caught.

I do not say “you will be caught” because you will be discovered. Sometimes you will not be discovered by human beings, but will you not be discovered by God? [Note: [Col. 1810] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “but you will be caught by God,” and so forth.]

You will be caught, dragged away, and killed. For everyone who does such things destroys himself.

There is the bait, therefore, and there is also the snare. Restrain your desire, and you will not fall into the snare. But if the desire for the bait overcomes you, it puts your neck into the snare, and the fowler of souls will catch you.

“Do not hand me over to the sinner through my own desire.” By this he is shaded on the day of battle. Desire produces heat, but the Lord’s shade moderates desire, so that we can restrain the thing toward which we were being carried away, and not become so overheated that we are led to the snare.

“They have plotted against me; do not abandon me, lest they perhaps be exalted.” You have elsewhere: “Those who press upon me will rejoice if I am shaken” (Ps. XII, 5). Such are these people, because such too is the devil. When he has seduced a person, he rejoices and triumphs over him; he himself is exalted because that person has been humbled.

But why has that person been humbled? Because he was wrongly exalted. And the one who triumphs over him will be humbled. Such are all who rejoice in evil. For a time they seem to glory, grow proud, and lift their necks. Do not let their exaltation delight you [Note: [Col. 1810] Augustine’s manuscripts and several others read “their rejoicing.”]; they have bait in their throats and a hook. There is what delights them, and there is what drags them away.

“Do not abandon me, lest they perhaps be exalted”—that is, lest they triumph over me, lest they rejoice over me.

13. [verse 10.] “The head of their circuit, the labor of their lips, will cover them.” “Me,” he says, “the shade of your wings will cover”; for you have overshadowed me on the day of battle. What will cover them? “The head of their circuit”—that is pride.

What is their “circuit”? It is that they go around and do not stand still; they move in the circle of error, where the journey has no end. For one who travels lengthwise begins somewhere and ends somewhere; one who travels in a circle never ends.

This is the labor of the impious, which is shown more clearly in another psalm: “The impious walk about in a circle” (Ps. XI, 9). But the head of their circuit is pride, because “the beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclus. X, 15).

But how is “the labor of their lips” derived from pride? Every proud person is counterfeit, and every counterfeit person is a liar. People labor to speak a lie, whereas they would speak the truth with complete ease. For the person who invents what he says labors; the person who wishes to speak the truth does not labor, because truth itself speaks without labor.

Therefore he said this to God concerning the human being: “Your shade will protect me; their own lie will cover them.” But their lie itself is the labor of their lips.

“Behold, he travailed with injustice, conceived pain, and gave birth to iniquity” (Ps. VII, 15). For there is labor in every evil work, and every evil work conceived has a lie as its guide. There is truth only in a good work.

And because everyone labors in falsehood, what did Truth cry out? “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28).

This is the voice that cries to those who labor, in another psalm: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. IV, 3).

Hear plainly elsewhere of labor in falsehood: “They taught their tongues to speak falsehood; they labored to act unjustly” (Jer. IX, 5).

“The head of their circuit, the labor of their lips, will cover them.”

14. [verse 11.] “Burning coals will fall upon them on the earth, and you will cast them down.” What does “on the earth” mean? Here, while they are still in this life. Here burning coals will fall upon them, and you will cast them down.

What burning coals are these? We know these coals. Or are these one kind and those another kind of which we are going to speak? I see that these serve for punishment, while those I am about to mention serve for salvation.

For something was said about certain coals when a man sought help against a deceitful tongue: “What will be given to you, or what will be added to you, against a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty one, together with consuming coals” (Ps. CXIX, 3–4). These are the words of God that pierce the heart and destroy its old condition and generate love; and they are the examples of people who had died and came back to life, who had been black and were made radiant.

Coals are darkness; their color indicates this. But when the flame of love has approached them and they have come back to life from the dead, let them hear from the Apostle: “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8).

These are the coals, brothers, whom we observe when we wish to change our life, pierced by God’s arrow, while the evil tongues of people—of the sort about whom he was complaining here—hinder us and wish to seduce us from the way of truth, or rather to lead us into their errors and say to us that, if we profess the faith, we will not fulfill it.

We look at those coals. The man who was drunk yesterday is sober today; the man who was an adulterer yesterday is chaste today; the man who was a robber yesterday is generous today. All these are burning coals.

The examples of the coals approach the wound made by the arrows—for I am not afraid to speak of a wound, since the bride herself cries out: “I am wounded by love” (Song II, 5, according to the Septuagint)—and there the hay is consumed; hence they are also called consuming coals.

The hay is consumed, but the gold is purified. A person changes from death to life and begins himself to be a burning coal. Such a coal was the Apostle, who had previously been a persecutor, blasphemer, and insolent man, black and extinguished; but after he obtained mercy (I Tim. I, 13), he was kindled from heaven. The voice of Christ kindled him; all his blackness perished, and he began, burning with the spirit by which he was kindled, to kindle others.

Are we, then, to understand here as well the burning coals that fall upon these wicked people and cast them down? Certainly we are not prevented from understanding it this way. I see shining forth here a plausible and irreproachable interpretation: I understand those coals to fall upon these people so that they may be cast down.

For upon some they come so that they may be kindled; upon others, so that they may be cast down. The same Coal said: “To some we are the aroma of death unto death; to others, the aroma of life unto life” (II Cor. II, 16).

They see the just burning with the Spirit and glowing with light, and through their envy they fall. This is what it means that “burning coals will come upon them on the earth, and they will be cast down.”

What does “on the earth” mean? They are still here, in this life. Apart from that punishment which is reserved for the impious, these coals cast them down before the eternal fire comes: “Burning coals will fall upon them on the earth, and they will cast them down.”

They will not stand in their miseries. Misery comes upon them, and they cannot endure it. But the just person stands. How does he stand? He says: “We also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 3–5).

But when some pressure or misery falls upon those people, they do not stand; they fall. When such people suffer pressures of this kind, they cannot endure them and fall into evil iniquities, because they are handed over by their own desire to the sinner.

[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence.]

### 15. [verse 12]

“A man of many words shall not be established upon the earth.” A man of many words loves lies. For what pleasure is there for him except speaking? He does not pay attention to what he says, so long as he speaks. [Note: Some manuscripts read this way; the editions read *loquitur*, “he speaks.”] It cannot happen that such a man is established.

What, then, should a servant of God be like, kindled by those coals and himself made into a saving coal? What should he be like? He should prefer listening to speaking, as it is written: “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak” (James 1:19). If possible, he should desire not to be obliged to speak, to say anything, or to teach.

For behold, I say to Your Charity: my brothers, we are speaking to you now in order to teach you something. How much better it would be if we all knew, and no one taught another—so that there would not be one speaking and another listening, but all would be listening to that one to whom it is said, “You will give gladness and joy to my hearing” (Psalm 50:10). Hence John also did not rejoice so much because he preached and spoke, but rejoiced because he listened; for he says: “The friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29).

Therefore, brothers, let me say briefly to Your Charity where each person may test himself: not by refusing to speak, but by requiring the ministry of speech from him, while possessing the joy of silence in his will and the voice of teaching when necessity demands it. When is the voice of teaching necessary? When you encounter an ignorant or uneducated person. If you are always delighted to teach, you always want to have someone ignorant whom you may teach. But if you are benevolent and want everyone to be educated, you do not want always to have people to teach; and the exercise or testing of your teaching will lie not in your will but in necessity.

Let your joy be in hearing God, and let necessity be involved in your speaking. Then you will not be a man of many words, lest you fail to be established. Why do you wish to speak but not to listen? You are always going out and refuse to return within. For the one who teaches you is within; when you teach, you go out, as it were, to those who are outside. From within we hear the truth, and to those who are outside our heart we speak.

When we are said to have in our heart those about whom we are thinking, this is said according to a certain image of them impressed upon us. For if they were altogether within us, they would certainly know what was in our heart, and there would be no need for us to speak to them. But if what you do outwardly delights you, take care lest you swell up outwardly and be unable to return through the narrow way. [Note: The editions read *per angustum*, “through the narrow [way].” The manuscripts read *per angustam*, “through the narrow [way/door],” with *portam* or *viam* understood. The allusion is to Matthew 7:13.] Then your God may be unable to say to you, “Enter into the joy of your Lord,” but may say to you, because what you loved was outside: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matthew 22:13).

For where he shows that it is evil to be sent outward, there he shows that it is good to enter inward. What did he say to the good servant? “Enter into the joy of your Lord.” But to the evil servant: “Cast him into the outer darkness” (ibid. 25:21, 23, 30). Let us therefore love not the outer things more, but the inner things. Let us rejoice in inward things; in outward things, let us have necessity, not will. [Note: This is the reading of the Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts; Erasmus and Lovanius read *voluptatem*, “pleasure.”]

“A man of many words shall not be established upon the earth.”

### 16

“Evil things shall hunt down the unjust man unto destruction.” Evils come, and he does not stand firm; therefore it says, “They shall hunt him down unto destruction.” Many good and many righteous people have suffered evils, and evils have, as it were, found them. For this reason it says “they shall hunt,” because each person wants to hide himself from evil; but when he is found by evil, he has, as it were, become the object of a hunt.

Do only the wicked flee from evils when they are pursued by evils? Was it not also said to the good: “If they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (ibid. 10:23)? Therefore, when the wicked persecuted the good—that is, our martyrs—and captured them, they hunted them, but not unto destruction. Their flesh was pressed, but their soul was crowned; the soul was expelled from the flesh, yet nothing happened to the flesh that would harm it afterward.

Let the flesh be burned, let the flesh be struck, let the flesh be torn apart: was it for that reason taken away from the Creator because it was handed over to the persecutor? Will the one who created it from nothing not restore it better than it was? Therefore, whenever the righteous were captured, the wicked did indeed hunt them, but not unto destruction. But those who will not be established and who are men of many words will be hunted by evils unto destruction. Why? Because they will not stand firm in miseries.

### 17. [verse 13]

“I have known that the Lord will execute judgment for the needy.” This needy person is not a man of many words: whoever is a man of many words wants to abound and does not know how to hunger. Those are needy to whom it is said: “Knock, and it shall be opened to you; seek, and you shall find; ask, and it shall be given to you” (Matthew 7:7). He is the needy one of whom it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (ibid. 5:6).

They groan amid the scandals of the wicked. They pray to their Head that they may be rescued from the evil man, delivered from the malignant man, and rescued from the hands of the unjust. They are the ones whose cause the Lord will not neglect. And if they now suffer afflictions, their glory will appear when their Head appears. For to such people, established here, it is said: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3).

We are therefore poor; our life is hidden. Let us cry out for bread, for there is living bread that came down from heaven (John 6:41); and he who refreshes us on the way will satisfy us in our homeland. For now, so that we may endure, we are refreshed; we must hunger until we are satisfied.

“I have known that the Lord will execute judgment for the needy.” This man was certain that the Lord would execute judgment for the needy and vindicate the cause of the poor. He will show the wicked how he loves his righteous people; he will show the rich how he loves his poor. By “rich” he meant the proud; by “poor,” the humble. By “rich” he meant those who, through abundance, do not seek; by “poor,” those who sigh through desire. The Lord will vindicate their cause.

### 18. [verse 14]

“Yet the righteous shall confess your name.” When you plead their cause and execute judgment for them, they will confess your name. They will attribute nothing to their own merits; they will ascribe everything only to your mercy.

“Yet the righteous shall confess your name.” And because they will confess your name, so that, however righteous they may be, they may claim nothing for themselves and attribute nothing to themselves, what will happen so that they may direct their heart? When they turn toward themselves, they twist their heart; but when they fix their attention upon the Lord, they direct their heart.

And where will pleasure, rest, joy, and blessedness be? In themselves? No, but in the one in whom they are light. “Now you are light in the Lord,” he says (Ephesians 5:8). Therefore see what follows; see where he concludes: “The upright shall dwell with your countenance.”

They fared badly in their own countenance; they will fare well with your countenance. When they loved their own countenance, “in the sweat of their countenance they ate their bread” (Genesis 3:19). Let them return, and when the sweat has been wiped away, their labors ended, and their groaning gone, your face will come to them with abundant sufficiency. They will seek nothing more, because they have nothing better; they will no longer abandon you, nor will they be abandoned by you. [Note: This is the reading of most manuscripts. The editions read: “They will not abandon you, lest they be abandoned by you.” Some manuscripts read: “May they not abandon you, nor be abandoned by you.”]
