For what was said about the Lord after the resurrection? “You will fill me with joy with your countenance” (Psalm 15:11). Without his countenance he would not give us joy. For this we cleanse our countenance, so that we may rejoice in his countenance.

For we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2)—because “the upright shall dwell with your countenance.”

Do we suppose this means with the countenance of the Father, and not with the countenance of the Son? Or with the countenance of the Son, and not with the countenance of the Father? Or is there, in some manner, one countenance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?

Let us see whether the Son himself does not promise us his countenance, by which he will make us joyful. Just now the Lord God inspired the reading of a passage in the Gospel that bears witness to this psalm. For the Lord himself says: “He who hears my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me; and he who loves me shall be loved by my Father, and I shall love him, and I shall show myself to him” (John 14:21).

What kind of reward did he promise, beloved? Did those to whom he promised that he would show himself not see him? Was he not before them? Did not the face of his flesh lie before their eyes? What, then, did he wish to show to those who saw him?

But because the disciples saw him as the Jews crucified him, while God was hidden in that flesh—and human beings could see the man but could not see God, although he was in the man, because “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8)—he gave the form of a man to both the devout and the impious, but reserved the form of God for those who had been cleansed and were devout, so that we might rejoice in him and be well with us eternally in his countenance.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 140

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1

You have heard, brothers, an admonition and petition from the mouth of the Apostle, when his Epistle was just read. For he says: “Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it; praying at the same time for us also, that God may open to us a door of the word, to speak his mystery, so that I may manifest it as I ought to speak” (Colossians 4:2–4).

Deign to reckon these words as mine also. For in the holy Scriptures there are profound mysteries. They are hidden so that they may not become cheap; they are sought so that they may exercise us; they are opened so that they may nourish us. The psalm we have just sung is obscure in many of its statements. When, with the Lord’s help, what has been said begins to be extracted and explained, you will see yourselves hearing what you already knew. But these things have been expressed in many ways so that variety of speech might remove weariness with the truth.

### 2

For what more or what more salutary will you hear and learn, brothers, than this: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind”; and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”? But do not think that these two commandments are small: “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22:37–40).

Whatever is conceived in the mind for our salvation, expressed by the mouth, or drawn out from any page of divine Scripture, has no end other than love.

Yet this love is not just any kind of love. For even people who live wickedly become entangled with one another in the fellowship of a ruined conscience; they are said to love one another, not to wish to part, to be drawn together by their conversations, to long for one another when absent, and to rejoice in one another’s presence. This love is Tartarean: it has birdlime by which to cast one into the depths, not wings by which to lift one into heaven.

What, then, is the love that is separated and distinguished from the other things called loves? The love called the true love of Christians was defined by Paul and enclosed within certain boundaries, although it is infinite in divinity, so that it may be completely distinguished from other forms of love.

“For the end,” he says, “of the commandment is love.” He could have stopped there. In other places, where he was speaking as to people who knew, he said only this much: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Romans 13:10); he did not say what kind of love. He did not say so there because he said it elsewhere. For not everything can or should be said everywhere.

Here, then: “Love is the fullness of the law.” Perhaps you were asking: What love? What kind of love? In another place you hear: “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart.” Now consider whether thieves have love from a pure heart among themselves.

A pure heart in love is present when you love a person according to God, because you must also love yourself in such a way that the rule does not go astray: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” For if you love yourself badly and uselessly, what good counsel do you give your neighbor by loving him in the same way?

How do you love yourself badly? Scripture, which flatters no one, indicates how: it convicts you that you do not love yourself—indeed, it proves that you hate yourself. “He who loves iniquity,” it says, “hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6). If, then, you love iniquity, do you think that you love yourself? You are mistaken. In the same way, if you love your neighbor while leading him toward iniquity, your love will be a snare for the one loved.

Therefore, love from a pure heart is that which is according to God, and from a good conscience, and from an unfeigned faith (1 Timothy 1:5). This love, defined by the Apostle, has two commandments: love of God and love of neighbor. Search for nothing else in the Scriptures; let no one prescribe anything else to you.

Whatever is obscure in Scripture is hidden there in this love; whatever is clear there is open there in this love. If it were nowhere open, it would not nourish you; if it were nowhere hidden, it would not exercise you.

This love cries out from a pure heart—from the heart of the kind of person who is praying in this psalm. And who is that? Let me say it briefly: it is Christ.

### 3

You are about to hear words that are wrongly understood as referring to our Lord Jesus Christ, and someone with little understanding may think that I have rashly said that Christ is the person speaking in this psalm.

For how can this be rightly understood of our Lord Jesus Christ—of that immaculate Lamb, in whom alone no sin was found, who alone could most truly say, “The prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30), that is, no fault, no guilt; who alone paid back what he had not stolen (Psalm 68:5); who alone shed innocent blood, the only Son of God taking flesh—not flesh by which he himself would be diminished, but flesh by which he would increase us?

How, then, can these words rightly be understood of that person: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips, so that you do not incline my heart toward wicked words, to excuse excuses in sins”?

For the meaning is perfectly clear: “Guard, O Lord, my mouth with a kind of door and entrance of your commandment, so that my heart may not turn toward wicked words.” What wicked words? Those by which sins are excused. “Let me not,” he says, “prefer to excuse my sins rather than accuse them.”

These words do not apply to our Lord Jesus Christ. What sins did he commit, which he ought to have confessed rather than defended? These are our words.

Certainly Christ is speaking. If they are our words, how does Christ speak? And where is the love of which I was speaking? Do you not know that love itself made us one in Christ? Love cries out to Christ on our behalf; love cries out from Christ for us.

How does love cry out to Christ on our behalf? “And it shall be that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel 2:32). How does love cry out from Christ for us? “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). “You are,” says the Apostle, “the body of Christ and members” (1 Corinthians 12:27).

Therefore, if he is the head and we are the body, one person speaks. Whether the head speaks or the members speak, it is one Christ who speaks. It belongs properly to the head to speak even in the person of the members.

Observe our ordinary way of speaking. First, consider how the head cannot speak except through our members. Then consider how our head speaks in the person of all the members.

Someone steps on your foot in a narrow place: “You are stepping on me,” says the head. Someone wounds your hand: “You have wounded me,” says the head. No one has touched your head, but the unity of the body’s structure speaks. That tongue, which is in the head, assumes the person of all your members; through the word it acts on behalf of them all.

Let us therefore hear Christ speaking, but let each person recognize his own voice there, as though clinging to Christ’s body. At times he will speak words in which none of us finds his own person, but which pertain to the head alone. Yet he does not separate himself from our words and take refuge in what belongs to him alone, nor does he fail to return from what belongs to him to what belongs to us.

For it was said of him and the Church: “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Hence he himself says in the Gospel concerning this very matter: “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6).

These things are not new; you have always heard them. [Note: The editions read “often”; the manuscripts, “always.”] But they must be recalled on appropriate occasions, first because the Scriptures we expound are so closely interwoven that many things are repeated in many places—and this is useful. For the care of the world has thorns and chokes the seeds; what the world compels us to forget must often be recalled by the Lord.

### 4. [verse 1]

“Lord, I have cried to you; hear me.” We can all say this. I say this: the whole Christ says it; yet it is said especially in the person of the body. For while he was here, bearing flesh, he prayed; and in the person of the body he prayed to the Father. When he prayed, drops of blood fell from his whole body.

Thus it is written in the Gospel: “Jesus prayed with intense prayer, and he sweated blood” (Luke 22:44). What is the outpouring of blood from the whole body except the suffering of the martyrs from the whole Church?

“Lord, I have cried to you; hear me. Attend to the voice of my supplication when I cry to you.” You thought that the business of crying out was already finished when you said, “I have cried to you.” You have cried out; do not yet be secure. If tribulation has ended, the cry has ended. But if the tribulation of the Church and the body of Christ remains until the end of the age, let it not merely say, “I have cried to you; hear me,” but also, “Attend to the voice of my supplication when I cry to you.”

### 5. [verses 2–4]

“Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice.”

Every Christian recognizes that this is ordinarily understood of the head himself. For as the day was already declining toward evening, the Lord gave up his spirit on the cross in order to receive it again; he did not lose it unwillingly.

Yet we too were represented there. For what of him hung upon the wood except what he received from us? And how could God the Father ever abandon and forsake his only Son, who is one God with him? Yet, fixing our weakness upon the cross—where, as the Apostle says, our old man was crucified with him—he cried out with the voice of that old man of ours: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 21:2; Matthew 27:46).

That, then, is the evening sacrifice: the passion of the Lord, the cross of the Lord, the offering of the saving victim, the holocaust acceptable to God. That evening sacrifice made, in the resurrection, a morning offering.

Prayer, therefore, directed purely from a faithful heart rises like incense from a holy altar. Nothing is more delightful than the fragrance of the Lord. [Note: Most manuscripts read *odoris*, “of the fragrance.”] May all who believe smell thus.

### 6

“Our old man,” then, “was crucified with him”—these are the Apostle’s words—“so that,” he says, “the body of sin might be destroyed, and that we might no longer serve sin” (Romans 6:6).

Hence, in the psalm itself, after it had said, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me, far from my salvation,” it immediately adds, “the words of my sins.” Whose sins, if you consider the head? Yet he himself testified on the cross that this was his voice in the psalm; he spoke the very words and pronounced the very verse.

There is no room for human conjecture, no opening for denial by any Christian. What I read in the psalm, I hear from the Lord. In the psalm itself I also recognize what I read in the Gospel: “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked and saw me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Psalm 21:17–19). All these things were fulfilled just as they had been foretold; as we heard, so also we saw (Psalm 47:9).

Therefore, if our Lord Jesus Christ, representing us in the love of his body, although he himself was without sin, said, “The words of my sins”—and he said this in the person of his body—who would dare say among his members that he has no sin, unless he dared to exalt himself in the name of a false righteousness and accuse Christ of falsehood?

Confess, then, O member, what your head pronounced on your behalf. And so that we may confess this, so that we may do this, and not justify ourselves before the sight of the only righteous one who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), he added the voice of his body: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips.”

He did not say “a barrier of restraint,” but “a door.” A door is both opened and closed. Therefore, if it is a door, let it be opened and closed: opened for confession of sin, closed for excuse of sin. In this way it will be a door of restraint, not of ruin.

### 7

For what benefit does this door of restraint bring us? What does Christ pray in the person of the body?

“So that you do not incline,” he says, “my heart toward wicked words.” What does “my heart” mean? The heart of my Church, certainly the heart of my body.

Notice the words in which the rule is fixed for us: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4), although no one had touched him personally. “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,” and so forth. And they said: “When did we see you hungry or thirsty?” And he replied: “When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:35, 37, 40).

These things ought not to be unfamiliar to Christians, especially since rules have been fixed in them for understanding the rest. They will either not be disturbed by them or will quickly be corrected.

Therefore, just as the righteous will say there, “Lord, why did you say, ‘I was hungry, and you gave me food’? When did we see you hungry?” and he will answer, “When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me,” so here also let us speak to Christ within [Note: The editions read *in Christo*, “in Christ”; the particle *in* is absent from some manuscripts.], in our inner person, where he deigns to dwell through faith (Ephesians 3:17).

For he is not absent from us, and we have one to whom we may speak, since he himself says: “Behold, I am with you until the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Let us therefore say to him also, since we have received his voice in this psalm—for no one denies that the words “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” are his voice—let us say accordingly: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips, so that you do not incline my heart toward wicked words, to excuse excuses in sins.”

Why do you pray thus, Lord? What sins of yours are you going to excuse? He answers: “When one of my members prays in this way, I pray in this way,” just as there he answered: “When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me.”

### 8

When, then, your heart has not been inclined, O member of Christ—when your heart has not been inclined “toward wicked words, to excuse excuses in sins, with men who work iniquity,” and you will not “join yourself to their chosen ones”—for this is what follows: “And I shall not join myself to their chosen ones.”

Who are their chosen ones? Those who justify themselves. Who are their chosen ones? Those who seem righteous to themselves and despise others, as that Pharisee in the temple said: “God, I give you thanks that I am not like the rest of men” (Luke 18:11).

Who are their chosen ones? If this man had been a prophet, he would have known what woman approached his feet.

You recognize the voice of another Pharisee who had invited the Lord, when that woman who was a sinner in the city came and approached his feet. She, shameless and brazen in fornication in former times, yet more brazen for salvation, burst into another person’s house. But the one reclining there was not a stranger. It was not an outsider who followed some guest to the banquet; the servant followed her Lord.

She approached his feet because she desired to follow his footsteps; she washed them with her tears and wiped them with her hair. What are the feet of Christ except those by which he traversed the whole world? “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (Isaiah 52:7; Romans 10:15)!

How many received the Lord’s feet, so that by receiving the righteous in the name of a righteous person they might receive the reward of a righteous person, and received a prophet in the name of a prophet so that they might receive a prophet’s reward! “And whoever gives,” he says, “to one of these least ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward” (Matthew 10:41–42).

Whoever welcomed the Lord’s feet with such kindness, what did he expend except the superfluities he had at home? Since hair is, as it were, superfluous, she rightly wiped the Lord’s feet with it. Your superfluities become necessities for you if you have rendered service to the Lord’s feet.

She therefore wished to be healed, conscious of a great wound. But was the wound great and the physician small?

The Pharisees, however, did not want to be touched by the unclean. They avoided every contact with sinners, and whenever they happened to be touched by necessity, they washed themselves. They nearly baptized not only themselves but also their vessels, beds, cups, and dishes every hour, as the Lord recalls in the Gospel (Matthew 23:25).

Since that Pharisee knew this woman—who, if she had approached the feet of that Pharisee, would certainly have been driven away lest his holiness be polluted—he had her in his body, not in his heart. And because he did not have her in his heart, he certainly had her falsely in his body.

Since he would have driven her away, while the Lord did not, he supposed that the Lord did not know what kind of woman she was, and said to himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would know what sort of woman has approached his feet.” He did not say, “He would have driven her away,” but “He would know what sort she was,” as though it necessarily followed that, if he knew, he would drive her away.

From the fact, therefore, that he did not drive her away, he confidently suspected that the Lord did not know her. But the Lord had his eyes upon the woman in such a way that he had his ears upon the Pharisee’s heart.

When he heard the Pharisee’s thought, he proposed the parable that you know:

“Two debtors owed money to a certain moneylender. One owed him five hundred denarii, the other fifty. When they both had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both. Tell me,” he said, “which of them loved him more?”

He answered, already compelled by the truth to pronounce judgment against himself: “I suppose, Lord, the one to whom he forgave more.”

And turning to the woman, he said to Simon: “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you did not give me a kiss, but she has not ceased kissing my feet. You did not give me water for my feet, but she washed my feet with her tears. You did not give me oil, but she anointed me with ointment. Therefore I tell you: her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:36–47).

Why? Because she confessed, because she wept, because her heart was not inclined toward wicked words to excuse excuses in sins; she was not joined to their chosen ones—that is, to those who defend themselves.

### 9

For this same woman would not have lacked a defense of her sins if her heart had been inclined toward wicked words. Do not her equals in depravity, though not her equals in confession—prostitutes, adulteresses, and shameless women—defend their sins every day?

If their sins have remained hidden, they deny them. But if they have been caught and convicted, or have committed them publicly, they defend them. And how easy their defense is, how quick, yet how rash; how habitual and how sacrilegious!

“Oh, if God did not want this, I would not do it! God wanted it; fortune wanted it; fate wanted it.”

She does not say: “I have said, Lord, have mercy on me,” as that sinful woman came to the physician’s feet and said: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Psalm 40:5).

And this defense, my brothers, belongs to what kind of people? Not only to the uneducated, but also to the educated. They sit and calculate the stars; they observe, describe, and conjecture their intervals, courses, revolutions, positions, and movements. [Note: One manuscript reads *siderum intervalla*, “the intervals of the stars.”] They are learned; they seem great. All this learning and greatness is a defense of sin.

“You will be an adulterer because you have Venus in this configuration; you will be a murderer because you have Mars in this configuration.” Mars, then, is the murderer, not you; Venus is the adulteress, not you. Take care lest you be condemned in place of Mars and Venus.

For God, who will judge, knows that it is you who say, “It is not I,” to a judge who knows.

Moreover, that astrologer who sells you stories about the snares of your own life—so that you may not even purchase death for free—for you have bought death from the astrologer at a price, having despised life, which Christ offered freely—if that astrologer should see his wife behaving somewhat too wantonly, or looking improperly at some other men, or repeatedly returning to the window, would he not seize her, beat her, and discipline her in his household?

Let his wife answer him: “If you can, beat Venus, not me.” Would he not reply: “Foolish woman, what belongs to the ruler is one thing, and what is offered to the customer is another”?

Who, then, are their chosen ones? The chosen ones of the wicked, the chosen ones of the impious, with whom one must not join oneself—that is, with whom one must not have fellowship.

Who are they? Those who judge themselves righteous and despise others as sinners, as those Pharisees did; or those who, because their sins are either manifestly detected or publicly committed, defend and assert them so that no blame may be attributed to them. In order that they themselves may not be judged to have done anything evil, they attribute everything either to God, who they say created human beings in this condition, or to the stars, which they say he arranged, or to his neglect of human affairs.

These are the defenses of the chosen ones of the world. But let the member of Christ speak; let the body of Christ speak; let Christ speak in the person of his body:

“Do not incline my heart toward wicked words, to excuse excuses in sins, with men who work iniquity; and I shall not join myself to their chosen ones.”

### 10

You know something that must not be passed over: among the Manichaeans, those who are regarded as holding within themselves a more eminent righteousness, as though occupying the first degree of righteousness, are called the “Elect.”

Those who know this may recognize it; those who did not know it, let them hear. All the saints are indeed God’s elect, and we have this in the Scriptures (Matthew 24:22, 24, 31). But they usurped that name for themselves and applied it to themselves as something especially belonging to them, so that they might now be called “Elect” in a proper sense.

Who are these Elect? If you say to them, “You have sinned,” they immediately bring forward that impious defense, worse and more sacrilegious than the others: “I did not sin; the nation of darkness did.”

What is this nation of darkness? The one that waged war against God.

“And it sins,” they say, “when you sin.”

“It does,” they reply, “because I have been mixed with it.”

The God who mixed you with it—what did he fear? For this is what they say: that the nation of darkness rebelled against God before the world existed; and that God, taking care lest his kingdoms should be devastated by the hostile assault when it arrived, sent here his own members, his own substance, that which he himself is—if it was gold, gold; if light, light; whatever it is, he sent it—and, they say, mixed it with the innermost parts of the nation of darkness, and fashioned the world from it.

“We souls,” they say, “are from those very members of God. But here we are oppressed by the innermost parts of the nation of darkness, and whatever we are said to sin, that nation sins.”

They seem to excuse themselves from sin, but they do not excuse their god from the charge of fear, nor do they excuse the substance of their god from the charge of corruptibility.

For if God is incorruptible, immutable, undefiled, spotless, and impenetrable, what could that nation do to him? Let it make whatever assault it wished: how could it terrify one who was impenetrable, inviolable, undefiled, immutable, and incorruptible?

If their god is such, then he is cruel, because he sent you here without cause, when nothing could harm him. Why did he send you? Behold, the nation of darkness could not harm him, but he himself gravely harmed you, and he himself was your enemy more than that nation was—although that nation too was able to harm you.

You could be oppressed, you could be taken captive, you could be defiled, you could be corrupted. Therefore he too could be harmed. For a fragment and portion, so to speak, of his nature proves the whole mass to be the same. What was sent here is of the same character as what remained there.

This is what they themselves say; they themselves admit that there are two substances: one of that kind and one of this. Their books contain this. And if they deny it, they are read and convicted.

### 11.

What then? To say nothing more at this opening—not to speak of worse things, not to speak of more criminal things—at this very opening in which they introduce the war, observe how they are defeated; and where they say that war was waged against God by the nation of darkness, they themselves are caught in the conflict of their words. For they have nothing to say, nor anywhere to retreat.

But do you wish, O impious and falsely elect one, to defend your sin, so that when you have done something evil you may not appear to have done it yourself? You seek someone onto whom you may cast your sin, and you cast it upon the nation of darkness. But consider God, and see whether you do not cast it back upon him. For if the nation of darkness that you invent could say this to you: “Why do you accuse me? Was I able to do something to your God, or was I not? If I was able, I am stronger than he; if I was not, why did he fear me? If he did not fear me, [Col. 1823] why did he send you here to suffer so much, when you are his member, when you are his substance? If he did not fear me, he acted out of envy; if he did not act out of this fear, he acted out of cruelty.”

How unjust, then, is he, when nothing could harm him, yet he caused his members to be harmed here in this way! Or could he be harmed? Then he is not incorruptible. When you wish, therefore, to defend yourself from your sin, you cannot praise God. You would not be caught in the praise of God unless you were boasting in your own praise. Turn instead to your own condemnation, and you will praise God.

Return to the words of the Psalms that you curse, and say: “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.” I said it; I sinned—not fortune, not fate, not the nation of darkness. If, then, you sinned, see now how the praise of God becomes clear—the praise in which you were constricted when you wished to defend yourself. It is better for you to be constricted by your sins and enlarged in his praise.

Now, having confessed your sin, see how God is praised: because he is just when he punishes you for persevering in sin, and merciful when he frees you after you confess. “Do not incline my heart,” he says, “to evil words, to make excuses for sins”—so that I might say that the nation of darkness did what I did.

### 12.

“With men who work iniquity.” What iniquity? Let us mention one of their infamous iniquities. Hear the public and unspeakable iniquity of the Manichaeans, which they confess. They say that it is more advantageous for a man to be a moneylender than a farmer. You ask the reason, and they give an explanation. See whether that explanation ought not to be called madness.

“For one who lends money at interest,” they say, “does not injure the cross of light” (many do not understand this, but I shall explain it); “whereas one who is a farmer greatly injures the cross of light.” You ask what cross of light they mean. “Those members of God,” they say, “which were captured in that battle were mixed throughout the whole world, and are in trees, herbs, apples, and fruits. He injures the members of God who tears the earth open with a plowshare; he injures the members of God who pulls grass from the ground; he injures the members of God who plucks an apple from a tree.”

To avoid committing these false murders in the field, he commits true murders in lending at interest. He does not offer bread to a beggar. See whether this justice can be a greater iniquity [Note: [Col. 1823] Thus most manuscripts. But the editions have: “this injustice.”]. [Col. 1824] He does not offer bread to a beggar. You ask why. So that the beggar may not receive the life that is in the bread—which they call a member of God, the divine substance—and bind it in the flesh.

What then of you? What? Why do you eat? Do you not have flesh? “But we,” they say, “because we have been enlightened by the faith of Manichaeus, purify through our prayers and psalms—the prayers and psalms of us who are the elect—the life that is in that bread, and send it from there to the treasuries of heaven.”

Such are their elect, that they need not be saved by God but are the saviors of God. And Christ himself, they say, is crucified throughout the whole world. In the Gospel I had received Christ as Savior; but in your books you are the saviors of Christ. You are plainly blasphemers of Christ, and for that reason you will not be saved by Christ.

So the morsel must not be given to the beggar, and the member of God must weep in the morsel while the beggar is destined to die of hunger! False mercy toward a morsel produces true murder of a human being [Note: [Col. 1824] Several manuscripts read: “False mercy toward a morsel produces true murder of a human being.”]. But who are these elect of theirs? “Do not incline my heart to evil words, and I shall not join myself to their elect.”

### 13. [verse 5]

“Let the righteous correct me in mercy and rebuke me.” Observe the sinner confessing [Note: [Col. 1824] Some manuscripts, with the Ambrosian manuscript, read: “the confessor of sinners.” Others: “the confession of sinners.” Still others: “the confession of the sinner.”]: he wishes to be corrected mercifully rather than praised deceitfully [Note: [Col. 1824] The word *rather* is absent in B; we have restored it from Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition. M.].

“Let the righteous correct me in mercy.” If he is righteous, if he is merciful, when he sees me sinning. Certainly certain members of Christ say this about certain members of Christ; they say it within one body. The Lord deigns to speak in the person of the one who corrects, and does not reject the person of the one corrected or to be corrected [Note: [Col. 1824] Thus the better manuscripts. The editions instead have: “or of the one correcting.”]. For all the members are in him, and he says: “Let the righteous correct me.”

What righteous person will correct you? The head corrects all the members. “Let the righteous correct me in mercy and rebuke me.” He will rebuke—but in mercy; he will rebuke—but he does not hate. Indeed, he will rebuke all the more because he does not hate. And why does this man give thanks for it? Because, “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. 9:8).

“Let the righteous correct me”—because he persecutes me? Far from it. Rather, the one who corrects out of hatred needs correction himself. Why, then, does he correct? “In mercy.” “And rebuke me”—in what? In mercy [Note: [Col. 1824] The Ambrosian manuscript and most manuscripts read: “In what mercy?”].

“But the oil of the sinner shall not fatten my head.” What is meant by “The oil of the sinner shall not fatten my head”? My head will not grow through flattery. False praise is flattery; the false praise of a flatterer is the oil of the sinner. Therefore, when people mock someone with false praise, they say of him: “I anointed his head.”

Love, then, to be rebuked by the righteous in mercy; do not love to be praised by the sinner in mockery. Have oil with you, and you will not seek the sinner’s oil. The wise virgins carried oil with them (Matt. 25:4): the wise virgins carried oil with them—that is, their conscience bore witness to them.

Oil is glory: it shines and gleams on the surface. But the glory must be good and true, so that it may be within, in its own vessels. Hear what is in the vessels: “Let a man examine himself, and then he will have glory in himself, and not in another” (Gal. 6:4).

What does “in his own vessels” mean? Hear the Apostle himself: “For our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12).

### 14.

Finally, because you are in the body of Christ and still bear a certain mortality, be righteous toward yourself, and be righteous within yourself [Note: [Col. 1824] The Louvain edition reads: “be there yourself,” etc., against the other editions and the manuscripts]. You are a sinner: take vengeance upon yourself; return to your conscience; exact penalties from yourself; torment yourself. For in this way you offer sacrifice to God.

“For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it,” says the sinner; “you will not delight in burnt offerings.” What then? Does he accept no sacrifice? “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:18–19). [Col. 1825]

Humble your heart, crush your heart, torment your heart; and you yourself will correct it in mercy. For you do not hate yourself when you rage against yourself. You will be righteous in the part that corrects [Note: [Col. 1825] Thus the better manuscripts. The editions have instead: “in the part corrected.”], although you are still a sinner in the part that is being corrected. For insofar as you are displeased with yourself, you are unjust; insofar as what is unjust in you is displeasing to you, you are righteous [Note: [Col. 1825] Thus most manuscripts. The Ambrosian manuscript instead has: “For insofar as you are displeased with yourself, you are righteous; insofar as what is unjust in you is displeasing to you, you are righteous.” Erasmus and the Louvain edition likewise have this, except that these two editions add: “and insofar as what is just in you is displeasing to you, you are unjust”; they then immediately add: “Do you wish to see,” etc.].

Do you wish to see how righteous you are? You are displeased with that in yourself which is displeasing to God. You have now joined yourself to God’s will, and within yourself you hate not what he made, but what he hates. Because you hate in yourself what you did—which he also hates, although he did not do it—you have begun to be severe toward yourself; he will be merciful. He will spare you, because you did not spare yourself.

Therefore, from the moment you have joined yourself to his eyes, and delight in his law, and rebuke in yourself what his law rebukes; from the moment what is displeasing to you in yourself is also displeasing to the eyes of God, see how righteous you are. But insofar as, having fallen, you have done things displeasing to God, and through a certain frailty of human weakness you slip into them, and still bear the weakness of the flesh, and your conscience groans under a certain resistance, in this respect you are unjust and a sinner [Note: [Col. 1825] Erasmus and the Louvain edition here added: “you are righteous, and in this respect”; this is rightly absent from the Ambrosian manuscript and the other manuscripts.].

### 15.

“How,” you will say, “am I righteous in one respect and a sinner in another? What are you saying?” We seem to be speaking contradictions unless apostolic authority comes to our aid. Hear it from the Apostle, lest a bad interpreter accuse me: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man.” There is the righteous person. Is one who delights in the law of God not righteous? From where, then, is he a sinner?

“I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin.” I am still waging war against myself; I have not yet been wholly restored to the image of my Maker. I have begun to be sculpted anew, and in the part by which I am being restored, what is deformed displeases me.

So while I remain this way, what do I hope for? “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:22–25). The grace of God has already begun to sculpt me anew; the grace of God pours in sweetness, so that through the inner man you may already delight in the law of God. The rest will be healed from the place where these things have also been healed. Still groan as one wounded; chastise yourself; be displeasing to yourself.

### 16.

“I do not fight as though beating the air,” he says, “but I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be found rejected” (1 Cor. 9:26–27).

Does one who chastises the body hate the body? If someone chastises a slave, does he hate the slave? If someone beats his son, does he hate his son? And to express the matter more closely, your flesh is like your wife. The Apostle himself says this: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church” (Eph. 5:29).

Certainly the flesh is like a wife, and no one [Col. 1826] hates his own flesh. Yet what does he say elsewhere? “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). It desires against you like your wife. Love it and chastise it until, in one restoration, one harmony comes to be.

When will this happen? Since now you cry out, “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death,” will this body be separated from you, and will you then be secure? What, then, means: “In ourselves we groan, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body” (Rom. 8:23)?

It is therefore restored from mortality to immortality, and it no longer resists, because it is no longer a mortality capable of resistance. Therefore chastise your body. Now discipline what you will later receive; now let it fail, so that then it may be sufficient [Note: [Col. 1826] Thus several manuscripts. Two others have: “now it is sufficient so that it may not fail.” The editions have: “now let it fail, and then it will be sufficient.”].

For it cannot be restored in this life so long as it is borne as mortal. Do not lay it down; do not break it off from yourself; bear it, educate it, chastise it. It will be restored at the end. And because no one has ever hated his own flesh, the flesh too will rise again.

But how? Will I still have to struggle even then? “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53).

### 17.

Therefore, when it is said, “Let him correct me and rebuke me”—whether it is a brother, a neighbor, someone nearby, or you yourself—you must be rebuked and corrected in mercy.

“But the oil of the sinner shall not fatten my head.” But what am I to do, you ask me? I suffer from flatterers; they do not cease their clamor. They praise in me what I do not want praised; they praise in me what I regard as insignificant; they criticize in me what I hold dear—flatterers, deceivers, impostors.

“For example, that great man Gaius Seius” [Note: [Col. 1826] The Louvain edition has: “Caius Cnaeus, great, learned, wise.” But why? Is it because he is a Christian? The words “Is it because he is” are absent from the Ambrosian and Erasmian editions, which have “Caius bronze,” and from the manuscripts, some of which read “Gaius bronze,” others “Gaius Gneus.” The expression is used as a generic name for any person, as above in Psalm 70, sermon 1, no. 14, and in Treatise 7 on John, no. 25. However, Tertullian’s *Apologeticus*, chapter 3, from which this passage appears to have been taken, reads in the editions: “The good man Gaius Seius, except that he is a Christian—or, ‘but bad only because he is a Christian.’”], great, learned, wise—but why a Christian? For he has great learning, great letters [Note: [Col. 1826] The manuscripts omit “and great letters.”], and great wisdom. If he has great wisdom, approve the fact that he is a Christian; if he has great learning, he chose learnedly [Note: [Col. 1826] Thus Erasmus and most manuscripts. The Ambrosian and Louvain editions have: “he read learnedly.”].

Finally, what you criticize is what pleases the one whom you praise. But what then? Let that praise not sweeten you [Note: [Col. 1826] Erasmus has: “induce.”]; it is the oil of the sinner.

But he does not cease speaking. Let it not fatten your head; that is, do not rejoice in such things; that is, do not nod assent, do not consent, do not congratulate yourself because of them. If he brought the oil of flattery, but your head remained sound, it was not inflated or swollen. For if it is inflated and swells, it creates weight and throws you down.

“But the oil of the sinner shall not fatten my head.”

### 18.

“For my prayer also shall still be in their good pleasure.” Wait. “Now they criticize me,” says Christ. In the earliest times of the Christians, Christians were reproached from every side. Still wait; “my prayer also shall be in their good pleasure.” The time will come when [Col. 1827] thousands of people, beating their breasts and saying, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12), will prevail [Note: [Col. 1827] Erasmus and the Louvain edition have “wickedness.” The Ambrosian manuscript and many manuscripts more correctly have “thousands.”].

How many remain now who are ashamed to beat their breasts? Let them, then, reproach us; let us endure it. Let them reproach, hate, accuse, slander: “My prayer also shall be in their good pleasure.” The time will come when my prayer will please them.

For they will raise themselves up as righteous by their own strength, but they will be defeated in the struggle. Because they raised themselves proudly, they will be struck down; they will be dragged along by their sins; they will see that they are unjust. What was spoken through the Prophets will be fulfilled. Fear of judgment will begin; the gaze of the soul will turn toward the consciousness of sins; and that prayer will please them: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

O wordy defense of iniquity! Certainly the peoples already say this, and the thunder of peoples beating their breasts does not cease. Rightly do the clouds thunder, in which God now dwells.

Where is that verbosity, where is that boasting: “I am righteous; I have done no evil”? Certainly, when you have contemplated the standard of righteousness in the holy Scriptures, no matter how much you have progressed, you will find yourself a sinner.

You have progressed: now you worship the one God—excellent. You do not fornicate away from him toward idols, astrologers, diviners, haruspices, augurs, or magicians; for these things are fornication away from the Lord God. You are already, in some measure, among the members of Christ.

Now begin also to see the sins of human society. You do not kill anyone; you do not commit adultery with another man’s wife; by going to another woman you do not wrong your own wife; you do not contaminate yourself with any shameful corruption; you have kept your hands from theft, your tongue from perjury, and your heart from desiring your neighbor’s property. Now you are righteous.

Attend to the rest; do not now become proud. Do you commit no sin with your tongue? Do you not slip into a harsh word? “But what great thing are you saying?” What great thing? “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:22). Now all that pride trembles.

Suppose you no longer do much by which God might be blasphemed through some impiety; you do not rush upon anyone to harm him; you do not do to another what you do not want to suffer yourself. What about the tongue? Who can tame it?

But suppose you have now also curbed it—although who is so great that he accomplishes this in every respect? Suppose you have now curbed it too. What do you do about your thoughts? What do you do about the tumult and crowd of rebellious desires? You do not give them your members. So I believe, and I see it. Yet sometimes thoughts incline and carry you away [Note: [Col. 1827] Thus several manuscripts. Others have: “they are inclined and carry you away.” The editions have: “they are inclined and present themselves.”], often while you are kneeling in prayer.

You prostrate your body, bend your neck, confess your sins, worship God. I see where the body lies; I ask where the mind is flying. I see the limbs lying there; let us see whether the conscience stands, whether it is fixed upon the one it worships—whether it is not often swept away by thoughts, like the surge of the sea, and carried by the storm now in one direction, now in another.

Suppose that you were speaking with me, and suddenly turned away to your servant and dismissed me—not someone from whom you were asking something, but someone with whom you had been speaking as an equal. Would I not [Col. 1828] regard this as an insult done to me?

See what you do to God every day.

What sort of person did I just describe, brothers? The person who worships the one God alone; who confesses Christ; who knows the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one God; who does not fornicate away from him; who does not worship demons; who does not seek help for himself from the devil [Note: [Col. 1828] Several manuscripts have: “who does not seek help for himself except from the Lord.”]; who holds to the Catholic Church; against whose dishonesty no one complains, and under whose oppression no weak neighbor groans; who does not tempt another man’s wife, but is content with his own—or even not with his own, but as apostolic discipline permits and allows, where there is the consent of both (1 Cor. 7:5), or where he has not yet married. Yet even one who is already such is still found in the things I have mentioned.

### 19. [verse 6]

The time has therefore come of which it was said: “My prayer also shall still be in their good pleasure”—whether it is the prayer he taught, or the prayer by which he intercedes for us.

In all these daily sins, then, what hope is there for us unless with humble heart we say in the Lord’s Prayer—which is now in our good pleasure, not in the good pleasure of those who defend our sins, but of those who confess them—“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” and have as advocate with the Father “Jesus Christ the righteous,” so that he himself may be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:1–2)?

Let the proud speak for now; they are defeated by numbers, defeated by the peoples, while the whole earth from the rising of the sun to its setting praises the name of the Lord. What can the few who argue otherwise do? They are judges of the impious.

But what is that to you? See what follows: “Their judges were swallowed up beside the rock.” [Col. 1829] What does “They were swallowed up beside the rock” mean? “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). They were swallowed up beside the rock.

“Beside” means compared with it. Those judges—great, powerful, learned—are called their judges, as though they were judging morals and delivering a verdict. Aristotle said this. Place him beside the rock, and he is swallowed up.

Who is Aristotle? Let him hear, “Christ said it,” and he trembles in the underworld. Pythagoras said this; Plato said this. Place them beside the rock; compare their authority with evangelical authority; compare men puffed up with the Crucified One.

Let us say to them: “You wrote your letters upon the hearts of the proud; he fixed his cross upon the hearts of kings” [Note: [Col. 1828] Three manuscripts have: “upon the foreheads of kings.”].

Finally, he died and rose again; you have died, and I do not wish to ask how you will rise. Therefore: “Their judges were swallowed up beside this rock.” They seem to say something for as long as they are not compared with the rock.

Therefore, if one of them is found to have said what Christ also said, we congratulate him, but we do not follow him. “But he existed before Christ.” If someone speaks the truth, is he earlier than Truth itself?

O man, look to Christ—not to when he came to you, but to when he made you. A sick man too may say: “But I fell into bed before the physician came to me.” Certainly the physician came later because you fell first.

### 20.

Observe, then, the text of the Psalm: “My prayer also shall still be in their good pleasure.” But there will be many who contradict it: “Their judges were swallowed up beside the rock.”

What, then, will happen? “They will hear my words, because they have prevailed.” My words have prevailed over their words. Certain things were spoken by them eloquently, but by me truthfully. It is one thing to praise a talkative man, another to praise a truthful man.

“They will hear my words, because they have prevailed.” How have they prevailed? Which of them was seized at a sacrifice, when those laws prohibited such things, and did not deny it? Which of them was caught worshiping an idol and did not cry out, “I did not do it,” fearing that he might be convicted? Such ministers the devil had [Note: [Col. 1829] Some manuscripts have: “the devil has.”].

But in what way did the words of the Lord prevail? “Behold, I send you like lambs among wolves. Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can cast both body and soul into the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 10:16, 28).

He gave fear, subjected hope, and kindled love. “Do not,” he says, “fear death.” You fear death? I die first. You are afraid that even a hair of yours may perish? I rise first, whole in the flesh.

Rightly you heard his words, because they prevailed. “They spoke,” and were killed; “they fell,” and stood. What came of all the deaths of the martyrs except that the words themselves might prevail, and that, as the earth was watered by the blood of Christ’s witnesses, the harvest of the Church might spring up everywhere?

“They will hear my words,” he says, “because they have prevailed.” How did they prevail? We have already said: when they are proclaimed by those who are not afraid.

Afraid of what? Neither exile, nor losses, nor death, nor the cross. Not death alone, but not even the kind of death that seemed more detestable than anything else. The Lord himself accepted the cross, so that his disciples would not fear death, and would not even dread its form.

Therefore, when these things are spoken by those who are not afraid, they prevail.

### 21. [verse 7]

What, then, did all those deaths of the martyrs accomplish? Hear: “As the fatness of the earth is broken up upon the earth, our bones were scattered [Note: [Col. 1829] The manuscripts generally have: “were dispersed.”] beside the underworld.” Beside the underworld the bones of the martyrs were scattered—that is, the bodies of Christ’s witnesses.

The martyrs were killed, and those who killed them seemed to have prevailed. They prevailed by persecuting, so that the words of Christ might prevail by being preached.

And what became of the deaths of the saints? “As the fatness of the earth is broken up upon the earth, our bones were scattered beside the underworld.”

What does “The fatness of the earth is broken up upon the earth” mean? We know the fatness of the earth: it consists of things regarded as contemptible. Those things that are, as it were, contemptible to human beings fertilize the earth. For it was also said in a certain psalm that the deaths of the saints lay exposed, and there was no one to bury them (Ps. 78:3).

But all those deaths became the fatness of the earth. Just as the earth receives a certain richness from things contemptible and cast off, so, from what the world despised, the earth received richness, so that from it the harvest of the Church might spring forth more abundantly.

You know already, brothers, that the contemptible things of this earth, from which the earth grows fat, I neither wish nor ought to name. Such is a certain nourishment and fatness of the earth; it is contemptible [Col. 1830] to human beings, as though filthy, and it is cast away.

But what did he do here, so that I may now use his own words? “He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to set him with princes, with the princes of his people” (Ps. 112:7–8).

For he was cast down upon the earth; like the fatness of the earth, he was broken up upon the earth. Thus that ulcerated Lazarus lay there, yet he was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:20–22).

“Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 116:15). Just as it is contemptible to the world, so it is precious to the farmer. For the farmer knows its usefulness and abundant nourishment; he knows what he seeks, what he chooses, and from what a fertile crop may arise. But this world despises it.

Do you not know that “God chose the contemptible things of the world, and things that are not, as though they were, to bring to nothing the things that are” (1 Cor. 1:28)?

Peter and Paul were raised from the dungheap, and when they were killed they were despised. Now, with the earth fattened by them and the harvest of the Church rising up, behold what is noble and eminent in the world: the emperor comes to Rome. Where does he hasten? To the emperor’s temple, or to the memorial of the fisherman?

“For as the fatness of the earth is broken up upon the earth, our bones were scattered beside the underworld.”

### 22. [verse 8]

“For my eyes are toward you, Lord; in you I have hoped; do not take away my soul.” For they were tortured [Note: [Col. 1830] Several manuscripts have: “they were bent down.”] in persecutions, and many fell away.

And because he had spoken of captivity under persecution—“As the fatness of the earth is broken up upon the earth, our bones were scattered beside the underworld”—the fact that many had fallen away and many had been endangered comes to mind. As though in the midst of the trials of persecution, the voice of one praying was sent forth:

“For my eyes are toward you, Lord.”

I do not care what those around me threaten: “My eyes are toward you, Lord.” I fix my eye more firmly upon your promises than upon their threats. I know what you suffered for me and what you promised me:

“My eyes are toward you, Lord; in you I have hoped; do not take away my soul.”

### 23. [verse 9]

“Guard me from the snare that they have set for me.” What was the snare? If you consent, I will spare you. The bait of this life has been placed in the snare. If the bird loves this bait, it falls into the snare. But if the bird is such that it says, “You know that I have not desired the day of man” (Jer. 17:16), its eyes will not turn away from God, and he himself will pull its feet out of the trap (Ps. 25:15).

“Guard me from the snare that they have set for me, and from the scandals of those who work iniquity.”

He mentioned two things, which must be distinguished from one another. He said that the persecutors had set the snare, but that the scandals came from those who consented and apostatized; and he wishes to be guarded from both.

From one side the threatenings rage; from the other the consenting fall away. I fear that this person may be the kind of person whom I should fear; that this person may be the kind of person whom I should imitate.

“I will do this to you if you do not consent.” “Guard me from the snare that they have set for me.” Behold, your brother has already consented: “And from the scandals of those who work iniquity.”

### 24. [verse 10]

“Sinners will fall into his nets.” What, then, brothers, does “Sinners will fall into his nets” mean? But not all sinners. Certain sinners—those who are sinners to such a degree that they love this life so much that they prefer it to eternal life—will fall into his snare.

“But what are you saying? Do you think that such people fall into his nets? What, then, of your disciples, O Christ?”

Behold, when persecution was raging, when they all left you alone and each went his own way—you foretold this because you foresaw it. For it was not because you foretold it that you caused it, nor did you deny yourself in any way—behold, those who clung to you failed in your trial and persecution, when your enemies were seeking to crucify you.

And that one bold man who had promised you that he would be with you even unto death heard from the physician what was happening within him as a sick man. For, feverish, he had declared himself healthy [Note: [Col. 1831] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition present the passage thus: “what was happening within him as a sick man; for, feverish, he had declared himself.” M.]. He was touching the vein of the heart.

The trial came; the testing came; the accusation came [Note: [Col. 1831] Some manuscripts of good authority have: “the approach.”]. And when he himself was questioned—not by some great authority, but by the lowest servant, and by a woman, by a slave woman—he succumbed.

He denied three times. After denying once, when it was mentioned again, he denied a second time; after denying twice, when it was mentioned again, he denied a third time.

The Lord had foretold this; he had not commanded it or compelled it. Or if Peter is thought to have acted rightly because the Lord had foretold it, then Judas too acted rightly when he betrayed him, because the Lord had foretold that as well.

Far from it, my brothers. This is the voice of those elect who defend their sins rather than confess them.

Let us look instead at Peter himself. If he committed no sin, why did he weep? Let us ask nothing about Peter except Peter’s tears; we find no more trustworthy witnesses concerning him. “He wept bitterly,” it says (Matt. 26:31–75).

He was not yet capable of passion. “You will follow me afterward” (John 13:36) had been said to him. He was still destined to become firm, strengthened by the Lord’s resurrection.

### 25.

Therefore, the time had not yet come for those bones to be scattered beside the underworld. For observe how many fell away—even those very first ones who clung to his mouth; they too fell away.

Why was this? “I am solitary until I pass over.” For this follows in the Psalm.

Earlier he had said: “Guard me, Lord, from the snare that they have set for me, and from the scandals of those who work iniquity.” From the snare and from the scandals; from those who terrify and from those who fall.

But because in his passion even those first men who were destined to be leaders of the Church and pillars of the earth fell away, what he says in another psalm had not yet taken place: “I established its pillars” (Ps. 75:4).

What does “I am solitary until I pass over” mean? This is the voice spoken in the person of the head: “I am solitary until I pass over.” What does “solitary” mean? In the passion, you alone suffer; you alone are killed by your enemies.

“I am solitary until I pass over.” What does “until I pass over” mean? The Evangelist says: “When the hour had come for Jesus to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13:1). What, then, is “until I pass over” except “from this world to the Father”?

For then I established its pillars—the pillars of the earth—when, through my resurrection, they clearly [Col. 1832] learned that death is not to be feared.

“Until I pass over, then, I am solitary. When I have passed over, I shall be multiplied; many will imitate me, many will suffer for my name. I alone am until I pass over; when I pass over, many will be one in me. I am solitary until I pass over.”

Hear also the mystery of his word. According to the Greek expression, *Pascha* appears to signify passion, for **πάσχειν** (*paschein*) means “to suffer.” But according to the Hebrew language, as those who know have interpreted it, *Pascha* is interpreted as “Passover” or “Passing Over.”

For if you ask learned Greeks, they deny that *Pascha* is Greek. It does sound there like **πάσχειν**, that is, “to suffer,” but it is not ordinarily inflected in that way. For “passion” in Greek is **πάθος** (*pathos*), not *pascha*.

Therefore *Pascha*, as those who know say, and as those who interpreted it for us so that we might read it, is interpreted as “Passover.” Thus, when the Lord’s passion was about to occur, it was as though the Evangelist were speaking through the very word: “When the hour had come,” he says, “for Jesus to pass from this world to the Father.”

Here, then, *Pascha* sounded in this verse: “I am solitary until I pass over.” After *Pascha*, I shall no longer be solitary; after the passing over, I shall no longer be solitary. Many will imitate; many will follow.

And if they will follow afterward, what will happen? “I am solitary until I pass over.”

What does the Lord say in this Psalm: “I am solitary until I pass over”? What does what we have explained mean? If we have understood it, attend to his own words in the Gospel:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”

He said this where he also said: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:24–25, 32).

“Unless a grain of wheat,” he says, “falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”

A great harvest, then, was owed to that grain. But wait: let it die first. For unless the grain falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone.

26. Therefore he was alone before he had been put to death. For this reason Peter, too, did not yet possess such strength: he was going to receive the strength to follow, but he did not have the strength to go before. For Christ’s sake—that is, for the confession of Christ’s name, by which we are Christians—no one died before Christ, lest perhaps this objection occur to you [Note: [Col. 1832] Er., Lug., Ven., and Lov. read *nobis* (“for us”), instead of *vobis* (“to you”). M.]. Many died and are martyrs; many Prophets suffered such things. Yet they did not die for the reason that they foretold Christ, but because they denounced the sins of human beings against them and resisted their iniquities more freely; and they are counted among the martyrs. For they were justly killed—not indeed for the confession of the name of Christ, but for the truth.

So completely did no one die for that very name—that is, for the confession of the name—before that grain fell into the ground, of which the words were spoken in the person of Christ, “I am alone until I pass over,” that even John himself, who had recently been killed, handed over by an unjust king to a dancing girl, was not killed because he had confessed Christ. Certainly he could have been killed for that reason too, and by many people. [Col. 1833] If he was killed by one man for another reason, how much more could he have been killed for Christ’s sake by those very people who killed Christ? For John bore witness to Christ. Those who heard Christ wanted to kill him, yet they did not kill the man who bore witness to him. For if an attack had been made upon John because of Christ, he would not have denied him. (For there were great powers in him, by which he was called the bridegroom’s friend [John 3:29]. Great was the grace in him, great his excellence: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” [Matthew 11:11].)

Therefore the attack was made upon the one who did not possess such strength: the attack was made upon Peter, not upon John. For Peter received those very powers only later; at that time he was weak. The man who did not possess the strength was questioned for Christ’s name; the man who possessed the strength did not suffer persecution for Christ’s sake, lest he go before Christ in the name of Christ. The Jews did not kill the man who bore free witness to Christ, whom the Jews killed; but Herod killed him because he said to him, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (ibid. 14:3–11). His brother had not died without offspring. He died for the law of truth, for equality [Note: [Col. 1833] Two manuscripts read *pro aequitate* (“for equity/justice”).], for righteousness: therefore he was holy, therefore a martyr; yet not for that name by which we are Christians. Why was this so, unless in order that the words “I am alone until I pass over” might be fulfilled?

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 141

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. To the solemnity of the martyrs, just as your devoted celebration demands it, so a sermon is owed by our ministry. But your Charity must remember how much was said yesterday. For although, because of your eagerness for the nourishment of your inner mouth, you were present throughout the whole sermon as though you were newly arrived, we must not therefore forget our common weakness. First, it is necessary to honor excellent words, as it is written: “Excellent words, however, belong to the wisdom of the Lord God.” [Note: [Col. 1833] The words *vox sapientiae* are absent in some manuscripts. Er., Lug., Ven., and Lov. read: “They are of wisdom, they are of the Lord God, which through us,” etc. M.] Through us, as through little vessels, they are served to you; and although the vessels are earthen, the bread is heavenly. The Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may be God’s” (2 Corinthians 4:7). The treasure is also the bread. For if the treasure and the bread were not the same, it would not elsewhere be written of that same treasure: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise, but a foolish man swallows it” (Proverbs 21:20).

Therefore we admonish your Charity to chew again, by turning over and pondering, the things that you store away by hearing, as though in the stomach of memory. This is what the statement means: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise, but a foolish man swallows it.” In brief, he said: The wise person chews again; the foolish person does not. What does this mean plainly and in Latin? The wise person reflects on what he has heard; the foolish person consigns what he has heard to forgetfulness.

For it was not for any other reason [Col. 1834] that, in the Law, those animals that chew the cud were called clean, and those that do not chew the cud unclean (Leviticus 11:2–8); for every creature of God is clean. To God the Maker, a pig is just as clean as a lamb. For he created all things “very good” (Genesis 1:31), and the Apostle says, “Every creature of God is good” (1 Timothy 4:4), and, “To the pure all things are pure” (Titus 1:15). Since, therefore, both are clean in nature, nevertheless by their symbolic meaning the lamb signifies something clean, while the pig signifies something unclean: the lamb signifies the innocence of wisdom that chews the cud; the pig signifies the uncleanness of folly that forgets.

A brief Psalm was delivered for the solemnity; let us see whether it can also be expounded briefly.

2. [Verse 2.] “With my voice I cried to the Lord.” “With my voice I cried to the Lord” would have been sufficient; perhaps *my* was not added without reason. Many cry to the Lord not with their own voice, but with the voice of their body. Therefore let the inner person, in whom Christ has begun to dwell through faith (Ephesians 3:17), cry to the Lord with his own voice—not in the noise of the lips, but in the affection of the heart. It is not the case that where a human being hears, there God hears. Unless you cry with the voice of your lungs, sides, and tongue, a human being does not hear you; your thought is a cry to the Lord.

“With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I pleaded with the Lord.” What he said—“I cried”—he explained when he said, “I pleaded.” For those who blaspheme also cry to the Lord. In the preceding verse he used the word “cry”; in the following verse he explained that cry. It is as though he were asked, “With what kind of cry did you cry to the Lord?” “To the Lord,” he says, “I pleaded”: my cry was my plea—not abuse, not murmuring, not blasphemy.

3. “I will pour out my prayer before him.” What does “before him” mean? In his sight. What does “in his sight” mean? Where he sees. But where does he not see? For we speak as though he saw somewhere, as though he did not see somewhere else. In this assembly of bodily things, human beings see, and animals see; but he sees even where a human being does not see. For no human being sees your thought, but God sees it. Pour out your prayer, therefore, where only he sees—the one who rewards.

For the Lord Jesus Christ commanded you to pray in secret. But if you recognize your inner room and cleanse it, there you ask God [Note: Most manuscripts read “where you ask God.” Some read “where you pray to God.”]. “When you pray,” he says, “do not be like the hypocrites, who stand praying in the streets and alleys so that they may be seen by human beings. But when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matthew 6:5–6).

If human beings are going to repay you, pour out your prayer before human beings; if God is going to repay you, pour out your prayer before him, and shut the door so that the tempter may not enter. The tempter never ceases knocking in order to break in; if he finds it shut, he passes on. Therefore the Apostle says—because it is in our power to shut the door, the door of the heart, not of walls; for the inner room is there too—“Do not give the devil an opportunity” (Ephesians 4:27). For if he has entered and taken possession, notice that you shut carelessly or neglected to shut.

[Col. 1835] 4. What does it mean to shut the door? This door has, as it were, two leaves: desire and fear. Either you desire something earthly, and he enters through that; or you fear something earthly, and he enters through that. Therefore shut the door of fear and desire against the devil; open it to Christ.

How do you open these leaves to Christ? By desiring the kingdom of heaven and fearing the fire of Gehenna. Through worldly desire the devil enters; through the longing for eternal life Christ enters. Through fear of temporal punishments the devil enters; through fear of eternal fire Christ enters.

Behold, the martyrs shut the door against the devil and opened it to Christ. This world promised them many things: they laughed at it and shut the leaf of desire against the devil. This world threatened them with beasts, fires, and crosses: they did not fear, and they shut the leaf of fear against the devil.

Let us see whether they opened them to Christ: “Whoever confesses me before human beings,” he says, “I also will confess before my Father who is in heaven.” They loved, therefore, the kingdom of heaven, where Christ will confess them. How will he confess them? “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). He will confess those placed at his right hand.

Let us see whether they also opened to Christ the leaf of fear that they had shut against the devil. In one and the same passage the Lord urges this: that it be shut against the devil and opened to him. “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul,” he says (Matthew 10:28). He urged that the leaf of fear be slammed in the devil’s face.

What, then, is there to fear? Is the entrance of fear not opened to Christ, though it is shut to the devil? At once he added, as though saying, “You have excluded him; open to me”: “But fear him,” he says, “who has power to kill both soul and body in the fire of Gehenna” (ibid. 10:28).

Now, then, if you have believed and opened to Christ, shut against the devil. Christ is within; there he dwells. Pour out your prayer before him; do not seek to be heard by him from afar. For the Wisdom of God is not far away; it “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1). Therefore, within you [Note: [Col. 1835] The editions read, “Behold, he is within you.” Most manuscripts lack *est* (“is”).], before him, pour out your prayer; there are his ears.

“For neither from the east nor from the west nor from the desert mountains; for God is judge” (Psalm 74:7). Since he is judge, consider what kind of case you are conducting in your heart.

5. “I will pour out my prayer before him; I will announce my tribulation in his sight.” There is repetition both in the two preceding verses and in those that follow: there are two statements, but each is said twice. One is: “With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I pleaded with the Lord.” The other is: “I will pour out my prayer before him; I will announce my tribulation in his sight.”

What is “before him” is “in his sight”; and what is “I will pour out my prayer” is “I will announce my tribulation.” When do you do this? He speaks as one placed in persecution: “When my spirit failed within me.” [Note: [Col. 1835] So most manuscripts read. But the editions read *deficit* (“fails”) both here and in the following passage.]

Why did your spirit [Col. 1836] fail, O martyr placed in tribulation? So that I might not claim my own strength, so that I might know that another works this power in me. “When they hand you over to judges”—thus the Lord instructed those whom he intended to make martyrs—“do not consider what you are to say; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:19–20).

Therefore let your spirit fail, and let the Spirit of God speak. He rightly wished to make them poor in spirit: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid. 5:3). Blessed, therefore, are those poor in their own spirit and rich in the Spirit of God. For every person who follows his own spirit is proud. Let him subject his spirit [Note: [Col. 1836] Am. and most manuscripts read: “Subject your spirit so that it may receive, etc.”], so that he may receive the Spirit of God.

He was ascending to the heights; let him sit down in the valley. If he goes up to the heights, the water flows away from him; if he sits down in the valley, he will be filled by it, and he becomes that belly of which it was said: “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

Therefore, “when my spirit failed within me, I announced my tribulation in your sight,” having been humbled and confessing to you as my spirit failed within me, while I am filled with your Spirit.

6. Perhaps people heard that my spirit had failed within me, despaired of me, and said, “We have seized him; we have overwhelmed him.” “But you knew my paths.” They thought I had been cast down; you saw me standing. Those who persecuted and seized me thought that my feet had become entangled; but their feet were bound, and they fell, while we rose and stood upright (Psalm 19:9).

“For my eyes are always toward the Lord, because he will draw my feet out of the snare” (Psalm 24:15). I persevered in walking: “For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22). They thought I was overwhelmed, but I was walking.

Where was I walking? On the paths they did not see, who thought I had been captured; on the paths of your righteousness, on the paths of your commandments. For you knew my paths; the persecutor did not know them. Otherwise he would not have envied me on them, but would have walked with me on them [Note: [Col. 1836] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read, “if on them,” etc.].

What are these paths, if not those ways of which it is said elsewhere: “The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly will perish” (Psalm 1:6)? He did not say, “He does not know the way of the ungodly”; he knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly will perish. For what he does not know perishes.

In many passages of Scripture we find that God’s knowing means preserving; God’s knowing means guarding; not knowing means condemning. For how will the one who knows all things say at the end, “I do not know you” (Matthew 7:23)? Let them not rejoice and say, “We will not be punished, because the judge does not know us.” They have already been punished if the judge does not know them.

The ways, therefore, that the Lord is said to know are here called “paths,” when he says, “You knew my paths.” Every path is a way, but not every way is a path. Why, then, are those ways called paths, except because they are narrow? The way of the ungodly is broad; the way of the righteous is narrow.

7. What is a way is also ways, just as what is Church is also churches, and what is heaven is also heavens. [Col. 1837] They are spoken of in the plural and in the singular. Because of the unity of the Church, there is one Church: “My dove, my perfect one, is one to her mother” (Song of Songs 6:8). Because of the fraternal congregations in different places, there are many churches: “The churches of Judea,” he says, “which are in Christ, were glorifying God because the man who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once ravaged” (Galatians 1:22–24).

Thus he speaks of churches, and he also speaks of one Church: “Be without offense to Jews and Greeks and the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 10:32). So there are ways and a way, paths and a path.

Why are there paths, and why is there a path? Just as we explained the reason for churches and the Church, so we must explain it here [Note: [Col. 1837] Er., Lug., Ven., and Lov. read *hic* (“here”) instead of *hinc* (“from here”). M.]. They are called God’s paths because there are many commandments.
