And because these many commandments are reduced to one—because “the fullness of the law is love” (Romans 13:10)—these ways, consisting of many commandments, are gathered into one; and it is called one because our way is love.

Let us see whether love is a way. Let us hear the Apostle: “And I will show you a still more excellent way” (1 Corinthians 12:31). “What way do you mean, O Apostle, a still more excellent way?” Hear what I mean: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions to the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (ibid. 13:1–3).

Therefore he called love the more excellent way. This is a great way, brothers, and it possesses a great mystery. Certainly, because it is more excellent, it is also loftier; for what surpasses is elevated. Nothing is higher than the way of love, and only the humble walk upon it.

These paths, therefore, he calls the commandments of love [Note: [Col. 1837] Er. and Lov. add here: “In me is all,” which is absent from the manuscripts.]. “You knew my paths,” he says: you knew that what I suffer for you, I suffer out of love; you knew that love endures all things in me; you knew that even if I hand over my body so that I may burn, I possess that love without which it profits a person nothing.

8. But who knows these human paths, my brothers, except the one to whom it was truly said, “You knew my paths”? For all human deeds are before the eyes of human beings, but the heart with which they are done is uncertain.

And how many ungodly people, measuring themselves by themselves [Note: [Col. 1837] Lug. and the Regius manuscript read *mentientes* (“lying”) instead of *metientes* (“measuring”). M.], say about us that we seek in the Church honors, praises, and temporal advantages? How many say that I speak to you for this reason, so that you may applaud and praise me, and that this is my goal and intention when I speak?

How can I show them that I do not speak with that intention? It remains for me to say, “You knew my paths.” How do they know what even you do not know? How do they know what I scarcely know myself? For I do not judge myself; “the one who judges me is the Lord” (1 Corinthians 4:3–4).

Peter, not knowing what he was presuming about himself, presumed something; and the physician saw something else in his strength. Therefore let us cry piously and purely to the Lord, because we truly cry, “You knew my paths.”

But do you want him to lead you along those paths? Be gentle, be meek; do not be savage [Note: [Col. 1838] So the Regius manuscript reads. In B. the word *esse* (“to be”) is omitted. Er., Lug., Ven., and Lov. read: “not savage, not proud, not with tossed-up, etc.” M.]. Do not be proud; do not have your neck tossed back and raised, like a horse and mule “which have no understanding” (Psalm 32:9). For when you are gentle and meek, the Lord mounts you and leads you along his ways: “He will direct the meek in judgment; he will teach the meek his ways” (Psalm 25:9). Therefore, you knew my paths.

9. “On this way on which I was walking, they hid a snare for me.” This way on which he was walking is Christ. There they hid a snare who persecute in Christ, on account of Christ’s name. There, therefore, they hid a snare for me [Note: [Col. 1838] Er. and Lov. add here: “who there cause me to stumble,” which is absent from Am. and the manuscripts.].

What do they envy in me? What do they persecute in me? That I am a Christian. If, then [Note: [Col. 1838] Thus Er., Lug., Ven., and Lov. In B. *ergo* (“then”) is absent.], they persecute this—that I am a Christian—“On the way on which I was walking, they hid a snare for me.” As far as it lies with them, on the way on which I was walking they themselves hid a snare for me; as far as their desire, their effort, and their intention were concerned, they wanted me to be caught by a snare on that very way.

But the Lord knows the way of the righteous, and you knew my paths. This is what they wanted; but you do not permit them to place a stumbling block in you, because you are my way.

For heretics also want to hide a stumbling block for us in the name of Christ, and they too are deceived. What they think they are placing on the way, they place outside the way, because they themselves are outside the way; they cannot place a snare where they themselves are not.

But this was said according to their desire, intention, and opinion. Elsewhere it is expressly said: “Beside the paths they placed stumbling blocks for me” (Psalm 140:6). What was said here, “on the way,” was said according to their desire and intention; what was said there, “beside the way,” that is, “beside the paths,” was said according to the truth.

In reality they do not place it in the path, nor on the way itself, because Christ is the way (John 14:6); but they do place it beside the paths. Christ does not allow them to place it on the way, lest there be no way by which we may walk; yet he allows them to place it beside the way, so that we may not turn away from the way.

A pagan thinks that he is placing a stumbling block on the way when he says to me, “You worship a crucified God.” He censures Christ’s cross, which he does not understand. He thinks he is placing in Christ what he places beside the way. I will not depart from Christ, and I will not fall from the way into the snare.

Let him mock Christ crucified; let me see Christ’s cross on the foreheads of kings. In what he mocks, there I am saved. Nothing is more arrogant than a sick person who mocks his medicine. If he did not mock it, he too would take it and be healed. That cross is a sign of humility; but in his excessive pride he does not recognize the means by which the swelling of his soul may be healed. But if I recognize it, I walk on the way.

So far am I from being ashamed of the cross that I do not keep Christ’s cross in a hidden place, but carry it on my forehead. We receive many sacraments in different ways: some, as you know, we receive with the mouth; some we receive through the whole body.

Since the forehead is a place of shame, the one who said, “Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, of him I will be ashamed before my Father who is in heaven” (Luke 9:26), placed that very disgrace, in a certain sense—the disgrace at which pagans laugh—in the place of our shame. You hear someone insult an impudent person and say, “He has no forehead.” What does “He has no forehead” mean? He is shameless. Let me not have a bare forehead; let the cross of my Lord cover it.

Therefore, “On the way on which I was walking, they hid a snare for me,” as far as it lies with them [Note: [Col. 1839] Am., Er., and some manuscripts read *nam* (“for”); some manuscripts omit it, while others with Lov. read *non* (“not”).]; for “they placed it beside the way.” But I will be safe if I do not depart from the way. “Do you not know that you are walking in the midst of snares?” says Scripture (Sirach 9:20).

What does “in the midst of snares” mean? On the way of Christ: snares on this side and snares on that side; snares on the right and snares on the left. Snares on the right: worldly prosperity; snares on the left: worldly adversity. Snares on the right: promises; snares on the left: terrors.

Walk in the midst of snares; do not depart from the way. Let neither promise catch you nor terror strike you down [Note: [Col. 1839] Most manuscripts read “let neither promise catch you nor terror strike you down,” using present forms instead of the editions’ perfect forms.].

“On the way on which I was walking, they hid a snare for me.”

10. [Verse 5.] “I looked to the right and saw.” He looked to the right and saw; the one who looks to the left is blinded. What does it mean to look to the right? To the place where those will be who are told, “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom.” For some will be on the left, to whom it will be said, “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34, 41).

While the whole world raged and threatened during the persecutions, while human insults and terrors multiplied everywhere, he despised the present, looked toward the future, and attended to the right, where he would be. He meditated on being there; he directed his attention there, and he saw, and for that reason he endured everything. But those who persecuted him did not see.

Therefore, when he said, “I looked to the right and saw,” he continued, “and there was no one who knew me.” For when you endure everything, who knows what you are attending to—whether you direct the eye to the right or to the left? If, in what you endure, you seek human praise, you have looked to the left; if, in what you endure, you seek God’s promises, you have looked to the right. You have looked to the right: you will see. You have looked to the left: you will be blinded.

But even when you see to the right, there will be no one who recognizes you. For who comforts you except the Lord, to whom you say, “You knew my paths”? “There was no one who knew me.”

11. “Escape has failed me.” He speaks as though surrounded: “Escape has failed me.” Let the persecutors mock [Note: [Col. 1839] Er. and Lov. read “The persecutors mock”; Am. and the manuscripts read “Let the persecutors mock.”]; he is overwhelmed, seized, surrounded, conquered [Note: [Col. 1839] Some manuscripts read “bound” instead of “conquered.”]; escape has failed him.

Escape has failed the one who did not flee. The one who does not flee suffers whatever he can for Christ—that is, he does not flee in spirit. For it is permitted and allowed to flee bodily, as the Lord said: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matthew 10:23).

The one who does not flee in spirit has lost escape. But it matters why he does not flee: whether because he is surrounded, because he is captured, or because he is brave. Escape fails both the captured person and the brave person.

What kind of escape, then, must be avoided? What escape must disappear from us? The kind of which the Lord says in the Gospel, that the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, but the hired man, who is not the shepherd, when he sees the wolf coming, flees. When he sees the robber, why does he flee? Because he does not care for the sheep (John 10:11–13).

Such escape had failed from this man—whether we understand this voice as coming from the person of Christ the Lord himself, who died for all, or from his members, our martyrs, because they too suffered for their brothers. Hear John saying: “As he laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (1 John 3:16).

But when they lay down their lives, Christ lays down his; for when they suffer persecution, he himself cries, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

“Escape has failed me; and there is no one who seeks my soul.” Is there, then, no one who seeks his soul? He sees human beings wishing to rage against his life, wishing to shed his blood; how is there no one who seeks his soul?

This is understood in two ways. Just as the loss of escape is understood in two ways—because escape fails both the captured person and the brave person—so a person’s soul is sought in two ways: either by persecutors or by those who love him.

Thus, when he says, “There is no one who seeks my soul,” he is speaking of those of whom he said [Note: [Col. 1840] Er., Lug., Ven., and Lov. read, “Of those, certainly, who persecute my soul.”], “Certainly they persecute my soul, but they do not seek my soul.” But if they seek my soul, they will find it clinging to you; and if they know how to seek it, they know how to imitate it.

So that you may know that a person’s soul is sought both by persecutors and by those who love him, elsewhere it is said: “Let those who seek my soul be put to shame and disgraced” (Psalm 40:15).

12. [Verse 6.] “I cried to you, Lord; I said, You are my hope.” When I was enduring, when I was in tribulation, I said, “You are my hope.” My hope is here; therefore I endure. But my portion is not here, but in the land of the living. God gives a portion in the land of the living, but not something from himself outside himself. What will he give to one who loves him, except himself?

13. [Verse 7.] “Attend to my prayer, for I have been greatly humbled.” Humbled by persecutors [Note: [Col. 1840] Lov. reads “humbled by sinners,” contrary to the other editions and the manuscripts.], humbled in confession. He humbles himself invisibly, having been humbled visibly by enemies. Therefore he is raised by him both visibly and invisibly.

The martyrs have already been raised invisibly; they will be raised visibly when this corruptible thing puts on incorruption in the resurrection of the dead, when even this very thing against which alone the persecutors could rage is restored (1 Corinthians 15:53).

“Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28). And what perishes? What do they kill? [Col. 1841] Is it even permitted to them that what they kill should perish? It will not perish. Hear the promise of the Lord himself: “Truly I say to you, not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:18). Why, then, are you anxious about the other members, when there will be no loss even of a hair?

14. “Deliver me from those who persecute me.” From whom do you think he is praying to be delivered? From the human beings who were persecuting him? Are those human beings really our enemies? We have other, invisible enemies who persecute in another way. One human being persecutes in order to kill the body; another persecutes in order to ensnare the soul.

And for this reason, through his vessels—because it is said of him, “He works in the sons of unbelief” (Ephesians 2:2)—through his vessels, that is, the human beings in whom he works, he carries out persecution of the body so that the ruin of the heart may take place within. For if the soul stands when the body falls, the snare has been broken, and we have been set free (Psalm 124:7).

Therefore we have other enemies as well, from whom we must entreat God to deliver us, lest they lead us astray, whether we have been broken by worldly troubles or enticed by seductions.

Who are these enemies? Let us see whether they are clearly described by some servant of the Lord, by some perfect soldier who engaged them in battle. Hear the Apostle saying: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood.” Do not turn your hatred against human beings, as though they were your enemies, and think that you are being crushed by their hostility. These human beings whom you fear are flesh and blood: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood.”

He wished to say this while despising the mortality of human beings. And against whom? “Against rulers,” he says, “and authorities and rulers of this world of darkness” (Ephesians 6:12).

You were frightened when you heard “rulers of the world.” If they are rulers of this world, are you going to pass beyond the world, where you will not suffer them? Are you going to pass beyond the world, where you will be delivered from them?

Understand, then, “rulers of the world and of this darkness” not as rulers of heaven and earth, for that entire structure is God’s creation. “World” is said both of heaven and earth and of wicked human beings.

Why are the latter also called the world? Because they love the world. And why are they called darkness? Because they are ungodly. Therefore, since many from their number have already become believers, what does the Apostle say? “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (ibid. 5:8).

Before you became light, then, when you were darkness, consider what ruler you had. Whom do the unrighteous have as their ruler, if not the devil, just as the devout and faithful have Christ as their ruler?

Therefore he called the devil and his angels “rulers of the world,” that is, rulers of those who love the world, rulers of sinners—which is to say, of this darkness. These are our enemies, from whom we must entreat the Lord to deliver us.

15. Hear “world” and “world” plainly distinguished in one passage of Holy Scripture, in the Gospel: the world made by God, and the world ruled by the devil—that is, those who love the world. God made human beings themselves; he did not make those who love the world. For to love the world is sin, and God did not make sin.

Hear, then, as I had begun to say, “world” and “world.” “He was in the world,” it is said. Of what was it said, “He was in the world,” except of the Wisdom of God, which is Christ Jesus? Of this it was said—as I recalled a little earlier—[Col. 1842] “It reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1). For “because of her purity she reaches everywhere, and nothing defiled enters into her” (Wisdom 7:24–25).

Therefore: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.” You have heard of two worlds: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:10).

The world that was made through Jesus is not ruled by those rulers and authorities of darkness; rather, the world that did not know Jesus is ruled by them—that is, those who love the world: sinners, unrighteous people, the proud, and unbelievers.

Why are sinners called the world? Because they love the world; and by loving it they inhabit the world, just as “house” can refer both to a building and to those who inhabit it.

A good house is often a good building; and a house is good because good people dwell in it. “Beware of this house, because it is bad” can be said in two ways. “This house is bad; beware,” perhaps because of its collapse, lest something fall and crush you. It can also be said in another way: “Beware of this bad house, lest you fall into the snare of hunters, lest you, being poor, be oppressed by the rich, lest you suffer some fraud.”

As there are two senses of “house,” so there are two senses of “world.” Why, then, are the righteous not also called the world, since they too are in the world? Because the Apostle says: “Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:3); for “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

The righteous person dwells here in the flesh, but in the heart he is with God. He too is called the world if he hears “Lift up your hearts” without cause; but if there is a reason why he hears it, let him dwell above [Note: [Col. 1842] Er., Lug., Ven., and Lov. read “let your hearts dwell above.” M.].

“For you have died,” he says, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). But those whose life is here—that is, whose desire and love cling here, are crushed here, and are entangled here—are rightly called inhabitants of the world; and those who inhabit the world are rightly called the world, just as those who inhabit a house are rightly called a house.

Therefore there is world and world: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him.” Behold the world made through the Lord; behold the world that did not know the Lord. Praise the work of creation and love the Creator; do not love dwelling in the creation, but dwell in the Creator.

16. “Deliver me from those who persecute me, for they have grown strong against me.” Who said, “They have grown strong against me”? The body of Christ cries out; it is the voice of the Church; the members of Christ cry out: “The number of sinners has greatly increased.” “Because lawlessness will abound, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12).

“Deliver me from those who persecute me, for they have grown strong against me.”

17. [verse 8.] “Bring my soul out of prison, so that it may confess your name.” This prison has been understood in various ways by earlier interpreters. Perhaps it is the very prison that is written in the title, “the cave.” For the title of this psalm reads: “An understanding of David, when he was in the cave: a prayer.” That cave is also the prison. We have proposed two things to be understood; but when we have understood one, it will be both. Merits make a prison. For in one and the same dwelling, it is a house for one person and a prison for another. Those who keep people shut up—even if they keep them in their own house—while those who are kept under closer guard are in prison: are the former also to be said to be in prison? The dwelling is one and the same for both; liberty makes it a house for one, servitude a prison for the other.

Some, then, have thought that this cave and prison is the world, and that the Church prays to be brought out of prison—that is, out of this world, from under the sun, where everything is vanity. For it is said: “All is vanity, and presumption of spirit in every work of man by which he labors under the sun” (Eccles. 1:2–3). Therefore, outside this world God promises that we shall be in some sort of rest; perhaps for this reason we cry out from this place, “Bring my soul out of prison.” Our soul is in Christ through faith and hope, as I said shortly before: “Your life is hidden with Christ in God.” But our body is in this prison, in this world. If he had said, “Bring my body out of prison,” we would readily understand the world as the prison. Nevertheless, perhaps because of certain earthly desires that hold us, against which we struggle and fight—for “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:23)—we rightly say, “Bring my soul out of this world,” that is, out of the labors and pressures of this age. It is not the flesh that you made, but the corruption of the flesh, its pressures, and its temptations that are a prison to me.

18. Others, however, have said that this prison and cave is this body, so that the meaning is, “Bring my soul out of prison.” But this interpretation too falters somewhat. For what great thing is it to say, “Bring my soul out of prison,” that is, “Bring my soul out of the body”? Do not the souls of thieves and criminals leave the body and go to worse punishments than those they endured here? What, then, is the great thing being requested: “Bring my soul out of prison,” when it must leave sooner or later? Perhaps the just man says, “I shall die now; bring my soul out of this bodily prison.” If he is in too great a hurry, he does not have charity. Certainly he ought to desire and long for this, as the Apostle says: “Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ, for that is much better” (Philipp. 1:23–24). But where is charity? Therefore he continues: “To remain in the flesh is necessary for you.”

God therefore brings him out of the body when he wishes. It could also be said that our body is a prison—not because what God made is a prison, but because it is subject to punishment and death. For two things must be considered in our body: God’s creation and the punishment deserved. This whole form, stature, gait, the ordered limbs, the arrangement of the senses—seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching—all this structure and differentiation of the workmanship could have been made only by God, who has worked all things, heavenly and earthly, highest and lowest, visible and invisible.

What, then, is punitive in it? That the flesh is corruptible, fragile, mortal, needy: this will not be present in the reward. It is not that there will be no body, since the body will rise again. But what will not be there? Corruption: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:53). Therefore, if the flesh is a prison to you, it is not your body that is your prison, but the corruption of your body. God made your body good, because he is good; the just one brought in corruption, because he is judge. The former you have from a benefit, the latter from punishment. Perhaps, then, he said, “Bring my soul out of prison,” meaning, “Bring my soul out of corruption.” If we understand it in this way, there is no blasphemy; the interpretation stands.

19. Finally, brothers, as I think, he said, “Bring my soul out of prison,” meaning, “Bring me out of distress.” For to a joyful person even a prison is spacious, while to a sorrowful person a meadow is narrow. He therefore prays to be brought out of distress. Although he possesses spaciousness in hope, in present reality he is confined.

Consider the Apostle’s distresses: “I had no rest in my spirit,” he said, “because I did not find Titus my brother” (2 Cor. 2:13). Elsewhere: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (ibid. 11:29). Since he was both weakened and burned, was he not in punishments and in prison? Yet these punishments, arising from charity, bring forth a crown. Hence he says again: “There remains for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:8).

This is the meaning of “Bring my soul out of prison, so that it may confess your name.” Once it has been brought out of corruption, what will it have to confess? There are no sins there, but praises. Confession, however, is understood in two ways: in our sins and in the praise of God. Confession concerning our sins is well known, and so familiar to all the people that whenever the word “confession” is heard in a reading—whether it is spoken of praise or of sins—fists immediately strike the breast. The word “confession” is therefore familiar in connection with sin; let us seek confession in praise.

Where do we find it? You have it in Scripture: “And you shall say this in confession: The works of the Lord are all very good” (Ecclus. 39:20–21). Here, then, confession is praise. Elsewhere the Lord himself says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth.” What was he confessing? Surely not sins. For Christ to confess was to praise. And hear the praise of the Father: “Because you have hidden these things,” he says, “from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to infants” (Matt. 11:25).

Since, then, after these narrow confines of corruption [Note: [Col. 1844] So the manuscripts. But Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “the narrow confines of corruptions.”] we shall dwell in the house of God, our whole life will be nothing but the praise of God. It has often been explained to you that, when necessity has passed away, all the business of necessity comes to an end, since there will be nothing for us to do there [Note: [Col. 1844] Above, in the exposition of Psalm 83.]. I do not say by day and night, where there is no night; but throughout the whole day, since there is one day, there will be nothing for us to do there except praise the one whom we love, because then we shall also see him. Now we desire the one whom we do not see, and praise him; then, when we see the one whom we love, how shall we praise him? Praise will be without end, because love will be without end.

Since this, then, is what we shall do there, therefore: “Bring my soul out of prison, so that it may confess your name.” For “blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). Now the prison hinders us, because “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15). It is not the body that weighs down the soul—for then also we shall have a body—but the body that is corrupted [Note: [Col. 1844] So Am. and many manuscripts. Lov., together with several manuscripts, reads: “Now the body weighs down my soul; for then also we shall have a body, but a body that is not corrupted.”]. Therefore it is not the body but corruption that makes a prison. “Bring my soul out of prison, so that it may confess your name.”

Now the voice that follows comes from the head, our Lord Jesus Christ. And it is of the same kind as yesterday’s final utterance. Yesterday’s final utterance, if you remember, was this: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140:10). And what is the final utterance here? “The righteous shall await me until you repay me.”

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 142

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. Concerning the psalm that we have sung, I shall say what the Lord grants to your Charity. Yesterday a shorter psalm was being treated, but the amount of time gave us the opportunity to say much even about a few things. Now, since the psalm is longer, we ought not to linger so long over each verse, lest the Lord perhaps not grant us the opportunity to complete the whole.

2. [verse 1.] The title of the psalm is: “For David himself, when his son was persecuting him.” We know from the Books of Kings that this happened: Absalom became an enemy to his father and waged against him not only a civil but also a domestic war. David, however, was not unjustly cast down but piously humbled; he received discipline from the Lord, submitted to the remedy, did not repay iniquity with iniquity, but kept his heart ready to follow the Lord’s will (2 Kings 15–16).

That David was thus praiseworthy. But another David, truly “Strong of Hand”—which is the interpretation of the name David—our Lord Jesus Christ must be recognized by us. For those past events were figures of things to come; and there is no need to commend at length what you have often heard and remember very well. Let us therefore seek in this psalm our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, announcing himself through this prophecy and proclaiming through events long ago enacted what would happen in this age.

He himself proclaimed himself in the Prophets, because he is the Word of God; and they did not say anything of this kind unless they were filled with the Word of God. They therefore announced Christ, filled with Christ; and those who went before him preceded his coming, yet he did not abandon those who preceded him.

Let us recognize, then, how his son also persecuted Christ. For he had sons, concerning whom he said: “The sons of the bridegroom do not fast while the bridegroom is with them; but when the bridegroom has been taken away from them, then they will fast, the sons of the bridegroom” (Matt. 9:15). The sons of the bridegroom are the Apostles; and among them is the persecutor Judas, the devil. Christ, then, is about to proclaim his Passion in this psalm. Let us listen.

3. Again we direct your Charity’s attention to this—not teaching you what you do not know, but reminding you of what you know—that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ is the head of his body; that he is the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), born from a virgin, as though in solitude, just as we heard in the Apocalypse. By “solitude,” I think, is meant that he alone was born in this way.

For this was the woman who gave birth to him who would rule the people with an iron rod (Rev. 12:5–6). This woman is the ancient city of God, of which the psalm says: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God.” This city begins with Abel himself, just as the evil city begins with Cain. This ancient city of God, always enduring the earth and hoping for heaven, is also called Jerusalem and Zion.

Certainly, concerning one born in Zion and the founder of Zion itself, a certain psalm says: “The mother Zion, a human being shall say.” What human being? “And a human being was made in her; and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:3, 5). Thus he himself was made human in Zion; but he was made a humble human being. And that same Most High founded the city in which he was made human.

Therefore that woman was also clothed with the sun—the sun of righteousness itself, whom the ungodly do not recognize and of whom they will say at the end: “Therefore we have gone astray from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. 5:6). There is, then, a certain sun of righteousness that does not rise for the ungodly. But this sun makes it rise upon the good and the evil (Matt. 5:45).

She was therefore clothed with the sun and carried in her womb the male child whom she was to bear. He himself was both founding Zion and being born in Zion; and that woman, the city of God, was protected by the light of the one whose flesh she carried. She rightly had the moon beneath her feet (Rev. 12:1–2), because she trampled underfoot, by her power, the mortality of the flesh that grows and wanes.

The Lord Jesus Christ is therefore both head and body. For he wished also to speak in us, having deigned to die for us; he made us his members. At times, therefore, he speaks from the person of his members; at times from his own person, as the head of us all. He has something to say without us; we can say nothing without him.

The Apostle says: “That I may complete what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ, in my flesh” (Col. 1:24). “That I may complete,” he says, “what is lacking in the afflictions,” not my afflictions, but Christ’s; “in the flesh,” not Christ’s flesh now, but mine. Christ, he says, still suffers affliction—not in his own flesh, in which he ascended into heaven, but in my flesh, which still labors on earth. Christ, he says, suffers affliction in my flesh: “For I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

For unless Christ himself suffered affliction in his members—that is, in his faithful ones—Saul on earth would not have persecuted Christ seated in heaven. Finally, explaining this openly in another place, he says: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (1 Cor. 12:12). He did not say, “So also are Christ and the body” [Note: [Col. 1846] Ambrose and some manuscripts read: “So also are Christ’s; but the body,” and so forth.]; rather, “One body, many members; so also is Christ.”

Christ, therefore, is the whole. And because Christ is the whole, the head cried from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Hold fast to this and impress it firmly upon your memory, as children of ecclesiastical instruction and catholic faith: recognize Christ as head and body, and recognize this same Christ as the Word of God, the only-begotten one equal to the Father. From this see how great is the grace by which you reach God: he himself willed to be one with us, although he is one with the Father.

How is he one with the Father? “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). How is he one with us? The Apostle says: “He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as referring to one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ.” But someone may say: If Christ is the seed of Abraham, are we also? Remember that Christ is the seed of Abraham; and therefore, if we too are the seed of Abraham, then we too are Christ.

Just as one body has many members, so also is Christ. And: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ.” Surely Christ is the seed of Abraham; nor can one contradict the Apostle’s extremely clear words: “And to your seed, which is Christ.” See what he says to us: “But if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Gal. 3:16, 27, 29).

That is why this is a great sacrament: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). The Apostle says: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak in reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32). Christ and the Church: two in one flesh. Relate the two to the difference in majesty. They are indeed two. For we are not the Word; we are not, in the beginning, God with God; we are not the one through whom all things were made (John 1:1, 3). We come to the flesh, and there Christ is both he and we.

Let us not, therefore, be surprised in the Psalms: for many things are said from the person of the head, many from the person of the members, and all this is spoken as though it were one person. Nor should you be surprised that there are two in one voice, since there are two in one flesh.

4. Judas, the son of the bridegroom, persecuting the bridegroom. Did this happen then only, or was it also set forth as an example of things to come? For the Church was going to suffer many false brothers, so that even now and until the end the son might persecute the bridegroom.

“For if an enemy had reproached me, I would certainly have endured it,” he says; “and if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would certainly have hidden myself from him.” Who is the enemy? Who is the one who hates me? The one who says: “Who is Christ? Christ was a human being, and he could not live when he wished to live; and, they say, he died unwillingly, overcome, crucified, killed.”

Enemies say these things. This is an open enemy, Christ says: he hates me and openly declares hostility against me. It is easy either to endure or to avoid such a person. What shall I do with Absalom? What shall I do with Judas? What shall I do with false brothers? What shall I do with evil sons who are nevertheless sons, who do not blaspheme Christ against us but worship Christ with us, and persecute Christ in us?

Concerning these, it is consequently said in the same psalm: “It would have been easy to endure the one who hated me, or to hide myself from him.” For you hide yourself from a pagan by entering the Church. But when you find there also what you fear, where will you seek to hide yourself? Indeed, the very Apostle who groans amid dangers from false brothers says: “Outside were conflicts, inside fears” (2 Cor. 7:5).

“If the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would certainly have hidden myself from him; but you, my like-minded one” (Ps. 54:13). He calls him like-minded, as one in Christ. The Church therefore has what it must endure outside and what it must lament within; yet it should count its enemies as being both outside and within—more easily avoided outside, more difficult to tolerate within.

[Col. 1848] 5. Let our Lord therefore speak; let Christ, the whole Christ with us, speak: “Lord, hear my prayer; receive my petition with your ears.” This is “hear,” namely, “receive with your ears”: the repetition is a confirmation. “Hear me in your truth, in your righteousness.”

Do not understand casually when it says, “in your righteousness.” For this commends grace, lest each one of us think that righteousness is his own. This is the righteousness of God, which God gave you in order that you might possess it. For what does the Apostle say about those who wished to glory in their own righteousness? “I bear them witness,” he says, “that they have a zeal for God.” Speaking of the Jews, he says: “They have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.”

What does “not according to knowledge” mean? What useful knowledge are you commending? Surely not that knowledge which, when it is alone, puffs up, and which, unless accompanied by charity, does not build up (1 Cor. 8:1). Certainly not that knowledge, but knowledge accompanied by charity, the teacher of humility.

See whether this is what he means: “They have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” Let him explain what knowledge he means: “Being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they have not submitted themselves to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:2–3).

Who, then, wish to establish their own righteousness? Those who attribute to themselves what they have done well and to God what they have done badly: utterly perverse people. They will finally become upright when they reverse this very order. A person is perverse because he attributes what is bad to God and what is good to himself; he will be upright when he attributes what he has done badly to himself and what he has done well to God.

For you would not live righteously after being ungodly unless you were made righteous by the one who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5). Therefore he says: “Hear me in your truth and in your righteousness,” not in mine, “so that I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through faith” (Philipp. 3:9). Behold: “In your righteousness hear me.” For when I look at myself, I find nothing of my own except sin.

6. [verse 2.] “And do not enter into judgment with your servant.” Who wish to enter into judgment with him except those who, being ignorant of God’s righteousness, wish to establish their own? What is this: “Why have we fasted, and you did not see; why have we humbled our souls, and you did not know?” (Isa. 58:3)—as though they were saying: “We did what you commanded; why do you not repay what you promised?”

God answers you: “To receive what I promised, I will give it; but to do what would make you worthy to receive it, I gave you the ability” [Note: [Col. 1848] So the manuscripts. The editions read: “I gave you the ability to do it; why you should receive it, I gave you”—except that Ambrose has, “why you should have received it.”].

Finally, the prophet speaks to such proud people: “Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all deserted me, says the Lord” (Jer. 2:29). Why do you wish to enter into judgment with me and enumerate your righteousnesses? Enumerate your righteousnesses; I know your crimes. How shall I approve righteousness where I condemn pride?

Rightly, then, this humble man in the body of Christ, learning from the head that he is meek and humble in heart (Matt. 11:29), says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant.” Let us not litigate; I do not want to have a case with you, so that I might put forward my righteousness and you might expose my iniquity: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant.”

Why this? Why does he fear? “Because no living person will be justified in your sight.” “Every living person”—surely every person living here, living in the flesh, living though destined to die, born as a human being, living from human beings, living as Adam from Adam. Every such person might perhaps be justified before himself, but not before you.

How before himself? He pleases himself and displeases you. But before you no living person will be justified. Do not, then, enter into judgment with me, Lord my God. However upright I may seem to myself, you bring forth your rule from your treasury and fit me to it, and I am found crooked. “Do not enter into judgment with your servant.”

Well said: “with your servant.” It is unworthy of you to enter into judgment with your servant, and not even with your friend—for you would not say, “I speak to you as my friends” (Luke 12:4), unless you yourself had made friends out of servants. You may call me a friend; I confess that I am a servant. I need mercy; I return as a fugitive; I seek peace; I am not worthy to be called your son (ibid. 15:21). “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, because no living person will be justified in your sight.”

“Before death, praise no one” (Ecclus. 11:30): absolutely no living person. What of the rams themselves, what of the Apostles themselves, concerning whose offspring it is said: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28:1)? Paul is one of these, and he says that he is not perfect: “Not that I have already received it,” he says, “or am already perfect” (Philipp. 3:12).

Finally, brothers, so that you may quickly recognize it, they themselves learned to pray what we pray; to them the heavenly Jurist gave the rule of petition. “Pray in this way,” he said. After prefacing certain things, he included this also, so that our rams—the leaders of the sheep and the chief members of the one Shepherd and gatherer of the flock [Note: [Col. 1849] Am. and most manuscripts read “gatherers.”]—might say it. They themselves learned to say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:9, 12).

They did not say: “We give you thanks, because you have forgiven us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”; rather: “Forgive us, as we forgive.” They were already believers, certainly; they were already Apostles. For this Lord’s Prayer is given especially to the faithful. If it referred only to those debts that are forgiven through Baptism, it would be more appropriate for catechumens to pray, “Forgive us our debts.”

Let the Apostles, then, say it; let them say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” And when they are asked, “Why do you say this? What debts of yours?” let them answer: “Because no living person will be justified in your sight.”

7. [verse 3.] “Because the enemy has pursued my soul; he has humbled my life to the earth.” See us; see our head on our behalf: “Because the enemy has pursued my soul.” The devil plainly pursued the soul of Christ, and Judas pursued the soul of his teacher. And now that same devil remains for the persecution of the body of Christ; Judas is succeeded by a Judas.

There is therefore no lack of a subject concerning which the body also may say: “Because the enemy has pursued my soul; he has humbled my life to the earth.” “He has humbled my life,” he says, “to the earth.” Elsewhere it is said: “They bent down my soul” (Ps. 56:7).

For what does whoever persecutes us seek to accomplish, except that, abandoning heavenly hope, we may think earthly thoughts and, yielding to the persecutor, love earthly things? They indeed strive to do this insofar as it lies within their power. But may this not happen to us, to whom it is said: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; think of the things that are above, not of those that are upon the earth. For you have died” (Col. 3:1–3).

“For no living person will be justified before God.” They therefore try, either by openly raging or by secretly laying traps, to bring our life down to the earth. Let us watch against them, so that we may say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philipp. 3:20). “The enemy,” he says, “has humbled my life to the earth.”

8. “They placed me in darkness, like the dead of the age.” You hear this more readily from the head, and you recognize it more readily in the head. For he was made dead on our behalf, but not one of the dead of the age.

Who are the dead of the age? And how was he not one of the dead of the age? The dead of the age are those who died deservedly, receiving the payment of iniquity and carrying death from the propagation of sin—from that utterance in which it is said: “For I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Ps. 50:7).

But he came through a virgin, taking flesh but not the iniquity of the flesh, taking clean flesh that cleanses. Yet the people who thought him a sinner counted him as one of the dead of the age.

But he who said in another psalm, “What I did not seize, then I repaid” (Ps. 68:5), and who said in the Gospel, “The prince of this world is coming”—the ruler of death, the persuader of evil works, the exactor of punishment—“and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30–31). What does “he will find nothing in me” mean? No guilt, nothing for which I ought to die.

“But so that all may know that I do the will of my Father,” he says, “rise, let us go from here.” “In order that I may die,” he says, “I do the will of my Father; but I am not worthy of death. I have done nothing for which I should die, but I do this so that I may die—so that by the death of the innocent those who had reason to die may be freed.”

“They placed me in darkness,” as though in the underworld, as though in the tomb, as though in the Passion itself; “like the dead of the age”—him who says: “I have become like a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. 87:5–6).

What does “free” mean? Why “free”? “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). Therefore he would not release others from bonds unless he himself were free from bonds. He, free, killed death; he bound the bond; he took captivity captive; and they placed him in darkness like the dead of the age.

9. [verse 4.] “And my spirit,” he says, “suffered weariness.” Remember: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38). See one voice [Note: [Col. 1850] So six manuscripts. The editions read, “my voice.” Shortly afterward Am., with some manuscripts, has, “Does it not appear?”].

Does it not clearly appear that there is a transition from the head to the members, and from the members to the head? “My spirit,” he says, “suffered weariness in me.” We recognize: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” But we were also there. For he transformed the body of our humiliation in himself, conforming it to the body of his glory (Philipp. 3:21); and “our old self was crucified with him” (Rom. 6:6).

“My heart was troubled in me.” “In me,” he says, not in others. For they had abandoned me; those who had clung to me had withdrawn; and when they saw me dying, they supposed something else. And they were defeated by the robber who believed at the very moment when they failed (Luke 23:40–42).

10. [verse 5.] From this point he turns to the members. “I remembered the days of old.” Did he remember the days of old, through whom every day was made? But the body speaks; each one who has been justified by his grace, clinging to him in charity and devoted humility, speaks and says: “I remembered the days of old; I meditated on all your works.”

For certainly you made all good things, and nothing would exist that was not established by you. Your creation has become a spectacle for me: I sought the craftsman in his work and the creator in all created things.

Why this? Why, except that he might understand that whatever good there was in himself had been made by him, lest, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish his own, he fail to submit to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10:3)? Thus he would be in accord with that earlier voice: “In your truth and in your righteousness.”

Therefore, in all God’s works and in meditation upon all God’s works, he suggests grace, commends grace, and boasts that he has found grace—the grace by which we have been saved freely. For we have indeed been saved freely. Why do you glory in your own righteousness? Why do you exalt yourself, being ignorant of God’s righteousness? Perhaps you gave something so that you might be saved; but what did you give so that you might be a human being?

Look, then, to the creator of your life, the author of your being, righteousness, and salvation. Meditate upon the works of his hands, because you will also find that the righteousness within you belongs to his hand [Note: [Col. 1851] Several manuscripts read, “belongs to the works of his hands.”].

Hear the Apostle teaching you this: “Not from works,” he says, “so that no one may boast.” Do we not have good works? Certainly we do. But see what follows: “For we are his workmanship,” he says. “We are his workmanship”: perhaps he wished to refer to the nature by which we are human beings, calling this workmanship? Certainly not; he was speaking of works: “Not,” he says, “from works, so that no one may boast.” But let us not conjecture; let him continue: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. 2:9–10).

Do not, then, think that you accomplish anything except insofar as you are evil. Turn yourself away from your own work to the work of the one who made you. He himself forms [Note: [Col. 1851] Erasmus, Lugdunensis, and Venetus read, “let him form.”]; and what he had formed and you destroyed, let him reform. For that you exist, he has worked; that you are good, if you are good, he works.

“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” If we work out our own salvation, why with fear, why with trembling, since what we work out is in our own power? Hear why with fear and trembling: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philipp. 2:12–13).

Therefore, with fear and trembling, so that it may please our craftsman to work in the valley. For he works as one in the lowly, he who judges among the nations and fills up the ruins. “I meditated on the works of your hands.” I saw, then, and examined your works, because nothing good can exist in us unless it is made by you, who made us.

[Col. 1852] 11. [verse 6.] And what did I do when I saw that every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration (James 1:17)? When I saw this, I turned away from the evil work that I had done in myself and stretched out my hands to you.

“I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is like land without water for you.” “Rain upon me,” he says, “so that I may produce good fruit.” For “the Lord will give sweetness, and our land will give its fruit” (Ps. 84:13).

“I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is like land without water”—not for me, but for you. I can thirst for you; I cannot irrigate myself. “My soul is like land without water for you,” because “my soul thirsted for the living God” (Ps. 41:3). When shall I come, except when he comes? “My soul thirsted for the living God,” because “my soul is like land without water for you.”

The sea is abundant, it overflows, it is plentiful, it surges—but it is bitter. The water was separated, and dry land appeared (Gen. 1:9): my soul. Irrigate it, because it is like land without water for you.

12. [verse 7.] “Hasten to hear me, Lord.” For what delay is possible when I thirst in this way, except one that intensifies my thirst? You delayed the rain so that, when I drew it in, I might drink it and not reject what you poured into me. If this is why you delayed, give now, because my soul is like land without water for you.

“Hasten to hear me, Lord; my spirit has failed.” May your spirit fill me, because my spirit has failed. This is the reason for you to hear quickly: my spirit has failed. I have now become poor in spirit; make me blessed in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:3).

For the one in whom his own spirit lives is proud; he is lifted up by his spirit against God. Let what is written elsewhere happen in him: “You will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust” (Ps. 103:29), so that, confessing, they may say: “Remember that we are dust” (Ps. 102:14).

When they have said, “Remember that we are dust,” let them then say: “My soul is like land without water for you.” For what is so much “land without water” as dust? “But hasten to hear me, Lord”: rain upon me, strengthen me, so that I may not be dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth (Ps. 1:4).

“Hasten to hear me, Lord; my spirit has failed.” Let my poverty not be delayed. You took away my spirit so that I might fail, return to my dust, and say to you: “My soul is like land without water for you.” Do also what follows in that psalm: “You will send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:30).

If, therefore, anyone is a new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away. In his spirit the old things have passed away; in your spirit new things have been made (2 Cor. 5:17).

13. Do not turn your face away from me. You have turned it away from the proud. For at one time I abounded, and in my abundance I was lifted up: for I once said in my abundance, “I shall never be shaken.” I said, “I shall not be shaken,” in my abundance, not knowing your righteousness and establishing my own; but you, Lord, in your goodwill, granted strength to my beauty. I said in my abundance, “I shall not be shaken”; yet whatever abundance I had came from you. [Col. 1853] And to prove that this had come to me from you, you turned your face away from me, and I became troubled (Ps. 29:7–8).

After this trouble into which I fell because you turned your face away; after the weariness of my spirit; after my heart was troubled within me because you turned your face away—now I have become like earth without water before you: “Do not turn your face away.” You turned it away from the proud; restore it to the humble. “Do not turn your face away from me”; for if you turn it away, I shall be like those who descend into the pit. What does “those who descend into the pit” mean? “When the sinner has come into the depths of evil, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). Those descend into the pit who even lose confession, contrary to what is said: “Let not the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. 68:16).

Scripture often calls this depth a pit; when the sinner comes into this depth, he despises. What does “he despises” mean? He no longer gives any thought to providence; or, if he does give it thought, he does not think that he belongs to it. He sets before himself license to sin, with the reins of wickedness cast loose and without hope of pardon. He does not say, “I shall return to God, so that he may return to me”; nor does he hear, “Turn to me, and I shall return to you” (Mal. 3:7), because, having come into the depths of evil, he despises. “For from the dead,” he says, “confession perishes, as though he did not exist” (Sir. 17:26). Therefore, do not turn your face away from me, lest I become like those who descend into the pit.

14. [Verse 8.] “Make me hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you.” Behold, I am in the night; but I have hoped in you until the iniquity of the night passes away (Ps. 56:2). “For,” as Peter says, “we have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Pet. 1:19).

He therefore calls “morning” the time after the end of the world, when we shall see what we believe in this world. “In the morning you shall hear my voice; in the morning I shall stand before you and contemplate” (Ps. 5:4–5). “Make me hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you.” For if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience (Rom. 8:25). The night demands patience; the day will grant joy. “Make me hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you.”

15. But what are we to do here until morning comes? For it is not enough to hope for morning. [Note: [Col. 1853] The word “morning” is absent from most manuscripts.] Something must be done. Why must something be done? Because he says in another psalm, “I sought God in the day of my tribulation”—as though during the time of my night I sought God. How did you seek him? “With my hands through the night before him, and I was not deceived” (Ps. 76:3).

God must be sought with the hands in the night. What does “with the hands” mean? By good works. “Before him”: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6:2, 4).

Since, then, we must hope for morning in this way, endure this night in this way, and persevere in this patience until the day dawns, what must be done here in the meantime? Perhaps you are going to accomplish something by yourself, so as to deserve to be brought to morning? “Make known to me, Lord, the way in which I should walk.” [Col. 1854]

Therefore he lights the prophetic lamp; therefore he sent the Lord himself, as though in a shell of flesh, who also said, “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21:16). Walk toward prophecy; walk toward the lamp of things foretold; walk toward the words of God. You do not yet see “the Word in the beginning, God with God” (John 1:1); walk toward the form of a servant, and you will be led to the form of the Lord.

“Make known to me, Lord, the way in which I should walk, for I have lifted up my soul to you.” I have lifted it up to you, not against you. “With you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:10). I have lifted up my soul to you; I have brought it like a vessel to the fountain. Fill me, therefore, since I have lifted up my soul to you.

16. [Verse 9.] “Deliver me from my enemies, Lord, for I have fled to you for refuge.” I once fled from you; now I have fled to you for refuge. Adam fled from the face of God and hid himself among the trees of paradise (Gen. 3:8), so that it might be said of him in the Book of Job: “Like a slave fleeing from his master and seeking the shade” (Job 7:2, LXX). He fled from the face of his master and sought the shade; for he fled into the shade among the trees of paradise. Woe if he remains in the shade, lest it afterward be said, “All things passed away like a shadow” (Wis. 5:9).

“Deliver me from my enemies.” Here I am not thinking of human enemies: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood.” But against whom? “Against rulers and authorities, against the powers of this world.” Of what world? Not of heaven and earth; for they do not rule what they did not make. “Rulers of the world”—but of what world? “Of this darkness.” What darkness? Certainly, of the wicked. “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

The rulers of this world of darkness are rulers of the wicked; against them you have your struggle. It is a great battle for you to conquer an enemy whom you do not see. “Against the rulers of this world of darkness”—that is, against the devil and his angels (ibid. 6:12): not the rulers of that world of which it is said, “The world was made through him,” but of that world of which it is said, “The world did not know him” (John 1:10).

“Deliver me from my enemies, Lord, for I have fled to you for refuge.” “From my enemies”—not Judas, but the one who filled Judas. I endure the one who is seen; I fight against the one who is unseen. For Judas received the morsel, and Satan entered into him (ibid. 13:27), so that this David might suffer persecution from his own son. How many Judases Satan fills—those who receive the morsel to their own judgment! “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29).

What is given is not evil, but what is good is given to the evil person for judgment. What is good cannot benefit one who receives it badly. Therefore: “Deliver me from my enemies, for I have fled to you for refuge.” [Note: [Col. 1854] Here the editions add: “Therefore, since I have fled to you for refuge, or where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there,” etc.; this is superfluous and is absent in some witnesses. It is found in the manuscripts.]

Where could I flee? “Where shall I go from your spirit? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.” What, then, remains? “If I take my wings like a dove and fly to the farthest parts of the sea”—that is, if in hope I dwell at the end of the world—“even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall bring me through” (Ps. 138:7–10). “Deliver me from my enemies, for I have fled to you for refuge, Lord.”

17. [Verses 10–12.] “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God.” O confession! O prescription! “For you are,” he says, “my God.” Shall I run to another to be restored, if I was made by another? You are my whole possession, because you are my God.

Shall I seek the Father for the sake of an inheritance? You are my God—not only the giver of the inheritance, but the inheritance itself: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15:5). Shall I seek the Lord for redemption? You are my God. Shall I seek a patron for deliverance? You are my God. Finally, though created, do I desire to be recreated? You are my God, my Creator, who created me through your Word and recreated me through the Word.

Yet you created me through the Word who remains God with you; you recreated me through the Word made flesh for us. Teach me, therefore, to do your will, for you are my God. If you do not teach me, I shall do my own will, and my God will abandon me. Teach me to do your will, for you are my God. Teach me: you are my God, and I shall not be my own teacher.

See how grace is commended. Hold fast to this; drink it in; let no one shake it from your heart. Do not have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; lest, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish your own [Note: [Col. 1855] The editions read “to establish the law.” The word “law” is absent from Amerbach and the manuscripts.], you fail to be subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:2–3). You recognize, surely, the words of the Apostle. Say, then: “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God.”

18. “Your good Spirit, not my evil spirit, shall lead me into a straight land.” For my evil spirit led me into a crooked land. [Note: [Col. 1855] Amerbach and several manuscripts read “will lead.”] And what did I deserve? What good works of mine, counted without your help, could there be by which I might obtain and deserve to be led by your Spirit into a straight land? What works of mine, or what merits of mine?

“For your name’s sake, Lord, you will give me life.” Consider, then, as far as you can, how greatly he commends grace, by which you have been saved freely. “For your name’s sake, Lord, you will give me life.” “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 112:1). “For your name’s sake, Lord, you will give me life”: in your righteousness, not in mine—not because I deserved it, but because you have mercy.

For if I were to display my merit, I would deserve nothing from you except punishment. You tore away my merits and grafted in your gifts. “For your name’s sake, Lord, you will give me life; in your righteousness you will bring my soul out of tribulation; and in your mercy you will destroy my enemies. And you will destroy all those who afflict my soul, for I am your servant.”

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 143

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. [Verse 1.] The title of this psalm is short in the number of its words, but weighty in the burden of its mysteries: “David himself, against Goliath.” Your Charity recalls with me from the Holy Scriptures the battle that took place in the time of our fathers. When foreigners were fighting against the people of God, one challenged one: Goliath challenged David. In that contest the will of God was demonstrated by the victory of either side.

But why do we concern ourselves with the victory, when we see who challenged and who was challenged? Impiety challenged piety; pride challenged humility; finally, the devil challenged Christ. Why are you surprised that the devil was defeated? One was large in bodily stature; the other was small in stature but great in faith.

Holy David took up military weapons to advance against Goliath. Because of his age and his small bodily stature, as we have said, he could not carry those weapons. He cast aside what weighed him down, not what helped him; he took five stones from the stream and placed them in a shepherd’s pouch. Armed with these bodily, but spiritually in the name of God, he advanced and conquered (1 Sam. 17).

This was indeed that David; but let us investigate the mysteries. We had proposed that this title was short in the number of its words, but weighty in the burden of its mysteries. Let that apostolic statement come to mind: “All these things happened to them symbolically” (1 Cor. 10:11), lest we seem rashly to seek something hidden where everything might simply be said without the depth of mystery.

We therefore have an authority that makes us attentive in seeking, watchful in investigating, devoted in hearing, faithful in believing, and diligent in doing. Christ is in David; but, as you who are educated in his school customarily understand, Christ is the head and the body. Therefore do not hear something spoken in the person of Christ as though it did not concern you, since you are members of Christ. With this laid down as a foundation, see what follows.

2. You know that the first people were burdened with many visible and bodily sacraments: circumcision, that rather laborious priesthood, and the temple full of figures, with its many kinds of burnt offerings and sacrifices.

Our David set these aside as weapons that pressed down rather than helped. For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly have come from the Law. Why, then, the Law? The text continues: “But Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 3:21–22).

Finally, what did this David—that is, Christ the head and the body—do at the time of the revelation of the New Testament, at the time when God’s grace was being disclosed and commended? He set aside the weapons and took up five stones. As we said, he set aside the weapons that weighed down; therefore he set aside the sacraments of the Law, those sacraments of the Law that were not imposed upon the Gentiles and that we do not observe.

For you remember how many things we read in the Old Law without observing them; nevertheless, we understand that they were set forth and prescribed for some symbolic purpose—not so that we reject God’s Law, but so that, once the promise has been fulfilled, we do not celebrate the sacraments that promised it. What they promised has come. The grace of the New Testament was veiled in the Law; it is revealed in the Gospel. We have removed the veil and recognized what was veiled; we have recognized it in the grace [Note: [Col. 1856] Erasmus and Louvain add: “in the grace, the grace of our Lord,” etc. “the grace” is absent from Amerbach and the manuscripts.] of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 1857] our head and Savior, who was crucified for us; and when he was crucified, the veil of the temple was also torn (Matt. 27:51).

Finally, he set aside the weapons, as burdens of the sacraments of the Old Law, and took up the Law itself. For the five stones signify the five books of Moses. He therefore took those five stones from the stream. You know what the stream is. Mortal time flows and runs past, and whatever comes into the world passes away.

The stones were therefore in the stream, as in that first people; there they were useless, idle, of no benefit; they passed over the streams. [Note: [Col. 1857] Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read: “they passed along like a stream.” Perhaps the reading should be: “the stream passed over the stones,” that is, over the stones.]

What did David do so that the Law itself might be useful? He received grace. For the Law cannot be fulfilled without grace: “The fullness of the Law is love” (Rom. 13:10). And where does this love come from? See whether it is not from grace. “The love of God,” he says, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (ibid. 5:5).

Since, then, grace caused the Law to be fulfilled, and grace is symbolized by milk—for this is what is freely given in the flesh, where the mother does not seek to receive but strives to give; this the mother gives freely, and she is distressed if there is no one to receive it—how else did David show that the Law cannot operate without grace except by wishing to join those five stones, which signified the Law in its five books, to grace, and placing them in the shepherd’s pouch in which he was accustomed to milk?

[Note: [Col. 1857] Louvain reads “in which.” The preposition “in” is absent from the other books.]

Armed with these—armed, certainly, with grace, and therefore relying not on himself but on his Lord—he advanced against proud Goliath, who boasted and trusted in himself. He took one stone, threw it, struck the enemy in the forehead, and he fell from that part of the body where he did not bear the sign of Christ.

You may also observe this: he placed five stones but sent one. Five books were read, but unity conquered. For, as we recalled a little earlier, “the fullness of the Law is love”; and the Apostle says, “Bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2–3).

Then, after striking and bringing him down, he took away his sword and cut off his head with it. This also our David did: he cast down the devil from his own people. But when his great ones, whom he held in his power and with whom he slaughtered the other souls, come to believe, they turn their tongues against the devil; and thus Goliath’s head is cut off with his own sword.

We have treated the mystery of the title as briefly as the time allowed. Let us see what the psalm itself contains.

3. “Blessed is the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war.” This is our voice, if we are the body of Christ. Let us bless the Lord our God, who teaches our hands for battle and our fingers for war.

The statement appears to be a repetition: “my hands for battle”—that is, “my fingers for war.” Is there some difference between hands and fingers? Hands certainly operate through the fingers; therefore we do not unreasonably understand “fingers” as standing for “hands.” Nevertheless, in the fingers we recognize a division of operation, while still recognizing the root of unity. [Note: [Col. 1857] Perhaps the reading should be: “and in the hand, the root of unity.”]

See that grace. The Apostle says: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings in one Spirit, to another kinds of tongues, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one his own as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:8).

To one this, to another that: these are divisions of operation. “One and the same Spirit works all these things”: this is the root of unity. With these fingers, then, the body of Christ fights as it advances into war and battle.

4. It would perhaps be too long to recount the kinds of battles and wars; it is easier to wage them than to explain them. We have one battle that the Apostle mentions: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood”—that is, against human beings from whom you seem to suffer troubles. You do not fight against them, but against “rulers and authorities and the powers of the world.”

And lest you understand “world” as heaven and earth, he shows what he means: “of this darkness,” he says (Eph. 6:12). That is, not of the world that was made through him, because “the world was made through him,” but of the world that did not know him, because “the world did not know him” (John 1:10).

These darknesses are not a matter of nature, but of will. The soul does not shine by itself, for it humbly and truthfully sings: “You will illumine my lamp, Lord; my God, illumine my darkness” (Ps. 17:29); and, “With you,” he says, “is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10)—not in our light, but in your light.

Our eyes, too, are called lights; yet if external light is absent, even healthy and open eyes will remain in darkness. Therefore we wage war against the rulers of this darkness—rulers, that is, of unbelievers: the devil and his angels, rulers of his sword, with which the devil fights against the faithful.

But just as, when Goliath has been struck down, his sword is taken up so that Goliath’s own head may be cut off with his sword, so when the unbelievers themselves come to believe, it is said to them: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). You fought from Goliath’s hand; now, in Christ’s hand, lift up Goliath’s head.

5. This is one battle. There is another, which each person wages within himself. The kind of battle was just read from the Apostle’s Letter: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish.” This too is a serious battle, and, what is more troublesome, an inward one.

If someone is victorious in this battle, he will immediately overcome the enemies whom he does not see. For the devil and his angels tempt nothing except what is carnal in you and rules over you. [Note: [Col. 1858] So the manuscripts; the editions read “rules carnally.”] How do we conquer those enemies whom we do not see, unless we feel the carnal movements within us? We struggle with these and strike them down. [Note: [Col. 1858] So several manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain read: “With these we struggle; by them we are struck, and we strike them.”]

In the love of money, avarice rules. When avarice rules you, the devil places before you externally a profit involving fraud. Often you do not reach profit unless you commit fraud. He therefore places before your avarice—which you have not overcome within, which you have not subdued, which you have not subjected to yourself—fraud and profit as work and reward, like an evil trainer placing them before his own athlete: “Do it, and take it.”

But if you trample avarice down, if it does not rule you inwardly, and you conquer it by recognizing it—for you do not perceive the devil lying in wait [Note: [Col. 1859] The manuscripts of better authority read “which you conquer by feeling it.” Amerbach reads “which, if you conquer it by feeling it, then the devil,” etc.; Erasmus and Louvain read “which, if you conquer it by feeling it, then you will conquer the devil,” etc.]—if, therefore, you have subdued avarice, you recognize another who places work and reward before you. What did the former propose? Fraud and profit. What does the latter propose? Innocence and a crown. “Do it, and take it,” says one; and the other says the same.

Now you are superior within, if you have not been conquered by avarice but have conquered avarice. You observe the one and conquer the other. You distinguish between them and say: “Here I see work and reward; there, bait and a snare.”

For you do not say anything within yourself that does not pertain to you. Indeed, through sin you have been divided against yourself. You bear the offspring of desire and the propagation of death. You have within yourself something against which to fight; you have within yourself something to conquer.

But you have someone to call upon, who helps you as you fight and crowns you when you conquer—the one who made you when you did not exist.

6. “How,” you ask, “shall I conquer?” Behold, the Apostle himself sets before you a most difficult battle and shows how laborious, or perhaps impossible, it would be if I did not understand it. “The flesh,” he says, “desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish.”

How do you command me to conquer, when he says, “so that you do not do the things you wish”? Do you ask how? Consider the grace of the shepherd’s pouch; place the stone from the stream in the milk-receptacle.

Behold, I too tell you—or rather, the Truth itself tells you: plainly, you do not do what you wish, while the flesh fights against your spirit. If you rely on yourself for this battle, you must be warned lest you have heard in vain, “Rejoice in God our helper” (Ps. 80:2). For if you could accomplish everything by yourself, a helper would not be necessary.

Again, if you yourself accomplished nothing by your own will, he would not be called a helper; for a helper assists one who is doing something. Finally, after saying, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish,” and setting you before yourself as though you were failing within yourself, he immediately sent you to the helper: “But if you are led by the Spirit, you are no longer under the Law.”

For whoever is under the Law does not fulfill the Law, but is burdened by the Law, just as that David was under the weapons. Therefore, if you are led by the Spirit, see who will help you fulfill what you wish: your helper, your protector, your hope, who teaches your hands for battle and your fingers for war.
