“For the works of the flesh,” he says, “are manifest: fornication, impurity, idolatry, luxury, sorcery, quarrels, enmities, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you, that those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:17–21).

He does not say those who struggle against such things, but those who do such things. When you struggle, one work is involved; when you conquer, another; when you have peace and rest, another.

As I demonstrate these things briefly by examples, pay attention. Some profit is suggested; it pleases you. It involves fraud, but the profit is great. It pleases you, but you do not consent. Observe the battle: you are still being persuaded, still being pressed, still deliberating. Therefore the one who fights is in danger.

We have seen the battle; let us see the rest. He despised justice in order to commit fraud: he was defeated. He despised profit in order to serve justice: he conquered. In these three cases, I grieve for the defeated, I fear for the one who is fighting, and I rejoice with the victor.

But even the one who conquered—did he act within himself so completely that money no longer tempted him at all, or aroused no pleasure in him, however conquerable and contemptible it might be; so that he not only did not consent to it, but did not even consider it worthy of a struggle? There is nevertheless some tickling of pleasure.

This tickling is present, and that enemy no longer fights or rules; nevertheless it remains, as though lingering in mortal flesh, which will not be so forever. Everything will be led into victory, but later. For now, “the body is dead because of sin,” and therefore sin is present in the same body, even though sin does not rule; “but the spirit is life because of righteousness. If the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:10 ff.).

There, there will be nothing left to fight and nothing to tickle; everything will yield to peace. [Note: [Col. 1860] Most manuscripts read “yield to peace.”]

For it is not one nature fighting against another nature, but something like a husband and wife in one household. If they disagree with each other, the labor is troublesome and dangerous; if the husband is defeated and the wife rules, the peace is perverse; but if the wife is subjected to the husband who rules, the peace is rightly ordered. Yet the one is not of a different nature from the other, since woman was made from man for the man.

Your flesh is your spouse, your servant. Consider it however you wish: it must be subjected; and if you fight [Note: [Col. 1860] Several manuscripts read “fight” in the imperative.], the battle must serve a purpose. For it is beneficial that what is lower be subjected to what is higher, so that the one who wishes the lower to be subjected to him may himself be subjected to what is higher than he is.

Recognize the order; seek peace. You to God, the flesh to you. What is more just? What is more beautiful? You to the greater, the lesser to you. Serve him who made you, so that what was made for you may serve you.

For we do not know or commend this order: the flesh to you and you to God—but, “you to God, and the flesh to you.” But if you despise “you to God,” you will never bring it about that “the flesh be subject to you.” [Note: [Col. 1860] So the manuscripts. The editions read: “But if you despise God, the flesh will never be subjected to you.”]

If you do not obey the Lord, you are tormented by a servant. If you are not first subject to God, so that afterward the flesh may be subject to you, can you say these words: “Blessed is the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war”? You wish to fight without being taught; defeated, you will be condemned.

First, then, submit yourself to God. Then, with him teaching and helping you, fight and say: “He teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war.”

7. [Verse 2.] And when you fight—for since you are in danger while you fight—say what follows, standing in the danger of battle: “My mercy.” I shall not be conquered. What does “my mercy” mean? Do you show me mercy and are merciful toward me? Or, “You have granted me to be merciful myself”?

For the enemy is conquered by nothing so much as by our being merciful. He prepares accusations for judgment but cannot bring false charges, because there is no one before whom he can do so. If he were conducting our case with him before a human judge, he could deceive the judge by lying and burden us with false accusations. But because our case with him is before such a judge as cannot be deceived, he seeks to lead us into sin, so that he may have true charges to bring against us.

And when human weakness perhaps succumbs to some of his frauds, let the work of humility follow in confession; let it be exercised in works of mercy and piety. [Note: [Col. 1861] Several manuscripts read: “let it be exercised in works of merciful piety.”]

Everything is erased when, from a true heart and with complete confidence, we say to the one who sees: “Forgive us, as we also forgive” (Matt. 6:12). Say it with your whole heart; say it with complete confidence; say it securely: “Forgive us, as we also forgive.” Or do not forgive, if we do not forgive.

Even if you do not say, “Do not forgive if we do not forgive,” he certainly does not forgive if we do not forgive. For he will not be a lying promiser in order that you, a sinner, may go unpunished. “Do you wish me to forgive?” he says. “Forgive.”

There is another work of mercy: “Do you wish me to give?” he says. “Give.” In one passage of the Gospel it is written: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38). “I hold something against you, and you hold something against another; forgive, and I forgive. You ask something from me, and another asks something from you; give, and I give.”

And what is it that forgives? What is it that gives? Is it not love? And where does love come from except through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5)?

If, then, our enemy is conquered through works of mercy, and we could not possess works of mercy unless we possessed love, and we would have no love unless we received the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1861] The manuscripts read “unless we received the Holy Spirit,” omitting “through.”], he teaches our hands for battle and our fingers for war. To him we rightly say, “My mercy,” since from him we have received even the ability to be merciful. “For judgment is without mercy to the one who has not shown mercy.”

8. Do you think works of mercy are insignificant? I would like to say something about them as well. First, attend to this statement drawn from Holy Scripture, which I just mentioned: “For judgment is without mercy to the one who has not shown mercy.” He will be judged without mercy who did not show mercy before he was judged.

What then? What follows? “But mercy triumphs over judgment” [Note: [Col. 1861] The editions read “mercy triumphs over judgment” with *judgment* in the accusative rather than the ablative.] (James 2:13). What does this mean, brothers: “Mercy triumphs over judgment”? Mercy is placed above judgment. Where a work of mercy is found, even if there is perhaps something in the judgment for which punishment is due, the fire of sin is extinguished, as it were, by a wave of mercy.

“For mercy triumphs over judgment.” But what of it? When he helps such people, frees such people, and forgives such people, is God unjust? Far be it. Even there he is just: mercy does not take justice away from him, nor does justice take mercy away from him.

See whether he is not just: “Forgive, and I forgive; give, and I give.” See whether he is not just: “In whatever measure you measure, it shall be measured out to you” (Matt. 7:2). The purpose of the words “in whatever measure” is not that the measure be of the same kind; rather, the same measure means this: “Forgive, and I forgive.”

There is with you a measure for granting forgiveness; you will find with me a measure for receiving forgiveness. There is with you a measure for giving what you have; you will find with me a measure for receiving what you do not have.

9. “My mercy and my refuge, my supporter and my deliverer.” This fighter struggles greatly, holding the flesh that desires against the spirit. Hold fast to what you hold. What you wish will be fully realized when death has been swallowed up in victory; when this mortal body, raised again, is transformed into an angelic condition and rises into a heavenly state.

“The dead,” he says, “in Christ shall rise first; then we who are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:15–16).

There death will be swallowed up in victory; there it will be said: “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Cor. 15:54–55). Nothing will remain, either in soul or in body, that rebels against the love of God. Full victory, full peace.

To us who are fighting this battle it is said: “Come, children, hear me; I shall teach you the fear of the Lord.” You are in battle; you are struggling in combat; yet you desire a certain rest. “Who is the person who desires life and loves to see good days?” Who is there who does not say, “I”? There is life and there are good days where nothing desires against the spirit [Note: [Col. 1862] The editions read “where the flesh desires nothing,” but “the flesh” is absent from the manuscripts.]; where it is not said, “Fight,” but “Rejoice.”

But who is the one who wishes for these days? [Note: [Col. 1862] The editions read “does not wish.”] Every person certainly says, “I.” Hear what follows. I see that you are laboring; I see that you are in battle and danger. Hear what follows: he teaches hands for battle and fingers for war.

“Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit; turn away from evil, and do good.” For how can you do good unless you turn away from evil? Why do I seek to have you clothe someone when you are still stripping another? Why do I seek to have you give when you are still robbing? “Turn away from evil, and do good.”

Do not first make a poor person weep beneath you so that another poor person may rejoice because of you. “Turn away from evil, and do good.” At what price? For now you are fighting. “Seek peace, and pursue it” (Ps. 33:12–15).

Learn to say: “My mercy and my refuge, my supporter and my deliverer, my protector.” My supporter, lest I fall; my deliverer, lest I remain trapped; my protector, lest I be struck. “My protector, and in him I have hoped.” In all these things—in all my labor, in all my battles, in all my difficulties—I have hoped in him.

“He subjects my people under me.” [Note: [Col. 1862] Several manuscripts read “has subjected”; most read “subjects.”] Behold, our head speaks with us.

### 10. [verse 3]

“Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him?” Everything that he is is contained in this: that you have made yourself known to him. What is man, that you have made yourself known to him? Or the son of man, that you take account of him? You take account of him: you value him, you esteem him so highly; you assign him his place, you know beneath what you should place him and above what you should place him. For estimation concerns the value of each thing.

How highly did he value man who poured out for him the blood of the Only-Begotten? “What is man, that you have made yourself known to him?” “To whom, who have you made yourself known?” [reading uncertain] [Note: [Col. 1863] So five manuscripts. The editions, however, read: “To whom have you made known what?”] “What is the son of man, that you take account of him?” Because you value him so highly, esteem him so highly, you show him to be something precious.

For God does not value man as man values man. When he finds a slave for sale, a man buys a horse at a higher price than a human being. Consider how highly God values you, so that you can say: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” And how highly did he value you, who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all? “How will he not also, together with him, graciously give us all things?” (Rom. 8:31–32).

He who gave this provision to the one who is fighting, what does he reserve for the victor? “I am,” he says, “the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41). This is the provision of those engaged in battle, brought in from the Lord’s storehouses, from which the angels are fed: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25).

But after the battles, and after this provision, what does he reserve? What will he give to the victors, except what is said in another psalm: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to be sheltered in his temple” (Ps. 26:4)?

“What is man, that you have made yourself known to him? Or the son of man, that you take account of him?”

### 11. [verse 4]

“Man has become like vanity”; and yet you have made yourself known to him, and you take account of him. Man has become like vanity. Like what vanity? Like times passing and flowing away. This is called vanity in comparison with the truth that always remains and never fails. For this creation too has its proper place. “God filled the earth with his good things,” as it is written (Sir. 16:30). What does “his” mean? Things suited to him.

But all these earthly, fleeting, transitory things, if they are compared with that truth where it is said, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14), everything that passes away is called vanity. For it vanishes with time, like smoke into the air.

And what more should I say than what the apostle James said, wishing to bring proud people down to humility? “What is your life?” he says. “It is a vapor appearing for a little while; afterward it will vanish away” (Jas. 4:15). Therefore, “Man has become like vanity.”

He became like vanity by sinning. For when he was first created, he was made like the truth; but because he sinned, because [Note: [Col. 1863] In Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain, “because” is absent. M.] he received what he deserved, he became like vanity. “For on account of iniquity you disciplined man,” he says in another psalm, “and you made his soul waste away like a spider’s.” Hence also this: “Man has become like vanity.” There what does he say? “Behold, you have made my days old” (Ps. 38:12, 6). Here what does he say? “His days pass away like a shadow.”

Let man be attentive to himself during the days of his shadow, so that he may do something worthy of the light he desires; and if he is in the shadow of night, let him seek the day. For, to the man who understands it, the day of this vanity is a day of tribulation—whether some adversity or distress harms us, or the world smiles upon us with some prosperity. Everything is to be feared and mourned, because “human life upon earth is a trial” (Job 7:1). Hence it is said: “All day long I walked in sorrow” (Ps. 37:7). [Note: [Col. 1864] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read: “For this is why it is said … I walked.”]

We need consolations, and whatever God now presents to us, when he presents it prosperously, is not the joy of the blessed but the consolation of the wretched.

Therefore, let man do something worthy of the light he desires during these days of his shadow, and in the night let him seek God, as it is written: “In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived” (Ps. 76:3). What day does he call the day of tribulation, except the one he also calls night? “With my hands by night before him.”

We are still in the night, and we keep watch by the lamp of prophecy. Something has been promised that is still awaited. But what does the apostle Peter say? “We have the prophetic word made more certain, and you do well to attend to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Pet. 1:19). That day itself is our reward there.

“In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you and contemplate” (Ps. 5:4–5). Therefore work with your hands, even in the night; that is, seek God through good works before that day comes which will gladden you, lest the day come which will sadden you.

See how securely you work, because you are not abandoned by the one whom you seek: “With my hands,” he says, “I sought God by night before him.” “So that your Father, who sees in secret, may repay you” (Matt. 6:4)—therefore, “before him.”

Have mercy and love within you; do nothing as though striving to please human beings. “With my hands”—that is, with my works; in the shadow, in this life; where he himself sees, not where I strive to please human beings.

And what follows? “And I was not deceived.”

“Man has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow”; and yet you have made yourself known to him, and you take account of him.

### 12. [verse 5]

“Lord, incline your heavens and descend; touch the mountains, and they will smoke. Flash forth flashes of lightning, and you will scatter them; send out your arrows, and you will trouble them. Send out your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me from many waters.”

The body of Christ, the humble David, full of grace and trusting in God, fighting in this age, invokes God’s help: “Incline your heavens and descend.”

What are the heavens that have been inclined? The apostles humbled. For these heavens declare the glory of God; and concerning these heavens that declare God’s glory it is immediately said: “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard; their sound has gone out through the whole earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:2, 4–5).

When, therefore, these heavens sent forth their voices throughout all the lands and performed miracles, while the Lord flashed and thundered through them by his miracles and commandments, they were thought to be gods who had come down from heaven to human beings. For some Gentiles, thinking this, even wished to sacrifice to them.

Then, seeing that an honor not due to them was being offered, and being terrified and abhorring it, and correcting those who were making such an error so that they might show them the movement of their hearts, they tore their garments and said: “Why are you doing this? We also are human beings subject to suffering, just as you are.” Then, with these words, they began to commend the greatness of our Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 14:7–17), humbling themselves so that God might be commended, because the heavens had been inclined so that God might descend.

Therefore: “Incline your heavens and descend.” It has happened.

“Touch the mountains, and they will smoke”: the proud mountains, earthly exaltation, swollen greatness. “Touch,” he says; “touch these mountains; from your grace give to these mountains—and they will smoke,” because they will confess their sins. The smoke of those confessing their sins will draw forth also the tears of humbled proud people.

“Touch the mountains, and they will smoke.” As long as they have not been touched, they seem great to themselves. They will say, “You are great, O Lord” (Ps. 47:2); and the mountains too will say, “You alone are Most High over all the earth” (Ps. 82:19).

### 13. [verse 6]

But there are certain people conspiring, assembling together against the Lord and against his Christ (Ps. 2:2; Acts 4:26–27). They assembled; they conspired.

“Flash forth flashes of lightning, and you will scatter them.” Increase your miracles, and their conspiracy will be dissolved. “Flash forth flashes of lightning, and you will scatter them.” Now terrified by the miracles, they will not dare do anything against you, and, astonished at the miracles themselves, they will hesitate. “Who is this who can do such things? Who is this who is so exalted, whose name has such power?”

When they say, “Who is this?” they will come to believe. You flashed forth in miracles, and you scattered their evil agreement.

“Send out your arrows, and you will trouble them.” “The arrows of the mighty are sharp” (Ps. 119:4): let your commandments and your words strike their hearts. “Send out your arrows, and you will trouble them.”

Let those who are wrongly healthy be wounded, so that those rightly wounded may be healed; and, now established in the Church and in the body of Christ, let them say with the Church: “For I am wounded in love” (Song 2:5, according to the Septuagint).

“Send out your arrows, and you will trouble them.”

### 14. [verse 7]

“Send out your hand from on high.” What follows? What happens at the end? How does the body of Christ conquer? [Note: [Col. 1865] Ambrose and Erasmus read, “How, he says?” Louvain reads, “How did he conquer?” The Floriacensis manuscript reads, “How does he conquer?” Several other manuscripts read, “How, then, does the body of Christ need …” Some have, “How here does the body of Christ need …”; in these latter manuscripts the verb “needs” is added.]

By heavenly assistance. For the Lord himself will come “with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God” and will descend from heaven (1 Thess. 4:15). He himself is the Savior of the body, the hand of God: “Send out your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me from many waters.”

What are “many waters”? Many peoples. Which peoples? Foreigners and unbelievers, whether attacking from without or lying in ambush within.

“Rescue me from many waters,” in which you were exercising me, in which you were rolling me about so that I might be stripped of my filth. This is that water of contradiction (Num. 20:13).

“Rescue me and deliver me from many waters.”

### 15. [verse 8]

Let us now hear about these many waters, from which God will rescue the body of his Christ, from which God will rescue the humility of David.

What does “from many waters” mean? What did you say, so that the waters would not be understood in another way? What did you say by “many waters”? Listen to what I said: “From the hand of foreign sons.”

Listen, brothers, to those among whom we are, among whom we live, and from whom we desire to be delivered: “Whose mouth has spoken vanity.”

Today, if all of you had not gathered for these divine spectacles of the word of God, and were living at this hour mingled with such people, what quantities of vanities would you hear! “Whose mouth has spoken vanity.”

When, finally, would those people who speak vanity hear you speaking the truth? “Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.”

### 16. [verse 9]

What are you doing among them with a shepherd’s vessel containing five stones? Tell me in another way: signify in another way the same Law that you signified by the five stones.

“O God, I will sing a new song to you.” A new song belongs to grace; [Note: [Col. 1866] So certain manuscripts. The editions read, “A new song is grace.”] a new song belongs to the new human being; a new song belongs to the New Testament.

“I will sing to you,” he says, “a new song.” But lest you think that grace departs from the Law, when rather the Law is fulfilled through grace: “On a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you.” On a ten-stringed psaltery—that is, in the Law of the ten commandments. There I will sing to you, there I will rejoice in you, there I will sing a new song to you, because “the fullness of the Law is love” (Rom. 13:10).

Those who do not have love can carry the psaltery; they cannot sing. Therefore I, he says, will sing to you a new song amid the waters of contradiction; and the waters of contradiction will never make my psaltery grow mute through their noise: “On a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you.”

### 17. [verses 10–11]

“To him who gives [Note: [Col. 1866] The editions read “gives,” and below, “redeemed.” Several manuscripts read “you give,” and afterwards “redeemed” or “you redeemed.” Some read “gives and redeems,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint, *tō didonti, tō lyttroumenō* (“to the one who gives, to the one who redeems”).] salvation to kings”—now that the mountains are smoking—“who redeems David his servant.”

You recognize David; be David. From what does he redeem David his servant? From what does he redeem Christ? From what does he redeem the body of Christ?

“Deliver me from the evil sword.” “From the sword” would not be enough; he adds “evil.” Without doubt, there is a good sword.

What is the good sword? The one of which the Lord says: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34). For he was going to separate the faithful from the unfaithful, children from parents, and to sever other relationships as well—a sword cutting away decay while healing the members of Christ.

There is therefore a good, double-edged sword, powerful with both edges: the Old and New Testaments, the narration of past events and the promise of future ones.

This, then, is the good sword. The evil sword, however, is the one with which those people speak vanity, because the sword with which God speaks truth is good.

Therefore: “Deliver me from the evil sword.” “The teeth of human beings are their weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5): from this evil sword deliver me.

The thing he has just called a sword he earlier called “many waters”: “Deliver me from many waters.” What I called many waters, I now call the evil sword.

Finally, after saying “from many waters,” he continued: “From the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity.” And so that you may know that the same people are meant, after saying here, “Deliver me from the evil sword,” he continued: “And rescue me from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity,” just as there.

And what follows—“Their right hand is a right hand of iniquity”—he had also placed earlier, when he called them many waters. For, lest you think that many waters were good, he explained them as the evil sword.

Now, therefore, let him explain what he said: “Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” What vanity did their mouth speak, and how is their right hand a right hand of iniquity?

### 18. [verses 12–14]

“Whose sons are like young plants, firmly established in their youth.”

He wishes to enumerate their prosperity. Pay attention, sons of light, sons of peace; pay attention, sons of the Church, members of Christ. Pay attention to whom he calls foreigners, whom he calls foreign sons, whom he calls waters of contradiction, whom he calls the evil sword.

Pay attention, I beg you, because you are endangered among such people; among their tongues you fight against the desires of your flesh. Among their tongues, placed in the devil’s hand and used by him in fighting, you have a struggle—not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities and the rulers of the darkness of this world (Eph. 6:12), that is, against the wicked.

Pay attention, so that you may distinguish yourselves; pay attention, lest you think that the true happiness is what weak or wicked people desire for themselves.

Behold, brothers: he certainly called them foreign sons; certainly, many waters; certainly, the evil sword. See the vanity they speak, and beware lest you speak such things; beware lest, while speaking such things, you imitate them.

“Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” What vanity did their mouth speak, and what right hand of theirs is a right hand of iniquity?

Listen: “Whose sons are like young plants, firmly established in their youth; their daughters are adorned and embellished like the likeness of a temple; their storerooms are full, overflowing from one thing into another; their sheep are fertile, multiplying at their outlets; their oxen are fat; there is no breach even of a fence, no exit, and no cry in their streets.”

So, is this not happiness? I ask the sons of the kingdom of heaven; I ask the offspring of the resurrection for eternity; I ask the body of Christ, the members of Christ, the temple of God: Is it not happiness to have healthy sons, adorned daughters, full storerooms, abundant herds, no collapse—not merely of a wall, but not even of a fence—no tumult or shouting in the streets, but quiet, peace, abundance, and plenty of possessions in houses and cities?

So, is this not happiness? Or should the righteous avoid it? Or do you not find the house of a righteous person also abounding in all these things, filled with this happiness?

Was not Abraham’s house abundant in gold, silver, sons, household, and flocks (Gen. 12:5; 13:2–6)? Did not the holy patriarch Jacob, fleeing from the face of his brother Esau into Mesopotamia, grow wealthy while serving, return, and give thanks to the Lord his God because he had crossed the river with only his staff and returned with such an abundance of flocks and children (Gen. 31:18; 32:7–10)?

What shall we say? Is this not happiness? Let it be happiness—but on the left. What does “on the left” mean? Temporal, mortal, bodily. I do not want you now to flee from it, but neither should you think it the right hand.

For these people are not wicked and vain because they abounded in such things, but because they placed on the right what ought to have been on the left. Therefore “their right hand is a right hand of iniquity”; therefore their mouth spoke vanity: because they placed on the right what they ought to have had on the left.

What ought they to have placed on the right? God, eternity, the years of God that do not fail, concerning which it is said: “Your years will not fail” (Ps. 101:28). There is the right hand; there our desire ought to be.

Let us use the left for a time; let us desire the right for eternity. “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11). For if you set your heart upon increasing riches, you will make what is left into what is right.

Correct yourselves; recognize Wisdom embracing you, to whom it was said: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2:6). See the holy love songs; see the Song of Songs, the heavenly marriage of Christ and the Church.

What does the bride say about the bridegroom? “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” The left hand is under the head, the right hand above the head. For the arm of one embracing from above is over the head, while the left hand is beneath the head.

“His left hand,” she says, “is under my head.” For he will not abandon me in the temporal necessities; nevertheless, that left hand will be under the head. It will not be placed above the head, but will be beneath the head, so that his right hand may embrace me, promising eternal life.

Thus the left hand is under the head if the right hand is above the head; and what is written to Timothy is fulfilled: [Note: [Col. 1868] Most manuscripts read: “For thus the left hand is under the head, the right hand above the head, and that which is written to Timothy is fulfilled,” etc.] “Having the promise of the present life and of the future” (1 Tim. 4:8).

“Having,” he says, “the promise of the present life and of the future.” What belongs to the present? The left hand under the head. What belongs to the future? “His right hand will embrace me.”

Are you seeking necessities for the present age? “Seek first the kingdom of God”—that is, the right hand—“and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). You will have here, he says, riches and glory, and in the age to come eternal life. “With my left hand I will hold your weakness, and with my right I will crown your perfection.”

Or perhaps the apostles, leaving everything they had or distributing to the poor what they possessed, remained without riches in this age? And where is that promise of the left hand: “He will receive in this age sevenfold”? [Note: [Col. 1868] Four manuscripts read, “He will receive a hundredfold.” Others, with the editions, read, “sevenfold.” Augustine likewise elsewhere cites this Gospel passage in this form; perhaps the Greek books had *heptaplasiona* (“sevenfold”) instead of *hekatontaplasiona* (“hundredfold”).]

He promised multiplication. And truly, what can the man of God lack? If some unbeliever possesses one house or a few, “the whole world is the wealth of the faithful person” [Note: [Col. 1868] Louvain reads, “is full of riches.” The word *plenus* (“full”) is absent from the other editions and from the manuscripts, nor is it found in the Greek Septuagint.] (Prov. 17:6, according to the Septuagint). See his left hand full beneath the head: “He will receive in this age sevenfold.” See the right hand embracing: “And in the age to come eternal life” (Matt. 19:29).

Rightly, in another passage, the same Wisdom is described: “Length of days is in her right hand, and in her left hand are riches and honor” (Prov. 3:16).

### 19. [verse 15]

Why, then, are these people vain talkers? Why did their mouth speak vanity? Because their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.

I do not therefore condemn them because their sons are like young plants firmly established in their youth, nor because their daughters are adorned like the likeness of a temple, nor because other abundance and earthly peace were present among them. Why, then, do I condemn them?

“They called the people blessed who possess these things.” O people speaking vanity! “They called the people blessed who possess these things.” They have lost the true right hand; wicked and perverse, they have put God’s gifts on backward. [Note: [Col. 1869] So several manuscripts. Some read, “having put themselves on backward.” The editions read, “having all put themselves on backward.”]

O wicked people, O vain talkers, O foreign sons! “They called the people blessed who possess these things.” They placed on the right what belonged on the left: “They called the people blessed who possess these things.”

But you, David—what do you say? You, body of Christ—what do you say? You, members of Christ—what do you say? You who are not foreign sons but sons of God—what do you say?

Since vain-talking foreign sons called the people blessed who possess these things, what do you say?

“Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God.”

Have the left hand, then, but keep it on the left; desire the right hand [Note: [Col. 1869] So most manuscripts. The editions punctuate the words as follows: “but keep it on the left, desire the right hand.” Below, Erasmus and Louvain read, “For they had Christ on the left, among whom …”; Ambrose, “For they had the left on the left.” Some manuscripts read, “From the left, then …”], so that you may be placed on the right.

For they had the left on the left, among whom he was hungry and they gave him food; he was thirsty and they gave him drink; he was a stranger and they welcomed him; he was naked and they clothed him (Matt. 25:35–36). They took all this from the left and transferred it to the works of the right, so that they might be placed on the right.

Therefore vain-talking foreign sons said, “Blessed is the people who possess these things”; but you say with us: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God.” [Note: [Col. 1869] The older manuscripts add this closing: “Turned toward God. Amen. Thanks be always to God.”]

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 144

### SERMON

[Note: [Col. 1869] Certainly he did not use this opening among his own people. Rather, as it is noted at the beginning of the very ancient Floriacensis manuscript, this sermon “was delivered at Utica, in the basilica of Massa Candida.” See below, no. 17, note a.]

### 1

We have desired to praise the Lord with you; and since he has deigned to grant this, so that the praise we offer him may have its proper order, lest perhaps through some excess we offend the one whom we praise, let us seek the better path of praise in God’s Scripture, so that we may not depart from that path either to the right or to the left.

For I dare say to your Charity: if God is to be praised well by a human being, God himself has praised himself; and because he has deigned to praise himself, human beings have found how to praise him.

For what was said to a human being cannot be said to God: “Let not your own mouth praise you” (Prov. 27:2). For a human being to praise himself is arrogance; for God to praise himself is mercy.

It benefits us to love the one whom we praise; by loving what is good, we become better. Therefore, because he knows that it benefits us to love him, by praising himself he makes himself lovable; and in doing so he cares for us, because he makes himself lovable.

He therefore urges our hearts to his praise; he filled his servants with his Spirit, so that they might praise him. And since his Spirit in his servants praises him, what else is this than God himself praising himself?

This psalm therefore begins as follows:

### 2. [verse 1]

“I will exalt you, my God, my king; and I will bless your name for age and age, and for the age of the age.”

You see that the praise of God has begun, and that this praise is carried through to the end of the psalm. Indeed, the title of the psalm is: “The praise itself of David.” And since David is understood as the one who came to us from the seed of David (Rom. 1:3), while he himself is our king, ruling us and leading us into his kingdom, “The praise itself of David” is understood as “The praise itself of Christ.”

Christ, according to the flesh, is David, because he is David’s son; but according to his divinity, he is David’s Creator and David’s Lord.

Finally, when the Apostle was honoring the first people of God—from whom the apostles themselves also believed and from whom many early churches were formed, carrying out among many thousands of people what the one rich man heard in the Gospel and went away sad (Matt. 19:21–22), namely, selling everything they had, distributing it to the poor, and seeking perfection in the Lord (Acts 2:41–47; 4:4, 32–35)—when, therefore, he was praising that first people, he said:

“Their fathers are theirs, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

Since Christ is from them according to the flesh, therefore he is David; but since he himself is God over all, blessed forever, therefore: “I will exalt you, my God, my king; and I will bless,” he says, “your name for age and age, and for the age of the age.”

Perhaps “for age” means here, while “for the age of the age” means forever. Begin praising now, then, if you are going to praise forever. Whoever does not wish to praise during the passing of this age will be silenced when the age of the age arrives.

Therefore, in the following verses he said almost this very thing.

### 3. [verse 2]

Lest anyone understand otherwise what he says, “I will praise your name for age,” and seek another age in which he would praise, he says: “Every day I will bless you.”

Praise and bless the Lord your God every day, so that when the individual days have been completed and the one day without end has arrived, you may go from praises to praise, just as from strength to strength (Ps. 83:8).

“Every day,” he says, “I will bless you”; no day will pass on which I do not bless you.

It is no wonder if you bless your God on your joyful day. But what if some sorrowful day should dawn, as human affairs are constituted, with scandals abounding and temptations multiplying? What if something sad should happen to a human being? Will you cease praising God? Will you cease blessing your Creator?

If you cease, you have lied by saying, “Every day I will bless you, Lord.” But if you do not cease, even if things seem bad for you on a sorrowful day, things will be well for you in your God.

There is indeed a place where, even when things are bad for you, things may be well. For if things are bad for you in some evil, they will undoubtedly be well for you in some good. And what is as good as your God, of whom it is said: “No one is good except one, God” (Luke 18:19)?

To understand how secure this praise is, and how secure this well-being is, consider the good itself. If you rejoice in some good that happens to you during the day, perhaps the good over which you rejoice will pass away on another day.

“It was good for me; I had a good day,” because perhaps profits came, or you were invited somewhere, or you spent a long time at a feast. You rejoice because you spent a long time at a feast; another person grieves because you were not ashamed.

Nevertheless, whatever such good you may rejoice in, it is certainly transitory. But if you rejoice in the Lord your God, you will hear Scripture saying: “Delight in the Lord” (Ps. 36:4). You will rejoice more firmly the more certain is the one in whom you rejoice.

If you rejoice in a coin, you fear a thief; but if you rejoice in God, what do you fear? That someone may take God away from you? No one will take God away from you if you do not abandon him.

For God is not like this light shining from heaven. We do not approach it whenever we wish, because it does not shine in every place. Because of our weakness, perhaps in winter we take pleasure in being in that very light; but now, in summer, you see that we have sought a place where we would not stand in that light.

But when you stand in your God and delight in the light of his truth, you do not seek a place by which to approach him; rather, the conscience approaches and the conscience withdraws.

What is said, “Approach him, and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:6), is said of the mind, not of a vehicle; of the affections, not of the feet.

And when you stand in him, you will not suffer the heat. For the Spirit will breathe upon you, and you will hope under his wings (Ps. 90:4).

### 4

You see, then, how you can delight every day. Your God will not abandon you, even if something sorrowful happens.

How grievous was what happened to the holy man Job! How sudden, how many were the evils! How everything in which he was thought to rejoice—not the things in which he actually rejoiced—was taken away when the devil tested him! How even his children died!

What was being preserved perished; those for whom it was being preserved perished. Yet the one who gave both the things and the people did not perish. The sons themselves perished from the present age, to be recognized and received in the future.

That man, however, had something else from which to rejoice, in which the words we have just recalled were true: “Every day I will bless you.” Did the fact that the day on which everything had perished dawned sorrowfully mean that the inner light in his heart failed?

For he stood in that light and said: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

Therefore he praised every day—the man who praised even on such a sorrowful day.

It is a brief lesson: always praise God, and say with a true heart, not falsely: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2).

It is a brief lesson, namely, that you should know that he gives mercifully when he gives and takes away mercifully when he takes away. Do not think that you are abandoned by his mercy: he either soothes you by giving, lest you fail, or corrects you when you are exulting, lest you perish.

Therefore, whether in his gifts or in his scourges, you yourself praise him. [Note: [Col. 1871] So the manuscripts. The editions read, “praise him.”] The praise of the one who scourges is medicine for the wound.

“Every day,” he says, “I will bless you.” Indeed, every day, brothers, bless him; whatever happens, bless God.

For he himself ensures that nothing happens which you cannot bear. Therefore you ought to be fearful when things are going well for you, and not prepare yourself as though you would never be tested.

For if you are never tested, you will never be proved. Is it not better to be tested and proved than, without being tested, to be rejected?

“And I will praise your name for age and age, and for the age of the age.”

### 5. [verse 3]

“Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise.”

How much was he about to say? What words was he going to seek? How great a thought did he enclose in the single word “exceedingly”? Think as much as you wish. But how can the one who cannot be comprehended be comprehended in thought?

He is “exceedingly worthy of praise,” and “his greatness has no end.” Therefore he said “exceedingly,” because “his greatness has no end,” lest you perhaps begin wishing to praise him and think that by praising you could bring to an end the greatness whose end cannot exist.

Do not, then, think that you can praise sufficiently the one whose greatness has no end. Is it not better that, just as he himself does not come to an end, neither should his praise come to an end?

His greatness is without end, and let your praise be without end. What is said of his greatness? “His greatness has no end.” What is said of your praise? “I will praise your name for age and age, and for the age of the age.”

Therefore, just as his greatness has no end, so your praise will have no end. For you will not cease praising the Lord when you have died in this flesh.

It is indeed said: “The dead will not praise you, Lord” (Ps. 113:17); but this concerns those of whom it is said: “From the dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes” (Sir. 17:26)—not those of whom he says: “Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live” (John 11:25). For “the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob is not God of the dead but of the living” (Matt. 22:32).

If you will belong to him forever, you will never be silent from his praise. Could you fear that, while you live here, you belong to him, but when you have died, you will not belong to him?

Hear the Apostle promising you security: “Whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.”

And how did it come about that you belong to him even when dead? Because he redeemed you and died at the price of his own blood. [Note: [Col. 1872] Several manuscripts read, “and redeemed the dead.”]

How can he lose a dead servant whose death is your price? Therefore, after saying, “Whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s,” to show that he himself was the price, he adds: “For to this end Christ died and rose again, so that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead” (Rom. 14:8–9).

6. [verse 4.] Yet, because there is no end to his greatness, and we ought to praise him whom we cannot comprehend—for if we comprehend him, there is an end to his greatness; but if there is no end to his greatness, we can comprehend something of him, though we cannot comprehend God in his entirety—let us, as though failing before his greatness, turn our attention to his works so that we may be refreshed by his goodness, and let us praise the one who works through his works, the Creator through created things, the Maker through his creation. Let us see what he has done here, what is known and evident to us. For how many other things has his boundless goodness and immeasurable greatness made that we do not know? We extend the range of our eyes only as far as heaven, and then draw it back from the sun, moon, and stars to the earth; and this whole expanse is where our sight wanders. Who can extend even the mind’s vision beyond the heavens, let alone that of the flesh? Therefore, insofar as his works are known to us, let us praise him through his works. For his invisible attributes, from the creation of the world onward, are perceived and understood through the things that have been made (Rom. I, 20).

“Generation and generation shall praise your works.” “Every generation shall praise your works.” Perhaps “every generation” is expressed by “generation and generation.” He was not going to keep saying “generation and generation” until he had completed the number of all generations; rather, the speaker’s repetition has sent the mind of the one thinking into infinity. Behold, this generation, which is now in the flesh and will pass from here as it came, praises the works of God; and the generation that succeeds it, taking its place, will surely praise the works of God; and after that there will be another. How many generations there will be until the end of the world! Indicating this, he says, “Generation and generation shall praise your works.”

Or did he perhaps wish by this repetition to indicate two particular generations? For we are in this generation children of God; in another generation we shall be children of the resurrection. Scripture calls them “children of the resurrection”; it called the resurrection itself “regeneration”: “In the regeneration,” he says, “when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty” (Matt. XIX, 28). Likewise, in another place: “For they shall neither marry nor be given in marriage, since they are children of the resurrection” (Luke XX, 35–36). Therefore: “Generation and generation shall praise your works.” We praise the works of the Lord now, while we live in this mortality; and if we praise him while fettered, how shall we praise him when crowned! Let us therefore now attend, in this generation, to the works of the Lord, in whose praise it is said, “Generation and generation shall praise your works,” because there is no end to your greatness. It is possible to contemplate your works, so that you may be praised, you who perform such works.

7. “And they shall proclaim your power.” For they will not praise your works unless they proclaim your power. Praises are set before boys in school, and all such things are put forward to be praised—things that God has made: praise of the sun, praise of heaven, praise of earth; and, to come down to smaller things, praise of the rose, praise of the laurel. All these are works of God; they are brought forward, received, and praised. The works are celebrated, while the maker is passed over in silence.

I wish the Creator to be praised in his works; I do not love a praiser who is ungrateful. You praise what he made, but are silent about the one who made it? As though, unless he were so great, you would find anything to praise. In what you see, what is being praised? The appearance, usefulness, some power, some capacity of these things. If beauty delights you, what is more beautiful than the one who made it? If usefulness is praised, what is more useful than the one who made all things? If power is praised, what is more powerful than the one by whom all things were made—by whom, moreover, the things made are not abandoned, but all are governed and directed?

Therefore, generation and generation does not praise you like certain eloquent mutes who praise the creature while forgetting the Creator, when it praises your works among your servants. But how does it praise you? “And they shall proclaim your power.” In praising your works, they shall proclaim your power.

These praisers—holy and good believers, true praisers, not ungrateful toward grace—when they praise this or that of God’s works, the highest and the lowest, heavenly and earthly, find themselves among the very works of God that they praise, because they too are among God’s works. For the one who made all things made us also among all things. Therefore, if you praise God’s works, you are going to praise yourself as well, because you too are a work of God.

Where, then, is “Let not your own mouth praise you” (Prov. XXVII, 2)? Behold, it has been found how you may both praise yourself and not be arrogant. Praise God in yourself, not yourself: not because you are such, but because he made you; not because you can do anything, but because he can act in you and through you. And so “they shall praise you and proclaim your power”—not their own, but yours.

Learn, then, how to praise. Looking upon works, marvel at the craftsman; give thanks, without boasting. Praise him because he made them, because he established them in this way, because he bestowed such gifts.

8. [verses 5–6.] Finally, see what follows: “They shall proclaim,” he says, “your power. And they shall speak of the magnificence of the glory of your holiness, and they shall recount your wonders. And they shall declare the power of your fearful deeds, and they shall tell of your greatness.” “They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness”—only yours.

This observer of works—see whether he has turned aside from the one who works to the work; see whether he has fallen from the one who made them to the things he made. From the things made he has made a step toward him, not a fall from him toward them. For if you love these things more than him, you will not have him. And what does it profit you to abound in works if the one who works abandons you? Certainly love these things too; but love him more, and love these things for his sake.

Proclaim his power; speak of the magnificence of the glory of his holiness; recount his wonders; declare the power of his fearful deeds. For he is both lovable and fearsome. If he did not flatter, there would be no exhortation; if he did not threaten, there would be no correction. Therefore your praisers will also declare the power of his fearful deeds: they will declare your power in punishing your creature and giving it discipline; they will not be silent.

For they will not preach your eternal kingdom and remain silent about eternal fire. The praise of God that sets you on the way ought to show you both what to love and what to fear, what to seek and what to avoid, what to choose and what to reject. The time for choosing is now; the time for receiving will come afterward. Let the power of fearful deeds, then, be declared.

“And they shall tell of your greatness,” he says. Thus infinite, just as there is no end to your greatness, they will not be silent about it. That greatness of yours, I say, of which I said above, “There is no end to your greatness,” they shall tell of it. How will they tell of it, if it has no end? They will tell of it when they praise it; and because it has no end, so there will be no end to its praise. Let us prove that there will be no end to its praise. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; throughout the ages of ages they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5). And that greatness of yours—that infinite greatness—they shall tell of it.

9. [verse 7.] “They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness.” O happy banquets! What will those who pour forth in this way eat? “The memory of the abundance of your sweetness.” What is “the memory of the abundance of your sweetness”? That you did not forget us when we had forgotten you. For all flesh had forgotten God; yet he did not forget his works.

This memory of him toward us—because he did not forget us—is to be proclaimed and recounted; and because it is exceedingly sweet, it is to be eaten and poured forth. Eat in such a way that you may pour forth; receive in such a way that you may give. You eat when you learn; you pour forth when you teach. You eat when you hear; you pour forth when you preach. Yet you pour forth only what you have eaten.

Finally, that most eager banqueter, the apostle John, for whom the Lord’s table itself was not enough unless he reclined upon the Lord’s breast (John XIII, 23) and drank divine secrets from his mystery—what did he pour forth? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John I, 1).

Therefore, “they shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness.” Why is “your memory” not enough, nor “the memory of your abundance,” nor “the memory of your sweetness,” but “the memory of the abundance of your sweetness”? For what good is abundance if it is without sweetness? Likewise, it is burdensome if it is sweet but scant.

10. Therefore, “they shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness,” because you did not forget us; and by not forgetting us, you reminded us, so that we too might remember. “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. XXI, 28).

Because, then, “they shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness,” understanding that there is nothing good in them that is not from you; that they could not have turned to you unless they had been reminded by you; and that they could not have been brought back to the memory of you if you had forgotten them—considering these things in your grace, “they shall rejoice in your righteousness.” Considering these things, I say, in your grace, they shall rejoice in your righteousness, not their own.

Brothers, if you wish to pour forth grace, drink grace. What does “drink grace” mean? Learn grace; understand grace. Before we existed, we were absolutely nothing; and we became human beings when previously we were nothing. Then, although already human beings, we were wicked and children of wrath by nature, like the rest (Eph. II, 3), through descent from that sinner.

Let us therefore attend to the grace of God—not only the grace by which he made us, but also that by which he remade us. To the one to whom we owe our existence, we also owe our justification. Let no one attribute to God merely that he exists, and attribute to himself that he is righteous. For what you wish to attribute to yourself is better: it is better to be something because you are righteous [Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read: “For it is better to be something, because you are rustus [‘rustic,’ probably corrupt].”] than because you are human. You give God what is lower, and yourself what is higher.

Give everything to him; praise him in everything. Do not fall from the hand of the craftsman. Who made you exist? Is it not written that God took clay from the earth and formed the human being (Gen. II, 7)? Before you were human, you were clay; before you were clay, you were nothing.

But do not give thanks to your craftsman only for this formation; hear of another formation in which he made you. “Not from works,” he says, “lest anyone should boast.” But the one who said, “Not from works, lest anyone should boast”—what did he mention earlier? [Note: In B: “But what did he say, ‘Not from works, lest anyone should boast’? What did he mention earlier?” We have followed Erasmus and the Venetian edition. M.]

“By grace you have been saved through faith; and this” [Note: Here the printed editions add “so that you might be saved through faith,” which is absent from the manuscripts.] “is not from yourselves.” These are the Apostle’s words, not mine: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this”—that is, “so that you might be saved through faith”—“is not from yourselves.” Although in saying “by grace” he had certainly already indicated “not from yourselves,” nevertheless, lest anyone understand it otherwise, he graciously clarified it more plainly.

Give me someone who understands, and he has said everything: “By grace you have been saved.” When you hear “by grace,” understand “freely.” If freely, then you contributed nothing and earned nothing; for if something has been given in return for merits, it is payment, not grace.

“By grace,” he says, “you have been saved through faith.” Explain this more clearly for the arrogant, for those who please themselves, for those who do not know God’s righteousness and wish to establish their own. Hear the same thing stated more clearly: “And this,” he says, “that you have been saved by grace, is not from yourselves, but is the gift of God.”

“But perhaps we did something so that we might deserve God’s gifts.” “Not from works,” he says, “lest anyone should boast.”

What then? Are we not to do good works? Indeed, we are to do them. But how? With him himself working in us, because through faith we make room in our hearts for the one who works good things in us and through us.

Hear, then, from where you may do good works: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, so that we might walk in them” (Eph. II, 8–10).

This is the abundant sweetness of his memory toward us. Pouring it forth, his preachers will rejoice in his righteousness, not their own.

What, then, in order that we might exist, praise, rejoice in your righteousness, and pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness—what have you done for us, Lord, whom we praise? Let us say it; and as we say it, let us praise.

11. [verse 8.] “The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and abundantly merciful. The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works.”

If he were not such, there would be no restoration of us [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read: “there would be no such restoration and renewal.” M.]. Look to yourself: what did you deserve as a sinner? What did you deserve as one who despised God? See whether anything comes before you except punishment, whether anything comes before you except chastisement.

You see, then, what was owed to you and what the one who gave freely has given. Forgiveness was given to the sinner; the spirit of justification was given; charity and love were given, in which you might do every good thing; and beyond these he will also give eternal life and fellowship with the angels—all from mercy.

Do not boast of your merits anywhere, because your very merits are his gifts: “They shall rejoice in your righteousness.”

“The Lord is compassionate and merciful”—you who made everything freely. “Patient”—for how many sinners does he endure! “The Lord is compassionate and merciful” toward those to whom he has granted forgiveness; toward those to whom he has not yet granted it, he is patient, not condemning but waiting, calling out through that very waiting: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Mal. III, 7); and in his excessive patience [Note: Most manuscripts read, “and excessive patience”]: “I do not desire the death of the wicked, but only that he return and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

He is indeed patient; but you, according to the hardness of your heart and your unrepentant heart, are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will render to each according to his works (Rom. II, 5–6). He is not now patient in enduring in such a way that he will never be just in judging [Note: Amalarius and Erasmus read “in judging”; so do several manuscripts, which shortly afterward, with the other witnesses, have “he waits until you repent.”].

He has appointed times. He calls you now; he exhorts you now; he waits until you repent—and you delay! Great is his mercy also in this, that he has made the day of your life uncertain, so that you do not know when you will depart from here; and while you expect each day to depart, you may at some point be converted. In this too his mercy is great.

Otherwise, if he had fixed one day for everyone, he would make sins abound through security. He therefore gave hope of forgiveness, lest you sin more through despair. Both hope and despair must be feared in sins.

Observe the voice of one who despairs and thereby increases sins, and observe the voice of one who hopes and thereby increases sins; and see how God’s providence and mercy meet both voices.

Hear the voice of one who despairs: “I am already going to be condemned; why should I not do whatever I want?” Hear also the voice of one who hopes: “The Lord’s mercy is great; whenever I turn, he will forgive me everything. Why should I not do whatever I want?” He despairs in order to sin; he hopes in order to sin. Both must be feared; both are dangerous. Woe to despair! Woe to perverse hope!

How does God’s mercy meet both these dangers and both these evils? What do you say, you who wished to sin in despair? “I am already going to be condemned; why should I not do whatever I want?” Hear Scripture: “I do not desire the death of the wicked, but only that he return and live.” By this word of God he is brought back to hope; but another snare must be feared, lest he sin more through that very hope.

What, then, did you say, you who sin more because of hope? “When I turn, God will forgive me everything; I will do whatever I want.” Hear Scripture too: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day; for suddenly his wrath will come, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Ecclus. V, 8–9).

Do not say, then, “Tomorrow I shall turn; tomorrow I shall please God; everything I have done today and yesterday will be forgiven me.” What you say is true, because God has promised forgiveness to your conversion; but he has not promised you tomorrow for your delay.

12. [verse 9.] “The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works.”

Why, then, does he condemn? Why does he scourge? Are those whom he condemns, those whom he scourges, not his works? They certainly are his works. And do you wish to know that his mercies are over all his works? From this comes that patience by which he makes his sun rise over the good and the evil. Are not his mercies over all his works, since he rains upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V, 45)? Are not his mercies over all his works?

He patiently awaits the sinner, saying, “Turn to me, and I will turn to you.” Are not his mercies over all his works? And when he says, “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41), this is not his mercy but his severity.

His mercy has been shown toward his works; his severity is not against his work, but against your work. Finally, if you remove your evil works, and nothing remains in you except his work, his mercy will not abandon you. But if you do not abandon your works, his severity will be directed against your work, not against his.

13. [verse 10.] “Let all your works confess to you, Lord, and let your saints bless you.”

Let all your works confess to you. What then? Is the earth not his work? Are the trees not his works? Are cattle, wild animals, fish, and birds not his works? They certainly are his works. And how will even these confess to him?

I see God’s works confessing him in the angels, for the angels are his works; and human beings are his works, and when human beings confess him, his works confess him. But do trees and stones have a voice of confession?

By all means, let all his works confess to him. What do you say? The earth and trees as well? They are all his works. If all praise him, why should they not all confess him? For confession is spoken not only of sins but also of praise. Perhaps whenever you hear “confession,” you think that it can refer only to sin. Indeed, this is so strongly assumed that whenever the word sounds forth from the divine utterances, it is immediately customary to beat one’s breast.

Hear that there is also a confession of praise. Did the Lord Jesus Christ have sin? Yet he said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI, 25). Confession, therefore, occurs in praise.

Accordingly, what should be understood by “Let all your works confess to you, Lord”? Let all your works praise you.

But a question like this returns to praise just as it did with confession. If the earth, trees, and all inanimate things cannot confess because they have no voice with which to confess, then for the same reason they cannot praise, because they have no voice with which to proclaim.

Yet do not those three young men enumerate all things as they walked unharmed amid the flames—young men who had room not only not to burn but also to praise God? To all things, from the heavenly to the earthly, they say: “Bless, sing a hymn, and exalt him above all forever” (Dan. III, 20, 90). Behold how they sing a hymn.

Let no one suppose that a mute stone or a mute animal possesses the reason required to understand God. Those who have thought this have strayed far from the truth.

God ordered and made all things. To some he gave sense, understanding, and immortality, as to the angels; to some he gave sense and understanding together with mortality, as to human beings; to some he gave bodily sensation but no understanding and no immortality, as to cattle; and to others he gave neither sensation, nor understanding, nor immortality, as to grasses, trees, and stones.

Nevertheless, even these cannot be absent from their own order; and he ordered creation by certain degrees [Note: Here Erasmus and the Louvain edition add, “and adorned,” which is absent from the other books], from earth to heaven, from visible things to invisible, from mortal things to immortal. This interweaving of creation, this most orderly beauty, rising from the lowest things to the highest and descending from the highest to the lowest, nowhere interrupted but harmonized through dissimilar things, praises God in its entirety.

Why, then, does it praise God in its entirety? Because when you contemplate it and see it as beautiful, you praise God in it. The appearance of the earth is a kind of voice of the mute earth.

You attend and see its appearance; you see its fertility; you see its strength—how it conceives seed, how it often produces what has not been sown. You see, and by your contemplation you somehow question it; and that very inquiry is a question. When, wondering, you have inquired, searched it out, and found great power, great beauty, and remarkable strength, then, since it could not possess this power from itself and by itself, it immediately comes to mind that it could not exist from itself except from that Creator.

And this which you have found in it is its voice of confession, so that you may praise the Creator. When you consider the whole beauty of this world, does not its very appearance answer you, as though with one voice: “I did not make myself, but God”?

14. [verse 11.] Therefore, “Let all your works confess to you, Lord, and let your saints bless you.” So that your saints may bless you in the confession of your works, let those same saints behold creation confessing. And hear the voice of those who bless you.

For when your saints bless you, what do they say? “They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom, and they shall tell of your power.”

How powerful is God, who made the earth! How powerful is God, who filled the earth with good things! How powerful is God, who gave animals their own lives! How powerful is God, who gave various seeds to the womb of the earth, so that they might produce such a variety of shrubs and such beauty of trees! How powerful is God, how great is God!

You question; creation answers. And from its answer, as from the confession of creation, you, holy one of God, bless God and speak of his power.

15. [verse 12.] “To make your power known to the children of men, and the glory of the magnificence of the beauty of your kingdom.”

Therefore your saints commend the glory of the magnificence of the beauty of your kingdom—the glory of the magnificence of its beauty. There is a certain magnificence of the beauty of your kingdom; that is, your kingdom possesses beauty, and great beauty. Since whatever possesses beauty has it from you, what beauty must your kingdom itself possess!

Let the kingdom not terrify us; it also has beauty with which we may be delighted. For what is the beauty with which the saints will be blessed, to whom it will be said, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV, 34)?

From where will they go? To where will they go? Observe, brothers, and, as much as you can, contemplate the beauty of that kingdom which is to come, for it is included in our prayer: “Your kingdom come” (Matt. VI, 10). We desire that kingdom itself to come; this is the kingdom that the saints proclaim.

Consider this world: it has beauty. What beauty the earth, the sea, the air, the sky, and the stars possess! Does all this not astonish every observer? Does its beauty not stand out in such a way that it seems that nothing more beautiful could be found?

And here, within this beauty, within this beauty that is almost ineffable, worms and mice and all the creeping things of the earth live with you; these too live with you amid this beauty.

What beauty must that kingdom have where none live with you except angels? Therefore it was not enough to say “the glory of beauty.” For one could also speak of the glory of the beauty of any form established in this world, whether of green things growing from the earth [Note: The Louvain edition reads “living,” contrary to the other editions and the manuscripts], or of things shining from heaven. But “the magnificence of the beauty of your kingdom” commends something that we do not yet see, which we believe without yet having seen, and which, once believed, we desire; for the sake of this desire we endure all things.

There is therefore a certain magnificence of beauty. Let it be loved before it is seen, so that when it has been seen it may be possessed.

16. [verse 13.] “Your kingdom.” What kingdom do I mean? “The kingdom of all ages.” The kingdom of this age also has its beauty; but it does not possess that magnificence of beauty which belongs to the kingdom of all ages.

“And your dominion is in every generation and generation.” This is that repetition, signifying either every generation or the generation that will exist after this generation.

17. “The Lord is faithful in his words, and holy in all his works.”

“The Lord is faithful in his words.” For what did he promise and not give? “The Lord is faithful in his words.” He has promised certain things that he has not yet given; but let him be believed on the basis of those things he has given.

“The Lord is faithful in his words.” We could believe him merely because he speaks; but he did not wish us to believe him only as one speaking. He wished us to hold fast to his Scripture, just as if you were to say to someone, when promising him something, “You do not believe me? Behold, I am writing it down for you.”

Since one generation departs and another comes, and the ages pass in this way as mortals yield place to those who succeed them, God’s Scripture had to remain—a kind of document of God that all who pass through this world might read and by which they might hold fast to the path of his promise [Note: Two manuscripts read “the force” rather than “the path.”].

How many things has he repaid from this document! Human beings hesitate to believe him concerning the resurrection of the dead and the future age, which alone now remains to be repaid. Yet if he should settle accounts with unbelievers, would not the unbelievers be ashamed?

If God says to you: “You hold my document. I promised judgment, the separation of good and evil, and an everlasting kingdom for the faithful, and you do not wish to believe? Read in my document everything I promised; settle accounts with me. Surely, by calculating what I have repaid, you can believe that I shall repay what I still owe.”

In that very document you have the promise of the only Son, whom I did not spare but handed over for all of you (Rom. VIII, 32). Now count that among the things repaid. Read the document: I promised there that through my Son I would give the pledge of the Holy Spirit. Count what has been repaid (Acts I, 8; II, 2–4).

I promised there the blood and crowns of the most glorious martyrs. Count what has been repaid; let the Massa [Note: Here the martyrs commonly called the Massa Candida are praised. We have discovered from a manuscript of Fleury that a sermon was delivered about them in their basilica near Utica. The same martyrs were discussed above in Psalm XLIX, no. 9. Compare Sermon 306 On Various Subjects, and Sermon 311, chapter 10, which calls them the “Utican White Mass”—Massa candida.] of my debt now repaid [Note: The editions had omitted “repaid”; we have restored it from several manuscripts] remind you of it.

But for this glory of the martyrs also to be repaid, it was promised to you in the document where it is written, “For your sake we are put to death all day long” (Ps. XLIII, 22). So that this might be repaid, “The nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things; the kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. II, 1–2). The rulers gathered together, conspiring against the Christians.

What then? Did I not also promise the faith of those very kings in the document, and repay it in its fulfillment? Notice where I promised it: “All the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. LXXI, 11; printed “Pasl.”). Ungrateful one, you read the debt, you see it repaid, and you do not believe the promise?

Read something else in my document: “For the nations raged”; “For my enemies spoke evil against me,” that is, against Christ: “When will he die, and his name perish?” (Ps. XL, 6). Because they did and said all these things, read what I promised, to which I bound myself as debtor: “The Lord will prevail against them, and he will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth; and they shall worship him, each one from his own place” (Zeph. II, 11).

Surely he has already prevailed; he has destroyed all the gods of the nations of the earth. Is he not also doing this, and repaying this? Before the eyes of all he displays the settlement of his debts. Some things he repaid in the time of our ancestors, which we did not see; some things he repaid in our time, which they did not see. Through every generation he has repaid what was written.

And what remains? Is he not believed after all these things have been repaid? What remains? Behold, you have settled the account; he has repaid so much. Has he become unfaithful because only a few things remain? Far be it! Why? Because “the Lord is faithful in his words, and holy in all his works.”

18. [verse 14.] “The Lord supports all who are falling.”

But whom does “all who are falling” mean? It means absolutely all who are falling, but falling in a certain way. For many fall away from him; but many “fall away from their own thoughts” (Ps. V, 11). If they had evil thoughts, they fall away from them, and the Lord supports all who are falling.

Those who lose something in this world and are holy—as though they are dishonored in this world; those who become poor from being rich, rejected from being honored, and yet remain holy people of God—are, as it were, falling. But the Lord supports all who are falling.

“For the righteous falls seven times and rises again; but the wicked shall be weakened by evils” (Prov. XXIV, 16). When evils befall the wicked, they are weakened by them; when evils befall the righteous, the Lord supports all who are falling.

Job had fallen from the former glory of the temporal goods by which he shone for a time; he had fallen from the glory of his household. Do you wish to know how far he had fallen? He sat on dung, and the Lord supported the one who had fallen.

How greatly did he support him? So greatly that, even in the grievous wound with which he had been struck throughout his body, he answered the wife who was tempting him—the only helper the devil had left him: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job II, 7–10). How firmly he had supported the one who was falling!
