“When the righteous falls,” he says, “he shall not be shaken, because the Lord supports his hand” (Ps. XXXVI, 24). “And he raises up all who have been crushed”—all who belong to him. For “God resists the proud” (James IV, 6).

19. [verse 15.] “The eyes of all hope in you, and you give them food in due season.”

It is just as when one restores a sick person at the proper time: when he ought to receive it, then you give; and you give what he ought to receive. Thus sometimes something is desired from him and he does not give it. The one who cares knows the hour for giving.

Why do I say this, brothers? So that no one, when he has perhaps not been heard by God while asking for something just—for when he asks for something unjust, he is heard to his own punishment—should lose heart or fail if, while asking for something not unjust, he is perhaps not heard. Let his eyes wait for the food that God gives in due season.

When he does not give, he does not give for this reason: lest what he gives should harm. For the Apostle was not asking for anything unjust when he begged that the thorn in his flesh, the angel of Satan by whom he was buffeted, be removed from him. Yet he asked and did not receive, because the time was still one for exercising weakness, not for food at the proper time.

“My grace is sufficient for you,” he said, “for power is perfected in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 7–9).

The devil asked that Job be put to the test, and received this (Job I, 9–12; II, 4–6). Attend, my brothers, to a great mystery—one to be learned, repeated, held in the mind, and never forgotten, because of the abundance of temptations in this world.

What shall I say? Is the Apostle really to be compared with the devil? The Apostle asks and does not receive; the devil asks and receives. But the Apostle did not receive for his perfection; the devil received for his condemnation.

Finally, Job himself received health at the proper time. It was delayed, however, so that he might be tested; he sat for a long time in his wound [Note: So the manuscripts. The editions read: “For he was delayed so that he might be tested, and he sat for a long time in the dust.”], and said many things. He asked God that these things be removed from him, and God did not remove them. He heard the devil more quickly when he sought permission to tempt Job than he heard Job himself when Job sought healing.

Learn, then, not to murmur against God; and when you are not heard, let what was written above not fail in you: “Every day I shall bless you.”

The Son himself, the only one [Note: So most manuscripts. The editions read “the only Son of the Father,” and so forth], had come to suffer, certainly to pay what he did not owe, to die in the hands of sinners, and with his blood to erase the document of our death. For this he had come. Yet, to show you an example of patience, he transformed “the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Phil. III, 21).

“Father,” he said, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” And, in order to fulfill “Every day I shall bless you,” although he did not receive what he seemed to be asking: “Nevertheless,” he said, “not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matt. XXVI, 39).

“The eyes of all hope in you, and you give them food in due season.”

20. [verse 16.] “You open your hand, and fill every living creature with blessing.”

Even if you do not give at some times, you nevertheless give at the proper time. You delay; you do not take away—and this at the proper time.

21. [verse 17.] “The Lord is righteous in all his ways.”

Both when he strikes and when he heals, he is righteous, and there is no iniquity with him. Finally, all the saints placed in tribulations first praised his righteousness, and then asked for his benefits.

First they said: “What you do is just.” Thus Daniel prayed, and so did the other saints: “Your judgments are just; we have suffered well, we have suffered rightly” (Dan. III, 27–31; IX, 5–19). They did not attribute injustice, iniquity, or folly to God. First they praised the one who scourged them, and so they experienced the one who fed them:

“The Lord is righteous in all his ways.”

Let no one think him unjust when he perhaps suffers something evil. Let him instead praise God’s righteousness and accuse his own injustice: “The Lord is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works.”

22. [verse 18.] The Lord is near to all who call upon him. And what of the statement, “For when they call upon me, I will not hear them” (Prov. 1:28)? Observe, then, what follows: “To all who call upon him in truth.” For many call upon him, but not in truth. They seek something else from him, and do not seek him himself.

[Col. 1883] Why do you love God? “Because he gave me health.” This is evident: he himself gave it, for no one has any salvation except from him. “Because,” he says, “he gave me a wealthy wife, when I had nothing, and one who serves me.” This too he himself gave; you speak truly. “He gave me children, many and good; he gave me a household; he gave me every good thing.” Is that why you love him? Is that why you seek nothing more? Be hungry; knock again at the householder’s door. He still has something to give. You are in poverty amid all these things you have received, and you do not know it. You still carry the ragged flesh of mortality. Have you received that robe of the glory of immortality, and, as though already satisfied, do you not ask for it? “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

Therefore, if God is good because he has given you these things, how much more blessed will you be when he has given you himself? You have desired so many things from him; I urge you, desire him also. For these things are not truly sweeter than he, nor can they be compared with him in any respect. Therefore, the person who places God himself—God from whom he received the things in which he rejoices—above all the things he has received, that person calls upon God in truth.

Now, so that you may understand: suppose it were proposed to such people and said, “What if God wished to take away from you all these things in which you rejoice?” Then God would no longer be loved. There would be no one to say, “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). But perhaps the one from whom he has taken them says, “God, what have I done to you? Why have you taken them from me and given them to those people? You give to the wicked and take away from your own.” [Note: Am. and nearly all manuscripts: “But perhaps, because he has taken them away, what does he say?”]

You accuse God as though he were unjust, and praise yourself as though you were just. Turn back: accuse yourself, praise him. Then you will be upright, when God pleases you in all the good things that he does for you [Note: Most manuscripts read, “the good things that you do”; Regius, “good things done”]; and when you suffer all evils, God does not displease you. This is to call upon God in truth.

Those who call upon the Lord in this way, he hears. He is near—that is, although he has not yet given what you want, he is nevertheless there [Note: Am., Er., and nearly all manuscripts read, “there he is.”]. It is like a physician who applies something to the eye or to the internal organs, something that heals by burning. If the sick person asks that it be removed, the physician waits for the proper time and does not do what the sick person asks; yet he does not go away. He is near, and does not do it; indeed, he does not do it precisely because he is near. He applied what he applied in order to heal, and in order to heal he does not do what he is asked.

He does not hear you with respect to your present desire, but by hearing you he attends to your future health; and this too is according to your will. For certainly even the person who does not wish to be burned wishes to be well. Therefore, “the Lord is near to all who call upon him.” But to which “all”? “To all who call upon him in truth.” He strengthens all such people who are falling, if they call upon him in truth.

23. [verse 19.] [Col. 1884] “He will do the will of those who fear him.” He will do it, he will do it: even if he does not do it at once, he will do it nevertheless. Certainly, if you fear God so that you may do his will, behold, he too in a certain sense serves you and does your will.

“And he will hear their prayers, and he will save them.” You see that the physician hears in order to save. When will this happen? Hear the Apostle say: “For in hope we have been saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25)—namely, the salvation that Peter says is “ready to be revealed in the last time” (1 Pet. 1:5).

24. [verse 20.] “The Lord guards all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners.” You see that there is severity with him in whom there is such great gentleness. He will save all who hope in him, all the faithful, all who fear him, all who call upon him in truth; and he will destroy all sinners.

Which sinners are these, except those who persist in their sins; who dare to blame God rather than themselves; who argue against God every day; who despair of the forgiveness of sins and, through that very despair, heap sin upon sin; or who perversely promise themselves forgiveness and, through that very promise, do not withdraw from sins and impiety?

The time will come when all these will be separated and will become two groups, one at the right hand and the other at the left. The righteous will receive the eternal kingdom; those others will go into the eternal fire (Matt. 25:32–33, 46): “And he will destroy all sinners.”

25. [verse 21.] Since these things are so, and we have heard of the Lord’s blessing, the Lord’s works, the Lord’s wonders, the Lord’s mercies, the Lord’s severity, his providence in all his works, and the confession of all his works, observe how the psalm concludes his praise: “My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 145

### SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. The delights of our spirit are the divine songs, in which even weeping is not without joy. For the faithful person and the pilgrim in this world, no remembrance is more pleasant than that of the city from which he is journeying; yet remembrance of the city during pilgrimage is not without pain and sighing. Nevertheless, the sure hope of our return consoles and encourages us even when we are saddened by our pilgrimage.

Let the words of God seize your hearts [Note: Am. and the manuscripts read, “Let the word of God seize your heart”], and let your possessor claim his possession for himself—that is, your minds—so that they may not be turned elsewhere. Let each one of you be wholly here in such a way that he may not be here; that is, let him be wholly in the word of God, which sounds upon earth so that he may be raised up by it and may not remain upon earth.

For this reason God is with us, so that we too may be with him. He who descended to us in order to be with us brings it about that we ascend to him so that we may be with him [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “so that we may be able to ascend to him with him.”]. Meanwhile, he himself did not disdain our pilgrimage, since the one who established all things is nowhere a pilgrim.

2. [verses 2–3.] Behold, the Psalm sounds forth. It is the voice of someone which, if you wish, is your voice: he encourages his soul to praise God and says to it, “Praise the Lord, my soul.” For sometimes, amid the tribulations and temptations of the present life, whether it wishes to or not, the soul is thrown into confusion. In another psalm he addresses its disturbance, saying, “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” But in order to remove that same [Col. 1885] disturbance from it, he suggests joy—not yet joy from possession, but from hope—and says to the troubled, anxious, sad, and grieving soul: “Hope in the Lord, for I shall yet confess him” (Ps. 42:5).

He establishes the hope by which he has raised himself up in confession, as though his soul, which was troubling him with sadness, were saying to him: “What do you mean by telling me, ‘Hope in the Lord’? My conscience recalls my sins; I know what I have committed, and you tell me, ‘Hope in the Lord’?” You have committed them; that is true. On what basis, then, do you hope? “Because I shall confess to him.” Just as God hates the person who defends his sins, so he raises up the person who confesses them.

Having therefore received this hope—which cannot exist without joy—although we are in difficult circumstances according to this life, full of storms and tempests, the soul is nevertheless raised up by this hope, because it rejoices in hope, as the Apostle says, “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12). It has received a certain elevation toward God, so that it may praise God, and it is told, “Praise the Lord, my soul.”

3. But who speaks, and to whom does he speak? What shall we say, brothers? Is the flesh saying, “Praise the Lord, my soul”? Can the flesh offer good counsel to the soul? Even if the flesh is thoroughly subdued and, through strength bestowed by the Lord, is subjected to our service, so that it serves us entirely like a slave under contract, it is enough if it does not hinder us.

Moreover, beloved, counsel is always sought from those who are better. And if our soul is something good, and our flesh is something good, because both were created by the one who made all things “very good” (Gen. 1:31), nevertheless the Apostle says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin.” There is also that body which is promised to us and which we do not yet possess, in whose redemption we rejoice in hope, as the Apostle says: “Within ourselves we groan, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body. For in hope we have been saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:10, 23–25).

Although, therefore, our body is in some respect good, yet as long as it is mortal because of sin, as long as it is needy, as long as it is corruptible, as long as it is so changeable that it does not remain in itself even for a moment, it is undoubtedly such that we desire its redemption, by which it may at some time cease to be such. But what will it eventually be like? The same Apostle says elsewhere: “This corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53).

But even when our body has become such—a heavenly and spiritual body, an angelic body in the fellowship of the angels—it will still not give counsel to the soul. For the body, precisely because it is body, is always beneath the soul; and any soul, however lowly, is found to be superior to the most excellent body.

4. [Col. 1886] Nor should this seem marvelous to you, since even any lowly, sinful soul is better than any great and most excellent body. It is not better in merit, but by nature. The sinful soul is indeed stained by certain filthy desires; nevertheless, even dirty gold is better than the purest lead.

Let your mind run through all creatures [Note: The manuscripts read, “through all things of creation”], and you will see that what we are saying is not incredible: although the soul may be blameworthy, it is nevertheless more praiseworthy than a praiseworthy body.

There are two things: soul and body. I blame the soul; I praise the body. I blame the soul because it is unjust; I praise the body because it is healthy. Yet within its own kind I praise the soul, or within its own kind I blame the soul; and within its own kind I praise the body, or within its own kind I blame it.

If you ask me which is better, the thing I blamed or the thing I praised, you are going to receive a surprising answer. I certainly blamed the one and praised the other; yet, when asked which is better, I answer that the thing I blamed is better than the thing I praised.

If you are surprised by these two, consider the two things I mentioned that are readily at hand: gold and lead. Behold, I blamed the gold: the gold is not good, it is dirty, it does not shine as it should, it is not sufficiently purified. This lead is excellent, nothing is more purified. I blamed one and praised the other, and placed both before you, blaming one and praising the other. After my blaming and praising, ask me which of the two is better. I shall answer: even dirty gold is better than purified lead.

Why is it better, and why did you blame it? Why did I blame it? Because it is not yet the gold that it can be. What can it be? Purified and better. Because it is not yet purified, it was blamed. Why was the lead praised? Because it has already been so purified that it cannot be better.

Similarly, you say that one horse is excellent and one person is worthless; yet, after praising the horse, you place the blamed person above it. For if you are asked which of these two is better, you will answer, “The person”—not by merit, but by nature.

In the arts, for example, you call one person an excellent shoemaker and criticize a jurist because he is ignorant of many laws. You praised the shoemaker and criticized the jurist; nevertheless, ask which of these two is better. The less knowledgeable jurist is preferred to the perfect shoemaker.

Let your Charity attend. Thus, after praising many things and blaming others, when questioned we often prefer the things we blamed to the things we praised.

The nature of the soul is more excellent than the nature of the body; it surpasses it greatly. It is a spiritual thing, an incorporeal thing, near to the substance of God. It is something invisible; it governs the body, moves the limbs, directs the senses, prepares thoughts, brings actions forth, and receives images of countless things. And who, finally, beloved brothers, is sufficient for praising the soul?

And if one falls short in praising the soul, what praise can be sufficient for the one who created the soul? Yet his grace is so great that this person says, “Praise the Lord, my soul.” Who can praise God? If he had said, “Praise yourself,” perhaps he would have fallen short. “Praise God,” he says. Try with a devout affection, and you will fall short in his praises. It is better for you to fall short while praising God than to advance while praising yourself. For when you praise God and cannot express what you wish, your thought is extended inward [Note: Am. and several manuscripts read “forward” (in anteriora)]; that very extension makes you more capable of the one whom you praise.

5. [Col. 1887] Who, then, as I had begun to say, is it that says, “Praise the Lord, my soul”? The flesh does not say it. Even if it were an angelic body, it would be inferior to the soul and could not give counsel to what is superior. The soul itself is miserable if it expects counsel from the body.

The flesh, when it obeys well, is the soul’s servant: the soul rules, and the flesh is ruled; the soul commands, and the flesh serves. When, then, can the flesh give this counsel to the soul?

Who, then, is it that says, “Praise the Lord, my soul”? We find nothing more in a human being than flesh and soul; the whole human being is this: spirit and flesh.

Or perhaps the soul itself speaks to itself, in a certain way commands itself, and encourages and arouses itself? For in certain disturbances it was flowing away through one part of itself; but through another part, which they call the rational mind—the part by which it thinks wisdom—already clinging to the Lord and sighing toward him, it noticed that certain lower parts of itself were being disturbed by worldly movements and, through a certain desire for earthly things, were going outward and abandoning the God within.

It calls itself back from outward things to inward things, from lower things to higher things, and says, “Praise the Lord, my soul.”

What pleases you in the world? What is it that you wish to praise? What is it that you wish to love? Wherever you turn through bodily senses, heaven confronts you, earth confronts you. Whatever you love on earth is earthly; whatever you love in heaven is corporeal. Everywhere you love, and everywhere you praise. How, then, should the one who made the things you praise be praised?

You have therefore lived long occupied with such things, beaten by the variety of your desires. You carry wounds, wounded [Note: Lugdunensis and Venetus read: “you carry the wounds of desires, wounded.” M.], divided among many loves, restless everywhere and secure nowhere. Gather yourself back to yourself [Note: Erasmus thus reads this passage: “Gather to yourself whatever pleased you outside; seek what author it has.” M.]. Whatever pleased you outwardly, seek to know who its author is.

There is nothing better on earth, for example, than this or that: gold, silver, animals, trees, pleasant places. Consider the whole earth. What is better in heaven than the sun, the moon, and the stars? Consider the whole heaven. All these things together are very good, because God made all things very good. Everywhere there is the beauty of the work, which commends the craftsman to you. You marvel at the structure; love the builder. Do not become occupied with what has been made and withdraw from the one who made it.

For he made these things with which you are occupied beneath you, because he made you beneath himself. If you cling to what is above, you will tread upon what is below; but if you withdraw from what is above, these things will be turned into punishment for you.

For this is how it happened, my brothers: the human being received a body as a servant, while having God as Lord; he had a servant body above which was the Creator, and beneath him that which had been created by the Creator. The rational soul was established in an intermediate position and received the law of clinging to what is above and ruling what is below.

It cannot rule what is below unless it is ruled by what is better. It is dragged by what is below and has therefore abandoned what is better. It cannot rule what it used to rule, because it refused to be ruled by the one by whom it was ruled.

Let it return now and praise. Through the rational mind, the soul itself receives counsel from the light of God, and from that light conceives a fixed counsel in the eternity of its Creator. There it reads something to be feared, praised, loved, desired, and sought. It does not yet possess it; it does not yet grasp it. It is struck by a certain flash, but it is not strong enough to remain there. And so it gathers itself toward a kind of health and says, “Praise the Lord, my soul.”

6. [Col. 1888] And what of it, brothers? Do we not praise the Lord? Do we not sing a hymn every day [Note: Some manuscripts read, “We do not sing every day.” Others read, “We sing a hymn.” Still others have, “We sing hymns.”]? Does not our mouth sound forth, according to our limited capacity, every day, and does not our heart give birth to the praises of God?

And what is it that we praise? The one we praise is great; but the one who praises is still weak. When does the praiser fulfill the excellence of the one praised?

Behold, a person stands and sings to God at somewhat greater length, and often his lips move in song while his thought flies off toward who knows what desires. Our mind was standing, in a certain way, in praise of God, while our soul was flowing here and there through various desires or the cares of business.

The mind itself, as though looking down from above upon the soul flowing here and there, addresses its restless distress as though turning toward it: “Praise the Lord, my soul.” What is it that makes you anxious about other things? What is it that occupies you—the care of earthly and mortal things? Stand with me; praise the Lord.

And as though the soul, weighed down and unable to stand as it ought, responds to the mind: “I will praise the Lord in my life.” What does “in my life” mean? Because at present I am in my death.

First, then, encourage yourself and say, “Praise the Lord, my soul.” Your soul answers you: “I praise him as much as I can—faintly, feebly, weakly.” Why? “Because while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6).

Why do you praise the Lord in this way—not perfectly, not steadily? Ask Scripture: “Because the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15).

Take away from me the body that weighs down my soul, and I praise the Lord. Take away from me the earthly dwelling that presses down the mind that thinks of many things, so that I may flow from many things into one, and I praise the Lord. But as long as I am thus, I cannot; I am weighed down.

What, then? Will you be silent and not praise the Lord perfectly? “I will praise the Lord in my life.”

7. [Col. 1889] What does “in my life” mean? “You are my hope here.” We say, “You are my hope here”; but my portion is not here, but “in the land of the living” (Ps. 142:6).

For this earth is the land of the dying. We pass from here, but where we go matters. The wicked person also journeys here, and the good person journeys here. It is not that the good person passes away while the wicked remains here, or that the wicked passes away while the good remains here. Both pass away, but they do not both go to the same place.

There were two people: a poor man covered with sores, lying at the gate of a rich man, and a rich man clothed in purple and fine linen, feasting splendidly every day. Both were here; both passed from here, but not to the same place. Different places receive them, because different merits lead them there.

The poor man passed into Abraham’s bosom, and the rich man passed into the torments of hell. They had been neighbors in body on earth: one inside the house, the other before the gate. After death they were so separated that Abraham says, “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed” (Luke 16:19–26).

Therefore, brothers, since hope feeds us here, and our life is not perfect except in that life which is promised—here there are groaning, temptations, distress, grief, and dangers—our soul will praise the Lord as he ought to be praised, according to what is said in another psalm: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 84:5), when our entire occupation will itself be praise.

But when will this happen? “In my life.” For what is the present life? It could say to you, “My death.” Why is it your death? Because I am away from the Lord. For if clinging to him is life, withdrawing from him is death.

But what consoles you? Hope. You already live in hope. Praise from hope; sing from hope. Do not sing from that which is your death; sing from that by which you live. Your death is the grief of this age; you live in the hope of the age to come. “I will praise,” he says, “the Lord in my life.”

8. And how will you praise your Lord? “I will sing to my God as long as I am.” What sort of praise is this: “I will sing to my God as long as I am”? Observe, my brothers, what that existence will be like. Where praise will be eternal, existence will be eternal.

Behold, now you exist. Do you sing to your God as long as you exist? Behold, you were singing; you turned your attention to some business, and you no longer sing, yet you exist. Behold, you exist and do not sing. Perhaps, having been bent toward something by desire, you not only do not sing but also offend his hearing; and yet you exist.

What will that praise be like where, as long as you exist, you praise? But what does “as long as I am” mean? Will there perhaps be a time when he is not? No. That “long” itself will be eternal, and therefore it will truly be long. For whatever has an end in time, however long it may be, is not truly long. “I will sing to my God as long as I am.”

9. Meanwhile, it is good: you will praise the Lord in your life; you will sing to your future God as long as you are. Good. Whatever is to be hoped for here, hope for from him. Let hope not abandon us in this pilgrimage and temptation, amid these wickednesses and ambushes of the enemy, with the temptations of the world resounding all around us, while we are placed everywhere amid labors and anguish.

What, then, shall we do? Hear what follows: “Do not put your trust in princes.”

Brothers, we are undertaking a great matter here. It is a divine voice, and it sounds down to us from above. For now, through some weakness of the human soul, when it has been troubled, it despairs of the Lord here and wishes to place its confidence in a human being.

Suppose someone in distress is told, “There is a certain great man through whom you can be delivered.” He smiles, rejoices, and is lifted up. But if he is told, “God delivers you,” he grows cold, as though in despair. Mortal help is promised, and you rejoice; immortal help is promised, and you are sad! You are promised that the one who is himself to be delivered will deliver you, and you exult as though at some great assistance; the Deliverer who needs no deliverer is promised, and you despair as though it were a mere tale.

Woe to such thoughts: they are wandering far away [Note: Several manuscripts read: “he is wandering far away.”]. Truly, a miserable and great death exists in them. Draw near; begin to desire, begin to seek and recognize the one by whom you were made. For he will not abandon his work if his work does not abandon him.

Turn, then, toward the one to whom you say, “I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing to my God as long as I am.” [Col. 1890] Filled with such a great spirit, the Psalmist now admonishes us and speaks as though to those who are far removed, to those who are journeying far away, and not only do not wish to praise God but do not yet even hope in God: “Do not put your trust in princes, nor in the sons of human beings, in whom there is no salvation” [Note: The editions read, “in whom.” The particle “in” is absent from the Septuagint and from the manuscripts, although below, at the third occurrence, they agree with the editions and have “from whom.”].

There is salvation in one Son of Man; and in him salvation exists not because he is the son of man, but because he is the Son of God—not on account of what he assumed from you, but on account of what he preserved in himself.

Therefore, there is salvation in no human being. In him, too, salvation exists because he is God, who is “God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. 9:5).

It was said of Christ: “From whom is Christ according to the flesh” (Rom. 9:5). From whom? From the Jews, from the patriarchs, Christ according to the flesh. But is Christ wholly what he is according to the flesh? No. For he is not, according to the flesh, “God over all, blessed for ever.” Therefore, salvation is in him because salvation belongs to the Lord.

Another psalm says: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Ps. 3:9). And people claim for themselves, without justification, that they give salvation. Let them give it to themselves. Say to the proud person: “You boast because you say that you give me salvation; give it to yourself. See whether you possess it.”

Considering your weakness properly, you see that you do not yet possess it. Therefore, do not urge me to expect it from you; expect it together with me. “Do not put your trust in princes, nor in the sons of human beings, in whom there is no salvation.”

Behold, certain princes come forward from who knows where and say: “I baptize, and what I give is holy; if you receive it from someone else, you have received nothing; if you receive it from me, you have received something.”

O human being, O prince, do you wish to be among the sons of human beings and among those princes in whom there is no salvation? Therefore, do I have salvation because you give it to me? For what you give is yours? Or do you in fact give it? Or should this even be said—that you give it?

Let the pipe also say that it gives water; let the channel also say that it itself flows; let the herald also say that he himself delivers. In the water I look for the fountain; in the voice of the herald I recognize the judge. You certainly will not be the author of my salvation. He will be, in whom I am secure; concerning you I am uncertain.

If you are not arrogant, I alone am not uncertain about you—you yourself are uncertain about yourself. Therefore, salvation comes to me from the one who is over all, because salvation belongs to the Lord.

You are among the sons of human beings; you are among the princes. But I hear the voice of the Psalm: “Do not put your trust in princes, nor in the sons of human beings, from whom there is no salvation.”

10. [verse 4.] [Col. 1891] According to the common condition of human beings, what are these sons of human beings? Do you want to know what they are? “His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth.”

Behold, all that he says, not knowing how long he will speak; he threatens, not knowing how long he will live. Suddenly his spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth. Does his spirit go forth when he wishes? It will go forth; it will go forth even when he does not wish it, and when he does not know it, he will return to his earth.

When the spirit goes forth, the flesh will return to the earth. But because it was flesh that was speaking in this way—“Rely on me, and I will give it to you”; they would not say this except those of whom it is said, “Because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3)—“his spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth; on that day all his thoughts will perish” [Note: Some manuscripts read “their thoughts.”].

Where is his arrogance? Where is his pride? Where is his boasting?

But perhaps he has passed to a good place, to the righteous—if indeed he has passed there. For I do not know where the one who spoke in this way has gone. Pride was speaking, and I do not know where such people go, except that I look at another psalm and see that their passing is evil: “I saw the wicked exalted like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 37:35–36).

The devout person who passed by and did not find the wicked reached the place where the wicked person is not.

Therefore, brothers, let us all hear; beloved brothers of God, let us all hear: in whatever tribulation, in whatever desire for a divine gift, let us not trust in princes, nor in the sons of human beings, in whom there is no salvation. All this is mortal, transitory, and fleeting. “His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth; on that day all his thoughts will perish.”

11. [verse 5.] What, then, shall we do, if we must not hope in the sons of human beings or in princes? What shall we do? “Blessed is he whose God is the God of Jacob, his helper.”

Not this person or that person, not this angel or that angel, but “Blessed is he whose God is the God of Jacob, his helper.” For he was Jacob’s helper in such a way that he made Israel out of Jacob (Gen. 32:28). A great help: Israel now sees God.

Therefore, if you are placed here as a pilgrim, not yet seeing God, and you have the God of Jacob as your helper, you will become Israel from Jacob, and you will be one who sees God. Every labor and every groaning will pass away; biting cares will pass away; joyful praises will follow.

“Blessed is he whose God is the God of Jacob, his helper”—the God of this Jacob. Why is he blessed, while still groaning in this life? “His hope is in the Lord his God.” He is blessed for this reason: his hope is in the Lord his God. The one in whom his hope lies will himself be his possession.

Brothers, have I perhaps made a mistake by saying that God will be our possession? What if I had said that he would be our inheritance? “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. 142:6). You will be my portion.

You will be the possession, and you will possess; you will be God’s possession, and God will be your possession. You will be his possession so that you may be cultivated by him; and he will be your possession so that you may cultivate him. For you cultivate God, and you are cultivated by God.

It is rightly said, “I cultivate God.” But how am I cultivated by God? We find this in the Apostle: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Cor. 3:9). And the Lord says, “I am the vine; you are the branches, and my Father is the cultivator” (John 15:1, 5).

God therefore cultivates you so that you may be fruitful, and you cultivate God so that you may be fruitful. It is good for you that God cultivates you; it is good for you that you cultivate God. If God, the cultivator, withdraws from a human being, the human being becomes abandoned; if the human being, the cultivator, withdraws from God, that same human being becomes abandoned.

God does not grow by your approach, nor diminish by your departure. Therefore, he will be our possession so that he may feed us, and we will be his possession so that he may govern us.

12. [verse 6.] [Col. 1892] “His hope is in the Lord his God.” Who is this Lord his God? Attend, brothers. Many people have many gods and call them their lords and their gods. But the Apostle says: “Although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:5–6).

Therefore, let him be your hope, the Lord your God; let your hope be in him. The hope even of the one who worships Saturn is in his lord and god; the hope of the one who worships Mars is in his lord and god, as is that of the one who worships Neptune and the one who worships Mercury. I add still more: the one who worships his belly, of whom it is said, “Their god is their belly” (Phil. 3:19).

Therefore, this is that person’s god, and that is the other’s god. Whose God is the God of this blessed person? “Because his hope is in the Lord his God.” But who is this? “The one who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them.”

My brothers, we have a great God! Let us bless his holy name, because he has deigned to make us his possession.

You do not yet see God; you cannot love fully what you do not yet see. The things you see, he himself made. You marvel at the world; why do you not seek the world’s craftsman [Note: Several manuscripts read: “seek the craftsman of the world”]? You look up at heaven and are awestruck; you consider the whole earth and tremble; when you occupy your thought with the vastness of the sea—what then? [Note: The editions read “when you occupy your thought”; the manuscripts, “when you occupy your thought” (cogitatione).]

Consider the countless stars; consider the many kinds of seeds, the many varieties of animals—whatever swims in the waters, crawls upon the earth, flies through the air, circles in the heavens. All these things: how great, how splendid, how beautiful, how astonishing!

Behold, the one who made all these things is your God. Place your hope in him so that you may be blessed: “His hope is in the Lord his God.” Whom? “The one who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them.” We have a great God!

13. [Col. 1893] Attend, brothers, to the great and good God who makes such things. What, then, did God have in mind when he made—if it is permissible to speak of God in terms of “having in mind”—heaven, earth, the sea, and all that is in them?

Perhaps this person might say: “I certainly see all these great things: God made heaven and earth and the sea. When does God count me among the things he made? Do I really belong to his care? Is God thinking about me now, or does he even know whether I am alive?”

What are you saying? Let no evil thought creep into your heart. Be one of those about whom we were speaking shortly before: “I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing to my God as long as I am.”

But this person addresses others, I do not know whom—some lukewarm people whom he encourages—and he is, as it were, afraid that they may despair of themselves because they are not included in God’s reckoning. For many people have thoughts of this kind.

But for this reason they abandon God and proceed through every kind of sin: because they do not believe that God cares what they do. Hear the divine utterances; do not despair of yourself. The one who took care to make you—does he not take care to restore you?

Is it not your God who made heaven, earth, and the sea? If he said only these things, perhaps you would answer: “The God who made heaven, earth, and the sea is a great God; but does he think about me?”

“It is he who made you,” you would be told. “How? Am I heaven, or am I earth, or am I the sea?”

It is indeed clear that I am neither heaven, nor earth, nor the sea; but I am on the earth. At least you grant me this, that you are on the earth. Hear that God made not only heaven, earth, and the sea: “For he made heaven, earth, and the sea, and all that is in them.”

If, then, he made all that is in them, he made you as well. I say too little when I say “you”: he made the sparrow, the locust, the little worm. There is nothing that he did not make, and he cares for everything.

His care is not expressed as a commandment, for he gave the commandment only to the human being. The Psalm says: “You will save human beings and animals, Lord, according to the abundance of your mercy” (Ps. 36:7–8).

“According to the abundance,” he says, “of your mercy: according to this you will save human beings and animals.”

And the Apostle says: “Does God care about oxen?” Here we have, “God does not care about oxen”; there we have, “You will save human beings and animals, Lord.” Are these statements contradictory?

What, then, does the Apostle say? “Does it pertain to God?” Where there is the commandment, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing” (1 Cor. 9:9; Deut. 25:4), did God not think about oxen? Thus, he wished certain oxen to be signified.

For God’s concern is not to instruct you about what you should do with oxen; human nature itself possesses this knowledge. The human being was made in such a way as to know how to provide for his animals. He did not receive commandments from God about this; rather, God implanted this understanding in his mind, so that he could do it even without a commandment. God made him such.

But just as he rules his animal, he himself must be ruled by another. From the one by whom he is ruled, he received a commandment. Therefore, with respect to the wording of the commandment, God is not concerned with oxen; but with respect to the providence of the universe by which he created all things and governs the world: “You will save human beings and animals, Lord.”

## 14. Let Your Charity Attend

Here perhaps someone may say to me [Note: [Col. 1893] The Manichaeans are indicated here.]: “It is from the New Testament, because it says, ‘God is not concerned about oxen’; but ‘You will save human beings and beasts, O Lord,’ is from the Old Testament.” There are people who slander these matters and say that the two Testaments do not agree with one another. Lest one Testament say one thing and the other something else, and lest he demand from me a statement from the New Testament corresponding to this one—“You will save human beings and beasts, O Lord”—what shall I do? Nothing stands at the head of the New Testament more prominently than the Gospel. In the Gospel I find that all these things pertain to God, and no one will now contradict this. For surely the Apostle will not be contrary to the Gospel. Let us hear the Lord himself, the prince and teacher of the Apostles. “Look,” he says, “at the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns; and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matt. 6:26). Therefore, apart from human beings, these animals too belong to God’s care—to be fed, not to receive a law. Thus, insofar as the giving of a law is concerned, God is not concerned about oxen; but insofar as creating, feeding, governing, and directing are concerned, everything belongs to God.

“Are not two sparrows sold for an assarius” (the Lord Jesus Christ says), “and not one of them will fall to the ground without the will of your Father” [Col. 1894]? “How much more valuable are you than they?” Therefore, do not say, “I do not belong to God.” Your soul belongs to God; your body belongs to God, because God made both your soul and your body. Perhaps you say, “God does not count me among the great multitude.” Here the Gospel adds something marvelous: “All the hairs of your head are numbered” (Matt. 10:29–31).

## 15. [Verses 7–8]

Therefore my God is he, and in him is my hope, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them. But as far as I am concerned, what does he do for me? “He keeps truth forever.” He has commended God both to be loved and to be feared. “He keeps truth forever.” What truth does he keep forever, and in whom does he keep truth? “He executes judgment for those who suffer wrong.” He vindicates those who suffer wrong, my brothers; he executes judgment for them. For whom? For those who suffer wrong, punishing all who do wrong. If, then, he will favor those who suffer wrong and punish those who do wrong, consider now to which group you wish to belong. Consider and pay attention whether you wish to be among those who suffer wrong or among those who inflict wrong.

At once the apostolic voice comes forward to you and says: “It is already altogether a fault in you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer wrong?” (1 Cor. 6:7). He rebukes people because they do not suffer wrong. He does not exhort you to suffer inconvenience, but to suffer wrong; for not every inconvenience is a wrong. Whatever you suffer justly is not a wrong.

Perhaps you might say, “I too am counted among those who have suffered wrong; for I suffered this in that place, and that in that case.” Consider whether you have suffered wrong. Robbers suffer many things, but not wrong; criminals, evildoers, burglars, adulterers, and seducers all suffer many evils, but there is no wrong in it. It is one thing to suffer wrong and another to suffer tribulation, punishment, hardship, or penalty. Consider where you are; look at what you have done; look at why you suffer—and there you will see what you suffer.

Right and wrong are opposites. Right is what is just. Yet not everything called “right” is right. What if someone establishes an unjust law? It should not be called right if it is unjust. True right, therefore, is what is also just. Consider what you have done, not what you suffer. If you have done right, you suffer wrong; if you have done wrong, you suffer what is right.

## 16.

Why have I said these things, brothers [Note: [Col. 1894] Against the Donatists.]? So that heretics may not exalt themselves when perhaps they suffer something as a result of the commands of earthly rulers; so that they may not count themselves among those who suffer wrong and say, “Behold, the Psalm consoles me: for I worship the God who will execute judgment for those who suffer wrong.”

I rightly ask whether you suffer wrong. If you have done right, what you suffer is wrong. Is it right to exsufflate Christ? Is it right, in rebellious pride, to erect an altar? Is it right, while sparing the persecutors of Christ’s tunic (John 19:24), to tear apart Christ’s Church? [Note: [Col. 1894] Most manuscripts read: “If it is right to exsufflate Christ; if it is right in rebellious pride to erect an altar; if it is right, while sparing the persecutors of Christ’s tunic (John 19:24), to tear apart Christ’s Church.”] If this is not right, then whatever you suffer on account of it is right. You are not, therefore, among those who suffer wrong.

I read something still clearer from the Gospel: “Blessed,” it says, “are those who suffer persecution.” Wait: why are you hurrying? Why do you say, “I am one of them”? Wait, I say; I shall read the whole passage. You have heard, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution”; already you had begun to claim something for yourself. If you permit me, I shall read the whole passage; see what follows: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness” (Matt. 5:10). Now say, “I am one of them.” If you dare to say, “I am one of them,” let us reconsider what I said above—or, to avoid length, I ask you only this: if you condemned one person whose case you did not know, would you dare say that you upheld justice? Or, if you suffered something on account of this, would you call it wrong? You raise yourself upon the rash tribunal of your heart, from which you will be thrown down, and you dare to pass judgment on a person whose case you do not know! If you did this concerning one person, you would be unjust; you do it concerning the whole world, and you are just?

Dearest brothers, what is it that suffers wrong except the Catholic Church, which endures so many such things? Amid so many scandals of heretics she groans; she sees the weak snatched from her bosom through evil persuasions and deceits, little ones dragged through I know not what hidden places and evil caves, rebaptized, with Christ exsufflated in them, and in them that part of their life killed which is not mortal—the part by which they were to live forever.

A man is persuaded to say, “I am not a Christian,” and this is called justice. “You are going to approach the bishop,” he tells him; “be careful not to say that you are a Christian. For if you say that you are a Christian, you will not receive what you seek; but in order to receive it, say that you are not one.” What are you advising, Christian? What are you teaching? Certainly you are suffering persecution. [Note: [Col. 1895] At this point Erasmus and Lovaniensis add, “all the more truly do you suffer persecution,” which is absent from the Amerbach edition and the manuscripts.] But how much more truly are you a persecutor! When emperors persecuted Christians, they compelled them by threats to do what you accomplish by persuasion. You persuade a Christian to deny that he is a Christian; what you accomplish by persuasion, a persecutor did not accomplish by killing.

Under your influence a man lives who denies that he is a Christian. He denies it—and lives? He has already lost his life; a corpse speaks to you. The one struck by the persecutor’s sword fell—and lives; the one to whom you speak stands—and has fallen. When you do these things, will whatever you suffer be wrong? I do not wish to flatter you: if all the things you do are unjust, whatever you suffer will be just. And for whom does he execute judgment, he who keeps truth forever? For those who suffer wrong.

## 17. [Verses 7–8]

Now come forward and bring out those good, apparently sharp and subtle arguments of yours, and say: “You feed; can a hungry man feed? That is, can a sinner give what is holy? Can a hungry man feed? Can one who is sick heal? Can one who is bound release?” These are the supposedly great and subtle arguments by which they deceive the inexperienced.

Let this Psalm close their mouths: “Giving food to the hungry” [Note: [Col. 1895] The editions have *dat*, “gives.” But the manuscripts have *dantem*, “giving,” in agreement with the Greek; this also corresponds to the earlier part of the verse, “executing judgment,” and so forth.]. Behold, I expect nothing from you; God gives food to the hungry. To which hungry people? To all. What does “all” mean? He himself gives food to all animals and all human beings; does he reserve no food for his beloved? If they have another hunger, they also have another food. Let us first seek their hunger, and we shall find their food: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (ibid., 6).

We must be God’s hungry ones. Before the sight of his door, let us beg in prayers; he himself gives food to the hungry. Why do you boast, heretic, that you release, raise up, and enlighten? Surely because you have already been released, stand upright, and are light? Far from it. Pay attention to what came before: “Do not put your trust in princes or in the sons of men, from whom there is no salvation.” They do not give salvation.

Therefore let the heretics withdraw from the midst. “The Lord releases those in chains; the Lord raises up those who have been cast down; the Lord makes the blind wise”—that is, he makes wise those who are blind. By this statement he has most excellently explained all the preceding statements. Lest, when he said, “The Lord releases those in chains,” we should refer this to those bound who perhaps are fastened with iron by their masters because of some offense, when he said, “He raises up those who have been cast down,” someone might come to mind who has stumbled and fallen, or fallen from a horse. There is another kind of fall and another kind of chain, just as there are other kinds of darkness and another kind of light.

When he said, “He makes the blind wise,” he did not wish to say, “He enlightens the blind,” lest you should understand this carnally, as when the Lord enlightened the man whose eyes he anointed with mud made from spittle and restored him to health (John 9:6–7). Lest you expect something of that sort, when he speaks of spiritual matters he shows a certain light of wisdom by which the blind are enlightened. Thus, just as the blind are enlightened by the light of wisdom, so those in chains are released and those cast down are raised up.

From what, then, are we bound? From what have we been cast down? Our body was our ornament; we sinned, and from it we received our chains. What are our chains? Mortality itself. Hear the Apostle Paul, for he too was still bound in this pilgrimage. How much this bound man traveled! His chains were not burdensome to him; with those very chains he preached the Gospel throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 1896] Some manuscripts have “throughout the whole world” in the singular form.]. The spirit of love carried away his chains and went as far as it could. Yet what does he say? “Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ.” What does “to depart” mean? To be released from the chains of mortality [Note: [Col. 1896] Lovaniensis adds “to be released.”]. And yet, out of mercy, he still wished to remain in chains for the sake of other people in chains, whom he might serve: “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:23–24).

The Lord, therefore, releases those in chains—that is, he makes mortals immortal. The Lord raises up those who have been cast down. Why were they cast down? Because they had stood upright. Why are they raised up? Because they had been humbled. Adam fell and was cast down; he fell, and Christ descended. Why did he who did not fall descend, except to raise up the one who fell? The Lord makes the blind wise; the Lord loves the just. Therefore he executes judgment for those who suffer wrong.

## 18. [Verse 9]

And who are these just people? In what sense are they just? As you have it: “The Lord watches over proselytes.” Proselytes are newcomers. The whole Church of the Gentiles is a proselyte. It is an outsider in relation to the patriarchs, not born from their flesh but made a daughter by imitation [Note: [Col. 1896] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition have “by imitating faith.”].

Nevertheless, the Lord watches over it, not some human being. “He will receive the orphan and the widow.” Let no one suppose that he receives an orphan because of an inheritance, or a widow because of I know not what personal business. God certainly helps these people too, and in all the duties of human society does good by caring for the orphan [Note: [Col. 1897] Thus the manuscripts; the editions have “consoling the orphan.”] and not abandoning the widow. But in a certain sense we are all orphans, with our father absent, though not dead. Among human beings, a person becomes an orphan when his father has died. And if you seek the truth, brothers, since the soul does not die, our parents are alive; and those who are orphans are more truly orphans because their fathers are absent. If they were evil, they live in punishments; if they were good, they live in rest [Note: [Col. 1897] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have: “With our fathers absent, we are orphans. Those who are orphans, if they have been evil, live in punishments; if they have been good, and so forth.”]. Everything remains intact for the Creator.

Nevertheless, as long as we are in this body and inhabit the place of pilgrimage, our Father is absent—to him we cry, “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). Therefore the Church is a widow, as though her bridegroom and husband were absent. He will come, the one who now protects her, unseen but desired. We are seized by great longing, and we desire the one whom we do not see [Note: [Col. 1897] Erasmus and several manuscripts have “in love of the one whom we do not know”; Erasmus has “in love of the one whom we do not know.” Shortly afterward Erasmus and the Lovaniensis edition have “with embraces seen, if not yet seen”; other manuscripts, more appropriately, have “seen.”]. We shall cling to the embraces of the one whom we shall see, if by faith we are held by him whom we do not yet see.

What, then, did he wish the orphan and the widow to be understood as, brothers? Those deprived of every support and aid. Let the soul, abandoned in the world, hope for God’s help for itself. Whatever you may have here—even if you have gold [Note: [Col. 1897] Manuscript B has “you have”; Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and Lovaniensis have “you may have.”]—have you relied upon it? Then you are no longer a proselyte, no longer an orphan, and you are not counted among widows. You have a friend: if you rely upon him and abandon God, you are not abandoned. You have all these things; do you not rely upon them or grow proud because of them? You are God’s orphan and God’s widow. He receives those who are abandoned. This is what he said: he receives the orphan, and he receives the widow.

## 19.

“And he will destroy the way of sinners.” What is the way of sinners? Mocking the things we say. “Who is an orphan? What widow? What kingdom of heaven? What punishment of hell? These are Christian fables. I shall live for what I see: ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.’”

Beware lest such people persuade you of anything. Let them not enter through your ear into your heart and find thorns in your ears; let anyone who begins to enter in this way depart after being pricked. “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:32–33).

But perhaps you will say, “Why, then, are they happy? Behold, they neither worship God nor cease committing every evil each day; they abound in the possessions for which I, in need, labor.” Do not be jealous of sinners. You see what they receive; you do not see what is being reserved for them.

“And how,” he says, “do I see what is not seen?” Faith certainly has eyes—and greater, more powerful, and stronger eyes. These eyes have deceived no one. Let these eyes be always upon the Lord, so that he too may pluck your feet from these snares (Ps. 24:15).

The way of sinners pleases you because it is broad and many walk along it; you see its breadth, but you do not see its end. Behold, where it ends there is a precipice; where it ends there is a certain abyss of the underworld. Rejoicing and straying widely along this road, they are plunged into that end. But [Col. 1898] you cannot extend your eyes far enough to see the end itself; believe the one who sees.

And who is the human being who sees? [Note: [Col. 1898] Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Lovaniensis have: “And who is the one who sees? A human being.” Perhaps, and so forth.] Perhaps no human being; but your Lord came to you so that you might believe God. Surely you will not believe your Lord and God, who says: “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it” (Matt. 7:13)? The Lord will destroy this way, because it is the way of sinners.

## 20. [Verse 10]

And once the way of sinners has been destroyed, what remains for us? “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid. 25:34). To this the Psalm concludes: “And he will destroy the way of sinners.”

And what of you? “The Lord will reign forever.” Rejoice, because he will reign for you; rejoice, because you will be his kingdom. Consider what follows. Surely you are a citizen of Zion, not of Babylon—that is, not of the perishing city of this age, but of Zion, which for a time labors and makes its pilgrimage, yet will reign forever.

You have heard the end; you belong there. “The Lord will reign forever, your God, O Zion.” O Zion, your God will reign forever. Will your God reign without you? “From generation to generation.” He said it twice because he could not say “forever” continually. Do not suppose that eternity ends when the words have ended. Eternity consists in four syllables in the word, but in itself it is without end. He could commend it to you only in this way: “Your God will reign from generation to generation.” He said too little. If he were to say it all day, it would be too brief; if he were to say it throughout his whole life, would he not eventually fall silent?

Love eternity. You will reign without end [Note: [Col. 1898] Some manuscripts read, “You will reign at that end.”] if Christ is your end, with whom you will reign forever and ever. Amen.

# Exposition of Psalm 146

## Sermon

[Note: [Col. 1898] Perhaps delivered to the people of Carthage, as appears from no. 17.]

### 1. [Verse 1]

We listened attentively while the present Psalm was being sung; and not all who listened also understood. How much more attentively, then, must it now be heard, if—as I hope and desire—with the prayers of all who are listening assisting us, whatever may perhaps be obscure here will be revealed by God’s gift, so that the hearing may be fruitful and the attentive hearer may not depart empty-handed?

Where did it begin? It says to us: “Praise the Lord.” This is said to all nations, not only to us. The Churches hear this voice, sounding through individual places, from the Readers one by one; yet one voice of God over all does not cease saying that we should praise him.

And as though we were asking why we ought to praise God, see what reason he gives: “Praise the Lord,” he says, “for the Psalm is good.” Is this the whole reward of those who praise? “Let us praise the Lord.” Why? “Because the Psalm is good.”

Someone might say, “I would like to praise the Lord if he would give me something for this praise. Who praises even a human being for nothing?” Those who praise human beings expect some reward; should the one who praises God expect, ask for, or hope for no reward? A weak person is praised, and something is expected from him; the Almighty is praised, and there is no reward?

Or perhaps I desire something that he cannot give? What does a human being desire that is not in God’s hand? When you praise a human being, perhaps you desire something he cannot provide. Praise God confidently; no one can say that he is unable to provide what you might desire.

With the hope of some reward set before us, therefore, we ought to praise God—but not with the expectation that he will give whatever we desire. For he is a father, and he does not give what his evil children desire. Let us praise, hope, and desire not this or that, but what the one whom we praise judges ought to be given. He knows what it is beneficial for us to receive; we should concern ourselves with what benefits us to receive.

The Apostle says: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should” (Rom. 8:26). The same Apostle Paul hoped that it would benefit him if the thorn in his flesh, the angel of Satan by whom he was buffeted, were taken away, as he himself confesses and says: “For this I entreated the Lord three times, that he might remove it from me; and he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness’” (2 Cor. 12:7–9).

He desired something; it was not granted according to his will, so that he might be cared for toward health [Note: [Col. 1899] The editions have “so that he might be consoled.” The manuscripts have “so that he might be cared for”; perhaps for “so that it might be granted.”].

What, then, is set before us here? “Praise,” he says, “the Lord.” Why should we praise the Lord? “Because the Psalm is good.” The Psalm itself is the praise of the Lord. Thus he says, “Praise the Lord, for it is good to praise the Lord.”

Let us not pass over praising the Lord in this way: it was said, and it passed; it was done, and we became silent; we praised, and we fell silent; we sang, and we rested. Do we now go on to some other task that remains, and, when other activities arise, will divine praise cease within us? Not so. Your tongue praises for an hour; let your life praise always. This, then, is why the Psalm is good.

### 2.

For a Psalm is a song—not just any song, but one played on the psaltery. The psaltery is a certain musical instrument, like the lyre, the cithara, and instruments of this kind, which were invented for singing. Therefore, whoever plays the psaltery does not play it with the voice alone; but, taking up an instrument called the psaltery, he makes his hands agree with his voice.

Do you wish, then, to play the psaltery? Let not only your voice sound the praises of God; let your works agree with your voice. When you sing with your voice, you will eventually become silent; let your life sing in such a way that you never become silent.

You conduct business and contemplate fraud: you have become silent with respect to the praise of God—and what is more serious, you have not merely fallen silent from praise but have proceeded into blasphemy. When God is praised because of your good work, you praise God by your work; and when God is blasphemed because of your evil work, you blaspheme God by your work.

Therefore, sing with your voice for the encouragement of your ears; do not become silent in your heart or mute in your life. If you do not contemplate fraud in business, you play the psaltery to God.

When you eat and drink, play the psaltery—not by introducing musical sweetness suited to the ears, but by eating and drinking modestly, frugally, and temperately, because the Apostle says: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Cor. 10:31).

If, therefore, you act well when you eat and drink, taking nourishment for your body and restoration for your limbs, giving thanks to the one who has provided these consolations of sustenance for you, mortal and fragile as you are, then your food and drink praise God. But if by immoderate greed you exceed the measure proper to nature and gorge yourself with drunkenness, then however many praises of God your tongue may utter, your life blasphemes.

After food and drink you rest in order to sleep. Do not do anything shameful in bed, and do not exceed the permission granted in God’s law. Let the marriage bed be chaste with your spouse; and if there is concern for begetting children, let there not be unrestrained luxury of lust. Be deferential in your bed to your spouse [Note: [Col. 1900] The editions read “show honor to your spouse”; the word “honor” is absent from the manuscripts.], because both of you are members of Christ (ibid. 6:15), both created by him, both restored by his blood. By doing these things you praise God, and your praise will not become silent at all.

What happens when sleep comes? When you sleep, let an evil conscience not rouse you from your rest; and the innocence of your sleep praises God.

If, then, you praise, do not sing with your tongue alone, but also take up the psaltery of good works, because the Psalm is good. You praise when you conduct business; you praise when you take food and drink; you praise when you rest in bed; you praise when you sleep. When do you not praise?

The praise of God will be perfected in us when we come to that city, when we have become equal to the angels of God (Matt. 22:30), when no bodily necessity troubles us in any way: no hunger, no thirst interrupts us; no heat tires us; no cold constricts us; no fever casts us down; no death brings us to an end. Let us train ourselves for that perfect praise through this praise in good works.

### 3.

Therefore, when he had said, “Praise the Lord, for the Psalm is good,” he continued: “Let praise be pleasing to our God.” How will praise be pleasing to our God? If he is praised by a good life. Hear that praise will then be pleasing to him. Elsewhere it is said: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9). If, then, praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner, it is not pleasing; for what is pleasing is beautiful.

Do you wish praise to be pleasing to your God? Do not contradict the good song of your praise with evil behavior. “Let praise be pleasing to our God.” What did he say? You who praise, live well. The praise of the ungodly offends God. He pays more attention to how you live than to what you sound like.

Certainly you wish to have peace with the one whom you praise. How do you seek peace with him when you are discordant with yourself? “How,” you ask, “am I discordant with myself?” Your tongue says one thing; your life indicates another.

“Let praise be pleasing to our God.” Praise can indeed be pleasing to a human being when he hears someone praising him with polished and pointed arguments and a pleasing voice. But let praise be pleasing to our God, whose ears are open not to the mouth but to the heart, not to the tongue but to the life of the one who praises.

### 4. [Verse 2]

Who is our God to whom praise is pleasing? He makes himself sweet to us and commends himself to us; thanks be to his condescension. For he deigns to commend himself to us—not as though we were going to provide something for him, but because we are instead going to receive many things from him.

How, then, does God commend himself to us? Hear the Apostle Paul: “But God commends,” he says, “his love toward us.” How does he “commend” it? Listen; let the Apostle himself speak, so that he may be compared with the Psalm: “God commends,” he says, “his love toward us.” How does he “commend” it? “Because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. 5:8–9).

What, then, does he reserve for those who praise him, when he commends himself in this way to sinners? Since the Apostle said that God commended his love to us by having Christ die for the ungodly—not so that the ungodly would remain ungodly, but so that through the death of the righteous they might be healed of unrighteousness—what do you hear here, when he said, “Let praise be pleasing to our God”? Let us see whether this is the same commendation that the Apostle described: that Christ died for sinners and for the ungodly.

“The Lord,” he says, “builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersed of Israel.” Behold, the Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersions of his people. For the people of Jerusalem are the people of Israel.

There is an eternal Jerusalem in heaven, where the angels too are citizens. What, then, is Israel there? If you consider that man, the grandson of Abraham, who was also called Jacob, how do we understand the angels as Israel? If we examine the interpretation of the name—for Jacob himself was called Israel after his name was changed (Gen. 32:28)—then the name “Israel” is found there more truly. May we also be followers of Israel!

For what does “Israel” mean? “Seeing God.” All the citizens of that city therefore rejoice in seeing God in that great, broad, and heavenly city; God himself is their spectacle.

But we are exiles from that city, expelled by sin so that we should not remain there, and weighed down by mortality so that we should not return there. God looked upon our exile, and he who builds Jerusalem restored the fallen part.

From where did he restore the fallen part? “Gathering the dispersions of Israel.” A certain part fell and became an exile. God mercifully saw this exile and sought those who were not seeking him. How did he seek them? Whom did he send into our captivity? He sent the Redeemer, according to what the Apostle says: “God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”

He therefore sent his Son, the Redeemer, into our captivity. “Carry a sack with you,” he says; “bring there the price of the captives.” For he put on the mortality of flesh, and there was the blood by whose outpouring we were to be redeemed. By that blood he gathered the dispersions of Israel [Note: [Col. 1901] The better manuscripts here and in the following passage have “he gathers.”].

And if he once gathered the dispersed, how must we now strive so that those who are dispersed may be gathered? If the dispersed were gathered so that they might be formed in the craftsman’s hand for the building, how are those to be gathered who have fallen from the craftsman’s hand through restlessness?

“The Lord builds Jerusalem.” Behold whom we praise; behold to whom we owe praise with our whole life: “The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersions of Israel.”

### 5. [Verse 3]

How does he gather them? What does he do in order to gather them? “He heals the brokenhearted.” Behold how the dispersions of Israel are gathered [Col. 1902]: so that those brokenhearted may be healed. Those who do not break their hearts are not healed.

What does it mean to break the heart? Let it be known, dearest ones; let it happen, so that you may be healed. It has been said in many other passages of Scripture. Most especially, in that passage, someone singing with our voice said: “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it.” He was saying to God: “If you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it; but you will not delight in burnt offerings.”

What, then? Shall we remain without offering sacrifice? Hear what he wishes you to offer. He continues and says: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:18–19).

He therefore “heals the brokenhearted,” because he draws near to them in order to heal them, as it is said elsewhere: “The Lord is near to those who have broken their heart” (Ps. 34:19).

Who have broken their heart? The humble. Who have not broken their heart? The proud. The broken heart will be healed; the exalted heart will be cast down. Perhaps it is cast down for this reason: so that, once broken, it may be healed.

Therefore, brothers, let us not want our heart to be raised up before it has been made upright [Note: [Col. 1902] Several manuscripts have “corrected.”]. What has not first been corrected is raised up wrongly.

### 6.

“He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their fractures.” He heals, he says, those brokenhearted; therefore he heals those humbled in heart, those who confess, those who punish themselves and exercise severe judgment upon themselves, so that they may be able to experience his mercy.

He heals such people; but their perfect healing will take place after mortality has passed, when “this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53–54), when there will be nothing arising from the corruption of the flesh to trouble us—not only nothing to which we consent, but nothing that is suggested by the flesh.

For now, my brothers, how many unlawful pleasures touch the mind! Even if we do not consent to them, so that our members may serve righteousness and not iniquity, nevertheless merely to take pleasure in such things, even without consenting to them, is not yet perfect health.

You will be healed; you will be healed with a broken heart. Do not be ashamed; break your heart. God heals such people.

“But what shall I do now?” you ask. “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin.”

What are you to do? Break your heart; confess. Go on, say what follows: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” To say this—“Wretched man that I am”—is already to break the heart. Let the one who confesses wretchedness hope for happiness. Say, then: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?”—so that the answer may be given to you: “The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:22–25).

But how will the grace of God itself deliver us, of which we have now received the pledge? Hear the same Apostle: “The body,” he says, “is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. If, therefore, the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (ibid. 8:10–11).

Our spirit has therefore received this pledge, so that we may begin to serve God by faith and be called righteous on the basis of faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17). Whatever still opposes and resists us derives from the mortality of the flesh, and this will be healed.

“For he will give life,” he says, “to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you.” He gave the pledge for this purpose: to fulfill what he promised.

What, then, will happen now in this life, while we are still confessors and not yet possessors? What will happen in this life? How will it be healed [Note: [Col. 1903] Erasmus and most manuscripts have “how will it endure?”]? “He heals the brokenhearted”; but perfect health will come when we have spoken as described. What, then, now? “He binds up their fractures.”

He heals, he says, those brokenhearted, whose perfect health will be in the resurrection of the righteous; for now he binds up their fractures.

### 7.

What are the bindings of these fractures? As physicians bind fractures. Sometimes—as Your Charity should understand, and as those who have observed or heard it from physicians know—when something has been set badly and crookedly, physicians break it in order to correct it, and they make a new wound because the previous healing was bad and crooked.

Thus, Scripture says, the ways of the Lord are straight, but “the crooked-hearted will stumble in them” (Hos. 14:10). What does “crooked-hearted” mean? One who has a twisted heart. He thinks that everything God says is twisted; he thinks that everything God has done is crooked; and all God’s judgments displease him, especially those in which he himself is corrected. He sits and argues about how badly God acts because God does not act according to his will.

A distorted heart—it is not enough that it does not correct itself toward God; it wants to distort God toward itself. [Note: [Col. 1903] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “A distorted heart is a crooked heart, which does not correct itself toward God,” and so forth.] What, then, does God say from above? “You are crooked; I am upright. If you were upright, you would perceive my fairness.”
