Just as, if you placed a crooked piece of wood on a level pavement, it would not settle but would totter and move in every direction—not because of any unevenness in the place, but because of the wood’s crookedness—so Scripture says: “How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart!” (Ps. 73:1).

What, then? How is a crooked heart straightened? It is crooked and hard; therefore let what is crooked and hard be broken and crushed, so that it may be straightened.

You cannot straighten your own heart. You break it; he straightens it. How do you break it? How do you crush it? By confessing and punishing your sins.

What else does the striking of the breast signify? Surely we do not think that our bones have committed some sin when we beat our breast. We signify that we break our heart so that it may be straightened by the Lord.

8. Therefore he heals the brokenhearted, those who have broken hearts; and the healing of that heart will then be complete when the restoration of the body also takes place, as has been promised. Meanwhile, what does the physician do? He binds up your wounds so that you may reach complete strength [Note: [Col. 1903] The Laudun manuscript reads *salutatem* (“health”).], until what has been broken and bound up is made firm. What are these bindings? Temporal sacraments. The temporal sacraments are medicinal bindings for our brokenness, by which we meanwhile have consolation; and all these things that we say to you—the very sounds that are uttered and pass away—whatever is performed temporally in the Church, are bindings for our wounds. [Col. 1904] For just as a physician removes the bandage when health is complete, so in that city, Jerusalem, when we have been made equal to the angels, do you suppose that we shall receive there what we receive here [Note: [Col. 1904] Augustine of Mainz, Erasmus, and several manuscripts: “For what do you suppose? Shall we receive there what we have received here?”]? Will the Gospel have to be read to us there, so that our faith may endure? Or will someone in authority have to lay hands upon us? All these things are bindings for a fracture; when health is complete, they will be removed. Yet one would not reach that health unless the fracture were bound up. Therefore he heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.

9. [Verse 4.] “He counts the multitude of the stars, and calls them all by name.” What great thing is it for God to count the multitude of the stars? Human beings have also attempted this; let them see whether they have been able to accomplish it. Yet they would not attempt it unless they hoped to accomplish it. Let us leave aside what they have been able to do and how far they have advanced. But I think it is not a great thing for God to count all the stars. Or does he review their number lest he forget? Is it a great thing for God to count the stars, when the hairs of our heads have been counted (Matt. 10:30)?

It is clear, brothers, that God wishes us to understand something in what he says: “He counts the multitude of the stars,” and, he says, “calls them all by name.” There are certain stars—lights in the Church—that comfort our night: all those of whom the Apostle says, “Among whom you appear as lights in the world.” In this “crooked and perverse generation,” he says, “among whom you appear as lights in the world, holding the word of life” (Phil. 2:15–16).

God counts these stars; he has counted all who will reign with him, all who are to be joined to the body of his Only-Begotten, and he counts them even now. Whoever is unworthy is not counted. “And many believed,” or many joined themselves to his people under some shadowy appearance of faith; yet he knows what he counts and what he winnows.

For the Gospel is of such great height that what was said has come to pass: “I have announced and spoken; they have multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39:6). Thus there are, in a sense, among the peoples some who are “beyond the number.” What does “beyond the number” mean? More than will ultimately be there. Within these walls there are more than will be in the kingdom of God, in that heavenly Jerusalem; they are beyond the number.

Let each person observe whether he shines in the darkness, whether he is not led astray by the darkness of the world’s wickedness. If he is neither led astray nor overcome, he will be like a star that God already counts.

10. “And calls them all,” he says, “by name.” There lies the whole reward. We have certain names before God. We ought to desire, to do, and to strive with all our strength that God may know our names—not to rejoice in other things, nor in certain spiritual gifts.

Let Your Charity observe: there are many gifts in the Church, as the Apostle says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings, to another the discernment of spirits—that is, the discernment between good and evil spirits—to another kinds of tongues, to another prophecy” (1 Cor. 12:8–10). How many things he has mentioned! How many indeed!

Many who have misused such gifts will hear at the end: “I never knew you.” And what will those who hear “I never knew you” say at the end? “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?” In your name—all these things. And what will he say to them? “I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:22–23).

What, then, is it to be already a light of heaven, comforting the night and not overcome by the night? “I will show you,” he says, “a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12:31). “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.” What a gift it is to speak in the tongues of angels and human beings! Yet, he says, if I do not have love, I am sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.

“If I know,” he says, “all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all prophecy and all faith, so that I could move mountains”—what great gifts these are!—“but do not have love, I am nothing.” What of the gift of martyrdom and of distributing one’s possessions? “And if I distribute,” he says, “all my goods to the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:1–3).

Therefore, whoever does not have love, even if he possesses these gifts for a time, will have them taken away. What he has will be taken from him because he lacks something; and he lacks this very thing by which the others are held fast and he himself does not perish [Note: [Col. 1905] The Floriacensis manuscript: “and he himself”—understand, “this very thing”—“does not perish.”]

What is that of which the Lord now says: “To the one who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Matt. 13:12)? Therefore, from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away. He has the grace of possessing, but he does not have the love by which to use it. Because he does not have that, even what he has will be taken from him.

For this reason, when the disciples returned to the place where they had been sent, he who counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name—he who knew that many would say, “Did we not cast out demons in your name?” and to whom he would say at the end, “I never knew you,” because he had not counted them among the multitude of the stars or called them by name—when the disciples returned, they rejoiced and said: “Lord, even the unclean spirits are subject to us because of your name.”

He said to them: “Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:17, 20). He counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name.

11. [Verse 5.] “Great is our Lord.” He was filled with joy and gave forth an ineffable utterance. I do not know what he was unable to say; how could he think it [Note: [Col. 1905] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venice edition read *cogitabat* (“he was thinking”). M.]. “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and his understanding has no number.”

He himself who counts the multitude of the stars cannot be counted: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and his understanding has no number.” Who could explain this? Who could worthily contemplate what has been said: “His understanding has no number”?

Would that he pour himself into you, and, where we fail, may he himself, who is powerful, enlighten your minds so that you may know what it means: “His understanding has no number.”

You see, brothers: is there a number to the sand? There is not one for us, but there is for God. The hairs of our heads have been counted, and the sand has been counted. Therefore, whatever this world contains that is infinite—even if it is infinite for human beings, it is not so for God [Note: [Col. 1906] Augustine of Mainz, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read *finitum* (“finite”). Shortly afterward, the same editions, together with Lovaniensis, read approximately: “even if it is not finite for human beings, nevertheless it is finite for God, and that is saying too little,” whereas most manuscripts read: “even if it is infinite for human beings, nevertheless…”]; Indeed, to say “for God” is too little: it has been counted even by the angels.

“His understanding has no number.” His understanding surpasses all those who count; it cannot be counted by us. Who counts number itself? Whatever is counted is counted by number. If whatever is counted is counted by number, number itself cannot be a number of something else; number cannot in any way be counted.

What, then, is with God, from which he made all things and in which he made all things, to whom it is said: “You have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight” (Wis. 11:21)? Who can count, measure, or weigh that very measure, that very number, and that very weight by which God ordered all things?

Therefore, “his understanding has no number.” Let human voices be silent; let human thoughts rest. Let them not extend themselves toward things incomprehensible as though they could comprehend them, but as though they were to participate in them—for we shall participate.

We shall not be what we comprehend, nor shall we comprehend the whole; but we shall participate. For something great was said about Jerusalem, whose dispersed people he gathers together: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in unity” (Ps. 121:3).

What does “in unity” mean except that which cannot be changed? Other created things can exist in different ways; but the one who created them cannot exist in different ways. He himself, therefore, is “in unity,” for it was said to him: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. 101:27–28).

Therefore, if he himself is the same and cannot be changed in any respect, then by participating in his divinity we too shall be immortal in eternal life. And this pledge was given to us through the Son of God, as I have already said to Your Holiness: before we were made participants in his immortality, he first became a participant in our mortality.

As he was mortal—not from his own substance, but from ours—so we shall be immortal, not from our substance, but from his. We shall therefore participate; let no one doubt it, for Scripture has said so.

And of what will we be participants? Are there parts in God, or is God divided into portions? Who, then, can explain how many participate in the one who is simple?

Therefore, do not demand what, I think, cannot suitably be said, because you see [Note: [Col. 1906] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venice edition, and Lovaniensis read: “Therefore, do not demand what, I think, cannot be clearly said before you see.” M.]. Instead, return to the remedy of the Savior. Break your heart; let the hardness of your spirit be shattered, let the obstinacy of your spirit be crushed; let it accuse itself in evil and be reborn in goodness.

He himself will set it straight, bind up the fracture, and restore health. Then what is now impossible for us will no longer be impossible. For it is good that the person who wishes to reach divinity should confess his weakness.

“His understanding has no number.”

12. [Verse 6.] Therefore he shows you what you must do when understanding is difficult, when he next says: “The Lord receives the meek.”

For example, you do not understand; you understand only a little; you do not grasp it. Honor the Scripture of God; honor the word of God, even when it is not clear. Through piety, defer understanding. Do not presumptuously accuse either the obscurity or the supposed perversity of Scripture.

There is nothing perverse here. Something is obscure, not so that it may be denied to you, but so that it may exercise you as one who will receive it. Therefore, when something is obscure, the physician has made it so that you may knock. He wanted you to be exercised in knocking; he wanted to open to the one who knocks (Matt. 7:7).

By knocking you will be exercised; once exercised, you will become broader; having become broader, you will receive what is given. Therefore, do not be indignant that it is closed. Be gentle; be meek. Do not kick against what is obscure and say, “It would have been better said if it had been said this way.” When can you say or judge how it ought to be said? It was said as it ought to have been said.

Let the sick person not correct his medicines; the physician knows how to measure them. Trust the one who is healing you.

What follows, then? “The Lord receives the meek.” Therefore, do not resist the things of God that are closed; be meek, so that he may receive you.

But if you resist, hear what follows: “But he humbles sinners to the ground.” There are many kinds of sinners: “But he humbles sinners to the ground.” Which sinners? Those opposed to the meek. By saying, “The Lord receives the meek, but humbles sinners to the ground,” he wished a particular kind of sinner to be understood from the preceding mention of meekness.

Therefore, in this place we understand sinners to mean the harsh and those who are not meek. Why does he humble them to the ground? They criticize intelligible things; they will have only earthly thoughts.

13. This happened to people who wished to ridicule the Law before they knew it; for they were not meek. Let Your Charity understand.

There arose a thoroughly corrupt sect, that of the Manichaeans. They ridiculed the Scriptures they had received and read. They wished to criticize what they did not understand, and by attacking and criticizing what they had not understood, they ensnared many.

But those who wished to do this were humbled to the ground. They were not permitted to understand heavenly things; they understood earthly things.

Whatever you hear in their fables is nothing but blasphemy and certain inventions of bodily images. Since they wished to understand God, they reached only the thought of this visible light; they could go no farther. They made fields of light in the kingdom of God like the sun they saw, as though it were a fruit of that light.

But all that is touched through the earth of the flesh is earth in relation to God. We have means by which we see, by which we hear, by which we smell, by which we taste, and by which we touch. This flesh, through five messengers whom we call the senses, perceives only bodily things; intelligible and spiritual things, however, are grasped by the mind.

Therefore, because they ridiculed the obscurity of the Scriptures—which were closed for the purpose of exercising those who knocked, not of denying them to the little ones—they were humbled to the ground, so that they could think of nothing beyond what is perceived through the earth.

What do I mean by “through the earth”? Through the flesh. This flesh is earth, and it was made from earth. Whatever you grasp through the eyes belongs to the earth; whatever through the ears, whatever through smell, whatever through taste, whatever through touch, belongs to the earth, because it is perceived through the earth.

They therefore were unable to understand the understanding that has no number, because “his understanding has no number.” They criticized the Scriptures, which wisely conceal understanding under certain mysteries so that the little ones may be exercised. Through that criticism they became harsh, the opposite of the meek, and were humbled to the ground, so that they could not perceive the incorporeal God, and whatever they thought about God, they thought only in bodily terms.

14. [Verse 7.] Therefore God humbles sinners to the ground. What must we do, then, if we do not wish to be humbled to the ground?

It is a great thing to advance as far as intelligible realities; it is a great thing to advance as far as spiritual realities; it is a great thing for the heart to reach the point at which it knows that something exists which is not extended through places and does not vary through times.

What form does wisdom have? Who can imagine it? Is it long? Is it square? Is it round? Is it now here and now there? Someone in the East thinks of wisdom; someone else in the West thinks of it. If they think of it rightly, it is wholly present to both, although they are situated in such a great diversity of places.

What is this? Who can grasp it? Who can grasp this substance, this divine and unchangeable nature?

Do not hurry; you will be able to grasp it. Hear what follows: “Begin to the Lord with confession.” Begin here if you wish to reach a clear understanding of the truth. If you wish to be led from the way of faith to possession of the vision, begin with confession.

First accuse yourself; after accusing yourself, praise God. Invoke the one whom you do not yet know, so that he may come to be known—not that he himself may come [Note: [Col. 1908] Most manuscripts read: “not that you yourself may come.”], but that he may lead you to himself.

How can he come from a place from which he never departs? This is the perfection of wisdom: it is everywhere, and it is far from the wicked. It is everywhere, I say, and it is far from those who are everywhere.

I ask you: from whom is that which is everywhere far? Where do you think they are, except that they lie in their own dissimilarity, driving out from themselves the likeness of God? Having been made unlike him, they withdrew; let them return, having been reformed.

“From where,” they say, “will we be reformed? When will we be reformed?” “Begin to the Lord with confession.”

What follows confession? Let good works follow. “Sing praise to our God on the lyre.” What does “on the lyre” mean? What I have already explained: as the psalm is sung on the psaltery, so also on the lyre—not only with the voice, but also in action. “Sing praise to our God on the lyre.”

15. [Verse 8.] Behold, confess; perform works of mercy; sing praise to our God. To which God? “To him who covers the heavens with clouds.”

What does “who covers the heavens with clouds” mean? He who veils Scripture with figures and mysteries. He who humbles sinners to the ground, he who receives the meek, covers the heavens with clouds.

And who can see a heaven covered with clouds? Do not be afraid. Hear what follows: “He who covers the heavens with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth.”

“He who covers the heavens with clouds”—you were alarmed because you do not see heaven. When it rains [Note: [Col. 1909] After *coelum* (“heaven”), the manuscripts have *complueris* (“you will be thoroughly rained upon”). Augustine of Mainz and Erasmus read *cum plueris* (“when you rain”).], you will bear fruit, and you will see clear skies.

“He covers the heavens with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth.” Perhaps this is what the Lord our God has done. If we did not have the occasion provided by the obscurity of Scripture, we would not be saying these things to you—things in which you rejoice.

Perhaps, then, this is the rain in which you rejoice. It could not be expressed to you through our tongue unless God covered the heaven of Scripture with clouds of figures.

For this purpose he covers the heavens with clouds: to prepare rain for the earth. For this purpose he wished the words of the prophets to be obscure, so that afterward God’s servants might have something to pour out through interpretation over the ears and hearts of people who receive from God’s clouds the nourishment of spiritual joy.

“He covers the heavens with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth.”

16. “Who makes grass sprout on the mountains, and plants for the service of human beings.”

Behold the fruit of the rain. “He makes grass,” he says, “sprout on the mountains.” Does he not also make it sprout on lowly ground? But what is great is that it sprouts on the mountains.

By “mountains” he means the exalted people of the world. Understand “mountains” here as those endowed with some great dignity.

It is no wonder that some widow put two small coins into the treasury (Mark 12:42); the earth brought forth grass, lowly earth—and the mountain brought it forth as well.

That Zacchaeus, a chief among the tax collectors, did so (Luke 19:2–8) was more remarkable, because the mountain brought forth grass. For the more elevated people are, the more greedy they are; and the greater they are in this world, the more they love their wealth.

That is why the man who was asking the Lord for counsel about eternal life went away sad. He called him “Good Teacher,” saying: “What must I do to have eternal life?” And he said: “Keep the commandments.” “Which ones?” He mentioned the commandments of the Law. “I have kept all these from my youth.” “One thing is lacking to you,” he said. “Do you wish to be perfect? Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”

What did the Lord say? “Behold, you are a mountain: receive the rain and produce grass.” For what will you produce? Will you not produce grass? Indeed, all the things that the rich give to the Church for the needs of those who serve God—what are they except grass? They are material and appear for a time; but no material thing is acquired from them.

Pay attention to what you buy with cheap things. The Apostle, showing that this is grass, says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9:11).

And hear that material things are grass: “All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6).

Therefore that man went away sad, and the Lord said: “How difficult it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of heaven!”

This, then, is great: that he makes grass sprout on the mountains. And how does he make grass sprout on the mountains if that rich man, upon hearing that he ought to give his possessions to the poor, went away sad? How did he later answer the sorrowful Apostles? “What is difficult for human beings is easy for God” (Matt. 19:16–26) [Note: [Col. 1910] All manuscripts read thus. The editions instead read *impossibilia* (“impossible”).]

Therefore he makes grass sprout on the mountains, for whom all things are easy. Indeed, nothing would be more barren than the hardest mountains. He rains who makes grass sprout on the mountains, “and plants for the service of human beings.”

For whose service? Consider Paul himself: “We,” he says, “are your servants through Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. 4:5). The one who said, “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?” called himself a servant. “For we serve you, brothers.”

Let none of us consider himself greater than you. We shall be greater if we are more humble: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you,” according to the Lord’s saying, “will be your servant” (Matt. 20:26).

Therefore he makes grass sprout on the mountains, and plants for the service of human beings.

The Apostle Paul, living by the work of his own hands, did not wish to accept that grass of the mountains; he wished to be in need [Note: [Col. 1910] Augustine of Mainz and several manuscripts read: “he did not wish to be in need.”]. Yet the mountains were giving grass.

Because he did not wish to receive it, should the mountains therefore not have given it, so that they would remain barren? The fruit is owed to the rain; food is owed to the servant, as the Lord says: “Eat what comes from them.” And lest they think that they are giving something of their own: “For the laborer,” he says, “is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:8, 7).

17. Therefore, brothers, since it has happened on this occasion that I have said something to you [Note: [Col. 1910] He dealt with this subject earlier among the people of Carthage, in Psalm 103, sermon 3, nos. 9–12.], especially since we are speaking about such matters without seeking anything from you, and therefore speak more freely—yet even if we were seeking something, we would seek your fruit, not your wealth [Note: [Col. 1910] Several manuscripts read: “not our wealth.”]—I nevertheless admonish you briefly, since we have already said much and the sermon must eventually end.

If you do not wish to be barren, but wish to return fruitfulness for the rain, lest your barrenness afterward be condemned—for God threatens the barren and thorny earth with fire (Heb. 6:7–8), while he prepares a granary for the fruitful—make yourselves exactors; become your own collectors.

Christ silently demands it, and the voice of one who is silent is greater, because he does not remain silent in the Gospel. He is not truly silent when he says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). He is not silent; hear his voice.

No one can exact anything from you—unless, perhaps, the servants who serve you in the Gospel must ask something of you. If it comes to this, that they must ask, see to it that what you ask from God is not asked in vain.

Therefore, be your own exactors, lest those who serve you in the Gospel be compelled—I do not say to suffer, for perhaps they do not ask even when compelled—but lest they accuse you by their silence.

Hence it is written: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Ps. 40:2). When it says, “who understands concerning the needy and the poor,” it does not wait for him to ask. Understand concerning him.

One needy person seeks you; another needy person you ought to seek. Both have been said, my brothers: “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6:30) was just read; and elsewhere Scripture says: “Let your alms sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give it.”

One person seeks you; another you ought to seek. Do not leave empty-handed the one who seeks you, for “give to everyone who asks you.” But there is another whom you ought to seek: “Let your alms sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give.”

You will never do this unless you have set aside something from your possessions, according to what each person wishes and according to the needs of his household, as though it were a debt to be paid to the treasury.

If Christ does not have his own commonwealth, he does not have his own treasury. Do you know what a *fiscus* is? A *fiscus* is a sack; hence the terms *fiscellae* and *fiscinae* are also used. Do not suppose that the treasury is some dragon, because the collector of the treasury is heard with fear. The treasury is a public sack.

The Lord himself had one here on earth when he had a money box; and that money box was entrusted to Judas (John 12:6). The Lord tolerated Judas the betrayer and thief, thereby displaying everywhere his own patience. Yet those who contributed were contributing to the Lord’s money box.

Unless perhaps you think that the Lord went about asking or was in need—he whom angels served, who fed so many thousands with five loaves. Why, then, did he wish to be in need? So that he might set an example to the mountains, that they should produce grass and not return barrenness for the rain.

Therefore cut off something and set aside a fixed amount [Note: [Col. 1911] Several manuscripts read *fisco* (“for the treasury”). Supply “of Christ.”], either from your annual produce or from your daily earnings. For when you seem to give as though from something living [Note: [Col. 1911] Several manuscripts read thus. The editions instead have approximately: “For you seem to give as though from something divine,” and below, where they had *devoveras*, they read *debueras* (“you ought to have”).], your hand necessarily trembles when you extend it toward something that you had not vowed.

Take out some part of your income. Do you want to give a tenth? Take out a tenth, although that is little. For it was said that the Pharisees gave tithes: “I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess” (Luke 18:12).

And what does the Lord say? “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20).

The one whose righteousness yours ought to exceed gives tithes; yet you do not even give a thousandth. How will you surpass one whom you do not equal?

“He who covers the heavens with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, who makes grass sprout on the mountains, and plants for the service of human beings.”

18. [Verse 9.] “And gives the cattle their food.” By these cattle he means God’s flocks. God does not defraud his flock of its food through the human beings for whose service he makes the grass sprout.

Hence the Apostle says: “Who feeds a flock and does not partake of the milk of the flock?” (1 Cor. 9:7).

“He gives the cattle their food, and to the young ravens that call upon him.”

Shall we perhaps think that ravens call upon God so that he may give them food? Do not think that an irrational soul calls upon God. No soul knows how to call upon God except the rational soul.

Understand the statement figuratively, lest you think, as certain impious people say, that human souls return into cattle, dogs, pigs, and ravens. Drive this from your hearts and from your faith. The human soul was made in the image of God (Gen. 1:26); it will not give its image to a dog or a pig.

What, then, does “to the young ravens that call upon him” mean? Who are the young ravens?

The Israelites claimed that they alone were righteous because they had received the Law; they called all the other people of the nations sinners. And indeed all the nations were in sin, in idolatry, in the worship of stones and wood. But did they remain so?

Even if our fathers themselves were not ravens, we ourselves are the young ravens who call upon God. “He gives the cattle their food, and to the young ravens that call upon him.”

They are the young ravens to whom Peter says: “You were not redeemed with perishable silver or gold from your futile way of life handed down from your ancestors” (1 Pet. 1:18).

As the young ravens progressed, they turned from worshiping the images of their ancestors and converted to God. And now you hear a young raven calling upon the one God.

“What, then? Have you abandoned your father?” you say to the young raven. “I have certainly abandoned him. For he was a raven who did not call upon God; I am a young raven who calls upon God.”

“And to the young ravens that call upon him.”

19. [Verse 10.] “He will not take pleasure in the strength of the horse.” The strength of the horse is pride. A horse appears to be fitted for the display of a human being, so that he may ride more exalted. Indeed, there is a neck in the horse that indicates a certain pride.

Let people not exalt themselves in their dignities; let them not think themselves elevated by their honors. Let them beware lest they be thrown by an untamed horse.

See what is said in another psalm: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will boast in the name of the Lord our God.” That is, they boast in temporal honors, but we will boast in the name of the Lord our God.

What happened to them? See what follows: “Their feet were bound, and they fell; but we rose and stood upright” (Ps. 19:8–9).

“He will not take pleasure in the strength of the horse; nor will he regard the tents of a man with favor.”

“In the tents of a man,” he says. There is the Lord’s tent, namely, the holy Church spread throughout the whole world. Heretics, separating themselves from the tents of the Church, have set up tents for themselves. God will not regard the man favorably in those tents.

But listen to the young raven who says: “I have chosen to be rejected in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83:11).

For if some good and pious person, confessing his weakness and calling upon God like a young raven, happens to lack temporal honor in the Church, he does not go outside the Church; he does not make for himself a tent outside the Church in which God would not take pleasure. Rather, what does he say? “I have chosen to be rejected in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.”

“Nor will he regard the tents of a man with favor.”

20. [Verse 11.] But what does he add? “The Lord will regard favorably those who fear him, and those who hope in his mercy.”

The Lord regards favorably those who fear him. But is God feared in the same way as a robber? A robber is feared; a wild beast is feared; an unjust and very powerful person is greatly feared.

“The Lord will regard favorably those who fear him.” But how are they to fear him? “And those who hope in his mercy.”

Behold, Judas the betrayer of Christ feared him, but he did not hope in his mercy. For afterward he regretted that he had betrayed the Lord and said: “I have sinned, because I betrayed innocent blood.”

You certainly feared rightly; but what if you had hoped in the mercy of the one whom you feared? He went away in despair and hanged himself with a noose (Matt. 27:4–5).

Therefore fear the Lord in such a way that you hope in his mercy. If you fear a robber, you hope for help from someone other than the one you fear; you ask help from one whom you do not fear against the one whom you fear.

If you fear God in this way, and therefore fear God because you are a sinner, from whom will you receive help against God? Where will you go? What will you do? Do you wish to flee from him? Flee to him. Do you wish to flee from the one who is angry? Flee to the one who has been appeased.

You will appease him if you hope in his mercy, and thereafter take care not to sin, while you plead that your past sins may be forgiven you by the Lord, to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 147

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. Your Charity remembers that, concerning the psalm we have just sung, we postponed the sermon until today. It was the psalm appointed for this day, and it was read on the Lord’s Day, and we undertook to expound it.

But because at that time we were moved by the Gospel reading, and because of the greatness of our fear and our concern for your benefit, we lingered over what the Lord commended to us concerning the last day. He wished us to await his coming with caution and watchfulness, terrifying us also by his example, lest he condemn us in judgment. He said that the coming of the Son of Man would be as it was in the days of Noah: “They were eating and drinking, buying and selling, marrying and taking wives, until Noah entered the ark; then the flood came and destroyed them all” (Matt. 24).

Therefore, anxious and shaken by great fear—for who, if he believes, would not be afraid?—we lingered over this as much as we could, so that a sermon might be drawn from your conduct and your life, and from the life of all of us, by which we might be able not only to await that day securely but also to desire it.

For if we love Christ, certainly we ought to desire his coming. It is perverse—and I do not know whether it is even true—to fear that the one whom you love may come; to pray, “Your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10); and to fear that your prayer may be heard.

But why the fear? Because the judge is coming? Is he unjust? Is he malicious? Is he envious? Or, finally, is he awaiting knowledge of your case from someone else, lest perhaps the one you have appointed either deceive you through betrayal or, failing through lesser eloquence and ability, be unable to demonstrate the goodness of your innocence in words?

None of this is so. Who, then, is coming? Why do you not rejoice? Who is coming to judge you except the one who came to be judged for you?

Do not fear the accuser of whom he himself said: “The prince of this world has been cast out” (John 12:31). Do not fear an evil advocate. The one who will then be your judge is your advocate now.

He will be there, and you will be there, and your case will be there: the statement of your case will be the testimony of your conscience. Therefore, whoever fears the future judge should correct his present conscience now.

Is it not enough for you that he will not inquire into the past? He will judge then without any further time remaining. But with how much time does he now admonish us? Then it will no longer be possible to correct ourselves; now, who prevents it?

As we strongly urged this on the Lord’s Day—for indeed, because it is truly almost the only thing that must be said—not a little time passed, and we were compelled to postpone until today this psalm that we had undertaken to expound.

Now it is present before us. Let us attend to it—or rather, let us attend to God, who in his mercy has deigned to distribute these sermons through his Spirit, in the manner he knows to be useful for our weakness. For what sick person dares give advice to a physician?

## 2.

When it was being read, I believe that either all or many of you noticed that it contains certain verses at which one must knock in order that they may be opened—especially where it says:

> “He gives snow like wool; he scatters mist like ashes;  
> he casts his ice like morsels of bread.  
> Who can withstand the face of his frost?”

For when these words are heard, anyone who takes them literally has certainly thought of divine works. For who gives snow, unless God? And who scatters mist, unless God? Who makes ice hard, unless he himself? These three things also have fitting and corresponding likenesses. For wool is not unlike snow, nor ash unlike mist, nor morsels of white bread unlike the brightness and whiteness of ice. [Note: [Col. 1914] The editions read candido nitori, “with white brightness,” with the manuscripts dissenting.] Ice is a certain substance resembling glass, but it is white. This is reported by those who know about such things; therefore we ought not to doubt it, since the most trustworthy Scripture bears witness to it. Ice is said, then, to become so frozen after being hardened for many years, and not thawing, that it cannot easily be dissolved. The snows of the previous winter are readily melted by the coming summer, for they have not been strengthened by the accumulation of years. But when great quantities of snow have been piled one upon another over many years, and by their mass have overcome the power of summer—not merely of one summer, but of many, especially in those regions of the earth, that is, in the northern quarter, where even in summer the sun is not found to be exceedingly hot—that long-lasting, age-old hardness produces this substance called ice.

Let Your Charity pay attention. What, then, is ice? It is snow hardened by frost over many years, so that it cannot easily be dissolved by the sun or by fire. We have explained this at somewhat greater length because many people are ignorant of it. Those who happen to know it should not find the discourse burdensome on account of a matter familiar to them, since it has been included not for their sake but for those who do not know.

When you heard these things as the Reader’s voice rang out, I do not doubt that you thought various thoughts. Some of you said—and said truly—“Great are the works of the Lord,” from which a certain portion was recalled: these earthly things, familiar to almost everyone, showing how God makes it snow, how he scatters mist, and how he also hardens ice. Others said to themselves, “Do you suppose that these things were placed in Scripture without reason? Or do all these words really mean what they sound like? Does this snow and wool, this mist and ash, this ice and bread perhaps signify something to us?”

But why did Scripture wish to speak in this way, through certain kinds of shadows cast by likenesses? How much better would it have spoken more plainly! Why do I either ask or hesitate over what those [Col. 1915] words demand? Why do I struggle while listening? Why do I so often leave after hearing a psalm uninstructed? This is what I said a little earlier: allow yourself to be treated; this is how you must be healed. A sick person is exceedingly proud and rash if he dares to instruct even a human physician. Would a sick person dare to give advice to a physician?

When a human being is sick and God is the healer, it is a great beginning of piety and health—before you know why something has been said—to believe that it ought to have been said in the manner in which it was said. [Note: [Col. 1915] This reading is found in the better manuscripts. The editions have instead: “and an indication of health. Before you know why something has been said, believe that it ought to have been said in this manner,” etc.] For this piety will make you capable of seeking what has been said; and when you have sought it, of finding it; and when you have found it, of rejoicing. May this disposition, then, be present for us through the Lord our God, in response to your prayers; and, if not for our sake, certainly for yours, may he deign to grant what lies hidden here.

For the moment, then, imagine that, since we promised a day devoted to a certain spectacle and divine production [Note: [Col. 1915] Erasmus and Lovaniensis omit the particle et, which occurs in the other books.], after these verses had been recited but not yet explained, we have brought forth some of the wrapped parcels of our Editor. Naturally, wrapped parcels are brought forth so that people may await their being unwrapped. [Note: [Col. 1915] The Floriacensis manuscript has spectentur, “may be viewed”; the meaning here is the same as exspectentur, “may be awaited.”] But you are preparing not merely to look at them, but also to clothe yourselves in them.

## 3.

On Sunday, if Your Charity remembers—you who were present—we said that the Gospel reading itself, which occupied us for so long that the exposition of the Psalm had to be postponed, had been read in a manner appropriate to this same Psalm. We said this then, but we could not demonstrate it, because we postponed the Psalm. Today, therefore, that correspondence itself must be shown.

In that Gospel reading we were terrified by the last day. That terror gives birth to security: terrified, we take precautions; taking precautions, we shall be secure. For just as disordered security drives one into terrors, so ordered concern produces security.

We were terrified lest we love this present life—which is failing, fleeting, and transitory—as though no other life existed. For if no other life exists, let us love this one. If there is no other life, those who have stayed awake today for the amphitheater are happier than we are. For what does the Apostle say?

> “If our hope in Christ is for this life only, we are more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Cor. 15:19).

There is, then, another life. Let each person question Christ in his faith. [Note: [Col. 1915] So the manuscripts. The editions have “your Christ” instead of Christum.] But faith is asleep. It is no wonder that you are tossed about, because Christ is asleep in the boat. For Jesus was sleeping in the boat, while the boat was being tossed on the waters amid many storms (Matt. 8:24–25).

The heart, therefore, is tossed about when Christ is asleep. Christ is always awake. What, then, does “Christ is asleep” mean? Your faith is asleep. Why are you still being thrown about by a storm of doubt? [Note: [Col. 1915] The manuscripts have dubitatione ut tempestate, “by doubt as by a storm,” or velut tempestate, “as by a storm.”] Awaken Christ; awaken your faith. With the eyes of faith, behold the future life for which you believed and for which you were marked with his sign—the one who lived this life in order to show you how contemptible is the life you loved, and how worthy of hope is the life you did not believe in.

If, then, you awaken your faith and turn its eyes toward the last things, toward the age to come in which we shall rejoice after the Lord’s second coming, after judgment has been completed, after the kingdom of heaven has been handed over to the saints—if you think of that life and of the business of that life, a business that is leisure, about which we have often spoken, dearest brethren—then our business will not be tossed about. It will be a leisurely business full of sweetness alone, interrupted by no distress, wounded by no weariness, disturbed by no cloud.

What will our business be? To praise God, to love him, and to praise him; to praise in love, and to love in praises.

> “Blessed are those who dwell in your house;  
> they shall praise you forever and ever” (Ps. 83:5).

Why, unless because they will love you forever and ever? Why, unless because they will see you forever and ever?

What a spectacle, then, my brethren, will this be in the vision of God! People see a hunter and are delighted: woe to the wretched if they do not correct themselves! For those who see a hunter and rejoice will see the Savior and be saddened. What could be more wretched than those for whom the Savior will not be salvation? It is therefore no wonder that, for those who take pleasure in a man fighting, God who delivers will not be salvation.

But we, brethren, if we remember that we are in his members, if we desire this, and if we persevere, shall see and rejoice. That city will be purified with all its citizens, with no seditious or turbulent person mixed into it. That enemy who now envies us and prevents us from reaching that homeland will not be able to lay snares for anyone there, because he is not even permitted to exist there. For if he is now excluded from the hearts of believers, how will he not be excluded from the city of the living?

What will it be, brethren—what will it be, I ask you—to be in that city, of which merely speaking is such a joy? We must prepare our hearts for this future life. Whoever prepares his heart for it despises this whole present life; and, having despised it, he awaits securely the day about which the Lord, by making us await it, has terrified us.

## 4.

Since this Psalm, then, speaks and sings to us of that future life, while the Gospel terrified us concerning the present one, the Psalm produces love of the future, and the Gospel produces fear of the present. Nor is the delight of the future left unmentioned in the writings of the New Testament—indeed, much more so there, where the things to be understood are not brought forth as though wrapped in coverings, but appear open, so that here they may be understood as obscure.

When the Gospel said to us, “Watch for the last day that is to come, the day of the Son of Man’s coming”—because it will find those who are secure in a bad condition, secure precisely because they are perversely secure—they are secure in the pleasures of the world, when they ought to be secure because the desires of the world have been subdued. The Apostle has already prepared us for that life in the words I recalled then:

> “From now on, brethren, the time is short. Let those who have wives live as though they had none; those who buy as though they were not buying; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who weep as though they did not weep; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away. I want you to be without anxiety” (1 Cor. 7:29–32).

The person who places all his joy and happiness in eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, and using this world is without anxiety—and such a person is so only outside the ark. Woe to him when the flood comes!

But whoever eats, drinks, or does anything else, does everything for the glory of God (1 Cor. 10:31). If there is some sorrow over worldly matters, he weeps in such a way that inwardly he rejoices in hope. If there is some joy over worldly matters, he rejoices in such a way that inwardly he fears spiritually. He neither gives himself over to be corrupted by prosperity nor allows himself to be broken by adversity. This is to weep as though not weeping and to rejoice as though not rejoicing.

If he has a wife, he has compassion on her weakness and renders the debt rather than demanding it; or, if he marries because of his own weakness, he mourns rather because he was unable to remain unmarried than rejoices because he married. Whoever sells what he knows would not have made him blessed even if it remained his; whoever knows that what he buys will pass away; whoever, even when surrounded and overflowing with possessions, does not presume upon them, but uses what he has to show mercy to the one who does not have, so that he too may receive what he does not have [Note: [Col. 1917] The American and manuscript witnesses omit “what he does not have.”] from the one who has everything—whoever is such a person awaits the last day securely, because he is not outside the ark. He is already counted among the imperishable timbers from which the ark is built (Gen. 6:14).

Let him therefore not fear the Lord who is to come, but hope for him and desire him. He will not come to inflict punishments upon him, but to bring his troubles to an end. This comes about through desire for that city. What the Gospel therefore warned us about is fulfilled through desire for the city that the Psalm sings. [Note: [Col. 1917] So the manuscripts. The editions have: “which the Psalm sings of.”] Thus the Gospel corresponds to this song.

## 5.

And what city does this Psalm sing? Let us listen. Let us listen and sing; when we hear this, our joy is the song of our God. For we do not sing only when we produce a song with voice and lips. There is also an inward song, because there are also certain inward ears. We sing with the voice in order to stir ourselves; we sing with the heart in order to please him.

It is called the Psalm of Haggai and Zechariah. [Note: [Col. 1917] This is the title of the Psalm in the Septuagint.] Haggai and Zechariah were prophets. These prophets were already in the captivity of that Jerusalem which, on earth, bore the shadow of a certain heavenly Jerusalem. While they were therefore in captivity in Babylonia, they prophesied the restoration of Jerusalem; they prophesied a new city arising from the restoration of the old, when the people had been freed from captivity (1 Esd. 5:1; 6:14).

We recognize this captivity too, if we truly recognize our own pilgrimage. For in this world, amid these tribulations of the age and this great multitude of scandals, we groan, in a certain sense, in captivity; but we shall be raised up. Our future new city, already equal in perfection, is foretold.

After the prophecy of these men, it also happened visibly, so that everything belonging to the fulfillment of the image might be made clear. Jerusalem was restored after seventy years of captivity. Thus the prophet Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 1917] Most manuscripts read, “prophesies after seventy years,” etc.], by the seventy years, marks with that number seven the whole cycle of this present time: for days revolve in the number seven, as you know; the same days depart and return.

After the seventy years, therefore, when Jeremiah prophesied that the city of Jerusalem would be restored (Jer. 25:12; 29:10), it came to pass that an image of future things was also signified there. It was signified to us that after all this revolving of time, which turns according to the number seven, our future city would exist in eternity, in a single day. For in that habitation time does not revolve, because its inhabitant does not fall.

When the Prophets saw this city in the spirit, they saw that one and spoke about this one. But they spoke about this one in such a way as to lead to that one; and all the things that occurred according to time, according to bodily movements, according to human actions, were signs and foreshadowings of future things.

## 6. [Verse 12]

Let us now hear that city being sung, and let us rise up toward it. The Spirit of God commends it to us greatly, pouring its love into us, so that we may sigh for it, groan in our pilgrimage, and desire to come to it. Let us love it; and to love it is itself to walk toward it.

Behold, let us love it through the holy mouth, through the prophetic mouth and the Spirit of God, saying:

> “Praise the Lord together, Jerusalem.”

While they are still in captivity, they see those flocks—or rather, the one flock of all the citizens gathered from every direction into that city. They see the joy of the mass of grain, already sent into the granary after threshing and winnowing, fearing nothing and enduring no labor or distress. Still placed here and living amid their own crushing, they send ahead the joy of hope and breathe toward that city, as though joining their hearts to the angels of God and to that future people who will remain with them in joy.

> “Praise the Lord together, Jerusalem.”

What will you do, O Jerusalem? Surely labor and groaning will pass away. What will you do? Will you plow, sow, renew your fields, sail, or conduct business? What will you do? Must you still be occupied with those works, even though they are good and arise from mercy?

Consider your number; consider your society gathered from every direction. See whether anyone is hungry to whom you may offer bread; see whether anyone is thirsty to whom you may give a cup of cold water; see whether there is any stranger among you whom you may receive as a guest; see whether anyone is sick whom you may visit; see whether anyone is quarrelling whom you may reconcile (Matt. 25:35–36); see whether anyone is dying whom you may bury.

What, then, will you do?

> “Praise the Lord together, Jerusalem.”

Behold, this is your business. As it is customary to write in inscriptions, “Use it happily”: “Praise the Lord together, Jerusalem.”

## 7.

Be Jerusalem. Remember those about whom it was said:

> “In your city you will reduce their image to nothing” (Ps. 72:20).

These are the people who now rejoice in such shows. Among them are those who did not come today because there is a spectacle. For whom is it a spectacle? For whom is it a loss? Or where does the spectacle come from, and where does the loss come from?

For not only those who produce such entertainments are struck by loss; those who willingly watch such things are struck by a greater loss. The coffers of the former are emptied of gold; the breast of the latter is stripped of the riches of righteousness.

Many producers mourn as they sell their estates. How ought sinners to mourn as they lose their souls! Did the Lord cry out for this purpose on Sunday, “Watch,” so that people would watch in this manner today?

I beg you, citizens of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the peace of Jerusalem, by its redeemer, its builder, and its ruler: turn prayers to God on their behalf. May they see and perceive that they are trifling; and, being intensely absorbed in those spectacles that please them, may they at some time look at themselves as well and become displeasing to themselves.

We rejoice that this has already happened in many cases. At one time we too sat there and went mad. And how many do we suppose are sitting there now who will become not only Christians but even bishops? From past events we infer future ones; from what has already happened we foretell what God will do.

Let your prayers keep watch; you do not groan in vain, brethren. Those who have escaped, praying for those who are in danger—because they too were once among those in danger—are certainly heard. God will withdraw his people from the captivity of Babylonia; he will entirely redeem and rescue them, and the number of the saints who bear the image of God will be completed.

Those will not be there whose image God despises in his city and reduces to nothing, because they too, in their city—that is, in Babylonia—reduced his image to nothing. [Note: [Col. 1919] So the manuscripts. Erasmus and Lovaniensis have: “because they too, in their captivity and in their city,” etc.]

There will be that people praising the Lord whom the Spirit of prophecy now foresees. It says this so that we may exult in hope and desire the reality itself:

> “Praise the Lord together, Jerusalem;  
> praise your God, Zion.”

Praise him together because you consist of many; praise him because you have been made one.

> “Many,” the Apostle says, “are one in Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 10:17).

Since we are many, therefore we praise together; since we are one, we praise. The many are the same as the one, because the one in whom they are one is always one.

## 8.

“Why,” says this Jerusalem, “do I praise the Lord together, and praise my God, Zion?”

Zion and Jerusalem are the same. The two names arise from different reasons. Jerusalem means “Vision of peace”; Zion means “Contemplation.” Consider whether these names signify anything other than spectacles, lest the nations think that they have spectacles while we do not.

Sometimes, after the crowd of the wicked has been poured out of the theater or amphitheater, they retain in their minds the fantasies of their vanity and feed their memory on things not merely useless but harmful, rejoicing in them as in sweet yet poisonous things. Then, as often happens, they see God’s servants passing by. They recognize them by their appearance, clothing, head, or forehead. [Note: [Col. 1919] Erasmus and several manuscripts have forte, “perhaps.”] They say to themselves and among themselves: “How wretched these people are! What are they missing!”

Brethren, let us pray to the Lord because of their goodwill, since they think that what they love is good. They wish us well. But:

> “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6).

If he hates his own soul, how will he love my soul? Nevertheless, in that perverse, empty, and vain goodwill—or, if it should be called goodwill—they grieve that we are losing what they love. Let us pray that they may not lose what we love.

See what kind of Jerusalem he exhorts to praise—or rather, what kind he anticipates will praise. For the praises of that city, when we shall see, love, and praise it, will not need to be exhorted and stirred by the prophetic voice. Rather, the Prophets say this now so that, insofar as they can while dwelling in this flesh, they may pour forth the future joys of the blessed into our ears and stir up love for that city. [Note: [Col. 1919] Some manuscripts have Sio; the editions have utpote, “as being,” and below: “pouring forth the joys of the blessed into our ears, so that they may stir up,” etc.]

Let us burn with desire; let us not be sluggish in spirit.

## 9. [Verse 13]

But see what kind of Jerusalem he says will praise God, and from what condition it will praise him: from a certain perfection of blessedness.

> “Praise the Lord together, Jerusalem;  
> praise your God, Zion.”

And as though it were saying, “From what shall I praise securely?”:

> “Because,” it says, “he has strengthened the bars of your gates.”

Pay attention, my brethren.

> “He has strengthened,” it says, “the bars of your gates.”

The strengthening of bars belongs not to open gates but to closed ones. Hence many copies have: “He has strengthened the bolts of your gates.”

Let Your Charity pay attention. It says that Jerusalem, enclosed, praises the Lord:

> “Praise the Lord together, Jerusalem;  
> praise your God, Zion.”

We praise together now; we praise now, but amid scandals. Many whom we do not wish to enter; many, even though we do not wish it, leave. Therefore scandals multiply.

> “Because iniquity has abounded,” Truth says, “the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12).

This is because of those who enter, whom we cannot judge, and those who leave, whom we cannot retain.

Why does this happen? Because perfection has not yet come; that blessedness has not yet come. Why does this happen? Because we are still the threshing floor, not yet the granary.

What, then, remains except that you should not fear that anything of this kind will happen in the future?

> “Praise the Lord together, Jerusalem;  
> praise your God, Zion;  
> because he has strengthened the bars of your gates.”

“He has strengthened.” He did not say merely, “He has added”; he said, “He has strengthened the bars of your gates.” [Note: [Col. 1920] So the African manuscripts and many others. Lovaniensis has: “He has not yet said, ‘He has added’; he has only said, ‘He has strengthened,’” etc. Shortly afterward the editions read: “Do not fear this when you have entered.” The text says only: “Let it be so,” etc.]

Let no one go out; let no one enter. We rejoice that no one goes out; we fear that no one enters. Do not fear this either. When you have entered, it will be said: only be among the virgins who carried oil with them.

## 10.

For the virgins signify souls. There were not truly five of them, but those five include thousands. In that number of five, thousands are understood—not women alone but men as well. Each sex is called feminine because it is the Church; and each sex, that is, the Church, is called a virgin.

> “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

Virginity of the flesh belongs to a few; virginity of the heart ought to belong to all. Virginity of the flesh means an untouched body; virginity of the heart means uncorrupted faith.

Thus the whole Church is called a virgin, while the people of God are named in the masculine gender. The people of God are both sexes, yet one people and a unique people; one Church and one dove. In this virginity are thousands of saints.

The five virgins, then, signify all the souls that will enter the kingdom of God. They are not numbered five without reason, since there are five bodily senses known to everyone. For through five gates something enters by the body into the soul: through the eyes enters what you may wrongly desire, or through the ears, or through the sense of smell, or through taste, or through touch.

Whoever does not admit corruption through these five gates is counted among the five virgins. Corruptions are admitted through unlawful desires. The books of Scripture are full of instruction about what is permitted and what is not. It is therefore necessary for you to be among those five virgins.

You will not fear what was said: “Let no one enter.” It is said, and it will happen—but once you have entered. No one will shut the gates against you; when you have entered, the gates of Jerusalem will be closed, and their bars will be strengthened.

But if you wish to be either no virgin in heart or, although a virgin, one of the foolish virgins, you will remain outside and knock in vain.

## 11.

Who are the foolish virgins? They too are five: souls, namely, that possess this continence of the flesh, avoiding the corruptions that come through all the senses I have already enumerated. They avoid the corruptions that come from every direction, as it were, but do not carry their good within their conscience before the eyes of God. Rather, they wish to please human beings by it and follow the judgment of others.

They seek the applause of the crowd. They are worthless in their own eyes when they wish to be precious to spectators; conscience is not enough for them. It is rightly said that they do not carry oil with them. Oil is precisely the glorying that produces radiance and splendor.

But what does the Apostle say? See the wise virgins carrying oil with them:

> “Let each one test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Gal. 6:4).

These, then, are the wise virgins. The foolish light their lamps; their works do indeed appear to shine, but they will fail and be extinguished, because they are not nourished by inward oil.

All fall asleep when the bridegroom delays, because people of both kinds fall asleep in death. As the Lord’s coming is delayed, both the foolish and the wise pass into this bodily and visible death, which Scripture is known to place in the position of sleep among all Christians.

When the Apostle was speaking about the sick, he said:

> “For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and a sufficient number sleep” (1 Cor. 11:30).

“Sleep,” he says; “they die.”

But behold, the bridegroom is coming, and all will rise, but not all will enter. The works of the foolish virgins, who do not possess the oil of conscience, will fail. They will not find anyone from whom to buy what flatterers used to sell them.

It is said by those who mock, not by those who envy:

> “Go instead to the sellers and buy some for yourselves.”

For the foolish had approached the wise and said to them:

> “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.”

What did the wise say?

> “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and you; go instead to the sellers and buy some for yourselves.”

This was a warning: “What use to you now are those from whom you are accustomed to buy flattery?”

And while they went, it says, the others entered, and the door was shut (Matt. 25:1–13). They go in their hearts, when they think such things, when they turn themselves away from that purpose and recall their past lives; they go, as it were, to the sellers. But then they do not find those who favor them; they do not find those who praise them, from whom they used to receive praise and be stirred to good works—not through the strength of a good conscience but through the stimulus of another person’s tongue.

## 12.

And what was said—“Perhaps there will not be enough for us and you”—was said with profound consideration of humility. For the oil we carry in our conscience is our judgment about ourselves, about what sort of people we are; and it is difficult for anyone to judge himself perfectly.

My brethren, however much a person may advance, however much he may stretch himself toward what lies ahead and forget what is behind (Phil. 3:13), if he now says to himself, “All is well,” the rule proceeds from God’s treasures and examines everything thoroughly:

> “Who can boast that he has a pure heart?  
> Who can boast that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. 20:9).

But what did Scripture say?

> “Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13).

However much you advance, you must hope in mercy. For if justice is brought forth without mercy, it will find something to condemn in anyone.

What Scripture consoles us? What Scripture urges us to show mercy, so that we may be all the more diligent in distributing what we possess in excess? We possess many surplus things if we retain only what is necessary. If we seek empty things, nothing is enough.

Brethren, seek what is sufficient for God’s work, not what is sufficient for your desire. Your desire is not God’s work. Your appearance, your body, your soul—this whole reality is God’s work. Seek what is sufficient, and you will see how little it is.

Two coins were sufficient for the widow to show mercy (Mark 12:42); two coins were sufficient to purchase the kingdom of God. What is sufficient for a producer to clothe hunters so many times? See that not only are the things sufficient for you few, but God himself does not ask much from you.

Seek how much he has given you, and from that take what is sufficient. The rest, lying there as surplus, belongs to others who need it. The surplus of the rich is the necessity of the poor. Another’s property is possessed whenever surplus is possessed.

## 13.

By showing such mercies—and especially that mercy which costs nothing:

> “Forgive, as we forgive” (Matt. 6:12),

in which you distribute nothing but love, and love grows as you distribute it; by showing mercy, then, and being fervent in those good works of mercy—which, as we have already said, will then no longer be necessary, because there will be no miserable person toward whom mercy must be shown [Note: [Col. 1922] Above, in Ps. 83, nos. 8 and 11]—you will await judgment securely.

You will not be so secure because of your own justice as because of God’s mercy, since you too have shown mercy beforehand.

> “Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy;  
> but mercy,” he says, “exults over judgment.”

Do not think, brethren, that he is not just when he shows mercy to us, [Note: [Col. 1922] So according to several manuscripts of good quality: nostri non miseretur, “shows no mercy to us.”] or that he departs from the rule of his justice. When he condemns, he is just; and when he shows mercy, he is just. For what is as just as to repay the one who has shown mercy? What is as just as that in the measure with which you have measured, it should be measured back to you (Matt. 7:2)?

Give to your needy brother. To what brother? To Christ. If it is to a brother, then to Christ; and if to Christ, then to God, who is blessed above all forever (Rom. 9:5). God wished to be in need of you, and you draw back your hand?

Certainly you stretch out your hand and ask from God. Hear Scripture:

> “Let your hand not be stretched out to receive and clenched when it comes to giving” (Sir. 4:36).

God wishes to have distributed from what he has given. For what do you give that he did not give? What do you have that you did not receive (1 Cor. 4:7)?

Or do you give something of your own—not to God, I say, but to anyone at all? You give from what belongs to him, who commands you to give. Be a distributor beforehand, not an invader.

Doing these things, then, and saying with good humility concerning that oil, “Perhaps there will not be enough for us,” you enter, and the door is shut.

Hear the Apostle saying this:

> “But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you” (1 Cor. 4:3).

For when could you judge my conscience? When could you examine the intention with which I do whatever I do? How much can human beings judge concerning another person? Certainly a person knows more about himself than another human being does; but God knows more about a person than that person knows about himself.

If you are such a person, you will enter; you will be among those five virgins. The other, foolish virgins will be shut out. For this is what you have in the Gospel: the door will be shut, and they will stand and cry out, “Open to us,” and it will not be opened:

> “Because he has strengthened the bars of your gates.”

“He has strengthened,” it says, “the bars of your gates.” Stand secure; praise securely; praise without end. Your gates have been firmly closed: a friend does not go out, and an enemy does not enter.

> “He has strengthened the bars of your gates.”

## 14.

> “He has blessed your children within you.”

They do not wander outside; they do not live as exiles. Within, they rejoice; within, they praise; within, they are blessed. [Note: [Col. 1923] So the African manuscripts and other witnesses. Erasmus and Lovaniensis have benedicunt, “they bless.”] Within, they do not give birth, because they now give birth to no one. They are children; they are holy. These holy children, now praising and rejoicing, were conceived and born by motherly love, and are enclosed by the love that gathers them.

Hear love giving birth to them. Paul the Apostle, endowed with it and bearing toward his children not only a father’s heart but also a mother’s, says:

> “My little children, for whom I am again in labor” (Gal. 4:19).

When Paul was in labor for them, love was in labor. When love was in labor for them, the Spirit of God was in labor; for:

> “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:6).

Let love, then, gather those whom it has conceived and brought forth. Now they are children within, secure. They have flown from the nest of fear; they have flown into the heavenly things; they have flown into the eternal things. They now fear nothing temporal.

## 15. [Verse 14]

> “He has blessed your children within you.”

Who has?

> “He has established peace as your borders.”

How you all exulted! [Note: [Col. 1923] Several manuscripts omit “all.”] Love of peace cries out from your hearts, and we are greatly delighted when it does so.

How did it delight you? I had said nothing; I had explained nothing. I merely recited the verse, and you cried out. What cried out from you? Love of peace. What did I show to your eyes? From where do you cry out if you do not love? From where do you love if you do not see?

Peace is invisible. What is the eye by which it was seen and therefore loved? For you would not acclaim it unless you loved it.

These are the spectacles that God provides of invisible things. With what beauty did the understanding of peace strike your hearts! What shall I now say about peace, or about the praise of peace? Your affection has anticipated all my words. I do not fill them; I cannot; I am weak. Let us defer all praise of peace to that homeland of peace. There we shall praise it more fully, where we shall possess it more fully.

If we love peace in its beginning within us in this way, how shall we praise it when it is perfected?

Behold, this is what I say, beloved children, children of love [Note: [Col. 1924] Several manuscripts have “children of charity.”], children of the kingdom, citizens of Jerusalem—for Jerusalem is the vision of peace—and all who love peace are blessed in it. They themselves enter when the gates are closed and the bars strengthened.

Follow and desire this peace, which you love and cherish under the name just given to it. Love it in the home, in business, in your wives, in your children, in your servants, in your friends, and in your enemies.

### 16

This is the peace which heretics do not possess. What does peace do in the uncertainties of this present region, in this pilgrimage of our mortality, when as yet no one is visible to another, no one sees another’s heart? What does peace do? It does not judge what is uncertain; it does not affirm what is unknown. It is more inclined to believe good of a person than to suspect evil. It does not grieve greatly at being mistaken when it believes good even of someone evil; but it is ruinous when, perhaps unknowingly, it thinks evil of someone good. “I do not know what he is like” [Note: [Col. 1924] Thus most manuscripts. But the editions read: “It is ruinous, however, when he has perhaps thought evil of a good person without knowing what he is like.”]. What do I lose if I believe that he is good? If the matter is uncertain, it is permissible for you to be cautious, lest it perhaps be true; but do not condemn him as though it were true. This is what peace commands. “Seek peace,” he says, “and pursue it” (Ps. 33:15).

What does heresy command? It condemns those it does not know; it condemns the whole world: “The whole world has perished; there is no Christian; Africa alone remains.” You have judged well! From what tribunal do you pronounce sentence upon the whole world? In what court did the world stand before you? I do not want anyone to believe me—but neither do I want anyone to believe you. Let Christ be believed; let the Spirit of God speaking through the Prophets be believed; let the Law of Moses be believed.

What did Moses say about these future times? It was said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Do you doubt what Abraham’s seed is? I think that, once the Apostle has spoken, you will not doubt. Or if you will doubt the Apostle as well, why is it said, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace (Jer. 6:14)? What does the Apostle say? “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” He does not say, “And to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: “And to your seed,” which is Christ (Gal. 3:16).

Behold, thousands of years ago it was said to Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” What was said thousands of years ago, and believed by one man, we now see fulfilled. We read this; we contemplate this; and you come from the side to resist it? What will you say? “Do not believe.” Whom should I not believe—the Spirit of God? God speaking to Abraham? And whom should I believe—you? “I am not saying that,” you will reply. You are not saying that? You are not saying, “Believe me rather than the Spirit of God and God speaking to Abraham”? What, then, are you saying to me? “He betrayed, and he betrayed.” Do you recite this from the Gospel, from the Apostle, from the Prophets? Examine all the Scriptures; read this to me from those writings which I believe—for I do not believe you. From where will you read it? “My father told me this,” he says; “my grandfather told me this; my brother told me this; my bishop told me this.” But the God of Abraham said: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.”

One man hears and believes, and after many ages it comes to pass among many. When it was said, it is believed; when it is fulfilled, is it doubted? Moses, then, said this; let the Prophets also speak. See the transaction by which we were purchased. Christ hangs upon the wood; see at what price he purchased, and thus you will see what he purchased. He is about to purchase something, but you do not yet know what that something is. Look, look at the price, and you will see what it is. He poured out blood; he purchased with his own blood; he purchased with the blood of the spotless Lamb; he purchased with the blood of the only Son of God.

What was purchased with the blood of the only Son of God? Look still at the price. The Prophet said long before it happened: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones.” I see a great price, O Christ [Note: [Col. 1925] Thus several manuscripts. The editions, however, read “of Christ.”]; let me see what you purchased: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.” In one and the same psalm I see the purchaser, the price, and the possession. The purchaser is Christ; the price is blood; the possession is the whole world.

Let us hear the very prophetic words contradicting the contentious heretics. Behold the possession of my Lord. I read the legal claim in the psalm [Note: [Col. 1925] This should be read thus with Erasmus and the better manuscripts. “[Uncertain: ‘Do you wish [it]? I read …],’ etc.”]: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence.” And see him contending; see him defending his right: “For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Ps. 21:17, 18, 28, 29). It is he who purchased, Christ—not Donatus, who apostatized.

“They shall worship”: rightly, “all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence.” Why rightly? “For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations.” Moses said that; the Prophets said this; and there are many thousands of other testimonies. Who can count the testimonies concerning the Church spread throughout the whole world? Who can count them?
