There are not as many heresies against the Church as there are testimonies of the Law for the Church. What page does not proclaim this? What verse does not speak of it? Everything cries out for the Lord’s unity, because he has established peace within the borders of Jerusalem.

You bark against these things, heretic! Hence it is rightly said of that city what is written in the Apocalypse: “Outside are the dogs” (Rev. 22:15). You bark against these things. From where did you judge the whole world, as I had begun to ask? From what tribunal? Evidently from the presumption of your heart. It is a lofty tribunal—but ruinous.

Moses said this; the Prophets said this; and still those who wish to appear Christians do not believe [Note: [Col. 1925] The Corbie manuscript reads, “do not wish to.”]!

### 17

A certain rich man was being tormented in hell. He desired a drop of water from the finger of the poor man whom he had despised before his gate, because he was burning in the flames. And when it was not given to him—for judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy—when, then, it was not given to him, he said to Abraham: “Father Abraham, send Lazarus. I have five brothers; let him announce to them what I am suffering here, lest they too come into this place of torment.” And what did Abraham say to him? “They have Moses and the Prophets there.” But he replied: “No, father Abraham; but if someone rises from the dead, they will believe.” And Abraham said: “If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead” (Luke 16:19–31).

Of whom did he say, “They have Moses and the Prophets there”? Surely of those who were still living, for whom ample time for correction still remained, who had not yet come to those places of torment. “They have there,” he said, “those whom they may hear, Moses and the Prophets.” They do not believe them, but if someone rises from the dead, they will believe. “If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.” This is Abraham’s judgment.

Where, and from what place, was Abraham’s judgment spoken? From a certain lofty place, full of rest and blessedness, which the man who was being tormented in the flame saw when he lifted up his eyes—when, in his bosom, that is, in his place of repose, he saw the poor man rejoicing in blessedness. From there this judgment was uttered. See from what tribunal it came. For God dwells there, because God dwells in the saints. Hence the Apostle desires and says, “To depart and be with Christ is far better” (Phil. 1:23); and to that thief it is said, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Therefore the Lord, being with Abraham and dwelling in Abraham, spoke this judgment: “They have Moses and the Prophets there; if they do not listen to them, neither will they believe him if someone rises from the dead.”

O heretics, here you have Moses and the Prophets! You are still alive; you can still hear; correction is still permitted; you are still allowed to restrain your contentiousness and hold to the truth. Debate among yourselves whether Moses and the Prophets should be heard, since they have offered such abundant testimonies to their faith, while we see human affairs proceeding just as they foretold. Why do you still hesitate to believe Moses and the Prophets? Why do you hesitate to listen?

Perhaps you are seeking someone risen from the dead, to see whether he too will tell you about his Church? This rich man in hell sought for someone to be sent from the dead to his brothers. He was rebuked for seeking this; Moses and the Prophets ought to have been sufficient for his brothers. He sought this in vain so that, now warned by his example, you might not suffer torment like him by seeking in vain and too late.

Listen to Moses and the Prophets. What did Moses say? “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” What did the Prophets say? “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.”

You will still say to me: “Let someone rise from the dead; I will not believe unless someone comes from there and tells me.” O Lord, thanks be to your mercy! You were willing to die so that someone might rise from the dead; and that someone—not just anyone, but the Truth—has risen from the dead. He who could speak truth about the underworld, even if he had not come to the underworld, nevertheless, because of the words of ignorant and evil people, behold, he himself died; behold, he has risen from the dead.

What do you say, heretic? What do you say? Now I will hear you; all your excuses are finished. Even if you were uttering [Note: [Col. 1926] The editions read “mocking,” with the manuscripts differing.] the words of the rich man situated in hell, Christ has risen from the dead. Will you deign at least to listen to him himself? Behold, he whom perhaps, while alive, you desired—like that dead rich man—to rise from the dead has risen from the dead [Note: [Col. 1926] Thus the manuscripts. But Augustine’s edition and Erasmus read: “Behold, because perhaps you are like the dead rich man, you desired the living to rise from the dead.” The Louvain edition likewise, except that it has “alive” instead of “the living.”]—not your father, not your grandfather, not those who, I do not know whom, have branded with the name of “tradition.”

But suppose they did not brand them; suppose they spoke the truth. Do you want to know how little that concerns me? Let us hear together what he who rose from the dead said. Why should I delay any longer? Let the Gospel now be opened; let what happened be read as though it were happening; let past events be placed before our eyes for the sake of avoiding future ones.

Behold Christ rising from the dead and showing himself to his disciples. This is his wedding: he is the bridegroom; the Church is the bride. Behold the bridegroom who was said to be dead, destroyed, finished; behold, he has risen whole; behold, he is shown to the eyes of his disciples; behold, he is offered to their hands to touch; behold, they touched the scars—the wounds whose healing had been despaired of [Note: [Col. 1927] Augustine’s edition reads, “whose wound had been despaired of.” Erasmus and several manuscripts read, “which had been despaired of as wounds.”].

He showed himself to their eyes to be seen and to their hands to be touched. They think he is a spirit, for they had despaired of their own salvation. He encourages them and confirms them in faith: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.”

They touch him, rejoice, and tremble. And while they were still trembling for joy, so you have it written. Even things that are certain, when they are exceedingly joyful, are scarcely believed. A certain hesitation, like that of one who believes more slowly, gives shape to the will of the one who possesses [Note: [Col. 1927] “Gives shape to the delight of the one who possesses” seems to be the preferable reading.]. It is necessary that a person rejoice more when what he had despaired of has come.

Indeed, to deepen and increase that joy, he did not wish to be recognized immediately. He restrained the sight of his disciples—those two whom he found speaking together on the road, already in despair, and saying: “But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.” They had thought this; now they no longer thought it. Hope was no longer with them, and Christ was with them—but he restored himself to them and restored hope.

Afterward, then, after they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread, he offered himself to his other disciples. When they thought he was a spirit, he said: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.” And while they were still trembling for joy, he said: “Do you have anything here to eat?” He took it, blessed it, ate it, and gave it to them. The reality of his body was made manifest; every suspicion of unreality was removed.

What follows? “Did you not know that it was necessary for everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms to be fulfilled?” And because they believed Moses and the Prophets—for what Abraham said was true, “If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead”—because, therefore, they believed Moses and the Prophets and were not among those whom Abraham rebuked, they heard what the Lord said: “Did you not know that it was necessary for everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms to be fulfilled?”

Behold those who believed Moses and the Prophets. See how, on the testimony of Moses and the Prophets themselves, they believe him who rose from the dead: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures; and he said to them, ‘Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day.’”

### 18

You now have the bridegroom of the Church. Moses was not silent about this, nor were the Prophets silent: that Christ would rise from the dead on the third day; that he would suffer and rise. The bridegroom has been portrayed for us, so that we may not go astray.

But certain people arise who, because we do not go astray concerning the bridegroom—and they themselves appear to believe about the bridegroom what we believe—say this to us in order to draw us away from the bridegroom’s members: “He is indeed the bridegroom whom you believe in, whom we too believe in; but the bride is not the Church which you hold.” And what is that bride? “The Party of Donatus.”

And is this what you say, or does the bridegroom say it? Is it you who say it, or God through Moses? Behold, through Moses I hold to the Church: Moses said, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.”

Is it you who say it, or the Spirit of God through the Prophets? Behold, through the Prophets I hold to the Church: the Prophet said, “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.”

Behold, I now hold the testimony of the Law and the testimony of the Prophets. Let us also hear him who rose from the dead. He showed himself to be the bridegroom; we hold fast to him. He confirmed this by demonstrating and presenting the testimonies. For Moses said this, and the Prophets said this: that Christ had to suffer and rise on the third day.

Since, then, we both hold the bridegroom from these very words—and I think that you are now beginning to believe with me both these words of Moses and the Prophets—let us also believe him who rose from the dead. Let him follow and speak.

“O Lord, I now see Christ the bridegroom; it has happened. Let no one draw me away from the members of your bride, and do not be my head if I am not among her members. Tell me something also about the Church, since I no longer doubt her bridegroom.”

Hear also about the Church. He continues and says: “Repentance and the forgiveness of sins must be preached in his name.” Nothing is truer: repentance and the forgiveness of sins must be preached in his name. But where?

Some say, “Behold, here”; others, “Behold, there.” And what does he himself say? “Do not believe them. False Christs and false prophets will arise and say, ‘Behold, here,’ and, ‘Behold, there’” (Matt. 24:23–24). They are not speaking of the head himself when they say, “Behold, here,” and, “Behold, there.” It is known that Christ is in heaven. Rather, they are speaking of the Church, where Christ is—the one who said, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (ibid. 28:20).

But the Lord says: “Do not believe them.” Whoever says, “Behold, here,” and, “Behold, there,” points out portions; I purchased the whole.

Let the Gospel tell me this; let him himself say this from the Gospel, since you have now risen from the dead, so that those who believe Moses and the Prophets may believe you. Say this to me yourself.

“I hear: It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:13–47).

What do you say, heretic? Certainly, when I was reciting Moses and reciting the Prophets, you deferred to him who was to rise from the dead. Behold, he has risen; behold, he has spoken. The Church of Christ and the wife of Christ possess as little uncertainty as the body of Christ possesses uncertainty when it has been displayed to the eyes and touched by the hands of the disciples.

Behold, he who rose from the dead displayed both. He displayed the head; he displayed the members. He displayed the bridegroom; he displayed the bride. Either believe both with me, or you believe the one to your condemnation.

What does it matter that he rose from the dead, and that he rose in the same body? You believe well because he showed his scars; because just as he was crucified and buried, so he was restored and displayed. You believe excellently. Listen to the one in whom you believe speaking: “Repentance and the forgiveness of sins must be preached in his name.” Where? Throughout the broad lands.

If I wished to say this myself, now struggling against heretics, now fighting, now engaged with them in a conflict over so great a question, I would not say it to the heretics present in the way that he said it against those who would come in the future. What more do you want? The forgiveness of sins is preached in Christ’s name. Where? “Among all nations.” From where? “Beginning from Jerusalem.”

Join yourself to this Church. Why do we quarrel? This Church began here on earth at Jerusalem so that from there it might rejoice in God in that heavenly Jerusalem. From this one it begins; in that one it ends. In that one the whole Church will be; from this one it took the beginning of its faith.

### 19

Read the Acts of the Apostles, if perhaps I am lying: how the disciples were gathered there when the Holy Spirit came, so that what the Lord said—“Beginning from Jerusalem”—might be shown to you; how they spoke in all the languages of those upon whom the Holy Spirit came (Acts 1:4–14; 2:1–12).

Why do you not wish to speak in all languages? Behold, all languages sounded there. Why now does the one who receives the Holy Spirit not speak in all languages? For at that time this was the sign that the Holy Spirit was coming upon human beings: that they should speak in all languages.

What will you say now, heretic? That the Holy Spirit is not given? I do not ask, “Where?” [Note: [Col. 1929] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Louvain edition read, “I do not tell you where.” M.] Is he given, or is he not given? If he is not given, what is it that you are doing by speaking, baptizing, and blessing? What is it that you are doing? You are celebrating empty rites.

Therefore he is given. If he is given, why do those to whom he is given not speak in all languages? Has God’s gift failed, or is its fruit less? The weeds have grown, but so has the wheat: “Let both grow until the harvest” (Matt. 13:30). He did not say, “Let the weeds grow and let the grain diminish”; both have grown.

Why, then, does the Holy Spirit not now appear in all languages? On the contrary, he does appear in all languages. At that time the Church had not yet been spread throughout the world, so that Christ’s members might speak in all nations. Then what was foretold concerning all was being fulfilled in one. Now the whole body of Christ speaks in all languages; and in those languages in which it does not yet speak, it will speak. The Church will grow until it occupies all languages.

What you abandoned—how far it has grown! Hold fast with us to how far it has advanced, so that with us you may reach what it has not yet reached.

I dare to say to you: I am in the body of Christ; I am in the Church of Christ. If the body of Christ now speaks in all languages, then I am in all languages. Greek is mine, Syriac is mine, Hebrew is mine; I belong to all nations, because I am in the unity of all nations.

### 20

Therefore, brothers, the Church began from Jerusalem and went throughout all nations. What could be clearer than this testimony of the Law, the Prophets, and the Lord himself? The voices of the Apostles resound everywhere, bearing witness to our hope in the unity of Christ’s body.

Rejoice in the grain; tolerate the weeds; groan in the threshing; sigh for the granary. The time will come when we shall rejoice, with the bars of Jerusalem’s gates secured. Let him enter who is to enter. Whoever will enter there openly does not enter here falsely. But whoever enters here falsely is outside. He is outside and does not know it. The winnowing fan will prove it; the bars will prove it.

Whoever is now truly and genuinely inside will be firmly inside there. Whoever is here inside by enduring will be there inside by rejoicing. “The borders of Jerusalem are peace,” because, he says, “he has established peace within your borders.”

Now we desire the peace which we possess here in hope. For what kind of peace is there yet within us? “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). When is there complete peace in one person? When it is complete in one person, then it will be complete in all the citizens of Jerusalem.

When will there be complete peace? When “this corruptible thing has put on incorruption, and this mortal thing has put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53). Then there will be complete peace; then firm peace. Nothing will contend against the soul in a person; the soul itself will not contend against itself, wounded in some part; there will be no frailty of the flesh, no bodily need, no hunger, no thirst, no cold, no heat, no weariness, no deprivation of any kind, no provocation to quarrel, and certainly not even that anxious care required to avoid an enemy and love him.

All these things, my brothers, contend against us; peace is not yet complete and perfect. When you cried out a little while ago at the mention of peace, you cried out from desire. Your cry arose from thirst, not from satiety, because perfect justice will be where perfect peace is.

Now we hunger and thirst for justice. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6). How shall they be satisfied? When we have come to peace. Therefore, after saying, “He has established peace within your borders”—because there will be satiety there and no deprivation—he immediately added, “And satisfying you with the fat of grain.”

### 21

Brothers, since the peace of which we are speaking is not yet wholly within us—that is, since it is not yet complete in each one of us—it may still delight your spirit to listen. But if nothing from the body resists and rebels, we shall finish the Psalm.

I never perceive you to be weary; nevertheless, God knows, I fear that I may be a burden to you or to some of the brothers. And I see the eagerness of many who demand from me this labor and this sweat, which I believe will not be fruitless in the Lord. I rejoice that the pleasure found in the truth of God’s word is so great that your good zeal, directed toward what is good and arising from what is good, surpasses the zeal of the madmen in the amphitheater. If they stood there for so long, would they still be watching?

Therefore, brothers, let us hear the rest, since this is what you wish. May the Lord be present—present both to our strength and to our minds.

“He has established peace within your borders” is said of that Jerusalem; “and satisfying you with the fat of grain.” Hunger and thirst for justice pass away; satiety follows. What will be the fat of grain there except that bread which descended from heaven to us (John 6:51)? In the homeland itself, how will he satisfy us who has fed us in such a way during our pilgrimage?

### 22. [verse 15]

Now he is going to speak of our pilgrimage itself, by which we come to that Jerusalem where we shall praise the Lord together, where we shall praise the Lord our God—when we, Jerusalem, we, Zion, shall have our gates’ bars secured.

For what does the one who will then satisfy us with the fat of grain do during this pilgrimage? This is what follows: “Who sends his word to the earth.”

Behold, on earth we labor, weary, languid, sluggish, cold. When would we rise to the fat of grain and satiety [Note: [Col. 1931] Augustine’s edition and the manuscripts read, “to the satisfying fat of grain.”] unless he sent his word to the earth by which we were weighed down, to the earth by which we were hindered from returning?

He sent his word; he did not abandon us even in the wilderness; manna rained from heaven. “Who sends his word to the earth.” And his word came to the earth. How? Or what is his word? “His word runs swiftly.” He did not say, “His word is swift”; his word runs “into swiftness.”

Let us understand, brothers. He could not have chosen a better word. A hot thing becomes hot through heat; a cold thing becomes cold through cold; a swift thing becomes swift through swiftness. What is hotter than the heat by which whatever becomes hot is made hot? What is colder than the cold by which whatever becomes cold is made cold? What, then, is swifter than the swiftness by which whatever runs swiftly becomes swift?

Many things can be called swift, some more and some less. Each thing is swift to the extent that it participates in swiftness. That thing participates more in swiftness; therefore it is swifter; or it participates less in swiftness; therefore it is less swift. What, then, is swifter than swiftness itself?

Therefore, how far does it run? Into swiftness. Increase the swiftness of the word as much as you wish, and say: “It is swifter than this or that, than birds, than winds, than angels.” Is any of these things as great as swiftness itself—reaching into swiftness itself?

What is swiftness itself, brothers? It is everywhere; it is not in a part. This pertains to the Word of God: the Word itself is not in a part but is everywhere, for it is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24), not yet having assumed flesh.

If we think of God in the form of God, the Word equal to the Father, it is that very Wisdom of God of which it was said: “She reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. 8:1). What swiftness! “She reaches mightily from end to end.”

But perhaps she reaches by immobility. If by immobility, as though some mass of stone filled a certain place, one may say that it reaches from one end of that place to the other, though not by movement.

What, then, shall we say? Does that Word have no movement, and is that Wisdom foolish? And what of what is said about the Spirit of Wisdom? After many things had been said, it says: “Sharp, mobile, certain, undefiled” (ibid. 7:22). Thus, surely, the Wisdom of God is mobile.

If, then, it is mobile, when it touches this, does it not touch that? Or does it touch this and abandon that? And where is its swiftness? Swiftness accomplishes this: that it is always everywhere and is nowhere confined.

But we cannot comprehend these things; we are sluggish. Who could comprehend them? And truly, brothers, since I have spoken as I was able—if indeed I was able, if indeed I understood—and as you were able to understand, what does the Apostle say? “To him who is able to do above all that we ask or understand” (Eph. 3:20).

What does he show here? That whenever we have understood, we have not understood as it truly is. Why is this? “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15).

Therefore, on earth we are cold. Swiftness is ardent; everything ardent is swifter, and everything cold is slower. We are slow, therefore we are cold. But that Wisdom runs into swiftness. Therefore it is most ardent, and “there is none who can hide from its heat” (Ps. 19:6).

### 23. [verse 16]

We, then, who are cold because of the slowness of the body, weighed down by the bond of this earthly and corruptible life—do we have no hope of grasping the Word that runs into swiftness? Or has he abandoned us, though by means of the body he has pressed us down into the lowest regions?

Did he not predestine us before we were born in this mortal and sluggish body? He who predestined us, then, gave the earth snow—us ourselves.

Let us now come to those somewhat obscure verses of the Psalm; let those coverings begin to be unfolded, since the more God’s word is spoken through us, the more eagerly it finds you.

Behold, sluggish on this earth, we have almost frozen here. And what happens with snow? It freezes above and falls down to the lower places. Thus, as love grew cold, human nature fell into these earthly regions and, wrapped in a sluggish body, became like snow.

But in this snow are the predestined children of God. For “he gives snow like wool.” What does “like wool” mean? It means that from the snow he gave—from those who are still sluggish and cold in spirit, whom he predestined—he is going to make something.

Wool is the material of a garment. When wool is seen, it is, as it were, a preparation for a garment. Therefore, because he predestined those who for a time crawl coldly upon the earth and do not yet burn with the fervor of love—for he is still speaking of predestination—God gave these as wool. He is going to make a garment from them.

It was fitting, therefore, that on the mountain Christ’s garment shone like snow (Matt. 17:2). Christ’s garment shone like snow, as though a tunic had already been made from that wool. From what wool? From the snow which he gave like wool. Those who were still predestined and sluggish were the wool; but wait and see what follows, because just as he gave them as wool, a tunic is made from them.

For just as the Church is called Christ’s body, so the Church itself is called Christ’s garment. Hence the Apostle says, “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27).

Let him therefore present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle; let him make himself a garment from that wool which he predestined in the snow. While they are still unbelieving, cold, and sluggish human beings, let him make a garment from this wool. So that it may be cleansed of spots, let it be washed by faith; so that it may have no wrinkle, let it be stretched upon the cross.

“He gives snow like wool.”

### 24

Now, if they have been predestined, they must be called. “Those whom he predestined, he also called” (Rom. 8:30). How, then, are they called from the sickness of that body so that they may be made well? How are they called? Hear the Gospel: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9:13).

Therefore, by the predestination of that snow, someone begins to recognize his torpor, to accuse his sin; by the calling, he begins to come to repentance [Note: [Col. 1932] Most manuscripts read, “by the predestination of the power of that one.” Others read, “by the predestination, someone begins to recognize.” Perhaps the reading should be, “that night.”].

Rightly, then, the one who gives snow like wool—because of the making of the future garment—also, because of the calling to repentance, “scatters mist like ashes.” “He scatters mist like ashes,” it says. Who does this? The one who gives snow like wool. For those whom he predestined, he calls to repentance, because those whom he predestined, he also called.

Ashes, moreover, pertain to repentance. Hear him calling to repentance when he reproached certain cities, saying: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were performed among you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, long ago,” he said, “they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11:21).

Therefore he scatters mist like ashes. What does “He scatters mist like ashes” mean? When someone is called to understand God and is told, “Grasp the truth,” he begins to wish to grasp the truth, but it is not enough. He sees that he is suffering from a certain darkness which he did not see before.

That mist exists so that you may know that you do not know, that you may know what ought to be known, and that you may see yourself unable to know what ought to be known. For if, while in this mist, you presume that you already know, you will hear from the Apostle: “Whoever thinks that he knows something does not yet know how he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2).

Therefore you have not yet comprehended; you are still suffering the mist. But the one who kindled for you the lamp of his flesh has not abandoned you. You do not go astray in the mist; follow by faith.

But because you strive to see and cannot, repent of your sins, because the mist has been scattered like ashes. Now repent that you were obstinate toward God; now repent that you followed your own evil ways. You have reached the difficulty of that blessed vision, and the mist which God scatters like ashes will be beneficial to you.

You yourself are still mist, but mist like ashes. For those who are still repenting roll about in ashes, my brothers, as though confessing that they are like them, saying to their God: “I am ashes.”

For a certain Scripture said: “I despised myself and wasted away, and I regarded myself as earth and ashes” (Job 30:19). This is the humility of the penitent.

When Abraham speaks to his God and wishes the destruction of Sodom to be disclosed to him, he says: “I am earth and ashes” (Gen. 18:27). How has this humility always existed in great and holy men?

Therefore he scatters mist like ashes. Why? Because those whom he predestined, he also called—the one who did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

### 25. [verses 17–18]

“He sends his ice like morsels of bread.”

There is no need to labor again to explain what the ice is. We have spoken beforehand, and I believe it has not escaped your Charity. What, then, does “He sends his ice like morsels of bread” mean?

Just as that snow is his because it belongs to the predestined; just as that mist is his because those who were predestined for salvation are called to repentance; so, in a certain manner, the ice is his.

What is ice? It has become very hard; it has frozen very deeply. It can no longer be dissolved easily like snow. Snow which has endured for many years and through a succession of ages is called ice. And this he sends like morsels of bread.

What does this mean? Some were exceedingly hard—not merely comparable to snow, but to ice. They too were predestined and called; and some of them were so formed that they might feed others and be useful to others.

Why should we count many whom we perhaps know, this person or that? Each person, reflecting on those he knows, will recall how hard, obstinate, and resistant to the truth they perhaps were, and how now they preach the truth. They have become morsels of bread.

Who is that one bread? The Apostle says, “We are one body in Christ” (Rom. 12:5). “One bread, one body—we who are many,” he says (1 Cor. 10:17). Therefore, if the one bread is the whole body of Christ, Christ’s members are morsels of bread.

From certain hard people he makes his members, useful for feeding others. Why go through many examples? Let us look at the Apostle Paul, so well known. Nothing is more familiar to us than this man, nothing sweeter, nothing more familiar in the Scriptures. And if there are people who, from as great a hardness as his, become bread [Note: [Col. 1934] Thus the better manuscripts. Erasmus and the Louvain edition read, “who are converted from as great a hardness as his and will become bread. By him,” etc.], let them all come to mind, with him set forth as an example, so that this meaning may be explained: “He sends his ice like morsels of bread.”

Behold, the Apostle Paul was ice: hard, resisting the truth, crying out against the Gospel, as though hardening himself against the sun. How hard he was, growing up in the Law, educated at the feet of Gamaliel, a teacher of the Law (Acts 22:3)!

Did he not hear Moses and the Prophets preaching Christ? Great hardness! Certainly the Gentiles had not heard the Prophets; they had not heard Moses. They were cold, but they were not ice. The man who believed in the words preaching Christ, yet did not believe in Christ when he came, had hardened himself exceedingly.

Because he was ice, therefore, he appeared bright and white—but hard and excessively cold. How was he bright and white? “A Hebrew of Hebrews; according to the Law, a Pharisee.” See the brightness of the ice.

Hear the hardness of the ice: “According to zeal, persecuting the Church of Christ” (Phil. 3:5–6). Among those stoning the holy martyr Stephen, this man was present—hard, and perhaps harder than the others. For he guarded the garments of all those who were stoning him, so that he might stone him with everyone’s hands (Acts 7:57).

26. Therefore we see snow, mist, and crystal: it is good that he breathe upon it and melt it. For if he does not breathe upon it, if he himself does not dissolve the hardness of this ice, “Who can withstand the face of his cold?” The face of whose cold? Of God. Whence comes his cold? See: he abandons the sinner; see: he does not call him; see: he does not open his understanding; see: he does not pour in grace. Let a person be released from the ice of his folly, if he can. He cannot. [Note: [Col. 1934] Thus the manuscripts. But Am. and Lov. read: “if he can receive grace, he cannot [be released from] folly. Why, then, etc.” Er. reads: “if he cannot receive grace, he cannot [be released from] folly: Why, then, etc.”]

Why can he not? “Who can withstand the face of his cold?” See, then, that person freezing and saying: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” See, I am growing cold; see, I am freezing. By what warmth shall I be melted, so that I may run? “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” “Who can withstand the face of his cold?” And who will deliver himself if he abandons him? And who delivers? “The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 23–25).

Hear grace here also: “He sends his crystal like [Col. 1935] morsels of bread: who can withstand the face of his cold?” Is there, then, despair? Far from it. For what follows is: “He will send forth his word, and melt them.” Therefore let not the snow despair; let not the mist despair; let not the crystal despair. For from snow, as from wool, a tunic is made. That mist finds salvation in repentance, because “those whom he predestined, he also called.” But even if there are among the predestined those who are extremely hard, and who have remained frozen for a very long time, as it were, and have become crystal, they will not be hard against the mercy of God. “He will send forth his word, and melt them.” What does “melt” mean? Lest you understand “melt” in a bad sense: he will liquefy them; he will dissolve them. For they are hard through pride. And deservedly pride is also called stupor; whatever is stupid is cold. People who have suffered from the cold say every day, “I was stupefied.” Therefore pride is stupor. “He will send forth his word, and melt them.” And indeed, when heaps of snow grow warm [Note: [Col. 1935] One manuscript reads “they melt” (tabefiunt).], they dissolve into water through humility. Just as stupor raises itself up like a mountain of snow, so pride raises up fools. “He will send forth his word, and melt them.”

See, that crystal, Saul, after the slaughter and stoning of Stephen, hardened in a kind of stupor against Christ, sought letters from the priests so that he might bring Christians from every quarter, panting for slaughter. He is hard and cold against the fire of God. But although he was hard, although he was cold [Note: [Col. 1935] The manuscripts here and below consistently read quanquam (“although”) rather than quantum (“as much as”).], see: he who would send forth his word and melt them cried out fervently from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 1–4). With that one voice, such great hardness of crystal was dissolved. Therefore, “he will send forth his word, and melt them.”

Let no one despair of crystal; still less of snow or mist. Let no one despair of crystal itself. Hear a certain voice of crystal: “I who formerly was a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and an injurious person.” But why did God melt the crystal? So that the snow itself might not despair of itself. For he says: “For this reason I obtained mercy, so that in me Christ Jesus might display all patience, as an example for those who would believe in him for eternal life” (I Tim. I, 13, 16).

Therefore God cries out to the nations: “I have melted the crystal; come, you snows.” “He will send forth his word, and melt them; his spirit will breathe, and the waters will flow.” See: crystal and snows are dissolved; they become waters. Let those who thirst come and drink. Saul, hard as crystal, persecuted Stephen to death; Paul now calls the nations to the fountain of living water. “His spirit will breathe, and the waters will flow.” A fervent Spirit: hence it is said in another psalm, “Turn our captivity, O Lord, like a stream in the south” (Ps. CXXV, 4). Jerusalem, captive, had frozen, as it were, in Babylonia; the south wind blows, the rigidity of captivity is dissolved, and the fervor of charity runs toward God. “His spirit will breathe, and the waters will flow.” “It will become in them a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John IV, 14).

27. [verse 19.] “Announcing his word to Jacob, his justifications and his judgments to Israel.”

What justifications? What judgments? Because everything that the human race has previously suffered here, when it was snow, mist, and crystal, it rightly suffered on account of its pride and exaltation against God. [Col. 1936] Let us return to the origin of our fall and see that the psalm most truly sings: “Before I was humbled, I transgressed.” But the one who says, “Before I was humbled, I transgressed,” himself says, “It is good for me that you have humbled me, so that I may learn your justifications” (Ps. CXVIII, 67, 71).

Jacob, then, learned these justifications from God—the Jacob whom he caused to wrestle with the Angel, in whose person the Lord himself had wrestled. He held him; he exerted force so as to hold him; he prevailed in order to hold him. Mercy allowed itself to be held, not weakness. Jacob therefore wrestled, prevailed, and held him; and the one whom he seemed to have defeated he asked to bless him (Gen. XXXII, 24–26).

How did he understand with whom he had wrestled and whom he had held? Why did he wrestle violently and hold him? Because “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use violence seize it” (Matt. XI, 12). Why, then, did he wrestle? Because it requires labor. Why do we scarcely hold what we easily lost? So that, by recovering easily what we lost, we might not learn to lose what we hold. Let a person labor to hold; what he has held after labor, he will hold firmly.

Therefore God manifested these judgments of his to Jacob and Israel. I will speak more plainly: that is, because even the righteous who are here suffer labors, dangers, troubles, and sufferings according to their merit, by the just judgment of God. For only that one can say that he suffered here without cause—although he did not suffer without cause, because he suffered for us—who alone could say, “What I did not seize, I then repaid” (Ps. LXVIII, 5); who alone could say, “The prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me.” And as if someone said to him, “Why, then, do you suffer?” he continues and says: “But so that all may know that I do the will of my Father: arise, let us go from here” (John XIV, 30, 31).

Let all the others who suffer according to their own merit, by the judgment of God and for righteousness, not arrogate to themselves, as though they possessed the suffering of innocence [Note: Thus several manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “and those who suffer for righteousness should not arrogate to themselves, as though they possessed the suffering of innocence,”] such as existed in Christ.

Hear the apostle Peter: “It is time,” he says, “for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord.” Exhorting the martyrs and witnesses of God to endure with the greatest patience all the threats of the roaring world, he said to them: “It is time for the beginning of judgment from the house of God. But if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the gospel of God? And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (I Peter IV, 4, 17, 18).

“Announcing his word to Jacob, his justifications and his judgments to Israel.”

28. [verse 20.] “He has not dealt so with every nation.”

Let no one deceive you: this judgment of God was not announced to any nation in such a way as to explain how both the righteous and the unrighteous suffer; how all suffer according to their merit; how the righteous themselves are delivered by the grace of God, not by their own merits. This was not announced to every nation, but only to Jacob, only to Israel.

What, then, shall we do, if he did not announce it to every nation but only to Jacob, only to Israel? Where shall we be? In Jacob and in Israel. “He did not manifest his judgments to them.” To whom? To all the nations.

And how were the snows called when the crystal was dissolved? How were the nations called when Paul was justified? How, unless they were to be in Jacob? “The wild olive was cut off so that it might be grafted into the olive” (Rom. XI, 17). Now they belong to the olive; now [Col. 1937] they should no longer be called nations, but one nation in Christ, the nation of Jacob, the nation of Israel.

Why the nation of Jacob and the nation of Israel? Because Jacob came from Isaac, and Isaac from Abraham. And what was said to Abraham? “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” The same was said to Isaac, and also to Jacob (Gen. XXII, 18; XXVI, 4; XXVIII, 14).

We therefore belong to Jacob, because we belong to Isaac; we belong to Abraham. For the seed of Abraham—not as interpreted by me or by any other person, but as interpreted by the holy Apostle—is Christ. And he says: “He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as of many, but as of one, ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. III, 16).

If there is one seed, there is one Jacob, one Israel, and all the nations are one [Note: [Col. 1937] The printed editions read unum (“one”); several manuscripts disagree.] in Christ. Therefore what he revealed to Jacob himself and to Israel himself pertains to all nations; and the only ones to be reckoned among the other nations are those who, refusing to believe in Christ, refuse to leave the wild olive and be grafted into the olive.

They will remain sterile and bitter branches among the woods [Note: Thus several manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “They will remain in the wooded branches, sterile and bitter.”]

Let Jacob rejoice. What is Jacob? “Supplanter,” because Jacob supplanted his brother (Gen. XXVII, 36). “For blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the nations enters” (Rom. XI, 25).

From Jacob Israel was made. What is Israel? Now let us all hear it—all Israel, whether you who are here in the members of Christ, or those who are outside and not outside, and throughout all nations everywhere outside, everywhere within. Let Israel himself hear, he who from Jacob was made Israel.

What is Israel? “Seeing God.” Where will he see God? In peace. In what peace? In the peace of Jerusalem; for, he says, “He has placed peace as your borders.” There we shall praise; all of us, one in the One, shall be directed to the One, because from then on we shall no longer be many and scattered.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 148

## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1. [verse 1.]

The meditation of our present life ought to be in the praise of God, because the eternal rejoicing of our future life will be the praise of God; and no one can become fit for the future life who has not trained himself for it now.

Now, therefore, we praise God, but we also ask God. Our praise has joy; our prayer has groaning. For something has been promised to us that we do not yet possess; and because the one who promised is truthful, we rejoice in hope. Yet because we do not yet possess it, we groan in desire. It is good for us to persevere in desire until what was promised comes, the groaning passes away, and praise alone takes its place.

On account of these two periods—one that is now, in the temptations and tribulations of this life, and the other that will then be, in security and perpetual rejoicing—we have also been given the observance of two seasons: before Easter and after Easter. What takes place before Easter signifies the tribulation in which we now are; what we do after Easter signifies the blessedness in which we shall later be.

Therefore, before Easter, what we celebrate, we also enact; but after Easter, what we celebrate, we signify, though we do not yet possess it. For this reason we spend that season [Col. 1938] in fasts and prayers; but this season we conduct with our fasts relaxed, in praises. This is what we sing: “Alleluia,” which, as you know, is interpreted in Latin as “Praise the Lord.”

That season, therefore, is the time before the resurrection; this is the time after the Lord’s resurrection. By this time the future life is signified, which we do not yet possess; for what we signify after the Lord’s resurrection, we shall possess after our own resurrection.

Both things have been figured and demonstrated for us in our Head. The Lord’s Passion shows us the life of present necessity, since we must labor, suffer tribulation, and finally die. But the Lord’s resurrection and glorification show us the life that we shall receive, when he comes to repay what is due to the deserving: evil to the evil, good to the good.

Indeed, now all the wicked can sing “Alleluia” with us. But if they persist in their wickedness, they will be able to speak with their lips the song of our future life; the life itself, however, which will then exist in the reality now signified, they cannot obtain, because they were unwilling to meditate upon it before it came and to hold what was going to come.

### 2.

Now, therefore, brothers, we exhort you to praise God; and this is what we all say to one another when we say, “Alleluia.” “Praise the Lord,” you say to another, and he says it to you. When all exhort one another, all do what they exhort.

But praise him with your whole selves [Note: Thus the manuscripts. But Am. and Lov. read: “But praise him with all your vows, that is, etc.” Er. reads: “But praise him with all your vows, with your whole selves, etc.”]—that is, let not only your tongue and your voice praise God, but also your conscience, your life, and your deeds.

For now we praise in the church when we assemble; when each person departs to his own affairs, he seems to cease praising God. Let him not cease to live well, and he always praises God. You cease to praise God when you turn aside from justice and from what pleases him.

For if you never turn aside from a good life, your tongue is silent, but your life cries out; and the ears of God are directed toward your heart. For just as our ears are directed toward our voices, so the ears of God are directed toward our thoughts.

It cannot happen that one who has good thoughts has evil deeds. Deeds proceed from thought; and no one can do anything, or move his limbs to do anything, unless the command of thought has first preceded it.

Just as from the inner palace whatever the emperor commands spreads throughout the Roman Empire—whatever you see being done throughout the provinces—so great is the movement produced by a single command of the emperor seated within. He merely moves his lips when he speaks, and the whole province is moved when what he says is done.

So also within each human being there is an emperor, seated in the heart. If he commands good things, good things are done; if he commands evil things, evil things are done. When Christ sits there, what can he command except good things? When the devil possesses it, what can he command except evil things?

But God willed that it should be in your power whom you prepare a place for: God or the devil. When you have made the preparation, whoever takes possession will command.

Therefore, brothers, do not attend only to sound. When you praise God, praise him with your whole selves: let the voice sing, let the life sing, let the deeds sing.

[Col. 1939] Although there is still groaning, tribulation, and temptation, hope that everything will pass away and that day will come when we shall praise without interruption.

See, this psalm, because it is clear, must be traversed by us. For it distributes the whole of creation as praising God, and seems to exhort it to praise, as though it had found it silent.

### 3.

“Praise the Lord from the heavens.”

As though he had found praise of the Lord silent in the heavens, he exhorts it to rise and praise. The heavenly things have never been silent in their praises of their Creator; earthly things have never ceased to praise God.

But there are plainly some things that possess the spirit of praising God in the affection with which God pleases them. For no one praises what does not please him.

There are other things, however, that do not possess the spirit of life and understanding with which to praise God. Yet because they too are good, arranged intact in their proper order, and referred to the beauty of the universe that God established, they themselves do not praise God with their own voice or heart; but when they are considered by those who understand, God is praised through them. And when God is praised through them, they too, in a certain way, praise God.

For example, all things in heaven that possess the spirit of life and a pure understanding for contemplating him and loving him without weariness or failure praise God in heaven.

But on earth, human beings praise God through the understanding by which they distinguish good and evil and recognize the creature and the Creator—those who reflect upon these things, to whom the Lord has given the mind to distinguish, delight in, and praise them.

Human beings can do this. Do animals perhaps possess such understanding? If animals possessed such understanding, God would not say to us: “Do not be like the horse and the mule, in which there is no understanding” (Ps. XXXI, 9).

When he exhorts us not to be like animals, without understanding, he shows us that he has given human beings understanding with which to praise God.

Do trees perhaps possess even the life by which they perceive, as animals do? For animals, although they do not possess the inner rational sense and intelligent, discerning mind that human beings possess in order to praise God, nevertheless possess manifest life: as we all know, they desire food, take what is useful, reject what is harmful, and possess bodily senses for distinguishing things—the sight of colors, hearing for sounds, smell for odors, taste for flavors, and movement either toward pleasures or away from troubles [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “or movement either for recognizing troubles.”]

We understand these things and see them before our eyes. Animals do not possess the reason that understands, but they do possess the spirit of an animate body and manifest life. Trees, however, do not even possess this; and yet all things praise God.

Why do they praise God? Because when we see and consider these things, and the Creator who made them, praise of God arises in us from them. And when God is praised through consideration of them, all things praise God.

He therefore began from heaven: all things praise, and he says, “Praise.” Why, when they are praising, does he say, “Praise”? Because he delighted in what they praise, and it pleased him, as it were, to add his own exhortation.

It is like coming upon people working joyfully—whether in a vineyard, in a harvest, or in some [Col. 1940] agricultural task. What they are doing pleases you, and you say, “Do it; work.” You do not mean that they should begin to do it only when you say so; rather, because you found them doing what pleased you, you add your own congratulation and exhortation.

By saying, “Do it,” and exhorting those who are already working, you make yourself, as it were, a participant with them by your good will. In this exhortation, therefore, the Prophet, full of the Spirit, says these things.

### 4.

It is also the psalm of Haggai and Zechariah; this is how its title reads.

These two prophets, at the time when the people were held captive in Babylonia, were already prophesying the future end of the captivity, so that the city of Jerusalem, which had fallen in war, might be restored (I Esdras V, 1, 2; and VI, 14).

In a mystery, therefore, they signified for us the future life, where we shall praise God after the captivity of the present life; where there will be the renewal of that great city, Jerusalem, from which we sigh as exiles, still held captive beneath the burden and weight of a mortal body. From there we still groan in exile, but in our homeland we shall rejoice.

Whoever does not groan as an exile will not rejoice as a citizen, because he has no desire.

These holy prophets therefore offered great consolation at that time to the people who were captive according to the flesh—that is, established in Babylonia under foreign kings. For through prophecy they showed the future time of release from captivity and of Jerusalem’s restoration.

But all those events took place as a figure (I Cor. X, 6); they possess their own truth. They were figured in the ancients; they are shown as present in us.

What, then, does the Apostle say now? “As long as we are in the body, we are exiles from the Lord” (II Cor. V, 6). We are not yet in our homeland.

When shall we be in our homeland? When we triumph after the enemy, the devil, has been conquered; when “the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed.” Then the saying that is written will take place: “Death is swallowed up in victory. Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (I Cor. XV, 26, 54, 55).

When, then, will there be no contention of death—the contention that now exists and makes us groan because of the failure and mutability of things, and because of the frailty of human flesh?

Temptations contend with us every day; pleasures contend with us every day. Even if we do not consent, we nevertheless suffer distress, contend, and face the great danger that the one who contends may be defeated. But even if we conquer by refusing consent, we still suffer distress in resisting pleasures.

The enemy does not cease and does not die except in the resurrection of the dead.

Let us anticipate it; let us trust. Haggai and Zechariah raise us up; they sing of our future liberation. If they sang to that people and it was fulfilled, will what is sung to the Christian people not be fulfilled?

Be confident. Only see how you conduct yourselves in this exile of life [Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “See not only how you conduct yourselves in this exile of this life, but how you conduct yourselves here.”]

Do not let the love of Babylonia please you, lest you forget the city of Jerusalem. Although your body is still held in Babylonia, let your heart be sent ahead to Jerusalem.

Let all creation, therefore, praise the Lord, because there we shall do what we now rehearse here in advance.

[Col. 1941]

### 5. [verse 1.]

“Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights.”

First he speaks of the heavens, then of the earth, for the God who made heaven and earth is praised.

The heavenly things are tranquil and peaceful. There is perpetual joy there, no death, no sickness, no trouble. The blessed always praise God.

But we are still below [Note: The printed editions read: “we sound in the depths.” The manuscripts read: “we are below”; compare also Treatise 8 on the First Epistle of John, §2.]. Yet when we consider how God is praised there, let us have our heart there, and let us not hear without reason, “Lift up your hearts.”

Let us lift our heart upward, lest it decay in the earth, since we are pleased by what the angels do there. Now we do so in hope; afterward, in reality, when we have arrived there. Therefore praise him in the heights.

### 6. [verses 2–5.]

“Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers. Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.”

When will he finish explaining everything by counting? Yet he has summarized and, as it were, touched upon everything, and concluded all the heavenly things that praise their Creator.

### 7.

And as though someone said to him, “Why do they praise him? What do they owe him? What has he conferred upon them, so that they should praise him?” he continues:

“For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.”

It is not surprising if works praise their worker; it is not surprising if things made praise their maker; it is not surprising if creation praises the Creator.

Christ too is named there, though it is as if we have not heard his name. Who is Christ?

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 1–3).

Through what were they made? Through the Word.

How does this passage show that they were made through the Word? “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” No one speaks or commands except by a word.

### 8. [verse 6.]

“He established them forever and throughout the age of the age.”

All the heavenly things, all the things above, all the powers and angels, a certain heavenly city—good, holy, blessed—from which, because we are exiles, we are still wretched; to which, because we shall return, we are blessed in hope; and in which, when we have returned, we shall be blessed in reality.

“He established them forever and throughout the age of the age.” He gave a commandment, and it shall not pass away.

What sort of commandment do you think the heavenly beings and holy angels have? What commandment did God give them? What else but that they should praise him?

Blessed are those whose occupation is to praise God. They do not plow, sow, grind, or cook; for these are works of necessity, and there is no necessity there. They do not steal, plunder, or commit adultery; for these are works of iniquity, and there is no iniquity there.

They do not break bread for the hungry, clothe the naked, receive the stranger, visit the sick, reconcile those who quarrel, or bury the dead; for these are works of mercy, and there is no misery there in which mercy may be performed.

O blessed ones! Do we think that we too shall be such? Come, let us sigh; from sighing let us groan.

And what are we, that we should be there? Mortal, cast out, rejected—earth and ashes. But the one who promised is omnipotent [Col. 1942].

If we attend to ourselves, what are we? If we attend to him, he is God; he is omnipotent. Will God, who made a human being from nothing, not make an angel from a human being? Or does God regard as a small thing the human being for whose sake he wished his Only-Begotten to die?

Let us attend to the evidence of love [Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “the evidence of God’s love and promise. Such things, etc.”]

We have received such pledges of God’s promise; we hold the death of Christ; we hold the blood of Christ.

Who died? The Only-Begotten. For whom did he die? Would that it had been for the good; would that it had been for the righteous! But what does the Apostle say? “Indeed, Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. V, 6).

He who gave his death to the ungodly—what does he preserve for the righteous except his life?

Let human frailty therefore rise up; let it not despair, let it not crush itself, let it not turn away, let it not say, “I shall not be.” The one who promised is God. And he came in order to promise; he appeared to human beings; he came to take our death and promise his life.

He came to the region of our exile to receive here what abounds here: insults, scourges, blows, spittle in the face, abuse, a crown of thorns, being hung upon wood, the cross, and death. These things abound in our region; he came for such an exchange.

What did he give here, and what did he receive? He gave exhortation, teaching, and remission of sins; he received insults, death, and the cross.

He brought us good things from that region and endured evil things in our region. Yet he promised us that we would be there where he came from, and he said: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24).

Such love went before us! Where we were, he was with us; where he is, we shall be with him.

What did God promise you, mortal human being? That you will live forever. Do you not believe it? Believe, believe. What he has already done is greater than what he promised.

What did he do? He died for you. What did he promise? That you would live with him. It is more incredible that the eternal one died than that a mortal should live forever. We already possess what is more incredible.

If God died for a human being, will a human being not live with God? Will a mortal not live forever, for whose sake the one who lives forever died?

But how did God die, and from where did God die? And can God die? He received from you that by which he could die for you. He could not die except as flesh; he could not die except as a mortal body. He clothed himself with that in which he would die for you; he will clothe you with that in which you will live with him.

Where did he clothe himself with death? In the virginity of his mother. Where will he clothe you with life? In the equality of the Father.

Here he chose for himself a chaste bridal chamber, where the bridegroom would be joined to the bride. “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14), so that he might become the head of the Church.

For the Word itself is not a part of the Church; but in order to be the head of the Church, he assumed flesh. Something of ours is already above, something that he received here, where he died, where he was crucified. The firstfruits of what is yours have already gone before, and you doubt that you will follow!

### 9. [verse 7.]

Therefore let him now turn also to earthly things, since he has already spoken the praises of heavenly things.

“Praise the Lord from the earth.”

From where did he begin above? “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” and he recounted the heavenly things. Now hear the earthly things:

[Col. 1943] “Dragons and all abysses.”

The abysses are the depths of the waters: all seas, and this cloud-filled air, belong to the abyss. Where there are clouds, winds, storms, rains, lightning, thunder, hail, snow, and whatever God wills to occur over the earth from this moist and dark air—all of this he called by the name of earth, because it is exceedingly changeable and mortal [Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “because it is in the depths.” Shortly afterward most manuscripts read: “it rains stars from above.”]

Unless perhaps you think that it rains stars from above. All these things occur here, near the earth. Sometimes people are on the peaks of mountains and see clouds beneath them, and often rains occur. To those who look carefully, all these things that are stirred up by disturbed air plainly appear to take place here, in this lowest region of the world.

For this reason the devil was condemned to these dark regions—that is, to this air—as to a prison, having fallen with his angels from the array of the higher angels. For the Apostle says this about him: “According to the prince of the power of this air, who now works in the sons of unbelief” (Eph. II, 2).

Another apostle says: “For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but thrust them into the prisons of darkness and delivered them to be kept for judgment and punishment” (II Peter II, 4)—calling this lower region hell, because it is the lower part of the world.

Do not consider what the devil received, but what he lost.

You see, then, what all these things are like: changeable, disturbed, terrifying, corruptible. Yet they have their place; they have their order; they too, according to their measure, complete the beauty of the universe; and therefore they praise the Lord.

Turning toward them, as though exhorting them also—or rather exhorting us, so that by considering them we may praise the Lord (for this is how they praise God: when, being considered, they produce praise of God)—he began to say: [Col. 1943] “Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all abysses.”

Dragons move about near the water, emerge from caves, and are carried through the air; the air is stirred on account of them. Dragons are great living creatures; there are none larger upon the earth. Therefore he began there: “Dragons and all abysses.”

There are caves of hidden waters, from which springs and rivers emerge. Some emerge in order to flow over the earth; others run secretly beneath it. All of this, and the entire moist nature of the waters, together with the sea and this lowest air, is called the abyss or abysses, where dragons live and praise God.

What? Do we think that dragons form choirs and praise God? Far from it. But you, as you consider dragons, attend to the craftsman of dragons, the creator of dragons. And when you marvel at dragons and say, “Great is God, who made these things,” the dragons praise God through your voices:

“Dragons and all abysses.”

### 10. [verse 8.]

“Fire, hail, snow, ice, the spirit of the tempest, which do his word.”

Why did he add here, “which do his word”? Many foolish people, unable to contemplate and discern creation acting in its proper places and order, and moving according to God’s nod and command, have thought that God governs all things above but despises, rejects, and abandons the things below, so that he neither cares for, governs, nor rules them. Instead, they think that these things are ruled by chance, however and wherever they can.

The things that they sometimes say to themselves move them [Note: [Col. 1944] Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read qui (“who”); the manuscripts read quae (“which”).]—but let them not say them to you; that is, do not consent when you hear them, for they are blasphemous and hateful to God:

“If God caused rain, would it rain upon the sea?”

“What sort of providence is that?” they say. “Getulia is thirsty, and the sea is drenched with rain.”

They think they are reasoning cleverly. They should be told: Getulia may be thirsty; but you are not thirsty [Note: Thus the manuscripts. But Am. and Er. read: “Getulia is thirsty, so that you might not be thirsty.” Lov. reads: “Getulia is thirsty, so that you would not be thirsty.”]

For it would be good for you to say to God: “My soul is like a waterless land for you” (Ps. CXLII, 6). Elsewhere it is said plainly: “My soul has thirsted for you; how often my flesh has thirsted for you” (Ps. LXII, 2). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. V, 6).

The one who argues in this way is already filled, as it were; he seems wise to himself and does not wish to learn, and therefore he does not thirst. For if he thirsted, he would wish to learn, and he would discover that everything is done by God’s providence on earth. He would marvel that even the limbs of a flea have been arranged.

Let Your Charity attend. Who arranged the limbs of a flea and a gnat, so that they have their order, their life, and their movement? Consider any small, tiny creature you wish.

If you consider the order of its limbs and the animation of the life by which it moves, so that of itself it flees death [Note: Perhaps it should be read: “by which it moves of itself and flees death”], loves life, seeks pleasures, avoids troubles, exercises different senses, and thrives in movement appropriate to itself—who gave the gnat its sting, with which it sucks blood? How slender is the tube through which it draws! Who arranged these things? Who made them?

You are amazed at the smallest things; praise the great one.

Hold fast to this, then, my brothers. Let no one shake you from the faith or from sound doctrine [Note: Most manuscripts read: “Let no one shake sound doctrine from you concerning the faith.”]

The one who made an angel in heaven made a worm on earth—but an angel in heaven for a heavenly dwelling, and a worm on earth for an earthly dwelling. Did he make an angel crawl in the mud and a worm in heaven? He distributed inhabitants to their dwelling places; he gave incorruption to incorruptible places, and corruptible things to corruptible places.

Consider everything; praise everything.

Therefore, the one who arranged the limbs of a worm does not govern the clouds? And why does it rain upon the sea? As though there were not things in the sea that are nourished by rain; as though he had not made fish there, as though he had not made living creatures there.

Observe how fish run toward fresh water. “And why,” he says, “does it rain upon a fish, while sometimes it does not rain upon me?” So that you may consider that you are in a desert region and in the exile of life, and that the present life may become bitter to you, so that you may desire the future one; or so that you may be scourged, admonished, and corrected.

But how does he distribute what belongs to each region? See: because we have spoken of Getulia, it rains here almost every year, and every year it produces grain. Grain cannot be stored here; it quickly spoils, because it is produced every year. There, because it is produced rarely and in abundance, it is stored for a long time.

But perhaps you think that God abandons the people there, or that there they do not praise and glorify God according to his good pleasure. Take a Getulian from there and place him among these pleasant trees: he wants to flee from here and return to bare [Col. 1945] Getulia [Note: Lov. reads: “to the bare land of Getulia”; the other books disagree.]

Therefore God has distributed and ordered to all places, regions, and times what belongs to each. It would be lengthy to recount a more careful consideration of all things. Who could explain it? Yet those who have eyes see many things there. When these things are seen, they please; when they have pleased, they are praised—not as though they themselves were praised, but the one who made them. Thus all things will praise God.

11. Considering these things, the prophet’s spirit, after saying, “Fire, hail, snow, ice, storm-wind,” all of which seem to certain foolish people to be confused and driven about as if by chance, added, “which perform his word.” Therefore, do not suppose that those things are moved by chance which in all their movement serve God’s word. Wherever God wills, there the fire shines [Note: [Col. 1945] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Lovaniensis: “there the fire shines.” M.]; there the cloud is carried, whether it bears rain, snow, or hail.

And why do lightning bolts sometimes strike a mountain and not strike a robber? Whatever I can say according to the capacity of my mind, insofar as God deigns to grant it—let those who are greater know greater things and understand more; and may God grant you to know more than I say, yet with moderation and without pride—I can therefore say, according to my modest ability, why they strike the mountain and do not strike the robber: because perhaps He is still seeking the robber’s conversion; and therefore the mountain that does not fear is struck, so that the human being who fears may be changed.

Sometimes you too, when you administer discipline, strike the ground so that a child may be frightened. And sometimes He strikes the very person whom He wishes.

But you say to me: “Look, He strikes someone more innocent and spares someone more wicked.” Do not be surprised: by whatever means death comes, it is good for the pious [Note: [Col. 1945] Manuscripts: “it is good.”]. But how do you know what punishments are secretly being reserved for that more wicked person if he refuses to change? Would they not rather wish to be burned by lightning [Note: [Col. 1945] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “to perish by lightning rather,” etc.], those to whom at the end it will be said, “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41)?

It is necessary that you be innocent. What then? Is it evil to die in a shipwreck and good to die of a fever? Whether he dies by this means or by that, consider what sort of person the one who dies is; consider where he is going after death, not from what cause he is departing this life. By whatever occasion, we shall depart from here. By what exits did the martyrs deserve to depart? Was it by fevers, as many wish to be released by fever? Some by a single stroke of the sword, others by fire, others by beasts. The beasts devoured the bodies of the martyrs, and they did not fear that their bodies would perish. For God will restore the bodies of His saints from every direction, He whose number includes even our hairs (ibid. 10:30).

And when He willed, He rescued the three youths from the fire (Dan. 3:24, 93). Did He therefore abandon the Maccabees in the fire (2 Macc. 7)? He openly delivered the former; He secretly crowned the latter. God knows, therefore, what He is doing.

You, fear and be good. By whatever means He wishes you to depart from here, may He find you ready. For you are a tenant (Ps. 118:19), not the possessor of the house. A house has been leased to you; this house has been leased to you, not given to you. Even if you do not wish it, you will move away; and you did not receive it under such a condition that, as it were, fixed times would belong to you. What did your Lord say? “When I wish, when I say, ‘Move out,’ be ready.” I am expelling you from your lodging, but I will give you a house: you are a tenant on earth; you will be a possessor in heaven.

12. Whatever happens here against our will, know that it happens only by God’s will, by His providence, His ordering, His command, and His laws. And if we do not understand why each thing happens, let us entrust this to His providence, because nothing happens without a cause, and let us not blaspheme [Note: [Col. 1946] In B., “we blaspheme.” Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Lovaniensis read, “let us not blaspheme.”].

For when we begin to argue about God’s works—“Why this? Why that?”—and say, “He ought not to have done it this way; He did this badly”: where then is God’s praise? You have lost your Alleluia. Consider everything in such a way that you may please God and praise the Craftsman.

For if you were to enter, perhaps, a blacksmith’s workshop, you would not dare criticize the bellows, anvils, or hammers. And suppose you bring in an ignorant person who does not know why each thing is there: he criticizes everything. But if he lacks the craftsman’s skill and at least possesses the discernment of a human being, what does he say to himself? “The bellows have not been placed here without reason; the craftsman knows why, even if I do not.”

In a workshop he does not dare disparage the smith, yet he dares criticize God in this world! Therefore, just as the fire, hail, snow, ice, and storm-wind “perform His word,” so everything that seems to foolish people to happen rashly in the order of nature performs only His word, because nothing happens except at His command.

13. [Verses 9–12.] Then he says that they should praise the Lord: “Mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds.” Then he turns to human beings: “Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth; young men and virgins, old men together with the young: let them praise the name of the Lord.” The praise from heaven has been unfolded; the praise from earth has been unfolded.

14. [Verse 13.] “For His name alone is exalted.” Let no human being seek to exalt his own name. Do you wish to be exalted? Submit yourself to Him who cannot be humbled: “His name alone is exalted.”

15. [Verse 14.] “His confession is in earth and heaven” [Note: [Col. 1946] Thus the manuscripts, according to the Septuagint. The printed editions instead read, “in heaven and on earth.”].

What does “His confession is in earth and heaven” mean? Is it the confession by which He Himself confesses? No, but the confession by which all things confess Him; all things cry out. The beauty of everything is, in a certain way, their voice, confessing God.

Heaven cries out to God: “You made me, not I myself.” Earth cries out: “You founded me, not I myself.” How do these things cry out? When they are considered and this is discovered: they cry out through your consideration; they cry out through your voice. “His confession is in earth and heaven.”

Look at heaven: it is beautiful. Look at earth: it is beautiful. Both together are exceedingly beautiful. He made them; He rules them; they are governed by His command; He brings the seasons to pass; He renews the moments; He renews them through Himself. [Note: [Col. 1946] Manuscripts: “through Him all things.”] Therefore all these things praise Him, whether in their standing still or their movement, whether from earth below or from heaven above, whether in decay or in renewal.

When you see these things and rejoice, and you are lifted up toward the Craftsman, and through the things that have been made you contemplate His invisible attributes as understood (Rom. 1:20), this is “His confession in earth and heaven”: that is, you confess Him on account of earthly things; you confess Him on account of heavenly things.

And because He Himself made all things, and nothing is better than He, whatever He made is beneath Him; and whatever pleases you in these things is less than He Himself. Therefore, do not let what He made please you in such a way that you withdraw from Him who made it. If you love what He made, love Him who made it much more. If the things He made are beautiful, how much more beautiful is He who made them? “His confession is in earth and heaven.”

16. “And He will exalt the horn of His people.” Behold what Haggai and Zechariah prophesied. Now the horn of His people is low in threshings, tribulations, temptations, and the beating of breasts. When will He exalt the horn of His people? When the Lord Himself comes and our sun has risen—not this sun that is seen by the eyes and rises upon the good and the evil (Matt. 5:45), but the one of whom it is said, “For you who fear God, the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing is in his wings” (Mal. 4:2); and of whom the proud and wicked will say, “The light of righteousness did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. 5:6).

That will be our summer. At present, fruit hidden through the winter in the root does not appear; you see trees, as it were, dry throughout winter. One who does not know how to see thinks the vine is dry; and perhaps there is another nearby that truly has dried up. They are alike throughout winter: one is alive, the other dead.
