But the life of one and the death of the other are hidden. Summer comes; the life of one is revealed, and the death of the other is manifested. The honor of leaves appears, the abundance of fruits; the vine is clothed in its outward form by what it possesses in the root.

Therefore now, brothers, we are such as other human beings are: just as they are born, eat, drink, dress, and pass through this life, so do the saints. Sometimes the very circumstance deceives people, and they say: “Look, he has begun to be a Christian—does his head not hurt? Or because he is a Christian, what more does he have than I do?”

O dry vine, you see beside you a vine that is bare in winter, but not dry. Summer will come [Note: [Col. 1947] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions: “but not dry through the force of summer. And the Lord will come,” etc.]; the Lord will come, our honor, who was hidden in the root; and then He will exalt the horn of His people, after the captivity in which we live mortally. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes and brings to light the hidden things of darkness; and then each one will have his praise from God” (1 Cor. 4:5).

But you say to me: “Where is my root? Where is my fruit?” If you believe, you know where your root is. It is there where your faith is, where your hope and your love are. Hear the Apostle: “For you have died.” They appeared dead, as it were, through winter; hear that they live: “And your life is hidden with Christ in God.” Behold where you have your root.

When, then, will you be adorned with honor? When will you be made fruitful with fruit? Hear what follows: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4). “And He will exalt the horn of His people.”

17. “A hymn for all His saints.” Do you know what a hymn is? It is a song with the praise of God. If you praise God but do not sing, you are not singing a hymn. If you sing but do not praise God, you are not singing a hymn. If you praise something else that does not pertain to the praise of God, even if you praise it by singing, you are not singing a hymn. A hymn therefore contains these three things: singing, praise, and God. Thus the praise of God in song is called a hymn.

What, then, is “a hymn for all His saints”? Let His saints receive a hymn; let His saints sing a hymn, because this is what they will receive at the end: an everlasting hymn. Therefore the psalm says elsewhere, “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49:23); and, “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5). This is “a hymn for all His saints.”

Who are His saints? “The sons of Israel, the people drawing near to Him.” Let no one say, “I am not a son of Israel.” Do not suppose that the Jews are sons of Israel and that we are not sons of Israel. I dare to say to you, my brothers: they are not, but we are. Hear why: because one born according to the spirit is greater than one born according to the flesh.

Where does “Israel” come from? From Abraham; for Isaac came from Abraham, and Israel from Isaac. How did Abraham please God? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:3). Whoever imitates Abraham is a son of Abraham; whoever degenerates from Abraham’s faith has lost Abraham’s lineage.

The Jews degenerated; they lost it. We imitated him; we found it. Hear that they lost it. What does the Lord say to those who say, “We are sons of Abraham”? They dared to display themselves and raise their necks because of the nobility of their righteous ancestry. And what does the Lord say to them? “If you were Abraham’s sons, you would do the works of Abraham” (John 8:33, 39).

If, therefore, they lost what it means to be sons of Abraham, we have found that we might be sons of Abraham. By believing, we found what they lost by not believing, because “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” “And the seed of Abraham is Christ” (Gal. 3:16), and we are in Christ. And from Israel came the people from whom came Mary; from Mary came Christ; in Christ are we. Therefore we are sons of Israel.

And how did he add the words by which he distinguished us? “The sons of Israel, the people drawing near to Him.” Consider the Jews: if they draw near, they are the ones. And perhaps they do draw near, someone says to me: “Every day they too sing the psalm and sing hymns to God.” Do you not hear what the prophet said to them? “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

If their heart is far away, but our heart is near—because we believe, because we hope, because we love, because we have been joined to Christ, because we have become His members—are members far from the head? If they were far away and separated, He would not say, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). If they were separated, He would not say from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). If He were not in us, He would not say, “I was hungry, and you gave me food”; and when they said to Him, “When did we see you hungry?” He replied, “When you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (Matt. 25:35, 37, 40).

Behold the people; behold Israel drawing near; and with Him now in hope, afterward in reality—[source breaks off].

# EXPOSITION ON PSALM 149

[Col. 1949]

SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. [Verse 1.] Let us praise the Lord both in voice, in understanding, and in good works; and, as this psalm exhorts us, let us sing a new song to Him. For thus it begins: “Sing to the Lord a new song.” The old person sings an old song; the new person, a new song. The Old Testament is an old song; the New Testament, a new song.

In the Old Testament there are temporal and earthly promises. Whoever loves earthly things sings an old song; whoever wishes to sing a new song should love eternal things. Love itself is new and eternal; therefore it is always new, because it never grows old.

For if you consider it carefully, this is ancient. How, then, is it new? Surely, my brothers, eternal life was not born only now. Eternal life is Christ Himself, and according to His divinity He was not born only now, because, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3).

If the things made through Him are ancient, what is He through whom they were made? What is He, if not eternal and coeternal with the Father? But we, having fallen into sin, came to old age. For our voice is in that psalm where it is said with a groan, “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6:8). Through sin the human being grows old; through grace he is renewed. Therefore all who are renewed in Christ, so that they may begin to belong to eternal life, sing a new song.

2. This song is also a song of peace; this song is a song of love. Whoever separates himself from the fellowship of the saints does not sing a new song. He has followed the old hostility, not the new love.

What is present in new love? Peace, the bond of holy fellowship, spiritual joining, a building made of living stones. Where is this? Not in one place, but throughout the whole world.

Hear this from another psalm: it says, “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. 95:1). From this it is understood that whoever does not sing with all the earth sings an old song, whatever words may come from his mouth.

For why should I attend to what he sounds like when I see what he thinks? “And you,” you say, “see what he thinks?” His deeds indicate it. For the eye does not penetrate the conscience. I attend to what he does, and there I understand what he thinks.

Indeed, if someone, for example, has been caught in theft, murder, or adultery, one does not see his thoughts in his heart, but in his deeds. Some things remain hidden within; but many also proceed into actions and become manifest even to human beings.

When those who had separated themselves from the bond of Christ’s love and from the fellowship of the holy Church were inwardly evil among themselves, no one knew this except God. Temptation came; it separated them [Note: [Col. 1949] Thus Ambrosianus and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “it overcame them.”], and it disclosed to human beings what God knew. For the fruit is not shown except in deeds. Hence it is said: “By their fruits you will know them” (Matt. 7:16).

For the Lord spoke to certain people who clothe themselves in sheep’s garments but inwardly are ravenous wolves. And lest human frailty perhaps be unable to recognize the wolf beneath the sheep’s skin, He said: “By their fruits you will know them.”

We seek the fruits of love and find the thorns of dissension. “By their fruits you will know them.” Therefore their song is old; let us sing a new song.

We have already said, brothers, that the whole earth sings a new song. Whoever does not sing a new song with the whole earth may say what he wishes, sound “Alleluia” with his tongue, say it all day and all night; my ears are not greatly inclined toward the voice of the singer, but I seek the conduct of the one who acts.

For I ask and say: “What is it that you sing?” He answers: “Alleluia.” “What is ‘Alleluia’?” “Praise the Lord.” Come, let us praise the Lord together. If you praise the Lord and I praise the Lord [Note: [Col. 1950] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read, “and I will praise the Lord. Why,” etc.], why are we in disagreement? Love praises the Lord; discord blasphemes the Lord.

3. And do you now wish to know where you are to sing the new song? Look at what the psalm itself is going to say, how and where these things are accomplished: whether they are accomplished among all nations or in some one part of the earth. From this you will understand more fully to whom the new song belongs.

What I recalled from another psalm is already clear: “Sing to the Lord a new song.” And to show that the fruit of love and unity is present in the new song, he added, “Sing to the Lord, all the earth.” Let no one separate himself; let no one withdraw. You are wheat; endure the chaff until the winnowing.

Do you wish to be shaken out of the threshing floor? Even if you were wheat outside the threshing floor, the birds would find you and carry you away (ibid. 3:12). Add that by the very fact that you depart [Note: [Col. 1950] Some manuscripts: “by the very fact that you go out,” etc. Others: “because you go out.”] and fly away, you show that you are chaff; and because you were light, the wind came and carried you away from beneath the feet of the oxen.

But those who are wheat endure the threshing. They rejoice because they are grains; they groan among the chaff; they await the winnower, whom they recognize as the redeemer.

“Sing to the Lord a new song: his praise is in the assembly of the saints.” This is the Church of the saints, the Church of grains spread throughout the whole world, sown across the Lord’s field, which is this world, as the Lord Himself explained when He spoke of the sower:

“‘A man sowed good seed in his field; and the enemy came and sowed weeds over it.’ And the servants said to the master of the household, ‘Did you not sow good seed in your field? From where, then, are the weeds?’ He answered them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ They wished to gather the weeds, but he restrained them, saying: ‘Let both grow until the harvest; and at harvest time I will say to the reapers, Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to burn them; but store my wheat in the barn.’”

Afterward the disciples asked Him, saying: “Explain to us the parable of the weeds.” And He explained everything, so that no one might attribute to his own heart what he understood there, but rather to the Teacher of heaven who was explaining it.

Let no one say: “He explained it for himself in whatever way he wished.” If the Lord were explaining a prophet’s parable, when He Himself was speaking through the prophets what they said, who would dare to say that it ought not to be explained in that way? Much more, when He Himself explained what He Himself had proposed, who dares to contradict manifest truth?

When, therefore, the Lord explained this parable, He said: “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man,” plainly indicating Himself. “The good seed, however, are the sons of the kingdom”: this is the Church of the saints. “The weeds are the sons of the evil one. The field is this world” (Matt. 13:24–30, 36–38).

Now see, brothers, that the good seed was sown throughout the world, and the weeds were sown throughout the world. Is wheat in one part and weeds in another? Wheat is throughout the whole, and weeds are throughout the whole. The Lord’s field is the world, not Africa.

It is not as when this land of Getulia produces sixtyfold or a hundredfold and Numidia produces tenfold; the Lord’s field is not like that. Everywhere it yields fruit to Him: a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. You must only see what you wish to be, if you are considering belonging to the Lord’s fruit [Note: [Col. 1951] Some manuscripts: “to belong to the Lord of fruits.”].

Therefore the Church of the saints is the catholic Church. The Church of the saints is not the Church of heretics. The Church of the saints is the one God marked out before it was seen, and displayed so that it might be seen.

The Church of the saints was formerly in the books; now it is among the nations. The Church of the saints was formerly only read; now it is both read and seen. When it was only read, it was believed; now that it is seen, it is contradicted. “His praise is in the assembly of the saints.”

4. [Verse 2.] “Let Israel rejoice in Him who made him.” What is Israel? “Seeing God”; for this is what the name Israel means. Let the one who sees God rejoice in Him by whom he was made.

What then, brothers? Since we have said that we belong to the Church of the saints, do we already see God? How are we Israel if we do not see Him? There is one kind of vision for the present time; there will be another vision in the future. The vision that exists now is through faith; the vision that will exist then will be by sight.

If we believe, we see; if we love, we see. What do we see? God. Where is God Himself? Ask John: “God is love” (1 John 4:16). Let us bless His holy name and rejoice in God, if we rejoice in love.

Whoever possesses love—why do we send him far away to see God? Let him attend to his conscience, and there he sees God. If love does not dwell there, God does not dwell there; but if love dwells there, God dwells there.

Perhaps he wishes to see Him seated in heaven. Let him have love, and He dwells in him as in heaven. Therefore let us be Israel and rejoice in Him who made us: “Let Israel rejoice in Him who made him.”

Let him rejoice in Him who made him, not in Arius [Note: [Col. 1951] Some manuscripts omit “not in Arius.”], not in Donatus, not in Caecilian, not in Proculeianus [Note: [Col. 1951] From this one may rightly infer that the sermon was delivered at Hippo while Proculeianus, or Proculeian, was alive—bishop of that city on the Donatist side, around the beginning of the fifth century. On him see Augustine, Letters 33, 34, 35, 78, and 88.], not in Augustine: [Col. 1952] “Let him rejoice in Him who made him.”

We, brothers, do not commend ourselves to you; rather, we commend God to you, because we commend you to God. How do we commend God to you? So that you may love Him for your own good, not for His; for you do not love Him to your own harm, nor to His harm.

God will not have less divinity if a human being does not have love for Him. You grow through God; He does not grow through you. And yet He loved us first so greatly (1 John 4:19), before we loved Him, that He sent His only Son to die for us (John 3:16).

He who made us was made among us. How did He Himself make us? “All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made.” How was He made among us? “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid. 1:3, 14).

Therefore He is the one in whom we ought to rejoice. Let no human being arrogate to himself the prerogatives of Him [Note: [Col. 1952] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “Let no one arrogate to himself, let no one diminish for himself, His prerogatives.”]; from Him comes the joy that makes us happy: “Let Israel rejoice in Him who made him.”

5. “And let the sons of Zion exult in their king.” Israel itself is the sons of the Church. Zion was indeed one city, which fell; in its remains the saints dwelt for a time. But true Zion and true Jerusalem—for Zion itself is Jerusalem—is eternal in heaven, and she is our mother (Gal. 4:26).

She gave us birth; she is the Church of the saints; she nourished us. In part she is a pilgrim; in the greater part she dwells in heaven. In the part that dwells in heaven, she is the blessedness of the angels; in the part that is a pilgrim in this age, she is the hope of the righteous.

Of that part it was said, “Glory to God in the highest”; of this part it was said, “And on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Therefore let those who groan in this life and desire that homeland run by love, not by the feet of the body. Let them seek not ships but wings; let them grasp the two wings of love. What are the two wings of love? Love of God and love of neighbor.

For we are pilgrims; we sigh and groan. Letters have come to us from our homeland; these very letters we read to you.

6. “Let Israel rejoice in Him who made him, and let the sons of Zion exult in their king.” What he said, “who made him,” he said also in “his king.” What you heard as “Israel” means the sons of Zion; and what you heard as “in Him who made him” means “in his king.”

The Son of God, who made us, was made among us. And our King rules us because our Creator made us. Yet He Himself is the one through whom we were made, and He is the one through whom we are ruled. Therefore we are Christians because He is Christ.

Christ is called from *chrisma*, that is, from anointing. Kings were anointed (1 Kings 10:1; 16:13), and priests also (Exod. 30:30). But He was anointed both King and Priest.

The King fought for us; the Priest offered Himself for us. When He fought for us, He appeared to be defeated, but in truth He conquered. For He was crucified, and from His cross, to which He was fastened, He killed the devil; and therefore He is our King.

But how is He Priest? Because He offered Himself for us. Give the Priest something to offer. What could a human being find to give as a clean victim [Note: [Col. 1952] The Corbie manuscript reads, “something clean to give? What victim?”]?

What victim? What clean thing can a sinner offer? O wicked person, O impious person! Whatever you bring is unclean, and something clean must be offered for you. Search within yourself for what you may offer; you will not find it. Search from yourself for what you may offer; He takes no pleasure in rams, goats, or bulls. Everything belongs to Him, even if you do not offer it.

Offer Him, therefore, a clean sacrifice. But you are a sinner, you are impious, you have a defiled conscience. Perhaps, once cleansed, you will be able to offer something clean; but in order that you may be cleansed, something must be offered for you. What, then, will you offer for yourself, so that you may be cleansed? If you have been cleansed, you will be able to offer what is clean.

Let the clean Priest therefore offer Himself and cleanse. This is what Christ did. He found nothing clean among human beings that He could offer for human beings; He offered Himself as a clean victim [Note: [Col. 1953] The editions add here “an unblemished sacrifice”; and below, after “true victim,” they read “clean victim.” These words have been removed on the authority of the manuscripts.].

Blessed victim, true victim, unblemished sacrifice! Therefore He did not offer what we gave Him; rather, He offered what He received from us, and He offered it clean. For He received flesh from us and offered it. But from where did He receive it? From the womb of the virgin Mary, so that He might offer it clean for the unclean.

He is both King and Priest; in Him let us rejoice.

7. [Verse 3.] “Let them praise His name in the chorus.” And what does “chorus” signify? Many know what a chorus is; and because we are speaking in a city, nearly everyone knows. A chorus is an agreement among singers.

If we sing in a chorus, let us sing harmoniously. In a chorus of singers, whoever disagrees in voice offends the ear and disturbs the chorus. If the voice of a singer who sings inappropriately disturbs the harmony of the singers, how does a discordant heresy disturb the harmony of those who praise?

The chorus of Christ is now the whole world. The chorus of Christ harmonizes from east to west [Note: [Col. 1953] Some manuscripts: “and from the west it harmonizes.”]. Let us see whether Christ’s chorus extends so far. Another psalm says: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 112:3). “Let them praise His name in the chorus.”

8. “Let them sing praise to Him with tambourine and psaltery.” Why does he take up the tambourine and psaltery? So that not only the voice may praise, but also the works. When the tambourine and psaltery are taken up, the hands harmonize with the voice.

So too you: if, whenever you sing “Alleluia,” you also extend bread to the hungry, clothe the naked, and receive the stranger, it is not only the voice that sounds; the hands also harmonize, because deeds agree with words. You have taken up an instrument, and the fingers agree with the tongue.

And the mystery of the tambourine and psaltery itself must not be passed over in silence. On the tambourine, leather is stretched; on the psaltery, strings are stretched. In both instruments the flesh is crucified.

How well did he sing on tambourine and psaltery who said: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14)! He who loves the new song, who teaches you when he says, “Whoever wishes to be my disciple, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24), wishes you to lift up the psaltery, as it were a tambourine [Note: [Col. 1953] Lovaniensis reads, “as it were a tambourine,” while the other books disagree.].

Do not lay down your psaltery; do not lay down your tambourine. Let yourself be stretched upon the wood and dried out from the desire of the flesh. The more tightly the strings are stretched, the more sharply they sound.

Therefore, so that the psaltery of the Apostle Paul might sound sharply, what did he say? “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. 3:13–14). He stretched himself; Christ touched him, and the sweetness of truth sounded.

“Let them sing praise to Him with tambourine and psaltery.”

9. [Verse 4.] “For the Lord has done good to His people.” What is as beneficial as dying for the ungodly? What is as beneficial as erasing the sinner’s bond with righteous blood? What is as beneficial as saying: “What you were does not concern me; become what you were not”?

The Lord has done good to His people by forgiving sins and promising eternal life. He does good by turning back the one who has turned away, helping the one who fights, and crowning the one who conquers: “The Lord has done good to His people.”

“And He will exalt the meek in salvation” [Note: [Col. 1954] Manuscripts read, “He exalted.”]. The proud too are exalted, but not in salvation. The meek are exalted in salvation, the proud in death. That is, the proud exalt themselves, and the Lord humbles them; the meek humble themselves, and God exalts them. “And He will exalt the meek in salvation” [Note: [Col. 1954] Thus the manuscripts, according to the Septuagint. The editions read, “in salvation” and below, “in death.”].

10. [Verses 5–6.] “The saints will exult in glory.” I wish to say something; listen more attentively about the glory of the saints. There is no one who does not love glory.

But the glory of fools—that popular glory, as it is called—has the allure of deception, so that each person, moved toward the praise of vain human beings [Note: [Col. 1954] Thus the manuscripts. Ambrosianus reads, “of pleasure, so that toward his own praise and the honor of human beings”; Erasmus reads, “of pleasure and deception, so that toward his own praise and the honor of vain human beings.” The Lovaniensis edition likewise, except that it omits “and deception.”], wishes to live in such a way that he may be praised by any people whatsoever, in whatever manner.

From this people become insane and swollen with conceit, empty within and puffed up outwardly. They even wish to lose their possessions by giving them to actors, stage performers, hunters, and charioteers. How much they give! How much they spend! They pour out their strength—not only that of their patrimony, but also that of their spirit.

These people disdain the poor, because the crowd does not shout for a poor man to receive anything; but the crowd shouts for the hunter to receive. Therefore, when no one shouts for them, they do not wish to distribute anything; when madmen shout, they become mad. Everyone becomes mad: the one who is watched, the one who watches, and the one who gives.

This insane glory is condemned by the Lord and rejected before the eyes of the Almighty. And yet, my brothers, Christ thus reproaches His own and says: “I have not received as much from you as the hunters received; and when you gave to them, you gave from what was mine. But I was naked, and you did not clothe me.”

And they say to Him: “When did we see you naked and not clothe you?” And He says to them: “When you did not do it for one of the least of mine, you did not do it for me” (Matt. 25:43–45).

But you wish to clothe one who pleases you. In whom does Christ displease you? You wish to clothe a hunter whom, if he is defeated, you might perhaps be ashamed to see defeated. Christ is never defeated: He conquered the devil, He conquered for you, He conquered for your sake, and He conquered in you. You do not wish to clothe such a victor.

Why? Because there is less shouting, because there is less madness. Therefore those who delight in such glory have nothing in their conscience. Just as they empty their chests in order to send clothing [Note: [Col. 1954] Ambrosianus and Erasmus read, “in order to change clothing.” Lovaniensis reads, “in order that they may shine.” The text has been corrected according to the manuscripts.], so they empty their very conscience, so that they have nothing precious there.

11. But how do the saints who exult in glory exult? It is not necessary for us to say; hear the following verse of the psalm itself: “The saints will exult in glory; they will rejoice in their chambers.”

Not in theaters, not in amphitheaters, not in circuses, not in trifles, not in public squares, but “in their chambers.” What does “in their chambers” mean? In their hearts.

Hear the Apostle Paul exulting in his chamber: “For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12).

Again, one must fear lest someone become self-satisfied before himself and, as though proud of his conscience, glory in it. For each person ought to exult with trembling (Ps. 2:11), because that in which he exults is God’s gift, not his own merit.

For there are many who please themselves and think themselves righteous. Against them another passage speaks, saying: “Who can boast of having a pure heart, or who can boast of being clean from sin?” (Prov. 20:9).

There is, then, a certain proper way of glorying in one’s conscience: you may know that your faith is sincere, that your hope is firm, and that your love is without pretense. But since there are perhaps still many things that can offend the eyes of God, praise God who has given you these things; He will perfect what He has given.

Therefore, after saying, “They will rejoice in their chambers,” lest they seem to be self-satisfied, he immediately added, “The exultations of God are in their throats.” Thus they will rejoice in their chambers without attributing their goodness to themselves, but praising Him from whom they received what they are, by whom they are called to arrive at what they are not yet, and from whom they hope for perfection; they give thanks to Him because He began the work: “The exultations of God are in their throats.”

Now behold the saints; behold their glory; behold it throughout the whole world; behold that the exultations of God are in their throats.

### 12

“And two-edged swords in their hands.” A *framea* is what is commonly called a sword. Some swords are sharpened on one side; these are *machaerae*. The same weapons are called *frameae*, *romphaeae*, and also *spathae*. This kind of iron weapon, sharpened on both sides, contains a great mystery.

“These are two-edged swords in their hands.” By the two-edged swords we understand the word of the Lord. It is one sword; but it is called “many” because there are many mouths and many tongues of the saints. Thus the word of God is a two-edged sword (Heb. 4:12). Why two-edged? It speaks of temporal things and speaks of eternal things. In both respects it proves what it says, and separates the one whom it strikes from the world.

Is this not the sword of which the Lord says, “I have not come to send peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34)? Consider how it comes to divide, how it comes to separate. It divides the saints; it divides the ungodly; it separates from you whatever hinders you. A son wishes to serve God, but his father does not: the sword comes, the word of God comes, and divides the son from his father. A daughter wishes to do so, but her mother does not: they are divided from one another by the sword. A daughter-in-law wishes to do so, but her mother-in-law does not: let the two-edged sword come, bringing the promise of the present life and of the future, the consolation of temporal things, and the enjoyment of eternal things. Behold the sword sharpened on both sides, promising temporal and eternal things.

In what has it deceived us [Note: [Col. 1956] Thus several manuscripts. But the editions read: “promising temporal things, in which it did not deceive us.”]? Was not the Church of God formerly throughout the whole world? Behold, it is now. Previously it was read about, but it was not seen; now, just as it is read, so it is perceived. Whatever has been promised to us temporally belongs to one side of the sword; whatever has been promised eternally belongs to the other side. You have hope of future things; you have consolation in the present. Do not let yourself be drawn back by anyone who wishes to draw you back: whether it is father, mother, sister, wife, or friend, let that person not draw you back; and the two-edged sword will be useful to you. It separates you beneficially; you join yourself together to your own harm.

Therefore our Lord comes bearing the two-edged sword, promising eternal things and fulfilling temporal ones. For this reason, too, there are said to be two Testaments. What, then, were the two-edged swords in their hands? The two Testaments belong to the two-edged sword: the Old Testament promises earthly things, the New eternal things. In both the word of God has been found true, like a two-edged sword.

Why, then, “in their hands,” and not “in their tongues”? “And two-edged swords,” he says, “in their hands.” By “in their hands” he meant “in their power.” They therefore received the word of God in their power, so that they might speak it where they wished and to whom they wished; they would not fear authority, nor despise poverty. For they held the sword in their hands; wherever they wished, they brandished it, wielded it, and struck with it. All this lay within the power of those who preached.

For if the word is not “in their hands”—lest someone perhaps say, “How is the word a two-edged sword, and how is it in their hands?”—if, then, the word is not in their hands, why is it written, “The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet” (Hag. 1:1)? Did God, brothers, make his word come into the prophet’s fingers? What does “it came by his hand” mean? He was given the power to preach the word of the Lord.

Finally, we can also understand these hands in another way. Those who spoke had the word of God on their tongue; those who wrote had it in their hands: “And two-edged swords in their hands.”

### 13

*[Verse 7.]* Now, brothers, you see the saints armed. Consider the slaughter; consider the glorious battles. For if there is a commander, there is a soldier; if there is a soldier, there is an enemy; if there is war, there is victory. What did these men do, who had two-edged swords in their hands? “To execute vengeance among the nations.”

See whether vengeance has not been executed among the nations. It is being executed every day; we are doing this by speaking. Consider how the Babylonian nations have been struck down. Double is repaid to her; for thus it is written of her: “Repay her double according to what she did” (Rev. 18:6). How is she repaid double? The saints wage war; they draw their two-edged swords; slaughter, killings, and separations take place. How is she repaid double? When she formerly had the power to persecute Christians, she killed the flesh but did not overthrow God; now double is repaid to her: the pagans are extinguished and the idols are broken.

“How,” you ask, “are the pagans killed?” How else than when they become Christians? I look for a pagan and do not find one; he is a Christian. Therefore the pagan has died. For if they are not killed, why was it said to Peter, “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13)? Why was Saul himself, the persecutor, killed, and Paul, the preacher, raised up? I look for Saul the persecutor and do not find him; he has been killed. By what means? By the two-edged sword.

But because he was killed in himself and made alive in Christ, he confidently says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). What happened to him happens through him to others. For when he became a preacher, he too received a two-edged sword in his hands, “to execute vengeance among the nations.”

And lest you should truly suppose that human beings were struck with iron, blood poured out, and wounds made in the flesh, what follows explains it: “Rebukes among the peoples.” What is a rebuke? Correction. Let the two-edged sword proceed from you; do not cease. God has given it to you according to your measure.

“What sort of person are you, worshiping idols?” Say to your friend—if indeed someone remains to whom you can say it—“What sort of person are you, who have abandoned the one by whom you were made and worship what you have made? The craftsman is better than what the craftsman makes. If you are ashamed to worship the craftsman, are you not ashamed to worship what the craftsman made?”

When he begins to be ashamed, when he begins to be pierced with remorse, you have made a wound with the sword. It has reached his heart; he is about to die so that he may live: “Two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples.”

### 14

*[Verse 8.]* “To bind their kings with fetters, and their nobles with iron chains. To execute upon them the written judgment.”

We have easily explained how people fall by the swords so that they may rise, are separated so that they may be gathered, wounded so that they may be healed, and die so that they may live. But what shall we do? How shall we explain, “To bind their kings with fetters”? The kings of the nations are to be bound with fetters; and he added “their nobles with chains,” specifying that they are iron.

Pay attention, so that you may recognize what you already know. These verses that we have begun to expound are obscure; but what I am going to say from them is not new. You already know it; now you do not need to learn it, but to be reminded of it. God wished to place some of his verses obscurely for this reason: not so that something new might be extracted from them, but so that what was already familiar might be renewed by the exposition of obscure passages [Note: [Col. 1957] Thus the manuscripts. The editions, however, read: “what was unfamiliar.”].

We know that kings have become Christians; we know that nobles of the nations have become Christians. They exist today, they existed [Note: [Col. 1957] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice: “There are today those who existed.” M.], and they will exist; and the two-edged swords in the hands of the saints do not cease.

How, then, do we understand them as bound with fetters and iron chains? Your Charity and learning know—for you have been nourished in the Church and are accustomed to hear the divine readings—that God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and he chose things that are not, as though they were, to bring to nothing the things that are.

Thus the Apostle says: “For consider your calling, brothers: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many are powerful, not many are noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the weak things of the world, and the lowly and despised things he chose, and things that are not, as though they were, to bring to nothing the things that are” (1 Cor. 1:26–28).

Christ God came to benefit everyone; but he chose to benefit the emperor through a fisherman, not the fisherman through the emperor. He chose things that had no importance in the world. He filled these men with his Spirit, gave them two-edged swords, commanded them to preach the Gospel, and sent them throughout the whole world (Matt. 28:19).

The world roared; the lion rose up against the lamb. But the lamb proved stronger than the lion. The lion was defeated by its savagery; the lamb conquered by suffering. Human hearts were turned toward the fear of Christ. Kings and nobles began to be moved by miracles, troubled by the fulfillment of prophecy, and to see the human race come together in one name.

And what were they to do? Many chose lowliness. They left their homes, distributed their possessions to the poor, and hastened toward perfection. For the Lord says to such an imperfect person: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give it to the poor; and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21). Many of the nobles did this; but they ceased to be nobles of the nations. They chose poverty in the world and nobility in Christ.

Others retain their nobility [Note: [Col. 1958] The editions add here, “in Christ,” which is absent from the manuscripts]; they retain royal authority, and are Christians in this condition. These are as though in fetters and as though in iron chains. Why? So that they might not advance toward unlawful deeds, they have received fetters: the fetters of wisdom, the fetters of the word of God.

### 15

Why, then, iron chains, and not golden chains? They are iron as long as they fear; let them love, and they will be golden. Let your Charity attend to what I am saying.

You have just heard the apostle John: “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has torment” (1 John 4:18). This is the iron chain. Yet unless a person begins to worship God through fear, he will not arrive at love. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). He therefore begins with iron chains and ends with a golden necklace. For it is said of Wisdom, “And a golden necklace around your neck” (Sir. 6:25). He would not place a golden necklace upon you unless he had first bound you in iron fetters. You began with fear; you are brought to completion in wisdom [Note: [Col. 1958] The editions read, “by wisdom.” But all the manuscripts have “to wisdom”; several of them read “bring to completion.”].

How many there are who do not wish to do evil because they fear hell and fear punishment! They do not yet love justice. If they were promised impunity and told, “Do whatever you wish; it will go unpunished,” they would unleash the advances of their lusts into every kind of wickedness.

And especially, my brothers, especially kings and nobles, to whom it is not easy to say, “What have you done?” A poor man, even if he does not fear God, because he has no power and no resources, refrains from acting out of fear of man, lest, when he becomes agitated, he be dragged off to punishment. But the powerful of the world—kings and nobles—unless they fear God, what will they fear?

Yet the word is preached to them, and they are struck by the two-edged sword. They are told that there is one who will place some at his right hand and others at his left, and that he will say to those on the left, “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:33, 41). They do not yet love justice, but they fear punishment; and by fearing punishment they have already received fetters and are being instructed in iron chains.

A powerful man from the world comes to us. His wife has offended him, or perhaps he has desired another woman who is more beautiful or another who is richer. He wishes to dismiss the wife he has, but he does not do so. He hears it from a servant of God, he hears it from a prophet, he hears it from an apostle, and he does not do it [Note: [Col. 1959] Most manuscripts read: “whom he has. You do not do it; he hears it from a servant of God, he hears it from a prophet, he hears it from an apostle: ‘You do not do it.’” And below: “You do not do it; it is not permitted to you,” etc.].

He hears from the one in whose hands is the two-edged sword: “You shall not do it. It is not permitted to you. God does not allow you to dismiss your wife, except on account of fornication” (Matt. 5:32). He hears this, fears, and does not do it. His feet, already free, were advancing toward a fall; they are held by fetters. He has iron chains; he fears God.

He is told, “God will condemn you if you do it. He is judge over all; he hears the groaning of your wife, and you will be held guilty in his sight.” On the one side lust flatters him; on the other punishment frightens him. He was going to consent to an evil desire unless iron chains held him back.

What is more, if he says, “I now wish to remain continent; I no longer want a wife”—you cannot. What if you wish it and she does not? Should she be made an adulteress by your continence [Note: [Col. 1959] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice have this passage as follows: “I will say what is more: but let him say, ‘I now wish to remain continent; I no longer want a wife.’ He cannot . . . Should you make her an adulteress by your continence?” M.]? If she marries another while you are alive, she will be an adulteress. God does not wish to compensate such a loss with such a gain.

Pay what is owed; even if you do not demand it, pay it. For perfect sanctification, God will count it to you if you do not demand what is owed, but return what is owed to your wife [Note: [Col. 1959] Thus several manuscripts. The editions instead read: “If you demand what is not owed.”]. You fear; you do not do it; your chains are shaken.

Hear that you are bound with iron chains: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (1 Cor. 7:39, 3, 27). It is hard; it is iron. For when the Lord said this, he showed that it is an iron chain.

“Listen, young men: they are iron chains; do not put your feet into them. Once you have put them in, you will be bound more tightly by fetters. Bishops’ hands reinforce such fetters for you. Do not men in fetters flee into the Church and get released here? Men flee here wishing to dismiss their wives; here they are bound more tightly. Let no one release these fetters” [Note: [Col. 1959] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “Let no one release them.”].

“What God has joined, let no human being separate.” But the chains are hard. Who does not know it? The Apostles themselves felt this hardness and said, “If such is the situation with a wife, it is not expedient to marry.” If they are iron chains, there is no need to put one’s feet into them. And the Lord says, “Not everyone can receive this word, but he who can receive it, let him receive it” (Matt. 19:6, 10, 11).

Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release, because you are bound with iron chains. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife (1 Cor. 7:27); do not bind yourself with iron chains.

### 16

*[Verse 9.]* “To execute upon them the written judgment.” This is the judgment that the saints execute among all the nations. Why “written”? Because these things were written beforehand [Col. 1960] and are now being fulfilled. Behold, they are now taking place; formerly they were read, but they did not take place.

And he concludes thus: “This honor belongs to all his saints.” Throughout the whole world, among all the nations, the saints do this and are glorified in this way: thus they exalt God in their throats; thus they rejoice in their dwelling places; thus they exult in their glory; thus they are exalted in salvation; thus they sing a new song; thus they say “Alleluia”—with heart, mouth, and life. Amen.

## Exposition of Psalm 150

### 1

Although the order of the Psalms—which seems to me to contain the secret of a great mystery—has not yet been revealed to me, nevertheless, since they are counted as one hundred and fifty, they suggest something even to us, who have not yet penetrated with the mind’s keen vision the height of their entire order, so that we may discuss it, insofar as the Lord helps us, without presumption.

First, the number fifteen, from which this number is multiplied—for what fifteen represents in the order of individual units, one hundred and fifty represents in the order of tens, since fifteen tens make one hundred and fifty; one thousand five hundred represents in the order of hundreds, since fifteen hundreds make one thousand five hundred; and fifteen thousand represents in the order of thousands, since fifteen thousands make fifteen thousand—the number fifteen therefore signifies the harmony of the two Testaments.

In the one, the Sabbath is observed, signifying rest (Exod. 20:10); in the other, the Lord’s Day, signifying resurrection. The Sabbath is the seventh day; but the Lord’s Day, following the seventh, is what but the eighth, which is also to be regarded as the first? For it is also called “the first day of the week” (Mark 16:2), so that afterward there are the second, third, and fourth, and so on up to the seventh Sabbath. From one Lord’s Day to the next, it is the eighth day. There the revelation of the New Testament is disclosed, which in the Old was hidden, as it were, beneath earthly promises.

Seven and eight together make fifteen. There are also that many songs called “Songs of Ascents,” since the temple likewise had that many steps.

Moreover, the number fifty itself carries a great mystery. It consists of a week of weeks, with one added—as the eighth itself, so to speak—to complete the number fifty. Seven times seven makes forty-nine; one is added to it, making fifty. This number fifty is so greatly significant that, after the days from the Lord’s resurrection had been completed, on that fiftieth day the Holy Spirit came upon those who had been gathered together in Christ (Acts 2:1–4).

The Holy Spirit is especially commended in Scripture by the number seven, both in Isaiah and in the Apocalypse (Rev. 1:20), where seven Spirits of God are most clearly mentioned, because of the sevenfold operation of one and the same Spirit. Isaiah the prophet recalls this sevenfold operation as follows: “The Spirit of God will rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, the Spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11:2–3).

This must be understood as “the pure fear of the Lord, enduring forever and ever” (Ps. 18:10). Perfect love casts out servile fear (1 John 4:18), and makes us free, so that we do not perform the servile works prohibited on the Sabbath. “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). For this reason also the Holy Spirit is commended by the number seven.

The Lord likewise distributed the fifty into forty and ten. On the fortieth day after his resurrection he ascended into heaven, and then, when ten days had been completed, he sent the Holy Spirit. By the number forty he commended the temporal dwelling with us in this world. Since the number four predominates in forty—and the world and the year have four parts—when ten is added, as a reward given for good works after the Law has been fulfilled, eternity itself is signified.

The number one hundred and fifty contains this fifty three times, as though the Trinity had multiplied it. For this reason also we understand, not inappropriately, that this is the number of the Psalms. In the number of fish caught in the nets cast after the resurrection, one hundred and fifty-three fish (John 21:11), there seems to have been given a reminder into how many parts this number should be divided, so that it might contain three fifties.

Although that number of fish also has another explanation, much more subtle and pleasing: when seventeen is put into a triangle—that is, when all the numbers from one through seventeen are counted—the same number is reached. In ten the Law is signified; in seven, Grace, because the Law is fulfilled only by love poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who is signified by the number seven.

### 2

Accordingly, those who have believed that all the Psalms comprise five books [Note: [Col. 1961] A Regius manuscript reads: “Some Greeks believed that all the Psalms comprise five books.”] followed the fact that at the end of a psalm it is said, “Let it be done, let it be done” (Pss. 40, 71, 88, and 105). But when I wished to understand the reason for this division, I could not do so; for the five parts are not equal to one another, at least not in the actual number of Psalms, even if they are not equal in the amount of writing, so that each might contain thirty.

And if the end of each book is “Let it be done, let it be done,” it may rightly be asked why the fifth book, which is also the last, does not end with the same formula.

But following the authority of canonical Scripture, where it is written, “For it is written in the book of Psalms” (Acts 1:20), we know that there is one book of Psalms. I see how both statements can be true, if the one does not conflict with the other. It may happen that, according to some usage of Hebrew writing, one book is called what consists of several books—just as one Church consists of many churches, and one heaven of many heavens.

For the one who said, “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 120:2), did not omit any heaven. And although Scripture says, “God called the firmament Heaven,” and that there are waters above the firmament (Gen. 1:8, 7), that is, above heaven, nevertheless the same Scripture does not lie when it says, “Let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:4–5), because it does not say “above heaven.”

There is also one earth composed of many lands. For in ordinary speech we say both “the globe of the earth” and “the globe of the lands.”

And when someone says, “It is written in the book of Psalms,” although the customary manner of speaking seems to indicate that he wished to say that there is one book, it can nevertheless be answered that the statement was made in the book of Psalms, that is, in one of their five books. This usage of speech is either absent or so rare that the twelve prophets are also believed to be one book because we read similarly, “As it is written in the book of the prophets” (Acts 7:42).

There are also those who call all the canonical Scriptures one book, because they agree with one another in a unity that is both marvelous and divine. Hence it is said, “In the beginning of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will,” so that this may be understood to mean that through the Son the Father made the world, whose creation is narrated at the beginning of the Scriptures in the book of Genesis.

Or, more appropriately, because this appears to be prophecy—not narrating what has happened, but foretelling what is to come—for it does not say “what I have done,” but “that I may do,” or “that I might do,” your will—this statement should be referred to what is written in the first parts of the same book: “The two shall become one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). The Apostle calls this a great mystery, referring it to Christ and the Church (Eph. 5:31–32).

This book of Psalms, however, can also be understood as being signified where it is said, “In the beginning of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will.” For what follows is, “My God, I have willed it, and your law is in the midst of my heart.” The first psalm itself is understood as having been prophesied about him at the beginning of this book: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence; but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:1–2). This is what is meant by, “My God, I have willed it, and your law is in the midst of my heart.”

What follows, “I have proclaimed your righteousness in the great assembly” (Ps. 39:8–10), more appropriately refers to, “And the two shall become one flesh.”

### 3

Whether, then, this or that is understood by the statement, “In the beginning of the book,” this book of Psalms, when questioned by fifties—if it is considered in those divisions of fifty—gives a great answer, very worthy of consideration.

For it does not seem to me accidental that the fiftieth Psalm concerns repentance, the hundredth mercy and judgment, and the one hundred fiftieth the praise of God in his saints. Thus we advance toward the blessed eternal life: first by condemning our sins, then by living well, so that after condemning an evil life and living a good one, we may deserve eternity.

According to the hidden purpose of his justice and goodness, God predestined those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he justified; and those whom he justified, he glorified (Rom. 8:30). Our predestination did not take place in us, but in secret with him, in his foreknowledge.

The remaining three take place in us: calling, justification, and glorification. We are called through the preaching of repentance; for the Lord began his preaching in this way: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2; 4:17).

We are justified in the calling of mercy and in the fear of judgment. Hence it is said, “O God, save me by your name, and judge me by your strength” (Ps. 53:3). The one who has first obtained salvation does not fear being judged.

When called, we renounce the devil through repentance, so that we may not remain under his yoke. When justified, we are healed through mercy, so that we may not fear judgment. When glorified, we pass into eternal life, where we praise God without end.

I believe this pertains to what the Lord says: “Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am brought to completion” (Luke 13:32) [Note: [Col. 1963] The editions read “on the third day.” “Day” is absent from the better manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Gospel.]. He also showed this in the three days of his passion, burial, and awakening. He was crucified, buried, and raised. On the cross he triumphed over principalities and powers; in the tomb he rested; in the resurrection he rejoiced.

Repentance torments; justice brings tranquility; eternal life glorifies.

The voice of repentance is: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity. This offers God the sacrifice of a troubled spirit, a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:3, 19).

The voice of Christ’s justice in his elect is: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord; I will sing psalms and understand in the blameless way, when you come to me.” Through mercy we are helped to do justice, so that we may come confidently to judgment, where “all who work iniquity” are destroyed from the city of the Lord (Ps. 100:1–2, 8). The verse with which this psalm concludes is the voice of eternal life [Note: [Col. 1963] The editions read, “and of eternal life,” but the conjunction “and” is redundant and is absent from the manuscripts.].

### 4

*[Verses 1–2.]* “Praise the Lord in his saints”—that is, in those whom he has glorified. “Praise him in the firmament of his strength.”

“Praise him in his strengths,” or, as others have translated it, “in his powers.” “Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness.”

All these are his saints. How does the Apostle say, “So that we may be the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:21)? If, then, the righteousness of God is what he has made in them, why should they not also be the strength of God, which he made in them so that they might rise from the dead?

For in Christ’s resurrection strength is especially commended, since in his passion there was weakness, as the Apostle says: “Although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4); and elsewhere, “To know him,” he says, “and the power of his resurrection” (Phil. 3:10).

He very aptly says, “In the firmament of his strength.” It is the firmament of strength because he will no longer die, and death will no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9).

Why should those powers which he made in them not also be called God’s powers? Indeed, let them themselves be his powers, just as it was said, “We are the righteousness of God in him.” For what is more powerful than to reign forever, with all enemies placed beneath one’s feet?

Why should they not also be the multitude of his greatness? Not the greatness by which he himself is great, but the greatness by which he made them great, so many in number—thousands of thousands. In another sense, righteousness is what he himself is as the righteous one; in another, it is what he makes in us, so that we may be his righteousness.

### 5

These same saints are signified successively by all the musical instruments, for the praise of God. What he proposed by saying, “Praise the Lord in his saints,” he carries out by signifying in various ways those same saints of his.

### 6

*[Verse 3.]* “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet,” because of the supreme clarity of praise.

“Praise him with the psaltery and lyre.” The psaltery praises God from above; the lyre praises God from below—as from heavenly and earthly things, as the one who made heaven and earth.

In another psalm we have already explained that the psaltery has its sounding wood above, upon which the series of strings rests so as to produce a better sound; the lyre has this wood below.

### 7

*[Verse 4.]* “Praise him with tambourine and chorus.” The tambourine praises God when, with the flesh already transformed, there is no weakness of earthly corruption. For a tambourine is made of leather that has been dried and strengthened.

The chorus praises God when a peaceful fellowship praises him.

“Praise him with strings and organ.” Both the psaltery and the lyre, which have already been mentioned, have strings.

*Organum* is a general name for all musical vessels, although usage has now established that *organs* properly means those instruments inflated by bellows. I do not think that this type is signified here. For although *organum*, as I said, is a Greek term general to all musical instruments, the Greeks call the instrument to which bellows are applied by another name. That it is called *organum* is rather a Latin and popular usage.

Therefore, when he says, “with strings and organ,” it seems to me that he wished to signify some organ that has strings. For psalteries and lyres alone do not have strings; but because in the psaltery and lyre, on account of the sound from above and below, something has been found that can be understood according to this distinction, he has directed us to seek something else in the strings themselves. They too are flesh, but flesh already freed from corruption [Note: [Col. 1964] Thus the better manuscripts. The editions read “freed,” feminine plural.].

Perhaps for this reason he added the organ—not so that the individual instruments might sound separately, but so that they might harmonize with the greatest concord through their diversity, as the parts are arranged in an organ. For even then the saints of God will have their distinct tones, harmonious rather than discordant—that is, agreeing rather than disagreeing—just as the sweetest harmony arises from sounds that are diverse but not opposed to one another.

“For star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:41–42).

### 8

*[Verses 5–6.]* “Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation.” Cymbals strike one another so that they may sound [Note: [Col. 1964] The editions read “so that they may sound well.” “Well” is absent from the manuscripts.]; for this reason some have compared them with our lips.

But I think it better understood as praising God, in a certain way, “with cymbals,” when each person is honored by his neighbor rather than by himself, and when, honoring one another, they give praise to God.

And lest anyone understand cymbals that sound without a soul, I think “with cymbals of jubilation” was added for this reason. For jubilation—that is, ineffable praise—proceeds only from the soul.

Nor should I pass over what musicians say, and what the thing itself makes evident: there are three kinds of sounds—voice, breath, and percussion. Voice is produced through the throat and arteries, as when a human being sings without any instrument; breath is produced through a flute or something similar; percussion is produced through a lyre or something similar.

No kind, then, has been omitted here. The voice is in the chorus, breath in the trumpet, percussion in the lyre—as mind, spirit, and body, but through likenesses, not in their proper senses.

What, then, did he mean by his opening statement, “Praise the Lord in his saints,” except those same saints? And where are they to praise God except in themselves? For he says: You are his saints; you are his strength, but the strength that he made in you; you are his power, and the multitude of his greatness, which he made and displayed in you.

You are the trumpet, the psaltery, the lyre, the tambourine, the chorus, the strings, the organ, and the cymbals of jubilation sounding well [Col. 1966], because they harmonize. Let nothing here be considered worthless, transitory, or playful. And because to think according to the flesh is death, “Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

## Prayer of Saint Aurelius Augustine

*(As it appears in the editions of Erasmus and Louvain at the end of this volume.)* The prayer which he was accustomed to say after each sermon and treatise.

Turning toward the Lord God, the almighty Father, let us give him, with a pure heart and insofar as our smallness permits, the greatest and truest thanks; beseeching with our whole soul his singular gentleness, that he may deign to hear our prayers according to his good pleasure; that by his power he may also drive the enemy away from our deeds and thoughts, multiply faith within us, govern our mind, grant us spiritual thoughts, and lead us to his blessedness: through Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord, who with him lives and reigns, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Exposition of Psalm 14 (G,S)*

[Col. 1965]

Found in three manuscripts—the Vatican, Regius, and another belonging to the Dominican convent at Clermont—immediately before the other exposition of the same Psalm, which you have in its proper place; and inserted for the most part into the commentary on the Psalms circulated under the name of Jerome.

[Col. 1965] ### 1

*[Verse 1.]* The fourteenth Psalm has appropriately been read; and according to the order it has happened in such a way that it seems almost to have been read deliberately. The Psalm was read according to the order, and I think it happened by God’s dispensation that what was beneficial to you should today be recited in the order of exposition.

The fourteenth Psalm was read, and its heading is “A Psalm of David.” Our David is Christ, as we have often said. Then we read in Exodus that the lamb is to be sacrificed on the fourteenth day (Exod. 12:5–6). It is sacrificed on the fourteenth day, when the moon is full, when none of its light is lacking. See, then, that Christ is sacrificed only in perfect and full light.

Since, therefore, the lamb is to be sacrificed for you on the fourteenth day, the Prophet now marvels, asks, and says:

2. **Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle?** You who wish to dwell in the Lord’s tabernacle, hear what is said. Who will dwell in your tabernacle? Or who will rest upon your holy mountain? Not first upon the mountain and afterward in the tabernacle, but first in the tabernacle, and so upon the mountain. A tabernacle is not a fixed house; a tabernacle has no foundation. Rather, it is moved here and there, and it migrates with the one who migrates. Therefore it is called *παροικία* (*paroikía*), “sojourning,” not habitation. Lord, who will sojourn in your tabernacle? Since it is a tabernacle, therefore it is called *παροικία*. Let us see, then, what the tabernacle is and what the mountain is. Since the tabernacle has no foundation, but is an uncertain dwelling, while mountains have firm foundations, the tabernacle seems to me to be the Church of this world.

The churches that you see now are tabernacles. For we do not remain here as inhabitants, but are going to migrate elsewhere. If “the outward form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7:31), and it is said elsewhere, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. 24:35), how much more will the stones of the churches that we see pass away? Thus the churches are now called tabernacles, because we are going to migrate from these [Col. 1966] to God’s holy mountain. What is this holy mountain of the Lord? Ezekiel says against the prince of Tyre: “You have been wounded,” he says, “by the mountain of the Lord.” And who will rest upon your holy mountain? (Ezek. 28:16, according to the Septuagint.) Since, then, we are going to migrate from the tabernacles to the mountains, we must learn who those are who are going to migrate to God’s holy mountain.

3. **[Verse 2.]** What he said—“Who will dwell in your tabernacle? Or who will rest upon your holy mountain?”—is the question of one asking. Therefore, what the Prophet asked, the Holy Spirit now answers. And what does he say to him? “Do you wish to know, O Prophet? Do you wish to know who dwells in my tabernacle, or who rests upon my holy mountain? Hear what follows: if you do what follows, you will dwell upon my holy mountain.”

You, therefore, who wish to dwell in the tabernacle and ascend God’s holy mountain, need not listen to my words; hear what the Lord answered the Prophet. Do what the Lord commanded, and you will ascend the Lord’s holy mountain.

**The one who walks without blemish and practices righteousness.** Therefore it is also said in the one-hundred-eighteenth psalm: “Blessed are the blameless in the way” (Ps. 118:1). At the very beginning it says, “Blessed are the blameless in the way.” Just as it says there, “blameless in the way,” so here also it says, “The one who walks without blemish.” The one who walks is on the way. “The one who walks without blemish.” See what is commanded: he did not say, “The one who reaches the end without blemish,” but, “The one who is still on the journey and has no blemish.”

Someone might say: “I have no blemish; I have done no evil.” It is not enough for us not to do evil unless we also do good. Thus what follows is: **“And practices righteousness.”** He did not say, “practices chastity”; he did not say, “practices wisdom” or “practices fortitude.” These virtues, indeed, are excellent. For example, wisdom benefits us so that we may be instructed by persecutions; fortitude benefits us so that we may resist persecutions; then temperance and [Col. 1967] chastity benefit us so that we do not lose our souls.

Righteousness alone is a great virtue and the mother of them all. Someone may say: “How is righteousness greater than the other virtues?” The other virtues delight the person who possesses them; righteousness does not delight the one who possesses it, but others. If I am wise, wisdom delights me; if I am strong, my strength delights me; if I am chaste, my chastity is my joy. But righteousness does not benefit the one who possesses it; it benefits the other wretched people who do not possess it.

Suppose that some poor man is quarreling with my brother; suppose that my brother is powerful, while another man—that is, a poor and wretched man unrelated to me—is being oppressed by his power. What benefit is my wisdom to the poor man? What benefit is my fortitude to the poor man? What benefit is my chastity to the poor man [Note: [Col. 1967] Thus the old codex in the Colbert Library, which in script, format, and size is very similar to the Royal volume praised by Petrarch and was copied at the same period—that is, seven hundred years ago—also presents the other exposition of Psalm 14, as well as certain other dubious works, indeed works that are certainly not Augustine’s. Such is Basil’s preface to the Psalms, contained in the same codices. [What benefit is my wisdom to the poor man? Righteousness benefits him, and so forth.]]? Righteousness benefits him, because I do not show favoritism toward my brother, but judge according to the truth.

Righteousness does not recognize brother, mother, or father; it recognizes truth. It does not show favoritism; it imitates the Lord. Therefore he said, “And practices righteousness,” so that he would not appear to have excluded the other virtues. The one who becomes angry for the sake of another’s relief, who does not take pleasure in the sufferings of others—that person is righteous.

4. **[Verse 3.]** Let us also state the other things that follow: **“The one who speaks truth in his heart.”** Many speak truth with their lips and not in their hearts; they appear to speak the truth, but their heart does not agree with their lips.

**“The one who has not practiced deceit with his tongue.”** For he has expressed in speech what he considered in his mind.

**“Nor has done evil to his neighbor.”** Some think that “neighbor” means a brother, or a nearby person, or a relative, or a blood relation. But our Lord teaches us in the Gospel, in that parable in which someone went down from Jerusalem to Jericho: a priest passed by, and a Levite passed by; neither showed compassion. A Samaritan passed by, and he showed compassion. The Lord then asks and says, “Which of these was the neighbor?” And the answer is immediately given: “The one who acted well.” The Lord adds: “Go, [Col. 1968] and you also do likewise” (Luke 10:30–37).

Therefore all human beings are neighbors to us, and we must do evil to no one. But if we understand “neighbors” to mean brothers and relatives, then it would be permissible for us to do evil to strangers. Far be it from us to believe this. All human beings are our neighbors, for we have one Father.

**“And has not received reproach against his neighbors.”** This is a great matter. “Never,” he says, “has a neighbor murmured against him; never,” he says, “has he found any opportunity to slander him.” This virtue surpasses human nature; it is the grace of God.

5. **[Verse 4.]** **“The wicked person is brought to nothing in his sight.”** Even if he is an emperor, even if he is a prefect, even if he is a bishop, even if he is a presbyter—for these are the dignities in the Church—whoever is wicked is counted as nothing in the sight of the holy person.

And immediately it follows: **“But he glorifies those who fear the Lord.”** This holy person, who walks without blemish and despises the powerful because they are evil, if he sees someone fearing God, he glorifies him, even if he is poor.

**“The one who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive him”** [Note: [Col. 1968] More correctly, according to the Colbert manuscript: “despises him.”]. Here also we must understand “neighbor” in the same way as above.

6. **[Verse 5.]** **“The one who has not lent his money at interest.”** There are many things that could be said, but the hour is shutting us out. Since the day before yesterday we said these things about the beginning of the catechesis [Note: [Col. 1968] Perhaps “of the catechesis.”], and, by God’s favor, you came out of Chaldea with Abraham (Gen. 11:31), you remember what we said: how you came out of Chaldea and entered the land of promise.

Finally, after Abraham came into the land of promise, adversaries were all around; enemies held the land. The Lord came, led him outside, set him upon a mountain, showed him the whole land, and said: “All this I will give to you and to your offspring” (ibid. 13:15). He promised it to him; he will restore it to us.

**Here ends the treatise of Aurelius Augustine, bishop, on Psalm 14.**

And immediately afterward, in the same manuscripts, another exposition of the same Psalm is appended, beginning: “Concerning this title,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 1967]

Since the one hundred and fifty psalms follow one another throughout this fourth volume in both cardinal and ordinal sequence, we have no need—and not even the ability—to append a separate index of them. Such an index would demonstrate nothing other than what anyone can very easily find in an open book, as the saying goes.

As for the matters that encompass and explain moral and dogmatic teaching, discipline and history, or that present and elucidate the literal, mystical, and other senses, all these will be fully indicated at the end of the final volume. They will be accompanied by a general alphabetical and analytical index, with which these complete works of the holy Doctor will be crowned. M.]

**Here ends the latter part of the fourth volume.**
